Neutral ibuprofen is more soluble in ether than in water, and the base converts it to its ionic form.
Both ibuprofen and caffeine in their neutral forms
Only the ionized species moves into water, so the two compounds are separated rather than remaining together.
qs.x: At pH 8.3 (well above pKa 4.4) ibuprofen is deprotonated to an ionic carboxylate that is water-soluble, while neutral caffeine stays in the ether. Trap: Forgetting that deprotonating an acid makes it ionic and water-soluble.

qs.q: A 100 mL aqueous caffeine solution is shaken once with 50 mL of DCM. What fraction of the caffeine is extracted into the DCM?
o: 80% is the result for equal volumes of the two solvents (K/(K + 1)).
50% would require K = 2.0 for these volumes, but K = 4.0 strongly favors DCM.
33% is the fraction left in the water, not the fraction extracted.
Correct: K = (n_DCM/50)/(n_aq/100) = 4.0, so n_DCM/n_aq = 2.0, and the fraction extracted is 2/(2 + 1) = 0.67.
qs.x: K = (n_DCM/50)/(n_aq/100) = 4.0, so n_DCM/n_aq = 2.0, and the fraction extracted is 2/(2 + 1) = 0.67. Trap: Ignoring the difference in volumes and using K/(K + 1), or reporting the fraction left behind.

graph.title: Figure 1. Rf versus percentage of ethyl acetate

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 9
text: A student examines how the structure of an alkyl bromide affects its rate of nucleophilic substitution. In one set of experiments, each alkyl bromide reacts with sodium iodide in acetone, a polar aprotic solvent, under conditions that favor a bimolecular mechanism (SN2). In a second set, the same alkyl bromides are allowed to react with a solvent of aqueous ethanol (solvolysis), under conditions that favor a unimolecular mechanism (SN1). Approximate relative rates, set to 1 for the slowest measurable reaction in each series, are shown in Table 1. In addition, the student treats optically pure (R)-2-bromobutane with sodium iodide in acetone and analyzes the product with a polarimeter. A second experiment compares the rate of the reaction of iodide with 1-bromobutane in acetone with the rate in water, a polar protic solvent. The student also plans to double the concentration of nucleophile in the solvolysis reaction of tert-butyl bromide. Throughout, the leaving group is bromide, and temperature is held constant. The student's goal is to connect each observation to the mechanism by which the reaction proceeds, and to the effects of substrate structure, solvent, and nucleophile on the rate.

qs.q: Why does tert-butyl bromide react so much faster than methyl bromide under SN1 conditions?
o: The tert-butyl carbon is less hindered, so the nucleophile attacks more easily.
The tertiary carbon is the most crowded, which is why it is slowest in SN2.
Bromide is a better leaving group from tertiary carbons because it is more basic there.
A better leaving group is a weaker base, and the leaving group is the same (Br⁻) in all cases.
The rate-determining step forms a tertiary carbocation, which is stabilized by electron donation from three alkyl groups.
Correct: In SN1 the slow step is ionization to a carbocation; alkyl groups stabilize the positive charge by hyperconjugation and induction, so tertiary is fastest and methyl is slowest.
The tert-butyl group can donate a proton to the solvent, which accelerates the reaction.
The mechanism is carbocation formation and capture, not proton donation.
qs.x: In SN1 the slow step is ionization to a carbocation; alkyl groups stabilize the positive charge by hyperconjugation and induction, so tertiary is fastest and methyl is slowest. Trap: Reasoning from steric hindrance, which controls SN2, instead of carbocation stability for SN1.

qs.q: What is the major product of the reaction of (R)-2-bromobutane with NaI in acetone?
o: (R)-2-iodobutane
Retention would result from a double-inversion or front-side attack, which is not the SN2 mechanism.
A racemic mixture of 2-iodobutane
A racemic product is characteristic of SN1 through a planar carbocation, not SN2.
(S)-2-iodobutane
Correct: SN2 proceeds by backside attack and inversion of configuration. Iodide takes the same CIP priority position as bromine, so R becomes S.
(S)-2-iodobutane and 1-iodobutane in equal amounts
No rearrangement or substitution at C1 occurs; iodide substitutes at the carbon bearing the bromine.
qs.x: SN2 proceeds by backside attack and inversion of configuration. Iodide takes the same CIP priority position as bromine, so R becomes S. Trap: Predicting racemization for every substitution at a stereocenter, rather than inversion for SN2.

qs.q: How would the rate of the SN2 reaction of iodide with 1-bromobutane change when the solvent is changed from acetone to water?
o: It would increase, because water is more polar and stabilizes the transition state more.
Greater polarity helps SN1 ionization, but SN2 nucleophiles lose reactivity when strongly solvated.
It would increase, because water can donate protons to the nucleophile.
Protonation of the nucleophile would make it less nucleophilic.
It would decrease, because water hydrogen bonds to iodide and lowers its nucleophilicity.
Correct: Polar protic solvents solvate anions through hydrogen bonds, creating a shell that hinders attack; polar aprotic solvents leave the nucleophile 'bare' and more reactive.
It would not change, because the substrate is the same.
Solvent strongly affects nucleophile reactivity even with the same substrate.
qs.x: Polar protic solvents solvate anions through hydrogen bonds, creating a shell that hinders attack; polar aprotic solvents leave the nucleophile 'bare' and more reactive. Trap: Assuming a more polar solvent always speeds substitution reactions.

qs.q: If the concentration of nucleophile is doubled in the solvolysis of tert-butyl bromide under SN1 conditions, how will the rate change?
o: It will double because the rate depends on both substrate and nucleophile.
A doubling would be seen for SN2, whose rate law is first order in each reactant.
It will not change appreciably, since the rate-determining step does not involve the nucleophile.
Correct: The SN1 rate law is rate = k[RBr]; ionization of the C–Br bond is slow, and the nucleophile attacks afterward in a fast step.
It will quadruple because the rate is second order in nucleophile.
There is no second-order dependence on nucleophile in either mechanism.
It will decrease because the added nucleophile competes with the solvent.
Added nucleophile does not slow ionization, which is the rate-determining step.
qs.x: The SN1 rate law is rate = k[RBr]; ionization of the C–Br bond is slow, and the nucleophile attacks afterward in a fast step. Trap: Applying the SN2 rate law, which includes nucleophile concentration, to an SN1 reaction.

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 10
text: A chemist studies the unimolecular isomerization of a compound in solution. The reaction is first order, and its rate constant k was measured at four temperatures, giving the data in Table 1. Figure 1 plots ln k against 1/T, where T is in kelvin, and the points fall on a straight line. The Arrhenius equation, k = A exp(−Ea/RT), describes the data, and R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). The overall reaction has ΔH° = −40 kJ/mol and ΔS° = −100 J/(mol·K), and both values are assumed to be independent of temperature over the range studied. In a second experiment, the chemist adds a catalyst that provides an alternative pathway for the same reaction, and she observes that the rate constant at 300 K increases substantially. The chemist reasons that the catalyst changes the kinetics of the reaction but not its thermodynamics. She also notes that the rate constant of a first-order reaction has units of inverse time, and that the half-life of such a reaction does not depend on the starting concentration. The same sample volume and solvent were used for all runs, and the temperature of each run was held constant by a thermostatted bath.

qs.q: The slope of the line in Figure 1 is approximately −7.2 × 10³ K. What is the activation energy of the reaction?
o: 7.2 kJ/mol
7.2 kJ/mol would result from ignoring R and converting units to kJ only.
0.87 kJ/mol
0.87 kJ/mol is the result of dividing by R rather than multiplying.
120 kJ/mol
120 kJ/mol is double the correct value and would come from an extra factor of 2 that is not in the Arrhenius relation.
60 kJ/mol
Correct: The slope equals −Ea/R, so Ea = (7.2 × 10³ K)(8.314 J/mol·K) = 6.0 × 10⁴ J/mol = 60 kJ/mol.
qs.x: The slope equals −Ea/R, so Ea = (7.2 × 10³ K)(8.314 J/mol·K) = 6.0 × 10⁴ J/mol = 60 kJ/mol. Trap: Dividing the slope by R rather than multiplying by it, or forgetting that the slope is −Ea/R.

qs.q: What is the half-life of the compound at 320 K?
o: 222 s is 1/k, which omits the factor of ln 2.
Correct: For first-order kinetics, t½ = ln 2 / k = 0.693 / (4.50 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹) = 154 s.
3.1 × 10⁻³ s is 0.693 × k, which multiplies instead of divides.
308 s is twice the correct half-life.
qs.x: For first-order kinetics, t½ = ln 2 / k = 0.693 / (4.50 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹) = 154 s. Trap: Using 1/k as the half-life and leaving out ln 2.

qs.q: How does the catalyst affect the reaction?
o: It lowers ΔG° of the reaction, making the products more stable.
ΔG° depends on the energies of reactants and products, which a catalyst does not change.
It lowers the activation energy and leaves ΔG° and the equilibrium constant unchanged.
Correct: A catalyst provides a pathway with lower Ea, speeding forward and reverse reactions equally, so K and the thermodynamic quantities (ΔH°, ΔG°) are unchanged.
It increases the equilibrium constant by increasing the forward rate only.
A catalyst accelerates the forward and reverse reactions equally, so K is not changed.
It raises the energy of the reactants so they are closer to the transition state.
A catalyst lowers the energy of the transition state relative to reactants; it does not raise the reactants' energy.
qs.x: A catalyst provides a pathway with lower Ea, speeding forward and reverse reactions equally, so K and the thermodynamic quantities (ΔH°, ΔG°) are unchanged. Trap: Believing a catalyst makes a reaction more spontaneous by changing ΔG°.

qs.q: What is ΔG° for the reaction at 300 K?
o: −10 kJ/mol
Correct: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = −40 kJ/mol − (300 K)(−0.100 kJ/mol·K) = −40 + 30 = −10 kJ/mol.
−70 kJ/mol
−70 kJ/mol results from a sign error, −40 − 30.
+10 kJ/mol
+10 kJ/mol would result from reversing the sign of the whole calculation.
−30 kJ/mol
−30 kJ/mol would arise from using a different temperature or neglecting the 300 K factor.
qs.x: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = −40 kJ/mol − (300 K)(−0.100 kJ/mol·K) = −40 + 30 = −10 kJ/mol. Trap: Mishandling the sign of ΔS° or forgetting to convert J to kJ.

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 1
text: Researchers examined the effect of acute sleep restriction on working memory. Sixty healthy adults aged 19 to 30 were randomly assigned to one of two groups. The control group slept 8 hours in the laboratory, and the restricted group was allowed only 4 hours. The next morning, each participant completed a computerized 2-back task, in which letters appear one at a time and the participant indicates whether the current letter matches the one shown two items earlier. Accuracy and mean reaction time on correct trials were recorded. The experimenters who scored the task did not know each participant's group, but participants knew how long they had been allowed to sleep. Group means were compared with independent-samples t-tests, using a significance threshold of p < 0.05. Results are shown in Table 1. In a separate sample of sleep-restricted adults, functional imaging showed reduced activation of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex during the same task, relative to well-rested adults. The investigators concluded that a single night of short sleep impairs the ability to hold and update information over a few seconds.

qs.q: Random assignment of participants to the two sleep conditions primarily served to:
o: ensure that every participant would respond identically to the 2-back task regardless of sleep condition.
Individuals still differ in their sensitivity to sleep loss; randomization does not remove that variability.
make the results generalize to all adults regardless of age, sex, or baseline sleep habits.
Generalizability depends on how participants were sampled, not on how they were assigned.
eliminate the need for a statistical test of the group difference in 2-back accuracy.
Randomization does not remove chance differences, so a statistical test is still needed.
distribute pre-existing differences, such as baseline memory ability, roughly equally across groups.
Correct: Random assignment makes the groups comparable on average before treatment, so confounders are balanced by chance rather than by design.
qs.x: Random assignment makes the groups comparable on average before treatment, so confounders are balanced by chance rather than by design. Trap: Confusing random assignment (internal validity) with random sampling (external validity).

qs.q: Relative to the control group mean, the percent decrease in accuracy in the restricted group was closest to:
o: 8 is the absolute difference in percentage points, not a relative percent change.
This divides 8 by the restricted mean (76) rather than by the control baseline.
Correct: The difference is 84 - 76 = 8 percentage points; 8/84 = 0.095, or about 9.5% of the control value.
This value does not follow from either mean; 8/84 is about 0.095.
qs.x: The difference is 84 - 76 = 8 percentage points; 8/84 = 0.095, or about 9.5% of the control value. Trap: Dividing the difference by the wrong baseline (the experimental mean) or reporting percentage points as a percent change.

qs.q: The imaging finding in the sleep-restricted adults is most consistent with the idea that the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex:
o: encodes new declarative memories into long-term storage after a delay.
Long-term declarative encoding relies chiefly on the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe.
controls the release of cortisol and other hormones during stress.
Cortisol release is governed by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.
supports the maintenance and manipulation of information in working memory.
Correct: The DLPFC is a core region for executive function and working memory, so reduced activation fits poorer 2-back performance.
coordinates the timing and sequencing of voluntary movements of the limbs.
Movement timing is associated with the cerebellum and basal ganglia.
qs.x: The DLPFC is a core region for executive function and working memory, so reduced activation fits poorer 2-back performance. Trap: Attributing every memory deficit to the hippocampus when the task is short-term manipulation of information.

qs.q: Which feature of the design most weakens the conclusion that sleep loss alone caused the group difference in accuracy?
o: The scorers of the task did not know the group assignments of the participants.
Blind scoring reduces experimenter bias and is a strength.
Both groups completed the same 2-back task in the morning under identical conditions of testing.
Identical tasks and timing hold the testing conditions constant, which is a strength.
Participants knew their sleep condition, so expectations or effort could have differed between groups.
Correct: Participant awareness permits demand characteristics or motivational differences, a threat that cannot be fully blinded in a sleep manipulation.
Participants were randomly assigned to the sleep-deprived or the rested group before any testing began.
Random assignment strengthens causal inference.
qs.x: Participant awareness permits demand characteristics or motivational differences, a threat that cannot be fully blinded in a sleep manipulation. Trap: Choosing a design strength because it sounds technical when the question asks for a weakness.

qs.q: The reaction-time results in Table 1 indicate that the restricted group:
o: responded faster but less accurately, showing a speed-accuracy trade-off in the sleep-deprived group.
Faster responding would show a lower mean RT, but the restricted mean RT is higher.
was slower and less accurate, so the deficit is not a speed-accuracy trade-off.
Correct: Reaction time rose from 612 to 668 ms (p = 0.01) while accuracy fell, so the group was impaired on both measures.
showed no reliable difference from controls in either measure because the SDs are large.
The reported p = 0.01 is below 0.05, so the difference is statistically significant despite the SDs.
was more accurate on trials with longer reaction times, as expected for a speed-accuracy trade-off.
Table 1 reports group means only and says nothing about accuracy as a function of trial RT.
qs.x: Reaction time rose from 612 to 668 ms (p = 0.01) while accuracy fell, so the group was impaired on both measures. Trap: Assuming overlapping SDs automatically mean a non-significant result.

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 2
text: Dark adaptation was measured in two groups of observers. Each observer first viewed an intense light for 5 minutes. The room was then darkened, and at set intervals the dimmest flash that the observer could detect was determined. The flash was a small dim 500-nm spot presented 10 degrees away from the point of fixation. Threshold is expressed in log units, where a lower value indicates greater sensitivity. Group N contained 10 observers with normal vision, and Group V contained 10 observers with a dietary deficiency of vitamin A. Mean thresholds are plotted in Figure 1. Normal observers reported that the flash appeared colorless at the later time points, although it appeared faintly colored at early time points. Observers in Group V had normal visual acuity under daylight conditions and did not differ from Group N in the size of the initial threshold elevation immediately after the bright light. In Group V, a clinical examination showed no damage to the optic nerve or to the cornea. The researchers wished to link the shape of each curve to the photoreceptor populations of the retina and to the photopigment that each population uses.

qs.q: The second downward phase of Group N's curve, after about 10 minutes, most likely reflects:
o: regeneration of rhodopsin in rods, which are more sensitive than cones in dim light.
Correct: The rod-cone break marks the point where rods, once their rhodopsin has regenerated, become more sensitive than cones; thresholds then keep falling.
regeneration of cone photopigment, which is more sensitive than rhodopsin in dim light.
Cones adapt quickly and account for the early plateau, not the later fall.
dilation of the pupil to its maximum diameter.
Pupil dilation takes seconds and explains little of a 30-minute change.
recovery of horizontal cells in the fovea.
The fovea contains cones and no rods, so it cannot explain the late rod-driven phase.
qs.x: The rod-cone break marks the point where rods, once their rhodopsin has regenerated, become more sensitive than cones; thresholds then keep falling. Trap: Reversing the roles: the early fast phase is cone-mediated and the late slow phase is rod-mediated.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for the flat later portion of Group V's curve?
o: Without enough vitamin A, retinal cannot be supplied to regenerate rhodopsin in the rods.
Correct: Retinal is derived from vitamin A and is the chromophore of rhodopsin; deficiency produces night blindness while the cone-based early phase is preserved.
Vitamin A deficiency destroys the cones first, so the early phase of dark adaptation does not occur.
Group V's early phase matches Group N's, indicating cones function.
Vitamin A is needed for transmission of visual signals across the optic chiasm to the cortex.
The examination showed no optic nerve damage, and vitamin A is not a chiasm transmitter.
The deficiency prevents the cornea and lens from refracting incoming light onto the retina.
The cornea was normal, and refraction does not explain a rod-specific deficit.
qs.x: Retinal is derived from vitamin A and is the chromophore of rhodopsin; deficiency produces night blindness while the cone-based early phase is preserved. Trap: Assuming a visual deficit must involve the optic nerve or the lens rather than the photopigment.

qs.q: At 30 minutes, the threshold for Group V is higher than that for Group N by 2.2 log units. Group V therefore needed a flash that was approximately how many times more intense?
o: 2.2 times
2.2 is the log difference, not the ratio of intensities.
160 times
Correct: Log units are powers of 10: 10^2.2 is about 158, so roughly 160 times more intense.
16 times
10^1.2 is about 16; the exponent of 10 is 2.2, not 1.2.
1,000 times
1,000 is 10^3, which would be a 3.0 log unit difference.
qs.x: Log units are powers of 10: 10^2.2 is about 158, so roughly 160 times more intense. Trap: Treating a difference in log units as a difference in the original units.

qs.q: The test flash was presented 10 degrees from fixation and appeared colorless at the later time points. These observations are best explained by the fact that:
o: cones, concentrated outside the fovea, contain three pigments and signal only brightness at low light.
Cones are concentrated in the fovea and the three cone types support color vision.
the fovea contains the highest density of rods, so peripheral light is not detected by the eye.
The fovea is rod-free and cone-dense, the opposite of the statement.
rods, concentrated outside the fovea, contain a single photopigment and thus do not signal color.
Correct: Rods predominate in the periphery, use one pigment (rhodopsin), and give achromatic vision; the late flash was detected by rods.
color is encoded only after the signal reaches the optic nerve, not in the photoreceptors.
Color coding begins in the retina with different cone types and opponent processing, not at the optic nerve.
qs.x: Rods predominate in the periphery, use one pigment (rhodopsin), and give achromatic vision; the late flash was detected by rods. Trap: Placing rods in the fovea; fovea is cone-only, rods are peripheral.

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 3
text: Stress responses were studied in 48 undergraduates using a 2 x 2 between-subjects design with 12 participants per cell. Participants were randomly assigned to perform either a stressful task (an unrehearsed, videotaped speech judged by a panel) or a non-stressful control task (reading aloud in an empty room). Within each task, participants waited beforehand either alone or with a supportive friend who was allowed to talk with them but who did not take part in the task. Saliva samples were collected 20 minutes after the task ended, and cortisol was measured. Participants also rated their anxiety on a 10-point scale. Mean cortisol is shown in Table 2. A two-way analysis of variance showed a significant main effect of task (p < 0.001), a significant main effect of support (p = 0.002), and a significant task by support interaction (p = 0.01). Anxiety ratings paralleled cortisol results. In a post-study questionnaire, participants in the speech task who waited with a friend reported being more confident that they could cope with the speech than did those who waited alone. Cortisol was sampled in the afternoon in all conditions.

qs.q: The hormone measured in this study is released as the final step of an axis in which:
o: the hypothalamus releases CRH, the anterior pituitary releases ACTH, and the adrenal cortex releases cortisol.
Correct: Cortisol is a glucocorticoid made by the adrenal cortex under control of ACTH (anterior pituitary), itself driven by hypothalamic CRH.
the posterior pituitary releases ACTH, which then stimulates the adrenal medulla to release cortisol directly into the blood.
ACTH comes from the anterior pituitary and acts on the cortex; the medulla makes catecholamines.
the adrenal medulla releases cortisol directly in response to sympathetic input.
The medulla releases epinephrine and norepinephrine, not cortisol.
the thyroid releases cortisol in response to TSH from the hypothalamus.
TSH acts on the thyroid, a different axis; the thyroid does not release cortisol.
qs.x: Cortisol is a glucocorticoid made by the adrenal cortex under control of ACTH (anterior pituitary), itself driven by hypothalamic CRH. Trap: Mixing up the adrenal cortex (cortisol, HPA axis) and adrenal medulla (epinephrine, sympathetic).

qs.q: The significant task by support interaction indicates that:
o: the speech task raised cortisol equally whether or not a friend was present.
Speech cortisol was 14.0 alone and 9.5 with a friend, so the rise was not equal.
the presence of a friend had no effect on cortisol in any condition tested.
The main effect of support was significant (p = 0.002), so a friend did matter overall.
anxiety ratings caused the cortisol differences between the friend and no-friend groups.
The design cannot show that anxiety ratings caused cortisol; they only paralleled it.
the effect of a friend on cortisol depended on whether the task was stressful.
Correct: A friend lowered cortisol by 4.5 nmol/L in the speech task but by only 0.2 nmol/L in the reading task, so the support effect depends on stress.
qs.x: A friend lowered cortisol by 4.5 nmol/L in the speech task but by only 0.2 nmol/L in the reading task, so the support effect depends on stress. Trap: Equating a main effect with an interaction; an interaction means one factor's effect changes across levels of the other.

qs.q: The post-study confidence ratings are most consistent with which view of how support reduced the stress response?
o: The James-Lange theory: support directly changed bodily arousal, which was then labeled as calm by the participant.
James-Lange begins with arousal; here the proposed first step is a change in cognitive evaluation (confidence).
Cognitive appraisal: support raised participants' perceived ability to cope, lowering perceived threat.
Correct: In appraisal models of stress, a stressor is judged against coping resources; support raises perceived resources and so lowers the stress response.
Classical conditioning: the friend became a conditioned stimulus for cortisol release.
Nothing in the design involves pairing a neutral stimulus with cortisol release; support reduced cortisol.
Learned helplessness: friends taught participants that outcomes are uncontrollable.
Learned helplessness would predict higher, not lower, stress responses.
qs.x: In appraisal models of stress, a stressor is judged against coping resources; support raises perceived resources and so lowers the stress response. Trap: Choosing a named theory because it is familiar without checking what the data say about timing.

qs.q: In the speech condition, the reduction in mean cortisol associated with waiting with a friend, expressed as a percentage of the 'alone' mean, was closest to:
o: 4.5 is the absolute reduction in nmol/L, not a percentage.
Correct: Reduction = 14.0 - 9.5 = 4.5 nmol/L; 4.5/14.0 = 0.32, or 32%.
47% divides 4.5 by 9.5, the 'friend' mean, not the baseline.
68% is the remaining fraction (9.5/14.0), not the reduction.
qs.x: Reduction = 14.0 - 9.5 = 4.5 nmol/L; 4.5/14.0 = 0.32, or 32%. Trap: Using the post-intervention mean as the denominator of a percent reduction.

tbl.cap: Table 2. Salivary cortisol 20 min after the task (nmol/L; mean, SD in parentheses; n = 12 per cell)

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 4
text: Researchers studied observational learning in 90 children aged 4 to 6 (45 boys, 45 girls). Each child watched a short film of an adult model who played with an inflatable doll by hitting it. Children were randomly assigned, within sex, to one of three versions of the film's ending: the model was praised and given candy (rewarded), the model was scolded and spanked (punished), or nothing happened (no consequence). There were 15 children per sex per condition. Each child was then taken to a playroom containing the same doll and other toys and observed through a one-way mirror for 10 minutes. Observers who did not know which film the child had seen counted the number of imitative aggressive acts. The mean counts are given in Table 3 and Figure 2. In a second phase, every child was told that they would get a sticker for each action by the model that they could reproduce, and almost all children, regardless of condition, then reproduced many of the model's aggressive acts. A statistical analysis showed significant main effects of condition (p < 0.01) and sex (p < 0.05), and no interaction.

qs.q: The lower imitation in the 'punished' condition is best explained by:
o: negative reinforcement: the film removed an aversive stimulus from the children after the behavior.
Negative reinforcement requires the child's own behavior to remove an aversive stimulus, which did not occur.
vicarious punishment: the model's observed consequences reduced the children's tendency to act.
Correct: In social learning theory, observed consequences change the likelihood that the observer performs the behavior (vicarious reinforcement and punishment).
classical conditioning of fear to the doll through direct pairing of the doll with spanking of the child.
The children were never spanked; the model was.
habituation to the film after repeated viewing, reducing the children's attention to the model.
Each child viewed the film once, so repeated exposure and habituation are not involved.
qs.x: In social learning theory, observed consequences change the likelihood that the observer performs the behavior (vicarious reinforcement and punishment). Trap: Treating observed consequences as if they were directly experienced by the learner.

qs.q: Among boys, the decrease in mean aggressive acts from the 'no consequence' condition to the 'punished' condition, as a percentage of the 'no consequence' mean, was closest to:
o: 3.6 is the absolute difference in acts.
47% divides 3.6 by 7.6, the rewarded mean, rather than the no-consequence baseline.
35% does not follow from any pairing of the table values.
Correct: Decrease = 6.8 - 3.2 = 3.6; 3.6/6.8 = 0.529, or about 53%.
qs.x: Decrease = 6.8 - 3.2 = 3.6; 3.6/6.8 = 0.529, or about 53%. Trap: Dividing by the wrong comparison condition when computing a relative decrease.

qs.q: Why is the observed sex difference a weaker basis for a causal claim than the condition difference?
o: Children cannot be randomly assigned to sex, so other differences in upbringing may be confounded with it.
Correct: Randomization supports causal claims for the manipulated variable only; sex is a quasi-independent (subject) variable.
Sex was measured with less precision than the film condition, which weakens the internal validity of the whole study.
Sex is easy to measure; the problem is lack of random assignment, not precision.
Observers knew each child's sex, but not each child's film condition, so scoring was blind to film.
Whether observers were aware of sex does not address causal attribution; it is still a non-manipulated variable.
The sex difference was non-significant, so no conclusion about it can be drawn from these data.
The text states the main effect of sex was significant (p < 0.05).
qs.x: Randomization supports causal claims for the manipulated variable only; sex is a quasi-independent (subject) variable. Trap: Assuming a significant effect of any factor in an ANOVA is causal.

qs.q: In the second phase, children in all conditions reproduced the model's behavior once they were offered stickers. This finding suggests that:
o: the children in the punished condition had not learned the behavior during the first phase.
If they had not learned it, they could not have reproduced it on request.
stickers acted as punishment and suppressed imitation in the second phase.
Stickers are positive reinforcement and increased, not suppressed, imitation.
observational learning requires direct reinforcement of the observer in order to be acquired.
Observational learning occurs without reinforcement of the observer; the model's consequences only influence performance.
the punished children had learned the behavior but were less likely to perform it spontaneously.
Correct: Learning and performance differ: acquisition occurred through observation, and incentives revealed it in children who had not shown it.
qs.x: Learning and performance differ: acquisition occurred through observation, and incentives revealed it in children who had not shown it. Trap: Equating a lack of performance with a lack of learning.

qs.q: Neural activity in premotor and inferior frontal regions that fires both when an individual performs an action and when the individual observes the same action performed by another is most closely associated with:
o: place cells.
Place cells in the hippocampus fire for a specific location in space.
Purkinje cells.
Purkinje cells are cerebellar output neurons involved in motor coordination.
grid cells.
Grid cells in the entorhinal cortex map space in a periodic pattern.
mirror neurons.
Correct: Mirror neurons respond during both execution and observation of actions and are proposed to support imitation.
qs.x: Mirror neurons respond during both execution and observation of actions and are proposed to support imitation. Trap: Selecting a well-known spatial cell type because it is also a named class of neuron.

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 5
text: A laboratory study examined how the number of people who witness an emergency affects helping. Participants (n = 200) were told they were in a study of reactions to a noisy office. Each sat in a cubicle and completed a questionnaire. After several minutes, they heard what appeared to be a worker in the next room dropping a shelf and crying out in pain. In the 'alone' condition, the participant was by himself or herself. In the other three conditions, the participant was in a room with one, two, or four other people who were research assistants instructed to continue working and to show no concern. There were 50 participants in each of the four conditions, and all conditions had the same distribution of age and sex. The experimenters recorded whether the participant left the cubicle to help within 2 minutes and the time to respond. Results are summarized in Table 4 and Figure 3. A chi-square test of helping (yes or no) by condition was significant (p < 0.001). In interviews afterward, many non-helping participants said that the emergency 'did not seem that serious' because the others seemed calm.

qs.q: The decline in helping as group size increased is best explained by:
o: social loafing, in which individuals reduce effort when they believe their output cannot be individually evaluated.
Social loafing concerns reduced effort on a shared task, not response to an emergency.
deindividuation, in which anonymity within a crowd raises aggression.
Deindividuation involves loss of self-awareness in a crowd, which was not the case in the cubicles.
diffusion of responsibility, in which each person feels less personally obligated to act when others are present.
Correct: The bystander effect is attributed to diffusion of responsibility, and here the research assistants' inaction also signals that action is unnecessary.
group polarization, in which discussion makes the group's view more extreme.
There was no group discussion, so polarization is not involved.
qs.x: The bystander effect is attributed to diffusion of responsibility, and here the research assistants' inaction also signals that action is unnecessary. Trap: Selecting a different well-known group phenomenon that sounds similar.

qs.q: Across all 200 participants, the overall percentage who helped within 2 minutes was:
o: 52.5% would correspond to 105 helpers.
62.5% would correspond to 125 helpers.
58.0% would correspond to 116 helpers; the total is 115.
qs.x: 42 + 32 + 24 + 17 = 115 helpers; 115/200 = 0.575, or 57.5%. Trap: Averaging the four percentages incorrectly or mis-summing the helper counts.

qs.q: Participants' statements that the event 'did not seem that serious' because others seemed calm best illustrates:
o: normative social influence driven by a desire for approval from the group.
Normative influence concerns conforming to gain acceptance; participants said they reinterpreted the event.
the foot-in-the-door technique, in which a small request precedes a larger one.
Foot-in-the-door involves a small request followed by a larger one.
social facilitation of a well-learned response in the presence of others.
Social facilitation is about performance in the presence of others on tasks, not interpretation of ambiguity.
informational social influence leading to pluralistic ignorance.
Correct: Participants used others' calm as information about whether the situation was an emergency, and the others' behavior was itself uninformed.
qs.x: Participants used others' calm as information about whether the situation was an emergency, and the others' behavior was itself uninformed. Trap: Equating all conformity with normative influence.

qs.q: A chi-square test was an appropriate choice for the analysis of helping because:
o: the outcome was a continuous variable with an approximately normal distribution within each group.
A continuous, normally distributed outcome would call for a t-test or ANOVA.
the outcome (helped or not) is categorical and was compared across independent groups.
Correct: Chi-square tests whether frequencies of a categorical outcome differ across categories or groups.
the same participants were measured repeatedly in all four conditions of the experiment.
Different participants were in each condition, so measures were independent.
the study compared the means of exactly two independent groups.
Four groups were compared, and means are not the unit of analysis.
qs.x: Chi-square tests whether frequencies of a categorical outcome differ across categories or groups. Trap: Picking a test by the number of groups without considering the type of outcome variable.

graph.title: Figure 3. Helping decreases with group size

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 6
text: A study examined whether a reminder about group stereotypes affects performance in a domain that is important to the test-taker's identity. Ninety-six undergraduates who rated mathematics as highly important to their self-concept were recruited: 64 women and 32 men. Women were randomly assigned to one of two conditions. In the 'threat' condition, they were told before a difficult 20-item math test that the test had shown gender differences in the past. In the 'no threat' condition, they were told that the test showed no gender differences. All 32 men received the 'threat' instructions. Participants were tested individually and then rated their anxiety during the test on a 7-point scale. Results are summarized in Table 5. Scores of the women in the 'threat' condition were significantly lower than those of women in the 'no threat' condition (p < 0.01), and the 'no threat' women and men did not differ significantly. A statistical mediation analysis found that test anxiety accounted for part of the effect of the instructions on women's scores. Prior math achievement, measured by self-reported scores on a college entrance exam, did not differ between the two groups of women.

qs.q: The lower scores of women in the threat condition are best interpreted as an example of:
o: stereotype threat, in which fear of confirming a negative group stereotype impairs performance.
Correct: Reminding a stereotyped group of the stereotype in a domain they care about can raise anxiety and lower performance.
the self-serving bias, in which people credit their own successes to internal causes.
The self-serving bias concerns attributions of success and failure, not a drop in test performance.
the Pygmalion effect, in which the high expectations of others raise a person's performance over time.
Pygmalion is a positive expectation effect, the opposite of the pattern seen here.
the fundamental attribution error, in which others' behavior is attributed to disposition.
The fundamental attribution error concerns explanations of other people's behavior, not performance changes.
qs.x: Reminding a stereotyped group of the stereotype in a domain they care about can raise anxiety and lower performance. Trap: Choosing an attribution bias because the scenario mentions explanation of performance.

qs.q: Using the pooled standard deviation of the two groups of women, the effect size (Cohen's d) for the difference between the threat and no threat conditions is closest to:
o: 2.4 is the raw difference in points, not standardized.
0.3 would correspond to a mean difference of about 1 point.
1.3 would require a pooled SD of only about 1.8 points.
qs.x: Difference = 13.6 - 11.2 = 2.4. Pooled SD (equal n) = sqrt((3.4^2 + 3.1^2)/2) = sqrt(10.6) = 3.25. d = 2.4/3.25 = 0.74. Trap: Reporting the raw mean difference as an effect size, or dividing by the wrong SD.

qs.q: What was the main purpose of including the group of men?
o: To serve as a group that was randomly assigned to the 'no threat' condition for comparison with women.
All men received the 'threat' instructions, so none were assigned to 'no threat'.
To test whether the anxiety measure is reliable across the threat and no-threat conditions.
A single administration of the anxiety scale in one group does not test its reliability.
To show that the 'threat' instructions alone do not reduce performance, so the effect depends on the stereotype.
Correct: Men heard the same instructions but scored like 'no threat' women, indicating that the instructions are not harmful per se.
To increase the sample size so that the sex difference in the main comparison would be significant.
The goal was a comparison control, not statistical power to produce significance.
qs.x: Men heard the same instructions but scored like 'no threat' women, indicating that the instructions are not harmful per se. Trap: Reading a comparison group as a way to boost sample size rather than as a control.

qs.q: Participants were chosen because mathematics was highly important to their self-concept. This selection criterion was most likely used because:
o: people who do not care about math cannot take a math test or be affected by its context in any way.
Someone who cares little about math can still take the test; the issue is the personal stakes.
self-concept is determined only by performance feedback received from other people.
Self-concept is shaped by multiple sources, including self-perception and social comparison, not only others' feedback.
identity is formed entirely during adolescence and is unchanging in adulthood.
Identity continues to develop and change across adulthood.
stereotype threat is expected to be stronger when the domain is central to identity.
Correct: Domain identification raises the stakes of a negative stereotype, so threat effects are most apparent among strongly identified individuals.
qs.x: Domain identification raises the stakes of a negative stereotype, so threat effects are most apparent among strongly identified individuals. Trap: Overgeneralizing a developmental claim to justify a selection criterion.

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 7
text: Researchers examined how implicit and explicit measures of attitudes toward an out-group predict behavior. A total of 120 participants completed an Implicit Association Test (IAT), in which faster pairing of out-group faces with negative words yields a higher D score, and a self-report scale on explicit attitudes toward the out-group, in which higher scores indicate more negative attitudes. Participants were told that the study concerned computer tasks and that a member of the out-group, who was a trained confederate, would join them for a second task. While the participant waited, the researchers measured how far (in cm) the participant placed his or her chair from the confederate's chair. Correlations among the measures are given in Table 6. Figure 4 plots a random subset of 8 participants' IAT scores against seating distance. The researchers argued that implicit attitudes reflect automatic associations that are less open to deliberate control. They also noted that participants were told the study was not about attitudes and that explicit responses were anonymous, but that the sample was drawn only from an undergraduate psychology subject pool.

qs.q: The proportion of variance in seating distance that is shared with IAT D scores is closest to:
o: 34% is r itself, not the proportion of variance.
3% would result from squaring 0.18 (or 0.12^2, which is about 1%), not 0.34.
58% is the square root of 0.34, not its square.
Correct: The coefficient of determination is r squared: 0.34^2 = 0.1156, or about 12%.
qs.x: The coefficient of determination is r squared: 0.34^2 = 0.1156, or about 12%. Trap: Reporting r as the percent of variance explained rather than r squared.

qs.q: Which statement is best supported by Table 6?
o: Implicit negative attitudes cause people to sit farther from out-group members in a waiting room.
Correlation does not establish causation; a third variable or reverse causation is possible.
Implicit attitudes were more strongly related to seating distance than were explicit attitudes.
Correct: The correlation with seating distance was significant for the IAT (0.34, p < 0.001) but not for explicit attitudes (0.12, p = 0.19).
Explicit attitudes are unrelated to implicit attitudes in the general population of adults.
The implicit-explicit correlation of 0.18 was reported at p = 0.05, indicating a weak relation, not proof of no relation.
Seating distance is a valid measure of explicit attitudes.
The data do not show that seating distance measures explicit attitudes; its correlation with them was non-significant.
qs.x: The correlation with seating distance was significant for the IAT (0.34, p < 0.001) but not for explicit attitudes (0.12, p = 0.19). Trap: Inferring causation from a correlation coefficient, however significant.

qs.q: Explicit self-reports of attitudes toward out-groups are often weaker predictors of behavior than implicit measures, most likely because explicit reports are:
o: subject to social desirability bias and limited introspective access.
Correct: Participants may hide or lack awareness of negative attitudes, so explicit responses can differ from automatic evaluation.
unaffected by participants' awareness of what is being measured by the questionnaire.
Explicit measures are affected by awareness, which is the weakness.
determined only by genetic factors rather than by learning and experience.
Attitudes are shaped by learning and social factors, not genetics alone.
only reliable when the scale has few items and a simple response format.
The number of items does not address the bias in reporting.
qs.x: Participants may hide or lack awareness of negative attitudes, so explicit responses can differ from automatic evaluation. Trap: Overlooking that responding in a socially acceptable way is a threat to self-report validity.

qs.q: The chair-placement behavior, if driven by negative attitudes toward the out-group, is best classified as:
o: prejudice.
Prejudice is the attitude (affect) that the IAT or scale assessed, not the chair placement.
a stereotype.
A stereotype is a cognitive generalization about a group, not an action.
a self-fulfilling prophecy.
A self-fulfilling prophecy requires a belief that leads to behavior that makes the belief true.
discrimination.
Correct: Discrimination is behavior, and prejudice is an attitude; avoidance by seating distance is a behavior.
qs.x: Discrimination is behavior, and prejudice is an attitude; avoidance by seating distance is a behavior. Trap: Mixing up the three components: stereotype (cognition), prejudice (affect), discrimination (behavior).

qs.q: Based on the line connecting the lowest and highest IAT points in Figure 4, the approximate increase in seating distance per 0.5 unit increase in IAT D score is:
o: 37 cm
37 cm is the change per full unit of D score.
18 cm
Correct: From (0.0, 60) to (1.3, 108): slope = 48/1.3 = about 37 cm per unit, so 0.5 unit corresponds to about 18 cm.
9 cm
9 cm would correspond to a slope of about 18 cm per unit.
48 cm
48 cm is the total rise across the whole range of 1.3 units.
qs.x: From (0.0, 60) to (1.3, 108): slope = 48/1.3 = about 37 cm per unit, so 0.5 unit corresponds to about 18 cm. Trap: Using the entire rise instead of the rise for the interval asked.

Explicit attitude score and seating distance

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 8
text: A variation of a classic conformity study examined the conditions under which individuals yield to a group. Each of 100 participants was seated with five confederates and judged which of three comparison lines matched a standard line. On 12 critical trials, all five confederates gave the same incorrect answer. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions (n = 25 each). In the 'unanimous' condition, participants answered aloud after hearing all confederates. In the 'ally' condition, one confederate gave the correct answer on every critical trial, and the other four gave the incorrect answer. In the 'dissenter' condition, one confederate gave a different incorrect answer, and the other four gave a common incorrect answer. In the 'private' condition, there were five unanimous confederates, but the participant wrote the answer on paper, without it being seen by others. The outcome was the number of conformist (incorrect) responses, out of 12. Results are shown in Table 7. When the lines are presented alone, participants make fewer than 1% errors. Afterwards, participants were fully debriefed about the deception.

qs.q: The lower conformity in the 'private' condition relative to the 'unanimous' condition suggests that:
o: conformity was due entirely to informational influence, because participants doubted their own perception.
If it were purely informational, private responding would not reduce it, because the group's information would still be available.
participants in the private condition had better vision.
Participants were randomly assigned, so vision should be equivalent across groups.
much of the conformity was due to normative influence, a desire to avoid disapproval from the group.
Correct: When answers are public, social pressure is greatest; removing public exposure reduced conformity, implicating normative influence.
conformity occurs only when the group is larger than ten people.
Group size was five confederates in every condition; the data say nothing about a threshold of ten.
qs.x: When answers are public, social pressure is greatest; removing public exposure reduced conformity, implicating normative influence. Trap: Treating any reduction in conformity as evidence of doubt about perception rather than of social pressure.

qs.q: The 'dissenter' condition was included to determine whether:
o: participants will conform less when the majority is correct than when it is incorrect.
In every condition, the majority gave an incorrect answer.
a correct answer from an ally is necessary in order to reduce conformity to the majority.
The result shows an ally is not necessary, because a wrong dissenter also lowered conformity.
confederates are more convincing in groups than when they respond alone.
The dissenter condition does not compare group and lone confederates.
breaking the unanimity of the majority reduces conformity even if the dissenter is wrong.
Correct: The dissenter gave a wrong answer yet conformity fell from 4.2 to 1.8, so lack of unanimity matters beyond the provision of correct information.
qs.x: The dissenter gave a wrong answer yet conformity fell from 4.2 to 1.8, so lack of unanimity matters beyond the provision of correct information. Trap: Assuming that only a correct dissenter provides a source of support.

qs.q: Relative to the 'unanimous' condition, the percent decrease in mean conformist responses in the 'ally' condition was closest to:
o: 3.1 is the absolute decrease in responses.
Correct: Decrease = 4.2 - 1.1 = 3.1; 3.1/4.2 = 0.738, or about 74%.
26% is the remaining proportion (1.1/4.2), not the decrease.
57% is the decrease for the dissenter condition (2.4/4.2), not for the ally condition.
qs.x: Decrease = 4.2 - 1.1 = 3.1; 3.1/4.2 = 0.738, or about 74%. Trap: Giving the fraction remaining rather than the fraction lost.

qs.q: Which of the following is a feature of the study that addresses an ethical concern raised by the deception?
o: Participants were randomly assigned to the four conditions.
Random assignment addresses internal validity, not ethics of deception.
The sample contained 25 participants per condition.
Sample size relates to statistical power, not the deception.
The outcome was recorded as the number of errors.
The dependent measure has no bearing on the ethical issue.
Participants were fully debriefed after the study.
Correct: Debriefing explains the deception and the purpose of the study and is the standard remedy when deception is necessary.
qs.x: Debriefing explains the deception and the purpose of the study and is the standard remedy when deception is necessary. Trap: Confusing methodological strengths with ethical safeguards.

tbl.cap: Table 7. Conformist responses out of 12 critical trials

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 9
text: A public health department compared mortality in four neighborhoods grouped by median household income quartile, from lowest (Q1) to highest (Q4). Each group contained 250,000 residents. The department reviewed death certificates for one calendar year and also computed the period life expectancy at birth for each group. The data are shown in Table 8, and life expectancy is plotted in Figure 5. Residents in the lowest-income neighborhoods were more likely to live near major highways and industrial sites, and fewer had employer-provided health insurance. Residents in the highest-income neighborhoods were more likely to have completed a college degree. The report noted that the analysis was cross-sectional, so each resident's income and health were measured at one time only, and that the data were aggregated by neighborhood. The department's authors stated that every step up the income ladder was associated with longer life, not only the step out of poverty, and discussed the idea that higher socioeconomic status gives people more flexible resources, such as money, knowledge, power, and social connections, that can be used to avoid risks and to benefit from new health advances.

qs.q: The crude death rate in the Q1 neighborhoods, per 1,000 residents, was:
o: 1 per 1,000 would correspond to 250 deaths.
100 per 1,000 would correspond to 25,000 deaths.
Correct: 2,500 deaths / 250,000 residents = 0.01, which is 10 per 1,000.
0.1 per 1,000 would correspond to 25 deaths.
qs.x: 2,500 deaths / 250,000 residents = 0.01, which is 10 per 1,000. Trap: Misplacing the decimal when converting a proportion to a rate per 1,000.

qs.q: According to Figure 5, the gap in life expectancy between the highest and lowest income quartiles is:
o: 8.2 years
Correct: 82.3 - 74.1 = 8.2 years.
5.5 years
5.5 years is the Q1-to-Q3 gap (79.6 - 74.1), not the Q1-to-Q4 gap.
5.3 years
5.3 years is the Q2-to-Q4 gap (82.3 - 77.0).
2.7 years
2.7 years is the Q3-to-Q4 gap (82.3 - 79.6), not Q1 to Q4.
qs.x: 82.3 - 74.1 = 8.2 years. Trap: Reading the wrong pair of bars from the graph.

qs.q: Because the study was cross-sectional, which alternative to the conclusion that low income causes poor health must be considered?
o: Poor health may reduce a person's ability to work and earn income (reverse causation).
Correct: A single time-point design cannot determine the direction of the association, and illness can lower earnings (health selection).
Mortality was measured in only four income groups, which is too few for any comparison.
The number of groups does not address direction of causation.
Residents of all neighborhoods have the same health risks regardless of income.
The report found differing exposures, such as highways and insurance, so risks are not the same.
Life expectancy is measured in years and income in dollars, so the two cannot be compared.
Differences in the units of measurement do not create any causal alternative.
qs.x: A single time-point design cannot determine the direction of the association, and illness can lower earnings (health selection). Trap: Taking an association at one point in time as proof of causal direction.

qs.q: The authors' idea that higher socioeconomic status provides flexible resources that can be used to avoid health risks and to gain from new advances is most consistent with:
o: the demographic transition model of population change.
The demographic transition model describes shifts in birth and death rates with industrialization.
symbolic interactionism as applied to everyday interaction.
Symbolic interactionism focuses on meanings created in everyday interaction.
the strain theory of deviance proposed by Merton.
Strain theory explains deviance as a result of a gap between goals and means.
the fundamental cause theory of health inequality.
Correct: Fundamental cause theory holds that SES gives access to flexible resources, so inequality persists even as specific disease mechanisms change.
qs.x: Fundamental cause theory holds that SES gives access to flexible resources, so inequality persists even as specific disease mechanisms change. Trap: Choosing a general sociological theory by name rather than matching to the argument.

qs.q: The conclusion that any individual resident of a Q1 neighborhood will die earlier than any resident of a Q4 neighborhood would be an example of:
o: a placebo effect, because participants expected the neighborhood to affect their health.
A placebo effect is a response to an inert treatment, which does not apply.
an ecological fallacy, because group-level data may not apply to individuals.
Correct: Aggregated neighborhood data describe groups; individual outcomes vary widely and cannot be inferred with certainty.
regression to the mean, because extreme neighborhood values drift toward the average.
Regression to the mean concerns extreme values drifting toward average on remeasurement.
a type II error, because a true difference between neighborhoods was missed.
A type II error is failing to reject a false null hypothesis, which is not what the statement describes.
qs.x: Aggregated neighborhood data describe groups; individual outcomes vary widely and cannot be inferred with certainty. Trap: Moving from a group-level pattern to a deterministic claim about individuals.

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 10
text: Researchers followed a national sample of 2,000 adults, each with documented family income during childhood, and recorded the income quintile of each adult at age 40. Parents' income quintiles were assigned from tax records when the participants were children. The researchers also recorded whether each participant earned a college degree. Table 9 shows, for each parental income quintile, the percentage of adult children who ended up in the bottom and top quintiles of the adult income distribution, and the percentage who earned a degree. In interviews with a subset of the participants, children from top-quintile families more often described receiving help from parents in selecting colleges, guidance on how to interact with admissions officers and employers, and introductions to professional contacts. Children from bottom-quintile families more often reported that they were the first in their families to apply to college and that they did not know how to ask for financial aid. The authors framed the results as showing both movement and persistence in social class position across generations, and discussed competing explanations from functionalist and conflict perspectives.

qs.q: The interview findings regarding parents' guidance and professional contacts are best described by which concept?
o: Cultural and social capital, which are passed on within families and advantage high-income children.
Correct: Bourdieu's cultural capital and social capital describe the knowledge, skills, and networks that families pass to children and that help reproduce class position.
Anomie, a breakdown of social norms in times of rapid social change or upheaval.
Anomie, as discussed by Durkheim, describes normlessness, not transmitted advantage.
Relative deprivation, the perception of being worse off than other comparable people or groups.
Relative deprivation refers to comparison with a reference group, not to family resources.
The looking-glass self, in which self-concept reflects imagined evaluations by other people.
The looking-glass self is a theory of self-concept formation, not of class reproduction.
qs.x: Bourdieu's cultural capital and social capital describe the knowledge, skills, and networks that families pass to children and that help reproduce class position. Trap: Selecting a famous sociological term that is not tied to the evidence given.

qs.q: The probability that a child from a top-quintile family reaches the top quintile, compared with a child from a bottom-quintile family, is about:
o: 30 times as high
30 is the difference in percentage points (38 - 8), not the ratio.
4.75 times as high
0.21 times as high
0.21 is the inverse ratio (8/38), which compares bottom to top.
3.2 times as high
3.2 does not follow from the table; the ratio of 38 to 8 is 4.75.
qs.x: 38%/8% = 4.75. Trap: Subtracting percentages instead of dividing to compare probabilities.

qs.q: Which interpretation of Table 9 is most consistent with a conflict perspective?
o: Unequal rewards motivate the most talented people to fill the most functionally important positions.
This is the functionalist (Davis-Moore) argument about talent and incentive.
Advantaged groups use their resources to preserve their position, which limits mobility for others.
Correct: Conflict theory views inequality as the result of competition in which dominant groups protect their advantages.
Class position has no effect on adult income once education is held constant.
The table shows parental quintile strongly related to adult outcomes.
Social stratification is beneficial because it promotes social stability and cohesion.
Emphasis on stability and cohesion is a functionalist claim.
qs.x: Conflict theory views inequality as the result of competition in which dominant groups protect their advantages. Trap: Selecting the functionalist claim when asked for the conflict reading.

qs.q: The study compares the class position of adults with that of their parents. This type of change is called:
o: intragenerational mobility.
Intragenerational mobility compares a person's own status over his or her lifetime.
structural mobility.
Structural mobility is movement caused by changes in the economy that shift many people at once.
social reproduction.
Social reproduction is the persistence of class across generations, not the term for a change.
intergenerational mobility.
Correct: Intergenerational mobility compares the status of children with that of their parents.
qs.x: Intergenerational mobility compares the status of children with that of their parents. Trap: Confusing intergenerational (across generations) with intragenerational (within one lifetime).

tbl.cap: Table 9. Adult outcomes by parental income quintile

passages.title: FL02 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 1
text: A research group purified protein Z from a bacterial lysate. The lysate was adjusted to pH 8.0 and loaded onto an anion-exchange column, whose beads carry positively charged groups. After washing, bound proteins were eluted with a gradient of increasing NaCl concentration, and absorbance at 280 nm was monitored (Figure 1). Peak fractions were then analyzed in three ways: SDS-PAGE in the presence of the reducing agent beta-mercaptoethanol (BME), SDS-PAGE without BME, and gel filtration under native conditions, which separates proteins by size and reports apparent native mass. SDS denatures proteins and disrupts noncovalent interactions, and BME breaks disulfide bonds. The four major proteins in the lysate are called X, Y, Z, and W. Their properties are summarized in Table 1. The isoelectric point (pI) of each protein was calculated from its amino acid sequence. All chromatography steps were performed at 4 degrees C with protease inhibitors present, and each experiment was repeated three times with similar results.

qs.q: Protein X appears in the flow-through at pH 8.0. Which statement best explains this?
o: X is too small to enter the pores of the beads and is excluded from the resin matrix entirely
pore-size exclusion is how gel filtration works, not ion exchange.
X carries a net positive charge at pH 8.0 and is repelled by the positively charged beads
Correct: X has a pI of 9.1, which is above 8.0, so it is protonated overall and positive, like the resin.
X is uncharged at pH 8.0 because its pI is above 8.0, so it passes through without binding
a protein is neutral only when pH equals pI; at pH below pI it is positive.
X contains no hydrophobic residues, so it cannot interact with the bead surface at all
hydrophobicity is irrelevant to binding of an ion-exchange resin.
qs.x: X has a pI of 9.1, which is above 8.0, so it is protonated overall and positive, like the resin. Trap: Confusing pore-size exclusion with charge-based binding, or assuming pH below pI means neutral.

qs.q: Protein W elutes at the highest NaCl concentration because:
o: it has the largest native mass, so it is retained longest inside the bead pores
size does not determine ion-exchange binding; Y and Z have the same subunit mass but elute earlier.
it forms a disulfide-linked dimer, which neutralizes its charge and weakens resin binding
disulfide formation does not neutralize charge and would not strengthen binding to the resin.
it has the lowest pI and therefore the greatest net negative charge at pH 8.0
Correct: At pH 8.0 proteins whose pI is below 8 are anionic, and W (pI 4.9) is the most negative and binds the cationic beads most tightly.
it is positively charged at pH 8.0 and binds the resin through ionic attraction
a positive protein would be repelled by positively charged beads, as X is.
qs.x: At pH 8.0 proteins whose pI is below 8 are anionic, and W (pI 4.9) is the most negative and binds the cationic beads most tightly. Trap: Equating larger size with stronger binding on an ion-exchange column.

qs.q: The SDS-PAGE results for protein W (45 kDa with BME, 90 kDa without BME) indicate that W is:
o: a single 90-kDa polypeptide with internal disulfide bonds
a single chain would run at 90 kDa with and without BME.
a noncovalent dimer of two 45-kDa chains
SDS would break noncovalent contacts, giving 45 kDa in both lanes, as seen for Z.
a 45-kDa monomer that aggregates only when BME is absent
the native mass of 90 kDa shows a stable dimer; BME-sensitive linkage indicates covalent disulfides.
two 45-kDa polypeptides linked by interchain disulfide bonds
Correct: Without BME the disulfide bond holds the chains together and they run as 90 kDa; BME cleaves the link and each chain runs at 45 kDa.
qs.x: Without BME the disulfide bond holds the chains together and they run as 90 kDa; BME cleaves the link and each chain runs at 45 kDa. Trap: Forgetting that SDS disrupts noncovalent but not disulfide bonds.

qs.q: Which description best fits protein Z?
o: A homodimer held together by noncovalent interactions
Correct: Native mass is 90 kDa but SDS-PAGE gives 45 kDa regardless of BME, so the subunits are not covalently linked.
A monomer of 90 kDa
a monomer would give 90 kDa on SDS-PAGE.
A homodimer joined by disulfide bonds
Z runs at 45 kDa without BME, so no disulfide links the subunits.
A homotetramer
four 45-kDa subunits would have a native mass near 180 kDa.
qs.x: Native mass is 90 kDa but SDS-PAGE gives 45 kDa regardless of BME, so the subunits are not covalently linked. Trap: Treating native mass alone as proof of a disulfide-linked or single-chain protein.

qs.q: If the chromatography were repeated at pH 5.0, how would protein Z most likely behave relative to pH 8.0?
o: It would bind more tightly because the solution is more acidic
lowering pH below the pI adds positive charge, which reduces anion-exchange binding.
It would behave identically because its mass does not change
ion exchange depends on charge, which depends on pH.
It would elute at the same salt concentration but as a monomer
pH change does not by itself dissociate the dimer or alter elution salt in that way.
It would bind much more weakly and elute at lower salt or in the flow-through
Correct: Near its pI of 5.2 Z has little or slightly positive net charge, so attraction to the anion-exchange beads falls sharply.
qs.x: Near its pI of 5.2 Z has little or slightly positive net charge, so attraction to the anion-exchange beads falls sharply. Trap: Assuming lower pH always increases binding to an anion exchanger.

graph.title: Figure 1. Anion-exchange elution profile

passages.title: FL02 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 2
text: Gene G encodes a metabolic enzyme and has five exons. The mature mRNA region amplified in this study spans exons 1 through 5; exon lengths in this region are 90, 120, 80, 150, and 105 base pairs, respectively. RNA was isolated from fibroblasts of a control subject and of three patients, each carrying a different single-nucleotide change at an intron-exon boundary, as confirmed by sequencing of genomic DNA. RNA was converted to complementary DNA (cDNA) using reverse transcriptase, and the cDNA was amplified by PCR using one primer in exon 1 and one in exon 5. PCR products were separated by gel electrophoresis, and each sample produced a single band. Product sizes and the location of each mutation are shown in Table 1. Researchers hypothesized that each mutation disrupts recognition of a splice site, causing the adjacent exon to be omitted from the mature mRNA. Translation of the control cDNA proceeds in the reading frame established at the start codon in exon 1.

qs.q: Based on the product sizes, which patient's mRNA most likely contains a frameshift downstream of the skipped exon?
o: Patient 1 only
exon 2 is 120 bp, a multiple of 3, so skipping it deletes whole codons without a frameshift.
Patient 2 only
Correct: Patient 2 lost exon 3 (80 bp, not a multiple of 3), shifting the reading frame; exons 2 (120 bp) and 4 (150 bp) are multiples of 3.
Patient 3 only
exon 4 is 150 bp, a multiple of 3, so the frame is maintained.
All three patients
only the patient missing the 80-bp exon has a length not divisible by 3.
qs.x: Patient 2 lost exon 3 (80 bp, not a multiple of 3), shifting the reading frame; exons 2 (120 bp) and 4 (150 bp) are multiples of 3. Trap: Assuming any exon skipping causes a frameshift instead of checking divisibility by 3.

qs.q: Why was reverse transcriptase included in the procedure?
o: To synthesize a DNA copy of the mature mRNA that can serve as a template for PCR
Correct: PCR polymerases need a DNA template, so spliced mRNA is first copied into cDNA.
To remove introns from the pre-mRNA so that the PCR primers can anneal to the exons
intron removal is done by the spliceosome in cells, not by reverse transcriptase.
To add a poly-A tail to the mature mRNA so that the primers can bind to it
primers here anneal to exon sequences, not a poly-A tail.
To transcribe genomic DNA into RNA that can then be amplified in the reaction
reverse transcriptase makes DNA from an RNA template, the opposite direction.
qs.x: PCR polymerases need a DNA template, so spliced mRNA is first copied into cDNA. Trap: Mixing up the direction of reverse transcription with splicing or transcription.

qs.q: The protein produced from Patient 1's mRNA is expected to differ from the control protein by:
o: a loss of 120 amino acids
120 is the number of base pairs, not codons; divide by 3.
a premature stop codon immediately after exon 1
the frame is maintained, so no new stop is created by this deletion.
an in-frame loss of about 40 amino acids
Correct: The 120-bp difference corresponds to 40 codons removed while the reading frame is retained.
no difference, because the genomic DNA sequence is intact
the mRNA, not the genomic DNA, determines the protein, and the mRNA lacks exon 2.
qs.x: The 120-bp difference corresponds to 40 codons removed while the reading frame is retained. Trap: Reporting base pairs lost as amino acids lost.

qs.q: The mutation in Patient 1 alters the 5' end of intron 2. Disruption of which interaction most directly explains exon skipping?
o: Binding of the ribosome to the start codon
translation initiation does not occur on introns and is unrelated to splice-site recognition.
Base pairing of U1 snRNA with the 5' splice site
Correct: The 5' donor site is recognized by U1 snRNP through RNA-RNA base pairing at the start of splicing.
Recognition of the poly-A signal by cleavage factors
the poly-A signal is at the 3' end of the transcript, not intron 2.
Addition of the 7-methylguanosine cap to the 5' end of the transcript
capping occurs at the 5' end of the whole transcript and not at internal introns.
qs.x: The 5' donor site is recognized by U1 snRNP through RNA-RNA base pairing at the start of splicing. Trap: Confusing the 5' splice site with the 5' cap of the transcript.

passages.title: FL02 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 3
text: Disorder D is caused by loss of function of an enzyme encoded on the X chromosome. Individual II-1, a male, is affected. His parents, I-1 and I-2, are unaffected, and there is no history of the disorder on either side of the family beyond II-1. His sister II-2 is unaffected and has married II-3, an unaffected man with no family history. Researchers measured enzyme activity in cultured skin fibroblasts from each family member (Table 1). Fibroblast colonies grown from single cells of I-2 and II-2 were also tested: about half of the colonies had normal enzyme activity and half had almost none. Disorder D follows a recessive pattern, and the family is not known to have any new mutation. Assume that II-2 and II-3 have not yet had any children and that the gene is not in the pseudoautosomal region. Written informed consent was obtained from all family members, and enzyme assays were performed in duplicate with the technician blinded to the pedigree and to the phenotype of each sample.

qs.q: Before enzyme activity was measured, what was the probability that II-2 is a carrier?
o: Correct: I-2 must be a carrier (she has an affected son and an unaffected father); each daughter receives the mutant X with probability 1/2, while I-1 passes his normal X to all daughters.
this would apply if the carrier status of I-2 were itself uncertain or two independent 1/2 events were needed.
this is the conditional probability used for an unaffected child of two autosomal carriers, not an X-linked pedigree.
II-2 would be a certain carrier only if her father were affected.
qs.x: I-2 must be a carrier (she has an affected son and an unaffected father); each daughter receives the mutant X with probability 1/2, while I-1 passes his normal X to all daughters. Trap: Applying the autosomal 2/3 rule to an X-linked pedigree.

qs.q: Assuming II-2 is a carrier, what is the probability that the first child of II-2 and II-3 is an affected boy?
o: this is the chance that any child inherits the mutant X, but daughters with II-3's normal X would be unaffected.
this double counts by multiplying in the 1/2 carrier probability, which is already given.
the father is unaffected, but the mother is a carrier and can transmit the allele to sons.
Correct: A carrier mother passes the mutant X to half of her children, and half of the children are male: 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.
qs.x: A carrier mother passes the mutant X to half of her children, and half of the children are male: 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4. Trap: Multiplying in the carrier probability again after being told she is a carrier.

qs.q: The intermediate enzyme activity in I-2 and II-2 and the mixed colony results are best explained by:
o: incomplete penetrance of the mutant allele, so only some carriers show any phenotype
penetrance describes whether a genotype produces a phenotype, not a cell-by-cell mix of enzyme activity.
inactivation of the paternal X in every cell, so all cells express the maternal allele
if the same X were inactivated in all cells, colonies would be uniform, not half and half.
random inactivation of one X chromosome in each cell early in female development
Correct: X inactivation yields a mosaic: roughly half of the cells express the normal X and half the mutant X.
codominance of two different alleles at an autosomal locus within each cell of the body
the gene is X-linked and one allele is inactive, not co-expressed in each cell.
qs.x: X inactivation yields a mosaic: roughly half of the cells express the normal X and half the mutant X. Trap: Treating mosaic expression as incomplete dominance rather than X inactivation.

qs.q: If II-1 had children with a woman who does not carry the mutation, what fraction of their daughters would be carriers?
o: None
daughters always receive the father's X, so they carry the allele.
All
Correct: II-1 gives his only X, bearing the mutant allele, to every daughter, who also receives a normal X from her mother.
Half
this is the expectation for daughters of a carrier mother, not an affected father.
One-fourth
this has no basis because the father's contribution is fixed rather than random.
qs.x: II-1 gives his only X, bearing the mutant allele, to every daughter, who also receives a normal X from her mother. Trap: Forgetting that affected fathers transmit their X to all daughters.

passages.title: FL02 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 4
text: Two children with fasting hypoglycemia were evaluated for inherited defects of hepatic glucose release. Patient A has a deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase, and Patient B has a deficiency of liver glycogen phosphorylase. A healthy child served as a comparison. Subjects were fed, then fasted for 12 hours, with blood glucose measured at intervals (Figure 1). At 8 hours of fasting, blood lactate was measured, and glucagon was injected to measure the change in blood glucose 30 minutes later. Liver glycogen content was measured by biopsy in the fed state. Results are in Table 1. Glucagon activates hepatic glycogen breakdown through a protein kinase A pathway. In the liver, gluconeogenesis uses lactate, amino acids, and glycerol as substrates, and glucose-6-phosphate produced by gluconeogenesis must be dephosphorylated before glucose can leave the cell. Gluconeogenesis was assumed to be intact in Patient B. Both children were otherwise growing normally and had normal kidney function, and all measurements were repeated on a second day to confirm that the results were reproducible and not due to illness.

qs.q: Why does glucagon fail to raise blood glucose in Patient A?
o: Glucagon cannot activate protein kinase A in the liver of this patient
the defect is in an enzyme downstream; the glucagon signal itself is not described as defective.
Glycogen synthase is overactive, converting all glucose to glycogen
glycogen synthase activity is inhibited by glucagon signaling, and does not explain the loss of release.
The liver lacks hexokinase, so it cannot take up glucose
uptake is irrelevant to glucose release during fasting.
Glycogen breakdown yields glucose-6-phosphate, which cannot be converted to free glucose without glucose-6-phosphatase
Correct: Glucagon still triggers glycogenolysis, but without dephosphorylation the product remains trapped in the hepatocyte.
qs.x: Glucagon still triggers glycogenolysis, but without dephosphorylation the product remains trapped in the hepatocyte. Trap: Assuming glucagon fails because the hormone pathway is broken.

qs.q: The elevated lactate in Patient A at 8 hours is best explained by:
