o: absence of lactate dehydrogenase, which prevents pyruvate from being converted to lactate
LDH activity is not missing; lactate is clearly being produced.
increased oxidative phosphorylation in the liver, which consumes lactate and lowers blood levels
greater oxidative phosphorylation would oxidize pyruvate, not raise lactate.
accumulation of glucose-6-phosphate that is diverted into glycolysis and yields pyruvate and lactate
Correct: Because glucose-6-phosphate cannot be released as glucose, it enters glycolysis, and the resulting pyruvate is reduced to lactate.
increased gluconeogenesis from lactate, which would lower rather than raise blood lactate
gluconeogenesis cannot be completed in this patient, so it does not clear lactate.
qs.x: Because glucose-6-phosphate cannot be released as glucose, it enters glycolysis, and the resulting pyruvate is reduced to lactate. Trap: Linking high lactate to oxygen shortage rather than diverted glucose-6-phosphate.

qs.q: Patient B maintains a higher fasting glucose than Patient A mainly because:
o: gluconeogenesis is intact and glucose-6-phosphatase is present
Correct: Patient B can still make glucose from lactate, amino acids, and glycerol, and release it.
Patient B stores less glycogen than Patient A
B actually stores more glycogen; the amount stored does not determine output when it cannot be broken down.
Patient B has a higher rate of glycogenolysis
the glucagon response of 4 mg/dL shows that glycogenolysis is largely absent.
Patient B oxidizes fatty acids to make glucose directly
animals cannot convert fatty acid acetyl-CoA into net glucose.
qs.x: Patient B can still make glucose from lactate, amino acids, and glycerol, and release it. Trap: Believing fatty acids can be converted to glucose.

qs.q: In healthy individuals, muscle glycogen cannot directly raise blood glucose primarily because muscle lacks:
o: glucose-6-phosphatase
Correct: Without this enzyme muscle cannot dephosphorylate glucose-6-phosphate for export.
glycogen phosphorylase
muscle has phosphorylase and uses it to degrade glycogen.
phosphoglucomutase
muscle uses it to convert glucose-1-phosphate into glucose-6-phosphate.
hexokinase
muscle expresses hexokinase for glucose phosphorylation.
qs.x: Without this enzyme muscle cannot dephosphorylate glucose-6-phosphate for export. Trap: Naming a glycogenolysis enzyme that muscle does have.

qs.q: Based on Figure 1, the approximate rate of fall in blood glucose for Patient B between 4 and 8 hours is:
o: 0.75 mg/dL per hour
this is approximately the rate for the healthy subject (88 to 85).
6 mg/dL per hour
Correct: From 75 to 52 is a drop of 23 mg/dL over 4 hours, or about 5.75, rounded to 6.
3 mg/dL per hour
this is the rate for Patient A (50 to 38).
23 mg/dL per hour
this is the total decline and has not been divided by the 4-hour interval.
qs.x: From 75 to 52 is a drop of 23 mg/dL over 4 hours, or about 5.75, rounded to 6. Trap: Reporting the total change instead of the rate, or reading the wrong curve.

graph.title: Figure 1. Blood glucose during fasting

passages.title: FL02 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 5
text: Uptake of two solutes, S and T, was studied in isolated red blood cells suspended in buffer. Both solutes are uncharged and are not metabolized in the cell. Initial uptake rates were measured over a range of external concentrations (Figure 1). Solute S is a small polar molecule, and solute T is a small nonpolar molecule that dissolves readily in lipids. In a second experiment, uptake rates were measured at an external concentration of 6 mM under four conditions (Table 1): untreated cells, cells treated with a compound that binds covalently to a membrane protein and blocks the carrier for S, cells in which ATP was depleted with metabolic poisons for 30 minutes, and cells chilled to 4 degrees C. The intracellular concentrations of both solutes were kept near zero by the assay design so that uptake rates reflect initial inward movement. Rates are reported in micromoles per liter of cells per minute.

qs.q: Which mechanism best accounts for the uptake of solute S?
o: Simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer
simple diffusion is not saturable and is not blocked by a carrier inhibitor.
Primary active transport
this would fall when ATP is depleted, but S uptake is unchanged.
Facilitated diffusion through a carrier protein
Correct: Uptake is saturable, blocked by a carrier inhibitor, and unaffected by ATP depletion, consistent with passive carrier-mediated transport.
Secondary active transport coupled to a Na+ gradient
this would need an ion gradient and is not supported by the data; ATP depletion eventually dissipates such gradients.
qs.x: Uptake is saturable, blocked by a carrier inhibitor, and unaffected by ATP depletion, consistent with passive carrier-mediated transport. Trap: Assuming any saturable transport is active transport.

qs.q: Based on Figure 1, the external concentration of S at which uptake is half-maximal is closest to:
o: 1 mM
the rate at 1 mM is 15, only a quarter of the maximum.
6 mM
at 6 mM the rate is already two-thirds of maximum.
12 mM
at 12 mM the rate is 48, which is 80 percent of maximum.
3 mM
Correct: The curve approaches about 60, and half of this (30) occurs at 3 mM.
qs.x: The curve approaches about 60, and half of this (30) occurs at 3 mM. Trap: Reading the half-maximal point from the y-axis value of the last data point.

qs.q: Which best explains why the uptake of T rises linearly over the range studied?
o: T crosses the bilayer by simple diffusion, so its rate is proportional to the concentration gradient
Correct: With no carrier to saturate, flux increases in proportion to the gradient.
T uses a carrier that is not yet saturated at 24 mM, so uptake still rises with concentration
the carrier for S saturates near 3 to 6 mM, and T is unaffected by the carrier blocker.
T uptake requires ATP hydrolysis at each step, so the rate depends on cellular ATP levels
ATP depletion did not change T uptake.
T enters through a gated channel that opens only at high concentrations of the solute
gating by concentration would produce a nonlinear curve.
qs.x: With no carrier to saturate, flux increases in proportion to the gradient. Trap: Reading a linear curve as evidence of a carrier that has not yet saturated.

qs.q: If the linear relationship for T continued at higher concentrations, at about what external concentration would T uptake reach 60, the maximum rate for S?
o: 24 mM
T uptake at 24 mM is only 36.
40 mM
Correct: The slope is 1.5 per mM (36/24), so 60/1.5 = 40 mM.
30 mM
this would give a rate of 45 at the observed slope.
60 mM
this treats slope as 1, the value of the rate itself.
qs.x: The slope is 1.5 per mM (36/24), so 60/1.5 = 40 mM. Trap: Setting concentration equal to the target rate without dividing by the slope.

graph.title: Figure 1. Uptake rate versus external concentration

passages.title: FL02 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 6
text: A bacterial culture in rich medium was divided into three flasks and incubated with shaking. At 2 hours, drug M was added to one flask and drug N to another, and the third served as a control. Viable counts were determined every 2 hours (Figure 1). Drug M inhibits the bacterial ribosome. Drug N blocks the final cross-linking step of peptidoglycan synthesis. A susceptible strain (A) and a strain (B) carrying a plasmid were compared by determining the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), the lowest drug concentration that prevents visible growth (Table 1). The plasmid in strain B encodes an enzyme that is secreted into the periplasm; its substrate specificity was not examined further. Colony counts are reported as log10 of colony-forming units per milliliter. In the control flask the culture grew exponentially during the 6 hours, and nutrients were not limiting. Counts for the culture in the first two hours were identical in all flasks.

qs.q: What is the approximate doubling time of the control culture? (A doubling increases log10 by about 0.3.)
o: 20 minutes
this would give 6 doublings (1.8 log units) in 2 hours.
60 minutes
this would give only 2 doublings (0.6 log units) in 2 hours.
120 minutes
this would give one doubling (0.3 log units) in 2 hours.
40 minutes
Correct: The count rises 0.9 log units in 2 hours, about 3 doublings, or one doubling per 40 minutes.
qs.x: The count rises 0.9 log units in 2 hours, about 3 doublings, or one doubling per 40 minutes. Trap: Treating the log-unit change as the number of doublings.

qs.q: Which classification fits drug M based on Figure 1?
o: Bactericidal, because the viable count is lower than that of the untreated control
M-treated cells are not killed; the count is simply not increasing.
Ineffective, because the viable count does not fall below the starting inoculum
stopping growth is an effect, and the count is far below the control by 6 hours.
Bacteriostatic, because it halts growth without substantially lowering the viable count
Correct: After addition the count stays near 5.9 rather than falling.
Selectively toxic to only dividing cells, so non-growing cells would be unaffected entirely
the data do not address which cells are affected.
qs.x: After addition the count stays near 5.9 rather than falling. Trap: Equating no decrease in viable count with no drug effect.

qs.q: Strain B has a 64-fold higher MIC for drug N but the same MIC for drug M. Which is the most likely explanation?
o: A mutation in the ribosome that prevents binding of both drugs
a ribosomal change would affect M and not N.
A plasmid-encoded enzyme that specifically inactivates drug N
Correct: Resistance limited to N implicates a drug-specific mechanism, such as a periplasmic enzyme that degrades N, while the ribosome target of M is unaltered.
Loss of the cell wall in strain B
the plasmid enzyme explains resistance; there is no evidence of wall loss, and wall loss would not specifically change only the N MIC.
A general efflux pump expelling both drugs
MIC for M is unchanged, so a general pump is unlikely.
qs.x: Resistance limited to N implicates a drug-specific mechanism, such as a periplasmic enzyme that degrades N, while the ribosome target of M is unaltered. Trap: Assuming resistance always arises from target alteration or general efflux.

qs.q: If drug M were added to a culture at the same time as drug N, the killing by drug N would most likely be:
o: increased, because both drugs target the same structure
M targets the ribosome, not the wall.
unchanged, because the drugs act independently
M halts growth, and growth is required for N to act.
increased, because M would stop repair of the cell wall
M's effect on protein synthesis stops growth, protecting the cells from N.
reduced, because drug N kills only actively growing cells that are synthesizing peptidoglycan
Correct: Drug M stops growth, and drug N needs cells that are building new wall to lyse them.
qs.x: Drug M stops growth, and drug N needs cells that are building new wall to lyse them. Trap: Assuming that two antibiotics together are always additive.

graph.title: Figure 1. Viable count over time

passages.title: FL02 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 7
text: In the developing vertebrate neural tube, cells at the ventral midline secrete the signaling protein Sonic hedgehog (Shh). Shh diffuses away from this source and binds the receptor Patched on nearby cells, relieving inhibition of the membrane protein Smoothened and ultimately activating transcription factors that specify cell fate. The measured concentration of Shh at increasing distance from the source is plotted in Figure 1, and the concentration thresholds associated with each fate are given in Table 1. In experiments on chick embryos, researchers treated embryos with cyclopamine, which inhibits Smoothened, and observed cell types after 48 hours. In another experiment, a second Shh-secreting tissue was grafted to the dorsal side of the neural tube. Concentration is expressed in arbitrary units, with 100 at the source. Shh concentration at a distance d (micrometers) fits the equation 100 x e^(-d/100). Embryos were staged by somite number, fixed, and stained for cell-type-specific markers, and each experimental group contained at least ten embryos, all of which gave consistent results.

qs.q: A cell located 100 um from the source would most likely become:
o: a motor neuron
Correct: At 100 um the concentration is about 37, within the 30 to 60 range for motor neurons.
a floor plate cell
floor plate fates require concentrations above 60, found within about 50 um.
a V2 interneuron
this fate requires concentrations of 15 to 30, found at greater distances.
a dorsal cell type
this requires concentrations below 15.
qs.x: At 100 um the concentration is about 37, within the 30 to 60 range for motor neurons. Trap: Reading the fate from the wrong concentration range.

qs.q: Cells at 25 um from the source in a cyclopamine-treated embryo would most likely adopt:
o: a floor plate fate, because Shh concentration is highest there
the cells cannot transduce the signal, so concentration is irrelevant.
a motor neuron fate, because cyclopamine reduces Shh concentration
cyclopamine blocks Smoothened and does not change Shh levels.
a dorsal fate, because they cannot respond to Shh
Correct: Blocking Smoothened prevents signal transduction, so cells take the fate that occurs without Shh signaling regardless of concentration.
apoptosis, because they lack the signal
the data do not indicate cell death; cells instead adopt default fates.
qs.x: Blocking Smoothened prevents signal transduction, so cells take the fate that occurs without Shh signaling regardless of concentration. Trap: Assuming cell fate follows the concentration even when the receptor pathway is blocked.

qs.q: What outcome is most likely after grafting a second Shh source to the dorsal side?
o: Ventral cell types, such as floor plate and motor neurons, would form near the graft
Correct: Cells near the graft experience high Shh and follow the same concentration-dependent fates.
Only the original ventral cell types would form because fate is fixed before Shh acts
fate depends on current signaling, as shown by the gradient.
Dorsal cell types would expand because Shh inhibits ventral fates
Shh promotes ventral fates.
No change, because Shh diffuses only ventrally
diffusion occurs in all directions from the source.
qs.x: Cells near the graft experience high Shh and follow the same concentration-dependent fates. Trap: Assuming developmental fate is predetermined and not induced by signals.

qs.q: Signaling by Shh from the midline to nearby cells is best described as:
o: endocrine signaling
this requires transport through the bloodstream to distant cells.
autocrine signaling
this means the cell responds to its own signal.
juxtacrine signaling
this requires direct contact between cell surfaces, while Shh diffuses through tissue.
paracrine signaling
Correct: Shh is secreted and acts on nearby cells over short distances.
qs.x: Shh is secreted and acts on nearby cells over short distances. Trap: Calling any secreted signal endocrine.

qs.q: Based on the equation or Figure 1, the Shh concentration falls by half over a distance of about:
o: 35 um
this is half the correct distance.
70 um
Correct: Half the source concentration (50) occurs at d = 100 ln2, about 69 um.
50 um
at 50 um the concentration is still about 61.
100 um
at 100 um the concentration is about 37, less than half.
qs.x: Half the source concentration (50) occurs at d = 100 ln2, about 69 um. Trap: Choosing the length constant of 100 um as the half-distance.

graph.title: Figure 1. Shh concentration versus distance

passages.title: FL02 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 8
text: The hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis was evaluated in three patients with suspected thyroid dysfunction. Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) from the hypothalamus stimulates the anterior pituitary to release thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which stimulates the thyroid to make and secrete thyroxine (T4). T4 and its more active derivative T3 feed back to inhibit TRH and TSH secretion. Baseline serum TSH and free T4 were measured (Table 1). Patients 2 and 3 and a healthy control were then given an intravenous dose of TRH, and serum TSH was measured over 2 hours (Figure 1). Reference ranges are 0.4 to 4.0 mU/L for TSH and 0.8 to 1.8 ng/dL for free T4. Patient 1 had antibodies that activate the TSH receptor on thyroid cells. Patient 2 had a thyroid gland that had been damaged by autoimmune inflammation. Patient 3 had a tumor that compressed the pituitary gland. Samples were drawn after an overnight fast, none of the patients was taking medications known to affect thyroid function, and all assays were run in the same laboratory using the same standards.

qs.q: Why is TSH nearly undetectable in Patient 1?
o: The antibodies destroy pituitary thyrotrophs, so TSH output falls despite low hormone
the antibodies act at the thyroid TSH receptor, not at the pituitary.
TRH secretion is increased, which should increase TSH and raise thyroid hormone output
high T4 reduces TRH and TSH secretion.
High circulating T4 and T3 exert negative feedback on the pituitary and hypothalamus
Correct: Because the thyroid is overstimulated by antibodies, hormone levels are high and suppress TSH.
The thyroid is unable to respond to TSH because its receptors are fully desensitized
the thyroid is overactive, as shown by T4 of 3.5.
qs.x: Because the thyroid is overstimulated by antibodies, hormone levels are high and suppress TSH. Trap: Assuming that low TSH means a primary pituitary problem.

qs.q: Patient 3's lack of TSH response to TRH most strongly suggests a defect in:
o: the thyroid gland
a thyroid defect would give a high TSH and a normal or large response to TRH, as seen in Patient 2.
the hypothalamus
a hypothalamic defect would still show a TSH rise when TRH is given.
the anterior pituitary
Correct: TRH acts directly on pituitary thyrotrophs, and a pituitary tumor prevents the TSH response.
the posterior pituitary
this does not secrete TSH.
qs.x: TRH acts directly on pituitary thyrotrophs, and a pituitary tumor prevents the TSH response. Trap: Choosing the hypothalamus because the TRH level is not measured.

qs.q: At 30 minutes, the TSH in Patient 2 is about how many times that of the control?
o: Correct: 60 mU/L divided by 12 mU/L equals 5.
2 is the control's baseline TSH in mU/L, not a ratio.
15 is the baseline TSH of Patient 2, not a ratio.
30 is 60/2, dividing Patient 2's 30-minute TSH by the control's baseline value rather than by its 30-minute value.
qs.x: 60 mU/L divided by 12 mU/L equals 5. Trap: Reporting the baseline value as the ratio.

qs.q: TSH stimulates thyroid cells by binding a receptor that:
o: diffuses into the nucleus and alters transcription directly
this describes thyroid hormone and steroid receptors.
activates a G protein coupled pathway raising cAMP
Correct: TSH is a glycoprotein hormone that acts on a cell-surface G protein coupled receptor.
is a ligand-gated ion channel
TSH acts through a G protein pathway, not ion channels.
has intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity
this describes insulin and growth factor receptors.
qs.x: TSH is a glycoprotein hormone that acts on a cell-surface G protein coupled receptor. Trap: Attributing nuclear receptor action to TSH, a peptide-type hormone.

graph.title: Figure 1. Serum TSH after TRH injection

passages.title: FL02 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 9
text: Hemodynamic measurements were obtained in a healthy adult at rest, the same adult during moderate exercise, and a patient with chronic systolic heart failure at rest (Table 1). End-diastolic volume (EDV) and end-systolic volume (ESV) are the ventricular volumes before and after contraction. Stroke volume (SV) is EDV minus ESV, ejection fraction (EF) is SV divided by EDV, cardiac output (CO) is heart rate (HR) times SV, and total peripheral resistance (TPR) is mean arterial pressure (MAP) divided by CO. The relationship between EDV and SV was also measured in ventricles from healthy and failing hearts by varying filling volume at constant heart rate (Figure 1). Systolic heart failure is characterized by reduced contractility. During exercise, sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine, which binds beta-1 receptors in the heart, and metabolites accumulate in active skeletal muscle. Pressures and volumes were obtained by catheterization and echocardiography, and the healthy adult had no history of cardiovascular disease and was not taking any medications during testing.

qs.q: What is the ejection fraction in the patient with heart failure?
o: 50/150 uses ESV as the denominator instead of EDV.
this is the stroke volume in mL, not a percentage of EDV.
this is the fraction that remains in the ventricle (ESV/EDV).
Correct: SV = 200 - 150 = 50 mL; EF = 50/200 = 25 percent.
qs.x: SV = 200 - 150 = 50 mL; EF = 50/200 = 25 percent. Trap: Dividing stroke volume by ESV or reporting ESV/EDV.

qs.q: What is the cardiac output of the healthy adult during exercise?
o: 10.5 L/min
150 x 70 uses the resting stroke volume, ignoring its rise during exercise.
19.5 L/min
this uses EDV of 130 mL as the stroke volume.
135 L/min
a decimal error: 13,500 mL is 13.5 L.
13.5 L/min
Correct: SV = 130 - 40 = 90 mL, and 150 x 90 = 13,500 mL/min.
qs.x: SV = 130 - 40 = 90 mL, and 150 x 90 = 13,500 mL/min. Trap: Using EDV instead of stroke volume.

qs.q: From rest to exercise in the healthy adult, which change contributed more to the rise in cardiac output?
o: The increase in stroke volume
SV increased by less than HR.
A decrease in end-systolic volume only
the ESV change is part of the stroke volume increase, which was smaller.
The increase in heart rate
Correct: HR rose about 2.1-fold (70 to 150) while SV rose about 1.3-fold (70 to 90).
A decrease in mean arterial pressure
MAP increased, not decreased.
qs.x: HR rose about 2.1-fold (70 to 150) while SV rose about 1.3-fold (70 to 90). Trap: Assuming stroke volume is the major driver of increased output.

qs.q: Based on Figure 1, which best explains the lower stroke volume in the failing heart at an EDV of 160 mL?
o: Reduced contractility
Correct: At the same filling volume the failing ventricle ejects less (40 versus 90 mL), shifting the curve down.
Reduced preload
the EDV is the same at 160 mL for both curves.
Increased sympathetic stimulation of beta-1 receptors
this would increase contractility and shift the curve up.
Higher venous return
the filling volume is already specified as equal.
qs.x: At the same filling volume the failing ventricle ejects less (40 versus 90 mL), shifting the curve down. Trap: Attributing a downward shift of the Starling curve to altered preload.

qs.q: What is the approximate TPR during exercise, and what likely accounts for its change from rest (about 20 mmHg min/L)?
o: About 8 mmHg min/L, due to sympathetic constriction of arterioles throughout the body
constriction would raise TPR, not lower it.
About 8 mmHg min/L, due to vasodilation of skeletal muscle arterioles by local metabolites
Correct: 110/13.5 is about 8; metabolites such as adenosine, potassium and lactate dilate arterioles in active muscle.
About 120 mmHg min/L, due to the increased MAP
this is not MAP divided by CO; resistance is MAP/CO.
About 20 mmHg min/L, unchanged from rest
resting TPR is 98/4.9 = 20, but exercise lowers it.
qs.x: 110/13.5 is about 8; metabolites such as adenosine, potassium and lactate dilate arterioles in active muscle. Trap: Multiplying MAP by CO instead of dividing, or ignoring local vasodilation.

graph.title: Figure 1. Stroke volume versus end-diastolic volume

passages.title: FL02 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 10
text: The neuromuscular junction was studied in isolated mouse nerve-diaphragm preparations. The motor nerve was stimulated while the end-plate potential (EPP) was recorded from the muscle fiber with an intracellular electrode, and muscle twitch was observed. In a separate test, the muscle was stimulated directly with electrodes placed on the fiber. Spontaneous miniature end-plate potentials (mEPPs), each resulting from release of one vesicle of acetylcholine (ACh), were also recorded. Toxin alpha, toxin beta, and neostigmine were tested individually, and neostigmine was also applied after toxin beta (Table 1). Toxin alpha reduced both the frequency and amplitude of mEPPs; toxin beta reduced mEPP amplitude but not frequency. Neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that degrades ACh in the synaptic cleft. The nicotinic ACh receptor is a ligand-gated channel permeable to Na+ and K+. EPP duration is the time for the potential to fall to half its peak amplitude. Preparations were bathed in oxygenated physiological saline at 35 degrees C, and each treatment was applied to at least six preparations, with representative values reported for each treatment.

qs.q: The mEPP data for toxin alpha most strongly suggest that it:
o: blocks nicotinic receptors on the muscle membrane
a receptor blocker would reduce mEPP amplitude but not frequency, as with toxin beta.
inhibits acetylcholinesterase
this would increase EPP duration, which did not change.
reduces the release of ACh from the presynaptic terminal
Correct: Fewer vesicles are released (lower frequency), while the preserved direct twitch shows the muscle remains excitable.
damages the contractile machinery of the muscle
twitch after direct stimulation is intact.
qs.x: Fewer vesicles are released (lower frequency), while the preserved direct twitch shows the muscle remains excitable. Trap: Ignoring the mEPP frequency and attributing the effect to the receptor.

qs.q: The longer EPP duration with neostigmine is best explained by:
o: increased reuptake of ACh into the presynaptic terminal
this would shorten the EPP.
slowed breakdown of ACh in the cleft, so it persists and keeps receptors activated
Correct: Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase prolongs ACh presence in the synaptic cleft.
increased synthesis of ACh by choline acetyltransferase
this would not change the duration of a single EPP.
direct opening of nicotinic receptor channels
neostigmine acts on the enzyme, not on the receptors.
qs.x: Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase prolongs ACh presence in the synaptic cleft. Trap: Assuming that reuptake rather than enzymatic degradation clears ACh at this synapse.

qs.q: Why does neostigmine partially reverse the effect of toxin beta?
o: Neostigmine irreversibly displaces toxin beta from the receptor
neostigmine acts on the enzyme and not on the receptor.
Neostigmine increases the frequency of vesicle release
there is no evidence for increased vesicle release.
Neostigmine blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels in the muscle
blocking channels would reduce excitation, not restore it.
Higher ACh concentrations in the cleft compete more effectively with the reversible antagonist
Correct: Toxin beta acts as a competitive receptor antagonist, and prolonging ACh action raises effective concentration.
qs.x: Toxin beta acts as a competitive receptor antagonist, and prolonging ACh action raises effective concentration. Trap: Assuming the rescue works at the receptor rather than through higher ACh.

qs.q: The EPP is a depolarization because ACh binding to the nicotinic receptor causes:
o: net inward movement of Na+ through the channel
Correct: Both Na+ and K+ pass, but the driving force on Na+ is much larger, producing net depolarization.
net outward movement of K+
this would hyperpolarize the membrane.
influx of Cl- through the channel
the channel is cation selective and does not carry Cl-.
release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum directly through the receptor
Ca2+ release occurs after action potentials, not from this ligand-gated channel.
qs.x: Both Na+ and K+ pass, but the driving force on Na+ is much larger, producing net depolarization. Trap: Forgetting that the channel is nonselective for cations but dominated by Na+ influx.

passages.title: FL02 · CARS · Passage 1
text: Oral historians have long contended with a suspicion that their sources are unreliable. People misremember dates, merge two events into one, and reshape the past to flatter the person they have become. Documents, by contrast, seem to sit still: a ledger records what was paid, and a minute book records what was decided. The suspicion is not groundless, but it rests on a mistaken picture of what an interview is for. To treat a recollection as a defective document is to ask of it something it was never going to provide.

Consider an interview with a retired textile worker about a strike that took place decades earlier. She places the walkout in the wrong year and credits a foreman with a speech that, according to the union records, was delivered by someone else. A historian interested only in establishing the sequence of events will log these as errors and move on. But the same account may contain things no ledger could: how it felt to stand outside the gates in winter, why the workers believed the foreman had betrayed them, which small humiliations made the walkout seem inevitable rather than merely advisable. The misattributed speech may itself be evidence. If the community came to remember the foreman as the voice of the company's contempt, then the error discloses how the strike was absorbed into collective understanding, which is a historical fact of considerable interest.

None of this licenses historians to abandon verification. A memory that cannot be reconciled with any surviving record is a claim, and claims call for scrutiny. The point is rather that error and meaning are not opposites. Some of the most revealing distortions are patterned: interviewees compress long processes into single dramatic moments, assign credit to figures who embody a movement's values, and smooth over conflicts that later became embarrassing. Such regularities tell us what people needed the past to mean.

Skeptics may reply that this reasoning makes oral history unfalsifiable, since any discrepancy can be redescribed as insight. The worry deserves a serious answer, and the answer lies in method. A careful interviewer compares accounts across many narrators and checks claims against independent evidence wherever it exists. Where narrators agree on a detail that the documents contradict, the discrepancy becomes a puzzle worth pursuing; where they disagree among themselves, the disagreement marks a contested memory. Interpretation is disciplined by comparison, not liberated from it.

There is also a deeper reason to resist the demand that testimony behave like a record. The archive is not a neutral repository but a product of choices about who was permitted to write things down and which papers were worth keeping. Those who kept the ledgers were seldom the ones who stood outside the gates. A history assembled only from documents will therefore tend to reproduce the perspective of those with the authority to produce them, and the apparent solidity of such sources is partly a reflection of whose voices were considered worth preserving.

It would be a mistake, then, to rank the two kinds of evidence on a single scale of reliability. Each answers different questions and fails in different ways. The ledger is precise about what was counted and silent about what was endured; the recollection is imprecise about the date and eloquent about the endurance. A historian who wishes to understand the strike, and not merely to date it, will need both, and will recognize that the tension between them is not an obstacle to understanding but one of its richest sources.

qs.q: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Oral history is unreliable and should be used only when written records are unavailable.
The author defends oral history and never limits it to cases without records.
Archives are biased toward the powerful and should be replaced by interviews with the people who actually lived through events.
The author calls archives partial, not worthless, and concludes that both sources are needed.
Historians should verify every memory against documents before treating it as evidence.
The author endorses verification but says it is not the whole task, so this narrows the thesis.
Oral testimony and documents answer different historical questions, so each should be valued for what it reveals.
Correct: This matches the author's argument that error and meaning are not opposites and that both kinds of evidence are needed.
qs.x: This matches the author's argument that error and meaning are not opposites and that both kinds of evidence are needed. Trap: Choosing the answer that picks one side; the author's closing move is to insist on both kinds of evidence.

qs.q: The author discusses the misattributed speech primarily in order to
o: demonstrate that the textile worker was an unreliable witness.
The author treats the error as informative, not as proof of unreliability.
show that an apparent factual error can itself serve as historical evidence about a community.
Correct: The author says the error discloses how the strike was absorbed into collective understanding.
argue that union records are more accurate than interviews and should therefore be given priority by historians.
The passage does not rank union records above interviews here.
suggest that foremen were generally resented by workers.
The foreman is a single example, and no general claim about foremen is made.
qs.x: The author says the error discloses how the strike was absorbed into collective understanding. Trap: Reading an illustration as a claim about the specific people in it, instead of as support for the larger argument.

qs.q: According to the passage, which of the following is true of the distortions found in oral testimony?
o: They occur only when narrators wish to flatter themselves or to present their own role in events in a favorable light.
Flattery is mentioned as one source, but the passage lists others, such as smoothing over conflicts.
Some of them follow recognizable patterns, such as compressing long processes into dramatic moments.
Correct: The passage states that some of the most revealing distortions are patterned.
They are random and therefore cannot be analyzed.
The passage says the opposite: they are patterned and informative.
They disappear when several narrators are interviewed.
Comparison across narrators helps interpret them but does not make them vanish.
qs.x: The passage states that some of the most revealing distortions are patterned. Trap: Overgeneralizing the first cause of error mentioned (self-flattery) to all distortions.

qs.q: The author's response to the charge that oral history is unfalsifiable is best described as
o: a denial that any discrepancy between memory and record can be a problem.
The author says that unreconciled memories are claims calling for scrutiny.
an acknowledgment that the concern is serious, followed by an appeal to comparison and independent checking.
Correct: The author calls the worry deserving of a serious answer and points to method.
a concession that oral history must be treated as less rigorous than documentary history and used only as a supplement.
The author says interpretation is disciplined, not that it is less rigorous.
a claim that falsifiability is an inappropriate standard for historical work.
The author never rejects the standard; the author argues oral history can meet it.
qs.x: The author calls the worry deserving of a serious answer and points to method. Trap: Assuming a defender of a method must dismiss criticism; here the author accepts the worry and answers it.

qs.q: Which of the following, if true, would most WEAKEN the author's claim about archives in the fifth paragraph?
o: Nearly all workers in the period kept detailed written accounts, many of which entered public archives.
Correct: If ordinary workers wrote and archived accounts, archives would not so clearly reflect those with authority.
Many archived ledgers contain arithmetic errors.
Arithmetic errors do not bear on whose voices the archive preserves.
Interviewees often disagree about dates.
Disagreement among interviewees concerns oral evidence, not the archive's selectivity.
Some historians prefer documents to interviews.
Historians' preferences do not show that archives represent all perspectives.
qs.x: If ordinary workers wrote and archived accounts, archives would not so clearly reflect those with authority. Trap: Picking a statement that criticizes some source in general rather than one that bears on the specific claim about whose perspective is preserved.

qs.q: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would regard a historian who dismissed an interviewee's account solely because it conflicted with a record as
o: correct, because written records are always more reliable than recollections and should override them.
The author rejects ranking the two on a single scale of reliability.
dishonest about the limits of the evidence.
Nothing suggests dishonesty; the criticism concerns missed insight.
overlooking what the discrepancy might reveal about how the event was remembered.
Correct: The author argues that conflict between memory and record can be informative rather than disqualifying.
guilty of ignoring the union's perspective.
The union records are the documents in question, not a perspective being ignored.
qs.x: The author argues that conflict between memory and record can be informative rather than disqualifying. Trap: Treating any disagreement with a document as automatic proof the narrator is wrong, which the author explicitly resists.

passages.title: FL02 · CARS · Passage 2
text: The word wilderness conjures an image of land untouched by human hands: ancient forest, empty valley, a place where nature persists in its original form. The image is so deeply embedded in conservation thought that it has shaped law, policy, and the boundaries of national parks. Yet a growing number of historians and ecologists argue that this picture is less a description of any actual landscape than an inheritance from a particular cultural moment, one in which educated city dwellers, anxious about industrial life, began to prize emptiness as a mark of purity.

The evidence for this claim is considerable. Many of the landscapes later designated as pristine were in fact managed for centuries by the peoples who lived in them. Burning to clear undergrowth, selective harvesting of plants, and the cultivation of favored species altered the composition of forests and grasslands in ways that persisted long after the managers had gone. When European travelers described open parkland and abundant game, they took for granted that they were seeing nature as it had always been, and they did not consider that the abundance might itself be an artifact of long human stewardship. The removal of those inhabitants, often by force, was then reinterpreted as the restoration of an original emptiness.

It does not follow, however, that the idea of wilderness should simply be discarded. Critics of the concept sometimes write as though exposing its cultural origins were enough to refute it, but the history of an idea does not settle its worth. Many valuable commitments, including the principle that persons possess rights, arose in particular times and places and were nonetheless worth keeping. The relevant question is not where the notion came from but what it now permits and what it forbids.

On that question the record is mixed. The wilderness ideal has protected vast areas from mining, logging, and development that would otherwise have transformed them, and those protections have benefited species that could survive nowhere else. At the same time, the ideal has encouraged a habit of mind in which nature is something to be visited rather than lived within. If the only authentic nature is that which lies far from human settlement, then the garden, the farm, and the vacant urban lot become unworthy of ecological concern, and the people who work the land are cast as intruders in it. Such a view can license the eviction of residents from protected areas, and it can lead a society to care intensely about distant forests while neglecting the rivers and fields it actually uses.

A more promising course is to retain what is valuable in the older idea while giving up its claim to describe a human-free past. Land can be protected because it shelters rare species, regulates water, or sustains traditions of care, and none of these justifications depends on pretending that no one ever lived there. Under this understanding, the aim of conservation is not to return a place to a state that never existed but to sustain the relationships, human and nonhuman, that make it valuable. The older ideal prized the absence of people. The revised one asks what kinds of presence are compatible with the flourishing of everything else, and in doing so it replaces a nostalgic picture with a question that can be answered through evidence and argument.

qs.q: The primary purpose of the passage is to
o: argue that the wilderness ideal should be revised rather than abandoned.
Correct: The author criticizes the ideal's premise but concludes it should be retained in modified form.
demonstrate that national parks should be dissolved.
The author credits the ideal with real protection and does not call for dissolving parks.
describe how indigenous peoples managed forests.
Land management is evidence used in service of a larger argument.
show that conservation law has been entirely ineffective at protecting the landscapes it targeted.
The author says the ideal has protected vast areas.
qs.x: The author criticizes the ideal's premise but concludes it should be retained in modified form. Trap: Picking a supporting detail (traditional management) as if it were the passage's goal.

qs.q: According to the passage, European travelers who described abundant game in open parkland
o: were aware that the land had been actively managed by its inhabitants for many generations.
The passage says they did not consider human stewardship.
deliberately concealed evidence of human activity.
No deliberate concealment is described; they simply assumed.
assumed that the landscape reflected nature as it had always been.
Correct: The passage says they took for granted that they saw original nature.
had been sent to study burning practices.
Nothing in the passage says they were sent to study anything.
qs.x: The passage says they took for granted that they saw original nature. Trap: Attributing intentional deception to people the passage describes as merely mistaken.

qs.q: The author mentions the principle that persons possess rights primarily to
o: suggest that conservation and human rights are equivalent causes.
The passage draws an analogy about origins, not an equivalence of causes.
show that wilderness is a legal concept.
The example is not about legal status of wilderness.
illustrate that an idea with a particular historical origin can still be worth retaining.
Correct: The author uses it as an analogy for an idea that arose at a specific time but remains valuable.
argue that the origin of an idea is irrelevant to every question.
The author says origin does not settle worth, not that it is irrelevant to everything.
qs.x: The author uses it as an analogy for an idea that arose at a specific time but remains valuable. Trap: Overextending a limited claim (origin does not settle worth) into an absolute one.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the author's attitude toward the wilderness ideal?
o: Qualified appreciation joined with criticism of its assumptions.
Correct: The author credits benefits yet identifies serious drawbacks and proposes revision.
Uncritical admiration of its protective record and its effects on local communities.
The author lists substantial costs, so admiration is not uncritical.
Scornful dismissal of its cultural origins.
The author specifically rejects dismissal based on origins.
Neutral indifference to its effects.
The author evaluates its effects in detail and with evident concern.
qs.x: The author credits benefits yet identifies serious drawbacks and proposes revision. Trap: Reading a balanced evaluation as one-sided because one half of it is more vivid.

qs.q: The passage suggests that the eviction of residents from protected areas is most directly supported by which belief?
o: That authentic nature exists only where people are absent.
Correct: The passage links the view that real nature is far from settlement to casting residents as intruders.
That rare species can survive in managed landscapes.
This belief would argue against eviction, not for it.
That farms deserve ecological protection.
Valuing farms ecologically would oppose the exclusionary view.
That water regulation is a valid reason for conservation even where people live on the land.
The author lists this as a justification that does not depend on exclusion.
qs.x: The passage links the view that real nature is far from settlement to casting residents as intruders. Trap: Choosing a statement that appears in the passage but supports the opposite conclusion.

qs.q: Suppose a recently protected valley is found to contain rare orchids that thrive only where local farmers have traditionally mowed the meadows. Which approach would be most consistent with the author's revised ideal?
o: Ban all human activity so the meadow returns to an original state.
This reflects the older ideal that prizes absence of people.
Permit commercial development, since the meadow is not pristine and has already been altered by people.
The author says lack of pristine status does not justify neglect.
Continue traditional mowing as part of protecting the orchids.
Correct: The revised ideal asks which kinds of presence are compatible with flourishing and sustains valuable relationships.
Ignore the orchids because the valley is a cultural landscape.
The author argues that cultural landscapes can warrant protection.
qs.x: The revised ideal asks which kinds of presence are compatible with flourishing and sustains valuable relationships. Trap: Applying the old ideal of exclusion because the question mentions protection.

passages.title: FL02 · CARS · Passage 3
text: Reading silently is now so ordinary that it is difficult to appreciate it as an achievement. A person sits with a book, and words enter the mind without passing through the mouth or ear. Yet for much of antiquity, reading was usually performed aloud, even when the reader was alone. A famous anecdote about a fourth-century bishop records the astonishment of a visitor who found him reading with his eyes moving over the page while his voice and tongue were at rest. Some scholars have taken the story as proof that silent reading was nearly unknown. Others, noting that ancient writers do refer to reading without sound, have concluded that the anecdote records only a personal habit that the visitor found curious. The truth is likely that both practices coexisted, with vocal reading dominant for reasons that were as much practical as cultural.

The practical reasons begin with the page itself. Early manuscripts commonly ran words together without spaces, so that a line of text resembled a continuous string of letters. To make sense of it, a reader needed to sound out the syllables and hear where one word ended and the next began. Only later, when scribes introduced gaps between words and eventually conventions of punctuation, did it become feasible to take in a line at a glance. The change was not instant, and it did not proceed uniformly. But as the visual layout grew easier to parse, the ear became less necessary, and the reader gained a kind of privacy that earlier readers had lacked.

The consequences of that privacy have been widely debated. Some historians contend that silent reading made possible a new inner life: a reader alone with a text could entertain doubts, pursue private devotions, and consider heretical ideas without an audience to hear them. Others point out that this account is too tidy. Heresy flourished in periods dominated by oral reading, and communal reading, in households or reading circles, has persisted into the present with no sign of loss. The more cautious conclusion is that silent reading widened the range of what a reader could do unobserved, without determining what any reader would in fact do.

It is tempting to treat the history as a story of progress from clumsy sounding-out to refined silent comprehension. That temptation should be resisted. Reading aloud was not a primitive stage that silent reading improved upon; it was a skill with its own virtues. A text that is read aloud is experienced as rhythm and cadence, and authors who expected their works to be heard composed accordingly, with repetitions and balanced clauses that aid listeners and now strike some modern readers as ornamental. To read such works silently is to miss part of what they were designed to do. Many poets still insist that a poem is incomplete until it is voiced.

What the history does show is that a technology as seemingly trivial as the space between words can alter the habits of a culture. Nothing in the human brain changed when scribes began leaving gaps; the new layout simply made possible a style of attention that had been available only with difficulty. The lesson is not that silent reading is superior, but that our most intimate practices are shaped by arrangements we seldom notice. The silence in which we read today is not a natural condition of reading. It is an inheritance, laid down gradually by scribes whose names we do not know.

qs.q: Which of the following best summarizes the author's view of the anecdote about the fourth-century bishop?
o: It is consistent with a past in which silent and vocal reading both existed.
Correct: The author concludes that both practices likely coexisted.
It proves that silent reading was unknown in antiquity.
The author notes that ancient writers refer to reading without sound.
It shows that the bishop was a heretic.
Heresy is not linked to the bishop in the passage.
It demonstrates that ancient writers never described anyone reading silently, even in private.
The passage states the opposite: ancient writers do refer to silent reading.
qs.x: The author concludes that both practices likely coexisted. Trap: Accepting the strongest claim made by one group of scholars, which the author does not endorse.

qs.q: According to the passage, the introduction of spaces between words most directly
o: caused silent reading to replace vocal reading entirely within a few generations of its adoption.
The author says the change was gradual and not uniform, and that communal reading persists.
altered the structure of the human brain.
The author explicitly says nothing in the brain changed.
made it possible to take in lines of text quickly without sounding them out.
Correct: The author says gaps made it feasible to take in a line at a glance.
eliminated communal reading.
The passage says communal reading has persisted.
qs.x: The author says gaps made it feasible to take in a line at a glance. Trap: Interpreting a facilitating change as a total replacement.

qs.q: The author's discussion of heresy in the third paragraph serves to
o: challenge an account that links silent reading too directly to a new inner life.
Correct: Heresy flourishing under oral reading is offered as evidence that the tidy account is incomplete.
prove that silent reading encouraged heresy.
The author uses heresy to complicate, not to prove, that link.
show that heresy could not exist without books.
The passage makes no claim that books are required for heresy.
criticize modern readers for the private, solitary habits that they have developed with silent reading.
No criticism of modern readers appears.
qs.x: Heresy flourishing under oral reading is offered as evidence that the tidy account is incomplete. Trap: Missing that the author presents the claim in order to qualify it.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the idea that history moved from sounding out to refined silent comprehension is best described as
o: enthusiastic, because it records genuine progress in human understanding over the centuries.
The author warns against treating the history as progress.
indifferent, because the history is uncertain.
The author argues the point with some force.
skeptical, because it wrongly treats reading aloud as inferior.
Correct: The author says the temptation should be resisted and defends reading aloud as a skill with virtues.
hostile, because silent reading is harmful.
The author does not claim silent reading is harmful; the author says it is not superior.
qs.x: The author says the temptation should be resisted and defends reading aloud as a skill with virtues. Trap: Overstating the author's criticism into a claim that silent reading is bad.

qs.q: Which of the following would the author most likely say about a speech composed to be delivered to a large crowd?
o: Its features show that the author lacked skill.
The author treats such features as purposeful.
Its repetitions and balanced phrases may be designed for listeners and could seem ornamental on the page.
Correct: The author explains that works composed for hearing use features that aid listeners.
It should be rewritten for silent readers.
The passage never recommends rewriting.
It is evidence that crowds lacked literacy.
The passage makes no inference about literacy rates.
qs.x: The author explains that works composed for hearing use features that aid listeners. Trap: Judging oral-style features by the standards of silent reading, the very error the author warns about.

qs.q: The final sentence of the passage most strongly suggests that the author regards silent reading as
o: an inborn ability that was released by the invention of spaces between words on the page, once scribes adopted them.
The author says nothing changed in the brain.
a practice that scribes deliberately planned to produce.
The scribes' names are unknown, and no plan is described.
a practice inferior to oral reading.
The author denies that either mode is simply superior.
a learned practice shaped by historical conditions rather than a natural state.
Correct: The author calls it an inheritance laid down gradually, not a natural condition.
qs.x: The author calls it an inheritance laid down gradually, not a natural condition. Trap: Reading 'inheritance' as implying planning, when the author stresses gradual and unnoticed change.

passages.title: FL02 · CARS · Passage 4
text: Every keyboard instrument embodies a compromise that most listeners never notice. The mathematics of sound dictates that stacking twelve perfect fifths, each a frequency ratio of three to two, does not return to the starting pitch exactly; it overshoots seven octaves by a small but audible amount. A tuner must therefore decide where to hide the discrepancy. For centuries Western musicians tuned their instruments in ways that made some keys beautifully pure and others harsh. A piece in a favored key sounded sweet, while a piece in a distant key might contain intervals so rough that composers avoided them or used them deliberately for effect.

The modern solution, equal temperament, divides the octave into twelve identical steps and thereby spreads the error evenly. Every key becomes equally usable, and a composer may modulate freely from any key to any other. This convenience is often presented as an unambiguous gain, and in practical terms it is hard to dispute. Orchestras, pianos, and the notation on which they depend would be unmanageable without a shared system in which any note can be reinterpreted as another. Yet the price of such freedom is that no interval except the octave is perfectly in tune. The listener's ear, accustomed to the compromise, has learned to accept thirds that are noticeably wider than the ratio found in nature.

Some historically minded performers have drawn from this a moral conclusion: that equal temperament has flattened the expressive palette of music, and that earlier systems preserved a variety of color now lost. There is something to the argument. When keys differ in character, a composer's choice of key becomes an expressive decision, and a listener attuned to the differences can hear a movement's tonal center as a kind of emotional signature. Players who revive older tunings report that familiar works acquire unexpected tension and relief.

But the argument invites caution. It is difficult to know how much of the color attributed to a key resided in the tuning and how much in the instrument, the performance practice, the pitch standard, or the expectations of the audience. Pitch itself has varied widely over time and place, so that a piece in a given key could have sounded considerably higher or lower than the same key does today. If the pitch moved, the character of the key cannot have been a simple function of its name. The claim that a key possessed a fixed emotional identity may therefore owe as much to later commentators, who enjoyed describing keys in vivid terms, as to the music itself.

The most reasonable position acknowledges both sides. Equal temperament did sacrifice something real: the sweetness of pure intervals and the individuality of keys. It also made possible styles of harmony that depend on unrestricted movement among keys, which would have been unplayable on the instruments of an earlier age. To mourn the loss without recognizing the gain is as one-sided as to celebrate the gain without recognizing the loss. Music has always advanced by exchanging one kind of beauty for another, and the interest of the history lies less in judging each exchange than in understanding what made it seem worthwhile to those who made it.

qs.q: The author's primary concern in the passage is to
o: evaluate the tradeoffs involved in the adoption of equal temperament.
Correct: The passage weighs what was lost and gained and concludes both must be acknowledged.
prove that equal temperament is mathematically flawed and should be abandoned by performers.
The author notes the mathematical problem but does not argue the system is simply flawed.
defend the use of historical tunings in all performances.
The author is cautious about the historical-performance argument.
explain how keyboard instruments are manufactured.
Manufacture is never discussed.
qs.x: The passage weighs what was lost and gained and concludes both must be acknowledged. Trap: Focusing on the opening mathematical point as though it were the thesis.

qs.q: According to the passage, stacking twelve perfect fifths
o: returns exactly to the starting pitch after passing through all twelve keys of the scale.
This is the opposite of the passage's claim.
falls short of seven octaves by a large amount.
The discrepancy is described as small, and it overshoots rather than falls short.
produces intervals identical to equal temperament.
Equal temperament is a solution to the discrepancy, not a result of stacking.
overshoots seven octaves by a small but audible amount.
Correct: The passage states that the stack overshoots seven octaves slightly.
qs.x: The passage states that the stack overshoots seven octaves slightly. Trap: Assuming that pure ratios must close exactly, which is the problem the passage describes.

qs.q: The author raises the fact that pitch has varied over time in order to
o: prove that equal temperament is superior.
The point is skeptical about key color, not a comparison favoring equal temperament.
argue that orchestras should adopt a lower pitch.
No recommendation about pitch standards is made.
cast doubt on the claim that each key had a fixed emotional character.
Correct: If pitch moved, the key's character cannot be a simple function of its name.
show that older instruments could not play in many keys without severe tuning problems.
The passage does not say that older instruments could not play in many keys.
qs.x: If pitch moved, the key's character cannot be a simple function of its name. Trap: Seeing a historical detail as support for the modern system rather than as an objection to the key-color claim.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the historically minded performers' conclusion is best characterized as
o: cautious acceptance of part of it combined with skepticism about its strength.
Correct: The author says there is something to the argument but invites caution.
complete agreement.
The author raises explicit objections.
contemptuous rejection of it as an unfounded belief invented by later commentators.
The author grants that there is something to the argument.
unconcern about the question.
The author spends two paragraphs evaluating it.
qs.x: The author says there is something to the argument but invites caution. Trap: Collapsing a mixed evaluation into agreement or rejection.

qs.q: Which of the following findings would most STRENGTHEN the claim that keys possessed fixed emotional identities?
o: Composers and theorists of the period wrote essays praising particular keys and describing the emotions that each key was supposed to convey.
This is the sort of later commentary the author suspects of distorting the picture.
Pianos today are tuned in equal temperament.
This is already assumed and does not bear on emotional identity.
Listeners unaware of key names describe pieces in one key with similar emotional terms across different pitch standards.
Correct: Independent agreement across pitch standards would show the effect is not an artifact of commentary or pitch.
Some older tunings contained rough intervals.
Rough intervals show differences exist but not that they carry fixed emotional character.
qs.x: Independent agreement across pitch standards would show the effect is not an artifact of commentary or pitch. Trap: Selecting evidence that merely repeats the contested claim instead of ruling out the author's alternative explanations.

qs.q: The passage implies that a composer writing for an instrument tuned to favor certain keys would most likely
o: make deliberate use of the roughness in remote keys for expressive purposes.
Correct: The passage says composers avoided harsh keys or used them deliberately for effect.
be unable to write in any but the favored keys.
The passage says composers could use the harsh keys deliberately.
regard all keys as identical in effect.
If keys sounded different, they could not be regarded as identical.
prefer to modulate freely among all keys without regard to how each one happened to sound.
Free modulation is described as a benefit of equal temperament.
qs.x: The passage says composers avoided harsh keys or used them deliberately for effect. Trap: Treating a tendency (avoidance) as an absolute impossibility.

passages.title: FL02 · CARS · Passage 5
text: A map appears to offer a plain report: here is a river, there is a road, and between them lies a town. The convention of presenting such information from above, in uniform colors and with a confident scale, encourages readers to treat the result as a mirror held up to the land. But every map is built through acts of selection, and selection is never innocent. A cartographer cannot show everything; she must choose which features deserve a mark, how large to draw them, and what to leave blank. Those choices reflect what the maker and the commissioning patron regarded as worth recording.

Historians of cartography have shown how such choices could serve ambitions that had little to do with navigation. Maps drawn for colonial administrations frequently portrayed territories as empty or only thinly settled, reducing established villages and routes to a few cursory symbols, or omitting them altogether. The effect was to make land appear available for claiming. A surveyor who drew a region as blank was not necessarily lying about what he had seen; he may have recorded faithfully what mattered to his employers. The distortion lay in the framework that told him what to count.

It would be a mistake to conclude, as some enthusiasts have, that all maps are therefore mere propaganda and that none can claim greater accuracy than any other. This inference confuses two separate matters. That a map reflects interests does not mean that it fails to correspond to the terrain. A coastal chart used by sailors to avoid rocks can be both the product of commercial interests and very reliable about where the rocks are, for the simple reason that its users would be punished by error. The more thoroughly a map's purpose demands accuracy about a particular feature, the more that feature will be rendered truthfully, whatever else the map omits.

What the critique of cartography establishes, then, is not the impossibility of accuracy but its relativity to purpose. A road map is accurate in showing which highways connect which towns and inaccurate, deliberately, in its disregard for elevation. A projection that preserves the shape of coastlines will distort areas, and one that preserves areas will distort shapes, because a sphere cannot be spread flat without sacrifice. No map can be faithful in every respect at once, so the question to ask of any map is not whether it is true but what it is true to, and what it asks the reader to ignore.

This habit of questioning is valuable well beyond the study of maps. Charts, diagrams, and statistical graphics all lend their subjects an air of authority through the neutrality of their form. A reader who learns to ask what a map omits will be better prepared to ask the same question of an unemployment figure or a poll. The point is not to become suspicious of every representation, which would be paralyzing, but to hold each one accountable to the purposes that shaped it. A representation that is understood in this way is more useful, not less, because its reader knows how far it can be trusted and where it must be supplemented.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
o: Maps are propaganda and cannot be trusted.
The author explicitly rejects this inference.
Maps are shaped by purpose, so their accuracy should be judged against what they are meant to show.
Correct: The author argues that accuracy is relative to purpose, neither absent nor absolute.
Accurate maps are impossible because the earth is a sphere that cannot be flattened without distortion.
The sphere is an illustration of one limit, not the thesis.
Colonial maps were drawn by dishonest surveyors.
The author says the surveyor was not necessarily lying.
qs.x: The author argues that accuracy is relative to purpose, neither absent nor absolute. Trap: Taking the author's rejected position (maps are mere propaganda) as the conclusion.

qs.q: According to the passage, a coastal chart tends to be reliable about rocks because
o: colonial administrations strictly regulate such charts and punish mapmakers who err.
No regulation is mentioned.
cartographers have no commercial interests.
The passage says such charts reflect commercial interests.
its users would suffer consequences if it were wrong.
Correct: The passage says that users would be punished by error.
projections preserve all shapes and areas.
The passage says no projection preserves both.
qs.x: The passage says that users would be punished by error. Trap: Reading the chart's commercial origin as a reason for inaccuracy rather than the stated reason for reliability.

qs.q: The author discusses the surveyor who drew a region as blank primarily to illustrate that
o: surveyors were unskilled observers.
His skill is not questioned; he recorded faithfully what mattered to his employers.
maps of unsettled land are always blank.
The point concerns villages omitted from maps of inhabited land.
colonial officials forbade accurate surveys of the region in order to protect their own claims to the land.
No prohibition is described.
distortion can arise from the framework guiding what is recorded rather than from deliberate falsehood.
Correct: The text says the distortion lay in the framework that told him what to count.
qs.x: The text says the distortion lay in the framework that told him what to count. Trap: Assuming that distortion requires lying or incompetence.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the claim that all maps are mere propaganda is best described as
o: critical, because it draws an unjustified inference from the fact that maps reflect interests.
Correct: The author says the inference confuses two separate matters.
approving, because it exposes the hidden motives and interests that lie behind every map ever produced.
The author accepts that interests shape maps but rejects the conclusion.
neutral, because the claim cannot be assessed.
The author assesses it directly and finds it flawed.
