The author maintains accuracy is possible relative to purpose.
qs.x: The author says the inference confuses two separate matters. Trap: Confusing the author's agreement with a premise (maps reflect interests) with agreement with the conclusion.

qs.q: Which of the following examples would best illustrate the author's final point about representations beyond maps?
o: A reader rejects a graph outright because it comes from a government agency with an interest in the result.
The author warns against blanket suspicion rather than source-based dismissal.
A reader accepts a poll because it uses precise decimals.
Precision of form is the kind of authority the author says should be questioned.
A reader ignores all statistics because they can be selectively reported by those who produce them.
The author calls blanket suspicion paralyzing.
A reader of a crime-rate graph asks which offenses were counted before trusting its message.
Correct: This reader holds the representation accountable to its purposes without dismissing it.
qs.x: This reader holds the representation accountable to its purposes without dismissing it. Trap: Choosing an answer that expresses distrust, when the author wants calibrated trust.

qs.q: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage about a projection that preserves areas?
o: It is the most accurate projection available.
The author says no map is accurate in every respect.
It must distort the shapes of some regions.
Correct: The passage says a map preserving areas will distort shapes since a sphere cannot be flattened without sacrifice.
It is useful only to colonial administrators and is of no value to other mapmakers.
No such restriction is implied.
It cannot be used for navigation.
Navigation is not discussed for this projection.
qs.x: The passage says a map preserving areas will distort shapes since a sphere cannot be flattened without sacrifice. Trap: Assuming that preserving one property makes a map generally best.

passages.title: FL02 · CARS · Passage 6
text: Modern democracies choose their legislators by election, and most citizens assume that this is the only method consistent with self-government. Yet in ancient Athens, many offices were filled by lot, and the practice was regarded not as a quaint superstition but as the signature of democracy itself. Elections, in the Athenian view, favored the wealthy, the eloquent, and the well connected, and thus tended toward oligarchy. Selection by lot gave every eligible citizen an equal chance of serving and prevented any faction from entrenching itself. Some contemporary theorists have revived the idea, proposing citizens' assemblies drawn by lottery to deliberate on difficult public questions.

The case for such assemblies rests on a simple observation about representation. An elected body does not mirror the population it serves. Legislators are older, wealthier, and more highly educated than the average citizen, and the demands of campaigning select for particular temperaments. A randomly chosen assembly, by contrast, would approximate a miniature of the public in its composition, so that its conclusions might be taken as an indication of what the public would think if it had the time to study the question carefully. Experiments in several countries have found that participants who hear from experts and from one another often change their minds, and that the resulting recommendations differ from the opinions held at the outset.

Defenders of election raise two main objections. The first is competence: governing requires knowledge, and chance cannot be expected to deliver it. The reply of the lottery's advocates is that an assembly does not need to be composed of experts, since it can consult them, just as a jury hears from witnesses without possessing their training. What the members must supply is judgment and impartiality, and these are not the monopoly of any class. The second objection concerns accountability. An elected official can be removed at the next election, whereas a member of a lottery assembly answers to no constituency. This objection has real force, and it is not fully answered by the observation that lottery members, lacking any need to be reelected, are freed from pressure by donors and party leaders. That freedom is also a freedom from the checks that voters impose.

The strongest version of the proposal therefore does not replace elections but supplements them. Assemblies chosen by lot would advise, set agendas, or review legislation, while elected bodies retained final authority and the accountability that comes with it. Under such an arrangement, the lottery would correct for the characteristic distortions of the electoral process without taking on duties for which it is ill suited.

Even this modest proposal faces a question that its supporters tend to underestimate: whether citizens will regard a recommendation produced by strangers they did not choose as legitimate. Elections confer a sense of authorship, since voters can say that the government is theirs. A lottery confers fairness in access but not that kind of ownership. Legitimacy may in the end depend less on whether a procedure is statistically representative than on whether those who live under its outcomes can recognize themselves in it. That is an empirical matter, and it will have to be settled by experience rather than by argument from first principles.

qs.q: The passage as a whole is primarily concerned with
o: proving that ancient Athens was more democratic than modern states, and that its practices should be copied.
Athens is background, not the thesis.
assessing a proposal to supplement elections with randomly selected citizens' assemblies.
Correct: The passage evaluates the case for and against, concluding with a supplementary role and open questions.
arguing that elections should be abolished.
The strongest version of the proposal retains elections.
describing how juries reach verdicts.
Juries serve only as an analogy.
qs.x: The passage evaluates the case for and against, concluding with a supplementary role and open questions. Trap: Mistaking the historical introduction for the focus of the passage.

qs.q: According to the passage, the Athenians believed elections tended toward oligarchy because
o: they allowed every citizen an equal chance to hold office regardless of wealth or standing.
That describes selection by lot.
they favored wealthy, eloquent, and well-connected candidates.
Correct: The passage says elections favored these groups.
they prevented factions from forming.
That also describes the effect of lot.
they were too costly to conduct.
Cost is not mentioned.
qs.x: The passage says elections favored these groups. Trap: Swapping the properties of the two methods.

qs.q: The author mentions the jury in the third paragraph in order to
o: show that juries are more accountable to the public than legislators are, and so make better decisions.
The jury analogy is about competence, not accountability.
argue that assemblies should have final authority.
The author gives final authority to elected bodies.
prove that lottery selection is always fair.
The analogy does not address fairness of selection.
support the claim that a body need not consist of experts in order to decide well.
Correct: The jury hears witnesses without having their training, paralleling an assembly consulting experts.
qs.x: The jury hears witnesses without having their training, paralleling an assembly consulting experts. Trap: Misreading an analogy's purpose by attending to a different feature of the example.

qs.q: The author's treatment of the accountability objection is best described as
o: granting it considerable weight while noting a partial response.
Correct: The author says the objection has real force and is not fully answered.
dismissing it as irrelevant.
The author calls it forceful.
conceding it completely and abandoning the proposal in favor of the existing electoral system.
The author keeps a modified proposal.
ignoring it in favor of the competence objection.
The author discusses both objections.
qs.x: The author says the objection has real force and is not fully answered. Trap: Treating the mention of a counterpoint as a rebuttal.

qs.q: Which of the following findings would most undermine the author's concluding concern about legitimacy?
o: Assemblies chosen by lot are statistically representative of the population.
Representativeness is already granted and does not address perceived legitimacy.
Citizens report that they regard recommendations from randomly chosen assemblies as authoritative as those of elected legislators.
Correct: That would show recognition and ownership are not obstacles, weakening the concern.
Members of lottery assemblies change their views after hearing experts.
Changing views bears on deliberation, not on acceptance by others.
Elected officials are older than the average citizen.
This is a premise of the case for lotteries, not evidence about legitimacy.
qs.x: That would show recognition and ownership are not obstacles, weakening the concern. Trap: Confusing statistical representativeness with perceived legitimacy, the very distinction the author draws.

qs.q: The author's discussion implies that freedom from donor pressure in a lottery assembly
o: comes at the cost of the checks that voters apply to elected officials.
Correct: The text says the freedom is also a freedom from the checks voters impose.
guarantees that members will be impartial.
Impartiality is not guaranteed by independence.
would also free elected legislators from the accountability that voters currently impose on them.
The passage does not suggest this for elected officials.
was a deliberate goal of the Athenians.
The passage does not attribute that goal to the Athenians.
qs.x: The text says the freedom is also a freedom from the checks voters impose. Trap: Seeing independence as a pure benefit, ignoring the tradeoff the author states.

passages.title: FL02 · CARS · Passage 7
text: Consider two drivers who leave a party equally intoxicated and equally careless. One arrives home without incident; the other, through no difference in intention or skill, strikes a child who runs into the road. Most people feel that the second driver deserves greater blame, and the law agrees, punishing the one far more severely than the other. Yet this reaction sits uneasily with a principle that seems almost self-evident: that people should be judged only for what lies within their control. The child's presence in the road was not within either driver's control. Philosophers who have dwelt on this puzzle call it moral luck, and it exposes a tension in our ordinary thinking about responsibility.

One response is to bite the bullet and hold that the principle must prevail. If control is what matters, then the two drivers are equally blameworthy, and our contrary feelings are a kind of cognitive mistake, perhaps a holdover from a time when harm itself was treated as a pollutant requiring cleansing. This view has the appeal of consistency. But it carries a high cost. If we strip away every contribution of fortune, little of what we routinely blame or praise survives. Our character, upbringing, and circumstances are not chosen, and neither are the opportunities that allow one person to display courage while another is never tested. A rigorous application of the control principle threatens to dissolve nearly all moral assessment.

A second response is to accept luck as part of morality and to deny that the principle ever applied without exception. On this view, to act is to stake oneself on a world one does not command, and the agent is answerable for what the action actually does. A person who fires a gun into a crowd cannot disown the result by pointing out that the bullet might have missed. The feeling of heightened responsibility after harm is not an error but a recognition that actions are made real by their effects. This view fits the reactions that people have, but it faces the charge of arbitrariness: why should a difference that the agent did not make make a difference to what the agent deserves?

The most promising reply may lie in distinguishing between blame and its distribution. One can hold that the two drivers are equally at fault in their choice to drive impaired, while recognizing that the harm they cause places different demands on them afterward. The driver who struck the child owes apology, compensation, and perhaps a lasting reckoning that the other does not owe, though the second driver might in fairness have owed the same had circumstances been different. The difference is one of what is owed rather than of how culpable each person was in deciding to drive. This does not remove all discomfort, but it relocates it, and the relocation has a real advantage: it lets us keep the control principle for questions of fault while granting that what happens afterward is partly a matter of fortune. We no longer ask why luck alters desert; we ask why harm generates obligations, and to that question there are familiar answers drawn from the ordinary practice of repairing wrongs.

qs.q: The passage is primarily concerned with
o: arguing that drunk driving should be punished more severely.
The drivers are an illustration, not a policy argument.
examining responses to a conflict between our judgments about blame and the principle that people are responsible only for what they control.
Correct: The author surveys responses to the puzzle and ends with a proposed reframing.
demonstrating that moral judgments are always mistaken.
The author does not claim all judgments are mistaken.
defending the law's treatment of the two drivers.
The author finds the law's pattern puzzling and does not simply defend it.
qs.x: The author surveys responses to the puzzle and ends with a proposed reframing. Trap: Treating the opening example as the topic rather than the puzzle it illustrates.

qs.q: The author claims that applying the control principle strictly would
o: confirm that harm is a pollutant.
The pollutant idea is offered as an explanation of intuitions, not a result.
make the two drivers equally innocent.
The strict view makes them equally blameworthy, not innocent.
support the law's different treatment of the two drivers, one of whom caused harm.
It conflicts with the law's different treatment.
eliminate most ordinary grounds for praise and blame.
Correct: The author says little of what we routinely praise or blame survives.
qs.x: The author says little of what we routinely praise or blame survives. Trap: Confusing 'equally blameworthy' with 'equally innocent'.

qs.q: The author refers to the person who fires a gun into a crowd in order to
o: illustrate the view that agents are answerable for what their actions actually do.
Correct: The example supports the second response, that a person cannot disown results by noting what might have been.
prove that intentions are irrelevant to blame, since only results determine what people are answerable for.
The author does not claim intentions are irrelevant.
show that the control principle is correct.
The example works against the strict control principle.
argue that firearms should be regulated.
Regulation is not the issue.
qs.x: The example supports the second response, that a person cannot disown results by noting what might have been. Trap: Overreading an illustration as a sweeping claim.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the second response is best characterized as
o: fully convinced of its correctness and unconcerned about the objections raised against it.
The author notes its difficulty and goes on to propose another reply.
sympathetic but aware of a serious objection.
Correct: The author says it fits reactions but faces the charge of arbitrariness.
mocking of its premises.
The author treats it respectfully.
indifferent to its implications.
The author weighs its implications at length.
qs.x: The author says it fits reactions but faces the charge of arbitrariness. Trap: Treating description of an objection as dismissal of the view.

qs.q: According to the proposal in the final paragraph, which of the following is most likely true of the second driver who did not strike a child?
o: The driver is entirely innocent of wrongdoing.
The proposal holds both equally at fault in the choice.
The driver owes more than the first driver.
Harm generates the obligations, so the first driver owes more.
As blameworthy for the choice to drive impaired but not currently obligated to compensate anyone.
Correct: The proposal separates culpability in the choice from what is owed after harm.
The driver should be punished equally in every respect, since the choice to drive impaired was identical.
Obligations to repair differ even though culpability is equal.
qs.x: The proposal separates culpability in the choice from what is owed after harm. Trap: Collapsing the distinction between culpability and what is owed.

qs.q: Which of the following situations would most clearly be analogous to the author's concluding proposal?
o: Two students cheat; both are expelled regardless of the outcome of the exam.
Here consequences play no role, so the analogy is missing.
Two doctors misdiagnose; neither is held responsible because patients recovered.
This denies responsibility where fault exists.
Two investors take a risk; the one who profits is declared more moral.
This ties moral worth to profit, which the proposal does not do.
Two contractors cut the same safety corner; one's building collapses, and only that contractor owes repairs, though both acted equally irresponsibly.
Correct: Equal fault in the decision but different obligations because of harm mirrors the proposal.
qs.x: Equal fault in the decision but different obligations because of harm mirrors the proposal. Trap: Picking a case with unequal outcomes but ignoring whether fault and obligation are distinguished.

passages.title: FL02 · CARS · Passage 8
text: Nineteenth-century natural history was conducted to a remarkable degree by people who held no university position. Clergymen catalogued beetles, physicians collected fossils, and women with leisure and keen eyes compiled records of seaweeds and mosses. These amateurs, as they are now called, supplied much of the raw material on which the major theories of the age were built. Yet during the twentieth century the amateur gradually lost status in most sciences, displaced by professionals whose training, salaries, and institutions seemed to promise rigor. The standard story presents this as a straightforward advance: as methods became more demanding, those without formal preparation could no longer contribute.

This story is only partly true. In fields such as particle physics, where the instruments cost billions, the retreat of the amateur was inevitable. But in other fields the explanation falls short. Astronomy, ornithology, and the study of insects have continued to benefit from the labor of unpaid observers, whose contributions include comets spotted before any professional noticed them and population counts covering regions no institution could afford to survey. If rigor were the only variable, these fields would have long since closed their doors. The persistence of amateurs shows that what mattered was not methodological sophistication in general but how much a given inquiry depended on expensive equipment or on information that only specialists could interpret.

A second feature of the standard story deserves attention: it measures the amateur against the professional's standards and finds the amateur wanting, without asking what the amateur offered that the professional did not. Volunteers can watch a field every day for years, an investment that no funded researcher could justify. They are scattered over wide territories, and they know local conditions intimately. Such advantages are not trivial. When a rare visitor appears at a pond, the amateur who walks past it each morning is more likely to notice than a specialist who visits twice a season.

Recent developments suggest that the line between the two groups may become more porous. Digital platforms now allow volunteers to submit observations that are pooled into databases of enormous size, and professionals have devised statistical methods to correct for the uneven skill and effort of contributors. These tools do not turn amateurs into professionals, but they convert their scattered observations into data that can answer questions that neither group could address alone. In some respects the arrangement resembles the older partnership between collector and theorist, now carried out at scale and with better safeguards.

It would be naive to idealize this relationship. Volunteers tend to cluster where it is pleasant to observe, so databases contain too many records from parks and roadsides and too few from remote or unwelcoming terrain. Contributors may report what is striking and neglect what is common. Professionals who rely on such data must therefore treat it with care, and sometimes they will be tempted to treat the volunteers as mere instruments of collection, not as partners in inquiry. If the collaboration is to endure, the relationship will need to rest on respect for what each side knows, since the history of science suggests that neglected observers do not remain in the field for long.

qs.q: Which of the following best captures the author's thesis?
o: Amateurs were never important to nineteenth-century science.
The author says amateurs supplied much of the raw material.
The decline of the amateur cannot be explained by rigor alone, and amateurs still offer distinctive contributions.
Correct: The author qualifies the standard story and highlights ongoing amateur value.
Professionals have largely been replaced by volunteers in modern science, which now relies mainly on unpaid amateur labor.
The author says volunteers supplement, not replace, professionals.
Digital databases make professional training unnecessary.
The author says the tools do not turn amateurs into professionals.
qs.x: The author qualifies the standard story and highlights ongoing amateur value. Trap: Overextending the argument that amateurs matter into the claim that they have replaced professionals.

qs.q: According to the passage, the retreat of the amateur from particle physics is best explained by
o: the decline of volunteer enthusiasm for the demanding work that the field requires.
Enthusiasm is not discussed.
statistical errors in volunteer data.
Statistical correction is discussed for databases of observations, not for physics.
the extremely high cost of the necessary instruments.
Correct: The author cites billion-dollar instruments as making the retreat inevitable.
the lack of local knowledge among physicists.
Local knowledge is an amateur advantage in other fields.
qs.x: The author cites billion-dollar instruments as making the retreat inevitable. Trap: Using a reason given for a different field.

qs.q: The author mentions the pond in the third paragraph primarily to
o: illustrate an advantage that frequent local observation gives volunteers.
Correct: The example shows the amateur who passes the pond daily is likelier to notice.
show that specialists lack scientific training.
It claims only that specialists visit less often.
argue that rare visitors to a site are more important to science than common ones are.
Importance of rarity is not argued.
criticize volunteers for neglecting remote areas.
The criticism of volunteers appears elsewhere and is not the point of the example.
qs.x: The example shows the amateur who passes the pond daily is likelier to notice. Trap: Reading a narrow illustration as a broad judgment about specialists.

qs.q: The author's tone in the final paragraph is best described as
o: celebratory, treating the collaboration between professionals and amateurs as flawless.
The author lists biases.
dismissive, treating volunteer data as worthless.
The author does not call the data worthless but advises care.
detached, avoiding any evaluation.
The author gives a clear recommendation.
cautious, acknowledging both the promise and the hazards of collaboration.
Correct: The author warns against idealizing the relationship while urging respect.
qs.x: The author warns against idealizing the relationship while urging respect. Trap: Taking the earlier optimistic paragraph as the author's overall tone.

qs.q: The passage most strongly suggests that if professionals ignored the biases in volunteer databases, the results would likely
o: be more reliable than data from funded surveys that follow standardized protocols.
The author suggests correcting biases, implying otherwise.
show fewer records from parks.
Parks are overrepresented, not underrepresented.
overrepresent pleasant and accessible locations.
Correct: The author says records cluster in pleasant places.
be free of reporting of unusual events.
Contributors report striking events, so unusual events would be overrepresented.
qs.x: The author says records cluster in pleasant places. Trap: Reversing the direction of the bias the passage describes.

qs.q: Which of the following developments would most weaken the author's claim that amateurs remain valuable in ornithology?
o: Volunteers submit observations through digital platforms.
Platforms are part of the author's account of continuing contributions.
Amateur observers occasionally misidentify species.
Occasional errors are already acknowledged and corrected statistically.
Some bird species live only in remote areas.
Remote species would make volunteers less useful in those areas only, and the author acknowledges this.
Automated recorders and cameras placed across the whole territory provide continuous observations at lower cost than volunteers can supply.
Correct: Continuous, cheap, comprehensive automated data would remove the amateur's advantages in coverage and persistence.
qs.x: Continuous, cheap, comprehensive automated data would remove the amateur's advantages in coverage and persistence. Trap: Choosing an acknowledged limitation instead of a development that removes the amateur's distinctive advantages.

passages.title: FL02 · CARS · Passage 9
text: In 1688 a Swiss medical student named Johannes Hofer coined the term nostalgia, combining Greek words for return and pain, to describe a condition he observed among Swiss soldiers and servants stationed far from their mountains. The sufferers were afflicted by melancholy, sleeplessness, and loss of appetite, and some, it was reported, declined fatally. For two centuries afterward, physicians treated nostalgia as a disease of the body and mind, debating whether its cause lay in damaged brain tissue or in the effects of altered air pressure. The remedy, naturally, was repatriation, or at least the threat of it.

By the twentieth century the word had changed beyond recognition. It no longer denoted a pathology but a mood: a wistful, often pleasant affection for a time that has gone. And its object had shifted, too. Hofer's soldiers longed for a place they could, in principle, return to. The modern nostalgic yearns for a period of time, which no journey can reach. This change is not merely a matter of vocabulary. It reflects a transformation in how societies understood the past. In a world of rapid change, the past appears not as a continuous presence but as a distinct country, separated from the present by innovations and upheavals, and therefore capable of being missed.

Critics have often treated nostalgia with suspicion. A common charge is that it falsifies history by selecting the pleasures of a former age and discarding its miseries. A person who yearns for the closeness of village life may forget the narrowness, the surveillance, and the want that accompanied it. This charge is justified in many cases, especially when nostalgia is exploited politically to promise the restoration of a golden age that never existed. Yet it would be wrong to assume that nostalgia is always an error of memory. A person who longs for a vanished community may be fully aware of its faults and still sense that something of value was lost with it. The longing, in such cases, is not a belief about the past but an expression of dissatisfaction with the present.

This second possibility suggests why nostalgia is so persistent and why attempts to dismiss it as sentimental have so often failed. Nostalgia can serve as a form of criticism, a way of voicing what a society lacks without possessing a program for supplying it. The nostalgic person may not want to return to the past, and often could not bear to, but wants the present to make room for goods that the past happened to contain. Whether such longing leads to reaction or to reform depends on whether it is turned toward fantasy or toward imagination: toward a picture of the past to be reinstated, or toward a question about what the present could learn from it.

If so, the history of the word is also a record of a change in ourselves. Hofer's patients suffered because they were absent from home. Today's nostalgics suffer, if that is the word, because home has changed while they stayed in place. In both cases the pain reveals an attachment, and attachments, whatever their risks, are among the conditions of a life that matters to the person who lives it.

qs.q: The passage is primarily concerned with
o: proving that nostalgia is a form of disease.
Nostalgia stopped being regarded as disease in the twentieth century.
condemning nostalgia as a political tool.
The author acknowledges political abuse but argues for a broader view.
tracing how the meaning of nostalgia has changed and assessing what the feeling can express.
Correct: The author traces the word's history and then evaluates the modern feeling.
describing the symptoms experienced by Swiss soldiers and the treatments that physicians prescribed.
The soldiers are the historical starting point only.
qs.x: The author traces the word's history and then evaluates the modern feeling. Trap: Treating the passage's opening anecdote as its subject.

qs.q: According to the passage, how did the object of nostalgia change between Hofer's time and the twentieth century?
o: It shifted from a time to a place.
This reverses the passage's account.
It shifted from the body to the mind.
Body and mind were both involved in early theories and this is not the object shift described.
It shifted from the home village to a foreign land, where the longing was first diagnosed.
Home was the original object, and longing for it as a place is what changed.
It shifted from a place that could be revisited to a period of time that cannot.
Correct: The author contrasts longing for a place with longing for a time.
qs.x: The author contrasts longing for a place with longing for a time. Trap: Reversing the direction of a historical shift.

qs.q: The author refers to the person who longs for a vanished community while recognizing its faults primarily to
o: prove that village life was better than modern life in nearly every respect that matters.
The author does not say the community was better.
argue that communities should be restored.
The author says nostalgics often would not want to return.
support the charge that nostalgia falsifies history.
The example is used against, not for, that charge as applied universally.
show that nostalgia need not rest on a false belief about the past.
Correct: The example separates longing from a mistaken belief.
qs.x: The example separates longing from a mistaken belief. Trap: Missing that the example is offered as a counterexample to the critics.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward critics who dismiss nostalgia as sentimental is best described as
o: entirely in agreement with them that nostalgia is merely a sentimental indulgence.
The author argues that dismissal has failed and is limited.
partly sympathetic but ultimately finding their view incomplete.
Correct: The author grants the charge in many cases yet argues it misses the critical function.
contemptuous.
The tone is measured, not contemptuous.
uninterested.
The author gives the critics sustained attention.
qs.x: The author grants the charge in many cases yet argues it misses the critical function. Trap: Equating partial concession with total agreement.

qs.q: According to the passage's reasoning, which of the following expressions of longing would most likely lead toward reform rather than reaction?
o: A politician who promises to restore a previous age exactly as it was, including its institutions, customs, and social hierarchies.
This is the fantasy of reinstatement the author associates with reaction.
A traveler who wants to relive a holiday by visiting the same hotel yearly.
This is a personal wish with no social orientation toward change.
A retiree who insists that earlier decades had no problems.
This reflects the falsifying idealization the author criticizes.
A resident who misses the shared public spaces of a former era and campaigns for new ones adapted to present needs.
Correct: This turns longing into a question about what the present could learn from the past.
qs.x: This turns longing into a question about what the present could learn from the past. Trap: Choosing a case that mentions the past favorably without asking whether it looks toward the present.

passages.title: FL02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 1
text: A student studies a mass-spring oscillator using a cart of adjustable mass on a horizontal, essentially frictionless air track. One end of an ideal spring is fixed to the track and the other end is attached to the cart. For each trial, the student pulls the cart 5.0 cm from equilibrium, releases it from rest, and uses a photogate to time 10 complete oscillations, from which the period T is calculated. The mass of the spring is negligible compared with that of the cart. The student varies the cart mass and repeats the measurement, then plots T² against mass to test the relationship between period and mass. Table 1 gives the periods and Figure 1 shows T² versus mass. In a separate demonstration, the same spring is hung vertically from a support and a 0.20 kg mass is attached to it. Use g = 10 m/s² where needed. Before each run, the student checks that the track is level by confirming that the cart does not drift, and each reported period is the average of three runs that agreed to within 1%.

qs.q: Based on the slope of the line in Figure 1, what is the spring constant?
o: 78 N/m
78 N/m multiplies the slope by 4π² instead of dividing.
2.0 N/m uses the slope itself as k and ignores the 4π² factor.
0.51 N/m takes the reciprocal of the slope without the 4π² factor.
20 N/m
Correct: The slope of T² vs m is 4π²/k, about 1.97 s²/kg, so k = 4π²/1.97 ≈ 20 N/m.
qs.x: The slope of T² vs m is 4π²/k, about 1.97 s²/kg, so k = 4π²/1.97 ≈ 20 N/m. Trap: Treating the slope of T² versus m as k directly, instead of recognizing that slope = 4π²/k.

qs.q: What is the maximum speed of the 0.20 kg cart during its oscillation at an amplitude of 5.0 cm?
o: 0.25 m/s is v², i.e., the square root was not taken.
Correct: Energy conservation: ½kA² = ½mv²max, so v = A√(k/m) = 0.050 × √(20/0.20) = 0.050 × 10 = 0.50 m/s.
0.71 m/s results from dropping the ½ from the spring energy only (kA² = ½mv²).
5.0 m/s uses v = Ak/m, which is dimensionally incorrect.
qs.x: Energy conservation: ½kA² = ½mv²max, so v = A√(k/m) = 0.050 × √(20/0.20) = 0.050 × 10 = 0.50 m/s. Trap: Forgetting to take the square root after solving ½kA² = ½mv² for v².

qs.q: If the student doubled the initial displacement of the cart from 5.0 cm to 10.0 cm, the period of oscillation would:
o: double.
double. Would require the period to be proportional to amplitude, which it is not.
remain unchanged.
Correct: For an ideal spring, T = 2π√(m/k) does not depend on amplitude, so the period stays the same.
increase by a factor of √2.
increase by a factor of √2. Confuses the amplitude dependence with the √m dependence.
decrease by half.
decrease by half. Incorrectly assumes a larger amplitude means a stiffer restoring force overall.
qs.x: For an ideal spring, T = 2π√(m/k) does not depend on amplitude, so the period stays the same. Trap: Assuming a larger amplitude means a longer trip and therefore a longer period.

qs.q: When the 0.20 kg mass hangs at rest from the same spring in the vertical demonstration, the spring is stretched from its relaxed length by approximately:
o: 0.010 m is m/k and omits g.
Correct: At equilibrium kx = mg, so x = mg/k = (0.20)(10)/20 = 0.10 m.
0.20 m is twice the equilibrium stretch, the maximum stretch if the mass were released from the unstretched position.
40 m multiplies mg by k instead of dividing.
qs.x: At equilibrium kx = mg, so x = mg/k = (0.20)(10)/20 = 0.10 m. Trap: Using x = m/k or x = mk/g and losing the weight force in the equilibrium condition.

qs.q: At what displacement from equilibrium are the kinetic and potential energies of the oscillating cart equal when the amplitude is 5.0 cm?
o: 2.5 cm
2.5 cm uses x = A/2, which gives PE = ¼ of the total, not half.
0 cm
0 cm at equilibrium the energy is entirely kinetic.
5.0 cm
5.0 cm at the turning point the energy is entirely potential.
3.5 cm
Correct: KE = PE means ½kx² = ½(½kA²), so x = A/√2 = 5.0/1.414 ≈ 3.5 cm.
qs.x: KE = PE means ½kx² = ½(½kA²), so x = A/√2 = 5.0/1.414 ≈ 3.5 cm. Trap: Assuming equal energies occur at half the amplitude rather than at A/√2.

graph.title: Figure 1. T² versus cart mass

passages.title: FL02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 2
text: Students investigate collisions between two carts on a low-friction track. Cart A has a mass of 0.50 kg and cart B has a mass of 0.30 kg. In each trial cart B starts at rest and cart A is launched toward it at 1.20 m/s. Velocities are measured with motion sensors just before and just after the carts interact, and the positive direction is the initial direction of cart A. In Trial 1, the carts are fitted with magnetic bumpers that repel one another, so the carts never actually touch. In Trial 2, the bumpers are replaced with Velcro strips so that the carts stick together after impact. The students then compare total momentum and total kinetic energy before and after each collision, assuming that external forces during the brief collisions are negligible. Results are given in Table 1. In a follow-up analysis of Trial 1, the students estimate that the repulsive interaction lasted 0.030 s.

qs.q: What is the total momentum of the two-cart system after the collision in Trial 2?
o: 0.38 kg·m/s
0.38 kg·m/s counts only cart A (0.50 × 0.75).
0.23 kg·m/s
0.23 kg·m/s counts only cart B (0.30 × 0.75).
0.75 kg·m/s
0.75 kg·m/s is the common velocity, not a momentum.
0.60 kg·m/s
Correct: Momentum is conserved: p = (0.50 + 0.30)(0.75) = 0.60 kg·m/s, equal to the initial 0.50 × 1.20 = 0.60 kg·m/s.
qs.x: Momentum is conserved: p = (0.50 + 0.30)(0.75) = 0.60 kg·m/s, equal to the initial 0.50 × 1.20 = 0.60 kg·m/s. Trap: Counting the momentum of only one cart after a collision in which both move together.

qs.q: How much kinetic energy is lost in the collision in Trial 2?
o: 0.36 J is the entire initial kinetic energy.
0.23 J is the final kinetic energy rather than the loss.
0 J
0 J assumes that momentum conservation also implies kinetic energy conservation.
qs.x: Initial KE = ½(0.50)(1.20)² = 0.360 J. Final KE = ½(0.80)(0.75)² = 0.225 J. Loss = 0.135 J ≈ 0.14 J. Trap: Assuming that because momentum is conserved, kinetic energy must be conserved too.

qs.q: Which observation best supports classifying Trial 1 as an elastic collision?
o: The carts move apart after the interaction.
The carts move apart after the interaction. Carts also separate in many inelastic collisions where they bounce with some energy lost.
The total kinetic energy after the collision equals the total kinetic energy before it.
Correct: KE after = ½(0.50)(0.30)² + ½(0.30)(1.50)² = 0.0225 + 0.3375 = 0.360 J, equal to the initial 0.360 J, which defines an elastic collision.
Total momentum is the same before and after.
Total momentum is the same before and after. Momentum is conserved in all collisions, elastic or not, when external forces are negligible.
Cart A's speed decreases while cart B's speed increases.
Cart A's speed decreases while cart B's speed increases. This occurs in any collision in which a moving cart strikes a stationary one.
qs.x: KE after = ½(0.50)(0.30)² + ½(0.30)(1.50)² = 0.0225 + 0.3375 = 0.360 J, equal to the initial 0.360 J, which defines an elastic collision. Trap: Using momentum conservation (true for every collision) as evidence that a collision is elastic.

qs.q: What is the average magnitude of the force exerted on cart B during the 0.030 s interaction in Trial 1?
o: Correct: Impulse = Δp of B = 0.30 × 1.50 = 0.45 kg·m/s, so F = 0.45/0.030 = 15 N.
50 N is Δv/Δt and ignores the mass of cart B.
0.45 N is the impulse (in N·s) and not divided by the time.
0.014 N multiplies the impulse by the time instead of dividing.
qs.x: Impulse = Δp of B = 0.30 × 1.50 = 0.45 kg·m/s, so F = 0.45/0.030 = 15 N. Trap: Dividing the change in velocity by time (an acceleration) and forgetting to multiply by mass.

passages.title: FL02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 3
text: A student uses a spring scale to study buoyant forces. A solid metal block of unknown composition is suspended from the scale and its weight is recorded in air. The block is then fully submerged, without touching the container, first in water (density 1000 kg/m³) and then in an unidentified liquid X, and the apparent weight is recorded each time. The scale reading is the tension in the string, which equals the weight of the block minus the buoyant force. Data are shown in Table 1. The student assumes that the block is incompressible and that neither liquid is absorbed by the block. In a second experiment, the student places a small cube of wood, with a density of 600 kg/m³, into liquid X and observes that it floats at rest. Use g = 10 m/s². The student repeats each reading three times and finds that the scale readings are reproducible to within 0.05 N. Care is taken to remove air bubbles from the surface of the block before it is submerged, and the block is suspended by a thin string whose volume and weight are assumed to be negligible.

qs.q: What is the density of the metal block?
o: 1.3 × 10³ kg/m³
1.3 × 10³ kg/m³ uses the apparent weight (3.0 N) as if it were the buoyant force.
3.0 × 10³ kg/m³
3.0 × 10³ kg/m³ divides the apparent weight by the volume, which is not the true weight.
8.0 × 10² kg/m³
8.0 × 10² kg/m³ is the density of liquid X, not of the block.
4.0 × 10³ kg/m³
Correct: In water B = 4.0 − 3.0 = 1.0 N = ρ_water·V·g, so V = 1.0/(1000 × 10) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³. Density = m/V = 0.40 kg/1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³ = 4.0 × 10³ kg/m³.
qs.x: In water B = 4.0 − 3.0 = 1.0 N = ρ_water·V·g, so V = 1.0/(1000 × 10) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³. Density = m/V = 0.40 kg/1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³ = 4.0 × 10³ kg/m³. Trap: Using the scale reading in a fluid as the buoyant force instead of the difference from the weight in air.

qs.q: What is the density of liquid X?
o: 3.2 × 10³ kg/m³
3.2 × 10³ kg/m³ reads the apparent weight as if it were a density.
1.25 × 10³ kg/m³ inverts the ratio of buoyant forces.
8.0 × 10² kg/m³
Correct: Buoyant force in X is 4.0 − 3.2 = 0.8 N. Since the same volume is displaced, ρ_X = 1000 × (0.8/1.0) = 800 kg/m³.
1.0 × 10³ kg/m³
1.0 × 10³ kg/m³ assumes the liquid is water because the block was fully submerged in both.
qs.x: Buoyant force in X is 4.0 − 3.2 = 0.8 N. Since the same volume is displaced, ρ_X = 1000 × (0.8/1.0) = 800 kg/m³. Trap: Inverting the ratio of buoyant forces when comparing two liquids.

qs.q: What fraction of the wooden cube's volume is submerged when it floats in liquid X?
o: 0.60 is the wood density as a fraction of water, not of liquid X.
Correct: Floating: ρ_wood·V·g = ρ_X·V_sub·g, so V_sub/V = 600/800 = 0.75.
1.33 exceeds 1, which is impossible for a floating object, and results from inverting the density ratio.
0.25 is the fraction of the cube above the surface.
qs.x: Floating: ρ_wood·V·g = ρ_X·V_sub·g, so V_sub/V = 600/800 = 0.75. Trap: Inverting the density ratio, or using the density of water instead of the fluid in which the object floats.

qs.q: What is the gauge pressure at a depth of 0.50 m in liquid X?
o: 5.0 kPa
5.0 kPa uses the density of water.
4.0 kPa
Correct: P_gauge = ρgh = (800)(10)(0.50) = 4000 Pa = 4.0 kPa.
105 kPa
105 kPa adds atmospheric pressure, which would give the absolute pressure, not the gauge pressure.
8.0 kPa
8.0 kPa corresponds to a depth of 1.0 m.
qs.x: P_gauge = ρgh = (800)(10)(0.50) = 4000 Pa = 4.0 kPa. Trap: Adding atmospheric pressure to a question that asks for gauge pressure.

passages.title: FL02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 4
text: A student builds an RC circuit from a 12.0 V battery, a resistor, a switch, and an initially uncharged capacitor connected in series. When the switch is closed at t = 0, a voltmeter placed across the capacitor records the voltage as a function of time. Circuit 1 uses R = 50 kΩ and C = 200 µF, and the data are plotted in Figure 1. The student then builds two more circuits and records the time needed for the capacitor voltage to reach 7.6 V, which is approximately 63% of the battery voltage. The results are given in Table 1. Throughout the experiment, the battery is considered ideal and the connecting wires have negligible resistance. The student also notes that the capacitor is a nonpolarized type and that the voltmeter has an internal resistance much larger than R, so that it draws a negligible current from the circuit. Before each trial, the capacitor is discharged by briefly shorting its leads, and the temperature of the room is held constant.

qs.q: What is the time constant of Circuit 1?
o: 6.9 s is τ ln 2, the half-time of charging, not the time constant.
Correct: τ = RC = (50 × 10³ Ω)(200 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 10 s, matching the time to reach about 63% of the final voltage.
1.0 × 10⁷ s multiplies kΩ by µF without converting units.
20 s is 2τ, when the voltage is about 86% of its final value.
qs.x: τ = RC = (50 × 10³ Ω)(200 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 10 s, matching the time to reach about 63% of the final voltage. Trap: Mixing up the time constant (63%) with a half-time (50%).

qs.q: What is the energy stored in the capacitor in Circuit 1 after it is fully charged?
o: 2.9 × 10⁻² J omits the factor of ½.
2.4 × 10⁻³ J is the charge Q = CV in coulombs, not an energy.
1.2 × 10⁻³ J uses ½CV without squaring the voltage.
qs.x: U = ½CV² = ½(200 × 10⁻⁶)(12)² = 1.44 × 10⁻² J. Trap: Forgetting to square the voltage or to include the ½ in the stored energy formula.

qs.q: A fourth circuit uses R = 25 kΩ and C = 400 µF. How long will it take the capacitor voltage to reach 7.6 V?
o: Correct: τ = RC = (25 × 10³)(400 × 10⁻⁶) = 10 s, identical to Circuit 1, so the time to reach 63% is the same.
20 s assumes that doubling C doubles the time without accounting for halving R.
5 s
5 s assumes that halving R alone sets the time.
40 s multiplies the effect of both changes instead of combining the product RC.
qs.x: τ = RC = (25 × 10³)(400 × 10⁻⁶) = 10 s, identical to Circuit 1, so the time to reach 63% is the same. Trap: Changing only one factor in RC mentally and ignoring that the other factor changed in the opposite direction.

qs.q: What is the current through the resistor in Circuit 1 at t = 10 s?
o: 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ A is the initial current V/R at t = 0.
1.5 × 10⁻⁴ A uses the capacitor voltage fraction (0.63 × 240 µA) rather than the remaining fraction.
1.2 × 10⁻⁴ A assumes that the current has dropped to half of its initial value.
Correct: At t = 10 s the capacitor voltage is 7.6 V, so the resistor has 12 − 7.6 = 4.4 V across it. I = 4.4/50,000 = 8.8 × 10⁻⁵ A.
qs.x: At t = 10 s the capacitor voltage is 7.6 V, so the resistor has 12 − 7.6 = 4.4 V across it. I = 4.4/50,000 = 8.8 × 10⁻⁵ A. Trap: Using the capacitor voltage rather than the voltage across the resistor to find the current.

qs.q: After Circuit 1 is fully charged, the battery is disconnected and a dielectric with κ = 2 is inserted to fill the space between the plates of the capacitor. The potential difference across the capacitor is now:
o: 12 V would be correct only if the battery stayed connected.
24 V assumes that the voltage doubles when C doubles.
3.0 V reduces the voltage by a factor of four.
Correct: With the battery disconnected, Q is constant. Inserting the dielectric doubles C, so V = Q/C halves to 6.0 V.
qs.x: With the battery disconnected, Q is constant. Inserting the dielectric doubles C, so V = Q/C halves to 6.0 V. Trap: Applying the constant-voltage condition (battery connected) when the battery has been removed.

graph.title: Figure 1. Capacitor voltage versus time (Circuit 1)

passages.title: FL02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 5
text: A student electroplates silver onto a small brass key in an electrolytic cell. The cell contains an aqueous solution of AgNO₃, a silver anode, and the key as the cathode, all connected to a constant-current power supply that delivers 0.500 A. The key is removed, rinsed, dried, and weighed at 10-minute intervals, and the increase in its mass is recorded as the mass of deposited silver. Table 1 and Figure 1 show the results. The molar mass of silver is 108 g/mol, and Faraday's constant is 96,500 C/mol e⁻. The student assumes that silver deposition is the only electrode process at the cathode, that the current efficiency is close to 100%, and that the mass of the silver anode decreases as the key's mass increases. Later the student wonders what would happen if the AgNO₃ solution were replaced with CuSO₄ under identical conditions. The key is cleaned with dilute acid before each run, and the power supply is checked with an ammeter to confirm that the current stays constant at 0.500 A.

qs.q: How many moles of electrons pass through the cell in 20 minutes?
o: 3.1 × 10⁻³ mol uses only 10 minutes (600 s).
1.2 × 10⁻² mol doubles the answer, as if two electrons were transferred per electron passed.
1.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol uses time in minutes instead of seconds.
qs.x: Q = It = (0.500)(1200 s) = 600 C. Moles of e⁻ = 600/96,500 = 6.2 × 10⁻³ mol. Trap: Using time in minutes in Q = It, which requires seconds.

qs.q: If the cell used CuSO₄(aq) instead of AgNO₃ under identical conditions, the mass of copper deposited in 20 minutes would be closest to:
o: 0.40 g forgets that two electrons are needed per Cu atom.
0.67 g is the silver mass at 20 min.
Correct: Moles of e⁻ = 6.2 × 10⁻³ mol, and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu gives 3.1 × 10⁻³ mol Cu. Mass = 3.1 × 10⁻³ × 63.5 ≈ 0.20 g.
0.10 g halves the copper amount a second time.
qs.x: Moles of e⁻ = 6.2 × 10⁻³ mol, and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu gives 3.1 × 10⁻³ mol Cu. Mass = 3.1 × 10⁻³ × 63.5 ≈ 0.20 g. Trap: Forgetting that Cu²⁺ requires two electrons per atom deposited.

qs.q: Which statement about the plating cell is correct?
o: The key is the anode, where Ag⁺ is oxidized.
The key is the anode, where Ag⁺ is oxidized. Reduction, not oxidation, occurs at the surface where metal deposits.
The key is connected to the negative terminal, and Ag⁺ is reduced at its surface.
Correct: In an electrolytic cell, the cathode is the site of reduction and is connected to the negative terminal of the power supply; Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag deposits on the key.
The silver electrode is the cathode, where Ag is reduced.
The silver electrode is the cathode, where Ag is reduced. The silver electrode dissolves, so it is the anode and undergoes oxidation.
Electrons flow through the solution from the silver electrode to the key.
Electrons flow through the solution from the silver electrode to the key. electrons flow through the external wire, while ions carry current in solution.
qs.x: In an electrolytic cell, the cathode is the site of reduction and is connected to the negative terminal of the power supply; Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag deposits on the key. Trap: Applying the galvanic-cell sign convention (cathode positive) to an electrolytic cell.

qs.q: If the current were increased to 1.00 A, the slope of the line in Figure 1 would be closest to:
o: 0.067 g/min
Correct: The present slope is about 0.0335 g/min. Mass deposited is proportional to current, so doubling the current doubles the slope to ≈ 0.067 g/min.
0.034 g/min
0.034 g/min assumes the deposition rate does not depend on current.
0.017 g/min
0.017 g/min halves the slope instead of doubling.
0.13 g/min
0.13 g/min quadruples the slope.
qs.x: The present slope is about 0.0335 g/min. Mass deposited is proportional to current, so doubling the current doubles the slope to ≈ 0.067 g/min. Trap: Assuming a rate that depends on charge is independent of current.

graph.title: Figure 1. Mass of silver deposited versus time

passages.title: FL02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 6
text: In a demonstration of wave interference, a student passes monochromatic light from a laser through a pair of narrow parallel slits and observes the resulting pattern on a screen placed 2.00 m from the slits. The pattern consists of evenly spaced bright and dark fringes near the center of the screen. The student changes the slit separation d, measures the distance Δy between adjacent bright fringes, and records the values in Table 1. For small angles, the fringe spacing is given by Δy = λL/d, where λ is the wavelength and L is the distance to the screen. The student then replaces the first laser with a second laser of a different color, uses the slits with d = 0.40 mm, and measures a fringe spacing of 2.5 mm. Finally, the student wonders how the pattern would change if the entire apparatus were submerged in water (refractive index 1.33). The slits are narrow compared with their separation, and the laser beam is wide enough to illuminate both slits uniformly.

qs.q: What is the wavelength of the first laser?
o: 300 nm
300 nm divides by an extra factor of 2.
1200 nm doubles the value by using 2L or 2d.
6.0 nm
6.0 nm has a power-of-ten error from mixing mm and m.
600 nm
qs.x: λ = Δy·d/L = (6.0 × 10⁻³ m)(0.20 × 10⁻³ m)/(2.00 m) = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m = 600 nm. Trap: Mixing millimeters and meters in Δy = λL/d.

qs.q: What is the wavelength of the second laser?
o: 720 nm
720 nm assumes spacing is inversely proportional to wavelength.
500 nm
1000 nm doubles the correct value.
250 nm
250 nm halves the correct value.
qs.x: λ = Δy·d/L = (2.5 × 10⁻³)(0.40 × 10⁻³)/2.00 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m = 500 nm. Trap: Inverting the proportionality between fringe spacing and wavelength.

qs.q: When the apparatus is submerged in water, the light's wavelength and frequency, relative to their values in air, are:
o: longer wavelength and the same frequency.
longer wavelength and the same frequency. Speed decreases in water, so wavelength cannot increase at constant frequency.
shorter wavelength and the same frequency.
Correct: Frequency is set by the source and does not change on entering a medium. Since v = c/n decreases, λ = v/f decreases by a factor of 1.33, and the fringe spacing decreases accordingly.
the same wavelength and lower frequency.
the same wavelength and lower frequency. Frequency is fixed by the source, not the medium.
shorter wavelength and higher frequency.
shorter wavelength and higher frequency. Frequency does not change when light changes media.
qs.x: Frequency is set by the source and does not change on entering a medium. Since v = c/n decreases, λ = v/f decreases by a factor of 1.33, and the fringe spacing decreases accordingly. Trap: Thinking that frequency changes when light enters a new medium.

qs.q: For the first laser, what is the path difference between light from the two slits at the first dark fringe on either side of the central bright fringe?
o: 600 nm
600 nm is one full wavelength, which gives the first bright fringe.
300 nm
Correct: Destructive interference first occurs at a path difference of λ/2 = 600/2 = 300 nm.
150 nm
150 nm is λ/4, which gives partial interference.
900 nm
900 nm is 3λ/2, the second dark fringe.
qs.x: Destructive interference first occurs at a path difference of λ/2 = 600/2 = 300 nm. Trap: Confusing the path difference for the first dark fringe (λ/2) with that for the first bright fringe (λ).

passages.title: FL02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 7
text: The emission spectrum of atomic hydrogen contains several series of lines. The Balmer series consists of visible lines produced when electrons relax from higher energy levels (n ≥ 3) to the n = 2 level. In the Bohr model, the energy of the nth level is Eₙ = −13.6 eV/n². A student heats hydrogen gas in a discharge tube, passes the emitted light through a diffraction grating, and measures the wavelengths of the four most prominent visible lines. The values, along with the transitions assigned by the student using the relationship λ (nm) = 1240 eV·nm/ΔE, are listed in Table 1. The student observes that the spacing between successive lines decreases toward shorter wavelength and that the lines appear to converge toward a limit. Further study extends the analysis to the Lyman series, in which electrons relax to the n = 1 level. The grating is calibrated with a lamp of known wavelengths, and the student uses a spectrometer to read each line to the nearest nanometer. The student also assumes the hydrogen nuclei are infinitely massive relative to the electron.

qs.q: What is the energy of the photon emitted in the n = 3 → n = 2 transition?
o: 4.91 eV adds the magnitudes of the two energy levels instead of subtracting.
1.51 eV is the magnitude of the n = 3 level only.
Correct: ΔE = E₃ − E₂ = −1.51 − (−3.40) = 1.89 eV (corresponding to 656 nm).
12.1 eV is the n = 3 → n = 1 energy, which belongs to the Lyman series.
qs.x: ΔE = E₃ − E₂ = −1.51 − (−3.40) = 1.89 eV (corresponding to 656 nm). Trap: Adding the magnitudes of the two levels rather than finding the difference.

qs.q: What is the shortest wavelength in the Balmer series (the series limit)?
o: 656 nm
656 nm is the longest Balmer wavelength (n = 3 → 2).
91 nm
91 nm is the Lyman series limit (n = ∞ → 1).
410 nm
410 nm is the n = 6 → 2 line, not the limit.
365 nm
Correct: The limit corresponds to n = ∞ → 2, ΔE = 3.40 eV, so λ = 1240/3.40 ≈ 365 nm.
qs.x: The limit corresponds to n = ∞ → 2, ΔE = 3.40 eV, so λ = 1240/3.40 ≈ 365 nm. Trap: Choosing the last observed line instead of the theoretical limit as n goes to infinity.

qs.q: What is the minimum photon energy needed to ionize a hydrogen atom that is initially in the n = 2 level?
o: Correct: Ionization requires raising the electron from E₂ = −3.40 eV to 0, so 3.40 eV is needed.
13.6 eV is the ionization energy from the ground state, n = 1.
10.2 eV is the energy of the n = 1 → 2 excitation.
1.89 eV is the n = 2 → 3 excitation energy.
qs.x: Ionization requires raising the electron from E₂ = −3.40 eV to 0, so 3.40 eV is needed. Trap: Using the ground-state ionization energy for an atom that is already excited.

qs.q: The n = 2 → n = 1 transition in hydrogen would emit light that is most likely:
o: visible, at about 656 nm.
visible, at about 656 nm. Is the n = 3 → 2 Balmer line.
ultraviolet, at about 122 nm.
Correct: ΔE = 13.6(1 − 1/4) = 10.2 eV, so λ = 1240/10.2 ≈ 122 nm, which is shorter than visible wavelengths, so it is ultraviolet.
infrared, at about 1900 nm.
infrared, at about 1900 nm. Would require an energy gap of only 0.65 eV.
X-ray, at about 1 nm.
X-ray, at about 1 nm. Would require roughly 1240 eV, far larger than any hydrogen transition.
qs.x: ΔE = 13.6(1 − 1/4) = 10.2 eV, so λ = 1240/10.2 ≈ 122 nm, which is shorter than visible wavelengths, so it is ultraviolet. Trap: Assuming that all hydrogen transitions to a lower level fall in the visible range.

passages.title: FL02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 8
text: A student titrates 25.0 mL of a 0.100 M solution of a weak monoprotic acid, HA, with 0.100 M NaOH at 25 °C. A calibrated pH meter is used to record the pH after each addition of titrant, and the solution is stirred throughout. The data are listed in Table 1 and plotted in Figure 1. The student identifies the equivalence point from the steepest part of the curve and uses the volumes before the equivalence point to analyze the buffer region. The student notes that the acid has only one acidic proton and that the activities of the ions in these dilute solutions can be approximated by their concentrations. Water's ion product is Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at this temperature. Several common indicators and their approximate transition ranges are: methyl orange (3.1–4.4), methyl red (4.4–6.2), bromothymol blue (6.0–7.6), and phenolphthalein (8.2–10.0). The pH meter is calibrated with buffers at pH 4.00 and 10.00 before the titration, and the burette is read to the nearest 0.01 mL. Carbon dioxide absorption from the air is assumed to be negligible.

qs.q: Based on the data, the acid dissociation constant of HA is closest to:
o: Correct: At the half-equivalence point (12.5 mL), [A⁻] = [HA], so pH = pKa = 4.76 and Ka = 10⁻⁴·⁷⁶ ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁵.
1.3 × 10⁻³ is the initial [H⁺] (from pH 2.88), not Ka.
5.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ is Kb of the conjugate base.
1.9 × 10⁻⁹ is [H⁺] at the equivalence point (pH 8.73), not Ka.
qs.x: At the half-equivalence point (12.5 mL), [A⁻] = [HA], so pH = pKa = 4.76 and Ka = 10⁻⁴·⁷⁶ ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁵. Trap: Reading the initial [H⁺] as Ka instead of using the half-equivalence point.

qs.q: Why is the pH at the equivalence point (25.0 mL) greater than 7?
o: Excess NaOH remains in the solution.
Excess NaOH remains in the solution. At equivalence NaOH has been added in exactly stoichiometric amount, with no excess.
Na⁺ hydrolyzes to produce OH⁻.
Na⁺ hydrolyzes to produce OH⁻. Na⁺ is the cation of a strong base and does not hydrolyze.
The conjugate base A⁻ reacts with water to produce OH⁻.
Correct: At equivalence all HA has been converted to A⁻, a weak base: A⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HA + OH⁻, so the solution is basic.
HA is completely dissociated at this point.
HA is completely dissociated at this point. HA has been consumed; it is not the species determining pH, and it is a weak acid anyway.
qs.x: At equivalence all HA has been converted to A⁻, a weak base: A⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HA + OH⁻, so the solution is basic. Trap: Thinking the equivalence point of any acid-base titration must have pH 7.

qs.q: What is the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] after 18.75 mL of NaOH has been added?
o: 0.33 is the ratio at 6.25 mL, where A⁻ is one-third of HA.
Correct: NaOH added = 1.875 mmol, so A⁻ = 1.875 mmol and HA remaining = 2.50 − 1.875 = 0.625 mmol, giving 3.0. Consistent with pH = 4.76 + log 3 = 5.24.
0.75 is the fraction of the equivalence volume added, not the concentration ratio.
1.5 incorrectly takes the ratio as 18.75/12.5.
qs.x: NaOH added = 1.875 mmol, so A⁻ = 1.875 mmol and HA remaining = 2.50 − 1.875 = 0.625 mmol, giving 3.0. Consistent with pH = 4.76 + log 3 = 5.24. Trap: Using the ratio of volumes added instead of the ratio of moles of conjugate base to remaining acid.

qs.q: Which indicator is most suitable for detecting the equivalence point of this titration?
o: Methyl orange
Methyl orange changes color at pH 3.1–4.4, well before the equivalence point.
Methyl red
Methyl red changes between 4.4 and 6.2, within the buffer region.
Bromothymol blue
Bromothymol blue changes between 6.0 and 7.6, before the equivalence point of a weak acid-strong base titration.
Phenolphthalein
Correct: The equivalence pH is 8.73 and the vertical region spans roughly pH 7 to 11. Phenolphthalein (8.2–10.0) changes color within that range.
qs.x: The equivalence pH is 8.73 and the vertical region spans roughly pH 7 to 11. Phenolphthalein (8.2–10.0) changes color within that range. Trap: Choosing an indicator with a midpoint near 7 for every titration.

qs.q: If a different weak acid with pKa = 3.2 at the same concentration and volume were titrated with the same NaOH solution, which change would be observed relative to Figure 1?
o: The equivalence point would still be at 25.0 mL, but the pH at 12.5 mL would be about 3.2.
Correct: The equivalence volume depends only on moles of acid and base (unchanged), while the half-equivalence pH equals pKa.
The equivalence point would occur at a smaller volume of NaOH.
The equivalence point would occur at a smaller volume of NaOH. a stronger weak acid has the same number of moles, so the same volume of base is needed.
The pH at 12.5 mL would still be 4.76.
The pH at 12.5 mL would still be 4.76. the half-equivalence pH equals the pKa of the acid, which is now lower.
The pH at the equivalence point would be higher than 8.73.
The pH at the equivalence point would be higher than 8.73. a weaker conjugate base is produced, so the equivalence pH would be lower.
qs.x: The equivalence volume depends only on moles of acid and base (unchanged), while the half-equivalence pH equals pKa. Trap: Assuming that a stronger acid reaches equivalence with less base.

passages.title: FL02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 9
text: A student separates a mixture containing 1.00 g each of benzoic acid (pKa ≈ 4.2), aniline (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 4.6), and naphthalene using liquid-liquid extraction. The mixture is dissolved in diethyl ether (density 0.71 g/mL) and shaken in a separatory funnel with 1 M NaOH(aq). The layers are separated, and the ether layer is next shaken with 1 M HCl(aq). The layers are again separated, and the remaining ether layer is dried and evaporated. The NaOH layer is acidified with concentrated HCl until it is strongly acidic, and a precipitate is collected by filtration. The HCl layer is made basic with NaOH, and the compound that separates is extracted back into fresh ether and recovered by evaporation. Each isolated compound is weighed and its identity is confirmed by melting point. The masses of each compound found in each fraction are shown in Table 1. The student is careful to vent the funnel after each shaking and to allow the layers to separate completely before draining.

qs.q: Which species is present in the aqueous NaOH layer after the first extraction?
o: Sodium benzoate
Correct: NaOH deprotonates benzoic acid (pKa 4.2), giving the ionic, water-soluble benzoate salt, which moves into the aqueous layer.
Benzoic acid
Benzoic acid the neutral acid would stay predominantly in the ether layer.
Anilinium chloride
Anilinium chloride no HCl has been added at this stage, and aniline is not protonated by NaOH.
Naphthalene
Naphthalene a neutral nonpolar hydrocarbon that remains in ether.
qs.x: NaOH deprotonates benzoic acid (pKa 4.2), giving the ionic, water-soluble benzoate salt, which moves into the aqueous layer. Trap: Forgetting that a charged species is what partitions into the aqueous phase.

qs.q: Why does a precipitate form when concentrated HCl is added to the NaOH extract?
o: Chloride ions react with sodium benzoate to form an insoluble salt.
Chloride ions react with sodium benzoate to form an insoluble salt. NaCl is soluble, and chloride does not form an insoluble salt with benzoate.
Naphthalene is oxidized by the acid.
Naphthalene is oxidized by the acid. Naphthalene is not in the NaOH layer, and HCl does not oxidize it.
Aniline is deprotonated to its neutral, insoluble form.
Aniline is deprotonated to its neutral, insoluble form. Aniline was not in the NaOH layer, and acid would protonate it, not deprotonate it.
Benzoate is protonated to neutral benzoic acid, which has low solubility in water.
Correct: Adding strong acid lowers the pH below the pKa, converting benzoate to the neutral acid, which is far less soluble in water and comes out of solution.
qs.x: Adding strong acid lowers the pH below the pKa, converting benzoate to the neutral acid, which is far less soluble in water and comes out of solution. Trap: Thinking the precipitate is a new compound rather than the re-protonated neutral acid.

qs.q: What percentage of the aniline in the original mixture is accounted for across all fractions in Table 1 (isolated HCl-layer fraction plus the aniline remaining in the ether layer)?
o: 88% counts only the aniline in the HCl fraction.
99% sums the aniline and naphthalene in the original ether fraction (0.01 + 0.98 g), which is not aniline recovery.
Correct: Recovered aniline = 0.88 g + 0.01 g = 0.89 g out of 1.00 g, or 89%.
12% is 100% minus the 88% in the HCl fraction, a loss figure that ignores the 0.01 g found in the ether layer.
qs.x: Recovered aniline = 0.88 g + 0.01 g = 0.89 g out of 1.00 g, or 89%. Trap: Ignoring the small amounts of a compound found in other fractions when computing total recovery.

qs.q: In the separatory funnel during the first extraction, the ether layer is located:
o: on top of the aqueous layer, because ether is less dense than water.
Correct: Diethyl ether (0.71 g/mL) is less dense than the aqueous solution, so it floats on top, and the aqueous NaOH layer is drained from the bottom.
below the aqueous layer, because ether is more polar than water.
below the aqueous layer, because ether is more polar than water. polarity does not determine layer position, and ether is less polar than water.
mixed with the aqueous layer, because ether dissolves in water.
mixed with the aqueous layer, because ether dissolves in water. ether is only slightly soluble in water and forms a separate layer.
below the aqueous layer, because the NaOH solution is less dense.
below the aqueous layer, because the NaOH solution is less dense. 1 M NaOH is denser than water, not less dense than ether.
qs.x: Diethyl ether (0.71 g/mL) is less dense than the aqueous solution, so it floats on top, and the aqueous NaOH layer is drained from the bottom. Trap: Assuming the organic layer is always the bottom layer.

r: Original ether layer after both washes

passages.title: FL02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 10
text: Dinitrogen tetroxide and nitrogen dioxide interconvert according to 2 NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g). NO₂ is a brown gas, while N₂O₄ is colorless. A student seals samples of the gas mixture in identical flasks at a total pressure of 1 atm and measures the equilibrium constant Kp (in atm⁻¹) at several temperatures by comparing the absorbance of NO₂ at its characteristic wavelength. Calorimetric experiments done separately give ΔH° = −57.2 kJ per mole of reaction as written, and the student assumes ΔH° and ΔS° are independent of temperature. The Kp values are given in Table 1, and a plot of ln Kp against 1000/T is shown in Figure 1. The student uses R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and a specific heat of water of 4.18 J/(g·K). The flasks are allowed to reach thermal equilibrium in a water bath for 30 minutes before each measurement, and the gases are assumed to behave ideally. Kp is defined as the equilibrium partial pressure of N₂O₄ divided by the square of the equilibrium partial pressure of NO₂.

qs.q: What is ΔG° at 298 K for the reaction as written?
o: −4.7 kJ/mol
+4.7 kJ/mol
+4.7 kJ/mol has the wrong sign; K > 1 means the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.
−2.1 kJ/mol
−2.1 kJ/mol uses log₁₀ K rather than the natural logarithm.
−57.2 kJ/mol
−57.2 kJ/mol is ΔH°, not ΔG°.
qs.x: ΔG° = −RT ln K = −(8.314)(298)(ln 6.8) = −(2478)(1.92) ≈ −4.7 × 10³ J/mol. Trap: Using log₁₀ instead of ln in ΔG° = −RT ln K, or getting the sign wrong.

qs.q: What is ΔS° for the reaction at 298 K?
o: +176 J/(mol·K) has the wrong sign; two moles of gas become one, so disorder decreases.
−192 J/(mol·K) is ΔH°/T, ignoring ΔG°.
Correct: ΔS° = (ΔH° − ΔG°)/T = (−57,200 + 4,700)/298 ≈ −176 J/(mol·K), consistent with fewer moles of gas on the product side.
−16 J/(mol·K)
−16 J/(mol·K) is ΔG°/T, not ΔS°.
qs.x: ΔS° = (ΔH° − ΔG°)/T = (−57,200 + 4,700)/298 ≈ −176 J/(mol·K), consistent with fewer moles of gas on the product side. Trap: Computing ΔS as ΔH/T or ΔG/T instead of (ΔH − ΔG)/T.

qs.q: A sealed flask of the gas mixture at equilibrium is moved from an ice-water bath (273 K) to a water bath at 350 K. Which observation is expected?
o: The color of the gas lightens as more N₂O₄ forms.
The color of the gas lightens as more N₂O₄ forms. Heating an exothermic reaction favors reactants, not products.
The color does not change because the pressure is the same.
The color does not change because the pressure is the same. Temperature, not pressure, controls K, and K changes with temperature.
The color of the gas darkens as more NO₂ forms.
Correct: The forward reaction is exothermic, so raising T shifts the equilibrium toward NO₂ (K decreases from 56 to 0.22), and the brown color intensifies.
The color first lightens and then darkens as equilibrium is reached.
The color first lightens and then darkens as equilibrium is reached. there is no basis for an initial opposing shift.
qs.x: The forward reaction is exothermic, so raising T shifts the equilibrium toward NO₂ (K decreases from 56 to 0.22), and the brown color intensifies. Trap: Thinking that a temperature increase always favors the products.

qs.q: What is the slope of a plot of ln Kp against 1/T (with T in kelvin)?
o: Correct: The van't Hoff relation is ln K = −ΔH°/(RT) + ΔS°/R, so the slope against 1/T is −ΔH°/R = 57,200/8.314 ≈ +6.9 × 10³ K (equivalent to +6.9 per unit of 1000/T, as in Figure 1).
−6.9 × 10³ K has the wrong sign for an exothermic reaction, whose ln K decreases as 1/T decreases.
+5.7 × 10⁴ K is ΔH° in J without dividing by R.
−1.8 × 10² K is ΔS°, not related to the slope.
qs.x: The van't Hoff relation is ln K = −ΔH°/(RT) + ΔS°/R, so the slope against 1/T is −ΔH°/R = 57,200/8.314 ≈ +6.9 × 10³ K (equivalent to +6.9 per unit of 1000/T, as in Figure 1). Trap: Forgetting the negative sign in −ΔH/R when the reaction is exothermic.

qs.q: The heat released when 0.50 mol of N₂O₄ forms is absorbed by 500 g of water. The temperature rise of the water is closest to:
o: Correct: 0.50 mol N₂O₄ formed releases 0.50 × 57.2 = 28.6 kJ. ΔT = 28,600/(500 × 4.18) = 13.7 K ≈ 14 K.
27 K uses the heat for 1.0 mol of reaction (57.2 kJ), i.e., does not scale to 0.50 mol.
6.8 K halves the correct answer by halving the heat a second time.
0.014 K uses kJ in place of J in the q = mcΔT equation.
qs.x: 0.50 mol N₂O₄ formed releases 0.50 × 57.2 = 28.6 kJ. ΔT = 28,600/(500 × 4.18) = 13.7 K ≈ 14 K. Trap: Mixing kJ with J when using q = mcΔT.

graph.title: Figure 1. van't Hoff plot

passages.title: FL02 · Psych/Soc · Passage 1
text: Researchers measured difference thresholds for lifted weight in 24 adults. On each trial, a blindfolded participant lifted a standard weight and then a comparison weight and reported which felt heavier. Comparison weights differed from the standard by small increments, and the just-noticeable difference (JND) was defined as the smallest increment judged heavier on 75% of trials. Five standard weights were tested, and the order of the standards was counterbalanced across participants. Weber's law states that the JND is a constant proportion of the standard intensity (JND = k x standard), where k is the Weber fraction. Participants were university students aged 18 to 25 with no neurological conditions. Mean results are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. In a separate session, participants who held a 400 g weight in the palm for several minutes reported that its felt heaviness gradually faded. Each participant completed all five standards in a single two-hour session with rest breaks between blocks, and lifts were made with the dominant hand using identical containers so that only the mass differed.

qs.q: Assuming Weber's law holds with the Weber fraction observed for the lighter standards, the predicted JND for a 300 g standard is closest to:
o: 3 g
This is the JND for the 100 g standard, not 300 g.
This treats k as 0.10 rather than 0.03.
This is a tenfold arithmetic slip; 0.03 x 300 is 9, not 90.
9 g
Correct: k = 0.03, so JND = 0.03 x 300 g = 9 g.
qs.x: k = 0.03, so JND = 0.03 x 300 g = 9 g. Trap: Using the JND of the nearest listed standard instead of multiplying the Weber fraction by the new standard intensity.

qs.q: Compared with the other standards, performance at the 800 g standard indicates that:
o: sensitivity to weight differences was higher, because the absolute JND was largest at the heaviest standard.
A larger JND means worse, not better, discrimination; the proportional value also rose.
sensitivity to weight differences was lower, because a larger proportional increment was needed.
Correct: The fraction rose from 0.03 to 0.05, so a relatively larger change was required, meaning lower sensitivity and a departure from Weber's law.
sensitivity was unchanged, because Weber's law holds exactly at every intensity.
The ratio changed from 0.03 to 0.05, so the law did not hold exactly.
participants adapted to the heavier weight, so the JND became zero at the 400 g standard.
Adaptation would not produce a JND of zero, and the table shows a JND of 12 g (not 0) at 400 g.
qs.x: The fraction rose from 0.03 to 0.05, so a relatively larger change was required, meaning lower sensitivity and a departure from Weber's law. Trap: Reading the larger absolute JND as greater sensitivity; only the ratio (and the direction of the change) matters for sensitivity.

qs.q: The sense of tension developed in the muscle and tendon while lifting the weights is most directly signaled by:
o: muscle spindles.
Spindles monitor muscle length and rate of stretch rather than tension.
Golgi tendon organs.
Correct: Golgi tendon organs sit at the muscle-tendon junction and respond to tension.
Pacinian corpuscles.
These skin receptors respond to deep pressure and vibration.
nociceptors.
These signal tissue damage, which was not part of the task.
qs.x: Golgi tendon organs sit at the muscle-tendon junction and respond to tension. Trap: Confusing muscle spindles (length) with Golgi tendon organs (tension).

qs.q: Counterbalancing the order of the standard weights across participants was done mainly to:
o: ensure that participants could not perceive the comparison weights at all during the lifting.
Participants could perceive them; the task depends on it.
prevent practice or fatigue effects from being confounded with standard weight.
Correct: If every person did standards in the same order, order and weight would be inseparable; counterbalancing spreads order effects across standards.
increase the number of observations collected for each standard weight in the study.
Counterbalancing changes order, not the number of observations.
replace the need to blind participants to the identity of the standards being compared.
It addresses order effects only, not knowledge of the stimuli.
qs.x: If every person did standards in the same order, order and weight would be inseparable; counterbalancing spreads order effects across standards. Trap: Mixing up counterbalancing (order effects) with random assignment (group equivalence).

qs.q: Which of the following describes a difference threshold rather than an absolute threshold?
o: The minimum weight on the palm that is felt on 50% of trials when nothing else is present.
This is the absolute threshold, the minimum detectable stimulus.
The point at which the lifted weight begins to feel painful rather than merely heavy.
Pain threshold is a different concept altogether.
The weight that cannot be distinguished from a 0 g stimulus.
This describes detection against nothing, again an absolute threshold.
The 12 g added to a 400 g weight before it feels heavier.
Correct: A difference threshold is the smallest detectable change between two stimuli, as in the JND.
qs.x: A difference threshold is the smallest detectable change between two stimuli, as in the JND. Trap: Treating any 'minimum amount' as an absolute threshold; a difference threshold compares two nonzero stimuli.
