passages.title: FL02 · Psych/Soc · Passage 2
text: Researchers compared two schedules for learning foreign-language vocabulary. One hundred twenty students with no prior exposure to the language were randomly assigned to a massed group or a spaced group (60 each). Every student studied the same 40 word pairs in three study sessions of equal length. Massed participants completed all three sessions back to back in one afternoon, whereas spaced participants completed one session per day on three consecutive days. Participants were later shown the native-language word and asked to write the translation. Each participant was tested at only one of four delays after the final session (15 per group per delay), so that earlier testing could not influence later recall. Mean percent correct is shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. The investigators interpreted the pattern as evidence that distributed practice strengthens long-term retention more than cramming does. Students were told only that they would be tested at some point and were not told the delay, and all testing took place in the same quiet room at the same time of day, with no feedback given during testing.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
o: Spaced study produced better recall than massed study at every delay tested, including the immediate test.
At day 0 the massed group scored higher.
Both groups forgot material at the same rate across the two days, differing only at the start.
The massed curve fell faster, from 88 to 20 versus 82 to 45.
Massed study prevented any meaningful forgetting for the full two days after the study session.
Massed recall fell from 88% to 62% by day 2.
The advantage of spaced study appeared only after a delay, not on the immediate test.
Correct: Massed was higher at day 0 (88 vs 82), but spaced was higher at every later delay.
qs.x: Massed was higher at day 0 (88 vs 82), but spaced was higher at every later delay. Trap: Overgeneralizing 'spacing is better' to all delays, ignoring the day 0 crossover.

qs.q: At the 30-day delay, the spaced group recalled how many times as many words as the massed group?
o: This would correspond to a 25% advantage, but 45 is 125% more than 20, not 25% more.
This is the difference in percentage points, not a ratio.
This is 20 / 45, the inverse ratio.
qs.x: 45 / 20 = 2.25. Trap: Reporting the percentage-point difference (25) or the inverted ratio (0.44) when a ratio of spaced to massed is requested.

qs.q: Successful recall of vocabulary after 30 days depends most heavily on consolidation of declarative memories by which structure?
o: Cerebellum
The cerebellum supports motor learning and conditioned reflexes.
Hippocampus
Correct: The hippocampus is critical for forming and consolidating explicit semantic memories such as word meanings.
Basal ganglia
These support procedural memory and habits.
Amygdala
The amygdala modulates emotional memory, which this task does not target.
qs.x: The hippocampus is critical for forming and consolidating explicit semantic memories such as word meanings. Trap: Assigning every memory task to the amygdala or basal ganglia rather than recognizing explicit semantic memory as hippocampal.

qs.q: A within-subjects version of this study, in which each student learned half the words by each schedule, would better control for:
o: individual differences in learning ability.
Correct: Each person serves as his or her own control, removing between-person variability.
differences in the language being learned by each group.
The language was the same for both groups already.
the length of the study sessions.
Session length was already equal.
the effect of testing delay on recall.
Delay would still affect recall; it is a manipulated factor.
qs.x: Each person serves as his or her own control, removing between-person variability. Trap: Thinking within-subjects designs remove order effects; they remove individual differences but can introduce carryover.

passages.title: FL02 · Psych/Soc · Passage 3
text: Thirty-six healthy adults viewed aversive photographs (such as images of injury) during functional MRI. On each trial, a written cue instructed participants either to 'view' the photograph naturally or to 'reappraise' it by imagining a more benign interpretation, for example that the injured person was an actor in a film. Each participant completed both trial types in counterbalanced order. After each trial, participants rated how negative they felt from 1 (not at all negative) to 9 (extremely negative). Activation in the amygdala and in the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (vlPFC) was expressed as percent signal change from a resting baseline. Paired-samples t-tests compared the two conditions for each measure, and results are shown in Table 1. Participants also reported how often they used reappraisal in daily life; frequent users showed greater vlPFC activation during reappraisal trials. Photographs were matched across conditions for rated unpleasantness and visual complexity in a pilot sample, and each participant saw 30 photographs per condition, with no photograph shown twice.

qs.q: The pattern of activation in Table 1 is most consistent with which interpretation?
o: The amygdala suppresses prefrontal activity in order to generate the emotional response.
The data show the opposite pairing: prefrontal up, amygdala down.
Emotion and cognition are processed by separate and unrelated brain systems that do not interact.
The inverse relationship suggests interaction.
Reappraisal works by increasing amygdala activity.
Amygdala signal fell by half.
Prefrontal regions exert top-down regulation.
Correct: vlPFC activity rose as amygdala activity and negative feeling fell, fitting prefrontal down-regulation of limbic responses.
qs.x: vlPFC activity rose as amygdala activity and negative feeling fell, fitting prefrontal down-regulation of limbic responses. Trap: Assuming a correlation between regions reveals the direction of influence; here the instruction manipulation supports the regulatory interpretation.

qs.q: The percent decrease in amygdala signal during reappraisal relative to viewing is closest to:
o: This reuses the reappraise value rather than a relative change.
This is not supported by the means given.
The signal did not fall to zero.
qs.x: (0.42 - 0.21) / 0.42 = 0.50, a 50% decrease. Trap: Using the raw value (0.21) or an absolute difference instead of dividing by the starting value.

qs.q: Paired-samples t-tests were appropriate for these comparisons because:
o: the dependent variables were categorical.
The measures were continuous.
the same participants were measured in both conditions.
Correct: Each person contributed a view and a reappraise score, so the scores are dependent.
three or more independent groups were compared.
There were two related conditions.
the study examined the correlation between two variables.
Group means were compared, not correlated.
qs.x: Each person contributed a view and a reappraise score, so the scores are dependent. Trap: Choosing an independent-samples test because there are two conditions, ignoring that the same people were in both.

qs.q: The finding that changing the interpretation of a photograph changed how negative it felt is best explained by which theory of emotion?
o: James-Lange theory, in which an emotion is simply the perception of bodily arousal.
This theory puts arousal first, not appraisal.
Lazarus's cognitive-mediational theory, in which appraisal determines the emotional response.
Correct: Appraisal of the stimulus shapes the emotion; changing the appraisal changed the emotion.
Cannon-Bard theory, in which arousal and emotion arise independently.
It does not assign a causal role to appraisal.
Yerkes-Dodson law, in which performance depends on arousal level.
This describes arousal and performance, not emotion generation.
qs.x: Appraisal of the stimulus shapes the emotion; changing the appraisal changed the emotion. Trap: Defaulting to James-Lange or Cannon-Bard whenever emotion is mentioned, without noting the role of cognitive appraisal.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Mean responses by instruction (n = 36)

passages.title: FL02 · Psych/Soc · Passage 4
text: In a double-blind randomized trial, 200 adults diagnosed with major depressive disorder received either a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) or an identical-looking placebo daily for 8 weeks (100 per group). Clinicians blind to assignment assessed severity with the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAM-D; higher scores indicate more severe depression) at baseline and at weeks 2, 4, and 8. 'Response' was defined as at least a 50% reduction from the baseline HAM-D score. Twelve SSRI participants and eight placebo participants withdrew before week 8, most citing side effects such as nausea and sleep disturbance. Primary analyses included all randomized participants, with the last available score carried forward for those who withdrew. Mean HAM-D scores are shown in Figure 1 and week 8 outcomes in Table 1. Participants were adults aged 25 to 60 who had not received antidepressant medication in the preceding three months, and all participants were offered brief supportive counseling at each clinic visit regardless of group.

qs.q: Based on response rates, the number of patients who must be treated with the SSRI rather than placebo for one additional patient to respond is closest to:
o: This inverts the relative improvement rather than the absolute risk difference.
Correct: Absolute difference = 45% - 30% = 15% (0.15); 1 / 0.15 = 6.7, about 7.
This is the percentage-point difference, not its reciprocal.
This is the SSRI response rate itself.
qs.x: Absolute difference = 45% - 30% = 15% (0.15); 1 / 0.15 = 6.7, about 7. Trap: Reporting the absolute difference (15) rather than its reciprocal when asked for a number needed to treat.

qs.q: SSRIs are thought to increase serotonergic signaling primarily by:
o: inhibiting the enzyme that degrades serotonin in the synaptic cleft.
This is how some other antidepressants, MAO inhibitors, act (intracellularly).
binding postsynaptic receptors and mimicking serotonin directly.
That describes a receptor agonist, not an SSRI.
blocking reuptake of serotonin into the presynaptic neuron.
Correct: Inhibiting the serotonin transporter raises synaptic serotonin.
increasing the synthesis of dopamine in the ventral tegmental area of the midbrain.
SSRIs act on serotonin, not dopamine synthesis.
qs.x: Inhibiting the serotonin transporter raises synaptic serotonin. Trap: Mixing up reuptake inhibitors, enzyme inhibitors, and direct receptor agonists.

qs.q: The placebo group's mean HAM-D score fell from 24 to 17. The most reasonable explanation is:
o: expectation of benefit together with the natural course of the disorder.
Correct: Placebo response reflects expectation and spontaneous improvement over time.
the placebo contained an active serotonergic compound.
An inert placebo is assumed; this does not follow from the data.
the SSRI group's improvement spilled over to the placebo group.
Participants were treated separately.
measurement error, because HAM-D cannot detect change.
Systematic change in a group is not explained by random error alone.
qs.x: Placebo response reflects expectation and spontaneous improvement over time. Trap: Assuming any improvement in a control group means the control was flawed rather than reflecting placebo and time effects.

qs.q: Suppose the trial had analyzed only participants who completed all 8 weeks. Because more SSRI participants withdrew for side effects, the SSRI effect would most likely be:
o: underestimated, since patients who withdraw from a trial are always the most improved ones.
Dropouts for side effects are not typically the most improved.
unchanged, because withdrawal from the trial is random with respect to drug response and outcome.
Withdrawal was related to the treatment itself.
eliminated, because double-blinding of the study corrects for any differential attrition between arms.
Blinding does not correct attrition bias.
overestimated, since those remaining may have tolerated and benefited from the drug.
Correct: Dropping non-completers can leave a more favorable subgroup in the drug arm, biasing the estimate upward.
qs.x: Dropping non-completers can leave a more favorable subgroup in the drug arm, biasing the estimate upward. Trap: Believing attrition is harmless if groups started equal; differential dropout breaks the benefit of randomization.

qs.q: The SSRI and placebo curves in Figure 1 differ little at week 2 but diverge more by weeks 4 to 8. This delay is most consistent with:
o: immediate depletion of serotonin stores that is later restored over several weeks.
Serotonin availability rises immediately with an SSRI.
participants gradually learning to guess which treatment assignment they had received.
Unblinding would not explain a gradual drug-specific divergence.
a failure of the drug to reach the brain in the first few weeks of dosing.
SSRIs begin acting within hours of dosing.
slower neural adaptations after blockade begins.
Correct: Reuptake blockade acts within hours, so the delayed benefit suggests slower downstream adaptations.
qs.x: Reuptake blockade acts within hours, so the delayed benefit suggests slower downstream adaptations. Trap: Assuming drug effects must appear as soon as the drug reaches its target.

passages.title: FL02 · Psych/Soc · Passage 5
text: Researchers studied whether effort declines when individual contributions are pooled. Two hundred forty undergraduates pulled on a rope attached to a force gauge, trying to pull as hard as possible, either alone or in groups of 2, 4, or 8. Participants were randomly assigned to group size and to one of two instruction conditions. In the anonymous condition, only total group force was recorded. In the identifiable condition, participants were told that each person's force would be measured by a separate gauge and posted afterward. Mean force per person is shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. Alone, participants produced a mean of 62 kg-force in both conditions. The investigators concluded that reduced effort in groups depends on whether individual outputs can be evaluated. Participants wore blindfolds and noise-canceling headphones so that they could not see or hear teammates, and the experimenter gave a countdown at the start of each pull so that all members began together.

qs.q: The decrease in per-person force with increasing group size in the anonymous condition illustrates:
o: social facilitation.
Facilitation is improved performance of simple tasks in the presence of others.
social loafing.
Correct: Individuals exert less effort in groups when their contributions are pooled and not individually evaluated.
group polarization.
This is the strengthening of a group's initial attitude after discussion.
deindividuation.
This is loss of self-awareness in groups, typically producing impulsive behavior, not the measured decline in effort.
qs.x: Individuals exert less effort in groups when their contributions are pooled and not individually evaluated. Trap: Choosing social facilitation because 'others are present'; facilitation predicts improved, not reduced, effort on simple tasks.

qs.q: In the anonymous condition, groups of 8 produced approximately what percentage of the total force that eight people would produce working alone?
o: This is the per-person force value, not a proportion of the alone total.
This is not supported by the table.
Correct: Group total = 8 x 38 = 304; eight alone = 8 x 62 = 496; 304 / 496 = 0.613.
This would mean no decrease in individual effort.
qs.x: Group total = 8 x 38 = 304; eight alone = 8 x 62 = 496; 304 / 496 = 0.613. Trap: Using the per-person force (38) as if it were a percentage.

qs.q: Per-person force was higher in the identifiable than in the anonymous condition mainly because identifiability:
o: increased diffusion of responsibility among the members of each group.
Identifiability does the opposite; it concentrates responsibility.
increased evaluation apprehension and accountability.
Correct: When outputs can be evaluated, people feel accountable, which reduces loafing.
reduced physical strength required of each individual person.
The task and strength requirement did not change.
caused participants to mimic the strongest member of the group.
No conformity mechanism is described.
qs.x: When outputs can be evaluated, people feel accountable, which reduces loafing. Trap: Confusing accountability (which reduces loafing) with diffusion of responsibility (which promotes it).

qs.q: The group size by instruction pattern in Figure 1 indicates an interaction because:
o: the effect of group size depends on whether contributions were identifiable.
Correct: The decline with group size is large for the anonymous but small for the identifiable condition, so the lines are not parallel.
both lines start at the same value for group size 1.
Equal starting points do not by themselves show an interaction.
both conditions show a decrease with group size.
A shared direction does not rule out different slopes, which is the interaction.
the identifiable condition produced the lowest force.
It produced the highest force at larger sizes.
qs.x: The decline with group size is large for the anonymous but small for the identifiable condition, so the lines are not parallel. Trap: Looking for an overall main effect instead of non-parallel lines.

passages.title: FL02 · Psych/Soc · Passage 6
text: Ninety students who had reported opposing a proposed tuition increase (attitude of 3 or lower on a 9-point scale; 1 = strongly oppose, 9 = strongly favor) were randomly assigned to three groups of 30. High-choice participants were asked to write a persuasive essay supporting the increase and were told the decision to write it was entirely theirs. Low-choice participants were told that writing the essay was a required part of the session. Control participants wrote an essay about campus parking. Afterward, each participant privately rated attitude toward the tuition increase. A one-way ANOVA found a significant effect of group, F(2, 87) = 27.4, p < 0.001. Group means and standard deviations are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. Participants in the high-choice group also reported that the essay task felt 'uncomfortable' more often than other participants. The essay session lasted 20 minutes, and the experimenter who collected attitude ratings was blind to group assignment. Participants were debriefed fully after the study and told that the tuition proposal was hypothetical.

qs.q: The attitude shift in the high-choice group is best explained by which process?
o: Conformity to a majority of peers who favored the increase.
No majority pressure was described.
Increased attention to peripheral cues in a persuasive message.
Participants wrote the message; they were not receiving one.
Classical conditioning of the tuition increase with positive feelings.
No pairing of stimuli is described.
Reducing the discomfort of acting against a held attitude by changing the attitude.
Correct: Freely choosing a behavior inconsistent with a belief creates dissonance, resolved by shifting the attitude toward the behavior.
qs.x: Freely choosing a behavior inconsistent with a belief creates dissonance, resolved by shifting the attitude toward the behavior. Trap: Attributing every attitude change to persuasion by others rather than to dissonance from one's own behavior.

qs.q: The low-choice group showed little attitude change most likely because:
o: they wrote a weaker essay than the high-choice group did, so they felt less committed.
Essay quality is not measured; the explanation lies in justification.
external justification (being required) explained their behavior.
Correct: With sufficient external justification, little dissonance arises, so there is little pressure to change attitude.
they had no prior attitude toward tuition before the study began.
Everyone began opposed to the increase.
being told what to do creates the most dissonance of all the conditions.
Compulsion reduces dissonance because the behavior is explained externally.
qs.x: With sufficient external justification, little dissonance arises, so there is little pressure to change attitude. Trap: Assuming more pressure produces more attitude change; in dissonance research, less external pressure does.

qs.q: After the significant ANOVA result, which additional analysis is needed to determine which groups differ?
o: A chi-square test of independence on the three groups' mean ratings.
The outcome is a continuous rating, not categorical counts.
A post hoc pairwise comparison with correction.
Correct: A significant omnibus F says only that at least one mean differs; post hoc tests identify the pairs.
A Pearson correlation between group membership and attitude score.
Group is categorical with three levels; correlation does not identify pairs.
No additional analysis, since a significant F shows that every pair differs.
F does not show that every pair differs.
qs.x: A significant omnibus F says only that at least one mean differs; post hoc tests identify the pairs. Trap: Reading a significant F as showing that every group differs from every other.

qs.q: Using a pooled standard deviation of about 1.5, the standardized difference (Cohen's d) between the high-choice and control groups is closest to:
o: This would be a medium effect, but the mean difference is much larger relative to SD.
This would require a mean difference of only 1.5.
This multiplies the mean difference by the SD instead of dividing.
qs.x: (4.8 - 2.1) / 1.5 = 2.7 / 1.5 = 1.8. Trap: Multiplying by the SD rather than dividing the mean difference by it.

qs.q: Which additional finding would most favor dissonance theory over Bem's self-perception theory, which proposes that people simply infer attitudes from their own behavior without any discomfort?
o: Higher attitude scores in the high-choice group than in the control group after writing.
Both theories predict this shift.
A significant ANOVA result for group on the final attitude rating.
This is the observed result and fits both theories.
Higher arousal in the high-choice group that falls after the attitude changes.
Correct: Dissonance predicts an aversive arousal state motivating change; self-perception predicts none.
A larger sample of participants in each of the three groups.
Sample size does not distinguish theories.
qs.x: Dissonance predicts an aversive arousal state motivating change; self-perception predicts none. Trap: Picking evidence that both theories predict.

passages.title: FL02 · Psych/Soc · Passage 7
text: In a 12-week community exercise program, 150 adults completed a questionnaire at enrollment measuring exercise self-efficacy, defined as confidence in one's ability to exercise regularly despite obstacles such as fatigue, bad weather, and time pressure. Scores ranged from 10 to 50. The program offered 36 scheduled sessions, and attendance was recorded. Across all 150 participants, the Pearson correlation between self-efficacy score and sessions attended was r = +0.60 (p < 0.001). Participants were divided into thirds based on baseline self-efficacy, and mean attendance for each third is shown in Table 1. Figure 1 plots a random sample of 10 participants. Participants who dropped out were counted as attending no further sessions. The investigators noted that participants with higher baseline fitness were also more likely to attend. Self-efficacy was measured before any session so that attendance could not influence the score. The questionnaire has shown high internal consistency in previous samples, and participants were not paid for attendance.

qs.q: Exercise self-efficacy, as defined in the passage, is best described as:
o: an overall evaluation of one's worth as a person across all domains.
This is self-esteem.
a belief that outcomes are controlled mostly by outside forces such as luck.
This is an external locus of control.
the full set of all beliefs one holds about oneself as a person.
This is self-concept.
a belief about one's capability to succeed.
Correct: Self-efficacy is task-specific confidence in one's ability to perform.
qs.x: Self-efficacy is task-specific confidence in one's ability to perform. Trap: Equating self-efficacy with global self-esteem; efficacy is specific to a task.

qs.q: The coefficient of determination for the relationship between self-efficacy and attendance is:
o: Correct: r squared = 0.60 x 0.60 = 0.36, so 36% of the variance in attendance is shared with self-efficacy.
This is r itself, not r squared.
This is approximately the square root of 0.60.
This is 1 - r, not r squared.
qs.x: r squared = 0.60 x 0.60 = 0.36, so 36% of the variance in attendance is shared with self-efficacy. Trap: Reporting r as if it were the proportion of variance explained.

qs.q: Which statement is a third-variable explanation of the observed correlation?
o: Greater self-efficacy causes participants to attend more sessions.
This is a direct causal explanation, not a third variable.
Higher baseline fitness raises both self-efficacy and attendance.
Correct: A third factor that influences both variables can produce a correlation without a direct link, as the passage's note on fitness suggests.
Attending more sessions raises self-efficacy.
This is reverse causation.
Random sampling error produced the correlation.
With p < 0.001 and n = 150, chance alone is unlikely, and this is not a third variable.
qs.x: A third factor that influences both variables can produce a correlation without a direct link, as the passage's note on fitness suggests. Trap: Calling reverse causation a third variable; a third variable must influence both measures.

qs.q: According to Bandura, which program change would most strongly increase participants' self-efficacy?
o: Starting with achievable goals to build success.
Correct: Mastery experiences are the strongest source of self-efficacy.
Removing all feedback on performance throughout the entire program.
Without feedback, success cannot be recognized.
Assigning very difficult goals to every participant from the first week.
Early failures reduce efficacy.
Telling participants that exercise is unimportant to their own health.
This undermines motivation without building confidence.
qs.x: Mastery experiences are the strongest source of self-efficacy. Trap: Favoring challenge over success; early mastery builds efficacy.

passages.title: FL02 · Psych/Soc · Passage 8
text: One hundred sixty strangers formed 80 pairs and played ten rounds of a two-person choice game, knowing in advance that there would be ten rounds. In each round, players chose simultaneously to cooperate or defect. If both cooperated, each earned 3 points; if both defected, each earned 1 point; if one defected and the other cooperated, the defector earned 5 points and the cooperator earned 0. Forty pairs were randomly assigned to a communication condition and spoke for two minutes before round 1, and 40 pairs were assigned to a no-communication condition. Players never revealed their choices during a round. Table 1 shows round 1 choices, and Figure 1 shows the percentage of players cooperating in selected rounds. No agreement made before the game was binding. Pairs sat in separate rooms and communicated only through the experimenter-supplied choice screen, and participants were paid in cash in proportion to the points they earned across all ten rounds.

qs.q: In a single round, a player who is certain that the partner will cooperate maximizes personal points by:
o: cooperating, which earns 3 rather than 1.
The comparison against a cooperating partner is 3 versus 5, not 3 versus 1.
cooperating, which earns 5 rather than 3.
Cooperating against a cooperator earns 3.
defecting, which earns 5 rather than 3.
Correct: Against a cooperator, defecting yields 5 versus 3 for cooperating.
defecting, which earns 1 rather than 0.
Defecting against a cooperator earns 5, not 1.
qs.x: Against a cooperator, defecting yields 5 versus 3 for cooperating. Trap: Comparing outcomes across different partner choices instead of fixing the partner's choice.

qs.q: Which test is most appropriate to compare the proportions of players who cooperated in round 1 across the two conditions?
o: Paired-samples t-test
The groups are independent and the outcome is not continuous.
Chi-square test
Correct: The outcome is categorical (cooperate or defect) in two independent groups.
Pearson correlation
This assesses a relationship between two continuous variables.
Repeated-measures ANOVA
Players were not measured repeatedly in this comparison.
qs.x: The outcome is categorical (cooperate or defect) in two independent groups. Trap: Using t-tests for categorical counts.

qs.q: The drop in cooperation in the communication condition at round 10 is most consistent with:
o: a gradual build-up of mutual trust between the players over the rounds.
Trust building would raise, not lower, cooperation.
a failure of the communication manipulation after the initial rounds.
The manipulation affected early rounds, and it persisted through round 7.
random measurement error occurring in round 10 only, for one group.
The drop is large and fits a known pattern.
no anticipated future retaliation on the last round.
Correct: Knowing the game ends removes the future cost of defection, producing end-game defection.
qs.x: Knowing the game ends removes the future cost of defection, producing end-game defection. Trap: Attributing a single-round drop to noise rather than to the incentive structure of a known final round.

qs.q: A pair mutually cooperates in 7 rounds and mutually defects in the other 3 rounds. Each player's total number of points is:
o: This ignores the 3 points from the mutual defection rounds.
This assumes mutual cooperation in all 10 rounds.
This incorrectly counts 5 points for some rounds.
qs.x: 7 x 3 + 3 x 1 = 21 + 3 = 24. Trap: Forgetting the points earned in mutual defection rounds.

passages.title: FL02 · Psych/Soc · Passage 9
text: Demographers compared two countries using national statistics, summarized in Table 1 and Figure 1. Crude birth rate (CBR) and crude death rate (CDR) are births and deaths per 1,000 people per year. Net migration is immigrants minus emigrants per 1,000 people per year. The age dependency ratio is the number of people younger than 15 or older than 64 for each person aged 15 to 64. Country X has a rapidly growing population, and many young workers leave seeking employment, sending money home. Country Y has an aging population and recruits foreign workers to fill labor shortages in its health care and service sectors. Population growth rate (%) is (CBR - CDR + net migration) / 10, using per-1,000 values. Figures are national estimates for the same calendar year, and neither country experienced war, famine, or major epidemics during the period reported. Remittances from emigrants are a major source of household income in Country X, whereas Country Y offers broad public pensions and universal health coverage.

qs.q: The age dependency ratio of Country Y is closest to:
o: This uses only the percentage of dependents, 36%, as a ratio rather than dividing by 64.
This is the dependency ratio of Country X, (35 + 4) / 61.
This is not supported by the data.
qs.x: (15 + 21) / 64 = 36 / 64 = 0.5625. Trap: Dividing dependents by the total population rather than the working-age population.

qs.q: The overall annual population growth rate of Country Y is closest to:
o: This is the natural increase alone, ignoring immigration.
+0.6% adds the size of the natural decrease (2 per 1,000) to net migration (4) instead of combining them with their correct signs.
This incorrectly subtracts migration from the natural decrease.
qs.x: (9 - 11 + 4) / 10 = +2 per 1,000 = +0.2% per year. Trap: Leaving net migration out of the growth calculation.

qs.q: Which of the following is a pull factor drawing workers from Country X to Country Y?
o: Limited employment opportunities in Country X.
This is a push factor at the origin.
High fertility in Country X.
This is a demographic condition, not a pull factor of Country Y.
Labor shortages and higher wages in Country Y.
Correct: Pull factors are attractions at the destination.
Remittances sent home to Country X.
These are consequences of migration, not a pull factor.
qs.x: Pull factors are attractions at the destination. Trap: Calling any factor related to migration a 'pull'; pull factors are located at the destination.

qs.q: Compared with Country X, which social institution in Country Y is most likely to face reduced demand because of the age structure?
o: Primary education
Correct: A smaller proportion aged 0-14 means fewer school-age children.
Health care for chronic illness
Demand rises with the larger share aged 65+.
Pension and social security systems
Pressure increases with a larger elderly group.
Long-term care services
Demand rises with more elderly people.
qs.x: A smaller proportion aged 0-14 means fewer school-age children. Trap: Choosing the institution with the largest absolute change rather than the one whose population shrinks.

qs.q: Using the rule of 70, if Country X maintained its current overall growth rate, its population would double in approximately:
o: 32 years
Correct: Growth = (32 - 8 - 2) / 10 = 2.2%; 70 / 2.2 = 31.8, about 32 years.
12 years
This is not supported by the growth rate.
29 years
This uses natural increase (2.4%) and ignores emigration.
35 years
This would correspond to a 2.0% growth rate.
qs.x: Growth = (32 - 8 - 2) / 10 = 2.2%; 70 / 2.2 = 31.8, about 32 years. Trap: Ignoring net migration, which gives 70 / 2.4 = 29.

passages.title: FL02 · Psych/Soc · Passage 10
text: To test for discrimination in hiring, researchers submitted 4,000 résumés in response to real entry-level job advertisements. Each résumé was designed at a higher or lower quality level (more or less experience and relevant skills). Names statistically associated with White or Black Americans were randomly assigned to résumés within each quality level, so 2,000 résumés carried White-sounding names and 2,000 carried Black-sounding names, each half higher and half lower quality. The outcome was a callback, meaning that the employer contacted the applicant. Overall callback rates were 14.0% for White-sounding names and 9.5% for Black-sounding names (chi-square test, p < 0.001). Table 1 gives results by quality level. The researchers noted that names may convey information beyond race, and that callbacks are not job offers. Contact information on each résumé, such as address and phone number, was held constant across names, and employers who responded did so within 30 days. Advertisements were sampled from several large metropolitan areas, and work histories were written to be equally plausible for the jobs advertised.

qs.q: The study measures which of the following?
o: Prejudice, meaning negative attitudes toward a group held by the employers.
Attitudes were not measured.
Institutional racism built into the legal system governing hiring.
Employers' hiring responses are not legal institutions.
Discrimination (differential treatment), not employers' attitudes.
Correct: Callback differences are behavior; the study cannot show whether prejudice (attitudes) motivated it.
Stereotype threat among applicants who anticipate being judged by their group.
Applicants did not take part; résumés were sent.
qs.x: Callback differences are behavior; the study cannot show whether prejudice (attitudes) motivated it. Trap: Using 'prejudice' and 'discrimination' interchangeably.

qs.q: The relative reduction in the overall callback rate for Black-sounding names compared with White-sounding names is closest to:
o: This is the absolute difference in percentage points.
This is the White rate relative to the Black rate minus one, (14.0 - 9.5) / 9.5, using the wrong baseline.
This is the ratio of rates, 9.5 / 14, not the reduction.
qs.x: (14.0 - 9.5) / 14.0 = 4.5 / 14.0 = 0.32. Trap: Dividing by the wrong baseline or reporting the absolute difference.

qs.q: Which conclusion about résumé quality is best supported by Table 1?
o: Higher-quality résumés with Black-sounding names got callbacks as often as lower-quality ones with White-sounding names.
Correct: Both were 11.0%.
Résumé quality had no effect on callbacks for either set of names.
Rates were higher for higher-quality résumés in both groups.
Higher résumé quality eliminated the gap between the two sets of names.
The gap remained, 17.0% versus 11.0%.
Black-sounding names received more callbacks than White-sounding names at the same quality level.
At each quality level, White-sounding names had the higher rate.
qs.x: Both were 11.0%. Trap: Assuming credentials remove the racial gap.

qs.q: A limitation affecting the construct validity of the study is that:
o: names may signal social class or other traits, not only race.
Correct: The manipulation may not isolate race, since names carry other information.
random assignment of names makes causal inference impossible.
Random assignment strengthens causal inference.
callback rates cannot be compared across groups.
Rates can be compared; the groups were equally sized.
the sample of 4,000 résumés is too small for a chi-square test.
The sample is large.
qs.x: The manipulation may not isolate race, since names carry other information. Trap: Mistaking a measurement-validity issue for a sampling-size issue.

passages.title: FL03 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 1
text: A dehydrogenase (Enzyme Q) was assayed at several substrate concentrations with no inhibitor, with Inhibitor A (40 micromolar), and with Inhibitor B (40 micromolar). Initial velocities (v, in micromoles of product per minute) are given in Table 1. Reciprocal values were then plotted as a Lineweaver-Burk (double-reciprocal) graph, with 1/v on the y-axis and 1/[S] on the x-axis; the plotted values are shown in the figure. Enzyme concentration was identical in all assays, each reaction was monitored for the first two minutes so that substrate depletion was negligible, and temperature and pH were held constant at the optimum for the enzyme. Each velocity is the mean of three replicate assays.

On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the y-intercept equals 1/Vmax and the x-intercept equals -1/Km. Inhibitor A resembles the substrate in structure, whereas Inhibitor B bears no resemblance to the substrate and was found to bind at a site distant from the active site. Neither inhibitor is consumed by the enzyme, and both bind reversibly. The investigators wished to classify each inhibitor and to estimate how strongly Inhibitor A binds the enzyme.

qs.q: The Lineweaver-Burk plot indicates that Inhibitor A is a:
o: noncompetitive inhibitor, because the lines share the same y-intercept while the slopes differ.
Noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax (raises the y-intercept) and leaves the x-intercept in place; the shared feature here is the y-intercept, which fits competitive inhibition.
competitive inhibitor, because the y-intercept is unchanged while the x-intercept moves closer to zero.

Correct: The A line crosses the y-axis at the same point as the uninhibited line (Vmax unchanged) but has a smaller-magnitude x-intercept, so the apparent Km is larger; this is competitive inhibition.
noncompetitive inhibitor, because Vmax is lowered and the x-intercept stays at the same position.
Vmax is not lowered with A; the plot shows that the y-intercept stays at 0.01.
uncompetitive inhibitor, because both intercepts shift while the slope remains the same as uninhibited.
Uncompetitive inhibition gives parallel lines; the A line has a steeper slope (0.06 versus 0.02).
qs.x: The A line crosses the y-axis at the same point as the uninhibited line (Vmax unchanged) but has a smaller-magnitude x-intercept, so the apparent Km is larger; this is competitive inhibition. Trap: Mixing up which intercept stays fixed: shared y-intercept means Vmax is unchanged (competitive), shared x-intercept means Km is unchanged (noncompetitive).

qs.q: Assuming simple competitive inhibition, with Inhibitor A at 40 micromolar, the inhibition constant (Ki) is closest to:
o: 13 micromolar
This results from 40/3, which treats the Km ratio of 3 as equal to [I]/Ki instead of 1 + [I]/Ki.
40 micromolar
This would require the apparent Km to double (1 + 40/40 = 2), but it tripled.
20 micromolar

Correct: The A line is 1/v = 0.06(1/[S]) + 0.01, so its x-intercept is -0.01/0.06, giving apparent Km = 6 mM. The uninhibited line gives Km = 2 mM. The ratio is 3 = 1 + [I]/Ki = 1 + 40/Ki, so Ki = 20 micromolar.
120 micromolar
This multiplies [I] by the Km ratio (40 x 3) rather than solving 3 = 1 + 40/Ki.
qs.x: The A line is 1/v = 0.06(1/[S]) + 0.01, so its x-intercept is -0.01/0.06, giving apparent Km = 6 mM. The uninhibited line gives Km = 2 mM. The ratio is 3 = 1 + [I]/Ki = 1 + 40/Ki, so Ki = 20 micromolar. Trap: Setting the Km ratio equal to [I]/Ki and forgetting the 1 in the factor (1 + [I]/Ki).

qs.q: What are the apparent Vmax and Km of Enzyme Q in the presence of Inhibitor B?
o: Vmax = 50 micromoles/min and Km = 2 mM

Correct: The B line has y-intercept 0.02, so Vmax = 1/0.02 = 50. Its slope is 0.04 and Km/Vmax = 0.04 gives Km = 2 mM, the same as without inhibitor (the line meets the uninhibited line at the x-intercept of -0.5).
Vmax = 100 micromoles/min and Km = 6 mM
These are the values obtained with Inhibitor A, not B.
Vmax = 50 micromoles/min and Km = 1 mM
Vmax is correct, but Km is unchanged by a noncompetitive inhibitor and is not halved.
Vmax = 100 micromoles/min and Km = 4 mM
The y-intercept of 0.02 gives Vmax of 50, not 100, and the x-intercept corresponds to Km = 2 mM.
qs.x: The B line has y-intercept 0.02, so Vmax = 1/0.02 = 50. Its slope is 0.04 and Km/Vmax = 0.04 gives Km = 2 mM, the same as without inhibitor (the line meets the uninhibited line at the x-intercept of -0.5). Trap: Taking the intercept values directly instead of inverting them (y-intercept = 1/Vmax, x-intercept = -1/Km).

qs.q: Substrate concentration is raised to 100 mM in assays that contain either inhibitor. Compared with the uninhibited enzyme at 100 mM, which prediction is best supported by the data?
o: Velocity with both inhibitors approaches the uninhibited value, because high [S] displaces any reversible inhibitor.
Only a competitor for the active site can be displaced; B acts elsewhere and lowers Vmax.
Velocity with Inhibitor B approaches the uninhibited value, whereas velocity with Inhibitor A remains near half of it.
The roles are reversed: A is competitive and is overcome, while B lowers Vmax.
Velocity with both inhibitors remains near half of the uninhibited value, because reversible inhibitors cannot be outcompeted.
Reversible competitive inhibitors can be outcompeted; A leaves Vmax unchanged.
Velocity with Inhibitor A approaches the uninhibited value, whereas velocity with Inhibitor B remains near half of it.
Correct: Competitive inhibition is overcome by high [S] (v = 100x100/106, about 94 with A, versus about 98 uninhibited), whereas B reduces Vmax to 50 and cannot be overcome by more substrate.
qs.x: Competitive inhibition is overcome by high [S] (v = 100x100/106, about 94 with A, versus about 98 uninhibited), whereas B reduces Vmax to 50 and cannot be overcome by more substrate. Trap: Assuming that any reversible inhibitor can be overcome with excess substrate, rather than only competitive ones.

qs.q: The data are most consistent with Inhibitor B decreasing the rate of catalysis by:
o: occupying the active site and preventing the substrate from binding, thereby raising the apparent Km.
This describes competitive inhibition, in which Km rises and Vmax is unchanged.
binding a site outside the active site and lowering the effective amount of functional enzyme.
Correct: Binding with similar affinity to free enzyme and enzyme-substrate complex, away from the active site, lowers Vmax without altering substrate binding (Km), which is noncompetitive inhibition.
binding only to the enzyme-substrate complex and locking the substrate in place, thereby lowering both Km and Vmax.
This describes uncompetitive inhibition, which would give parallel lines; the B line is not parallel to the control.
covalently modifying the active-site residue and permanently destroying part of the enzyme.
The passage states that B binds reversibly, and covalent modification would be irreversible.
qs.x: Binding with similar affinity to free enzyme and enzyme-substrate complex, away from the active site, lowers Vmax without altering substrate binding (Km), which is noncompetitive inhibition. Trap: Equating any decrease in Vmax with irreversible damage, even though noncompetitive inhibitors bind reversibly at a remote site.

graph.title: Lineweaver-Burk plot of Enzyme Q

passages.title: FL03 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 2
text: The lac operon of E. coli encodes beta-galactosidase (lacZ). In the wild-type operon, the lac repressor (encoded by lacI) binds the operator and blocks transcription unless allolactose, an isomer of lactose, is present. The catabolite activator protein (CAP, encoded by crp) binds cAMP and stimulates transcription from the lac promoter; cAMP levels are low when glucose is abundant.

Researchers grew several strains in three media: glycerol without lactose, glycerol with lactose, and glucose with lactose. Beta-galactosidase activity was measured in arbitrary units (Table 1). The lacO-c strain carries a mutation in the operator, and the lacI-s strain carries a mutation that alters the repressor so that it no longer binds allolactose. In the partial diploid strains, a second copy of the operon was carried on an F' plasmid; the genotype written before the slash is on the chromosome, and the genotype after the slash is on the plasmid. Assume that the strains differ only in the genotypes listed and that cultures were harvested in the exponential growth phase.

qs.q: The high beta-galactosidase activity of the lacI- strain in glycerol without lactose is best explained by the fact that in this strain:
o: allolactose is produced at a high basal rate even without lactose in the medium.
The strain's behavior reflects the repressor defect, not a source of inducer.
no functional repressor is made, so lacZ is transcribed continuously.
Correct: Loss of the repressor removes the block at the operator, producing constitutive expression when cAMP is high (glycerol medium).
CAP is permanently inactive, so the lac promoter is never activated at all.
Inactive CAP would lower expression, as in the Delta-crp strain.
the operator sequence cannot be bound by RNA polymerase under any condition.
A defective polymerase-operator interaction would lower, not raise, expression.
qs.x: Loss of the repressor removes the block at the operator, producing constitutive expression when cAMP is high (glycerol medium). Trap: Thinking the repressor is an activator, so that its loss should lower expression.

qs.q: The lacI- lacZ+ / lacI+ lacZ- partial diploid shows inducible expression like the wild type. This result indicates that the lacI+ product:
o: replaces the operator sequence on the chromosome by homologous recombination.
Proteins do not replace DNA sequences; they bind to them.
is an enzyme that degrades the beta-galactosidase made from the lacZ+ gene.
Nothing in the data suggests degradation; regulation is of transcription.
is a diffusible protein that can act on the lacZ+ operator in trans.
Correct: The repressor made from the plasmid copy reaches the chromosomal operator, restoring regulation, so lacI acts in trans.
acts only on the same DNA molecule that encodes it, as a cis-acting site.
A cis-only action would leave the lacZ+ copy unrepressed and constitutive.
qs.x: The repressor made from the plasmid copy reaches the chromosomal operator, restoring regulation, so lacI acts in trans. Trap: Confusing the trans-acting repressor with the cis-acting operator, which affects only its own DNA.

qs.q: Wild-type cells grown in glucose plus lactose show low beta-galactosidase activity (2 units) even though allolactose is present. The most likely explanation is that:
o: glucose lowers cAMP, so CAP does not bind and the promoter is poorly activated.
Correct: Without cAMP-CAP, RNA polymerase binds the lac promoter weakly; the Delta-crp strain shows the same dependence.
glucose induces mutations in the lacZ gene during growth.
The effect is reversible regulation, not mutation.
glucose causes the repressor to bind allolactose more tightly and remain off the operator.
If the repressor remained bound, the lacI- strain would not also show low expression in glucose.
lactose cannot be taken into cells that are growing in glucose.
This does not account for lacI- and lacO-c strains also being low in glucose.
qs.x: Without cAMP-CAP, RNA polymerase binds the lac promoter weakly; the Delta-crp strain shows the same dependence. Trap: Attributing the low expression in glucose to the repressor, even though lacI- cells are also low.

qs.q: In the lacI-s lacZ+ / lacI+ lacZ+ partial diploid with glycerol and lactose, expression is only 2 units. This indicates that lacI-s is:
o: a loss-of-function allele that impairs binding of the repressor to the operator DNA.
The mutant binds DNA tightly; it fails to respond to the inducer.
an operator mutation that acts only in cis on the same DNA molecule as the mutation.
Operator mutations are cis-acting and cause constitutive expression, as in lacO-c.
dominant, because the mutant repressor stays bound to both operators.
Correct: The mutant repressor cannot release in response to allolactose, so even in the presence of the wild-type repressor both operators remain blocked.
recessive, because the wild-type repressor still releases the operators in lactose.
A recessive allele would allow normal induction in the presence of the lacI+ copy.
qs.x: The mutant repressor cannot release in response to allolactose, so even in the presence of the wild-type repressor both operators remain blocked. Trap: Assuming a repressor mutation must be recessive as with loss-of-function lacI- alleles.

passages.title: FL03 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 3
text: In Labrador retrievers, coat color depends on two genes. At the B locus, the dominant allele B produces black pigment and the recessive allele b produces brown pigment. At the E locus, the dominant allele E allows pigment to be deposited in the hair, while dogs that are homozygous ee are yellow regardless of their genotype at the B locus.

Breeders crossed dogs heterozygous at both loci (BbEe x BbEe) and recorded the coat colors of 640 puppies. In a separate test cross, a BbEe dog was crossed with a bbee dog. The observed and expected results for the dihybrid cross are shown in Table 1. A chi-square test was performed to determine whether the observed numbers fit the expected ratio; with 2 degrees of freedom, the critical value at p = 0.05 is 5.99.
The two loci were found to be on different chromosomes. Assume complete penetrance and no other modifying genes.

qs.q: The inheritance pattern at the E locus relative to the B locus is an example of:
o: incomplete dominance, giving a 1:2:1 ratio.
Heterozygotes are not intermediate in this cross.
recessive epistasis, giving a 9:3:4 ratio.
Correct: Genotype ee masks the B-locus alleles, so the 9 B_E_ : 3 bbE_ : 4 (B_ee + bbee) dihybrid ratio emerges.
complete dominance at both loci, giving a 9:3:3:1 ratio.
Four distinct phenotypes are not seen; the two yellow classes are indistinguishable.
codominance, giving a 1:1 ratio.
No heterozygote shows both parental phenotypes.
qs.x: Genotype ee masks the B-locus alleles, so the 9 B_E_ : 3 bbE_ : 4 (B_ee + bbee) dihybrid ratio emerges. Trap: Expecting the classical 9:3:3:1 ratio without recognizing that one gene masks the other.

qs.q: Among the yellow puppies from the BbEe x BbEe cross, what fraction is expected to be genotype BBee?
o: Correct: Yellow puppies are 4/16 of the total (BBee, 2 Bbee, bbee); BBee is 1 of those 4, or 1/4.
Only the Bbee genotype is 2 of 4.
This divides by 3, as if only three yellow genotypes were equally likely.
This is the fraction of all puppies, not of the yellow ones.
qs.x: Yellow puppies are 4/16 of the total (BBee, 2 Bbee, bbee); BBee is 1 of those 4, or 1/4. Trap: Using the fraction of the total offspring (1/16) instead of the fraction within the yellow class.

qs.q: Using the observed and expected values in Table 1, the chi-square statistic is closest to:
o: This is half the correct value; dividing by degrees of freedom is not part of the statistic.
This is off by a factor of 10.
This is double the correct value, as if the deviations were counted twice.
qs.x: Chi-square = (352-360)^2/360 + (118-120)^2/120 + (170-160)^2/160 = 0.178 + 0.033 + 0.625, which is about 0.84, below 5.99. Trap: Dividing by the observed instead of the expected values, or forgetting to square the deviations.

qs.q: Based on the chi-square statistic, which conclusion is justified?
o: The results should be rejected because observed and expected values are not identical.
Small deviations are expected from random sampling.
The data do not differ significantly from the 9:3:4 ratio, so the null hypothesis is not rejected.
Correct: A statistic of 0.84 is lower than the 5.99 critical value at 2 degrees of freedom, so the deviation can be due to chance.
The data prove that epistasis is present with certainty.
Statistics fail to reject the null, but do not prove a hypothesis.
The data differ significantly from 9:3:4, so the loci are linked.
The statistic is below the critical value; linkage would not be implied even if it were above.
qs.x: A statistic of 0.84 is lower than the 5.99 critical value at 2 degrees of freedom, so the deviation can be due to chance. Trap: Treating any difference between observed and expected values as evidence against the model.

qs.q: In the test cross BbEe x bbee, what fraction of the puppies is expected to be yellow?
o: Correct: All ee puppies are yellow; Ee x ee gives 1/2 ee, regardless of B-locus genotype. Black and brown are each 1/4.
This would require three independent heterozygous crosses.
This would apply to a cross between two Ee parents, where the E_ fraction is 3/4.
This is the expected fraction of black or brown puppies, not yellow.
qs.x: All ee puppies are yellow; Ee x ee gives 1/2 ee, regardless of B-locus genotype. Black and brown are each 1/4. Trap: Using the 4/16 result from the dihybrid cross rather than the Ee x ee ratio.

passages.title: FL03 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 4
text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) catalyzes the first, rate-limiting step of the oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway. Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and depend on this pathway for NADPH, which glutathione reductase uses to regenerate reduced glutathione (GSH) from its oxidized form (GSSG). GSH is needed to detoxify hydrogen peroxide.

Researchers incubated red blood cells from healthy volunteers and from volunteers with a partial G6PD deficiency with or without an oxidant drug that generates hydrogen peroxide. They measured NADPH production rate, the GSH/GSSG ratio, and the percentage of cells lysed (hemolysis) after 4 hours. Results are in Table 1.

Cells from both groups maintained similar glycolytic flux and ATP levels. Deficient cells had normal levels of glutathione reductase and total glutathione. Heinz bodies (precipitates of oxidized hemoglobin) formed only in cells with a low GSH/GSSG ratio. The oxidant did not change the number of cells in any sample at the start of the incubation, and hemolysis was determined by release of hemoglobin into the medium.

qs.q: The reaction catalyzed by G6PD directly produces:
o: ATP and ribulose-5-phosphate from ADP and glucose-6-phosphate.
The pathway does not generate ATP, and ribulose-5-phosphate is formed later.
NADH and pyruvate from glucose-6-phosphate and NAD+.
These products are of glycolysis, not the pentose phosphate pathway.
NADPH and 6-phosphogluconolactone from glucose-6-phosphate and NADP+.
Correct: G6PD oxidizes glucose-6-phosphate and reduces NADP+ to NADPH in the first committed step of the pathway.
FADH2 and fructose-6-phosphate from glucose-6-phosphate.
Fructose-6-phosphate arises by isomerization in glycolysis without FAD.
qs.x: G6PD oxidizes glucose-6-phosphate and reduces NADP+ to NADPH in the first committed step of the pathway. Trap: Mixing up NADPH of the pentose phosphate pathway with NADH of glycolysis.

qs.q: Erythrocytes are especially vulnerable to G6PD deficiency because they:
o: synthesize large amounts of fatty acids that require NADPH.
Red cells do not synthesize fatty acids in bulk.
have the highest rate of oxidative phosphorylation of any cell.
Red cells have no mitochondria, so no oxidative phosphorylation.
do not carry out glycolysis, relying only on the pentose phosphate pathway.
Red cells depend on glycolysis for ATP; the data say flux was similar.
lack mitochondria and have no other major source of NADPH.
Correct: Without mitochondria, red cells cannot use mitochondrial NADPH-generating routes, so the pentose phosphate pathway is the main source.
qs.x: Without mitochondria, red cells cannot use mitochondrial NADPH-generating routes, so the pentose phosphate pathway is the main source. Trap: Assuming red cells are rich in mitochondria because they carry oxygen.

qs.q: Which statement best explains why hemolysis rises to 45% in deficient cells exposed to the oxidant?
o: Total glutathione is lower in deficient cells, so less peroxide can be neutralized.
Total glutathione was normal; the problem is its reduction state.
Low NADPH production limits regeneration of GSH, so peroxide damage to cell components is unchecked.
Correct: Glutathione reductase needs NADPH; without it GSSG accumulates (ratio drops to 10), Heinz bodies form, and membranes are damaged.
The oxidant lowers ATP levels in deficient cells only.
ATP levels were similar in both groups.
The oxidant inhibits glutathione reductase specifically in deficient cells.
Glutathione reductase levels were normal and the oxidant affected normal cells much less.
qs.x: Glutathione reductase needs NADPH; without it GSSG accumulates (ratio drops to 10), Heinz bodies form, and membranes are damaged. Trap: Blaming total glutathione or ATP content when the data show the problem is NADPH supply for regeneration.

qs.q: Compared with normal cells, the fall in the GSH/GSSG ratio caused by the oxidant in deficient cells is approximately how many times greater (fold decline)?
o: 7.5 times
Correct: Normal ratio fell 400 to 150, a 2.67-fold decline; deficient fell 200 to 10, a 20-fold decline; 20/2.67 is about 7.5.
20 times
This is the fold decline in deficient cells only.
1.9 times
This does not correspond to the ratio of the two fold declines.
2.7 times
This is the fold decline in normal cells only.
qs.x: Normal ratio fell 400 to 150, a 2.67-fold decline; deficient fell 200 to 10, a 20-fold decline; 20/2.67 is about 7.5. Trap: Reporting one group's fold change instead of the ratio of the two fold changes.

passages.title: FL03 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 5
text: A family has a recessive disorder caused by a single-nucleotide substitution in exon 4 of a gene. The substitution destroys the only EcoRI recognition site in a 1,200-bp region surrounding the exon. DNA from each family member was amplified by PCR with primers that flank the region, using a heat-stable DNA polymerase and 30 cycles of denaturation at 95 degrees C, annealing at 58 degrees C, and extension at 72 degrees C. Each product was digested with EcoRI and resolved on an agarose gel stained with a DNA-binding dye. A no-template control was run in parallel, containing all reagents except genomic DNA.

The wild-type allele yields fragments of 800 bp and 400 bp after digestion. The mutant allele remains 1,200 bp. Fragment sizes seen on the gel are listed in Table 1. A student calculated that PCR doubles the number of target molecules in each cycle under ideal conditions. Samples were loaded in adjacent lanes, and a ladder of known fragment lengths was included so that the sizes of the bands could be estimated. The sample from the unrelated control was known not to carry the mutation.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, which individuals are heterozygous for the mutation?
o: The unrelated control and the affected child
The control shows only 800 and 400 bp (homozygous wild type) and the child shows only 1,200 bp (homozygous mutant).
The affected child only, because the child displays the disease
The child has only the 1,200-bp band, indicating two mutant alleles; a heterozygote would also show cut fragments.
The mother and the father
Correct: Heterozygotes carry one uncut mutant allele (1,200 bp) and one cut wild-type allele (800 and 400 bp), which is the pattern in lanes 4 and 5.
The mother, the father, and the affected child, because all three carry at least one mutant allele
The child carries two mutant copies and is therefore homozygous, not heterozygous.
qs.x: Heterozygotes carry one uncut mutant allele (1,200 bp) and one cut wild-type allele (800 and 400 bp), which is the pattern in lanes 4 and 5. Trap: Counting everyone who carries the mutant allele as heterozygous, including the homozygous affected child.

qs.q: A DNA polymerase from a thermophilic bacterium is used in the PCR because it:
o: remains active after repeated exposure to the 95 degrees C denaturation step.
Correct: Each cycle melts the double-stranded template at 95 degrees C, which would denature most polymerases; a thermostable enzyme avoids replenishing it every cycle.
is able to copy RNA templates directly into cDNA without primers.
Reverse transcriptase copies RNA, and all DNA polymerases require a primer.
can initiate synthesis de novo without a primer when the template is sufficiently long.
DNA polymerases cannot start synthesis without a primer, which is why primers flank the region.
has proofreading and unwinds the helix using ATP at the annealing step.
Heat, not an ATP-driven helicase, separates the strands in PCR, and the annealing step only lets primers bind.
qs.x: Each cycle melts the double-stranded template at 95 degrees C, which would denature most polymerases; a thermostable enzyme avoids replenishing it every cycle. Trap: Believing that the polymerase itself separates the strands, rather than the heat of the denaturation step.

qs.q: A reaction begins with 100 copies of the target region. Assuming perfect doubling every cycle, approximately how many copies of the amplified region exist after 6 cycles?
o: This multiplies by the number of cycles (100 x 6), which would be linear growth.
This is 100 x 12 (6 cycles x 2), treating doubling as adding a constant amount each cycle.
This uses 2^7, one cycle too many (100 x 128).
Correct: Copies = 100 x 2^6 = 100 x 64 = 6,400.
qs.x: Copies = 100 x 2^6 = 100 x 64 = 6,400. Trap: Treating amplification as linear (multiplying by cycle number) instead of exponential (2 to the power of cycle number).

qs.q: On the agarose gel, which statement correctly describes the lane 6 band and the direction of its movement?
o: The 1,200-bp fragment migrates faster than the 400-bp fragment and moves toward the positive electrode.
Larger fragments are retarded more by the gel matrix, so the 1,200-bp fragment moves more slowly than the smaller fragments.
The 1,200-bp fragment migrates more slowly than the 400-bp fragment and moves toward the positive electrode.
Correct: DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate backbone, so it moves to the anode, and in the gel matrix smaller fragments move farther.
The 1,200-bp fragment migrates more slowly than the 400-bp fragment and moves toward the negative electrode.
DNA is negatively charged and moves to the positive electrode.
The 1,200-bp fragment migrates at the same rate as the 400-bp fragment because the two carry the same charge-to-mass ratio.
Charge-to-mass is similar, but the sieving effect of agarose separates fragments by length.
qs.x: DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate backbone, so it moves to the anode, and in the gel matrix smaller fragments move farther. Trap: Applying size-exclusion column logic (large molecules first) to a gel, where the smallest fragments run farthest.

qs.q: If a band at 1,200 bp had appeared in lane 2 (no-template control), the most likely explanation would be that:
o: reagents or pipetting introduced contaminating template DNA or amplified product.
Correct: With no genomic DNA added, any product must have come from contaminating template or earlier amplicons, so the experiment lacks a clean negative control.
the mutant allele was present in the reagents, which means the primers never bound.
A product forms only if primers bind to some template, so primer binding did occur.
EcoRI digestion was incomplete and generated the larger band from the smaller pieces.
Digestion cannot produce a larger fragment, and no template was present for it to arise from.
the size ladder migrated unevenly and appeared as a false band in the next lane.
The ladder lane is separate and does not account for a band absent a template.
qs.x: With no genomic DNA added, any product must have come from contaminating template or earlier amplicons, so the experiment lacks a clean negative control. Trap: Assuming the polymerase can create products without a template, rather than recognizing contamination.

passages.title: FL03 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 6
text: A bacteriophage infects E. coli and produces progeny by the lytic cycle. In a one-step growth experiment, phage were mixed with bacteria at a low ratio so that nearly all infected cells were infected by one phage. After a short adsorption period, unadsorbed phage were neutralized with antiserum and the culture was diluted, so that the initial concentration of infected cells was 2 x 10^6 per mL and free phage was essentially zero.

At intervals, two samples were taken. One sample was plated directly to measure free phage. The other was treated with chloroform, which lyses cells and releases intracellular mature phage, and then plated to measure total infectious phage (free plus intracellular). Results are in Figure 1, with phage titer given in units of 10^6 plaque-forming units (PFU) per mL.

A second phage strain, which carries a mutation in a gene encoding a lysis protein, was tested in the same way. Its chloroform-treated titer rose as shown for the wild-type phage, but its free phage titer remained near zero.

qs.q: Based on Figure 1, the latent period of this phage (time before release of progeny phage) is approximately:
o: 25 minutes
Correct: Free phage titer remains zero until about 25 minutes, when the first cells lyse.
50 minutes
This is the last time point, at which the plateau is established.
40 minutes
This is when the burst is complete.
5 minutes
At 5 minutes total infectivity is at its lowest, which marks the eclipse period, not the end of latency.
qs.x: Free phage titer remains zero until about 25 minutes, when the first cells lyse. Trap: Using the first rise of the chloroform curve instead of the first rise of the free-phage curve.

qs.q: The average burst size (progeny phage per infected cell) is approximately:
o: Correct: The plateau is 100 x 10^6 PFU/mL from 2 x 10^6 infected cells per mL, so 100/2 = 50 phage per cell.
This inverts the ratio.
This ignores the number of infected cells, using the plateau titer alone.
This is the initial infected cell concentration, not the burst.
qs.x: The plateau is 100 x 10^6 PFU/mL from 2 x 10^6 infected cells per mL, so 100/2 = 50 phage per cell. Trap: Reading the plateau value as the burst size without dividing by the number of infected cells.

qs.q: The drop in the chloroform-treated titer during the first 5 to 10 minutes (eclipse) is best explained by the fact that:
o: the cells are not yet infected.
The infected centers were already established at 2 x 10^6 per mL.
the phage has lost its genome through mutation.
Infection subsequently proceeds normally, so the genome remains.
infecting virions are disassembled as their genomes enter the host, so infectious particles are absent until new virions assemble.
Correct: Before assembly, the parental particles have released their nucleic acid and progeny have not yet formed, so there is little infectivity even inside intact cells.
most phage are destroyed by the host's immune system.
Bacteria lack an adaptive immune system of this type, and the antiserum acted only on free phage.
qs.x: Before assembly, the parental particles have released their nucleic acid and progeny have not yet formed, so there is little infectivity even inside intact cells. Trap: Interpreting the loss of infectivity as loss of the virus, when it reflects the intracellular stage in which no complete virions exist.

qs.q: The mutant phage with a defective lysis protein would be expected to produce which result in the one-step growth experiment?
o: Neither titer rises, because the phage cannot replicate.
Replication and assembly are normal, since the chloroform titer rises.
Only the free-phage titer rises, because phage bud from cells.
Bacteriophages of this type exit by lysis, not budding.
Both titers rise normally, because lysis is not required to release progeny.
The free titer stays near zero.
Infectious progeny accumulate inside intact cells, so the chloroform-treated titer rises while the free titer stays low.
Correct: Without lysis the mature virions remain trapped in the cell; chloroform releases them for counting, as the passage describes.
qs.x: Without lysis the mature virions remain trapped in the cell; chloroform releases them for counting, as the passage describes. Trap: Assuming a lysis defect would prevent virion assembly, rather than release.

graph.title: Figure 1. One-step growth curve

passages.title: FL03 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 7
text: Trisomy 21 arises when a gamete carries two copies of chromosome 21. To study the origin of the extra chromosome, researchers examined 150 affected children in whom the extra chromosome was of maternal origin. A DNA marker located close to the centromere of chromosome 21 was typed in each child and mother. In 108 children, the two maternal copies of the marker carried different alleles. In the remaining 42 children, the two maternal copies carried identical alleles. Crossing over near the centromere is rare and was ignored.

The researchers also examined the frequency of trisomy 21 births in relation to maternal age (Table 1; Figure 1). In humans, oocytes begin meiosis before birth and arrest in prophase I until ovulation, which may occur decades later. Each primary oocyte completes meiosis I at ovulation and then arrests again in metaphase II until fertilization. The age data are approximate population averages and were collected from many centers over several years.

qs.q: In the 42 children whose two maternal marker copies were identical, the nondisjunction most likely occurred during:
o: meiosis I, when homologous chromosomes failed to separate.
Failure of homologs to separate gives a gamete with one copy from each homolog, producing two different marker alleles.
meiosis I, when sister chromatids failed to separate during prophase.
Sister chromatids do not separate in meiosis I during any phase, and this is not the event that nondisjunction involves.
mitosis in the zygote, because identical alleles can arise only from mitotic errors.
Identical alleles are expected from meiosis II errors; mitotic errors need not be invoked.
meiosis II, when sister chromatids failed to separate.
Correct: Sister chromatids are identical copies (apart from rare crossover), so a disomic gamete from failed sister-chromatid separation carries two identical marker alleles near the centromere.
qs.x: Sister chromatids are identical copies (apart from rare crossover), so a disomic gamete from failed sister-chromatid separation carries two identical marker alleles near the centromere. Trap: Remembering that homologs separate in meiosis I and sister chromatids in meiosis II, then reversing the two.

qs.q: What percentage of these 150 maternal-origin cases is attributable to errors in meiosis I?
o: Correct: Different maternal alleles indicate meiosis I error: 108/150 = 0.72, or 72%.
This is 42/150, the meiosis II fraction.
This is the raw count of meiosis II cases written as a percent, instead of dividing by 150.
This halves the correct value, as if only one of two meiosis I products carried the error.
qs.x: Different maternal alleles indicate meiosis I error: 108/150 = 0.72, or 72%. Trap: Using the count of one category as the percentage or choosing the complementary category.

qs.q: According to Table 1, the risk of trisomy 21 at age 40 is approximately how many times the risk at age 30?
o: 2.9 times
This is the ratio for age 35 (2.9/1.0), not for age 40.
33 times
This uses the age 45 value rather than age 40.
10 times
Correct: 10 per 1,000 divided by 1.0 per 1,000 is 10.
1.25 times
This is the ratio of age 30 to age 25 (1.0/0.8), not age 40 to age 30.
qs.x: 10 per 1,000 divided by 1.0 per 1,000 is 10. Trap: Reading the neighboring row of the table rather than the row for age 40.

qs.q: Which feature of oogenesis best explains the pattern in Figure 1?
o: Mutations accumulate in the mitotic divisions of oogonia throughout adult life, as in spermatogenesis.
Oogonia complete mitosis before birth; there are no adult mitotic divisions to accumulate mutations.
Primary oocytes stay arrested in prophase I for decades while cohesion deteriorates.
Correct: Prolonged arrest with age-related loss of chromosome cohesion makes missegregation more likely at resumption of meiosis.
Meiosis I is completed before birth, and meiosis II occurs shortly after ovulation.
Meiosis I is completed only at ovulation; the oocyte arrests in prophase I from fetal life.
Older mothers produce more polar bodies, which carry extra copies of chromosome 21 into the egg.
Polar bodies are discarded and do not donate chromosomes to the egg.
qs.x: Prolonged arrest with age-related loss of chromosome cohesion makes missegregation more likely at resumption of meiosis. Trap: Importing the spermatogenesis model of continuous divisions, when oocytes are arrested from fetal life.

graph.title: Trisomy 21 frequency versus maternal age

passages.title: FL03 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 8
text: Glucagon and epinephrine both raise blood glucose, in part by stimulating glycogen breakdown in the liver. Isolated hepatocytes were treated for 10 minutes with several agents. Intracellular cAMP, the fraction of glycogen phosphorylase in the active form, and glucose output were then measured (Table 1; Figure 1).

Glucagon binds a Gs-coupled receptor. Epinephrine acts on beta-adrenergic receptors (Gs-coupled) and on alpha-1 receptors (Gq-coupled). Propranolol is a beta-receptor antagonist. Forskolin directly activates adenylyl cyclase. Cholera toxin permanently locks the alpha subunit of Gs in its GTP-bound state. IBMX inhibits phosphodiesterase, the enzyme that degrades cAMP to AMP. Glucagon and epinephrine were each used at saturating doses. Cells were first incubated in glucose-free buffer for 30 minutes to establish a stable baseline. Cells for each treatment came from the same liver preparation, so that differences between treatments reflect the agent used. Glycogen phosphorylase is activated by phosphorylation by phosphorylase kinase, which is itself activated by protein kinase A or by calcium.

qs.q: Forskolin raises cAMP and glucose output without a receptor ligand. This indicates that forskolin acts at which step of the pathway?
o: Directly on adenylyl cyclase, downstream of the receptor and the G protein.
Correct: Forskolin bypasses the receptor and Gs and activates the enzyme that makes cAMP from ATP, so the downstream response (PKA, phosphorylase kinase, phosphorylase) follows.
On the glucagon receptor, as a ligand mimic that activates Gs.
If forskolin acted at the receptor, it would be blocked by receptor antagonists; the passage states it activates the cyclase directly.
On phosphodiesterase, by increasing the rate at which cAMP is degraded to AMP.
Increasing degradation would lower cAMP, but cAMP rose with forskolin.
On glycogen phosphorylase, by directly phosphorylating it to the active form.
Phosphorylase is activated by phosphorylase kinase, which itself requires PKA; cAMP rose with forskolin, so the effect begins upstream.
qs.x: Forskolin bypasses the receptor and Gs and activates the enzyme that makes cAMP from ATP, so the downstream response (PKA, phosphorylase kinase, phosphorylase) follows. Trap: Assuming any compound that raises cAMP must bind the receptor, ignoring that the cyclase can be activated directly.

qs.q: When propranolol was added, epinephrine still raised active phosphorylase from 10% to 20%, even though cAMP stayed near basal. The most likely explanation is that epinephrine:
o: binds the glucagon receptor and activates a second pool of adenylyl cyclase that propranolol cannot reach.
Epinephrine does not bind the glucagon receptor, and cAMP would have risen if a cyclase were activated.
also activates alpha-1 receptors, which signal through Gq, IP3, and Ca2+ to activate phosphorylase kinase.
Correct: Propranolol blocks beta receptors (cAMP rises are lost), but alpha-1 receptors remain, giving a cAMP-independent Ca2+ pathway that partially activates phosphorylase kinase.
inhibits phosphodiesterase, leaving a small amount of cAMP that was not detected by the assay.
cAMP stayed near basal, and a phosphodiesterase block would raise cAMP, not leave it unchanged.
is converted to glucagon by hepatocyte enzymes, producing a small cAMP-independent response.
Epinephrine is not converted to glucagon, a peptide hormone with a different structure.
qs.x: Propranolol blocks beta receptors (cAMP rises are lost), but alpha-1 receptors remain, giving a cAMP-independent Ca2+ pathway that partially activates phosphorylase kinase. Trap: Assuming cAMP must account for every effect of epinephrine, overlooking its second receptor class.

qs.q: Compared with glucagon alone, adding IBMX increased cAMP by approximately how much, and why?
o: 2.5-fold, because IBMX activates adenylyl cyclase directly.
The ratio is right, but the passage says IBMX inhibits phosphodiesterase; forskolin activates adenylyl cyclase.
0.4-fold, because IBMX blocks the glucagon receptor and lowers cAMP.
0.4 is 80/200, the inverse ratio, and cAMP rose rather than fell.
2.5-fold, because cAMP degradation by phosphodiesterase was blocked.
Correct: 200/80 = 2.5. With phosphodiesterase inhibited, cAMP made by adenylyl cyclase accumulates.
40-fold, because IBMX inhibits the Gs protein and amplifies the signal.
The 40-fold value is 200/5, which compares to basal, and IBMX does not act on Gs.
qs.x: 200/80 = 2.5. With phosphodiesterase inhibited, cAMP made by adenylyl cyclase accumulates. Trap: Inverting the ratio or comparing with basal rather than with the glucagon-treated cells.

qs.q: Cholera toxin raises cAMP in the absence of hormone because it:
o: directly phosphorylates adenylyl cyclase on a serine residue to increase its activity.
The passage describes an effect on the Gs alpha subunit, not a kinase-like action on the cyclase.
blocks cAMP phosphodiesterase, preventing the breakdown of cAMP.
The passage attributes the effect to the Gs alpha subunit; IBMX is the phosphodiesterase inhibitor.
mimics glucagon by binding to the glucagon receptor and activating Gs.
Cholera toxin acts on the G protein itself, not on the receptor.
keeps the Gs alpha subunit in its active GTP-bound form, so adenylyl cyclase stays on.
Correct: By blocking GTP hydrolysis by Gs alpha, the toxin leaves it constitutively active, giving persistent cyclase activation and sustained cAMP.
