qs.x: By blocking GTP hydrolysis by Gs alpha, the toxin leaves it constitutively active, giving persistent cyclase activation and sustained cAMP. Trap: Confusing the G protein locked in its GTP-bound state with receptor activation by a ligand.

graph.title: Intracellular cAMP by treatment

passages.title: FL03 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 9
text: An indirect ELISA was used to follow the antibody response to a vaccine antigen. Antigen was coated on a plastic plate, wells were blocked with an irrelevant protein, and serial dilutions of a volunteer's serum were added. After washing, an enzyme-linked antibody that recognizes human IgG was added, followed by a substrate that turns yellow. Absorbance (optical density, OD) is proportional to the amount of bound antibody. The titer is the highest dilution with an OD of at least 0.20, the cutoff set at three standard deviations above the mean of blank wells.

The volunteer received a first dose at day 0 and a booster at day 21. Serum was collected on days 0, 14, and 28 (Table 1; Figure 1). Each serum sample was assayed in duplicate on the same plate, and the values shown are means. Wells that received buffer instead of serum served as blanks. The plate was washed several times between each step to remove unbound material.

qs.q: What is the antibody titer on day 28?
o: The OD at 1:2,700 is 0.80, but a higher dilution (1:8,100) is still above the cutoff.
Correct: At the highest dilution tested (1:8,100) the OD is 0.30, which exceeds the 0.20 cutoff, so the titer is at least 8,100.
The OD at 1:900 is above cutoff, but higher dilutions are as well.
This is the day 14 titer, where OD at 1:900 (0.15) has already fallen below 0.20.
qs.x: At the highest dilution tested (1:8,100) the OD is 0.30, which exceeds the 0.20 cutoff, so the titer is at least 8,100. Trap: Selecting the dilution with the highest OD instead of the highest dilution that remains above the cutoff.

qs.q: By what factor did the titer increase from day 14 to day 28?
o: 3-fold
This compares neighboring dilution steps, which differ threefold, rather than the full change between titers.
9-fold
This results from taking the day 14 titer as 900, even though the OD at 1:900 is below the cutoff.
81-fold
This uses a day 14 titer of 100, ignoring that the 1:300 dilution is above cutoff.
27-fold
Correct: Day 14 titer is 300 (OD 0.32, whereas 1:900 gives 0.15), and day 28 titer is 8,100, so 8,100/300 = 27.
qs.x: Day 14 titer is 300 (OD 0.32, whereas 1:900 gives 0.15), and day 28 titer is 8,100, so 8,100/300 = 27. Trap: Using a dilution step or the wrong day 14 end point rather than comparing the two true titers.

qs.q: The higher and faster antibody response after the booster is best explained by the action of:
o: memory B cells from the first dose, which respond rapidly and have undergone affinity maturation.
Correct: Primed memory B and T cells give a faster, larger secondary response with higher-affinity, class-switched IgG.
natural killer cells, which produce IgG directly after recognizing the antigen.
Natural killer cells are innate lymphocytes and do not secrete antibodies.
complement proteins, which store the antigen shape and generate new antibodies on the booster.
Complement helps clear opsonized antigens, but it does not generate or remember antibodies.
neutrophils, which carry antigen to the spleen and replace the plasma cells that decay after the first dose.
Neutrophils are short-lived, innate phagocytes, and they do not provide immunologic memory.
qs.x: Primed memory B and T cells give a faster, larger secondary response with higher-affinity, class-switched IgG. Trap: Attributing memory to innate cells, when only B and T lymphocytes provide it.

qs.q: A well with no serum, blocked but otherwise treated identically, shows an OD of 0.04. If this value were high (for example, 1.5), the most likely cause would be:
o: high concentration of IgG in the serum that was added to the well.
No serum was added to this well.
the antigen coating failed, so no antibody could bind and the enzyme remained inactive.
Failed coating would reduce signal in sample wells, not increase signal in a no-serum well.
inadequate blocking, so the enzyme-linked antibody bound directly to the plastic.
Correct: Without serum, signal comes from nonspecific binding of the detection antibody, and this is what blocking is intended to reduce.
a booster dose that raised the titer of antigen-specific antibody.
A well with no serum cannot reflect the volunteer's immune response.
qs.x: Without serum, signal comes from nonspecific binding of the detection antibody, and this is what blocking is intended to reduce. Trap: Reading any signal as specific antibody binding, when blank wells measure background.

qs.q: The detection antibody recognizes only human IgG. Which statement best explains the low OD at day 14 relative to day 28?
o: IgM predominates early in a primary response, and the detection antibody does not recognize IgM.
Correct: Class switching to IgG takes time; at day 14, antigen-specific IgM, undetected by an anti-IgG reagent, makes up much of the response.
IgG predominates early in a primary response, but its affinity is too low to bind antigen on the plate.
IgM, not IgG, predominates early, and the OD reflects amount of binding rather than the lack of any binding.
The detection antibody binds IgM more strongly than IgG, which suppresses the day 28 signal.
The anti-IgG reagent does not bind IgM, and the day 28 signal is high, not suppressed.
The antibody-secreting plasma cells at day 14 produce IgE, which cannot be adsorbed to plastic.
IgE is a minor isotype in a vaccine response, and it can bind to coated antigen if present.
qs.x: Class switching to IgG takes time; at day 14, antigen-specific IgM, undetected by an anti-IgG reagent, makes up much of the response. Trap: Forgetting that an isotype-specific detection reagent reports only that isotype, not the total antibody response.

graph.title: Anti-antigen IgG ELISA signal

passages.title: FL03 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 10
text: Rod photoreceptors contain rhodopsin, a G protein-coupled receptor bound to 11-cis-retinal, in the membranes of their outer segments. In the dark, cyclic GMP (cGMP) levels are high and cGMP binds to channels in the plasma membrane, holding them open. In light, 11-cis-retinal is converted to all-trans-retinal, which activates rhodopsin, which in turn activates the G protein transducin and a phosphodiesterase (PDE) that hydrolyzes cGMP.

Researchers recorded from isolated rods under four conditions: darkness, dim light, bright light, and bright light in the presence of IBMX, a PDE inhibitor. Membrane potential, relative cGMP concentration, and glutamate release from the synaptic terminal were measured (Table 1). Relative cGMP in darkness was set to 100.

The channel opened by cGMP is nonselective for cations, and the rod also contains Na+/K+ pumps in the inner segment and K+ channels that are not regulated by cGMP. Glutamate release from rods is voltage-dependent and rises with depolarization.

qs.q: The relatively depolarized potential of the rod in darkness (-40 mV) is the result of:
o: Cl- exit through open voltage-gated chloride channels in the outer segment.
Cl- is not described as the cause of the dark current.
K+ entry through open cGMP-gated channels down its gradient.
K+ would exit down its gradient and the channels are nonselective, dominated by Na+ influx.
activity of the Na+/K+ pump alone, without any open ion channels.
The pump is electrogenic but hyperpolarizing and cannot produce the depolarization.
Na+ entry through open cGMP-gated channels.
Correct: High cGMP keeps nonselective cation channels open, and the inward Na+ current (dark current) depolarizes the cell compared with the K+ equilibrium potential.
qs.x: High cGMP keeps nonselective cation channels open, and the inward Na+ current (dark current) depolarizes the cell compared with the K+ equilibrium potential. Trap: Thinking photoreceptors are hyperpolarized at rest, as most neurons are.

qs.q: In bright light, the hyperpolarization of the rod arises because:
o: rhodopsin directly closes the cGMP-gated cation channels by binding them.
The effect is mediated by the cGMP decrease through a G protein cascade.
glutamate released in the light binds and inhibits the rod directly.
Glutamate release is the output, and falls in light.
PDE activation lowers cGMP, closing the channels.
Correct: Light activates transducin and PDE, cGMP falls to 10, and channel closure removes the depolarizing dark current.
light increases cGMP, which opens K+ channels and lets potassium leave.
cGMP decreases in light, as in Table 1.
qs.x: Light activates transducin and PDE, cGMP falls to 10, and channel closure removes the depolarizing dark current. Trap: Assuming light activates a channel directly, as in ionotropic receptors.

qs.q: The result with bright light plus IBMX supports the conclusion that:
o: cGMP breakdown is required for light-induced hyperpolarization.
Correct: With PDE blocked, cGMP stays at 90 and the rod remains near -42 mV with high glutamate release despite bright light.
glutamate release is independent of membrane potential in rods.
Release tracked potential in all four conditions.
cGMP breakdown is not involved, because light is still present in the assay.
The persistence of depolarization indicates the opposite.
IBMX activates rhodopsin even without a photon.
The cell still behaves as in darkness, so there is no activation.
qs.x: With PDE blocked, cGMP stays at 90 and the rod remains near -42 mV with high glutamate release despite bright light. Trap: Concluding that the presence of the stimulus (light) alone determines the response.

qs.q: A diet deficient in vitamin A would be expected to impair night vision mainly because:
o: vitamin A is the metabolic precursor from which rods synthesize cGMP.
cGMP is made from GTP.
vitamin A is the precursor of retinal, which rhodopsin requires.
Correct: Retinal derives from vitamin A; without it, rhodopsin cannot be regenerated, and rods in dim light are affected first.
vitamin A activates the PDE directly, independent of transducin.
Activation of PDE depends on transducin.
vitamin A serves as the neurotransmitter released by rods.
Rods use glutamate.
qs.x: Retinal derives from vitamin A; without it, rhodopsin cannot be regenerated, and rods in dim light are affected first. Trap: Linking vitamin A deficiency to cones or the lens rather than to rhodopsin in rods.

passages.title: FL03 · CARS · Passage 1
text: Architects have long admired buildings that no architect designed. The farmhouses of a mountain valley, the courtyard houses of a desert town, the stilted dwellings of a tidal village: such structures are praised for their economy, their fit with climate, and a kind of visual calm that professionally designed buildings rarely achieve. The usual explanation is that vernacular builders were wiser than their modern successors, that generations of trial and error had distilled into every roof pitch a knowledge that no drawing board could replace. This explanation flatters the past, and like most flattery it conceals as much as it reveals.

The surviving vernacular buildings we photograph are survivors in a literal sense. Houses that leaked, collapsed, or burned were not preserved as models of regional wisdom; they were abandoned and, within a generation, forgotten. What remains is a filtered sample, and filtering by itself can produce the appearance of design without any designer, much as a riverbed sorts its stones by size without intending to. To say that the builders knew what they were doing is therefore partly to mistake the output of selection for the content of understanding.

Yet the opposite conclusion, that vernacular architecture is merely accident dressed in nostalgia, is no better. Tradition is not a lottery. Builders worked with a small repertoire of materials and techniques, and they could observe at close range how their neighbors' choices fared in storms and winters. Errors were visible, and they were costly enough to be remembered. A community that rebuilt after every flood learned to build on higher ground, and the learning was real even if it was never written down. What distinguishes this knowledge from the professional's is its form: it is tacit, local, and slow. It cannot be transferred to another climate without loss, and it offers no guidance when conditions change, as the tradition of timber construction discovered when the forests that supplied it were cut.

This last point exposes a weakness in the romantic view that is rarely acknowledged. Vernacular forms are well adapted only to the conditions that shaped them. When a village acquires cheap cement, a road, and a new set of expectations about comfort, the old wisdom has nothing to say, because it was never wisdom about alternatives. The same people who built a flawless thatched roof may build a poor concrete one, not from decline but because the feedback that refined the first has not yet had time to refine the second. Modern architecture's characteristic confidence, its willingness to design for conditions that have no precedent, is the reverse side of this limitation. Professionals can reason about novel situations precisely because they have abstracted principles from particular cases, at the price of sometimes abstracting away something the particular cases contained.

It would be a mistake, then, to treat the two modes as rivals in a contest for the title of true architecture. They are better seen as complementary answers to different problems. Tradition is excellent at refining a solution under stable conditions; theory is better when conditions are unstable or unknown. The architects who have learned most from vernacular building have generally not copied its surfaces, the mud walls and deep eaves, but have tried to reproduce its habit of attending closely to how a building actually performs once people live in it. That habit, more than any pattern of walls or windows, is what the best anonymous builders possessed, and it is the one thing professional training can easily neglect.

qs.q: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?
o: Vernacular buildings are admired only because the poorly built ones have vanished, so surviving examples teach architects almost nothing about building well.
The author grants that selection plays a role but insists that the learning was real.
Vernacular building embodies real but tacit, local knowledge that fails under changed conditions, so it complements professional design.
Correct: This covers the author's rejection of both the romantic and the dismissive views and the closing claim of complementarity.
Modern architects should imitate the materials and visible forms of vernacular buildings wherever possible, since those forms hold the accumulated wisdom of builders.
The author says the best learners copied the habit of attending to performance, not the surfaces.
Professional architecture is superior to vernacular building because it can reason from first principles about conditions for which no precedent exists in any tradition.
The author calls the two modes complementary and credits tradition with strengths theory lacks.
qs.x: This covers the author's rejection of both the romantic and the dismissive views and the closing claim of complementarity. Trap: Latching onto the survivorship argument of the second paragraph and treating it as the thesis, when the author goes on to qualify it.

qs.q: The author compares the filtering of surviving buildings to a riverbed sorting stones by size in order to illustrate that:
o: the appearance of design can arise from a selection process without anyone intending it.
Correct: The comparison is introduced right after the point that surviving structures are a filtered sample.
vernacular builders deliberately sorted their methods by performance over many generations.
The riverbed sorts without intention; the analogy denies deliberate design.
natural forces, not human choices, determined the form of traditional buildings.
The author says builders did learn from observation; only the survival pattern is compared to a natural process.
old buildings are as predictable in their shapes as river stones are in theirs.
Predictability of form is not the point; the point is the origin of apparent order.
qs.x: The comparison is introduced right after the point that surviving structures are a filtered sample. Trap: Reading the analogy as saying that nature, not people, made the buildings, rather than as a point about selection.

qs.q: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that vernacular builders' learning was real?
o: Surviving vernacular buildings in snowy regions have steeper roofs than those in dry regions.
This fits the claim that local conditions shaped practice, so it supports rather than weakens.
Builders in many regions could not explain in words why they chose particular roof pitches.
The author already says the knowledge was tacit and unwritten.
Cement houses in newly modernized villages often perform worse than the thatched houses they replaced.
The author predicts this and attributes it to lack of feedback time, not to a lack of earlier learning.
Communities repeatedly rebuilt on the same flood-prone sites for centuries despite recurrent losses.
Correct: If feedback from visible, costly errors did not alter practice, then the claim that tradition refined solutions through observation is undermined.
qs.x: If feedback from visible, costly errors did not alter practice, then the claim that tradition refined solutions through observation is undermined. Trap: Choosing evidence that the knowledge was unspoken; the author concedes that it was tacit.

qs.q: Based on the passage, which of the following would the author most likely predict about a vernacular builder who moved to a region with a very different climate?
o: The builder would quickly outperform local professionals because tacit knowledge of one climate adapts easily to the conditions of any other.
The author says such knowledge is slow and local, not easily adaptive.
The builder would apply abstract principles of physics to design for the new conditions, since tacit knowledge transfers poorly but theory does not.
Abstracting principles is described as the professional's mode, not the vernacular builder's.
The builder's methods would work equally well in the new region because good building practice is universal across climates and materials.
This contradicts the claim that vernacular forms are adapted only to the conditions that shaped them.
The builder's inherited methods would offer little guidance, so good results would depend on new feedback.
Correct: The author says tradition cannot be transferred to another climate without loss and gives no guidance when conditions change.
qs.x: The author says tradition cannot be transferred to another climate without loss and gives no guidance when conditions change. Trap: Assuming that wisdom accumulated in one place is general wisdom, which the passage explicitly denies.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the view that vernacular builders were wiser than modern architects is best described as:
o: outright rejection based on the claim that tradition is a lottery whose successes owe nothing to learning.
The author explicitly says tradition is not a lottery.
qualified skepticism that grants a basis of truth while exposing what the view omits.
Correct: The author calls the view flattering and incomplete yet affirms that the learning was real.
enthusiastic endorsement tempered only by concern for modern building materials and their weaker durability.
The first paragraph says the explanation flatters the past and conceals as much as it reveals.
indifference, since the author thinks the two modes of building cannot be meaningfully compared with one another.
The author compares them at length and calls them complementary.
qs.x: The author calls the view flattering and incomplete yet affirms that the learning was real. Trap: Treating the criticism of the romantic view as total rejection, and missing the author's concession in the third paragraph.

qs.q: Which of the following practices by an architect would best reflect the approach the author recommends in the final paragraph?
o: Building houses with mud walls and deep eaves in every climate in order to honor local tradition and its accumulated lessons.
The author says the best learners did not copy surfaces such as mud walls and deep eaves.
Preparing designs entirely from physical models and computer simulations and never visiting finished sites afterward.
This ignores performance in use, which the author says training tends to neglect.
Measuring energy use and occupant comfort in completed buildings and adjusting later designs accordingly.
Correct: This reproduces the vernacular builders' habit of attending to how a building performs once people live in it.
Rejecting all new materials and relying only on techniques that have been proven over many centuries of use.
The author says tradition offers no guidance for new materials and conditions.
qs.x: This reproduces the vernacular builders' habit of attending to how a building performs once people live in it. Trap: Picking the answer that copies vernacular forms, the exact approach the author says is not the useful lesson.

passages.title: FL03 · CARS · Passage 2
text: Linguists who study how grammar arises have noticed a curious regularity: the small, colorless words that hold sentences together tend to be worn-down remnants of words that once meant something vivid. English will, now a marker of the future, began as a verb of wanting, and one can still hear the older sense in the phrase "willing participant." The French future tense, as in chanterai, is the fossil of a Latin construction meaning roughly "I have to sing," in which the verb habere was fused onto the infinitive until no speaker could detect the seam. Such cases are examples of what is called grammaticalization, the process by which lexical items acquire grammatical functions and, in doing so, lose phonetic substance and concrete meaning.

The standard account holds that the process is driven by frequency and by a kind of economy. A phrase used constantly is pronounced quickly; quickly pronounced phrases are slurred; slurred phrases fuse. "Going to" becomes "gonna," and once the reduced form is available, speakers no longer hear "going" as motion at all. Meanwhile the meaning bleaches. A verb of motion toward a place becomes a marker of intention, then a mere signal of what will happen, so that one can say that the sky is going to rain without implying that the sky is going anywhere. Grammar, on this picture, is perpetually being renewed from the vocabulary below it.

The account is attractive, but it invites an overstatement that some linguists have resisted. If grammar emerges from erosion, one might conclude that grammatical systems are mere debris, the accidental residue of speech habits, and that nothing about them reflects the structure of thought. This conclusion does not follow. That a form originates in slurred speech tells us nothing about whether it later takes on a systematic role. A coastline is shaped by erosion, but it does not follow that a harbor is a random feature of the map; once it exists, ships organize around it. Likewise, once a marker of the future has become obligatory, other parts of the language are arranged around it, and speakers acquire expectations about where it will appear and what it may combine with. Origins and functions are separate questions.

A second difficulty concerns direction. The pathway from concrete to abstract seems so common that some have treated it as a law: body parts become spatial prepositions, as when "back" yields "behind"; spatial terms become temporal ones; temporal terms become logical connectives. Yet the evidence for such a law is, by its nature, drawn from languages with long written records, where changes can be traced. It is possible that the reverse pathway, from abstract to concrete, occurs too and is simply harder to detect, because the resulting words look like ordinary vocabulary and attract no notice. The unidirectionality of grammaticalization may thus be partly an artifact of how linguists have looked.

Neither difficulty undermines the central insight, which is that grammar is not a separate layer laid on top of vocabulary but a continuation of it. What the debate shows is that the insight can be pressed too far in two ways: by treating the origin of a form as the explanation of its present role, and by treating a pattern observed in well-documented languages as a universal. The more cautious position is also the more interesting one. It asks why concrete meanings so often become abstract ones without insisting that they must, and it treats the answer as something to be discovered in the speech of living communities and not simply asserted from the armchair.

qs.q: Which of the following best summarizes the author's position on grammaticalization?
o: It reveals real continuity between vocabulary and grammar, but does not show that origins explain function or that one direction is universal.
Correct: The final paragraph accepts the central insight and names two overextensions.
It shows that grammatical systems are accidental debris of worn-down words, with no systematic connection to thought or to meaning.
The author says this conclusion does not follow.
It is a universal law, applying in every language without exception, by which concrete meanings always become abstract and then grammatical.
The author suggests the unidirectional pattern may be partly an artifact of sources.
It is best studied through languages with long written records, because only such languages provide reliable evidence of change over time, the author holds.
The author notes this reliance as a source of bias, not as a recommendation.
qs.x: The final paragraph accepts the central insight and names two overextensions. Trap: Accepting the 'law' phrasing in the second half of the passage as the author's view, when the author questions it.

qs.q: The author mentions the phrase "willing participant" in the first paragraph primarily to show that:
o: the word "will" has recently reversed course in English, moving from a grammatical use back to a lexical one.
No such reversal is claimed; the lexical sense is older.
English grammar is more resistant to erosion than French grammar, which has worn down its older forms faster.
No comparison of resistance is made.
traces of an older lexical meaning can persist in forms that have become grammatical.
Correct: The sentence says one can still hear the older sense of wanting in that phrase.
speakers cannot reliably tell the future marker apart from the adjective in ordinary conversation.
The point is that an older sense is audible, not that speakers confuse them.
qs.x: The sentence says one can still hear the older sense of wanting in that phrase. Trap: Reading the example as evidence of recent change rather than as a surviving trace of the origin.

qs.q: The author compares a coastline and a harbor in the third paragraph in order to argue that:
o: how a feature originated does not settle what role it plays once it exists.
Correct: The text states that origins and functions are separate questions, and the harbor organizes ships regardless of how it was formed.
grammar is shaped by speech habits in the same way waves shape a shoreline.
This is the premise being granted, not the point of the analogy.
grammatical markers, like harbors, are placed where speakers need them most.
Nothing suggests markers are placed purposefully.
grammatical change occurs too slowly for speakers to observe it directly.
The analogy is not about the rate of change.
qs.x: The text states that origins and functions are separate questions, and the harbor organizes ships regardless of how it was formed. Trap: Taking the erosion half of the analogy as the point rather than the contrast between origin and function.

qs.q: Which of the following discoveries would most directly challenge the claim that grammaticalization is unidirectional?
o: A language in which the word for "hand" has become a preposition meaning "beside," as in several well-studied families.
This is a concrete-to-abstract change, which fits the pattern.
A language in which a future marker fused with the verb stem and was worn down over several centuries of use.
Fusion and erosion are the standard pattern.
A documented language in which a grammatical suffix has become an independent noun with a concrete meaning.
Correct: This is a documented abstract-to-concrete change, the reverse pathway the author thinks may be underdetected.
A language with no written records in which words for spatial relations are also used to express time.
This is concrete-to-abstract again and would not conflict with the pattern.
qs.x: This is a documented abstract-to-concrete change, the reverse pathway the author thinks may be underdetected. Trap: Choosing an example of the pattern itself rather than a counterexample to its direction.

qs.q: According to the passage, the evidence for the unidirectionality of grammaticalization is problematic because it:
o: comes mainly from languages with long written records, so it may reflect where linguists could look.
Correct: The author says such evidence is drawn from languages with records, and that the reverse pathway may be undetected.
has been contradicted by studies of French and Latin that found grammatical markers turning into full words.
The French example is cited as support for the standard account, not as a contradiction.
rests on frequency counts that cannot be verified in living languages with no written history.
Frequency is part of the standard account, not the evidence for direction.
applies only to grammatical markers of the future tense and not to other grammatical categories.
The passage names several pathways, such as body parts to spatial terms.
qs.x: The author says such evidence is drawn from languages with records, and that the reverse pathway may be undetected. Trap: Overlooking the sampling problem and assuming the objection concerns the data's quality rather than its coverage.

qs.q: Which of the following is the best example of grammaticalization as the passage describes it?
o: A new word for a computer program enters the language and is adopted by most speakers within a generation.
This is an addition to vocabulary, not a shift to a grammatical function.
A noun is borrowed from another language and keeps its original pronunciation, spelling, and meaning.
Borrowing retains meaning and form; no grammatical function is acquired.
A verb meaning "to finish" comes to mark completed action and is gradually shortened to a particle.
Correct: A lexical item loses concrete meaning and acquires a grammatical function while reducing in form.
A particle that once marked tense becomes a verb with a vivid concrete meaning and full inflection.
This would be the reverse pathway, not the pattern described.
qs.x: A lexical item loses concrete meaning and acquires a grammatical function while reducing in form. Trap: Selecting the reverse pathway because it also involves a word changing category.

passages.title: FL03 · CARS · Passage 3
text: Few episodes in the history of chemistry are retold as often, or as unfairly, as the rise and fall of phlogiston. In the textbook version, eighteenth-century chemists believed that combustible bodies contained an invisible substance, phlogiston, released during burning; Lavoisier then weighed the products of combustion, showed that they were heavier than the original metals, and in a single stroke replaced fantasy with oxygen and measurement. The story is tidy, and it makes the phlogiston theorists look like men who refused to weigh things.

They weighed things. Their difficulty was that the theory they held explained a great deal that chemists then needed explained. Phlogiston unified a set of apparently unrelated processes: metals calcined when heated and could be restored by heating with charcoal; sulfur burned and could be regenerated from its acid; respiration, fermentation, and rusting all seemed to be slow forms of the same loss. A chemist who held that metals were compounds of a calx and phlogiston could explain why charcoal, a substance rich in the principle of flammability, returned the metal from its calx. This was not a fanciful claim but an organizing principle that guided experiments and predicted outcomes, and it produced real discoveries, among them the isolation of several gases that Priestley described in terms derived from the theory.

The gain in weight on calcination was a genuine anomaly, but it was not obviously fatal. Some defenders proposed that phlogiston had negative weight, an idea that sounds absurd to the modern ear but was not absurd to those who thought of fire as a buoyant, upward-tending principle. Others observed that weight was not yet universally accepted as the measure of material quantity, since chemists also relied on properties such as color, texture, and reactivity to identify what a substance was. To insist that mass must be conserved in every reaction was to import a commitment that Lavoisier's own program, not the evidence alone, supplied. The evidence did not compel his assumption; his assumption made the evidence compelling.

What eventually decided the matter was not a single decisive experiment but the accumulating cost of keeping the older theory alive. Each anomaly could be accommodated, but accommodation required additional hypotheses, and the additional hypotheses did not predict anything new. The oxygen account, by contrast, handled the weight gains without adjustment, explained combustion and respiration with one mechanism, and proved extensible to the new quantitative methods that chemists increasingly valued. Within a generation, the question of which theory was correct had become, for most practitioners, a question of which theory was useful for the work they wished to do.

It would be a mistake to draw from this history the cynical lesson that scientific theories win by fashion. The oxygen theory prevailed because it was better, in ways that can be specified. But it would be equally mistaken to conclude that its rival was foolish. The phlogiston chemists were responding to the same world with the same instruments, and many of their reasoning patterns, such as seeking a common principle behind diverse phenomena, are the same patterns that later chemists would use to good effect. A history that makes losers into fools is also a history that cannot explain why the debate lasted so long, or why intelligent people took part in it. The most useful way to read the episode is as a case in which a reasonable theory was displaced by a more productive one, a transition far more instructive, and far more common, than the replacement of error by truth.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
o: Lavoisier's weighing experiments conclusively refuted phlogiston theory in a single stroke, after which chemists abandoned it.
The author calls this the unfair textbook version.
Scientific theories are accepted mainly because of fashion and influence rather than because of evidence.
The author calls this a cynical lesson and says oxygen theory won because it was better.
Phlogiston chemists were mistaken because they did not use the balance in their work, relying on qualitative impressions alone, as the textbook says.
The author's opening point is that they weighed things.
Phlogiston theory was reasonable and productive but was displaced by a more productive rival, so its history should not be told as truth defeating folly.
Correct: This matches the final paragraph's reading of the episode.
qs.x: This matches the final paragraph's reading of the episode. Trap: Accepting the textbook narrative of the first paragraph as the author's own conclusion.

qs.q: According to the passage, how did a phlogiston chemist explain the restoration of a metal when its calx was heated with charcoal?
o: Charcoal absorbed oxygen from the calx, leaving behind the pure metal and carbon dioxide.
Oxygen belongs to the rival theory.
Charcoal, rich in the principle of flammability, supplied phlogiston to the calx.
Correct: The second paragraph gives this explanation directly.
The calx lost weight as phlogiston of negative weight was driven off by the heat of the charcoal fire.
Negative weight was a response to weight gain on calcination, not the explanation for restoration.
Heating decomposed the calx into sulfur and its acid, which then recombined with the charcoal.
Sulfur is mentioned for a separate example.
qs.x: The second paragraph gives this explanation directly. Trap: Mixing the rival oxygen explanation into the phlogiston account.

qs.q: The statement that "his assumption made the evidence compelling" most directly suggests that:
o: Lavoisier invented or altered his data in order to make the evidence fit his preferred theory.
The passage does not suggest any fabrication.
the weight evidence persuaded only those who already accepted conservation of mass as a guide.
Correct: The author says conservation of mass was Lavoisier's commitment, not something the evidence alone supplied.
the weight measurements were too imprecise to carry real force in the argument, whatever he assumed.
The author calls the weight gain a genuine anomaly, not a measurement problem.
phlogiston theorists did not understand how to interpret the readings of the balance.
The author says they weighed and had reasonable responses.
qs.x: The author says conservation of mass was Lavoisier's commitment, not something the evidence alone supplied. Trap: Reading the claim as an accusation of dishonesty instead of a point about assumptions.

qs.q: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that oxygen theory prevailed because it was better in specifiable ways?
o: Oxygen theory explained combustion and respiration with a single mechanism, whereas phlogiston theory needed several separate hypotheses.
This supports the author's claim.
Most chemists who adopted oxygen theory did so because of a few prominent figures, without evaluating the quantitative evidence.
Correct: If adoption was driven by influence rather than evaluation of explanatory merits, the claim of prevailing on specifiable merits is weakened.
Some phlogiston theorists proposed adjustments that predicted no new phenomena and were never tested.
The author already says this and uses it as support.
Priestley, who isolated several gases, continued to defend phlogiston theory for the rest of his life, even after most colleagues had abandoned it.
One holdout does not show that the majority were not persuaded by specifiable merits.
qs.x: If adoption was driven by influence rather than evaluation of explanatory merits, the claim of prevailing on specifiable merits is weakened. Trap: Choosing evidence that merely repeats the passage's support for oxygen theory.

qs.q: The sentence "They weighed things" serves primarily to:
o: directly contradict an impression created by the textbook account.
Correct: The preceding paragraph said the story makes them look like men who refused to weigh things, and this short sentence rebuts it.
introduce a list of the instruments used by eighteenth-century chemists.
No list follows; the paragraph is about the theory's explanatory power.
concede that phlogiston chemists were less rigorous than Lavoisier.
The sentence asserts rigor, not a deficit.
suggest that weight was the only evidence phlogiston chemists valued.
The author notes they also relied on color, texture, and reactivity.
qs.x: The preceding paragraph said the story makes them look like men who refused to weigh things, and this short sentence rebuts it. Trap: Treating the short sentence as a transition rather than as a rebuttal of the first paragraph.

qs.q: Which situation is most analogous to the way the phlogiston theory was eventually displaced?
o: A model is abandoned after a single experiment gives a result that contradicts it, and no rival model is needed.
The author says no single decisive experiment decided the matter.
Researchers adopt a theory because it is simpler to teach, even though it explains fewer of the observations that matter.
The author says the winner explained more with one mechanism.
A theory is retained because its supporters hold prestigious posts, even though it handles all observations well and has no competitor.
This is about status, which the author does not give as the reason for displacement.
A model gets a new patch after each conflicting observation, none of the patches predicts anything new, and a rival needs none.
Correct: This repeats the structure of the fourth paragraph: accommodation by additional hypotheses that predict nothing new, set against a rival that needs no adjustment.
qs.x: This repeats the structure of the fourth paragraph: accommodation by additional hypotheses that predict nothing new, set against a rival that needs no adjustment. Trap: Choosing the single-decisive-experiment picture the passage explicitly rejects.

passages.title: FL03 · CARS · Passage 4
text: The unreliable narrator is usually introduced to students as a kind of puzzle. A story is told in the first person by someone who, as the reader gradually discovers, is deceiving others, deceiving himself, or simply failing to understand what he reports. The reader's task is to detect the gap between what the narrator says and what the story shows, and to recover the truth the narrator conceals. The critic who prizes such narratives often praises them for their ironies, the pleasure of seeing farther than the speaker sees. This account is accurate as far as it goes, but it encourages a narrow view of what unreliability does.

The puzzle model assumes that behind the narrator's account lies a stable set of facts, which the attentive reader can reconstruct as a detective reconstructs a crime. In some novels this assumption holds. When the butler who narrates a memoir of loyal service lets slip details revealing that his employer sympathized with a hateful cause, the reader can fill in what the butler cannot bring himself to say. But in other works, no such reconstruction is possible. The narrator's version may be contradicted by a second version, and the second by a third, with no authoritative account to adjudicate among them. In such cases, to speak of unreliability is almost misleading, for the concept presupposes a standard of reliability against which the narrator can be measured, and the text declines to supply one.

The difference matters because it changes what the reader is invited to do. With the puzzle, the reader is a solver, and the pleasure lies in the click of the solution. With the irresolvable narrative, the reader is asked to dwell in uncertainty, and the interest shifts from what happened to why a person would need to tell the story in this way. The distortions become the subject. A narrator who recalls a childhood summer as idyllic while the details he supplies point to neglect is not only concealing a fact; he is displaying the machinery by which memory protects the self. Here unreliability is not a barrier between the reader and the truth but a form of truth about the narrator, one that no straightforward report could convey.

Some critics worry that this second kind of reading licenses anything. If no account is authoritative, they say, the interpreter may attribute any motive to the narrator and find confirmation everywhere. The worry is real, but it overlooks the constraints that remain. A reading must still account for the particular words on the page, for which details are offered and which omitted, for where the narrator's syntax tightens or his tone turns defensive. These features are as available to checking as the clues in a mystery; the difference is that they support a portrait of a mind and not the solution to a crime. An interpretation of a mind can be better or worse, though it cannot be final.

None of this requires abandoning the older view. The detective's pleasure is real and the novels that provide it are worth reading. What it requires is a recognition that unreliability is not one device but a family of them, and that a reader who approaches every deceptive narrator as a riddle will mistake some of the subtlest fiction for a failure of clarity. To read well is partly to learn which kind of narrator one is dealing with, and to adjust one's expectations of the story accordingly: to look for an answer where an answer exists, and for a portrait where it does not.

qs.q: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Unreliable narrators are best understood as puzzles in which the reader detects and then corrects the narrator's deceptions to recover what happened.
The author calls this account accurate as far as it goes but too narrow.
Unreliable narration takes two forms, one inviting reconstruction of facts and one offering a portrait of a mind, and readers must tell them apart.
Correct: The final paragraph states this directly.
Interpreters of unreliable narrators may attribute any motive they wish to the narrator, since no account of a novel is ever authoritative.
The author says this worry overlooks constraints from the text.
Novels with irresolvable narratives are more subtle than those with reconstructable facts and so are superior works of literary art, the author holds.
The author values both kinds and does not rank them.
qs.x: The final paragraph states this directly. Trap: Choosing the puzzle model, which the passage introduces first, then qualifies.

qs.q: The author says that speaking of unreliability can be "almost misleading" in some works because:
o: the narrators in such works are actually telling the truth, so that nothing in their accounts needs to be corrected.
The text does not claim the narrators are truthful, only that no standard exists.
readers cannot detect any gap between the narrator's words and the story the text itself tells.
Readers can detect distortions; what is missing is an authoritative version.
the concept presupposes a standard of reliability that such texts never supply.
Correct: The second paragraph gives this reason.
critics have used the term too broadly in the past and so drained it of precise meaning.
The reason given is conceptual, not historical.
qs.x: The second paragraph gives this reason. Trap: Confusing the absence of an authoritative account with the presence of an honest narrator.

qs.q: Which of the following would the author most likely say about a novel in which three narrators give conflicting versions of an event, none confirmed by the text?
o: It is a failure of clarity, because the reader cannot recover what actually happened in the event.
The author says this is the mistake of treating all such narrators as riddles.
It is best read as a portrait of why each narrator needs to tell the story as he does, not as a puzzle.
Correct: This is the author's treatment of irresolvable narratives in the third paragraph.
It should be reread until one narrator is shown, from clues in the text, to be the reliable one.
The text declines to supply a standard that would settle this.
It is a poor example of unreliability because none of the narrators is deceiving anyone about anything at all.
Deception is not required; the narrators' distortions become the subject.
qs.x: This is the author's treatment of irresolvable narratives in the third paragraph. Trap: Applying the detective approach where the text provides no authoritative account.

qs.q: The author's response to the worry that the second kind of reading "licenses anything" depends on which assumption?
o: Readers are generally more skilled at interpreting minds than at solving puzzles, so their readings of narrators can be trusted.
The author does not compare reader skills.
Interpretations of narrators' minds can eventually be made final if enough textual evidence is gathered.
The author says an interpretation can be better or worse but not final.
Features of the text, such as omissions and shifts in tone, can be checked even without a final account of the facts.
Correct: The author answers by pointing to textual constraints that make some readings better than others.
The narrator's motives are always stated openly somewhere in the novel, where the reader can check them.
The author's examples concern what the narrator conceals or fails to say.
qs.x: The author answers by pointing to textual constraints that make some readings better than others. Trap: Overlooking the author's statement that such interpretation is not final.

qs.q: According to the passage, critics who prize the puzzle model typically praise unreliable narration for:
o: the unreliability of memory as a theme.
This is a feature the author associates with the second kind of reading.
the irony of seeing farther than the speaker sees.
Correct: This is stated in the first paragraph.
the absence of any authoritative version of events.
This characterizes the irresolvable narratives, not the puzzle model.
the accuracy with which it depicts how memory protects the self.
This belongs to the author's discussion of the second kind of reading, not to the critics' praise.
qs.x: This is stated in the first paragraph. Trap: Attributing the author's own second-kind reading to the critics who prize the puzzle model.

qs.q: A narrator insists that he felt no resentment toward his brother, yet describes in detail each occasion on which he declined to help him. Which description best fits the passage's idea of unreliability as "a form of truth about the narrator"?
o: The narrator is a liar whose real actions can be reconstructed by the reader as in a detective story.
This describes the puzzle model, not the second kind of unreliability.
The contradiction reveals the narrator's need to deny a feeling that his own account displays.
Correct: The distortion itself conveys something about the narrator, as in the idyllic-summer example.
The narrator's account is simply unclear and so cannot be interpreted.
The author says such accounts can be interpreted by attending to the text.
The narrator has been replaced by a more authoritative speaker midway through the story.
Nothing suggests a change of narrator.
qs.x: The distortion itself conveys something about the narrator, as in the idyllic-summer example. Trap: Reducing the example to a simple lie that the reader can solve.

passages.title: FL03 · CARS · Passage 5
text: Economists who study asset bubbles face a problem that physicians would recognize: the condition can be diagnosed with certainty only after it has ended. A bubble is conventionally defined as a rise in an asset's price far above its fundamental value, the value justified by the income the asset can be expected to produce. By this definition, the Dutch fervor for tulip bulbs in the 1630s, in which single bulbs were said to sell for the price of a house before prices collapsed in early 1637, has long served as the archetype. It is cited in textbooks and in popular warnings against speculation as the clearest case of collective irrationality in market history.

Recent scholarship has complicated that picture in two ways. First, the surviving records suggest that the episode was narrower than the legend. Many of the most dramatic prices appear in contracts for future delivery that were never settled, and the people involved seem to have been a small circle of traders and prosperous craftsmen, not the whole of Dutch society. When the market fell, the authorities were reluctant to enforce the unsettled contracts, which limited the losses that individuals actually bore. The story of ruined families and a damaged national economy rests largely on moralizing pamphlets written by observers who disapproved of the trade, and such sources are not neutral witnesses to economic outcomes.

Second, and more fundamentally, the notion of fundamental value is less secure for rare bulbs than for shares or bonds. A rare variety could be propagated, and a bulb that produced distinctive flowers could in principle yield offspring that would be sold in later seasons. Under such conditions, a high price might reflect a reasonable, if optimistic, expectation about future sales and not a collective delusion. Whether the expectation was reasonable cannot be settled by observing that prices fell, because prices fall after many forecasts that were sensible when made. To call a price irrational because it later declined is to judge a decision by its outcome, which is precisely the error that forecasters are trained to avoid.

The skeptic about bubbles draws a strong conclusion from this: that the concept is a retrospective label with no explanatory power, applied to any decline that disappoints investors. That conclusion goes too far. The difficulty of identifying a bubble in advance does not show that no market has ever been driven by expectations detached from any plausible income stream. Where traders can be shown to have held and expressed beliefs that rested on nothing except the expectation that others would pay more, the label has content. The right lesson is a more modest one: the concept is a demanding one, and a historian who wishes to apply it must show not just that a price rose and fell but that participants' expectations were unreasonable at the time they were formed, on information available to them.

This standard is harder to meet than popular accounts suggest, and for that reason it should make us more cautious about the lesson routinely drawn from tulips. If the episode was smaller, shorter, and more defensible than the legend, then it is a poor basis for the claim that markets periodically lose their minds. It may still be true that they do. But the evidence for that proposition will have to come from cases that have been examined with the care now being applied to this one, and from a definition of irrationality that does not depend on knowing how the story ended.

qs.q: Which of the following best summarizes the main argument of the passage?
o: The tulip episode is a weaker case of a bubble than believed, and invoking the concept requires showing expectations were unreasonable when formed.
Correct: This captures both the reassessment of the tulip case and the standard proposed for using the concept.
Asset bubbles are a myth, because every price that later falls was reasonable when set, so the concept has no use in economics.
The author says the skeptic's conclusion goes too far.
Tulip prices were fully reasonable, since rare bulbs could be propagated and sold at high prices in later seasons, and the episode shows that no market is ever driven by detached expectations.
The author says a high price might have reflected reasonable expectations, not that it was.
The Dutch authorities caused the collapse by refusing to enforce contracts for future delivery, which panicked the buyers of bulbs.
The refusal is said to have limited losses; it is not blamed for the collapse.
qs.x: This captures both the reassessment of the tulip case and the standard proposed for using the concept. Trap: Moving from 'might have been reasonable' to 'was reasonable,' a stronger claim than the author makes.

qs.q: The author mentions the "moralizing pamphlets" to suggest that:
o: accounts of widespread ruin may be unreliable because their authors disapproved.
Correct: The author says such sources are not neutral witnesses to economic outcomes.
the Dutch population was largely unaware of the trade in bulbs until it was over, so losses were small.
The text says the participants were a small circle, not that the public was unaware.
pamphlets provide the best available evidence for the scale of losses suffered by Dutch households.
The author discounts them for this purpose.
contracts for future delivery were never recorded, so the extent of the trading cannot be estimated.
The text says the contracts were unsettled, not unrecorded, and does not link that point to the pamphlets.
qs.x: The author says such sources are not neutral witnesses to economic outcomes. Trap: Reading the pamphlets as supporting evidence because they are contemporary sources.

qs.q: The author describes calling a price irrational "because it later declined" as an error. Which of the following is most analogous?
o: Concluding that a forecast was sound because its author is widely respected in the field.
This appeals to authority, not outcome.
Concluding that a medicine works because the patients who take it later say they feel better.
This is a causal reasoning error, not outcome-based judging of a decision.
Concluding that a poem is excellent because a great many people have read it over the years.
This infers quality from popularity, not from the outcome of a decision.
Concluding that a surgeon erred because a patient died after a low-risk operation.
Correct: Both judge a decision by its outcome rather than by the information available when it was made.
qs.x: Both judge a decision by its outcome rather than by the information available when it was made. Trap: Matching on surface features such as medicine or forecasting rather than the outcome-based fallacy.

qs.q: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the claim that the tulip episode was narrower than the legend?
o: Many of the most dramatic prices were recorded in contracts that were never settled, so that little money ever changed hands afterward.
This is already part of the author's evidence for a narrow episode.
Moralizing pamphlets of the time exaggerated the extent of ruin to make a point about greed and speculation.
This supports the author's view.
Rare varieties of bulbs could be propagated into new bulbs that were sold in later seasons.
This bears on fundamental value, not on how many people took part.
Probate records show many households of every social class held settled bulb contracts and lost large sums.
Correct: This would show broad participation and real losses, contrary to the narrow, mostly unsettled picture.
qs.x: This would show broad participation and real losses, contrary to the narrow, mostly unsettled picture. Trap: Choosing facts already used in the passage's case instead of evidence against it.

qs.q: The author's response to the skeptic who calls bubbles a mere retrospective label rests on the claim that:
o: traders of rare assets always form irrational expectations, because scarcity itself distorts their judgment of value over time.
The author says nothing so general.
prices rarely fall after forecasts that were sensible, so every decline signals earlier irrationality.
The author says prices do fall after many sensible forecasts.
historians have already shown, in a large number of documented cases, that bubbles are common in markets.
The author says the evidence will need to come from carefully examined cases.
the difficulty of spotting a bubble beforehand is separate from whether detached expectations ever drive a market.
Correct: The author says the difficulty does not show that no market was driven by expectations detached from income streams.
qs.x: The author says the difficulty does not show that no market was driven by expectations detached from income streams. Trap: Treating the author's partial agreement with the skeptic as complete agreement.

qs.q: Based on the passage, which of the following episodes would the author most readily classify as a bubble?
o: A market in which participants stated that they bought a useless, income-free asset solely to resell it at a higher price.
Correct: This meets the author's criterion of beliefs resting on nothing except expected resale at higher prices.
A market in which prices for a rare asset rose steeply for several months and then fell sharply back to levels near where they had started, ruining many holders.
The author says rising and falling alone does not establish a bubble.
A market in which many investors lost large sums of money after a sharp decline in the price of an asset.
Losses after a decline do not show irrational expectations when formed.
A market in which an asset could be reproduced and sold in later seasons at prices that remained high.
This resembles the tulip case, where high prices could be reasonable.
qs.x: This meets the author's criterion of beliefs resting on nothing except expected resale at higher prices. Trap: Using price rise and collapse as the test, which the author explicitly rejects.

passages.title: FL03 · CARS · Passage 6
text: Readers weep for characters who never lived. Philosophers have long found this puzzling because three plausible claims seem to conflict. First, we feel real emotions toward fictional characters. Second, to feel an emotion such as pity or fear toward someone, one must believe that the person exists and is actually suffering or in danger. Third, we do not believe that fictional characters exist. If all three were true, our emotional responses to novels would be impossible, yet they occur daily. At least one claim must give way, and the history of the debate is largely the history of which one to give up.

One response denies the first claim. On this view, what we feel in front of a film or a novel is not real fear or pity but a quasi-emotion, a make-believe version that we engage in voluntarily and that carries no risk. The viewer who grips her seat during a horror film does not really fear the monster; she pretends to, and the pounding heart is an accompaniment of the pretense. The weakness of this solution is that it sits poorly with how we describe our experience. People who cry at the end of a novel do not report that they pretended to cry; the tears are no more make-believe than tears at a funeral. Moreover, the physiological signs of fear in the cinema are not noticeably different from those of fear elsewhere, and a theory that treats them as merely accompanying a pretense must explain why the body participates so faithfully in a game.

A second response denies the third claim, holding that we suspend disbelief and temporarily believe in the characters while we read. This avoids the awkwardness of denying that the emotions are real, but it fits our behavior badly. A person who believed that a murderer was loose in the room would telephone the police, whereas the reader of a thriller keeps turning pages. The absence of the actions that belief would ordinarily produce is a strong reason to doubt that belief is present. Defenders of the view reply that suspension of disbelief is a special state in which belief is cut off from action, but this reply risks making the notion of belief so thin that it no longer explains anything.

The third response, and the one that has attracted most recent attention, denies the second claim. Emotions, it says, do not require belief in the existence of their objects; they require only that we vividly entertain thoughts about them. We can be moved by the thought of a loss we are merely imagining, as when we dread a conversation that has not occurred and may never occur. If imagining is sufficient to produce emotion in those cases, nothing prevents it from doing so in the case of fiction. Its cost is that it requires a more liberal account of what emotions are than the traditional one, and critics ask whether such an account can still distinguish between pity for a character and mere sentimentality about an idea.

None of these solutions is wholly satisfactory, and it may be that the paradox is not a single puzzle but several. What the debate has accomplished is to show that our ordinary notions of belief, emotion, and imagination are less tightly connected than they first appear, and that a theory of fiction must be a theory of the mind before it can be a theory of art.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the primary purpose of the passage?
o: To argue that the emotions readers feel toward fictional characters are not genuine emotions in any sense.
This is one response the author critiques.
To defend the view that readers never actually believe in the existence of fictional characters.
This is a premise of the puzzle, not the author's argument.
To show that the debate has been settled in favor of the third of the three responses.
The author says none of the solutions is wholly satisfactory.
To present a philosophical puzzle about emotional responses to fiction and evaluate three responses.
Correct: The passage frames the paradox and then assesses each response.
qs.x: The passage frames the paradox and then assesses each response. Trap: Taking the most recent response, given more attention, as the author's endorsed view.

qs.q: The author criticizes the quasi-emotion response mainly on the grounds that it:
o: requires that readers believe in the characters, which the author thinks readers plainly do not.
This is the second response, not the first.
conflicts with how people describe their experience and with the body's apparent participation.
Correct: The author cites people's reports of real tears and the physiological similarity to ordinary fear.
cannot explain why some people enjoy horror films while others find the same films unbearable.
The passage does not discuss this.
treats emotion as a matter of thought and not feeling, so that no physiological response is expected.
This describes the third response.
qs.x: The author cites people's reports of real tears and the physiological similarity to ordinary fear. Trap: Confusing the features of the first response with those of the second or third.

qs.q: The author's treatment of the second response suggests that the response is weak primarily because:
o: readers cannot recall the characters clearly after finishing a long novel, so no belief could have formed.
The passage makes no such claim.
readers of fiction do not act as they would if they believed the danger was real.
Correct: The thriller reader keeps turning pages instead of calling the police.
belief cannot be suspended by any reader, even briefly, so the response collapses at once.
The author says defenders reply that it can, in a special state.
emotion is not required for belief in a character, so the response mislocates the problem.
This would concern the third response and reverses the relation.
qs.x: The thriller reader keeps turning pages instead of calling the police. Trap: Overlooking the behavioral argument and substituting a general claim about belief.

qs.q: Which of the following findings would most undermine the third response?
o: People who vividly imagine difficult future conversations often experience genuine dread and rehearse what they will say.
This supports the response.
People who watch horror films have raised heart rates and sweaty palms while the film is playing.
This is consistent with any of the responses, particularly the first and third.
People rarely feel dread when they vividly imagine an upcoming conversation, though they weep at fictional deaths.
Correct: The third response leans on the claim that vivid imagining produces emotion in ordinary life; this undercuts that continuity with fiction.
People who believe a danger is real usually take protective action, such as calling for help.
This supports the argument against the second response, not the third.
qs.x: The third response leans on the claim that vivid imagining produces emotion in ordinary life; this undercuts that continuity with fiction. Trap: Selecting evidence that supports the third response because it mentions imagination.

qs.q: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument against the second response?
o: Readers of thrillers report feeling suspense but not terror, and many describe the feeling as pleasant and safe.
This leaves the argument intact or concerns degree of emotion.
Most readers know that the characters in the novels they read are invented by the author.
This is the third claim of the puzzle, which the second response denies, so it does not weaken the argument.
People who believe in a faraway disaster they cannot avert often take no action, though the belief is real.
Correct: The argument assumes that belief ordinarily produces action; this shows belief can exist without action.
People call the police when they believe an intruder is nearby, and they do so within minutes.
This supports the author's argument.
qs.x: The argument assumes that belief ordinarily produces action; this shows belief can exist without action. Trap: Choosing facts that restate premises instead of challenging the inference from missing action to missing belief.

qs.q: The author's concluding remark that a theory of fiction "must be a theory of the mind before it can be a theory of art" implies that:
o: works of art should be evaluated chiefly by the strength of the emotions they produce in their readers.
The passage does not discuss evaluation.
explaining responses to fiction requires clarifying the relations among belief, emotion, and imagination.
Correct: The preceding sentence says the debate has shown these notions are less tightly connected than they seemed.
psychologists are better placed than literary critics to resolve the paradox through experiments.
The text does not rank disciplines.
the paradox disappears once readers fully understand that the events in fiction are invented.
The author says none of the solutions is wholly satisfactory.
qs.x: The preceding sentence says the debate has shown these notions are less tightly connected than they seemed. Trap: Taking the conclusion as a claim about art criticism rather than about psychology.

passages.title: FL03 · CARS · Passage 7
text: Literary histories often begin the novel with a birth certificate: a date, a title, an author. Yet the quarrel over which book was the first novel has lasted for centuries without resolution, which suggests that the question is badly formed. Ancient prose romances, medieval tales of chivalry, and the Spanish picaresque narratives of the sixteenth century all have their champions, and each claim rests on a prior decision about what the form requires. If a novel must depict ordinary private life, the romances fall out; if it need only be long, prose, and fictional, nearly any extended tale qualifies. The dispute is therefore less about facts than about definitions, and definitions are chosen to serve the argument of whoever proposes them.

A more productive approach treats the novel as a bundle of conventions that came together gradually under changing conditions of reading. Consider the expansion of print in eighteenth-century Europe. Cheaper paper, a growing class of literate city dwellers, and the spread of circulating libraries created a market for narratives that could be read privately, at leisure, and without the classical education that older genres presumed. Writers who supplied this market borrowed freely: the letter from commerce, the diary from religious self-examination, the travel report from the merchant's log. The pretense of authenticity, whether a "found" manuscript or an editor's preface insisting that the events were true, was not a trick played on naive readers. It was an economical way of persuading a public that still regarded invented stories as frivolous, even morally suspect, that a tale about people like themselves deserved their attention.

Critics once held that this market explains the novel's realism, as though the form were simply a mirror held up to the rising middle class. The claim is too simple. Realism, in the sense of close attention to everyday objects and motives, is a technique, and techniques can serve many ends. Some of the most scrupulous early realists wrote satire; others wrote sensational tales of seduction and crime. The same readers who wanted plausibility devoured improbable adventures. What the market supplied was demand for narratives that could be consumed in volume, and that demand rewarded whatever held attention across hundreds of pages, whether or not it resembled life. Realism became the dominant convention later, in the nineteenth century, partly because serial publication rewarded characters whom readers could follow for months and come to regard as acquaintances.

None of this means that economics dictates literary form. Authors resisted the market, imitated one another, and invented techniques, such as the narrator who enters a character's thoughts, that no reader had requested. But inventions endured only if they found readers, and the circumstances of reading helped determine which did. A history that begins with a genius and a masterpiece will therefore mislead, as will one that reduces the form to a response to demand. The better account follows the conventions themselves: which were borrowed, which were abandoned, and which hardened into expectations so familiar that later readers mistook them for the nature of the form. On this account there was no first novel, only a period in which enough conventions stabilized that readers began to recognize a kind of book when they saw it.

qs.q: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?
o: The first novel can be identified once scholars agree on a definition, and the eighteenth-century book market then explains everything about its realism.
The author says the dispute over the first novel is about definitions and ultimately ill-formed, and calls the realism-as-mirror claim too simple.
Economic conditions fully determined the techniques of early novelists, who responded to the demand of readers without inventing anything themselves.
The author states that authors invented techniques that no reader had requested.
The novel is better understood as a set of conventions that stabilized under changing conditions of reading than as a form with a single first example or a simple reflection of its market.
Correct: The passage rejects both the search for a first novel and the reduction of the form to demand, and offers the convention-based account instead.
Realism was the defining feature of the novel from its beginnings, and later conventions such as serial publication merely refined it.
The author says realism became dominant later, in the nineteenth century, and that early realists often served other ends.
qs.x: The passage rejects both the search for a first novel and the reduction of the form to demand, and offers the convention-based account instead. Trap: Choosing the answer that keeps the search for a 'first novel' alive, when the author calls the question itself badly formed.

qs.q: The author discusses ancient romances, medieval tales, and picaresque narratives in the first paragraph primarily to suggest that:
o: disagreement over the first novel reflects different definitions of the form rather than disagreement about facts.
Correct: The paragraph says each claim depends on a prior decision about what the form requires, so the dispute concerns definitions.
the novel emerged from these earlier forms by a slow process in which each was gradually refined into the next.
The paragraph is about competing claims to be first, not about a lineage of refinement.
scholars who defend these earlier forms as novels have misread the surviving manuscripts of the period in question.
No misreading of manuscripts is alleged; the disagreement is about criteria.
private life was a theme that all of these earlier forms treated with approximately equal seriousness and care.
The author notes the romances fall out if the novel must depict ordinary private life, so they did not treat it equally.
qs.x: The paragraph says each claim depends on a prior decision about what the form requires, so the dispute concerns definitions. Trap: Reading a list of candidate ancestors as evidence of a single line of descent rather than of competing definitions.

qs.q: According to the passage, writers often presented their stories as found manuscripts or true accounts because:
o: readers of the period were generally unable to tell the difference between invented stories and genuine documents.
The author says the pretense was not a trick played on naive readers.
booksellers of the period required writers to submit evidence that the events in a narrative had actually occurred.
Nothing in the passage mentions any such requirement by booksellers.
the device allowed the author to borrow the letter, the diary, and the travel report from other fields of writing.
The borrowing of those forms is a separate point; the pretense of authenticity had a persuasive purpose.
the device helped persuade a public that doubted invented stories that such tales were worth reading.
Correct: The author calls the pretense an economical way of persuading a public that regarded fiction as frivolous or suspect.
qs.x: The author calls the pretense an economical way of persuading a public that regarded fiction as frivolous or suspect. Trap: Assuming that readers of the period were naive about fiction, which the author explicitly denies.

qs.q: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the circumstances of reading helped determine which technical inventions endured?
o: Techniques that spread widely among eighteenth-century novelists were often borrowed from letters, diaries, and merchants' logs.
This concerns the origin of conventions, not their survival, and is part of the author's own account.
Narrative techniques that were widely imitated by later writers had often first appeared in books that sold almost no copies and were read by very few people.
Correct: If inventions endured despite finding almost no readers, then reader circumstances would not be what decided their survival.
Many of the most successful serial novels of the nineteenth century featured characters whom readers followed for months.
This is consistent with, and supports, the author's point about serial publication rewarding certain characters.
Some early writers who were skeptical of the market for fiction produced technical experiments that readers had not asked for.
The author already grants that writers invented techniques no one requested; survival is the issue.
qs.x: If inventions endured despite finding almost no readers, then reader circumstances would not be what decided their survival. Trap: Picking evidence that the author already accepts (authors invented techniques) instead of evidence about which inventions survived.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the view that the novel's realism simply mirrors the rising middle class is best described as:
o: complete agreement, since the growth of a literate urban public explains why realism came to dominate the form.
The author says the claim is too simple and gives counterexamples.
scornful dismissal, since the author regards any explanation that mentions readers or markets as fundamentally mistaken.
The author says economics matters; what the author denies is that it dictates form.
qualified rejection, since the view captures a real market influence but mistakes a technique for an essential feature.
Correct: The author calls the claim too simple and notes that early realists also served satire and sensation, yet credits the market with a real role.
neutral reporting, since the author describes the claim without indicating whether the evidence supports or opposes it.
The author evaluates the claim explicitly as too simple.
