qs.x: The author calls the claim too simple and notes that early realists also served satire and sensation, yet credits the market with a real role. Trap: Treating criticism of one explanation as rejection of every market-based explanation, which overstates the author's position.

qs.q: A historian wanted to apply the author's approach to the origins of the podcast. Which research plan would be most consistent with that approach?
o: Tracing which conventions were borrowed from radio and other earlier media, which were dropped, and which hardened into listener expectations as listening habits changed.
Correct: This follows conventions as they were borrowed, abandoned, and stabilized, without a single first example or pure determinism.
Identifying the first recording that deserves to be called a podcast and showing that its creator conceived the whole form in advance.
This is the genius-and-masterpiece history the author warns will mislead.
Showing that the technology of cheap digital distribution fully determined the length, structure, and subject of every episode produced.
This reduces the form to a response to technology, as the author rejects for the market.
Arguing that every podcast format is a mirror of its audience and then ranking formats by how accurately they reflect listeners.
This repeats the mirror claim the author calls too simple.
qs.x: This follows conventions as they were borrowed, abandoned, and stabilized, without a single first example or pure determinism. Trap: Choosing the plan that hunts for a first example or a single cause, which the author specifically warns against.

passages.title: FL03 · CARS · Passage 8
text: The phrase "tragedy of the commons" has become shorthand for the claim that resources held in common are doomed. Each user gains the full benefit of taking one more unit while the cost of depletion is spread across everyone, so rational individuals collectively ruin what they share. The argument is logically tidy, and for open-access resources, where there are no rules and no means of excluding outsiders, it often holds. As a general statement about history, however, it is badly incomplete. Historians of rural economies have found common pastures, forests, and irrigation systems that survived for centuries, some of them far longer than the private estates around them. The question for historians is not whether such incentives exist but whether they always overwhelm the arrangements that people build to manage them.

Their survival is not mysterious once one notices what the tidy argument leaves out. A village pasture was not open to the world. Membership was defined, often by residence or inherited right. Each household's grazing was limited by a stint, a quota commonly tied to the number of animals the household could feed through the winter from its own land. Violations were noticed because neighbors watched one another's animals daily. Fines were small at first and rose with repetition, and in some villages surplus animals were impounded until the fine was paid. The officials who imposed the fines were chosen from among the users. Such arrangements cost something to maintain, but the cost was low relative to the value of the pasture, because the users were few, knew one another, and expected to share the village for life.

This does not mean that commons were idyllic or egalitarian. Stints were often proportioned to landholding, so that the wealthiest households received the largest share, while the landless, who might depend most on gleaning and fuel gathering, held the weakest claims. Nor were such regimes durable under all circumstances. Where population grew rapidly, where markets for wool or timber suddenly opened to distant buyers, or where a central authority displaced local rules without replacing the monitoring they provided, the same institutions could fail. A commons that endured in one century could collapse in the next, and the cause was rarely the mere fact of common ownership.

The more accurate lesson is therefore conditional. Common-pool resources are vulnerable when users cannot be identified or excluded, cannot observe one another, or can profit from extraction faster than rules can adapt. Where those conditions hold, privatization or state control may be a remedy; where they do not, the same remedies can destroy the local knowledge and monitoring on which the resource depended. Enclosure was not a single event but a long series of local bargains and legal acts that proceeded unevenly across regions. A policy that begins from the assumption that commons always fail risks dismantling working institutions. The history of enclosure, in which common lands were converted to private holdings, suggests that whatever efficiency gains appeared were often purchased at the expense of the people who had used the land, and were not always as large as its advocates predicted.

qs.q: Which of the following best summarizes the main argument of the passage?
o: Common ownership is the cause of resource depletion in open-access settings, and private ownership should therefore replace it wherever resources are at risk.
The author says privatization may help under some conditions but can destroy working institutions under others.
Common resources are not inevitably ruined; whether they endure depends on conditions such as exclusion and monitoring, so policy should not assume they always fail.
Correct: This combines the author's conditional lesson with the policy warning in the last paragraph.
Historical commons survived because their users were more cooperative and less self-interested than people in modern economies.
The author attributes survival to rules, exclusion, and monitoring, not to unusual goodwill; users are still described as rational.
The tragedy of the commons is a logically invalid argument that has been shown to be wrong in every case where it has been applied.
The author says the argument often holds for open-access resources, so it is not invalid or always wrong.
qs.x: This combines the author's conditional lesson with the policy warning in the last paragraph. Trap: Overgeneralizing the author's criticism into the claim that the tragedy argument is always wrong, when the author grants it for open-access resources.

qs.q: The author states that a village pasture "was not open to the world" in order to show that:
o: village pastures were more productive than the private estates that surrounded them in the same region.
Productivity relative to estates is not at issue; only the survival of commons is compared.
outsiders were never permitted to graze animals on the pasture under any circumstances during any season.
The author says membership was defined, often by residence or inherited right, not that every outsider was barred in every case.
residents were unable to use the pasture during winter, when animals had to be fed from their own land.
Winter feeding is mentioned as a basis for stints, not as a restriction on use.
the open-access assumption behind the tidy argument did not describe such pastures.
Correct: The sentence follows the remark that the tidy argument leaves things out; the omitted element is limited membership.
qs.x: The sentence follows the remark that the tidy argument leaves things out; the omitted element is limited membership. Trap: Over-reading 'not open to the world' as an absolute ban on all outsiders rather than as defined membership.

qs.q: According to the passage, a household's stint was commonly tied to:
o: the number of animals it could feed through the winter from its own land.
Correct: The second paragraph states this directly.
the size of the fine that it had paid for earlier violations of the village rules over the years.
Fines are described as rising with repetition, but they are not the basis of stints.
the number of households in the village that were willing to monitor its animals every day of the year.
Monitoring was done by neighbors as a matter of course; it is not described as determining stints.
the market price of wool at the time that the household registered its animals with the village officials.
Wool prices appear later, as a force that could destabilize commons, not as a basis for stints.
qs.x: The second paragraph states this directly. Trap: Confusing the mechanisms the passage lists (stints, monitoring, fines) with one another.

qs.q: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that monitoring by neighbors helped commons survive?
o: Commons in which the wealthiest households received the largest stints were more likely to survive than those with equal stints.
This concerns inequality, which the author already says existed, and says nothing about monitoring.
Commons that were opened to distant buyers of wool and timber were more likely to collapse than commons that were not.
This is the author's own point about market pressure and does not touch monitoring.
Commons whose users lived in distant towns and rarely saw one another's animals lasted as long as commons whose users watched each other daily.
Correct: If commons without observation did as well as those with it, then monitoring would not explain survival.
Commons in which fines rose with repeated violations had fewer violations than commons that charged the same fine every time.
This supports the role of graduated sanctions and does not weaken the role of observation.
qs.x: If commons without observation did as well as those with it, then monitoring would not explain survival. Trap: Picking a finding that the author already accepts or that is irrelevant to monitoring instead of one that would undercut it.

qs.q: Based on the passage, which of the following resources would the author most likely expect to be overused?
o: A mountain pasture used by a few families who have shared it for generations and who graze limited numbers of animals.
Few, long-term users with limits resemble the successful village pasture.
A forest managed by local users who elect officials, impose graduated fines, and observe one another's harvests of fuel.
Elected officials, graduated fines, and mutual observation are the features the author credits for survival.
An irrigation system run by farmers who know one another, expect to live nearby for life, and monitor the flow of water.
Known neighbors with long horizons and monitoring match the conditions for survival.
A fishery used by boats from many distant ports, with no means of identifying vessels or checking catches.
Correct: Users who cannot be identified, excluded, or observed fit the conditions the author names as making a commons vulnerable.
qs.x: Users who cannot be identified, excluded, or observed fit the conditions the author names as making a commons vulnerable. Trap: Choosing a resource that is 'common' in name only, when the author's criteria are about exclusion and observation.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the claim that commons are doomed is best described as:
o: wholehearted agreement, since the author believes that every shared resource faces the same incentive to overuse it.
The author lists cases of long-lived commons that the argument does not fit.
accepting its logic for open-access resources while rejecting it as a general account of history and policy.
Correct: The author says the argument often holds for open-access resources but is incomplete as a general statement.
complete rejection, since the author considers the claim to be contradicted by the survival of any single commons.
The author grants that it often holds for open-access resources and that some commons failed, so rejection is not complete.
indifference, since the author thinks that the claim concerns economics and cannot be tested against historical evidence.
The author uses historical evidence from rural economies to evaluate the claim.
qs.x: The author says the argument often holds for open-access resources but is incomplete as a general statement. Trap: Treating a qualified critique as complete agreement or complete rejection.

passages.title: FL03 · CARS · Passage 9
text: Historians are trained to trust documents, and the training carries a hidden cost. Where the archive is full, the historian feels on firm ground; where it is thin, there is a temptation to conclude that little of importance occurred. Yet the contents of an archive are not a sample of everything that happened. They are the residue of what someone thought worth recording, what someone thought worth keeping, and what survived fire, flood, and the periodic clearing of cellars. Governments record taxes, property, and crimes; churches record baptisms and burials; merchants record debts. Those whose lives crossed none of these institutions, or crossed them only at the margins, leave faint traces or none at all.

The resulting silences are often treated as a limit on what can be known, a regrettable gap to be acknowledged in a footnote and then ignored. A more demanding approach treats the silence itself as evidence. Consider a town whose court records show, across two centuries, a steady stream of disputes among landowners and almost no complaints from tenants. A naive reading concludes that tenants were content. A more careful one asks what it would have cost a tenant to bring a complaint, whether a court would have heard it, and whether a clerk would have written it down. If the answers are that the cost was prohibitive, the court unwilling, and the clerk indifferent, then the absence of complaints tells us not about tenants' contentment but about their lack of access to the institution that produced the record. The silence is informative, though it reports on the archive and not on the past.

Some historians draw from this a more radical conclusion: that since the archive reflects the interests of the powerful, the historian can do no more than reproduce their view of events. This is too pessimistic. Documents created for one purpose may reveal things their authors had no wish to disclose. A landlord's account books, kept to track rents, may show by their annual arrears that tenants were regularly unable to pay; a priest's burial register, kept to record fees, may show by its seasonal peaks that a hungry winter was followed by a wave of deaths. Such evidence is incidental in the strict sense, being a byproduct of record-keeping and not its aim, and for that reason it is often more trustworthy on the matters at issue than the author's explicit testimony. The historian's skill lies in reading sources against the grain, using them to answer questions their makers never asked.

Reading against the grain has limits, however, and a responsible practitioner should state them. Incidental evidence can show that tenants fell behind in their rents; it cannot show how they felt about it, or what they said to one another in the evening. The historian who claims to recover such interior experience from records of this kind is typically supplying it from imagination, however disciplined. The honest course is to distinguish between what the sources establish, what they make plausible, and what they leave unknown, and to resist the pressure to turn every gap into a story.

What emerges is a practice of reading that is neither credulous nor despairing. The archive is neither a window onto the past nor a wall in front of it, but a set of partial and interested accounts that can be interrogated, and whose silences can themselves be made to speak, provided that the historian is clear about the difference between what has been found and what has been inferred.

qs.q: Which of the following best captures the main idea of the passage?
o: Archives are so biased toward the powerful that historians cannot recover anything reliable about the lives of ordinary people, whatever methods they use.
The author calls this too pessimistic.
Silences in the archive should be filled in by the historian's disciplined imagination of what people must have felt.
The author warns against supplying interior experience from imagination.
Official records are reliable when they include explicit testimony given by those who lived through events.
The author says incidental evidence is often more trustworthy than explicit testimony.
Historians should read archives critically, treating silences and incidental evidence as informative while stating the limits of inference.
Correct: This reflects the passage's practice of reading neither credulously nor despairingly.
qs.x: This reflects the passage's practice of reading neither credulously nor despairingly. Trap: Choosing the pessimistic view, which the author mentions only to reject.

qs.q: The example of the town's court records is intended to show that:
o: the absence of tenants' complaints may reflect their lack of access to the court, not contentment.
Correct: The author says the silence reports on the archive, not on the past.
tenants in the town were generally content with their landlords, since few of them ever brought a case.
This is the naive reading the author rejects.
clerks routinely destroyed the records of disputes in order to protect landowners.
Clerks' indifference is a possibility raised, but not destruction.
landowners fabricated records to avoid scrutiny from the crown.
The passage doesn't suggest fabrication.
qs.x: The author says the silence reports on the archive, not on the past. Trap: Accepting the naive reading that the passage presents in order to criticize it.

qs.q: According to the passage, incidental evidence is often more trustworthy than explicit testimony because:
o: it is produced by institutions with no interests of their own to serve in the matters recorded.
The author says the archive reflects interested accounts.
it describes the interior experience of ordinary people more directly and vividly than any official testimony could.
The author says it cannot show feelings.
it is a byproduct of record-keeping, not shaped by its author's wish to persuade on the question at issue.
Correct: The author says such evidence is a byproduct, not the aim, of record-keeping.
it is more abundant than explicit testimony and so allows far wider statistical sampling.
Abundance is not mentioned as a reason.
qs.x: The author says such evidence is a byproduct, not the aim, of record-keeping. Trap: Assuming incidental evidence is reliable because institutions are neutral, rather than because authors had no motive to shape it.

qs.q: Which of the following is the best example of reading against the grain?
o: Using a governor's published speech to learn what the governor said about his own policies and motives.
This uses the document for its stated purpose.
Using insurance ledgers, kept to track payments, to estimate how often storms damaged cargo.
Correct: Documents kept for one purpose answer a question their makers never asked.
Assuming that a town whose court records list no crimes must have had no crime at all.
This reads silence naively.
Inventing a diary entry for an imagined tenant in order to illustrate hardships of the period.
The author warns against supplying experience from imagination.
qs.x: Documents kept for one purpose answer a question their makers never asked. Trap: Choosing a use of a source for its explicit purpose instead of an incidental one.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward historians who claim to recover the interior experience of ordinary people from incidental records is best described as:
o: admiring of their skill in reconstructing the inner lives of people who left no writing.
The author says the honest course is to distinguish evidence from inference.
hostile to any use of incidental evidence at all, even for questions it can address.
The author endorses incidental evidence for questions it can address.
indifferent, because documents never reveal feelings and so the matter is of no importance.
The author says records can show some matters but not feelings; the attitude is concern, not indifference.
cautious, because such claims typically rely on imagination more than on sources.
Correct: The author says they are typically supplying the experience from imagination.
qs.x: The author says they are typically supplying the experience from imagination. Trap: Treating the author's praise of reading against the grain as unlimited.

passages.title: FL03 · Chem/Phys · Passage 1
text: A student reproduces a Joule-type experiment. A 10.0 kg mass hangs from a string that passes over a pulley and turns a paddle wheel inside an insulated container of water. The mass is lowered slowly at constant speed through 1.50 m, then lifted back by hand with the paddle disengaged, and this cycle is called one drop. The water has mass 0.500 kg (c = 4184 J/(kg·K)), and the paddle and container add a heat capacity of 108 J/K, so the total heat capacity is 2200 J/K. Assume g = 9.8 m/s². The student assumes all the gravitational energy lost by the mass is converted to thermal energy. After 20, 40, 60, and 80 drops, the temperature rise of the water is measured with a digital thermometer. Table 1 gives the predicted and measured values, and Figure 1 plots them against the number of drops. The student suspects that the small shortfall in the measured values arises from heat exchanged with the surroundings.

qs.q: How much gravitational potential energy does the 10.0 kg mass lose in one drop?
o: 15 J multiplies mass by height and omits g.
98 J omits the 1.50 m height.
Correct: ΔU = mgh = (10.0 kg)(9.8 m/s²)(1.50 m) = 147 J, which matches 2940 J / 20 drops in Table 1.
1470 J is a factor of ten too large.
qs.x: ΔU = mgh = (10.0 kg)(9.8 m/s²)(1.50 m) = 147 J, which matches 2940 J / 20 drops in Table 1. Trap: Leaving out g or the height, or dropping a factor in a three-variable product such as mgh.

qs.q: During one slow descent at constant speed, the work done by the string tension on the 10.0 kg mass is:
o: +147 J, because the tension supplies the energy that heats the water in the container
The sign is wrong; the string does negative work on the mass.
−147 J, because the mass accelerates downward under gravity throughout the descent
The mass does not accelerate; the −147 J arises because T = mg, not because of acceleration.
0 J, because the net force on the mass is zero at constant speed and so no work is done by any force
The net work is zero, but the tension alone still does work.
−147 J, because tension points up, the displacement is down, and T equals mg
Correct: At constant speed T = mg, directed upward, while the displacement is downward, so W = −(98 N)(1.50 m) = −147 J; the negative sign means the mass loses energy to the paddle.
qs.x: At constant speed T = mg, directed upward, while the displacement is downward, so W = −(98 N)(1.50 m) = −147 J; the negative sign means the mass loses energy to the paddle. Trap: Concluding that zero net force means zero work by each individual force.

qs.q: At 80 drops, the measured temperature rise is closest to what percentage of the predicted rise?
o: 85% does not match the table values.
Correct: 5.04 / 5.35 = 0.942, or about 94%. The 6% shortfall is consistent with heat loss to the surroundings.
106% would require the measured rise to exceed the predicted rise.
6% is the shortfall, not the fraction obtained.
qs.x: 5.04 / 5.35 = 0.942, or about 94%. The 6% shortfall is consistent with heat loss to the surroundings. Trap: Reporting the percentage lost rather than the percentage obtained.

qs.q: Using the measured trend in Table 1, about how many drops would be needed to raise the water temperature by 10.0 K?
o: 142 drops uses only the water's heat capacity (2092 J/K) and ignores the apparatus.
150 drops assumes 100% conversion (2200 J/K × 10.0 K / 147 J = 150).
Correct: The measured rise is 5.04 K / 80 = 0.063 K per drop, so 10.0 K / 0.063 K = about 159 drops.
168 drops overcorrects for losses.
qs.x: The measured rise is 5.04 K / 80 = 0.063 K per drop, so 10.0 K / 0.063 K = about 159 drops. Trap: Using the predicted rate per drop and ignoring the measured shortfall.

qs.q: The student replaces the 10.0 kg mass with a 20.0 kg mass lowered through 0.75 m per drop, and performs 40 drops under the same conditions. The predicted temperature rise would be:
o: half of 2.67 K, because the height is halved
Halving only h ignores the doubled mass.
one-quarter of 2.67 K, because both quantities change
The changes multiply to give a factor of one, not one-quarter.
double 2.67 K, because the mass is doubled
Doubling only m ignores the halved height.
unchanged at 2.67 K, because mgh per drop is unchanged
Correct: mgh = (20.0)(9.8)(0.75) = 147 J, the same energy per drop, so 40 drops still dissipate 5880 J and raise the temperature by 2.67 K.
qs.x: mgh = (20.0)(9.8)(0.75) = 147 J, the same energy per drop, so 40 drops still dissipate 5880 J and raise the temperature by 2.67 K. Trap: Changing one variable in a product and ignoring the compensating change in the other.

graph.title: Figure 1. Temperature rise of the water versus number of drops

passages.title: FL03 · Chem/Phys · Passage 2
text: A student builds a simple hydrometer from a uniform solid cylinder of mass 60 g, length 20 cm, and cross-sectional area 4.0 cm², giving it a density of 0.75 g/cm³. The cylinder is placed upright in four different liquids and allowed to float at rest, as shown in Table 1. For each liquid, the student records the density and the depth to which the cylinder is submerged. The cylinder floats upright in every liquid. The student then tests an unknown liquid in which the cylinder floats with 12.0 cm submerged. Assume that the density of water is 1.00 g/cm³ (1000 kg/m³), that g = 9.8 m/s², and that atmospheric pressure acts equally on the liquid surface and the top of the cylinder, so that only gauge pressure needs to be considered. The student wants to use the results to understand how the density of a liquid determines how deeply a floating body sinks, and to connect that depth to the forces acting on the cylinder and to the pressure of the liquid at its bottom face. The cylinder is dry before each trial and is left to settle for one minute before the depth is read from a ruler along its side.

qs.q: What is the magnitude of the buoyant force on the floating cylinder in water?
o: 0.78 N would be the buoyant force if the entire 80 cm³ were submerged, but only 60 cm³ is.
0.059 N is off by a factor of 10 from a unit conversion error.
1.2 N is twice the weight and would make the cylinder accelerate upward.
Correct: A floating object is in equilibrium, so the buoyant force equals the weight: 0.060 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 0.59 N.
qs.x: A floating object is in equilibrium, so the buoyant force equals the weight: 0.060 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 0.59 N. Trap: Using the cylinder's full volume instead of the submerged volume to find buoyant force.

qs.q: How does the buoyant force on the cylinder in the sugar solution compare to that in water?
o: It is 1.5 times larger in the sugar solution.
Greater density alone would raise the force only if displaced volume stayed fixed, but the submerged depth decreases.
It is the same in both liquids.
Correct: In both liquids the cylinder floats at rest, so the buoyant force equals its weight. The denser liquid simply needs less displaced volume to supply the same force.
It is 1.5 times smaller in the sugar solution.
The force cannot be smaller; it must still balance the unchanged weight.
It is larger in the sugar solution because the liquid is denser, but by a factor of 1.2.
1.2 is the density ratio of the salt solution to water and is unrelated to the equilibrium condition.
qs.x: In both liquids the cylinder floats at rest, so the buoyant force equals its weight. The denser liquid simply needs less displaced volume to supply the same force. Trap: Assuming a denser fluid exerts more buoyant force even when the object floats in both.

qs.q: The unknown liquid submerges the cylinder to a depth of 12.0 cm. What is its density?
o: 1.25 g/cm³
Correct: Weight equals ρgAh, so ρ = m/(Ah) = 60 g/(4.0 cm² × 12.0 cm) = 1.25 g/cm³.
0.80 g/cm³
0.80 g/cm³ is 12/15, a ratio that is inversely related to the correct form.
1.67 g/cm³
1.67 g/cm³ is 20/12 and uses the full cylinder length instead of mass.
1.20 g/cm³
1.20 g/cm³ is the density of the salt solution, which submerges the cylinder 12.5 cm, not 12.0 cm.
qs.x: Weight equals ρgAh, so ρ = m/(Ah) = 60 g/(4.0 cm² × 12.0 cm) = 1.25 g/cm³. Trap: Picking the nearest table entry instead of calculating from m = ρAh.

qs.q: What is the gauge pressure at the bottom face of the cylinder when it floats in water?
o: 2.0 × 10³ Pa uses the full 0.20 m length rather than the submerged depth.
1.0 × 10⁵ Pa is roughly atmospheric pressure, which is not part of gauge pressure.
1.5 × 10⁴ Pa results from a power-of-ten error when converting 15 cm to meters.
Correct: The bottom face is 0.150 m below the surface: P = ρgh = 1000 × 9.8 × 0.150 = 1.47 × 10³ Pa, which gives a force of 0.59 N on 4.0 cm², matching the weight.
qs.x: The bottom face is 0.150 m below the surface: P = ρgh = 1000 × 9.8 × 0.150 = 1.47 × 10³ Pa, which gives a force of 0.59 N on 4.0 cm², matching the weight. Trap: Using cylinder length rather than submerged depth in P = ρgh.

passages.title: FL03 · Chem/Phys · Passage 3
text: A galvanic cell is assembled from a zinc strip in 1.0 M Zn(NO₃)₂ and a silver wire in AgNO₃ of variable concentration. The two half-cells are joined by a salt bridge containing KNO₃ in agar, and a high-impedance voltmeter connects the metals. Standard reduction potentials are E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V and E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V. At 25 °C the Nernst equation can be written E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q. The student prepares AgNO₃ solutions at four concentrations, keeps [Zn²⁺] at 1.0 M, and records the cell potential once the reading stabilizes. Table 1 lists the results, and Figure 1 plots the potential against log[Ag⁺]. In a second experiment, the student replaces the voltmeter with a small resistor and lets the cell discharge for several hours with [Ag⁺] initially 1.0 M. The Faraday constant is 96,485 C/mol e⁻. Each solution is freshly prepared by dilution from the 1.0 M stock, and the electrodes are polished with fine abrasive and rinsed between trials. The temperature of the room is 25 °C.

qs.q: Toward which half-cell do the nitrate ions in the salt bridge migrate while the cell operates?
o: Toward the silver half-cell, because the cathode attracts anions
In a galvanic cell the cathode is positive, but its charge is balanced by cation flow into it.
Toward the silver half-cell, where Ag⁺ is being consumed from solution
Removal of Ag⁺ leaves excess negative charge in the silver half-cell, so cations, not anions, move there.
Toward the zinc half-cell, where oxidation produces excess positive charge
Correct: Zn is oxidized at the anode, increasing [Zn²⁺]; anions flow toward the anode compartment to preserve neutrality (and K⁺ flows toward the cathode).
Neither; the bridge only carries electrons between the electrodes
Electrons travel through the external wire; the bridge carries ions.
qs.x: Zn is oxidized at the anode, increasing [Zn²⁺]; anions flow toward the anode compartment to preserve neutrality (and K⁺ flows toward the cathode). Trap: Thinking the salt bridge conducts electrons, or sending anions toward the cathode.

qs.q: Using the Nernst equation, what is the cell potential when [Ag⁺] = 0.010 M and [Zn²⁺] = 1.0 M?
o: 1.32 V uses 0.0592 without dividing by n.
1.50 V treats Q as 1/[Ag⁺] instead of 1/[Ag⁺]².
1.68 V has the wrong sign for the correction.
qs.x: E° = 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V; Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Ag⁺]² = 1/(1.0×10⁻⁴) = 1.0×10⁴, so E = 1.56 − (0.0592/2)(4) = 1.44 V. Trap: Forgetting that Ag⁺ is squared in Q when the half-reactions are balanced for 2 electrons.

qs.q: The slope of the line in Figure 1 is closest to:
o: +0.030 V per unit log[Ag⁺]
0.030 V ignores the squared term in Q.
+0.059 V per unit log[Ag⁺]
Correct: E = E° + (0.0592/2)(2)log[Ag⁺], so the slope is +0.0592 V per tenfold change; the data fall 0.06 V per decade.
−0.059 V per unit log[Ag⁺]
The slope is positive because E rises with [Ag⁺].
+0.118 V per unit log[Ag⁺]
0.118 V doubles the factor and does not match the data.
qs.x: E = E° + (0.0592/2)(2)log[Ag⁺], so the slope is +0.0592 V per tenfold change; the data fall 0.06 V per decade. Trap: Using 0.0592/n for the slope without accounting for the exponent of 2 on [Ag⁺].

qs.q: What is the standard free energy change for the cell reaction Zn(s) + 2 Ag⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag(s)?
o: −150 kJ/mol
−150 kJ uses n = 1.
−301 kJ/mol
+301 kJ/mol
The sign is wrong for a spontaneous cell.
−602 kJ/mol
−602 kJ uses n = 4.
qs.x: ΔG° = −nFE° = −(2)(96,485 C/mol)(1.56 V) = −3.01×10⁵ J/mol. Trap: Using n = 1 because each silver ion accepts only one electron, ignoring the 2 e⁻ transferred per reaction.

qs.q: During the long discharge through the resistor with no replenishment of solutions, the cell potential is expected to:
o: remain at 1.56 V, because E° is a constant of the electrode materials
E° is constant, but E depends on Q.
drop to zero immediately, because the resistor removes the potential difference
The resistor draws current but the potential persists until reactants are depleted.
rise gradually, because Zn²⁺ accumulation increases the driving force
Increasing [Zn²⁺] raises Q and lowers E.
fall gradually toward zero, because Q increases toward K as Ag⁺ is consumed
Correct: Ag⁺ is consumed and Zn²⁺ is produced, so Q grows toward K and E falls toward 0 at equilibrium.
qs.x: Ag⁺ is consumed and Zn²⁺ is produced, so Q grows toward K and E falls toward 0 at equilibrium. Trap: Equating E with E° and forgetting that cell potential depends on concentrations as the reaction proceeds.

graph.title: Figure 1. Cell potential versus log[Ag⁺]

passages.title: FL03 · Chem/Phys · Passage 4
text: A student studies image formation with a thin converging lens. An illuminated arrow 2.0 cm tall is placed on an optical bench at several distances d₀ from the lens, and a screen is moved until a sharp image appears at distance dᵢ. The student uses the convention that distances for real objects and real images are positive. Table 1 lists the measured values and the image height. The student then plots 1/dᵢ against 1/d₀ in Figure 1. Finally, the lens is removed and replaced with a concave spherical mirror at the same location, and the arrow is again placed 15.0 cm in front of the reflecting surface. The mirror has a radius of curvature of 20.0 cm. Throughout, the student uses the relation 1/d₀ + 1/dᵢ = 1/f and the magnification m = −dᵢ/d₀. All images discussed are formed with paraxial rays. The bench is shielded from stray light, the lens is mounted on a vertical holder at the 0 cm mark, and each image distance is judged as the screen position that gives the sharpest edges.

qs.q: With the object at 15.0 cm, which description fits the image on the screen?
o: Real, inverted, and reduced
The image is larger than the object, not smaller.
Real, upright, and the same size
Upright real images do not occur with a single lens, and the sizes differ.
Virtual, upright, and enlarged
A virtual image cannot be projected on a screen.
Real, inverted, and enlarged
Correct: A real image captured on a screen is inverted; the image height of 4.0 cm exceeds the object's 2.0 cm, so m = −2.0.
qs.x: A real image captured on a screen is inverted; the image height of 4.0 cm exceeds the object's 2.0 cm, so m = −2.0. Trap: Forgetting that a real image formed on a screen by a single lens is always inverted.

qs.q: From the intercept of the line in Figure 1, the focal length of the lens is:
o: 5.0 cm
5.0 cm would correspond to an intercept of 0.20 cm⁻¹, twice the observed value.
10 cm
Correct: The line obeys 1/dᵢ = 1/f − 1/d₀, so the y-intercept is 1/f = 0.100 cm⁻¹ and f = 10 cm.
20 cm
20 cm is the d₀ where dᵢ = d₀ (twice the focal length).
0.10 is the intercept itself, 1/f, not f.
qs.x: The line obeys 1/dᵢ = 1/f − 1/d₀, so the y-intercept is 1/f = 0.100 cm⁻¹ and f = 10 cm. Trap: Reporting the intercept 1/f directly as the focal length.

qs.q: If the arrow were placed 5.0 cm from the lens, the image would be:
o: real, inverted, and located 10 cm behind the lens
The sign of dᵢ is negative, not positive.
virtual, inverted, and located 3.3 cm on the object side
Virtual images from a converging lens are upright.
real, upright, and located 3.3 cm behind the lens
3.3 cm results from adding rather than subtracting reciprocals, and a real image requires d₀ > f.
virtual, upright, and located 10 cm on the object side of the lens
Correct: 1/dᵢ = 1/10 − 1/5 = −1/10, so dᵢ = −10 cm; the negative sign marks a virtual image on the object side, with m = +2 (upright).
qs.x: 1/dᵢ = 1/10 − 1/5 = −1/10, so dᵢ = −10 cm; the negative sign marks a virtual image on the object side, with m = +2 (upright). Trap: Dropping the sign of dᵢ when the object lies inside the focal length.

qs.q: With the concave mirror (R = 20.0 cm) and the object 15.0 cm in front of it, the image is located:
o: 60 cm behind the mirror and is virtual
60 cm uses f = R = 20 cm.
30 cm behind the mirror and is virtual
A positive dᵢ for a mirror is on the reflecting side, so it cannot be behind the mirror.
30 cm in front of the mirror and is real
Correct: f = R/2 = 10.0 cm, so dᵢ = 30.0 cm, positive, in front of the mirror, as for the lens at the same d₀ (real, inverted).
20 cm in front of the mirror and is real
20 cm would apply when the object is at 2f = 20 cm.
qs.x: f = R/2 = 10.0 cm, so dᵢ = 30.0 cm, positive, in front of the mirror, as for the lens at the same d₀ (real, inverted). Trap: Using the radius of curvature as the focal length of a mirror.

graph.title: Figure 1. Reciprocal of image distance versus reciprocal of object distance

passages.title: FL03 · Chem/Phys · Passage 5
text: Iodine-131 (Z = 53) is used to treat thyroid disease. It decays by beta emission, accompanied by gamma rays. To measure its half-life, a technician places a small sealed I-131 source at a fixed distance from a detector and records the activity (background already subtracted) at intervals over 24 days. Table 1 lists the corrected activity, and Figure 1 plots activity against time. The technician states that the detector response is proportional to the number of decays per second and that the geometry did not change. In a separate calculation, the technician needs to estimate the remaining activity of a similar sample at a time between measurements. Use ln 2 = 0.693 and 2^(−2.5) = 0.177 where needed. A patient who receives I-131 also loses it by biological excretion, but only the physical decay of the isolated source is studied here. The source is kept in a shielded container between readings, and each reading is taken for a counting time long enough to make statistical fluctuations small.

qs.q: Which nuclide is the product of the beta decay of I-131?
o: ¹³¹₅₄Xe
Correct: Beta-minus decay converts a neutron to a proton, so Z rises from 53 to 54 and A stays 131, giving xenon-131.
¹³¹₅₂Te
Te-131 (Z = 52) would result from positron emission or electron capture.
¹²⁷₅₁Sb
Sb-127 (Z = 51, A = 127) would result from alpha emission.
¹³⁰₅₃I
I-130 would require loss of a neutron, which is not beta decay.
qs.x: Beta-minus decay converts a neutron to a proton, so Z rises from 53 to 54 and A stays 131, giving xenon-131. Trap: Lowering Z in beta-minus decay, as occurs in beta-plus decay or electron capture.

qs.q: From Figure 1, the half-life of I-131 is closest to:
o: 4 days
At 4 days, the activity is 283 MBq, about 71% of the initial value, not 50%.
8 days
Correct: Activity falls from 400 to 200 MBq in 8 days, and again from 200 to 100 MBq between 8 and 16 days.
12 days
At 12 days, the activity is 141 MBq, which is about 35% of the initial value.
16 days
At 16 days, the activity has fallen to 25% of its initial value (two half-lives).
qs.x: Activity falls from 400 to 200 MBq in 8 days, and again from 200 to 100 MBq between 8 and 16 days. Trap: Choosing the time at which the activity reaches 25%, which corresponds to two half-lives.

qs.q: What is the decay constant of I-131?
o: 0.125 d⁻¹ is 1/t½, which omits the ln 2 factor.
Correct: λ = ln 2 / t½ = 0.693 / 8.0 d = 0.087 d⁻¹.
0.69 d⁻¹ is ln 2 without division by the half-life.
11.5 is t½ / ln 2, which is the mean lifetime in days, not a rate.
qs.x: λ = ln 2 / t½ = 0.693 / 8.0 d = 0.087 d⁻¹. Trap: Taking the decay constant as 1/t½ rather than ln 2/t½.

qs.q: Which value is closest to the activity of the source at 20 days?
o: 50 MBq
50 MBq is the activity at 24 days (3 half-lives).
71 MBq
75 MBq
75 MBq is the linear average of the 16-day and 24-day readings, but decay is exponential, not linear.
100 MBq
100 MBq is the activity at 16 days.
qs.x: 20 d is 2.5 half-lives: 400 × 2^(−2.5) = 400 × 0.177 = 71 MBq. Trap: Interpolating linearly between data points on an exponential decay curve.

graph.title: Figure 1. Activity of the I-131 source versus time

passages.title: FL03 · Chem/Phys · Passage 6
text: A student studies a phosphate buffer made from NaH₂PO₄ (H₂PO₄⁻, the acid) and Na₂HPO₄ (HPO₄²⁻, the conjugate base), for which pKa = 7.21 at 25 °C. Four buffers are prepared, each with a total volume of 100 mL and a total phosphate content of 10.0 mmol, but with different ratios of base to acid. The pH of each is measured with a calibrated meter. Then 1.0 mL of 1.0 M HCl (1.0 mmol H⁺) is added to each buffer and the pH is measured again. Table 1 shows the composition and results, and Figure 1 plots the magnitude of the pH change against the initial pH. The student assumes that volume changes are negligible and that activity coefficients are close to 1. Use log 2 = 0.30 and log 3 = 0.48. The meter is calibrated with standards at pH 4.00, 7.00, and 10.00 before each use, and the solutions are stirred gently for 30 seconds after the acid is added so that the reading is stable.

qs.q: Which statement best explains why buffer 1 resists the added acid most effectively?
o: Its pH equals the pKa, so both components are present at their highest combined capacity
Correct: At pH = pKa, [HPO₄²⁻] = [H₂PO₄⁻], so the buffer can absorb the greatest amount of either acid or base before the ratio changes much.
Its pH is nearest 7.4, the pH of blood, so it contains the largest total phosphate
All four buffers contain the same total phosphate (10.0 mmol), and the pH of blood is not a factor.
It contains the most HPO₄²⁻, which is the component that neutralizes the acid
Buffer 4 contains more HPO₄²⁻ (9.0 mmol) yet changed pH more.
It has the lowest ionic strength, so the added HCl is diluted to the greatest extent
Ionic strength does not differ by design, and dilution is the same for each buffer.
qs.x: At pH = pKa, [HPO₄²⁻] = [H₂PO₄⁻], so the buffer can absorb the greatest amount of either acid or base before the ratio changes much. Trap: Assuming that the buffer with the most base is the strongest buffer against acid.

qs.q: What is the initial pH of buffer 2?
o: 6.61 inverts the ratio (2.0/8.0).
7.51 uses a ratio of 2 instead of 4.
8.16 corresponds to a ratio of 9, which belongs to buffer 4.
qs.x: pH = 7.21 + log(8.0/2.0) = 7.21 + log 4 = 7.21 + 0.60 = 7.81. Trap: Inverting the base to acid ratio in the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.

qs.q: Which reaction primarily accounts for the small pH change when HCl is added to these buffers?
o: H⁺ + HPO₄²⁻ → H₂PO₄⁻
Correct: The conjugate base HPO₄²⁻ accepts the proton and converts to H₂PO₄⁻, so the ratio changes only modestly.
H⁺ + H₂PO₄⁻ → H₃PO₄
Protonating H₂PO₄⁻ to H₃PO₄ would need a pH near pKa₁ (about 2).
H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
At pH 6 to 8, [OH⁻] is about 10⁻⁷ M or less, so it cannot neutralize 1.0 mmol of H⁺.
H₂PO₄⁻ + HPO₄²⁻ → H₃PO₄ + PO₄³⁻
This is not a net acid-base reaction in the buffer and does not absorb added acid.
qs.x: The conjugate base HPO₄²⁻ accepts the proton and converts to H₂PO₄⁻, so the ratio changes only modestly. Trap: Choosing the reaction of H⁺ with the acid form, which cannot neutralize additional acid.

qs.q: Why does buffer 3 show a larger |ΔpH| than buffer 1 when the same 1.0 mmol of HCl is added?
o: Its pKa is lower than that of buffer 1, so it is a weaker acid and less effective
The pKa is a property of the acid and is the same in all buffers.
Its H₂PO₄⁻ concentration is high, so it dissociates and consumes the added acid
H₂PO₄⁻ does not consume H⁺ at this pH.
Its HPO₄²⁻ supply is small, so 1.0 mmol of H⁺ shifts the base to acid ratio from 1:4 to 1:9
Correct: Buffer 3 has only 2.0 mmol HPO₄²⁻; after 1.0 mmol H⁺ the ratio goes from 2.0:8.0 to 1.0:9.0, so the logarithm falls by 0.35. In buffer 1 the ratio only goes from 1:1 to 4:6.
The HCl is not completely neutralized in buffer 3, leaving free H⁺ at 0.01 M
HCl is completely consumed because 2.0 mmol of base exceeds 1.0 mmol of acid.
qs.x: Buffer 3 has only 2.0 mmol HPO₄²⁻; after 1.0 mmol H⁺ the ratio goes from 2.0:8.0 to 1.0:9.0, so the logarithm falls by 0.35. In buffer 1 the ratio only goes from 1:1 to 4:6. Trap: Treating the pKa as variable between buffers made of the same conjugate pair.

qs.q: How much HCl could buffer 1 absorb before its pH falls to 6.21 (one unit below the pKa)?
o: 0.91 mmol
0.91 mmol is the HPO₄²⁻ remaining, not the amount consumed.
4.1 mmol
Correct: At pH = pKa − 1, the base to acid ratio is 1:10; with 10.0 mmol total, HPO₄²⁻ = 10.0/11 = 0.91 mmol. HPO₄²⁻ consumed = 5.0 − 0.91 = 4.1 mmol, which equals the H⁺ added.
4.5 mmol
4.5 mmol would leave only 0.5 mmol HPO₄²⁻ (a 1:19 ratio), overshooting the target pH of 6.21.
5.0 mmol
5.0 mmol would remove all the base, leaving no buffer.
qs.x: At pH = pKa − 1, the base to acid ratio is 1:10; with 10.0 mmol total, HPO₄²⁻ = 10.0/11 = 0.91 mmol. HPO₄²⁻ consumed = 5.0 − 0.91 = 4.1 mmol, which equals the H⁺ added. Trap: Reporting the amount of base remaining instead of the amount of acid absorbed.

graph.title: Figure 1. Magnitude of pH change versus initial pH

passages.title: FL03 · Chem/Phys · Passage 7
text: An unknown liquid with molecular formula C₄H₈O₂ has a boiling point of 77°C. Its infrared spectrum shows a very strong, sharp absorption at 1740 cm⁻¹ and strong absorptions near 1240 and 1050 cm⁻¹, but no broad absorption between 2500 and 3500 cm⁻¹. The 1H NMR spectrum, recorded in CDCl₃, gives three signals, summarized in Table 1. A student considers two structural isomers consistent with the formula: ethyl acetate and butanoic acid. Butanoic acid boils at 164°C and displays a very broad IR absorption centered near 3000 cm⁻¹ along with a one-proton NMR singlet near 11 ppm. The student uses the data to assign the structure of the unknown and to rationalize the difference in boiling points between the two isomers. All spectra were obtained on a purified sample that had been dried over anhydrous sodium sulfate. The student reasons from the molecular formula to the degree of unsaturation, then uses the IR spectrum to identify the functional group before using the NMR integration and splitting to determine connectivity, and finally compares the physical properties of the two isomers.

qs.q: How many degrees of unsaturation does C₄H₈O₂ have?
o: Correct: DoU = (2C + 2 − H)/2 = (10 − 8)/2 = 1, accounted for by one C=O.
0 would be a fully saturated acyclic compound such as C₄H₁₀O₂.
2 counts the two oxygen atoms as unsaturations.
4 uses the carbon count directly.
qs.x: DoU = (2C + 2 − H)/2 = (10 − 8)/2 = 1, accounted for by one C=O. Trap: Counting oxygen atoms in the degrees of unsaturation formula.

qs.q: Which functional group is indicated by the IR data for the unknown?
o: A carboxylic acid
A carboxylic acid would show a very broad O–H stretch from 2500 to 3500.
An ester
Correct: A strong C=O stretch at 1740 cm⁻¹, C–O stretches near 1240 and 1050, and no O–H band are characteristic of an ester.
A ketone
A ketone would not account for both oxygen atoms and has no C–O stretches near 1240 and 1050.
An alcohol
An alcohol would show a broad O–H absorption near 3300.
qs.x: A strong C=O stretch at 1740 cm⁻¹, C–O stretches near 1240 and 1050, and no O–H band are characteristic of an ester. Trap: Assigning any 1700–1750 cm⁻¹ peak to a ketone without checking for C–O and O–H signals.

qs.q: Why does the signal at 4.12 ppm appear as a quartet and at a relatively downfield position?
o: It is a CH₃ next to a CH₂ (n + 1 = 3) and is shielded by the carbonyl.
A CH₃ would have 3H integration, not 2H.
It is a CH₂ with four neighboring protons and is bonded to carbon only.
A carbon-bonded CH₂ would not shift to 4.12, and four neighbors would give a quintet.
It is a CH₂ next to a CH₃ (n + 1 = 4) and is deshielded by the adjacent oxygen.
Correct: The 2H signal is the O–CH₂ of the ethyl group, split by three CH₃ protons into a quartet and shifted downfield by oxygen's electronegativity.
It is a single proton split by three equivalent neighbors and deshielded by the carbonyl.
A single proton would integrate for 1H.
qs.x: The 2H signal is the O–CH₂ of the ethyl group, split by three CH₃ protons into a quartet and shifted downfield by oxygen's electronegativity. Trap: Using the number of neighbors as the multiplicity instead of n + 1.

qs.q: Which statement best explains why butanoic acid boils at a much higher temperature than ethyl acetate?
o: Butanoic acid has a greater molar mass than ethyl acetate, so its dispersion forces are much stronger
Both isomers have the same formula and therefore the same molar mass.
Ethyl acetate has stronger London dispersion forces than butanoic acid because of its branched structure
Both have similar dispersion forces; that is not the difference.
Ethyl acetate is nonpolar while butanoic acid is polar, so only butanoic acid has dipole-dipole attractions
Esters are polar as well, since they contain C=O and C–O bonds.
Butanoic acid forms hydrogen-bonded dimers through O–H and C=O groups, which ethyl acetate cannot do
Correct: Carboxylic acids form hydrogen-bonded dimers, which require much more energy to separate than the dipole-dipole forces in the ester.
qs.x: Carboxylic acids form hydrogen-bonded dimers, which require much more energy to separate than the dipole-dipole forces in the ester. Trap: Overlooking that isomers have equal masses so hydrogen bonding must account for the difference.

passages.title: FL03 · Chem/Phys · Passage 8
text: A biochemist separates a mixture of four amino acids on a cation-exchange column. The resin contains fixed sulfonate groups (−SO₃⁻), and the column is equilibrated and loaded at pH 3.0. The amino acids are then eluted with a buffer whose NaCl concentration is gradually increased. At pH 3.0, aspartate is close to neutral or slightly negative, glutamate is nearly neutral with slight positive charge, glycine is about +0.2, and lysine is about +1.1. Table 1 lists the isoelectric point (pI) and the elution volume for each. Figure 1 plots elution volume against pI. For lysine, the pKa values are 2.18 (α-COOH), 8.95 (α-NH₃⁺), and 10.53 (side-chain NH₃⁺). For comparison, a second column of anion-exchange resin, with fixed positively charged groups, is considered for the same sample at pH 3.0. Samples of each amino acid are detected as they leave the column by reaction with ninhydrin, and the elution volume is taken at the center of each peak. Flow rate, column length, and temperature are kept constant, so differences in elution volume reflect differences in the strength of binding to the resin.

qs.q: Why does lysine elute last from the cation-exchange column?
o: It has the lowest pI of the four amino acids, so it is the most strongly retained by the resin
Lysine has the highest pI (9.74) of the four.
It carries the greatest net negative charge at pH 3.0 and is therefore pulled toward the resin by the sulfonate groups
Lysine is not negatively charged at pH 3.0, and a negative net charge would cause weaker retention, not stronger.
It carries the greatest net positive charge at pH 3.0 and binds most tightly to the resin

Correct: Cation-exchange resin retains positively charged molecules. Lysine's net charge near +1.1 gives the strongest electrostatic attraction, so a higher salt concentration is needed to displace it.
It is the smallest of the four amino acids and so diffuses most slowly through the resin pores
Lysine is larger than glycine, and size is not the basis of ion-exchange separation.
qs.x: Cation-exchange resin retains positively charged molecules. Lysine's net charge near +1.1 gives the strongest electrostatic attraction, so a higher salt concentration is needed to displace it. Trap: Assuming elution order tracks size instead of charge.

qs.q: Which change to the elution conditions would cause lysine to elute sooner?
o: Increasing the NaCl concentration of the eluting buffer
Correct: Na⁺ competes with lysine for the sulfonate groups, so a higher salt concentration displaces it more quickly.
Lowering the pH of the buffer to 1.5
A lower pH increases the positive charge and retention.
Lowering the NaCl concentration of the eluting buffer
Lower salt reduces competition for resin sites, so lysine elutes later.
Switching the column to a size-exclusion resin without changing the buffer
A size-exclusion resin separates by size rather than charge, so it does not address how fast lysine leaves an ion-exchange column.
qs.x: Na⁺ competes with lysine for the sulfonate groups, so a higher salt concentration displaces it more quickly. Trap: Thinking that more positive charge makes elution faster.

qs.q: On an anion-exchange column at pH 3.0, which amino acid would elute first?
o: Glycine
Glycine has a slight positive charge (+0.2) and is weakly repelled, so it elutes after lysine.
Glutamate
Glutamate is close to neutral, so it is retained more than the positively charged lysine.
Lysine
Correct: The anion-exchange resin is positively charged and retains negatively charged species. Lysine is net positive and is repelled, so it passes through first.
Aspartate
Aspartate is the most negative at this pH and is retained most strongly by the positive resin.
qs.x: The anion-exchange resin is positively charged and retains negatively charged species. Lysine is net positive and is repelled, so it passes through first. Trap: Reversing the logic from the cation-exchange column.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for glutamate eluting after aspartate on the cation-exchange column?
o: Glutamate has a lower molar mass than aspartate, so it moves through the resin bed more slowly
Glutamate is the larger of the two, so mass cannot explain it; mass does not determine ion-exchange retention.
The side chain of glutamate is positively charged at pH 3.0, so it binds the sulfonate resin more strongly
The carboxyl side chain is neutral or negative, never positive at this pH.
Glutamate is more hydrophobic than aspartate, so it dissolves in the mobile phase and is carried along less
Hydrophobicity is not the main factor in ion-exchange retention.
Glutamate's side-chain carboxyl has a higher pKa, so it is less deprotonated at pH 3.0 and the amino acid is less negative
Correct: Glutamate's side-chain pKa (about 4.25) is higher than aspartate's (about 3.65), so at pH 3.0 more of it is protonated and the net charge is closer to positive, which binds the resin more.
qs.x: Glutamate's side-chain pKa (about 4.25) is higher than aspartate's (about 3.65), so at pH 3.0 more of it is protonated and the net charge is closer to positive, which binds the resin more. Trap: Ignoring side-chain pKa differences between Asp and Glu.

qs.q: Using the pKa values given, what is the pI of lysine?
o: Correct: The neutral zwitterion lies between deprotonation of the α-NH₃⁺ and side-chain, so pI = (8.95 + 10.53)/2 = 9.74.
5.57 averages the first two pKa values and applies to a neutral side chain.
7.22 averages all three pKa values.
10.53 is the pKa of the side chain, not the pI.
qs.x: The neutral zwitterion lies between deprotonation of the α-NH₃⁺ and side-chain, so pI = (8.95 + 10.53)/2 = 9.74. Trap: Averaging the wrong pair of pKa values for a basic amino acid.

passages.title: FL03 · Chem/Phys · Passage 9
text: A chemist compares the rates of base-promoted hydrolysis (saponification) of several esters, RCO₂R′, in aqueous ethanol containing excess NaOH at 25°C. The reaction is monitored by the disappearance of hydroxide. The mechanism involves addition of hydroxide to the carbonyl carbon to give a tetrahedral intermediate, followed by loss of the alkoxide (R′O⁻) and an acid-base reaction between the resulting carboxylic acid and a base. The approximate relative rates, referenced to methyl acetate, are given in Table 1. The tert-butyl ester is hydrolyzed very slowly under these basic conditions. The chemist also notes that, when ethyl acetate is hydrolyzed with a stoichiometric amount of NaOH, the hydroxide is consumed completely, and that the same hydrolysis in dilute aqueous acid is reversible. Each ester is used at the same initial concentration, and the temperature is controlled with a water bath so that the rate comparisons are valid. Rates are determined from the change in hydroxide concentration over the first several minutes of reaction, before the concentrations have changed appreciably.

qs.q: What is the first step in the mechanism of saponification?
o: Hydroxide adds to the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate
Correct: Hydroxide is a strong nucleophile that adds to the electrophilic C=O carbon, producing a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate.
Water protonates the alkoxy oxygen, converting the alkoxide into a better leaving group
Protonation of the alkoxy oxygen to make a better leaving group occurs in acid-catalyzed hydrolysis, not under basic conditions.
Hydroxide displaces the alkoxide group by SN2 attack at the carbon of the R′ group
SN2 displacement at the R′ carbon is not the pathway; attack at the acyl carbon is much faster.
Hydroxide removes an α-hydrogen, generating an enolate that is then protonated by water
Enolate formation is a side equilibrium that does not cleave the ester.
qs.x: Hydroxide is a strong nucleophile that adds to the electrophilic C=O carbon, producing a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate. Trap: Mixing up the acid-catalyzed and base-promoted mechanisms.

qs.q: Which statement best explains the slow rate of hydrolysis of tert-butyl acetate?
o: tert-Butoxide is a better leaving group than methoxide, which should speed the collapse of the intermediate.
tert-Butoxide is a stronger base and therefore a poorer leaving group, so a better leaving group would not explain a slower rate; the observed trend follows sterics.
The tert-butyl group donates electron density into the carbonyl carbon by resonance, making it less electrophilic.
Alkyl groups donate through induction, not resonance, and the effect is small.
tert-Butyl acetate lacks a carbonyl group and therefore cannot form a tetrahedral intermediate.
tert-Butyl acetate does contain a carbonyl group.
Steric crowding from the tert-butyl group raises the energy of the tetrahedral transition state.
Correct: Bulky R′ groups crowd the tetrahedral intermediate and the approach of OH⁻, increasing the activation energy and lowering the rate.
qs.x: Bulky R′ groups crowd the tetrahedral intermediate and the approach of OH⁻, increasing the activation energy and lowering the rate. Trap: Attributing the rate trend to leaving-group acidity when the observed trend follows sterics.

qs.q: Why is methyl chloroacetate hydrolyzed much faster than methyl acetate?
o: Chlorine is a bulky substituent that crowds the carbonyl carbon and stabilizes the intermediate by shielding.
Steric crowding would slow the reaction, not accelerate it, and shielding does not stabilize a negatively charged intermediate.
Chlorine donates electrons by resonance to the carbonyl carbon, making addition of hydroxide easier.
Chlorine withdraws electrons inductively; donation would reduce the electrophilicity and slow the reaction.
Electron-withdrawing chlorine makes the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic and stabilizes the intermediate.
Correct: The inductive effect of Cl makes the carbonyl carbon more positive and the intermediate more stable, so addition of OH⁻ is faster.
Chloride is a better leaving group than methoxide, so the intermediate collapses more rapidly.
The leaving group is methoxide in both esters; Cl remains on the acyl carbon chain.
qs.x: The inductive effect of Cl makes the carbonyl carbon more positive and the intermediate more stable, so addition of OH⁻ is faster. Trap: Treating the chlorine as the leaving group because it is a halogen.

qs.q: Why is the saponification of ethyl acetate effectively irreversible, while acid-catalyzed hydrolysis is reversible?
o: Ethanol is volatile and escapes from the reaction mixture, so the reverse reaction cannot occur.
Volatility is not required; the reaction is irreversible even in a sealed vessel.
The tetrahedral intermediate is more stable under basic conditions, so it never reverts to the ester.
The stability of the intermediate does not determine reversibility.
Hydroxide deprotonates the acid product to a carboxylate, which ethanol cannot attack.
Correct: The final acid-base step forms acetate, which resists attack by nucleophiles because of resonance and charge, so the reaction proceeds to completion. Base is consumed, not catalytic.
Hydroxide is regenerated at the end of the mechanism and acts as a catalyst, driving the reaction forward.
Hydroxide is consumed in the process, not regenerated.
qs.x: The final acid-base step forms acetate, which resists attack by nucleophiles because of resonance and charge, so the reaction proceeds to completion. Base is consumed, not catalytic. Trap: Calling hydroxide a catalyst even though it is consumed.

passages.title: FL03 · Chem/Phys · Passage 10
text: Crystal violet, a purple dye, is bleached by hydroxide: CV⁺ + OH⁻ → colorless product. A student follows the reaction in a spectrophotometer at 590 nm using a cuvette of path length 1.00 cm. The molar absorptivity of CV⁺ at this wavelength is 8.7 × 10⁴ M⁻¹cm⁻¹, and the product does not absorb. The initial [CV⁺] is 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ M, and [OH⁻] is 0.050 M, which is in large excess. Absorbance is recorded at 30 s intervals at 25 °C. Table 1 lists the absorbance (A) and its natural logarithm, and Figure 1 plots ln A against time. In a second run at the same temperature with [OH⁻] = 0.100 M and the same [CV⁺], the half-life was 15 s. The student assumes the rate law is rate = k[CV⁺][OH⁻] and treats the data as pseudo-first-order. The solutions are thermostatted in a water bath, and the spectrophotometer is zeroed with a blank containing only hydroxide solution before each run.

qs.q: What is [CV⁺] at 60 s?
o: Correct: c = A/(εb) = 0.217/[(8.7×10⁴)(1.00)] = 2.5×10⁻⁶ M, one quarter of the initial concentration (two half-lives).
5.0×10⁻⁶ M is the concentration at 30 s (one half-life).
7.5×10⁻⁶ M is the amount consumed, not remaining.
2.5×10⁻⁵ M is larger than the initial concentration of 1.0×10⁻⁵ M.
qs.x: c = A/(εb) = 0.217/[(8.7×10⁴)(1.00)] = 2.5×10⁻⁶ M, one quarter of the initial concentration (two half-lives). Trap: Misplacing the decimal when converting absorbance to concentration with a large ε.

qs.q: What is the pseudo-first-order rate constant for the first run?
o: Correct: The slope of ln A versus t is (−2.912 − (−0.139))/120 s = −0.0231 s⁻¹, so k_obs = 0.023 s⁻¹ (also ln 2/30 s).
0.033 s⁻¹ equals 1/t½, which omits ln 2.
0.69 s⁻¹ is ln 2 and omits division by the half-life.
43 s⁻¹
43 s⁻¹ is the reciprocal of the correct value, with the wrong units.
qs.x: The slope of ln A versus t is (−2.912 − (−0.139))/120 s = −0.0231 s⁻¹, so k_obs = 0.023 s⁻¹ (also ln 2/30 s). Trap: Using 1/t½ as the first-order rate constant.

qs.q: What is the second-order rate constant k for the bleaching reaction?
o: 0.46 M⁻¹s⁻¹
Correct: k = k_obs/[OH⁻] = 0.0231/0.050 = 0.46 M⁻¹s⁻¹; the second run gives (ln 2/15)/0.100 = 0.46 M⁻¹s⁻¹, confirming first order in OH⁻.
1.2×10⁻³ comes from multiplying k_obs by [OH⁻].
0.023 reuses k_obs and does not divide by [OH⁻].
0.92 M⁻¹s⁻¹
0.92 comes from dividing the second-run constant by the first concentration.
qs.x: k = k_obs/[OH⁻] = 0.0231/0.050 = 0.46 M⁻¹s⁻¹; the second run gives (ln 2/15)/0.100 = 0.46 M⁻¹s⁻¹, confirming first order in OH⁻. Trap: Multiplying rather than dividing k_obs by the hydroxide concentration.

qs.q: Why was [OH⁻] kept in large excess over [CV⁺]?
o: So the product also absorbs at 590 nm and amplifies the signal
The product is colorless and does not absorb.
So the reaction becomes zero order in CV⁺ and the plot of A against time is linear
The reaction remains first order in CV⁺, so A versus t is exponential.
So the activation energy falls and the reaction is completed within the 120 s observed
Concentration does not change the activation energy; only the rate is affected.
So [OH⁻] stays nearly constant, making the rate depend only on [CV⁺]
Correct: With [OH⁻] ≫ [CV⁺], [OH⁻] barely changes, so rate = k_obs[CV⁺] and ln A is linear in time.
qs.x: With [OH⁻] ≫ [CV⁺], [OH⁻] barely changes, so rate = k_obs[CV⁺] and ln A is linear in time. Trap: Believing that excess reagent changes the activation energy rather than the apparent order.

graph.title: Figure 1. ln A versus time for the bleaching of crystal violet

passages.title: FL03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 1
text: Researchers studied conditioned taste aversion in 40 adult laboratory rats. On the conditioning day, each rat drank a novel saccharin-flavored solution for 20 minutes. Rats were then randomly assigned (n = 10 per group) to receive an injection of lithium chloride, a drug that causes nausea, either 30 minutes, 6 hours, or 24 hours after drinking, or an injection of saline 30 minutes after drinking. Two days later, each rat was offered the saccharin solution again for 20 minutes, and the volume consumed was measured. Lithium chloride produced nausea lasting about 2 hours, and no rat received a second injection. Results are shown in Table 1. In a follow-up, rats from the 30-minute lithium group were offered saccharin for five consecutive daily tests with no further injections. Their mean intake rose steadily across the tests, reaching 11.9 mL on the fifth day. The investigators noted that rats rarely develop aversions to the sounds or lights present in the testing room, even when these accompany the nausea.

qs.q: After conditioning, the saccharin solution in the lithium groups is best described as a:
o: unconditioned stimulus that naturally elicits nausea.
The nausea-inducing drug is the unconditioned stimulus; saccharin did not cause illness on its own.
conditioned response that reflects the rats' learned avoidance.
The avoidance is the response; saccharin is the stimulus that triggers it.
conditioned stimulus that now elicits an aversive response.
Correct: Saccharin began as a neutral taste and, through pairing with nausea, acquired the ability to elicit avoidance, which defines a conditioned stimulus.
negative reinforcer that increases the drinking of saccharin.
Intake fell, and a stimulus that is removed to strengthen a behavior is not what was manipulated here.
qs.x: Saccharin began as a neutral taste and, through pairing with nausea, acquired the ability to elicit avoidance, which defines a conditioned stimulus. Trap: Confusing the learned stimulus (CS) with the learned response (CR), or calling the drug the CS because it was the 'treatment.'

qs.q: Intake in the 6-hour lithium group (5.4 mL) was far below that of the saline group (14.2 mL). This result is notable because it shows that:
o: conditioning occurred only because the saccharin and the lithium injection were presented at the same moment.
The injection came 6 hours after drinking, so the two stimuli were not simultaneous.
the rats had habituated to the saccharin solution during conditioning.
Habituation would not lower intake relative to the saline control, which drank the same solution.
learning of a flavor-illness association can form despite a delay of hours between the CS and US.
Correct: Most classical conditioning requires the CS and US to be close in time, but taste-illness learning is biologically prepared and tolerates long delays.
the lithium injection acted as a conditioned stimulus for the saccharin taste.
Lithium is the unconditioned stimulus; the saccharin taste is the one that gained meaning.
qs.x: Most classical conditioning requires the CS and US to be close in time, but taste-illness learning is biologically prepared and tolerates long delays. Trap: Assuming that all classical conditioning needs a half-second-to-seconds interval and so reading the 6-hour effect as a methodological flaw.

qs.q: The gradual rise in saccharin intake to 11.9 mL across five tests without further injections illustrates:
o: spontaneous recovery, because the aversion reappeared after a rest period.
Spontaneous recovery is the return of an extinguished response after a pause; here the aversion was weakening, not returning.
extinction, because the CS was repeatedly presented without the US.
Correct: Repeated presentation of the CS alone weakens the conditioned response, so intake gradually returns toward baseline.
stimulus generalization, because the rats drank similar flavors.
Generalization concerns responses to stimuli resembling the CS, which were not tested.
sensitization, because exposure heightened the rats' responses.
Sensitization would increase responsiveness to stimuli and would not produce increased drinking.
qs.x: Repeated presentation of the CS alone weakens the conditioned response, so intake gradually returns toward baseline. Trap: Reading any change in a conditioned response over time as spontaneous recovery rather than recognizing the decline as extinction.

qs.q: The saline-injected group was included primarily to:
o: rule out that handling or injection alone reduced saccharin intake.
Correct: Because that group went through the same procedure except for the drug, differences in intake can be attributed to pairing with lithium.
measure how much saccharin intake rises after repeated extinction trials without lithium.
Extinction was assessed in the lithium group, not the saline group.
increase the sample size available for the comparison with the 24-hour delay group.
The saline group was a separate comparison and did not add to the 24-hour group.
confirm that lithium chloride acts as an unconditioned stimulus that produces nausea.
That lithium causes nausea is known from prior work and is not tested by a saline group.
qs.x: Because that group went through the same procedure except for the drug, differences in intake can be attributed to pairing with lithium. Trap: Thinking a control group exists to enlarge the sample or to test the drug itself instead of isolating the manipulated variable.

qs.q: Relative to the saline group, the percentage reduction in saccharin intake in the 30-minute lithium group was closest to:
o: This is 3.1 / 14.2, the intake as a fraction of control rather than the reduction.
This is the reduction for the 6-hour group, (14.2 - 5.4) / 14.2.
This would require intake of about 1.6 mL; it is not supported by the table.
qs.x: (14.2 - 3.1) / 14.2 = 11.1 / 14.2, or about 78%. Trap: Reporting the remaining intake (22%) as the reduction instead of subtracting it from 100%.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Saccharin intake at test (mL, mean with SD in parentheses)

passages.title: FL03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 2
text: Pure-tone audiometry was used to measure hearing thresholds in three groups of adults with no history of ear disease or noisy occupations: young (ages 20 to 29), middle-aged (50 to 59), and older (70 to 79), with 40 participants per group. Each participant listened through headphones to tones at four frequencies, and the threshold was defined as the lowest intensity, in decibels hearing level (dB HL), detected on 50% of presentations. Higher values therefore indicate poorer hearing. Mean thresholds are shown in Figure 1. To determine the site of the loss, thresholds at 4000 Hz were also measured by bone conduction, in which a vibrator on the skull bypasses the outer and middle ear. These results are shown in Table 1 for the older group and for a comparison group of 10 adults with fluid behind the eardrum. Postmortem examination of cochleae from a separate set of older donors showed that loss of hair cells was greatest near the cochlear base and minimal near the apex.

qs.q: Which structural change best accounts for the greater high-frequency loss in older adults?
o: Loss of hair cells near the apex of the cochlea, where the basilar membrane is wide and floppy
The apex encodes low frequencies, and the donor cochleae showed minimal apical loss.
Stiffening of the tympanic membrane and ossicles, which impairs transmission of sound to the cochlea
Conductive changes would raise bone-conduction thresholds less than air thresholds, which was not the pattern in the older group.
Degeneration of the vestibular hair cells in the semicircular canals that sense head rotation
The vestibular system contributes to balance, not to detecting tones.
Loss of hair cells along the stiff basilar membrane near the cochlear base
Correct: High frequencies maximally displace the basilar membrane near the base, so hair-cell loss there impairs high-pitched hearing first.
qs.x: High frequencies maximally displace the basilar membrane near the base, so hair-cell loss there impairs high-pitched hearing first. Trap: Choosing the apex because 'older' suggests low sounds, forgetting that high frequencies are coded at the base.

qs.q: The elevation in threshold of older adults relative to young adults at 8000 Hz is about how many times the elevation at 1000 Hz?
o: 1.5 does not match any pair of readings in Figure 1 and understates the 8000 Hz elevation relative to 1000 Hz.
Correct: At 8000 Hz the elevation is 70 - 12 = 58 dB; at 1000 Hz it is 22 - 5 = 17 dB; 58 / 17 is about 3.4.
Neither pair of read values gives this ratio; it would underestimate the difference at 8000 Hz.
This is far too large; the older group's thresholds are 70 versus 22 dB, a ratio of about 3.2 even before subtracting baselines.
qs.x: At 8000 Hz the elevation is 70 - 12 = 58 dB; at 1000 Hz it is 22 - 5 = 17 dB; 58 / 17 is about 3.4. Trap: Dividing raw thresholds (70/22) instead of first subtracting each frequency's young-adult baseline.

qs.q: The older group's air-conduction (52 dB) and bone-conduction (49 dB) thresholds at 4000 Hz indicate that their loss is mainly:
o: sensorineural, because bypassing the middle ear does not help.
Correct: If the problem were in the outer or middle ear, bone conduction would be much better than air conduction, as in the middle-ear fluid group (5 versus 40 dB).
conductive, because the air-conduction threshold is elevated above normal.
Elevated air thresholds occur in both types; the air-bone gap distinguishes them, and the gap here is only 3 dB.
conductive, because damage to the ossicles reduces sound transmission.
Ossicle damage would produce a large air-bone gap, which is absent.
cortical, because the sound reaches the inner ear normally.
The elevated bone-conduction threshold points to the cochlea or auditory nerve, and the histology supports a cochlear cause.
qs.x: If the problem were in the outer or middle ear, bone conduction would be much better than air conduction, as in the middle-ear fluid group (5 versus 40 dB). Trap: Seeing high air-conduction thresholds and concluding 'conductive' without comparing air and bone values.

qs.q: The threshold values measured in this study correspond to the psychophysical concept of:
o: difference threshold, the smallest detectable change between two stimuli of different intensity.
Difference thresholds involve comparing two stimuli, not detecting a single tone.
sensory adaptation, the reduced responsiveness of receptors to constant stimulation.
Adaptation concerns declining responses during sustained stimulation and was not measured.
signal detection, the separation of sensitivity from response bias in a decision.
No catch trials or bias measures were described.
absolute threshold, the minimum intensity detected 50% of the time.
Correct: The study defined threshold as the lowest intensity detected on half of presentations, which is the standard definition of absolute threshold.
qs.x: The study defined threshold as the lowest intensity detected on half of presentations, which is the standard definition of absolute threshold. Trap: Mixing absolute threshold with the just-noticeable difference because both are called 'thresholds.'

qs.q: For an older adult whose profound loss is due to destruction of cochlear hair cells, which intervention directly addresses the deficit?
o: A cochlear implant that stimulates the auditory nerve
Correct: The implant bypasses damaged hair cells and delivers electrical signals to auditory nerve fibers.
Tympanostomy tubes inserted to drain fluid from the middle ear
Tubes treat middle-ear fluid, a conductive problem.
An ossicular prosthesis to replace the damaged middle-ear bones
This would address conductive loss, which this group did not have.
Surgical removal of impacted earwax from the ear canal
Earwax blockage affects sound transmission to the eardrum, not hair-cell function.
qs.x: The implant bypasses damaged hair cells and delivers electrical signals to auditory nerve fibers. Trap: Matching any ear procedure to 'hearing loss' without checking whether the site is conductive or sensorineural.
