passages.title: FL03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 3
text: Fourteen healthy adults slept for two consecutive nights in a sleep laboratory while polysomnography recorded EEG, eye movements, and chin muscle tone. The first night was used for adaptation, and data were taken from the second night. Recordings were scored in 30-second epochs as wakefulness, stage N1, N2, or N3 (non-REM sleep), or REM sleep. During each stage, an experimenter played a 1-second tone that began at 40 dB and rose in 5-dB steps every 30 seconds until the participant awoke; the loudness at awakening was the arousal threshold. Mean values are shown in Table 1. During N2 sleep, participants also heard the same 50-dB tone every 10 seconds. The amplitude of the EEG response to the tone declined over the first several minutes of repetition, but a recording of the sleeper's own name, played afterward, produced a large response. Total sleep time averaged 420 minutes. Participants avoided caffeine and alcohol on study days, and the scorers did not know when the tones were played.

qs.q: A participant is awakened during the stage marked by low-amplitude, mixed-frequency EEG activity, rapid eye movements, and loss of chin muscle tone. The participant is most likely to report:
o: a vivid, story-like dream.
Correct: REM sleep combines wake-like cortical activity with muscle atonia, and awakenings from it yield vivid, narrative dreams most often.
a brief sensation of falling, with no organized imagery.
Hypnic jerks and falling sensations occur at sleep onset in N1, which shows theta waves and slow rolling eye movements.
no mental activity, but a short period of sleepwalking.
Sleepwalking arises from deep N3 sleep, when muscle tone is preserved, not from REM, when voluntary muscles are paralyzed.
a clear memory of the tones played during the night.
Sleeping people do not form lasting memories of ordinary external stimuli, and this stage has no special link to remembering tones.
qs.x: REM sleep combines wake-like cortical activity with muscle atonia, and awakenings from it yield vivid, narrative dreams most often. Trap: Matching low-amplitude, mixed EEG to light non-REM sleep because the waves are small, rather than recognizing the wake-like pattern of REM.

qs.q: What percentage of total sleep time was spent in stage N3?
o: This is the share for N1 (21/420), the shortest stage.
This is the share for REM sleep (105/420), not N3.
Correct: 84 min / 420 min = 0.20, or 20%.
This is N3 divided by N2 (84/210), which uses the wrong denominator instead of total sleep time.
qs.x: 84 min / 420 min = 0.20, or 20%. Trap: Dividing by the time in another stage instead of by the total sleep time.

qs.q: The declining EEG response to the repeated 50-dB tone, together with the large response to the sleeper's own name, is best described as:
o: sensitization to the tone, in which repeated exposure produces a progressively stronger response to it and to similar stimuli.
Sensitization would raise the response with repetition; the data show a decline.
habituation to the repeated tone, with the personally meaningful name still capturing attention.
Correct: Repeated exposure to a harmless stimulus reduces responding, and a novel, meaningful stimulus is not habituated to, so the name evokes a large response.
extinction of a conditioned response, in which a learned association fades when the tone is presented repeatedly without its usual consequence.
Extinction requires an earlier learned association that stops being reinforced; no association was trained here.
spontaneous recovery of a learned response, in which a response reappears after a rest period, here when the name replaced the tone.
Spontaneous recovery refers to a conditioned response reappearing after a rest period, which does not describe a new stimulus (the name) evoking a response.
qs.x: Repeated exposure to a harmless stimulus reduces responding, and a novel, meaningful stimulus is not habituated to, so the name evokes a large response. Trap: Calling any decline in responding extinction, even though extinction requires an earlier learned association.

qs.q: Why did the researchers use data from the second night rather than the first?
o: Sleep stages cannot be scored reliably until a participant has been recorded for at least two nights.
Scoring in 30-second epochs is possible from any recording; no minimum number of nights is needed.
Total sleep time always doubles on the second night, so its data give a larger sample of epochs.
Sleep duration does not systematically double; the adaptation night addresses sleep quality, not sample size.
Participants on the first night would have heard tones that altered the arousal thresholds measured later.
The tones were played on the data night, not before it; the adaptation night addressed environment effects.
An unfamiliar room and equipment can disturb first-night sleep, which would distort stage durations.
Correct: A first-night effect (lighter, more fragmented sleep in an unfamiliar setting) is a known confound, and an adaptation night reduces it.
qs.x: A first-night effect (lighter, more fragmented sleep in an unfamiliar setting) is a known confound, and an adaptation night reduces it. Trap: Treating the adaptation night as a way to collect more data instead of a control for an unfamiliar environment.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by Table 1?
o: The loudest tone was needed to awaken sleepers from the delta-wave stage, indicating the deepest sleep.
Correct: N3 had the highest mean threshold (78 dB) and slow, high-amplitude delta waves, consistent with deep slow-wave sleep.
Arousal threshold fell steadily from N1 through REM as the night went on, so sleep became lighter with each successive stage.
Thresholds rose from N1 (52) to N3 (78) before falling to 66 in REM; they did not fall steadily, and the table does not track time across the night.
REM sleep is the deepest stage because its EEG pattern differs most from that of wakefulness.
REM thresholds (66 dB) are lower than N3 (78 dB), and its wake-like EEG suggests a more active brain, not a deeper sleep by this measure.
N2 is the stage from which participants were hardest to awaken, because it accounted for the longest share of the night.
Duration does not determine arousal difficulty; N2 had a threshold of 62 dB, below both N3 (78) and REM (66).
qs.x: N3 had the highest mean threshold (78 dB) and slow, high-amplitude delta waves, consistent with deep slow-wave sleep. Trap: Equating the stage with the longest duration with the deepest sleep, instead of using the arousal-threshold column.

r: Theta waves with sleep spindles and K-complexes

passages.title: FL03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 4
text: A university research team surveyed 1,200 undergraduates about their social media use. Students reported their average daily hours on social platforms and completed a 20-item loneliness scale (score range 20 to 80; higher scores indicate greater loneliness) and a sleep diary. Participants were recruited through an introductory psychology course at one university and received course credit. Pearson correlations are shown in Table 1. Six months later, 900 of the students completed the same measures again, and the researchers computed cross-lagged correlations between the two time points (Table 2). Figure 1 shows mean loneliness scores for students grouped by reported daily use at the first survey. The authors cautioned against causal conclusions but proposed that heavy use might displace time spent in face-to-face contact and invite unfavorable comparisons with peers. They also noted that participants may have misjudged their own hours of use and that students who completed the second survey were somewhat less lonely at baseline than those who did not.

qs.q: Approximately what proportion of the variance in loneliness is shared with daily use at the first survey?
o: This treats r itself as the proportion of variance shared.
Correct: The coefficient of determination is r squared: 0.24 x 0.24 = 0.058, or about 6%.
Doubling r would not give the shared variance.
Doubling the correlation again mistakes r for a percentage.
qs.x: The coefficient of determination is r squared: 0.24 x 0.24 = 0.058, or about 6%. Trap: Reading r = 0.24 as 24% of variance explained instead of squaring it.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the Table 1 data?
o: Heavy use causes loneliness, because the correlation between the two is statistically significant at p < 0.001.
Significance shows that the association is unlikely due to chance, not that one variable causes the other.
Use and loneliness are associated, but a third variable such as poor sleep could contribute to both.
Correct: The data are correlational, and sleep is related to both use and loneliness, so it is a plausible confounder.
Use and loneliness are unrelated, because the correlation coefficient is below 0.30 in magnitude.
An r of 0.24 with n = 1,200 is a significant, if modest, association.
Loneliness reduces sleep, which in turn causes heavier use, as shown by the signs of the correlations.
Correlation signs cannot establish a causal chain.
qs.x: The data are correlational, and sleep is related to both use and loneliness, so it is a plausible confounder. Trap: Equating statistical significance with demonstration of causation.

qs.q: Compared with the use-to-loneliness path, the loneliness-to-use path in Table 2 suggests that:
o: social media use clearly causes later loneliness, because use was measured at the first time point.
Temporal order is necessary but not sufficient for causal inference, and the larger path runs the other way.
neither path is statistically significant at the conventional 0.05 level.
Both p-values are below 0.05.
earlier loneliness predicted later use somewhat more strongly than the reverse.
Correct: The correlation from loneliness to later use (+0.17) exceeds the correlation in the other direction (+0.09), though neither proves causation.
the two variables had no relationship at either of the two time points.
All correlations in both tables are significant.
qs.x: The correlation from loneliness to later use (+0.17) exceeds the correlation in the other direction (+0.09), though neither proves causation. Trap: Assuming the variable measured first must be the cause, despite the larger cross-lagged path going the other way.

qs.q: Which feature of the sampling most limits generalization of these findings to all adults?
o: The sample included more than 1,000 students, which exceeds many comparable surveys.
Large samples improve precision and do not limit generalization by themselves.
Loneliness was measured with a 20-item scale instead of a single question.
Scale length relates to reliability, not to which population was sampled.
Some students were lost between the first and second surveys, six months apart.
Attrition threatens internal validity of the longitudinal analysis, rather than generalization to adults as a whole.
Participants were volunteers from one university's introductory course.
Correct: A convenience sample of young students at one school may differ in age, education, and social context from the broader population.
qs.x: A convenience sample of young students at one school may differ in age, education, and social context from the broader population. Trap: Confusing a large sample size with a representative sample.

qs.q: Which psychological process best fits the authors' proposal about 'unfavorable comparisons with peers'?
o: The looking-glass self, in which a person is shaped by the unconscious reactions of strangers.
The looking-glass self concerns imagined judgments of others, not comparisons of self to peers.
The fundamental attribution error, in which dispositions are overemphasized in explaining others' behavior.
This is about explaining others' behavior.
Cognitive dissonance, in which conflicting attitudes produce discomfort.
Dissonance concerns inconsistency between beliefs or between beliefs and behavior.
Social comparison, in which people evaluate their own abilities and status against those of others.
Correct: According to social comparison theory, upward comparisons with peers who appear more successful or more connected can lower self-evaluation.
qs.x: According to social comparison theory, upward comparisons with peers who appear more successful or more connected can lower self-evaluation. Trap: Choosing the looking-glass self because it also involves other people, without noting the process is comparison to peers.

passages.title: FL03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 5
text: In a study of short-term retention, 120 adults were shown a list of 20 unrelated common nouns, one word every 2 seconds at the center of a computer screen. Participants were tested individually in a quiet room and were told in advance that they would be asked to recall the list. They were randomly assigned to one of two conditions (n = 60 each). In the immediate condition, participants wrote down as many words as they could remember, in any order, as soon as the list ended. In the delay condition, participants first counted backward by threes from a three-digit number for 30 seconds and then began writing. For each condition, researchers computed the percentage of participants who correctly recalled the word at each serial position. Figure 1 shows results for selected positions. Mean total recall was 11.4 words in the immediate condition and 8.1 words in the delay condition.

qs.q: The loss of the advantage for the final list items in the delay condition is best explained by:
o: the final items having been poorly encoded into long-term memory because the list was long and fast.
Early and middle items were not affected by the delay, which does not support a general encoding failure.
the final items having been held in short-term memory and then lost during counting.
Correct: Late items are recalled from working memory in the immediate condition; counting prevents rehearsal and displaces them, so the recency advantage disappears.
retroactive facilitation from the counting task strengthening the earlier items in the list.
Early-item recall was nearly unchanged, and a distraction task would not strengthen any item.
a decline in implicit procedural memory caused by the interruption after the list ended.
Procedural memory concerns skills, not recall of words.
qs.x: Late items are recalled from working memory in the immediate condition; counting prevents rehearsal and displaces them, so the recency advantage disappears. Trap: Attributing the recency loss to long-term forgetting, when the surviving primacy items show long-term storage was intact.

qs.q: The high recall of the first few words in both conditions most likely reflects:
o: their storage in the sensory register, which holds the first items for several seconds.
Sensory memory lasts only a second or two and could not survive the counting task.
greater rehearsal of early items, promoting their transfer to long-term memory.
Correct: Early items receive more rehearsal before the list fills working memory, so they are stored more durably and are unaffected by the delay.
their encoding as a single chunk of seven items in working memory.
Chunking is not suggested by a list of unrelated words.
the serial position curve being created by the interference from the counting task.
Primacy was present in the immediate condition, which had no counting task.
qs.x: Early items receive more rehearsal before the list fills working memory, so they are stored more durably and are unaffected by the delay. Trap: Assigning the primacy effect to short-term storage rather than to long-term transfer.

qs.q: At serial position 20, the percentage-point difference between the immediate and delay conditions is:
o: Correct: 88% - 34% = 54 percentage points.
This is the delay condition's value alone.
This arises from misreading one of the values at position 20 by 10.
Misreading either value by 10 would give 64; neither is shown by the graph.
qs.x: 88% - 34% = 54 percentage points. Trap: Reporting one condition's value instead of subtracting the two.

qs.q: Why did participants in the delay condition count backward rather than simply wait for 30 seconds?
o: To increase the number of words stored in long-term memory.
Counting would not enhance storage.
To make the delay and immediate conditions equal in total time.
The delay condition lasted 30 seconds longer by design.
To measure working-memory capacity through the counting performance.
Counting accuracy was not analyzed.
To prevent rehearsal of the last items during the delay.
Correct: Without a distractor, participants could keep rehearsing recent words, preserving the recency effect and confounding the effect of time with that of rehearsal.
qs.x: Without a distractor, participants could keep rehearsing recent words, preserving the recency effect and confounding the effect of time with that of rehearsal. Trap: Assuming that a filler task is intended to improve learning rather than block rehearsal.

passages.title: FL03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 6
text: In a variant of an obedience experiment, 120 adults were randomly assigned to four conditions (n = 30 each). Each participant, cast as a "teacher," was told to deliver electric shocks of rising intensity, up to 450 V, to a "learner" (a confederate who received no shocks) for each wrong answer on a word-pair test. If the teacher hesitated, an experimenter gave a series of standard verbal prods, such as "The experiment requires that you continue." In the first condition, the experimenter wore a lab coat and sat in the room. In the second, he gave the same instructions by telephone from another room. In the third, he sat in the room but wore ordinary clothes. In the fourth, a second "teacher" (a confederate) refused to continue partway through the session. All participants were debriefed and told that no shocks were delivered. The proportion who delivered the maximum shock is shown in Table 1. Participants had no prior coursework in psychology, and the same two experimenters ran all sessions using a written script.

qs.q: The lower rate of full obedience in the telephone condition than in the in-room, lab coat condition best supports which conclusion?
o: Obedience depends mainly on the learner's apparent suffering, which was the same in both conditions.
The learner's behavior was not varied across these conditions, so it cannot account for the difference between them.
Obedience reflects the authority figure's attire, which the telephone condition removed entirely.
Attire was varied only in the third condition; a telephone instruction differs from the in-room condition mainly in how present and watchful the authority is, not in attire alone.
Obedience is greater when the authority figure is physically close and able to monitor compliance.
Correct: Proximity and surveillance of the authority increase compliance, so remote instruction produced fewer maximum shocks (23% vs. 67%).
Obedience reflects the group size, which the telephone condition reduced from two people to one.
Group size was not manipulated between these two conditions; in each, one participant faced one experimenter.
qs.x: Proximity and surveillance of the authority increase compliance, so remote instruction produced fewer maximum shocks (23% vs. 67%). Trap: Attributing a difference to a variable (such as attire or suffering) that was not manipulated between the two conditions compared.

qs.q: The sharp drop in obedience when a peer teacher refused to continue is best explained by:
o: the presence of a dissenting peer, which legitimizes disobedience and reduces pressure to comply.
Correct: A model of defiance shows that refusal is possible and weakens the authority's influence, as in research on resistance to authority.
social facilitation, in which the presence of an audience or co-actors improves performance on simple or well-learned tasks.
Social facilitation concerns performance effects of an audience, not a decision to continue or refuse an order.
deindividuation, in which immersion in a group lowers self-awareness and personal accountability for harmful acts.
Deindividuation would increase harmful compliance in a group; here the peer's refusal reduced it.
groupthink, in which a cohesive group suppresses dissent and overrides realistic appraisal of alternatives to preserve unanimity.
Groupthink describes cohesive groups suppressing dissent; the dissenting peer here was followed rather than suppressed.
qs.x: A model of defiance shows that refusal is possible and weakens the authority's influence, as in research on resistance to authority. Trap: Choosing a familiar group-behavior term (groupthink, deindividuation) without checking whether its predicted direction matches the result.

qs.q: Approximately how many times as large was the proportion delivering 450 V in the lab coat, in-room condition as in the telephone condition?
o: This is the inverse ratio (7/20), which compares the telephone condition to the in-room condition.
This is the difference in the number of participants (20 - 7), not a ratio.
This is the difference between the percentages (66.7 - 23.3 = 43.3), which is in percentage points, not a ratio.
Correct: 20 / 7 = 2.86, or about 2.9 times.
qs.x: 20 / 7 = 2.86, or about 2.9 times. Trap: Subtracting two values when the question asks for a ratio, or inverting the ratio.

qs.q: Which design feature most directly allows a comparison of the lab coat and ordinary clothes conditions to isolate the effect of attire?
o: Debriefing of all participants, which equalized their knowledge of the study afterward.
Debriefing occurs after the data are collected and cannot affect behavior during the experiment.
Random assignment, with location, prods, and learner responses held constant across the two conditions.
Correct: Only attire differed between the two conditions, and random assignment spread participant characteristics evenly.
Use of a confederate as the learner, which ensured that no shocks were actually delivered.
Using a confederate protects participants' welfare and standardizes the learner's responses but does not isolate attire.
The inclusion of 30 participants per condition, which makes any difference statistically significant.
A sample of 30 per group does not guarantee statistical significance, and sample size does not isolate a variable.
qs.x: Only attire differed between the two conditions, and random assignment spread participant characteristics evenly. Trap: Confusing ethical or procedural safeguards with features that control confounding variables.

passages.title: FL03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 7
text: Pigeons were trained to peck a key for food. Thirty-two pigeons, each reduced to 85% of free-feeding body weight, were randomly assigned to four groups (n = 8 each) that differed only in the reinforcement schedule. Fixed-ratio 10 (FR-10): food after every 10th peck. Variable-ratio 10 (VR-10): food after an unpredictable number of pecks that averaged 10. Fixed-interval 30 s (FI-30): food for the first peck after 30 seconds had elapsed since the last food. Variable-interval 30 s (VI-30): food for the first peck after an unpredictable interval averaging 30 seconds. After 20 daily sessions, mean peck rate was recorded. Food was then withheld entirely, and the experimenters counted total pecks until 5 minutes passed with no peck. Results are shown in Table 1. Responding on the FI-30 schedule showed a pause after each food delivery, followed by an increasing rate as the end of the interval approached. Sessions lasted 40 minutes, and the chamber, key, and food hopper were identical for every group.

qs.q: Gambling on a slot machine, which pays out after an unpredictable number of plays, most resembles which schedule?
o: Variable-ratio
Correct: Payoff depends on the number of responses, which varies unpredictably; this is variable-ratio and it sustains high, steady rates.
Fixed-ratio
Fixed-ratio pays after a set number of responses, which a slot machine does not do.
Variable-interval
Variable-interval depends on elapsed time, not on the number of plays, so playing faster would not bring a payout sooner.
Fixed-interval
Fixed-interval depends on a predictable amount of elapsed time, not on the number of plays.
qs.x: Payoff depends on the number of responses, which varies unpredictably; this is variable-ratio and it sustains high, steady rates. Trap: Choosing fixed-ratio because payouts are tied to responses, overlooking the unpredictability of the required number.

qs.q: The much lower peck rate on FI-30 than on the ratio schedules is best explained by the fact that on an interval schedule:
o: food is delivered after a fixed number of pecks, which lets the bird rest once it has completed that required number.
A set number of pecks defines a fixed-ratio schedule, not a fixed-interval one.
the unpredictability of food delivery makes each peck equally likely to be reinforced.
Fixed-interval schedules are predictable in timing, and the pecks made early in the interval are never reinforced.
extra pecks before the interval ends do not bring food sooner, so rate is not tied to number of pecks.
Correct: Reinforcement depends on time passing, so fast pecking does not increase food; the bird pecks little early in the interval.
punishment is delivered for pecks made before the interval has elapsed, which suppresses responding early in the interval.
No punisher was used; early pecks are simply not reinforced, which is extinction-like, not punishment.
qs.x: Reinforcement depends on time passing, so fast pecking does not increase food; the bird pecks little early in the interval. Trap: Assuming that all intermittent schedules produce similarly high response rates.

qs.q: By approximately what percent did the mean peck rate on VR-10 exceed that on FR-10?
o: The difference was divided by the larger rate (16/78 = 20.5%); the comparison group's rate should be the base.
16 is the raw difference in pecks per minute, not a percent of the FR-10 rate.
Correct: The percent excess is (78 - 62) / 62 = 0.258, or about 26%.
This is the ratio 78/62 expressed as a percent (about 126%), which is the rate itself as a percent of FR-10 rather than the excess.
qs.x: The percent excess is (78 - 62) / 62 = 0.258, or about 26%. Trap: Dividing by the wrong baseline or reporting the raw difference as a percent.

qs.q: Which result in Table 1 is best explained by the unpredictability of reinforcement on the variable schedules?
o: Fewer total pecks after food was withheld, because variable schedules weaken the link between pecking and food.
The table shows the opposite: variable groups pecked more after food was withheld (410 vs. 95; 260 vs. 120).
Greater persistence of pecking after food was withheld, because the absence of food is harder to detect.
Correct: Birds on variable schedules were used to long, irregular runs without food, so extinction does not stand out; they pecked 410 and 260 times, more than their fixed counterparts.
A faster peck rate on VI-30 than on FR-10 during training, because interval schedules deliver food more often.
VI-30 birds pecked 36 times per minute, slower than FR-10 birds at 62, so this result does not occur.
A pause after each food delivery, because the bird knew when the next food would be available.
The post-reinforcement pause is described for the fixed-interval schedule, where timing is predictable.
qs.x: Birds on variable schedules were used to long, irregular runs without food, so extinction does not stand out; they pecked 410 and 260 times, more than their fixed counterparts. Trap: Expecting weaker responding from the less predictable schedule, which reverses the partial-reinforcement extinction effect.

passages.title: FL03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 8
text: Researchers tested whether intergroup contact reduces prejudice. Two hundred forty adolescents from two ethnic groups that had little prior contact were randomly assigned (n = 80 per condition) to a four-week program. In the cooperative contact condition, mixed-group teams of equal status worked toward a shared goal that no single group could reach alone, with support from program leaders. In the unstructured contact condition, adolescents shared a facility and meals but chose their own activities, and teams were not formed. In the no-contact condition, adolescents stayed in their own groups. Warmth toward the out-group was measured at baseline, at 4 weeks, and at 24 weeks, on a 0 to 100 thermometer (higher scores indicate warmer feelings). Results are summarized in Table 1 and Figure 1. The research assistants who collected the ratings did not know the condition assignments. Participants completed the ratings privately, and none left the program before the final assessment.

qs.q: Which feature of the cooperative contact condition is most consistent with the conditions that the contact hypothesis says are needed to reduce prejudice?
o: Equal-status teams pursuing a common goal with institutional support.
Correct: Equal status, cooperation toward shared goals, and authority support are the classic conditions for contact to improve intergroup attitudes.
Frequent, casual exposure to out-group members in shared settings.
Mere exposure was present in the unstructured condition, where warmth did not rise, so it is not sufficient.
Random assignment of participants to a program instead of self-selection.
Random assignment strengthens the design but is not a feature of the contact conditions that the theory describes.
Measurement of attitudes at several time points after the program began.
Repeated measurement is a design feature and does not itself change attitudes.
qs.x: Equal status, cooperation toward shared goals, and authority support are the classic conditions for contact to improve intergroup attitudes. Trap: Assuming that simply being together reduces prejudice, even though the unstructured group shows little change.

qs.q: Which change would most likely allow the unstructured contact condition to produce attitude gains similar to the cooperative condition?
o: Increasing the number of meals that adolescents from both groups share in the facility.
More shared meals add exposure only; the unstructured group already had meals and shows no gain.
Adding a competition between the two ethnic groups to increase the salience of group identity.
Competition between groups increases hostility, as in Sherif's realistic conflict findings.
Assigning mixed-group teams a goal that requires the efforts of members from both groups.
Correct: Superordinate goals that require cooperation, as in Sherif's studies, convert two groups into one team and reduce bias.
Reminding adolescents of their ethnic group membership before each activity.
Emphasizing category membership strengthens in-group versus out-group distinctions rather than reducing them.
qs.x: Superordinate goals that require cooperation, as in Sherif's studies, convert two groups into one team and reduce bias. Trap: Choosing more exposure, which fails to separate cooperation from simple contact.

qs.q: In the cooperative contact condition, by approximately what percent did mean warmth decline from week 4 to week 24?
o: This is the raw decline in points (4), not the percent.
This divides the 4-point decline by the 19-point gain (4/19), which gives the share of the gain lost rather than the percent decline from week 4.
This is the net gain from baseline relative to baseline (15/42), not the decline from week 4.
Correct: (61 - 57) / 61 = 0.066, or about 7%.
qs.x: (61 - 57) / 61 = 0.066, or about 7%. Trap: Dividing by the wrong reference value.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of including the no-contact condition?
o: To ensure that every adolescent receives the same amount of out-group exposure.
The no-contact group received no exposure, so the condition does not equalize exposure.
To show whether warmth changes with time and repeated testing even when no contact occurs.
Correct: A control group that receives no contact reveals changes due to time, repeated measurement, or outside events, so program effects can be separated.
To show that unstructured contact is more effective than cooperative contact.
The data show the opposite: cooperative contact produced the largest gain.
To eliminate the need for random assignment to the other two conditions.
Random assignment is needed for every group and cannot be replaced by a control group.
qs.x: A control group that receives no contact reveals changes due to time, repeated measurement, or outside events, so program effects can be separated. Trap: Treating a control group as something that substitutes for random assignment.

passages.title: FL03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 9
text: To study the development of conservation, researchers tested 180 children, 30 at each age from 4 to 9 years. In the number task, each child first agreed that two rows of six coins were equal, then watched as one row was spread out; the child was asked whether the rows still held the same number. In the liquid task, a child agreed that two identical glasses held equal amounts of juice, and then the juice from one glass was poured into a tall, thin glass; the child was asked whether the amounts were still equal. A child passed a task only by answering that the quantities were equal and giving a reason. Each child was tested once. Pass counts are shown in Table 1, and the percent passing is plotted in Figure 1. Testers followed a fixed script and scored the children's reasons using written criteria; any child who did not understand the instructions was retested on another day.

qs.q: How many more 6-year-olds passed the number task than passed the liquid task?
o: Correct: 13 - 7 = 6 children.
13 is the number passing the number task alone, not the difference.
20% is the difference in percentages (43% - 23%), which is in percentage points, not a count of children.
7 is the number passing the liquid task, not the difference between tasks.
qs.x: 13 - 7 = 6 children. Trap: Reporting one of the two table values or a percentage-point gap instead of the difference in counts.

qs.q: A 4-year-old says the tall, thin glass holds more juice because it looks "taller." According to Piaget, this response most directly reflects:
o: egocentrism, an inability to take another person's perspective, typical of the sensorimotor stage (birth to age 2).
Egocentrism is a preoperational feature, but it concerns perspective-taking, and the sensorimotor stage covers roughly birth to age 2.
lack of object permanence, typical of the formal operational stage, which arises in adolescence.
Object permanence develops in the sensorimotor stage; it is not tied to the formal operational stage, which comes after conservation.
centration on one dimension, typical of the preoperational stage.
Correct: Preoperational children center on one salient feature (height) and cannot yet coordinate height with width, so they fail to conserve.
reversible logic that applies only to abstract hypotheses, typical of the concrete operational stage.
Concrete operational thinking allows reversible reasoning about real objects and is what passing the task reflects; hypothetical reasoning belongs to the formal operational stage.
qs.x: Preoperational children center on one salient feature (height) and cannot yet coordinate height with width, so they fail to conserve. Trap: Matching the child's age to the wrong stage label, or confusing centration with egocentrism.

qs.q: Which statement is a limitation of using these data to describe how an individual child develops?
o: Only two tasks were used, so no clear developmental trend can be seen across the six ages that were tested.
Two tasks still show a clear trend, as the figure shows; the issue is the design, not the number of tasks.
The numbers of children differed across the ages, so percentages cannot be compared from one age group to another.
The groups were equal (30 each), so percentages are directly comparable.
Each child was tested only once, which makes percentages an invalid summary of how children perform on the tasks.
Testing once is not invalid; percentages of passing in each age group are appropriate summaries.
Different children were tested at each age, so age differences may reflect cohort effects, not individual change.
Correct: A cross-sectional design compares different children and cannot show within-child change; a longitudinal design would be needed.
qs.x: A cross-sectional design compares different children and cannot show within-child change; a longitudinal design would be needed. Trap: Citing a flaw that the data do not have, instead of the inability of a cross-sectional design to track individuals.

qs.q: A teacher helps a 6-year-old succeed on the liquid task by guiding her to compare the width and height of the glasses, and the child then solves it. Which concept best describes the range of tasks the child can complete only with such guidance?
o: The sensitive period for language
A sensitive period describes a time when learning of a skill, such as language, is most efficient, not guided task performance.
The zone of proximal development
Correct: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development is the gap between what a child can do alone and what she can do with a more skilled helper.
Assimilation of a new schema
Assimilation fits new information into an existing schema, and the passage describes a task the child cannot yet complete alone.
Authoritative scaffolding of attachment
Attachment styles describe the bond between infant and caregiver, not guided cognitive performance.
qs.x: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development is the gap between what a child can do alone and what she can do with a more skilled helper. Trap: Applying Piaget's terms (assimilation) to a social-guidance process described by Vygotsky.

passages.title: FL03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 10
text: A national health survey of 6,000 adults examined access to care by insurance and income. Respondents were grouped as uninsured, covered by public insurance, covered by private insurance with household income below the median, or covered by private insurance with household income above the median. Each respondent reported whether, in the past year, cost had caused them to delay needed medical care, and whether they had a routine checkup. Results are shown in Table 1. The survey was observational, and respondents were selected by a random sample of households. Uninsured respondents were younger on average and more often worked in jobs that did not offer coverage. Researchers noted that clinics in several low-income neighborhoods had long waits and few evening hours, and that interviews with clinicians indicated that some assumed patients who missed appointments simply did not value care. Interviews were conducted by telephone in English and Spanish with adults aged 25 to 64, and the response rate was 62%.

qs.q: Approximately what percent of all 6,000 respondents delayed care because of cost?
o: This is the rate for the largest group alone (above-median private), which is not the overall rate.
This is the unweighted average of the four percentages ((42 + 22 + 15 + 6)/4 = 21.25), which ignores the different group sizes.
This is the rate for the uninsured group alone.
qs.x: Delayers: 336 + 264 + 240 + 144 = 984; 984 / 6,000 = 16.4%, or about 16%. Trap: Averaging group percentages without weighting by group size.

qs.q: Why can the survey not show that lack of insurance causes lower checkup rates?
o: The sample was selected at random, which makes any comparison across the insurance groups impossible.
Random sampling supports generalization to the population and does not prevent group comparisons.
The checkup percentages were not reported separately for each group, so no comparison of the groups is possible.
The table reports checkup rates separately for each group, so comparison is possible.
Insured and uninsured respondents also differ in income, age, and job type, which could explain the gap.
Correct: An observational comparison has uncontrolled confounders such as income, age, and job type, so insurance status cannot be isolated as the cause.
Self-reported checkups are unrelated to actual health service use, which limits all survey research.
Self-report can be inaccurate, but it is not unrelated to service use; it would not by itself explain the inability to infer causation.
qs.x: An observational comparison has uncontrolled confounders such as income, age, and job type, so insurance status cannot be isolated as the cause. Trap: Treating an association between insurance status and outcomes as proof that insurance is the cause.

qs.q: The pattern in Table 1, in which access to care rises with insurance coverage and income, is best described as an example of:
o: a demographic transition, in which falling mortality and fertility shift the age structure of a population.
The demographic transition describes shifts in birth and death rates, which are not shown here.
anomie, in which the weakening of social norms leads to deviance.
Anomie (Durkheim) describes normlessness, not resource differences in access to care.
a self-fulfilling prophecy, in which expectations about a group produce the behavior expected.
The self-fulfilling prophecy concerns how expectations shape behavior; it fits the clinician example rather than the group differences in the table.
a health disparity arising from social stratification, with unequal distribution of resources.
Correct: Unequal access to health care by social class reflects stratification, which affects health outcomes through resource differences.
qs.x: Unequal access to health care by social class reflects stratification, which affects health outcomes through resource differences. Trap: Choosing a theory term that matches a different detail from the passage instead of the pattern the question asks about.

qs.q: The clinicians who assumed that patients who missed appointments simply did not value care are most clearly making which error?
o: The self-serving bias: crediting successes to internal causes and failures to external causes.
Self-serving bias concerns how people explain their own successes and failures, not how they judge others.
The fundamental attribution error: explaining behavior by disposition and overlooking situational barriers.
Correct: Clinicians ignored situational causes (cost, wait times, hours) and blamed patients' character, the fundamental attribution error.
The actor-observer effect: attributing one's own behavior to dispositions and others' behavior to situations.
The actor-observer effect contrasts explanations for one's own behavior with those for others; here only judgments about other people are described, so it does not fit.
The just-world hypothesis: assuming that favorable outcomes are always deserved.
Just-world beliefs concern deserved outcomes; the clinicians' explanation is about the cause of a specific behavior.
qs.x: Clinicians ignored situational causes (cost, wait times, hours) and blamed patients' character, the fundamental attribution error. Trap: Choosing actor-observer effect, which contrasts self and other, when only judgments about others are described.

passages.title: FL04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 1
text: Myoglobin (Mb) is a monomeric oxygen-storage protein in muscle, whereas hemoglobin (Hb) is a tetramer that transports oxygen in blood. Oxygen saturation of purified Mb and of purified adult Hb was measured at several partial pressures of oxygen (pO2) at 37°C. For Hb, measurements were made at pH 7.4 and pH 7.2, with all other conditions, including the concentration of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG), held constant. Results are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. In the lungs, alveolar pO2 is approximately 100 mmHg; in resting skeletal muscle capillaries, pO2 is approximately 40 mmHg.

The pO2 at which a protein is 50% saturated (P50) was estimated for each curve. Researchers also examined fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which has two α chains and two γ chains. In the presence of physiological 2,3-BPG, HbF was more saturated than adult HbA at any given pO2. A variant hemoglobin (HbS) with a single substitution at the surface of the β chain, Glu6 to Val, was also studied. Its oxygen-binding curve was similar to that of HbA, but deoxygenated HbS formed fibers at high concentration.

qs.q: The difference in shape between the Mb curve and the Hb curves in Figure 1 is best explained by which of the following?
o: Mb binds O2 with lower affinity than Hb, so Mb saturates at higher pO2 values.
Mb is saturated at much lower pO2 (78% at 10 mmHg), so its affinity is higher, not lower.
Hb contains iron in the ferric state, which binds O2 in a sigmoidal manner, whereas Mb contains ferrous iron that binds O2 with a single affinity
Both proteins bind O2 on ferrous (Fe2+) heme; ferric iron does not bind O2.
Hb binds O2 cooperatively because O2 binding at one heme raises the affinity of the other subunits, whereas Mb has a single heme

Correct: Hb is a tetramer whose subunits shift together from the T state toward the R state as O2 binds, giving a sigmoidal curve; Mb has one heme and no subunit interactions, so its curve is hyperbolic.
Mb binds O2 at several interacting sites on its chain, producing a hyperbolic curve with a high P50 value compared with Hb
Mb has one binding site; interacting sites would produce a sigmoidal curve.
qs.x: Hb is a tetramer whose subunits shift together from the T state toward the R state as O2 binds, giving a sigmoidal curve; Mb has one heme and no subunit interactions, so its curve is hyperbolic. Trap: Reading the left-shifted Mb curve as 'lower affinity' reverses the meaning of a low P50.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, the P50 of Hb at pH 7.2 is closest to which value?
o: 20 mmHg
At 20 mmHg, saturation is only 21%.
26 mmHg
26 mmHg is the approximate P50 at pH 7.4 (50% falls between 33% at 20 and 60% at 30), not at pH 7.2.
45 mmHg
At 45 mmHg saturation would be well above 63%, so P50 is lower than this.
33 mmHg
Correct: At pH 7.2, saturation is 44% at 30 mmHg and 63% at 40 mmHg; 50% lies about one-third of the way between, near 33 mmHg.
qs.x: At pH 7.2, saturation is 44% at 30 mmHg and 63% at 40 mmHg; 50% lies about one-third of the way between, near 33 mmHg. Trap: Using the pH 7.4 P50 for the pH 7.2 curve ignores the rightward shift.

qs.q: Assuming blood leaving the lungs has pO2 of 100 mmHg and venous blood has pO2 of 40 mmHg, the amount of O2 released per Hb at pH 7.2 compared with pH 7.4 is approximately:
o: 10% greater
A 10% difference would correspond to roughly 23 points released at pH 7.2.
50% greater
Correct: At pH 7.4, Hb releases 97 − 76 = 21 saturation points; at pH 7.2 it releases 95 − 63 = 32 points. 32/21 is about 1.5, or 50% greater (Bohr effect).
the same
The release is not equal because the curves differ at 40 mmHg (63% vs 76%) but nearly coincide at 100 mmHg.
three times greater
Three times would require releasing about 63 points.
qs.x: At pH 7.4, Hb releases 97 − 76 = 21 saturation points; at pH 7.2 it releases 95 − 63 = 32 points. 32/21 is about 1.5, or 50% greater (Bohr effect). Trap: Comparing only the venous saturations (63 vs 76) rather than the difference from arterial values gives the wrong magnitude.

qs.q: Which statement best explains why HbF is more saturated than HbA at a given pO2 in the presence of 2,3-BPG?
o: γ chains bind 2,3-BPG less strongly than β chains, so HbF is less stabilized in the T state

Correct: 2,3-BPG binds in the central cavity of deoxyHb and favors the T state. γ chains lack a positively charged residue that interacts with 2,3-BPG, so HbF binds it less well and has higher O2 affinity.
γ chains lack heme groups, so HbF binds O2 only through its α chains and therefore has a higher apparent affinity
γ chains contain heme; HbF remains a tetramer with cooperative binding.
HbF binds 2,3-BPG more strongly than HbA does, which stabilizes the R state and favors oxygen release to the tissues
Stronger 2,3-BPG binding would lower O2 affinity.
HbF is a monomer with a hyperbolic binding curve like Mb, so it is more saturated at every pO2 regardless of 2,3-BPG
HbF is a tetramer (α2γ2) with a sigmoidal curve.
qs.x: 2,3-BPG binds in the central cavity of deoxyHb and favors the T state. γ chains lack a positively charged residue that interacts with 2,3-BPG, so HbF binds it less well and has higher O2 affinity. Trap: Assuming that anything with higher affinity must bind the allosteric effector more tightly.

qs.q: The Glu6 to Val substitution in HbS most likely promotes fiber formation in the deoxygenated state because it:
o: introduces a disulfide bond between adjacent β chains, covalently cross-linking the tetramers into long polymers
Valine has no sulfhydryl group and cannot form disulfides.
replaces a charged residue with a nonpolar one that can form hydrophobic contacts with a pocket on another Hb molecule
Correct: Valine is nonpolar; at the protein surface it creates a sticky hydrophobic patch that fits a complementary pocket on another deoxyHb molecule, leading to polymerization.
eliminates the heme-binding histidine of the β chain, causing a loss of O2 binding and a collapse of the tetramer into aggregates
The passage states the oxygen-binding curve was similar to HbA, and Glu6 is not the heme-binding histidine.
replaces a hydrophobic residue with a charged residue at the surface, increasing solubility and driving fiber formation
Glu is the charged residue and Val the nonpolar one; the change is in the opposite direction.
qs.x: Valine is nonpolar; at the protein surface it creates a sticky hydrophobic patch that fits a complementary pocket on another deoxyHb molecule, leading to polymerization. Trap: Reversing which residue is charged and which is hydrophobic.

passages.title: FL04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 2
text: Cultured human fibroblast lines were compared for their response to ultraviolet (UV-C) light, which produces cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers between adjacent thymines. Line W is wild type. Line N lacks XPA, a protein required for nucleotide excision repair (NER). Line M lacks MSH2, a component of the mismatch repair (MMR) system that detects base mismatches and small insertion/deletion loops formed by replication errors.

Cells were irradiated with increasing UV doses, and survival was measured by colony formation (Table 1, Figure 1). Separately, unirradiated cells were grown for many generations and plated in 6-thioguanine, which kills cells with a functional HPRT gene; colonies therefore represent cells that acquired loss-of-function mutations in HPRT. Mutant frequency is expressed per 10^6 cells. The UV doses used deliver damage to the DNA of every cell in the dish, and cells were allowed to recover for 24 hours before being replated at low density so that each surviving cell could form a colony. Each value is the mean of three independent experiments, and the standard error was less than 3 percentage points for all survival values.

qs.q: Line N is hypersensitive to UV light most likely because it cannot:
o: reverse the dimer in place by direct photoreactivation using a light-dependent enzyme present in human cells
Human cells lack photolyase, and the defect in N is in the NER pathway rather than in a direct-reversal pathway.
recognize mismatched bases and remove the newly synthesized strand after replication errors arise
That describes MMR, which is intact in N; N has a normal mutant frequency in Table 1.
excise an oligonucleotide containing the distorting dimer and resynthesize the gap using the intact strand as template
Correct: NER removes bulky helix-distorting lesions such as pyrimidine dimers; without XPA the dimers persist and block replication and transcription.
repair double-strand breaks by joining broken ends of the two DNA molecules without a template
UV primarily produces intrastrand dimers, not double-strand breaks, and end joining is not the defect in N.
qs.x: NER removes bulky helix-distorting lesions such as pyrimidine dimers; without XPA the dimers persist and block replication and transcription. Trap: Assigning UV damage to mismatch repair because both pathways correct DNA errors.

qs.q: Compared with line W, the spontaneous HPRT mutant frequency in line M is approximately:
o: 20-fold higher, consistent with accumulation of uncorrected replication errors
Correct: 40 divided by 2 equals 20; without MMR, polymerase errors that escape proofreading become permanent after the next round of replication.
2-fold higher, a modest difference expected from the small variation between cell lines
The ratio is 40/2 = 20, far larger than 2-fold.
10-fold higher, reflecting the loss of both excision repair and mismatch repair functions
The ratio is 20, not 10, and only MMR is missing in M.
40-fold higher, because line M carries 40 mutants compared with a baseline of one
The wild-type baseline is 2 mutants, not 1, so the ratio is 20.
qs.x: 40 divided by 2 equals 20; without MMR, polymerase errors that escape proofreading become permanent after the next round of replication. Trap: Reporting the mutant count itself as the fold change.

qs.q: Unrepaired dimers in line N that are bypassed during DNA replication would most likely lead to which outcome?
o: silent mutations only, because the genetic code is degenerate and dimers never alter coding sequences
Mutations at dimers occur at random positions and can change amino acids or create stop codons; they are not restricted to silent changes.
large chromosomal deletions generated each time a dimer causes the replication machinery to stall
Stalling does not usually produce large deletions; bypass by translesion synthesis causes point mutations.
insertions of repeated units in microsatellites, which is the characteristic lesion of unrepaired dimers
Slippage at repeats is characteristic of MMR deficiency, not of unrepaired dimers.
base substitutions, typically C to T changes at dipyrimidine sites, introduced by error-prone translesion synthesis
Correct: Dimers block high-fidelity replicative polymerases; translesion polymerases bypass them but frequently insert incorrect bases, usually adenine opposite cytosine, which yields C to T changes.
qs.x: Dimers block high-fidelity replicative polymerases; translesion polymerases bypass them but frequently insert incorrect bases, usually adenine opposite cytosine, which yields C to T changes. Trap: Linking pyrimidine dimers to microsatellite slippage.

qs.q: In line M, which type of mutation would be expected to accumulate in repetitive microsatellite sequences?
o: pyrimidine dimers resulting from direct absorption of UV photons by adjacent thymines in the repeat
Dimers form on UV exposure and are handled by NER; they are not slippage products.
small insertions and deletions arising from polymerase slippage
Correct: Slippage on repeats creates unpaired loops that MMR normally corrects; without MSH2 these persist as length changes.
whole-chromosome gains and losses produced by failure of the spindle to attach to kinetochores
Aneuploidy arises from segregation errors, which are unrelated to loss of MSH2.
single-strand breaks from oxidative damage that are normally sealed by DNA ligase after base excision
Oxidative damage is handled by base excision repair, which is intact in M.
qs.x: Slippage on repeats creates unpaired loops that MMR normally corrects; without MSH2 these persist as length changes. Trap: Choosing the answer that sounds like generic DNA damage rather than the MMR substrate.
