passages.title: FL04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 3
text: In Drosophila melanogaster, three recessive alleles on chromosome 2 were studied: black body (b), vestigial wings (vg), and cinnabar eyes (cn). Female flies heterozygous for two of the genes, with both wild-type alleles on one homolog and both recessive alleles on the other, were crossed to males homozygous recessive for both genes (a testcross). Because crossing over does not occur in male Drosophila, the heterozygous parent in each cross was female. For each of three crosses, 1000 progeny were scored (Table 1). Map distance is expressed in map units, where 1 map unit equals 1% recombinant progeny.

In a separate cage population that was large, randomly mating, and free of selection, migration, and mutation, 4% of the flies had vestigial wings, which is an autosomal recessive trait. The researchers wanted to place the three genes in order on a linkage map and also to estimate the fraction of wild-type flies in the cage that carry the vestigial allele. Parental-type progeny are the two most common classes in each cross.

qs.q: What is the map distance between the b and vg genes?
o: 8.5 map units
8.5% is the frequency of a single recombinant class (85/1000); both reciprocal classes must be counted.
17 map units
Correct: In cross 1 the recombinants are 85 + 85 = 170 of 1000 progeny, or 17%, which equals 17 map units.
83 map units
83% is the frequency of parental types.
34 map units
34 doubles the recombinant frequency incorrectly.
qs.x: In cross 1 the recombinants are 85 + 85 = 170 of 1000 progeny, or 17%, which equals 17 map units. Trap: Counting only one of the two reciprocal recombinant classes.

qs.q: Based on the three crosses, what is the order of the genes on the chromosome?
o: b - cn - vg
Correct: b-vg (17) equals b-cn (8) plus cn-vg (9), so cn lies between b and vg.
cn - b - vg
This puts b in the middle; then cn-vg would equal 8 + 17 = 25, not 9.
b - vg - cn
If vg were in the middle, b-cn would equal 17 + 9 = 26, not 8.
vg - b - cn
This also puts b in the middle; then vg-cn would equal 17 + 8 = 25, not 9.
qs.x: b-vg (17) equals b-cn (8) plus cn-vg (9), so cn lies between b and vg. Trap: Choosing the order from the single largest distance without checking additivity.

qs.q: If crossovers between b and cn and between cn and vg occurred independently, about how many double-crossover progeny per 1000 would be expected?
o: 17 is the b-vg distance.
72 comes from multiplying frequencies as percentages without converting to fractions.
Correct: Expected double crossovers = 0.08 × 0.09 × 1000 = 7.2, about 7.
0.7 is an arithmetic slip of a factor of ten.
qs.x: Expected double crossovers = 0.08 × 0.09 × 1000 = 7.2, about 7. Trap: Adding instead of multiplying probabilities of independent events.

qs.q: Recombinant progeny in these testcrosses arise primarily from crossing over between:
o: sister chromatids of the same chromosome during prophase of mitosis
Exchanges between sister chromatids give identical alleles and no new combinations.
nonhomologous chromosomes during metaphase II of meiosis
Nonhomologous chromosomes do not exchange alleles at the same loci; independent assortment is at metaphase I.
nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes in prophase I
Correct: Homologs synapse in prophase I and exchange segments between nonsister chromatids, producing recombinant chromatids.
sister chromatids of one chromosome during anaphase I of meiosis
Sister chromatids remain attached in anaphase I; homologs separate.
qs.x: Homologs synapse in prophase I and exchange segments between nonsister chromatids, producing recombinant chromatids. Trap: Confusing independent assortment with crossing over, or sister with nonsister exchange.

qs.q: In the cage population, what fraction of the wild-type flies are heterozygous for the vestigial allele, assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
o: 0.32, which is 32%
0.32 is the fraction of all flies, not of wild-type flies.
Correct: q² = 0.04, so q = 0.2 and p = 0.8. Heterozygotes are 2pq = 0.32 of all flies. Wild-type flies make up 0.96, so the fraction among them is 0.32/0.96 = 33%.
0.2 is the allele frequency q.
0.16 is pq, omitting the factor of 2.
qs.x: q² = 0.04, so q = 0.2 and p = 0.8. Heterozygotes are 2pq = 0.32 of all flies. Wild-type flies make up 0.96, so the fraction among them is 0.32/0.96 = 33%. Trap: Forgetting to restrict the denominator to phenotypically wild-type flies.

passages.title: FL04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 4
text: During fasting, the liver oxidizes fatty acids released from adipose tissue and produces ketone bodies that other tissues use as fuel. To test the role of mitochondrial fatty acid import, researchers gave mice either saline or etomoxir, an irreversible inhibitor of carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I), and then fasted them for 24 hours. A fed control group received saline. Plasma insulin was low in both fasted groups. Blood and liver samples were collected (Table 1). Etomoxir-treated mice became lethargic and hypothermic during the fast, and several required early removal from the study because of severe weakness. Food was withheld in all fasted groups, and water was available at all times.

Liver mitochondria from fasted control mice, incubated with palmitoyl-CoA and carnitine, consumed oxygen readily. Mitochondria from etomoxir-treated mice did not unless they were supplied with octanoate, a medium-chain fatty acid that enters mitochondria without the carnitine shuttle. The researchers concluded that long-chain fatty acid oxidation is required both for ketogenesis and for maintenance of blood glucose during fasting.

qs.q: In fasted control mice, the rise in β-hydroxybutyrate is best explained by:
o: conversion of glucose to acetoacetate by glycolysis in the liver, which increases when blood glucose is low
Glucose is low, and ketone bodies derive from acetyl-CoA, not directly from glycolysis.
inhibition of β-oxidation by the high plasma free fatty acid concentration, which forces acetyl-CoA into ketone body synthesis
Free fatty acids are the substrate for oxidation, not an inhibitor.
increased conversion of ketone bodies back to fatty acids in the liver, which releases β-hydroxybutyrate into the blood
The liver releases ketone bodies and lacks the enzyme needed to use them; it does not make fatty acids from them.
acetyl-CoA from β-oxidation exceeding the capacity of the citric acid cycle, because oxaloacetate is diverted to gluconeogenesis
Correct: During fasting the liver oxidizes large amounts of fatty acids while oxaloacetate is drawn into gluconeogenesis. Excess acetyl-CoA condenses to HMG-CoA and then ketone bodies.
qs.x: During fasting the liver oxidizes large amounts of fatty acids while oxaloacetate is drawn into gluconeogenesis. Excess acetyl-CoA condenses to HMG-CoA and then ketone bodies. Trap: Assuming ketone bodies come from carbohydrate rather than from fatty acid breakdown.

qs.q: Octanoate restores oxygen consumption in mitochondria from etomoxir-treated mice because it:
o: can cross the inner mitochondrial membrane without conversion to acylcarnitine
Correct: CPT-I on the outer mitochondrial membrane converts long-chain acyl-CoA to acylcarnitine for transport. Medium-chain fatty acids enter the matrix without this step and are oxidized there.
is oxidized in the cytosol by peroxisomal enzymes, which do not depend on CPT-I for substrate entry
The experiment measured mitochondrial oxygen consumption, so oxidation occurs in mitochondria.
is converted to glucose in the cytosol before entering mitochondria for oxidation by the citric acid cycle
Fatty acids cannot be converted net to glucose in animals.
directly donates electrons to complex IV of the electron transport chain, bypassing the need for β-oxidation
Electrons from fatty acid oxidation enter via FADH2 and NADH, not directly at complex IV.
qs.x: CPT-I on the outer mitochondrial membrane converts long-chain acyl-CoA to acylcarnitine for transport. Medium-chain fatty acids enter the matrix without this step and are oxidized there. Trap: Thinking the carnitine shuttle blocks all fatty acids rather than long-chain ones.

qs.q: Which statement best explains the hypoglycemia in etomoxir-treated mice?
o: Elevated ketone bodies suppress glucagon release, which prevents the liver from stimulating gluconeogenesis during the fast
Ketone bodies are low (0.2 mM) in this group.
Without fatty acid oxidation, the liver lacks the ATP, NADH, and acetyl-CoA that support gluconeogenesis

Correct: β-oxidation supplies ATP and NADH and acetyl-CoA, which allosterically activates pyruvate carboxylase. Blocking it impairs gluconeogenesis, and fatty acids are instead stored as triacylglycerol, as shown by the sixfold rise in liver triacylglycerol.
Fatty acids are converted directly to glucose by the liver, and blocking this route lowers the blood glucose concentration
Animals cannot convert fatty acids to glucose net.
Etomoxir increases insulin secretion from pancreatic β cells, which drives glucose uptake into peripheral tissues
Insulin was stated to be low in both fasted groups.
qs.x: β-oxidation supplies ATP and NADH and acetyl-CoA, which allosterically activates pyruvate carboxylase. Blocking it impairs gluconeogenesis, and fatty acids are instead stored as triacylglycerol, as shown by the sixfold rise in liver triacylglycerol. Trap: Believing fatty acids can be a net carbon source for glucose.

qs.q: Complete oxidation of one palmitate (16 carbons) to CO2, using 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 ATP per FADH2, yields a net ATP of approximately:
o: 96 would omit part of the NADH or FADH2 yield.
108 omits the 2 ATP equivalents spent on activation.
129 uses older P/O ratios (2.5 and 1.5 are given here).
Correct: Seven cycles give 7 FADH2 (10.5) and 7 NADH (17.5), and 8 acetyl-CoA give 10 each (80), for 108. Activation to palmitoyl-CoA costs 2 ATP equivalents, so net is 106.
qs.x: Seven cycles give 7 FADH2 (10.5) and 7 NADH (17.5), and 8 acetyl-CoA give 10 each (80), for 108. Activation to palmitoyl-CoA costs 2 ATP equivalents, so net is 106. Trap: Forgetting the two ATP equivalents consumed activating the fatty acid.

passages.title: FL04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 5
text: Cholesterol is a major lipid of animal plasma membranes. To study its effect on bilayer fluidity, unilamellar liposomes were prepared from dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC; two saturated 16-carbon chains; gel-to-fluid transition near 41°C) or dioleoylphosphatidylcholine (DOPC; two cis-monounsaturated 18-carbon chains; transition near -17°C), each containing 0 to 30 mol% cholesterol.

The fluorescent probe diphenylhexatriene (DPH), which partitions into the hydrophobic core, was added to each preparation. The steady-state fluorescence anisotropy of DPH was measured; a higher anisotropy means that the probe rotates less freely and the bilayer is less fluid (Table 1, Figure 1). Measurements were made at 25°C and at 50°C, after each sample had been equilibrated for 10 minutes. The lipid concentration and probe-to-lipid ratio were the same in every sample, so that differences in anisotropy reflect the bilayer and not the amount of probe.
In a final experiment, the passive leak rate of a small polar dye from DPPC liposomes at 50°C was measured, and it decreased as cholesterol content increased.

qs.q: In DPPC bilayers at 50°C, cholesterol most likely alters membrane properties by:
o: increasing the spacing between phospholipids so that acyl chains move more freely and fluidity rises
Anisotropy increased with cholesterol at 50°C, indicating reduced, not increased, fluidity.
forming covalent bonds with phospholipid head groups that anchor the lipids to the underlying cytoskeleton
Cholesterol associates with lipids noncovalently; it does not form covalent links to head groups.
restricting motion of the fatty acyl chains near the head groups, which decreases fluidity
Correct: The rigid steroid ring packs against the upper acyl chains, so DPH anisotropy rises from 0.06 to 0.20 as the bilayer becomes more ordered.
lowering the temperature of the gel-to-fluid transition so that the bilayer becomes a gel at 50°C
The bilayer becomes more ordered but the data do not show gel formation; the effect is intermediate ordering, not a shift into the gel phase.
qs.x: The rigid steroid ring packs against the upper acyl chains, so DPH anisotropy rises from 0.06 to 0.20 as the bilayer becomes more ordered. Trap: Assuming cholesterol always makes a membrane more fluid.

qs.q: The decrease in DPPC anisotropy with added cholesterol at 25°C is best explained by cholesterol:
o: disrupting the tight packing of the saturated chains in the gel phase
Correct: Below the transition temperature, saturated chains are crystalline; the bulky sterol ring interrupts their ordered packing and increases motion, lowering anisotropy.
increasing hydrogen bonding between the saturated chains so that they rotate more freely
Saturated acyl chains do not form hydrogen bonds with one another, and added bonding would reduce motion rather than increase it.
converting saturated chains to unsaturated chains, which introduces kinks into the bilayer
Cholesterol cannot alter the chemical structure of the acyl chains; no desaturation occurs in liposomes.
raising the transition temperature so that DPPC melts at 25°C instead of 41°C
Cholesterol broadens the transition rather than raising it; DPPC remains in the gel phase at 25°C.
qs.x: Below the transition temperature, saturated chains are crystalline; the bulky sterol ring interrupts their ordered packing and increases motion, lowering anisotropy. Trap: Applying the fluid-phase effect of cholesterol to the gel phase.

qs.q: From Table 1, the percent decrease in DPPC anisotropy at 25°C between 0 and 30 mol% cholesterol is closest to:
o: This is the absolute change in anisotropy (0.12) written as a percentage, not the fractional change.
This results from dividing the change by 0.22 rather than by the starting value of 0.34.
This is the remaining fraction (0.22/0.34), not the percent decrease.
qs.x: (0.34 - 0.22)/0.34 = 0.12/0.34 = 35%. Trap: Dividing by the final value rather than the initial value.

qs.q: Many organisms that are shifted to a lower growth temperature respond by increasing the proportion of unsaturated fatty acids in their membranes. The data for DOPC are consistent with this because:
o: saturated chains pack more loosely than unsaturated chains and so remain the more fluid lipid below their transition
Saturated chains pack tightly, and DPPC is the less fluid lipid at 25°C (0.34 versus 0.07).
cholesterol eliminates all effect of fatty acid structure, so DOPC and DPPC behave identically at 25°C
The 0% rows differ greatly (0.07 versus 0.34), so chain structure matters.
unsaturated chains prevent tight packing, so DOPC is fluid at 25°C with anisotropy near 0.07
Correct: cis double bonds create kinks that keep lipids spaced apart, so fluid membranes can be maintained at low temperature.
unsaturated chains raise the transition temperature, allowing DOPC to remain in the gel phase at 25°C
DOPC melts near -17°C, so it is fluid, not gel, at 25°C.
qs.x: cis double bonds create kinks that keep lipids spaced apart, so fluid membranes can be maintained at low temperature. Trap: Reversing which fatty acid type lowers the transition temperature.

qs.q: A leak rate of a small polar dye that decreases with cholesterol at 50°C most directly indicates that cholesterol:
o: creates aqueous channels that let the dye diffuse out through protein-lined pores in the bilayer
Liposomes contain no proteins here, and channels would increase leakage.
reduces the passive permeability of the fluid bilayer to small polar solutes
Correct: More ordered packing leaves fewer transient gaps for polar molecules to cross the hydrophobic core, consistent with the higher anisotropy at 50°C.
increases the flip-flop rate of phospholipids so the dye is carried across with lipids moving between leaflets
Dye is not carried by lipids, and a lower leak rate argues against increased disruption.
converts the DPPC bilayer into a micelle with a hydrophobic interior that traps the polar dye
Phospholipids with two acyl chains form bilayers, and cholesterol does not convert them into micelles.
qs.x: More ordered packing leaves fewer transient gaps for polar molecules to cross the hydrophobic core, consistent with the higher anisotropy at 50°C. Trap: Confusing reduced permeability with reduced fluidity being impossible together.

graph.title: Figure 1. DPH anisotropy versus cholesterol content

passages.title: FL04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 6
text: The Ames test screens chemicals for mutagenicity using Salmonella typhimurium strains that cannot synthesize histidine (his-). Strain TA100 carries a base-pair substitution in the histidine operon, and strain TA98 carries a frameshift mutation in the same operon. Cells were plated on minimal agar containing a trace of histidine, which permits a few divisions, and colonies that grow represent his+ revertants.

Chemical X was tested with and without S9, a rat liver extract that contains cytochrome P450 enzymes. Bacteria do not express these enzymes. Revertant colonies per plate were counted after 48 hours (Table 1). Plates with no chemical show spontaneous reversion. In a dose-response experiment with S9 (Figure 1), a plate with at least twice the spontaneous count is typically scored as positive. All plates were prepared in triplicate and the mean counts are shown, and a separate set of plates containing only the solvent used to dissolve chemical X gave counts identical to the no-chemical plates.

qs.q: Plating the strains on agar that lacks histidine except for a trace amount serves to:
o: induce new mutations in all cells by starving them of an essential amino acid until the operon is damaged
Starvation selects among existing cells; it is not what generates the mutations being counted.
kill all cells carrying a frameshift mutation, leaving only strains with base-pair substitutions on the plate
Both TA98 and TA100 grow when they revert, and selection acts on reversion, not on mutation class.
select for revertants, because only cells that regained histidine synthesis continue to divide into colonies
Correct: Once the trace histidine is exhausted, only his+ cells keep growing, so colony number reports reversion frequency.
activate the cytochrome P450 enzymes in the bacteria so that chemical X is converted to a mutagen
Bacteria lack these enzymes; S9 supplies them.
qs.x: Once the trace histidine is exhausted, only his+ cells keep growing, so colony number reports reversion frequency. Trap: Thinking the medium generates the mutations rather than selecting them.

qs.q: The data in Table 1 best support which conclusion about chemical X?
o: It is a direct-acting frameshift mutagen that damages the histidine operon of TA98 without metabolic activation
TA98 counts did not change (30 versus 33), so frameshifts are not induced.
It is a direct-acting mutagen of both strains because counts with S9 exceed those without S9 in each strain
TA98 did not increase with S9, and without S9 TA100 did not increase either (125 versus 120).
It is not mutagenic, because the revertants in the S9 plates arise from a toxic effect that selects for his+ cells
Toxicity cannot create his+ cells, and the effect is dose dependent for TA100 only.
It is converted by liver enzymes into a mutagen that causes base-pair substitutions
Correct: Revertants rise only for TA100 and only with S9, so a metabolite, not X itself, induces substitutions rather than frameshifts.
qs.x: Revertants rise only for TA100 and only with S9, so a metabolite, not X itself, induces substitutions rather than frameshifts. Trap: Concluding the compound is a direct mutagen from the S9 plate alone.

qs.q: With S9, the fold increase in TA100 revertants at 100 µg of chemical X compared with spontaneous reversion is approximately:
o: Correct: 485/120 = 4.04, which exceeds the twofold criterion for a positive result.
This is the ratio without S9 (125/120), not with S9.
This is the difference in colonies (485 - 120), not a fold change.
This results from the ratio of the TA100 value to the TA98 value (485/30).
qs.x: 485/120 = 4.04, which exceeds the twofold criterion for a positive result. Trap: Reporting the difference in counts rather than the ratio.

qs.q: A single point mutation can be detected in this assay soon after it occurs mainly because bacteria:
o: contain multiple copies of the chromosome in each cell that are repaired by recombination between homologs
Typical bacterial cells contain one circular chromosome during most of the growth cycle, and the change is detected because there is no second allele.
carry the histidine genes on mitochondrial DNA that is inherited from the mother in many generations
Bacteria have no mitochondria.
are haploid, so a recessive-type change in the single copy of the gene is expressed immediately
Correct: With one chromosome there is no second allele to mask the mutation, so the his+ phenotype is displayed directly.
package the histidine operon into nucleosomes whose structure allows mutations to be silenced
Bacteria lack histones and nucleosomes, and silencing would hide mutations.
qs.x: With one chromosome there is no second allele to mask the mutation, so the his+ phenotype is displayed directly. Trap: Applying eukaryotic features such as mitochondria to bacteria.

graph.title: Figure 1. Dose response of chemical X with S9

passages.title: FL04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 7
text: The tumor suppressor p53 is stabilized after DNA damage and acts as a transcription factor. To study its role, researchers treated isogenic cell lines, either wild type or null for p53, with a DNA-damaging drug for 24 hours. Cells were fixed, stained with a fluorescent DNA-binding dye, and analyzed by flow cytometry. Cells were classified by DNA content: G1 (2n), S (between 2n and 4n), G2/M (4n), and sub-G1 (less than 2n), where sub-G1 represents cells with fragmented DNA. The four categories sum to 100% for each sample (Table 1). Western blotting showed that p21, a protein that inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases, rose about eightfold in treated wild-type cells and was undetectable in p53-null cells with or without drug.

Additional assays in treated wild-type cells found release of cytochrome c from mitochondria into the cytosol, activation of caspase-9 and caspase-3, and exposure of phosphatidylserine on the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane. Plasma membrane integrity remained intact for most sub-G1 cells at 24 hours.

qs.q: The increase in G1 cells among treated wild-type cells is most likely due to p21-mediated:
o: activation of cyclin B-CDK1, which drives cells through G2
CDK1 activation would promote mitotic entry, not G1 arrest.
inhibition of cyclin E-CDK2, which keeps Rb hypophosphorylated and bound to E2F
Correct: p21 inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes, preventing Rb phosphorylation, so E2F-dependent S-phase genes remain off and cells arrest in G1.
phosphorylation of Rb, which releases E2F
Phosphorylated Rb releases E2F and promotes S entry.
degradation of p53 by Mdm2
Mdm2 degrades p53; DNA damage stabilizes p53.
qs.x: p21 inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes, preventing Rb phosphorylation, so E2F-dependent S-phase genes remain off and cells arrest in G1. Trap: Mixing up the direction of Rb phosphorylation and E2F release.

qs.q: The sub-G1 population in treated cells most likely reflects:
o: cleavage of chromosomal DNA into fragments by caspase-activated nucleases
Correct: Caspase-activated DNase cuts DNA between nucleosomes, producing small fragments that leak out of fixed cells, giving less than 2n DNA content.
cells arrested in G0 with decondensed chromatin and a reduced rate of transcription
G0 cells have 2n DNA and fall in the G1 peak.
cells that have replicated only half of their DNA before being arrested by a checkpoint in S phase
Cells midway through S phase fall between 2n and 4n, not below 2n.
necrotic cells with intact DNA and ruptured membranes that release their contents into the medium
Necrosis is not indicated, since membranes remained intact in most cells.
qs.x: Caspase-activated DNase cuts DNA between nucleosomes, producing small fragments that leak out of fixed cells, giving less than 2n DNA content. Trap: Mistaking low DNA content for cell-cycle position instead of DNA degradation.

qs.q: Compared with treated wild-type cells, treated p53-null cells show a much larger G2/M fraction and a small G1 fraction. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: p53 is required for any cell cycle arrest after DNA damage, since arrest requires p53-dependent transcription
The G2/M arrest in null cells shows arrest is possible without p53.
p53-null cells do not respond to DNA damage in any way, because the damage cannot be detected without p53
Null cells show a changed distribution (G2/M 55% compared with 14% untreated), so they do respond.
p53-null cells arrest in G1 because they have more p21 than wild-type cells after damage, which blocks S phase entry
p21 was undetectable in p53-null cells.
p53 is required for the G1 arrest after DNA damage, but a G2/M arrest can occur without it
Correct: Without p53, G1 arrest fails (15% G1), and damaged cells proceed through S phase to a p53-independent G2/M arrest (55%).
qs.x: Without p53, G1 arrest fails (15% G1), and damaged cells proceed through S phase to a p53-independent G2/M arrest (55%). Trap: Concluding that failure of one checkpoint means all checkpoints are lost.

qs.q: Which observation distinguishes apoptosis from necrosis in these cells?
o: Swelling of organelles and rupture of the plasma membrane, with passive loss of cell contents
Swelling and rupture are characteristic of necrosis.
Cytochrome c release and caspase activation with preserved plasma membrane integrity

Correct: Apoptosis involves the mitochondrial pathway (cytochrome c, apoptosome, caspase-9 then caspase-3) and an intact membrane until late, with phosphatidylserine flipped outward to mark cells for phagocytosis.
Release of intracellular contents that recruits immune cells and causes inflammation in surrounding tissue
Inflammation from leaked contents is characteristic of necrosis.
Random degradation of DNA without any requirement for energy or for activation of specific enzymes
Apoptotic DNA cleavage is orderly and energy requiring, not random.
qs.x: Apoptosis involves the mitochondrial pathway (cytochrome c, apoptosome, caspase-9 then caspase-3) and an intact membrane until late, with phosphatidylserine flipped outward to mark cells for phagocytosis. Trap: Attributing the features of necrosis to apoptosis.

passages.title: FL04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 8
text: Renin, released by juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney in response to low renal perfusion pressure, cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) converts this to angiotensin II, which constricts arterioles and stimulates the adrenal cortex (zona glomerulosa) to release aldosterone. Aldosterone increases Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion in the distal nephron, and the resulting water retention expands extracellular volume. Together, these actions raise arterial pressure.

Four adults were studied while seated (Table 1). The control subject was healthy. Patient A had stenosis of a single renal artery. Patient B had an aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma. Patient C was a healthy adult given the ACE inhibitor lisinopril for one week. In healthy volunteers, dietary Na+ intake was varied and morning plasma renin activity (PRA) was measured (Figure 1). All blood samples were drawn after 30 minutes of seated rest, and subjects on the drug or on each diet had been at steady state for at least one week. Mean arterial pressure was calculated from three seated cuff readings.

qs.q: The high PRA and high aldosterone of Patient A are best explained by:
o: autonomous aldosterone production by the adrenal cortex that suppresses renin through volume expansion
That describes Patient B, whose PRA is low; Patient A has high renin.
reduced perfusion pressure in the affected kidney, which activates renin release
Correct: Poor flow past the juxtaglomerular cells signals volume depletion, so renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone all rise and cause hypertension.
loss of angiotensin II formation, which removes negative feedback on renin secretion by the kidney
That describes ACE inhibition (Patient C), which lowers aldosterone, whereas Patient A has high aldosterone.
excess antidiuretic hormone, which raises renin by increasing water reabsorption in the collecting duct
ADH does not directly raise renin or aldosterone, and Patient A's data point to a renal cause.
qs.x: Poor flow past the juxtaglomerular cells signals volume depletion, so renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone all rise and cause hypertension. Trap: Mistaking secondary aldosterone excess for a primary adrenal disorder.

qs.q: The low PRA in Patient B most likely reflects:
o: destruction of the juxtaglomerular cells by prolonged high pressure, which permanently abolishes renin
The cells are functioning, since renin is suppressed by feedback and would rise if volume were lowered.
increased conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, which directly inhibits adrenal aldosterone release
Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone release; in Patient B aldosterone is autonomous.
hyperkalemia that stimulates renin release, matching the high aldosterone value and the high pressure
Patient B has hypokalemia (3.1 mM), not hyperkalemia.
volume expansion and high pressure resulting from aldosterone-driven Na+ retention
Correct: Excess aldosterone retains Na+ and water; increased renal perfusion and pressure suppress renin release despite hypertension.
qs.x: Excess aldosterone retains Na+ and water; increased renal perfusion and pressure suppress renin release despite hypertension. Trap: Expecting renin to rise whenever blood pressure is abnormal.

qs.q: In Patient C, the ACE inhibitor produced the observed pattern of low aldosterone and high PRA because:
o: angiotensin II normally stimulates renin, so blocking it should lower renin, and the high PRA must be an error
Angiotensin II feeds back negatively on renin; the high PRA is expected.
lisinopril blocks the aldosterone receptor in the distal nephron, so the adrenal gland releases less hormone
ACE inhibitors act upstream on angiotensin I conversion; they do not block the aldosterone receptor.
angiotensin II normally inhibits renin, so blocking its formation removes this feedback while also lowering aldosterone
Correct: Less angiotensin II means less vasoconstriction and less aldosterone, which lowers blood pressure and, by removing feedback and lowering pressure, raises renin.
lisinopril directly stimulates the juxtaglomerular cells, and aldosterone falls because of the increased blood pressure
Pressure fell to 80 mm Hg in Patient C, and the drug does not act on juxtaglomerular cells directly.
qs.x: Less angiotensin II means less vasoconstriction and less aldosterone, which lowers blood pressure and, by removing feedback and lowering pressure, raises renin. Trap: Forgetting that angiotensin II inhibits renin release.

qs.q: From Figure 1, PRA at the lowest Na+ intake is approximately how many times its value at the highest intake?
o: This results from dividing the Na+ intakes (200/10) rather than the PRA values.
This is the PRA at 50 mmol/day, not a ratio.
This is the difference in PRA (5.0 - 0.4), not a ratio.
qs.x: 5.0/0.4 = 12.5. Trap: Subtracting values when a fold change is asked.

qs.q: Aldosterone acts on cells of the distal nephron mainly by:
o: binding a G protein-coupled receptor and rapidly generating cAMP to open Na+ channels
Steroid hormones typically act through intracellular receptors, which is why their effect develops over hours.
binding a receptor tyrosine kinase that phosphorylates ENaC channels already present in the membrane
Aldosterone does not act through a receptor tyrosine kinase.
entering the cell and directly inhibiting the Na+/K+ ATPase so that K+ secretion into the lumen is reduced
Aldosterone increases, not inhibits, the pump, and it increases K+ secretion.
binding an intracellular receptor and increasing transcription of Na+ channel and Na+/K+ ATPase genes
Correct: As a steroid hormone it crosses the membrane, binds a cytoplasmic receptor, and acts on DNA to increase Na+ reabsorption.
qs.x: As a steroid hormone it crosses the membrane, binds a cytoplasmic receptor, and acts on DNA to increase Na+ reabsorption. Trap: Assigning peptide-hormone signaling to a steroid hormone.

graph.title: Figure 1. Plasma renin activity and dietary sodium

passages.title: FL04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 9
text: Purified digestive enzymes were assayed at 37°C in buffers across a range of pH values, mimicking the lumen of different segments of the gastrointestinal tract. Pepsin, trypsin and salivary amylase activities were measured as a percentage of each enzyme's maximum (Table 1, Figure 1). Fasting gastric lumen pH is about 2. Chyme entering the duodenum is neutralized by bicarbonate secreted by the pancreas, raising duodenal pH to about 6 to 7. Bicarbonate release is stimulated by the hormone secretin, which is released by duodenal cells in response to acid.

Pepsin is secreted as the inactive zymogen pepsinogen, which is cleaved to pepsin when exposed to acid. Trypsin is secreted by the pancreas as trypsinogen and activated by enteropeptidase, a brush-border enzyme of the duodenum. Salivary amylase digests starch to maltose and dextrins, and a related amylase is secreted by the pancreas into the duodenum. Enzyme activity is defined as the rate of product formation, and the buffers did not change the ionization of the substrates. All assays used equal amounts of enzyme and saturating concentrations of substrate (a protein for pepsin and trypsin, starch for amylase).

qs.q: Based on Table 1, starch digestion by salivary amylase most likely:
o: continues unchanged in the stomach, because amylase has its highest activity at the pH of gastric juice
Activity at pH 2 is 0%, and the maximum is at pH 6.
accelerates in the stomach because pepsin cleaves amylase into fragments that act more quickly on starch
Pepsin would degrade amylase, not activate it, and amylase shows no activity at pH 2.
stops in the stomach, where the acidic pH inactivates the enzyme
Correct: Activity is 0% at pH 2, so swallowed amylase cannot work in the acidic lumen; digestion resumes with pancreatic amylase in the duodenum.
is completed in the mouth because amylase fully hydrolyzes starch to glucose before swallowing
Amylase yields maltose and dextrins, and digestion is finished by pancreatic amylase and brush-border enzymes.
qs.x: Activity is 0% at pH 2, so swallowed amylase cannot work in the acidic lumen; digestion resumes with pancreatic amylase in the duodenum. Trap: Assuming an enzyme remains active wherever it travels.

qs.q: Secretion of pepsin and trypsin as the zymogens pepsinogen and trypsinogen most directly serves to:
o: allow the enzymes to function at both acidic and basic pH instead of being limited to a single optimum
Zymogens are inactive; they do not alter the pH optimum of the active enzyme.
prevent digestion of the secretory cells and ducts until the enzymes reach the lumen
Correct: Inactive precursors are activated by acid or enteropeptidase only after secretion, so the proteases do not digest the cells that make them.
increase the rate at which the active enzymes cleave peptide bonds once they reach the intestinal lumen
Zymogen cleavage controls timing and location of activation, not catalytic rate.
allow the stomach to absorb whole proteins directly through the gastric epithelium before they are digested
Protein absorption occurs in the small intestine as amino acids and small peptides.
qs.x: Inactive precursors are activated by acid or enteropeptidase only after secretion, so the proteases do not digest the cells that make them. Trap: Thinking activation of a zymogen improves its catalytic speed.

qs.q: A patient whose pancreas fails to secrete bicarbonate would most likely have impaired digestion of dietary protein in the duodenum because:
o: duodenal pH would remain acidic, where trypsin is nearly inactive
Correct: Without neutralization the lumen stays near pH 2 to 4, where trypsin is at 0 to 2% of maximum, so pancreatic proteases cannot function.
acidic chyme would raise trypsin activity to its maximum, which would digest the intestinal wall
Trypsin is essentially inactive at acidic pH (0% at pH 2).
pepsin would be inactivated by the acidic chyme, leaving no protease active in the stomach or duodenum
Pepsin is most active at pH 2, so it would remain active in acidic chyme.
enteropeptidase would be unable to cleave trypsinogen, because acid is the only trigger for its activation
Enteropeptidase is an intestinal enzyme; acid activates pepsinogen, not trypsinogen.
qs.x: Without neutralization the lumen stays near pH 2 to 4, where trypsin is at 0 to 2% of maximum, so pancreatic proteases cannot function. Trap: Assuming an enzyme that is active in acid must be the one that continues to work in the intestine.

qs.q: At pH 6, trypsin activity compared with pepsin activity is approximately:
o: 1.7 times as high
This results from dividing 50 by 30 instead of by 3.
47 times as high
This is the difference between the two percentages (50 - 3), not a ratio.
17 times as high
Correct: 50/3 = 16.7, so trypsin is about 17-fold more active than pepsin at pH 6.
0.06 times as high
This inverts the ratio (3/50) and so compares pepsin with trypsin.
qs.x: 50/3 = 16.7, so trypsin is about 17-fold more active than pepsin at pH 6. Trap: Subtracting percentages or inverting the ratio.

passages.title: FL04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 10
text: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) recognize viral peptides presented on class I major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules. The peptide lies in a groove formed by two alpha helices over a beta-sheet floor, and side chains at positions 2 and 9 (anchor residues) insert into hydrophobic pockets. Other residues point upward toward the T-cell receptor (TCR), an alpha-beta heterodimer, and T-cell activation requires both stable presentation of the peptide on the target cell and engagement of the TCR by exposed residues.

Variants of a nine-residue viral peptide (wild type, WT, ALYKTEAVV) were synthesized. Each was tested for competition with a reference peptide for binding to the MHC molecule (IC50; lower values mean tighter binding) and for ability to induce killing of target cells by a CTL clone (Table 1). Position 2 of WT is Leu, and Lys occupies position 4.
The purified TCR was analyzed by SDS-PAGE. Without reducing agent, one band appeared at about 85 kDa. With beta-mercaptoethanol, two bands appeared at about 45 and 40 kDa.

qs.q: The loss of MHC binding by the L2D peptide is best explained by:
o: loss of the peptide backbone, because Asp is not one of the standard amino acids encoded by the genetic code
Asp is a standard amino acid with a normal peptide backbone.
creation of a disulfide bond between the Asp side chain and cysteines in the groove that locks the peptide
Asp lacks a thiol and cannot form disulfides.
replacement of a hydrophobic side chain by a basic side chain whose positive charge repels the helices
Asp is acidic, not basic.
placement of a charged carboxylate side chain into a hydrophobic anchor pocket
Correct: Leu fits the nonpolar pocket through hydrophobic interactions; Asp is negatively charged at physiological pH and cannot be accommodated.
qs.x: Leu fits the nonpolar pocket through hydrophobic interactions; Asp is negatively charged at physiological pH and cannot be accommodated. Trap: Calling Asp basic or confusing charge type.

qs.q: The K4A peptide binds MHC normally (18 nM) but induces little lysis (6%). This is most consistent with Lys at position 4:
o: being a residue whose side chain projects toward the TCR and contributes to recognition
Correct: Binding is unaffected, so the peptide is still displayed, but loss of the Lys contact prevents TCR engagement and CTL activation.
serving as an anchor residue whose loss would be expected to weaken binding to the MHC molecule
Anchor residues are at positions 2 and 9, and K4A binding is unchanged.
being required for the CTL clone to kill because the peptide is unable to reach the cell surface
Binding to MHC is normal (IC50 18 nM), so the peptide can be presented.
being phosphorylated in the groove, a modification that K4A prevents and that is required for lysis
Nothing in the data indicates phosphorylation; lysis depends on TCR contact.
qs.x: Binding is unaffected, so the peptide is still displayed, but loss of the Lys contact prevents TCR engagement and CTL activation. Trap: Assuming any residue that matters functionally must matter for MHC binding.

qs.q: The SDS-PAGE results most likely indicate that the TCR:
o: is a single polypeptide of 85 kDa that is cleaved into two pieces by beta-mercaptoethanol through proteolysis
Beta-mercaptoethanol reduces disulfides; it does not cleave peptide bonds.
contains two identical subunits held together by hydrophobic interactions that SDS did not disrupt
SDS disrupts noncovalent interactions, and the two bands differ in size.
consists of two different polypeptides linked by an interchain disulfide bond
Correct: Without beta-mercaptoethanol the linked chains migrate as one 85 kDa species; reduction breaks the disulfide and releases chains of about 45 and 40 kDa.
is composed of two chains joined by peptide bonds, which are broken only by treatment with a reducing agent
Reducing agents break S-S bonds rather than peptide bonds.
qs.x: Without beta-mercaptoethanol the linked chains migrate as one 85 kDa species; reduction breaks the disulfide and releases chains of about 45 and 40 kDa. Trap: Thinking reducing agents break peptide bonds.

qs.q: Assuming IC50 reflects relative binding affinity, V9L binds the MHC molecule more tightly than WT by a factor of about:
o: This is the inverse (9/15) and so the affinity of WT relative to V9L.
This is the difference in IC50 values (15 - 9), not a ratio.
This is the ratio of lysis to IC50 for WT (62/15), which does not compare the affinities of the two peptides.
Correct: 15/9 = 1.67; the lower IC50 indicates higher affinity.
qs.x: 15/9 = 1.67; the lower IC50 indicates higher affinity. Trap: Inverting the ratio because lower IC50 means tighter binding.

passages.title: FL04 · CARS · Passage 1
text: Students of religion have long worked from an assumption so intuitive that it seldom receives defense: that ritual is the outward expression of inner belief. On this view, a community first holds convictions about the divine, the cosmos, or the afterlife, and then devises gestures, recitations, and festivals to dramatize those convictions. The ritual is a kind of illustrated textbook, and the scholar's task is to read the pictures back into the doctrine that produced them. The model has the advantage of tidiness, and it flatters the modern habit of imagining religion as primarily a matter of what one affirms.

The difficulty is that the model sits poorly with much of the evidence. Consider the pilgrimage circuits of many traditions, in which participants walk for weeks, circle shrines in prescribed directions, and bathe at designated places. When ethnographers ask walkers why they circle to the left rather than the right, the usual answer is not a doctrine but a shrug and the remark that this is how it is done. If ritual were an illustrated textbook, one would expect participants to be able to read it. Instead they perform with great exactness and little commentary, and the exactness seems to be the point.

A minority of scholars have therefore proposed reversing the order of explanation. Ritual, they argue, is the more stable element, and belief the more fluid one. Doctrines are reinterpreted every generation, abandoned in schism, and translated into new idioms, while the gestures persist almost unchanged for centuries. Communities often supply new explanations for old actions, much as a family may invent a story to account for an inherited recipe whose original purpose is forgotten. On this account, belief is frequently a retrospective gloss: people act together first, and then reach for reasons.

This reversal should not be accepted too quickly, because it inherits the tidiness of the view it replaces. To say that ritual comes first is also to offer a single arrow of causation, merely pointing the other way. The historical record contains cases in which a reforming movement altered doctrine and, within a generation, rewrote the liturgy to match; here belief plainly led. It also contains cases in which a ritual was abandoned because it came to seem incompatible with what the community thought true. Neither order of explanation can claim the field.

What the evidence supports, I think, is a more modest claim: that ritual and belief are mutually shaping, and that their relation varies with the tradition, the period, and even the individual worshipper. A participant may arrive at a festival with firm convictions, find them altered by the experience of standing among thousands, and leave with a different account of what the festival means. Another may attend for years from habit, and only under questioning discover that she holds an opinion about it. To describe both people, we need a vocabulary that does not force their experience into a sequence.

This has a practical consequence for the study of unfamiliar traditions. A researcher who assumes that practice illustrates doctrine will tend to seek out the priest, the text, and the articulate informant, and will treat the silent majority as imperfectly informed. A researcher who assumes the reverse will do the opposite, and risk dismissing the sophisticated theology that many communities do possess. The wiser course is to treat each as a hypothesis to be tested against the particular case, remaining alert to the possibility that the participants themselves have never settled the matter, and have no need to.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
o: Ritual precedes belief, and doctrines are mostly after-the-fact rationalizations of communal practice, so texts deserve little attention.
The author presents this as a reversal that should not be accepted too quickly.
Ethnographers should rely on priests and texts because ordinary worshippers cannot explain what they do, and observation adds little.
The author warns that this strategy risks misjudging silent participants, and also notes the opposite error.
Neither the claim that ritual expresses belief nor the claim that belief follows ritual adequately describes the relation, which is better treated as variable and mutual.
Correct: The author critiques both causal orders and ends by endorsing a mutual, context-dependent relation.
Modern readers misunderstand religion because they emphasize what is affirmed rather than what is performed, and should study only ritual.
This is a side remark about the appeal of the older model, not the passage's thesis.
qs.x: The author critiques both causal orders and ends by endorsing a mutual, context-dependent relation. Trap: Picking the reversal view because it receives sympathetic, detailed treatment in the middle of the passage; the author rejects it as one-sided too.

qs.q: The author mentions pilgrims who answer questions about circling direction with a shrug in order to:
o: demonstrate that pilgrims are ignorant of their own religion and should therefore be ignored by researchers.
The author does not call pilgrims ignorant; the point concerns the model, not the pilgrims.
prove that the direction of circling has no real significance for the tradition or for the people who follow it.
Exactness is described as the point, so the direction is plainly significant to them.
show that participants often perform exactly without being able to supply doctrinal explanations.
Correct: The shrug illustrates exact performance without commentary, which strains the illustrated-textbook model.
argue that ethnographers ask poorly designed questions of worshippers and should adopt better methods of interviewing.
No criticism of ethnographic questions is offered.
qs.x: The shrug illustrates exact performance without commentary, which strains the illustrated-textbook model. Trap: Reading the shrug as evidence of ignorance or insignificance rather than as evidence about how practice and explanation relate.

qs.q: According to the passage, which of the following is true of the view that belief is a retrospective gloss on ritual?
o: It offers a single direction of causation, just as the view it replaces does.
Correct: The fourth paragraph says the reversal merely points the arrow the other way.
It is contradicted by every historical case in which doctrine changed.
The author says it fits some cases and fails in others, not that every case contradicts it.
It is supported by cases in which liturgy was rewritten after a reform.
Liturgy rewritten after doctrinal reform is cited as a case where belief led.
It was first proposed by the scholars who defended the illustrated-textbook model.
The reversal is proposed by a minority opposed to the older model.
qs.x: The fourth paragraph says the reversal merely points the arrow the other way. Trap: Overgeneralizing from the counterexample cases to claim they refute the view entirely.

qs.q: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the relation between ritual and belief varies across traditions?
o: Some worshippers attend festivals for years before forming any opinion about them, and then adopt the opinions of their neighbors.
This is consistent with the author's examples and does not threaten variation.
Across a large sample of traditions and periods, doctrine changed first in virtually every documented case of liturgical change.
Correct: A uniform order across traditions would undercut the claim of variation and favor the older model.
Several communities invent new explanations for inherited gestures whose origins are forgotten, while continuing to perform the gestures unchanged.
The author already cites this and it fits the variation claim.
Some ritual practices were abandoned in particular communities because they seemed inconsistent with the truths those communities accepted.
The author cites this as a case where belief led, consistent with variation.
qs.x: A uniform order across traditions would undercut the claim of variation and favor the older model. Trap: Selecting a statement already used as supporting evidence in the passage rather than one that challenges the conclusion.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the illustrated-textbook model is best described as:
o: dismissive and contemptuous of its proponents.
The tone is measured and concedes advantages.
enthusiastic, with minor reservations about its method.
The author rejects the model as inadequate, not as nearly right.
indifferent, treating it as equal to its rival.
The author finds both models inadequate but does not treat them as equals in the pilgrimage evidence.
critical but acknowledging its appeal.
Correct: The author grants its tidiness and flattery of modern habits, yet argues it fits poorly with evidence.
qs.x: The author grants its tidiness and flattery of modern habits, yet argues it fits poorly with evidence. Trap: Mistaking sustained disagreement for scorn when the author actually credits the model's advantages.

qs.q: Suppose a researcher studying a village festival finds that residents readily describe its theology in detail yet cannot explain several of its gestures. This finding would be most consistent with:
o: the author's view that the relation between practice and belief may differ even within one tradition.
Correct: Mixed articulacy fits the author's picture of varying, mutually shaping relations.
the claim that ritual is simply an illustrated textbook of doctrine, in which gestures merely repeat what believers already affirm.
If gestures cannot be explained, the textbook reading fails for them.
the claim that sophisticated theology is absent from communities that perform exact rituals, since exact performance requires no reflection.
The researcher found detailed theology, so this is contradicted.
the claim that belief is always a retrospective gloss on practice, invented afterward by participants to explain what they already do.
Detailed theology existing alongside unexplained gestures does not show belief is always a gloss.
qs.x: Mixed articulacy fits the author's picture of varying, mutually shaping relations. Trap: Treating a partial confirmation of the older model as full confirmation of one side, ignoring the mixed evidence.

passages.title: FL04 · CARS · Passage 2
text: Legal systems are often praised for their rationality, yet they have always relied on fictions: statements that the law treats as true while knowing them to be false. A corporation is a "person" that can sue and be sued. A child found abandoned is "deemed" to have been born in the place where she was found. In older English practice, a plaintiff seeking access to a court that did not hear his sort of claim would allege that the defendant had trespassed, whether or not any trespass had occurred, so that the court could take jurisdiction. The defendant was not permitted to deny the allegation. Critics from Bentham onward have found such devices embarrassing, and have urged that a rational system say what it means.

The critics are right that fictions can conceal. When a court pretends that a seller always knew of a defect, it may obscure the actual policy choice, which is that sellers ought to bear the cost of defects they are better placed to discover. A false statement placed in the middle of an opinion invites later judges to take it literally and to draw conclusions that its inventors never intended.

Yet the more careful defenders of fictions observe that they do work that plain speech cannot easily do. Law faces a standing problem of adaptation. Its rules are inherited from circumstances that no longer exist, and its institutions cannot simply rewrite them whenever they seem unsuited to the present. Legislatures act slowly, and judges are constrained by precedent and by their own claims to apply rather than make law. A fiction permits a court to preserve the verbal form of an old rule while altering its effect, so that continuity is maintained even as substance changes. The corporation-as-person device, for instance, allowed courts to extend familiar rules about contracts and property to new organizations without first drafting a comprehensive code for them.

It is tempting to conclude that fictions are therefore a harmless convenience, a kind of lubricant for the machinery. But this conclusion also moves too quickly. A lubricant is invisible when it works, and a fiction that remains in use long after its purpose has lapsed becomes a source of friction rather than relief. Legal history records many such cases, in which a formula devised to avoid a harsh rule survived the repeal of that rule and continued to produce odd results because no one remembered what it had been meant to avoid.

One way of reconciling the two positions is to distinguish between fictions that are transparent and those that are opaque. A transparent fiction is one that all parties understand to be a convention, as when a jurist says "let us treat the company as a person for this purpose." Its falsity is acknowledged, and so its limits are visible: everyone knows that the company cannot be imprisoned or married. An opaque fiction, by contrast, is believed, or at least not examined, and it tends to expand beyond the purpose for which it was created. The practical lesson is not that fictions should be abolished, but that they should be made to carry labels, and that courts should periodically ask whether the problem they were invented to solve still exists.

Such a standard would not satisfy a thoroughgoing rationalist, who would prefer that every rule justify itself in the language of its actual purpose. But the demand for perfect candor underestimates how much of social life depends on useful pretenses, and how often the alternative to a fiction is not truth but paralysis.

qs.q: The primary purpose of the passage is to:
o: evaluate criticisms of legal fictions and propose a way of keeping their benefits while limiting their costs.
Correct: The author weighs the critics and defenders and then recommends transparency and periodic review.
trace the history of corporate personhood from early English practice to the present and show how its legal uses have steadily expanded.
Corporate personhood is only one example among several.
argue that legal systems should abandon fictions in favor of plain statements of policy, since candor always serves the public better.
The author rejects the rationalist demand for perfect candor.
show that judges invent fictions mainly to expand their own authority, and that legislatures should therefore take over the practice.
The passage says nothing about judicial self-aggrandizement; fictions are tied to adaptation.
qs.x: The author weighs the critics and defenders and then recommends transparency and periodic review. Trap: Taking a prominent example as the subject of the whole passage.

qs.q: In the passage, the example of the defendant who could not deny an alleged trespass serves to illustrate:
o: a fiction that was transparent because all parties understood it as a convention.
The defendant was forbidden to deny it, which fits an opaque rather than transparent device.
a case in which a court deliberately punished an innocent party in order to secure a harsh rule's intended effect.
The passage does not describe punishment of an innocent party.
a fiction that survived because legislators could not repeal it, even after its original purpose had been forgotten.
Nothing is said about legislative repeal in this example.
a fiction used to give a court jurisdiction over claims it would not otherwise hear.
Correct: The allegation was false but allowed the court to take jurisdiction, and the defendant could not contest it.
qs.x: The allegation was false but allowed the court to take jurisdiction, and the defendant could not contest it. Trap: Assuming a fiction that is formally accepted by everyone is transparent; transparency requires acknowledged falsity.

qs.q: Which of the following is most strongly implied by the author's discussion of the corporation-as-person device?
o: Corporations should be treated as persons for every purpose, including imprisonment, because the fiction reflects what they actually are.
The author notes that a company cannot be imprisoned or married.
The device is now an example of an opaque fiction that should be dropped, because courts have forgotten that it is only a convenience.
The author uses it as a transparent example, not as one to drop.
Legislatures have never been able to regulate corporations, which is why courts were forced to develop the fiction on their own.
The passage says legislatures act slowly, not that they cannot regulate.
Treating organizations as persons let courts reuse existing rules without first writing a new code.
Correct: The third paragraph states that it extended familiar rules to new organizations without a comprehensive code.
qs.x: The third paragraph states that it extended familiar rules to new organizations without a comprehensive code. Trap: Treating a helpful device as endorsed without limit.

qs.q: The author claims that a fiction that lingers after its purpose has lapsed becomes a source of friction. Which of the following would most support this claim?
o: A formula designed to evade a harsh rule continues to yield odd outcomes after that rule has been repealed.
Correct: This directly matches the surviving formula that produces odd results.
A court openly states that it is treating a company as a person for a limited purpose, and explains the convenience that justifies doing so.
This is a transparent fiction functioning as intended.
A legislature replaces a fiction with a detailed statute that states its purpose, so that courts no longer need to pretend anything.
This is an alternative to fictions, not evidence of friction from a lingering one.
A fiction is abandoned once judges recognize that the problem it solved has disappeared, and the old formula is dropped without comment.
This shows the successful removal of a fiction, which gives no evidence of friction.
qs.x: This directly matches the surviving formula that produces odd results. Trap: Choosing a case showing a fiction working well rather than one persisting beyond its purpose.

qs.q: The author would most likely respond to a rationalist who demands that every rule be justified in the language of its actual purpose by arguing that:
o: fictions are in fact more truthful than direct statements of policy, because they reveal how judges actually reason about hard cases.
The author concedes fictions are false statements.
only legislatures should be permitted to use fictions, since they alone are accountable to the public for what the fictions conceal.
The passage does not restrict fictions to legislatures.
citizens benefit from not knowing the real rationale of rules, because open discussion of that rationale weakens respect for law.
The author acknowledges that fictions can conceal the real policy choice and does not praise ignorance.
perfect candor is not always attainable, and the real alternative to a fiction is sometimes stalled adaptation.
Correct: The final sentence says the alternative to fiction is often paralysis, not truth.
qs.x: The final sentence says the alternative to fiction is often paralysis, not truth. Trap: Overstating the author's defense into a claim that fictions are good in themselves.

qs.q: Which of the following is the best description of the author's distinction between transparent and opaque fictions?
o: A transparent fiction is written into statute and thereby approved by legislators, while an opaque one appears only in judicial opinions.
The source of the fiction is not the basis of the distinction.
A transparent fiction acknowledges its own falsity and thereby reveals its limits, while an opaque one is taken as true and tends to spread.
Correct: This restates the fifth paragraph's contrast of acknowledged versus unexamined fictions.
A transparent fiction is always harmless to the parties before the court, while an opaque one always causes a clear injustice.
The author says opaque fictions tend to expand, not that all cause injustice or that transparent ones never fail.
A transparent fiction serves questions of jurisdiction in the courts, while an opaque one serves only the law of property and inheritance.
Subject matter plays no role in the distinction.
qs.x: This restates the fifth paragraph's contrast of acknowledged versus unexamined fictions. Trap: Importing a distinction by source or subject matter instead of by whether falsity is acknowledged.

passages.title: FL04 · CARS · Passage 3
text: Few arts are as stubbornly resistant to preservation as dance. A painting hangs on a wall, a poem sits on a page, a symphony is captured in a score that any trained musician can realize. A dance, by contrast, seems to vanish in the instant of its performance, leaving only memory in the bodies of those who danced it. For centuries this impermanence was treated as the essence of the form, and choreographers took a certain pride in working in a medium that could not be hoarded.

Yet efforts to notate movement are old. Renaissance dancing masters devised shorthand for the steps of court dances, and in the twentieth century several comprehensive systems were developed, some using abstract symbols arranged on a staff that records the direction, level, and duration of each movement. Advocates argued that notation would give dance what music had long possessed: a text, independent of any particular performer, from which works could be revived and studied. Libraries now hold notated scores of major ballets, and some companies stage works on the strength of the score alone.

The results have been mixed, and the reasons are instructive. A musical score succeeds because music has a relatively small set of dimensions, pitch and duration chief among them, that can be written down with great precision, and because performers are trained in a shared set of conventions for supplying the rest. A dancer's body, however, moves in many dimensions at once, and the qualities that audiences value most, the weight of a step, the arc of a gesture, the timing of a breath, are the very qualities that notation captures least well. A score may specify that an arm rises to shoulder height over two beats and say nothing about whether the rise is a surrender or a challenge. Two companies working from the same score can produce performances that look like different works.

Some conclude from this that notation has failed and that dance can only be passed from body to body. That conclusion is too sweeping, and it rests on a mistaken comparison. The fair comparison is not between a score and a performance but between a dance score and the way that works are actually transmitted in the absence of one. Without notation, a choreographer's work is carried by a single repetiteur, or by a handful of dancers who remember it, and it changes with each retelling. Details drift, steps are simplified to suit new bodies, and a work can be lost entirely within a generation when its keepers retire. Notation, imperfect as it is, serves as a check against such drift, since it fixes what can be fixed, and gives later interpreters something to argue with.

This suggests a more productive way to think about the dance score. It is less like a recording than like a legal constitution: a document that constrains without determining, that must be interpreted by successive generations, and that remains authoritative precisely because it does not settle every question. Its value lies not in making performances identical but in making the disagreements among them legible. When a company departs from the score, it can do so knowingly, and the audience that cares to look can see where the departure occurred.

On this view, the old pride in dance as an unhoardable art may be only half right. Dance is fleeting, but the fleetingness is not total, and the arts of memory, whether in the body or on the page, have always worked together.

qs.q: Which of the following best summarizes the author's position on dance notation?
o: Notation cannot fully capture dance, but it provides a useful constraint on drift and makes departures from a work visible.
Correct: The author concedes limits yet defends notation as a check and an object of interpretation.
Notation has failed as a method of preservation because it cannot record qualities such as weight and timing, and should be abandoned.
The author calls this conclusion too sweeping.
Notation makes dance as permanent and reproducible as a musical score, so that performances no longer depend on the memories of dancers.
The author says notation is imperfect and that performances may look like different works.
Notation is unnecessary because dancers transmit works reliably from body to body, with little change across successive generations of performers.
The author describes oral transmission as prone to drift and loss.
qs.x: The author concedes limits yet defends notation as a check and an object of interpretation. Trap: Treating the acknowledged limits as the author's conclusion rather than as a concession.

qs.q: According to the passage, a musical score is more effective than a dance score for which of the following reasons?
o: Musicians are more disciplined than dancers about following written instructions, and therefore depart less from what a score prescribes.
Discipline is not discussed.
Musical notation was invented centuries earlier than any system for dance, and has had far more time to become a standard.
Renaissance dance notations are mentioned; chronology is not the explanation.
Music is not subject to differences between performances, because a score completely determines every aspect of how it is played.
Different performances of the same score obviously exist, and the passage does not deny this.
Music has fewer dimensions that must be specified and performers share conventions for supplying the rest.
Correct: The third paragraph says music has few dimensions that can be written precisely, plus shared conventions.
qs.x: The third paragraph says music has few dimensions that can be written precisely, plus shared conventions. Trap: Substituting a plausible but unmentioned explanation about performer attitude.

qs.q: The author compares the dance score to a legal constitution in order to:
o: argue that dance companies are obligated by law to follow scores exactly, and may be penalized for any deviation.
The comparison is figurative, not about legal obligations.
suggest that a score constrains without determining, and gains authority by requiring interpretation.
Correct: The analogy stresses constraint without determination and successive interpretation.
imply that choreographers should resolve every disagreement before a performance, so that interpretation is never needed.
The author says value lies in making disagreements legible, not in eliminating them.
claim that dance scores are more precise than constitutional text, and therefore leave less room for interpretation.
The author says precision is limited; the analogy concerns interpretation.
qs.x: The analogy stresses constraint without determination and successive interpretation. Trap: Reading the analogy literally as a claim about enforcement.

qs.q: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage about works transmitted without notation?
o: They are more likely to change as they pass through successive keepers.
Correct: The author describes drift, simplification, and loss without a notated check.
They are always performed identically by every company, because the steps are fixed once they have been taught to the first dancers.
The author says details drift, the opposite of identity.
They are valued more by audiences than notated works, since viewers prefer performances that depend on the memory of living dancers.
Audience preference is not discussed.
They cannot be revived once the last dancer who learned them has retired, because no other form of record can exist.
The passage says works may be lost, not that revival is impossible in every case.
qs.x: The author describes drift, simplification, and loss without a notated check. Trap: Stretching 'can be lost' to 'cannot be revived' in all cases.

qs.q: Which of the following would most weaken the author's argument that notation acts as a check against drift?
o: Two companies using the same score produce performances that look different from each other.
The author already grants this and still says the score fixes what can be fixed.
Libraries hold scores of major ballets that are rarely consulted.
Rare consultation does not show that consulted scores fail to constrain.
Companies working from notated scores alter the works as much as companies relying on memory do.
Correct: If notation reduced no more drift than memory, the claimed checking function would be undermined.
Some choreographers prefer that their works not be preserved.
Choreographer preferences do not bear on whether notation checks drift.
qs.x: If notation reduced no more drift than memory, the claimed checking function would be undermined. Trap: Choosing a point the author already concedes instead of one that attacks the check-on-drift claim itself.

qs.q: The final paragraph suggests that the pride in dance as an 'unhoardable art' is:
o: entirely justified, since notation cannot preserve anything essential about a work and dance therefore disappears with each performance.
The author denies that notation preserves nothing.
entirely mistaken, since dance is as permanent as painting once it has been recorded in any form, whether notated or remembered.
The author does not claim dance equals painting in permanence.
partly justified, since dance is fleeting, but overstated since memory in body and page can preserve some of it.
Correct: The author says the view is 'only half right' because the fleetingness is not total.
irrelevant to the choice between memory and written scores, since the permanence of an art form has no bearing on how it is kept.
The author connects the pride to the role of memory arts, not dismisses it as irrelevant.
qs.x: The author says the view is 'only half right' because the fleetingness is not total. Trap: Taking 'half right' to mean either all right or all wrong.

passages.title: FL04 · CARS · Passage 4
text: When a farmer's plow turns up a bronze vessel, or a construction crew breaks into a burial chamber, the object that emerges is already half transformed. It has been removed from the soil that surrounded it, and with that removal has gone much of what an archaeologist would most like to know: what lay beside it, at what depth, in what arrangement, and in association with what other remains. A vessel in a museum case may be admired as a work of craft, but as evidence it is nearly mute. This is why archaeologists insist, sometimes to the annoyance of collectors, that the context of an artifact is more valuable than the artifact itself.

The claim is easy to misunderstand. It does not say that objects are unimportant, nor that a beautiful piece has no value to scholarship. Its point is that knowledge in archaeology is produced by relations rather than by things. A single coin found in a layer of ash tells almost nothing, but the same coin found beneath a collapsed roof, above a floor of beaten earth, and beside a hoard of similar coins can date a destruction, identify a trade route, and suggest the wealth of a household. The information lies in the pattern, and the pattern is destroyed when any element is extracted without record.

This principle underlies the strong condemnation of looting, which strips sites of objects for the antiquities market. Defenders of the market sometimes reply that museums and private collectors preserve objects that would otherwise decay or be lost, and that many looted pieces are now better cared for than they would have been in the ground. The reply has force as far as the object is concerned. But it overlooks the fact that the loss imposed by looting is not primarily a loss of objects. A looted tomb may yield a handsome pot, while the scholar's chance of learning who was buried there, and how the community regarded the dead, is permanently reduced.

Yet an insistence on context can itself become a dogma, and some archaeologists have begun to question its more absolute forms. Excavation is destructive. Every trench removes the very layers that it records, and the record that remains is a product of the excavator's choices about what to notice and what to ignore. Early excavators discarded animal bones and seeds that modern specialists consider invaluable, and recorded nothing about soil that is now routinely analyzed chemically. If context is the true repository of meaning, then a careless modern excavation may be no better, in principle, than a plunderer's, since both destroy what the next generation might have read with better tools.

This is not a reason to abandon excavation, but it does recommend humility. Context is not a fixed quantity waiting to be recovered; it is something that is defined by the questions currently asked of it. Which features count as relevant evidence changes as methods change, and the excavator therefore acts not only as a reader of the past but as a custodian whose decisions bind later readers. Responsible practice means leaving portions of a site untouched whenever the research aim permits, and keeping records detailed enough to allow future scholars to evaluate the interpretations built from them.

The ethical weight of the principle is thus double. It condemns the person who destroys context for profit, and it also disciplines the professional who destroys context for knowledge, by reminding both that a site can be excavated only once.

qs.q: The passage is primarily concerned with:
o: arguing that museums should return looted objects to their countries of origin, regardless of how the objects were acquired.
Repatriation is never discussed.
explaining why context matters more than objects in archaeology and what responsibilities follow from this.
Correct: The passage develops the principle, applies it to looting, and extends it to excavators.
showing that early excavators were more careless than modern ones, and that the discipline has improved steadily as methods advanced.
Early excavators are an illustration, not the subject.
defending the antiquities market against charges of causing destruction, since collectors preserve objects that would otherwise be lost.
The market's defense is acknowledged and then answered.
qs.x: The passage develops the principle, applies it to looting, and extends it to excavators. Trap: Focusing on the looting discussion because it is the most emotionally charged part, rather than the full argument.

qs.q: The example of the coin found beneath a collapsed roof is used to show that:
o: coins are the most informative kind of artifact, because they can be dated by the inscriptions and rulers they carry.
The coin is just an example, with no ranking of artifact types.
a destruction layer can be dated only by coins, since no other objects found at a site can fix a date.
The passage says coins can help date, not that only coins can.
wealthy households are always identifiable from hoards, because only the rich owned enough valuables to bury them.
The passage says the pattern 'suggests' wealth, not that hoards always identify it.
the information in a find depends on its relations to surrounding features.
Correct: The same coin gains meaning from its associations.
qs.x: The same coin gains meaning from its associations. Trap: Overgeneralizing a single illustration into a universal rule.

qs.q: According to the passage, the reply of the market's defenders is limited because it:
o: is contradicted by evidence that looted objects are poorly cared for once they have been removed from the ground and sold.
The author grants that the objects may be better cared for.
addresses the physical survival of objects but not the loss of information about their context.
Correct: The author grants it has force for objects but says the real loss is contextual.
wrongly assumes that archaeologists value objects too little, when in fact they care only about the objects themselves.
The author says archaeologists do value objects, as the earlier paragraph shows.
ignores the fact that museums are not interested in beauty, and so cannot be trusted to protect the finest objects.
Beauty is not at issue.
qs.x: The author grants it has force for objects but says the real loss is contextual. Trap: Assuming the author denies the factual claim when she in fact accepts it and challenges its relevance.

qs.q: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage about the claim that 'context is the true repository of meaning'?
o: It was abandoned by archaeologists once chemical analysis of soil became routine, because such analysis made context unnecessary to record.
The author keeps the principle and refines it.
Because what counts as context changes with methods, the claim cannot justify treating current practice as final.
