Correct: The author says context is defined by current questions and therefore recommends humility.
It implies that excavation should never occur, since any digging destroys information that later researchers might be able to read.
The author says this is not a reason to abandon excavation.
It applies to looters but not to professional excavators, since professionals are trained to recognize and preserve every kind of evidence.
The final paragraph applies the principle to both groups.
qs.x: The author says context is defined by current questions and therefore recommends humility. Trap: Concluding that a criticism of absolutism is a rejection of the principle altogether.

qs.q: Which of the following new findings would most support the author's point about the excavator as custodian?
o: A looted vessel is shown to have been well maintained in a private collection and to have been kept free of damage for decades.
This supports the market's defenders' point about objects, not the custodian point.
A dig team finds a coin beside a hoard of similar coins and dates the whole group of objects to a single reign.
This reflects the importance of association, not later reinterpretation.
A site is protected by law from all excavation, so that no future team can recover information that present methods cannot detect.
Complete protection is not what the author recommends; she urges leaving portions untouched where aims permit.
Seeds discarded in a past excavation are later shown to indicate the diet of the people who lived at the site.
Correct: Discarded material later proving valuable shows how decisions bind later readers.
qs.x: Discarded material later proving valuable shows how decisions bind later readers. Trap: Choosing evidence about context in general rather than evidence about how excavators' choices affect later scholars.

qs.q: The author's concluding sentence suggests that the principle:
o: applies to professional excavators as well as to looters, because excavation is unrepeatable.
Correct: A site can be excavated only once, so both parties destroy context.
exempts professionals because they record what they remove, so that no information is lost when a layer is dug away.
The fourth paragraph says careless modern excavation may be no better in principle.
is irrelevant where sites have been excavated more than once, since repeated digging provides the missing context for every find.
The sentence asserts that a site can be excavated only once.
should be replaced by a principle that values objects over context, since objects are the only finds that museums can display.
The author does not endorse valuing objects over context.
qs.x: A site can be excavated only once, so both parties destroy context. Trap: Letting professional purpose excuse the destruction the author says both groups cause.

passages.title: FL04 · CARS · Passage 5
text: Theories of civil disobedience usually begin by distinguishing it from ordinary lawbreaking. The civil disobedient, we are told, acts publicly, accepts the legal consequences of her act, and appeals to a shared sense of justice rather than to private advantage. She breaks a law in order to draw attention to its wrongness, and her willingness to be punished is meant to show that she respects the legal order even as she challenges one of its parts. The most influential versions of this account, developed in the twentieth century, add that the disobedience should be nonviolent and should come only after legal avenues of reform have been tried and have failed.

This picture has a clear moral logic. It reconciles the demand that citizens obey the law with the recognition that majorities sometimes enact injustice. By accepting punishment, the protester signals that she does not regard herself as exempt from the rules that bind others, and by acting openly, she invites her fellow citizens to evaluate her claim. The act becomes a form of address, a speech delivered in the language of conduct to an audience that has not been persuaded by words.

But the standard account has been criticized for presupposing a society in which the legal order is basically just and responsive. Where a government systematically excludes a group from the political process, the requirement that protesters first exhaust legal avenues amounts to telling them to petition an authority that has no obligation to listen. Likewise, the insistence on accepting punishment assumes that courts will treat the disobedient fairly. If sentences are used to silence a movement, submission to them may serve the repression rather than the protest. Critics conclude that the conditions of the standard account describe a particular kind of political circumstance, namely a reasonably healthy liberal democracy, and not a universal ethics of dissent.

Defenders of the standard account have two replies. First, they say, the conditions are not meant to be applied mechanically, but to mark the conduct that is most clearly justified, leaving other forms of protest to be judged by other standards. A theory that identifies the central case does not claim that everything outside it is wrong. Second, they argue that the conditions have a strategic rationale that survives imperfect circumstances. A protest that is public, nonviolent, and accepting of penalty is hard to portray as mere criminality, and thus it keeps the sympathy of bystanders whom a more aggressive tactic would alienate.

The second reply, however, depends on an empirical assumption about how audiences respond, and the assumption is not always borne out. Authorities have repeatedly succeeded in labeling peaceful protest as disorder, while some disruptive campaigns have won public support by the evident gravity of their cause. The strategic defense, then, is a hypothesis about particular audiences rather than a general truth, and it must be tested case by case.

What may be learned from this dispute is that the standard account is best read as an ideal type, describing what dissent looks like when circumstances are favorable, and offering a vocabulary for assessing departures from it. To insist that it either governs all cases or none misconceives the kind of claim it makes. A map of a well-surveyed region is no less useful for failing to cover the whole continent, so long as one does not mistake its borders for the edge of the world.

qs.q: The author's main purpose is to:
o: assess criticisms of the standard account of civil disobedience and argue that it is best treated as an ideal type.
Correct: The author evaluates criticism and two defenses, then proposes the ideal-type reading.
prove that civil disobedience is justified only in liberal democracies, where the legal order is fair enough to deserve respect.
The author says the account describes conditions in such societies, not that disobedience is justified only there.
argue that nonviolence is strategically superior to disruptive protest, because it wins more public support and sympathy for a cause.
The author calls the strategic claim a hypothesis that must be tested.
show that accepting punishment is an essential component of any justified dissent, however unjust the system that imposes the penalty.
The author questions whether accepting punishment is always appropriate.
qs.x: The author evaluates criticism and two defenses, then proposes the ideal-type reading. Trap: Treating the critics' position as the author's own.

qs.q: According to the standard account, the willingness of the protester to accept punishment serves to:
o: persuade courts to reduce the severity of sentences, since judges look more favorably on those who do not resist arrest.
Leniency is not mentioned.
demonstrate that her cause has majority support, because willingness to bear a penalty shows that many others share her view.
Support is not shown by accepting punishment.
signal respect for the legal order even as she challenges part of it.
Correct: The first paragraph says it shows respect for the legal order.
avoid the need for further protest once her act has been made known to the public.
Further protest is not discussed in this connection.
qs.x: The first paragraph says it shows respect for the legal order. Trap: Importing a practical motive for a symbolic act.

qs.q: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the strategic defense described in the fourth paragraph?
o: Peaceful protests that accept penalties are frequently dismissed by the public as the work of criminals.
Correct: The defense says such protest is hard to portray as criminality; contrary evidence undermines it.
Disruptive campaigns sometimes lose public support, particularly when their tactics inconvenience people who are indifferent to the cause.
This weakens the case for disruption, not the strategic defense of the standard conduct.
Courts occasionally treat protesters fairly, even when the laws that the protesters broke were passed by large majorities of voters.
Fair courts do not bear on audience response.
Nonviolent protests are generally less expensive to organize, which explains why they are more common than disruptive campaigns.
Cost is not part of the defense.
qs.x: The defense says such protest is hard to portray as criminality; contrary evidence undermines it. Trap: Selecting evidence about disruptive protest, which supports rather than weakens the defense.

qs.q: The author's reference to a map of a well-surveyed region serves to:
o: suggest that the standard account is geographically limited to certain countries.
The domain is conditions, not literal geography.
imply that critics have misread the facts of particular protests.
The analogy concerns the nature of the theory, not factual misreading.
indicate that a theory may be valuable within a domain without governing all cases.
Correct: The map analogy makes the point about a model's useful but bounded scope.
argue that theories of dissent should be replaced by detailed case studies.
The author keeps the theory as an ideal type.
qs.x: The map analogy makes the point about a model's useful but bounded scope. Trap: Reading the map metaphor literally.

qs.q: Which of the following would the author most likely agree with?
o: A protest that departs from the standard conditions is not thereby shown to be unjustified.
Correct: Defenders and the author treat the conditions as marking the central case, with departures judged by other standards.
Any protest that breaks the law is justified if its cause is just, whatever means are used and whoever may be harmed.
The author does not endorse such a sweeping claim.
Legal avenues should never be exhausted before protest begins, because delay always makes the underlying injustice worse than the lawbreaking.
The author does not reject the exhaustion condition; she questions its universality.
Protesters who flee punishment forfeit all moral standing, and nothing they say afterward deserves to be taken seriously by others.
No such claim is made.
qs.x: Defenders and the author treat the conditions as marking the central case, with departures judged by other standards. Trap: Hearing a rejection of strict conditions as endorsement of no conditions.

qs.q: The criticism in the third paragraph depends on which of the following assumptions?
o: That protesters in unjust societies never have access to courts, so that the standard account cannot apply to them at all.
The critics say courts may be unfair, not that access is always absent.
That the conditions of the standard account presuppose institutions that are fair and responsive.
Correct: The critics say the account presupposes a basically just and responsive order.
That nonviolence is always ineffective under repressive regimes, because such governments respond only to threats of force.
Effectiveness of nonviolence is not their claim.
That majorities never enact unjust laws, so that the standard account describes only protests against rules that are fair.
The first paragraph already grants that majorities sometimes enact injustice.
qs.x: The critics say the account presupposes a basically just and responsive order. Trap: Making the critics' claim absolute when they reason from specific circumstances.

passages.title: FL04 · CARS · Passage 6
text: A common complaint about modern poetry is that it is difficult, and the complaint is often delivered with the suspicion that the difficulty is a pose. Why should a poem not say plainly what it means? The question assumes that a poem's meaning can be stated in other words, that beneath the imagery and syntax lies a message which a more forthright writer would simply have delivered. If this were so, difficulty would indeed be a kind of dishonesty, a withholding of something the poet could have handed over.

Poets and critics have long resisted this assumption. In a well-known formulation, a poem should not mean but be, which is to say that its significance is inseparable from the particular words, rhythms, and silences in which it is embodied. Paraphrase is possible, as every teacher knows, but the paraphrase is to the poem as a map is to a landscape: useful for orientation, incapable of being walked through. To ask what a poem means in other words is already to have changed the subject, since the experience that the poem provides is not a conclusion arrived at by a route that might be shortened.

This defense, though, can be pushed too far. If poems cannot be paraphrased at all, nothing can be said about them, and criticism becomes pointless. Readers do discuss poems, agree on interpretations, and sometimes persuade one another that a reading is mistaken. The truth appears to be that paraphrase is possible but partial: it recovers some of what a poem does while necessarily losing the rest. What distinguishes a poem from an essay is not that it has no paraphrasable content but that the content is not its chief achievement, which lies in how the content is held.

Consider the effect of line breaks. A poet who ends a line in the middle of a sentence creates a small pause that does not exist in prose, and in that pause a reader may entertain a meaning that the next line then revises. A line that reads "she left the house behind" may suggest abandonment until the following line adds "her at the window," whereupon the first meaning is not canceled but shadowed by the second. The reader experiences both, in sequence, and the resulting ambiguity is part of what the poem communicates. A paraphrase would have to choose, and in choosing would eliminate precisely the instability that the poet had arranged.

Difficulty, on this account, is not a barrier erected between the poem and the reader, but a feature of the kind of attention that the poem requires. It slows reading so that the words may be encountered as words, rather than as vehicles to be discarded on arrival. That is not to say that every obscure poem is successful. Obscurity may result from private reference that the poet failed to make accessible, or from carelessness mistaken for depth. The test is whether the reader's effort is rewarded: whether, after sustained attention, the poem yields more than its first appearance promised.

The skeptic who suspects a pose is therefore half right. Some difficulty is affected. But to treat all difficulty as affectation is to demand that poetry become a more efficient delivery system for statements, and to forget that efficiency was never the point.

qs.q: The author's central claim about difficult poetry is that:
o: its difficulty is often a legitimate feature of the attention it demands, though not every obscure poem succeeds.
Correct: The author defends difficulty as a feature while admitting that obscurity may fail.
its difficulty is nearly always an affectation by poets who wish to appear profound, and readers are right to dismiss it.
The author says the skeptic is only half right.
its meaning cannot be discussed or paraphrased in any form, so critics can offer readers no help in approaching it.
The author explicitly rejects the claim that nothing can be said.
it should be simplified so that readers can reach its message more quickly, since efficiency is the proper goal of reading.
The author argues against treating poetry as efficient delivery of statements.
qs.x: The author defends difficulty as a feature while admitting that obscurity may fail. Trap: Adopting the skeptic's view because the author concedes some difficulty is affected.

qs.q: In the passage, the comparison of paraphrase to a map is used to suggest that paraphrase:
o: is useful for orientation but cannot reproduce the experience of the poem itself.
Correct: A map orients but cannot be walked through.
is deceptive and should be avoided by careful readers, since any restatement of a poem in plain terms misleads its audience.
The author calls it useful.
is more accurate than the poem because it is clearer, and so is the better guide to what the poet meant.
Clarity is not equated with accuracy to the poem's achievement.
can substitute for the poem when time is limited, since the plain statement carries all that the poem communicates.
The author says it cannot capture the experience.
qs.x: A map orients but cannot be walked through. Trap: Treating a limited tool as a worthless one.

qs.q: According to the passage, the line 'she left the house behind' followed by 'her at the window' illustrates that:
o: poets should avoid ending a line mid-sentence, because such breaks interrupt the reader and make the sense harder to follow.
The author presents the effect as a poetic resource.
the second line corrects an error in the first, so that the reader must discard the first meaning entirely.
The first meaning is shadowed, not corrected as an error.
a line break can allow a first meaning to be shadowed rather than canceled by a second.
Correct: The author says both meanings are experienced in sequence.
ambiguity in poetry is always unintentional, and readers should resolve it by choosing whichever meaning is the most common.
The author says the poet arranged the instability.
qs.x: The author says both meanings are experienced in sequence. Trap: Reading revision as correction rather than layering.

qs.q: The author would most likely agree that a criticism that insists a poem 'cannot be discussed' is:
o: correct, since poems are inseparable from their words and no two readers can ever arrive at the same understanding of one.
Inseparability does not mean silence on the subject.
correct, since paraphrase always distorts a poem and therefore no interpretation can be better or worse than another.
Paraphrase is partial, not useless.
irrelevant, since poems do not communicate anything to readers and so cannot be understood in the first place.
The author says poems communicate through ambiguity.
mistaken, since readers do reach shared interpretations and correct one another.
Correct: The third paragraph rejects this extreme.
qs.x: The third paragraph rejects this extreme. Trap: Following the first half of the defense without noting its limit.

qs.q: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as a justified criticism of a poem?
o: The poem rewards repeated reading with new layers of meaning that were not evident on the first encounter.
This is the success test.
The poem depends on a private reference that readers cannot recover, so sustained attention yields nothing more.
Correct: The author names inaccessible private reference and unrewarded effort as failures.
The poem contains a line break that produces ambiguity, so that two meanings are held together at once.
This is praised as a poetic effect.
The poem cannot be paraphrased in full, and the reader's sense of it changes as the poem is reread.
Partial paraphrasability is expected of poems.
qs.x: The author names inaccessible private reference and unrewarded effort as failures. Trap: Confusing difficulty itself with the kind of difficulty the author criticizes.

qs.q: The final paragraph's reference to efficiency suggests that the skeptic's demand rests on the view that poetry should be:
o: entirely free of rhythm and imagery, since such features distract from the message that is being conveyed.
Rhythm and imagery are not the target.
written only by trained critics, who alone are able to decide what a given text is supposed to communicate.
Authorship is not discussed.
read only by those who already understand it, since no one else could be expected to follow its meaning.
Readership limits are not discussed.
a means of transmitting statements as quickly as possible.
Correct: The author says the skeptic would turn poetry into a delivery system for statements.
qs.x: The author says the skeptic would turn poetry into a delivery system for statements. Trap: Choosing an option about form rather than purpose.

passages.title: FL04 · CARS · Passage 7
text: The arrival of synchronized sound in the late 1920s is conventionally told as a story of progress: silent film was a promising but incomplete art, and the talkies completed it. The story is so familiar that it is easy to overlook how many of the period's filmmakers and critics regarded the change as a catastrophe. They did not object to sound as such. Their complaint was that early sound technology, which required actors to speak toward concealed microphones and cameras to be sealed in soundproof booths, froze a medium that had only recently learned to move.

By the mid-1920s, silent cinema had developed a sophisticated visual grammar. Directors used the moving camera, rapid cutting, and carefully composed images to convey emotion and thought without a word of dialogue, and the intertitle, which had once been a crutch, had become in skilled hands a sparing and sometimes poetic device. Audiences had learned to read faces, gestures, and the rhythms of editing. The loss of this grammar in the first years of sound was real: films of the early talkie period are often static, dominated by people standing near a microphone and talking.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that silent film was a complete art that sound merely spoiled. Silent film was never silent; theaters employed pianists, organists, and sometimes full orchestras, and the experience of the film varied with the musicians and the audience. The "silent" form was therefore already a performance medium in which each screening differed, and its apparent purity is partly a creation of later archives, which preserve the film but not the music that accompanied it. The art that the sound-era critics mourned was in some respects an art that survives only in reconstruction.

Nor did the early limitations of sound last. Within a few years, microphones became portable, cameras were freed from their booths, and directors discovered that sound could do things that images could not. A sound heard from off screen could suggest a presence that the picture withheld; a conversation could overlap another in a way that no intertitle could represent; and silence itself, deliberately introduced into a soundtrack, could gain a force that it never had when silence was the default. Filmmakers who had mastered the visual grammar of the silent era often proved the best at exploiting these resources, since they understood that the image should continue to carry meaning even when speech was available.

The most defensible account of the transition, then, is neither a triumph nor a tragedy. It was a disruption that destroyed some achievements and made others possible, and the ledger cannot be balanced by an appeal to a single standard of artistic completeness. The idea that an art form has a destination, toward which it moves when its technology permits, is attractive, but it imposes a purpose that the artists themselves did not share. They were not completing a form; they were responding, with varying success, to the materials available.

Seen this way, the persistence of silent filmmaking as an occasional deliberate choice in later decades is not a nostalgic eccentricity. It is evidence that the capacities of the earlier form never became obsolete, only optional.

qs.q: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Silent cinema was a complete art that was ruined by synchronized sound, which brought nothing of value to the medium.
The author says it is a mistake to call silent film a complete art spoiled by sound.
Early sound technology was so limiting that it should never have been adopted, and the industry would have been better without it.
The limits did not last, and the author notes gains.
The shift to sound is better understood as a disruption with both losses and gains than as either simple progress or simple decline.
Correct: The author rejects both triumph and tragedy narratives.
Archives have distorted our understanding of the silent era by omitting images, which is why its achievements are widely misjudged.
Archives omitted the music, not the images.
qs.x: The author rejects both triumph and tragedy narratives. Trap: Identifying the main idea with the opening critics' claim rather than the author's balanced conclusion.

qs.q: According to the passage, early talkie films were often static because:
o: directors had forgotten the visual grammar of silent film, so that scenes became static after the industry adopted sound.
The author says directors who mastered silent grammar proved best at using sound later.
actors had to speak toward hidden microphones and cameras were enclosed in soundproof booths.
Correct: The first paragraph names the microphone and booth requirements.
audiences preferred dialogue to movement, so studios deliberately chose to keep the camera in place for speaking scenes.
Audience preference is not given as the reason.
intertitles had become too elaborate, so that studios required directors to replace them with spoken lines of dialogue.
Intertitles are not blamed.
qs.x: The first paragraph names the microphone and booth requirements. Trap: Blaming filmmakers' skill rather than the technology.

qs.q: The author's point that silent film 'was never silent' primarily serves to:
o: argue that live musicians were better than recorded sound, and that sound film therefore marked a decline in musical quality.
The author does not rank live over recorded music.
show that audiences disliked silent films shown without accompaniment, which is why theaters hired musicians to perform with them.
Audience dislike is not mentioned.
undermine the idea that silent cinema was a pure, uniform art form.
Correct: The live music made each screening differ, complicating the picture of purity.
claim that sound film is therefore not a new medium, since it simply continued the practices of silent exhibition.
The author acknowledges that sound brought new possibilities.
qs.x: The live music made each screening differ, complicating the picture of purity. Trap: Reading a historical correction as a preference claim.

qs.q: Which of the following can be inferred about the author's view of intertitles?
o: They were a mark of artistic failure in all silent films, because they showed that images could not tell the story alone.
The author says they began as a crutch but could improve.
They were unnecessary once the camera moved, since moving images made written explanation of the story redundant.
The passage does not tie them to camera movement.
They were eliminated before 1920, after directors learned to tell stories entirely through gesture and framing.
Dates are not given and they were used into the mid-1920s.
They could become an effective, restrained artistic device when used skillfully.
Correct: The second paragraph says they had become sparing and sometimes poetic in skilled hands.
qs.x: The second paragraph says they had become sparing and sometimes poetic in skilled hands. Trap: Taking the 'crutch' remark as the author's final judgment.

qs.q: The author's discussion of off-screen sound and deliberate silence most directly supports which claim?
o: Directors of the silent era could not adapt to sound, and their careers declined once the new technology was introduced.
The author says silent-era filmmakers often adapted best.
Soundtracks are more important than images, because modern audiences respond more strongly to what they hear than to what they see.
The author says the image should still carry meaning.
Sound opened expressive possibilities that images alone could not provide.
Correct: These are examples of things sound could do that images could not.
Silence was impossible in silent film, since live music or commentary accompanied every showing of every film ever made.
Silence gained force only once it was deliberately introduced, not that it was impossible earlier.
qs.x: These are examples of things sound could do that images could not. Trap: Turning a claim about added resources into a claim about priority.

qs.q: Which of the following, if true, would most challenge the author's argument that sound brought genuine expressive gains?
o: Some directors continued to make silent films for artistic reasons, even after sound had become standard in commercial cinema.
The author uses this as evidence that the earlier capacities remained.
Early sound films were often static, because the recording equipment limited where actors and cameras could be placed.
The author already grants this.
Film archives preserve the images but not the original music, so modern viewers must supply accompaniment of their own choosing.
The author cites this about archives and it does not bear on sound's gains.
Critics of the period agreed that films with off-screen sound and overlapping speech were less expressive than silent films.
Correct: Evidence that these techniques lacked expressive worth would undercut the claim, though the author's own judgment stays contestable.
qs.x: Evidence that these techniques lacked expressive worth would undercut the claim, though the author's own judgment stays contestable. Trap: Choosing a fact the author already accepts.

passages.title: FL04 · CARS · Passage 8
text: Few features of schooling are as widely used and as little understood as the grade. A letter or number placed at the top of a paper is treated by students, parents, universities, and employers as a compact measurement of learning. It is also, for most of those who read it, a judgment: it tells them where a student stands relative to some standard, or relative to peers. Yet any teacher can testify that the same piece of work might earn different marks from different markers, or from the same marker on different days, and that a single grade often blends what the student knows with how hard she worked, how neatly she wrote, and whether she turned the assignment in on time.

Reformers have long argued that this blending makes grades poor instruments. A grade that mixes mastery with compliance, they say, tells us neither accurately, and a student who understands a subject but neglects homework may be recorded as failing it. Their remedy is to separate the components: report achievement against clearly stated standards in one place, and behaviors such as punctuality and effort in another. Schools that have adopted such systems often find that their grades become more consistent across classrooms, and that conversations with students shift from negotiating points to identifying what remains to be learned.

The reform, however, rests on an assumption that deserves more scrutiny than it usually receives: that learning can be cleanly detached from the habits that produce it. In many fields the distinction is artificial. A student who cannot meet deadlines may be unable to complete the extended projects through which advanced skills are developed, and effort may be less a separate virtue than one of the mechanisms by which knowledge is acquired. To report mastery without regard to such habits risks describing a student's current state while leaving unstated the process on which her future progress depends.

There is a further complication. The act of measuring changes the thing measured. When students know that a grade will count toward a transcript, they adjust their behavior to the grade rather than to the learning it was meant to track, a phenomenon familiar to anyone who has studied for a test by memorizing what was likely to appear on it. Standards-based reporting does not eliminate this tendency; it only relocates it. Students who are told that they must demonstrate each of thirty standards may simply learn to demonstrate thirty standards, whether or not the demonstration reflects understanding.

None of this shows that grades should be discarded. Institutions require some means of summarizing performance, and the alternatives, such as narrative evaluations, are expensive in teachers' time and difficult for outside readers to compare. The sensible position is that a grade is a communication with several audiences, and that no single design can serve all of them equally. What teachers can do is be candid about what a given grade is meant to convey, and resist the temptation to treat it as an objective fact. A mark is a summary written by a person, using criteria chosen by a person, and its authority depends on that person's willingness to explain how it was reached.
The challenge for schools is therefore less to perfect the grade than to ensure that students and families understand what it is.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the author's central view of grades?
o: Grades are useful summaries whose design involves unavoidable trade-offs, so their meaning must be made explicit.
Correct: The author endorses grades with candor about their limits.
Grades are inaccurate and should be replaced by narrative evaluations, since no number can summarize what a student has learned.
Narrative evaluations are called costly and hard to compare.
Grades should measure only mastery, apart from effort and behavior, because anything else corrupts the meaning of the mark.
The author questions the assumption that mastery can be cleanly separated.
Grades are objective facts about a student's learning, and so can be compared directly across schools and teachers.
The author tells teachers to resist treating a grade as objective fact.
qs.x: The author endorses grades with candor about their limits. Trap: Choosing the reformers' position, which the author examines critically rather than adopts.

qs.q: According to the reformers described in the passage, a student who understands a subject but neglects homework:
o: should be given a higher grade for understanding, since mastery of the material is the only thing a grade ought to reflect.
The reformers want separation, not a bonus.
may be recorded as failing under a grading system that blends mastery with compliance.
Correct: This is the reformers' example of the blending problem.
will always improve if effort is graded separately, because students respond only to what is formally counted in their grades.
Improvement is not asserted.
should be excluded from standards-based reporting, since such systems are designed only for students who comply with routines.
Exclusion is not discussed.
qs.x: This is the reformers' example of the blending problem. Trap: Confusing the problem described with the remedy.

qs.q: The author raises the example of studying by memorizing likely test content to show that:
o: measurement can shift behavior toward the measure rather than the learning it was meant to track.
Correct: The example illustrates adjusting to the grade, as the paragraph states.
tests are unfair to students who memorize well, because memorization is a skill that schools ought not to reward at all.
Fairness is not at issue.
teachers deliberately encourage memorization, since they believe that recall of facts is the highest form of understanding.
Teacher intention is not mentioned.
standards-based reporting prevents this kind of behavior, because students cannot adjust their efforts to a measure that is detailed.
The author says standards-based reporting only relocates it.
qs.x: The example illustrates adjusting to the grade, as the paragraph states. Trap: Missing that the author sees the problem persisting under the reform.

qs.q: The third paragraph suggests that the reformers' assumption is questionable because:
o: effort and punctuality are never relevant to achievement, and should be excluded from every account of how students learn.
The author argues they may be relevant.
habits such as meeting deadlines may be part of how learning is achieved in many fields.
Correct: The author says effort may be a mechanism of acquiring knowledge.
teachers cannot measure mastery objectively, so that any grade will inevitably reflect the personal impressions of the teacher.
The point concerns the detachment of habits, not measurability.
students with poor habits cannot learn, and so schools are justified in lowering grades for any lapse in routine.
The author says they may impede extended projects, not make learning impossible.
qs.x: The author says effort may be a mechanism of acquiring knowledge. Trap: Overextending 'may be related' to 'always prevents'.

qs.q: Which of the following findings would most undermine the author's claim that standards-based reporting only relocates the tendency to adjust behavior to the grade?
o: Students under both systems study mainly what is likely to be assessed, and do so with comparable levels of effort and success.
This would support the author's claim.
Students under standards-based reporting show deeper understanding on unfamiliar tasks than students under traditional grading.
Correct: Deeper transfer would suggest the system does change what students learn.
Teachers under standards-based reporting spend more time on grading, though their students show no difference in understanding.
Time spent does not address behavior toward the measure.
Grades become more consistent across classrooms under both systems, so that comparisons between teachers become more reliable.
Consistency is a separate benefit the author already grants.
qs.x: Deeper transfer would suggest the system does change what students learn. Trap: Selecting a result that is true of the reform but does not bear on the claim.

qs.q: The author's concluding recommendation for teachers is most consistent with which of the following?
o: A teacher who adopts whichever system produces the highest grades.
Grade inflation is not discussed.
A teacher who refuses to assign grades.
The author says grades remain necessary.
A teacher who explains to students how a grade was reached and what it is intended to show.
Correct: The author says authority depends on the willingness to explain.
A teacher who tells students their grades are objective measurements.
The author says teachers should resist treating grades as objective fact.
qs.x: The author says authority depends on the willingness to explain. Trap: Reading the criticism of grades as support for abolishing them.

passages.title: FL04 · CARS · Passage 9
text: Compilers of encyclopedias have always had to decide, before anything else, how to arrange what they know. The choice looks like a matter of convenience, but it is better understood as a claim about the nature of knowledge. Ancient and medieval compilers generally arranged their material by subject, descending from the heavens to the earth, from God to angels to humans to animals to minerals. A reader moving through such a work was meant to experience the order of creation itself, and the book's structure taught as much as its entries did. The drawback was practical: someone who wanted to learn about a single plant had to know where in the cosmic hierarchy it belonged before the book could be of any help.

The alphabetical encyclopedia solved that problem by giving up on the cosmic hierarchy. Arranged by the first letter of each heading, it required nothing of its reader except the name of the thing sought. Its early modern advocates praised it as neutral, since no one's theory of the world determined where an entry would fall. Yet neutrality had a cost. Alphabetical order scatters related topics across the volumes, so that "anatomy" and "surgery" stand far apart while "anatomy" sits beside "anchor." Knowledge, which had been a structure, became a collection of fragments.

The editors of the great eighteenth-century French Encyclopédie were acutely aware of this cost and tried to repair it with two devices. They prefaced the work with a diagram, a tree of knowledge, showing how the disciplines were thought to descend from the human faculties of memory, reason, and imagination. And they threaded the entries with cross-references directing readers from one article to another. The cross-references did more than assist. A reverent article on an approved doctrine could point the reader toward another, ostensibly unrelated, that treated the same doctrine with irony; an entry on a sacred rite might send the curious to a plain description of similar rites among other peoples. The alphabetical order thus concealed an argument conducted in the links, one that censors examining the work entry by entry could not easily detect.

It would be tempting to conclude that alphabetical arrangement is simply liberating because it lets readers assemble their own order. But the reader's freedom is partial. A person who consults an encyclopedia arrives with a question already formed, and the alphabetical format rewards only those questions whose terms the editors anticipated. A reader who does not know that a phenomenon has a name cannot look it up. The thematic encyclopedia, for all its rigidity, can expose a reader to subjects never sought, since browsing a single chapter reveals its neighbors. Each format therefore favors a different kind of curiosity: the alphabetical serves the person who knows what is missing, while the thematic serves the person who does not yet know what to ask.

Digital reference works have revived this debate rather than ended it. Search engines function as an alphabetical index of unprecedented reach, and hyperlinks resemble the Encyclopédie's cross-references, but an unbounded index has no editor to decide what is worth including, and a reader can follow links indefinitely without ever grasping how the subjects fit together. The history suggests that no arrangement is innocent; each embodies a view of what a reader should be able to do with knowledge. The sensible response is not to search for a perfect order but to ask of any arrangement what it makes easy, what it makes hard, and who decided.

qs.q: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to:
o: argue that alphabetical arrangement has made encyclopedias more reliable than thematic ones.
The author does not rank reliability and notes costs of alphabetical order.
show that the ordering of an encyclopedia reflects assumptions about knowledge and readers, so each arrangement has costs and benefits.
Correct: The passage traces several arrangements and concludes that none is innocent and each favors something.
demonstrate that eighteenth-century editors disguised their real views from the public.
The Encyclopédie is one example, not the passage's main point.
claim that digital reference works have solved problems of arrangement that print could not.
The final paragraph says digital works revived the debate rather than ended it.
qs.x: The passage traces several arrangements and concludes that none is innocent and each favors something. Trap: Choosing a detailed example (the Encyclopédie) as the main point instead of the passage-wide argument.

qs.q: According to the passage, a drawback of the alphabetical encyclopedia is that it:
o: requires readers to understand the hierarchy of creation before they can locate an entry.
That is the drawback of the subject-ordered work.
assigns each topic to a position that depends on the compiler's own theory of the world.
Neutrality is the alphabetical order's claimed advantage.
separates related subjects and depends on readers already knowing the name of what they seek.
Correct: The second and fourth paragraphs say it scatters related topics and rewards only anticipated, named questions.
prevents editors from including cross-references between articles on different subjects.
The Encyclopédie used cross-references within alphabetical order.
qs.x: The second and fourth paragraphs say it scatters related topics and rewards only anticipated, named questions. Trap: Attributing the thematic format's drawback to the alphabetical format by reversing the comparison.

qs.q: The author mentions the cross-references in the Encyclopédie primarily to illustrate how:
o: an apparently neutral arrangement could still carry an argument that readers might miss.
Correct: The cross-references conducted an argument that entry-by-entry censors could not easily detect.
editors compensated for the fragmentation of knowledge by restoring a cosmic hierarchy.
The tree diagram, not the links, addressed fragmentation, and it was not a cosmic hierarchy.
censors of the period were generally unable to understand the works they reviewed.
The passage says the links were hard to detect, not that censors lacked understanding.
links between articles are less useful to readers than a tree of knowledge diagram.
No comparison of usefulness is made.
qs.x: The cross-references conducted an argument that entry-by-entry censors could not easily detect. Trap: Reading a statement about what was hard to detect as a general claim about the censors' competence.

qs.q: Which of the following claims about readers is most clearly supported by the fourth paragraph?
o: Readers prefer browsing to searching because browsing is faster and more reliable.
Speed and reliability are not discussed.
Readers who consult alphabetical works are usually more curious than those who read thematic ones.
The author says the formats favor different kinds of curiosity, not more or less.
Readers of thematic works may encounter useful subjects that they would not have thought to request.
Correct: Browsing a chapter reveals neighbors, exposing readers to subjects never sought.
Readers of every format ultimately assemble the same order of knowledge for themselves.
The author denies that the freedom to assemble one's own order is complete.
qs.x: Browsing a chapter reveals neighbors, exposing readers to subjects never sought. Trap: Turning a claim of different strengths into a claim that one group is simply better.

qs.q: Suppose a modern reference site lets users reach any article only by typing its exact title, with no categories or links. Based on the passage, the author would most likely say that this site:
o: resembles the medieval encyclopedia because it teaches the order of creation.
The medieval work was ordered by subject, which this site lacks.
serves readers who know what they are missing but offers little to those who do not know what to ask.
Correct: Such a site extends the alphabetical logic and rewards only anticipated, named questions.
is the most neutral possible design and therefore free of any assumptions about readers.
The author says no arrangement is innocent, since each embodies a view of what readers should do.
would undermine censorship because it prevents editors from deciding what is included.
Editors still decide what is included; the passage notes only that unbounded indexes lack an editor.
qs.x: Such a site extends the alphabetical logic and rewards only anticipated, named questions. Trap: Equating a neutral-looking design with one that makes no assumptions about readers.

passages.title: FL04 · Chem/Phys · Passage 1
text: A student studies the stability of a uniform ladder of mass 20 kg and length 4.0 m that leans against a smooth vertical wall, with its foot on a rough horizontal floor. The ladder makes an angle θ with the floor. Use g = 10 m/s². Because the wall is smooth, it exerts only a horizontal normal force on the ladder, whereas the floor exerts a vertical normal force N and a horizontal static friction force f. The student applies the conditions for static equilibrium, taking torques about the foot of the ladder, to find the friction force required at several angles when the ladder is on the verge of slipping. The smallest coefficient of static friction that prevents slipping is μ = f/N. Results for the unloaded ladder are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. The student then asks how the requirement changes when a 60 kg person stands on the ladder at various heights.

qs.q: According to Table 1, which expression gives the friction force needed at 60° for the unloaded ladder?
o: f = mg/tan θ ≈ 115 N
f = mg/tan θ ≈ 115 N omits the factor of 1/2 that comes from the weight acting at the ladder's midpoint.
f = mg/(2 tan θ) ≈ 58 N
Correct: Torque about the foot gives N_w(L sin θ) = mg(L/2)cos θ, so N_w = mg/(2 tan θ) = 200/(2 × 1.73) = 58 N, and f equals N_w by horizontal balance.
f = mg/2 ≈ 100 N ignores the angle dependence that enters through the lever arms of the wall force and the weight.
f = (mg/2) tan θ ≈ 173 N
f = (mg/2) tan θ ≈ 173 N inverts the tangent, which would predict more friction at steeper angles, contrary to Table 1.
qs.x: Torque about the foot gives N_w(L sin θ) = mg(L/2)cos θ, so N_w = mg/(2 tan θ) = 200/(2 × 1.73) = 58 N, and f equals N_w by horizontal balance. Trap: Forgetting that the weight acts at L/2 (so the factor of 2) or inverting the tangent when solving for the wall force.

qs.q: A student's floor has μs = 0.40 with the ladder. Using Figure 1, which angle is approximately the smallest at which the unloaded ladder remains at rest?
o: About 39° with the floor
About 39° with the floor comes from inverting the relationship (tan θ = 2μ instead of 1/(2μ)); at 39° the requirement is above 0.60.
About 22° with the floor
About 22° with the floor uses θ = arctan μ, which ignores the torque balance, and is far below the angle where μ_min drops to 0.40.
About 51° with the floor
Correct: The requirement μ = 1/(2 tan θ) = 0.40 gives tan θ = 1.25, so θ ≈ 51°; Figure 1 shows μ_min of 0.42 at 50° and 0.29 at 60°, bracketing 0.40.
About 68° with the floor
About 68° with the floor is stable but not the smallest angle; μ_min is only about 0.20 there, well under 0.40.
qs.x: The requirement μ = 1/(2 tan θ) = 0.40 gives tan θ = 1.25, so θ ≈ 51°; Figure 1 shows μ_min of 0.42 at 50° and 0.29 at 60°, bracketing 0.40. Trap: Reading the graph backward and choosing the angle where μ_min exceeds the available friction, which would cause slipping.

qs.q: Why is the foot of the ladder a convenient axis for the torque equation?
o: The unknown floor forces act at the axis, so they exert no torque and drop out
Correct: Both the normal force and the friction force from the floor act at the foot, so their lever arms are zero and they do not appear in the equation, leaving only the wall force and the weight.
The ladder's weight acts at the axis, so it contributes no torque and drops out
The ladder's weight acts at the axis, so it contributes no torque and drops out is false; the weight acts at the center of mass, 2.0 m from the foot, and supplies the main torque.
The wall force and the floor friction force have equal lever arms and cancel in the torque sum

The wall force and the floor friction force have equal lever arms and cancel in the torque sum is wrong; the wall force acts at the top, with a lever arm L sin θ, while the friction force acts at the axis.
Torque can only be calculated about a point where a surface exerts a force on the object

Torque can only be calculated about a point where a surface exerts a force on the object is wrong; any point may serve as the axis for an object in equilibrium, and this one is just the most convenient.
qs.x: Both the normal force and the friction force from the floor act at the foot, so their lever arms are zero and they do not appear in the equation, leaving only the wall force and the weight. Trap: Believing the weight acts at the pivot or that an axis must be placed at a contact point.

qs.q: A 60 kg person (weight 600 N) stands 80% of the way up the 20 kg ladder, which is at 60°. About what friction force does the floor need to supply?
o: About 580 N
About 580 N is the sum (mg/2 + weight × 0.8) without dividing by tan θ, so it is the torque-like numerator rather than a force.
About 231 N
About 231 N uses a person standing at the midpoint (50% up) instead of 80%, which gives a smaller torque from the person.
About 58 N
About 58 N is the friction for the unloaded ladder in Table 1 and ignores the person's added torque.
About 335 N
Correct: Torque about the foot: N_w(L sin 60°) = 200(L/2)cos 60° + 600(0.8L)cos 60°, so N_w = (100 + 480)/tan 60° = 580/1.73 ≈ 335 N, and f = N_w.
qs.x: Torque about the foot: N_w(L sin 60°) = 200(L/2)cos 60° + 600(0.8L)cos 60°, so N_w = (100 + 480)/tan 60° = 580/1.73 ≈ 335 N, and f = N_w. Trap: Using the person's weight at the midpoint, or giving the answer without dividing by tan θ.

qs.q: Suppose the wall were rough instead of smooth. How would the floor friction force required to hold the unloaded ladder at a given angle compare with the smooth-wall case?
o: It would be larger, because the wall's friction force adds a second horizontal force the floor must cancel

It would be larger, because the wall's friction force adds a second horizontal force the floor must cancel is wrong; wall friction is directed along the wall (vertical), so it is not a horizontal force.
It would be smaller, because wall friction supplies an upward force and an additional torque
Correct: Wall friction acts upward, adding a torque about the foot that helps balance the weight, so the wall's normal force, which equals the floor friction, can be smaller.
It would be the same, because the ladder's weight and angle fix the floor friction independent of wall properties

It would be the same, because the ladder's weight and angle fix the floor friction independent of wall properties is wrong; the wall's friction force adds a torque about the foot, changing the balance.
It would be zero, because any wall friction at all makes the floor friction unnecessary
It would be zero, because any wall friction at all makes the floor friction unnecessary overstates the effect; the wall still needs a horizontal normal force that the floor friction must balance.
qs.x: Wall friction acts upward, adding a torque about the foot that helps balance the weight, so the wall's normal force, which equals the floor friction, can be smaller. Trap: Treating all wall forces as horizontal or thinking wall properties cannot affect the torque balance.
