passages.title: FL04 · Psych/Soc · Passage 4
text: The facial feedback hypothesis proposes that changes in facial muscle activity can influence the emotions a person experiences. One hundred twenty adults were told that the study concerned motor coordination while performing tasks with the mouth. Participants were randomly assigned to hold a pen in one of three ways while rating 12 cartoons for funniness on a scale from 0 (not at all funny) to 9 (extremely funny). Holding the pen between the teeth with the lips open forced the muscles of a smile (n = 40). Holding it with the lips only prevented a smile or produced a pout (n = 40). In the neutral condition, participants held the pen in the non-dominant hand and did not use the mouth (n = 40). Mean ratings are shown in Table 1. The authors argued that sensory feedback from the face contributes to the experience of emotion, and they noted that other laboratories have reported smaller effects with this procedure.

qs.q: Which theory of emotion most directly predicts that the facial posture manipulation would change reported amusement?
o: The Cannon-Bard theory, which holds that emotional experience and bodily responses arise simultaneously and independently.
This theory predicts that body state does not drive emotion, so it would predict no effect of posture.
The James-Lange theory, which holds that emotional experience follows from the perception of bodily responses.
Correct: If feedback from facial muscles is perceived as a bodily response and shapes the feeling, emotion follows the body, as the James-Lange theory proposes.
The Lazarus appraisal theory, which holds that a cognitive appraisal of the stimulus must precede any emotional experience.
Appraisal theory places cognition before emotion and does not predict that muscle posture alone changes feelings.
The Yerkes-Dodson law, which holds that performance is best at a moderate level of physiological arousal.
This is a relationship between arousal and task performance, not a theory of how emotions arise.
qs.x: If feedback from facial muscles is perceived as a bodily response and shapes the feeling, emotion follows the body, as the James-Lange theory proposes. Trap: Choosing the most familiar emotion theory rather than the one in which bodily feedback precedes the feeling.

qs.q: What does the inclusion of the neutral condition allow the researchers to conclude?
o: The smiling posture raised ratings and the non-smiling posture lowered them relative to baseline.
Correct: Relative to the neutral mean of 5.2, the teeth condition was 0.6 higher (5.8) and the lips condition was 0.6 lower (4.6), so both directions of change are seen.
Only the smiling posture altered ratings, because the lips condition was equal to the neutral baseline.
The lips mean (4.6) is below the neutral mean, not equal to it.
Only the non-smiling posture altered ratings, because the teeth condition was equal to the neutral baseline.
The teeth mean (5.8) is above the neutral mean, not equal to it.
Neither posture altered ratings, because the neutral condition fell between the other two condition means.
A middle position for the neutral condition is expected if both postures have effects in opposite directions.
qs.x: Relative to the neutral mean of 5.2, the teeth condition was 0.6 higher (5.8) and the lips condition was 0.6 lower (4.6), so both directions of change are seen. Trap: Interpreting the middle value of a baseline group as evidence that the manipulation had no effect.

qs.q: What is the standard error of the mean rating for the teeth (smile) condition? (Use the square root of 40 = 6.3.)
o: This divides the SD by n (1.2 / 40) rather than by the square root of n.
This divides the SD by 4, which is not a function of the sample size here.
This multiplies the SD by the square root of n (1.2 x 6.3) rather than dividing.
Correct: SEM = SD / square root of n = 1.2 / 6.3, which is about 0.19.
qs.x: SEM = SD / square root of n = 1.2 / 6.3, which is about 0.19. Trap: Dividing the standard deviation by n instead of by the square root of n.

qs.q: The participants were told the study concerned motor coordination. This feature of the design most directly reduces which threat to validity?
o: Selection bias, in which the groups already differ before the manipulation because of nonrandom assignment.
Selection bias is handled by random assignment, not by a cover story.
Demand characteristics, in which participants guess the hypothesis and respond accordingly.
Correct: A cover story keeps participants from realizing that smiling and amusement are the focus, so their ratings are less likely to reflect what they think the study predicts.
Regression to the mean, in which extreme initial scores drift toward the average when participants are retested.
Regression to the mean concerns repeated measures on extreme scorers, and there was a single rating session.
Attrition, in which participants drop out of one condition more often than they drop out of another.
Attrition concerns participants leaving the study and is unaffected by what they are told about its purpose.
qs.x: A cover story keeps participants from realizing that smiling and amusement are the focus, so their ratings are less likely to reflect what they think the study predicts. Trap: Naming a generic validity threat without linking it to the specific feature of the procedure.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Mean funniness ratings (0-9)

passages.title: FL04 · Psych/Soc · Passage 5
text: Researchers presented a hypothetical moral dilemma to 200 participants in four age groups (n = 50 each): a man considers stealing an expensive drug he cannot afford to save his dying wife. Each participant explained whether the man should steal and why. Two trained raters, blind to age, classified the reasoning as preconventional (focused on punishment or personal gain), conventional (focused on social approval, laws, and duty to maintain order), or postconventional (focused on abstract principles of justice that may override specific laws). The percentage of participants in each age group whose reasoning fell into each level is shown in Figure 1. The authors proposed that, as adolescents take on more social roles and learn the expectations of peers, schools, and communities, reasoning shifts from self-interest toward shared social norms. They noted that each participant was interviewed only once. Agreement between the two raters was high (kappa = 0.85), and participants were told that there were no right or wrong answers.

qs.q: A participant says the man should not steal the drug because breaking the law would damage the order that holds society together. This reasoning is best classified as
o: preconventional, because it is motivated by avoiding punishment.
The participant does not mention punishment to the self.
preconventional, because it treats the exchange of favors as a fair bargain.
Nothing in the answer concerns an exchange of favors for personal benefit.
postconventional, because it is based on universal principles that can override the law.
A postconventional answer would place abstract justice above the law, whereas this answer defends the law.
conventional, because it is based on upholding laws and the social order.
Correct: Appeals to law and the maintenance of social order are the hallmark of conventional reasoning.
qs.x: Appeals to law and the maintenance of social order are the hallmark of conventional reasoning. Trap: Matching on the word law to the wrong level without noticing that the law is being defended rather than judged by a higher principle.

qs.q: How many of the 16-year-olds used conventional reasoning?
o: This reports the percentage as if it were a count.
This is 20% of 50, the number using preconventional reasoning.
Correct: 68% of 50 participants = 34.
This is half of 34 and has no basis in the data.
qs.x: 68% of 50 participants = 34. Trap: Reporting a percentage as a count when each group has 50 rather than 100 participants.

qs.q: The rise in conventional reasoning between the ages of 10 and 16 is most consistent with the influence of which process?
o: Socialization, in which family, peers, and schools transmit the norms of the society.
Correct: Learning the norms of one's society through interaction with family, peers, and institutions is socialization, which the authors propose as the driver.
Deindividuation, in which anonymity within a crowd reduces the sense of personal responsibility.
Deindividuation concerns reduced restraint in anonymous groups, which would not increase adherence to norms.
Social facilitation, in which the presence of an audience improves performance on simple tasks.
Social facilitation concerns task performance in the presence of others.
Groupthink, in which a cohesive group suppresses dissent in order to reach quick agreement.
Groupthink describes decision making in a cohesive group, not individual moral development.
qs.x: Learning the norms of one's society through interaction with family, peers, and institutions is socialization, which the authors propose as the driver. Trap: Picking a group-behavior term because it sounds social without checking whether it describes the learning of norms.

qs.q: Which statement about the data in Figure 1 is supported?
o: Preconventional reasoning was more common than conventional reasoning among the 13-year-olds.
At age 13 conventional (50%) exceeded preconventional (45%).
Postconventional reasoning was the most common level among the 20-year-olds.
At age 20 postconventional was 22% and conventional was 70%.
The percentage of participants using preconventional reasoning increased with each older age group.
Preconventional reasoning fell from 70% to 8% with age.
At age 16, conventional reasoning was more than three times as common as preconventional reasoning.
Correct: At age 16 the values are 68% and 20%, a ratio of 3.4.
qs.x: At age 16 the values are 68% and 20%, a ratio of 3.4. Trap: Reading the wrong series or age group, or reversing the direction of a trend.

graph.title: Figure 1. Reasoning level by age group

passages.title: FL04 · Psych/Soc · Passage 6
text: Researchers tested compliance among 300 homeowners in similar neighborhoods. Each was randomly assigned to one of three conditions (n = 100 each). In the small-request condition, a canvasser asked the resident to sign a short petition supporting safer streets, which all residents agreed to do. A week later, a different canvasser asked the resident to install a large 'Drive Carefully' sign in the front yard. In the paid-small-request condition, the first request was the same, but residents were given a $5 voucher for signing. The second request was identical. In the large-request-only condition, residents were approached only with the sign request. Compliance with the sign request, scored by whether a sign was installed within two days, is shown in Table 1. A chi-square test across the three conditions was significant (p < 0.001). The investigators concluded that agreeing to a small request can change how people see themselves, increasing later compliance with larger requests, unless the first action can be attributed to an outside reward.

qs.q: Asking for a small request first, then a larger one, is an example of which compliance technique?
o: Door-in-the-face
This starts with a large request that is refused before a smaller one is made.
Lowballing
This involves changing the terms of an agreed request to be less favorable.
Foot-in-the-door
Correct: Agreement with a small initial request increases the likelihood of agreement with a later larger request.
That's-not-all
This sweetens an offer before the target decides, and no sweetener was used here.
qs.x: Agreement with a small initial request increases the likelihood of agreement with a later larger request. Trap: Mixing up foot-in-the-door and door-in-the-face because both involve two requests.

qs.q: The lower compliance in the paid-small-request condition is best explained by:
o: classical conditioning, because the voucher became a conditioned stimulus.
No pairing procedure was used, and this would predict higher compliance.
the mere exposure effect, because they saw the petition twice.
Exposure was equal in both small-request conditions.
reactance, because the canvassers refused to pay more.
No data indicate that residents sought more money or that freedom was threatened.
self-perception: with an external reward available, residents attributed signing to the voucher rather than to their own beliefs.
Correct: Payment provides sufficient external justification for the first act, so people do not infer a strong personal commitment to the cause.
qs.x: Payment provides sufficient external justification for the first act, so people do not infer a strong personal commitment to the cause. Trap: Assuming a reward always increases later cooperation, when it can undercut intrinsic attribution.

qs.q: The compliance rate in the small-request condition was approximately how many times that in the large-request-only condition?
o: Correct: 46% / 17% is about 2.7.
This is the percentage-point difference (46 - 17), not a ratio.
This is the ratio of the small-request to paid condition (46/24), not to the large-request-only condition.
This is the inverse ratio (17/46).
qs.x: 46% / 17% is about 2.7. Trap: Subtracting percentages when asked for how many times larger.

qs.q: Why is a chi-square test an appropriate analysis for these data?
o: The outcome is a continuous measure that is normally distributed.
Installing a sign is a yes/no outcome, so the data are not continuous.
The same residents were measured repeatedly over time.
Each resident belonged to only one condition, so groups are independent.
The outcome is categorical (sign installed or not), and the test compares frequencies across independent groups.
Correct: Chi-square assesses whether observed counts across categories differ from what would be expected by chance.
The researchers wanted to calculate a correlation between two continuous variables.
The analysis compares group frequencies, not two continuous variables.
qs.x: Chi-square assesses whether observed counts across categories differ from what would be expected by chance. Trap: Defaulting to a t-test or ANOVA without checking whether the outcome is categorical.

qs.q: A different team first asks residents to host a large billboard, which is almost always refused, and then asks for the yard sign. This approach would most directly rely on:
o: self-perception of consistent commitment to the cause.
This explains foot-in-the-door because it relies on an agreed first action.
the central route of persuasion through strong arguments.
The technique alters social pressure rather than argument quality.
the norm of reciprocity, because the second request appears to be a concession.
Correct: The door-in-the-face technique works because a person who sees a concession feels pressure to reciprocate.
operant extinction of the refusal behavior.
No reinforcement schedule is involved.
qs.x: The door-in-the-face technique works because a person who sees a concession feels pressure to reciprocate. Trap: Applying the same explanation (consistency) to both techniques, rather than concession and reciprocity here.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Compliance with the sign request

passages.title: FL04 · Psych/Soc · Passage 7
text: A school-based study examined whether giving students graded mastery experiences changes math self-efficacy. A total of 160 seventh-graders were randomly assigned to an intervention group (n = 80) or a control group (n = 80). Intervention students completed a 6-month program of problems that began at a manageable level and increased in difficulty only after success. Controls attended regular class. At baseline, 3 months, and 6 months, students rated their confidence in solving specific types of math problems on a scale from 1 (not at all confident) to 7 (completely confident). A standardized math test was given at baseline and at 6 months. Self-efficacy over time is shown in Figure 1. Mean math test scores (out of 100) were 62 at baseline and 74 at 6 months for the intervention group, and 61 at baseline and 65 at 6 months for the control group. Across all students, the change in self-efficacy from baseline to 6 months correlated with the change in test score at r = 0.52. The investigators discussed that self-efficacy differs from global self-esteem.

qs.q: The intervention's design of graded successes is most directly based on which source of self-efficacy proposed by Bandura?
o: Vicarious experience
This arises from watching similar others succeed, which was not part of the program.
Mastery experiences
Correct: Repeated personal success at a task is the strongest source of efficacy beliefs.
Verbal persuasion
This involves encouragement from others, not completed successes.
Physiological and emotional states
This refers to interpreting arousal and mood, which was not manipulated.
qs.x: Repeated personal success at a task is the strongest source of efficacy beliefs. Trap: Choosing a source that sounds supportive rather than the one defined by one's own successes.

qs.q: What was the difference between the groups in mean improvement in math test score from baseline to 6 months?
o: 12 points
This is the intervention group's improvement alone.
8 points
Correct: Intervention improved 74 - 62 = 12 and control 65 - 61 = 4, and 12 - 4 = 8.
9 points
This is the difference in final scores (74 - 65), which ignores baseline differences.
4 points
This is the control group's improvement alone.
qs.x: Intervention improved 74 - 62 = 12 and control 65 - 61 = 4, and 12 - 4 = 8. Trap: Comparing final scores instead of comparing change from each group's own baseline.

qs.q: Approximately what proportion of the variance in math score change is shared with self-efficacy change?
o: This is the correlation coefficient itself, not r squared.
This is a decimal-shift error.
This is the variance not shared (1 - 0.27).
Correct: The coefficient of determination is r squared, 0.52 x 0.52 = 0.27.
qs.x: The coefficient of determination is r squared, 0.52 x 0.52 = 0.27. Trap: Reading r as the proportion of variance explained.

qs.q: Which statement best distinguishes self-efficacy from self-esteem?
o: Self-efficacy is the discrepancy between the actual self and the ideal self, whereas self-esteem is the actual self-concept.
This is a description of self-discrepancy, not efficacy.
Self-efficacy is determined at birth, whereas self-esteem is learned.
Efficacy beliefs are learned and changed, as shown in this study.
Self-efficacy refers to how others evaluate a person, whereas self-esteem is private.
Both are self-evaluations; the distinction is in scope, not audience.
Self-efficacy is a belief about one's ability to succeed at specific tasks, whereas self-esteem is a global evaluation of one's own worth.
Correct: Efficacy is task-specific and tied to capability, while esteem is a broad affective appraisal of the self.
qs.x: Efficacy is task-specific and tied to capability, while esteem is a broad affective appraisal of the self. Trap: Treating the two as synonyms for confidence rather than task-specific versus global.

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean math self-efficacy

passages.title: FL04 · Psych/Soc · Passage 8
text: Researchers examined how outcomes affect explanations of behavior. In a laboratory study, 120 students took a bogus 'social perceptiveness' test and were randomly told they had either succeeded or failed, regardless of their actual answers. Actors (n = 60) received feedback on their own test, 30 told of success and 30 of failure. Observers (n = 60) watched an actor of the same sex receive the feedback and were told only the actor's result, again 30 in each outcome condition. All participants then rated, on 1 to 7 scales, how much the result was due to internal causes (the actor's ability and effort) and how much to external causes (luck and test difficulty). Higher numbers indicate stronger agreement. Mean ratings are shown in Table 1. The investigators measured self-esteem before the study and found no differences between conditions. They suggested that the actors' pattern helps to protect or enhance self-esteem, while observers tend to under-weight situational factors when explaining another person's outcome.

qs.q: The actors' ratings are an example of which attributional bias?
o: Self-serving bias
Correct: Actors credited success to internal causes and blamed failure on external ones, protecting self-esteem.
Just-world hypothesis
This is the belief that people get what they deserve, which would involve judging others' outcomes.
Confirmation bias
This is a preference for evidence that matches expectations, not a pattern of causal attributions.
Halo effect
This is a general positive impression generalizing to other traits.
qs.x: Actors credited success to internal causes and blamed failure on external ones, protecting self-esteem. Trap: Choosing a bias that matches the word 'self' or 'bias' without matching the direction of attributions.

qs.q: Which interpretation of the observers' ratings is most consistent with the table?
o: Observers favored internal over external explanations of the actor's outcome, whether the actor succeeded or failed.
Correct: Internal ratings exceeded external ratings in both observer conditions (4.9 vs 4.0 and 4.8 vs 4.2), a pattern consistent with the fundamental attribution error.
Observers favored external explanations whenever the actor failed.
In the observer-failure row, internal (4.8) exceeded external (4.2).
Observers' ratings were identical for success and failure.
The ratings were close but not identical, and the claim about the pattern is about direction rather than equality.
Observers attributed outcomes mainly to luck.
Luck is an external cause, and external ratings were below internal ones.
qs.x: Internal ratings exceeded external ratings in both observer conditions (4.9 vs 4.0 and 4.8 vs 4.2), a pattern consistent with the fundamental attribution error. Trap: Reading the actor rows when asked about observers, since the actors show the opposite pattern.

qs.q: Why were participants told they had succeeded or failed regardless of their actual answers?
o: So that every participant would think they were performing well.
Half of the actors were told they failed.
So that observers would have the same abilities as actors.
Observers were not tested and abilities were not the point.
So that the outcome would be independent of real ability, isolating the effect of the outcome itself on attributions.
Correct: Random feedback removes real performance differences as a confound, so differences in attribution can be tied to the outcome.
To avoid the need for a control condition.
Random assignment to success or failure serves as the comparison, and it does not replace controls.
qs.x: Random feedback removes real performance differences as a confound, so differences in attribution can be tied to the outcome. Trap: Assuming real feedback would be more valid, when it would confound ability with outcome.

qs.q: In the failure conditions, by how much did actors' mean internal rating fall below observers' mean internal rating?
o: This is the difference in external ratings (5.4 - 3.1), mixing rows and columns.
This is the difference in actor and observer external ratings for failure (5.4 - 4.8).
Correct: Observer failure internal (4.8) minus actor failure internal (3.1) equals 1.7, reflecting the actor-observer difference.
This is the actors' internal difference between success and failure (5.8 - 3.1).
qs.x: Observer failure internal (4.8) minus actor failure internal (3.1) equals 1.7, reflecting the actor-observer difference. Trap: Subtracting values from the wrong rows or columns in a two-factor table.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Mean attribution ratings (1-7)

passages.title: FL04 · Psych/Soc · Passage 9
text: In a longitudinal study, researchers observed 120 mothers at home when their infants were 3 and 6 months old and rated each mother's sensitivity (prompt, accurate responses to the infant's signals) as high (n = 60) or low (n = 60). At 12 months each infant took part in the Strange Situation, a laboratory procedure with brief separations from and reunions with the caregiver in an unfamiliar room. Observers classified each infant as secure, insecure-avoidant, insecure-resistant, or disorganized; classifications are shown in Table 1. Observers also rated infant distress (0 = none, 7 = extreme) at baseline, during the first separation, and at the first reunion. Mean ratings for the three organized patterns are shown in Figure 1. The raters of infant behavior were unaware of the maternal sensitivity ratings. All families were recruited from one large metropolitan area in a single region and were closely similar in income and in maternal education.

qs.q: Across all 120 infants, what percentage were classified as secure?
o: This is the number of secure infants (60) written as a percentage.
This is the proportion secure in the high-sensitivity group alone (42 / 60).
This is the proportion secure in the low-sensitivity group alone (18 / 60).
Correct: Secure infants = 42 + 18 = 60, and 60 / 120 = 50%.
qs.x: Secure infants = 42 + 18 = 60, and 60 / 120 = 50%. Trap: Using the percentage from one subgroup, or the raw count, instead of pooling both groups and dividing by the total.

qs.q: Which series in Figure 1 represents the pattern in which the infant seeks contact at reunion but is not comforted and remains distressed?
o: Secure, because the infant is upset at separation and returns to the caregiver for comfort.
Secure infants calm at reunion (4.0 to 1.5), showing that contact comforts them.
Avoidant, because the infant shows little distress and turns away from the caregiver on reunion.
Avoidant infants show little distress at any point and do not seek contact.
Resistant, because the infant is highly distressed at separation and remains so at reunion.
Correct: The resistant (ambivalent) pattern shows distress that rises at separation and stays high at reunion (4.5 to 4.8).
None of the series, because that pattern is defined only for disorganized infants.
Disorganized infants show contradictory or confused behavior and were not plotted in Figure 1, so the claim is false and the pattern still appears.
qs.x: The resistant (ambivalent) pattern shows distress that rises at separation and stays high at reunion (4.5 to 4.8). Trap: Matching on distress at separation alone and ignoring what happens at reunion, which is what separates the patterns.

qs.q: Compared with the high-sensitivity group, how many times as large was the proportion of infants in the low-sensitivity group who were classified as insecure (any type)?
o: About 1.4
This is 70 / 50, comparing the low group with the overall rate.
About 0.43
This inverts the ratio (30 / 70).
About 40
This is the difference in percentage points (70 - 30) rather than a ratio.
About 2.3
Correct: Insecure in the low group = 18 + 12 + 12 = 42 of 60 (70%). Insecure in the high group = 8 + 4 + 6 = 18 of 60 (30%). 70 / 30 is about 2.3.
qs.x: Insecure in the low group = 18 + 12 + 12 = 42 of 60 (70%). Insecure in the high group = 8 + 4 + 6 = 18 of 60 (30%). 70 / 30 is about 2.3. Trap: Inverting the ratio or reporting a difference in percentage points when the question asks for a ratio.

qs.q: Which alternative explanation could account for the association between maternal sensitivity and infant security even though sensitivity was measured before the Strange Situation?
o: Insecure attachment at 12 months could have caused the lower maternal sensitivity that was measured at 3 and 6 months.
Sensitivity was measured at 3 and 6 months, before the 12-month classification, so a later outcome cannot cause it.
Infant temperament, such as irritability, could both hinder caregiving and increase insecure behavior.
Correct: A third variable, such as an infant trait that affects both caregiving and attachment behavior, is a confound that the observational design does not rule out.
The Strange Situation observers could have been influenced by knowing each mother's earlier sensitivity rating.
The passage states that behavior raters were unaware of the sensitivity ratings.
The measure of distress may not have been reliable, because it used only a 0 to 7 rating scale.
A rating scale of this kind does not make the measure unreliable and would not by itself explain a group association.
qs.x: A third variable, such as an infant trait that affects both caregiving and attachment behavior, is a confound that the observational design does not rule out. Trap: Proposing reverse causation or rater bias without checking the timeline and the blinding described in the passage.

qs.q: A secure infant explores the room while the caregiver is present but returns to the caregiver when upset. According to attachment theory, this behavior shows that the caregiver serves as
o: a conditioned stimulus that has become associated with feeding through classical conditioning.
Attachment theory emphasizes responsiveness and not pairing with feeding as a conditioning process.
a secure base for exploration and a safe haven for comfort.
Correct: Ainsworth described the attachment figure as a secure base for exploration and a safe haven in distress.
a model whose behavior the infant imitates and is later reinforced for imitating.
Imitation and reinforcement belong to social learning theory, not to this description.
a source of contact comfort that matters mainly when the infant is hungry.
Harlow's work showed that contact comfort is valued independent of feeding.
qs.x: Ainsworth described the attachment figure as a secure base for exploration and a safe haven in distress. Trap: Explaining attachment as feeding or conditioning rather than as responsive caregiving that supports exploration.

passages.title: FL04 · Psych/Soc · Passage 10
text: Demographers reviewed national statistics for one country across four years, shown in Table 1. Crude birth rate (CBR) and crude death rate (CDR) are births and deaths per 1,000 people per year. The net migration rate (NMR) is immigrants minus emigrants per 1,000 people per year. The total growth rate per 1,000 equals CBR - CDR + NMR. During this period, the country built clean water systems and vaccination programs, and many young adults left rural villages to work abroad before return migration began in the 2010s. Figure 1 plots CBR and CDR. The researchers noted that the later fall in CBR coincided with the shift in NMR from negative to positive, but cautioned that the data came from only four time points for a single country. Return migrants were counted as immigrants, and all rates came from official national registries that used the same standard definitions in each year.

qs.q: What was the country's total annual growth rate in 2000, as a percentage?
o: This leaves the rate per 1,000 as if it were a percentage.
This is the rate of natural increase (17 per 1,000) with migration ignored.
This adds the emigration term (24 - 7 + 3 = 20 per 1,000) when it should be subtracted.
Correct: Total growth = 24 - 7 + (-3) = 14 per 1,000, which is 1.4%.
qs.x: Total growth = 24 - 7 + (-3) = 14 per 1,000, which is 1.4%. Trap: Forgetting that rates per 1,000 must be divided by 10 to give a percentage, or mishandling the sign of net migration.

qs.q: Which stage of the demographic transition and which process best explain the large gap between CBR and CDR in 1985?
o: Stage 1, because both birth and death rates were still high and the population was roughly stable.
In stage 1 both rates are high and nearly equal, but here they differ by 26 per 1,000.
Stage 2, because mortality fell with sanitation and medicine while fertility stayed high.
Correct: In 1985 the CDR (10) had fallen well below the CBR (36), which is characteristic of the early expanding stage where public health measures cut death rates first.
Stage 3, because declining fertility had already brought the birth rate close to the death rate.
In stage 3 fertility has declined substantially, whereas the CBR here is still 36.
Stage 4, because both rates were low and population growth had nearly stopped completely.
In stage 4 both rates are low and similar, which does not match a CBR of 36.
qs.x: In 1985 the CDR (10) had fallen well below the CBR (36), which is characteristic of the early expanding stage where public health measures cut death rates first. Trap: Choosing a stage from the size of one rate rather than from the relationship between the birth and death rates.

qs.q: Approximately how many people did the country gain or lose through net migration in 2000?
o: A net gain of about 156,000 people
This has the right size but the wrong sign, as emigrants outnumbered immigrants.
A net loss of about 1,560,000 people
This is off by a factor of 10.
A net loss of about 156,000 people
Correct: NMR = -3 per 1,000 and the population was 52 million (52,000 thousand), so net migration = -3 x 52,000 = -156,000.
A net loss of about 3,000 people
This is the rate itself (3 per 1,000) and has not been multiplied by the population.
qs.x: NMR = -3 per 1,000 and the population was 52 million (52,000 thousand), so net migration = -3 x 52,000 = -156,000. Trap: Using the rate per 1,000 as if it were a number of people, or losing track of the sign and the factor of 1,000.

qs.q: The researchers noted that CBR fell while NMR shifted from negative to positive. Why does this not show that immigration lowered the birth rate?
o: Both trends could reflect broader development, such as urbanization, so causation is unsupported.
Correct: Two variables that change over time together can both be driven by a third process, and correlation from four points in one country cannot establish causation.
Net migration rates cannot be meaningfully compared with birth rates because they are measured in different units.
Both are rates per 1,000 people, so the units do not prevent comparison.
The birth rate had already reached its lowest possible value before the direction of migration changed.
The CBR continued to fall from 24 to 12 after 2000, when NMR was still negative.
Four years of data are enough to prove an association but not enough to calculate any rate.
The rates are given for each year, and the limitation concerns inferring causation rather than computing rates.
qs.x: Two variables that change over time together can both be driven by a third process, and correlation from four points in one country cannot establish causation. Trap: Treating a temporal association between two trends as proof that one caused the other.

passages.title: FL05 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 1
text: Molecular chaperones prevent aggregation of unfolded proteins and assist folding. A researcher tested the Hsp70 system using firefly luciferase, which is enzymatically active only when natively folded. Luciferase (100 nM) was denatured by heating at 42 degrees C for 10 minutes and then diluted into refolding buffer at 25 degrees C. The buffer contained the components listed in Table 1, with Hsp70 (1 uM), the co-chaperone Hsp40 (0.5 uM), and either ATP or the nonhydrolyzable analog ATP-gamma-S (2 mM each) as indicated. Luciferase activity was measured over time and expressed as a percentage of the activity of an equal amount of never-denatured enzyme. Figure 1 shows recovery over 60 minutes for three of the conditions. In all tubes, a fraction of the denatured luciferase formed visible aggregates; the aggregate fraction was lowest in the tubes containing Hsp70 and ATP. Reactions were run in triplicate and the values shown are means; the standard deviation of each mean was below 4 percentage points. Luciferase activity was measured by adding luciferin and ATP immediately before reading luminescence.

qs.q: By how much did adding Hsp40 to the Hsp70 plus ATP system increase the luciferase activity recovered at 60 minutes?
o: 70 percentage points, the difference between condition 4 and the no-chaperone control
this is the total effect of the full system over no chaperone (78 - 8), not the added effect of Hsp40.
17 percentage points, the average gain per 15 minutes shown in Figure 1
this is not a quantity tied to the comparison; the gain from Hsp40 is the difference in 60-minute recoveries.
45 percentage points, the activity recovered by Hsp70 plus ATP alone in condition 3
this is the recovery without Hsp40, not the increment gained by adding it.
33 percentage points, the difference between 78% (condition 4) and 45% (condition 3)
Correct: 78 - 45 = 33 percentage points.
qs.x: 78 - 45 = 33 percentage points. Trap: Subtracting the wrong pair of conditions (such as condition 4 minus condition 1) and reporting the total effect of the whole system as the effect of Hsp40.

qs.q: The very low recovery in condition 5 compared with condition 4 is best explained by which conclusion?
o: Hsp40 is inactivated by nonhydrolyzable nucleotides, so Hsp70 can no longer bind exposed hydrophobic segments
Hsp40 delivers substrate and stimulates Hsp70 ATPase activity; the data do not show it is inactivated, and Hsp70 binding is not the problem.
Hsp70 acts as a kinase that covalently phosphorylates luciferase using the terminal phosphate of ATP
Hsp70 is not a kinase here; ATP hydrolysis powers conformational cycling of the chaperone itself.
ATP-gamma-S binds Hsp70 more tightly than ATP and therefore speeds substrate release from the chaperone
tight binding of a nonhydrolyzable analog locks the closed, substrate-holding state; it does not speed release.
ATP hydrolysis, not ATP binding alone, is needed for Hsp70 to release substrate
Correct: ATP-gamma-S binds but is not hydrolyzed, so Hsp70 stays locked on the substrate and recovery stays near baseline.
qs.x: ATP-gamma-S binds but is not hydrolyzed, so Hsp70 stays locked on the substrate and recovery stays near baseline. Trap: Assuming that binding of ATP is enough to drive the chaperone cycle, overlooking that the analog binds but cannot be hydrolyzed.

qs.q: Which feature of an unfolded luciferase molecule is most directly recognized by Hsp70?
o: Branched oligosaccharides attached to asparagine residues in the unfolded chain
N-linked glycans are added in the ER lumen and are not present on cytosolic luciferase.
Exposed hydrophobic side chains that are normally buried in the native core
Correct: Hsp70 binds short hydrophobic stretches exposed on non-native proteins, shielding them from aggregation.
Disulfide bonds formed between cysteine side chains on the protein surface
disulfide bonds are not what Hsp70 recognizes, and luciferase folding in this buffer does not depend on them.
An N-terminal signal sequence directing the protein toward the endoplasmic reticulum
signal sequences direct targeting to the ER and are not the general chaperone recognition feature.
qs.x: Hsp70 binds short hydrophobic stretches exposed on non-native proteins, shielding them from aggregation. Trap: Selecting a targeting or modification feature because it is a memorable protein signal, rather than the exposed hydrophobic patches that define a non-native protein.

qs.q: Which additional control would best test whether the benefit of Hsp70 is due to its chaperone activity rather than to nonspecific protein crowding?
o: Measure luciferase aggregation by light scattering in the no-chaperone condition only
this characterizes aggregation in one tube and offers no matched comparison for crowding.
Add bovine serum albumin at the same mass concentration as Hsp70, together with ATP
Correct: A non-chaperone protein at equal mass with ATP controls for crowding or nonspecific stabilization.
Add Hsp70 at ten times the concentration without ATP and measure recovery at 60 minutes
this varies chaperone dose without a nonchaperone protein, so crowding is still not distinguished.
Repeat condition 3 with luciferase that was never heated before dilution into the buffer
this tests native enzyme stability, not whether the benefit depends on the chaperone.
qs.x: A non-chaperone protein at equal mass with ATP controls for crowding or nonspecific stabilization. Trap: Choosing a control that varies the chaperone itself instead of one that replaces the chaperone with an irrelevant protein.

qs.q: Compared with the Hsp70 system, the bacterial chaperonin GroEL/GroES promotes folding primarily by which mechanism?
o: Specifying the native conformation by supplying information absent from the amino acid sequence
the native fold is encoded by the sequence; chaperones only prevent off-pathway aggregation.
Enclosing one unfolded polypeptide in an ATP-gated cavity so it can fold in isolation
Correct: GroEL/GroES forms a barrel-like chamber that isolates one substrate protein while it folds.
Inserting new disulfide bonds into the substrate through reversible thiol-disulfide exchange
disulfide formation is catalyzed by protein disulfide isomerase, a different folding enzyme.
Cleaving the polypeptide at proline residues to remove misfolded segments
chaperonins do not cleave substrates; proteolytic trimming is not part of folding assistance.
qs.x: GroEL/GroES forms a barrel-like chamber that isolates one substrate protein while it folds. Trap: Believing chaperones carry structural information for the fold, contrary to the principle that the amino acid sequence determines the native structure.

passages.title: FL05 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 2
text: A transcription factor (TF) is hypothesized to activate a gene by binding a response element in the promoter. To test this, researchers cloned the promoter upstream of a firefly luciferase gene and transfected the construct into cells that express little endogenous TF. A second plasmid with Renilla luciferase under a constitutive promoter was co-transfected in every dish. After 24 hours, firefly luminescence was divided by Renilla luminescence to give relative luciferase units (RLU), and values were normalized so that the wild-type promoter without added TF equals 1.0. Constructs included the wild-type promoter, a promoter with point mutations in the response element, and TF variants lacking either the DNA-binding domain (dDBD) or the activation domain (dAD). Table 1 shows results with 100 ng of TF plasmid. Figure 1 shows RLU for the wild-type promoter as the amount of TF plasmid was varied. Each condition was performed in triplicate wells, and values shown are means. Cell viability was above 90 percent in all conditions, and expression of each TF variant was confirmed by immunoblot to be comparable to that of the full-length protein.

qs.q: The fold activation caused by full-length TF on the wild-type promoter is about how many times greater than the fold activation on the mutant promoter?
o: 9 times, because 12.4 divided by about 1.4 is approximately 9
Correct: Mutant fold activation is 1.3/0.9, about 1.4; 12.4/1.4 is about 9.
1.4 times, because the mutant and wild-type promoters give similar absolute RLU with TF
the RLU with TF differ by roughly tenfold, so the two promoters are not similar.
14 times, because 12.4 divided by the mutant baseline of 0.9 gives about 14
this divides by the baseline of the mutant without TF rather than by the mutant's own fold activation.
12 times, because the wild-type fold activation is 12.4 and the mutant shows no activation
the mutant is not zero; it shows a modest 1.4-fold change, and the question asks for a ratio of fold changes.
qs.x: Mutant fold activation is 1.3/0.9, about 1.4; 12.4/1.4 is about 9. Trap: Using raw RLU or the wrong baseline instead of calculating fold activation for each promoter before comparing them.

qs.q: The finding that the dAD TF reduced RLU to 0.4, below the value of the promoter without added TF, is best explained by which of the following?
o: The dAD protein binds the Renilla promoter and lowers the normalization signal in every dish
a drop in Renilla would raise, not lower, the firefly/Renilla ratio; the effect is specific to the response element.
dAD occupies the response element but cannot recruit machinery, blocking endogenous TF
Correct: a DNA-binding but activation-defective TF can act as a dominant negative at its binding site.
The dAD protein cannot enter the nucleus, so it degrades firefly luciferase mRNA in the cytoplasm
dAD lacks only the activation domain; nothing suggests it is excluded from the nucleus or targets mRNA.
The dAD protein increases initiation by acting as a general transcription factor at all promoters
loss of the activation domain would remove, not add, stimulation of transcription.
qs.x: a DNA-binding but activation-defective TF can act as a dominant negative at its binding site. Trap: Treating a value below baseline as noise or as a loss of function only, rather than recognizing competition with endogenous activator at the binding site.

qs.q: In Figure 1, RLU rises only slightly when TF plasmid is increased from 100 ng to 200 ng. Which explanation is most reasonable?
o: Renilla luminescence doubles between these points, exactly offsetting the added firefly activity
Renilla is a constitutive control and there is no evidence it doubles with TF dose.
The response element is deleted when TF concentration exceeds about 100 ng of plasmid per dish
TF binding does not delete DNA elements; plateau does not imply loss of the site.
Another component, such as coactivators or promoter template, becomes limiting
Correct: a plateau indicates that some other factor or the available promoter sites limit expression.
The additional TF protein is degraded because it can no longer bind DNA at the mutant element
the mutant element is not present in this wild-type series, and degradation is not indicated by the data.
qs.x: a plateau indicates that some other factor or the available promoter sites limit expression. Trap: Assuming that more activator must always give more output and attributing a plateau to a technical artifact.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of co-transfecting the Renilla luciferase plasmid in every dish?
o: To confirm that the TF binds the response element directly rather than through other proteins
a second luciferase does not report DNA binding; that requires assays such as gel shift or ChIP.
To correct firefly luminescence for differences in transfection efficiency and cell number between dishes
Correct: the constitutive control normalizes variation unrelated to the response element.
To prevent the firefly luciferase reaction from consuming ATP needed by the transfected cells
the control does not protect ATP supplies; it serves as a normalizing reference.
To provide a second promoter whose activity should rise in proportion to the amount of TF
a constitutive control is expected to stay constant, not respond to the TF.
qs.x: the constitutive control normalizes variation unrelated to the response element. Trap: Thinking the second reporter measures a second regulated target rather than serving as a constitutive loading and transfection control.

qs.q: Most DNA-binding domains of transcription factors recognize a specific sequence primarily through which interaction?
o: Covalent bonds between lysine side chains and the deoxyribose hydroxyl groups of the DNA backbone
transcription factors bind noncovalently, and backbone contacts do not provide sequence specificity.
Base stacking between aromatic residues and the bases after the helix is melted in the promoter
binding to a response element does not require melting the double helix.
Ionic attraction between positively charged side chains and the negatively charged phosphates alone
phosphate contacts add affinity but are the same for every sequence, so they cannot supply specificity.
Hydrogen bonds and van der Waals contacts between side chains and base edges in the major groove
Correct: the major groove exposes distinctive patterns of base functional groups to protein side chains.
qs.x: the major groove exposes distinctive patterns of base functional groups to protein side chains. Trap: Choosing electrostatic phosphate contacts because DNA is highly charged, forgetting that sequence specificity comes from base contacts.

passages.title: FL05 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 3
text: In Drosophila, body color (gray, b+, dominant; black, b) and wing shape (normal, vg+, dominant; vestigial, vg) are encoded by genes on chromosome 2. A researcher crossed true-breeding gray, normal-winged flies with true-breeding black, vestigial-winged flies and obtained F1 offspring that were all gray with normal wings. In cross 1, F1 females were mated with black, vestigial males, and 1000 progeny were scored. In cross 2, F1 males were mated with black, vestigial females, and 1000 progeny were scored. Results are shown in Table 1. Recombination frequency between two genes is the number of recombinant progeny divided by total progeny, and 1% recombination corresponds to 1 map unit. The researcher also noted that, for genes on separate chromosomes, a test cross of a dihybrid would give four phenotypic classes in equal numbers. Flies were reared on standard medium at 25 degrees C, and progeny were scored by an observer who did not know which parent carried which allele. Only flies that eclosed within 14 days were counted, and males and females of each phenotype were pooled.

qs.q: What is the distance between the body color and wing shape genes, based on cross 1?
o: 50 map units, since the genes assort independently in the F1 female
independent assortment would give 50% recombinants, but only 17% were observed.
83 map units, since 830 of 1000 progeny show the parental combinations
parental progeny are not used for distance; recombinants are counted.
8.5 map units, since only 85 progeny of each recombinant class are counted
each recombinant class contributes, so both classes must be added before dividing.
17 map units, since 170 of 1000 progeny are recombinant
Correct: (85 + 85)/1000 = 0.17, or 17 map units.
qs.x: (85 + 85)/1000 = 0.17, or 17 map units. Trap: Counting only one recombinant class, or using the parental fraction to compute map distance.

qs.q: If the two genes had been located on different chromosomes, how many gray, vestigial progeny would be expected from 1000 progeny in cross 1?
o: 170, because recombinants would make up 17% of the progeny regardless of linkage
17% is the observed recombination with linkage; unlinked genes give 50% recombinants split across two classes.
85, because the number of recombinants is fixed by the F1 parent
85 is the observed number with linkage; independent assortment predicts a different count.
250, because the four phenotypic classes would appear in equal numbers
Correct: independent assortment of a dihybrid test cross gives a 1:1:1:1 ratio.
500, because half of the progeny would carry the dominant wing allele and half the gray allele
gray, vestigial is one specific class, a quarter of progeny, not half.
qs.x: independent assortment of a dihybrid test cross gives a 1:1:1:1 ratio. Trap: Applying the observed recombination frequency to the unlinked expectation instead of the 1:1:1:1 ratio.

qs.q: The absence of recombinant progeny in cross 2 is most consistent with which explanation?
o: Crossing over does not occur in male Drosophila, so only parental chromosomes are transmitted
Correct: male Drosophila lack meiotic recombination, so the linked alleles are inherited together.
Gray, vestigial and black, normal males die before the progeny are scored
there is no evidence of lethality; total progeny are 1000 in each cross.
The genes are much closer together in males than in females, so recombination is below 1 percent
map distance is a property of the chromosomal region and does not differ by sex in this manner.
The F1 male is homozygous at both loci, so recombinant gametes cannot be distinguished
the F1 male is a heterozygote because its parents were both homozygous for different alleles.
qs.x: male Drosophila lack meiotic recombination, so the linked alleles are inherited together. Trap: Assuming a different gene distance in males instead of recognizing a sex-specific absence of crossing over.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes the arrangement of alleles on the chromosomes of the F1 female in cross 1?
o: One homolog carries b+ and vg+ and the other carries b and vg (cis arrangement)
Correct: the most frequent progeny classes reflect the parental chromosome arrangement (cis).
The arrangement cannot be deduced because both parental classes occur in equal numbers
equal parental classes are expected; their identity as the majority classes defines the arrangement.
Both b+ and b are on one chromosome and both vg+ and vg on the other chromosome
a chromosome carries only one allele per gene, so both alleles of one gene cannot lie on one chromosome.
One chromosome carries b+ and vg and the other carries b and vg+, because recombinants are least common
if that were the arrangement, gray, vestigial and black, normal progeny would be parental and most common.
qs.x: the most frequent progeny classes reflect the parental chromosome arrangement (cis). Trap: Confusing which classes are parental and which are recombinant, then reversing the cis and trans arrangement.

qs.q: If the F1 female were mated with a black, vestigial male and 600 progeny were scored, about how many gray, vestigial progeny would be expected?
o: 150, because one quarter of the 600 progeny would show this phenotype
one quarter is the unlinked expectation, not the linked result.
51, because 8.5% of 600 are expected in this recombinant class
Correct: recombination is 17%, split evenly between two classes: 8.5% each, or 51 of 600.
102, because 17% of 600 progeny would be gray and vestigial
17% is the total of both recombinant classes, not one class.
85, because the same count of gray, vestigial progeny occurs at any sample size
counts scale with the total number of progeny.
qs.x: recombination is 17%, split evenly between two classes: 8.5% each, or 51 of 600. Trap: Using the whole 17% for one class instead of halving it between the two reciprocal recombinant phenotypes.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Progeny phenotypes

passages.title: FL05 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 4
text: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) catalyzes the committed step of glycolysis, converting fructose 6-phosphate (F6P) to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate. A muscle extract containing PFK-1 was assayed with saturating Mg-ATP as the phosphoryl donor, and velocity was measured at varied F6P. Figure 1 shows velocity (in arbitrary units, with 100 equal to Vmax) for a control containing 1 mM ATP and for a reaction containing 5 mM ATP. Table 1 reports the F6P concentration giving half-maximal velocity (S0.5) in the presence of the effectors indicated, all in 5 mM ATP unless stated. Vmax was unchanged in every condition. The investigator also noted that the liver isoform is activated by fructose 2,6-bisphosphate (F2,6BP), a product of PFK-2, and that cytosolic citrate rises when the citric acid cycle is saturated. Assays were performed at 30 degrees C and pH 7.0 in triplicate, and velocity was calculated from the initial linear rate in a coupled enzyme system. Standard deviations were below 5 percent of each mean, and S0.5 values were obtained by fitting a sigmoidal curve.

qs.q: Which effector in Table 1 most completely overcame the inhibition produced by 5 mM ATP?
o: AMP, which lowered S0.5 to the same value as the 1 mM ATP control
AMP lowered S0.5 to 0.9 mM, still above the 0.5 mM control.
F2,6BP, which lowered S0.5 below the value of the 1 mM ATP control
Correct: S0.5 of 0.3 mM is lower than both 2.4 mM (5 mM ATP) and 0.5 mM (control).
Citrate, which raised S0.5 to a value above that of 5 mM ATP alone
citrate raised S0.5 further to 4.8 mM, deepening the inhibition.
None of the effectors, because Vmax was unchanged in every condition tested
an unchanged Vmax does not preclude relief of inhibition, which is reported by S0.5.
qs.x: S0.5 of 0.3 mM is lower than both 2.4 mM (5 mM ATP) and 0.5 mM (control). Trap: Reading the unchanged Vmax as meaning that effectors have no effect, when allosteric effectors act by shifting S0.5.

qs.q: The effect of 5 mM ATP in Figure 1 is best described as which type of regulation?
o: Competitive inhibition at the active site that lowers Vmax as ATP concentration rises
ATP is also a substrate, but the data show unchanged Vmax and a raised S0.5, with a regulatory site involved.
Feedforward activation by product that increases the rate at low F6P concentration
velocity is lower, not higher, at low F6P with 5 mM ATP.
Allosteric inhibition at a regulatory site that raises S0.5 without changing Vmax
Correct: ATP at high concentration binds a separate regulatory site, lowering affinity for F6P.
Covalent modification by phosphorylation that irreversibly decreases enzyme turnover
a rise in S0.5 with unchanged Vmax in vitro does not indicate covalent modification.
qs.x: ATP at high concentration binds a separate regulatory site, lowering affinity for F6P. Trap: Labeling any decrease in rate as inhibition at the active site, ignoring the unchanged Vmax and the separate regulatory site.

qs.q: In the liver of a fasting person with high glucagon, how would F2,6BP and glycolytic flux most likely change?
o: F2,6BP is unchanged, because F2,6BP regulates only the muscle isoform of PFK-1
F2,6BP is a major regulator of the liver isoform, as the passage states.
F2,6BP rises, so PFK-1 activity increases and glycolytic flux rises
high F2,6BP is a fed-state, insulin-driven signal, the opposite of the fasting condition.
F2,6BP falls, so PFK-1 activity declines and gluconeogenesis is favored
Correct: glucagon, via PKA, shifts PFK-2/FBPase-2 toward degrading F2,6BP, removing activation of PFK-1.
F2,6BP rises, so fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase is activated and glucose is released
F2,6BP inhibits fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase; a rise would suppress, not activate, gluconeogenesis.
qs.x: glucagon, via PKA, shifts PFK-2/FBPase-2 toward degrading F2,6BP, removing activation of PFK-1. Trap: Remembering that F2,6BP activates PFK-1 but forgetting that glucagon lowers its level through PKA-mediated phosphorylation.

qs.q: Which interpretation of the effect of citrate in Table 1 is most consistent with cellular energy metabolism?
o: Citrate is the product of PFK-1, so inhibition is simple product inhibition at the active site
citrate is not a product of the PFK-1 reaction; fructose 1,6-bisphosphate is.
Citrate signals low energy charge, so strong inhibition of PFK-1 prevents ATP synthesis
low energy charge would raise AMP and activate PFK-1, not inhibit it.
Citrate signals insulin action, so inhibition of PFK-1 diverts F6P to the pentose phosphate pathway
citrate is not an insulin signal and its effect on PFK-1 is not designed to divert flux that way.
Citrate signals abundant precursors and acetyl-CoA flux, so slowing glycolysis conserves glucose
Correct: high cytosolic citrate indicates the citric acid cycle is saturated, a feedback signal to reduce glycolysis.
qs.x: high cytosolic citrate indicates the citric acid cycle is saturated, a feedback signal to reduce glycolysis. Trap: Assuming any metabolite that inhibits PFK-1 must signal low energy, instead of recognizing it as a sign of plentiful fuel.

qs.q: The sigmoidal shape of the velocity curves in Figure 1 is most consistent with which property of PFK-1?
o: Irreversible inactivation of the enzyme by substrate at high F6P concentration
substrate inactivation would produce a decline at high F6P, which is not observed.
A single active site obeying Michaelis-Menten kinetics with a hyperbolic velocity curve
Michaelis-Menten kinetics gives a hyperbola, not a sigmoid.
Cooperative substrate binding among subunits of the tetrameric enzyme
Correct: binding of F6P to one subunit increases the affinity of the others, producing a sigmoidal curve.
Competitive binding of ATP and F6P to the same site on a monomeric enzyme
a monomeric enzyme with competition at one site would not show sigmoidal behavior.
qs.x: binding of F6P to one subunit increases the affinity of the others, producing a sigmoidal curve. Trap: Assuming all enzymes give hyperbolic curves and attributing a sigmoid to experimental error.

passages.title: FL05 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 5
text: The Na+/K+ ATPase uses ATP to export three Na+ ions and import two K+ ions per cycle, and cardiac glycosides such as ouabain bind its extracellular face and block it. Cultured epithelial cells that express an Na+-dependent glucose transporter (SGLT) were incubated under four conditions. Intracellular Na+ and K+ were measured by atomic absorption, membrane potential by patch-clamp recording, and Na+-dependent glucose uptake by a radiolabeled glucose analog. Control cells had normal ion gradients. Ouabain (100 uM) was applied for 1 hour or 6 hours. In a fourth group, ATP synthesis was blocked for 1 hour with oligomycin and 2-deoxyglucose. Extracellular Na+ was 145 mM and extracellular K+ was 5 mM throughout. Table 1 gives the measurements and Figure 1 shows intracellular Na+ over time in control cells and in ouabain-treated cells. Each measurement was repeated on three separate cultures, and values are means. Cell viability, assessed by dye exclusion, exceeded 95 percent in every condition, and glucose uptake was measured over a 5 minute window at the end of each incubation.

qs.q: By what factor did intracellular Na+ increase after 6 hours of ouabain treatment relative to control cells?
o: About 3.3-fold, since 40 mM was gained and 12 mM was the starting concentration
40/12 is 3.3 and gives the increment relative to baseline, while the fold change is final divided by initial.
About 4.3-fold, since 52 mM divided by 12 mM is approximately 4.3
About 2.3-fold, since the cell lost 70 mM K+ and gained a comparable amount of Na+
K+ loss is not used to compute Na+ fold change, which is the ratio of 52 to 12.
About 5.2-fold, since the final concentration of 52 mM is compared with 10 mM
the control concentration is 12 mM, not 10 mM.
qs.x: 52/12 = 4.33. Trap: Computing the change (40 mM) over baseline instead of the final value divided by baseline when a fold increase is requested.

qs.q: The depolarization of the ouabain-treated cells from -70 mV to -28 mV is best explained by which mechanism?
o: Increased extracellular K+ because the cells release K+ faster than the medium can buffer it
extracellular K+ was held at 5 mM throughout the experiment.
Opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels because intracellular Na+ is higher than extracellular Na+
intracellular Na+ (52 mM) is still far below extracellular Na+ (145 mM).
Direct electrogenic pumping that adds negative charge, which is lost when the pump is blocked
the pump's electrogenic contribution is small; the main effect of blocking it is dissipation of the gradients.
Loss of the K+ gradient as intracellular K+ falls, since resting potential is set mainly by K+ leak channels
Correct: less K+ inside shifts the K+ equilibrium potential toward zero and the membrane depolarizes.
qs.x: less K+ inside shifts the K+ equilibrium potential toward zero and the membrane depolarizes. Trap: Attributing the resting potential mainly to the pump's electrogenic effect rather than to the K+ gradient and leak channels.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for the fall in Na+-dependent glucose uptake in ouabain-treated cells?
o: The inward Na+ gradient that powers the SGLT symporter is dissipated as intracellular Na+ rises
Correct: SGLT is secondary active transport that depends on the Na+ gradient set by the pump.
Ouabain binds the SGLT transporter and directly blocks the glucose binding site
ouabain is specific to the Na+/K+ ATPase and does not bind SGLT.
Hyperpolarization of the membrane reduces the driving force for glucose entry via SGLT
the cells depolarize rather than hyperpolarize in the ouabain groups.
Intracellular K+ falls, which blocks the entry of glucose through facilitated diffusion carriers
K+ is not a cosubstrate for SGLT, and the uptake measured is the Na+-dependent component.
qs.x: SGLT is secondary active transport that depends on the Na+ gradient set by the pump. Trap: Assuming ouabain acts on every transporter directly instead of inferring the indirect loss of the Na+ gradient.

qs.q: Cardiac glycosides increase the force of cardiac muscle contraction. Which mechanism best explains this effect using the data above?
o: Reduced intracellular Na+ increases Ca2+ extrusion by the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger and shortens relaxation
ouabain raises, not lowers, intracellular Na+ according to Table 1.
Elevated intracellular K+ depolarizes the membrane and triggers sustained opening of ryanodine receptors
intracellular K+ falls with ouabain, as the table shows.
Raised intracellular Na+ reduces Na+/Ca2+ exchange, so cytosolic Ca2+ rises and enhances contraction
Correct: less Na+ gradient reduces Ca2+ extrusion, so more Ca2+ is available for contraction.
Higher ATP levels in the cell increase cross-bridge cycling because the pump no longer uses ATP
ATP is not the limiting factor in this effect, and pump inhibition does not make ATP the explanation for greater contractility.
qs.x: less Na+ gradient reduces Ca2+ extrusion, so more Ca2+ is available for contraction. Trap: Reading the rise in intracellular Na+ as a direct activator of contraction instead of connecting it to reduced Ca2+ extrusion.

passages.title: FL05 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 6
text: Bacteria in batch culture pass through lag, exponential, stationary, and death phases. An investigator inoculated a nutrient broth with Escherichia coli, incubated it at 37 degrees C with shaking, and measured viable counts (colony-forming units, CFU, per mL) at the times in Table 1. Three flasks were prepared. The control flask received no drug. In the second flask, ampicillin, an inhibitor of peptidoglycan cross-linking, was added at 2 hours. In the third flask, chloramphenicol, an inhibitor of the bacterial ribosome, was added at 2 hours. Viable counts are expressed as log10 CFU per mL. Figure 1 plots the same data. Colonies recovered at 10 hours from the ampicillin flask were picked, regrown, and exposed again to ampicillin, and the new culture was killed with the same kinetics as the original strain. Cultures were started from a single colony grown overnight and diluted to the same starting density. Samples were serially diluted in saline and plated on drug-free agar, and colonies were counted after 24 hours. Each point is the mean of three replicate flasks.

qs.q: What is the approximate doubling time of the untreated culture during exponential growth?
o: 30 minutes, since log10 CFU rises by 0.6 per hour, equal to two doublings per hour
Correct: 0.6/0.301 = 2 doublings per hour.
60 minutes, since the count rises by 0.6 log units, which equals one doubling per hour
one doubling is 0.301 log units; 0.6 log units is two doublings.
15 minutes, since the count rises by 0.6 log units per hour, equal to four doublings per hour
this would require a 1.2 log increase per hour.
120 minutes, since the count rises by 0.6 log units over the 2 hours of the log phase
the 0.6 log increase occurs per hour, not over two hours.
qs.x: 0.6/0.301 = 2 doublings per hour. Trap: Treating a 1 log10 or 0.6 log10 change as one doubling instead of converting with log10 of 2 (0.301).

qs.q: Between 2 and 4 hours, approximately what percentage of viable cells in the ampicillin flask were killed?
o: 50%, since the counts fell from 5.6 to 3.6 and 3.6 is about half of 5.6
log values cannot be compared as simple fractions; each unit is a tenfold change.
90%, since a 1 log decrease means that 1 cell in 10 survives
the decrease from 5.6 to 3.6 is 2 log units, not 1.
99%, since a 2.0 log decrease means that 1 cell in 100 survives
Correct: 5.6 to 3.6 is a 2-log fall, a 100-fold decrease.
99.9%, since a 3 log decrease means that 1 cell in 1000 survives
the fall is 2 log units, not 3.
qs.x: 5.6 to 3.6 is a 2-log fall, a 100-fold decrease. Trap: Reading the log scale as linear and comparing 3.6 with 5.6 directly as a percentage.

qs.q: The plateau at about 2.2 log10 CFU/mL in the ampicillin flask, together with the final regrowth experiment, is best explained by which of the following?
o: A small subpopulation of dormant persister cells that survive without heritable resistance
Correct: the survivors give a susceptible culture on regrowth, the signature of phenotypic tolerance.
A subpopulation carrying heritable beta-lactamase genes that grows normally in the drug
the regrown cells were killed with the original kinetics, arguing against heritable resistance.
Complete degradation of ampicillin by 6 hours, allowing the surviving cells to grow again
counts stay flat rather than rising, and the drug effect persists.
Conversion of the survivors into spores that resist the antibiotic through a thick coat
E. Coli does not form endospores.
qs.x: the survivors give a susceptible culture on regrowth, the signature of phenotypic tolerance. Trap: Equating any survivors of an antibiotic with genetic resistance, ignoring that the regrown cells were susceptible.

qs.q: Compared with a culture treated at 2 hours, an identical culture treated with ampicillin at 10 hours would most likely show which result?
o: Bacteriostatic behavior with flat counts, because ampicillin inhibits DNA gyrase in nongrowing cells
DNA gyrase is the target of quinolones, not ampicillin.
Faster killing, because stationary cells have a thinner outer membrane that admits more drug
there is no basis for a thinner membrane in stationary cells, and growth state is the key factor.
Much less killing, because cells in stationary phase are not actively synthesizing new peptidoglycan
Correct: beta-lactams kill by corrupting cell wall synthesis in growing cells, so stationary cells are relatively tolerant.
The same killing rate, because ampicillin acts on the ribosome irrespective of growth rate
ampicillin targets cell wall cross-linking, not the ribosome.
qs.x: beta-lactams kill by corrupting cell wall synthesis in growing cells, so stationary cells are relatively tolerant. Trap: Assuming that bactericidal antibiotics kill equally well regardless of growth state of the target cells.

passages.title: FL05 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 7
text: Apoptosis is a regulated cell death program carried out by caspases. To dissect the pathway, human T-lymphoma cells were treated with etoposide, a DNA-damaging drug, and sampled over 8 hours. Cytosolic cytochrome c was measured by immunoblot after subcellular fractionation, caspase-9 and caspase-3 activities were measured with fluorogenic substrates and normalized to untreated cells (1.0), and the percentage of cells staining with Annexin V was measured by flow cytometry. Figure 1 shows caspase activities over time. Table 1 shows results after 8 hours for etoposide alone, etoposide plus the pan-caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-FMK, and etoposide in cells that overexpress the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2. Untreated cells had cytosolic cytochrome c of 1.0 and 4% Annexin V-positive cells. Cytochrome c is reported relative to untreated cells. Each condition was run in three independent experiments, and values are means with variation below 10 percent. Equal protein was used in every enzyme reaction, and Z-VAD-FMK was added 1 hour before etoposide.

qs.q: By approximately what percentage did Z-VAD-FMK reduce the proportion of Annexin V-positive cells after etoposide treatment at 8 hours?
o: 86%, since the 14% remaining is subtracted from 100% to give the reduction
this ignores that the starting value is 62%, not 100%.
48%, since the difference between 62% and 14% is 48 percentage points
48 is the absolute difference, not the percentage reduction relative to 62%.
23%, since 14% divided by 62% gives the proportion of cells left after treatment
14/62 is 23% remaining, not the percentage reduced.
77%, because 48 of the 62 starting percentage points were lost
qs.x: (62 - 14)/62 = 0.77. Trap: Reporting the percentage-point difference or the fraction remaining rather than the relative reduction.

qs.q: What do the results in the Bcl-2 cells indicate about the position of Bcl-2 in the pathway?
o: Bcl-2 acts upstream of cytochrome c release, since cytochrome c stays low and caspases stay off
Correct: with Bcl-2, cytosolic cytochrome c stays near baseline, so release from mitochondria is blocked.
Bcl-2 activates caspase-9 directly, since caspase-9 activity is higher than in untreated cells
caspase-9 activity is 1.2, close to baseline, not elevated.
Bcl-2 acts as a caspase inhibitor like Z-VAD-FMK, since cytochrome c release is unaffected
in Bcl-2 cells cytochrome c release is reduced, whereas Z-VAD-FMK leaves it high (7.8).
Bcl-2 acts downstream of caspase-3, since caspase-3 activity is cleaved into inactive fragments
caspase-3 activity is low because upstream events are blocked, not because Bcl-2 acts after it.
qs.x: with Bcl-2, cytosolic cytochrome c stays near baseline, so release from mitochondria is blocked. Trap: Comparing Bcl-2 with Z-VAD-FMK as if both blocked caspases directly, missing that cytochrome c release is blocked only by Bcl-2.

qs.q: In Figure 1, caspase-3 activity ends higher than caspase-9 activity. Which statement best accounts for this difference?
o: Caspase-3 is activated first and then cleaves procaspase-9, forming a positive feedback loop
caspase-9 activity rises earlier in Figure 1, so caspase-3 follows rather than precedes it.
Each active caspase-9 molecule cleaves many procaspase-3 molecules, amplifying the signal
Correct: a protease cascade amplifies because one active enzyme can activate many downstream zymogens.
Caspase-3 is produced by new transcription of the gene after the DNA damage is detected
the caspases exist as inactive zymogens and are activated by cleavage.
Caspase-9 is degraded more quickly than caspase-3 by the proteasome in the first 4 hours
caspase-9 activity keeps rising to 6.5, not falling.
qs.x: a protease cascade amplifies because one active enzyme can activate many downstream zymogens. Trap: Reversing the order of the cascade because the downstream enzyme shows the larger signal.

qs.q: Annexin V staining marks cells in early apoptosis because Annexin V binds which cellular change?
o: Cleavage of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase by active executioner caspases
PARP cleavage is detected by immunoblot, and Annexin V is a phospholipid-binding protein.
Phosphatidylserine moving from the inner to the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane
Correct: phosphatidylserine exposure is an early apoptotic signal for phagocytes.
Release of cytochrome c into the cytosol after mitochondrial permeabilization
cytochrome c release is measured by fractionation and immunoblot, as in Table 1.
Fragmentation of nuclear DNA into nucleosome-sized pieces inside the nucleus
DNA laddering is detected by other assays such as TUNEL and gel electrophoresis, not by Annexin V.
qs.x: phosphatidylserine exposure is an early apoptotic signal for phagocytes. Trap: Mixing up the markers of apoptosis and assigning a nuclear or mitochondrial event to the membrane stain.
