passages.title: FL05 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 8
text: Serotonin (5-HT) released at synapses is cleared mainly by reuptake through the serotonin transporter (SERT) and degraded by monoamine oxidase (MAO). Researchers used in vivo microdialysis in the prefrontal cortex of adult rats and measured extracellular 5-HT as a percentage of baseline. Drug X is a selective SERT inhibitor, drug Y is an MAO inhibitor, and WAY-100635 blocks inhibitory 5-HT1A autoreceptors on serotonergic neurons in the raphe nuclei. Drugs were given by injection at time 0. Table 1 lists the peak extracellular 5-HT in each group, and Figure 1 shows the time course for drug X at 5 mg/kg compared with saline. Peak values were reached 60 minutes after injection in the groups receiving drug X, and 90 minutes after injection of drug Y. Each group contained eight animals. Probes were implanted one day before the experiment, and animals moved freely during sampling. Dialysate samples were collected every 30 minutes and analyzed by high-performance liquid chromatography, with baseline defined as the mean of three samples before injection.

qs.q: The increase above baseline produced by 5 mg/kg of drug X is about how many times the increase produced by 1 mg/kg?
o: 5.0 times, because the dose was raised from 1 to 5 mg/kg and the response is proportional
the response is not proportional to dose, as the data show.
1.6 times, because 340 divided by 210 is approximately 1.6
this compares the peak values, not the increases above the 100% baseline.
2.2 times, because 240 divided by 110 is approximately 2.2
Correct: increase above baseline is 240 versus 110.
3.4 times, because the peak at 5 mg/kg is 340% of the baseline value
this restates the peak relative to baseline instead of comparing the two doses.
qs.x: increase above baseline is 240 versus 110. Trap: Comparing peak levels rather than the increase above baseline, which understates the dose effect.

qs.q: Why did adding the 5-HT1A antagonist WAY-100635 to drug X produce a larger peak (520%) than drug X alone?
o: The antagonist inhibits MAO, so that cytosolic 5-HT is degraded more slowly in terminals
WAY-100635 acts at 5-HT1A receptors; MAO inhibition was the action of drug Y.
Blocking autoreceptors removes inhibitory feedback on raphe neuron firing, so more 5-HT is released
Correct: autoreceptor activation by increased extracellular 5-HT normally reduces serotonergic firing and release.
The antagonist is converted into 5-HT in the terminal, adding to the endogenous transmitter
WAY-100635 is a receptor antagonist, not a serotonin precursor.
The antagonist stimulates SERT in the presynaptic membrane, so that 5-HT reuptake increases
stimulating SERT would lower, not raise, extracellular 5-HT.
qs.x: autoreceptor activation by increased extracellular 5-HT normally reduces serotonergic firing and release. Trap: Forgetting that presynaptic autoreceptors provide negative feedback, so blocking them increases release.

qs.q: If drug X and drug Y were administered together at 5 mg/kg, which outcome is most likely?
o: Extracellular 5-HT would exceed either drug alone, raising serotonin syndrome risk
Correct: two mechanisms (blocked reuptake and blocked degradation) are additive or synergistic.
Extracellular 5-HT would return to baseline, because reuptake and degradation offset each other
the two drugs both increase availability, so their effects do not cancel.
Extracellular 5-HT would be lower than with either drug alone, because the drugs compete at SERT
drug Y acts on MAO, not at SERT, so they do not compete for the same target.
Extracellular 5-HT would equal the drug X value, because MAO acts only in the synaptic cleft
MAO is located on mitochondria in the presynaptic neuron and glia, not within the cleft.
qs.x: two mechanisms (blocked reuptake and blocked degradation) are additive or synergistic. Trap: Assuming that two drugs affecting the same transmitter must be redundant or competing, instead of acting through different steps.

qs.q: The energy that drives serotonin uptake by SERT is most directly derived from which source?
o: The inward Na+ gradient, which is maintained by the Na+/K+ ATPase
Correct: SERT is a secondary active transporter coupled to Na+ and Cl- influx.
The outward H+ gradient generated in the synaptic vesicle membrane by the V-ATPase
the vesicular H+ gradient drives packaging into vesicles (VMAT), not plasma membrane reuptake.
The concentration gradient of 5-HT itself, so that uptake is passive facilitated diffusion
uptake occurs against a large concentration gradient and is therefore not passive.
Direct hydrolysis of ATP by SERT during each transport cycle
SERT is not an ATPase; it is coupled to ion gradients.
qs.x: SERT is a secondary active transporter coupled to Na+ and Cl- influx. Trap: Treating reuptake as passive or ATP-driven, instead of secondary active transport using the sodium gradient.

passages.title: FL05 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 9
text: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) controls urine concentration by acting on the collecting duct. Five groups of adult rats were studied. Water-loaded rats were given a large volume of water by gavage. Dehydrated rats were deprived of water for 24 hours. A third group had surgical removal of the posterior pituitary (central diabetes insipidus model) and a fourth group were the same animals after injection of dDAVP, a long-acting V2 receptor agonist. The fifth group carried a mutation that eliminates the V2 receptor in the kidney (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus model). Urine flow, urine osmolality, plasma osmolality, and plasma ADH were measured and are shown in Table 1. Figure 1 plots urine osmolality against plasma ADH concentration for rats with intact kidneys and pituitaries across several levels of hydration. Rats were housed in metabolic cages for timed urine collection, and blood was drawn at the end of each collection period. Each group contained six animals and values are group means. Osmolality was determined by freezing-point depression, and ADH by radioimmunoassay.

qs.q: By approximately what percentage did urine flow fall between the water-loaded and the dehydrated groups?
o: 90%, since the flow dropped from 60 to 6 uL/min
10%, since the dehydrated flow of 6 is one tenth of the value in the water-loaded group
6 is 10% of 60, which is the fraction remaining, not the decrease.
54%, since the difference between the two values is 54 uL/min
54 is the absolute difference in uL/min, not a percentage.
99%, since the urine osmolality rose by a factor of 11 between the groups
this confuses osmolality with flow and gives an unsupported percentage.
qs.x: (60 - 6)/60 = 0.90. Trap: Reporting the fraction remaining or the absolute change instead of the percentage decrease.

qs.q: Which conclusion about the nephrogenic diabetes insipidus group is best supported by Table 1?
o: The defect would be corrected by dDAVP, since that drug acts on the V2 receptors in the kidney
this group lacks the V2 receptor, so dDAVP could not act.
The defect lies in ADH secretion, since plasma ADH is lower than in the dehydrated group
plasma ADH is 12.0 pg/mL, higher than in the dehydrated group (6.0).
The defect lies in the collecting duct response, since ADH is high but urine stays dilute
Correct: high plasma ADH with dilute urine shows that target cells cannot respond.
The defect lies in the hypothalamic osmoreceptors, since plasma osmolality is below normal
plasma osmolality is high (311), not below normal.
qs.x: high plasma ADH with dilute urine shows that target cells cannot respond. Trap: Attributing dilute urine to a lack of hormone without checking that plasma ADH is actually elevated.

qs.q: Concentrated urine depends on a steep osmotic gradient in the renal medulla. Which segment makes the major contribution to this gradient by actively reabsorbing solute without water?
o: The descending limb of the loop of Henle, via active secretion of urea into the lumen
the descending limb is water-permeable and has little active solute transport.
The proximal convoluted tubule, via sodium-coupled cotransport of glucose and amino acids
the proximal tubule reabsorbs solute and water in proportion, so it does not build the gradient.
The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, via the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter
Correct: this segment is water-impermeable and reabsorbs NaCl, generating the medullary gradient.
The distal convoluted tubule, via the aquaporin-2 channels inserted in response to ADH
aquaporin-2 channels operate in the collecting duct and use the gradient rather than create it.
qs.x: this segment is water-impermeable and reabsorbs NaCl, generating the medullary gradient. Trap: Choosing the proximal tubule because most reabsorption occurs there, instead of the segment that creates the gradient.

qs.q: What stimulus most directly triggered the rise in plasma ADH in the dehydrated rats?
o: Increased plasma osmolality sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors, leading to release from the posterior pituitary
Correct: plasma osmolality rose from 285 to 305, the main trigger for ADH release.
Increased plasma glucose sensed by pancreatic beta cells, leading to release from the hypothalamus
glucose is not the stimulus for ADH, and beta cells do not control its release.
Decreased plasma ADH feedback on the adrenal cortex, leading to release of aldosterone
ADH release is not controlled by adrenal feedback in this way.
Decreased urine osmolality sensed by receptors in the collecting duct, leading to release from the anterior pituitary
urine osmolality was high, and ADH is released from the posterior pituitary.
qs.x: plasma osmolality rose from 285 to 305, the main trigger for ADH release. Trap: Assigning ADH release to the anterior pituitary or to renal sensors rather than to hypothalamic osmoreceptors.

passages.title: FL05 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 10
text: Vaccines exploit immune memory. Mice were immunized intramuscularly on day 0 with a protein antigen combined with an adjuvant, and received an identical booster on day 28. Serum antigen-specific antibody titers (reciprocal of the highest dilution giving a positive signal) were measured by ELISA on the days shown in Table 1. A second group of mice was treated with an antibody that depletes CD4+ T cells before the first immunization and throughout the study; only IgG titers are shown for these mice. Titers of 10 are the assay detection limit. Figure 1 shows the IgM and IgG responses of the control group. In the control mice, IgM was the main class early in the primary response, while after the booster the IgG response was both faster and larger. Antibody affinity measured separately was about 20 times higher at day 35 than at day 14. Each group contained ten mice, and sera from individual animals were pooled by group at each time point. Each sample was assayed in duplicate and values shown are geometric means.

qs.q: The peak IgG titer after the booster is how many times larger than the peak IgG titer of the primary response in control mice?
o: 32 times, since 5120 divided by 160 equals 32
Correct: peak primary IgG is 160 at day 14; peak secondary is 5120 at day 35.
16 times, since 5120 divided by the day 7 IgM titer of 320 equals 16
this divides an IgG value by an IgM value and uses the wrong time.
2 times, since 5120 divided by the day 42 titer of 2560 equals 2
this compares the secondary peak with its own later decline.
64 times, since 5120 divided by the day 28 titer of 80 equals 64
day 28 is a decayed value just before the booster, not the primary peak.
qs.x: peak primary IgG is 160 at day 14; peak secondary is 5120 at day 35. Trap: Dividing by a titer measured just before the booster rather than by the peak of the primary response.

qs.q: The weak IgG response in CD4-depleted mice most directly supports which conclusion?
o: Helper T cells are the cells that secrete antibody, so removal eliminates the IgG supply
plasma cells derived from B cells secrete antibody, not T cells.
CD4+ T cells present antigen on MHC class I, so that depletion prevents antigen recognition by B cells
CD4+ T cells recognize antigen on MHC class II and do not present it.
Helper T cells provide CD40 ligand and cytokines that drive class switching and memory
Correct: B cells need T cell help for isotype switching and affinity maturation to protein antigens.
Cytotoxic T cells kill the antibody-secreting plasma cells unless helper T cells are present
the data do not suggest cytotoxic killing of plasma cells.
qs.x: B cells need T cell help for isotype switching and affinity maturation to protein antigens. Trap: Thinking T cells make antibody, instead of recognizing that helper T cells instruct B cells.

qs.q: Which process best accounts for the roughly 20-fold higher antibody affinity measured at day 35 compared with day 14?
o: V(D)J recombination in the bone marrow that generates new receptor specificities after each booster
V(D)J recombination occurs before antigen exposure and does not change affinity after activation.
Negative selection of self-reactive B cells in the spleen, which raises the average affinity for antigen
negative selection removes self-reactive cells and is not the cause of improved affinity to the immunizing antigen.
Complement binding to antibody, which increases the intrinsic binding strength for the antigen
complement acts after antibody binds and does not alter affinity.
Somatic hypermutation in germinal centers, with selection of B cells that bind antigen best
Correct: mutated B cell clones with better binding survive, giving affinity maturation.
qs.x: mutated B cell clones with better binding survive, giving affinity maturation. Trap: Confusing V(D)J recombination, which creates diversity before antigen exposure, with somatic hypermutation after exposure.

qs.q: Why was an adjuvant included with the antigen in the immunization?
o: To supply preformed IgG that neutralizes the antigen and prevents local tissue damage
adjuvants do not supply antibody; passive immunity would be provided by transferred antibody.
To prevent processing of the antigen so that the protein is displayed intact on B cells
antigen processing is needed for T cell help; adjuvants do not prevent it.
To deplete CD4+ T cells at the injection site so that tolerance to the antigen is avoided
adjuvants enhance rather than deplete T cell responses.
To activate innate immune cells, increasing costimulation and T cell help
Correct: adjuvants provide danger signals that enhance antigen-presenting cell activation.
qs.x: adjuvants provide danger signals that enhance antigen-presenting cell activation. Trap: Believing that an adjuvant delivers antibody or antigen rather than boosting the innate signals needed for adaptive activation.

passages.title: FL05 · CARS · Passage 1
text: Philosophers who write about lying tend to begin with a hard case: a murderer arrives at the door and asks where your friend is hiding. Nearly everyone's first instinct is that one may deceive him, and the instinct is so strong that it is often treated as a test any ethical theory must pass. Immanuel Kant notoriously failed it, or appeared to, by insisting that even here a lie is forbidden. His critics have found in this stubbornness a reductio of duty-based ethics: a theory that cannot permit a small falsehood to save a life, they say, has mistaken a rule for a reason.

The critics' conclusion is too quick, and the error lies in how they describe what is wrong with lying. The usual consequentialist account says that lies are bad because of what they cause: false beliefs, damaged relationships, eroded confidence in one's word. On this account the murderer case is trivial, since the harm of the lie is negligible and the harm of the truth is enormous. But the account has an awkward consequence of its own. It implies that a lie told in perfect secrecy and never discovered, is not wrong at all, or is wrong only to the extent that it risks exposure. Most people who reflect on having been lied to by a trusted friend sense that the wrong was done at the moment of the lie, whatever followed.

A better account locates the wrong in the nature of assertion itself. To assert something to another person is to invite her to rely on your word instead of on her own evidence. Assertion works only because a background practice exists in which speakers are presumed to say what they believe; the liar trades on that presumption while privately exempting himself from it. He treats the listener's trust as a resource to be spent, and treats the practice as something that others uphold for his benefit. This wrong is done to a particular person and also to the shared institution.

Does this account recover Kant's severity? Not entirely. Once we see that the wrong consists in abusing a listener's entitled trust, we can ask whether the murderer has such an entitlement. A person who asks a question in order to commit violence has himself stepped outside the practice of honest inquiry; he is not requesting information but seeking a tool. To answer him falsely is not to exploit his trust, because he has not extended the kind of trust that assertion presupposes. On this reading the deception is more like refusing to hand over a weapon than like cheating a business partner. The lie is permitted not because its consequences are good but because the relationship that would make lying wrong is absent.

This conclusion should not be stretched. The exception is narrow, and it is easily abused by anyone who wishes to classify an inconvenient questioner as an enemy. White lies told to spare a colleague's feelings, or lies to a customer who asks an honest question about a product, involve real trust and are therefore wrong on this view, even if forgivably so. The account thus yields a verdict between Kant's and the consequentialist's: lying is wrong in a way that outcomes cannot fully cancel, yet the wrongness depends on the relationship between speaker and listener rather than on an exceptionless rule. What it asks of us is not that we never deceive but that we notice whom we are deceiving, and whether they have given us the trust we are about to spend.

qs.q: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?
o: Lying is wrong only to the degree that it produces harmful consequences, so a lie that saves a life is never objectionable on any ethical theory.
The author criticizes the pure consequentialist account for its implication about secret lies and does not endorse it.
Kant's prohibition on lying should be accepted without exception, because any exemption would destroy the practice of assertion on which communication depends.
The author calls Kant's critics too quick but also holds that an exception is possible, so Kant's absolutism is not accepted.
Ordinary intuitions about lying are unreliable guides to ethical theory, since the murderer case shows that moral judgment conflicts with duty.
The author treats the murderer intuition as a legitimate test, not as an unreliable one.
Lying is wrong because it abuses the trust that an assertion invites, so its wrongness depends on the speaker-listener relationship rather than on outcomes.
Correct: The author rejects both the consequentialist and the Kantian accounts in favor of locating the wrong in the abuse of trust that assertion invites.
qs.x: The author rejects both the consequentialist and the Kantian accounts in favor of locating the wrong in the abuse of trust that assertion invites. Trap: Choosing the consequentialist option because the murderer case seems to favor outcomes; the author uses that case to qualify Kant, not to endorse outcome-based ethics.

qs.q: The author mentions a lie that is told in perfect secrecy and never discovered primarily in order to:
o: show that Kant's absolute prohibition would condemn even a lie that no person ever suspects or is harmed by.
The example is aimed at consequentialism, not at Kant; the author does not say Kant's view is troubled by secret lies.
argue that most lies are never found out, so their practical consequences are usually too small to matter morally.
The author makes no empirical claim about how often lies are discovered.
expose an implication of the consequentialist account that conflicts with how people judge having been lied to.
Correct: A secret lie causes no bad outcomes, so a purely consequentialist view would call it harmless, which clashes with the sense that the wrong occurs at the moment of lying.
support the claim that a murderer who asks a question has forfeited any entitlement to be told the truth.
The secret-lie example concerns consequentialism; the murderer's entitlement is discussed later, using a different argument.
qs.x: A secret lie causes no bad outcomes, so a purely consequentialist view would call it harmless, which clashes with the sense that the wrong occurs at the moment of lying. Trap: Reading the example as an attack on Kant, because Kant is the first philosopher named; the example is introduced under the consequentialist account.

qs.q: According to the passage, Kant's critics regard his position on the murderer case as a reductio because they believe that:
o: a theory of duty cannot explain why false beliefs and damaged relationships make lying wrong in ordinary cases.
Explaining ordinary harms of lying is the consequentialist's strength, not the critics' charge against Kant.
a theory forbidding a small falsehood that would save a life has treated a rule as though it were a reason.
Correct: The passage says critics think such a theory 'has mistaken a rule for a reason.'
any ethical theory that begins from hard cases must eventually supply an exception for each conceivable emergency.
The critics' complaint concerns Kant's refusal in this case, not a general claim about exceptions to every theory.
Kant's argument implicitly shows that the murderer is entitled to receive an honest answer to any question he asks.
Critics do not argue that the murderer is entitled to the truth; they argue Kant's rule is too rigid.
qs.x: The passage says critics think such a theory 'has mistaken a rule for a reason.' Trap: Confusing the critics' objection with the author's later point about entitlement to trust; the reductio charge is only that a rule is being followed against its purpose.

qs.q: Based on the passage, the author would most likely characterize a lie told to spare a colleague's feelings as:
o: permissible, because the harm done is negligible and the colleague is unlikely ever to discover the falsehood.
Negligible harm is the consequentialist test, which the author rejects as the source of the wrong.
permissible, because the colleague has implicitly agreed to a practice in which kind falsehoods are exchanged freely.
The passage says white lies involve real trust, not a mutual agreement to exchange falsehoods.
wrong, because it spends the colleague's real trust, though the kindly motive makes it forgivable.
Correct: The final paragraph says white lies involve real trust and are wrong on this view, 'even if forgivably so.'
as grave as the murderer's case, because every lie violates an exceptionless rule regardless of the relationship.
The author rejects exceptionless rules and says wrongness depends on the relationship.
qs.x: The final paragraph says white lies involve real trust and are wrong on this view, 'even if forgivably so.' Trap: Assuming that rejecting Kant's absolutism means small lies are acceptable; the author says white lies remain wrong, only forgivably so.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's account of why deceiving the murderer is permitted?
o: Most people who have been lied to by a trusted friend report that the wrong was done at the moment of the lie.
That supports the trust-based account rather than weakening it.
Many philosophers who defend Kant's view have not offered any account of the harm that a lie does to the listener.
Philosophers' failure to explain harm is irrelevant to whether absent trust makes the lie permissible.
Societies in which lying is widespread tend to show lower confidence in institutions than societies in which it is rare.
Social consequences of lying are outcome-based and do not bear on the trust-based exception.
Most people who agree that the murderer has extended no trust to the speaker still judge that lying to him is wrong.
Correct: The author's permission depends on the absence of entitled trust; if people still judge the lie wrong without trust, that premise is undermined.
qs.x: The author's permission depends on the absence of entitled trust; if people still judge the lie wrong without trust, that premise is undermined. Trap: Picking the option about consequences for institutions, which sounds damaging to lying generally but is irrelevant to the exception for the murderer.

qs.q: Which of the following lies would the author's account most clearly treat as permitted?
o: A physician tells a frightened patient that a painful procedure will be quick, hoping to steady the patient's nerves.
The patient relies on the physician's word, so the lie spends real trust.
A job candidate claims more experience than she has, in order to compete with applicants who have stronger credentials.
The interviewer is entitled to rely on honest statements of qualifications.
A negotiator assures a counterpart that no better offer exists, so that the counterpart will agree to terms quickly.
The counterpart is relying on the negotiator's assurance, so the relationship is one of trust.
A pharmacist tells an armed robber who demands narcotics that the shelves were emptied earlier that morning.
Correct: The robber seeks a tool for violence and has not extended the trust that assertion presupposes, as with the murderer.
qs.x: The robber seeks a tool for violence and has not extended the trust that assertion presupposes, as with the murderer. Trap: Picking a kind-motive lie such as the physician's; the author's exception turns on the listener's lack of entitled trust, not on the speaker's good intentions.

passages.title: FL05 · CARS · Passage 2
text: The standard story of the Reformation is a story about a machine. In 1517 a university professor in a small Saxon town circulated objections to the sale of indulgences; within weeks, the story goes, printers had carried them across the German lands, and within a few years a movement that would once have been smothered, as earlier dissent had been, escaped the control of the Church. The press, on this telling, was the cause that made the difference. Jan Hus had been burned a century earlier without a press to spread his teaching, and Martin Luther lived because printed pamphlets made him too famous to silence.

There is something right in this account, and a good deal that is misleading. The figures are impressive: the number of German-language pamphlets rose from a trickle to many thousands of titles within a decade, and Luther himself accounted for a remarkable share of them. But a statistic about output tells us nothing about demand. Printers in this period were commercial gamblers who financed expensive print runs on borrowed money, and a book that did not sell could ruin a shop. They printed Luther in such quantity precisely because readers were buying him. The press did not create the appetite for reform; it responded to an appetite already formed by decades of anticlericalism, by humanist scholarship, and by resentment of papal taxation. A technology that merely supplies what the market wants cannot be the sole explanation of the market.

The reliance on print also conceals how much of the movement was oral. Most inhabitants of sixteenth-century towns could not read, yet they encountered the new ideas constantly: in sermons, in hymns set to familiar tunes, in crude woodcuts that conveyed a satire of the pope to anyone who could look at a page. Pamphlets were frequently read aloud in taverns and workshops, so that one purchased copy might serve dozens of listeners. The press was one element in a system of communication that also included the pulpit, the street, and the marketplace, and the elements reinforced one another. A printed sermon gave a preacher's words a second life, but it was the preacher's performance, and the audience's readiness to hear it, that gave the printed version its force.

None of this makes the press incidental. Print allowed arguments to be fixed in a stable form, so that a text could be quoted, answered, and attacked point by point, and this encouraged a style of public controversy that earlier dissent had lacked. It made it far more difficult for authorities to suppress an idea by seizing a single manuscript or silencing a single speaker, because copies had already scattered. And it gave Luther's opponents a reason to print as well, so that the argument became a contest conducted in public, with the educated laity as an audience. These are real effects, but they are effects of speed and replication, which magnify a message rather than generate it.

The sensible conclusion is that the press and the Reformation made each other. The movement gave printers a product that sold; the printers gave the movement a reach that no earlier dissenting group had enjoyed. To ask which of the two came first, or which deserves the credit, is to assume that causes must be ranked in a line. Historical change of this kind is better imagined as a feedback loop in which a new tool and a new demand amplify one another until the combination can no longer be reversed. The machine mattered, but only because people were already prepared to use it.

qs.q: The central claim of the passage is that the printing press:
o: and the Reformation reinforced each other, since the press magnified a demand for reform that already existed rather than creating it.
Correct: The passage concludes that the press and the movement 'made each other' in a feedback loop.
was the decisive cause of the Reformation, because it allowed Luther's objections to reach a reading public that earlier dissenters never had.
The author denies that the press was the sole cause.
was largely incidental to the Reformation, since sermons, songs, and images carried the new ideas to most townspeople without any printing.
The author says the press was not incidental; it fixed arguments and made suppression harder.
created a market for religious controversy that printers then exploited, so that commercial motives explain the spread of reformist ideas.
The author argues demand preceded the pamphlets; printers responded to readers.
qs.x: The passage concludes that the press and the movement 'made each other' in a feedback loop. Trap: Overcorrecting to the view that the press was unimportant; the author explicitly says 'None of this makes the press incidental.'

qs.q: The reference to Jan Hus in the first paragraph serves mainly to:
o: show the reasoning behind the standard account, in which dissent without a press was suppressed but Luther's was not.
Correct: Hus is cited as part of how the standard story explains why the press made the difference.
suggest that the Church had grown more tolerant of dissent by the time of Luther than it was in Hus's day.
The passage does not claim the Church had become more tolerant.
demonstrate that popular resentment of papal taxation had been building for a century before the Reformation began.
Resentment of taxation is mentioned later, not through Hus.
establish that Hus's teaching spread widely by oral means even though no printed copies of it survived.
The passage says Hus lacked a press; it does not discuss oral spread of his teaching.
qs.x: Hus is cited as part of how the standard story explains why the press made the difference. Trap: Treating a sentence from the account the author goes on to qualify as the author's own conclusion.

qs.q: According to the passage, printers published Luther's pamphlets in such quantity mainly because:
o: they sympathized with his objections and accepted likely losses in order to help the reform movement succeed.
The passage attributes the quantity to demand, not to sympathy.
Church officials had commissioned replies to the indulgence controversy and paid printers to produce them promptly.
No commissioning by Church officials is mentioned.
improvements in the technology had lowered production costs so far that unsold books carried little financial risk.
The passage says print runs were expensive and risky.
readers were purchasing them, and an unsold edition financed by borrowed money could ruin a printing shop.
Correct: The passage says printers were commercial gamblers who printed Luther because readers were buying him.
qs.x: The passage says printers were commercial gamblers who printed Luther because readers were buying him. Trap: Attributing printers' behavior to ideology; the passage explains it with commercial incentives.

qs.q: The passage most strongly suggests that a printed pamphlet in a sixteenth-century town could:
o: influence people who never read it, because it might be read aloud to listeners in taverns and workshops.
Correct: The passage says pamphlets were read aloud so one copy might serve dozens of listeners.
be understood by most inhabitants of the town, because literacy rates had risen sharply after the invention of print.
The passage says most inhabitants could not read.
replace the pulpit as the main channel of reform, because printed words were harder for authorities to contradict.
The author says the media reinforced one another and that the pulpit remained important.
persuade readers of its message without any help from preaching, because its arguments were fixed in stable form.
The passage says printed versions gained force from the preacher's performance and audience readiness.
qs.x: The passage says pamphlets were read aloud so one copy might serve dozens of listeners. Trap: Assuming print implied a literate audience; the passage notes most townspeople could not read.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that the press responded to an existing demand for reform?
o: Luther's most widely printed works were also the ones that he composed most quickly and revised least.
Speed of composition is irrelevant to whether demand preceded the press.
Towns that first acquired a press in the 1520s became centers of reform soon afterward, whatever their earlier sentiment.
Correct: If reform followed the arrival of presses regardless of earlier sentiment, the press would be creating demand, contrary to the author's view.
Pamphlets written by Luther's Catholic opponents were printed in smaller numbers than pamphlets written by Luther himself.
Smaller opposition print runs do not show that the press created demand.
Anticlerical writing had circulated in manuscript form in German towns for decades before the Reformation began.
Earlier anticlerical manuscripts support the claim that demand existed beforehand.
qs.x: If reform followed the arrival of presses regardless of earlier sentiment, the press would be creating demand, contrary to the author's view. Trap: Choosing the manuscript option because it concerns pre-Reformation sentiment; it strengthens the author rather than weakens.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the standard story of the Reformation is best described as:
o: scornful rejection, treating it as a legend with no support in the evidence that historians have gathered.
The author grants that the account has merit and that the press had real effects.
qualified acceptance, crediting what is right in it while arguing that it is incomplete and misleading in emphasis.
Correct: The author says there is 'something right in this account, and a good deal that is misleading.'
neutral summary, reporting its main claims and leaving readers to decide how much weight to give them.
The author argues against the account rather than merely reporting it.
enthusiastic endorsement, offering new statistics in order to confirm what historians have long believed.
The author questions the account's conclusion and does not endorse it.
qs.x: The author says there is 'something right in this account, and a good deal that is misleading.' Trap: Reading the opening paragraph's neutral summary as the author's whole stance; the author turns critical in paragraph two.

passages.title: FL05 · CARS · Passage 3
text: Readers who meet stream of consciousness for the first time usually take it to be a form of realism. The novelist, they assume, has discovered that real minds do not think in tidy paragraphs and has decided to transcribe what actually happens: associations that wander, sentences that break off, perceptions interrupted by memory. The technique is praised for its fidelity, and the difficulty of the resulting books is excused as the price of honesty. This account is attractive, and it is mistaken. Whatever else it is, the stream of consciousness in the fiction of Virginia Woolf or James Joyce is not a recording.

The simplest way to see this is to notice how unlike actual thought the printed result is. Real inner experience, to the extent that we can report on it at all, is largely wordless: it consists of images, moods, half-formed intentions, and a continuous pressure of bodily sensation that language cannot easily capture. A page of Modernist interior monologue, by contrast, is composed of articulate and often beautifully rhythmic sentences, arranged with a care that no passing thought could possess. The writer has selected, ordered, and polished. To call the outcome a transcript is like calling a landscape painting a photograph of a field simply because it includes grass.

What the technique actually accomplishes is a formal solution to a problem that nineteenth-century fiction had left unresolved: how to represent the experience of time. The realist novel measured time by the clock and the calendar; chapters advanced from morning to evening, from one year to the next, and the inner life was reported in summary by an authoritative narrator. But anyone who has waited anxiously, or been absorbed in a conversation, knows that experienced duration does not match the clock. An hour can pass in a moment, and a moment, remembered, can expand to fill a chapter. Modernist writers saw that sentences, unlike clocks, could stretch and compress. By letting a single afternoon occupy hundreds of pages, or by compressing years into a subordinate clause, they made the reader feel time as it is lived rather than as it is measured.

This explains some features that the realism account cannot. It explains why the novels so often concentrate on ordinary days, a party, a walk through a city, a visit to a lighthouse, since a trivial external occasion is the best background against which internal duration shows up. It also explains the characteristic movement between minds. When a narrative slides from one character's thoughts to another's within a single paragraph, the reader is not being offered a more accurate map of consciousness; she is being shown that private worlds overlap, that a single moment is experienced differently by each person who stands in it, and that no one of those experiences has authority over the others.

None of this requires us to abandon the word realism, only to hold it more loosely. The Modernists were faithful to something, but the something was the texture of experience, not the surface of thought. Their art was a deliberate construction, built from the rhythms and syntax of an invented language, whose purpose was to give readers an impression they could not otherwise have had. If the books are demanding, it is not because the authors were being honest about the mess of the mind, but because they were asking readers to do something unfamiliar: to attend to time itself.

qs.q: Which statement best captures the central argument of the passage?
o: Stream of consciousness is a crafted formal technique for conveying experienced time, not a faithful transcription of how minds work.
Correct: The author argues that the technique is constructed and solves the problem of representing lived time.
Modernist novelists invented a deliberately obscure language in order to show that realism cannot be reconciled with inner life.
The author says the language serves a purpose, to let readers feel time, not to obscure.
Real consciousness is so largely wordless that the prose of Woolf and Joyce fails as a representation of private experience.
The author uses wordlessness to show the prose is not a recording, not that it fails.
Nineteenth-century realism represented the relation between clock time and inner experience better than Modernism managed to.
The author says realism left the time problem unresolved.
qs.x: The author argues that the technique is constructed and solves the problem of representing lived time. Trap: Taking the observation that thought is wordless as the author's conclusion, rather than as evidence that the technique is artificial.

qs.q: The comparison between a landscape painting and a photograph of a field is used to:
o: suggest that selection and arrangement make a work an artifact, not a record, even if it includes real elements.
Correct: The analogy makes the point that including real features (grass) does not make a composed work a transcript.
argue that Modernist prose resembles painting more than it resembles any other form of narrative fiction written in English.
The analogy concerns artifice versus recording, not similarity to painting as a genre.
concede that stream of consciousness borrows its raw material from ordinary experience, as landscapes do.
The author's point is about construction, not about borrowed raw material.
criticize readers who prefer visual art to literature because they undervalue the difficulty of writing.
No criticism of readers' preferences between arts is made.
qs.x: The analogy makes the point that including real features (grass) does not make a composed work a transcript. Trap: Reading the analogy as about visual similarity; it is about the difference between composition and recording.

qs.q: According to the passage, the nineteenth-century realist novel typically presented the inner life:
o: in summary, through an authoritative narrator, while time was marked by the clock and calendar.
Correct: The passage states that the inner life 'was reported in summary by an authoritative narrator.'
through fragmentary associations that broke off, wandered, and were interrupted by memories of earlier events.
That describes Modernist techniques, as the passage portrays them.
through overlapping perspectives of several characters, none of whom held authority over the others' experience.
Overlapping minds are attributed to Modernist writers.
by stretching a single afternoon across hundreds of pages in order to render the feel of lived duration.
Dilating an afternoon is a Modernist device.
qs.x: The passage states that the inner life 'was reported in summary by an authoritative narrator.' Trap: Attributing Modernist features to the realists the passage contrasts them with.

qs.q: The author would most likely say that a reader who finds a Modernist novel difficult:
o: has discovered that the author failed to select and polish the material before presenting it to the public.
The author stresses the care and polish of the prose.
can remove the difficulty by rereading the book as a literal record of a single mind's uninterrupted thoughts.
The author rejects the transcript reading.
is meeting the unavoidable cost of fidelity to the wordless and disorderly character of ordinary inner experience.
The final paragraph explicitly rejects this 'price of honesty' explanation.
is being asked to attend to experienced duration in an unfamiliar way, not to decode a transcript.
Correct: The final paragraph says the difficulty reflects asking readers to attend to time, not honesty about mental mess.
qs.x: The final paragraph says the difficulty reflects asking readers to attend to time, not honesty about mental mess. Trap: Accepting the 'difficulty as honesty' explanation that the author's first paragraph attributes to naive readers and then rejects.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that Modernist interior monologue does not resemble actual thought?
o: Manuscript evidence shows that Woolf and Joyce revised their interior passages repeatedly before they were published.
Repeated revision supports the claim that the prose is crafted.
Studies in which people speak their thoughts aloud yield reports in fluent, grammatical sentences much like Modernist monologue.
Correct: If real thought-reports look like Modernist monologue, the author's claim of dissimilarity is undermined.
Surveys show that many readers find Modernist novels more difficult to follow than novels written in the realist tradition.
Reader difficulty does not bear on whether the prose resembles thought.
Literary historians note that some realist novelists occasionally depicted a character's private thoughts in direct form.
Realist depictions of thought do not address whether Modernist prose resembles it.
qs.x: If real thought-reports look like Modernist monologue, the author's claim of dissimilarity is undermined. Trap: Choosing the manuscript-revision option; it sounds relevant to Modernist technique but actually supports the author.

qs.q: Which of the following works would the author most likely say uses a technique similar to that of the Modernist novelists?
o: A documentary that records a dinner party with a fixed camera and presents the entire event in real time without cuts.
A fixed real-time recording is the transcript model the author rejects.
A film in which one dinner party fills forty minutes, with scenes lengthening and shortening with a character's anxiety.
Correct: The film lets experienced duration stretch and compress against the clock, as the Modernist writers did.
A memoir that summarizes a decade of the writer's life in chronological chapters introduced by short dated headings.
Chronological summary resembles the realist treatment of time.
A novel told by a detached historian who explains to the reader what each character felt at every stage of a gathering.
An authoritative narrator explaining feelings resembles the realist approach.
qs.x: The film lets experienced duration stretch and compress against the clock, as the Modernist writers did. Trap: Picking the real-time documentary because it sounds 'faithful'; the author contrasts clock time with experienced duration.

passages.title: FL05 · CARS · Passage 4
text: It has long been repeated that photography liberated painting. Once a machine could record a face or a street with perfect accuracy, the argument runs, painters no longer needed to imitate nature and were free to explore color, light, and the act of seeing, and Impressionism was the first great result. The tidiness of this story explains its longevity. A single invention is made to explain a revolution in art, and the usual sense of cause and effect is satisfied. But the chronology is awkward, and the economics worse, and a closer look suggests that the relationship between the two media was less a rescue than a rivalry that changed both.

Consider first what photography could actually do in the middle of the nineteenth century. Early processes required long exposures, so that crowds blurred into emptiness and people had to be clamped still for portraits. Images were monochrome, and they could not be printed in quantity without considerable expense. These limits meant that photography competed seriously with painters only in a narrow market, chiefly small portraits for the middle class. The prestigious branches of painting, such as large historical canvases and commissioned portraits of the wealthy, were not threatened. Painters who feared for their livelihoods might have been rational to worry about the future, but there is little evidence of a sudden collapse in demand in the years when the Impressionists began to develop their style.

A more persuasive explanation of the movement points to pressures within painting itself. The official Salon, which controlled access to buyers, favored polished surfaces and edifying subjects, and younger painters who disliked its conservatism had every reason to organize exhibitions of their own. Meanwhile, the invention of paint in portable metal tubes allowed artists to work outdoors and to capture changing light in a single session. Railways took painters to the coast and the suburbs, and the modern city of cafes, boulevards, and leisure supplied new subjects. These developments would have encouraged quick, broken brushwork and bright color whether or not a camera had ever existed.

What photography did provide, however, was a visual vocabulary. Snapshots and early street views showed scenes cropped arbitrarily at the edges, figures cut off by the frame, and viewpoints from above or at odd angles. Impressionist compositions use precisely such devices: a dancer's leg intrudes from the margin, a boulevard is seen from a balcony, a group of figures is caught in mid-gesture. The painters were not copying photographs so much as absorbing a new sense of what a picture could look like, a sense that the camera made familiar to everyone. In that respect, photography changed what seemed natural to see before it changed what painting needed to do.

The deepest influence may have been a reorientation of ambition. Faced with a machine that could record outward appearances, painters began to emphasize what a machine could not: the particular sensation of a moment, as registered by one nervous and attentive observer. The visible brushstroke became a kind of signature, evidence that a person had stood at this spot and seen this light. Photography therefore did not free painting from imitation so much as sharpen a question that painters had always faced, namely what a hand and an eye could offer that a mechanism could not. The answer they gave redefined their art, and, by sending photographers in turn to imitate painterly effects, it altered the camera's ambitions as well.

qs.q: The primary purpose of the passage is to:
o: propose that Impressionism arose chiefly from economic pressure, as photographic studios drove painters out of the market for portrait commissions.
The passage says photography did not threaten the prestigious market in the relevant years.
argue that Impressionist painters rejected photographic devices such as cropping because they undermined claims that a painting records personal sensation.
The passage says Impressionists used photographic devices such as cropping.
argue that photography shaped Impressionism by supplying compositional habits and sharpening painters' claims for eye and hand, not by freeing them from imitation.
Correct: The passage rejects the 'liberation' story and describes subtler influences of photography.
claim that the Salon system, and not any technological development, was the single cause of the Impressionists' distinctive style of painting.
The Salon is one pressure among several, alongside paint tubes, railways, and urban subjects.
qs.x: The passage rejects the 'liberation' story and describes subtler influences of photography. Trap: Replacing one single-cause story with another; the author describes multiple pressures plus photography's indirect influence.

qs.q: The passage cites all of the following as developments that encouraged Impressionist methods independently of photography EXCEPT:
o: inexpensive photographic prints that persuaded buyers to abandon painted canvases.
Correct: The passage says photographs were expensive to print in quantity and did not collapse demand, so cheap prints are not cited.
the invention of paint packaged in portable metal tubes that allowed work outdoors.
Tube paint is cited.
railways that carried painters to the coast and the suburbs where they sought subjects.
Railways are cited.
the rise of a modern city of cafes, boulevards, and leisure that offered new subjects.
The modern city is cited as a source of subjects.
qs.x: The passage says photographs were expensive to print in quantity and did not collapse demand, so cheap prints are not cited. Trap: Missing the word EXCEPT and choosing a cited development; three options are directly stated in the third paragraph.

qs.q: The passage suggests that, when Impressionism developed, large historical canvases and commissioned portraits of the wealthy:
o: were being abandoned by painters who saw that photographs recorded events and faces more accurately than paint could.
The passage says there is little evidence of a sudden collapse in demand.
were the main subjects of the first independent exhibitions organized by painters who disliked the Salon's conservatism.
The independent exhibitions are described as a reaction against Salon taste, not as showing these genres.
were made newly practical by portable tube paints that allowed large works to be completed within a single session.
Tube paint is linked to outdoor work, not to large canvases.
were not yet seriously threatened by photography, which then competed mainly in a narrow market for small portraits.
Correct: The passage says prestigious branches of painting were not threatened.
qs.x: The passage says prestigious branches of painting were not threatened. Trap: Accepting the standard story that photography's accuracy immediately displaced the most prestigious painting.

qs.q: The author refers to a dancer's leg intruding from the margin of a picture in order to:
o: show that Impressionist compositions use framing devices of the kind that photographs had made familiar.
Correct: The detail is offered as an example of cropped, arbitrary framing resembling snapshots.
illustrate a specific case in which a painter copied a particular photograph in order to complete a canvas.
The passage says painters absorbed a new sense of pictures, not that they copied photographs.
demonstrate that the Salon favored unconventional framing in works that it accepted for official exhibition.
The Salon is described as favoring polished surfaces and edifying subjects.
support the claim that outdoor work, made possible by tube paint, changed what painters chose to depict.
Outdoor work is discussed separately in the third paragraph.
qs.x: The detail is offered as an example of cropped, arbitrary framing resembling snapshots. Trap: Reading 'influence' as 'copying'; the author explicitly says painters were not copying photographs.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the claim that photography liberated painting is best described as:
o: hostile, regarding the claim as a deliberate distortion by historians who ignore the contributions of painters.
The author gives no hint of accusing historians of deliberate distortion.
indifferent, presenting the claim as one of several theories that cannot be weighed on the available evidence.
The author weighs evidence and reaches a conclusion.
skeptical, regarding the claim as neat but poorly supported by the chronology and economics of the period.
Correct: The first paragraph praises its tidiness but says 'the chronology is awkward, and the economics worse.'
appreciative, regarding the claim as basically sound but in need of a few details to account for its exceptions.
The author considers the claim largely inadequate, not basically sound.
qs.x: The first paragraph praises its tidiness but says 'the chronology is awkward, and the economics worse.' Trap: Mistaking 'hostile' for 'critical'; the author is measured and acknowledges why the story endures.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that photography did not seriously threaten painters' livelihoods before Impressionism?
o: Records showing that many Impressionist painters also submitted works to the official Salon during the same decade of the 1860s.
Salon submissions do not bear on market competition from photography.
Evidence that several leading Impressionists purchased photographic equipment and experimented with it in their own studios between exhibitions.
Owning cameras does not show that painters' livelihoods were threatened.
A steep fall in wealthy patrons' portrait commissions in the decade before the first Impressionist show, as cheap photo studios multiplied.
Correct: A collapse in wealthy portrait commissions linked to photography would contradict the author's economic claim.
Evidence that some photographers of the period imitated painterly effects such as soft focus and visible texture in their finished prints.
Photographers imitating painters is part of the author's closing point and does not concern livelihood.
qs.x: A collapse in wealthy portrait commissions linked to photography would contradict the author's economic claim. Trap: Selecting evidence that links painters to photography generally; the claim at issue is specifically economic.

passages.title: FL05 · CARS · Passage 5
text: Jazz improvisation is often described in the language of pure freedom. A soloist steps forward, the story goes, and invents music out of nothing, answerable to no score and no rule except the inspiration of the moment. The romance of this picture has been useful to jazz's advocates, who have used it to defend the music against the charge that it is mere entertainment. But the romance is misleading, and it has led listeners to misunderstand what improvisers do and why their best work is admired. The truth is that improvisation is a highly disciplined activity, closer to fluent speech than to free invention.

Consider how people talk. A speaker constructing a sentence does not invent words or grammar on the spot; she draws on a vocabulary and a set of syntactic habits acquired over years, and combines them into utterances that are new but not unprecedented. Jazz players work in much the same way. A young musician learns tunes, chord progressions, and rhythmic conventions, and memorizes the phrases of admired predecessors, often by transcribing recorded solos note for note. This stock of material, sometimes called a vocabulary, is not an obstacle to originality but its precondition. A soloist with nothing to draw upon would not sound free; he would sound lost. What the listener hears as spontaneity is a skilled recombination, produced at speed, of material the player knows thoroughly.

If improvisation resembles speech, it should also resemble conversation, and here the music's social character appears. The rhythm section does not merely accompany; it listens, and it answers. A drummer who hears a soloist hesitate may leave a space, and a pianist who hears an unexpected substitution may alter the harmony beneath it. These exchanges can be so close that it becomes difficult to say who initiated an idea and who responded. For this reason the value of a performance cannot be assessed by examining the soloist's lines alone. A solo that seems unremarkable on paper may be thrilling in context because it is exactly right for what the other players had just done, and a technically brilliant solo that ignores the ensemble may seem arid.

The recording industry has complicated this picture in a curious way. Because the music was preserved on discs, solos that were once fleeting became permanent objects, studied, transcribed, and in some cases played back by later musicians as though they were compositions. Some critics regret this, arguing that to freeze a solo is to betray the spirit of improvisation. But the history of the music suggests a different reading. The recordings became a shared library from which each generation builds its vocabulary, and thereby extended the conversation across decades. Players who learn a famous solo are not necessarily imitators; they are often students acquiring a language they will use to say something of their own.

None of this diminishes the achievement of the great improvisers. If anything, it clarifies where that achievement lies. The remarkable thing about a fine solo is not that it appears from nowhere, which no music does, but that a player has taken a shared language and made it answer to a particular moment, with particular companions, in a way that could not have been planned. Freedom, in that sense, is not the absence of constraint but mastery within it. To appreciate jazz is to listen not for the absence of rules, but for the intelligence with which rules are bent.

qs.q: Which of the following best summarizes the passage?
o: Jazz improvisation is a disciplined recombination of a shared learned language, and its value lies in responsiveness to the moment and to other players.
Correct: The passage rejects the 'pure freedom' picture and describes improvisation as fluent, conversational use of a shared vocabulary.
Jazz improvisation is spontaneous invention from nothing, which is why it deserves to be taken more seriously as art than composed music.
This is the romantic view the author calls misleading.
Recordings have damaged jazz improvisation by turning fleeting solos into fixed compositions that later players merely copy without understanding.
The author argues recordings enriched the shared library.
Rhythm section players contribute more to a performance than soloists do, because they determine the harmony on which every solo depends.
The author says the players respond to one another, not that one group matters more.
qs.x: The passage rejects the 'pure freedom' picture and describes improvisation as fluent, conversational use of a shared vocabulary. Trap: Choosing the romantic 'freedom' picture, which the passage introduces only to correct.

qs.q: The comparison of improvisation to fluent speech is used primarily to:
o: suggest that jazz players are able to speak more fluently than other musicians because of their training.
The comparison is about the nature of improvisation, not about fluency of jazz players versus others.
show that listeners cannot judge a solo without knowing the words of the song on which it is based.
The passage does not mention lyrics.
argue that originality depends on a stock of learned material that is recombined rather than invented.
Correct: Speakers use inherited vocabulary and grammar to say new things, as improvisers do.
indicate that the phrases of admired predecessors should be quoted exactly in every performance.
Transcribed phrases are material to be recombined, not quoted exactly.
qs.x: Speakers use inherited vocabulary and grammar to say new things, as improvisers do. Trap: Reading 'speech' literally as about words and lyrics.

qs.q: According to the passage, why do some critics regret that solos have been recorded?
o: They believe young players now learn solos note for note and so no longer develop any vocabulary of their own.
The author rejects the idea that learners are merely imitators, but this is not the critics' stated complaint.
They believe that freezing a solo into a permanent object betrays the spirit of improvisation.
Correct: The passage says critics argue that 'to freeze a solo is to betray the spirit of improvisation.'
They believe the rhythm section's contribution is lost when recordings emphasize the soloist at the expense of the group.
Nothing is said about recordings and the rhythm section.
They believe that listeners judge performances on technical brilliance instead of how well players respond to one another.
Technical brilliance versus responsiveness is a separate point about evaluation.
qs.x: The passage says critics argue that 'to freeze a solo is to betray the spirit of improvisation.' Trap: Mixing the critics' complaint with the author's rebuttal about learners acquiring a language.

qs.q: The author would most likely agree that a simple solo could be judged better than a technically dazzling one if:
o: the simple solo answered what the other players had just done, while the dazzling one ignored them.
Correct: The passage says a solo that ignores the ensemble may seem arid while a modest one fitted to the moment can be thrilling.
the simple solo used fewer phrases borrowed from earlier recorded solos than the dazzling one did.
The author says borrowed vocabulary is the precondition of originality, not a defect.
the dazzling solo was based on a chord progression with which the audience was already familiar.
Familiar progressions are normal and do not count against a solo.
the simple solo had been written out in advance, so that no part of it depended on chance.
Writing out a solo would contradict improvisation.
qs.x: The passage says a solo that ignores the ensemble may seem arid while a modest one fitted to the moment can be thrilling. Trap: Equating quality with novelty of material; the author prizes responsiveness.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that improvisation resembles conversation?
o: Evidence that many accomplished soloists learned their craft by transcribing the recorded solos of earlier players.
Transcription supports the vocabulary claim, not the conversation claim.
Recordings showing a rhythm section plays nearly the same accompaniment whatever the soloist plays.
Correct: If accompaniment does not respond to the soloist, the exchange is not conversational.
Surveys indicating that audiences report greater enjoyment of live jazz performances than of recorded jazz.
Audience enjoyment does not bear on interaction among players.
Biographical evidence that several early jazz players had little formal training in music theory or notation.
Formal training is irrelevant to whether players respond to each other.
qs.x: If accompaniment does not respond to the soloist, the exchange is not conversational. Trap: Picking the training or transcription options because they concern jazz learning rather than the interaction claim.

qs.q: Which of the following activities is most analogous to improvisation as the author describes it?
o: A novelist invents a new language and then writes an entire book in it for a small audience of enthusiasts.
Inventing a language is the 'invention from nothing' picture the author rejects.
A public speaker answers an unscripted question using familiar phrases arranged to suit that particular questioner.
Correct: The speaker recombines learned material fluently and responsively, as the author says improvisers do.
A pianist performs a memorized score exactly as written, taking care to match the tempo of a famous recording.
A fixed performance is the opposite of improvisation.
A chess player calculates every move in advance and then plays through the planned sequence regardless of the opponent.
Ignoring the opponent lacks responsiveness.
qs.x: The speaker recombines learned material fluently and responsively, as the author says improvisers do. Trap: Equating improvisation with sheer invention; the author compares it with fluent speech.

passages.title: FL05 · CARS · Passage 6
text: Since Emile Durkheim, social theorists have been inclined to see ritual as a kind of social glue. In his account of early religion, collective ceremonies bring scattered individuals together, focus their attention on a common symbol, and produce a heightened emotional state he called effervescence. Participants leave feeling that they belong to something larger than themselves, and the group's solidarity is renewed. The idea has proved durable because it fits so much ordinary experience: the hush of a funeral, the roar of a stadium, the shared awkwardness and warmth of a wedding. But a durable idea is not necessarily a complete one, and the glue metaphor conceals as much as it reveals.

Consider first the question of what exactly does the binding. It is tempting to suppose that the content of a ritual, its myth or doctrine, is what unites those who perform it. Yet in many societies participants offer quite different interpretations of the same ceremony, and some admit that they do not know what it means. What they share is not a belief but an action: they stand, chant, move, and sometimes suffer together. Researchers who measure the physiology of people taking part in synchronized activities report that heart rates and breathing tend to converge, and that participants subsequently behave more generously toward fellow participants. If this is correct, ritual cohesion is produced less by agreement about meaning than by the experience of coordinated bodies, which would explain why rituals can unite people who disagree about nearly everything else.

A second complication is cost. Many rituals are demanding: they require fasting, expense, pain, or long hours of repetitive work. A cynic might regard the costs as an unfortunate by-product, but a more illuminating suggestion is that the costs are the point. Anyone can claim to be committed to a group, but only a person who is willing to pay a price can convincingly demonstrate it. A demanding initiation therefore screens out the half-hearted and reassures the committed that their companions will not abandon them. This would explain why groups that ask the most of their members, within limits, often show the strongest loyalty, and why ceremonies that are made too easy lose their capacity to bind.

Neither of these points overturns Durkheim, but they qualify the notion that cohesion is an unqualified good. The same mechanisms that create trust within a group can sharpen the line between insiders and outsiders. A ritual that signals loyalty to one community also signals that others do not belong, and the very costliness that reassures members can make it difficult for newcomers to join. Ceremonies have been used to consecrate peace between rivals, but they have also been used to prepare men for war. The cohesion that a ritual generates, in other words, is directed somewhere, and the direction is not determined by the ritual itself.

It follows that the question to ask of a ceremony is not simply whether it brings people together, but whom it brings together, at what price, and against whom. The glue metaphor encourages us to treat solidarity as a substance that a ritual deposits, as uniform and as harmless as adhesive. A better picture would be that of a current, which can power a community or sweep it away. To understand rituals, we should examine how they channel shared feeling, since the channel, rather than the feeling alone, determines whether a society flourishes or fractures.

qs.q: The main argument of the passage is that:
o: rituals bind people together mainly through the beliefs they share, so a ceremony's myth matters more than the actions that participants perform.
The passage says participants often disagree on meaning, and shared action does the binding.
Durkheim's view of ritual as social glue is sound but incomplete, because cohesion comes from shared action and cost and can be aimed against outsiders.
Correct: The author accepts Durkheim but qualifies the glue metaphor.
demanding rituals are harmful to communities, because the costs they impose discourage newcomers and encourage hostility toward neighboring groups.
The author says costs can be the reason rituals bind; the harm is only that cohesion can be directed against outsiders.
Durkheim's theory should be abandoned, since modern research on physiology has shown that rituals do not produce any real feeling of solidarity.
The author says the points 'neither overturn Durkheim'.
qs.x: The author accepts Durkheim but qualifies the glue metaphor. Trap: Overgeneralizing the warning about outsiders into a rejection of ritual or of Durkheim.

qs.q: According to the passage, researchers who measure the physiology of people in synchronized activities report that these participants:
o: tend to show converging heart rates and breathing and afterward behave more generously toward one another.
Correct: This is stated directly in the second paragraph.
tend to agree more closely about the meaning of the ceremony and then become less generous toward outsiders.
The passage says people often disagree on meaning, and no result about generosity to outsiders is reported.
tend to experience a heightened emotional state only when they hold the same beliefs about the symbol being honored.
Belief is not stated as a requirement.

Nothing is reported about repetition weakening responses.
qs.x: This is stated directly in the second paragraph. Trap: Importing the author's later point about outsiders into the research findings.

qs.q: The author describes the cynic's view that ritual costs are an unfortunate by-product in order to:
o: show that skeptics of Durkheim have correctly identified the main weakness in his theory of effervescence.
The cynic is not presented as correct about Durkheim.
prove that groups making the greatest demands on members eventually lose their capacity to bind them.
The passage says demanding groups often show the strongest loyalty, within limits.

The passage says easy ceremonies lose their capacity to bind.
