Correct: The cynic's view is set up so the author can offer the signaling account.
qs.x: The cynic's view is set up so the author can offer the signaling account. Trap: Treating the cynic's view as the author's own.

qs.q: If the author's account is correct, which of the following would be LEAST likely to build strong loyalty among members of a group?
o: A long initiation involving fasting and repetitive labor, followed by a shared meal for all of those who finish it.
Costly initiation is said to screen out the half-hearted.
A synchronized procession in which participants hold differing views about the meaning of the symbols that they carry.
Disagreement about meaning does not prevent synchrony from binding.
A brief, free ceremony open to anyone, requiring no sacrifice and no coordinated activity.
Correct: Such a ceremony lacks both costly signaling and coordinated bodies, the two mechanisms the author describes.
A costly ceremony that is understood by everyone to signal loyalty to a single community rather than to outsiders.
Signaled loyalty is exactly what the cost mechanism produces.
qs.x: Such a ceremony lacks both costly signaling and coordinated bodies, the two mechanisms the author describes. Trap: Thinking shared interpretation is required for solidarity; the author says shared action matters more.

qs.q: Which finding would most strengthen the author's claim that coordinated action, rather than shared belief, produces cohesion?
o: Randomly assigned to move in unison, participants donated more to fellow participants than those moving out of time, with identical explanations.
Correct: Random assignment to synchrony with identical explanations isolates action from belief.
Participants who rated their belief in a ritual's founding myth as very strong contributed more money to the group's common fund afterward.
That would suggest belief matters, weakening the claim.
Groups whose rituals include an elaborate and detailed myth have survived longer, on average, than groups whose rituals include no myth at all.
Myth detail and survival point toward belief.
Members of groups that perform ceremonies regularly report greater pride in their communities than members of groups that do not.
Pride after regular ceremonies does not separate action from belief.
qs.x: Random assignment to synchrony with identical explanations isolates action from belief. Trap: Choosing evidence that merely links ritual to cohesion without separating action from belief.

qs.q: Which of the following best illustrates the author's concluding point that the 'channel' of shared feeling determines its effects?
o: A seasonal festival attracts visitors from distant regions and raises revenue for the shops and inns of a small town.
Revenue is not about direction of solidarity.
A mourning ceremony is performed by participants who offer conflicting accounts of what its symbols are meant to signify.
This illustrates the point about differing interpretations.
A harvest festival strengthens a village's internal bonds while also reinforcing its hostility toward a neighboring village.
Correct: The festival creates cohesion that is directed against outsiders, illustrating that the direction is not fixed by ritual alone.
A funeral brings together relatives who had been estranged and prompts them to resolve a long-running quarrel.
Reconciliation shows cohesion but not its direction toward or against others.
qs.x: The festival creates cohesion that is directed against outsiders, illustrating that the direction is not fixed by ritual alone. Trap: Picking an example that shows ritual producing cohesion but not its direction.

passages.title: FL05 · CARS · Passage 7
text: No one has ever signed the social contract. This simple observation has been the standard objection to social contract theory since the eighteenth century, and it seems fatal. If the legitimacy of government is supposed to rest on an agreement, then the lack of any actual agreement leaves the state without a foundation. Philosophers have responded in various ways. John Locke suggested that anyone who accepts the benefits of living under a government, by traveling its roads or owning its land, has given tacit consent. But a citizen who has never had a realistic option to leave, and who has never been asked a question, can hardly be said to have consented to anything. Tacit consent of this sort is consent in name only.

The better response is to concede the objection and deny that it touches the theory's real purpose. The classic contract theorists, Thomas Hobbes and Jean-Jacques Rousseau among them, were not writing history. When Hobbes imagined a state of nature in which life was solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short, he was not reporting an anthropological discovery; he was constructing a thought experiment designed to isolate what political order provides. The question of the experiment is not "what did people agree to?" but "what could people in these circumstances reasonably accept?" The contract is a device for testing institutions: if a rule could not be justified to each of the free and equal persons who must live under it, then the rule lacks the authority it claims.

A critic will reply that a hypothetical agreement binds no one. If I would have agreed to buy your car at a reasonable price, that does not oblige me to pay for it. The remark is witty, and it identifies a real distinction, but it mistakes the contract theorist's claim. The theory does not say that a hypothetical contract creates an obligation in the way an actual contract does. It says that the reasons which would lead rational persons to accept a certain arrangement are themselves the grounds of the state's legitimacy. The thought experiment does not supply the obligation; it reveals where the justification lies. What carries the weight is the argument, not the imaginary signature.

This reading has the further virtue of explaining why contract theory has been so productive as a critical instrument. If legitimacy depends on what could be justified to everyone affected, then it is natural to ask whether the arrangements actually in place satisfy that test. Those who are excluded from a political community, or whose interests are systematically ignored, have standing to complain that the supposed contract was never offered to them on acceptable terms. The device has been used to attack slavery, the denial of the vote to women, and the exclusion of the poor from political life, precisely because it requires a justification that survives the scrutiny of the least advantaged.

Of course, the hypothetical contract has its own difficulties. The results depend heavily on how we describe the parties and what they are allowed to know, and different descriptions have produced rival conclusions, from Hobbes's near-absolute sovereign to the limited and accountable governments favored by Locke. Critics are right that this flexibility makes the contract less a proof than a framework for argument. But a framework for argument is no small thing. The social contract does not tell us what the state has done; it asks what it could say for itself, and it holds the state's answer open to inspection by those it governs.

qs.q: The author's main point about social contract theory is that it:
o: succeeds in establishing legitimate political obligation, because rational persons would in fact have agreed to the contract if they had been asked.
The author says the hypothetical contract does not itself create obligations.
fails to ground legitimacy, since neither actual nor tacit consent can be shown to have been given by citizens who never signed anything.
The author concedes the objection but denies it touches the theory's purpose.
is best understood as a thought experiment testing whether institutions can be justified to those they govern, not as a record of agreement.
Correct: The passage concedes that no one signed and defends the contract as a device for justification.
should be restricted to the work of Hobbes, whose account of the state of nature reflects historical findings about early societies.
The author says Hobbes was not reporting history.
qs.x: The passage concedes that no one signed and defends the contract as a device for justification. Trap: Choosing the 'theory fails' answer because the passage opens with the strongest objection.

qs.q: The discussion of Locke's tacit consent serves mainly to:
o: provide the author's preferred solution to the problem that no one has ever signed a contract with the state.
The author rejects it and prefers conceding the objection.
show that Locke and Hobbes agreed about the actual historical origins of legitimate government in the state of nature.
The passage does not claim Locke and Hobbes shared a historical thesis.
illustrate how a hypothetical agreement can generate obligations in the same way that an actual contract would.
The passage says hypothetical contracts do not create obligations in that way.

Correct: The author argues that tacit consent is 'consent in name only.'
qs.x: The author argues that tacit consent is 'consent in name only.' Trap: Treating Locke's view as the author's own; the author calls it consent in name only.

qs.q: The author replies to the claim that a hypothetical contract binds no one by arguing that:
o: a hypothetical contract binds people just as an actual contract does, because the parties would have signed it if asked.
The author explicitly denies that hypothetical contracts create obligation in that way.
the analogy to purchasing a car is mistaken, since governments, unlike private sellers, have a right to demand payment from every citizen.
The passage does not argue that governments have a special right to payment.
the objection is correct, but it applies only to Rousseau, whose version of the theory depends on the consent of the people.
The objection is said to mistake the theory's claim for every theorist, not only Rousseau.
the reasons that would lead rational persons to accept an arrangement ground the state's legitimacy, not the imagined agreement itself.
Correct: The passage says the thought experiment reveals where justification lies; the argument carries the weight.
qs.x: The passage says the thought experiment reveals where justification lies; the argument carries the weight. Trap: Believing the author defends hypothetical consent as real consent.

qs.q: The author would most likely say that a law which benefits the majority but cannot be justified to a particular minority:
o: is valid so long as the minority has remained in the country and so has tacitly agreed to the rules that govern it.

lacks the authority it claims, on the contract theorist's test of what could be justified to each person affected.
Correct: The passage says a rule that could not be justified to each person lacks the authority it claims.
is invalid unless the minority has been asked to sign an actual document accepting its terms and conditions.
The author says actual signatures are not the test.
qs.x: The passage says a rule that could not be justified to each person lacks the authority it claims. Trap: Falling back on tacit consent, which the author rejects.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that the force of the contract lies in the argument rather than in an imagined agreement?
o: Evidence that Hobbes and Locke reached different conclusions because they described the parties to the contract in different ways.
The author already concedes this variation.
Evidence that arguments from the contract were used in the past to criticize slavery and the exclusion of women from voting.
This supports the claim that the contract works as a critical instrument.
Evidence that most citizens would decline to sign a document accepting the terms of the government under which they live.
Refusal to sign is irrelevant to the argument-based reading.
Evidence that people find a thought experiment persuasive only when they believe its parties actually agreed.
Correct: If the reasoning persuades only because of imagined agreement, then agreement, not argument, is doing the work.
qs.x: If the reasoning persuades only because of imagined agreement, then agreement, not argument, is doing the work. Trap: Choosing the option that matches an objection the author already grants in the last paragraph.

qs.q: The author's response to the remark that a hypothetical contract is no contract at all is best described as:
o: dismissing it as a trivial point that confuses the theory with the claim that legitimacy has an anthropological source.
The author grants it identifies a real distinction and does not call it trivial.
accepting it as decisive against the classical theorists but not against modern versions of the contract theory.
The author does not accept it as decisive against anyone.
acknowledging its wit and its force while denying that it targets what the theory actually claims.
Correct: The author calls it witty and identifies a real distinction but says it mistakes the theorist's claim.
welcoming it as a refinement that shows the theory can survive only if it abandons its appeal to consent.
The author does not say the theory must abandon consent.
qs.x: The author calls it witty and identifies a real distinction but says it mistakes the theorist's claim. Trap: Reading the author's reply as a dismissal rather than a qualified rebuttal.

passages.title: FL05 · CARS · Passage 8
text: When a scientific claim is published in a reputable journal, readers tend to assume that it has been checked. The assumption is understandable, since the phrase peer-reviewed is routinely used as a kind of certificate, and public discussions of research often turn on whether a study has passed that hurdle. The difficulty is that peer review was never designed to certify truth. It emerged as a way for editors with limited space and limited expertise to decide which submissions were worth printing, and in that role it is a filter for plausibility, relevance, and competence. A reviewer typically reads a manuscript, sometimes alongside summary tables, and judges whether the methods seem reasonable and the conclusions follow from the reported data. The reviewer rarely sees the raw data, almost never repeats an analysis, and cannot know what the authors chose not to report.

Why, then, has the certificate come to be mistaken for a guarantee? Part of the reason is that the system has legitimately succeeded at what it was built to do. Reviewers do catch errors of logic, missing controls, and exaggerated interpretation, and manuscripts frequently improve as a result. Another part is that journals and universities have found it convenient to let the label stand for more than it means. Funding agencies and hiring committees need a quick measure of quality, and the count of published papers provides one. When the reward system pays for publication rather than for reliability, researchers are encouraged to produce results that look publishable, which means results that are new, clean, and statistically significant.

Replication is the natural remedy, since an effect that exists should appear whenever a competent laboratory looks for it. Large coordinated efforts to repeat published findings in some fields have reported that a surprisingly high proportion of results could not be reproduced, and the finding has been widely discussed as a crisis. Yet it would be an error to interpret every failed replication as the refutation of the original claim. The second laboratory may have used a slightly different population, a different procedure, or an instrument with different sensitivity, and any of these differences may matter. Conversely, a successful replication supports a claim only if both studies avoided the same systematic bias. A single repetition, in either direction, is evidence, but it is not a verdict.

The lesson to draw is not that science is unreliable, but that its reliability lives in a process that is slower and more distributed than the label suggests. A finding becomes trustworthy as independent groups test it, extend it, and fail to break it, and the confidence we can place in it increases with every such test. What the institution needs is to reward that work. One promising proposal is that journals should evaluate a study's question and design before the results are known, committing to publish it regardless of outcome. Such an arrangement removes the temptation to polish a null result into a discovery and gives replication the same standing as novelty.

For the public, the practical implication is modest but important. A single study, however prestigious its venue, should be treated as a promising lead rather than a settled fact. The more relevant questions are whether the result has been repeated, whether the methods were specified in advance, and whether the effect is large enough to survive minor changes in procedure. Peer review is a necessary stage in that long conversation. It is not the end of it.

qs.q: The passage as a whole argues that:
o: peer review certifies the truth of published findings, but replication is needed because modern journals publish too many studies for any reviewers to read.
The author says review was never designed to certify truth.
the replication crisis shows that most published science is unreliable, and so the public should disregard findings that appear in journals.
The author says science is not unreliable and that public should treat a single study as a lead.

The author argues for publishing regardless of outcome and says failed replications are not verdicts.
peer review filters submissions for plausibility rather than certifying truth, so reliability depends on slower replication that institutions should reward.
Correct: The author contrasts the filtering role of review with the process of replication and proposes rewarding the latter.
qs.x: The author contrasts the filtering role of review with the process of replication and proposes rewarding the latter. Trap: Treating the replication crisis as proof that science is unreliable; the author says reliability lives in a slower process.

qs.q: The passage states that peer reviewers do all of the following EXCEPT:

repeat the authors' analyses and examine the raw data on which the reported results are based.

catch errors of logic, missing controls, and interpretations that exaggerate what the results show.

The passage says manuscripts frequently improve as a result.

qs.q: According to the passage, a successful replication would provide weaker support for a claim if:
o: the replicating laboratory was less prestigious than the laboratory that had published the original finding.
Prestige is not mentioned as relevant.
the original and the replicating study shared the same systematic bias, such as one flawed measurement.

qs.q: The author discusses registered, pre-evaluated studies in the fourth paragraph in order to:
o: show that peer review has failed completely and should therefore be replaced by a system run by funding agencies.
The author says review is necessary and not a failure.

Correct: The passage presents it as a promising proposal that removes the temptation to polish null results.
