The passage says reviewers cannot detect fraud and does not propose this.
qs.x: The passage presents it as a promising proposal that removes the temptation to polish null results. Trap: Interpreting the proposal as a replacement for peer review rather than a change in what is evaluated and when.

qs.q: Which finding would most support the author's claim that rewarding publication encourages publishable, statistically significant results?
o: Surveys showing that most working researchers regard peer review as an essential component of the whole scientific enterprise today.
Researchers' valuation of peer review is irrelevant to incentives.
Analyses showing that the share of published papers reporting significant results far exceeds what chance and typical study power predict.
Correct: An excess of significant results suggests selection for publishable results.
Reports that some reviewers recommend additional controls or analyses before they will approve a manuscript for printing.
Reviewer recommendations do not bear on incentives for significance.
Evidence that replication projects reproduced results at lower rates in fields where studies typically use small samples and flexible methods.
Sample size and reproducibility is a different issue.
qs.x: An excess of significant results suggests selection for publishable results. Trap: Choosing an option about the replication crisis in general rather than about incentive-driven selection.

qs.q: A person reads news of a single new study reporting a surprising health benefit. The passage suggests the most reasonable response is to:
o: accept the finding as reliable because it has been peer-reviewed and published in a respected journal.
The author says peer review is not a guarantee.
reject the finding because peer review cannot detect fraud and most surprising results fail to replicate.
The author says science is not unreliable and does not recommend blanket rejection.
wait to learn whether the result has been repeated and whether the methods were specified in advance before changing any habits.
Correct: The final paragraph advises treating a single study as a promising lead and asking about repetition and pre-specified methods.
accept the finding if the reported effect reached statistical significance and the sample was reasonably large.
Significance alone does not address the concerns raised in the passage.
qs.x: The final paragraph advises treating a single study as a promising lead and asking about repetition and pre-specified methods. Trap: Treating peer review as a certificate, the assumption the passage opens by challenging.

passages.title: FL05 · CARS · Passage 9
text: A familiar picture of judging holds that a court decides a case by finding the applicable rule and applying it,. Another picture, favored by cynics, holds that the real reasons for decisions are political preferences, and that the doctrine of precedent, which instructs judges to follow earlier decisions, is a decorative cover. Neither picture describes what judges in common law systems actually do, and neither can explain why lawyers treat the past decisions of courts as something more than a source of examples. A better account begins by noticing that precedent is neither a rule nor a pretext, but a discipline of justification.

Consider how a precedent operates. A court that decides a case announces a result together with its reasons, and later courts are expected to treat like cases alike. But what counts as a like case is never obvious. Suppose an earlier court held that the owner of a shop is liable to a customer who slips on a wet floor. A later case involves a customer who slips on a wet floor in the parking lot of a shop that does not own the lot. The later judge must decide whether the earlier reasoning, which perhaps emphasized the owner's control over the premises, extends to a situation in which control is divided. In doing so she is neither applying a fixed rule nor deciding what she prefers; she is reasoning by analogy, asking which features of the earlier case supplied its justification and whether they are present again.

This explains the importance of the technique known as distinguishing. A judge who finds the earlier case relevantly different may decline to follow it without overruling it, by showing that the difference matters in light of the principle at stake. Skeptics view this flexibility as evidence of manipulation, since a clever judge can always find some difference. But the practice is constrained by the requirement that the difference be defended publicly, in a written opinion that other judges, lawyers, and the losing party can read and criticize. A distinction that no one finds plausible will be recognized as evasion, and a judge who relies on too many of them will lose authority. The constraint is not mechanical, but it is real.

The doctrine also has a forward-looking function. Because courts know that their reasons will bind future courts, they are encouraged to state those reasons in terms general enough to be applied consistently and narrow enough to be defended. Individuals and businesses, for their part, can organize their affairs in the expectation that similar disputes will be resolved in similar ways. Stability of this kind is valuable even when the rule chosen is not the best one imaginable, since people can plan around a rule they can predict. Yet the doctrine is not designed to freeze the law. When circumstances change or a past decision proves unworkable, courts may overrule it, though they are expected to explain why the benefits of correction outweigh the costs of disturbing settled expectations.

Precedent, then, works less like a chain than like a conversation in which each judge adds to what has been said while remaining answerable to it. The past does not dictate the result, but it supplies the vocabulary of the argument and the standards by which an answer will be judged. That is a more modest form of constraint than the formalist imagines, and a more demanding one than the cynic allows. It requires judges to reason in the open, in a way that connects the present dispute to the ones that came before.

qs.q: The primary claim of the passage is that precedent is:
o: a discipline of public justification, in which judges reason by analogy from earlier cases.
Correct: The author calls precedent 'neither a rule nor a pretext, but a discipline of justification.'
a mechanical device by which judges find the applicable rule and apply it to the facts of the case before them.
That is the formalist picture the author rejects.
a decorative cover for decisions that judges reach on political grounds, since earlier cases can always be distinguished.
That is the cynical picture the author rejects.
a chain of decisions that bind later courts so strictly that overruling a past decision is never permitted.
The passage says courts may overrule decisions with an explanation.
qs.x: The author calls precedent 'neither a rule nor a pretext, but a discipline of justification.' Trap: Picking one of the two pictures the author sets up and then rejects.

qs.q: The example of the customer who slips in the parking lot is used to:
o: show that courts routinely overrule earlier decisions when the facts of a later case are not identical to those of the first.
The passage says distinguishing is not overruling.
demonstrate that judges decide such cases according to their own preferences about which parties ought to be liable.
The author says the judge is neither applying a rule nor deciding what she prefers.
illustrate reasoning by analogy, in which a judge asks which features justified an earlier decision and whether they recur.
Correct: The example shows the judge asking whether the earlier reasoning about control extends to divided control.
prove that an owner who does not control a premises can never be held liable for harm suffered there by customers.
The passage poses a question and does not state an outcome.
qs.x: The example shows the judge asking whether the earlier reasoning about control extends to divided control. Trap: Concluding that the example resolves the case rather than illustrating the method.

qs.q: According to the passage, what restrains a judge's use of the technique of distinguishing?
o: The rule that a judge may distinguish a case only after the higher court has approved of the proposed difference.
No such approval requirement is mentioned.
The prohibition on finding any difference between cases that were decided within the preceding decade of the court's own case law.
No such time-based prohibition is mentioned.
The expectation that a judge who distinguishes an earlier case must also overrule it in the very same written opinion.
The passage says distinguishing is done without overruling.
The requirement that any difference be defended in a written opinion open to criticism by lawyers, judges, and the losing party.
Correct: The passage says distinctions must be defended publicly and implausible ones lose authority.
qs.x: The passage says distinctions must be defended publicly and implausible ones lose authority. Trap: Assuming a formal procedural limit; the constraint is the discipline of public reasoning.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that precedent is not merely a pretext?
o: A study showing that judges' decisions in similar cases track their political affiliations, whatever precedents or reasons they give.
Correct: If outcomes track politics irrespective of precedent, precedent looks like a cover, as the cynic says.
A study showing that judges frequently cite earlier decisions in their opinions in their written opinions when deciding cases with similar facts.
Frequent citation is compatible with either view and does not show constraint.
A study showing that businesses regularly consult past decisions in order to plan their affairs around the predicted outcomes of disputes.
Planning by businesses supports the stability function.
A study showing that judges who distinguish earlier cases generally write longer opinions than judges who follow them.
Longer opinions are irrelevant to whether precedent constrains.
qs.x: If outcomes track politics irrespective of precedent, precedent looks like a cover, as the cynic says. Trap: Choosing evidence that precedent is used, which does not show whether it constrains outcomes.

qs.q: Under the author's account, a court's decision to overrule a decades-old precedent would be most consistent with the doctrine if the court:
o: announced that its members preferred a different rule and saw no need to give reasons for departing from the earlier decision.
The doctrine demands reasoned justification.
claimed a minor factual difference that it did not defend, so that it could avoid following the earlier decision altogether.
An undefended distinction is evasion, not overruling.
kept the earlier decision despite its being clearly unworkable, because its outcomes could be predicted by people planning ahead.
The author says the doctrine is not designed to freeze the law.
explained that the decision had proved unworkable and that correcting it outweighed the cost of disturbing settled expectations.
Correct: The passage says courts may overrule when circumstances change or a decision proves unworkable, explaining why the benefits outweigh the costs.
qs.x: The passage says courts may overrule when circumstances change or a decision proves unworkable, explaining why the benefits outweigh the costs. Trap: Treating predictability as an absolute value; the author says overruling is allowed with justification.

passages.title: FL05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 1
text: A physics class studies a spring-loaded launcher that fires a small steel ball from ground level over level ground. The launch speed is fixed at 20 m/s, and the launch angle θ above the horizontal is varied. Air resistance is first neglected, and g = 10 m/s². Students treat the horizontal and vertical motions independently: the horizontal velocity is constant, while the vertical velocity changes at a constant rate g downward. For each angle, they recorded the horizontal range, the maximum height, and the total time of flight (Table 1). Figure 1 plots range against launch angle; the range expression is R = v₀² sin 2θ / g. In a second trial, the launcher is mounted horizontally on a platform 45 m above the ground and fires the ball at 12 m/s. Finally, the students repeat the 45° launch with a light foam ball, for which air resistance is significant, and compare it with the steel ball.

qs.q: According to Table 1 and Figure 1, the ball has the same range when launched at 15° and at 75°. The best explanation is that:
o: the two launches have the same time of flight, because flight time depends only on the horizontal velocity component
Table 1 lists flight times of 1.04 s and 3.86 s, which differ greatly; flight time depends on the vertical component v₀ sin θ.
the horizontal velocity component is equal at the two angles, so the ball covers equal distance in equal time
The horizontal components are v₀ cos 15° = 19.3 m/s and v₀ cos 75° = 5.2 m/s; equal range arises because the flight times compensate.
the two launches reach the same maximum height, so the ball falls through equal distances and spends equal time aloft
Table 1 lists maximum heights of 1.34 m and 18.7 m, which are very different.
the angles are complementary, so sin 2θ takes the same value (sin 30° = sin 150°) in the range expression
Correct: R = v₀² sin 2θ / g, and 2θ = 30° or 150° gives sin 2θ = 0.5 in both cases, so R = 400(0.5)/10 = 20 m.
qs.x: R = v₀² sin 2θ / g, and 2θ = 30° or 150° gives sin 2θ = 0.5 in both cases, so R = 400(0.5)/10 = 20 m. Trap: Assuming equal range implies equal flight time or equal horizontal speed; only the product of the two is equal.

qs.q: Using Table 1, approximately how long does the ball launched at 45° take to reach the top of its path?
o: About 0.7 s, one quarter of the listed time, because the ball must decelerate vertically twice before landing
Nothing in the motion gives a quarter-time; the rise and fall each take half of the total.
About 2.0 s, the flight time of the 30° launch, because both trajectories share the same vertical acceleration
The 30° flight time depends on a different vertical component (10 m/s), so it does not apply to the 45° launch.
About 2.8 s, the full time of flight listed in Table 1, because the ball reaches the top at the end of its flight
2.83 s is the total time for the up-and-down trip, not the time to the apex.
About 1.4 s, half of the 2.83 s total flight time, because the rise and fall of the path are symmetric
Correct: At the top the vertical velocity is zero: t = v₀ sin 45°/g = 14.1/10 = 1.41 s, which is half of 2.83 s.
qs.x: At the top the vertical velocity is zero: t = v₀ sin 45°/g = 14.1/10 = 1.41 s, which is half of 2.83 s. Trap: Reading the total flight time from the table as the time to maximum height.

qs.q: In the second trial, the ball is fired horizontally at 12 m/s from a platform 45 m high. How far from the base of the platform does it land?
o: 108 m, obtained by using a fall time of 2h/g = 9.0 s in the horizontal distance calculation
2h/g also ignores the square root; solving h = ½gt² for t gives t = √(2h/g).
36 m, because the ball falls for 3.0 s while moving horizontally at a constant 12 m/s
Correct: The vertical motion starts with zero vertical speed: 45 = ½(10)t², so t = 3.0 s, and x = 12 × 3.0 = 36 m.
25 m, obtained by using a fall time of √(h/g) ≈ 2.1 s in the horizontal distance calculation
√(h/g) omits the factor of 2 in h = ½gt².
54 m, obtained by using a fall time of h/g = 4.5 s in the horizontal distance calculation
h/g is not what the kinematic equation gives; the correct expression is √(2h/g).
qs.x: The vertical motion starts with zero vertical speed: 45 = ½(10)t², so t = 3.0 s, and x = 12 × 3.0 = 36 m. Trap: Using h/g or 2h/g for the fall time instead of √(2h/g).

qs.q: Compared with the steel ball in Table 1, a foam ball launched at 45° and the same speed in air will most likely:
o: land short of 40 m but on a perfectly symmetric path, because drag removes equal speed on the way up and the way down
Drag is largest when the ball is fastest and loses less speed on the way down in the horizontal direction; the path is skewed, not symmetric.
land short of 40 m and descend more steeply than it rose, because drag reduces the horizontal velocity throughout the flight
Correct: Drag opposes the velocity, so it slows the horizontal motion, shortening the range and making the descent steeper than the ascent.
land beyond 40 m, because drag reduces the downward acceleration and lengthens the time the ball remains in the air
Drag adds to gravity on the way up and subtracts from it on the way down; the flight cannot be longer overall than the vacuum case.
land at 40 m, because the horizontal and vertical motions remain independent even when a velocity-dependent drag force acts
Drag has horizontal and vertical components, so the two motions are no longer independent.
qs.x: Drag opposes the velocity, so it slows the horizontal motion, shortening the range and making the descent steeper than the ascent. Trap: Assuming the independence of horizontal and vertical motion still holds with air resistance.

qs.q: At the highest point of the 60° trajectory in Table 1, what fraction of the ball's initial kinetic energy remains as kinetic energy?
o: One-half, because kinetic and potential energy are shared equally by the ball at the highest point of its path
The split of energy depends on the launch angle; at 60° it is 1/4 to 3/4, not 1/2 to 1/2 (that occurs at 45°).
One-quarter, because only the horizontal component v₀ cos 60° = 10 m/s remains and KE scales with speed squared
Correct: KE_top/KE₀ = (10)²/(20)² = 1/4; the remaining three-quarters has become gravitational potential energy (check: mgh = m(10)(15) = 150m = ¾ × 200m).
None, because the velocity of the ball at the top of the path is zero and so its kinetic energy is zero
Only the vertical velocity is zero at the top; the horizontal velocity is still 10 m/s.
Three-quarters, because the vertical component v₀ sin 60° ≈ 17.3 m/s is the part of the velocity that remains at the top
The vertical component is the part that is lost at the apex; three-quarters is the potential energy fraction.
qs.x: KE_top/KE₀ = (10)²/(20)² = 1/4; the remaining three-quarters has become gravitational potential energy (check: mgh = m(10)(15) = 150m = ¾ × 200m). Trap: Thinking the ball is momentarily at rest at the top; the horizontal velocity persists.

graph.title: Figure 1. Range versus launch angle (no air resistance)

passages.title: FL05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 2
text: A thermochemistry student wants the standard enthalpy of formation of liquid ethanol, which cannot be measured directly because carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen do not combine cleanly to give ethanol. Instead, the student applies Hess's law to combustion data collected at 298 K and listed in Table 1. Hess's law states that the enthalpy change of an overall reaction equals the sum of the enthalpy changes of the steps into which it can be divided, because enthalpy is a state function. All combustion products are assumed to be CO₂(g) and H₂O(l). The student also burns a 2.30 g sample of ethanol (molar mass 46.1 g/mol) in a bomb calorimeter whose total heat capacity, including its water bath, is 10.0 kJ/K, and records the temperature rise. A teacher points out that a bomb calorimeter operates at constant volume and measures ΔU, but that ΔH and ΔU differ only slightly for this reaction, so the difference is neglected here.

qs.q: Which value is the standard enthalpy of formation of liquid ethanol, 2 C(graphite) + 3 H₂(g) + ½ O₂(g) → C₂H₅OH(l), obtained from Table 1?
o: −277 kJ/mol, from 2(−393.5) + 3(−285.8) − (−1367), with reaction (3) reversed so that ethanol is a product
Correct: Multiply (1) by 2 and (2) by 3, and reverse (3) so that ethanol appears as a product: −787 − 857.4 + 1367 = −277 kJ/mol.
−3011 kJ/mol, from 2(−393.5) + 3(−285.8) + (−1367), adding reaction (3) as written without reversing it
Reaction (3) has ethanol as a reactant, so it must be reversed (sign changed) rather than added as written.
+277 kJ/mol, from 2(−393.5) + 3(−285.8) + (−1367) with the sign of the final result then reversed, as for an endothermic step
A sign error: the formation reaction of ethanol is exothermic by the Hess's law sum, not endothermic.
+294 kJ/mol, from 2(−393.5) + (−285.8) − (−1367), counting only one mole of H₂ and so one mole of H₂O(l)
Three moles of H₂ are required to supply the six hydrogens in 3 H₂O; using one mole of water leaves the cycle unbalanced.
qs.x: Multiply (1) by 2 and (2) by 3, and reverse (3) so that ethanol appears as a product: −787 − 857.4 + 1367 = −277 kJ/mol. Trap: Forgetting to reverse the combustion reaction (change the sign) or to multiply by the stoichiometric coefficients.

qs.q: What temperature rise does the student record when the 2.30 g sample of ethanol burns completely in the calorimeter?
o: 3.4 K, since only half of the sample is assumed to burn and release its heat to the calorimeter
Combustion is stated to be complete, so the full 0.0499 mol contributes.
6.8 K, since 0.0499 mol of ethanol releases about 68 kJ and the calorimeter absorbs 10.0 kJ per kelvin
68 K, since the heat released in kilojoules is read directly as the temperature change of the bath
The heat must be divided by the heat capacity (10.0 kJ/K) to get ΔT; 68 is the heat in kJ.
3.0 K, since the heat released per gram of ethanol (29.7 kJ) is divided by the heat capacity instead of the heat for 2.30 g
29.7 kJ is the heat for only 1.00 g; the sample is 2.30 g, so the heat is 2.30 × 29.7 = 68.2 kJ.
qs.x: n = 2.30/46.1 = 0.0499 mol; q = 0.0499 × 1367 = 68.2 kJ; ΔT = 68.2/10.0 = 6.8 K. Trap: Forgetting to convert grams to moles or to divide the heat by the calorimeter's heat capacity.

qs.q: Suppose the combustion of ethanol in reaction (3) produced H₂O(g) instead of H₂O(l). Compared with −1367 kJ/mol, the enthalpy change would be:
o: more negative, because the greater entropy of gaseous products makes the reaction more exothermic than the one forming liquid
Entropy affects ΔG, not ΔH; gas-phase products absorb heat on forming from liquid, making ΔH less negative.
unchanged, because enthalpy is a state function and the identity or phase of the products does not matter to ΔH
State function means ΔH is path-independent, not independent of the final state; different product phases have different enthalpies.
less negative, because vaporizing the three moles of water absorbs about 3 × 44 kJ that the liquid-product reaction does not require
Correct: H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) is endothermic (about +44 kJ/mol), so forming gas instead of liquid leaves the overall reaction about 132 kJ less exothermic (≈ −1235 kJ/mol).
more negative, because forming a gas releases the energy that was stored in the attractions between liquid water molecules
Forming a gas from a liquid requires energy input (breaking intermolecular attractions), not release.
qs.x: H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) is endothermic (about +44 kJ/mol), so forming gas instead of liquid leaves the overall reaction about 132 kJ less exothermic (≈ −1235 kJ/mol). Trap: Treating 'state function' as meaning that product phases do not affect ΔH.

qs.q: What is ΔH for the reaction 4 CO₂(g) + 6 H₂O(l) → 2 C₂H₅OH(l) + 6 O₂(g)?
o: −2734 kJ, since the reaction is reaction (3) doubled but not reversed
Not reversing leaves ethanol as a reactant and gives an exothermic value; the written reaction forms ethanol, so the sign flips.
+2734 kJ, since the reaction is reaction (3) reversed to form ethanol and then doubled for two moles
Correct: Reversing (3) changes the sign to +1367 for 1 mol of ethanol; doubling all coefficients doubles the enthalpy change to +2734 kJ.
+683.5 kJ, since the reaction is reaction (3) reversed and halved to give one mole of ethanol per two moles of CO₂
Halving would give 0.5 mol ethanol from 1 mol CO₂, not 2 mol ethanol from 4 mol CO₂.
+1367 kJ, since the reaction is reaction (3) reversed with the coefficients left unchanged
The written equation produces 2 mol ethanol, so the value for 1 mol must be doubled.
qs.x: Reversing (3) changes the sign to +1367 for 1 mol of ethanol; doubling all coefficients doubles the enthalpy change to +2734 kJ. Trap: Multiplying the coefficients without doubling ΔH, or forgetting to change the sign when reversing.

h: ΔH° (kJ per mole of reaction as written)

passages.title: FL05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 3
text: A laboratory studies how a gas in a rigid flask exerts pressure by attaching an open-end mercury manometer to it. The flask is sealed at 300 K when its gas is at atmospheric pressure (760 mm Hg), so the mercury levels in both arms of the U-tube are equal. The flask is then heated, and the height difference h between the mercury levels in the two arms is recorded (Table 1, Figure 1). Mercury has a density of 13,600 kg/m³, so 1 mm Hg corresponds to 133 Pa; take g = 9.8 m/s². The gas is ideal, and the temperature of the mercury is assumed constant, the flask volume is constant, and the change in manometer fluid volume is ignored. On a later day, a storm lowers the atmospheric pressure to 740 mm Hg, and the student repeats the measurement at 360 K. The student also considers replacing mercury with water (density 1,000 kg/m³) in the same arrangement.

qs.q: At 360 K, which value is the gauge pressure of the gas in the flask?
o: 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa, the absolute pressure of the gas (912 mm Hg) rather than its excess over atmospheric pressure
912 mm Hg × 133 Pa/mm Hg ≈ 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa is the absolute pressure; gauge pressure subtracts the 760 mm Hg atmosphere.
1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, the atmospheric pressure alone, which the open arm of the manometer contributes
The atmospheric pressure is the reference, not the gauge value; the gauge value is the excess due to heating.
2.0 × 10⁷ Pa, obtained by using the height of 152 in millimeters rather than 0.152 in meters in ρgh
h must be in meters (0.152 m) for SI; using 152 gives a value 1000 times too large.
2.0 × 10⁴ Pa, the hydrostatic pressure ρgh of a 152 mm column of mercury
qs.x: P_gauge = ρgh = (13,600)(9.8)(0.152) = 2.03 × 10⁴ Pa. Trap: Reporting absolute pressure as gauge pressure, or forgetting to convert millimeters to meters.

qs.q: At 360 K, how do the mercury levels in the two arms compare?
o: The level in the open arm is 912 mm higher than in the flask arm, because the manometer reads the absolute pressure
An open-end manometer shows the difference between gas and atmospheric pressure, not the absolute pressure.
The levels remain equal, because the gas pressure and the atmospheric pressure both act on the mercury surface
The levels are equal only when the gas pressure equals atmospheric pressure (300 K).
The level in the flask arm is 152 mm higher than in the open arm, because the heated gas is drawn upward into the tube
Gas pressure pushes the mercury surface down in the flask arm; the gas does not pull mercury upward.
The level in the open arm is 152 mm higher than in the flask arm, because the gas pressure exceeds atmospheric pressure
Correct: Higher gas pressure pushes mercury down in the flask arm and up in the open arm, and the difference equals the gauge pressure, 152 mm Hg.
qs.x: Higher gas pressure pushes mercury down in the flask arm and up in the open arm, and the difference equals the gauge pressure, 152 mm Hg. Trap: Thinking a higher gas pressure raises the mercury level on the gas side.

qs.q: If the mercury were replaced by water, what height difference would the gauge pressure at 360 K produce?
o: About 11.2 mm, obtained by dividing 152 mm by 13.6 instead of multiplying by the density ratio
A less dense fluid needs a taller column, not a shorter one; 152/13.6 inverts the ratio.
About 0.152 m, because the same pressure difference produces the same column height in any fluid
For a fixed pressure, h = P/ρg depends on the fluid's density.
About 2.07 m, because column height scales inversely with fluid density and water is 13.6 times less dense
About 12.4 m, obtained by multiplying the absolute pressure of 912 mm Hg by 13.6 instead of the gauge pressure
The difference of the manometer levels reflects gauge pressure; using the absolute pressure gives 12.4 m.
qs.x: h = P/ρg = 20,260/(1000 × 9.8) = 2.07 m, i.e., 152 mm × 13.6. Trap: Believing the column height is independent of the fluid, or inverting the density ratio.

qs.q: Figure 1 is extended linearly to h = −760 mm. Which temperature does this point represent, and what does it signify?
o: 0 K, where the absolute pressure of the ideal gas in the rigid flask extrapolates to zero on the linear plot
Correct: The slope is 76/30 = 2.53 mm/K; h = P − 760, so h = −760 means P = 0, which occurs at T = 300 − 760/2.53 = 0 K.
760 K, where the absolute pressure of the gas rises to equal atmospheric pressure in the manometer
At h = −760 the gas pressure is zero, not equal to atmospheric pressure (which occurs at 300 K, h = 0).
273 K, where the gas pressure falls below 760 mm Hg and the gas condenses to a liquid in the flask
273 K is the freezing point of water in kelvin and has no special meaning for this gas at constant volume.
300 K, where the gauge pressure vanishes and the mercury columns stand at equal levels in the two arms
h = 0 at 300 K, not −760 mm; −760 mm corresponds to zero absolute pressure.
qs.x: The slope is 76/30 = 2.53 mm/K; h = P − 760, so h = −760 means P = 0, which occurs at T = 300 − 760/2.53 = 0 K. Trap: Reading the x-intercept of the line as the temperature where the pressure is zero.

qs.q: During the storm (atmospheric pressure 740 mm Hg) the student measures the height difference at 360 K. What value is observed, assuming the gas pressure is unchanged?
o: 172 mm, with the open arm higher, because the gas pressure of 912 mm Hg exceeds the lowered atmospheric pressure by 172 mm Hg
Correct: h = P_gas − P_atm = 912 − 740 = 172 mm Hg.
20 mm, with the open arm higher, because the height difference equals the change in atmospheric pressure alone
The height difference is the full gauge pressure, 912 − 740, not just the atmospheric change.
132 mm, with the open arm higher, because the lower atmospheric pressure reduces the pressure difference across the manometer
Lower atmospheric pressure presses less on the open arm, so the mercury is pushed up higher in it; the difference increases.
152 mm, with the open arm higher, because the gas pressure at 360 K is unchanged and so the height difference is also unchanged
The gas pressure is unchanged, but the reference (atmosphere) fell, so the difference increases.
qs.x: h = P_gas − P_atm = 912 − 740 = 172 mm Hg. Trap: Assuming the manometer reading is a property of the gas only and does not depend on atmospheric pressure.

graph.title: Figure 1. Manometer height difference versus flask temperature

passages.title: FL05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 4
text: Students build a circuit from two ideal batteries and three resistors and use it to test Kirchhoff's rules. Battery 1 (ε₁ = 12 V) in series with R₁ = 2.0 Ω forms the left branch. A single resistor R₃ = 3.0 Ω forms the middle branch. Battery 2 (ε₂ = 2.0 V) in series with R₂ = 4.0 Ω forms the right branch. The three branches are connected between the same top and bottom nodes, and the positive terminal of each battery faces the top node. Current I₁ flows upward through the left branch into the top node, and I₃ and I₂ flow downward through the middle and right branches. An ammeter in each branch and a voltmeter across each resistor gave the readings in Table 1. The students then opened a switch in the right branch, so that no current flowed through Battery 2 and R₂, and they remeasured the circuit. Wires have negligible resistance, and the meters are assumed to be ideal. The students also check the readings against the junction rule at the top node.

qs.q: Which loop-rule equation for the loop containing Battery 1, R₁, and R₃ is satisfied by the data in Table 1?
o: 12 + 2.0 I₁ − 3.0 I₃ = 0, since the potential rises across R₁ when moving with the current through it
Moving with the current through a resistor lowers the potential, so R₁ enters with a negative sign; 12 + 6 − 6 = 12 V, not zero.
12 − 2.0 I₁ − 3.0 I₃ = 0, since 12 − 6.0 − 6.0 = 0 for the left loop
Correct: Going around the loop from the positive terminal of Battery 1 through R₁ and R₃ with the current, the potential falls across each resistor: ε₁ − I₁R₁ − I₃R₃ = 0, and 12 − 6.0 − 6.0 = 0.
12 − 2.0 I₁ − 3.0 I₂ = 0, since the right branch carries the current that flows through R₃
R₃ carries I₃ = 2.0 A, not I₂ = 1.0 A; the equation would give 12 − 6 − 3 = 3 V, not zero.
12 − 2.0 I₁ + 3.0 I₃ = 0, since moving through R₃ against the current raises the potential
Traversing R₃ in the direction of the current lowers the potential; the sign is wrong and 12 − 6 + 6 = 12 V, not zero.
qs.x: Going around the loop from the positive terminal of Battery 1 through R₁ and R₃ with the current, the potential falls across each resistor: ε₁ − I₁R₁ − I₃R₃ = 0, and 12 − 6.0 − 6.0 = 0. Trap: Using the wrong branch current in a resistor term or giving a resistor drop the wrong sign.

qs.q: In Table 1, Battery 1 delivers 36 W, but the resistors dissipate a total of 34 W. Where does the remaining 2.0 W go?
o: Into heat in the connecting wires, which have small but nonzero resistance, so that part of the power is lost in the circuit
The wires are stated to have negligible resistance, so they dissipate no measurable power.
Into chemical energy stored in Battery 2, because current enters its positive terminal and the battery is being charged
Correct: Current I₂ = 1.0 A enters the positive terminal of Battery 2 (ε₂ = 2.0 V), so it absorbs P = ε₂I₂ = 2.0 W; 36 = 18 + 4 + 12 + 2.
Into radiation from the meters, whose internal resistances dissipate part of the power supplied by the batteries
The meters are assumed to be ideal, so they dissipate no power; the missing 2.0 W is accounted for by Battery 2.
Into the top node, where the current divides and a portion of the energy remains with the charge that returns to Battery 1
A node stores no energy; charge conservation holds there, and energy is accounted for by the elements.
qs.x: Current I₂ = 1.0 A enters the positive terminal of Battery 2 (ε₂ = 2.0 V), so it absorbs P = ε₂I₂ = 2.0 W; 36 = 18 + 4 + 12 + 2. Trap: Assuming a battery can only deliver power, never absorb it.

qs.q: After the switch in the right branch is opened, what is the potential difference across R₃?
o: 6.0 V, since the voltage across the middle branch is unaffected by opening a different branch of the circuit
The middle branch's voltage is set by the circuit as a whole; with Battery 2 removed, the current through R₃ rises to 2.4 A.
4.8 V, since this is the potential difference across R₁ rather than across R₃ in the remaining circuit
4.8 V is the drop across R₁ (2.4 A × 2.0 Ω); R₃ drops (2.4 A × 3.0 Ω) = 7.2 V.
7.2 V, since the remaining series circuit carries 12/(2.0 + 3.0) = 2.4 A through R₃
Correct: With the right branch open, Battery 1 drives I = 12/5.0 = 2.4 A through R₁ and R₃ in series, so V₃ = (2.4)(3.0) = 7.2 V.
12 V, since with no current in the right branch the full emf of Battery 1 appears across R₃
R₁ still carries 2.4 A and drops 4.8 V, so R₃ receives only the remaining 7.2 V.
qs.x: With the right branch open, Battery 1 drives I = 12/5.0 = 2.4 A through R₁ and R₃ in series, so V₃ = (2.4)(3.0) = 7.2 V. Trap: Assuming the node voltage does not change when a branch is removed.

qs.q: Why must the ammeters be connected as they were in this experiment?
o: In series with each branch, with a resistance much larger than that of the branch, so that the current through them is easily detected
A large series resistance would reduce the branch current and disturb the measurement.
In parallel with each branch, with a resistance much larger than that of the branch, so that they divert very little of the current
Parallel connection measures a potential difference (voltmeter use), and a large resistance is the voltmeter requirement.
In series with each branch, with a resistance much smaller than that of the branch, so that they do not alter the current being measured
Correct: An ammeter measures the current passing through it, so it must be in series; a small internal resistance leaves the branch current essentially unchanged.
In parallel with each resistor, with a resistance much smaller than that of the resistor, so that the full potential difference appears across them
A small resistance in parallel would act as a short circuit across the resistor, diverting almost all the current.
qs.x: An ammeter measures the current passing through it, so it must be in series; a small internal resistance leaves the branch current essentially unchanged. Trap: Mixing up the connection and resistance requirements for ammeters and voltmeters.

passages.title: FL05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 5
text: A laser beam is directed into a semicircular glass block of refractive index n = 1.50 so that it travels along a radius of the curved face and strikes the center of the flat face from inside the glass, where the glass meets air (n = 1.00). Because the beam enters along a radius, it is not bent at the curved surface. A student varies the angle of incidence θ₁ in the glass, measured from the normal, and records the angle θ₂ of the refracted ray in air (Table 1, Figure 1). At the largest angle, no refracted ray emerged, and the reflected ray became bright. In a second experiment, the student replaces the air with water (n = 1.33) on the flat face and repeats the measurements. Finally, the student examines a thin glass fiber in which a core is surrounded by a cladding of different refractive index, and asks how light is guided along it. The refractive index of a medium is n = c/v, where v is the speed of light in that medium. Use c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

qs.q: Which value is the critical angle for the glass–air interface?
o: 56.3°, from tan θc = 1.50/1.00 in place of the sine ratio in Snell's law
Snell's law uses sines, and the ratio must be n₂/n₁ = 1/1.5, not 1.5.
48.2°, from taking the complement of the correct critical angle as the angle measured from the interface surface
48.2° would be the angle between the ray and the interface, not from the normal.
33.7°, from tan θc = 1.00/1.50 in place of the sine ratio that appears in Snell's law
Snell's law uses sines of the angles, not tangents.
41.8°, from sin θc = n(air)/n(glass) = 1.00/1.50, the angle at which the refracted ray grazes the surface
Correct: At the critical angle θ₂ = 90°, so n₁ sin θc = n₂ sin 90°, and sin θc = 1/1.5 = 0.667, giving θc = 41.8°. This agrees with Table 1, since 40° refracts and 45° does not.
qs.x: At the critical angle θ₂ = 90°, so n₁ sin θc = n₂ sin 90°, and sin θc = 1/1.5 = 0.667, giving θc = 41.8°. This agrees with Table 1, since 40° refracts and 45° does not. Trap: Using tangent instead of sine, or measuring the angle from the surface instead of the normal.

qs.q: A beam of wavelength 600 nm in air enters the glass. Which pair gives its wavelength and frequency in the glass?
o: 400 nm and 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz, since the frequency increases in proportion to the refractive index of the glass
The frequency does not change at a boundary; only speed and wavelength change.
900 nm and 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz, since the wavelength increases in proportion to the refractive index of the glass
The wavelength decreases when light slows in a denser medium (λ = λ₀/n).
400 nm and 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz, since the speed drops to c/1.5 while the frequency stays fixed
Correct: Frequency is set by the source: f = c/λ = (3.0 × 10⁸)/(600 × 10⁻⁹) = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. In glass λ = λ₀/n = 600/1.5 = 400 nm.
600 nm and 3.3 × 10¹⁴ Hz, since the wavelength is fixed while the frequency decreases as the speed drops
The frequency is unchanged; the wavelength shrinks as the speed decreases.
qs.x: Frequency is set by the source: f = c/λ = (3.0 × 10⁸)/(600 × 10⁻⁹) = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. In glass λ = λ₀/n = 600/1.5 = 400 nm. Trap: Thinking that the frequency, rather than the wavelength, changes on entering a new medium.

qs.q: In Table 1, why is the refracted angle θ₂ in air larger than the incident angle θ₁ in glass?
o: Part of the beam energy is absorbed by the glass at the interface, so the emergent ray is deflected away from the normal
Refraction does not depend on absorption; the angle is fixed by the ratio of refractive indices.
Light travels faster in air than in glass, so the ray bends away from the normal on leaving the glass
Correct: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ with n₁ > n₂ requires sin θ₂ > sin θ₁; the ray goes from a slower medium to a faster one, bending away from the normal.
Light travels slower in air than in glass, so the ray bends away from the normal to keep its wavefronts continuous
Light is faster, not slower, in air (v = c/n).
The frequency of light increases on entering air, so the ray bends away from the normal in proportion to that change
The frequency is unchanged across the boundary.
qs.x: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ with n₁ > n₂ requires sin θ₂ > sin θ₁; the ray goes from a slower medium to a faster one, bending away from the normal. Trap: Believing refraction toward or away from the normal depends on absorption or on frequency change.

qs.q: In the second experiment, the glass faces water (n = 1.33). What is the new critical angle?
o: 27.5°, the complement of the correct angle, measured from the surface instead of the normal
27.5° is 90° − 62.5°, which is the angle from the surface.
48.6°, the refracted angle observed for a 30° incident ray in the glass–air experiment
48.6° is a refracted angle in air, unrelated to the water interface.
41.8°, the value found for the glass–air interface since the glass is unchanged
The critical angle depends on both media; water's index of 1.33 raises it.
62.5°, from sin θc = n(water)/n(glass) = 1.33/1.50 for light incident from the glass side
Correct: sin θc = n₂/n₁ = 1.33/1.50 = 0.887, so θc = 62.5°; the smaller index contrast gives a larger critical angle than for glass–air.
qs.x: sin θc = n₂/n₁ = 1.33/1.50 = 0.887, so θc = 62.5°; the smaller index contrast gives a larger critical angle than for glass–air. Trap: Applying the glass–air critical angle to a different interface.

qs.q: In the glass fiber, light is confined by total internal reflection. Which condition is required?
o: The core must have a higher refractive index than the cladding, and rays must strike the boundary at angles greater than the critical angle
Correct: TIR requires light traveling from higher to lower n at an angle of incidence above θc.
The core must have a lower refractive index than the cladding, so that rays bend toward the normal at the boundary and return to the core
Light going from a lower-n core to a higher-n cladding is always refracted and cannot undergo TIR.
The core must have a higher refractive index than the cladding, and rays must strike the boundary at angles smaller than the critical angle
Angles smaller than the critical angle allow the light to refract out of the core.
The core must have the same refractive index as the cladding, and the boundary must be rough enough to scatter light back inward
Equal indices give no reflection at all; the light would pass into the cladding.
qs.x: TIR requires light traveling from higher to lower n at an angle of incidence above θc. Trap: Confusing which medium must have the higher index, or which side of the critical angle gives TIR.

graph.title: Figure 1. Refracted angle in air versus incident angle in glass

passages.title: FL05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 6
text: The Bohr model explains the line spectrum of hydrogen by assuming that the electron occupies quantized energy levels given by Eₙ = −13.6 eV/n², and that a photon is emitted when the electron drops between levels. A student examines the visible Balmer series, in which all transitions end on n = 2, by passing the light of a hydrogen discharge tube through a diffraction grating and measuring the wavelengths. Photon wavelengths are calculated from λ = hc/E, with hc = 1240 eV·nm. The results are given in Table 1 and Figure 1, where the wavelength is plotted against the quantum number n of the starting level. The student then considers the He⁺ ion, a one-electron ion with nuclear charge Z = 2, for which Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV, and predicts how its spectrum compares with that of hydrogen. Finally, the student asks which photons a ground-state hydrogen atom can absorb.

qs.q: How much energy is required to ionize a hydrogen atom whose electron is in the n = 2 level?
o: 13.6 eV, the ionization energy of an atom whose electron is in the ground state
13.6 eV ionizes ground-state hydrogen; an excited atom needs less.
10.2 eV, the photon energy for the transition from n = 2 down to n = 1
10.2 eV is the energy released in a transition between bound levels, not the energy to reach E = 0.
3.4 eV, the magnitude of the energy of the n = 2 level
Correct: E₂ = −13.6/4 = −3.4 eV, so 3.4 eV raises the electron to E = 0 (ionization).
1.89 eV, the photon energy for the transition from n = 3 down to n = 2
1.89 eV is the red Balmer line energy, equal to E₃ − E₂, which only reaches n = 3.
qs.x: E₂ = −13.6/4 = −3.4 eV, so 3.4 eV raises the electron to E = 0 (ionization). Trap: Using the ground-state ionization energy for an excited atom.

qs.q: Which energy is released when a He⁺ ion drops from n = 2 to n = 1?
o: 40.8 eV, because the levels scale with Z² = 4 relative to hydrogen
Correct: ΔE = 13.6(4)(1/1² − 1/2²) = 54.4(0.75) = 40.8 eV, four times the hydrogen value (10.2 eV).
10.2 eV, since the transition energy is the same as for hydrogen when only one electron is present
Eₙ scales with Z², so the He⁺ energies are four times those of hydrogen even with one electron.
54.4 eV, because the ion's electron falls from the n = 2 level all the way to the ionization limit
54.4 eV is the ground-state binding energy of He⁺, not the 2 → 1 transition energy.
13.6 eV, because the ion's electron is in a state with the same energy as the hydrogen ground state
13.6 eV is the hydrogen ground-state energy; He⁺ levels are deeper by a factor Z².
qs.x: ΔE = 13.6(4)(1/1² − 1/2²) = 54.4(0.75) = 40.8 eV, four times the hydrogen value (10.2 eV). Trap: Forgetting the Z² scaling of energy levels for hydrogen-like ions.

qs.q: Extrapolating Figure 1 to very large n, the Balmer wavelengths approach which limiting value?
o: About 656 nm, since the red line of Table 1 sets the long-wavelength limit that the series approaches
656 nm is the longest wavelength in the series, not the limit as n increases.
About 410 nm, since the n = 6 line is the last Balmer line that can be observed in the visible region
410 nm is the n = 6 line; the lines keep converging to shorter wavelengths.
About 365 nm, corresponding to the 3.4 eV needed to move from n = 2 to the ionization limit
Correct: As n → ∞, the photon energy → 3.4 eV and λ = 1240/3.4 = 365 nm; wavelengths decrease and converge toward this series limit.
About 91 nm, corresponding to the 13.6 eV needed to move from n = 1 to the ionization limit
91 nm is the Lyman series limit (transitions to n = 1), which lies in the ultraviolet.
qs.x: As n → ∞, the photon energy → 3.4 eV and λ = 1240/3.4 = 365 nm; wavelengths decrease and converge toward this series limit. Trap: Confusing the Balmer series limit with the Lyman series limit.

qs.q: Which photon can be absorbed by a ground-state hydrogen atom, assuming each photon is absorbed only if it exactly fits an allowed transition or exceeds the ionization energy?
o: 10.2 eV, which promotes the electron from n = 1 to n = 2
Correct: E₂ − E₁ = −3.4 − (−13.6) = 10.2 eV, an allowed transition. The other energies match no level difference and are below the 13.6 eV ionization energy.
9.0 eV, which promotes the electron to a level below n = 2 that lies between the allowed levels
There is no allowed level 9.0 eV above the ground state.
11.5 eV, which promotes the electron to a level between n = 2 and n = 3
11.5 eV lies between the n = 2 (10.2 eV) and n = 3 (12.09 eV) transition energies, so it is not absorbed.
12.4 eV, which promotes the electron to a level between n = 3 and n = 4
12.4 eV lies between the n = 3 (12.09 eV) and n = 4 (12.75 eV) transition energies, so it is not absorbed.
qs.x: E₂ − E₁ = −3.4 − (−13.6) = 10.2 eV, an allowed transition. The other energies match no level difference and are below the 13.6 eV ionization energy. Trap: Assuming an atom can absorb any photon energy above the first excitation energy.

graph.title: Figure 1. Balmer line wavelength versus starting level

passages.title: FL05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 7
text: A beverage chemist studies how carbon dioxide dissolves in water. Henry's law states that the concentration of a dissolved gas is proportional to its partial pressure above the solution: [CO₂] = k_H·P(CO₂). Sealed vessels containing 1.00 L of pure water were pressurized with CO₂ at 25 °C until equilibrium was reached, and the dissolved CO₂ was measured. The same measurement was then made at a fixed CO₂ pressure of 1.0 atm while the temperature was varied (Table 1). Figure 1 shows the concentration at 25 °C versus pressure. Reaction of dissolved CO₂ with water to form carbonic acid is ignored. In a final test, a 0.50 L sealed bottle of the beverage carbonated at 3.0 atm is opened and the contents are poured into a glass. The temperature was held constant by a water bath, and the gas phase contained only CO₂. The molar mass of CO₂ is 44 g/mol, and one mole of gas occupies 24.5 L at 25 °C and 1.0 atm.

qs.q: According to Figure 1, which concentration is expected at 25 °C when P(CO₂) = 2.5 atm?
o: 0.33 mol/L, obtained by multiplying the pressure by 0.13, the highest concentration listed in the table
0.13 is the concentration at 4.0 atm, not a multiplier; no such factor applies.
0.13 mol/L, the value at 4.0 atm, because the dissolved concentration levels off once the solution is saturated
The data show no plateau; the concentration rises proportionally up to 4.0 atm.
0.083 mol/L, found by interpolating the linear plot that passes through the origin with k_H = 0.033 mol/(L·atm)
Correct: The plot is linear through the origin: 0.033 × 2.5 = 0.083 mol/L.
0.066 mol/L, the value at 2.0 atm, because the concentrations are measured only at whole-number pressures
Interpolation between 0.066 and 0.099 gives 0.083 mol/L; 2.5 atm lies between the listed values.
qs.x: The plot is linear through the origin: 0.033 × 2.5 = 0.083 mol/L. Trap: Assuming the concentration only takes listed values or plateaus at high pressure.

qs.q: What mass of CO₂ is dissolved in the 0.50 L bottle carbonated at 3.0 atm and 25 °C?
o: 1.1 g, from using the 1.5 atm value of 0.050 mol/L for the dissolved CO₂ concentration
The bottle was carbonated at 3.0 atm, not 1.5 atm.
4.4 g, from using the 1.00 L concentration without scaling for the 0.50 L bottle volume
The bottle holds only 0.50 L, so the moles are halved relative to 1.00 L.
0.049 g, from multiplying the number of moles in the bottle by the molar mass in kg/mol
Molar mass in kg/mol is 0.044; using it with moles gives 0.0022 kg (2.2 g), not 0.049 g.
qs.x: n = 0.099 × 0.50 = 0.0495 mol; mass = 0.0495 × 44 = 2.18 g ≈ 2.2 g. Trap: Forgetting to scale by the volume or misusing the molar mass units.

qs.q: When the bottle carbonated at 4.0 atm is opened to a room with a CO₂ partial pressure near zero, the solution is allowed to equilibrate at 1.0 atm total CO₂ (assume 25 °C). What volume of CO₂ gas leaves 1.00 L of solution?
o: About 2.4 L, from (0.132 − 0.033) mol × 24.5 L/mol, counting only the CO₂ that leaves the solution
Correct: At 1.0 atm the solution retains 0.033 mol/L; 0.099 mol escapes, occupying 0.099 × 24.5 = 2.4 L at 25 °C and 1 atm.
About 1.6 L, from half of the CO₂ that was dissolved before opening, since pressure halves on opening
Pressure falls by a factor of four, not two, and solubility is proportional to pressure.
About 0.81 L, from 0.033 mol × 24.5 L/mol, counting only the CO₂ that remains dissolved
0.033 mol is what remains dissolved, not what leaves.
About 3.2 L, from 0.132 mol × 24.5 L/mol, assuming all of the dissolved CO₂ escapes
Some CO₂ stays dissolved at 1.0 atm (0.033 mol/L), so not all of it escapes.
qs.x: At 1.0 atm the solution retains 0.033 mol/L; 0.099 mol escapes, occupying 0.099 × 24.5 = 2.4 L at 25 °C and 1 atm. Trap: Assuming all the dissolved gas leaves when a bottle is opened.

qs.q: Table 1 shows lower dissolved [CO₂] at 35 °C than at 5 °C at the same pressure. Which statement best explains this?
o: Dissolution of CO₂ is endothermic, so adding heat shifts the equilibrium toward gaseous CO₂ and lowers k_H
If dissolving were endothermic, heating would increase solubility.
Dissolution of CO₂ is exothermic, so adding heat shifts the equilibrium toward gaseous CO₂ and lowers k_H
Correct: Gas solubility generally decreases with temperature because dissolving a gas releases heat (CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq) + heat); by Le Chatelier's principle heating favors the reverse.
Dissolution of CO₂ is exothermic, so adding heat shifts the equilibrium toward dissolved CO₂ and raises k_H
If heat shifted the equilibrium toward dissolved CO₂, solubility would rise with temperature, contrary to the data.
Dissolution of CO₂ is entropy-driven, so a higher temperature makes the process less favorable by lowering ΔS
Dissolving a gas decreases entropy; higher temperature makes −TΔS less favorable, but the key point is that the enthalpy of solution is negative.
qs.x: Gas solubility generally decreases with temperature because dissolving a gas releases heat (CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq) + heat); by Le Chatelier's principle heating favors the reverse. Trap: Choosing the direction of the shift that does not match the sign of ΔH.

qs.q: A gas mixture of 80% N₂ and 20% CO₂ by moles at a total pressure of 5.0 atm is equilibrated with water at 25 °C. Assuming only CO₂ matters, what is the dissolved [CO₂]?
o: 0.0066 mol/L, since the 20% mole fraction is multiplied by 0.033 rather than by the total pressure
The mole fraction must be multiplied by the total pressure first (1.0 atm), then by k_H.
0.033 mol/L, since the partial pressure of CO₂ is 20% of 5.0 atm, which is 1.0 atm
Correct: P(CO₂) = 0.20 × 5.0 = 1.0 atm (Dalton's law), so [CO₂] = 0.033 × 1.0 = 0.033 mol/L.
0.132 mol/L, since the mole fraction of N₂ sets the partial pressure of CO₂
0.80 × 5.0 = 4.0 atm is the N₂ partial pressure, not the CO₂ partial pressure.
0.165 mol/L, since the total pressure of 5.0 atm determines the concentration of dissolved gas
Henry's law uses the partial pressure of the gas, not the total pressure.
qs.x: P(CO₂) = 0.20 × 5.0 = 1.0 atm (Dalton's law), so [CO₂] = 0.033 × 1.0 = 0.033 mol/L. Trap: Using total pressure instead of partial pressure in Henry's law.

graph.title: Figure 1. Dissolved CO₂ concentration versus pressure at 25 °C

passages.title: FL05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 8
text: A chemistry class uses the valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) model to predict molecular shapes and compares the predictions with measured dipole moments (Table 1). In the model, regions of electron density around a central atom, both bonding pairs and lone pairs, arrange themselves to minimize repulsion, and lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs. The steric number is the number of bonded atoms plus the number of lone pairs on the central atom. Experimentally, a molecule's dipole moment is measured in debye (D). A molecule is polar only if its bond dipoles do not cancel when summed as vectors. Students are asked to explain why molecules with polar bonds, such as BF₃ and CCl₄, can still be nonpolar, to account for the bond angle in water (104.5°, compared with the ideal tetrahedral angle of 109.5°), and to predict the geometries of molecules not in the table, including ClF₃ and the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺.

qs.q: BF₃ has polar B–F bonds but a dipole moment of zero, whereas NH₃ has a dipole moment of 1.47 D. Which statement explains this?
o: BF₃ is bent while NH₃ is linear, so the bond dipoles cancel in BF₃ but add in NH₃ because of their different shapes
BF₃ is trigonal planar, not bent, and NH₃ is trigonal pyramidal, not linear.
BF₃ has less polar bonds than NH₃, so its dipole moment is zero even though the bond dipoles do not cancel as vectors
The B–F bond is actually more polar than N–H; the cancellation is due to symmetry.
BF₃ is trigonal planar, so its bond dipoles cancel, whereas the lone pair on NH₃ leaves a nonzero vector sum
Correct: Molecular polarity depends on geometry, not bond polarity alone. Symmetric, lone-pair-free BF₃ has cancelling dipoles; pyramidal NH₃ has a net dipole.
BF₃ has three bonded atoms and NH₃ has three bonded atoms, so the dipole moments differ because of the lone pair's electron count alone
Both have three bonded atoms; the difference is the geometry resulting from the lone pair, not a simple count of electrons.
qs.x: Molecular polarity depends on geometry, not bond polarity alone. Symmetric, lone-pair-free BF₃ has cancelling dipoles; pyramidal NH₃ has a net dipole. Trap: Equating polar bonds with a polar molecule without considering geometry.

qs.q: Why is the H–O–H bond angle in water (104.5°) smaller than the ideal tetrahedral angle?
o: The two lone pairs on oxygen attract the hydrogen atoms, pulling the bonded atoms closer together and shrinking the angle
Lone pairs repel the bonding electron pairs; they do not attract the hydrogen nuclei.
The two lone pairs on oxygen repel the bonding pairs more strongly than the bonding pairs repel each other, compressing the H–O–H angle
Correct: Lone pair–bonding pair repulsion exceeds bonding pair–bonding pair repulsion, so the lone pairs occupy more space and squeeze the bonded atoms together.
The hydrogen atoms repel each other more strongly than the lone pairs, which pushes the bonded atoms toward a smaller angle
The lone pairs, not the hydrogen atoms, are the stronger source of repulsion.
The oxygen atom is sp² hybridized, so the bond angle is closer to 120° but is reduced by the hydrogen bonds in the liquid
Oxygen in water is approximately sp³, and sp² hybridization would give an angle larger than 109.5°, not smaller.
qs.x: Lone pair–bonding pair repulsion exceeds bonding pair–bonding pair repulsion, so the lone pairs occupy more space and squeeze the bonded atoms together. Trap: Thinking lone pairs attract bonded atoms rather than repel bonding pairs.

qs.q: SF₄ has five electron domains, one of them a lone pair, and the geometry in Table 1 is seesaw. Why does the lone pair occupy an equatorial position?
o: An equatorial lone pair has two 90° interactions with bonding pairs, whereas an axial lone pair would have three, so the equatorial site minimizes repulsion
Correct: In a trigonal bipyramid, the equatorial site has two 90° neighbors while the axial site has three; the lone pair takes the site with fewer close repulsions.
An axial lone pair has two 90° interactions with bonding pairs, so it is favored, and the seesaw shape results from the other four atoms bending
Because the axial site has more 90° contacts, the axial position is disfavored for lone pairs.
An equatorial lone pair has three 90° interactions with bonding pairs, whereas an axial lone pair would have two, so equatorial minimizes repulsion
The counts are reversed: it is the axial site that has three 90° interactions.
An equatorial lone pair has no 90° interactions with bonding pairs, whereas an axial lone pair would have four, so equatorial minimizes repulsion
An equatorial site still has two axial neighbors at 90°.
qs.x: In a trigonal bipyramid, the equatorial site has two 90° neighbors while the axial site has three; the lone pair takes the site with fewer close repulsions. Trap: Reversing the count of 90° repulsions at axial and equatorial positions.

qs.q: Using the same reasoning, which description fits ClF₃, which has five electron domains including two lone pairs?
o: T-shaped and polar, since both lone pairs occupy equatorial positions and the dipoles do not cancel
Correct: With two lone pairs equatorial, the three F atoms lie in a T shape (one equatorial, two axial); the bond dipoles do not cancel, so ClF₃ is polar.
Seesaw and polar, since two lone pairs occupy axial positions and the remaining atoms form a see-saw
A seesaw has only one lone pair; ClF₃ has two, and axial lone pairs are disfavored.
Square planar and nonpolar, since the two lone pairs occupy axial positions and the four atoms form a square
Square planar has six domains (e.g., XeF₄); ClF₃ has five.
Trigonal planar and nonpolar, since the two lone pairs and three fluorines lie in the same plane and cancel
Planar trigonal arrangement would require only three domains; ClF₃ has five, and its dipoles do not cancel.
qs.x: With two lone pairs equatorial, the three F atoms lie in a T shape (one equatorial, two axial); the bond dipoles do not cancel, so ClF₃ is polar. Trap: Placing lone pairs in axial positions or confusing geometries across steric numbers.

passages.title: FL05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 9
text: A student separates a mixture of hexane and heptane by fractional distillation. At 90 °C the vapor pressures of the pure liquids are 1,400 torr for hexane and 600 torr for heptane, and the liquid mixtures are assumed to obey Raoult's law. Table 1 gives, for several liquid compositions at 90 °C, the total vapor pressure and the mole fraction of hexane in the vapor in equilibrium with the liquid. Figure 1 plots the vapor composition (y) against the liquid composition (x) together with the line y = x. The student uses a column packed with glass beads between the boiling flask and a condenser. Each complete vaporization and condensation cycle on the packing is equivalent to one theoretical plate. The student follows the composition of the condensed vapor through successive cycles, starting with a liquid of hexane mole fraction 0.40. Finally, the student asks whether ethanol–water mixtures, which show positive deviations from Raoult's law, can be separated completely by the same method.

qs.q: What is the total vapor pressure at 90 °C above a liquid mixture with a hexane mole fraction of 0.30?
o: 840 torr, from 0.30(1,400) + 0.70(600), the sum of the two partial pressures
Correct: By Raoult's law, P = x_hex P°_hex + x_hept P°_hept = 420 + 420 = 840 torr (also 600 + 800x = 840).
1,000 torr, the simple average of the two pure-liquid vapor pressures, with no regard to the composition of the liquid
The total pressure depends on the composition; the simple average applies only to a 50:50 mixture.
420 torr, the partial pressure of one component rather than the sum of both partial pressures
420 torr is only one of the two partial pressures; the total is their sum.
1,160 torr, from 0.70(1,400) + 0.30(600), which reverses the mole fractions of the two components
The mole fraction of hexane is 0.30, not 0.70; the reversed fractions give a different mixture.
qs.x: By Raoult's law, P = x_hex P°_hex + x_hept P°_hept = 420 + 420 = 840 torr (also 600 + 800x = 840). Trap: Averaging the pure vapor pressures or reversing the mole fractions.

qs.q: Starting with liquid of x = 0.40, the vapor is condensed and re-vaporized once more. What is the approximate hexane mole fraction in the second vapor, using Table 1?
o: About 0.40, since re-vaporizing a condensed liquid returns it to the original composition of the boiling flask
Each vaporization enriches the more volatile component, so the composition does not return to 0.40.
About 0.61, since the vapor over the original liquid already has the final composition after the first cycle
0.61 is the composition after one plate; a second plate enriches the vapor further.
About 0.78, since the first vapor (y = 0.61) condenses to a liquid with x ≈ 0.60, which gives vapor with y ≈ 0.78
Correct: Cycle 1 gives y = 0.61; condensing yields a liquid with x = 0.61 ≈ 0.60, whose vapor is y = 0.78 (row x = 0.60).
About 0.90, since two cycles are needed to reach the composition of the vapor above liquid with x = 0.80
The second vapor reflects the liquid x = 0.60 row, not x = 0.80.
qs.x: Cycle 1 gives y = 0.61; condensing yields a liquid with x = 0.61 ≈ 0.60, whose vapor is y = 0.78 (row x = 0.60). Trap: Stopping after one cycle or not using the condensate as the new liquid composition.

qs.q: Why does packing the fractionating column with glass beads improve the separation?
o: It acts as a selective filter that traps molecules of the less volatile component by adsorbing them irreversibly on the glass surface
The glass beads do not adsorb the components permanently; the separation arises from vapor–liquid equilibrium.
It lowers the boiling point of the mixture, so the more volatile component can be driven off without any heating of the flask
Packing does not change the boiling point of the mixture; the pressure and composition set it.
It provides a large surface for repeated condensation and re-vaporization, adding theoretical plates and enriching the more volatile component
Correct: Each condensation–vaporization on the packing is one equilibrium stage; more surface means more plates and a purer distillate.
It prevents the two components from mixing in the vapor phase, so that each component moves through the column separately
Vapor components do mix; the separation is via repeated equilibria, not by keeping vapors apart.
qs.x: Each condensation–vaporization on the packing is one equilibrium stage; more surface means more plates and a purer distillate. Trap: Attributing separation to a filtering or adsorption effect rather than repeated vapor–liquid equilibria.

qs.q: Ethanol–water mixtures form a minimum-boiling azeotrope at about 95.6% ethanol by mass. What is the expected result of fractionally distilling a 50% ethanol mixture with an efficient column?
o: The distillate approaches the azeotrope (about 95.6% ethanol) but not pure ethanol, since it vaporizes without changing composition
Correct: At the azeotrope, vapor and liquid have the same composition, so further plates give no more enrichment; the distillate approaches 95.6% ethanol.
The distillate remains at 50% ethanol, since a positive deviation from Raoult's law removes any difference in volatility between the two liquids
Positive deviations raise the vapor pressure; the vapor is initially enriched in ethanol up to the azeotrope.
The distillate is pure water, since water has the lower vapor pressure and therefore vaporizes first from the boiling flask at the start
Water has the higher boiling point and lower volatility, so it is not the first to distill.
The distillate is pure ethanol, since an efficient column with enough theoretical plates can always separate any two volatile liquids completely
Pure ethanol cannot be obtained by ordinary fractional distillation from a mixture lying below the azeotrope.
qs.x: At the azeotrope, vapor and liquid have the same composition, so further plates give no more enrichment; the distillate approaches 95.6% ethanol. Trap: Believing a long column can always give pure components, even for azeotropes.

graph.title: Figure 1. Vapor composition versus liquid composition at 90 °C

passages.title: FL05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 10
text: Glucose in water exists mostly as cyclic hemiacetals, formed when the C5 hydroxyl group adds to the aldehyde carbon (C1) of the open-chain form. The two ring forms, called anomers, differ in configuration at C1: in α-D-glucopyranose the C1 hydroxyl group is axial, and in β-D-glucopyranose it is equatorial. The open-chain form is present at much less than 0.01%. A student dissolves pure crystalline α-D-glucopyranose in water at a concentration of 0.10 g/mL and 25 °C, with a trace of acid catalyst, and follows the optical rotation in a polarimeter tube of 1.0 dm path length. The observed rotation is α_obs = [α]·c·l, with c in g/mL and l in dm. The specific rotations are +112° for the α anomer and +18.7° for the β anomer. The measured rotations are given in Table 1 and Figure 1. The rotation changes with time and settles at a constant value; this phenomenon is called mutarotation.

qs.q: Which process explains the change in rotation seen in Table 1?
o: Ring opening to the open-chain aldehyde followed by ring closure at C1, which interconverts the α and β anomers until equilibrium is reached

Correct: Hemiacetals are reversible: the pyranose ring opens to the aldehyde and re-closes, producing either anomer. The different specific rotations of the anomers cause the observed rotation to change.
Oxidation of the aldehyde carbon by dissolved oxygen in the water, which converts glucose into gluconic acid and changes the rotation
No oxidant is present, and an oxidation would not stop at a constant rotation near the value shown.
Epimerization at C2 through an enediol intermediate, which converts glucose into mannose and fructose until the rotation stabilizes
Epimerization through enediols requires base and is much slower; it is not the cause of the mutarotation described.
Racemization at C5 through a planar carbocation, which converts D-glucose into L-glucose and gradually reduces the observed rotation of the solution
The C5 stereocenter is not involved in the interconversion of anomers, and no L-glucose forms.
qs.x: Hemiacetals are reversible: the pyranose ring opens to the aldehyde and re-closes, producing either anomer. The different specific rotations of the anomers cause the observed rotation to change. Trap: Attributing the rotation change to a different stereocenter or an oxidation instead of ring opening at C1.

qs.q: From the final rotation in Table 1, what percentage of the glucose is present as the α anomer at equilibrium?
o: About 63%, since this is the fraction of the β anomer rather than of the α anomer at equilibrium
64% is roughly the β fraction (1 − 0.37 = 0.63).
About 53%, since the equilibrium specific rotation of +53° is read directly as a percentage
Specific rotations are not percentages; the fraction comes from a weighted average.
About 37%, since the equilibrium specific rotation of +53° gives (53 − 18.7)/(112 − 18.7)
Correct: The equilibrium specific rotation is 5.3/(0.10 × 1.0) = 53°. With x as the α fraction, 112x + 18.7(1 − x) = 53 gives x = 34.3/93.3 = 0.37.
About 47%, since the percentage is obtained by subtracting the equilibrium rotation of 53 from 100
Subtracting from 100 has no basis; the fraction must be calculated from the weighted average of the two specific rotations.
qs.x: The equilibrium specific rotation is 5.3/(0.10 × 1.0) = 53°. With x as the α fraction, 112x + 18.7(1 − x) = 53 gives x = 34.3/93.3 = 0.37. Trap: Using a rotation value as a percentage instead of a weighted average of the two specific rotations.

qs.q: Using Figure 1, what is the approximate half-life of the approach to equilibrium?
o: About 30 min, since the rotation has fallen to roughly 60% of its initial value by that time
At 30 min, the excess is 1.5°, about one quarter of the initial excess, not half.
About 7 min, since the rotation falls by about 2° per 7 min at the start and then continues linearly
The decay is exponential, not linear; half the excess is gone by 15 min, not 7.
About 45 min, since the rotation has nearly leveled off near the final value by that time
At 45 min the excess is 0.7°, about one eighth, so half has been passed long before.
About 15 min, since the excess rotation over the final value falls from 5.9° to about 3° by then
Correct: Initial excess = 11.2 − 5.3 = 5.9°; half is about 3.0°, reached at 8.2 − 5.3 = 2.9° at 15 min.
qs.x: Initial excess = 11.2 − 5.3 = 5.9°; half is about 3.0°, reached at 8.2 − 5.3 = 2.9° at 15 min. Trap: Taking half of the observed rotation instead of half of the excess over the final value.

qs.q: Why does the β anomer predominate over the α anomer at equilibrium (about 64% versus 36%)?
o: In β-D-glucopyranose the anomeric hydroxyl is axial, which allows it to hydrogen bond with the ring oxygen and stabilizes the chair
The anomeric hydroxyl of the β form is equatorial, not axial; the axial hydroxyl is in the α form.
In β-D-glucopyranose the ring is a planar five-membered furanose, which has less angle strain than the six-membered chair of the α form
Both anomers are six-membered pyranose chairs; the furanose is a different ring form and is a minor component.
In β-D-glucopyranose the C1 carbon is an sp² carbonyl carbon, which is more stable than the sp³ anomeric carbon of the α form
Both anomers have an sp³ anomeric carbon; the carbonyl carbon exists only in the very minor open-chain form.
In β-D-glucopyranose all substituents, including the anomeric hydroxyl, are equatorial, which minimizes 1,3-diaxial strain in the chair
Correct: The β anomer places the C1 hydroxyl equatorial, like all other substituents; the α anomer has it axial, adding steric strain.
qs.x: The β anomer places the C1 hydroxyl equatorial, like all other substituents; the α anomer has it axial, adding steric strain. Trap: Mixing up which anomer has the axial anomeric hydroxyl.

passages.title: FL05 · Psych/Soc · Passage 1
text: Researchers recruited 200 pairs of monozygotic (MZ) and 200 pairs of dizygotic (DZ) same-sex adult twins who were reared together. Each twin completed a validated Big Five inventory, and the within-pair correlation for each trait was computed separately for MZ and DZ pairs. Heritability was estimated with Falconer's formula, h² = 2(rMZ − rDZ). Under the simple model used, the variance not explained by heritability and shared environment was attributed to nonshared environment plus measurement error, estimated as 1 − rMZ. In a second analysis, a separate longitudinal sample of 1,500 adults completed the same inventory twice, ten years apart, and the rank-order stability (test–retest correlation) of composite trait scores was computed within each starting-age group. Zygosity was confirmed by genotyping, and all participants gave informed consent. Twins were recruited from a national registry, and pairs in which either twin had a diagnosed psychiatric disorder were excluded. The inventory used 60 items per trait rated on a five-point agreement scale, and all scores were standardized and adjusted for age and sex before correlations were computed. The authors caution that the estimates describe the sampled population and its range of environments. Twin correlations are shown in Table 1, and ten-year stability by starting age is shown in Figure 1.

qs.q: According to Falconer's formula and the data in Table 1, what is the estimated heritability of Openness?
o: This is simply the MZ correlation, which includes shared environment and genes together.
This adds the two correlations instead of subtracting them.
This is the raw MZ–DZ difference and omits the doubling step.
qs.x: 2(0.58 − 0.31) = 0.54. Trap: Forgetting to double the MZ–DZ difference (reporting 0.27) or using rMZ alone as if it were heritability.

qs.q: Under the model described, which trait has the largest proportion of variance attributable to nonshared environment plus measurement error?
o: Extraversion
1 − 0.52 = 0.48, which is smaller than the Agreeableness residual.
Openness
1 − 0.58 = 0.42, the smallest residual, since Openness has the highest MZ correlation.
Neuroticism
1 − 0.46 = 0.54, which is large but still below the Agreeableness residual.
Agreeableness
Correct: 1 − rMZ = 0.60, the largest among the five traits.
qs.x: 1 − rMZ = 0.60, the largest among the five traits. Trap: Choosing the trait with the largest heritability or the largest rMZ − rDZ gap instead of the largest 1 − rMZ residual.

qs.q: Which statement best describes what Figure 1 shows about personality stability?
o: Individuals' relative standing on traits becomes more consistent across a decade as people age, though average levels could still change
Correct: rank-order stability rose from 0.55 to 0.77, which concerns relative position, not mean-level change.
The decreasing stability of older adults indicates that genetic influence on personality weakens in later decades as experiences accumulate
The curve increases with age; it does not decrease, and the figure says nothing about genetic influence.
Personality traits are fully fixed by age 20, and the positive correlations at every starting age mainly reflect measurement error in the inventory
Correlations well below 1.0 at all ages show that substantial change in rank order still occurs, including at age 20.
Test-retest correlations rise with age mainly because older adults score higher on every trait at the second testing than at the first one
Rank-order correlations are insensitive to uniform shifts in mean level, so higher scores would not raise them.
qs.x: rank-order stability rose from 0.55 to 0.77, which concerns relative position, not mean-level change. Trap: Confusing rank-order stability (relative position) with mean-level stability, or reading a correlation below 1 as 'no stability'.

qs.q: The twin data estimate the heritability of Extraversion at 0.56. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
o: About 56% of any one person's Extraversion is caused by that person's genes, with the remaining 44% caused by upbringing and chance
Heritability does not partition an individual's trait into causal percentages.
The estimate would be the same in every population and every environment in which Extraversion is measured by the inventory
Heritability depends on the genetic and environmental variance of the specific population studied.
Extraversion cannot be changed by experience in the 56% of people who carry the relevant genetic variants for the trait
Heritability does not identify subgroups with fixed traits or imply immutability.
In this population, about 56% of the variation in Extraversion scores among individuals is associated with genetic differences
Correct: heritability is a population-level variance statistic.
qs.x: heritability is a population-level variance statistic. Trap: Treating heritability as the percent of an individual's trait that is 'genetic' or as fixed across populations.

qs.q: Suppose MZ twins' parents treat them more alike than DZ twins' parents in ways that influence personality. How would this violation of the equal-environments assumption most likely affect the Falconer estimate?
o: It would inflate the estimate, because the extra MZ similarity due to environment would be attributed to genes
Correct: the larger rMZ − rDZ gap is partly environmental.
It would leave the estimate unchanged, because Falconer's formula already subtracts out all environmental effects
The formula assumes equal environments and cannot remove unequal environmental similarity.
It would make the estimate negative, because environmental correlations are always larger in DZ pairs
There is no basis for DZ pairs having larger environmental correlations here.
It would deflate the estimate, because shared treatment would make MZ and DZ pairs equally similar
Greater MZ than DZ treatment similarity widens, not narrows, the correlation gap.
qs.x: the larger rMZ − rDZ gap is partly environmental. Trap: Assuming twin methods automatically remove environmental confounds, rather than relying on the equal-environments assumption.

graph.title: Figure 1. Ten-year rank-order stability of composite Big Five scores

passages.title: FL05 · Psych/Soc · Passage 2
text: In a replication of classic helping research, 320 undergraduates took part in a computer-mediated study of 'online group discussions.' Each participant sat in an individual cubicle and was randomly assigned to one of four conditions (n = 80 each). Through headphones, the participant heard another discussant, actually a recording, begin to choke and call for help. In the Alone condition, the participant believed the choking discussant was the only other person in the discussion.
