In the Two-bystander condition, the participant believed one additional discussant was listening; in the Five-bystander condition, four additional discussants. In the Five-bystander-with-model condition, a second recorded voice announced within 5 seconds, 'I'm going for help.' Helping was defined as leaving the cubicle to alert the experimenter within 60 seconds. Latency to help was recorded for participants who helped. Results are shown in Table 1. All participants were fully debriefed afterward. Before the session, participants completed a brief questionnaire on prior first-aid training, which did not differ across conditions. Sessions were run individually over two weeks, and the order of conditions was randomized across time slots to avoid confounds with the day or the experimenter.

qs.q: By how many percentage points did helping decrease from the Alone condition to the Five-bystander condition?
o: 40 percentage points
36 percentage points
36 is the number of helpers in the Five-bystander group, not a difference in percentages.
47 percentage points
40 / 85 is a 47% relative decrease, which is not a percentage-point difference.
20 percentage points
This is the drop from Alone to the Two-bystander condition (85% − 65%).
qs.x: 85% − 45% = 40. Trap: Reporting a relative percent decrease (47%) as if it were a difference in percentage points.

qs.q: The high helping rate in the Five-bystander-with-model condition (80%) most strongly suggests that:
o: participants in groups helped more because they were deindividuated and so lost awareness of their personal moral standards
Deindividuation lowers self-awareness and would predict less, not more, prosocial action.
social facilitation raised arousal so that participants in the model condition performed the dominant response of not helping at all
This misapplies social facilitation; the dominant response here was increased helping, not the reverse.
seeing another person act reduced diffusion of responsibility and defined the situation as an emergency, so the bystander effect is not inevitable
Correct: a model who helps changes both responsibility and interpretation.
group size has no causal influence on helping, because the same number of bystanders was present as in the Five-bystander condition and the effect disappeared
The 45% versus 80% contrast occurs at equal group size, but the Alone versus Five-bystander contrast still shows an effect of group size.
qs.x: a model who helps changes both responsibility and interpretation. Trap: Concluding that equal group size means group size never matters, instead of seeing that modeling moderates the bystander effect.

qs.q: Why was random assignment to the four conditions important in this study?
o: It prevents participants from guessing the purpose of the study, thereby removing demand characteristics entirely
Random assignment does not hide the study's purpose or remove demand characteristics.
It makes preexisting differences such as helpfulness approximately equal across conditions, supporting causal inference about condition effects
Correct: random assignment equates groups on average.
It eliminates the need for a control condition, because every participant experiences every level of the independent variable in turn
Assignment to separate groups is a between-subjects design, so a comparison condition (Alone) is still needed.
It guarantees the participants are representative of all adults, allowing the observed helping rates to be generalized to the public
Random assignment affects internal validity, whereas representativeness depends on random sampling.
qs.x: random assignment equates groups on average. Trap: Mixing up random assignment (internal validity) with random sampling (external validity).

qs.q: A critic argues that helping a recorded voice through headphones differs from helping a person in a real emergency. This criticism most directly concerns the study's:
o: internal validity, because random assignment cannot establish whether group size actually changed helping
Random assignment protects internal validity; the criticism concerns realism.
construct validity of the independent variable, because the number of bystanders was never manipulated by the experimenters
The number of bystanders was manipulated; the criticism concerns realism of the emergency.
external validity, because the laboratory setting and recorded emergency may not generalize to real helping
Correct: the concern is about generalizing beyond the lab.
reliability, because repeated helping responses by the same participant were inconsistent across trials
Participants were measured once, and the criticism does not concern consistency.
qs.x: the concern is about generalizing beyond the lab. Trap: Calling every methodological criticism a threat to internal validity.

passages.title: FL05 · Psych/Soc · Passage 3
text: Undergraduates (N = 240) read a persuasive message advocating a new comprehensive-examination requirement for graduation. The study used a 2 × 2 × 2 between-subjects design with 30 participants per cell. The message contained either strong arguments (specific, verifiable evidence) or weak arguments (vague, anecdotal claims). It was attributed either to a professor of education who chairs a university board (high expertise) or to a high-school student (low expertise). Finally, participants were told that the requirement would take effect either next year, so it would apply to them (high personal relevance), or in ten years, so it would not (low personal relevance). Afterward, participants rated their agreement with the policy on a scale from 1 (strongly oppose) to 9 (strongly favor). Mean agreement for each cell is shown in Table 1. The expertise and relevance manipulations were checked with a brief questionnaire at the end of the session, and participants who failed to recall the source of the message were excluded and replaced. Argument strength was pretested with an independent sample who rated the arguments' quality. All messages were of equal length (about 300 words) and were read on a computer screen at the participant's own pace in a quiet room.

qs.q: Averaging across source expertise, how much higher was agreement with strong arguments than with weak arguments among high-relevance participants?
o: 4.8 points
This subtracts mismatched cells (7.8 − 3.0) rather than averaging across both sources.
0.9 points
This is the strong-versus-weak difference for the low-relevance participants, not the high-relevance participants.
4.4 points
This subtracts mismatched cells (7.6 − 3.2) rather than averaging across both sources.
4.6 points
Correct: strong mean = (7.8 + 7.6)/2 = 7.7; weak mean = (3.2 + 3.0)/2 = 3.1; difference 4.6.
qs.x: strong mean = (7.8 + 7.6)/2 = 7.7; weak mean = (3.2 + 3.0)/2 = 3.1; difference 4.6. Trap: Using single cells rather than averaging across both source conditions, or reading the low-relevance rows by mistake.

qs.q: Which statement best describes the low-relevance results?
o: Agreement did not depend on either argument quality or source expertise, consistent with no message processing
Agreement changed by about 1.8 to 2.2 points with source expertise, so processing cues clearly mattered.
Agreement depended more on source expertise than on argument quality, consistent with peripheral processing
Correct: expert minus nonexpert averages about 2.0 while strong minus weak averages 0.9.
Agreement depended more on argument quality than on source expertise, consistent with central-route processing
This describes the high-relevance pattern, in which the quality difference was 4.6 points.
Agreement depended on argument quality only when the source was an expert, consistent with systematic processing
The quality difference was small for both sources (1.1 for the nonexpert source and 0.7 for the expert source), not selective to experts.
qs.x: expert minus nonexpert averages about 2.0 while strong minus weak averages 0.9. Trap: Assuming any attitude change reflects careful processing; peripheral cues such as expertise can drive change when motivation is low.

qs.q: How many participants read a message containing weak arguments?
o: This counts only one relevance level, or half of the weak-argument participants.
Correct: two relevance levels × two source levels × 30 participants = 120.
This is the size of a single cell, not all cells with weak arguments.
This is the entire sample and includes participants who read strong arguments.
qs.x: two relevance levels × two source levels × 30 participants = 120. Trap: Reading a single cell size or the total N rather than summing the cells that share a level of one factor.

qs.q: A follow-up testing the same participants one month later would most likely find that attitudes formed by high-relevance participants were:
o: more persistent only for participants who read weak arguments, because those arguments required more effort
Weak arguments were rejected by high-relevance participants, and extra effort does not explain durability.
more persistent, more resistant to counter-persuasion, and more predictive of behavior than low-relevance attitudes
Correct: central-route attitudes are generally more durable.
less persistent, because attitudes formed through careful thought are easily overturned by later persuasive messages from others
Central-route attitudes are generally more resistant, not less.
equally persistent, because the durability of an attitude depends only on how large the initial change in attitude was
Durability depends on the processing route, not just on the amount of change.
qs.x: central-route attitudes are generally more durable. Trap: Assuming the size of initial change, not the processing route, determines how durable an attitude is.

qs.q: Participants high in need for cognition read the same messages under the low-relevance condition. Compared with participants low in need for cognition, they would most likely show:
o: a smaller difference between strong and weak arguments, because they would rely more heavily on source expertise as a mental shortcut
People high in need for cognition rely less on peripheral cues.
a larger difference between expert and nonexpert sources, because they are more sensitive to social status cues in persuasion
This reverses the expected effect of dispositional motivation to think.
a larger difference between strong and weak arguments, because they enjoy effortful thinking and process centrally despite low relevance
Correct: need for cognition raises elaboration.
no difference in processing, because need for cognition affects the route only when the message is personally relevant
Need for cognition is a dispositional motivator that operates across relevance levels.
qs.x: need for cognition raises elaboration. Trap: Assuming low personal relevance forces peripheral processing for everyone, ignoring dispositional motivation.

passages.title: FL05 · Psych/Soc · Passage 4
text: Undergraduates (N = 200; 40 per condition) took part in what they believed was a study of impression formation. Each participant read a short profile of a fellow student and then completed a 7-point state self-esteem scale (1 = very low, 7 = very high). The profile described a student who was academically superior (upward comparison) or struggling (downward comparison), and who was either similar to the participant (same major and class year) or dissimilar (different major and class year). A fifth control group read a neutral weather report. Participants were randomly assigned to conditions, and the scale was completed privately. The standard deviation in each condition was approximately 1.0. Condition means are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. Profiles were matched for length and writing style, and a manipulation check confirmed that participants perceived upward targets as more successful and similar targets as more like themselves. Participants were told the study concerned first impressions, and a debriefing followed.

qs.q: Using the control group as the reference, what is the approximate magnitude of Cohen's d for the upward, similar condition?
o: 1.0, a large effect
4.0, a very large effect
This multiplies by 4 rather than dividing the mean difference by the SD.
0.1, a negligible effect
This would correspond to a 0.1-point mean difference, not a 1.0-point difference.
0.4, a small-to-medium effect
This does not match the 1.0-point mean difference when the SD is 1.0.
qs.x: (4.9 − 3.9)/1.0 = 1.0. Trap: Reporting the raw mean difference without standardizing, or misapplying the SD.

qs.q: The upward, dissimilar condition (4.8) did not differ meaningfully from the control (4.9). Which explanation best fits social comparison theory?
o: People form their self-concept primarily through reflected appraisals from parents, which a stranger's profile cannot supply
This describes the looking-glass self, which does not explain why similarity mattered here.
People protect their self-esteem by attributing a dissimilar target's success to luck, which the data directly demonstrate
No attribution measure was collected, so the data do not demonstrate this process.
People adjust their self-esteem only when a downward comparison is available, so any upward comparison is ignored
The similar upward target did lower self-esteem, so upward comparisons are not ignored.
Comparisons are most informative with similar others, so a dissimilar high achiever is not relevant to one's own standing
Correct: comparison is most informative and threatening when targets are similar.
qs.x: comparison is most informative and threatening when targets are similar. Trap: Assuming any upward comparison threatens self-esteem regardless of the target's relevance.

qs.q: The researchers next want to test whether the effect of comparison direction depends on participants' pre-measured trait self-esteem (high versus low). Which design would best address this?
o: Add trait self-esteem as a second between-subjects factor and test its interaction with comparison direction
Correct: a moderator is tested as an interaction.
Correlate trait self-esteem with state self-esteem within the control group alone to test the effect of comparison
The control group has no comparison manipulation.
Measure state self-esteem twice for each participant and test for a main effect of time in the five conditions
A time effect does not test whether trait level changes the comparison effect.
Compare only the high-trait-self-esteem participants across conditions, because this isolates the main effect of comparison direction
Dropping low-trait participants cannot test whether trait self-esteem changes the effect.
qs.x: a moderator is tested as an interaction. Trap: Testing a main effect in one subgroup rather than an interaction, which is what moderation requires.

qs.q: Which finding from a real-world setting would best parallel the big-fish-little-pond effect?
o: Students in a less selective school report lower academic self-concept because their classmates have lower test scores
Lower-achieving peers provide downward comparisons that tend to raise self-concept.
Students in both types of school report the same academic self-concept because it depends solely on absolute ability
Self-concept depends on relative standing, as the comparison data show.
Students enrolled in a highly selective school report higher academic self-concept than equally able students in a less selective school
This reverses the effect; selective schools supply upward comparisons.
Equally able students enrolled in a highly selective school report lower academic self-concept than those in a less selective school
Correct: upward comparison with high achievers lowers self-concept.
qs.x: upward comparison with high achievers lowers self-concept. Trap: Assuming prestigious environments always raise self-concept, ignoring social comparison with higher-achieving peers.

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean state self-esteem by condition

passages.title: FL05 · Psych/Soc · Passage 5
text: Researchers administered a race Implicit Association Test (IAT) to 150 White participants. In the IAT, participants rapidly sort face and word stimuli using two response keys. In the 'compatible' block, one key was assigned to White faces and pleasant words and the other key to Black faces and unpleasant words; in the 'incompatible' block, the pairings were reversed. The order of the two blocks was counterbalanced across participants. Participants also completed an explicit feeling-thermometer measure of attitudes toward each group. In a separate laboratory task, the distance at which each participant chose to sit from a Black confederate was recorded as a behavioral index. Two weeks later, participants repeated the IAT. A larger IAT D score indicates a stronger association of White with pleasant. Results are summarized in Table 1. All participants completed the IAT on a laptop in a quiet laboratory, performed practice trials before each block, and were instructed to respond as quickly and accurately as possible. The confederate was blind to participants' IAT scores, and the seating task occurred in a waiting room before the participants believed the study had started. Latencies were averaged after removing responses that were extremely fast or slow.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the block latencies in Table 1?
o: Participants paired White faces with pleasant words faster than Black faces with pleasant words, indicating a stronger automatic White-pleasant association
Correct: faster compatible responses (720 ms versus 905 ms) reflect easier pairings.
Participants consciously endorsed more negative attitudes toward Black individuals, as indicated by the 185 ms latency difference between blocks
The IAT measures response speed, which does not show conscious endorsement; explicit attitudes were measured separately.
Participants had more practice in the incompatible block, which lowered their accuracy relative to the compatible block
Practice effects were handled by counterbalancing, and accuracy was not reported.
Participants were slower in the compatible block because they had to override their stereotype-consistent responses on each trial
The incompatible block, not the compatible block, was slower.
qs.x: faster compatible responses (720 ms versus 905 ms) reflect easier pairings. Trap: Equating a faster implicit pairing with consciously held prejudice.

qs.q: Approximately what proportion of the variance in explicit thermometer scores is shared with IAT D scores?
o: About 9%
This is the shared variance for r = 0.30, not r = 0.18.
About 36%
This squares 0.6 or doubles the correlation, neither of which matches r = 0.18.
About 3%
Correct: r² = 0.18² = 0.032.
About 18%
This treats the correlation coefficient itself as the proportion of shared variance.
qs.x: r² = 0.18² = 0.032. Trap: Reading r as the proportion of shared variance instead of squaring it.

qs.q: The two-week test-retest correlation of 0.50 for the IAT suggests that:
o: the explicit measure is more reliable than the IAT, because the explicit measure correlates 0.12 with seating distance
Correlation with behavior reflects predictive validity, not test-retest reliability.
the IAT is a valid measure of discriminatory behavior, because scores are partly stable over a two-week interval
Reliability does not establish validity.
an individual's IAT score is only moderately reliable, so one score is a limited basis for classifying a person
Correct: moderate reliability limits individual-level inference.
the IAT is perfectly reliable, because the correlation is statistically different from zero
Statistical significance does not equal high reliability.
qs.x: moderate reliability limits individual-level inference. Trap: Equating a statistically significant correlation with high reliability or validity.

qs.q: Why did the researchers counterbalance the order of the compatible and incompatible blocks?
o: To increase the correlation between the IAT and explicit attitudes by matching task conditions
Counterbalancing is not designed to raise correlations.
To ensure that participants could not form conscious attitudes about the groups while sorting words
Counterbalancing does not prevent conscious attitudes.
To make the test-retest correlation equal across the first and second administrations
Counterbalancing block order does not equalize test-retest correlations.
To keep practice or fatigue effects from being confounded with the type of pairing
Correct: order effects would otherwise bias the latency comparison.
qs.x: order effects would otherwise bias the latency comparison. Trap: Thinking counterbalancing controls participants' beliefs rather than order effects.

r: Correlation, IAT D with explicit thermometer difference
Correlation, IAT D with seating distance
Correlation, explicit thermometer with seating distance
Test-retest correlation of IAT D (two weeks)

passages.title: FL05 · Psych/Soc · Passage 6
text: In a study of cooperation, 300 undergraduates (75 per condition) played a prisoner's dilemma for points later exchanged for lottery tickets. On each round, each player privately chose to Cooperate or Defect. Payoffs (own points, partner's points) were: both cooperate, 3 and 3; one defects while the other cooperates, 5 for the defector and 0 for the cooperator; both defect, 1 and 1. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions. In the first, they played a single anonymous round with a stranger with no communication. In the second, they played a single round after two minutes of face-to-face discussion with their partner. In the third, they played ten rounds against a programmed partner using tit-for-tat (cooperate on round 1, then copy the participant's previous move). In the fourth, they played ten rounds against a programmed partner who always defected. Table 1 gives the mean percentage of cooperative choices. Participants in all conditions received written instructions and a payoff chart before play, and they were told that partners would never be identified afterward. Programmed partners were described only as other participants in an adjoining room. Participants who had played a similar game before were not recruited, so that familiarity with the strategies would not influence the results.

qs.q: In the single-round, no-communication condition, why is defection the rational choice by payoff alone?
o: Defection earns more only when the partner also defects, because mutual defection yields 1 point each and cooperation yields 3 each
3 > 1, so mutual defection is worse than mutual cooperation, and defection still beats cooperation against a cooperating partner.
Defection pays more than cooperation whatever the partner does (5 versus 3 if the partner cooperates, 1 versus 0 if not)
Correct: defection is a dominant strategy.
Defection earns more than cooperation only after the first round, once the partner's strategy can be observed
In a one-round game there is no later round, and the dominance holds for any partner choice.
Defection guarantees the highest joint payoff for the pair, because the defector's gain exceeds the partner's loss
Joint payoff is highest (6) under mutual cooperation, not when one defects (5).
qs.x: defection is a dominant strategy. Trap: Confusing the individually rational choice (defect) with the jointly best outcome (mutual cooperation).

qs.q: Over ten rounds, how many points would a player using tit-for-tat earn against a partner who always defects?
o: 30 points
This is the total for ten rounds of mutual cooperation, which the defecting partner prevents.
14 points
This is the always-defect partner's total (5 + 9), not the tit-for-tat player's.
9 points
Correct: round 1: 0 (cooperate versus defect); rounds 2-10: 1 each (mutual defection) = 9.
10 points
This assumes mutual defection (1 point) occurs on all ten rounds, ignoring the opening cooperation that earned 0.
qs.x: round 1: 0 (cooperate versus defect); rounds 2-10: 1 each (mutual defection) = 9. Trap: Forgetting that tit-for-tat cooperates on the first round and is exploited exactly once.

qs.q: The rise in cooperation from 38% to 71% after a two-minute discussion is best explained by:
o: communication allowing participants to build trust and make verbal commitments, though not binding
Correct: 'cheap talk' raises trust and cooperation.
communication producing deindividuation, which reduced concern over the partner's welfare
Discussion makes partners more identifiable, not less, and generally increases concern.
communication changing the payoffs so that cooperation became the dominant strategy in the single round of play
The payoff matrix was unchanged.
communication increasing the number of rounds, which allowed reciprocity to develop over time
The condition still had a single round.
qs.x: 'cheap talk' raises trust and cooperation. Trap: Assuming cooperation rises only when incentives change.

qs.q: The very low cooperation (15%) with the always-defect partner is most consistent with:
o: the mere-exposure effect, in which repeated exposure to the partner increased liking
Liking would raise cooperation, which was low in this condition.
frustration-aggression, in which a lack of reward from cooperation led participants to harm the partner
The data do not show aggression; the drop in cooperation is consistent with a simple payoff-based response.
a superordinate goal, in which participants shifted toward a shared objective with the partner, which would reduce cooperation
A shared goal would increase cooperation, not decrease it.
reciprocity, in which people match a partner's behavior
Correct: participants returned defection with defection.
qs.x: participants returned defection with defection. Trap: Reading lowered cooperation as aggression rather than reciprocity.

h: Mean % of participants' choices that were cooperative

passages.title: FL05 · Psych/Soc · Passage 7
text: Sociologists used a national longitudinal dataset to compare the percentage of young adults who had completed a bachelor's degree by age 25, grouped by childhood family-income quartile, for two birth cohorts (1970 and 1990). For the 1990 cohort, the researchers also recorded the number of books in the home, as a proxy for cultural capital, and the percentage of students whose teachers expected them to attend college, measured at age 15. Degree completion by cohort is shown in Figure 1, and the 1990-cohort indicators are in Table 1. The authors note that families in higher income quartiles also differ in parental education, neighborhood school funding, and access to tutoring, and that income cannot be randomly assigned. Quartile 1 is the lowest-income group and Quartile 4 the highest. Each quartile contained several thousand respondents, and the survey weights were applied so the estimates represent all young adults in each cohort. Respondents were followed through annual interviews until age 25, and cases with missing degree information were excluded. Teachers' expectations were reported independently of the students' own grades or test scores.

qs.q: Which statement about the change from the 1970 to the 1990 cohort is best supported by Figure 1?
o: Degree completion rose in every quartile, and the top-minus-bottom gap shrank by roughly half across the two cohorts
The absolute gap was nearly unchanged, although the ratio of Q4 to Q1 fell.
Completion rose in every quartile, but the top-minus-bottom gap stayed about the same (49 versus 50 points)
Degree completion rose only in the lowest quartile, which closed the gap in educational attainment
The other quartiles rose too (14 to 24, 26 to 38, 55 to 62), and the gap remained about 50 points.
Degree completion rose in every quartile, and the top-minus-bottom gap widened by about ten percentage points
49 to 50 points is a one-point change, not ten.
qs.x: 55 − 6 = 49 and 62 − 12 = 50. Trap: Judging inequality by the ratio between groups alone and missing that the absolute gap did not change.

qs.q: The pattern of books in the home across quartiles in Table 1 is best used by sociologists to illustrate which concept?
o: Anomie, in which a rapid change in norms leaves members of a group without clear guidelines for behavior
Anomie describes normlessness, which is not shown by book ownership.
Relative deprivation, in which people judge their own situation by comparing it to a reference group of similar others
The data do not measure subjective comparison.
Social capital, in which a child's network of relationships gives access to jobs and institutional resources
Books are cultural resources, not network ties.
Cultural capital, in which higher-status families pass on knowledge and habits valued by schools
Correct: Bourdieu's concept.
qs.x: Bourdieu's concept. Trap: Mixing up cultural capital (knowledge, tastes, books) with social capital (networks).

qs.q: Why can the researchers not conclude from these data that raising a family's income would, by itself, raise a child's chance of completing a degree?
o: The dataset is longitudinal, and longitudinal designs cannot adequately measure an outcome that occurs after childhood
Longitudinal designs are especially well suited to later outcomes.
Degree completion is a categorical outcome, so its relationship to a quartile variable cannot be described statistically
Categorical outcomes can be related to ordinal predictors.
Income is confounded with parental education and school funding and was not randomly assigned, so the data show association only
Correct: confounding prevents causal claims.
The data are drawn from two separate birth cohorts, which makes any comparison across quartiles within one cohort invalid
Comparison within a cohort is valid; cohort differences do not undermine it.
qs.x: confounding prevents causal claims. Trap: Assuming a large longitudinal dataset establishes causation.

qs.q: The higher percentage of teachers in Q4 who expect college attendance (82% versus 31%) could widen outcome gaps through which process?
o: Cognitive dissonance, in which students change their attitudes after being induced to act against their beliefs
Dissonance concerns attitude-behavior conflict, not expectation effects.
The halo effect, in which one favorable trait of a student leads teachers to infer other favorable traits
This is a perceptual bias and does not describe how expectations become outcomes.
A self-fulfilling prophecy, in which expectations shape treatment and effort, so students confirm them
Correct: teacher expectation effect.
Social loafing, in which students reduce effort when their contributions are pooled in a group
Social loafing is about group work, not teacher expectations.
qs.x: teacher expectation effect. Trap: Naming a related social psychology bias rather than the mechanism by which expectations produce confirming outcomes.

graph.title: Figure 1. Bachelor's degree completion by age 25, by childhood income quartile

passages.title: FL05 · Psych/Soc · Passage 8
text: Demographers compared two countries with similar total populations of about 40 million. Country X is a low-income country; Country Y is a high-income country. Indicators were drawn from national censuses and vital registration systems. The total dependency ratio was defined as the number of people aged 0-14 plus those aged 65 and older, per 100 people aged 15-64. The total fertility rate (TFR) is the average number of children a woman would have over her lifetime at current age-specific rates; the replacement level in low-mortality countries is about 2.1. Table 1 gives the indicators, and Figure 1 shows the age distribution. Country Y has had net immigration of near zero over the past decade. Mortality statistics were adjusted for incomplete death registration in Country X using survey data. Life expectancy at birth is the average number of years a newborn would live if current age-specific death rates persisted. Both countries' fertility rates were measured in the same recent year, and the percentages in each age group are rounded to whole numbers.

qs.q: What is the total dependency ratio for Country X?
o: About 42 dependents per 100 people aged 15-64
This is the sum of the percentages (38 + 4) without dividing by the working-age share.
About 72 dependents per 100 people aged 15-64
About 58 dependents per 100 people aged 15-64
This is the working-age percentage itself, not the dependency ratio.
About 66 dependents per 100 people aged 15-64
38/58 = 0.66 is only the youth dependency ratio.
qs.x: (38 + 4)/58 = 0.72. Trap: Giving the youth dependency ratio alone or leaving out the division by the working-age population.

qs.q: Country X's age structure, with a broad base, implies that even if its TFR fell immediately to replacement level, its population would likely:
o: continue growing for decades, because large youth cohorts will move into childbearing ages (population momentum)
Correct: large youth cohorts keep births high.
become older at a faster pace than Country Y, because a broad base leads to a larger proportion of older adults
The broad base would keep the population young for a long time.
stop growing immediately, because growth depends only on the current TFR and not on the age structure
Age structure produces momentum.
begin shrinking within a decade, because replacement fertility always causes immediate population decline in a country
Replacement fertility leads to stability only after the age structure adjusts.
qs.x: large youth cohorts keep births high. Trap: Assuming population growth stops the moment fertility reaches replacement level.

qs.q: With a TFR of 1.3 and near-zero net immigration, Country Y's population is expected to:
o: shrink and age over time, because fertility is well below replacement and the 65+ group is large
Correct: TFR below 2.1 without migration means decline.
grow slowly over time, because the proportion aged 15-64 is larger than that of Country X
Working-age share does not determine growth; births are too few.
grow rapidly over time, because life expectancy at birth is high and deaths are infrequent
Low mortality alone does not drive growth when births are far below replacement.
remain constant over time, because high-income countries always reach a stable stationary population
Stability would need about replacement fertility, not 1.3.
qs.x: TFR below 2.1 without migration means decline. Trap: Assuming low mortality implies growth regardless of fertility.

qs.q: The causes of death listed in Table 1 are consistent with which stage description from the epidemiologic transition?
o: Country Y is earlier in the transition, dominated by infectious disease, while Country X is later, dominated by chronic disease
This reverses the countries' positions.
Both countries are in the same stage, because leading causes of death do not change as life expectancy increases
Causes of death change as life expectancy rises.
Country X is earlier, dominated by infectious disease, while Country Y is later, dominated by chronic degenerative disease
Correct: the shift from infectious to chronic disease marks the transition.
Country X is later in the transition, because high fertility is associated with deaths from heart disease and cancer in young adults
High fertility and infectious disease go together in early stages.
qs.x: the shift from infectious to chronic disease marks the transition. Trap: Reversing the order of the transition: infectious disease comes first, chronic disease later.

graph.title: Figure 1. Percentage of population by age group

passages.title: FL05 · Psych/Soc · Passage 9
text: Economists compared household income distributions in two countries, A and B. Households were ranked by pre-tax income and divided into quintiles, and the share of total national income held by each quintile is shown in Table 1. Figure 1 plots each country's Lorenz curve, which gives the cumulative percentage of income held by the poorest cumulative percentage of households, together with the line of perfect equality. The Gini coefficient equals 1 minus twice the area under the Lorenz curve, with the area expressed as a fraction of the unit square; here, the area was approximated with the trapezoid rule across the quintile points. A Gini of 0 indicates perfect equality and a Gini of 1 indicates that a single household holds all income. Later, a policy simulation transferred income through taxes and benefits within Country A. Income was measured at the household level before taxes and transfers, and households were adjusted for size so that large and small households could be compared. Ten million households were ranked in each country, and the data came from comparable national income surveys. The authors report shares as percentages that sum to 100 within each country.

qs.q: Using the trapezoid approximation described, what is the Gini coefficient of Country A?
o: About 0.57
This is the area under the curve doubled (2 × 0.286), not 1 minus that number.
About 0.43
About 0.71
This is 1 minus the area (1 − 0.286), which omits the doubling step.
About 0.29
This is Country B's Gini coefficient (1 − 2 × 0.356 = 0.29).
qs.x: area ≈ 0.1 × (0.04 + 0.17 + 0.40 + 0.76 + 1.49) = 0.286; Gini = 1 − 2(0.286) = 0.43. Trap: Reporting twice the area under the Lorenz curve instead of 1 minus twice that area.

qs.q: What is the ratio of the richest to the poorest quintile's income share in Country B?
o: About 0.2
This inverts the ratio, giving poorest to richest (8/39).
About 4.9
About 12.8
This is Country A's ratio (51/4), not Country B's.
About 3.0
This is 39/13, comparing the richest quintile with the second-poorest instead of the poorest.
qs.x: 39/8 = 4.875. Trap: Using the other country's column or inverting the ratio.

qs.q: How many more percentage points of national income does the poorest 60% of households hold in Country B than in Country A?
o: 12 percentage points
This is the difference in the richest-quintile shares (51 − 39), not the cumulative share held by the poorest 60%.
4 percentage points
This is the difference in the poorest-quintile shares (8 − 4), not the cumulative share held by the poorest 60%.
11 percentage points
Correct: B holds 38% and A holds 27%; 38 − 27 = 11.
8 percentage points
This is the gap at the poorest 40% of households (21 − 13), not at 60%.
qs.x: B holds 38% and A holds 27%; 38 − 27 = 11. Trap: Using single-quintile shares instead of cumulative shares at the 60% mark.

qs.q: Which statement identifies a limitation of using the Gini coefficient alone to compare countries?
o: The Gini coefficient measures only the income share of the richest quintile and ignores the shares of all other households
It uses the entire distribution, not only the top share.
The Gini coefficient cannot be computed unless every household in the country has exactly the same income as the others
It is defined for unequal distributions and equals 0 only for exact equality.
Two countries with very different Lorenz curves, such as one with a poor bottom and one with a rich top, can share a Gini
Correct: the Gini summarizes the whole curve in one number.
The Gini coefficient ranges from -1 to 1, so negative values cannot be directly compared with positive values
The Gini ranges from 0 to 1.
qs.x: the Gini summarizes the whole curve in one number. Trap: Assuming a single summary index reveals where in the distribution inequality is located.

qs.q: In the simulation, 5 percentage points of national income are moved from the richest quintile to the poorest quintile in Country A. What is the new approximate Gini coefficient?
o: About 0.25
This assumes a much larger redistribution than 5 percentage points of national income.
About 0.35
Correct: new shares 9, 9, 14, 22, 46 give cumulative 0.09, 0.18, 0.32, 0.54, 1.00; area = 0.326; Gini = 0.35.
About 0.38
A transfer of only 3 percentage points would give about 0.38, which is smaller than the stated shift.
About 0.43
This is the original Gini, as if the transfer made no difference.
qs.x: new shares 9, 9, 14, 22, 46 give cumulative 0.09, 0.18, 0.32, 0.54, 1.00; area = 0.326; Gini = 0.35. Trap: Assuming a transfer between the extreme quintiles leaves the Gini unchanged, or miscalculating the new cumulative shares.

graph.title: Figure 1. Lorenz curves

passages.title: FL05 · Psych/Soc · Passage 10
text: A university health office estimated nightly sleep duration (hours) among its 40,000 students. Sample A was a simple random sample (n = 400). Sample B was a simple random sample (n = 1,600). Sample C was a volunteer sample recruited by an online posting (n = 1,600). Standard errors were computed as SD/√n, and 95% confidence intervals as mean ± 1.96 SE. The population is assumed to have a standard deviation of about 1.6 hours. Results are shown in Table 1. Figure 1 shows how the half-width of the 95% confidence interval would change with sample size if the standard deviation stays at 1.6 hours. The health office sent the random samples by email to students drawn from the full enrollment list, and the response rate was close to 100% for both random samples because participation was a course requirement. Sleep duration was self-reported using a one-week diary and averaged across nights. Volunteers for Sample C responded to a posting on a social-media page about student wellness.

qs.q: To reduce the 95% CI half-width in Sample B (0.078 h) by half, the health office would need a random sample of about:
o: 3,200 students
Doubling n reduces the SE only by a factor of √2, not by half.
6,400 students
Correct: halving the SE requires quadrupling n: 1,600 × 4 = 6,400.
4,000 students
This is an arbitrary increase and gives an SE of about 0.025, not 0.02.
2,400 students
This adds half to n, which reduces the half-width by far less than half.
qs.x: halving the SE requires quadrupling n: 1,600 × 4 = 6,400. Trap: Assuming that doubling n halves the interval; precision improves with the square root of n.

qs.q: Which is the correct interpretation of the 95% confidence interval for Sample A (6.64 to 6.96 hours)?
o: About 95% of repeated samples of 400 students would have a sample mean of exactly 6.8 hours
Sample means vary around the population mean.
About 95% of individual students in the population sleep between 6.64 and 6.96 hours per night
The interval concerns the mean, not individual values; individuals vary with an SD of 1.6 hours.
There is a 95% probability that the true population mean lies between 6.64 and 6.96 hours for this particular interval
The true mean is fixed, so a computed interval either contains it or not.
If sampling were repeated many times, about 95% of the intervals constructed would contain the true population mean
Correct: this is the frequentist meaning of the interval.
qs.x: this is the frequentist meaning of the interval. Trap: Reading a 95% CI as the range containing 95% of individual observations.

qs.q: Sample C has the same n as Sample B and a similarly narrow interval, yet its mean differs by 0.7 hours. The best explanation is that:
o: self-selection bias in a volunteer sample is not fixed by a large n, so the interval is precise but may be inaccurate
Correct: bias is distinct from sampling error.
the narrow interval proves that Sample C is representative of all 40,000 students in the university
A narrow interval reflects precision, not representativeness.
the larger sample size of Sample C produces a smaller mean through the central limit theorem, even though n is the same
Sample size does not shift the mean; n is equal across B and C.
the difference arises only from random sampling error, which is expected to be about 0.7 hours at n = 1,600
The SE is about 0.04, so a 0.7 hour difference is far larger than expected from random error.
qs.x: bias is distinct from sampling error. Trap: Believing that a large sample size or narrow CI fixes bias from a non-random sample.

qs.q: What would be the approximate 99% confidence interval for Sample A, using a multiplier of 2.58?
o: About 6.39 to 7.21 hours
This divides the SD by 10 instead of by 20 to get the SE, which doubles the margin.
About 6.72 to 6.88 hours
This is the 95% interval for Sample B (SE = 0.04), not the 99% interval for Sample A.
About 6.59 to 7.01 hours
About 6.64 to 6.96 hours
This is the 95% interval, whose multiplier is 1.96.
qs.x: 2.58 × 0.08 = 0.206; 6.8 ± 0.21. Trap: Using the right multiplier but forgetting that the interval is symmetric, or using the 95% interval.

qs.q: According to Figure 1, about how much does the half-width decrease when n increases from 900 to 2,500?
o: About 0.04 hours
About 0.17 hours
This is the decrease from n = 100 to n = 400 (0.314 − 0.157).
About 0.10 hours
This is nearly the entire half-width at n = 900, rather than the decrease.
About 0.01 hours
This is much smaller than the plotted decrease of about 0.04 hours.
qs.x: 0.105 − 0.063 = 0.042. Trap: Overlooking diminishing returns: later increases in n buy much smaller gains in precision than early ones.

graph.title: Figure 1. Half-width of 95% CI versus sample size (SD = 1.6 h)

passages.title: FL06 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 1
text: Hemoglobin A (HbA) binds oxygen cooperatively. A hematology group characterized a patient-derived variant, Hb-V, in which a single amino acid substitution weakens a salt bridge that normally stabilizes the T (tense) conformation of the tetramer. Purified HbA and Hb-V were equilibrated with defined partial pressures of O2 at 37 degrees C and pH 7.4, and fractional saturation (Y) was measured spectrophotometrically. Data were fit with the Hill equation, log[Y/(1 - Y)] = n log pO2 - n log P50, where P50 is the pO2 at half saturation and n is the Hill coefficient. In the lungs, alveolar capillary blood is exposed to a pO2 of about 100 mmHg, while resting systemic tissues operate at a pO2 of about 40 mmHg. The patient has a hematocrit above the reference range and a normal arterial pO2. Table 1 lists saturation values, and Figure 1 plots the two saturation curves. Investigators also confirmed by mass spectrometry that the two proteins have the same subunit composition apart from the single substitution, and that heme content per tetramer is identical, so differences in the curves reflect allosteric behavior.

qs.q: Compared with Hb-V, how much more O2 does HbA release (in percentage points of saturation) when blood moves from the lungs (100 mmHg) to resting tissue (40 mmHg)?
o: About 9 percentage points more, since HbA falls about 21 points and Hb-V falls about 12 points
Correct: HbA drops from 97.8% to 77.0% saturation, a 20.8-point fall, whereas Hb-V drops from 95.0% to 82.8%, a 12.2-point fall; the difference is about 8.6 points.
About 9 percentage points more, but Hb-V is the one that falls about 21 points and HbA about 12
This reverses the two curves; HbA is the steeper, right-shifted curve and so unloads more.;
About 1 percentage point more, since both curves reach near 95 to 98 percent saturation in the lungs
Equal loading in the lungs does not mean equal unloading; the curves differ markedly at 40 mmHg.;
About 35 percentage points more, since HbA falls from near 98 percent to near 62 percent saturation
HbA is 77% saturated at 40 mmHg, not 62%; this overstates the unloading.
qs.x: HbA drops from 97.8% to 77.0% saturation, a 20.8-point fall, whereas Hb-V drops from 95.0% to 82.8%, a 12.2-point fall; the difference is about 8.6 points. Trap: Comparing only the saturation at the lungs (both near 95-98%) and forgetting that unloading is the difference between lung and tissue values.

qs.q: The Hill coefficient of Hb-V (1.5) is lower than that of HbA (2.8). Which statement best interprets this difference?
o: Each Hb-V subunit binds O2 independently, so the curve is hyperbolic exactly like that of monomeric myoglobin
n = 1.5 is still above 1, so some cooperativity remains; only n = 1 is non-cooperative.;
Binding of O2 to one subunit of Hb-V lowers the O2 affinity of the remaining subunits, as in negative cooperativity
n greater than 1 indicates positive, not negative, cooperativity (negative would be n less than 1).;
Binding of O2 to one subunit of Hb-V raises the O2 affinity of the remaining subunits less than it does in HbA
Correct: A lower n means weaker positive cooperativity; the destabilized T-state salt bridge means less energy is stored to be released on the first binding event.
Hb-V carries fewer total O2 binding sites per tetramer than HbA, which flattens its saturation curve at high pO2
Both tetramers have four heme groups; both approach near-full saturation at 100 mmHg.
qs.x: A lower n means weaker positive cooperativity; the destabilized T-state salt bridge means less energy is stored to be released on the first binding event. Trap: Treating any n greater than 1 as equal to full cooperativity, or reading a left shift (P50) as a change in the Hill coefficient.

qs.q: Which response is most likely in the patient with Hb-V, whose arterial pO2 is normal?
o: Decreased erythropoietin secretion, because arterial O2 saturation in the lungs is not reduced
EPO is driven by renal tissue oxygenation, not by lung saturation alone.;
Decreased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate synthesis in red cells, because the curve is already shifted to the right
Hb-V curve is shifted left, not right.;
Increased erythrocyte pH, because protons released by Hb-V stabilize the R conformation of the tetramer
Hb-V does not release excess protons in a way that explains polycythemia; the hematocrit rise reflects hypoxia sensing.
Increased renal erythropoietin secretion, because impaired O2 release lowers pO2 in kidney tissue
Correct: High-affinity Hb-V unloads less O2 (P50 14 mmHg), so renal interstitial pO2 falls and the kidney raises erythropoietin, raising hematocrit.
qs.x: High-affinity Hb-V unloads less O2 (P50 14 mmHg), so renal interstitial pO2 falls and the kidney raises erythropoietin, raising hematocrit. Trap: Assuming a normal arterial pO2 means normal tissue oxygenation, ignoring that high-affinity hemoglobin withholds O2 from tissues.

qs.q: During heavy exercise, muscle capillary blood is more acidic (pH near 7.2). Which molecular event best explains the resulting rightward shift of the HbA curve?
o: Deprotonation of His146 on the beta chains breaks a salt bridge and stabilizes the high-affinity R state
The direction is reversed; acid promotes protonation, not deprotonation.;
Protons displace O2 competitively at the heme iron of each subunit, lowering saturation by simple mass action
Protons bind to amino acid side chains, not at the heme O2 site; the effect is allosteric.;
Protonation of His146 on the beta chains promotes a salt bridge that stabilizes the T state
Correct: The Bohr effect: protons bind beta His146 and other residues, favoring the low-affinity T conformation and raising P50.
Protonation of the proximal histidine oxidizes the heme iron to Fe3+, which cannot bind O2 until it is reduced
Oxidation to methemoglobin is not the Bohr mechanism and would not be reversible by pH alone.
qs.x: The Bohr effect: protons bind beta His146 and other residues, favoring the low-affinity T conformation and raising P50. Trap: Picturing protons as competitive ligands at the heme rather than as allosteric effectors on side chains that stabilize the T state.

qs.q: Using the HbA data at 20 and 40 mmHg, what is the approximate slope of a Hill plot, log[Y/(1 - Y)] versus log pO2, over this interval?
o: Half the true slope; arises from dividing by 0.602 (log 4) instead of 0.301 (log 2).;
This is the rise on the y axis only; the slope also requires dividing by the change in log pO2.;
A slope of 1 describes non-cooperative binding, which does not fit HbA.
Correct: Y = 0.324 gives log(0.479) = -0.32; Y = 0.770 gives log(3.35) = +0.52; the rise is 0.84 over a log pO2 change of 0.301, so slope = 2.8.
qs.x: Y = 0.324 gives log(0.479) = -0.32; Y = 0.770 gives log(3.35) = +0.52; the rise is 0.84 over a log pO2 change of 0.301, so slope = 2.8. Trap: Forgetting to divide the y change by the x change in log units, or using a doubling of pO2 as 4-fold.

graph.title: Figure 1. Oxygen saturation curves of HbA and Hb-V

passages.title: FL06 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 2
text: Many human genes contain exons whose inclusion depends on recognition of the 5' splice site, which begins with the dinucleotide GU at the first two bases of the intron. A patient with a hereditary enzyme deficiency carries a G-to-A change at the first nucleotide of intron 4 in gene G (GU becomes AU). To test its effect, researchers built minigenes containing exons 3, 4, and 5 with their flanking introns, transfected them into cultured cells, and amplified spliced mRNA by RT-PCR using a forward primer in exon 3 and a reverse primer in exon 5. The amplified region contributes 80 nucleotides from exon 3 and 70 nucleotides from exon 5; exon 4 is 100 nucleotides long. Products were resolved on a gel and band intensities were quantified (Table 1). In a fourth condition, an engineered U1 snRNA whose 5' end was made complementary to the mutant sequence was co-expressed. Cells were harvested 36 hours after transfection, and each condition was repeated in three independent transfections with similar results; values in Table 1 are means. Primer positions were chosen so that every spliced form of the transcript could be amplified with equal efficiency.

qs.q: Which spliceosomal component normally recognizes the intronic GU at the 5' splice site by base pairing and is therefore most directly affected by this mutation?
o: U1 snRNP, whose RNA component base pairs with the 5' splice site sequence
Correct: U1 snRNA pairs with the conserved 5' splice site; an AU at the intron start weakens this pairing and exon 4 is not defined.
U2 snRNP, whose RNA component base pairs with the 3' splice site at the intron-exon junction
U2 recognizes the branch point adenine, not the 5' splice site.;
U6 snRNP, whose RNA component pairs with the polypyrimidine tract upstream of exon 5
U6 replaces U1 at the 5' splice site later, but the initial recognition of GU is by U1; the polypyrimidine tract binds U2AF.;
The exon junction complex, which is deposited after splicing and positions the intron for lariat formation
The exon junction complex is deposited after splicing and does not recognize splice sites.
qs.x: U1 snRNA pairs with the conserved 5' splice site; an AU at the intron start weakens this pairing and exon 4 is not defined. Trap: Confusing the branch point (U2) and 3' splice site machinery with the 5' splice site, which is recognized by U1.

qs.q: Assuming equal total mRNA in the wild-type and mutant conditions, the mutant minigene produces what fraction of the exon-4-containing mRNA made by the wild-type minigene?
o: About 93 percent, because the 150-nt band is the one containing exon 4 in the mutant
The 150-nt band equals 80 + 70 and lacks exon 4; it is the skipped product.;
About 7 percent, because 7 divided by 94 is approximately 0.07
Correct: Exon-4-containing mRNA is the 250-nt (80 + 100 + 70) product: 7% in mutant versus 94% in wild type, a ratio of about 0.074.
About 15-fold higher, because the 150-nt band in the mutant (93) divided by that in wild type (6) is roughly 15
That is the increase in skipped product, not the change in included product.;
About 50 percent, because the mutation affects only one of two alleles in the minigene system
The minigene is a single copy construct in each cell; no allelic dilution is involved.
qs.x: Exon-4-containing mRNA is the 250-nt (80 + 100 + 70) product: 7% in mutant versus 94% in wild type, a ratio of about 0.074. Trap: Identifying the wrong band as the exon-inclusion product; 250 = 80 + 100 + 70 includes exon 4, while 150 skips it.

qs.q: If the 150-nt skipped mRNA were translated in the full gene, what is the most likely consequence for the encoded enzyme?
o: An in-frame deletion of 33 amino acids, because the removal of 100 nucleotides preserves the reading frame
100 is not a multiple of 3; a 99-nt exon would preserve frame, not 100.;
A frameshift downstream of exon 3, because 100 nucleotides is not divisible by 3, and a truncated protein
Correct: Loss of 100 nt shifts the reading frame (100 = 33 x 3 + 1), so codons in exon 5 are misread and a premature stop is likely.
No change in the protein, because exon 4 is replaced by sequences from the adjacent introns during splicing
Introns are removed, not substituted, and exon skipping does not insert intron sequence.;
A longer protein that retains exon 4 and adds the intron, because the mutant 5' splice site cannot be cleaved
Skipping removes exon 4; it does not add sequence, and the 150-nt band is shorter, not longer.
qs.x: Loss of 100 nt shifts the reading frame (100 = 33 x 3 + 1), so codons in exon 5 are misread and a premature stop is likely. Trap: Counting the 100-nt loss as in-frame without checking divisibility by 3.

qs.q: What does the partial rescue by the engineered U1 snRNA (61% included product) most strongly indicate?
o: The mutation acts by creating a cryptic 3' splice site inside exon 4 that the engineered U1 snRNA suppresses
U1 acts at 5' splice sites; the data give no evidence for a cryptic 3' site.;
The mutation disrupts the polyadenylation signal of the transcript, and the engineered U1 restores 3' end processing
Polyadenylation signals are not involved here; both amplified products were spliced mRNAs.;
Base pairing between U1 snRNA and the 5' splice site is required for inclusion of exon 4, and restoring complementarity restores it in part
Correct: The control U1 gave no rescue, while a U1 complementary to AU did; this supports a causal role for U1-5' splice site pairing.
Exon 4 inclusion depends on the translation of the minigene, and the engineered U1 stabilizes the mutant mRNA by blocking decay
Splicing occurs on the pre-mRNA before translation; stability was not tested.
qs.x: The control U1 gave no rescue, while a U1 complementary to AU did; this supports a causal role for U1-5' splice site pairing. Trap: Over-reading a rescue as full restoration; 61% inclusion versus 94% shows only partial repair, and the control U1 is what proves specificity.

passages.title: FL06 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 3
text: A growth-restriction disorder was traced to a deletion allele (D) of an autosomal gene that is imprinted: in normal tissues only the copy inherited from the father is transcribed, and the maternal copy is silenced by DNA methylation at a differentially methylated region. Clinicians studied a three-generation family (Table 1). The deletion removes the coding sequence, so a person who inherits D from the father has no functional copy expressed, whereas a person who inherits D from the mother expresses the normal paternal copy. Among people who inherit D from the father, the disorder appears in 80 percent (penetrance 0.8); no person who inherited D from the mother was affected. II-2 and II-4 are the parents of generation III. Assume no new mutations, that all individuals were genotyped by PCR, and that penetrance and imprinting apply equally to both sexes. I-1 inherited D from his own mother, who was not a family member.

qs.q: Which comparison in Table 1 most directly shows that the phenotype depends on the parent of origin of D rather than on the D/+ genotype alone?
o: II-1 and II-2 are both affected, which shows the disorder is more common in people who have an affected sibling in the family
Two affected siblings do not separate parental origin from genotype; both inherited D from the father.
I-1 and III-1 are both unaffected D/+ men, which proves that D acts as a recessive allele in men but not in women
The unaffected D/+ men inherited D from mothers; the pattern follows parent of origin, not recessiveness or the sex of the carrier.
I-1 and II-1 are both D/+ men, yet only II-1 is affected; II-1 received D from his father and I-1 received it from his mother
Correct: Identical genotypes with different phenotypes, sorted by the sex of the transmitting parent, are the signature of imprinting.
I-2 and II-3 are both unaffected +/+ women, which shows the normal allele is dominant over D in every generation
+/+ individuals carry no D, so they cannot test an effect of parental origin.
qs.x: Identical genotypes with different phenotypes, sorted by the sex of the transmitting parent, are the signature of imprinting. Trap: Reading identical genotypes with different phenotypes as simple incomplete penetrance, when the phenotype sorts perfectly by the sex of the transmitting parent.

qs.q: II-2 (D/+) and II-4 (+/+) plan another child. What is the probability that the child is affected?
o: 0, because any D allele from II-2 would be maternal in the child and silenced
Correct: A child of II-2 who receives D gets it from the mother; that copy is silenced and the paternal copy from II-4 is normal and expressed, so the risk is 0 (as seen for III-1 and III-2).
0.2, because half of the children inherit D and penetrance is then halved again for maternal origin of the allele
No further halving applies; maternal D never causes disease in this family.
0.4, because half of the children inherit D and penetrance in D/+ carriers is 0.8, regardless of the parent
0.5 x 0.8 = 0.4 applies only when the carrier parent is the father.
0.5, because half of the children inherit D from the parent who carries it, and all carriers are affected
0.5 is only the chance of inheriting D; it ignores that maternal D is not expressed.
qs.x: A child of II-2 who receives D gets it from the mother; that copy is silenced and the paternal copy from II-4 is normal and expressed, so the risk is 0 (as seen for III-1 and III-2). Trap: Using the Mendelian 1/2 chance of inheriting D as the disease risk, even though II-2 is the carrier and her allele will be silenced in the child.

qs.q: III-1 is an unaffected D/+ man who has a child with a +/+ woman. What is the probability that the child is affected?
o: 0, because III-1 is unaffected and so cannot pass on an expressed copy of D to any of his children
His own phenotype does not predict his child's; his silenced state is not transmitted.
0.2, because III-1 inherited D from his mother and the effect is therefore reduced by half in the child
Nothing halves the effect; 0.2 has no basis in the given penetrance.
0.5, because every child who inherits D from III-1 is certain to be affected, as penetrance is complete
0.5 ignores the stated penetrance of 0.8 for paternally inherited D.
0.4, because the imprint is reset in his germline, so D is paternal in his child (0.5 x 0.8 = 0.4)

Correct: Imprints are erased and re-established in the germline by the sex of the carrier, so D passed by III-1 is expressed as a paternal allele; 0.5 chance of inheriting D x 0.8 penetrance = 0.4 (as when I-1 had affected II-1 and II-2).
qs.x: Imprints are erased and re-established in the germline by the sex of the carrier, so D passed by III-1 is expressed as a paternal allele; 0.5 chance of inheriting D x 0.8 penetrance = 0.4 (as when I-1 had affected II-1 and II-2). Trap: Assuming an unaffected carrier cannot have affected offspring, which forgets that the imprint is reset in the germline of each generation.

qs.q: Which molecular mechanism best explains why the maternal copy of the gene is not expressed in normal tissues?
o: Acetylation of histones across the maternal gene, which compacts the chromatin and blocks transcription
Histone acetylation loosens chromatin and promotes, not blocks, transcription.
Methylation of cytosines at a differentially methylated region on the maternal allele, reset in gametes
Correct: DNA methylation at a differentially methylated region silences one parental allele, and the mark is reset in the germline.
Random inactivation of one chromosome in each cell, producing a mosaic of maternal and paternal expression
Random choice in each cell describes X inactivation; imprinting always silences the same parental allele.
Loss of the maternal gene by deletion in the egg, which is later corrected by repair after fertilization
The maternal allele is intact and silenced epigenetically, not deleted.
qs.x: DNA methylation at a differentially methylated region silences one parental allele, and the mark is reset in the germline. Trap: Confusing imprinting with random X inactivation; imprinting always silences the same parental allele in every cell.

passages.title: FL06 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 4
text: Mitochondria were isolated from rat liver and suspended in a sealed chamber fitted with an oxygen electrode. Substrates and inhibitors were added as indicated in Table 1, and the rate of O2 consumption was recorded. With pyruvate and malate (which generate NADH in the matrix), respiration is slow until ADP is added (state 3). Each condition was run in a fresh sample. Rotenone, antimycin A, and oligomycin are inhibitors of different components of oxidative phosphorylation: rotenone binds the ubiquinone site of Complex I, antimycin A blocks electron transfer through Complex III, and oligomycin blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase (Fo). 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) is a lipophilic weak acid that carries protons across the inner membrane. Succinate donates electrons through Complex II. Rates are expressed as nmol O2 per minute per mg mitochondrial protein. Respiratory buffer contained phosphate, magnesium, and a fixed concentration of mitochondrial protein, and the chamber was maintained at 30 degrees C. Preparations with a respiratory control ratio below 5 in the pyruvate and malate control were discarded.

qs.q: The data in conditions 3 and 4 support which conclusion about the mitochondria?
o: Complex I is blocked, but electron flow through Complex II, Complex III, and Complex IV remains intact
Correct: Rotenone drops respiration to 8, and succinate, which feeds electrons into ubiquinone via Complex II, restores 90, so downstream complexes work.
Complex II is blocked, but electron flow through Complex I, Complex III, and Complex IV remains intact
Succinate is oxidized by Complex II, and respiration recovers on adding it; Complex II is functional.;
ATP synthase is blocked, but electron flow through Complexes I to IV remains intact in the presence of ADP
Rotenone does not target ATP synthase, and respiration is low because NADH oxidation is blocked.;
Complex IV is blocked, but the other complexes are able to pass electrons to ubiquinone and cytochrome c
If Complex IV were blocked, succinate could not restore respiration.
qs.x: Rotenone drops respiration to 8, and succinate, which feeds electrons into ubiquinone via Complex II, restores 90, so downstream complexes work. Trap: Assuming that an inhibitor that stops respiration blocks the whole chain, when a bypass substrate (succinate) can restore flow beyond the block.

qs.q: In condition 5, which change in the redox state of carriers is expected?
o: Ubiquinone and the carriers upstream of Complex III become more oxidized, while cytochrome c becomes more reduced
This reverses the backup; upstream carriers cannot pass electrons and stay reduced.;
All carriers of the chain, including cytochrome c and Complex IV, become more reduced as O2 is no longer consumed
Complex IV and cytochrome c lie downstream of the block and are drained of electrons by the remaining O2.;
All carriers of the chain, including ubiquinone and Complex I, become more oxidized because electron input has stopped
Succinate is still present and feeds electrons in; upstream carriers are reduced, not oxidized.
Ubiquinone and upstream carriers become more reduced, while cytochrome c and Complex IV become more oxidized
Correct: Antimycin A blocks electron exit from the cytochrome b-c1 complex, so electrons back up in upstream carriers while downstream carriers lose their electrons to O2 until they are oxidized.
qs.x: Antimycin A blocks electron exit from the cytochrome b-c1 complex, so electrons back up in upstream carriers while downstream carriers lose their electrons to O2 until they are oxidized. Trap: Forgetting that an inhibitor makes everything upstream reduced and everything downstream oxidized.

qs.q: Why does DNP restore O2 consumption (condition 7) after oligomycin has inhibited it (condition 6)?
o: DNP removes oligomycin from the Fo channel, so ATP synthase resumes making ATP at the state 3 rate
DNP does not reverse oligomycin; ATP synthesis is not required for the rate.;
DNP dissipates the proton gradient, so electron transport proceeds without ATP synthase flux
Correct: Oligomycin lets the gradient build until it opposes proton pumping; DNP carries protons back across the membrane, uncoupling respiration from ATP synthesis.
DNP donates electrons directly to cytochrome c oxidase, which bypasses the need for Complexes I through III
DNP is a protonophore, not an electron donor.;
DNP raises the proton gradient across the inner membrane, which activates Complex I in the absence of ADP
DNP lowers, not raises, the gradient.
qs.x: Oligomycin lets the gradient build until it opposes proton pumping; DNP carries protons back across the membrane, uncoupling respiration from ATP synthesis. Trap: Thinking that respiration depends on ATP synthesis itself, when electron flow is limited by the proton gradient (respiratory control).

qs.q: What is the respiratory control ratio (state 3 to state 4) for pyruvate and malate in this preparation?
o: This results from dividing 120 by 90 (the succinate condition) instead of 15.;
Correct: State 3 (with ADP) is 120 and state 4 (no ADP) is 15; 120/15 = 8.
This is the difference 120 - 15 rather than the ratio.;
This is the inverse ratio, 15/120.
qs.x: State 3 (with ADP) is 120 and state 4 (no ADP) is 15; 120/15 = 8. Trap: Subtracting instead of dividing, or inverting the ratio of rates.

qs.q: Malonate is a competitive inhibitor of succinate dehydrogenase. In mitochondria oxidizing pyruvate and malate with ADP, malonate would most directly cause which change?
o: Succinyl-CoA accumulates because the cycle is blocked before the succinyl-CoA synthetase step
Succinyl-CoA lies upstream of succinate and would be depleted/limited rather than the intermediate that accumulates.;
Fumarate accumulates while succinate falls because the reaction runs in reverse in the matrix
SDH is inhibited, not reversed; fumarate is downstream and would fall.;
Citrate synthase activity increases because oxaloacetate becomes more available once the cycle is blocked
Oxaloacetate regeneration depends on the full cycle; blockage lowers it.
Succinate accumulates while fumarate and malate formed from it decline, slowing the TCA cycle
Correct: SDH converts succinate to fumarate; blocking it halts the cycle at that step and succinate builds up.
qs.x: SDH converts succinate to fumarate; blocking it halts the cycle at that step and succinate builds up. Trap: Mixing up which intermediates lie upstream and downstream of a blocked step.

passages.title: FL06 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 5
text: Microtubule-targeting drugs are used in cancer chemotherapy. Paclitaxel binds the beta-tubulin subunit within the polymer and stabilizes microtubules; colchicine binds free alpha/beta-tubulin dimers and prevents their addition to polymers. In an in vitro assay, purified tubulin plus GTP was warmed to 37 degrees C and polymerization was followed by turbidity (absorbance at 350 nm) with vehicle, paclitaxel, or colchicine (Figure 1). Separately, dividing cultured cells were exposed to each drug for 18 hours, fixed, stained for DNA and tubulin, and scored for mitotic index (percent of cells in mitosis) and the percentage of mitotic cells with a bipolar spindle (Table 1). Neurons in non-dividing culture were also treated; they showed reduced delivery of vesicles to distal axon terminals. Cell experiments used a concentration of each drug that produced a maximal effect without detectable cell death over this interval, and at least 500 cells were scored per condition by observers blind to treatment.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for the high mitotic index with both drugs?
o: Defective spindle attachment inactivates the G1/S checkpoint, which prevents cells from reaching mitosis at all
Drug-treated cells accumulate in mitosis, so they do pass G1/S.;
Defective spindle attachment keeps the spindle assembly checkpoint active, inhibiting the APC/C and delaying anaphase
Correct: Unattached or untensioned kinetochores generate a checkpoint signal that blocks APC/C-mediated degradation of securin and cyclin B, so cells remain in mitosis.
Defective spindle attachment activates the APC/C, which degrades cyclin B and drives early exit from metaphase
APC/C activation promotes anaphase, which is opposite to the observed arrest.;
Drug binding to centromeric DNA blocks replication in S phase and arrests cells with 4N content before mitosis
The drugs bind tubulin, not DNA, and arrested cells are in mitosis, not S phase.
qs.x: Unattached or untensioned kinetochores generate a checkpoint signal that blocks APC/C-mediated degradation of securin and cyclin B, so cells remain in mitosis. Trap: Treating a mitotic arrest as a G1 or S arrest, instead of a spindle checkpoint response.

qs.q: At 10 minutes in Figure 1, the absorbance in the paclitaxel sample is how many times that of the vehicle sample, and what does the ratio suggest?
o: About 0.36-fold, indicating that paclitaxel slows polymerization
0.36 is the inverse ratio (0.10/0.28); the paclitaxel signal is higher.;
About 2.8-fold, indicating that paclitaxel accelerates polymerization
Correct: 0.28/0.10 = 2.8; paclitaxel promotes assembly and stabilizes the polymer, shortening the lag phase.
About 14-fold, indicating that paclitaxel completely blocks depolymerization
The ratio is 2.8, not 14; 14 would come from comparing 0.28 with colchicine (0.02).;
About 1.0-fold, indicating that paclitaxel has no effect on the lag phase of polymerization
The two curves diverge markedly by 10 min.
qs.x: 0.28/0.10 = 2.8; paclitaxel promotes assembly and stabilizes the polymer, shortening the lag phase. Trap: Reading the ratio upside down; a larger turbidity means more polymer.

qs.q: Neurons treated with the drugs show reduced delivery of vesicles to axon terminals. Which statement best explains this effect?
o: Kinesin motors carry vesicles toward microtubule plus ends, and disrupted dynamics impair anterograde transport
Correct: Axonal microtubules have plus ends oriented away from the soma; kinesin walks toward plus ends, so tracks that are altered by the drugs reduce delivery.
Dynein motors carry vesicles toward the plus ends of axonal microtubules, and the drugs inactivate this retrograde motor
Dynein moves toward minus ends (retrograde, toward the soma).;
Kinesin motors carry vesicles toward the minus ends of axonal microtubules, which lie at the axon terminal
Minus ends lie near the cell body; kinesin moves toward plus ends.;
Actin-based myosin motors carry vesicles along axonal microtubule bundles and require tubulin GTP hydrolysis for movement
Myosins use actin tracks; this does not explain a tubulin-targeting effect.
qs.x: Axonal microtubules have plus ends oriented away from the soma; kinesin walks toward plus ends, so tracks that are altered by the drugs reduce delivery. Trap: Reversing kinesin and dynein polarity relative to the axon.

qs.q: Out of 1,000 cells scored, approximately how many paclitaxel-treated cells were in mitosis with a bipolar spindle?
o: This counts all mitotic cells, not only those with bipolar spindles.;
Correct: Mitotic cells = 0.30 x 1000 = 300; 40% of these have bipolar spindles: 300 x 0.40 = 120.
This applies the bipolar percentage to the total cell count rather than to the mitotic fraction.;
This multiplies 0.30 by 0.40 by 100 instead of by 1000.
qs.x: Mitotic cells = 0.30 x 1000 = 300; 40% of these have bipolar spindles: 300 x 0.40 = 120. Trap: Applying a percentage of mitotic cells to the whole population or mixing the denominators.
