passages.title: FL06 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 6
text: Bacteria regulate gene expression according to nutrient availability. In E. coli, the lac operon (lacZ, lacY, lacA) is controlled by the LacI repressor, which binds the operator (lacO), and by the CAP-cAMP activator, whose levels rise when glucose is scarce. The trp operon encodes enzymes for tryptophan synthesis and is controlled by the TrpR repressor and by attenuation within a leader region (trpL). A student measured beta-galactosidase (lacZ product) activity as a percent of the wild-type induced level, and tryptophan synthesis enzyme activity as a percent of the level in tryptophan-free medium (Table 1). Lactose, or its isomer allolactose, is the natural inducer; 'O^c' is a mutation in the operator that prevents repressor binding. 'I^s' encodes a repressor that cannot bind allolactose. Glycerol provides carbon without lowering cAMP. All strains were grown to mid-log phase at 37 degrees C in minimal medium with the indicated carbon sources, and each activity was normalized to cell density. Values are the mean of three independent cultures that differed by less than 10 percent.

qs.q: Why is beta-galactosidase activity of the lacI- strain only 6% in glucose plus lactose, although the repressor is absent?
o: Glucose raises allolactose levels, and allolactose binds the operator to block RNA polymerase from the promoter
Allolactose releases the repressor from the operator; it does not block transcription, and LacI is absent here.;
Glucose induces additional LacI synthesis from a second gene, which restores repression of the operon
The strain lacks functional LacI, so no repressor can be restored.;
Glucose directly inhibits beta-galactosidase enzyme activity by binding the active site of the lacZ product
The measured effect is on expression and is shared by other strains with different lac defects.
Glucose lowers cAMP, so the CAP-cAMP activator is not available to stimulate transcription of the lac promoter
Correct: Without repression, the lac promoter is still weak; high glucose reduces adenylyl cyclase activity and CAP-cAMP, so output remains low (catabolite repression).
qs.x: Without repression, the lac promoter is still weak; high glucose reduces adenylyl cyclase activity and CAP-cAMP, so output remains low (catabolite repression). Trap: Assuming that without the repressor the operon must be maximally expressed regardless of the carbon source.

qs.q: A merodiploid carries lacO^c lacZ+ on the chromosome and lacO+ lacZ- on an F' plasmid, with functional LacI. In glycerol without lactose, which result is expected?
o: Beta-galactosidase activity is low, because the diffusible LacI repressor from the F' plasmid binds the mutant operator
LacI cannot bind O^c, so repressor diffusion does not help.;
Beta-galactosidase activity is low, because the lacZ- allele on the F' plasmid is dominant over the chromosomal lacZ+
Mutations in a structural gene are recessive when a functional copy exists.;
Beta-galactosidase activity is high, because O^c acts in cis on the lacZ+ gene on the same DNA molecule
Correct: The operator mutation affects only the genes on the same DNA, so the chromosomal lacZ+ is constitutively expressed despite repressor.
Beta-galactosidase activity is intermediate, because the F' operator and the chromosomal operator compete for the activator
Operators are not shared between DNA molecules; effect is in cis.
qs.x: The operator mutation affects only the genes on the same DNA, so the chromosomal lacZ+ is constitutively expressed despite repressor. Trap: Treating an operator mutation as trans-acting like a repressor mutation; only lacI mutations are diffusible.

qs.q: Which explanation fits the activity of the lacI^s strain (1% in all conditions)?
o: The mutant repressor cannot bind the operator but binds allolactose, so lactose is sequestered and induction fails
A repressor that cannot bind the operator would give constitutive expression, as in lacI-.;
The mutant repressor binds CAP-cAMP, and prevents it from activating the promoter in any carbon source
No evidence indicates repressor-CAP interaction; the phenotype is lack of induction.;
The mutant repressor binds the operator but not allolactose, so it is never released
Correct: A superrepressor remains locked on the operator, so even lactose cannot induce transcription.
The mutant gene produces too much beta-galactosidase, which then feeds back to block its own mRNA
Enzyme product does not feed back on mRNA in this way; activity is low, not high.
qs.x: A superrepressor remains locked on the operator, so even lactose cannot induce transcription. Trap: Confusing superrepressor (I^s) with I- (no operator binding), which would be constitutive.

qs.q: In Table 1b, the trpR- strain still shows 30% activity with tryptophan rather than 100%. Which mechanism most likely accounts for the reduction?
o: Attenuation: abundant tryptophan lets ribosomes translate the leader quickly, so a terminator hairpin forms
Correct: Charged tRNA-Trp is plentiful, so the ribosome moves past the Trp codons in the leader; the 3-4 terminator hairpin forms and RNA polymerase falls off.
Attenuation: with abundant tryptophan, ribosomes stall at the Trp codons in the leader, allowing the 2-3 antiterminator hairpin to form
Stalling at Trp codons occurs when tryptophan is scarce and favors antitermination.;
Tryptophan binds the operator directly and blocks RNA polymerase, a role that remains when TrpR is absent
Tryptophan acts through TrpR, which is absent here.;
Tryptophan raises cAMP and the CAP-cAMP complex activates the trp promoter, which would increase activity
The trp operon is not controlled by CAP-cAMP in this way, and activation would raise rather than lower activity.
qs.x: Charged tRNA-Trp is plentiful, so the ribosome moves past the Trp codons in the leader; the 3-4 terminator hairpin forms and RNA polymerase falls off. Trap: Linking ribosome stalling to high, rather than low, tryptophan; stalling allows transcription to continue.

qs.q: Which statement correctly contrasts the lac and trp operons?
o: The lac operon is inducible because its inducer inactivates the repressor, whereas the trp operon is repressible because its corepressor activates the repressor
Correct: Allolactose binds LacI and releases it from the operator; tryptophan binds TrpR and enables operator binding.
The lac operon is repressible because its end product activates the repressor, whereas the trp operon is inducible because its substrate inactivates the repressor
This assigns each operon the other's control mode.;
Both operons are inducible because in each case the small-molecule effector releases the repressor from the operator
Tryptophan promotes, rather than prevents, TrpR binding to the operator.;
Both operons are controlled only by positive regulators because the repressor lacks a role in either regulatory circuit
Both operons have a repressor with a defined role; CAP only adds to lac regulation.
qs.x: Allolactose binds LacI and releases it from the operator; tryptophan binds TrpR and enables operator binding. Trap: Swapping inducible and repressible, or assuming both small molecules inactivate their repressors.

passages.title: FL06 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 7
text: Pluripotent mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) express the transcription factor Oct4 and self-renew in culture. Withdrawal of leukemia inhibitory factor and addition of retinoic acid (RA) induces differentiation toward neural ectoderm, marked by the transcription factor Pax6. Researchers collected cells every 2 days after RA addition and measured Oct4 and Pax6 mRNA by qPCR, expressed as a percent of each gene's maximum (Figure 1). In a second experiment, cells were treated for 6 days with RA under four conditions, and mRNA levels were normalized to a day-0 or maximal reference (Table 1). Brachyury, a mesodermal marker, was also measured. siRNA was introduced by transfection; the Oct4 transgene lacks its native promoter and was driven by a constitutive promoter. Each time point was measured in three biological replicates, and the plotted values are means. Cells were maintained in monolayer culture at identical density and with identical medium changes across all conditions to avoid differences caused by crowding.

qs.q: Pax6 induction after RA, with low Brachyury, indicates that the cells are differentiating toward which germ layer and derivatives?
o: Mesoderm, which gives rise to muscle, bone, and the circulatory system
Mesoderm is marked by Brachyury, which stays at about 3%.;
Ectoderm, which gives rise to the nervous system and epidermis
Correct: Pax6 marks neural ectoderm, which forms the neural tube, brain, and eye; Brachyury marks mesoderm, which stays low.
Endoderm, which gives rise to the lining of the gut and the liver and pancreas
Endoderm markers (Sox17, Foxa2) were not measured, and Pax6 is not an endoderm marker.;
Trophectoderm, which gives rise to the placenta and chorion outside the embryo proper
Trophectoderm is an extra-embryonic lineage marked by other factors such as Cdx2.
qs.x: Pax6 marks neural ectoderm, which forms the neural tube, brain, and eye; Brachyury marks mesoderm, which stays low. Trap: Choosing mesoderm because of the name 'ectoderm' versus 'mesoderm'; marker gene identity decides, and Pax6 is neural.

qs.q: Based on the Oct4 transgene condition in Table 1, which conclusion is best supported?
o: Oct4 is a direct transcriptional activator of Pax6, because Pax6 rises when Oct4 is expressed
Pax6 falls, not rises, with sustained Oct4.;
Sustained Oct4 expression suppresses RA-driven induction of Pax6, so loss of Oct4 is needed for neural differentiation
Correct: With constitutive Oct4, Pax6 stays at 15% compared with 85% in controls, even though RA is present.
Oct4 expression converts the cells to mesoderm, because Brachyury rises to the highest level when Oct4 is retained
Brachyury is only 8%, scarcely above the 3% baseline.;
Oct4 is dispensable for the pluripotent state, because Pax6 induction occurs normally in the transgene group
Pax6 induction is blunted in the transgene group, and its absence in the no-RA group shows the state is maintained.
qs.x: With constitutive Oct4, Pax6 stays at 15% compared with 85% in controls, even though RA is present. Trap: Reading Oct4 as a driver of the neural program rather than a barrier to it.

qs.q: According to Figure 1, when do the Oct4 and Pax6 mRNA levels cross?
o: Between days 1 and 2, when both are near 70% of maximum
At day 2, Oct4 is 70 but Pax6 is only 10.;
Between days 5 and 6, when both are near 10% of maximum
At day 6 Pax6 is already 85.;
They do not cross, because Oct4 falls below 10% before Pax6 rises above 50%
Pax6 reaches 45 by day 4 while Oct4 is still 30; the lines cross.
Between days 3 and 4, when both are near 40% of maximum
Correct: Interpolating, Oct4 falls from 70 to 30 and Pax6 rises from 10 to 45 between days 2 and 4; they are equal near day 3.6 at about 38%.
qs.x: Interpolating, Oct4 falls from 70 to 30 and Pax6 rises from 10 to 45 between days 2 and 4; they are equal near day 3.6 at about 38%. Trap: Reading the crossing from the endpoints rather than interpolating between plotted points.

qs.q: Which mechanism most plausibly silences the Oct4 gene during differentiation?
o: Demethylation of its promoter, together with histone acetylation, which opens chromatin
These marks are associated with active transcription.;
Mutation of the Oct4 coding sequence by RA, which prevents synthesis of a functional protein
RA does not mutate DNA; the effect is on mRNA levels and is reversible in principle.;
Increased telomerase activity, which shortens telomeres and prevents Oct4 transcription
Telomerase lengthens telomeres, and it is not a transcriptional silencing mechanism.
CpG methylation of its promoter, together with histone deacetylation, which compacts chromatin
Correct: Differentiating cells recruit DNA methyltransferases and deacetylases to pluripotency gene promoters, producing stable silencing.
qs.x: Differentiating cells recruit DNA methyltransferases and deacetylases to pluripotency gene promoters, producing stable silencing. Trap: Associating differentiation with demethylation of all genes; silencing of pluripotency genes requires repressive marks.

graph.title: Figure 1. Marker mRNA after retinoic acid addition

passages.title: FL06 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 8
text: Cortisol secretion is controlled by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) stimulates anterior pituitary release of ACTH, which stimulates the adrenal cortex; cortisol exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary. ACTH is cleaved from proopiomelanocortin (POMC), which also yields melanocyte-stimulating hormone. Dexamethasone is a synthetic glucocorticoid that suppresses ACTH when feedback is intact. In an endocrine clinic, patients with suspected hypercortisolism received 1 mg dexamethasone (low dose) or 8 mg (high dose) at night; serum cortisol was measured the next morning (Table 1). A patient with primary adrenal insufficiency, who had a damaged adrenal cortex, was also evaluated. Values are means for each diagnostic group. Reference morning cortisol is 5 to 23 micrograms per deciliter. Blood was collected at 8 AM after an overnight fast, and none of the patients was taking exogenous steroids, estrogen, or any drug that interferes with dexamethasone metabolism. Group sizes were comparable, and results are expressed as group means.

qs.q: Why is ACTH low (4 pg/mL) in patients with an adrenal adenoma?
o: The adenoma secretes ACTH autonomously, which inhibits cortisol release from the opposite adrenal gland
Adrenal tumors secrete cortisol, not ACTH.;
Excess cortisol from the autonomous adenoma suppresses CRH and ACTH through negative feedback
Correct: The adenoma secretes cortisol independent of ACTH; high cortisol inhibits the hypothalamus and pituitary, so ACTH falls.
Low cortisol removes feedback from the pituitary, so corticotrophs are inactive and ACTH output falls
Cortisol is high (32), not low, and low cortisol would raise ACTH.;
Dexamethasone given at night destroys corticotrophs, which lowers ACTH measured in the baseline sample
Baseline ACTH was drawn before dexamethasone and dexamethasone does not destroy cells.
qs.x: The adenoma secretes cortisol independent of ACTH; high cortisol inhibits the hypothalamus and pituitary, so ACTH falls. Trap: Assuming that high cortisol always accompanies high ACTH; autonomous cortisol production lowers ACTH.

qs.q: By what percentage does high-dose dexamethasone lower cortisol in the pituitary adenoma group, compared with baseline?
o: About 27 percent
This is the remaining fraction (8/30), not the decrease.;
About 22 percent
This is the absolute drop (22 ug/dL), not a percentage.;
About 93 percent
This would be the fall for the control group on high-dose dexamethasone (15 to 1.0), not for the adenoma group.
About 73 percent
qs.x: (30 - 8)/30 = 22/30 = 0.733, a 73% decrease. Trap: Reporting what remains rather than the fractional decrease.

qs.q: Why does cortisol in the ectopic ACTH group remain unsuppressed after high-dose dexamethasone?
o: The tumor cells secrete CRH, which overrides dexamethasone at the level of the pituitary corticotrophs
The tumor is described as ACTH-secreting and CRH from a tumor is a far rarer mechanism not suggested by the table.;
The adrenal glands lack glucocorticoid receptors, so they cannot respond to the signal in any group
Dexamethasone acts on the pituitary and hypothalamus, and adrenal receptors are not the explanation.;
The tumor metabolizes dexamethasone completely, preventing any effect in normal pituitary tissue
No evidence of drug metabolism; the explanation is lack of feedback sensitivity.
The tumor secretes ACTH without regard to glucocorticoid feedback, so cortisol output stays high
Correct: Ectopic tumor cells lack the glucocorticoid-sensitive regulation of pituitary corticotrophs, so even high-dose dexamethasone cannot decrease ACTH.
qs.x: Ectopic tumor cells lack the glucocorticoid-sensitive regulation of pituitary corticotrophs, so even high-dose dexamethasone cannot decrease ACTH. Trap: Attributing nonsuppression to receptor loss in the pituitary; the key difference is the tumor's autonomy from feedback.

qs.q: Which finding is expected in primary adrenal insufficiency?
o: Hyperpigmentation of the skin, because high POMC-derived peptides activate melanocytes
Correct: Low cortisol removes feedback, so ACTH is high (380); cleavage of POMC also generates MSH-related peptides that darken skin.
Hypernatremia and hypokalemia, because aldosterone deficiency increases potassium excretion
Aldosterone deficiency causes hyponatremia and hyperkalemia.;
Central obesity and striae, because chronic low cortisol increases fat deposition in the abdomen
Central obesity and striae are signs of cortisol excess.;
Elevated blood glucose, because low cortisol increases hepatic gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance
Cortisol deficiency lowers, not raises, blood glucose.
qs.x: Low cortisol removes feedback, so ACTH is high (380); cleavage of POMC also generates MSH-related peptides that darken skin. Trap: Linking low cortisol to the excess-cortisol phenotype, or reversing the sodium and potassium changes of aldosterone loss.

qs.q: Which metabolic effect is expected in the pituitary adenoma group because of chronic cortisol elevation?
o: Increased hepatic gluconeogenesis and muscle protein catabolism, causing hyperglycemia and muscle wasting
Correct: Cortisol raises blood glucose by stimulating gluconeogenic enzyme expression and mobilizing amino acids from muscle.
Decreased hepatic gluconeogenesis and increased glycogen deposition, causing fasting hypoglycemia
Cortisol opposes insulin and raises blood glucose.;
Increased peripheral glucose uptake and increased muscle protein synthesis, causing muscle growth
Cortisol decreases glucose uptake in muscle and favors protein breakdown.;
Increased lipolysis in all adipose tissue with suppressed appetite, causing weight loss in the trunk
Cortisol promotes central fat deposition and increases appetite.
qs.x: Cortisol raises blood glucose by stimulating gluconeogenic enzyme expression and mobilizing amino acids from muscle. Trap: Mixing up cortisol's catabolic actions with anabolic actions of insulin or growth hormone.

passages.title: FL06 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 9
text: Breathing is regulated by central chemoreceptors in the medulla, which respond to hydrogen ion concentration in cerebrospinal fluid, and by peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies, which respond to low arterial pO2 and to arterial pH and PaCO2. Volunteers inhaled mixtures that raised PaCO2 stepwise, and minute ventilation was recorded in three conditions: normal oxygen, hypoxia (arterial pO2 near 50 mmHg), and after an opioid (Figure 1). Arterial blood gas values from four clinical groups are shown in Table 1; pH was calculated from the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, pH = 6.1 + log[HCO3-/(0.03 x PaCO2)]. Opioids depress respiratory neurons in the medulla. Assume the people in Table 1 are at steady state. Subjects were studied at rest, and end-tidal PCO2 was used as an estimate of PaCO2. For the clinical groups, PaCO2 and bicarbonate were measured at steady state, at least one week after the condition began except for the acute group.

qs.q: Which sequence best describes how a rise in arterial PaCO2 increases ventilation through central chemoreceptors?
o: Blood hydrogen ions cross the blood-brain barrier readily and stimulate the medullary chemoreceptors directly
H+ and HCO3- cross the blood-brain barrier poorly; CO2 does.;
CO2 binds the glomus cells of the carotid body, which signal the medulla through the vagus nerve
Carotid body afferents travel via the glossopharyngeal nerve and these are peripheral, not central, chemoreceptors.;
CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier and forms carbonic acid in CSF, and the resulting hydrogen ions stimulate medullary chemoreceptors
Correct: Dissolved CO2 diffuses into CSF, is hydrated by carbonic anhydrase to H2CO3, and dissociates; central chemoreceptors sense the lowered CSF pH.
Rising CO2 lowers CSF bicarbonate, which depolarizes pulmonary stretch receptors that signal the medulla
Stretch receptors report lung inflation, not CO2.
qs.x: Dissolved CO2 diffuses into CSF, is hydrated by carbonic anhydrase to H2CO3, and dissociates; central chemoreceptors sense the lowered CSF pH. Trap: Assuming blood H+ acts directly on central chemoreceptors, when CO2 is the diffusible stimulus.

qs.q: From Figure 1, what is the ventilatory sensitivity (slope) for normal oxygen between PaCO2 of 45 and 55 mmHg?
o: 0.9 L/min per mmHg
This is the opioid slope (17 - 8)/10.;
3.7 L/min per mmHg
This divides the final ventilation (37) by 10 rather than the change.;
2.0 L/min per mmHg
Correct: (37 - 17)/(55 - 45) = 20/10 = 2.0 L/min per mmHg; opioid slope is only 0.9.
20 L/min per mmHg
This is the total rise in ventilation without dividing by the 10 mmHg interval.
qs.x: (37 - 17)/(55 - 45) = 20/10 = 2.0 L/min per mmHg; opioid slope is only 0.9. Trap: Dividing a single value rather than a change by the interval, or confusing the two curves.

qs.q: Group 3 (chronic hypercapnia) has a PaCO2 of 60 mmHg but a nearly normal pH. Which process explains this?
o: Increased CO2 elimination by the lungs over several days, lowering PaCO2 to normal
PaCO2 is still 60 mmHg; lung elimination has not improved.;
Increased renal excretion of bicarbonate over several days, which lowers plasma HCO3- and buffers the acidosis
Excreting bicarbonate would lower pH further.;
Renal retention of bicarbonate over several days raises plasma HCO3-, buffering the pH
Correct: Kidneys excrete H+ and generate new HCO3-, so HCO3- rises to 34 and the ratio, and thus pH, returns toward normal (7.38).
Hemoglobin buffering in red cells alone, which fully compensates within minutes and does not need the kidney
Hemoglobin buffering is limited and does not fully correct a chronic acidosis; HCO3- change is renal.
qs.x: Kidneys excrete H+ and generate new HCO3-, so HCO3- rises to 34 and the ratio, and thus pH, returns toward normal (7.38). Trap: Thinking the lungs or immediate buffers produce a normal pH in a chronic respiratory acidosis; compensation is renal and slow.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for the higher ventilation in the hypoxia curve at every PaCO2?
o: Low arterial pO2 hyperpolarizes carotid body glomus cells, which reduces input to the medulla through the vagus nerve
Hypoxia depolarizes glomus cells (K+ channel closure) and increases input.;
Low arterial pO2 directly stimulates medullary central chemoreceptors, which become more sensitive than the peripheral ones
Central chemoreceptors respond to CSF H+, and directly depress rather than stimulate at severe hypoxia.;
Low arterial pO2 depolarizes carotid body glomus cells, which signal the medulla through the glossopharyngeal nerve
Correct: Peripheral chemoreceptors respond to hypoxia and add drive on top of the CO2 response.
Low arterial pO2 raises plasma bicarbonate, which lowers CSF pH and stimulates the central chemoreceptors
Hypoxia does not raise bicarbonate; it triggers a respiratory alkalosis when ventilation rises.
qs.x: Peripheral chemoreceptors respond to hypoxia and add drive on top of the CO2 response. Trap: Attributing the hypoxic drive to central chemoreceptors rather than the carotid bodies.

graph.title: Figure 1. Ventilatory response to carbon dioxide

passages.title: FL06 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 10
text: Fetal blood must extract oxygen from maternal blood across the placenta. Adult hemoglobin (HbA, alpha2beta2) binds 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) in the central cavity of the deoxygenated tetramer, using beta-chain residues including His143. Fetal hemoglobin (HbF, alpha2gamma2) has serine at the corresponding position of the gamma chain. A physiology laboratory compared maternal and umbilical cord blood at 37 degrees C, pH 7.4, and equal 2,3-BPG concentrations, and measured hemoglobin concentration and P50 (Table 1). Oxygen saturation curves are plotted in Figure 1. Each gram of hemoglobin carries up to 1.34 mL O2 when fully saturated; ignore dissolved oxygen. Placental venous (fetal) pO2 is approximately 30 mmHg. After birth, gamma-globin expression is repressed and beta-globin expression rises. The cord blood samples came from term deliveries without complications, and maternal samples were drawn from the same patients shortly before delivery. Blood was oxygenated in a tonometer to generate each point on the curves, and temperature and pH were fixed.

qs.q: Which molecular difference best explains the higher O2 affinity of HbF than of HbA at equal 2,3-BPG concentration?
o: The gamma chain lacks His143, so HbF binds 2,3-BPG weakly and the T state is less stabilized
Correct: Less 2,3-BPG binding means less stabilization of the low-affinity T conformation, leaving a lower P50.
The gamma chain has an extra histidine, so HbF binds 2,3-BPG more tightly and favors the R state
Tighter 2,3-BPG binding would lower O2 affinity (stabilizing T).;
The gamma chain binds oxygen at a different heme iron oxidation state, which increases the affinity per site
HbF uses the same Fe2+ heme chemistry as HbA.;
The gamma chain forms disulfide bonds across the tetramer, which locks the molecule in the R conformation
Disulfide cross-links are not the mechanism; the difference lies in 2,3-BPG binding.
qs.x: Less 2,3-BPG binding means less stabilization of the low-affinity T conformation, leaving a lower P50. Trap: Assuming that higher affinity means tighter binding of 2,3-BPG; 2,3-BPG lowers O2 affinity.

qs.q: What is the approximate O2 content of cord blood at pO2 30 mmHg (mL O2 per dL)?
o: This is the fully saturated capacity; at 30 mmHg saturation is only about 77%.;
This uses maternal hemoglobin (12.5 g/dL) or a lower saturation and does not match cord blood.;
Correct: Capacity = 16.0 g/dL x 1.34 = 21.4 mL/dL; saturation at 30 mmHg is 76.6%; 21.4 x 0.766 = 16.4.
This is closer to the maternal blood value at 30 mmHg (16.75 x 0.571), not the cord blood value.
qs.x: Capacity = 16.0 g/dL x 1.34 = 21.4 mL/dL; saturation at 30 mmHg is 76.6%; 21.4 x 0.766 = 16.4. Trap: Using maternal hemoglobin concentration or skipping the saturation factor.

qs.q: In the placenta, fetal CO2 enters maternal blood, lowering maternal pH and raising fetal pH. Which effect on the saturation curves does this produce?
o: The maternal curve shifts left and the fetal curve shifts right, which together increase O2 transfer to the fetus
The directions are reversed; this would impair transfer.;
The maternal curve shifts right and the fetal curve shifts left, which together increase O2 transfer to the fetus
Correct: This is the double Bohr effect: acidified maternal blood unloads O2 more easily, while fetal blood becoming more alkaline loads O2 more easily.
Both curves shift right, which together increase the amount of O2 bound by the fetus
A right shift in fetal blood would reduce O2 loading.;
Neither curve shifts, because the Bohr effect applies only to myoglobin in skeletal muscle
The Bohr effect applies to hemoglobin and operates in the placenta.
qs.x: This is the double Bohr effect: acidified maternal blood unloads O2 more easily, while fetal blood becoming more alkaline loads O2 more easily. Trap: Applying Bohr shifts in the wrong direction to each blood compartment.

qs.q: Raising HbF expression after birth is a strategy in sickle cell disease. Which mechanism best explains why HbF is protective?
o: Gamma chains bind oxygen so tightly that they never release it, which prevents any HbS from becoming deoxygenated
HbF does release O2 to fetal tissues, and HbS deoxygenation still occurs in the mixed cell.;
Gamma chains do not take part in the contacts that polymerize deoxygenated HbS, so HbF dilutes and interrupts the polymer
Correct: Beta^S Val6 contacts are absent in gamma chains; hybrid and HbF tetramers resist polymerization.
Gamma chains cross-link HbS tetramers by disulfide bonds, which stabilizes the soluble form of the red cell
Disulfide cross-linking would not prevent polymerization.;
Gamma chains increase 2,3-BPG binding by HbS, which keeps HbS in the R state and soluble
HbF binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so it would not push HbS toward the R state by this route.
qs.x: Beta^S Val6 contacts are absent in gamma chains; hybrid and HbF tetramers resist polymerization. Trap: Believing HbF helps because of oxygen affinity alone; the benefit is blocking HbS polymer contacts.

graph.title: Figure 1. Maternal and fetal O2 saturation curves

passages.title: FL06 · CARS · Passage 1
text: For several decades, a small set of laboratory findings has been cited as evidence that free will is an illusion. In the best known of these experiments, volunteers were asked to flex a wrist whenever they felt the urge and to note the position of a rapidly moving clock hand at the moment they became aware of deciding. Electrodes on the scalp registered a slow negative drift in electrical activity, the readiness potential, that began roughly half a second before movement and well before the reported moment of decision. Many commentators inferred that if the brain begins preparing an act before the agent is aware of choosing it, the choice was made by neural machinery, and consciousness merely watches.

The argument rests heavily on a narrow empirical base, so its parts should be separated. The first is the claim that the readiness potential marks a decision. This has been challenged by researchers who point out that when the signal is averaged across many trials, it is aligned to the movement, a procedure that can manufacture a gradual ramp out of random fluctuations. On this account, spontaneous neural noise crosses a threshold at an unpredictable moment, and the act follows; the ramp reflects nothing more than what such fluctuations look like when they are selected backward from their outcome. If so, the early signal is not a hidden verdict awaiting delivery but a background condition that makes a movement more likely without settling it.

The second part is the claim that the reported time of awareness is trustworthy. Judging a clock hand's position is retrospective estimation, which shifts with attention and expectation. A finding that awareness of deciding lags brain activity by a few hundred milliseconds may therefore say as much about the unreliability of introspective timing as about the causal order of events.

The third and most important part is the move from the laboratory to ordinary life. The tasks in question were deliberately arbitrary: nothing hung on whether the wrist moved now or a moment later. Yet the choices that matter to those who defend free will, such as whether to change careers, involve extended deliberation, the weighing of reasons, and revision in light of argument. To generalize from one to the other is to assume that all decisions are of the same kind, which is exactly what needs to be shown.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that neuroscience is irrelevant to the debate. Defenders of free will have often spoken as though the self were a command post standing outside the causal order of the brain and issuing orders to it. Evidence that conscious experience arrives late, or that unconscious processes shape which options even come to mind, damages this picture. But it damages only a particular version of the picture. Compatibilists have long held that freedom consists not in escaping causation but in acting from one's own reasons, remaining responsive to considerations that bear on what to do, and being able to revise one's course when those considerations change. On this view, to discover that deliberation is carried out by neurons is no more a threat to freedom than to discover that digestion is carried out by enzymes is a threat to nourishment.

What the experiments most plausibly show, then, is not that we are puppets but that our ordinary self-understanding is partly mistaken about how choosing works. It is a long way from the conclusion that choosing does not exist.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the central thesis of the passage?
o: Laboratory studies of the readiness potential have conclusively shown that conscious deliberation plays no causal role in any human action.
Overstates the passage; the author denies the experiments show this.
Compatibilism is the only defensible account of free will because every other account is refuted by timing studies of the brain.
The author favors compatibilism but does not claim it is the only defensible view or that timing studies refute rivals.
Neuroscientific findings correct a mistaken picture of how choosing works but fall well short of showing that choosing is an illusion.
Correct: The passage ends by saying the experiments show a partly mistaken self-understanding, not that choosing does not exist.
Philosophers who defend free will should abandon their position because introspective reports of decision timing cannot be trusted at all.
The author questions timing reports but does not tell philosophers to abandon their position.
qs.x: The passage ends by saying the experiments show a partly mistaken self-understanding, not that choosing does not exist. Trap: Choosing the answer that takes the experiment's popular conclusion as the author's own.

qs.q: The author's discussion of averaging a signal aligned to the movement serves primarily to
o: demonstrate that the readiness potential is absent when volunteers make a deliberate choice instead of responding to a spontaneous urge.
The passage never says the signal disappears for deliberate choices.
show that the clock-hand method of timing awareness is less accurate than methods based on electrical recordings from the scalp.
The clock-hand issue is discussed separately and is not compared with electrical methods here.
argue that random neural fluctuations are unrelated to the production of movement and can safely be ignored by researchers.
The passage says noise makes movement more likely, so it is not unrelated.
suggest that the apparent early ramp may be an artifact of how the data are processed rather than a marker of decision.
Correct: The averaging point supports the claim that a ramp can be manufactured from noise selected backward from movement.
qs.x: The averaging point supports the claim that a ramp can be manufactured from noise selected backward from movement. Trap: Confusing the first objection (what the signal means) with the second (timing of awareness).

qs.q: The author's treatment of the third part of the argument assumes which of the following?
o: Any decision that is made after extended deliberation must be free, regardless of how its neural preparation is organized.
The author claims only that deliberation has not been shown ineffective, not that it must be free.
Participants in laboratory studies are generally unable to follow instructions about when to move or when to report awareness.
Nothing suggests participants cannot follow instructions.
The significance of a decision for a person's life determines how quickly the corresponding brain activity begins.
The passage makes no claim about timing of brain activity relative to stakes.
Arbitrary flicks of the wrist and long deliberation about a career may involve different kinds of decision processes.
Correct: The author says generalizing from capricious flicks assumes all decisions are of one kind, which must be shown.
qs.x: The author says generalizing from capricious flicks assumes all decisions are of one kind, which must be shown. Trap: Reading the author's caution as a positive claim that deliberate choices are free.

qs.q: Suppose later studies found that brain signals reliably predicted, many seconds in advance, which job offer people would accept after weeks of deliberation. How would this finding bear on the passage?
o: It would confirm the author's view that the readiness potential is nothing more than averaged random neural fluctuation.
The finding concerns prediction of weighty choices, not the noise account of the ramp.
It would show that compatibilists are wrong to define freedom in terms of responsiveness to reasons and revision of one's course.
Prediction alone does not show reasons-responsiveness is absent, so compatibilism is not refuted.
It would weaken the author's objection that results from arbitrary tasks cannot be extended to weighty, deliberate choices.
Correct: The third objection says arbitrary-task data do not speak to deliberation; such a finding would supply data on deliberation.
It would be irrelevant, because the author holds that evidence about the brain can never bear on questions about free will.
The author explicitly says neuroscience is not irrelevant.
qs.x: The third objection says arbitrary-task data do not speak to deliberation; such a finding would supply data on deliberation. Trap: Treating any neural predictability as automatically refuting compatibilism.

qs.q: The comparison of digestion and enzymes to deliberation and neurons is intended to illustrate that
o: discovering the physical basis of a process does not by itself show that the process fails to do what it appears to do.
Correct: The analogy shows that a mechanism underlying a function does not threaten the function.
deliberation and digestion are equally automatic processes that occur largely outside conscious awareness and voluntary control.
The analogy is about mechanism and function, not automaticity.
neurons and enzymes are the only components in the body whose activity is relevant to philosophical questions about agency.
No claim of exclusivity is made.
compatibilists believe that freedom and nourishment are both illusions that science will eventually be able to explain away.
Compatibilists are said to defend freedom, not call it an illusion.
qs.x: The analogy shows that a mechanism underlying a function does not threaten the function. Trap: Taking the analogy to claim that deliberation is as automatic as digestion.

qs.q: Which of the following claims would the author be most likely to accept?
o: Evidence that unconscious processes determine which options come to mind counts against the command-post picture of the self.
Correct: The author says such evidence damages the command-post picture, though only a particular version of the picture.
Evidence that consciousness arrives late would prove that people are not responsible for the consequences of their choices.
The author never links late consciousness to loss of responsibility.
Evidence from timing studies is the best available basis for deciding whether deliberation is causally effective in daily life.
The author says such studies do not speak directly to deliberation.
Evidence that decisions have neural causes would leave the command-post picture entirely untouched while harming compatibilism.
The author says the evidence does damage the picture and not compatibilism.
qs.x: The author says such evidence damages the command-post picture, though only a particular version of the picture. Trap: Overreaching from late awareness to claims about moral responsibility.

passages.title: FL06 · CARS · Passage 2
text: The phrase "Silk Road" suggests a single highway along which caravans carried bolts of cloth from China to Rome. The image is vivid and misleading. The term itself was coined in 1877 by a German geographer, and it entered popular usage only in the twentieth century. No ancient traveler would have recognized it. What existed instead was a shifting web of routes across deserts, mountain passes, steppe, and sea lanes, and almost nobody traveled its whole length. Goods moved in relays, passing through the hands of many intermediaries, each of whom took a margin and each of whom shaped what was passed on.

This relay structure matters for the question of what, exactly, was exchanged. Silk was certainly traded, and it was prized in distant courts, but it was far from the only commodity, and for much of the period it was not the most important one. Horses from Central Asia were of intense strategic interest to Chinese dynasties, which paid for them in textiles. Glassware, spices, gold, incense, medicinal plants, and precious stones moved in several directions. Bulky goods rarely traveled far overland, since the cost of transport quickly exceeded their value, which is why the overland trade favored items of high value and low weight. Much of the exchange of heavier goods took place by sea, a fact that the overland metaphor tends to conceal.

If goods were only part of the story, ideas and techniques were arguably the larger part. Buddhism traveled from northern India across Central Asia into China, changing as it went and absorbing local forms of art and ritual. Manichaean, Christian, and later Islamic communities followed similar paths. Papermaking spread westward over several centuries, eventually transforming record-keeping and scholarship in the Islamic world and Europe. Crops, instruments, and mathematical methods traveled alongside. Disease traveled too, and the diffusion of plague along trading routes is one of the sharper reminders that connection has costs as well as benefits.

The people who carried these things were not passive conduits. Merchants from Sogdiana, in what is now Uzbekistan, acted for centuries as brokers between cultures, writing in their own language, founding communities in Chinese cities, and translating religious texts. Historians who read the exchange as a contest between two great empires miss the contribution of smaller societies in the middle. Oasis towns have yielded documents in a half-dozen languages recording contracts, loans, and letters concerning ordinary business.

Skeptics argue that the romantic story has been inflated by modern interest. Governments now promote the idea for diplomatic and commercial reasons, and the label is attached to initiatives that bear little relation to the historical record. There is some justice in the complaint, but it should not be pushed too far. That the name is a modern invention does not show that the phenomenon was imaginary, any more than the coining of the word "Renaissance" long after the fact shows that nothing changed in fifteenth-century Italy. The more reasonable conclusion is that the metaphor of a road should be replaced by something more accurate, such as a network or an ecology of exchange, and that the importance of the connections should be assessed by their consequences instead of by the glamour of their name.

The lesson, then, is about method as much as about trade. Historians should be wary of metaphors that make complicated processes look tidy. A road implies a beginning and an end, a direction, a traveler. A network implies none of these, and the history it describes is better for the lack.

qs.q: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to
o: argue that overland trade across Eurasia was economically insignificant compared with the exchange of goods carried by sea.
Sea trade is mentioned as underrepresented, but the passage does not call overland trade insignificant.
replace a misleading metaphor with a more accurate account of how goods, ideas, and diseases moved across Eurasia.
Correct: The passage corrects the road metaphor and argues for a network picture while describing what moved.
defend the traditional picture of the Silk Road against modern skeptics who regard it as a diplomatic invention.
The author partly agrees with skeptics and proposes revising, not defending, the traditional picture.
demonstrate that Chinese dynasties dominated long-distance exchange and that smaller societies played only a supporting role.
The author stresses the role of smaller societies such as Sogdiana.
qs.x: The passage corrects the road metaphor and argues for a network picture while describing what moved. Trap: Seizing on one detail (sea trade or skeptics) rather than the overall aim.

qs.q: According to the passage, overland trade favored items of high value and low weight because
o: rulers along the routes imposed heavy taxes on bulky goods but allowed lightweight luxuries to pass without any duties.
No taxation is mentioned.
merchants in oasis towns refused to handle goods that could not be carried by a single traveler from end to end.
Goods moved in relays, not by a single traveler.
the expense of moving bulky goods over long distances by land would soon exceed what they were worth.
Correct: The passage states transport cost quickly exceeded the value of bulky goods.
demand for heavy goods such as grain and timber was lower in China than demand for textiles and horses.
The passage gives no comparison of demand for heavy goods.
qs.x: The passage states transport cost quickly exceeded the value of bulky goods. Trap: Importing a plausible-sounding economic reason not given in the text.

qs.q: The reference to the coining of the word "Renaissance" most nearly serves to
o: suggest that fifteenth-century Italy was more closely connected to Asian trade networks than historians have acknowledged.
The analogy is not about Italian links with Asia.
illustrate how governments use historical labels to promote contemporary diplomatic and commercial initiatives abroad.
Government promotion is a separate point.
indicate that most historical periods are named by writers who had little knowledge of the events they described.
The passage makes no claim about writers' knowledge.
show that a name invented after the fact does not prove that the thing it names never happened.
Correct: The analogy answers the skeptics: late coinage of a term does not make the phenomenon imaginary.
qs.x: The analogy answers the skeptics: late coinage of a term does not make the phenomenon imaginary. Trap: Missing that the example is an analogy about naming, not about Italy.

qs.q: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the exchange of ideas and techniques was arguably the larger part of the story?
o: Documents from oasis towns showing that contracts and loans were written in several different languages by local traders.
Multilingual documents support the importance of cultural intermediaries.
Archaeological evidence that almost all religious and technical change in China was homegrown and predated contact.
Correct: Evidence that borrowed ideas and techniques were largely not borrowed would undercut the claim.
Evidence that Sogdian merchants founded settlements in Chinese cities and translated religious texts into local languages.
Translation and settlement support the idea-exchange claim.
Records showing that horses from Central Asia were purchased by Chinese dynasties in exchange for large quantities of textiles.
Horse-for-textile trade concerns goods, and does not bear on the ideas claim.
qs.x: Evidence that borrowed ideas and techniques were largely not borrowed would undercut the claim. Trap: Picking evidence about goods that merely seems related instead of evidence that contradicts the claim.

qs.q: The passage suggests that the "contest between two great empires" reading of Eurasian exchange is flawed because it
o: overlooks intermediary societies that acted as brokers, translators, and settlers between the larger powers.
Correct: The Sogdian example shows smaller societies in the middle were significant.
exaggerates the amount of silk that reached the Roman world relative to the amount of glassware and incense.
The passage does not tie the flaw to silk quantities.
assumes that Buddhism spread to China through military conquest and not through the movement of merchants.
Conquest is never mentioned as the assumed route of Buddhism.
relies on documents from oasis towns that the author considers too unreliable to support firm conclusions.
The author calls oasis documents rich evidence.
qs.x: The Sogdian example shows smaller societies in the middle were significant. Trap: Attributing to the text claims about conquest or document unreliability.

qs.q: The author's concluding statement that the history described by a network is "better for the lack" of a beginning, end, and traveler implies that
o: an accurate account of this exchange has to describe many interacting participants and directions, not one journey.
Correct: The network image is preferred because the real process lacked a single direction or traveler.
historians of trade should avoid describing individual merchants and focus only on large impersonal economic forces.
The author praises Sogdian merchants as agents.
the Silk Road never had any identifiable starting points such as cities, ports, or mountain passes along its routes.
The author names oasis towns and routes, so identifiable places existed.
metaphors should be avoided in historical writing altogether because they cannot represent complicated processes.
The author recommends a better metaphor, not abandoning metaphor.
qs.x: The network image is preferred because the real process lacked a single direction or traveler. Trap: Over-generalizing a warning about one metaphor to all metaphors.

passages.title: FL06 · CARS · Passage 3
text: When Michel de Montaigne retired to his tower in the 1570s and began writing short, wandering prose pieces about cannibals, thumbs, idleness, and friendship, he called them essais, a word meaning trials or attempts. The name was a statement of method. A treatise advances from definitions to conclusions and expects the reader to accept both. Montaigne offered something less secure: a mind testing a question against its own experience, reporting what happened, and frequently ending where it had not expected to be. The essay has been defined ever since by this refusal to pretend that thought arrives finished.

That provisional quality is easily mistaken for a lack of rigor. Defenders of the treatise tradition have complained that the essay permits writers to evade the burden of proof. An essayist may digress, change his mind, or leave a question open, and no one can say he has broken a rule. But the criticism assumes that the only rigor worth having is the rigor of deduction. A good essay has another kind: fidelity to the way a question actually looks from a particular position, with its complications left in. Montaigne's reflections on cruelty, for example, are persuasive precisely because he admits his own squeamishness and then reasons from it, rather than hiding it behind an abstract principle. The essay's discipline lies in honesty about the process.

The form also has a distinctive relation to its reader. The treatise addresses a student who must be instructed; the essay addresses a companion who is invited to watch someone think. This explains why the great essayists are so often remembered as voices and not as systems. We read Johnson, Hazlitt, Woolf, and Baldwin partly for what they say and partly for the company of the sensibility saying it. The personal essay in particular depends on a calculated intimacy, one in which the writer discloses enough to be believed and withholds enough to avoid self-absorption. When that balance fails, the result is confession without insight, the self displayed rather than used.

It is tempting to conclude that the essay is therefore a purely literary form, unconcerned with knowledge. That would be a mistake. The essay has been a vehicle for serious intellectual work, from Bacon's compressed advice on statecraft to modern writing on science and law. Its advantage in such domains is that it can hold together considerations that systematic argument must separate. A treatise on grief must choose a definition of grief; an essay can follow a loss through memory, ritual, and embarrassment without deciding in advance which of these is the real subject. What it offers is not a conclusion that can be cited but an understanding that must be experienced.

The present danger to the form is less its critics than its imitators. The commercial appetite for opinion has produced a great deal of writing that borrows the essay's first-person voice while abandoning its method. The opinion column begins with a conclusion and recruits experience as decoration. The reader learns what the author thinks but never watches the thinking happen. In a genuine essay the conclusion is a discovery, however modest, and the reader can tell. Where the writer already knows what he will find, the trial is a performance, and the word has lost its meaning.

Montaigne's own motto, which he is said to have kept inscribed in his library, was a question: what do I know? The essay, at its best, keeps that question open without making it an excuse for saying nothing.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
o: A chronological history of the essay from Montaigne to the present, with each period's major writers evaluated in turn.
The structure is thematic, not chronological.
A comparison of the treatise and the essay concluding that the treatise is more rigorous but less pleasant to read.
The author does not conclude the treatise is more rigorous.
A defense of Montaigne's reputation followed by a series of examples of modern essayists who surpass his achievements.
Montaigne is not said to be surpassed.
A statement of the form's method, replies to objections, remarks on reader and scope, and a warning about imitation.
Correct: The passage defines the form, answers the charge of laxity, discusses reader and scope, then warns about opinion writing.
qs.x: The passage defines the form, answers the charge of laxity, discusses reader and scope, then warns about opinion writing. Trap: Reading the passage as a historical survey because it begins with Montaigne.

qs.q: The author's response to the charge that the essay evades the burden of proof is that
o: the essay does not have to meet any standard of rigor because its purpose is literary pleasure rather than knowledge.
The author rejects the idea that the essay is purely literary and unconcerned with knowledge.
the essay has its own kind of rigor, which lies in honestly reporting how a question appears from a given position.
Correct: The author claims a different rigor: fidelity to how a question looks, complications included.
most essays are in fact organized as deductive arguments, although their digressions can make this difficult to notice.
The author says the essay does not proceed by deduction.
the burden of proof is lighter in domains such as statecraft and law than it is in the natural sciences.
No comparison with the natural sciences is drawn.
qs.x: The author claims a different rigor: fidelity to how a question looks, complications included. Trap: Choosing the concession that the essay is exempt from standards.

qs.q: According to the passage, the personal essay fails when the writer
o: withholds so much personal experience that the reader cannot tell what the writer's position on the question is.
Withholding too much is not described as the failure; self-absorption is.
discloses so much of the self that nothing is learned from the disclosure about the question under discussion.
Correct: Failure is 'confession without insight, the self displayed rather than used.'
borrows the first-person voice from earlier essayists instead of developing a style that reflects an individual sensibility.
Imitation of voice is attributed to opinion writing, not to this failure.
reaches a conclusion that the reader finds modest or unexpected at the end of a long and wandering chain of thought.
Modest or unexpected conclusions are praised, not criticized.
qs.x: Failure is 'confession without insight, the self displayed rather than used.' Trap: Reversing the balance the author describes between disclosure and withholding.

qs.q: The passage suggests that an opinion column differs from a genuine essay in that the column
o: treats the author's experience as support for a conclusion already reached, instead of as material for discovery.
Correct: The column 'begins with a conclusion and recruits experience as decoration.'
avoids the first-person voice and presents its claims as though they were established by impersonal methods.
The column borrows the first-person voice.
addresses a student who must be instructed rather than a companion who is invited to watch someone think.
That contrast describes the treatise, not the column.
leaves its central question open and therefore cannot offer readers any understanding of the topic discussed.
Leaving questions open is characteristic of the essay.
qs.x: The column 'begins with a conclusion and recruits experience as decoration.' Trap: Confusing the opinion column with the treatise.

qs.q: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that the essay can handle considerations that systematic argument must separate?
o: A survey showing that most readers can name more essayists than they can name authors of philosophical treatises.
Name recognition does not bear on cognitive range.
A history showing that Bacon wrote his essays after completing longer and more systematic works on the same subjects.
Bacon's order of composition is irrelevant to the claim.
An analysis showing that modern opinion columns are more widely read than the essays of Johnson, Hazlitt, or Woolf.
Popularity of columns does not address the essay's capabilities.
A study in which readers of essays about bereavement reported grasping aspects of grief that definitions had left out.
Correct: Evidence that essays convey aspects of a subject that definitions miss directly supports the claim.
qs.x: Evidence that essays convey aspects of a subject that definitions miss directly supports the claim. Trap: Picking evidence about popularity rather than about what the form can accomplish.

qs.q: The reference to Montaigne's motto in the final paragraph primarily serves to
o: suggest that Montaigne himself doubted that any essay could succeed in producing knowledge about human nature.
The author says the essay can yield understanding, so doubt about knowledge is not implied.
show that the form was invented as a response to the scholarly skepticism that dominated sixteenth-century libraries.
No historical claim about scholarly skepticism is made.
support the claim that a writer who asks a question cannot also be said to have reached a conclusion of any kind.
The author says conclusions in essays are discoveries, so questions and conclusions can coexist.
illustrate that the essay's commitment to inquiry is compatible with leaving questions unresolved.
Correct: The motto is a question kept open, matching the author's final sentence about the essay not using openness as an excuse.
qs.x: The motto is a question kept open, matching the author's final sentence about the essay not using openness as an excuse. Trap: Equating an open question with complete skepticism.

passages.title: FL06 · CARS · Passage 4
text: The modern public museum presents itself as a neutral custodian: a place where objects of lasting value are kept safe, arranged sensibly, and shown to anyone who walks in. Few institutions have been so thoroughly shaped by the circumstances of their founding. The ancestors of the museum were private cabinets of curiosities, assembled by princes and scholars in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, in which fossils, coins, instruments, and exotic artifacts were displayed together as evidence of the collector's reach. The institution acquired its public character only later, most dramatically when revolutionary France converted royal and church property into a national collection open to citizens. From the start, then, the museum was bound up with questions of who owns the past and for whom it is displayed.

This history complicates the claim of neutrality. To collect is to select, and to display is to arrange; every gallery embodies a judgment about what belongs together and what deserves a room of its own. Nineteenth-century museums frequently sorted human cultures on a scale of progress, placing European art at the summit and the artifacts of colonized peoples in the category of ethnography. Visitors who passed from one wing to another were being taught a theory, though the theory was rarely stated.

Critics have drawn from this a severe conclusion: that museums are instruments of power whose authority rests on concealment. The argument has force in particular cases. Many celebrated collections were assembled through conquest, coercive purchase, or the removal of objects from communities that did not consent. But the severe conclusion overreaches when it treats the museum's origins as a complete account of its function. Institutions are not prisoners of their beginnings. The public art gallery that began as a display of royal wealth has become, in many cities, one of the few spaces where people of different backgrounds meet in the presence of the same objects.

A more useful response is to ask what a museum can honestly claim to do. It cannot claim to present the past as it was, for the past does not arrive in glass cases. What it can do is preserve material that would otherwise be lost, make that material accessible, and offer interpretations that are open to challenge. The third of these is the one that most needs emphasis. A label that says "Greek, fifth century" invites the visitor to treat the object as a fact, whereas a label that says how the piece was acquired, what is uncertain about its dating, and why curators have placed it beside its neighbors invites the visitor to treat the display as an argument. The latter does not make the museum less authoritative. It moves the source of authority from the building to the quality of the reasons offered.

Some curators fear that such candor will erode public confidence. The evidence suggests the opposite risk. Trust that depends on visitors not knowing how collections were formed is fragile, and it is likely to collapse when the facts become known, as they increasingly do. Trust that rests on a record of acknowledging uncertainty and correcting error is sturdier, since it was never staked on perfection. Scientific institutions have found this to be true, and there is no reason to think museums are different.

The museum is therefore best understood neither as a temple of neutral value nor as a mere apparatus of domination, but as an institution that makes claims and ought to be held accountable for them. That standard is more demanding than neutrality, and it is also more honest.

qs.q: The main idea of the passage is that museums
o: are fundamentally instruments of power whose collections cannot be justified in light of the circumstances under which they were assembled.
The author rejects the severe conclusion as overreaching.
have succeeded in becoming neutral custodians of the past by moving away from their origins in private collections.
The author denies that neutrality is an accurate description.
should be understood as interpretive institutions whose authority depends on the reasons they offer, not on a claim of neutrality.
Correct: The final paragraph presents the museum as an institution that makes claims and should be accountable for them.
should reduce public confidence in their holdings by emphasizing how much of the historical record remains uncertain.
The author argues candor strengthens, not reduces, trust.
qs.x: The final paragraph presents the museum as an institution that makes claims and should be accountable for them. Trap: Taking the critics' severe view as the author's own.

qs.q: The passage suggests that nineteenth-century museums taught visitors a theory primarily through
o: explicit labels that stated the supposed scale of progress and explained where each culture belonged on it.
The passage says the theory was rarely stated.
the physical arrangement of objects, which put European art and colonized peoples' artifacts in separate categories.
Correct: The passage says the theory was 'rarely stated' and conveyed by how the wings were arranged.
public lectures delivered by curators who defended the hierarchy of cultures in front of the collections.
Lectures are not mentioned.
the removal of objects from communities, which showed visitors that some cultures were unfit to keep their heritage.
The removal of objects is discussed separately and is not said to teach this theory.
qs.x: The passage says the theory was 'rarely stated' and conveyed by how the wings were arranged. Trap: Assuming a theory must be taught through explicit statement.

qs.q: The author mentions the public art gallery that began as a display of royal wealth in order to
o: show that an institution's present function cannot be inferred from the conditions of its origin alone.
Correct: The example supports the claim that institutions are not prisoners of their beginnings.
prove that the claim of neutrality is justified because many cities now have galleries open to all citizens.
The author denies neutrality; the example concerns function, not neutrality.
argue that private collections have always been more beneficial to the public than institutions founded by states.
No comparison of private and state collections is made.
support the claim that revolutionary governments were more concerned with public access than earlier collectors.
The example is not about revolutionary governments' motives.
qs.x: The example supports the claim that institutions are not prisoners of their beginnings. Trap: Interpreting a point about change over time as endorsement of neutrality.

qs.q: Which of the following best illustrates the kind of label the author would prefer?
o: A card stating the culture and century of a vase and its measurements, with no additional commentary that might distract viewers.
This resembles the 'Greek, fifth century' label the author criticizes.
A card describing a vase as one of the finest examples of its type and praising the skill of the craftsperson who made it.
Praise offers no reasons open to challenge.
A card noting that a vase was purchased from a dealer in 1890, that its date is disputed, and why it hangs beside two other works.
Correct: The preferred label discloses acquisition, uncertainty, and curatorial reasoning.
A card asking visitors to decide for themselves what a vase means, with no information about its origin or acquisition.
The author wants offered reasons, not their absence.
qs.x: The preferred label discloses acquisition, uncertainty, and curatorial reasoning. Trap: Mistaking minimal information for neutrality.

qs.q: The author's argument about public trust is based on which of the following assumptions?
o: Visitors place greater trust in museums that avoid discussing their history of acquiring objects through conquest.
The author argues the opposite about concealment.
Scientific institutions have generally avoided admitting uncertainty because doing so reduces public confidence in results.
The author says scientific institutions confirm that acknowledging uncertainty builds trust.
Information about how collections were formed is likely to become widely known over time.
Correct: Trust built on ignorance collapses 'when the facts become known, as they increasingly do.'
Curators who fear a loss of confidence are mistaken about how many people actually visit museums.
Visitor numbers are not at issue.
qs.x: Trust built on ignorance collapses 'when the facts become known, as they increasingly do.' Trap: Reading a fear the author rejects as a premise of the argument.

qs.q: Which of the following would most undermine the author's claim that a museum's origins do not fully determine its function?
o: Evidence that some museums have returned objects to communities from which they were removed in earlier centuries.
Returns show institutions changing, supporting the claim.
Evidence that visitors to old galleries consistently describe them as expressions of the culture that founded them.
Correct: If visitors consistently see galleries as expressions of the founding culture, origins would still be driving function, contrary to the claim.
Evidence that visitors from different backgrounds meet in public galleries more often than in other civic spaces.
Diverse meeting supports the claim.
Evidence that cabinets of curiosities included fossils and instruments in addition to coins and artifacts.
The contents of cabinets are irrelevant.
qs.x: If visitors consistently see galleries as expressions of the founding culture, origins would still be driving function, contrary to the claim. Trap: Picking evidence about change that actually supports the author.

passages.title: FL06 · CARS · Passage 5
text: Few art forms have been so closely identified with the idea of a nation as opera. Textbooks routinely present Giuseppe Verdi as the musical voice of Italian unification, Richard Wagner as the embodiment of German cultural aspiration, and Bedrich Smetana as the founder of a Czech national style. The pattern seems to confirm a simple thesis: a people discovers its identity, and its composers give that identity sound. Yet a closer look at how particular works came to be regarded as national suggests that the relation between music and nation runs largely in the opposite direction. Nations, or at least their mythologies, are often assembled from music, and the assembling is done not by composers but by audiences, critics, and later historians.

Consider the best-known case. The chorus of Hebrew slaves in Verdi's early opera Nabucco, sung in the 1840s, is often said to have been taken up on the spot by Italian patriots as an anthem of resistance to Austrian rule. The story is stirring, and much of it appears to have been added in later decades, when Verdi had become a national monument and the unification movement had victory to commemorate. Contemporary reports show enthusiastic audiences, but the political meaning of that enthusiasm was uncertain, and the opera's biblical subject matter was not obviously a coded message. The legend tells us less about what happened in a Milan theater in 1842 than about what Italians later needed to remember.

This does not mean that opera played no role in nation-building. It means that the role was subtler than the legend suggests. Opera was a public art, performed in cities where the educated classes gathered, and its choice of language mattered. In regions where the language of the ruling court differed from the language of the people, composing an opera in the vernacular was itself a political act, since it asserted that the local tongue was fit for the grandest of forms. Smetana's operas, written in Czech for a theater built partly by public subscription, are a better example of this than anything in Verdi, and their significance is institutional as much as musical: they gave an audience a reason to gather and to see itself gathering.

There is a further complication. The characteristics that listeners most readily call national are not stable. A folk-like melody, a dance rhythm, or an orchestral color that seems quintessentially Czech or Russian was frequently borrowed from elsewhere or invented to meet a market that expected exoticism. The result is a feedback loop: audiences abroad identify a sound as typical of a country, composers at home reinforce it, and over time the sound comes to seem an ancient inheritance.

None of this diminishes the works themselves. A listener moved by the exiles' chorus does not need to believe in the legend to be moved, and a composer who draws on local idioms may do so out of sincere attachment. But a historian should be careful not to treat the stories that nations tell about their art as evidence of how that art was first heard. The relation between opera and national identity is better described as a long negotiation than as a simple expression, and its history is full of retrospective revision.

What emerges, in short, is a reminder that cultural memory edits the past in favor of a satisfying plot. Opera did not simply reflect nations; it supplied the occasions, the language, and the stories from which they learned to imagine themselves.

qs.q: The author's primary claim about the relation between opera and national identity is that
o: composers of the nineteenth century were generally indifferent to politics and wrote operas solely for commercial success.
The author grants that composers could be sincere in drawing on local idioms and that opera did play a role.
national meanings attributed to operas were often built by later audiences and historians, not expressed by the works at first.
Correct: The opening says the relation runs largely in the opposite direction, with audiences and later historians assembling national meaning.
opera had no meaningful influence on the development of national consciousness in countries that were ruled by foreign courts.
The author says opera did play a role, especially vernacular opera.
the national character of an opera can be determined by identifying folk melodies that the composer borrowed from local traditions.
The passage argues such 'national' melodies were often borrowed or invented.
qs.x: The opening says the relation runs largely in the opposite direction, with audiences and later historians assembling national meaning. Trap: Treating a revisionist argument as a denial of any role for opera.

qs.q: According to the passage, the Nabucco legend
o: probably grew later, when Verdi was a national monument and the unification movement could celebrate success.
Correct: The author says much of the story seems to have been added later, when commemoration was needed.
was invented by Austrian officials who wished to portray Italian patriots as threats to public order in Milan.
Austrian invention is not mentioned.
is entirely false, because contemporary reports show that early audiences were indifferent to the chorus of slaves.
Contemporary reports show enthusiastic audiences, so the passage does not call everything false.
is supported by the opera's biblical subject matter, which was widely understood as a coded message of resistance.
The author says the subject matter was not obviously a coded message.
qs.x: The author says much of the story seems to have been added later, when commemoration was needed. Trap: Overcorrecting from 'partly legendary' to 'entirely false.'

qs.q: The author regards Smetana's operas as a better example of nation-building than Verdi's because Smetana's operas
o: contained more melodies derived from authentic Czech folk traditions than Verdi's work did from Italian sources.
The author suggests national melodies are unreliable, and makes no claim of more authentic folk material.
were performed more frequently in foreign theaters, where audiences were eager to hear a distinctly national sound.
Foreign demand is cited as part of the feedback loop, not as Smetana's advantage.
expressed political aspirations more explicitly than Verdi's work, which was concerned mainly with biblical subjects.
The author does not claim Smetana's works were more explicit politically.
were sung in the vernacular and gave audiences an institution in which to gather and see themselves doing so.
Correct: The significance is described as institutional: Czech language, public subscription, and gathering.
qs.x: The significance is described as institutional: Czech language, public subscription, and gathering. Trap: Equating national significance with folk content.

qs.q: The 'feedback loop' described in the fourth paragraph refers to a process in which
o: composers at home borrow melodies from foreign sources, which then persuade audiences abroad that the melodies are original.
Borrowing is mentioned but the loop is not about persuading foreigners of originality.
critics who write about national style are influenced by composers' statements, which in turn depend on critics' earlier judgments.
Critics' statements are not part of this loop.
foreign listeners label a sound as typical, composers at home reinforce it, and the sound later appears to be an ancient inheritance.
Correct: The paragraph describes foreign identification, home reinforcement, and later perception of antiquity.
audiences at home demand exotic sounds from composers who learn to avoid anything that would remind listeners of foreign music.
The loop concerns foreign audiences' expectations, not audiences at home avoiding foreign sounds.
qs.x: The paragraph describes foreign identification, home reinforcement, and later perception of antiquity. Trap: Garbling the direction of influence between audiences abroad and composers at home.

qs.q: Which of the following claims is most consistent with the author's view of cultural memory?
o: Legends about works of art are usually reliable because they were preserved by people who had direct experience of events.
The author doubts such legends.
Stories communities tell about their art may reveal more about later needs than about early reception.
Correct: The author says the legend reveals what Italians later needed to remember.
Cultural memory is less reliable for music than for literature because music cannot be preserved in written records.
No comparison of music with literature is made.
Listeners who are moved by a work should abandon any belief in legends associated with it in order to appreciate it.
The author says one need not believe the legend to be moved, but does not require abandoning it.
qs.x: The author says the legend reveals what Italians later needed to remember. Trap: Choosing a claim stronger than the one the author endorses.

qs.q: Which of the following findings would most weaken the author's account of the Nabucco legend?
o: Theater records showing that Nabucco was performed to full houses in Milan during its first season and in later revivals.
Full houses fit the passage's report of enthusiastic but politically uncertain audiences.
Letters from Verdi's contemporaries describing the music of the slaves' chorus as unusually moving and memorable to listeners.
Praise of the music does not bear on political meaning.
Newspaper reports from 1842 showing that audiences explicitly linked the chorus to Austrian rule and demanded it be repeated as a protest.
Correct: Contemporary evidence of explicit political reading would undermine the claim that the political meaning was added later.
Evidence that Verdi was honored as a national figure only after unification, when the movement had succeeded in its aims.
This agrees with the author's claim that the legend grew after Verdi became a monument.
qs.x: Contemporary evidence of explicit political reading would undermine the claim that the political meaning was added later. Trap: Choosing evidence of popularity, which the author already accepts.

passages.title: FL06 · CARS · Passage 6
text: Anyone who has called a father's brother and a mother's brother by the same word, uncle, has taken part in a system of kinship classification without noticing. English speakers group together a surprisingly diverse set of relatives under a handful of terms, and the grouping seems so natural that it takes effort to see it as a choice. Other languages divide the same relatives differently. In some, a father's brother is called by the same word as the father, while a mother's brother has a separate term. In others, all cousins are called by sibling terms, or a mother's sister is addressed as mother. The study of such systems was among the earliest projects of anthropology, and it has yielded two lessons that pull in opposite directions.

The first lesson, associated with the nineteenth-century American lawyer and ethnologist Lewis Henry Morgan, was that terminology is a window onto social organization.
