passages.title: FL06 · Chem/Phys · Passage 10
text: A student studies the elimination reactions of 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, a tertiary alkyl bromide, under three sets of conditions at 55 °C: (a) 0.50 M sodium ethoxide in ethanol, (b) pure ethanol with no added base, and (c) 0.50 M potassium tert-butoxide in tert-butanol. Product mixtures are analyzed by gas chromatography to determine the percentage of 2-methyl-2-butene (the more substituted, Zaitsev alkene), 2-methyl-1-butene (the less substituted, Hofmann alkene), and ethyl tert-pentyl ether (a substitution product). In separate kinetic runs, the student doubles the concentration of the alkyl bromide alone, or of the base alone, and records how the overall rate changes. The student knows that a strong base favors a concerted elimination, whereas ionization of the leaving group without a strong base gives a carbocation intermediate. Table 1 summarizes the observations. Percentages are of total products. Every run begins with an alkyl bromide concentration of 0.10 M, and each is allowed to proceed until no alkyl bromide remains. Each analysis is repeated three times and averaged, and the standard deviations are below 2 percentage points.

qs.q: In conditions (a), by what factor does the rate change if both [RBr] and [ethoxide] are doubled?
o: A factor of 1 would require the rate to be zero order in both species.
A factor of 2 would apply if the rate were first order in only one species, as for E1 in condition (b).
A factor of 8 would require a third-order rate law.
Correct: The rate law is rate = k[RBr][EtO⁻] (first order in each, as for a bimolecular E2), so doubling both increases the rate by 2 × 2 = 4.
qs.x: The rate law is rate = k[RBr][EtO⁻] (first order in each, as for a bimolecular E2), so doubling both increases the rate by 2 × 2 = 4. Trap: Using only one concentration term in the rate law, or applying the E1 rate law to a strong-base reaction.

qs.q: Which statement best explains why condition (b) gives mostly ether and some alkene?
o: Ethanol reacts first with the alkyl bromide in a single step in which the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group.
A single-step backside attack describes SN2, which is blocked at a tertiary center and would give rate dependence on ethanol concentration as well.
Slow ionization of the C–Br bond forms a tertiary carbocation, which is captured by ethanol as a nucleophile (SN1) or loses a proton to the solvent (E1).
Correct: The rate-limiting step is unimolecular ionization (rate depends only on [RBr]); the common carbocation then partitions between SN1 and E1 products, with substitution dominating.
Ethanol is a poor base and a poor nucleophile, so the reaction proceeds by free radical chain steps that give a mixture of alkene and ether.
No radical initiators are present; ionic polar-protic conditions give ionic mechanisms.
Ethanol acts as a strong base that removes a β-hydrogen in a concerted step, and the ether forms by backside attack at the tertiary carbon.
Ethanol is a weak base, and backside attack at a tertiary carbon is too hindered for SN2.
qs.x: The rate-limiting step is unimolecular ionization (rate depends only on [RBr]); the common carbocation then partitions between SN1 and E1 products, with substitution dominating. Trap: Treating a weak base/nucleophile solvent as if it caused a concerted E2 or SN2 reaction at a tertiary substrate.

qs.q: Why does potassium tert-butoxide give mostly the Hofmann alkene (c) while sodium ethoxide gives mostly the Zaitsev alkene (a)?
o: The tert-butoxide is a better nucleophile than ethoxide, and it attacks the tertiary carbon directly to eject the leaving group.
Bulk makes tert-butoxide a poorer nucleophile, and E2 does not involve attack on the carbon bearing the leaving group.
The bulky tert-butoxide removes the more accessible hydrogens of the methyl group more readily than the hindered internal hydrogens, favoring the less substituted alkene.
Correct: Steric hindrance in the base controls which β-hydrogen can be reached in the concerted E2 transition state, so the less hindered β-hydrogens are removed.
The tert-butoxide forms a carbocation more quickly than ethoxide, and the cation rearranges to the less substituted alkene.
E2 is concerted and does not involve a carbocation; rearrangement is not the cause.
The tert-butoxide is a much weaker base than ethoxide, and weaker bases favor the less stable alkene product.
tert-Butoxide (conjugate acid pKa about 17 to 18) is at least as strong a base as ethoxide.
qs.x: Steric hindrance in the base controls which β-hydrogen can be reached in the concerted E2 transition state, so the less hindered β-hydrogens are removed. Trap: Treating a bulky base as weaker or as a better nucleophile instead of recognizing steric control of selectivity.

qs.q: Which geometric arrangement of the leaving group and the β-hydrogen is required in the transition state of an E2 reaction?
o: The β-hydrogen and the leaving group must be gauche, with a dihedral angle of 60° so that the departing base is stabilized by the substituents.
A gauche arrangement does not permit good overlap between the breaking bonds.
The β-hydrogen and the leaving group must be perpendicular, with a dihedral angle of 90° so that sp³ orbitals are not aligned with the π system.
At 90°, the orbitals are orthogonal and cannot overlap to form a π bond.
The β-hydrogen and the leaving group must be anti-periplanar, with a dihedral angle of 180° so that the orbitals overlap to form the π bond.
Correct: Anti-periplanar alignment (the staggered conformation) permits smooth overlap of the C–H bonding orbital with the C–LG antibonding orbital as the π bond forms.
The β-hydrogen and the leaving group must be syn-periplanar, with a dihedral angle of 0° so that the orbitals are eclipsed during bond formation.
Syn-periplanar elimination is possible in some rigid systems but is higher in energy because the groups are eclipsed.
qs.x: Anti-periplanar alignment (the staggered conformation) permits smooth overlap of the C–H bonding orbital with the C–LG antibonding orbital as the π bond forms. Trap: Remembering that E2 requires an eclipsed geometry instead of the staggered anti arrangement.

qs.q: When 2-bromo-3-methylbutane (a secondary bromide) undergoes solvolysis in ethanol, which alkene is expected to be a major elimination product, and why?
o: 2-Methyl-1-butene, formed after a 1,2-methyl shift converts the secondary cation into a tertiary carbocation.
The methyl group shift would give a different, less stable cation, and the hydride shift is the more direct path to a tertiary center.
3-Methyl-1-butene, formed because E1 reactions always follow the Hofmann rule when the carbocation is secondary.
E1 reactions generally give the more substituted (Zaitsev) alkene, and the carbocation can rearrange before proton loss.
2-Methyl-2-butene, formed after a 1,2-hydride shift converts the secondary carbocation to a more stable tertiary carbocation.
Correct: Ionization gives a secondary carbocation, which rearranges by a 1,2-hydride shift to the tertiary cation; loss of a proton gives the most substituted alkene.
2-Methyl-2-butene, formed by a concerted anti elimination in which no carbocation is involved because ethanol is a good nucleophile.
Ethanol is a weak base, so the concerted E2 pathway is not favored; the carbocation mechanism accounts for the rearranged skeleton.
qs.x: Ionization gives a secondary carbocation, which rearranges by a 1,2-hydride shift to the tertiary cation; loss of a proton gives the most substituted alkene. Trap: Ignoring carbocation rearrangement in E1/SN1 reactions of secondary substrates.

passages.title: FL06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 1
text: Opponent-process theory proposes that, after three cone types transduce light, downstream neurons encode color along red-green, blue-yellow, and black-white axes. A researcher tested whether afterimage strength reflects fatigue in these opponent channels. Thirty participants with normal trichromatic vision and 30 participants with deuteranopia (absent medium-wavelength cones) fixated a saturated red disk or, on a separate day, a saturated blue disk for 10, 30, or 60 s. Immediately afterward, each viewed a uniform white field and pressed a key when the afterimage faded. Participants also named the dominant hue of the afterimage. Viewing distance, disk luminance, and room lighting were held constant, and the order of colors was counterbalanced. Mean afterimage durations appear in Table 1 and Figure 1. All trichromats reported a greenish afterimage after red adaptation and a yellowish afterimage after blue adaptation. Deuteranopes reported a yellowish afterimage after blue adaptation but described only a faint, colorless dark patch after red adaptation.

qs.q: The greenish afterimage reported by trichromats after red adaptation is best explained by which process?
o: Long-wavelength cones permanently lose their photopigment during adaptation, so short-wavelength cones alone signal green once the white field appears
Pigment bleaching is temporary and cannot by itself generate a green hue; the complementary color arises from opponent channels.
Feature detectors in primary visual cortex for red habituate fully, so the blue-yellow channel takes over and labels the white field as green
The blue-yellow channel signals blue or yellow, not green; green belongs to the red-green axis.
Prolonged stimulation fatigues the red-signaling side of the red-green channel, so the green-signaling side dominates when the white field appears

Correct: Prolonged stimulation fatigues the red-signaling side of the red-green channel, so the green-signaling side dominates when the white field appears - sustained red input fatigues one pole of the red-green opponent channel, producing a rebound toward green on a neutral field.
Rods saturate during red fixation and send a green-labeled signal to visual cortex through the dorsal stream when the white field is shown
Rods do not mediate color, and the dorsal stream is not a color pathway.
qs.x: Prolonged stimulation fatigues the red-signaling side of the red-green channel, so the green-signaling side dominates when the white field appears - sustained red input fatigues one pole of the red-green opponent channel, producing a rebound toward green on a neutral field. Trap: Attributing the afterimage to photopigment bleaching alone rather than to rebound in an opponent channel.

qs.q: Compared with trichromats, deuteranopes showed much shorter afterimages after red adaptation but nearly normal afterimages after blue adaptation. Which explanation best accounts for this pattern?
o: Deuteranopes have fewer rods than trichromats, so the dark-adapted system contributes weaker afterimages for long-wavelength stimuli only
Rods are not color-specific and would not selectively affect red afterimages.
Without short-wavelength cones the blue-yellow channel receives little input, so afterimages of every hue are shortened in deuteranopes
Deuteranopia involves M cones; blue afterimages were normal, contradicting a blue-yellow deficit.
Without medium-wavelength cones the red-green channel receives little differential input and fatigues weakly, while the blue-yellow channel is intact

Correct: Without medium-wavelength cones the red-green channel receives little differential input and fatigues weakly, while the blue-yellow channel is intact - the deficit is specific to the red-green axis, whereas blue-yellow input from S cones is preserved.
Deuteranopes have impaired blue-yellow processing, which is why their blue afterimages were reduced relative to trichromats in Table 1
Table 1 shows blue durations for deuteranopes (3.3, 7.1, 10.5 s) nearly equal to trichromats, so this misreads the data.
qs.x: Without medium-wavelength cones the red-green channel receives little differential input and fatigues weakly, while the blue-yellow channel is intact - the deficit is specific to the red-green axis, whereas blue-yellow input from S cones is preserved. Trap: Confusing which cone type is missing in deuteranopia and which opponent channel it affects.

qs.q: In trichromats, by how much did afterimage duration after red adaptation increase between 10 s and 60 s of adaptation?
o: This is roughly the ratio 11.6/3.8, not the difference.
Correct: 7.8 s - 11.6 s minus 3.8 s equals 7.8 s.
This is the increase for the blue series (10.9 - 3.5), not red.
This is the 60 s value itself, not the increase.
qs.x: 7.8 s - 11.6 s minus 3.8 s equals 7.8 s. Trap: Reading the wrong series or reporting a ratio instead of a difference.

qs.q: Which finding is most difficult to explain with a purely trichromatic account and best supports opponent-process coding?
o: Trichromats and deuteranopes both perceive the white field as colorless once the afterimage has completely faded away
Perceiving white as colorless does not distinguish between the theories.
Deuteranopes show weaker red-green discrimination than trichromats, as expected when one of three cone classes is missing
Reduced discrimination with a missing cone class is exactly what trichromacy predicts.
Afterimage duration increases as adaptation time increases for every group tested, from 10 s through 60 s of fixation
Longer adaptation producing stronger fatigue is compatible with either theory.
Afterimages appear in complementary hues, green after red and yellow after blue, rather than in the hue of the adapting stimulus

Correct: Afterimages appear in complementary hues, green after red and yellow after blue, rather than in the hue of the adapting stimulus - cone responses alone predict reduced sensitivity, not a complementary hue; paired opposing channels explain the rebound.
qs.x: Afterimages appear in complementary hues, green after red and yellow after blue, rather than in the hue of the adapting stimulus - cone responses alone predict reduced sensitivity, not a complementary hue; paired opposing channels explain the rebound. Trap: Choosing a result that fits both theories equally well.

qs.q: Opponent processing of color first appears at which level of the visual pathway?
o: The outer segments of cones, where three photopigments are already arranged in opposing excitatory and inhibitory pairs
Cones are trichromatic; opponency arises when their outputs are compared downstream.
Retinal ganglion cells and the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus
Correct: Retinal ganglion cells and the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus - cone signals are recombined into opponent channels in ganglion cells and LGN neurons, before cortical processing.
The medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, which relays color signals toward the primary visual cortex for integration
The MGN is part of the auditory pathway.
The superior colliculus, which compares cone outputs to direct eye movements toward objects of a particular hue
The superior colliculus guides orienting, not color opponency.
qs.x: Retinal ganglion cells and the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus - cone signals are recombined into opponent channels in ganglion cells and LGN neurons, before cortical processing. Trap: Assuming opponent coding occurs in photoreceptors because the theory is often presented alongside cone types.

passages.title: FL06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 2
text: The Stroop task requires participants to name the ink color of a stimulus while ignoring its meaning. Forty-eight undergraduates completed three trial types on a computer: congruent (the word BLUE printed in blue ink), neutral (a row of Xs printed in blue ink), and incongruent (the word RED printed in blue ink). Participants pressed one of four keys to report ink color, and response time (RT) and errors were recorded for each trial. In Part 1, congruent, neutral, and incongruent trials appeared equally often. In Part 2, researchers varied the proportion of incongruent trials across separate blocks that contained only congruent and incongruent trials: 25% incongruent in one block and 75% incongruent in another. Block order was counterbalanced across participants, and each block contained 120 trials. The researchers hypothesized that participants would adjust their level of attentional control according to how likely conflict was. Mean RTs and error rates are shown in Table 1.

qs.q: In Part 1, what was the interference effect, defined as incongruent RT minus neutral RT?
o: 127 ms
Correct: 127 ms - 782 ms minus 655 ms equals 127 ms.
203 ms
This is the 25% block difference (801 - 598), a different block and baseline.
43 ms
This is neutral minus congruent (655 - 612), the facilitation effect.
170 ms
This subtracts the congruent RT (782 - 612), which includes facilitation, not interference alone.
qs.x: 127 ms - 782 ms minus 655 ms equals 127 ms. Trap: Using the congruent condition as the baseline when the question specifies neutral.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for slower and less accurate responses on incongruent trials?
o: Word reading is a highly practiced, automatic process that competes with the slower, controlled process of naming ink color

Correct: Word reading is a highly practiced, automatic process that competes with the slower, controlled process of naming ink color - the automatic word response conflicts with the task-relevant color response and must be suppressed by selective attention.
Color naming is the automatic process and word reading is the controlled one, so the word must be inhibited before the ink color is named
The automaticity is reversed; reading is the more practiced response.
Holding four response keys in working memory exceeds capacity only on incongruent trials, producing errors unrelated to the printed words
The key mapping was identical across trial types, so memory load cannot explain the difference.
Conflicting words physically mask the ink color, so participants cannot perceive the color on incongruent trials without extra viewing time
Participants see the ink color clearly; the problem is response competition, not perception.
qs.x: Word reading is a highly practiced, automatic process that competes with the slower, controlled process of naming ink color - the automatic word response conflicts with the task-relevant color response and must be suppressed by selective attention. Trap: Reversing which process is automatic.

qs.q: In Part 2, the interference effect (incongruent minus congruent RT) was smaller in the 75% incongruent block (105 ms) than in the 25% block (203 ms). What is the most reasonable interpretation?
o: Participants learned to ignore ink color and respond to the words instead, which removes conflict because the words are now the target
Responding to words would produce errors on the ink-color task; error rate actually fell to 6%.
Frequent incongruent trials make word reading faster, so automatic reading becomes stronger and interference shrinks through added practice
More practice reading words would strengthen, not weaken, the competing response.
When conflict is frequent, participants increase top-down attentional control, which reduces the influence of the irrelevant word

Correct: When conflict is frequent, participants increase top-down attentional control, which reduces the influence of the irrelevant word - conflict-adaptive control lowers interference where conflict is expected.
Participants in the 75% block were more fatigued, so slower congruent responses artificially compressed the difference between the conditions
Fatigue is speculative and not supported; the congruent RT difference is small relative to the shift in incongruent RT.
qs.x: When conflict is frequent, participants increase top-down attentional control, which reduces the influence of the irrelevant word - conflict-adaptive control lowers interference where conflict is expected. Trap: Interpreting reduced interference as more automatic reading rather than more control.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of including the neutral condition in Part 1?
o: It controls for order effects by separating the congruent and incongruent trials so that participants cannot predict the next stimulus
Counterbalancing, not a neutral trial type, handles order effects.
It equalizes the number of trials per block so that error rates can be compared directly across the three conditions
Trial counts are not the purpose of a neutral condition.
It serves as a manipulation check showing that participants can see ink color when no word is present to distract them
A check on perception is not what the neutral baseline is for; it isolates facilitation versus interference.
It provides a baseline that separates speeding from congruent words (facilitation) from slowing caused by conflicting words (interference)

Correct: It provides a baseline that separates speeding from congruent words (facilitation) from slowing caused by conflicting words (interference) - comparing neutral with congruent and incongruent trials partitions the Stroop effect into two components.
qs.x: It provides a baseline that separates speeding from congruent words (facilitation) from slowing caused by conflicting words (interference) - comparing neutral with congruent and incongruent trials partitions the Stroop effect into two components. Trap: Treating the neutral condition as a mere filler or perception check.

passages.title: FL06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 3
text: In the transactional model of stress, stress arises when a person appraises situational demands as exceeding available resources. Researchers tested whether changing appraisal alters the hormonal stress response. Sixty healthy adults were randomly assigned to a reappraisal group, who were told that physiological arousal before a public speech improves performance, or to a control group, who received no instruction. All participants prepared and delivered a 5-minute speech and completed mental arithmetic in front of a stern evaluation panel. Saliva samples were collected before the task (0 min) and 20, 40, and 60 min afterward, and cortisol was measured in nmol/L. Participants also rated perceived task demands and perceived coping resources; a resources-to-demands ratio above 1.0 was classified as a challenge appraisal and a ratio below 1.0 as a threat appraisal. Mean cortisol appears in Figure 1, and appraisal results appear in Table 1. Sampling occurred in the afternoon, when baseline cortisol is relatively stable.

qs.q: Which appraisal process was most directly altered by the instruction given to the reappraisal group?
o: Primary appraisal, because participants decided that the speech task was irrelevant to their well-being and therefore not worth evaluating
The speech remained relevant; the instruction changed perceived resources, not relevance.
Neither appraisal process, because cortisol responses are driven only by the physical features of the stressor and not by interpretation
The data show that interpretation altered cortisol, contradicting a purely physical account.
Primary appraisal, because participants judged the evaluation panel to be benign and therefore classified the situation as harmless
Panel behavior was identical across groups, so primary appraisal of the situation was not what changed.
Secondary appraisal, because participants reinterpreted their arousal as a resource available for coping with the speech

Correct: Secondary appraisal, because participants reinterpreted their arousal as a resource available for coping with the speech - secondary appraisal evaluates coping resources, and the instruction recast arousal as helpful.
qs.x: Secondary appraisal, because participants reinterpreted their arousal as a resource available for coping with the speech - secondary appraisal evaluates coping resources, and the instruction recast arousal as helpful. Trap: Mixing up primary appraisal (is it a threat?) with secondary appraisal (can I cope?).

qs.q: Cortisol released in response to the speech task is the end product of which sequence?
o: Sympathetic neurons stimulate the thyroid, whose hormones then trigger cortisol secretion from the posterior pituitary gland
Thyroid hormones and the posterior pituitary are not part of the cortisol cascade.
Hypothalamic CRH stimulates adrenal medullary release of epinephrine, which then triggers cortisol secretion from the anterior pituitary
Epinephrine is a medullary catecholamine and the pituitary does not secrete cortisol.
Hypothalamic CRH stimulates pituitary ACTH release, which stimulates cortisol secretion from the adrenal cortex
Correct: Hypothalamic CRH stimulates pituitary ACTH release, which stimulates cortisol secretion from the adrenal cortex - this is the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.
Pituitary ACTH stimulates hypothalamic CRH release, which stimulates cortisol secretion from the adrenal medulla through sympathetic nerves
The order is reversed and cortisol comes from the cortex, not the medulla.
qs.x: Hypothalamic CRH stimulates pituitary ACTH release, which stimulates cortisol secretion from the adrenal cortex - this is the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. Trap: Confusing the adrenal cortex (cortisol) with the adrenal medulla (epinephrine).

qs.q: Relative to baseline, how large was the 20-minute cortisol increase in the reappraisal group compared with the control group?
o: About half as large, roughly 3.2 versus 6.5 nmol/L
Correct: About half as large, roughly 3.2 versus 6.5 nmol/L - reappraisal rise 11.0 - 7.8 = 3.2; control rise 14.5 - 8.0 = 6.5; 3.2/6.5 is about 0.49.
About three-quarters as large, roughly 4.9 versus 6.5 nmol/L
This does not match the figure values; the rise was 3.2, not 4.9.
About twice as large, roughly 13.0 versus 6.5 nmol/L
This reverses the groups; the reappraisal group had the smaller rise.
Nearly identical, roughly 6.0 versus 6.5 nmol/L
The groups differed clearly at 20 min (11.0 versus 14.5 nmol/L).
qs.x: About half as large, roughly 3.2 versus 6.5 nmol/L - reappraisal rise 11.0 - 7.8 = 3.2; control rise 14.5 - 8.0 = 6.5; 3.2/6.5 is about 0.49. Trap: Comparing the raw 20-min values instead of the change from baseline.

qs.q: Why does peak cortisol occur roughly 20 minutes after the stressor rather than immediately, as heart rate does?
o: Cortisol is stored in salivary glands and released only after the stressor ends, whereas heart rate is controlled by hormones in blood
Cortisol is not stored in salivary glands; saliva only reflects blood levels.
The parasympathetic system initially suppresses cortisol for several minutes, whereas heart rate is unaffected by parasympathetic output
The parasympathetic system does not gate cortisol release this way, and it does affect heart rate.
Participants anticipate the stressor and release cortisol before it begins, so the later peak reflects only measurement delay in the assay
Baseline was low before the task, so there was no anticipatory peak; the delay is physiological.
The HPA axis relies on a slower hormonal cascade, whereas the sympathetic-adrenal medullary response acts within seconds through neural signaling

Correct: The HPA axis relies on a slower hormonal cascade, whereas the sympathetic-adrenal medullary response acts within seconds through neural signaling - endocrine cascades and steroid secretion take minutes, while sympathetic neural activation is nearly immediate.
qs.x: The HPA axis relies on a slower hormonal cascade, whereas the sympathetic-adrenal medullary response acts within seconds through neural signaling - endocrine cascades and steroid secretion take minutes, while sympathetic neural activation is nearly immediate. Trap: Assuming all stress hormones act at the same speed.

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean salivary cortisol before and after the speech task

passages.title: FL06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 4
text: Erikson proposed that adolescence centers on a crisis of identity versus role confusion, whereas Marcia operationalized identity with two dimensions: exploration of alternatives and commitment to chosen roles. Combining these yields four statuses: diffusion (low exploration, low commitment), foreclosure (low exploration, high commitment), moratorium (high exploration, low commitment), and achievement (high exploration, high commitment). Researchers surveyed two separate samples of 150 emerging adults each, one aged 18 to 20 and one aged 24 to 26, recruited from the same community. Participants completed structured interviews about occupation, values, and relationships, which trained raters coded into the four statuses. Participants also completed a 100-point well-being scale. Raters were blind to well-being scores, and interviews were conducted individually by researchers who did not know participants' ages in advance. Participants received a small payment, and all responses were anonymized before coding. Table 1 shows the percentage of each sample in each status and the mean well-being score for each status across both samples combined.

qs.q: According to Erikson, which psychosocial stage follows the identity versus role confusion stage?
o: Intimacy versus isolation, in which young adults seek close commitments to others
Correct: Intimacy versus isolation, in which young adults seek close commitments to others - intimacy versus isolation is the young-adult stage after adolescence.
Integrity versus despair, in which older adults reflect on whether their lives have been meaningful and well spent
This is the final stage of late adulthood.
Industry versus inferiority, in which school-age children develop competence by mastering tasks valued by their society
This precedes adolescence.
Generativity versus stagnation, in which adults seek to guide and contribute to the next generation through work and family
This is the middle-adulthood stage, two stages later.
qs.x: Intimacy versus isolation, in which young adults seek close commitments to others - intimacy versus isolation is the young-adult stage after adolescence. Trap: Mixing up the order of Erikson's eight stages.

qs.q: How many participants in the 24-26 sample were classified as identity achievement?
o: This is the percentage itself, not the number of participants.
This is 18% of 150, the 18-20 achievement figure.
Correct: 66 - 44% of 150 is 66.
This is 56% of 150, the combined share of the other three statuses.
qs.x: 66 - 44% of 150 is 66. Trap: Reporting the percentage instead of converting to a count, or using the wrong sample.

qs.q: Which pattern in Table 1 is most consistent with identity development across emerging adulthood?
o: The share in moratorium rises with age because exploration increases, while the share in achievement remains below one quarter
Moratorium fell from 28% to 20% and achievement reached 44%.
Foreclosure becomes the most common status in the older sample because commitments are made without exploring other alternatives
Achievement, not foreclosure, was most common at ages 24-26.
The share in diffusion stays about the same in both samples, indicating that lack of exploration is a stable trait through the 20s
Diffusion dropped from 24% to 14%.
The share in identity achievement rises sharply while the shares in diffusion, foreclosure, and moratorium all decline
Correct: The share in identity achievement rises sharply while the shares in diffusion, foreclosure, and moratorium all decline - achievement rose from 18% to 44% while each other status fell.
qs.x: The share in identity achievement rises sharply while the shares in diffusion, foreclosure, and moratorium all decline - achievement rose from 18% to 44% while each other status fell. Trap: Assuming exploration status increases with age instead of resolving into commitment.

qs.q: What is the main limitation on concluding from these data that identity achievement increases with age within individuals?
o: Both samples were recruited from the same community, so the results cannot be compared and a different design is required to compare ages
Sampling from the same community helps comparability; it is not the limitation.
Different people were studied at each age, so group differences may reflect cohort effects rather than change; following the same people over time would address this

Correct: Different people were studied at each age, so group differences may reflect cohort effects rather than change; following the same people over time would address this - a cross-sectional design confounds age with cohort.
The well-being scale ranges from 0 to 100, which is too broad a range to detect differences among the four identity statuses
A 100-point scale is adequate; the problem is the age comparison, not scale range.
The interviews were coded by trained raters, so coding errors are unavoidable and would make any comparison of percentages meaningless
Rater coding with blinding is a strength; it does not prevent age comparisons.
qs.x: Different people were studied at each age, so group differences may reflect cohort effects rather than change; following the same people over time would address this - a cross-sectional design confounds age with cohort. Trap: Overlooking that cross-sectional samples confound age with cohort.

passages.title: FL06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 5
text: In the minimal group paradigm, people are divided into groups on trivial bases and then allocate resources. Sixty-six students were told they would join one of two groups. In the random condition, membership was decided by a coin toss; in the preference condition, by a purported preference for paintings by Klee or Kandinsky; and in the control condition, no group labels were used. Participants never met other members, were identified only by code numbers, and could not benefit personally from their allocations. Each participant divided 100 points between two anonymous recipients, one from the participant's own group and one from the other group (in the control condition, two unlabeled recipients). Allocations were made privately in booklets, and the scorer did not know each participant's condition. Participants then completed a 7-point group identification scale. Table 1 shows mean allocations with 22 participants per condition. Figure 1 shows mean in-group bias (points to in-group minus points to out-group) by identification score among all labeled participants.

qs.q: What do the results of the random and preference conditions most directly demonstrate?
o: Participants allocate points according to personal gain, because they expect to receive resources from members of their own group later
Participants could not benefit personally, by design.
Competition over scarce resources between groups is required before members will favor their own group over an outsider
Participants did not compete; favoritism arose anyway.
Favoritism appears only when group membership reflects a meaningful shared preference, since coin-toss groups show no allocation bias
The random condition also showed bias (56.2 versus 43.8).
Mere categorization into groups, without contact, competition, or personal gain, is sufficient to produce in-group favoritism

Correct: Mere categorization into groups, without contact, competition, or personal gain, is sufficient to produce in-group favoritism - favoritism appeared even though groups were arbitrary and anonymous.
qs.x: Mere categorization into groups, without contact, competition, or personal gain, is sufficient to produce in-group favoritism - favoritism appeared even though groups were arbitrary and anonymous. Trap: Assuming intergroup conflict over resources is required for in-group bias.

qs.q: What was the mean in-group bias in the preference condition?
o: 16.2 points
Correct: 16.2 points - 58.1 minus 41.9 is 16.2.
8.1 points
This is half of 16.2, which divides the difference by two.
58.1 points
This is the in-group allocation itself, not the bias.
12.4 points
This is the random condition bias (56.2 - 43.8).
qs.x: 16.2 points - 58.1 minus 41.9 is 16.2. Trap: Using one allocation rather than the difference between allocations.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of the control condition?
o: To demonstrate that out-group members are always treated worse than in-group members regardless of how groups were created
The control shows no group-based difference, and it cannot show anything about all groups.
To show that unequal allocation arises from group labels rather than from a general tendency to divide points unevenly between recipients

Correct: To show that unequal allocation arises from group labels rather than from a general tendency to divide points unevenly between recipients - near-even allocation (50.3 versus 49.7) without labels gives the baseline.
To increase the sample size of the study so that the allocation means in the labeled conditions can be estimated with more precision
The control does not contribute to estimates of the labeled conditions.
To ensure that participants understand the instructions for dividing points because they are told which recipient belongs to their group
Control participants received no group information; the purpose is a baseline.
qs.x: To show that unequal allocation arises from group labels rather than from a general tendency to divide points unevenly between recipients - near-even allocation (50.3 versus 49.7) without labels gives the baseline. Trap: Seeing a control condition as extra data rather than a baseline for comparison.

qs.q: Social identity theory would explain the allocation pattern in which way?
o: People reduce cognitive dissonance after choosing a group, so they justify the choice by sending more points to recipients in the chosen group
Dissonance reduction is a different theory and does not predict identification-related bias.
People are born with an instinct to harm outsiders, so the allocation reflects an aggressive drive released by seeing any other group
Social identity theory is not an instinct theory; it concerns self-esteem and categorization.
People derive part of their self-esteem from group membership, so favoring the in-group raises the perceived worth of their own social identity

Correct: People derive part of their self-esteem from group membership, so favoring the in-group raises the perceived worth of their own social identity - this explains why identification tracks bias.
People imitate others they have seen rewarded for favoring their own group, so the allocation reflects social learning from observed models
No models were observed in this study.
qs.x: People derive part of their self-esteem from group membership, so favoring the in-group raises the perceived worth of their own social identity - this explains why identification tracks bias. Trap: Attributing in-group favoritism to aggressive instinct or dissonance rather than self-esteem from group membership.

qs.q: Using the endpoints of Figure 1, what is the approximate increase in in-group bias per one-point increase in identification score?
o: 4.5 points
18 points
This is the total rise in bias, not the rate per unit of identification.
3.6 points
This divides by 5 (the number of points on the x-axis) rather than 4 intervals.
5.4 points
This is the increase from 5 to 6 of 5.0, not the average slope across the range.
qs.x: 4.5 points - (19.0 - 1.0)/(6 - 2) is 4.5. Trap: Dividing by the wrong number of intervals or using the total rise.

h: Mean points to in-group (or recipient A)
Mean points to out-group (or recipient B)

graph.title: Figure 1. In-group bias by group identification score

passages.title: FL06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 6
text: The frustration-aggression hypothesis holds that blocking a goal increases the likelihood of aggression, and the weapons effect suggests that aggressive cues can prime aggressive responses. Eighty undergraduates were randomly assigned to cells of a 2 x 2 design (20 per cell). Frustration was manipulated by having participants work on puzzles under time pressure while a confederate repeatedly interrupted and insulted them; the puzzles were unsolvable (high frustration) or solvable (low frustration). Cue was manipulated by placing either a handgun or a badminton racquet on a nearby table, described as left over from another study. Participants then played a reaction-time game in which they could deliver noise blasts to the confederate and chose an intensity from 1 (very quiet) to 10 (very loud). Participants were told the confederate was another student, and the confederate wore headphones. No noise was actually delivered, and participants were fully debriefed afterward. Experimenters recording intensity were unaware of the cue condition. Mean intensity is shown in Table 1.

qs.q: Averaged across both cues, how much higher was mean noise intensity under high frustration than under low frustration?
o: 1.5 points
This compares only the racquet cells (5.1 - 3.6).
1.7 points
This is the handgun-minus-racquet difference under high frustration.
2.9 points
This compares only the handgun cells (6.8 - 3.9).
2.2 points
qs.x: 2.2 points - (6.8 + 5.1)/2 = 5.95; (3.9 + 3.6)/2 = 3.75; the difference is 2.2. Trap: Comparing a single pair of cells instead of the marginal means.

qs.q: Which statement best describes the effect of the handgun cue?
o: The handgun raised intensity by about the same amount under both frustration levels, indicating a cue effect independent of anger
The increases (1.7 versus 0.3) differ markedly.
The handgun raised intensity by 2.9 points under high frustration, which shows the cue alone can account for the frustration effect
2.9 is the high-versus-low frustration difference for handgun cells, not the cue effect.
The handgun raised intensity by 1.7 points under high frustration but only 0.3 under low frustration, suggesting cues prime aggression mainly when anger is aroused

Correct: The handgun raised intensity by 1.7 points under high frustration but only 0.3 under low frustration, suggesting cues prime aggression mainly when anger is aroused - the cue effect depended on frustration level, an interaction.
The handgun lowered intensity under low frustration because participants were inhibited by the weapon, which reversed the cue effect
Intensity was slightly higher with the handgun (3.9 versus 3.6), not lower.
qs.x: The handgun raised intensity by 1.7 points under high frustration but only 0.3 under low frustration, suggesting cues prime aggression mainly when anger is aroused - the cue effect depended on frustration level, an interaction. Trap: Describing main effects when the pattern is an interaction.

qs.q: Which limitation applies most directly to the use of noise-blast intensity as the outcome measure?
o: The outcome was measured on a 10-point scale, which prevents any statistical comparison across the four cells of the design
Ordinal-like scales are routinely analyzed this way; the issue is validity of the measure.
Random assignment of participants to the four cells makes it impossible to compare mean intensity between the high and low frustration groups
Random assignment is what permits causal comparison.
A laboratory game rating may not capture real-world harmful aggression, which limits external validity of the conclusions

Correct: A laboratory game rating may not capture real-world harmful aggression, which limits external validity of the conclusions - operational definitions of aggression in the lab may not generalize.
The confederate knew the hypothesis of the study, which guarantees that participants will deliver the maximum intensity in every cell
Nothing in the design implies this, and results varied across cells.
qs.x: A laboratory game rating may not capture real-world harmful aggression, which limits external validity of the conclusions - operational definitions of aggression in the lab may not generalize. Trap: Confusing random assignment (internal validity) with external validity of an outcome measure.

qs.q: Which finding would be most consistent with social learning theory rather than the frustration-aggression hypothesis?
o: Participants with higher baseline testosterone delivered louder blasts regardless of the condition to which they had been assigned
This implicates biological factors, not learning from models.
Participants who watched a model rewarded for delivering loud blasts then delivered louder blasts, even when they were not frustrated

Correct: Participants who watched a model rewarded for delivering loud blasts then delivered louder blasts, even when they were not frustrated - aggression learned through observation and reinforcement occurs without frustration.
Participants who were blocked from completing puzzles delivered louder blasts than participants who completed puzzles without interruption
This is the frustration-aggression prediction.
Participants given an alternative outlet for frustration, such as a punching bag, subsequently delivered quieter blasts
This resembles catharsis, not social learning.
qs.x: Participants who watched a model rewarded for delivering loud blasts then delivered louder blasts, even when they were not frustrated - aggression learned through observation and reinforcement occurs without frustration. Trap: Choosing an observed correlate of aggression that is not about observational learning.

passages.title: FL06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 7
text: Sociologists treat healthcare as a social institution that organizes how societies define illness, distribute treatment, and train practitioners. A survey of 4,500 adults in a mid-sized metropolitan region compared access to care across household income levels. Respondents were grouped as low income (n = 1,500), middle income (n = 1,500), and high income (n = 1,500). Each reported whether they currently held health insurance, whether they had received a routine checkup in the previous 12 months, and whether they had delayed needed care in the previous year because of cost. Table 1 shows the results. Interviewers also asked how often respondents consulted a physician for conditions such as back pain or sleeplessness; the investigators noted that such experiences have increasingly been defined as medical problems over recent decades, and that physicians now hold primary authority over how they are labeled and treated. Respondents were selected by random-digit dialing, and the three income groups were similar in age and sex distribution.

qs.q: Which sociological perspective most directly interprets the income gradient in Table 1?
o: Rational choice theory, because low-income adults weigh costs and benefits and voluntarily decide to forgo care that has little value
Cost delay reflects constrained resources, not freely chosen low valuation of care.
Functionalism, because health care efficiently allocates services to those who are most in need and thereby maintains social stability
Functionalism would not predict systematic disadvantage for low-income groups.
Conflict theory, because differential access to care reflects an unequal distribution of resources and power in society

Correct: Conflict theory, because differential access to care reflects an unequal distribution of resources and power in society - conflict theory emphasizes inequality in access to scarce social resources.
Symbolic interactionism, because patients and physicians construct shared meanings of illness during each individual clinical encounter
This perspective concerns micro-level meanings, not the group-level gradient.
qs.x: Conflict theory, because differential access to care reflects an unequal distribution of resources and power in society - conflict theory emphasizes inequality in access to scarce social resources. Trap: Selecting functionalism, which emphasizes stability, for a pattern of unequal access.

qs.q: How many low-income respondents reported delaying care because of cost?
o: This is 52% of 1,500, the checkup percentage.
This is 78% of 1,500, the insured count.
This is 11% of 1,500, the middle-income percentage.
qs.x: 360 - 24% of 1,500 is 360. Trap: Applying the wrong column or income group.

qs.q: The investigators' observation about back pain and sleeplessness best illustrates which concept?
o: Anomie, in which rapid social change weakens norms and leaves individuals without clear guidance on acceptable behavior
Anomie concerns normlessness, not medical labeling.
Rationalization, in which social life becomes organized by efficiency, calculability, and impersonal rules over tradition
This is Weber's concept of bureaucratic organization, not defining conditions as medical.
Medicalization, in which a human experience becomes defined and treated as a medical problem under professional authority

Correct: Medicalization, in which a human experience becomes defined and treated as a medical problem under professional authority - medicalization is the expansion of medical definitions to ordinary experiences.
Deinstitutionalization, in which people formerly cared for in large facilities are moved to community settings with less supervision
This concerns moving patients out of institutions.
qs.x: Medicalization, in which a human experience becomes defined and treated as a medical problem under professional authority - medicalization is the expansion of medical definitions to ordinary experiences. Trap: Confusing medicalization with rationalization because both concern institutional authority.

qs.q: Among low-income respondents, 78% were insured but 24% still delayed care for cost. What does this suggest?
o: Insurance coverage alone does not remove cost barriers such as deductibles and copayments, so access remains unequal
Correct: Insurance coverage alone does not remove cost barriers such as deductibles and copayments, so access remains unequal - being insured is not equivalent to affording care.
Surveys of delayed care are inherently invalid, since respondents cannot be expected to recall whether cost delayed care during the previous year
Self-report has limits, but nothing here shows it is invalid.
Insurance is unrelated to access to care, since delays occur at similar rates among insured and uninsured adults in every income group
The data do not separate insured from uninsured, so this overstates the data.
Low-income respondents value preventive care less than higher-income respondents, which explains their lower checkup rates
Cost-related delay points to structural barriers, not valuation.
qs.x: Insurance coverage alone does not remove cost barriers such as deductibles and copayments, so access remains unequal - being insured is not equivalent to affording care. Trap: Equating insurance coverage with the ability to use care.

passages.title: FL06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 8
text: Demographic transition theory describes a shift from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as societies industrialize. Researchers compiled national statistics for one country over four decades: the percentage of the population living in urban areas, the total fertility rate (TFR; average number of births per woman), and the infant mortality rate (IMR; deaths per 1,000 live births). During this period, female secondary-school enrollment rose steadily, and wage labor in cities replaced farming as the main source of household income, so children shifted from being economic assets in farming households to costly dependents in cities. The crude death rate was already below 10 per 1,000 by 1980. Data are shown in Table 1, and Figure 1 plots TFR against percent urban for the four years. Replacement-level fertility in low-mortality countries is about 2.1. All figures come from census and vital registration records, and the four years were chosen at equal 20-year intervals.

qs.q: Between 1980 and 2000, the country is best described as being in which stage of the demographic transition?
o: Stage 4, in which birth and death rates are both low and nearly equal, producing a stable and slowly changing population
TFR of 3.3 is well above replacement, so growth was still substantial.
Stage 1, in which both birth and death rates are high and population grows slowly because mortality offsets fertility
Death rates were already low.
Stage 2, in which death rates fall sharply while birth rates remain high, producing the most rapid population growth
Birth rates were declining by 2000.
Stage 3, in which death rates are already low and birth rates are falling, so population growth is slowing
Correct: Stage 3, in which death rates are already low and birth rates are falling, so population growth is slowing - death rate was low by 1980 and TFR fell from 5.1 to 3.3.
qs.x: Stage 3, in which death rates are already low and birth rates are falling, so population growth is slowing - death rate was low by 1980 and TFR fell from 5.1 to 3.3. Trap: Choosing stage 2 because death rates fell, ignoring the fall in births.

qs.q: Which explanation best links rising urbanization to the decline in fertility shown here?
o: In cities children generate costs rather than farm labor, and education and wage work raise the opportunity cost of childbearing for women

Correct: In cities children generate costs rather than farm labor, and education and wage work raise the opportunity cost of childbearing for women - urban living and women's schooling reduce the economic value of children.
Cities have higher death rates than rural areas, so parents have fewer children because fewer infants survive to be counted
Infant mortality fell during this period.
Urban residents have less access to schooling, so women marry later and have fewer children because of lower educational attainment
Female enrollment rose, and education typically lowers fertility.
Governments forced urban families to limit births, so the decline in TFR reflects coercion rather than any change in family economics
Nothing in the passage describes coercive policy.
qs.x: In cities children generate costs rather than farm labor, and education and wage work raise the opportunity cost of childbearing for women - urban living and women's schooling reduce the economic value of children. Trap: Assuming lower fertility reflects higher mortality rather than changed incentives.

qs.q: By approximately what percentage did TFR decrease from 1960 to 2020?
o: This is not derived from the table values.
This is the absolute decline (4.2 births) read as a percentage.
This is the 2020 TFR as a proportion of 1960 (2.0/6.2).
qs.x: 68% - (6.2 - 2.0)/6.2 is about 0.68. Trap: Mixing an absolute change with a percentage change.

qs.q: Even after TFR fell to 2.0, which factor best explains why the national population is still likely to grow for decades?
o: Urbanization itself raises the birth rate, so continued migration to cities raises TFR again in the years after 2020
The data show urbanization accompanying lower fertility.
Replacement-level fertility is 2.1, so a TFR of 2.0 is above replacement and directly guarantees that each generation is larger
2.0 is slightly below 2.1.
Infant mortality is rising sharply, which increases the number of births needed to replace each family and keeps total births high
IMR fell to 12 per 1,000.
A large cohort of young women born during high-fertility years is entering childbearing age, producing population momentum
Correct: A large cohort of young women born during high-fertility years is entering childbearing age, producing population momentum - age structure keeps births exceeding deaths for a time.
qs.x: A large cohort of young women born during high-fertility years is entering childbearing age, producing population momentum - age structure keeps births exceeding deaths for a time. Trap: Assuming that near-replacement TFR means immediate population stability.

qs.q: Using the 1960 and 2020 points in Figure 1, what is the approximate change in TFR for each 10-percentage-point increase in urban population?
o: A decrease of about 0.09 births per woman
This is the change per single percentage point.
A decrease of about 0.9 births per woman
Correct: A decrease of about 0.9 births per woman - (2.0 - 6.2)/(68 - 22) is about -0.091 per point, or -0.9 per 10 points.
A decrease of about 1.8 births per woman
This corresponds to a slope twice as steep as the data indicate.
A decrease of about 4.2 births per woman
This is the total decline over the whole period.
qs.x: A decrease of about 0.9 births per woman - (2.0 - 6.2)/(68 - 22) is about -0.091 per point, or -0.9 per 10 points. Trap: Reporting per-point change or total change instead of per 10 points.

graph.title: Figure 1. Total fertility rate by percent urban

passages.title: FL06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 9
text: Residential segregation is often quantified with the dissimilarity index (D), which ranges from 0 (even distribution of two groups across neighborhoods) to 1 (complete separation). Researchers examined 40 U.S. metropolitan areas, divided them into tertiles of Black-white segregation, and computed asthma-related emergency department (ED) visits per 10,000 residents for Black and white residents. They also obtained the average poverty rate in majority-Black neighborhoods. All analyses were conducted at the level of the metropolitan area. Results are shown in Table 1, and Figure 1 plots the Black-white difference in ED visit rate against D for six metropolitan areas. The authors suggest that segregation concentrates poverty, older housing, and traffic-related air pollution in particular neighborhoods, affecting residents regardless of their individual behaviors. Rates were age-adjusted, and metropolitan areas were drawn from the same set of large cities in each tertile to keep population size comparable. The authors cautioned that the study was observational and that individual-level records were not available to them.

qs.q: A dissimilarity index of 0.68 indicates which of the following?
o: About 68% of one group would need to move to a different neighborhood for the two groups to be evenly distributed

Correct: About 68% of one group would need to move to a different neighborhood for the two groups to be evenly distributed - D is the proportion of one group that would have to relocate for even distribution.
The Black-white difference in asthma ED visits equals 0.68 times the rate among white residents in the same metropolitan area
D is not a multiplier of ED rates.
Black residents have a poverty rate of 68% in the majority-Black neighborhoods of the metropolitan area on average
Poverty rate is a separate column.
Black residents make up about 68% of the population of the metropolitan area and white residents make up the remaining 32%
D measures distribution, not group share.
qs.x: About 68% of one group would need to move to a different neighborhood for the two groups to be evenly distributed - D is the proportion of one group that would have to relocate for even distribution. Trap: Interpreting D as a group's population share or as a rate.

qs.q: In the high-segregation tertile, the Black asthma ED rate was approximately how many times the white rate?
o: This inverts the ratio (19/63).
Correct: 3.3 - 63/19 is about 3.3.
This is the low tertile ratio (28/17).
This is the medium tertile ratio (41/18).
qs.x: 3.3 - 63/19 is about 3.3. Trap: Using the wrong tertile or inverting the ratio.

qs.q: Which mechanism best supports the authors' suggestion that segregation affects health independent of individual behavior?
o: Residents of segregated areas choose to smoke more often, which raises asthma risk through a behavioral pathway at the individual level
This is an individual-behavior explanation, contrary to the claim.
Segregation concentrates poverty and environmental hazards in particular neighborhoods, exposing all residents there to higher respiratory risk

Correct: Segregation concentrates poverty and environmental hazards in particular neighborhoods, exposing all residents there to higher respiratory risk - neighborhood-level exposures act on residents irrespective of personal choices.
Hospitals in segregated areas record more ED visits per person because they use broader diagnostic criteria for asthma than other hospitals
No data indicate differences in diagnostic criteria.
White residents in segregated areas are genetically less susceptible to asthma, which explains why their rates are flat across tertiles
Genetic explanations are unsupported and do not fit the pattern.
qs.x: Segregation concentrates poverty and environmental hazards in particular neighborhoods, exposing all residents there to higher respiratory risk - neighborhood-level exposures act on residents irrespective of personal choices. Trap: Defaulting to individual behavior to explain health disparities.

qs.q: Why can these results not show that an individual Black resident's asthma risk rises when that person lives in a more segregated area?
o: The data describe metropolitan areas, and relationships between aggregate measures may not hold for individuals, an ecological fallacy

Correct: The data describe metropolitan areas, and relationships between aggregate measures may not hold for individuals, an ecological fallacy - inference from group-level to individual-level data is unsafe.
Poverty is reported only for majority-Black neighborhoods, which proves that poverty has no relationship to asthma outcomes
Missing comparison data limit inference but do not prove no relationship.
Emergency department visits are measured per 10,000 residents, so the data cannot reflect any association with individual health
Rates per 10,000 are standard; the limit is aggregation level.
The tertiles contain unequal numbers of metropolitan areas, which invalidates any comparison of group means for individual residents
Tertiles are by design nearly equal in size, and size does not address the individual-level issue.
qs.x: The data describe metropolitan areas, and relationships between aggregate measures may not hold for individuals, an ecological fallacy - inference from group-level to individual-level data is unsafe. Trap: Applying aggregate relationships directly to individuals.

graph.title: Figure 1. Black-white difference in asthma ED visit rate by segregation

passages.title: FL06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 10
text: A cohort study followed 1,000 adults aged 55 to 65 for five years to examine whether regular herbal tea drinking (at least one cup daily) is related to cardiovascular events (heart attack or stroke). At baseline, 500 participants reported drinking tea regularly and 500 did not. Researchers also recorded socioeconomic status (SES) as high or low and noted that high-SES participants were far more likely to drink tea. Participants were not randomized, and tea habits were self-reported once at baseline. Table 1 presents the number of participants, events, and five-year incidence overall and within SES strata. The risk ratio (RR) is the incidence among tea drinkers divided by the incidence among non-drinkers. The investigators also noted that, in general, low SES is associated with higher cardiovascular risk because of differences in diet, stress, and access to care. Participants with prior cardiovascular events were excluded at baseline, and follow-up was complete for all 1,000 participants.

qs.q: In this study, SES is best described as which of the following?
o: A confounder, because it is associated with both tea drinking and cardiovascular events without being a consequence of tea drinking

Correct: A confounder, because it is associated with both tea drinking and cardiovascular events without being a consequence of tea drinking - SES relates to exposure and outcome and is not on the causal pathway.
A mediator, because tea drinking causes higher SES, which in turn lowers the risk of cardiovascular events over the follow-up period
Tea does not plausibly cause SES.
A dependent variable, because researchers measured it after cardiovascular events had occurred in each participant
SES was recorded at baseline and is not the outcome.
An effect modifier only, because the risk ratio differs across strata and therefore SES cannot be associated with tea drinking
SES clearly differs in tea use across groups.
qs.x: A confounder, because it is associated with both tea drinking and cardiovascular events without being a consequence of tea drinking - SES relates to exposure and outcome and is not on the causal pathway. Trap: Confusing a confounder with a mediator or an outcome.

qs.q: What was the crude risk ratio for cardiovascular events comparing tea drinkers with non-drinkers?
o: This is the absolute risk reduction as a proportion of 10%, 1 - 0.60.
This is the inverse (10.0/6.0).
Correct: 0.60 - 6.0/10.0 equals 0.60.
This is the risk ratio within the high-SES stratum, not the crude value.
qs.x: 0.60 - 6.0/10.0 equals 0.60. Trap: Inverting the ratio or using the stratum-specific value.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the stratified results?
o: Tea drinking increases cardiovascular risk in all participants because the risk ratio in the low-SES stratum exceeds 1.0
The high-SES RR is 1.0 and the low-SES difference is not enough to claim a general harm.
SES has no relationship to cardiovascular events, because incidence among tea drinkers in the high-SES stratum equals that of non-drinkers
Incidence differs by SES (4.0% versus 11.5% to 14.0%), so SES is related to risk.
The apparent protective association is largely explained by confounding, since within the high-SES stratum incidence was equal and within the low-SES stratum it was not lower among tea drinkers

Correct: The apparent protective association is largely explained by confounding, since within the high-SES stratum incidence was equal and within the low-SES stratum it was not lower among tea drinkers - stratum-specific RRs are 1.0 and about 1.2, compared with the crude 0.60.
Tea drinking protects against cardiovascular events because the crude risk is lower among tea drinkers, and stratifying cannot change that finding
Stratification can reveal confounding that reverses or removes a crude association.
qs.x: The apparent protective association is largely explained by confounding, since within the high-SES stratum incidence was equal and within the low-SES stratum it was not lower among tea drinkers - stratum-specific RRs are 1.0 and about 1.2, compared with the crude 0.60. Trap: Trusting the crude association without checking stratum-specific results.

qs.q: Which design would best establish whether tea drinking causes a change in cardiovascular risk?
o: A larger cohort study with the same self-reported tea habits, because greater sample size removes bias from confounding variables
Sample size reduces random error, not confounding.
A randomized controlled trial in which participants are randomly assigned to drink tea or an alternative beverage and followed for events

Correct: A randomized controlled trial in which participants are randomly assigned to drink tea or an alternative beverage and followed for events - random assignment balances both measured and unmeasured confounders across groups.
A cross-sectional survey of tea habits and cardiovascular history at one time point, because it avoids the delay of a long follow-up
Cross-sectional data cannot establish temporal order.
A case study of one heavy tea drinker followed in detail, because intensive observation can isolate the effect of a single exposure
A single case cannot isolate a causal effect.
qs.x: A randomized controlled trial in which participants are randomly assigned to drink tea or an alternative beverage and followed for events - random assignment balances both measured and unmeasured confounders across groups. Trap: Believing that larger observational samples remove confounding.

qs.q: Even after stratifying by SES, why might the association between tea and cardiovascular events remain confounded?
o: Risk ratios cannot be calculated within strata, so the within-stratum comparisons are not valid for evaluating the role of SES
Risk ratios are routinely computed within strata, as in Table 1.
Unmeasured factors such as diet and exercise may differ between tea drinkers and non-drinkers within each SES stratum, leaving residual confounding

Correct: Unmeasured factors such as diet and exercise may differ between tea drinkers and non-drinkers within each SES stratum, leaving residual confounding - stratifying by one variable adjusts only for that variable.
Stratification increases the correlation between the exposure and the outcome, so it adds bias to a previously unbiased comparison
Stratification does not add bias in this way.
Events were counted for only five years, so any difference in incidence is explained entirely by the length of the observation period
Follow-up length does not create a confounder.
qs.x: Unmeasured factors such as diet and exercise may differ between tea drinkers and non-drinkers within each SES stratum, leaving residual confounding - stratifying by one variable adjusts only for that variable. Trap: Assuming that adjusting for one confounder eliminates all confounding.

passages.title: FL07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 1
text: Allosteric enzymes often show sigmoidal rather than hyperbolic saturation kinetics. A researcher purified a hexameric enzyme (E) that catalyzes the first committed step in the synthesis of amino acid Z. Initial velocities were measured at a fixed enzyme concentration across a range of substrate concentrations under three conditions: no effector, 2 mM Z (the pathway end product), and 1 mM compound M, a substrate analog that binds a regulatory site distinct from the active site. Results are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. Extrapolated maximal velocity was 100 umol/min in every condition. Without effectors, the Hill coefficient was 2.5. With compound M present, the curve became hyperbolic with a Hill coefficient of 1.0. Structural studies indicated that Z stabilizes the low-affinity tense (T) conformation of the hexamer, whereas compound M stabilizes the high-affinity relaxed (R) conformation. The researcher concluded that E is regulated by feedback from the pathway product.

qs.q: Which statement best describes how Z affects enzyme E?
o: It raises the substrate concentration needed for half-maximal velocity without changing the maximal velocity.
Correct: Table 1 shows velocity at 8 mM falling from 85 to 36 umol/min while the extrapolated maximum stays 100 umol/min, so the apparent K0.5 rises (a K-type effect).
It lowers the maximal velocity of the enzyme while leaving the substrate concentration for half-maximal velocity unchanged.
Vmax was the same in every condition, and the half-maximal point clearly shifted.
It converts the sigmoidal curve into a hyperbolic one by stabilizing the high-affinity relaxed conformation of the hexamer.
That describes compound M; Z stabilizes the T state and keeps the curve sigmoidal.
It competes with substrate at the active site, so its effect is fully overcome by saturating substrate and cooperativity is lost.
Z binds a separate regulatory site, and cooperativity is retained; the lower velocity at 16 mM reflects the shifted K0.5, not a lower Vmax.
qs.x: Table 1 shows velocity at 8 mM falling from 85 to 36 umol/min while the extrapolated maximum stays 100 umol/min, so the apparent K0.5 rises (a K-type effect). Trap: Mistaking a rightward shift of the curve for a drop in Vmax, because the curve looks lower at intermediate [S].

qs.q: In the absence of any effector, what is the velocity at a substrate concentration of 4 mM?
o: 50 umol/min
Correct: With a Hill coefficient of 2.5 and K0.5 = 4 mM, v = Vmax x [S]^n/(K^n + [S]^n); when [S] = K0.5 the velocity is exactly half of Vmax, 50 umol/min (Table 1).
25 umol/min
This would be the velocity at one quarter of Vmax, well below the [S] equal to K0.5.
75 umol/min
This would occur at an [S] above 4 mM (about 6 mM for this curve).
85 umol/min
This is the velocity at 8 mM, not 4 mM.
qs.x: With a Hill coefficient of 2.5 and K0.5 = 4 mM, v = Vmax x [S]^n/(K^n + [S]^n); when [S] = K0.5 the velocity is exactly half of Vmax, 50 umol/min (Table 1). Trap: Reading the next row of the table or assuming Michaelis-Menten hyperbolic behavior.

qs.q: Which feature of enzyme E best explains the sigmoidal curve observed without effectors?
o: Substrate binding at the active site covalently modifies the enzyme and permanently increases its turnover number.
Allosteric cooperativity is reversible and conformational, not a permanent covalent change.
Each subunit of the hexamer binds substrate independently, with identical affinity regardless of the occupancy of other sites.
Independent identical sites would give a hyperbolic curve with n = 1, as seen with compound M.
Substrate binding to one subunit shifts neighboring subunits toward the high-affinity R conformation.
Correct: Positive cooperativity among subunits makes affinity rise as sites fill, producing a sigmoidal curve with n > 1.
The product Z is formed during the assay and progressively inhibits the enzyme as substrate concentration is raised.
No Z was present in the no-effector condition, and product inhibition would not generate cooperativity.
qs.x: Positive cooperativity among subunits makes affinity rise as sites fill, producing a sigmoidal curve with n > 1. Trap: Choosing independent binding because the enzyme has several subunits, ignoring communication between them.

qs.q: At a substrate concentration of 2 mM, approximately how many times greater is the velocity with compound M than with no effector?
o: About 1.5-fold
This would be the ratio if the curves differed little at low [S], but they differ substantially there.
About 2.5-fold
This misreads one of the table entries; the ratio of 57.1 to 15.0 is higher.
About 8-fold
This overstates the ratio; 8 is not supported by the two table values.
About 4-fold
Correct: Table 1 gives 57.1 umol/min with compound M and 15.0 umol/min with no effector: 57.1/15.0 is about 3.8, or roughly 4-fold.
qs.x: Table 1 gives 57.1 umol/min with compound M and 15.0 umol/min with no effector: 57.1/15.0 is about 3.8, or roughly 4-fold. Trap: Comparing the ratio at saturating [S], where curves converge, instead of at 2 mM.

qs.q: Why is inhibition of E by Z advantageous to the cell?
o: It ensures the pathway runs fastest when Z is already abundant, to build a reserve of the end product.
This is the opposite of feedback inhibition; abundant Z reduces enzyme activity.
It lowers flux through the pathway when Z is abundant, saving substrate and energy for other uses.
Correct: Feedback inhibition of the committed step matches synthesis to demand for Z.
It permanently inactivates enzyme E so that the cell no longer needs to express the gene encoding it.
Allosteric inhibition is reversible, and the enzyme resumes activity when Z falls.
It raises the Vmax of E so that the intermediates of the pathway cannot accumulate when Z levels are high.
Z did not alter Vmax; it shifted K0.5.
qs.x: Feedback inhibition of the committed step matches synthesis to demand for Z. Trap: Assuming regulation by an end product must increase activity to keep supply high.
