passages.title: FL07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 2
text: Many antibiotics selectively target bacterial protein synthesis. A researcher used a cell-free E. coli translation system programmed with an mRNA encoding firefly luciferase and containing a Shine-Dalgarno sequence upstream of the start codon. Four reactions were run for 30 minutes, each containing one test compound at 50 uM: puromycin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, and Drug D, an experimental compound. Luciferase activity was measured as a readout of full-length protein. Formation of 70S initiation complexes, containing fMet-tRNA in the P site, was measured by a primer-extension inhibition (toeprint) assay. Short peptides that were released from ribosomes were collected on filters after the reactions were labeled with [35S]-methionine. All values are expressed relative to the no-drug control in Table 1. The researcher also noted that the translation system contains no 5' cap-binding factors, and that charged initiator tRNA was supplied in all reactions. Each reaction contained identical amounts of ribosomes, initiation factors, elongation factors, GTP, and an energy-regenerating system, so differences between reactions reflect only the added compound. Reactions were performed in duplicate and the means are shown.

qs.q: Which compound most likely acts by preventing assembly of the 70S initiation complex?
o: Puromycin, because luciferase activity fell to 3% of control.
Luciferase activity fell with every compound; initiation complexes were still 95% with puromycin.
Drug D, because it is the only compound that sharply reduced the initiation complex signal.
Correct: Only Drug D reduced the toeprint signal to 10%, while the other three allowed initiation complexes to form (95-98%).
Chloramphenicol, because it produced only 4% of the short peptide signal.
Its initiation complex level of 98% shows initiation proceeded normally and a later step was blocked.
Tetracycline, because it is the only compound that left short peptide release at control levels.
Its short peptide level was 4%, not elevated, and initiation complexes formed normally.
qs.x: Only Drug D reduced the toeprint signal to 10%, while the other three allowed initiation complexes to form (95-98%). Trap: Choosing any compound with low luciferase activity, which cannot distinguish initiation from elongation blocks.

qs.q: The large increase in released short labeled peptides with puromycin is best explained by which property?
o: It blocks the peptidyl transferase center so that peptide bonds cannot form, trapping the nascent chain on the ribosome.
This describes chloramphenicol, which did not increase released peptides.
It resembles the 3' end of an aminoacyl-tRNA and accepts the nascent chain, causing premature termination.
Correct: Puromycin enters the A site, the peptidyl transferase links the growing chain to it, and the peptidyl-puromycin dissociates.
It binds the 30S subunit and prevents aminoacyl-tRNA from entering the A site, leaving fMet-tRNA in the P site.
This describes tetracycline, which did not release short peptides.
It inhibits release factors, so that completed chains remain attached to the tRNA at the stop codon of the mRNA.
Release factors act at stop codons on full-length chains, not at short, truncated products.
qs.x: Puromycin enters the A site, the peptidyl transferase links the growing chain to it, and the peptidyl-puromycin dissociates. Trap: Confusing premature chain release with inhibition of peptide bond formation.

qs.q: Which mutation in the luciferase mRNA would most likely abolish translation in this cell-free system?
o: A deletion of the Shine-Dalgarno sequence that normally base pairs with 16S rRNA of the 30S subunit
Correct: Initiation in bacteria depends on pairing between the Shine-Dalgarno sequence and 16S rRNA to position the start codon in the P site.
Loss of a 5' 7-methylguanosine cap, which normally recruits the 30S subunit through eIF4E before scanning to the start codon
The system lacks cap-binding factors; the cap is a eukaryotic feature, so its absence would not matter.
Addition of a poly(A) tail, which normally pairs with 23S rRNA to stabilize the 50S subunit on the transcript
Bacterial translation does not need a poly(A) tail, and 23S rRNA does not pair with it.
Replacement of the AUG start codon with a second AUG, which would shift the position of initiation by a few codons
Another AUG would simply move the start site or leave translation of the downstream gene intact.
qs.x: Initiation in bacteria depends on pairing between the Shine-Dalgarno sequence and 16S rRNA to position the start codon in the P site. Trap: Applying eukaryotic initiation features (cap, scanning) to a bacterial system.

qs.q: Chloramphenicol allows initiation complex formation but blocks luciferase synthesis. At which step does it most likely act?
o: Peptide bond formation by the 23S rRNA peptidyl transferase center in the large subunit
Correct: The initiation complex (98%) formed, but no elongation occurred, consistent with inhibition of peptide bond formation on the 50S subunit.
Joining of the 50S subunit to the 30S initiation complex, which is mediated by hydrolysis of GTP by IF2
Joining occurred, as indicated by 98% initiation complexes.
Binding of fMet-tRNA to the 30S subunit, which requires IF3 to prevent premature association of the subunits
The toeprint assay shows fMet-tRNA positioned normally.
Recognition of the stop codon by release factors, which hydrolyze the bond joining the peptide to the tRNA
Luciferase never reached a stop codon; synthesis was blocked much earlier.
qs.x: The initiation complex (98%) formed, but no elongation occurred, consistent with inhibition of peptide bond formation on the 50S subunit. Trap: Assuming that blocked protein synthesis always means blocked initiation.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Effects of test compounds on in vitro translation (% of no-drug control)

passages.title: FL07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 3
text: A heteroplasmic point mutation in the mitochondrial tRNA-Leu(UUR) gene, similar to variants that cause MELAS syndrome, was identified in a family. Clinical status and the percentage of mutant mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) in blood were determined for each member. The pedigree contained the following people. I-1 is an unaffected man and I-2 is his affected wife. Their children are II-1 (a daughter), II-2 (a son), and II-3 (a daughter). II-1 has two children, III-1 and III-2. II-2 has a son, III-3, and a daughter, III-4. Affected individuals show lactic acidosis, stroke-like episodes, and muscle weakness. Table 1 lists clinical status and blood heteroplasmy. Muscle biopsies in affected individuals showed ragged-red fibers and reduced activity of respiratory chain complex I. No pathogenic mutation was found in the nuclear genes that encode complex I subunits. The researchers noted that mutant fraction in tissues other than blood was not measured, so blood values may not exactly reflect tissue burden.

qs.q: Why do the children of affected male II-2 (III-3 and III-4) carry no mutant mtDNA?
o: The mutation is recessive, and III-3 and III-4 inherited a normal copy of the allele from their unaffected mother.
mtDNA is not inherited in a Mendelian recessive fashion with two alleles from two parents.
The mutation is carried on the Y chromosome, so only sons could inherit it, and III-3 has 0% mutant mtDNA.
A Y-linked trait would pass to all sons, and mtDNA is not on the Y chromosome.
Meiotic recombination in II-2 separated the mutation from the mtDNA that was packaged into the sperm during spermatogenesis.
Recombination of mtDNA does not occur in meiosis; mtDNA is not packaged with the nuclear chromosomes.
Sperm mitochondria are typically eliminated or diluted, so offspring inherit mtDNA essentially from the mother.
Correct: Paternal mitochondria in the zygote are degraded or too few to matter, so mtDNA transmission is maternal.
qs.x: Paternal mitochondria in the zygote are degraded or too few to matter, so mtDNA transmission is maternal. Trap: Treating mtDNA like an autosomal recessive gene because the unaffected mother appears to 'rescue' the children.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, the threshold level of mutant mtDNA required for symptoms most likely lies between
o: Correct: The highest unaffected value is 30% (III-2) and the lowest affected value is 60% (II-1, mildly), so the threshold lies in this interval.
III-2 at 30% is unaffected, so the threshold must be above 30%.
II-1 at 60% is already affected, so the threshold must be at or below 60%.
Individuals with 60% and 70% are affected, so symptoms appear well below this range.
qs.x: The highest unaffected value is 30% (III-2) and the lowest affected value is 60% (II-1, mildly), so the threshold lies in this interval. Trap: Using the average heteroplasmy of affected people instead of the boundary between affected and unaffected.

qs.q: II-1, II-2, and II-3 have the same mother but very different mutant mtDNA percentages. This variation is best explained by
o: independent assortment of the maternal chromosomes during meiosis I, which separates mutant from normal mitochondria
mtDNA is not on nuclear chromosomes and does not independently assort.
crossing over between maternal and paternal mtDNA in the zygote, which produces a different mix in each child
Paternal mtDNA is essentially absent, so there is no meaningful recombination with it.
somatic mutation of nuclear DNA in each child during development, which differs among siblings at random
The percentages reflect the inherited mtDNA mix, and no nuclear mutations were found.
random segregation of mtDNA molecules into oocytes through a genetic bottleneck during oogenesis
Correct: Few mtDNA copies populate each developing oocyte, so the mutant fraction drifts widely between siblings.
qs.x: Few mtDNA copies populate each developing oocyte, so the mutant fraction drifts widely between siblings. Trap: Invoking meiotic independent assortment for a genome that is not on chromosomes.

qs.q: Which observation in the pedigree argues most strongly against X-linked dominant inheritance?
o: Affected male II-2 has an unaffected daughter, III-4, but an X-linked dominant father would pass the allele to all daughters.
Correct: An X-linked dominant affected father transmits his X to every daughter, so unaffected III-4 is inconsistent.
Affected female I-2 has an unaffected daughter, II-3, whereas X-linked dominance requires all daughters of an affected mother to be affected.
An affected heterozygous mother transmits the allele to about half of her children, so II-3 is not inconsistent.
Unaffected male III-2 has an affected mother, which cannot occur in X-linked dominant inheritance.
An affected heterozygous mother can have unaffected sons.
Affected female III-1 has an affected mother, which is only possible if the trait is autosomal dominant.
An affected daughter of an affected mother fits X-linked dominant inheritance.
qs.x: An X-linked dominant affected father transmits his X to every daughter, so unaffected III-4 is inconsistent. Trap: Using affected mothers with unaffected children as evidence, though that fits many modes of inheritance.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Clinical status and blood mutant mtDNA

passages.title: FL07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 4
text: Gluconeogenesis in the liver converts lactate released from exercising muscle into glucose (the Cori cycle). Isolated rat hepatocytes were incubated for 30 minutes with 10 mM lactate unless otherwise noted, and glucose released into the medium was measured (Table 1). Conditions were: glucagon (100 nM), insulin (10 nM), ethanol (20 mM), and 3-mercaptopicolinate (MPA), a selective inhibitor of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK). In two additional incubations, 10 mM glycerol replaced lactate as the substrate, with or without MPA. Ethanol is oxidized in hepatocytes by alcohol dehydrogenase, which converts NAD+ to NADH. Glycerol is phosphorylated by glycerol kinase and then oxidized to dihydroxyacetone phosphate. The investigators also noted that hepatocytes express glucose-6-phosphatase but that skeletal muscle cells, used in a separate comparison, release no glucose under any of these conditions. Hepatocyte viability, assessed by trypan blue exclusion, exceeded 95% in all conditions, and cell number per dish was equal, so the differences reflect metabolic effects rather than cell loss. Each value is the mean of three independent preparations from different animals.

qs.q: Ethanol decreased glucose production from lactate most likely because it
o: raises the NADH/NAD+ ratio, which shifts the lactate dehydrogenase reaction away from pyruvate formation
Correct: Converting lactate to pyruvate needs NAD+; excess NADH slows it and limits pyruvate for gluconeogenesis.
inhibits PEPCK directly, as 3-mercaptopicolinate does, so oxaloacetate cannot be converted to phosphoenolpyruvate
If ethanol acted like MPA, glycerol-derived glucose would also be unaffected and the mechanisms differ; ethanol acts through redox state.
lowers the NADH/NAD+ ratio, which activates pyruvate dehydrogenase and diverts pyruvate into the citric acid cycle
Ethanol oxidation raises, not lowers, NADH, and PDH is not the explanation.
activates glucagon signaling, which phosphorylates pyruvate kinase and shuts down the formation of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate
Glucagon increased glucose output; ethanol does not mimic it, and pyruvate kinase is a glycolytic enzyme.
qs.x: Converting lactate to pyruvate needs NAD+; excess NADH slows it and limits pyruvate for gluconeogenesis. Trap: Overlooking the redox consequence of alcohol metabolism and assuming a direct enzyme inhibitor.

qs.q: Glucagon increases hepatic gluconeogenesis in part by
o: raising fructose-2,6-bisphosphate through insulin-dependent dephosphorylation of the bifunctional enzyme PFK-2/FBPase-2
Insulin, not glucagon, favors that direction and the effect is on glycolysis.
activating glucokinase through cAMP so that glucose is trapped within the hepatocyte as glucose-6-phosphate
That would reduce glucose release; glucagon decreases glucose phosphorylation.
lowering fructose-2,6-bisphosphate through cAMP-dependent phosphorylation of the bifunctional enzyme PFK-2/FBPase-2
Correct: Lower F2,6BP relieves activation of PFK-1 and inhibition of FBPase-1, favoring glucose synthesis.
inhibiting glucose-6-phosphatase through protein kinase A so that glucose-6-phosphate accumulates in the endoplasmic reticulum
Inhibiting glucose-6-phosphatase would decrease output of free glucose, opposite to the observation.
qs.x: Lower F2,6BP relieves activation of PFK-1 and inhibition of FBPase-1, favoring glucose synthesis. Trap: Reversing the effects of glucagon and insulin on fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.

qs.q: Why did MPA drastically reduce glucose production from lactate but not from glycerol?
o: Glycerol is converted to pyruvate by glycerol kinase and then to oxaloacetate by pyruvate carboxylase, bypassing PEPCK.
That route would still require PEPCK; glycerol does not follow it.
Glycerol activates PEPCK allosterically, which overcomes the inhibition produced by MPA at the 10 mM concentration used.
Competition by glycerol at PEPCK is not supported; the rate is just not dependent on PEPCK.
Glycerol enters gluconeogenesis as dihydroxyacetone phosphate, downstream of the PEPCK step.
Correct: Lactate must pass pyruvate, oxaloacetate and PEP, but glycerol feeds into the pathway below PEPCK.
Glycerol is converted to glucose by glucokinase in a single step, which does not depend on any gluconeogenic enzyme.
Glucokinase phosphorylates glucose and cannot form glucose from glycerol.
qs.x: Lactate must pass pyruvate, oxaloacetate and PEP, but glycerol feeds into the pathway below PEPCK. Trap: Assuming all gluconeogenic substrates must pass through every enzyme of the pathway.

qs.q: How many high-energy phosphate bonds (ATP plus GTP) are consumed to synthesize 3 molecules of glucose from lactate?
o: This is the cost for one glucose, not three.
Correct: Each glucose from 2 pyruvate costs 4 ATP and 2 GTP (6 total); 3 glucose cost 18.
This counts 4 per glucose and omits the 2 GTP used by PEPCK.
This would double count by using 8 per glucose.
qs.x: Each glucose from 2 pyruvate costs 4 ATP and 2 GTP (6 total); 3 glucose cost 18. Trap: Computing the cost for one glucose or leaving out the GTP-dependent PEPCK step.

qs.q: Skeletal muscle cannot contribute free glucose to the blood from lactate because muscle
o: lacks lactate dehydrogenase, so that pyruvate cannot be formed from lactate in the cytosol
Muscle has abundant lactate dehydrogenase.
lacks hexokinase, so that glucose cannot be phosphorylated after uptake from the blood
Muscle has hexokinase and takes up glucose.
lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so glucose-6-phosphate cannot be dephosphorylated and exported
Correct: Free glucose can leave a cell only after glucose-6-phosphatase acts, and this enzyme is mainly in liver and kidney.
lacks GLUT4 transporters, which must be present for any glucose to be taken up into cells after meals
Muscle expresses GLUT4, and the question concerns export, not uptake.
qs.x: Free glucose can leave a cell only after glucose-6-phosphatase acts, and this enzyme is mainly in liver and kidney. Trap: Confusing uptake with release of glucose and blaming a glycolytic enzyme.

passages.title: FL07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 5
text: To follow the secretory pathway, cultured pancreatic acinar cells were pulse-labeled for 5 minutes with [35S]-methionine and then chased with excess unlabeled methionine. At each time point, cells were fractionated, and the percentage of total labeled secretory protein (digestive enzyme precursor) found in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), the Golgi apparatus, secretory vesicles, and extracellular medium was measured (Table 1 and Figure 1). In a second experiment, cells expressing a temperature-sensitive mutant of Sec23, a component of COPII coat, were shifted to the nonpermissive temperature before the pulse. After a 60-minute chase, 90% of the label remained in the ER, 8% was in the Golgi, 2% was in vesicles, and none was in the medium. The secretory protein was also found to carry N-linked oligosaccharides while still in the ER, and a version lacking its N-terminal signal sequence was not found in the ER at all. Cells were maintained at 37 degrees C except where noted. Fractions were validated using marker proteins, and the total recovered label did not change over the 60-minute chase, indicating little degradation.

qs.q: Why was a brief pulse followed by a chase with excess unlabeled methionine used?
o: It prevents the labeled proteins from being degraded by lysosomes, so that all of the label persists in the Golgi.
A chase does not prevent degradation or hold label in a single compartment.
It ensures that the ribosomes synthesize proteins only on the rough ER, so the label is restricted to that organelle.
Ribosome location is determined by signal sequences, not by the labeling protocol.
It creates a single cohort of labeled proteins whose movement through compartments can be followed over time.
Correct: Short labeling plus a chase prevents new labeled protein from entering, so the cohort's transit is tracked.
It increases the specific activity of the secretory protein, which allows detection of low levels in the medium.
A chase dilutes the label rather than increasing specific activity of newly made protein.
qs.x: Short labeling plus a chase prevents new labeled protein from entering, so the cohort's transit is tracked. Trap: Thinking that the chase raises labeling, when its role is to stop new label from being incorporated.

qs.q: At 30 minutes, what percentage of the labeled protein has already left the ER?
o: This is the fraction still in the ER, not the fraction that left.
This adds the vesicles and medium and omits the proteins that are in the Golgi, which also left the ER.
This is the fraction in the Golgi or in vesicles alone, not the total.
Correct: 20% is in the ER at 30 min; the remaining 35 + 35 + 10 = 80% has moved to the Golgi, vesicles, or medium (Table 1).
qs.x: 20% is in the ER at 30 min; the remaining 35 + 35 + 10 = 80% has moved to the Golgi, vesicles, or medium (Table 1). Trap: Reporting the ER fraction or only one compartment instead of the sum of all later compartments.

qs.q: Why did the Sec23 mutant accumulate label in the ER?
o: COPI-coated vesicles carry cargo from the Golgi to the plasma membrane, and their formation was blocked.
COPI mediates retrograde transport, and Sec23 is part of COPII.
Clathrin-coated vesicles carry cargo from the plasma membrane to endosomes, and their formation was blocked.
Clathrin acts in endocytosis and trans-Golgi sorting, not ER export.
COPII-coated vesicles carry cargo from the ER to the Golgi, and their formation was blocked.
Correct: COPII mediates anterograde ER-to-Golgi transport, so its loss traps cargo in the ER.
Signal recognition particle cannot bind the signal sequence, so that translation arrests before entry into the ER.
The protein was in the ER, so cotranslational targeting worked.
qs.x: COPII mediates anterograde ER-to-Golgi transport, so its loss traps cargo in the ER. Trap: Mixing up COPI, COPII, and clathrin coats and their directions of transport.

qs.q: An ER-resident protein carrying a C-terminal KDEL sequence is engineered to lack this sequence. Where is this protein most likely found?
o: Entirely in the cytosol, because KDEL is the signal that directs the protein to enter the ER during translation.
KDEL is a retrieval signal, while the N-terminal signal sequence directs entry.
In the nucleus, because the loss of the sequence exposes a nuclear localization signal in the C-terminus.
No nuclear signal is exposed; loss of KDEL does not target proteins to the nucleus.
Increasingly in the secretory vesicles and extracellular medium, because it is no longer retrieved from the Golgi.
Correct: KDEL receptors in the Golgi return escaped residents to the ER via COPI vesicles; removing KDEL lets it be secreted.
In the ER lumen at the same level as before, because retention depends only on the size of the protein.
Retention depends on active retrieval, not size alone.
qs.x: KDEL receptors in the Golgi return escaped residents to the ER via COPI vesicles; removing KDEL lets it be secreted. Trap: Treating KDEL as an import signal rather than a retrieval signal.

qs.q: Which statement best accounts for the finding that the protein is glycosylated while still in the ER?
o: Oligosaccharyltransferase adds a preassembled oligosaccharide to asparagine residues as the polypeptide enters the ER lumen.
Correct: N-linked glycosylation begins cotranslationally in the ER lumen, before the protein ever reaches the Golgi.
Glycosyltransferases in the cytosol attach the sugars to serine and threonine, and the protein is then imported into the ER.
That describes neither N-linked glycosylation nor its compartment; it occurs in the lumen.
The Golgi sends glycosylation enzymes back to the ER in COPII vesicles, where they modify all proteins on the cytosolic face.
COPII is anterograde, and N-linked sugars are added to the luminal side.
The signal peptidase attaches the sugar chain to the signal sequence as it is cleaved off the polypeptide in the ER.
Signal peptidase cleaves the signal sequence and does not add sugars.
qs.x: N-linked glycosylation begins cotranslationally in the ER lumen, before the protein ever reaches the Golgi. Trap: Assuming that all glycosylation occurs in the Golgi.

passages.title: FL07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 6
text: HIV-1 is a retrovirus whose single-stranded RNA genome is converted to DNA in the host cell. To dissect the replication cycle, CD4+ T cells were infected with an HIV-1-derived virus in the presence of one of three antiretroviral drugs: an RT inhibitor (AZT), an integrase inhibitor, and a protease inhibitor. After 48 hours, four measurements were made: late reverse transcription products (viral DNA), integrated provirus (Alu-LTR PCR), circular viral DNA containing two LTRs (2-LTR circles, formed only in the nucleus when integration fails), and p24 capsid protein released in the supernatant. Viruses in the supernatant were then used to infect fresh cells, and infectivity was scored. Data are in Table 1 as percent of untreated controls. Control infected cells in which CCR5 and CD4 were absent showed no viral DNA at all. Each condition was run in triplicate, drugs were added two hours before infection, and cell viability was unaffected by any drug at the concentrations used, so the differences reflect specific effects on viral replication.

qs.q: The integrase inhibitor increased 2-LTR circles while decreasing integrated provirus. This pattern is best explained by
o: failure of reverse transcription, which leaves viral RNA in the cytoplasm and prevents any DNA from forming
Viral DNA was 98% of control, so reverse transcription occurred.
failure of capsid assembly at the plasma membrane, which causes viral DNA to accumulate in released virions
Assembly is not the step blocked, and 2-LTR circles form only in the nucleus.
increased activity of RT in the presence of the drug, which synthesizes extra copies of viral DNA that circularize
RT activity (total viral DNA) did not rise; only the circular fraction did.
viral DNA being imported into the nucleus but unable to be inserted into host chromosomes, so it is circularized
Correct: Unintegrated nuclear viral DNA is a substrate for circularization, so 2-LTR circles accumulate when integration is blocked.
qs.x: Unintegrated nuclear viral DNA is a substrate for circularization, so 2-LTR circles accumulate when integration is blocked. Trap: Assuming the drug stops DNA synthesis because integrated DNA is low.

qs.q: Cells treated with the protease inhibitor released normal amounts of p24 but the progeny virus was nearly noninfectious. This is because
o: the viral envelope glycoprotein could not bind CD4, so that progeny virions could not enter new cells
Envelope binding is not affected by a protease inhibitor.
Gag and Gag-Pol polyproteins were not cleaved, so the released virions remained immature
Correct: Viral protease cleaves the polyproteins during and after budding to produce mature capsid, RT and integrase.
the viral genome was not reverse transcribed, so that the progeny contained no usable nucleic acid
Reverse transcription proceeded normally (100% viral DNA).
the provirus was excised from the host genome, which prevented the production of new viral transcripts
Integration was unaffected at 99%, and p24 production was normal.
qs.x: Viral protease cleaves the polyproteins during and after budding to produce mature capsid, RT and integrase. Trap: Thinking normal p24 release means the progeny virus must be normal.

qs.q: Which property of reverse transcriptase most directly contributes to rapid evolution of drug resistance in HIV?
o: It can only copy DNA templates, which restricts replication to a few cell types in the host.
RT copies RNA into DNA, and it can also copy DNA.
It lacks 3' to 5' exonuclease proofreading activity, producing a high rate of copying errors.
Correct: Errors made by RT during each replication cycle generate a diverse viral population from which resistant variants are selected.
It integrates the viral DNA into the host genome at a specific sequence, which creates a single stable genotype.
Integrase, not RT, mediates integration, and insertion is not sequence specific.
It requires a host RNA primer that is replaced by a DNA repair enzyme, which introduces random mutations into the viral genes.
RT uses a host tRNA primer, but repair of the primer does not generate the mutation rate.
qs.x: Errors made by RT during each replication cycle generate a diverse viral population from which resistant variants are selected. Trap: Attributing mutations to integrase or to host repair rather than to RT's lack of proofreading.

qs.q: A latently infected resting T cell contains integrated provirus but does not make viral proteins. Treatment with the RT inhibitor, integrase inhibitor, and protease inhibitor would be expected to
o: leave the provirus intact, because integrated DNA is replicated with the host genome and these drugs act on later events
Correct: Latent proviral DNA persists in host chromosomes and these drugs only block new rounds of replication, not the existing provirus.
eliminate the provirus within hours, because the integrase inhibitor reverses integration of viral DNA from the host chromosome
Integrase inhibitors block integration but do not excise provirus.
eliminate the provirus after cell division, because RT is required to maintain viral DNA in dividing cells
Host DNA polymerase, not RT, replicates the provirus.
degrade viral RNA in the cytoplasm of the cell, because protease inhibitors activate host ribonucleases
Protease inhibitors do not activate ribonucleases and no viral RNA is being made in latency.
qs.x: Latent proviral DNA persists in host chromosomes and these drugs only block new rounds of replication, not the existing provirus. Trap: Assuming that drugs blocking replication enzymes will clear integrated DNA.

passages.title: FL07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 7
text: The spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) delays anaphase until all kinetochores are attached to spindle microtubules. Cultured human cells were transfected with a control siRNA, an siRNA against Mad2 (a SAC component), or the Mad2 siRNA together with an siRNA-resistant Mad2 gene. Cells were grown for 12 hours with or without nocodazole, a drug that depolymerizes microtubules, and the mitotic index (percentage of cells with condensed chromosomes and no nuclear envelope) was determined. Separate cultures were released from nocodazole-free growth, and 2,500 daughter cells per condition were scored for abnormal chromosome number. Results are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. In mitosis, the checkpoint signal inhibits the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) bound to its activator Cdc20. The investigators also compared these findings to oocyte meiosis, in which cohesin along chromosome arms is cleaved at anaphase I but centromeric cohesin is protected until anaphase II. Cells were synchronized by a double thymidine block before each experiment so that most entered mitosis together. Mitotic index was scored by an observer unaware of the condition, and at least 500 cells were counted for each point.

qs.q: Why did the mitotic index remain low in Mad2-depleted cells exposed to nocodazole?
o: Nocodazole stabilizes microtubules, so that the cells complete mitosis faster than control cells.
Nocodazole depolymerizes microtubules.
Without the checkpoint, cells exited mitosis despite unattached kinetochores instead of arresting.
Correct: Mad2 is needed for the checkpoint arrest, so cells lacking it proceed through anaphase even without spindles.
Mad2 depletion blocks entry into mitosis, so that the cells remain in G2 and never condense their chromosomes.
The mitotic index without drug is equal to control (6%), so entry is normal.
Cells lacking Mad2 arrest in metaphase but the arrest is not counted, since the chromosomes are no longer visibly condensed.
Arrested cells keep condensed chromosomes and would be counted.
qs.x: Mad2 is needed for the checkpoint arrest, so cells lacking it proceed through anaphase even without spindles. Trap: Assuming a low mitotic index means cells did not enter mitosis.

qs.q: The checkpoint prevents anaphase by directly inhibiting which process?
o: Phosphorylation of lamins by cyclin B-Cdk1, which prevents the nuclear envelope from breaking down in prophase
This occurs in prophase, before the checkpoint operates, and promotes mitosis.
Replication of DNA by polymerase delta, which prevents cells from entering mitosis with incompletely duplicated chromosomes
That is an S phase process and a different checkpoint.
Ubiquitination of securin by APC/C-Cdc20, which prevents release of the protease separase
Correct: Securin degradation frees separase to cleave cohesin; the checkpoint blocks APC/C-Cdc20, keeping securin intact.
Assembly of the contractile ring by actin and myosin, which prevents cytokinesis before chromosomes have been segregated
The ring forms later and is not the checkpoint's direct target.
qs.x: Securin degradation frees separase to cleave cohesin; the checkpoint blocks APC/C-Cdc20, keeping securin intact. Trap: Confusing the SAC with the G2/M DNA damage checkpoint or with cytokinesis control.

qs.q: Of the 2,500 Mad2-depleted daughter cells scored, how many are expected to be aneuploid?
o: This misplaces the decimal point.
This corresponds to 6%, the mitotic index, rather than the aneuploidy rate.
This is about 68% of 2,500, the mitotic index of control cells with nocodazole.
qs.x: 18% of 2,500 = 0.18 x 2,500 = 450 (Table 1). Trap: Using the wrong column of the table.

qs.q: A primary spermatocyte undergoes nondisjunction of one chromosome pair in meiosis I. What fraction of the sperm will have an abnormal number of that chromosome?
o: This is the fraction if only one product were affected.
Correct: Both homologs go to one secondary spermatocyte, so all four sperm are abnormal: two n+1 and two n-1.
This is the fraction for nondisjunction in meiosis II.
No meiosis I outcome produces three abnormal and one normal gamete.
qs.x: Both homologs go to one secondary spermatocyte, so all four sperm are abnormal: two n+1 and two n-1. Trap: Applying the meiosis II result (half abnormal) to a meiosis I error.

qs.q: In oocyte meiosis I, sister chromatids stay together while homologous chromosomes separate. This is possible because
o: centromeric cohesin is protected from cleavage by separase until anaphase II, whereas arm cohesin is cleaved
Correct: Loss of arm cohesin resolves chiasmata, letting homologs segregate; protected centromeric cohesin holds the sisters together.
DNA replication is skipped before meiosis I, so that each chromosome consists of only one chromatid at that stage
DNA is replicated once before meiosis I and chromosomes have two chromatids.
the APC/C is permanently inactive in meiosis I, so that separase is never activated until fertilization
APC/C is active at the metaphase-anaphase I transition, and separase cleaves arm cohesin.
kinetochores of sister chromatids attach to opposite spindle poles in meiosis I, so that sisters are pulled apart
In meiosis I, sister kinetochores attach to the same pole.
qs.x: Loss of arm cohesin resolves chiasmata, letting homologs segregate; protected centromeric cohesin holds the sisters together. Trap: Believing that sisters separate in meiosis I because homologs separate there.

passages.title: FL07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 8
text: Conduction velocity of an action potential depends on axon diameter and myelination. An electrophysiologist measured velocities in several nerve fiber types (Table 1) and plotted velocity against diameter for myelinated and unmyelinated axons (Figure 1). In myelinated axons, voltage-gated Na+ channels are concentrated at the nodes of Ranvier, and the internodal membrane is wrapped by many layers of oligodendrocyte or Schwann cell membrane. In a further experiment, an anti-myelin antibody was injected near a myelinated A-alpha fiber, producing focal demyelination; conduction velocity in that fiber fell from 90 to 40 m/s, and some impulses failed to cross the lesion. Application of 4-aminopyridine (4-AP), which blocks voltage-gated K+ channels, restored conduction across the lesion in some fibers. Recordings with two electrodes showed the impulse always traveled away from the stimulation site, never back toward it. All measurements were made at 37 degrees C in isolated preparations bathed in physiological saline, and each velocity is the mean of at least ten fibers.

qs.q: Which feature best explains why myelinated axons conduct faster than unmyelinated axons of the same diameter?
o: Action potentials are regenerated only at nodes, and current spreads rapidly through the insulated internodes between them.
Correct: Myelin increases membrane resistance and decreases capacitance, so depolarization passes quickly to the next node (saltatory conduction).
Voltage-gated Na+ channels are distributed evenly along the myelin, so depolarization is regenerated at every point on the axon.
The channels are clustered at nodes, which is why conduction is saltatory.
Myelin actively pumps Na+ out of the axon, so the resting membrane potential is more negative than in unmyelinated axons.
Myelin is an insulator, and does not pump ions to hyperpolarize the axon.
The myelinated axon has a larger number of K+ leak channels, so repolarization is completed sooner after each impulse.
Leak channels would shunt current and slow propagation, not speed it.
qs.x: Myelin increases membrane resistance and decreases capacitance, so depolarization passes quickly to the next node (saltatory conduction). Trap: Believing that myelin boosts the number of channels rather than insulating the internodes.

qs.q: At an axon diameter of 16 um, the conduction velocity of a myelinated axon is about how many times that of an unmyelinated axon?
o: This is the unmyelinated velocity itself and not a ratio.
This is the ratio of velocity to diameter for the myelinated fiber (96/16).
Correct: Figure 1 gives 96 m/s for the myelinated axon and 4 m/s for the unmyelinated axon at 16 um; 96/4 = 24.
This is the value for the A-alpha fiber in Table 1, not a ratio at 16 um.
qs.x: Figure 1 gives 96 m/s for the myelinated axon and 4 m/s for the unmyelinated axon at 16 um; 96/4 = 24. Trap: Reading the wrong curve or reporting a single value instead of a ratio.

qs.q: Why did 4-AP restore conduction across the demyelinated lesion in some fibers?
o: Blocking K+ channels remyelinates the axon, so that the original conduction velocity of 90 m/s is restored.
4-AP does not cause remyelination, and velocity may recover only partially.
Blocking K+ channels raises the Na+ concentration outside the axon, which increases the driving force for Na+ entry.
K+ channel block does not change the extracellular Na+ concentration.
Blocking K+ channels converts the lesion into a node of Ranvier, so that a normal action potential is generated.
The membrane does not become a node; Na+ channels are not redistributed by 4-AP.
Blocking K+ channels exposed by demyelination reduces repolarizing current loss, so more depolarization reaches the next node.
Correct: Exposed internodal K+ channels shunt current; blocking them prolongs depolarization and helps the impulse cross the lesion.
qs.x: Exposed internodal K+ channels shunt current; blocking them prolongs depolarization and helps the impulse cross the lesion. Trap: Thinking a K+ channel blocker repairs the myelin rather than modifying membrane currents.

qs.q: The impulse traveled only away from the stimulation site. Which property accounts for this?
o: Voltage-gated Na+ channels are present only on the side of the axon farthest from the cell body, so conduction is one-way.
Channels are present along the axon, and the direction is set by refractoriness.
The sodium-potassium ATPase restores ion gradients before the wave front reaches each node, so that the impulse is never reversed.
The pump acts too slowly, and it is not responsible for one-way travel.
Myelin only allows current to flow toward the axon terminal, because it is a rectifying, ion-conducting layer.
Myelin is an insulator and does not rectify current.
Voltage-gated Na+ channels behind the impulse are inactivated, so the membrane there cannot fire again immediately.
Correct: The refractory period behind the wavefront ensures one-way propagation.
qs.x: The refractory period behind the wavefront ensures one-way propagation. Trap: Crediting the Na+/K+ pump for the direction of propagation.

passages.title: FL07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 9
text: Bile acids are synthesized from cholesterol in hepatocytes, conjugated, secreted into bile, and largely reabsorbed in the ileum (enterohepatic circulation). Four groups of rats were studied: controls, rats with surgical ligation of the common bile duct (BDL), rats fed cholestyramine (a resin that binds bile acids in the intestine and is not absorbed), and rats given a hemolysis-inducing agent. Serum bilirubin, fecal fat excretion (as a percentage of ingested fat), serum cholesterol, and hepatic expression of CYP7A1 (the rate-limiting enzyme of bile acid synthesis) were measured (Table 1). Bile acids activate the nuclear receptor FXR in the ileum and liver, which represses CYP7A1 transcription. Urine was also tested for bilirubin: it was positive in BDL rats but negative in all other groups. Stool from BDL rats was pale, whereas stool from the other groups was brown. Animals were fed the same diet, fasted overnight before blood sampling, and housed individually for fecal collection over three days. Values are group means with five animals per group.

qs.q: The high fecal fat and pale stool in BDL rats are best explained by
o: excess pancreatic lipase, which digests fats too rapidly to be absorbed and gives stool its pale color
Lipase was not measured, and increased lipase would not cause steatorrhea.
failure of hepatocytes to conjugate bilirubin, which causes unconjugated bilirubin to be excreted in the feces
Conjugated bilirubin was high in BDL, so conjugation was intact.
absent delivery of bile to the duodenum, which impairs micelle formation and prevents the bilirubin pigments from reaching the gut
Correct: Without bile salts, dietary lipids are poorly emulsified and absorbed, and bilirubin cannot reach the gut to form stercobilin.
increased reabsorption of bile acids in the ileum, which removes the lipids from the intestinal lumen before digestion
Bile acids cannot be reabsorbed if they never reach the intestine.
qs.x: Without bile salts, dietary lipids are poorly emulsified and absorbed, and bilirubin cannot reach the gut to form stercobilin. Trap: Blaming pancreatic enzymes or conjugation defects instead of loss of bile flow.

qs.q: Why did cholestyramine lower serum cholesterol and raise CYP7A1 expression?
o: Binding bile acids increases their return to the liver, which activates FXR and lowers CYP7A1 so that cholesterol is conserved.
This is the opposite of the data; CYP7A1 rose 3.5-fold.
Cholestyramine is absorbed in the ileum and inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, so that less cholesterol is synthesized.
Cholestyramine is not absorbed, and CYP7A1 would not rise by this mechanism.
Cholestyramine increases fecal fat by blocking pancreatic lipase, which reduces the cholesterol absorbed from the diet only.
Fecal fat rose modestly from bile acid loss, and the CYP7A1 change shows a hepatic effect.
Binding bile acids interrupts enterohepatic recycling, relieving FXR repression so the liver converts more cholesterol into bile acids.
Correct: Reduced bile acid return lowers FXR signaling, increasing CYP7A1 and pulling cholesterol into bile acid synthesis.
qs.x: Reduced bile acid return lowers FXR signaling, increasing CYP7A1 and pulling cholesterol into bile acid synthesis. Trap: Reversing the sign of FXR feedback on CYP7A1.

qs.q: Which laboratory pattern in Table 1 distinguishes hemolysis from bile duct obstruction?
o: Elevated bilirubin that is mostly conjugated with pale stool, as seen in hemolysis because hepatocytes secrete bilirubin normally.
Hemolysis produced mostly unconjugated bilirubin with brown stool.
Elevated bilirubin with a doubling of serum cholesterol, which is found in hemolysis as well as obstruction.
Serum cholesterol was unchanged (70 mg/dL) in hemolysis.
Normal bilirubin with reduced CYP7A1 expression, which is characteristic of hemolytic conditions in the liver.
Bilirubin was elevated in hemolysis and CYP7A1 was normal.
Elevated bilirubin that is mostly unconjugated and absent from urine, in contrast to the mostly conjugated, urine-positive pattern in BDL.
Correct: Unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and not filtered, so it is not found in urine; conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and appears in urine.
qs.x: Unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and not filtered, so it is not found in urine; conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and appears in urine. Trap: Reading all raised bilirubin as the same and overlooking the conjugated fraction.

qs.q: In the liver, bile acids are conjugated to glycine or taurine before secretion. What is the main benefit of conjugation?
o: It raises the pKa so the bile acids remain uncharged in the duodenum, letting them diffuse across the epithelium.
Conjugation lowers the pKa and keeps the bile salts charged.
It converts cholesterol directly into bilirubin, so that the pigments can be excreted along with the bile acids.
Bilirubin is derived from heme, not from cholesterol.
It prevents the bile acids from activating FXR, which would otherwise shut down all of the bile production in the liver.
Conjugation does not prevent FXR signaling.
It lowers the pKa so the bile acids stay ionized in the intestine, making them more water soluble and better detergents.
Correct: Conjugated bile salts remain charged at intestinal pH, which improves amphipathic behavior and micelle formation, and limits passive absorption in the upper intestine.
qs.x: Conjugated bile salts remain charged at intestinal pH, which improves amphipathic behavior and micelle formation, and limits passive absorption in the upper intestine. Trap: Assuming conjugation makes the molecule less polar.

passages.title: FL07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 10
text: Brown adipose tissue (BAT) produces heat during cold exposure. Wild-type mice and mice lacking uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1-/-) were moved from 30 degrees C to 4 degrees C, and rectal temperature was recorded hourly (Figure 1). Mitochondria were then isolated from BAT of each genotype and from wild-type liver, and oxygen consumption was measured with pyruvate and malate as substrates (Table 1). Oligomycin, an inhibitor of ATP synthase, was added to some samples, and GDP, a purine nucleotide that inhibits UCP1, was added to others. Rates are given relative to the baseline in each tissue (set to 100). During cold exposure, sympathetic neurons release norepinephrine onto brown adipocytes, which raises intracellular cAMP and releases fatty acids from stored triglycerides. Fatty acids serve both as fuel for oxidation and as activators of UCP1. Mice were individually housed, had free access to food, and were of equal age and body mass. Mitochondrial preparations were of comparable purity, as judged by citrate synthase activity per milligram of protein.

qs.q: How does UCP1 generate heat?
o: It pumps protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space, using ATP hydrolysis to build a larger gradient.
UCP1 dissipates the gradient rather than building it.
It lets protons flow back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase, so the energy of the gradient is released as heat.
Correct: Proton leak through UCP1 uncouples electron transport from ATP synthesis; respiration continues and the energy is dissipated as heat.
It transfers electrons directly from NADH to oxygen, bypassing complexes III and IV, so that less water is formed.
UCP1 is not an electron carrier; it conducts protons.
It inhibits ATP synthase through binding of GDP, which makes the electron transport chain stop completely.
GDP inhibits UCP1, not ATP synthase, and the chain continues to run.
qs.x: Proton leak through UCP1 uncouples electron transport from ATP synthesis; respiration continues and the energy is dissipated as heat. Trap: Confusing uncoupling with inhibition of the electron transport chain.

qs.q: Oligomycin reduced oxygen consumption by wild-type liver mitochondria to 20% but only to 85% in wild-type BAT mitochondria. This difference is best explained by
o: lower activity of complex I in BAT, which makes the oligomycin binding site on ATP synthase inaccessible
Complex I activity does not affect oligomycin binding, and respiration was high.
greater ATP synthase activity in BAT, which makes the tissue less sensitive to oligomycin at the concentration used
Greater ATP synthase would make BAT more oligomycin-sensitive, not less.
continued proton re-entry through UCP1 in BAT, which relieves the proton gradient that would otherwise slow electron transport
Correct: In liver, blocking ATP synthase builds a large gradient that restricts respiration; in BAT, UCP1 provides an alternative proton path.
absence of an electron transport chain in liver mitochondria, which reduces baseline oxygen consumption to a very low level
Liver mitochondria had normal baseline respiration of 100% and a functional chain.
qs.x: In liver, blocking ATP synthase builds a large gradient that restricts respiration; in BAT, UCP1 provides an alternative proton path. Trap: Overlooking respiratory control, whereby ATP synthase inhibition normally slows electron flow.

qs.q: Which chain of events links cold exposure to heat production in brown adipocytes?
o: Norepinephrine binds alpha-1 receptors, cAMP falls, triglyceride synthesis rises, and fatty acids inhibit UCP1.
Brown fat is activated through beta receptors, with increased cAMP and lipolysis.
Acetylcholine binds muscarinic receptors on brown adipocytes, which closes UCP1 and increases ATP synthesis.
The sympathetic neurotransmitter is norepinephrine and UCP1 is activated.
Insulin binds its receptor, glucose uptake rises, glycogen is stored, and heat is generated by the glycogen synthase reaction.
Insulin does not mediate the cold response, and glycogen synthesis is not a major heat source.
Norepinephrine binds beta-adrenergic receptors, cAMP rises, lipolysis releases fatty acids, and fatty acids activate UCP1.
Correct: Sympathetic stimulation through a Gs-coupled receptor increases cAMP and PKA activity, which drives lipolysis; fatty acids activate UCP1.
qs.x: Sympathetic stimulation through a Gs-coupled receptor increases cAMP and PKA activity, which drives lipolysis; fatty acids activate UCP1. Trap: Choosing parasympathetic or insulin signaling for a sympathetic thermogenic response.

qs.q: After 4 hours at 4 degrees C, the fall in temperature of UCP1-/- mice is about how many times that of wild-type mice?
o: About 2-fold
This would be a much smaller difference than shown in Figure 1.
About 20-fold
Correct: The knockout fell 37.0 - 26.5 = 10.5 degrees C and wild type fell 0.5 degrees C; 10.5/0.5 = 21.
About 7-fold
This would result from comparing the 3-hour drop in KO to a drop of about 1 degree.
About 70-fold
This would require a wild-type drop of only about 0.15 degrees C.
qs.x: The knockout fell 37.0 - 26.5 = 10.5 degrees C and wild type fell 0.5 degrees C; 10.5/0.5 = 21. Trap: Dividing final temperatures (26.5/36.5) instead of the temperature drops.

passages.title: FL07 · CARS · Passage 1
text: Kant's claim that only actions done from duty have moral worth strikes many readers as cold. The shopkeeper who gives correct change because honesty is good for business acts in accordance with duty, Kant says, but not from duty; his action would vanish the moment cheating became profitable and safe. Even the sympathetic person who delights in helping others, Kant continues, deserves praise and encouragement but not esteem in the strict sense, because inclination is a fortunate accident of temperament rather than an achievement of the will. Critics have heard in this a demand that we suppress affection, and Schiller's quip that Kant would have us help our friends with a sigh of reluctance has become the standard summary of the objection.

The objection, however, misreads what Kant is isolating. He is not recommending that we cultivate reluctance; he is asking what, in a good action, makes it good. His answer is that the worth lies in the principle on which the agent acts, not in the outcome and not in the feeling that accompanies it. A person moved by pity who helps a stranger has done something admirable in its effects, but if we ask whether she would have helped when pity failed, we learn whether her conduct was governed by a principle or merely by a mood. Kant's famous thought experiment of the person whose sympathy has been extinguished by grief, who nevertheless helps others purely because it is right, is a test device. It strips away the motive that normally accompanies helping so that the contribution of duty can be seen alone, as one isolates a single variable in an experiment. It does not follow that a life without inclination is the ideal.

What, then, does duty require? Kant's categorical imperative asks whether the maxim of one's action could be willed as a universal law. A maxim of making false promises to escape difficulty fails, since if everyone adopted it the practice of promising would collapse and the maxim would defeat itself. This procedure is often presented as a mechanical decision rule, and as such it generates well-known embarrassments: maxims can be described so narrowly that almost anything passes, or so broadly that harmless actions fail. Defenders reply that the imperative is better read as a constraint on deliberation than as an algorithm. It does not tell us what to do; it screens out proposals that make an exception of ourselves, that claim for our own case a license we would not extend to anyone else.

Seen this way, Kantian duty is less a rival to compassion than a safeguard against its unreliability. Compassion is selective: we feel more for the one child in a well than for thousands in a famine, more for those who resemble us than for strangers. A morality grounded in feeling inherits these biases. Duty, by contrast, binds us equally toward persons whom we do not love and cannot see. The price is that Kant's ethics seems to leave little room for moral luck, for the way outcomes and temperament shape how we are judged. A will that is good even if wholly lacking power to accomplish its purpose shines, he says, like a jewel for its own sake. Whether that picture is noble or evasive remains the central dispute between Kant and his critics, and perhaps it is a dispute about whether morality is chiefly about who we are or about what we bring about in the world.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?
o: Kant held that acting from compassion is morally worthless, and the passage endorses this view because feelings are always unreliable guides.
Kant says sympathy deserves praise; the passage says it is merely not what confers strict worth, and it never calls feelings worthless.
Kant's emphasis on duty is a claim about where moral worth lies, and it can be defended against the charge of demanding emotional coldness.
Correct: the passage defends duty-based worth against the coldness objection while noting a remaining dispute.
Kant's categorical imperative is a mechanical decision procedure that settles every moral question without any need for judgment from the agent.
The passage says the imperative is better read as a constraint than as an algorithm.
Kant's ethics succeeds because it gives outcomes and temperament the central place in how we should evaluate individual moral agents.
Kant locates worth in the principle of the will, and the passage says his ethics leaves little room for outcomes and luck.
qs.x: the passage defends duty-based worth against the coldness objection while noting a remaining dispute. Trap: Choosing the extreme version of Kant's view (feelings are worthless) instead of the passage's more qualified claim that inclination is not the source of strict moral worth.

qs.q: According to the passage, the thought experiment of the person whose sympathy has been extinguished by grief is intended to
o: recommend that moral agents try to cultivate emotional detachment so that their helping behavior becomes more reliably principled over time.
The passage says explicitly that it does not follow that a life without inclination is ideal.
show that people who are grieving are exempt from the ordinary demands of the categorical imperative toward strangers in need.
Nothing in the passage suggests an exemption; the person in the example helps anyway.
isolate the contribution of duty by removing the motive that usually accompanies helping, much as an experiment isolates a single variable.
Correct: the passage calls the case a test device that strips away inclination so duty can be seen alone.
demonstrate that sympathy and duty always produce conflicting recommendations, so that one of them must be abandoned in practice.
The passage argues duty and compassion need not be rivals, and often coincide.
qs.x: the passage calls the case a test device that strips away inclination so duty can be seen alone. Trap: Reading a diagnostic thought experiment as a recommendation for how people should live.

qs.q: The shopkeeper example is used in the passage to illustrate an action that is
o: in accordance with duty but not from duty, because its motive would disappear if cheating became safe and profitable.
Correct: correct change given only because honesty pays matches duty in outward result but not in motive.
from duty and also from inclination, because the shopkeeper's honesty is both principled and pleasurable to him in each transaction.
The shopkeeper is moved by profit, not by duty, so the action is not from duty.
contrary to duty but beneficial, because the shopkeeper's concern with profit corrupts what would otherwise be a perfectly neutral act.
The act itself is what duty requires; the problem lies in the motive, not the act.
from duty but morally unremarkable, because giving correct change is such a trivial act that no moral worth could attach to it.
Triviality is not the issue; the issue is the motive behind the action.
qs.x: correct change given only because honesty pays matches duty in outward result but not in motive. Trap: Confusing the outward conformity of an action with duty with the agent's motive for performing it.

qs.q: Which of the following findings, if true, would most undermine the defenders' reading of the categorical imperative as a constraint rather than an algorithm?
o: Most people who apply the test to their own proposed actions reach different verdicts than their friends reach about the same proposals, even after discussing them at length.
Disagreement in verdicts is consistent with a constraint that does not fix a single answer.
The universalization test rules out some proposals, such as false promising, that many people already regard as wrong for other reasons.
Screening out some proposals is exactly what a constraint on deliberation does.
Kant himself sometimes disagreed with later interpreters about how to describe maxims in applying the imperative to specific cases.
Interpretive disagreement does not show the test is an algorithm; it fits the constraint reading.
Applying the universalization test to any situation always yields exactly one permissible action, whatever description of the maxim is chosen.
Correct: if the test always produced a unique answer regardless of description, it would function as a decision algorithm, contradicting the defenders' reading.
qs.x: if the test always produced a unique answer regardless of description, it would function as a decision algorithm, contradicting the defenders' reading. Trap: Treating any fact about disagreement as damaging, rather than asking which fact would show the procedure is mechanical.

qs.q: The passage suggests that a Kantian would most likely criticize a charity that distributes aid solely according to which appeals stir donors' strongest feelings because such a policy
o: treats recipients as means to the donors' pleasure, which the passage identifies as the sole ground of Kant's concern with charity.
The passage never says that using persons as means is the sole ground of the concern; it focuses on selectivity.
inherits the selectivity of compassion, favoring those who resemble us or are vividly presented over others in equal need.
Correct: the passage says compassion is selective and a morality grounded in feeling inherits those biases, whereas duty binds equally.
fails to calculate the total amount of welfare produced, which the passage describes as the chief test of a morally good action.
The passage rejects outcomes as the source of worth, so welfare totals are not Kant's test.
relies on universal laws that cannot be willed without contradiction, as in the example of the false promise to escape difficulty.
The false-promise example concerns self-defeating maxims, not the biases of feeling-driven aid.
qs.x: the passage says compassion is selective and a morality grounded in feeling inherits those biases, whereas duty binds equally. Trap: Importing a different Kantian doctrine from outside the passage instead of using the passage's own argument about compassion's selectivity.

qs.q: The final sentence of the passage serves mainly to
o: conclude that Kant's critics are mistaken because moral luck has no genuine influence on how people are judged by others.
The passage says the ethics leaves little room for moral luck, and it does not argue moral luck is illusory.
restate the claim that duty is a safeguard against the unreliability of compassion in the cases of strangers and friends alike.
That safeguard point was made earlier; the last sentence moves to the larger dispute.
frame the unresolved dispute between Kant and his critics as a question about whether morality concerns character or consequences.
Correct: it raises the broader issue, who we are versus what we bring about, that underlies the disagreement.
propose a compromise in which actions are judged by their outcomes when sympathy is present and by principle when it is absent.
No compromise is offered; the passage ends by leaving the dispute open.
qs.x: it raises the broader issue, who we are versus what we bring about, that underlies the disagreement. Trap: Mistaking a closing reflection that leaves a question open for a conclusion that settles it.

passages.title: FL07 · CARS · Passage 2
text: Since Gibbon, the fall of the Roman Empire has served as a mirror in which each age sees its own anxieties. Gibbon, writing in the Enlightenment, blamed the loss of civic virtue and the rise of Christianity, which he thought redirected loyalty from the state to the afterlife. Nineteenth-century nationalists preferred racial and migratory explanations, picturing a vigorous Germanic north overwhelming a tired Mediterranean south. Twentieth-century scholars, living through world wars and economic crises, pointed to fiscal strain, inflation, and the burdens of a vast military. That the same events could support such varied narratives should make us cautious, but it has not stopped historians from continuing to look for a master explanation.

The most influential recent revision is the idea of late antiquity, associated with Peter Brown, which treats the centuries between roughly 250 and 800 not as a decline but as a transformation. On this view, Roman institutions did not collapse so much as mutate: bishops assumed the functions of municipal magistrates, barbarian kings ruled through Roman law and Roman administrators, and Latin evolved into new languages without ceasing to be a living medium. The framework has the merit of directing attention to religious creativity, to art, and to continuities in everyday life that older narratives ignored. It also rescued the period from the condescension implied by the phrase Dark Ages.

Yet critics argue that the transformation model is too comfortable. Bryan Ward-Perkins and others have pointed to archaeological evidence that seems to resist euphemism: in Britain and parts of the western Mediterranean, the quality and quantity of pottery, coinage, and building declined sharply in the fifth century, and standards of material life fell to levels not seen for centuries. Mass-produced wares that had been available to ordinary households disappeared. Such evidence suggests that a complex economy of long-distance exchange genuinely contracted, and that people living through the change would hardly have described it as a mere transformation. To call this a transition, the critics say, is to let the vocabulary of continuity conceal real loss.

The disagreement is partly empirical and partly a matter of what counts as the thing that ended. If the empire is understood as a political organization with a central tax-collecting state, then it plainly ended in the West, and its disappearance had consequences for those who lived under it. If it is understood as a cultural and religious community, much survived and even flourished. Neither side can simply refute the other with facts, because each selects different facts as the relevant ones. A historian who studies the papyri of Egypt, where administrative continuity under new rulers is abundant, will see a different past than one who excavates a Kent villa abandoned and never reoccupied.

This does not mean that every interpretation is equally good. Some, such as claims of a single cause like lead poisoning or moral decadence, fail because they cannot explain the uneven timing: the eastern empire, subject to the same alleged moral decay, endured for another millennium. A good account must explain regional variation as well as general trends. The most persuasive recent work therefore combines elements of both camps, treating the West's political collapse as swift and its cultural adaptation as gradual, and asking why the same crisis produced such different outcomes in different places.

qs.q: The primary purpose of the passage is to
o: survey rival explanations of Rome's fall, show why they persist, and argue that adequate accounts must address regional variation.
Correct: the passage surveys views, explains the split, and concludes with a regional-variation criterion.
defend the late antiquity model against its critics by showing that archaeological evidence for economic decline is unreliable and incomplete.
The passage presents the critics' evidence as serious and does not dismiss it.
argue that the fall of the Western empire was caused chiefly by fiscal strain, with cultural and religious changes playing only minor roles.
Fiscal strain is mentioned as one twentieth-century explanation, not as the passage's thesis.
demonstrate that all interpretations of Rome's fall are equally valid because each reflects the concerns of the period that produced it.
The author explicitly says that not every interpretation is equally good.
qs.x: the passage surveys views, explains the split, and concludes with a regional-variation criterion. Trap: Taking the passage's early observation that interpretations reflect their eras as its final claim, overlooking the later rejection of relativism.

qs.q: The author mentions Gibbon, nineteenth-century nationalists, and twentieth-century scholars in the first paragraph in order to
o: suggest that explanations of Rome's fall have repeatedly mirrored the preoccupations of the periods in which they were written.
Correct: the opening calls Rome a mirror for each age's anxieties and urges caution.
show that the study of Rome's fall has progressed steadily, with each generation correcting the errors of the generation before it.
The paragraph urges caution about the varied narratives rather than praising progress.
prove that Christianity, migration, and fiscal strain were each independently sufficient causes of the Western empire's collapse.
The passage does not claim any factor was sufficient by itself; it later rejects single causes.
establish that historians who lived through wars and economic crises were better qualified than earlier scholars to judge Rome's decline.
No claim is made that wartime experience gave scholars superior qualifications.
qs.x: the opening calls Rome a mirror for each age's anxieties and urges caution. Trap: Reading a list of historical views as a progress narrative rather than as evidence of how context shapes interpretation.

qs.q: Which of the following discoveries would most weaken the critics' use of the pottery evidence from Britain?
o: Pottery manufacture in Britain had been declining slowly for more than a century before the empire's political authority ended there.
A longer prior decline does not remove the sharp fifth-century drop and might even support contraction.
Coin finds from fifth-century Britain are rarer than those from the fourth century but are still found at many sites in the region.
Fewer but still present coins would not undermine the claim of decline.
Households in fifth-century Britain shifted to wooden and leather containers made locally, which survive poorly in the archaeological record.
Correct: if households switched to perishable local goods, the archaeological disappearance of pottery would not show economic contraction.
Pottery production in the eastern Mediterranean continued without interruption throughout the fifth century and long afterward.
Eastern continuity is irrelevant to Britain's pottery, and fits the point about regional variation.
qs.x: if households switched to perishable local goods, the archaeological disappearance of pottery would not show economic contraction. Trap: Choosing evidence that is merely related to the topic instead of evidence that offers an alternative explanation for the specific data.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward single-cause explanations such as lead poisoning is best described as
o: dismissive, because they cannot account for the East's survival under the same alleged conditions that supposedly doomed the West.
Correct: the passage says single causes fail to explain uneven timing, citing the enduring eastern empire.
sympathetic, because they offer a simple and elegant unifying principle that the more complicated transformation model cannot provide.
The author criticizes rather than praises these explanations.
neutral, because the author considers all claims about the empire's decline equally difficult to test with the surviving evidence.
The author explicitly distinguishes better from worse interpretations.
cautiously approving, because they could be combined with the transformation model to give a complete account of the cultural changes.
The passage states that such single causes fail; it does not propose merging them with other views.
qs.x: the passage says single causes fail to explain uneven timing, citing the enduring eastern empire. Trap: Overgeneralizing from the passage's tolerance for multiple perspectives to tolerance for every explanation.

qs.q: The passage implies that the historian who studies Egyptian papyri and the one who excavates a Kent villa are likely to disagree because
o: one of them has misread the evidence, since archaeology and papyrology cannot both produce reliable conclusions about the empire.
The passage does not say either evidence type is unreliable; it says each yields a different past.
the Egyptian evidence concerns the eastern empire only, so it is irrelevant to any question about the western provinces.
The passage uses the contrast to illustrate differing evidence, not geographic irrelevance.
each works with evidence that makes a different part of the historical record, continuity or abandonment, appear to be typical.
Correct: the passage says each side selects different facts as relevant, so evidence base shapes the story.
the papyri show administrative continuity while excavations show economic collapse, so the two cannot be reconciled by any account.
The final paragraph says the strongest work combines both camps, so reconciliation is possible.
qs.x: the passage says each side selects different facts as relevant, so evidence base shapes the story. Trap: Concluding that conflicting evidence means one side is wrong, when the passage treats both as accurate but selective.

qs.q: A study finds that eastern cities kept a functioning tax-collecting administration while western cities lost theirs, and that long-distance trade persisted only where administration persisted. How does this finding relate to the passage?
o: It supports the claim that lead poisoning caused the western collapse, since eastern cities were presumably exposed to less lead.
Nothing about lead exposure appears in the finding, and the passage rejects that explanation.
It supports the combined approach by linking political collapse to economic contraction and helps explain different regional outcomes.
Correct: the finding connects political structure to economic contraction and accounts for regional variation, matching the most persuasive recent work.
It undermines the late antiquity model entirely, because that model denies that political institutions had any effect on trade patterns.
The late antiquity model emphasized continuity, not a denial that institutions affected trade.
It supports the nineteenth-century migration thesis, because it shows that peoples from the north destroyed western tax systems.
The finding says nothing about migrating peoples as the cause of the administrative loss.
qs.x: the finding connects political structure to economic contraction and accounts for regional variation, matching the most persuasive recent work. Trap: Matching the finding to an explanation named in the passage by surface association rather than by what it actually shows.

passages.title: FL07 · CARS · Passage 3
text: Robert Frost is often reported to have said that poetry is what gets lost in translation. Whether or not he said it, the remark expresses a widespread belief that poems are uniquely resistant to being carried from one language into another, since their meaning cannot be separated from the sounds, rhythms, and associations of the words that carry it. If a poem were merely a prose statement dressed in ornament, a translator could extract the statement and re-dress it. But in a poem the dress is part of the body. The pun, the rhyme, the line break, the echo of an older text, all contribute to what the poem says, and none has an exact counterpart in another tongue.

Translators have responded to this predicament in three broad ways. The first, the literalist approach, aims at fidelity to the words, often at the expense of the target language's idiom; the resulting version may read awkwardly, but it allows the reader to see how the original was built. Vladimir Nabokov defended this approach so fiercely that he produced a translation of Pushkin's Eugene Onegin that sacrificed rhyme and meter entirely and loaded the page with footnotes. The second approach, the formalist, tries to reproduce the form: the rhyme scheme, the meter, the stanza. It risks distortion, because rhymes in the new language drag in words the poet never chose. The third, the imitative or free approach, treats the original as an occasion for a new poem, seeking the effect the original had on its first readers rather than its literal content. Ezra Pound's versions of Chinese verse, made without any real knowledge of the language, are the notorious example, and yet they altered English poetry more than most faithful renderings did.

Each strategy implies a theory of what a poem is. The literalist treats it as a document, the formalist as an artifact, the imitator as an event. None captures everything, and it would be a mistake to suppose that a single correct method awaits discovery. A more productive question is what a given translation is for. A version meant to help students read the original line by line has different obligations from one meant to give an English-speaking audience the pleasure of a poem. The same translator may reasonably offer both, as when a bilingual edition places a plain prose crib beside an ambitious verse rendering.

Pessimism about translation also tends to forget that poets themselves are great translators and great borrowers. Much of the English tradition was formed by translations: Chapman's Homer, which Keats praised in a famous sonnet, the King James Bible, and Dryden's Virgil all became part of the language they translated into. In these cases what was lost was less important than what was made. A translation is not a diminished copy but a second work, standing in a relation of dependence and rivalry to the first. Frost's remark, understood this way, is not an indictment but a description of where the translator's labor must go: not into retrieving what cannot be carried over, but into inventing in the new language an equivalent poem that has earned its own life.

qs.q: Which of the following best summarizes the passage's view of translating poetry?
o: Translation is better understood as the creation of a second poem for a particular purpose than as the failed transfer of an original.
Correct: the passage concludes that a translation is a second work standing in relation to the first.
Translation is impossible for poetry because form and meaning are inseparable, so any attempt at it should be abandoned by serious readers.
The author rejects pessimism about translation, citing its role in English literature.
Translation is best accomplished by the formalist method, which reproduces the original rhyme and meter most accurately in the new language.
The author says formal reproduction risks distortion and that no single method is correct.
Translation succeeds only when translators know the original language well, as the example of Pound's Chinese verse versions demonstrates.
Pound's versions are cited as influential despite his lack of knowledge, not as a model of success.
qs.x: the passage concludes that a translation is a second work standing in relation to the first. Trap: Picking the view the passage introduces (poetry resists translation) rather than the view it argues for.

qs.q: When the author says that in a poem 'the dress is part of the body,' the author means that
o: ornamental features of a poem are unimportant, so translators may safely discard them without any loss to the poem's meaning.
That is the view the metaphor denies.
a poem's author usually has a bodily or personal experience in mind, which a translator from another culture cannot fully share.
The metaphor concerns form and meaning, not the author's bodily experience.
the translator must wear the style of the original poet, imitating the manner in which that poet lived as well as wrote.
The metaphor is about words and form, not about the translator's lifestyle.
a poem's sounds, rhythms, and associations contribute to what it says, so its meaning cannot be separated from its wording.
Correct: the sentence follows the claim that prose statements could be re-dressed, and says that form is part of meaning.
qs.x: the sentence follows the claim that prose statements could be re-dressed, and says that form is part of meaning. Trap: Reading a metaphor in isolation instead of in light of the preceding sentences that set up its meaning.

qs.q: The passage uses Ezra Pound's versions of Chinese verse primarily to show that
o: a translator's lack of knowledge of the source language is the best qualification for producing a lively and original translation.
The passage calls the example notorious; it does not recommend ignorance.
a free rendering can be unfaithful to the original's content and still exert a lasting influence on the target language's poetry.
Correct: the passage calls Pound notorious yet more influential than most faithful renderings.
the imitative approach is superior to the literalist and formalist approaches in every circumstance in which translators may work.
The author says no single method is correct, so superiority in every circumstance is not claimed.
English poetry changed more because of translations from Chinese than because of translations from any other language.
The comparison is with faithful renderings, not with other languages' translations.
