qs.x: the passage calls Pound notorious yet more influential than most faithful renderings. Trap: Taking an illustrative example as support for a broader, stronger claim than the passage makes.

qs.q: The author mentions the bilingual edition with a prose crib beside a verse rendering in order to
o: argue that the literalist method is ultimately more useful to readers than the imitative method for nearly all poems.
The passage declines to rank methods.
demonstrate that the verse rendering is merely a decorative addition that depends entirely on the accuracy of the prose version.
The verse rendering is described as ambitious and a work with its own aims.
show that bilingual editions are generally preferred by scholars to translations published without the original text alongside.
The passage makes no claim about scholars' preferences.
illustrate that a single translator may serve two different purposes by offering separate versions suited to each of them.
Correct: the example follows the claim that different purposes carry different obligations.
qs.x: the example follows the claim that different purposes carry different obligations. Trap: Assuming an example shows a preference when the passage only uses it to illustrate coexistence of purposes.

qs.q: A translator replaces a pun in a Spanish poem with a pun in English that relies on entirely different words but produces a similar comic effect. This approach is most similar to
o: the literalist approach, because it preserves the structure of the original so that readers can see how the poem was built.
Literalism would keep the words even at the cost of English idiom.
the formalist approach, because it keeps the original rhyme scheme and meter intact while changing only the vocabulary.
The example does not concern rhyme or meter, which formalism targets.
none of the approaches described, because puns are said to have no counterpart in another tongue and cannot be translated.
The passage says puns lack an exact counterpart, but a translator can still seek an equivalent effect.
the imitative approach, because it seeks to reproduce the effect on readers rather than the original's words.
Correct: swapping the words to preserve the effect is how the passage defines imitative translation.
qs.x: swapping the words to preserve the effect is how the passage defines imitative translation. Trap: Matching on the mention of a device (pun, rhyme) rather than on the translator's goal.

qs.q: Which of the following is an assumption on which the author's claim that no single correct method awaits discovery depends?
o: Every poem contains a core statement that survives translation in any method, so the methods differ only in their manner of presenting it.
The author denies that a poem is a prose statement in ornament.
Readers who cannot read the original will always judge a translation by its literal accuracy rather than by its poetic effect in English.
The passage says audiences may want pleasure, not literal accuracy.
Translators who adopt one method consistently produce better results than translators who switch among methods from one poem to the next.
The passage notes that one translator may reasonably offer both versions.
Translations serve different readers and aims, and a method suited to one aim may be poorly suited to another.
Correct: the author ties method to what the translation is for, so differing aims is the premise.
qs.x: the author ties method to what the translation is for, so differing aims is the premise. Trap: Selecting a claim that sounds related to translation instead of one needed by the specific argument.

passages.title: FL07 · CARS · Passage 4
text: When Kandinsky painted what is often called the first abstract watercolor around 1910, he did not think he was abandoning meaning; he believed he was releasing it. Colors and shapes, he argued, act directly on the soul, as musical tones do, without needing to depict anything. The comparison with music was crucial to early abstractionists, since music had long been admired as the art that said what it said without representing the world. If a symphony needed no picture of a thunderstorm to move its audience, a canvas might need no landscape. Abstraction, on this account, is not an absence of subject matter but a discovery of a different kind of subject: the inner life, rendered in pure form.

A second tradition understood abstraction less as expression than as inquiry. Mondrian, moving through a series of increasingly stripped-down paintings of a tree, arrived at a grid of black lines and primary colors that he regarded as the visual structure underlying all appearances. His project resembled a philosophical reduction: remove the accidental, and the essential is left. Later, critics such as Clement Greenberg gave this impulse a different rationale. For Greenberg, modernist painting advanced by discarding everything that was not unique to the medium itself, such as illusionistic depth and storytelling, until it concentrated on the flat surface and the arrangement of pigment upon it. Abstraction was the logical end point of painting's attempt to know its own nature.

Skeptics have long objected that abstract painting is easy to fake and impossible to judge. If a canvas of splashed paint carries no recognizable skill in drawing, how can one distinguish achievement from accident? The objection has some force against the careless claim that abstract works can mean anything the viewer wants. But it overlooks the fact that abstract painters work under severe constraints of their own. Without a represented object to supply coherence, the painter must make the relations of color, weight, and edge do all the work, and the result either holds together or visibly fails. Viewers often detect the difference quickly, even when they cannot explain it, in the way listeners hear a wrong note without being trained musicians. Jackson Pollock's drip paintings, which looked random to many contemporaries, display on close study a controlled density and rhythm that imitators have rarely matched.

There remains a more sociological doubt. Abstraction, some historians point out, flourished in the postwar United States partly because institutions found it congenial: it was apolitical, it seemed to embody individual freedom, and it could be exhibited abroad as a contrast to officially mandated realism elsewhere. Those who hold this view do not claim the paintings were insincere. Their point is that the meaning of an artwork is not exhausted by the intentions of its maker, for institutions, critics, and governments confer meanings of their own. What began as a spiritual or analytic quest could thus become an emblem of a political ideal. That an art form may serve purposes its practitioners never foresaw is no reason to deny it value; it is, rather, a reminder that painting, like every human activity, exists in a world that uses it.

qs.q: The main point of the passage is that
o: abstract painting is the highest form of art because it expresses the inner life without relying on the limits of representation.
The passage never ranks abstraction as the highest art form.
abstract painting has several justifications, resists the charge of arbitrariness, and acquires meanings its makers never intended.
Correct: the passage covers expressive and analytic rationales, replies to skeptics, and the sociological point.
abstract painting flourished in the postwar United States only because institutions promoted it for political purposes they favored.
The historians do not claim the paintings were insincere or only political, and the passage says institutions merely conferred additional meanings.
abstract painting is widely misunderstood because viewers lack the training to see the technical skill that its practitioners possess.
The passage says viewers often detect quality without training.
qs.x: the passage covers expressive and analytic rationales, replies to skeptics, and the sociological point. Trap: Selecting the claim from one section of the passage as if it were the claim of the whole passage.

qs.q: According to the passage, the views of Kandinsky and Greenberg differ in that
o: Kandinsky saw abstraction as expressing inner life directly, whereas Greenberg saw it as painting's concentration on what is unique to its medium.
Correct: the passage ties Kandinsky to the soul and music analogy, and Greenberg to the medium's self-knowledge.
Kandinsky regarded abstraction as an inquiry into hidden structure, whereas Greenberg regarded it as a rejection of all rules of composition.
The structural inquiry belongs to Mondrian, and Greenberg valued the medium's own properties, not lawlessness.
Kandinsky wished to eliminate emotion from painting, whereas Greenberg wished to restore emotion by returning to illusionistic depth and storytelling.
Kandinsky valued emotion, and Greenberg wanted to discard illusionistic depth.
Kandinsky defended abstraction by analogy with music, whereas Greenberg defended it by analogy with philosophical reduction of experience.
The philosophical reduction is attributed to Mondrian, not Greenberg.
qs.x: the passage ties Kandinsky to the soul and music analogy, and Greenberg to the medium's self-knowledge. Trap: Swapping the attributions of the rationales among the painters and critics named in the passage.

qs.q: The author responds to the skeptics' charge that abstract painting cannot be judged by arguing that
o: abstract painters face their own constraints, since color and form relations must alone hold the work together.
Correct: the passage says the work either holds together or visibly fails, a detectable difference.
abstract painting is judged by the same standards as representational painting, such as the skill of drawing and accuracy of likeness.
The skeptics' point was that such skill is absent; the author does not reply by asserting it.
the judgments of trained critics are the only reliable way of telling accomplished abstract works from works produced by accident.
The author says untrained viewers can detect differences, like hearing a wrong note.
viewers who dislike abstract works usually change their opinions after they learn about the intentions and biographies of the painters.
Nothing in the passage addresses changes in viewers' opinions.
qs.x: the passage says the work either holds together or visibly fails, a detectable difference. Trap: Offering a reply that concedes the skeptics' premise rather than answering it.

qs.q: The comparison to listeners who hear a wrong note without musical training functions to
o: suggest that abstract painting is a form of music and should be judged exclusively by the standards of musical criticism.
The analogy concerns perception of quality, not a merger of the arts.
illustrate Kandinsky's claim that colors act on the soul in the same way that musical tones do without depicting anything.
That earlier music comparison concerned expression, not the detection of quality.
support the claim that viewers can often perceive a difference in quality without being able to explain it.
Correct: the analogy follows the claim that viewers detect the difference quickly without explaining it.
argue that only specialists can reliably tell a successful abstract painting from a failed one, as in the case of music.
The analogy says training is not needed.
qs.x: the analogy follows the claim that viewers detect the difference quickly without explaining it. Trap: Confusing two separate uses of music analogies in the passage.

qs.q: The historians mentioned in the last paragraph would most likely agree with which of the following?
o: An artwork can come to carry significance, such as political symbolism, that its creator did not intend and never anticipated.
Correct: the passage says meaning is not exhausted by intentions and that institutions confer meanings.
Abstract painters in the postwar United States insincerely adopted their style because they knew that institutions would reward it.
The historians explicitly do not claim the paintings were insincere.
An artwork's meaning is determined entirely by the response of critics, governments, and institutions rather than by its maker.
The claim is that meaning is not exhausted by intent, not that it is determined solely by others.
Abstraction should be regarded as less valuable than realist painting because it served political ends it was not meant to serve.
The author says that serving unforeseen purposes is no reason to deny value.
qs.x: the passage says meaning is not exhausted by intentions and that institutions confer meanings. Trap: Choosing an extreme restatement (entirely determined) of a moderate claim (not exhausted).

qs.q: Which of the following findings would most undermine the author's response to the skeptics?
o: Viewers with art training, shown pairs of Pollock paintings and skilled imitations, preferred the imitations about half of the time they were tested.
Trained viewers' preferences do not test the claim about untrained detection, and imitation differs from random splatters.
Viewers with no art training, shown pairs of Pollock paintings and random splatters, identified the genuine Pollocks no more often than chance would predict.
Correct: chance-level discrimination by untrained viewers contradicts the claim that the difference between success and failure is often detected quickly.
Viewers shown abstract paintings reported that they found the works emotionally moving but could not explain their reactions in words.
Being moved without being able to explain is exactly what the author describes.
Viewers shown a series of Mondrian grids and the same grids with lines shifted preferred the originals only when they knew the artist.
That result is about knowledge of the artist and Mondrian, not about untrained detection of quality; it does not directly address Pollock versus randomness.
qs.x: chance-level discrimination by untrained viewers contradicts the claim that the difference between success and failure is often detected quickly. Trap: Selecting a result about experts or emotion when the author's claim concerned untrained viewers' detection of quality.

passages.title: FL07 · CARS · Passage 5
text: In 1966, the Beach Boys' Pet Sounds and then the Beatles' Revolver made it clear that the recording studio had ceased to be a place where performances were merely captured. Tape loops, varied playback speeds, and layered overdubs produced sounds that no group of musicians could have played together in a room. The producer and theorist Brian Eno later gave this development its most quoted formulation, describing the studio as a compositional tool, an instrument in its own right, that could be played as a guitar is played. The claim is more than a metaphor, and it explains why bands of this period began to book studio time as they once booked concert halls. A guitarist's craft consists in exploiting the physical properties of strings, wood, and amplification; a studio artist exploits the properties of tape saturation, reverberation chambers, and microphone placement, and develops comparable skill in doing so.

The idea unsettles an older view of recording as a window onto a performance. According to that view, the best recording is the most transparent one, and engineering ought to disappear, preserving as faithfully as possible an event that occurred in a particular hall. Classical labels long worked under this ideal, sending engineers to hide their equipment and keep it out of the artists' sight, and live-in-concert albums still invoke it. Yet even the transparent recording involves choices. Where the microphones are placed, how many are used, and whether the room's reverberation is included alter the sound dramatically, and a listener at home hears something no member of the audience ever heard. The window, on inspection, is a painted window.

If the studio is an instrument, then questions about authorship become tangled. Who plays it? Phil Spector, with his dense wall of sound, was credited as the author of records that others sang and played. George Martin shaped the Beatles' arrangements with scoring and tape editing. Later, hip-hop producers built entire tracks from fragments of earlier recordings, treating the turntable and sampler as instruments. In each case the person at the console contributes something that cannot be traced to any musician's hands. Some critics respond by narrowing the idea of musical authorship to composition and performance, and treating engineering as craft service. This distinction seems increasingly arbitrary, since a record's most identifiable feature, its sound, is often precisely what the engineer and producer have made.

There is also a cost to the studio as instrument. Because editing allows any imperfection to be corrected, listeners may come to expect a polish that live musicians cannot supply, and performers sometimes find themselves judged against recordings that were themselves composites. Pitch correction software, which can adjust a singer's intonation note by note, has made this concern more urgent. Some artists have responded by deliberately preserving flaws, recording live to tape in one take as a statement of authenticity. Even this gesture, however, depends on the studio's resources: the choice of one take is a decision about how the recording will sound, and an act of production like any other. The studio cannot be switched off; it can only be used with more or less visible intention.

qs.q: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: The recording studio has been harmful to music because editing tools have led listeners to expect a polish that live performers cannot give.
The cost of polish is discussed but is only one part of the argument.
The recording studio functions as an instrument that shapes the sound of music, which complicates ideas about authorship and authenticity.
Correct: the passage argues the studio is an instrument and traces its consequences for authorship and authenticity.
The recording studio should be used only to capture live performances transparently, as classical labels have long attempted to do.
The transparency ideal is the view the passage unsettles.
The recording studio became important only after 1966, when tape techniques first allowed producers to credit themselves as authors.
The passage dates one development to 1966 but does not say the studio only then became important or that credit was the aim.
qs.x: the passage argues the studio is an instrument and traces its consequences for authorship and authenticity. Trap: Selecting a detail from one paragraph as the passage's main idea.

qs.q: When the author calls the transparent recording 'a painted window,' the author means that
o: recordings made to appear faithful are in fact dishonest because they conceal the actual identity of the musicians performing.
The point concerns technical choices, not the musicians' identity.
listeners typically admire the decoration of a recording more than the performance that the recording is meant to preserve.
The metaphor says nothing about admiration for decoration over performance.
even recordings that aim to disappear involve choices about microphones and room sound that shape what the listener hears.
Correct: the author says microphone placement and reverberation alter the sound so the listener hears what no audience member heard.
classical recordings are inferior to studio-constructed albums because they are limited by the acoustics of a single hall.
The author does not rank classical recordings as inferior.
qs.x: the author says microphone placement and reverberation alter the sound so the listener hears what no audience member heard. Trap: Reading the metaphor as a moral charge of dishonesty rather than a point about unavoidable mediation.

qs.q: The author discusses Spector, Martin, and hip-hop producers in order to
o: show that producers and engineers contribute to records in ways that cannot be attributed to the hands of any performing musician.
Correct: the passage states that in each case the person at the console contributes something untraceable to the musicians.
prove that the best recordings result from having a producer who is also the principal performer and composer of the music.
Spector and Martin are described as shaping records others played; they are not described as performers.
argue that sampling and tape editing have no value unless they are used to reproduce earlier performances exactly.
Hip-hop producers are said to build new tracks from fragments, not reproduce them.
illustrate how the older view of recording as a window onto performance was gradually perfected by more skilled engineers.
These cases are offered as challenges to, not perfections of, the window view.
qs.x: the passage states that in each case the person at the console contributes something untraceable to the musicians. Trap: Assuming that illustrations of producers' roles imply that producers should also be the performers.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward recording live to tape in a single take as a statement of authenticity is best described as
o: fully supportive, because the gesture restores the performers' control over the sound that the studio had previously taken away.
The author denies that the gesture escapes the studio's influence.
scornful, because the gesture is dishonest in pretending that engineers and producers played no part in the resulting record.
The tone is measured; the author does not accuse artists of dishonesty.
indifferent, because the author regards all questions of authenticity as irrelevant to the use of the studio as an instrument.
The author discusses authenticity at length and treats it as a real concern.
appreciative but unpersuaded, since the choice is itself a production decision made with the studio's resources.
Correct: the passage says the gesture still depends on the studio and is an act of production like any other.
qs.x: the passage says the gesture still depends on the studio and is an act of production like any other. Trap: Taking a nuanced evaluation to be wholly positive or wholly negative.

qs.q: A photographer chooses a lens, exposure, and darkroom technique to produce an image that no unaided eye would see. The author would most likely regard this as
o: a contrast with the studio artist's work, since photographers merely record scenes while studio artists compose entirely new sounds.
The author denies that engineering is mere recording; so the contrast fails.
evidence that photography is superior to recording, because photographers receive credit for all the choices made in their art.
The passage makes no comparison of credit among arts.
irrelevant to the passage, because the argument concerns only music and cannot be extended to any other art form.
The argument is about shaping through instruments, so it does extend by analogy.
analogous to the studio artist's work, since both shape the final product through the properties of the medium's equipment.
Correct: the passage's argument about microphone placement and tape properties parallels these technical choices shaping the result.
qs.x: the passage's argument about microphone placement and tape properties parallels these technical choices shaping the result. Trap: Rejecting a fitting analogy because it comes from a different domain.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that engineers and producers make a record's most identifiable feature, its sound?
o: Listeners asked to rate records preferred those with more elaborate production when the underlying songs were of equal quality.
Preference for elaborate production would suggest production matters to listeners.
Musicians asked to describe their own albums said that producers had substantial influence over the sounds heard on the recordings.
Musicians' reports of producer influence would support the claim.
Listeners asked to identify famous records relied overwhelmingly on melody and lyrics rather than on production textures.
Correct: if identification rests on melody and lyrics rather than sonic texture, the sound is not what makes a record most identifiable.
Listeners shown pitch-corrected and uncorrected versions of the same vocal performance often could not tell which version was which.
Failure to hear pitch correction concerns one effect and does not show that the sound is not identifiable.
qs.x: if identification rests on melody and lyrics rather than sonic texture, the sound is not what makes a record most identifiable. Trap: Choosing a result that bears on production in general rather than on what makes records identifiable.

passages.title: FL07 · CARS · Passage 6
text: Marcel Mauss's 1925 essay on the gift began from a puzzle. In many societies he surveyed, goods were exchanged not through markets but through elaborate cycles of giving, receiving, and reciprocating, and yet these transfers were neither free nor purely voluntary. A gift, Mauss argued, creates an obligation to return something, and the sense of obligation is as binding as a contract. The Trobriand Islanders' kula, in which shell necklaces and armbands circulate in opposite directions among islands for years, was his central example. Participants did not keep the valuables; honor came from holding one briefly and passing it on. Reciprocity here is not haggling; to calculate the return too openly would be an insult to the partner. Mauss concluded that the gift is a total social phenomenon, simultaneously economic, religious, legal, and moral.

Modern readers frequently take from Mauss the thought that there is no such thing as a pure gift. If a gift places the recipient in debt, then every gift contains a hidden transaction. Jacques Derrida pressed this to a paradoxical conclusion: a true gift would have to be unrecognized by both the giver, who would gain no credit, and the receiver, who would feel no debt, but then it would not be a gift at all. The argument is ingenious, but it may mistake a feature of gifts for a flaw. That gifts create relationships is precisely what distinguishes them from sales. A purchase ends the connection between buyer and seller, since the goods change hands and the account is settled. A gift, by leaving the account open, keeps the parties bound to each other.

This difference explains why attempts to convert gifts into money often offend. In a well-known study of day care centers in Haifa, researchers introduced a fine for parents who arrived late to collect their children. Lateness increased rather than declined, and it remained high even after the fine was removed. One interpretation is that the fine altered the nature of the relationship: lateness, once a favor requiring apology, became a service with a posted price. Where teachers had relied on parents' sense of obligation, the fine replaced obligation with payment, and the moral cost of being late vanished. The case is commonly cited in support of the claim that market incentives can crowd out social norms, though critics note that it was a single study in a small number of centers.

Gift exchange is not confined to traditional societies. Blood donation, which in many countries relies on unpaid volunteers, was the subject of Richard Titmuss's argument that a system of voluntary donation produces a safer supply than payment and also expresses social solidarity. Open-source software, in which programmers contribute code that others may use freely, shows a similar logic. Contributors gain reputation and belonging, which are not prices but do function as returns. Such examples suggest that the gift and the market are not alternatives dividing the world into two zones; they are different ways of organizing the same activities, with different effects on how people regard one another, and societies choose, often unconsciously, between them.

qs.q: The primary purpose of the passage is to
o: explain Mauss's idea of the gift and argue that gifts and markets are different ways of organizing similar activities.
Correct: the passage moves from Mauss to consequences and concludes that gift and market are different organizations of activity.
refute Mauss's claim that gifts create obligations by showing that modern gift-giving is voluntary and disinterested.
The passage supports, rather than refutes, the idea that gifts bind.
argue that market incentives should never be applied to activities such as childcare, blood donation, or open-source programming.
The author cites the Haifa case cautiously and does not make an absolute claim.
defend Derrida's argument that gifts are impossible because every apparently generous act contains a concealed transaction.
The author says Derrida's argument mistakes a feature of gifts for a flaw.
qs.x: the passage moves from Mauss to consequences and concludes that gift and market are different organizations of activity. Trap: Treating a position the author discusses (Derrida's) as the author's own.

qs.q: The author says that Derrida 'may mistake a feature of gifts for a flaw' because
o: Derrida failed to notice that recipients of gifts normally feel no sense of debt to the giver of the gift.
The passage accepts that gifts create debt.
Derrida overlooked the fact that gifts are always exchanged in cycles, as in the kula, across several different islands.
The kula example does not address Derrida's point about purity.
creating a continuing relationship through obligation is what distinguishes a gift from a sale, so it is not a defect.
Correct: the passage contrasts open accounts in gifts with settled accounts in purchases.
Derrida wrongly assumed that the giver of a gift gains no reputation or credit from the giving of the gift.
Derrida's own argument said the giver would gain no credit in a true gift; that is not what the author criticizes.
qs.x: the passage contrasts open accounts in gifts with settled accounts in purchases. Trap: Mixing up Derrida's premises with the author's objection to his conclusion.

qs.q: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the crowding-out interpretation of the Haifa day care study?
o: Parents at the centers reported that they felt guilty about arriving late both before and after the fine was introduced.
Guilt both before and after is not clearly inconsistent with the interpretation, and could even support it.
Lateness remained elevated after the fine was removed, even though teachers reminded parents that lateness imposed costs on staff.
Persisting lateness after removal fits the idea that norms were damaged.
Similar fines in other countries, in settings such as libraries, reduced the frequency of overdue returns by borrowers.
Results in other settings do not address what happened in the Haifa centers.
When the fine was introduced, centers also extended their official closing time, and parents read the fine as payment for the extra hours.
Correct: a change in the closing time offers a different explanation for the rise in lateness, independent of any moral shift.
qs.x: a change in the closing time offers a different explanation for the rise in lateness, independent of any moral shift. Trap: Choosing an outside case instead of a confound within the study itself.

qs.q: The discussion of open-source software mainly serves to
o: demonstrate that programmers who contribute code receive no benefit from their contributions beyond the satisfaction of giving.
The passage says that contributors do gain reputation and belonging.
prove that voluntary contribution always produces higher-quality products than the commercial software developed by firms.
The passage compares blood donation safety with payment, but it does not make a general quality claim about software.
show that gift logic operates in modern settings and that returns to giving need not take the form of prices.
Correct: the passage says contributors gain reputation and belonging, which function as returns but are not prices.
illustrate the argument that Trobriand kula exchange and open-source programming rely on the same specific set of rules.
The parallel is one of logic, not of identical rules.
qs.x: the passage says contributors gain reputation and belonging, which function as returns but are not prices. Trap: Over-reading a parallel as an identity or as a claim about quality.

qs.q: Which of the following is the best example of the passage's idea that the same activity can be organized as a gift or as a market?
o: A shopkeeper selling goods at a discount to a customer who happens to be a close friend of the family.
This is a sale with a personal discount, not a different organization of the same activity.
A neighbor who borrows tools and keeps them permanently, which the owner regards as an unfair taking of property.
This is a dispute over taking property, not an alternative organization of one activity.
A museum that charges admission on most days but waives the entrance fee for all visitors on the first Sunday of each month.
A fee waiver is a pricing practice and does not shift the relationship from market to gift.
Care for an aging parent given by family out of obligation versus by a paid nursing agency under contract.
Correct: the same activity, caring for a parent, can be organized by obligation or payment, with differing effects on relationships.
qs.x: the same activity, caring for a parent, can be organized by obligation or payment, with differing effects on relationships. Trap: Choosing an example involving money and friendship by surface features rather than the underlying parallel.

qs.q: According to the passage, a purchase differs from a gift in that a purchase
o: involves no obligation of any kind, whereas a gift creates obligations that are binding only in traditional societies.
Purchases have obligations like payment, and the passage says obligations in gifts exist in modern settings too.
requires equal value to change hands, whereas a gift requires only that the recipient accept the thing offered.
The passage does not claim a purchase needs equal value or that a gift needs only acceptance.
depends on the legal system for enforcement, whereas a gift depends solely on the private feelings of the giver.
The passage says gift obligations are as binding as contract, not merely private feeling.
settles the account between the parties and ends their connection, whereas a gift leaves the account open.
Correct: the passage states that goods change hands and the account is settled in a purchase.
qs.x: the passage states that goods change hands and the account is settled in a purchase. Trap: Attributing to the passage a contrast it does not draw.

passages.title: FL07 · CARS · Passage 7
text: Defenders of federalism often begin with an argument about information: governments close to the people know local conditions better than a distant capital can. Madison's Federalist No. 10 gave the idea a different, more surprising turn. Rather than praising small units for their cohesion, he argued that a large republic is safer than a small one against the dangers of faction, since in an extended territory many interests will compete and no single one is likely to dominate. Both arguments treat the division of authority as a tool for managing human limitations rather than as a good in itself. The federal structure of the United States has been defended ever since on both grounds: as a way of keeping government responsive and as a way of preventing any group from capturing all its power at once.

A third argument, associated with Justice Brandeis's remark that a state may serve as a laboratory of democracy, emphasizes experimentation. Different jurisdictions may try different policies, and others can observe the results at little cost. Welfare reform, minimum wage increases, and the legalization of various activities have each spread from a few states to many. The argument assumes, however, that lessons transfer: that a policy that succeeds in one state would succeed in another. Where populations, industries, and institutions differ greatly, the experiment may prove nothing, and the confidence of reformers who cite a neighbor's success may be misplaced.

Critics of federalism have pointed to costs that its defenders tend to underplay. The most serious is historical: in the United States, the doctrine of states' rights was invoked to defend slavery and later to resist civil rights legislation, and the protection of local self-government in these cases meant the protection of local oppression. A second cost is competition among jurisdictions. If states compete for businesses by lowering taxes or relaxing regulations, the result may be a race to the bottom in which every state offers less protection to its citizens than any would choose on its own. Economists remain divided about how often such races actually occur, since businesses weigh many factors besides regulation, but the possibility has been used to justify national standards in areas such as environmental protection.

The attempt to decide in the abstract whether federalism is good is therefore probably misguided. The relevant question is which functions are better assigned to which level. Matters whose effects stay within a locality, such as the layout of streets or the management of a school, seem suited to local control. Matters whose effects spill across borders, such as air pollution or the regulation of interstate commerce, seem to require a wider authority. Matters involving basic rights seem to demand a uniform floor that no locality may breach. Even this division invites disagreement, for the classification of any given issue is often itself a contested political question. Federalism, in the end, is less a settled doctrine than a continuing negotiation about where to draw lines, with the lines moving as the circumstances and the stakes change.

qs.q: The passage as a whole is best described as
o: a defense of federalism based on the claim that local governments always know local conditions better than any distant national authority could.
The passage lists problems with that argument and does not say it holds always.
a historical account of how the doctrine of states' rights was used to resist civil rights legislation in the United States.
That history is one criticism, not the passage's overall subject.
an evaluation of arguments for and against federalism that ends by recasting the issue as one of assigning functions to levels of government.
Correct: the passage reviews defenses and criticisms and ends with a function-assignment framing.
an argument that national standards should replace state authority in matters such as environmental protection and interstate commerce.
The passage says some matters suit local control, so replacement is not its thesis.
qs.x: the passage reviews defenses and criticisms and ends with a function-assignment framing. Trap: Choosing one part of the passage as its overall purpose.

qs.q: According to the passage, Madison's argument in Federalist No. 10 is surprising because it
o: claims that governments close to the people have better information, whereas one might expect distant governments to have more resources.
The information argument is the opening one and not Madison's turn.
claims that states may serve as laboratories of democracy, whereas one might expect national governments to have more experience.
The laboratory remark is attributed to Brandeis.
claims that states' rights protect local self-government, whereas one might expect them to endanger the rights of minorities.
The states' rights issue belongs to the critics' section.
claims that a large republic is safer than a small one against faction, whereas one might expect small units to be more cohesive and safer.
Correct: the passage says Madison argued that many competing interests in a large territory prevent domination.
qs.x: the passage says Madison argued that many competing interests in a large territory prevent domination. Trap: Attributing arguments to the wrong person among those named in the passage.

qs.q: The laboratory-of-democracy argument, as presented in the passage, assumes that
o: state governments always choose policies that are better than those which would be selected by the national government.
No assumption about states' superiority is stated.
a policy that works in one jurisdiction would also work in another, so observers can learn from the neighboring experiment.
Correct: the passage says the argument assumes lessons transfer.
policy experiments should be limited to the legalization of activities that are currently prohibited in most jurisdictions.
The passage lists welfare reform and minimum wages too, so no such limit exists.
citizens of different states hold the same preferences about taxes and regulation, which makes competition unnecessary.
The assumption concerns transfer of results, not preferences.
qs.x: the passage says the argument assumes lessons transfer. Trap: Selecting a plausible-sounding premise not stated or needed in the passage.

qs.q: Which of the following situations is most clearly a function that the author would assign to a wider authority?
o: A town decides how wide its streets should be and where to place its crosswalks near the schools.
Street layout is a local matter in the passage.
A school district chooses between two reading curricula for its elementary schools on the basis of local test results.
School management is named as suited to local control.
A factory in an upstream state discharges waste into a river, harming the water supply of a downstream state.
Correct: effects that spill across borders, such as pollution, require a wider authority.
A county decides on the hours during which its public library will be open on weekends throughout the year.
Library hours are a purely local matter whose effects stay within the community.
qs.x: effects that spill across borders, such as pollution, require a wider authority. Trap: Choosing examples that share the setting of the passage's local examples rather than its spillover criterion.

qs.q: The author's view on whether federalism can be judged good or bad in the abstract is that
o: the question has a clear answer, since the historical costs of federalism clearly outweigh the benefits that its defenders cite.
The author does not weigh the totals in that way.
the question is poorly posed, because the real issue is which functions are better assigned to which level of government.
Correct: the passage calls abstract judgment misguided and recasts the question in terms of assigning functions.
the question has a clear answer, since the three standard defenses of federalism are sufficient to establish its general value.
The author does not claim the defenses suffice.
the question cannot be answered because economists disagree about whether races to the bottom actually occur among states.
The economists' disagreement is a side point and not the reason the question is misguided.
qs.x: the passage calls abstract judgment misguided and recasts the question in terms of assigning functions. Trap: Taking an unresolved empirical dispute as the author's reason for a conceptual objection.

qs.q: Which of the following findings would most weaken the race-to-the-bottom worry described in the passage?
o: Firms choose locations mostly for workforce skills and nearness to customers, and rarely change those choices over regulatory differences.
Correct: if regulations rarely affect firms' location, states have little incentive to compete by relaxing them.
States that lowered business taxes subsequently reported that their revenue available for schools and road repair was smaller than before.
Reduced revenue would support concern about harms from competing on taxes.
States with stricter environmental rules were more likely to be sued by firms than states with looser rules over the same period, mostly over permit disputes.
Lawsuits do not address whether states relax rules to attract firms.
Citizens of states with weaker protections reported that they would prefer stronger protections if the national government required them.
Citizen preference for stronger protection fits the worry that states provide less than residents would choose.
qs.x: if regulations rarely affect firms' location, states have little incentive to compete by relaxing them. Trap: Choosing evidence about consequences of competition rather than evidence about whether the competition occurs.

passages.title: FL07 · CARS · Passage 8
text: Thomas Kuhn's The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) proposed that science does not advance by the steady accumulation of facts. Instead, long periods of normal science, in which researchers solve puzzles within a shared framework, are punctuated by revolutions in which the framework itself is replaced. A paradigm, in Kuhn's usage, is not merely a theory but a package of exemplary achievements, methods, and assumptions that tells practitioners which questions are worth asking and what counts as an answer. Anomalies, results that the paradigm cannot absorb, accumulate until a crisis arises and a rival framework gains adherents. The transition is not simply a matter of weighing evidence, Kuhn claimed, because the competing paradigms disagree about what the evidence is.

This last claim, the incommensurability of paradigms, provoked the fiercest criticism. If scientists on opposite sides of a revolution cannot even agree on the meaning of terms such as mass or planet, then it seems that they cannot rationally persuade one another, and the choice between theories would resemble a religious conversion. Critics such as Karl Popper and Imre Lakatos worried that this made science irrational. Kuhn later insisted he had been misread: he held that theory choice involves shared values such as accuracy, consistency, and fruitfulness, which guide scientists even when they cannot be applied as an algorithm. Reasonable scientists may weigh the values differently, and for that reason early disagreement during a transition is rational rather than a symptom of mass irrationality.

Historians of science have also challenged the neatness of Kuhn's picture. The Copernican revolution, his favorite example, took more than a century, and Copernicus's own system used epicycles and was hardly simpler or more accurate than Ptolemy's. No single moment divides the old from the new. In some fields, such as geology, the acceptance of plate tectonics in the 1960s resembled a revolution, with a long-resisted hypothesis rapidly winning over a field after new evidence from the ocean floor. In others, such as the development of molecular biology, change came through a series of overlapping refinements with no clear crisis. It may be that revolution describes the extreme end of a continuum, and that much scientific change is intermediate.

Whatever its limitations, Kuhn's account altered how scientists and the public think about science. It undermined the image of the scientist as a lone reasoner confronting nature without presuppositions, and it drew attention to the role of education, community, and institutions in sustaining a research tradition. It also gave a name to a familiar experience: that younger researchers are often quicker than their elders to adopt a new framework. That observation can be abused, as when fringe thinkers cite Kuhn to claim that their rejection by the mainstream proves they are the next revolutionaries. But rejection by one's peers is not evidence of being right. Kuhn himself would have insisted that the vast majority of challenges to a paradigm fail, and that a paradigm's resistance to change, though sometimes a vice, is also what allows normal science to make steady progress.

qs.q: Which of the following best summarizes the passage?
o: Kuhn's account of scientific revolutions has been influential, criticized, and refined, yet remains useful for understanding scientific change.
Correct: the passage presents the theory, criticisms, historians' complications, and lasting influence.
Kuhn showed that scientific theories are chosen by irrational conversion, which proves that science has no more authority than other beliefs.
The passage reports that Kuhn insisted theory choice involves shared values.
Kuhn's account has been entirely discredited by historians, who have shown that scientific change always proceeds through gradual refinement.
The passage says some fields did see revolutions, such as geology.
Kuhn argued that younger scientists are always right about new frameworks, so that established researchers should defer to them.
The passage says younger researchers are quicker to adopt, not that they are always right.
qs.x: the passage presents the theory, criticisms, historians' complications, and lasting influence. Trap: Selecting an extreme conclusion that the passage itself contradicts.

qs.q: According to the passage, a paradigm is best understood as
o: a single scientific theory that has been confirmed by enough evidence to be accepted by all of the members of a research community.
The passage says it is not merely a theory.
a package of exemplary achievements, methods, and assumptions that guides which questions practitioners ask and what counts as an answer.
Correct: the passage defines it as more than a theory, a package of achievements, methods, and assumptions.
a set of anomalies that a research community has agreed to ignore until a rival framework gains more adherents.
Anomalies are what paradigms cannot absorb, not what they define.
an institutional arrangement for educating young scientists, with textbooks, laboratories, and journals all organized around one particular discipline.
Education is mentioned as an influence in the last paragraph, not as the definition.
qs.x: the passage defines it as more than a theory, a package of achievements, methods, and assumptions. Trap: Reducing a defined term to its most familiar sense.

qs.q: Critics worried that incommensurability made science irrational because it implied that
o: scientists would never abandon a paradigm no matter how many anomalies accumulated, since each paradigm defines its own evidence.
The passage describes revolutions occurring, so paradigms are abandoned.
scientists in normal science could not solve puzzles, since the puzzles of a paradigm would not be acknowledged by its practitioners.
Puzzle-solving is the activity of normal science, not at issue here.
scientific values such as accuracy and consistency had been abandoned, leaving scientists with no standards for assessing theories.
Kuhn later said shared values guide choice, in response to the critics.
scientists on opposite sides of a revolution could not rationally persuade each other, making theory choice resemble conversion.
Correct: the passage states the critics' concern about the terms and persuasion.
qs.x: the passage states the critics' concern about the terms and persuasion. Trap: Confusing the criticism with Kuhn's later reply to it.

qs.q: The author contrasts plate tectonics with molecular biology primarily to suggest that
o: geology is a more mature science than molecular biology because it experienced a genuine crisis and revolution during its history.
Maturity of fields is not discussed.
Kuhn's account is correct for the physical sciences but incorrect for the biological sciences, which develop by different rules.
The contrast is between episodes, not a general division of sciences.
scientific change varies, some episodes resembling revolutions and others overlapping refinements, so change may lie on a continuum.
Correct: the passage ends the paragraph by suggesting revolution is an extreme on a continuum.
the acceptance of plate tectonics resulted from new evidence, while molecular biology advanced without any use of evidence.
Both fields use evidence; the contrast is the pace and pattern of change.
qs.x: the passage ends the paragraph by suggesting revolution is an extreme on a continuum. Trap: Turning a contrast of two cases into a general rule about disciplines.

qs.q: Which of the following would the author most likely say about a researcher whose unorthodox theory is rejected by her peers?
o: The rejection is evidence she is right, since a paradigm's defenders always resist whatever threatens their framework.
The passage says that this reasoning can be abused by fringe thinkers.
The rejection is evidence she is wrong, since a paradigm's resistance to change reflects the soundness of its methods.
The passage says resistance can be a vice as well as a virtue, so it is not simple evidence of soundness.
The rejection is not evidence she is right, since most challenges to a paradigm fail.
Correct: the passage warns that rejection by peers is not evidence of being right.
The rejection is irrelevant, since scientific theories are chosen by shared values and never by the opinions of the community.
The passage says institutions and communities matter in sustaining research.
qs.x: the passage warns that rejection by peers is not evidence of being right. Trap: Treating a warning against one inference as support for its opposite.

qs.q: Which of the following findings would most undermine the claim that scientists on opposite sides of a revolution cannot rationally persuade one another?
o: Several prominent opponents of a new theory abandoned their position after a specific experiment whose relevance both sides accepted beforehand.
Correct: conversion by an experiment accepted as relevant by both sides shows rational persuasion across frameworks.
Several prominent opponents of a new theory retired from research without ever having published a reply to the arguments of its supporters or conceding anything.
Retirement without reply says nothing about whether persuasion was possible.
Several prominent supporters of a new theory disagreed with one another about which of its predictions should be tested most urgently.
Disagreement among supporters does not bear on persuasion across the divide.
Several prominent opponents of a new theory continued to reject it for decades, while a younger generation adopted it without hesitation.
Continued rejection and generational turnover fit the claim, and the passage itself notes the generational pattern.
qs.x: conversion by an experiment accepted as relevant by both sides shows rational persuasion across frameworks. Trap: Choosing evidence about the sociology of scientists instead of evidence of persuasion across the divide.

passages.title: FL07 · CARS · Passage 9
text: The doctrine of precedent holds that courts should decide present cases in line with earlier decisions on similar facts. Its familiar justification is that it promotes equality, since like cases are treated alike, and predictability, since people can plan their affairs with confidence about how the law will be applied. Yet precedent is more subtle than the slogan suggests, because no two cases are identical, and the judge who follows a precedent must first decide what the earlier case stands for. This is the work of distinguishing: a judge who wishes to avoid an earlier ruling may argue that its facts differ in some material way, while a judge who wishes to follow it argues that the differences are immaterial. Much of legal reasoning consists in arguments over which similarities count.

Critics sometimes infer that precedent is therefore a sham, a mask for judges to reach conclusions they favor on other grounds. The inference is hasty. That a rule requires interpretation does not show that it places no constraint on the interpreter. A judge who must explain why a prior case does not apply, in a written opinion that will be read by colleagues, litigants, and appellate courts, faces a real discipline. Opinions that rely on strained distinctions are criticized, reversed, or ignored by later courts. Constraint in law is less like a wall than like a current; it does not forbid movement but makes some directions harder to take than others.

Within the common law tradition, the usual way of explaining how precedent develops is through the analogy of a chain novel. Each judge adds a chapter to a story begun by predecessors, and must try to write one that makes the whole narrative as coherent as possible. Ronald Dworkin used this image to argue that judges are bound not only by the specific holdings of earlier cases but by the principles that best justify them. The image has its limits, since law is made by many authors working under strong institutional pressures, but it captures the sense in which a judge is both free and constrained. A judge may extend the story in a new direction, but not tear out the chapters already written.

How, then, can precedent ever be overruled? Courts do so, though sparingly, when a past decision has proved unworkable, rested on facts that have changed, or conflicts with principles that have grown up around it. Brown v. Board of Education's repudiation of the separate but equal rule is the best-known American example. The justification for overruling turns on a tension between stability and correctness: a court that never corrects its errors perpetuates injustice, but one that corrects them too readily deprives citizens of the reliance that precedent was meant to supply. There is no formula for resolving this tension. The practice of precedent works by teaching judges to feel its weight, and to depart from it only when the reasons for doing so can be stated in terms that others can recognize as legal rather than merely personal.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Precedent is a mask for judicial preference, since every ruling can be distinguished from earlier ones whenever a judge wishes to do so.
The author calls that inference hasty.
Precedent should never be overruled, since the stability it provides is always more valuable than correcting an earlier mistaken decision.
The author says courts may overrule when decisions are unworkable or rest on changed facts.
Precedent is an algorithm that tells judges how to decide present cases by matching them with the facts of earlier ones.
The passage says cases are never identical and require judgment about what counts.
Precedent constrains judges through interpretive judgment rather than mechanical rules, and is overruled only for reasons others recognize as legal.
Correct: the passage defends precedent as a real but non-mechanical constraint.
qs.x: the passage defends precedent as a real but non-mechanical constraint. Trap: Choosing the position the passage rejects instead of the one it defends.

qs.q: The statement that constraint in law is 'less like a wall than like a current' means that precedent
o: is flexible enough that judges can always move in whichever direction they prefer without any real resistance.
Strained distinctions face criticism, so the resistance is real.
does not forbid every departure, but makes some directions of decision harder to take than others.
Correct: a current permits movement but with greater difficulty in some directions.
moves judges steadily toward better decisions as the body of earlier cases becomes larger and more complete.
The current metaphor concerns resistance, not progress toward correctness.
blocks all departures from earlier decisions, though it can be bypassed by reversing the lower court's ruling.
A wall would forbid all departures; the author rejects that image.
qs.x: a current permits movement but with greater difficulty in some directions. Trap: Reading a metaphor as meaning either total freedom or total prohibition.

qs.q: The chain novel analogy is used to illustrate that
o: judges are entirely free, since each new chapter can take the story in whichever direction its author finds most appealing.
The passage says the judge cannot tear out earlier chapters.
judges are both free and constrained, because each must extend the story coherently without tearing out earlier chapters.
Correct: the passage says the image captures how a judge is both free and constrained.
judges working in the common law tradition collaborate closely with their predecessors and agree on the shape of the whole.
The passage says law has many authors working under institutional pressures, so close collaboration is not claimed.
judges are bound only by the specific holdings of earlier cases and not by the principles that might justify them.
Dworkin's point was that judges are bound by principles as well as holdings.
qs.x: the passage says the image captures how a judge is both free and constrained. Trap: Choosing a statement that captures only half of the analogy's point.

qs.q: According to the passage, which of the following would most justify a court's overruling a precedent?
o: The judges hearing the new case believe that they would have decided the original case differently if they had heard it.
That reason is personal, which the passage says is not enough.
The earlier decision rested on factual conditions that have changed and has proved difficult to apply consistently.
Correct: the passage lists unworkability and changed facts as grounds, stated in legal terms.
The earlier decision is old enough that most of the citizens who relied on it have since died or moved elsewhere.
Age or the passing of relying citizens is not a ground in the passage.
The earlier decision was criticized in the press, and the outcome of the new case will please a large number of citizens.
Popularity and press criticism are not legal reasons.
qs.x: the passage lists unworkability and changed facts as grounds, stated in legal terms. Trap: Choosing a reason that sounds sensible but is not among those the passage names.

qs.q: Which of the following findings would most support the critics who regard precedent as a sham?
o: Judges' votes in precedent-governed cases are predictable from politics alone, and strained distinctions are rarely criticized or reversed.
Correct: predictability from politics and no cost for strained distinctions would show precedent exerts little constraint.
Judges in precedent-governed cases wrote longer opinions than judges in cases without precedent, citing many earlier decisions and discussing their facts at length.
Longer opinions with more citations are consistent with a real discipline.
Judges who overruled precedent were criticized by colleagues more often than judges who followed precedent in similar cases.
Criticism of overruling indicates the weight of precedent.
Judges' opinions in cases governed by precedent were read by litigants, and appellate courts sometimes reversed those decisions.
Reversals show that appellate courts enforce constraint.
qs.x: predictability from politics and no cost for strained distinctions would show precedent exerts little constraint. Trap: Selecting evidence that merely involves judges' behavior rather than evidence that constraint is absent.

passages.title: FL07 · Chem/Phys · Passage 1
text: A student investigates an Atwood machine consisting of a light string passed over a low-friction pulley, with a block of mass m1 hanging on one side and a block of mass m2 on the other. In each trial the blocks are held at rest, released, and the acceleration of the heavier block is determined from video analysis. The pulley and string are treated as massless in the ideal model, and g is taken as 10 m/s². The masses used and the measured accelerations are given in Table 1. In the ideal model, both blocks share the same acceleration magnitude, and the string tension is the same on both sides of the pulley. The student also plots the measured acceleration against the dimensionless quantity (m1 − m2)/(m1 + m2) for each trial, shown in the figure. The student releases each pair from rest, keeps the string taut, makes sure the heavier block does not strike the floor, and averages three repetitions of each trial. Air resistance is neglected.

qs.q: In the ideal model, what is the acceleration of the blocks in Trial 1 (m1 = 0.50 kg, m2 = 0.30 kg)?
o: 2.5 m/s²
Correct: The net force on the system is (m1 − m2)g = 2.0 N and the total mass being accelerated is 0.80 kg, so a = 2.0/0.80 = 2.5 m/s².
4.0 m/s²
This option divides the net force by m1 alone (2.0/0.50), ignoring that both blocks accelerate together.
6.7 m/s²
This option divides the net force by m2 alone (2.0/0.30), ignoring the heavier block's inertia.
5.0 m/s²
This option gives a = g/2, which would apply only if m1 were three times m2 rather than 5/3 times m2.
qs.x: The net force on the system is (m1 − m2)g = 2.0 N and the total mass being accelerated is 0.80 kg, so a = 2.0/0.80 = 2.5 m/s². Trap: Dividing the net force by only one of the masses instead of the total mass of both blocks.

qs.q: In the ideal model, what is the tension in the string during Trial 1?
o: Correct: For the lighter block, T − m2g = m2a, so T = 0.30(10 + 2.5) = 3.75 N; this is between m2g = 3.0 N and m1g = 5.0 N, as expected for accelerating blocks.
This option equals m1g, which would hold only if the heavier block were in equilibrium rather than accelerating downward.
This option equals m2g, which would hold only if the lighter block were not accelerating upward.
This option equals the total weight (m1 + m2)g, which would be the tension only if one block were supported entirely by the other.
qs.x: For the lighter block, T − m2g = m2a, so T = 0.30(10 + 2.5) = 3.75 N; this is between m2g = 3.0 N and m1g = 5.0 N, as expected for accelerating blocks. Trap: Assuming tension equals the weight of one block, as in static equilibrium, when both blocks are accelerating.

qs.q: If both masses in Trial 1 were doubled (m1 = 1.0 kg, m2 = 0.60 kg), how would the ideal acceleration change?
o: It would double to 5.0 m/s², since the net force doubles
This option counts the doubled net force but neglects the doubled inertia of the system.
It would fall to 1.25 m/s², since the total mass doubles
This option counts the doubled inertia but neglects the doubled net driving force.
It would be unchanged at 2.5 m/s², since the mass ratio is the same
Correct: a = g(m1 − m2)/(m1 + m2) depends only on the ratio, which stays 0.25. The net force and the total mass both double, so their effects cancel.
It would rise to 3.75 m/s², since the tension increases
This option is wrong because tension does increase (to 7.5 N), but acceleration depends on the net force divided by total mass, not tension alone.
qs.x: a = g(m1 − m2)/(m1 + m2) depends only on the ratio, which stays 0.25. The net force and the total mass both double, so their effects cancel. Trap: Considering only the change in net force or only the change in total mass rather than both together.

qs.q: The best-fit line through the origin in the figure has a slope closest to which quantity?
o: 4.8 m/s², approximately g/2
This option is the value of the y-axis at the largest ratio, not the slope (change in y per unit x).
19 m/s², approximately 2g
This option would require measured accelerations roughly twice those observed, as when the ratio is doubled.
0.10 s²/m, approximately 1/g
This option has units of s²/m, so it is the reciprocal of the slope and cannot be a slope on this plot.
9.6 m/s², approximately g

Correct: Ideal theory gives a = g × [(m1 − m2)/(m1 + m2)], so the slope equals g. Fitting the points (e.g., 4.8/0.50 and 3.9/0.40) gives about 9.6 m/s²; the slight deficit is consistent with small pulley friction and inertia.
qs.x: Ideal theory gives a = g × [(m1 − m2)/(m1 + m2)], so the slope equals g. Fitting the points (e.g., 4.8/0.50 and 3.9/0.40) gives about 9.6 m/s²; the slight deficit is consistent with small pulley friction and inertia. Trap: Reading the largest y-value as the slope instead of calculating rise over run.

qs.q: In Trial 1 the 0.50 kg block is released from rest and descends 0.80 m. Using the ideal model, what is its speed at that point?
o: This option is √2, the result of v² = ad without the factor of 2 in v² = 2ad.
Correct: Energy conservation: (m1 − m2)gh = ½(m1 + m2)v², so 1.6 J = 0.40v² and v² = 4.0, giving v = 2.0 m/s. Kinematics gives the same: v² = 2ad = 2(2.5)(0.80).
This option is v², not v; the square root was not taken after solving for v².
This option is √8, which results from using the speed formula with a = 5.0 m/s² or doubling the energy released.
qs.x: Energy conservation: (m1 − m2)gh = ½(m1 + m2)v², so 1.6 J = 0.40v² and v² = 4.0, giving v = 2.0 m/s. Kinematics gives the same: v² = 2ad = 2(2.5)(0.80). Trap: Forgetting that the kinetic energy belongs to both blocks, or stopping at v² without taking the square root.

passages.title: FL07 · Chem/Phys · Passage 2
text: Industrial ammonia is made by the Haber-Bosch reaction, N2(g) + 3 H2(g) ⇌ 2 NH3(g). A chemical engineer models a reactor fed with N2 and H2 in the stoichiometric 1:3 mole ratio and treats all gases as ideal, with Kp defined using partial pressures in atmospheres. For each condition in Table 1, the engineer calculates the mole fraction of NH3 once the mixture has stopped changing. Conditions A through C use an uncatalyzed reactor. In Condition D, a finely divided iron catalyst is added to the reactor of Condition B, with temperature and pressure unchanged. Figure 1 shows the equilibrium NH3 mole fraction as a function of total pressure at 400 °C and at 500 °C. Because the reaction is carried out in a closed reactor, the total pressure is held constant by adjusting the volume as ammonia forms, and the feed gases are assumed to contain no NH3 at the start. The times in Table 1 are the engineer's estimates for the reactor to reach a constant composition.

qs.q: Which statement best explains why the NH3 mole fraction in Condition B is greater than in Condition A?
o: Raising the pressure increases Kp, so the equilibrium mixture contains a larger fraction of NH3
Kp depends only on temperature, and both conditions are at 400 °C.
Raising the pressure increases the rate of the forward reaction only, so more NH3 accumulates
Compression speeds both forward and reverse reactions; the position shifts because Q is temporarily displaced below K, not because only one rate changes.
Raising the pressure favors the side with fewer moles of gas, NH3
Correct: The reactants contain 4 moles of gas and the product 2 moles, so higher pressure favors the product side and raises the NH3 fraction while Kp is unchanged.
Raising the pressure makes the exothermic forward reaction release heat, which favors NH3
Temperature is fixed at 400 °C in both conditions, and a heat change would not explain a pressure effect at constant temperature.
qs.x: The reactants contain 4 moles of gas and the product 2 moles, so higher pressure favors the product side and raises the NH3 fraction while Kp is unchanged. Trap: Thinking that a pressure change alters the equilibrium constant instead of only the equilibrium position.

qs.q: Using the data for Condition B, what is Kp at 400 °C?
o: Correct: In B, P(NH3) = 0.349 × 200 = 69.8 atm; the remaining 0.651 is split 1:3, so P(N2) = 32.6 atm and P(H2) = 97.7 atm. Kp = (69.8)²/[(32.6)(97.7)³] = 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ atm⁻².
This value results from squaring P(H2) instead of cubing it.
This value is calculated from mole fractions rather than partial pressures, which gives a dimensionless Kx and not Kp.
6.2 × 10³ atm²
This value is the inverse of Kp, with the products and reactants placed in the wrong positions.
qs.x: In B, P(NH3) = 0.349 × 200 = 69.8 atm; the remaining 0.651 is split 1:3, so P(N2) = 32.6 atm and P(H2) = 97.7 atm. Kp = (69.8)²/[(32.6)(97.7)³] = 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ atm⁻². Trap: Using the H2 coefficient incorrectly or inverting the expression so reactants are in the numerator.

qs.q: Comparing Conditions B and C, which conclusion is best supported?
o: Kp is larger at 500 °C, and the forward reaction is endothermic
The NH3 fraction decreased, so Kp cannot have increased.
Kp is unchanged at 500 °C, because the total pressure is the same
Kp depends on temperature, and the temperature changed, so Kp changed even though pressure was equal.
Kp is lower at 500 °C, and the reaction is endothermic
Kp is correctly smaller, but an endothermic forward reaction would be favored by heating and would give more NH3.
Kp is smaller at 500 °C, and the forward reaction is exothermic

Correct: At the same pressure, the NH3 fraction falls from 0.349 to 0.170 when heated, so Kp decreases. Heating shifts a reaction toward the endothermic direction, so the forward reaction must be exothermic.
qs.x: At the same pressure, the NH3 fraction falls from 0.349 to 0.170 when heated, so Kp decreases. Heating shifts a reaction toward the endothermic direction, so the forward reaction must be exothermic. Trap: Mixing up which direction heat favors for exothermic and endothermic reactions.

qs.q: The results for Conditions B and D show that the iron catalyst:
o: raises the equilibrium yield of NH3 by lowering the activation energy of only the forward reaction
A catalyst cannot lower the barrier of only one direction, and the yield did not change.
reaches the same equilibrium composition sooner by lowering both activation energies

Correct: The mole fraction is 0.349 in both, so the position of equilibrium and Kp are unchanged, while the time falls from 60 min to 4 min because the catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions equally.
reaches equilibrium sooner by raising Kp, so that more NH3 forms at equilibrium
Kp depends only on temperature, and a catalyst does not alter it.
lowers the equilibrium yield of NH3 but compensates by greatly increasing the rate
The yield stayed at 0.349 and did not decrease.
qs.x: The mole fraction is 0.349 in both, so the position of equilibrium and Kp are unchanged, while the time falls from 60 min to 4 min because the catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions equally. Trap: Believing a catalyst increases the equilibrium yield or shifts the equilibrium.
