passages.title: FL07 · Psych/Soc · Passage 5
text: Groupthink describes a pattern in which pressure for agreement leads cohesive groups to make poor decisions. A researcher assigned 36 four-person groups of university students to three conditions (12 groups each). Each group read a case file about three candidates for a research position and had 30 minutes to choose one. The file was written so that the best candidate could be identified only if members combined information that had been given to individual members alone (unshared information). Groups in the first condition were composed of friends and led by a member who was instructed to state a preferred candidate at the start. Groups in the second condition were also composed of friends, but one member was randomly assigned the role of devil's advocate and told to challenge the emerging consensus. Groups in the third condition were composed of strangers with no leader. Recorded discussions were coded for the percentage of unshared information items mentioned. After deciding, each member rated confidence in the group's choice from 1 to 10. Results are in Table 1.

qs.q: Which result in Table 1 is most characteristic of groupthink?
o: Friends with a devil's advocate reported the lowest confidence while choosing the best candidate most often.
The devil's advocate groups did not have the lowest confidence (the strangers did), and high accuracy is not a sign of groupthink.
Strangers with no leader mentioned more unshared information than friends with a directive leader and chose correctly more often.
This pattern is the expected result of less cohesion and no directive pressure; it is not itself a symptom of groupthink.
Friends with a devil's advocate mentioned the largest share of unshared items and rated their confidence below the directive-leader groups.
This describes a group in which dissent was encouraged and decisions were better, the opposite of groupthink.
Friends with a directive leader reported the highest confidence while choosing the best candidate least often.
Correct: Groupthink involves illusions of invulnerability and unanimity and self-censorship, which show up as high confidence alongside poor decisions and little sharing of dissenting information.
qs.x: Groupthink involves illusions of invulnerability and unanimity and self-censorship, which show up as high confidence alongside poor decisions and little sharing of dissenting information. Trap: Choosing a result that shows better decisions rather than the combination of high confidence and low quality.

qs.q: By what factor was the proportion of groups choosing the best candidate greater in the devil's advocate condition than in the directive leader condition?
o: 1.1 is the ratio of the devil's advocate groups to the stranger groups (8 / 7), which is a different comparison.
0.5 is the inverse ratio (4 / 8).
Correct: 8/12 divided by 4/12 equals 2.
4 is the number of successful groups in the directive condition, not the ratio.
qs.x: 8/12 divided by 4/12 equals 2. Trap: Inverting the ratio or reporting a raw count instead of the comparison.

qs.q: Assigning one member to challenge the emerging consensus most likely improved decisions by doing which of the following?
o: Increasing the group's cohesiveness so that members felt more committed to the first candidate named.
Greater cohesiveness is an antecedent of groupthink; the friends in both conditions were equally cohesive.
Increasing deindividuation so that members felt less personally accountable for the choice.
Deindividuation relates to loss of self-awareness in crowds, not to reasoned dissent in a small discussion.
Reducing self-censorship and normative pressure so that unshared information entered the discussion.
Correct: A designated dissenter makes disagreement legitimate, weakens conformity pressure, and encourages sharing of information that contradicts the early preference.
Increasing social facilitation so that members performed the well-learned task more quickly.
Social facilitation concerns performance of simple or well-learned tasks in the presence of others, not complex judgment.
qs.x: A designated dissenter makes disagreement legitimate, weakens conformity pressure, and encourages sharing of information that contradicts the early preference. Trap: Naming a social-psychology term that sounds related to group effects without matching the described mechanism.

qs.q: Which limitation of the design most weakens the conclusion that cohesion by itself caused the poor decisions in the first condition?
o: Cohesion was varied together with leader directiveness, so the two factors cannot be separated.
Correct: The directive-leader condition differs from the stranger condition in both cohesion and leadership, so a factorial design would be needed to isolate cohesion.
Each group contained only four members, so no group was large enough to show conformity pressure.
Conformity pressure operates in small groups, and four-person groups are typical in such research.
Confidence ratings were collected after the decision, so members' ratings could not be influenced by the outcome.
Collecting confidence after the decision is a procedural choice and does not confound cohesion with leadership.
Groups were assigned to conditions at random, so differences among the groups would not reflect chance.
Random assignment is a strength of the design, not a limitation, and it is not the main concern.
qs.x: The directive-leader condition differs from the stranger condition in both cohesion and leadership, so a factorial design would be needed to isolate cohesion. Trap: Citing a generic procedural detail instead of the confound that links two manipulated factors.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Group decision outcomes (12 groups per condition)

passages.title: FL07 · Psych/Soc · Passage 6
text: Evaluative conditioning refers to changes in liking that result from pairing a neutral stimulus with a stimulus that already evokes a positive or negative reaction. In one study, 90 adults saw images of an unfamiliar brand of pen (Brand X) on a computer screen. Participants were randomly assigned to three groups (n = 30 each). In the positive group, each Brand X image was shown immediately before a pleasant image such as a puppy or a sunset. In the negative group, each Brand X image preceded an unpleasant image such as a spoiled meal. In the random group, Brand X images and pleasant or unpleasant images were shown in random order with no consistent pairing. Before and after the session, participants rated their attitude toward Brand X from -5 (very negative) to +5 (very positive). Table 1 shows mean ratings after 16 pairings. In a second set of participants, ratings were measured after different numbers of pairings, shown in Figure 1. Afterward, all participants rated a similar pen from Brand Y, which had never been shown.

qs.q: In the positive pairing group, which element of the procedure is the unconditioned stimulus?
o: The image of Brand X shown before the pleasant image.
Brand X is the neutral stimulus that becomes the conditioned stimulus.
The positive attitude toward Brand X after the session.
The learned positive attitude toward the pen is the conditioned response.
The computer screen on which the images were presented.
The screen is constant across all groups and does not elicit the response.
The pleasant image shown after the pen.
Correct: The pleasant image already evokes a positive response without learning, so it is the unconditioned stimulus; the pen becomes the conditioned stimulus.
qs.x: The pleasant image already evokes a positive response without learning, so it is the unconditioned stimulus; the pen becomes the conditioned stimulus. Trap: Confusing the neutral stimulus that acquires meaning with the stimulus that already carries it.

qs.q: By how many rating points did the mean attitude toward Brand X change in the negative pairing group between the start and the end of the session?
o: -1.9 is the final rating, not the change from the starting rating.
-2.0 results from adding the baseline instead of subtracting it.
1.8 gives the magnitude but loses the direction of the change.
qs.x: -1.9 - (-0.1) = -1.8. Trap: Reporting the final value or mishandling the sign of a negative baseline.

qs.q: The purpose of the random group was primarily to rule out which alternative explanation?
o: That participants' attitudes changed because of operant reinforcement for choosing the pleasant images.
No responses were reinforced in this procedure, so operant reinforcement is not an alternative explanation here.
That mere exposure to Brand X and to the images, rather than their consistent pairing, altered the ratings.
Correct: The random group sees the same stimuli as the other groups but without contingency, so any change due to exposure alone would appear there too; its ratings barely moved (0.0 to 0.2).
That participants in the positive and negative groups differed from one another in the amount of social desirability bias they showed.
Social desirability would be similar in all groups; the random group does not specifically test it.
That the pleasant and unpleasant images had different intensities, which changed the order effects.
Image intensity is a feature of the stimuli and is not addressed by removing the contingency.
qs.x: The random group sees the same stimuli as the other groups but without contingency, so any change due to exposure alone would appear there too; its ratings barely moved (0.0 to 0.2). Trap: Treating a control group as a check against every possible bias instead of the specific contingency being tested.

qs.q: Which statement about learning is best supported by Figure 1?
o: Each additional pairing produced a smaller change in attitude as the number of pairings increased.
Correct: The positive group's rating rose by 0.8 over the first 2 pairings but only 0.2 over the last 8, a negatively accelerated acquisition curve.
The attitude changed at a constant rate across the 16 pairings in both groups.
A constant rate would give a straight line, but the curves flatten.
Negative pairings produced a larger change in attitude than positive pairings at every number of pairings.
The positive ratings were larger in magnitude than the negative ratings at 16 pairings (2.3 versus 1.9).
Attitudes changed little during the first four pairings and then changed rapidly.
The largest changes occurred in the earliest pairings, not later.
qs.x: The positive group's rating rose by 0.8 over the first 2 pairings but only 0.2 over the last 8, a negatively accelerated acquisition curve. Trap: Reading a flattening curve as a constant rate of learning.

qs.q: The ratings of Brand Y in Table 1 (1.1 in the positive group and -0.8 in the negative group) are most consistent with which phenomenon?
o: Extinction of the conditioned attitude because Brand Y was never paired with an image.
Extinction requires repeated presentation of the conditioned stimulus without the unconditioned stimulus, and Brand Y was never conditioned.
Stimulus generalization of the conditioned attitude to a similar pen.
Correct: A conditioned response can transfer to stimuli similar to the conditioned stimulus, so Brand Y took on a milder form of the attitudes toward Brand X.
Spontaneous recovery of the conditioned attitude after a rest period.
Spontaneous recovery refers to the return of an extinguished response after a delay, and no extinction occurred.
Sensitization to all pens as a result of repeated exposure to emotional images.
Sensitization would raise responses to all stimuli in the same direction, whereas the ratings diverged by group.
qs.x: A conditioned response can transfer to stimuli similar to the conditioned stimulus, so Brand Y took on a milder form of the attitudes toward Brand X. Trap: Naming a conditioning process that involves a different procedure than the one described.

passages.title: FL07 · Psych/Soc · Passage 7
text: Sociologists consider the family the primary agent of socialization, the process through which children learn the norms and expectations of their society. A research team analyzed a survey of 2,400 adolescents in a metropolitan region who were sorted by household type: two biological parents, a single parent, a stepfamily, or a multigenerational household that included grandparents. Adolescents reported the average weekly hours that at least one adult in the home directly supervised their activities. The researchers obtained grade point average (GPA, 4.0 scale) from school records and asked whether each adolescent expected to complete a four-year college degree. They also recorded household income, which was lowest on average in single-parent households and highest in two-parent households. The researchers were interested in whether differences in supervision and educational outcomes across household types persisted after the survey was weighted to match the region's population, and whether the patterns could be interpreted as evidence of causal effects of family structure. Table 1 presents the unweighted results by household type.

qs.q: Approximately how many single-parent adolescents in the sample expected to complete a four-year college degree?
o: 61 is the percentage, not the number of adolescents.
390 is 0.65 x 600 and is not based on the Table 1 percentage for this group.
234 is the number who did not expect a degree (0.39 x 600).
qs.x: 0.61 x 600 = 366. Trap: Reporting the percentage as a count or computing the complement.

qs.q: What is the mean weekly supervision across all 2,400 adolescents in the sample?
o: About 22 hours, the midpoint of the highest and lowest group means
The midpoint of the extreme group means ignores how many adolescents are in each household type.
About 24 hours, the value for the largest group
The largest group's mean describes only that group, not the entire sample.
About 17 hours, the mean for stepfamily adolescents
The stepfamily mean describes only one subgroup, not the entire sample.
About 21 hours
qs.x: The weighted mean is (1,200 x 24 + 600 x 15 + 360 x 17 + 240 x 29) / 2,400 = 50,880 / 2,400 = 21.2 hours. Trap: Averaging group means without weighting by group size.

qs.q: A reader concludes that growing up in a single-parent household reduces educational outcomes. Which additional information from the passage most seriously challenges this causal claim?
o: Multigenerational households had the highest supervision, which shows that more adults always lead to better grades.
The multigenerational GPA (3.1) was below the two-parent GPA (3.2), so more adults do not 'always' improve grades; this also does not address the confound.
Single-parent households also had the lowest average income, which could explain both the household type and the outcomes.
Correct: Household income is a plausible confounder that is related to both family structure and educational outcomes, so the association cannot be read as causal.
Stepfamilies had GPAs similar to single-parent households, which shows that household structure itself has no effect on grades.
Similar GPAs in two household types does not show that structure has no effect and does not address confounding by income.
Two-parent households contained the largest number of adolescents, which makes their mean GPA more precise.
Precision from sample size is unrelated to whether a correlation reflects causation.
qs.x: Household income is a plausible confounder that is related to both family structure and educational outcomes, so the association cannot be read as causal. Trap: Treating a correlation between family type and outcomes as causal without considering shared third variables.

qs.q: Which statement best reflects the conflict perspective on these findings?
o: Families transmit unequal resources and advantages across generations, so differences in outcomes reproduce existing social class inequality.
Correct: Conflict theory emphasizes how institutions such as the family distribute power and resources unequally and help reproduce social stratification.
Families perform essential functions such as raising children, and differences in outcomes reflect temporary problems of adaptation by the institution.
This describes the structural-functionalist view of the family as a stable institution performing needed functions.
Families create meanings through everyday interaction, and the adolescent's outcome depends on how the adolescent defines the household.
This describes the symbolic interactionist emphasis on meanings created in interaction.
Families maintain solidarity through shared rituals, so each household type contributes in the same way to social cohesion.
This is closer to a Durkheimian functionalist argument about ritual and cohesion.
qs.x: Conflict theory emphasizes how institutions such as the family distribute power and resources unequally and help reproduce social stratification. Trap: Confusing the functionalist and conflict perspectives on institutions.

passages.title: FL07 · Psych/Soc · Passage 8
text: Migration scholars distinguish push factors, which drive people away from an origin, from pull factors, which attract them to a destination. A national statistics office compiled data on emigration from four provinces of a middle-income country to a wealthier neighboring country over one year. For each province, officials calculated the emigration rate per 1,000 residents using population and the number of recorded emigrants. They also recorded the provincial unemployment rate and the percentage of households with a relative already living in the destination country (a measure of established migrant networks). The average wage in the destination country was about three times the wage in any of the four provinces. The recorded emigrants were those who registered a change of residence with consular offices, so informal moves were not counted. Population figures came from the most recent national census. Table 1 gives the data. Figure 1 plots each province's emigration rate against its unemployment rate.

qs.q: What was the emigration rate for Province B, in emigrants per 1,000 residents?
o: 0.6 is the rate per 100 residents (0.6%), not per 1,000.
60 is a misplaced decimal; the rate per 10,000 would be 60.
16.7 is the population per emigrant divided by 10 and is not a rate.
qs.x: 9,000 / 1,500,000 = 0.006, or 6 per 1,000. Trap: Misplacing the decimal when converting a proportion to a per-1,000 rate.

qs.q: Which of the following is best classified as a pull factor in this scenario?
o: High unemployment rates in Provinces A and D.
Unemployment at the place of origin is a push factor.
Low wages relative to living costs in each province of origin.
Low purchasing power at the origin is a push factor, since it is a condition of the origin.
Average wages in the destination country about three times those in the provinces.
Correct: Pull factors are attractive features of the destination, such as higher wages and job availability.
The lack of available jobs for new graduates in Province C.
A scarcity of jobs at home is a push factor.
qs.x: Pull factors are attractive features of the destination, such as higher wages and job availability. Trap: Labeling any economic factor as a pull factor without checking whether it describes the origin or the destination.

qs.q: The higher emigration rates in provinces where more households have a relative abroad are most consistent with which concept?
o: Urban ecology, in which cities develop concentric zones that attract new migrants to specific neighborhoods of a city.
Urban ecology concerns spatial patterns within cities, not the effect of networks on emigration from provinces.
Demographic transition, in which falling mortality is followed by falling fertility as a country industrializes.
Demographic transition addresses birth and death rates, not network effects on migration.
Rationalization, in which social life becomes increasingly governed by efficiency and formal rules.
Rationalization is a Weberian concept about the organization of institutions and does not explain network migration.
Chain migration, in which established migrants provide information, housing, and jobs that lower the cost and risk of moving.
Correct: Social networks of earlier migrants reduce barriers for those who follow, which produces chain migration and clustering of origin communities.
qs.x: Social networks of earlier migrants reduce barriers for those who follow, which produces chain migration and clustering of origin communities. Trap: Selecting a demography or sociology term that sounds relevant but describes a different process.

qs.q: The researchers conclude that unemployed individuals are the ones most likely to emigrate. Why is this conclusion not justified by Figure 1?
o: The scatter plot contains only four points, so a pattern in the data can never be detected.
Four points are few, but the issue is the level of analysis, and a pattern can be seen in them.
Unemployment and emigration rates are both expressed as percentages, so they cannot be compared directly.
Variables measured in different units can still be correlated and plotted together.
The relationship in the figure is negative, which contradicts the claim that unemployment promotes emigration.
The figure shows a positive relationship: higher unemployment goes with higher emigration.
The data are at the province level, so they cannot show that the people who left were the unemployed ones.
Correct: Inferring individual behavior from group-level correlations is the ecological fallacy; individual-level data on migrants' employment would be needed.
qs.x: Inferring individual behavior from group-level correlations is the ecological fallacy; individual-level data on migrants' employment would be needed. Trap: Reading an aggregate-level association as proof about the individuals within the aggregate.

passages.title: FL07 · Psych/Soc · Passage 9
text: Sociologists studying gender stratification often compare women's and men's earnings after statistically adjusting for differences in worker characteristics. A researcher analyzed payroll records for 8,000 full-time employees (4,000 women and 4,000 men) at a large set of firms. The outcome was median hourly wage. All firms used similar full-time job classifications, and wages excluded bonuses and overtime pay. Women and men in the sample were similar in age on average. Table 1 reports the ratio of women's to men's wages (1.00 would indicate equal pay) under four statistical models that added control variables cumulatively. The researcher also computed the unadjusted ratio separately by age group, shown in Figure 1. Occupational data showed that 70% of employees in the lowest-paying job categories were women, and that the median hourly wage of occupations with a majority of women was lower than that of occupations with a majority of men even when the two types of occupations required the same level of education.

qs.q: According to Table 1, women earned what percentage less than men per hour after all of the controls in Model 4 were included?
o: 18% is the unadjusted gap from Model 1.
14% is the gap after Model 2's education and experience controls and is not the final model.
Correct: 1.00 - 0.94 = 0.06, a 6% shortfall remained after controls.
94% is the women's earnings as a share of men's, not the shortfall.
qs.x: 1.00 - 0.94 = 0.06, a 6% shortfall remained after controls. Trap: Reporting the ratio itself or an intermediate model's gap instead of the final residual gap.

qs.q: What fraction of the unadjusted gap (Model 1) is accounted for by the difference between Model 2 and Model 4, namely weekly hours, occupation, and industry?
o: About 8%
8% is the percentage-point change itself, not its share of the unadjusted gap.
About 33%
33% would be 6 / 18, the remaining unexplained part of the gap, rather than the part accounted for.
About 67%
67% would be 12 / 18, which is not tied to the model differences.
About 44%
Correct: The ratio rises from 0.86 to 0.94, an 8-point change, out of an unadjusted gap of 18 points: 8 / 18 = 0.44.
qs.x: The ratio rises from 0.86 to 0.94, an 8-point change, out of an unadjusted gap of 18 points: 8 / 18 = 0.44. Trap: Using the percentage-point change rather than a proportion of the total gap.

qs.q: Which interpretation of Figure 1 is most consistent with sociological research on gender and work?
o: The widening gap at older ages is consistent with women's wages falling in real terms as they retire from the labor force.
The data are for full-time employees and show a wider gap rather than retirement-related decline.
The widening gap at older ages is consistent with older men having less education than older women in every cohort.
The passage reports no education differences by age, and education was controlled in Model 2 without eliminating the gap.
The narrowing of the gap at older ages reflects younger women entering higher-paying occupations over time.
The figure shows the gap widening (the ratio falls) with age, not narrowing.
The widening gap at older ages is consistent with career interruptions and caregiving penalties that accumulate over a woman's working life.
Correct: Mothers often face wage penalties, reduced hours, and slower promotion, so a gap that widens through the child-rearing and mid-career years is consistent with these cumulative effects.
qs.x: Mothers often face wage penalties, reduced hours, and slower promotion, so a gap that widens through the child-rearing and mid-career years is consistent with these cumulative effects. Trap: Reading the direction of a trend backward or assuming a cohort explanation not supported by the data.

qs.q: Why might Model 4 understate the role of discrimination in the wage gap?
o: Controlling for occupation increases the sample size and so changes the meaning of the median wage.
Adding controls does not change the sample size of a regression with complete data.
Occupation is measured at the firm level and so cannot be compared across the different firms in the sample.
Nothing in the passage says occupation was measured at the firm level; it was a variable for each employee.
Discrimination can occur only when employers know the gender of the workers, and occupation hides this information.
Discrimination can occur through many processes, including structural ones, and does not require such secrecy.
Sorting into lower-paying occupations may itself reflect barriers and the devaluation of work done mostly by women.

Correct: If women are channeled into occupations that pay less because of hiring practices, expectations, or devaluation of female-dominated work, adjusting for occupation removes part of the gap that is itself an outcome of discrimination.
qs.x: If women are channeled into occupations that pay less because of hiring practices, expectations, or devaluation of female-dominated work, adjusting for occupation removes part of the gap that is itself an outcome of discrimination. Trap: Assuming that an adjusted gap measures only discrimination-free pay differences.

passages.title: FL07 · Psych/Soc · Passage 10
text: A sleep-hygiene program was tested for its effect on a standardized attention score (higher is better; population SD about 15 points). Three independent two-group randomized trials compared the program with usual care, using the same outcome measure and the same two-sided significance level (alpha = 0.05). Study A enrolled 100 participants per group, Study B enrolled 2,000 per group, and Study C enrolled 20 per group. For each study, the researchers calculated the difference between group means, Cohen's d (the mean difference divided by the pooled standard deviation), the 95% confidence interval for the difference, and a p value from a two-sample test. Results are shown in Table 1. The pre-specified primary analysis in every study was the difference between group means on the attention score at 12 weeks, and all participants were analyzed in the groups to which they were randomized. A news report on Study B described the program as having a 'significant benefit,' and a report on Study C described the program as having 'no effect.'

qs.q: Which statement best compares Study B with Study A?
o: Study B has a larger effect size and a larger p value because its sample is much larger.
Study B's effect size (0.07) is smaller, not larger, than that of A.
Study B has a smaller effect size but is statistically significant because its sample is much larger.
Correct: Cohen's d is 0.07 for B versus 0.40 for A, but the large sample (2,000 per group) shrinks the standard error so that even a tiny difference gives p = 0.035.
Study B has the same effect size and the same p value because both studies used the same outcome measure.
The effect sizes and p values in Table 1 differ between the two studies.
Study B has a smaller effect size and a nonsignificant p value because its confidence interval is narrower.
Study B's p value of 0.035 is below 0.05, so it is significant, and a narrower interval does not imply nonsignificance.
qs.x: Cohen's d is 0.07 for B versus 0.40 for A, but the large sample (2,000 per group) shrinks the standard error so that even a tiny difference gives p = 0.035. Trap: Equating statistical significance with a large or practically important effect.

qs.q: The news report that Study C found 'no effect' is a misinterpretation mainly because:
o: The p value of 0.21 means there is a 21% chance that the program has no effect on attention.
A p value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis is true, not the probability that the null is true.
The mean difference of 6.0 points is the same as in Study B, so the program must have a significant effect.
Study B's difference was 1.0, not 6.0; the mean difference of 6.0 was in Studies A and C.
The interval includes both no effect and a large benefit, so the study was too small to rule out an effect the same size as Study A's.
Correct: A nonsignificant result with a wide interval (-3.3 to 15.3) is inconclusive; Study C has the same d (0.40) as Study A but only 20 per group, so it lacked power.
The confidence interval is centered at 6.0 and therefore proves that the true difference equals 6.0 points.
An interval gives a range of plausible values and does not prove that the true value equals the center.
qs.x: A nonsignificant result with a wide interval (-3.3 to 15.3) is inconclusive; Study C has the same d (0.40) as Study A but only 20 per group, so it lacked power. Trap: Reading a p value as the probability that the null hypothesis is true or a nonsignificant result as proof of no effect.

qs.q: Using Table 1, what is the Cohen's d for Study A?
o: 0.06 results from dividing by a pooled SD that is too large, such as 100 instead of 15.
2.5 is the inverse ratio (15 / 6).
0.20 is half the effect size and comes from dividing the difference by 30.
Correct: d = mean difference / SD = 6.0 / 15 = 0.40.
qs.x: d = mean difference / SD = 6.0 / 15 = 0.40. Trap: Inverting the ratio or dividing by the wrong standard deviation.

qs.q: Suppose the sleep program has no true effect and 20 independent trials like these are each tested at alpha = 0.05. About how many are expected to be statistically significant?
o: Zero would require a Type I error rate of 0, which alpha = 0.05 does not provide.
Correct: With a true null, the Type I error rate is 5%, so 0.05 x 20 = 1 trial is expected to give a significant result by chance.
Five would be 25% of the trials, not 5%.
Nineteen is the expected number of nonsignificant results.
qs.x: With a true null, the Type I error rate is 5%, so 0.05 x 20 = 1 trial is expected to give a significant result by chance. Trap: Assuming that when the null is true no trial will reach significance, or reversing significant and nonsignificant counts.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Results of three trials

passages.title: FL08 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 1
text: Bovine ribonuclease A (RNase A) is a 124-residue enzyme stabilized by four disulfide bonds formed by its eight cysteine residues. A researcher measured catalytic activity under several treatments to test how the native fold is specified. Samples were treated as described in Table 1, and activity was assayed both during treatment and after dialysis that removed urea and beta-mercaptoethanol (beta-ME) from the sample. In a second experiment, fully reduced and denatured enzyme was dialyzed free of beta-ME and allowed to reoxidize in air, either in buffer or in the continued presence of 8 M urea. Activity recovery was followed over 24 hours (Figure 1). Native RNase A is a compact single polypeptide with no bound cofactors, and the assay buffer contained no other proteins. Activity was measured by following hydrolysis of cyclic cytidine 2',3'-phosphate at 25 C and pH 7.0, and each value is the mean of three independent samples. Dialysis was carried out against a large volume of buffer for 24 hours at 4 C, using a membrane permeable to urea and beta-ME but not to the enzyme.

qs.q: According to Table 1, which statement best explains why activity returns after 8 M urea alone is removed?
o: Urea cleaves peptide bonds in the chain, and dialysis allows the enzyme to re-ligate them in the original order.
Urea disrupts hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic packing; it does not hydrolyze peptide bonds, and peptide bonds do not re-ligate on dialysis.
Disulfide bonds remain intact, so the covalently constrained chain can re-form its noncovalent interactions after urea is removed.
Correct: The disulfides were never broken in urea alone, which is why the chain is held near its native topology and refolds (96% recovery).
Urea reduces the disulfide bonds to thiols, which spontaneously reoxidize into the native pairs once urea is removed.
No reducing agent was present, so the disulfides stay intact; urea does not reduce them.
Urea only masks the active site without altering the structure of the protein, so removal restores activity immediately.
Activity was 3% during treatment, which reflects global unfolding, not simple masking of the active site.
qs.x: The disulfides were never broken in urea alone, which is why the chain is held near its native topology and refolds (96% recovery). Trap: Assuming urea breaks covalent bonds; urea disrupts only noncovalent interactions.

qs.q: What is the role of beta-ME in the second treatment of Table 1?
o: It oxidizes cysteine side chains to form additional disulfide bonds between the chains.
This is the opposite of its action; a reducing agent breaks disulfides rather than forming them.
It reduces each disulfide bond to a pair of free thiol groups.
Correct: Beta-ME is a thiol reducing agent that converts S-S bonds to two -SH groups through thiol-disulfide exchange, allowing complete unfolding in urea.
It hydrolyzes the peptide backbone adjacent to each cysteine residue.
Reducing agents act on S-S bonds, not on peptide bonds.
It disrupts hydrogen bonds in the secondary structure by acting as a chaotrope, as urea does.
Urea is the chaotrope; beta-ME is added specifically to cleave the covalent cross-links.
qs.x: Beta-ME is a thiol reducing agent that converts S-S bonds to two -SH groups through thiol-disulfide exchange, allowing complete unfolding in urea. Trap: Confusing a reducing agent with an oxidizing agent when describing disulfide chemistry.

qs.q: If the eight cysteines of fully reduced RNase A paired at random to form four disulfide bonds, about what percentage of the molecules would form the native pairing?
o: About 12%
1/8 treats the problem as choosing one partner for a single cysteine.
About 25%
1/4 counts only the four disulfide bonds, not the possible pairings.
About 1%

Correct: Eight cysteines can be paired into four disulfides in 7 x 5 x 3 x 1 = 105 ways, only one of which is native, so about 1/105, or roughly 1%. This matches the 1% recovery after oxidation in urea.
About 50%
1/2 assumes only two possible pairing arrangements.
qs.x: Eight cysteines can be paired into four disulfides in 7 x 5 x 3 x 1 = 105 ways, only one of which is native, so about 1/105, or roughly 1%. This matches the 1% recovery after oxidation in urea. Trap: Counting only the number of bonds rather than the number of possible pairings.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by Figure 1?
o: Disulfide bonds by themselves dictate the native fold, regardless of the surrounding solvent conditions.
Oxidation in urea formed disulfides but produced inactive protein, so disulfides alone do not specify the fold.
Refolding of RNase A requires a chaperone supplied by the buffer, and without it oxidation cannot yield the native pairs.
The assay buffer contained no other proteins, and no ribosomes or chaperones were involved.
The native fold is determined by the order in which the polypeptide emerges from a ribosome.
The experiment began with a complete polypeptide, so translation order was not tested.
The sequence encodes the fold, which forms when native noncovalent contacts are favored.
Correct: In buffer, reduced enzyme recovered 90% activity, whereas in urea (which prevents native noncovalent contacts) it recovered about 2%. Sequence plus favorable conditions suffice.
qs.x: In buffer, reduced enzyme recovered 90% activity, whereas in urea (which prevents native noncovalent contacts) it recovered about 2%. Sequence plus favorable conditions suffice. Trap: Attributing structure to the disulfide bonds alone; they stabilize the fold but pairing depends on the folded state.

qs.q: In a eukaryotic cell, where would the disulfide bonds of a secreted protein like RNase A most likely form?
o: The cytosol
The cytosol is kept reducing by high glutathione levels, which disfavors stable disulfides.
The mitochondrial matrix
The matrix is a reducing compartment, and RNase A is not a mitochondrial protein.
The lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum
Correct: The ER lumen is oxidizing and contains protein disulfide isomerase, which catalyzes formation and rearrangement of disulfides in secreted proteins.
The nucleoplasm
The nucleoplasm is reducing, and secreted proteins do not fold there.
qs.x: The ER lumen is oxidizing and contains protein disulfide isomerase, which catalyzes formation and rearrangement of disulfides in secreted proteins. Trap: Assuming disulfides form wherever cysteines are present; the redox state of the compartment matters.

r: 8 M urea + 0.1 M beta-ME, then air oxidation in 8 M urea

passages.title: FL08 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 2
text: Silencing of the tumor suppressor gene RGS-7 is frequent in a colon cancer cell line. Bisulfite sequencing of the RGS-7 promoter CpG island, chromatin immunoprecipitation for acetylated histone H3, and quantitative RT-PCR were performed on normal colonic fibroblasts and on the tumor line. Tumor cells were then cultured for 72 hours with 5-azacytidine (a cytidine analog that is incorporated into replicating DNA and covalently traps DNA methyltransferases), with trichostatin A (TSA, an inhibitor of histone deacetylases), or with both. Doubling time of the tumor cells was approximately 24 hours. Results are shown in Table 1. Histone acetylation is given relative to normal fibroblasts, and RGS-7 mRNA was normalized to a housekeeping transcript and expressed relative to normal fibroblasts. The researcher concluded that DNA methylation and histone deacetylation both contribute to repression of the gene. Each condition was run in triplicate, and the drug concentrations used had no effect on cell viability over the treatment period. Bisulfite conversion deaminates unmethylated cytosine to uracil but leaves methylated cytosine unchanged, so methylation at individual CpG sites can be read by sequencing. All cells were grown in the same medium.

qs.q: Which mechanism best explains how promoter CpG methylation represses transcription?
o: Methyl-CpG-binding proteins recruit histone deacetylases that compact chromatin and exclude transcription factors.
Correct: Methylated CpGs recruit MBD proteins with HDAC and remodeling complexes, producing condensed chromatin (the pattern of low acetylation in untreated tumor cells).
Methylated cytosine cannot base-pair with guanine, so RNA polymerase stalls at the promoter during elongation.
Methylated cytosine still base-pairs with guanine; methylation acts on chromatin accessibility and factor binding, not elongation.
Methylation converts the CpG island into RNA, so the gene is silenced through hybridization to the transcript.
Methylation is a covalent DNA modification and does not turn DNA into RNA.
Methylation of the template strand introduces stop codons into the mRNA, which then undergoes nonsense-mediated decay.
Methylation does not alter the coding sequence, so no codons change.
qs.x: Methylated CpGs recruit MBD proteins with HDAC and remodeling complexes, producing condensed chromatin (the pattern of low acetylation in untreated tumor cells). Trap: Thinking methylation changes the DNA sequence or base-pairing rather than recruiting chromatin-modifying proteins.

qs.q: Why did the tumor cells need to be cultured for 72 hours with 5-azacytidine for methylation to decrease?
o: The analog traps methyltransferase on replicating DNA, so new strands stay unmethylated after each division.
Correct: With a 24-hour doubling time, 72 hours allows about three rounds of replication; each round dilutes methylation because trapped DNMT1 cannot maintain it on new strands.
The analog must first be transcribed into RNA and translated into a demethylase enzyme before methyl groups can be removed.
The analog is incorporated into DNA, not translated, and it acts by inhibiting methyltransferase, not by inducing a demethylase.
The analog directly removes methyl groups from existing cytosines within minutes, but its effect is detected only after 72 hours.
The analog does not chemically remove methyl groups from existing cytosines.
The analog binds histones and gradually displaces methylated DNA from nucleosomes during interphase, independent of DNA replication.
The analog works through DNA incorporation, not histone binding, and nucleosomes remain bound to DNA.
qs.x: With a 24-hour doubling time, 72 hours allows about three rounds of replication; each round dilutes methylation because trapped DNMT1 cannot maintain it on new strands. Trap: Assuming the drug erases methyl marks directly; it depends on DNA replication.

qs.q: TSA alone increased RGS-7 mRNA even though promoter methylation stayed at 90%. Which explanation is most consistent with this result?
o: Greater histone acetylation loosens chromatin enough for partial transcription despite methylation.
Correct: Inhibiting HDACs preserves acetyl groups on lysines, neutralizing histone positive charge and loosening nucleosomes; methylation remained at 90%, so activation was only partial (0.18).
TSA removes methyl groups from CpG sites, but the net effect is partially masked by increased mRNA degradation.
Methylation was unchanged at 90%, so TSA did not remove methyl groups.
TSA increases methylation of histones, which directly activates RNA polymerase at the methylated promoter.
TSA inhibits deacetylases and does not increase histone methylation; the result involves acetylation.
TSA acts as a transcription factor that binds the methylated CpG island and recruits the general transcription machinery.
TSA is a small-molecule enzyme inhibitor, not a DNA-binding transcription factor.
qs.x: Inhibiting HDACs preserves acetyl groups on lysines, neutralizing histone positive charge and loosening nucleosomes; methylation remained at 90%, so activation was only partial (0.18). Trap: Believing the TSA effect must come through lower DNA methylation, ignoring the table value of 90%.

qs.q: Which comparison from Table 1 best supports the conclusion that methylation and deacetylation act together to repress RGS-7?
o: Both drugs alone increased mRNA above the untreated tumor level, but neither reached the normal level of 1.00.
Failure to reach 1.00 does not by itself show cooperation between the two mechanisms.
The increase in mRNA with both drugs (0.80) is greater than the sum of the increases with each drug alone (0.60).
Correct: Combined treatment raised mRNA from 0.05 to 0.85 (+0.80), whereas the single treatments gave +0.47 and +0.13 (sum 0.60), so the effects are greater than additive.
5-azacytidine increased mRNA more than TSA did, which shows that methylation is the only repressive mechanism.
TSA also increased expression, so methylation is not the only mechanism.
Normal fibroblasts have low methylation and high acetylation, which proves both marks are required for gene expression.
Correlation in normal cells does not show how the marks interact in treated tumor cells.
qs.x: Combined treatment raised mRNA from 0.05 to 0.85 (+0.80), whereas the single treatments gave +0.47 and +0.13 (sum 0.60), so the effects are greater than additive. Trap: Ranking which single drug worked better instead of comparing combined and summed effects.

passages.title: FL08 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 3
text: A researcher used a simulation to study genetic drift. Each replicate population contained N diploid individuals, random mating, no selection, no mutation, and no migration, and began with allele A at frequency 0.5. For each population size, 20 replicates were run for 50 generations. Expected heterozygosity declines in a finite population by a factor of (1 - 1/2N) each generation, so that H at generation t equals H(0) x (1 - 1/2N)^t, where H(0) = 2pq at the start. Table 1 gives the number of replicates in which allele A became fixed (frequency 1.0) or lost (frequency 0) by generation 50 and the mean heterozygosity at generation 50 across replicates. Figure 1 shows the expected decline of heterozygosity over time for each size. A replicate was scored as fixed if every individual carried only A, and as lost if no individual carried A. Heterozygosity was calculated from allele frequencies in each replicate at the end of generation 50 and then averaged. Generations were discrete and nonoverlapping, and each generation drew its parents at random from the previous one.

qs.q: Why do the N = 10 populations lose heterozygosity so much faster than the N = 1000 populations?
o: Small populations experience stronger natural selection against heterozygotes than large populations.
The simulation specified no selection.
Small populations have higher mutation rates, which convert heterozygotes into homozygotes.
The simulation specified no mutation.
Random sampling of gametes each generation causes larger chance fluctuations in allele frequency when few individuals reproduce.
Correct: With 20 gene copies, each generation's allele frequency is a small random sample of the previous one, so fixation or loss occurs quickly (17 of 20 replicates).
Inbreeding depression in small populations causes heterozygotes to leave fewer offspring.
Differential fitness was excluded; the loss is due to sampling error in a neutral model.
qs.x: With 20 gene copies, each generation's allele frequency is a small random sample of the previous one, so fixation or loss occurs quickly (17 of 20 replicates). Trap: Attributing the effect to selection or mutation when drift is a sampling-error process.

qs.q: Using the formula given, what is the expected heterozygosity at generation 50 for a population with N = 25?
o: Correct: (1 - 1/50)^50 = 0.98^50, about 0.36; multiplying by H(0) = 2(0.5)(0.5) = 0.50 gives about 0.18.
0.36 is the retained fraction and omits multiplying by the starting heterozygosity of 0.50.
0.30 is the approximate value for N = 50, not N = 25.
0.02 reflects the per-generation loss of 1/2N, not the cumulative result.
qs.x: (1 - 1/50)^50 = 0.98^50, about 0.36; multiplying by H(0) = 2(0.5)(0.5) = 0.50 gives about 0.18. Trap: Forgetting to multiply the retained fraction by the initial heterozygosity.

qs.q: Which change would most effectively counteract divergence in allele frequency among several small populations?
o: A reduction in the population size to increase the effect of sampling
Smaller populations would show more drift and diverge more.
A shift to self-fertilization in every population
Self-fertilization increases homozygosity within each population without restoring shared alleles.
A single strong bottleneck in each population
A bottleneck reduces diversity further and increases random divergence.
Exchange of about one migrant per population each generation
Correct: Gene flow introduces alleles from other populations, offsetting local fixation or loss and homogenizing allele frequencies.
qs.x: Gene flow introduces alleles from other populations, offsetting local fixation or loss and homogenizing allele frequencies. Trap: Assuming any demographic change reduces drift; only larger size or gene flow does.

qs.q: A few individuals from a large island population colonize a new island. Compared with the source population, the new population is most likely to show which pattern?
o: Allele frequencies identical to the source because all alleles are neutral
Small samples rarely mirror source frequencies even for neutral alleles.
Greater heterozygosity because mating occurs between unrelated founders
Founders carry a limited subset of alleles, so heterozygosity is usually lower.
Allele frequencies that differ from the source by chance, with reduced allelic diversity
Correct: This is the founder effect: a small sample carries only some alleles at chance frequencies, and a small size increases later drift.
Allele frequencies shifted toward the alleles with the highest fitness in the source
Chance, not fitness in the source, determines which alleles the founders carry.
qs.x: This is the founder effect: a small sample carries only some alleles at chance frequencies, and a small size increases later drift. Trap: Assuming a sample reproduces the source frequencies exactly.

qs.q: In one simulated N = 1000 population at generation 50, the frequency of A is 0.8. If mating is random, what is the expected frequency of heterozygotes among offspring?
o: 0.16 omits the factor of 2 (pq).
0.64 is p squared, the frequency of AA homozygotes.
0.20 is the frequency of the minor allele, not of heterozygotes.
Correct: Heterozygote frequency is 2pq = 2(0.8)(0.2) = 0.32 under Hardy-Weinberg conditions.
qs.x: Heterozygote frequency is 2pq = 2(0.8)(0.2) = 0.32 under Hardy-Weinberg conditions. Trap: Forgetting the factor of 2 or reporting a homozygote frequency.

h: Replicates with A fixed or lost

passages.title: FL08 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 4
text: Skeletal muscle stores glucose as glycogen, and its turnover is controlled by hormones that act through opposing covalent modifications. To study this, cultured differentiated myotubes were loaded with glycogen and then incubated for 60 minutes in medium containing 5 mM glucose with no hormone (control), 100 nM epinephrine, 100 nM insulin, or both hormones. Cyclic AMP, the fraction of glycogen phosphorylase in the active phosphorylated form (phosphorylase a), the fraction of glycogen synthase in the active form, and glycogen content were measured (Table 1). Glycogen content over time is shown in Figure 1. In a separate group, myotubes were pretreated with propranolol, a beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist, before epinephrine was added. Myotubes lack the glucagon receptor and glucose 6-phosphatase. Glycogen content is expressed as nmol glucosyl units per mg protein, and all values are means of four independent cultures. Initial glycogen content was 400 nmol/mg in every group, and cultures were handled identically apart from the additions listed.

qs.q: Which sequence best explains how epinephrine raised phosphorylase a in the myotubes?
o: Receptor activation inhibits adenylyl cyclase, lowering cAMP and releasing phosphatase inhibition, which phosphorylates phosphorylase.
cAMP rose rather than fell, so adenylyl cyclase was stimulated, not inhibited.
Receptor activation opens calcium channels, and calcium directly binds glycogen phosphorylase and converts it to the a form.
Calcium can activate phosphorylase kinase in muscle, but it does not bind phosphorylase to convert it directly, and the cAMP data point to the PKA route.
Receptor activation raises cAMP, which activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates phosphorylase kinase, which phosphorylates phosphorylase b.
Correct: cAMP rose from 5 to 60 pmol/mg; this activates PKA, which phosphorylates phosphorylase kinase, which in turn phosphorylates and activates phosphorylase (70% in the a form).
Receptor activation stimulates glucose uptake, and the rise in glucose 6-phosphate converts phosphorylase b into phosphorylase a.
Glucose 6-phosphate is an allosteric inhibitor of phosphorylase b, and the conversion is covalent, not driven by substrate level.
qs.x: cAMP rose from 5 to 60 pmol/mg; this activates PKA, which phosphorylates phosphorylase kinase, which in turn phosphorylates and activates phosphorylase (70% in the a form). Trap: Skipping the intermediate kinase cascade and linking the receptor directly to phosphorylase.

qs.q: Based on Figure 1, what was the mean rate of net glycogen loss in epinephrine-treated myotubes between 30 and 60 minutes?
o: 2.7 nmol/mg/min
Correct: Glycogen fell from 270 to 190 nmol/mg over 30 minutes: 80/30 = 2.7 nmol/mg/min.
3.5 nmol/mg/min
3.5 is the average over the full 60 minutes, (400 - 190)/60.
4.3 nmol/mg/min
4.3 is the rate from 0 to 30 minutes, 130/30, so it ignores the slowing of loss.
8.0 nmol/mg/min
8.0 comes from dividing 80 by 10 rather than by 30 minutes.
qs.x: Glycogen fell from 270 to 190 nmol/mg over 30 minutes: 80/30 = 2.7 nmol/mg/min. Trap: Using the whole-experiment average instead of the specified interval.

qs.q: In myotubes given both hormones, glycogen synthase was only 15% active, compared with 75% with insulin alone. Which interpretation is best supported?
o: Insulin and epinephrine bind the same receptor, so the two hormones compete and cancel each other out.
The hormones use distinct receptors and signaling pathways; they are not competitors at one receptor.
Insulin cannot activate glycogen synthase in the presence of any glucose, so the result reflects glucose rather than hormone.
Insulin alone raised synthase to 75% in the same 5 mM glucose.
Epinephrine activates glycogen synthase by phosphorylation, and insulin reverses this effect only at much higher doses.
Phosphorylation inactivates glycogen synthase, so epinephrine decreases its activity, and no dose comparison was made.
Sustained cAMP and PKA activity keeps glycogen synthase phosphorylated and inactive despite insulin.

Correct: With both hormones cAMP stayed high (55 pmol/mg), PKA-dependent phosphorylation of synthase (and phosphatase inhibition) predominated, so synthase remained mostly inactive and glycogen fell to 230.
qs.x: With both hormones cAMP stayed high (55 pmol/mg), PKA-dependent phosphorylation of synthase (and phosphatase inhibition) predominated, so synthase remained mostly inactive and glycogen fell to 230. Trap: Believing that phosphorylation activates every enzyme in the glycogen pathway.

qs.q: Myotubes pretreated with propranolol and then given epinephrine would most likely show which pattern at 60 minutes?
o: cAMP near 60 pmol/mg, phosphorylase a near 70%, and glycogen near 190 nmol/mg (as with epinephrine alone)
This is the unblocked epinephrine result.
cAMP near 5 pmol/mg, phosphorylase a near 10%, glycogen still near 400 nmol/mg
Correct: Blocking the beta-adrenergic receptor prevents epinephrine from raising cAMP, so phosphorylase and synthase stay near control values and glycogen is not mobilized.
cAMP near 60 pmol/mg, phosphorylase a near 10%, and glycogen near 520 nmol/mg
This mixes high cAMP with low phosphorylase a, which is not consistent with the cascade, and 520 is the insulin value.
cAMP near 4 pmol/mg, phosphorylase a near 70%, and glycogen near 190 nmol/mg
Phosphorylase a cannot rise to 70% without a rise in cAMP in this pathway, so low cAMP with high phosphorylase a is inconsistent.
qs.x: Blocking the beta-adrenergic receptor prevents epinephrine from raising cAMP, so phosphorylase and synthase stay near control values and glycogen is not mobilized. Trap: Forgetting that a receptor antagonist acts upstream and blocks every downstream effect.

passages.title: FL08 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 5
text: Fibronectin is an extracellular matrix glycoprotein containing a cell-binding region with the tripeptide Arg-Gly-Asp (RGD). To investigate how fibroblasts attach to fibronectin, researchers coated 96-well plates with bovine serum albumin (BSA) or fibronectin and added fibroblasts for 60 minutes. Nonadherent cells were washed away, and the percentage of cells remaining was determined (Table 1). Conditions included the soluble peptide GRGDS, a control peptide GRGES in which Asp is replaced by Glu, a function-blocking antibody against the integrin beta-1 subunit, nonimmune IgG, or EDTA, which chelates divalent cations. In a separate experiment, the GRGDS peptide was titrated into wells coated with fibronectin (Figure 1). Fibronectin-coated wells had no other adhesive proteins present, and the peptides were present throughout the assay. Cells were serum starved before the assay so that adhesive proteins in serum would not contribute, and every well received the same number of cells. Antibodies and peptides were added to cells 15 minutes before plating. Adherent cells were fixed and stained, and absorbance was converted to percent of the cells added using a standard curve. Each condition was run in sextuplicate.

qs.q: Which conclusion about the GRGDS and GRGES results is best supported?
o: Attachment depends on specific recognition of the RGD sequence, not just any similar short peptide.
Correct: GRGDS lowered adhesion from 88% to 21%, whereas GRGES, differing by one methylene in the side chain, left it at 85%, showing sequence specificity.
Cell attachment is mediated by electrostatic attraction between acidic peptides and the plasma membrane.
Both peptides are similar in charge, yet only one blocked adhesion; charge alone cannot explain this.
Cell attachment depends on fibronectin being phosphorylated within the RGD region of the cell-binding domain.
Phosphorylation was not examined, and the peptides are not modified.
GRGDS destroys the fibronectin coating on the plate, which would prevent adhesion of cells to the surface.
The control peptide did not impair adhesion, and the RGD peptide competes with fibronectin for binding rather than degrading it.
qs.x: GRGDS lowered adhesion from 88% to 21%, whereas GRGES, differing by one methylene in the side chain, left it at 85%, showing sequence specificity. Trap: Assuming any similar peptide would block adhesion; the control peptide differs by one residue and does not.

qs.q: Why does EDTA reduce adhesion to 12%?
o: EDTA cleaves the peptide bond between arginine and glycine in the RGD motif.
EDTA is a chelator and does not hydrolyze peptide bonds.
EDTA cross-links integrins into aggregates that cannot bind ligand.
Chelating cations does not cross-link proteins.
EDTA activates proteases that digest fibronectin on the plate.
No protease activation is implied; the effect is on the ion requirement of integrin binding.
Integrin binding to RGD ligands requires divalent cations such as Mg2+ or Ca2+, which EDTA removes.
Correct: Integrin ligand-binding sites coordinate a divalent cation (a metal ion-dependent adhesion site), so chelation prevents binding and cells wash away.
qs.x: Integrin ligand-binding sites coordinate a divalent cation (a metal ion-dependent adhesion site), so chelation prevents binding and cells wash away. Trap: Believing EDTA damages the substrate protein rather than integrin cation dependence.

qs.q: In Figure 1, adhesion falls halfway from its untreated value to its value at the highest GRGDS concentration at which of the following concentrations?
o: Below 10 micromolar
At 10 micromolar adhesion is still 81%, a minor reduction.
Between 10 and 30 micromolar
At 30 micromolar adhesion is still 62%, above the 54% midpoint.
Above 300 micromolar
Adhesion is already near the 21% plateau by 300 micromolar.
Between 30 and 100 micromolar
Correct: Adhesion falls from 88% to about 21% at saturation, a midpoint of about 54%. Adhesion is 62% at 30 micromolar and 38% at 100 micromolar, so 54% lies between those points.
qs.x: Adhesion falls from 88% to about 21% at saturation, a midpoint of about 54%. Adhesion is 62% at 30 micromolar and 38% at 100 micromolar, so 54% lies between those points. Trap: Reading the midpoint from the starting value of 88% instead of the midpoint between starting value and plateau.

qs.q: After binding fibronectin, integrins promote cell spreading by which intracellular mechanism?
o: Linking to actin filaments through adaptor proteins such as talin and vinculin
Correct: Integrin clustering assembles focal adhesions that anchor actin stress fibers and activate FAK and downstream pathways (outside-in signaling).
Opening ligand-gated ion channels in the plasma membrane that depolarize the cell and trigger calcium entry
Integrins are not ion channels.
Binding directly to intermediate filaments of the nuclear lamina, which transmits tension straight to chromatin
Integrins do not connect directly to nuclear lamins; their major cytoplasmic link is to actin.
Releasing calcium from the Golgi apparatus through IP3 receptors, which activates myosin light chain kinase
IP3 receptors are found chiefly on the endoplasmic reticulum, not the Golgi, and are not central to integrin adhesion.
qs.x: Integrin clustering assembles focal adhesions that anchor actin stress fibers and activate FAK and downstream pathways (outside-in signaling). Trap: Confusing integrin outside-in signaling with ion channel or second messenger release.

passages.title: FL08 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 6
text: Escherichia coli cells were made competent by treatment with ice-cold CaCl2 and transformed with pAR1, a high-copy plasmid carrying an origin of replication and the bla gene, which confers ampicillin resistance. In each tube, 100 microliters of competent cells and plasmid DNA were incubated on ice, heat shocked at 42 C for 45 seconds, returned to ice, and then given 900 microliters of nutrient broth and 1 hour of growth at 37 C. For each condition, 100 microliters of the 1 mL culture were spread on a plate. Controls are shown in Table 1, with 10 ng of plasmid used where plasmid was added. Figure 1 shows colonies per plate on ampicillin plates when the DNA amount was varied. Transformation efficiency is defined as transformants per microgram of plasmid DNA. Plates were incubated at 37 C overnight before colonies were counted. Wild-type cells of this strain are sensitive to ampicillin and carry no plasmid. Colony counts are means of duplicate plates. The plasmid DNA was purified and supercoiled, and the same preparation was used in every transformation. Competent cells were prepared in a single batch and kept on ice until use.

qs.q: What is the transformation efficiency, in transformants per microgram of DNA, for the 10 ng condition in Table 1?
o: 8.5 x 10^3 omits correcting for the one-tenth of the culture that was plated.
8.5 x 10^5 treats 10 ng as 0.001 microgram.
Correct: Only 1/10 of the culture was plated, so total transformants = 85 x 10 = 850; 850 / 0.01 microgram = 8.5 x 10^4 per microgram.
8.5 x 10^2 is the total number of transformants and is not divided by the amount of DNA.
qs.x: Only 1/10 of the culture was plated, so total transformants = 85 x 10 = 850; 850 / 0.01 microgram = 8.5 x 10^4 per microgram. Trap: Not correcting for the fraction of the culture plated, or mixing up ng and micrograms.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of the CaCl2 treatment and heat shock?
o: They activate the bla gene so that the cells become resistant to ampicillin.
The bla gene is expressed from the plasmid after uptake and is not turned on by these treatments.
They sterilize the culture so that only transformed cells remain.
These treatments permit survival; they do not kill nontransformed cells (the ampicillin does).
They increase the permeability of the cell envelope to plasmid DNA.
Correct: Divalent cations neutralize the repulsion between DNA and the lipopolysaccharide-containing envelope, and the brief heat shock helps DNA enter; without it only 2 colonies appeared.
They cut the plasmid at specific sites so that it can integrate into the chromosome.
Neither treatment is a restriction digestion, and the plasmid replicates on its own origin.
qs.x: Divalent cations neutralize the repulsion between DNA and the lipopolysaccharide-containing envelope, and the brief heat shock helps DNA enter; without it only 2 colonies appeared. Trap: Thinking the treatments select for transformants; selection comes from the antibiotic.

qs.q: What is the purpose of the 'cells, no DNA' control on the LB + ampicillin plate?
o: It measures the number of viable cells in the competent cell stock before any DNA is added to the cells.
The viable count is measured by the lawn on antibiotic-free LB, not by the ampicillin plate.
It confirms the recipient cells are ampicillin sensitive and the plates are uncontaminated.
Correct: Zero colonies show that colonies on the experimental plate result from the plasmid.
It shows that the heat shock step alone can cause the cells to acquire resistance to ampicillin.
No colonies grew, so heat shock alone did not confer resistance.
It confirms that the plasmid replicates in the recipient cells after heat shock and the recovery period.
No plasmid was added to this control.
qs.x: Zero colonies show that colonies on the experimental plate result from the plasmid. Trap: Confusing the negative control with the control that measures viable cell number.

qs.q: Which statement best explains the trend in efficiency seen at 50 and 100 ng in Figure 1?
o: Plasmid DNA at high concentration is toxic to ampicillin, which reduces colony number.
Plasmid DNA does not interact with ampicillin in this way.
Ampicillin is degraded more at high DNA concentrations, so colonies cannot form.
The antibiotic's stability is unrelated to DNA concentration.
High plasmid amounts inactivate the bla gene by recombination with the chromosome.
No recombination into the chromosome is described, and plasmids replicate autonomously.
The number of cells able to take up DNA is limited, so each additional nanogram yields fewer transformants.
Correct: Colonies rose only from 85 to 310 and 390 as DNA rose tenfold, so efficiency fell from 8.5 x 10^4 to 3.9 x 10^4 per microgram, consistent with a limited number of competent cells.
qs.x: Colonies rose only from 85 to 310 and 390 as DNA rose tenfold, so efficiency fell from 8.5 x 10^4 to 3.9 x 10^4 per microgram, consistent with a limited number of competent cells. Trap: Assuming colony number should rise in proportion to DNA at all amounts.

qs.q: How does the bla gene product allow the transformed cells to grow on ampicillin plates?
o: It prevents ampicillin from crossing the outer membrane by blocking porins.
Beta-lactamase is an enzyme and not a porin regulator.
It hydrolyzes the beta-lactam ring of ampicillin, inactivating the drug.
Correct: The bla gene encodes beta-lactamase, which cleaves the beta-lactam ring; ampicillin otherwise inhibits transpeptidases that cross-link peptidoglycan.
It pumps ampicillin out of the cell using ATP hydrolysis.
This describes efflux pumps, not beta-lactamase.
It modifies the ribosome so that ampicillin no longer inhibits translation.
Ampicillin targets cell wall synthesis, not the ribosome.
qs.x: The bla gene encodes beta-lactamase, which cleaves the beta-lactam ring; ampicillin otherwise inhibits transpeptidases that cross-link peptidoglycan. Trap: Confusing the mechanism of ampicillin with ribosome-targeting antibiotics.

passages.title: FL08 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 7
text: Mutations in RAS oncogenes and in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene frequently co-occur in cancers. To test how these alterations cooperate, researchers introduced into non-transformed fibroblasts either an empty vector, a constitutively active HRAS-G12V allele, a short hairpin RNA that knocks down p53 (shp53), or both HRAS-G12V and shp53. Cells were scored for colony formation in soft agar, a measure of anchorage-independent growth (Table 1), and counted over 8 days in culture (Figure 1). The G12V substitution abolishes the GTPase activity of Ras, which leaves the protein in the GTP-bound state. Cells expressing HRAS-G12V alone eventually stopped dividing and expressed senescence markers. Colonies were counted from three replicate plates per condition, and the means are reported. Cells were selected with antibiotics so that every cell counted carried the introduced constructs, and cells were grown in standard medium containing 10% serum. Efficiency of p53 knockdown was confirmed by immunoblotting, which showed an approximately 90% reduction in p53 protein. Senescence was assessed by staining for beta-galactosidase activity at pH 6. Soft agar colonies were counted after 3 weeks.

qs.q: Why does the G12V mutation make Ras behave as an oncogene?
o: The mutation eliminates Ras expression, so growth inhibitory signals are no longer relayed.
Loss of expression would be a loss-of-function change typical of a tumor suppressor, not an oncogene.
The protein stays GTP-bound and so signals constitutively, a gain of function that acts dominantly at the level of one allele.
Correct: Ras is active when GTP-bound; without GTPase activity it cannot switch off, so a single mutant allele promotes proliferation.
The mutant protein is stuck in the GDP-bound state, which activates downstream kinases.
The GDP-bound form is the inactive form.
The mutation disrupts both alleles, because tumor suppressor genes require two hits.
The two-hit pattern applies to tumor suppressors; an oncogenic mutation acts dominantly.
qs.x: Ras is active when GTP-bound; without GTPase activity it cannot switch off, so a single mutant allele promotes proliferation. Trap: Confusing oncogene gain of function with tumor suppressor loss of function.

qs.q: Which interpretation best accounts for the difference between the HRAS-G12V curve and the HRAS-G12V + shp53 curve in Figure 1?
o: Loss of p53 increases the GTPase activity of Ras, which restores normal growth control.
Ras remained mutant and GTPase-defective; p53 loss does not repair it.
Loss of p53 allows cells to bypass the senescence and growth arrest triggered by oncogenic Ras.
Correct: p53 mediates the senescence response to oncogenic stress; removing it allowed continued growth (45 x 10^5 cells at day 8 versus 3.2 x 10^5).
The shp53 construct itself encodes an oncogene that drives proliferation.
A short hairpin RNA only reduces expression of p53 and does not encode an oncogene.
The cells with shp53 are no longer dependent on nutrients, which allows indefinite growth.
Nutrient dependence was not measured, and cells still needed medium to grow.
qs.x: p53 mediates the senescence response to oncogenic stress; removing it allowed continued growth (45 x 10^5 cells at day 8 versus 3.2 x 10^5). Trap: Treating p53 as a growth promoter instead of a barrier against transformation.

qs.q: The shp53 construct alone produced only 6 colonies, far fewer than the HRAS-G12V + shp53 combination. What does this suggest about p53?
o: It is required for basic cell cycle progression, so loss of p53 slows the growth of every cell regardless of Ras status.
Cells with shp53 alone were not impaired, as indicated by their ability to form colonies.
It acts as an oncogene whose knockdown triggers apoptosis in cells with normal Ras, which limits colony formation.
p53 is a tumor suppressor, and the data do not show apoptosis.
It activates the Ras pathway, so loss of p53 is lethal to the cell unless Ras is also mutated by a second event.
Ras does not depend on p53 for activation.
It restrains proliferation but does not drive growth signaling, so its loss matters when a driver is present.
Correct: Loss of a brake alone causes little transformation (6 vs 2 colonies) but permits unrestrained growth when a driver such as Ras is active (187).
qs.x: Loss of a brake alone causes little transformation (6 vs 2 colonies) but permits unrestrained growth when a driver such as Ras is active (187). Trap: Expecting loss of a tumor suppressor to be strongly transforming on its own.

qs.q: A child inherits one mutant RB1 allele. Why is the child at high risk of retinoblastoma?
o: Only one additional somatic mutation or loss of the normal allele is needed in a retinal cell to eliminate RB1 function.
Correct: Per the two-hit model, the germline mutation is the first hit, and a single somatic second hit in any retinal cell unmasks the recessive loss of function.
The mutant allele is an oncogene that is dominant in its effect on every cell.
RB1 is a tumor suppressor that is recessive at the cellular level, not a dominant oncogene.
A normal RB1 allele cannot compensate for the mutant protein, which blocks the normal one in a dominant-negative manner.
Dominant-negative interference is not the usual mechanism for this risk.
Both RB1 alleles are inactivated in all cells by the inherited mutation.
The inherited mutation affects one allele; the second must be lost somatically.
qs.x: Per the two-hit model, the germline mutation is the first hit, and a single somatic second hit in any retinal cell unmasks the recessive loss of function. Trap: Treating the inherited allele as a dominant cause rather than as a first hit.

passages.title: FL08 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 8
text: Insulin and glucagon coordinate blood glucose between meals and after eating. In a study, ten healthy adults and ten adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus fasted overnight and then ingested 75 g of glucose. Blood was sampled at the times listed, and mean plasma glucose, insulin, and glucagon concentrations were measured (Table 1; glucose in mg/dL, insulin in microunits/mL, glucagon in pg/mL). Figure 1 plots the glucose data. For adults, a plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher two hours after a 75 g glucose load is diagnostic of diabetes. The type 2 diabetes group had a body mass index higher than that of the healthy group, and no participant was taking insulin or an insulin secretagogue on the day of the test. Participants were matched for age and sex, and venous blood was drawn through an indwelling catheter. Insulin and glucagon were measured by immunoassay, and glucose by an enzymatic method. All measurements were made in the same laboratory on the same day, and values are group means.

qs.q: Why does plasma glucagon fall after glucose ingestion in the healthy group?
o: Glucagon is rapidly taken up by skeletal muscle, which consumes it as a fuel after a meal.
Muscle does not clear glucagon as a fuel; the effect is on secretion.
Elevated glucose and the rise in insulin suppress glucagon secretion by pancreatic alpha cells.
Correct: Glucagon fell from 65 to 45 pg/mL at 30 minutes as insulin peaked at 60; high glucose and paracrine insulin inhibit alpha cells, appropriately reducing hepatic glucose output.
Insulin directly degrades glucagon in the circulation, which eliminates it within minutes.
Insulin does not degrade glucagon; it inhibits its release.
Glucose stimulates beta cells to convert glucagon to proinsulin.
Glucagon is not a precursor of proinsulin; they are separate hormones.
qs.x: Glucagon fell from 65 to 45 pg/mL at 30 minutes as insulin peaked at 60; high glucose and paracrine insulin inhibit alpha cells, appropriately reducing hepatic glucose output. Trap: Assuming glucagon is removed by the periphery rather than suppressed at the alpha cell.

qs.q: The diabetes group had high insulin but also high glucose. Which explanation is most consistent with these data?
o: Target tissues are resistant to insulin, so glucose uptake is impaired despite high insulin levels.

Correct: Insulin concentrations were equal to or higher than in the healthy group (peak 60 vs 60, with higher fasting values), yet glucose remained elevated, indicating reduced responsiveness (for example, impaired GLUT4 translocation).
Insulin secretion is essentially absent, so glucose cannot enter muscle and adipose cells in the usual manner.
Insulin was present at 45-60 microunits/mL, so it was not absent.
The insulin in this group is rapidly converted to glucagon in the liver soon after it is secreted into blood.
Insulin is not converted to glucagon.
The beta cells secrete too much glucagon, which blocks the insulin receptor on the surface of target cells.
Glucagon is made by alpha cells, not beta cells, and it does not block insulin receptors.
qs.x: Insulin concentrations were equal to or higher than in the healthy group (peak 60 vs 60, with higher fasting values), yet glucose remained elevated, indicating reduced responsiveness (for example, impaired GLUT4 translocation). Trap: Equating hyperglycemia with a lack of insulin secretion, as in type 1 diabetes.

qs.q: By what factor was the glucose rise from baseline to the peak value larger in the diabetes group than in the healthy group?
o: About 2.0
2.0 is the ratio of the peak values (285/140) and does not correct for the higher fasting baseline.
About 1.8
1.8 is the ratio of the 30-minute values (250/140) and also ignores baseline.
About 2.5
Correct: Rise in healthy group: 140 - 85 = 55 mg/dL. Rise in diabetes group: 285 - 150 = 135 mg/dL. 135/55 is about 2.5.
About 5.4
5.4 compares the diabetes rise with the healthy rise at 60 minutes (135/25), which is not the peak.
qs.x: Rise in healthy group: 140 - 85 = 55 mg/dL. Rise in diabetes group: 285 - 150 = 135 mg/dL. 135/55 is about 2.5. Trap: Comparing raw peak values instead of rises from each group's baseline.

qs.q: Which of the following responses is stimulated by glucagon in hepatocytes?
o: Activation of a receptor tyrosine kinase that promotes glycogen synthesis
This describes insulin signaling.
Increased glucose uptake through insulin-dependent GLUT4 transporters
GLUT4 is found in muscle and adipose tissue and is insulin-dependent; the liver uses GLUT2.
Inhibition of gluconeogenesis through reduced expression of PEPCK
Glucagon increases, not decreases, gluconeogenic gene expression.
Activation of a G protein-coupled receptor that raises cyclic AMP and promotes glycogen breakdown
Correct: Glucagon binds a Gs-coupled receptor, raising cAMP and activating PKA, which activates phosphorylase kinase and glycogenolysis and promotes gluconeogenesis.
qs.x: Glucagon binds a Gs-coupled receptor, raising cAMP and activating PKA, which activates phosphorylase kinase and glycogenolysis and promotes gluconeogenesis. Trap: Attributing insulin-like actions to glucagon or vice versa.

qs.q: Which statement about the 120-minute results is most accurate?
o: The healthy group meets the diagnostic threshold, because its glucose fell back below its fasting baseline by that time.
The healthy value was 90 mg/dL, far below 200.
Neither group meets the diagnostic threshold, because the glucose of both groups rose above fasting levels after the load.
All values that exceed fasting levels are not diagnostic; the criterion is 200 mg/dL at two hours.
The diabetes group does not meet the diagnostic threshold, because its glucose had already fallen from the 60-minute peak.
A decline from the peak does not matter; 240 mg/dL still exceeds 200.
The diabetes group meets the diagnostic threshold, with glucose still elevated despite higher insulin.
Correct: At 120 minutes, glucose was 240 mg/dL (at least 200) in the diabetes group, with insulin at 55 compared with 10 in the healthy group.
qs.x: At 120 minutes, glucose was 240 mg/dL (at least 200) in the diabetes group, with insulin at 55 compared with 10 in the healthy group. Trap: Applying the diagnostic criterion to the change from peak instead of the absolute value.
