Documented campaigns by industries have sought to create the appearance of scientific doubt about the hazards of their products, deliberately emphasizing uncertainty that the research community did not share. The existence of such campaigns complicates the argument above, since it shows that doubt can be cultivated for advantage and that it is not always a sign of an honest response to a past betrayal. Telling the two apart is difficult for a layperson, and it is a task for which no simple rule exists.

What follows for scientists is uncomfortable. It is not enough to be right; they must also be seen to be trustworthy, and that may mean admitting uncertainty openly, disclosing financial ties, and listening to communities rather than lecturing them. Some will regard such steps as a concession to unreason. But if trust is a relationship rather than a verdict on a set of claims, the maintenance of the relationship is part of the scientific enterprise, not a public-relations afterthought.

qs.q: The deficit model, as described in the passage, assumes that
o: public distrust of science results from a lack of knowledge
Correct: the passage defines it as the assumption that distrust arises from ignorance, so supplying facts is the remedy.
scientists distrust the public because it cannot evaluate evidence
The model concerns the public's distrust of science, not the reverse.
knowledge of a technology reliably increases worry about its risks
The passage reports that knowledgeable people may be more worried, which is a finding against the model, not part of it.
distrust arises mainly from the commercial alignment of institutions
This is part of the alternative approach.
qs.x: the passage defines it as the assumption that distrust arises from ignorance, so supplying facts is the remedy. Trap: Attributing the alternative approach's explanation to the deficit model.

qs.q: Which finding described in the passage most directly challenges the deficit model?
o: Communities that were subjects of unethical research may pass their suspicion on to people who never took part
This supports the institutional-history explanation but does not address whether knowledge raises trust.
Industries have run documented campaigns to create an appearance of scientific doubt about the hazards of their products
Manufactured doubt complicates the alternative account and does not test the deficit model directly.
Few ordinary people can personally verify more than a minuscule fraction of the scientific findings they rely on
This supports the testimony argument, not a test of knowledge against trust.
People who know a good deal about a technology may be more worried about it than people who know little
Correct: if knowledge and trust are weakly related, or inversely related, supplying facts will not reliably produce trust.
qs.x: if knowledge and trust are weakly related, or inversely related, supplying facts will not reliably produce trust. Trap: Choosing evidence that supports the alternative view without bearing on the deficit assumption.

qs.q: The author regards distrust among communities that were subjects of unethical research as
o: an irrational reaction that scientists can correct by disclosing more facts
The author says it is not irrational and that facts alone may not address it.
a reasonable response to evidence about how institutions have behaved
Correct: the author says this distrust is not irrational, being a response to evidence about institutions.
a form of manufactured doubt created by industries seeking commercial advantage
Manufactured doubt is a separate category, and the author says no such mechanism is claimed here.
a consequence of ignorance about the competence of research scientists
The author says such doubt concerns motives and history more than competence.
qs.x: the author says this distrust is not irrational, being a response to evidence about institutions. Trap: Equating all distrust with either ignorance or manipulation.

qs.q: The author mentions industry campaigns to manufacture doubt in order to
o: prove that every expression of public skepticism about science has been deliberately produced by commercial interests
The author says some skepticism is manufactured, not all.
qualify the claim that distrust reflects honest responses to past betrayals, since some doubt is cultivated for advantage
Correct: the author says the campaigns complicate the earlier argument by showing doubt can be cultivated and is not always honest.
argue that scientists should avoid disclosing financial ties so that campaigns cannot exploit them
The author recommends disclosure, not avoiding it.
show that the philosophical account of trust as tracking trustworthiness has been refuted by the evidence
The author says the argument is complicated, not refuted.
qs.x: the author says the campaigns complicate the earlier argument by showing doubt can be cultivated and is not always honest. Trap: Overextending a qualification into a sweeping claim.

qs.q: Which of the following findings would most support the claim that trust tracks perceived trustworthiness rather than knowledge?
o: Public trust in an institution rose after a campaign that repeated its findings, with the same reported conflicts of interest
A rise after repeating findings would fit the deficit model.
Public trust in an institution was lower among citizens who had read more of its published reports
Lower trust among those with more knowledge challenges the deficit model but does not isolate trustworthiness as the cause.
Public trust in an institution rose after it disclosed its financial ties, with public knowledge of the facts unchanged
Correct: a rise in trust after disclosure, with facts held constant, points to trustworthiness as the operative factor.
Public trust in an institution did not differ between citizens who owned shares in industry and citizens who did not
Shareholding does not test either factor.
qs.x: a rise in trust after disclosure, with facts held constant, points to trustworthiness as the operative factor. Trap: Choosing evidence that is merely against the deficit model rather than for the trustworthiness account.

qs.q: The phrase "not a public-relations afterthought" in the last sentence suggests that maintaining trust is
o: a task that scientists should delegate to professional communicators
The author places the responsibility on scientists, not on communicators.
part of the scientific enterprise itself rather than a secondary task
Correct: the author says that if trust is a relationship, maintaining it is part of the enterprise.
unnecessary when the scientific evidence on a question is strong
The author says it is not enough to be right.
a concession to unreason that scientists should make only reluctantly
The author reports that some scientists regard it as a concession to unreason but disagrees.
qs.x: the author says that if trust is a relationship, maintaining it is part of the enterprise. Trap: Adopting the objection the author reports as if it were the author's own view.

passages.title: FL08 · CARS · Passage 9
text: In the nineteenth century, John Henry Newman defended the university as a place devoted to the cultivation of the intellect for its own sake. Knowledge, he argued, is its own end, and a liberal education forms habits of judgment that outlast any particular subject. Around the same time, in the German states, a rival conception was emerging: the research university, in which the professor was not merely a teacher but an investigator, and students were initiated into the production of new knowledge. The modern university is a hybrid of these two, and like many hybrids it is prone to internal tension.

The tension is most visible in debates about the value of what universities do. Governments and families increasingly ask what a degree is for, and the answers they expect are economic: higher earnings, employability, contributions to innovation. Universities have responded by publicizing their role in the economy, in some cases by creating offices to license patents and attract industrial partners. Such activities can be defended as extending the benefits of research to society. But they raise a worry that the university's distinctive value, the disinterested pursuit of understanding, will be crowded out by what can be measured and sold. Fields that cannot promise a return, such as the study of ancient languages, are first to feel pressure.

Defenders of the economic emphasis reply that the older ideal was always an idealization. Newman's university served the sons of a narrow elite for whom the leisure to pursue knowledge for its own sake was a privilege, and the research university's ties to state and industry date back to its origins in the training of officials and the support of national projects. To insist on purity, they say, is to forget who was excluded. Expanding access to higher education has required justifying it to taxpayers in terms they understand.

There is another consideration that tends to fall between the two camps. The usefulness of knowledge is notoriously hard to predict. Mathematical results once thought to be curiosities have later become the foundation of cryptography; studies of the behavior of bacteria in unusual environments have yielded tools of molecular biology. If the practical payoff of inquiry is often unforeseeable, then a university that organized itself strictly around foreseeable returns would be worse at producing useful results, not better. On this argument, the case for unfettered inquiry can be made on utilitarian grounds, which may be more persuasive to a skeptical public than an appeal to the intrinsic dignity of the mind.

The argument has a limit, though. It justifies freedom of inquiry as a means, and what is justified only as a means may be abandoned when a better means appears. A university that defends itself solely by its eventual usefulness has conceded the premise of its critics, namely that its worth is to be measured by its outputs. Newman's insistence that knowledge is an end is therefore not merely nostalgic; it names a commitment that cannot be derived from any calculation of benefit, and without which the calculation itself would lose its point.

qs.q: According to the first paragraph, the modern university is prone to internal tension because it
o: pairs learning pursued for its own sake with research aimed at producing knowledge
Correct: the passage describes the university as a hybrid of Newman's ideal and the German research university.
has abandoned the study of established subjects in favor of the creation of new knowledge
The passage does not say established subjects were abandoned.
serves governments that ask for economic returns and families that ask for liberal education
The economic demand comes from both governments and families in the second paragraph.
inherited its structure from German professors who rejected the teaching of undergraduates
The German professor was an investigator as well as a teacher, not one who rejected teaching.
qs.x: the passage describes the university as a hybrid of Newman's ideal and the German research university. Trap: Taking the economic pressures in paragraph two as the source of the hybrid tension in paragraph one.

qs.q: The defenders of the economic emphasis argue that Newman's ideal
o: was available only to a narrow, privileged elite
Correct: they say the leisure to pursue knowledge for its own sake was a privilege of the elite students Newman's university served.
ignored the value of liberal habits of judgment
Newman's view is that liberal education forms such habits, and defenders do not deny it.
could never be defended on utilitarian grounds
The utilitarian defense is introduced later and is not part of the defenders' reply.
was introduced to justify industrial patents
Patents are a later development in universities' economic role.
qs.x: they say the leisure to pursue knowledge for its own sake was a privilege of the elite students Newman's university served. Trap: Confusing the defenders' historical point with the later utilitarian argument.

qs.q: The mathematics and bacteria examples are used to support which claim?
o: The practical value of inquiry is often unforeseeable, so a strict focus on foreseeable returns could reduce useful results
Correct: the passage says that if payoffs are unforeseeable, organizing around foreseeable returns would be worse at producing useful results.
Universities should teach only the subjects that have already been shown to produce commercial technologies
This reverses the point of the examples.
Researchers who pursue curiosities do so with the intention of producing cryptography and laboratory tools
The passage says the results were once thought to be curiosities, not that researchers intended these uses.
The intrinsic dignity of the mind is a stronger argument than any appeal to practical benefit
The passage says the utilitarian argument may be more persuasive to a skeptical public.
qs.x: the passage says that if payoffs are unforeseeable, organizing around foreseeable returns would be worse at producing useful results. Trap: Reading examples of surprising usefulness as an endorsement of targeted research.

qs.q: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument from unforeseeable usefulness?
o: Most major practical advances in recent decades came from projects funded partly by private industry
Source of funding does not show whether the work was directed.
Many mathematical results remain without any practical application after more than a century
Unused results are consistent with unpredictability.
Funding for the humanities has fallen faster than funding for engineering at most universities
Funding trends do not address how useful results arise.
Most major practical advances in recent decades came from projects aimed at a specific application from the start
Correct: if practical advances usually come from directed work, targeting foreseeable returns would not reduce useful results.
qs.x: if practical advances usually come from directed work, targeting foreseeable returns would not reduce useful results. Trap: Choosing a fact about funding that has a similar theme but does not test the claim.

qs.q: The author concludes that a university which defends itself solely by its eventual usefulness
o: will be more persuasive to the public than one that appeals to the dignity of the mind
The author grants persuasiveness earlier, but says the defense has a limit.
will necessarily abandon research in fields that cannot promise a financial return
The passage says such fields are pressured, but does not say they are necessarily abandoned.
concedes its critics' premise that its worth lies in what it produces
Correct: the final paragraph says such a defense concedes that worth is measured by outputs.
has shown that Newman's ideal can be derived from a calculation of benefit
The author says the commitment cannot be derived from a calculation of benefit.
qs.x: the final paragraph says such a defense concedes that worth is measured by outputs. Trap: Taking the persuasiveness point from paragraph four as the author's conclusion.

passages.title: FL08 · Chem/Phys · Passage 1
text: A physics class investigates energy conservation with a simple pendulum: a 0.50 kg brass bob hanging from a light, inextensible string of length 1.60 m. The bob is released from rest at a chosen angle θ0 from the vertical, and a photogate at the lowest point of the swing measures its speed. Take g = 9.8 m/s² and treat the bob as a point mass. Table 1 lists the height h of the release point above the lowest point, the speed predicted by assuming that mechanical energy is conserved, and the measured speed for four release angles. Figure 1 plots the square of the measured speed against h. The students notice that the measured speeds are consistently a little lower than the predictions and that the discrepancy grows as the release angle increases. They also plan a follow-up run in which the brass bob is replaced by a 1.0 kg bob of the same size, released from the same angles.

qs.q: If the bob is released from θ0 = 60°, what is its speed at the lowest point, ignoring air resistance?
o: 2.8 m/s, from v = √(gh) with h = 0.80 m
Dropping the factor of 2 gives √7.84 = 2.8 m/s, but ½mv² = mgh requires v² = 2gh.
4.0 m/s, from v = √(2gh) with h = 0.80 m
Correct: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2 × 9.8 × 0.80) = 3.96 m/s ≈ 4.0 m/s.
5.6 m/s, from v = √(2gL) with the full string length as the drop
The bob falls only L(1 − cos 60°) = 0.80 m, not the whole 1.60 m string length.
16 m/s, the numerical value of 2gh in m²/s²
2gh = 15.7 m²/s² is v², so the square root must still be taken.
qs.x: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2 × 9.8 × 0.80) = 3.96 m/s ≈ 4.0 m/s. Trap: Using the string length L instead of the vertical drop L(1 − cos θ0), or forgetting the square root or the factor of 2 in mgh = ½mv².

qs.q: At the lowest point of the 60° release, what is the tension in the string?
o: 4.9 N, since the tension at the bottom equals the weight mg
The bob is moving along a circular arc, so T must exceed mg to supply the centripetal force.
9.8 N, since T = mg + mv²/L = 4.9 N + 4.9 N
Correct: At the bottom the net upward force supplies the centripetal force: T − mg = mv²/L, so T = 4.9 + (0.50)(15.7)/1.60 = 9.8 N.
14.7 N, since T = 3mg at the bottom of every swing
T = 3mg holds only for release from the horizontal (θ0 = 90°); at 60° T = mg(3 − 2cos 60°) = 2mg.
19.6 N, since T = mg + 2mv²/L
The centripetal term is mv²/L, with no extra factor of 2.
qs.x: At the bottom the net upward force supplies the centripetal force: T − mg = mv²/L, so T = 4.9 + (0.50)(15.7)/1.60 = 9.8 N. Trap: Assuming the tension at the bottom of the swing is just mg, or applying the 3mg result that is valid only for a horizontal release.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for the measured speeds in Table 1 being slightly lower than the predicted speeds?
o: The string tension does negative work on the bob throughout the swing, removing kinetic energy.
Tension is always perpendicular to the bob's velocity, so it does no work.
Part of the energy is stored as elastic potential energy as the string stretches.
The string is described as inextensible, so it stores no elastic energy.
Air drag and friction at the pivot do negative work on the bob, converting some mechanical energy to thermal energy.
Correct: Nonconservative forces remove mechanical energy, and the loss grows with the path length traveled, which is larger for larger release angles.
The bob's mass lowers its speed through v = √(2gh/m), so a heavier bob falls more slowly.
Mass cancels from mgh = ½mv², so the predicted speed does not depend on mass.
qs.x: Nonconservative forces remove mechanical energy, and the loss grows with the path length traveled, which is larger for larger release angles. Trap: Thinking that tension does work on a pendulum bob, even though it is perpendicular to the motion at every instant.

qs.q: The slope of the line through the data in Figure 1 is closest to which quantity?
o: 9.8 m/s², the free-fall acceleration g
G would be the slope of v² versus 2h, not of v² versus h.
4.9 m/s², half the free-fall acceleration
The factor is 2g, not g/2.
0.05 s²/m, the reciprocal of 2g
The slope of v² (m²/s²) versus h (m) has units of m/s², not s²/m.
19 m/s², approximately 2g, because v² = 2gh
Correct: Since v² = 2gh, a plot of v² against h is a line of slope 2g ≈ 19.6 m/s²; the measured slope is about 19 m/s².
qs.x: Since v² = 2gh, a plot of v² against h is a line of slope 2g ≈ 19.6 m/s²; the measured slope is about 19 m/s². Trap: Reading the slope of v² versus h as g instead of 2g, or inverting the axes.

qs.q: In the follow-up run, the 1.0 kg bob is released from 60°. Compared with the 0.50 kg bob, its bottom speed and kinetic energy there will be
o: a speed lower by a factor of √2 and unchanged kinetic energy.
The speed does not depend on mass, and KE = mgh scales with mass.
doubled speed and quadrupled kinetic energy.
Speed is independent of mass, so KE only doubles.
unchanged speed and doubled kinetic energy.
Correct: v = √(2gh) is independent of mass, while KE = mgh doubles when m doubles.
unchanged speed and unchanged kinetic energy.
The speed is unchanged but the larger mass gives twice the kinetic energy at the same speed.
qs.x: v = √(2gh) is independent of mass, while KE = mgh doubles when m doubles. Trap: Believing that heavier objects gain more speed, rather than more energy, when they fall through the same height.

graph.title: Figure 1. Square of measured bottom speed versus release height

passages.title: FL08 · Chem/Phys · Passage 2
text: A student studies the gas-phase reaction 2 NO + Cl2 → 2 NOCl in a rigid vessel at 25 °C by the method of initial rates. In each experiment, known starting concentrations of NO and Cl2 are mixed, and the initial rate of NOCl formation is determined from the early pressure change. Table 1 lists the results of four experiments. The student proposes the following two-step mechanism: Step 1 is a fast, reversible equilibrium, NO + Cl2 ⇌ NOCl2, with equilibrium constant K. Step 2 is slow, NOCl2 + NO → 2 NOCl, with rate constant k2. The student wants to determine whether the experimental rate law is consistent with this mechanism and then use it to predict rates under new conditions. Rates are expressed as the rate of disappearance of Cl2, in M/s, so that no stoichiometric factor is needed in the rate law. The vessel is thermostatted so that the temperature stays constant, and each initial rate is measured before more than a few percent of the reactants have been consumed, so the listed concentrations can be taken as constant during a measurement.

qs.q: Based on Experiments 1 and 2, what is the reaction order with respect to NO?
o: Second order, because doubling [NO] at constant [Cl2] quadruples the rate
Correct: The rate rises from 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ to 8.0 × 10⁻⁵ M/s, a factor of 4 = 2², so the order in NO is 2.
First order, because the rate increases when [NO] is increased
A first-order dependence would only double the rate when [NO] doubles.
Zero order, because NO is a reactant that is consumed to make product
The rate clearly changes with [NO]; order cannot be read from the stoichiometric coefficient or from consumption.
Third order, because the overall reaction is third order
The order in each reactant comes from the data; 2 NO's overall coefficient does not fix the order in NO alone.
qs.x: The rate rises from 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ to 8.0 × 10⁻⁵ M/s, a factor of 4 = 2², so the order in NO is 2. Trap: Equating the order with the stoichiometric coefficient or confusing the rate ratio (4) with the order (2).

qs.q: What is the value of the rate constant k for the rate law rate = k[NO]²[Cl2]?
o: 20 M⁻² s⁻¹
Correct: k = rate / ([NO]²[Cl2]) = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ / (1.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.010) = 20 M⁻² s⁻¹ (units for a third-order reaction).
0.20 M⁻¹ s⁻¹
This results from dividing by [NO]² only, and the units are those of a second-order constant.
This results from dividing by a single concentration of 0.010 M, which would be first order.
This is simply the initial rate in Experiment 1, not the rate constant.
qs.x: k = rate / ([NO]²[Cl2]) = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ / (1.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.010) = 20 M⁻² s⁻¹ (units for a third-order reaction). Trap: Dividing the rate by too few concentration terms, which also produces the wrong units for k.

qs.q: What is the predicted initial rate when [NO] = 0.030 M and [Cl2] = 0.020 M?
o: 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, from 3² × 2 × rate₁
Correct: Relative to Experiment 1, [NO] is tripled (factor 9) and [Cl2] is doubled (factor 2): 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 9 × 2 = 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ M/s.
1.2 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, from 3 × 2 × rate₁ (first order in NO)
This treats the reaction as first order in NO (3 × 2 × 2.0 × 10⁻⁵).
5.4 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, from 3² × 3 × rate₁ (Cl2 also tripled)
This applies a factor of 3 rather than 2 for Cl2, as if [Cl2] had also been tripled.
7.2 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, from 3² × 2² × rate₁ (second order in Cl2)
This treats the reaction as second order in Cl2 (9 × 4 × 2.0 × 10⁻⁵).
qs.x: Relative to Experiment 1, [NO] is tripled (factor 9) and [Cl2] is doubled (factor 2): 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 9 × 2 = 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ M/s. Trap: Applying the concentration ratios without raising them to the correct reaction orders.

qs.q: Assuming that Step 1 is a fast pre-equilibrium and Step 2 is rate-limiting, which rate law does the proposed mechanism predict?
o: Rate = k1[NO][Cl2], which treats Step 1 as rate-limiting
Step 1 is fast and reversible, so it does not set the overall rate.
Rate = k2K[NO]²[Cl2], matching the experimental rate law
Correct: Rate = k2[NOCl2][NO], and the fast equilibrium gives [NOCl2] = K[NO][Cl2], so rate = k2K[NO]²[Cl2].
Rate = k2[NOCl2][NO], the rate law of the slow step as written
An intermediate cannot appear in the final rate law; it must be replaced using the equilibrium.
Rate = k2K[NO][Cl2]², since Cl2 appears in the pre-equilibrium
Cl2 enters Step 1 once, so it appears with a power of 1.
qs.x: Rate = k2[NOCl2][NO], and the fast equilibrium gives [NOCl2] = K[NO][Cl2], so rate = k2K[NO]²[Cl2]. Trap: Leaving a reaction intermediate in the final rate law instead of substituting from the fast equilibrium.

passages.title: FL08 · Chem/Phys · Passage 3
text: Students measure the rise of water in clean glass capillary tubes of different inner radii r, each dipped vertically into a beaker of water at 20 °C. The liquid rises until the upward force from surface tension balances the weight of the raised column, giving h = 2γcosθ / (ρgr), where γ is the surface tension, θ is the contact angle, and ρ is the liquid density. For water on clean glass, θ ≈ 0°, ρ = 1,000 kg/m³, and g = 9.8 m/s². Table 1 and Figure 1 show the measured heights. In a second set of measurements, the students compare other liquids in a tube of r = 0.50 mm: mercury (γ = 0.48 N/m, ρ = 13,600 kg/m³, θ = 140° on glass) and a dilute detergent solution whose surface tension is 0.025 N/m but which otherwise behaves like water (ρ = 1,000 kg/m³, θ ≈ 0°). The effect of the thin film of liquid on the tube wall is ignored.

qs.q: According to the equation, what rise is expected for water in a tube of inner radius 0.10 mm?
o: About 74 mm, with the factor of 2 left out
This omits the factor of 2 in the numerator.
About 15 mm, with r misread as 1.0 mm
This is the height for r = 1.00 mm, from a decimal-place error in the radius.
About 149 mm, from h ∝ 1/r
Correct: h = 2γcosθ/(ρgr) = 2(0.0728)/(1,000 × 9.8 × 1.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.149 m, in agreement with h ∝ 1/r from Figure 1.
About 298 mm, with 0.10 mm read as a diameter
This arises from treating 0.10 mm as the diameter, using r = 0.05 mm.
qs.x: h = 2γcosθ/(ρgr) = 2(0.0728)/(1,000 × 9.8 × 1.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.149 m, in agreement with h ∝ 1/r from Figure 1. Trap: Mis-converting millimeters to meters, or confusing the tube radius with its diameter.

qs.q: Using the slope of Figure 1, what is the surface tension of water?
o: Correct: The slope is h·r = 14.9 mm² = 1.49 × 10⁻⁵ m²; γ = slope × ρg/2 = 1.49 × 10⁻⁵ × 9,800 / 2 ≈ 0.073 N/m.
This omits the 1/2 that comes from the factor 2 in 2γ.
This divides by 4 rather than by 2.
This uses the slope in mm² without converting it to m².
qs.x: The slope is h·r = 14.9 mm² = 1.49 × 10⁻⁵ m²; γ = slope × ρg/2 = 1.49 × 10⁻⁵ × 9,800 / 2 ≈ 0.073 N/m. Trap: Forgetting to convert the slope from mm² to m², or dropping the factor of 2 in the equation.

qs.q: In the tube with r = 0.50 mm, the mercury meniscus will most likely be
o: raised by about 11 mm, because the density of mercury is high
The magnitude is right but a contact angle above 90° gives a depression.
depressed by about 14 mm, because mercury is a nonwetting liquid
This ignores the cos 140° factor (−0.766); the magnitude should be 11 mm.
neither raised nor depressed, because ρ appears in the denominator
Density affects the magnitude of the height but the sign is set by cosθ.
depressed by about 11 mm, because cosθ is negative for θ = 140°.
Correct: h = 2(0.48)(cos 140°)/(13,600 × 9.8 × 5.0 × 10⁻⁴) = −0.011 m; the negative sign means a depression, as cohesion exceeds adhesion.
qs.x: h = 2(0.48)(cos 140°)/(13,600 × 9.8 × 5.0 × 10⁻⁴) = −0.011 m; the negative sign means a depression, as cohesion exceeds adhesion. Trap: Ignoring the sign of cosθ for a nonwetting liquid, which turns a capillary rise into a depression.

qs.q: The detergent solution is drawn into the tube with r = 0.50 mm. What rise is expected?
o: About 30 mm
This assumes the rise is unaffected by the surface tension.
About 87 mm
This inverts the ratio of surface tensions, so that the rise increases.
About 10 mm
Correct: h is proportional to γ: 29.7 mm × (0.025/0.0728) = 10.2 mm.
About 3.5 mm
This squares the ratio of surface tensions, but h is linear in γ.
qs.x: h is proportional to γ: 29.7 mm × (0.025/0.0728) = 10.2 mm. Trap: Inverting or squaring the ratio of surface tensions when scaling the capillary rise.

graph.title: Figure 1. Capillary rise of water versus reciprocal radius

passages.title: FL08 · Chem/Phys · Passage 4
text: A Hofmann voltameter contains 0.1 M aqueous Na2SO4 between two inert platinum electrodes. A constant current of 2.00 A is passed through the cell, and the H2 and O2 gases are collected in separate inverted tubes at 25 °C and 1.00 atm, where the molar gas volume is 24.5 L/mol. The Faraday constant is 96,485 C per mole of electrons. Table 1 and Figure 1 give the volumes of gas collected at four times. Water vapor and gas solubility are ignored. The overall reaction is 2 H2O → 2 H2 + O2. The sulfate and sodium ions are not consumed. A few drops of universal indicator, which is green near pH 7, red in acid, and blue-violet in base, are added to the solution before the current is started. The student keeps the current constant by adjusting a variable resistor in series with the cell and holds the temperature at 25 °C with a water bath. Stirring is not used, so local pH changes near each electrode remain observable.

qs.q: How many moles of electrons have passed through the cell after 600 s?
o: 6.2 × 10⁻³ mol, the moles of H2 formed
This is the moles of H2 formed (n(e⁻)/2), not of electrons.
2.5 × 10⁻² mol, the value at 1,200 s
This corresponds to 1,200 s (2,400 C), not 600 s.
2.1 × 10⁻⁴ mol, with t in minutes
This treats the time as 10 minutes, giving 20 C instead of 1,200 C.
qs.x: n(e⁻) = Q/F = (2.00 A × 600 s)/96,485 C/mol = 1,200/96,485 = 1.24 × 10⁻² mol. Trap: Mixing up moles of electrons with moles of H2, or leaving the time in minutes.

qs.q: Why is the volume of H2 collected about twice the volume of O2?
o: H2 has half the molar mass of O2 and so occupies twice the volume at the same T and P.
At the same T and P, a mole of any ideal gas has the same volume regardless of its mass.
Oxygen is far more soluble in water than hydrogen, so half the O2 stays dissolved.
Solubility is ignored in this setup, and neither gas is that soluble.
Forming H2 takes 2 mol e⁻ per mole while forming O2 releases 4 mol e⁻ per mole, so the same charge makes twice as many moles of H2.
Correct: The same charge makes n(H2) = Q/2F and n(O2) = Q/4F, and equal moles of ideal gases occupy equal volumes at the same T and P.
Hydrogen forms at the anode, where the current density is larger.
Hydrogen forms at the cathode, and the same current passes through both electrodes.
qs.x: The same charge makes n(H2) = Q/2F and n(O2) = Q/4F, and equal moles of ideal gases occupy equal volumes at the same T and P. Trap: Attributing the 2:1 ratio to gas properties such as molar mass, when it follows from the electrons transferred per mole.

qs.q: In this neutral Na2SO4 solution, which half-reaction occurs at the cathode?
o: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na(s)
E° = −2.71 V is much more negative than the reduction of water, so Na⁺ is not reduced in water.
This is an oxidation, which occurs at the anode.
Correct: Water is reduced (E° ≈ −0.83 V at pH 14, about −0.41 V at pH 7), far more easily than Na⁺ (−2.71 V), forming H2 gas.
SO4²⁻ + 4 H⁺ + 2 e⁻ → SO2 + 2 H2O
Sulfate is not reduced under these conditions, and its reduction is kinetically very slow.
qs.x: Water is reduced (E° ≈ −0.83 V at pH 14, about −0.41 V at pH 7), far more easily than Na⁺ (−2.71 V), forming H2 gas. Trap: Selecting the reduction of the metal cation (Na⁺) rather than the reduction of water in an aqueous solution of an active metal salt.

qs.q: If the current is increased to 4.00 A, about how long does it take to collect 152 mL of H2 under the same conditions?
o: Correct: At 2.00 A, 152 mL of H2 takes 600 s; volume is proportional to charge (I × t), so doubling I halves the time to 300 s.
This quarters the time, as if the volume depended on the square of the current.
The current does affect how fast the gas is produced, so the time should change.
This doubles the time, inverting the effect of a larger current.
qs.x: At 2.00 A, 152 mL of H2 takes 600 s; volume is proportional to charge (I × t), so doubling I halves the time to 300 s. Trap: Misapplying the proportionality n = It/(nF) by thinking more current slows, or has no effect on, gas production.

qs.q: As the electrolysis proceeds, what color changes are expected in the indicator-containing solution?
o: Blue-violet near the anode and red near the cathode
This reverses the products; H⁺ forms at the anode and OH⁻ at the cathode.
Blue-violet near both electrodes, since water is converted into OH⁻
Only the cathode makes OH⁻; the anode makes H⁺.
Red near the anode (acidic) and blue-violet near the cathode (basic)
Correct: Anode: 2 H2O → O2 + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻ generates H⁺; cathode: 2 H2O + 2 e⁻ → H2 + 2 OH⁻ generates OH⁻.
No change near either electrode, since Na2SO4 is a neutral salt
The ions of the salt only carry current; water itself is oxidized and reduced, shifting local pH.
qs.x: Anode: 2 H2O → O2 + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻ generates H⁺; cathode: 2 H2O + 2 e⁻ → H2 + 2 OH⁻ generates OH⁻. Trap: Assuming a neutral salt solution cannot change in pH during electrolysis.

graph.title: Figure 1. Gas volume collected versus electrolysis time

passages.title: FL08 · Chem/Phys · Passage 5
text: A student studies standing waves in a metal pipe that is closed at one end and open at the other. A small speaker held near the open end is swept through a range of frequencies, and the loudest responses are recorded as resonances. The pipe has length L = 0.600 m and inner radius r = 0.025 m. The air temperature is 20 °C, and the speed of sound is v ≈ 331 + 0.6T m/s, where T is in °C. Because the pressure antinode at the closed end is a displacement node, and the displacement antinode at the open end actually lies slightly outside the pipe, the effective length is L + 0.6r. Table 1 compares the three lowest measured resonances with predictions made with the uncorrected length L and with the corrected effective length. The student wonders how the resonance pattern and the frequencies would change if the pipe were open at both ends or if the room were warmer.

qs.q: Which set of resonant frequencies is expected for this pipe?
o: Only odd multiples of the lowest frequency, because the closed end is a displacement node and the open end a displacement antinode
Correct: The pipe supports λ = 4L_eff/n for odd n only, giving f, 3f, 5f, as in the measured 139, 418, and 696 Hz.
All integer multiples of the lowest frequency, as in a pipe open at both ends
A pipe with one closed end cannot support the even harmonics.
Only even multiples of the lowest frequency, because the closed end is a displacement antinode
The closed end is a node, and the data (139, 418, 696 Hz) show odd multiples.
Only odd multiples of the lowest frequency, because the closed end is a displacement antinode
The odd harmonics are correct, but the closed end is a displacement node, not an antinode.
qs.x: The pipe supports λ = 4L_eff/n for odd n only, giving f, 3f, 5f, as in the measured 139, 418, and 696 Hz. Trap: Reversing which end of the pipe is the node and which is the antinode, or applying the open-open harmonic series.

qs.q: Ignoring the end correction, what would be the lowest resonance of an open-open pipe of the same length?
o: 143 Hz, from f = v/(4L)
This is the closed-pipe fundamental.
572 Hz, from f = v/L
This takes the wavelength to be L, but the fundamental has λ = 2L.
429 Hz, from f = 3v/(4L)
This is the third resonance of the closed pipe.
286 Hz, from f = v/(2L)
Correct: For a pipe open at both ends, λ = 2L, so f = 343/(2 × 0.600) = 286 Hz.
qs.x: For a pipe open at both ends, λ = 2L, so f = 343/(2 × 0.600) = 286 Hz. Trap: Using the closed-pipe relationship f = v/4L for a pipe that is open at both ends.

qs.q: If the air warms to 30 °C and the pipe length is unchanged, the lowest resonance will be closest to
o: 139 Hz, because the pipe length alone fixes the resonant frequency
The frequency depends on v/λ, so a change in v changes it.
137 Hz, because warmer air is less dense and carries sound more slowly
Sound travels faster, not slower, in warmer air.
144 Hz, because the frequency is proportional to the Celsius temperature
F is proportional to v, which is not proportional to the Celsius temperature; v = 349 m/s gives 142 Hz.
142 Hz, because v rises by about 2% while L_eff is fixed.
qs.x: v = 331 + 0.6(30) = 349 m/s, so f = 349/(4 × 0.615) = 142 Hz, up from 139 Hz. Trap: Assuming the resonant frequency is set only by the pipe length, ignoring its dependence on the speed of sound.

qs.q: Why are the measured frequencies lower than those predicted from the uncorrected length L?
o: The open-end antinode forms slightly beyond the pipe, so the standing wave fits a longer effective length.
Correct: A longer effective length gives a longer wavelength (λ = 4L_eff) and thus a lower frequency for the same sound speed.
The closed end reflects the wave with a delay, shortening the effective length.
A shorter effective length would raise, not lower, the frequency.
The speed of sound inside the pipe is lower than 343 m/s because of friction against the walls.
Wall effects are far too small to account for a 2.5% shift and are not the origin of the end correction.
The speaker adds energy that lowers the natural frequency of the air column.
A driving source selects resonances but does not shift the natural frequencies of the column.
qs.x: A longer effective length gives a longer wavelength (λ = 4L_eff) and thus a lower frequency for the same sound speed. Trap: Believing the end correction shortens the pipe, rather than lengthening its effective length.

passages.title: FL08 · Chem/Phys · Passage 6
text: The binding energy of a nucleus equals the energy equivalent of its mass defect, Δm = Z·m(¹H) + N·m(n) − m(atom), where atomic masses are used so that electron masses cancel. Take m(¹H) = 1.007825 u, m(n) = 1.008665 u, and 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c². Table 1 lists the atomic masses of four nuclides together with their calculated mass defects and binding energies, and Figure 1 plots the binding energy per nucleon against mass number A. Nuclear energy can be released by splitting a heavy nucleus (fission) or by joining light nuclei (fusion), because in both cases the products have greater binding energy per nucleon. For the fission of ²³⁵U, assume the two fragments each have A ≈ 118 and a binding energy of about 8.5 MeV per nucleon, and neglect any emitted neutrons. Students compare reactions by subtracting the total binding energy of the reactants from that of the products, because a positive difference corresponds to energy released as kinetic energy and radiation.

qs.q: What is the mass defect of ⁴He?
o: 4.0326 u, the mass of the free nucleons
This is the mass of the separated nucleons (2 H atoms + 2 neutrons), not the defect.
0.0152 u, half the mass defect
This halves the correct mass defect, counting only one pair of nucleons.
28.3 u, the binding energy in MeV
This is the binding energy in MeV mistakenly written with the unit u.
qs.x: Δm = 2(1.007825) + 2(1.008665) − 4.002603 = 4.032980 − 4.002603 = 0.0304 u. Trap: Confusing the mass defect (in u) with the total mass of the nucleons or with the binding energy in MeV.

qs.q: Which of the four nuclides has the most stable nucleus per nucleon, according to Table 1?
o: ²³⁵U, because it has the largest total binding energy
Total binding energy grows with the number of nucleons; BE per nucleon is the stability measure.
⁴He, because it has the smallest mass defect
A smaller mass defect means less binding, and ⁴He has much lower BE/A than ⁵⁶Fe.
⁵⁶Fe, because it has the highest binding energy per nucleon
Correct: Stability per nucleon is measured by BE/A, which peaks near A ≈ 56–62; ⁵⁶Fe has 8.79 MeV per nucleon.
²H, because it has the lowest atomic mass
Atomic mass alone says nothing about stability; ²H has the lowest BE/A.
qs.x: Stability per nucleon is measured by BE/A, which peaks near A ≈ 56–62; ⁵⁶Fe has 8.79 MeV per nucleon. Trap: Comparing total binding energies of nuclei with different numbers of nucleons rather than binding energy per nucleon.

qs.q: Approximately how much energy is released when one ²³⁵U nucleus splits into two A ≈ 118 fragments?
o: About 1,780 MeV
This is the total binding energy of ²³⁵U, not the energy released.
About 210 MeV
Correct: ΔE = 235 × (8.5 − 7.59) ≈ 214 MeV, the difference between the fragments' and ²³⁵U's total binding energies.
About 2,000 MeV
This is the total binding energy of the fragments, not the difference.
About 0.9 MeV
This is the gain per nucleon; it must be multiplied by 235 nucleons.
qs.x: ΔE = 235 × (8.5 − 7.59) ≈ 214 MeV, the difference between the fragments' and ²³⁵U's total binding energies. Trap: Reporting the binding energy of one nucleus, or the per-nucleon gain, as the energy released in the reaction.

qs.q: How much energy is released when two ²H nuclei fuse to form one ⁴He nucleus?
o: About 28 MeV
This is the binding energy of ⁴He alone, neglecting the binding energy already present in the two deuterons.
About 6 MeV
This is roughly the difference of per-nucleon values, 7.1 − 1.1 = 6, not the difference of totals.
About 4.4 MeV
This is the combined binding energy of the two deuterons.
About 24 MeV
Correct: ΔE = BE(⁴He) − 2 × BE(²H) = 28.3 − 2(2.2) = 23.9 MeV.
qs.x: ΔE = BE(⁴He) − 2 × BE(²H) = 28.3 − 2(2.2) = 23.9 MeV. Trap: Not subtracting the initial binding energy of the reactants from that of the products.

graph.title: Figure 1. Binding energy per nucleon versus mass number

passages.title: FL08 · Chem/Phys · Passage 7
text: A chemist adds dilute AgNO3 dropwise to a solution containing 0.050 M NaCl and 0.0050 M Na2CrO4 at 25 °C. Both silver salts are sparingly soluble: AgCl is white and Ag2CrO4 is brick red. Table 1 lists their solubility products and the minimum [Ag⁺] needed to begin precipitation from this solution. Volume changes on addition are negligible, and a precipitate begins to form when the ion product exceeds Ksp. In a separate test, the chemist adds concentrated aqueous NH3 to a suspension of solid AgCl, and the solid dissolves as the complex ion forms: Ag⁺ + 2 NH3 ⇌ Ag(NH3)2⁺, with a large formation constant Kf = 1.6 × 10⁷. The chemist also asks what happens to the solubility of AgCl if the water is replaced by 0.10 M NaCl. The temperature is held at 25 °C so that the Ksp values stay constant, and the chemist assumes ideal behavior of all ions and ignores any hydrolysis of chromate.

qs.q: Which solid precipitates first as AgNO3 is added, and why?
o: Ag2CrO4, because its Ksp is smaller than that of AgCl
The Ksp values cannot be compared directly for salts with different formulas; the required [Ag⁺] decides.
AgCl, because it needs a much lower [Ag⁺] (3.6 × 10⁻⁹ M) to begin precipitating
Correct: Precipitation begins when Q exceeds Ksp; AgCl reaches that point at 3.6 × 10⁻⁹ M Ag⁺, well before the 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ M required for Ag2CrO4.
Ag2CrO4, because its minimum [Ag⁺] is the larger value
A larger required [Ag⁺] means that the salt precipitates later.
Both precipitate together, because they come from the same Ag⁺ source
The two salts have different thresholds, so they precipitate sequentially.
qs.x: Precipitation begins when Q exceeds Ksp; AgCl reaches that point at 3.6 × 10⁻⁹ M Ag⁺, well before the 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ M required for Ag2CrO4. Trap: Ranking the precipitation order by comparing Ksp values of salts with different stoichiometries instead of the ion concentration needed.

qs.q: At the moment Ag2CrO4 first appears, what is [Cl⁻] in solution?
o: 3.6 × 10⁻⁹ M, the [Ag⁺] for AgCl
This is the [Ag⁺] at which AgCl begins to precipitate, not [Cl⁻].
Correct: [Ag⁺] = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ M at that point, so [Cl⁻] = Ksp(AgCl)/[Ag⁺] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰/1.5 × 10⁻⁵ = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ M.
2.4 × 10⁻⁴ M, the fraction remaining
This is the fraction of chloride that remains, not its concentration.
5.0 × 10⁻² M, the starting [Cl⁻]
This is the starting [Cl⁻], ignoring the AgCl that has already precipitated.
qs.x: [Ag⁺] = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ M at that point, so [Cl⁻] = Ksp(AgCl)/[Ag⁺] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰/1.5 × 10⁻⁵ = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ M. Trap: Mixing up the [Ag⁺] threshold with the remaining anion concentration, or ignoring the chloride already removed.

qs.q: What percentage of the original chloride has precipitated when Ag2CrO4 begins to form?
o: This overstates the remaining chloride by a factor of about 50.
Correct: Remaining fraction = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵/0.050 = 2.4 × 10⁻⁴, so 99.98% has precipitated; the separation is nearly quantitative.
This treats the remaining fraction as 24%, confusing 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ with 0.24.
This is the percent of chloride that remains, not the percent that precipitated.
qs.x: Remaining fraction = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵/0.050 = 2.4 × 10⁻⁴, so 99.98% has precipitated; the separation is nearly quantitative. Trap: Reporting the percentage left in solution rather than the percentage precipitated.

qs.q: What is the molar solubility of AgCl in 0.10 M NaCl?
o: This is √Ksp, the solubility in pure water, ignoring the common ion.
This is the Ksp value itself, not a concentration.
This multiplies Ksp by [Cl⁻] instead of dividing.
Correct: s = [Ag⁺] = Ksp/[Cl⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰/0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M, far lower than in pure water because of the common ion effect.
qs.x: s = [Ag⁺] = Ksp/[Cl⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰/0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M, far lower than in pure water because of the common ion effect. Trap: Using √Ksp in a solution that already contains a common ion.

qs.q: Why does AgCl dissolve in concentrated NH3?
o: Complexation by NH3 lowers [Ag⁺], so Q falls below Ksp and more AgCl dissolves.
Correct: Formation of Ag(NH3)2⁺ removes free Ag⁺, shifting the dissolution equilibrium AgCl ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ to the right.
NH3 raises the Ksp of AgCl by acting as a polar solvent.
Ksp depends only on temperature; NH3 does not change it.
NH3 reduces Ag⁺ to Ag(s), which leaves Cl⁻ free in solution.
NH3 is a ligand, not a reducing agent, and Ag(NH3)2⁺ retains silver in the +1 state.
NH3 reacts with Cl⁻ to form NH4Cl, which is more soluble than AgCl.
Cl⁻ is a spectator-type anion here and does not react with NH3; the complexation of Ag⁺ drives dissolution.
qs.x: Formation of Ag(NH3)2⁺ removes free Ag⁺, shifting the dissolution equilibrium AgCl ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ to the right. Trap: Believing a ligand changes Ksp rather than shifting the equilibrium by removing a product ion.

passages.title: FL08 · Chem/Phys · Passage 8
text: Hybridization of carbon influences molecular geometry as well as bond lengths, strengths, and acidities. Table 1 summarizes data for ethane, ethene, and ethyne. Each carbon atom mixes its 2s and 2p orbitals to form hybrid orbitals: sp³ (25% s character) in ethane, sp² (33% s) in ethene, and sp (50% s) in ethyne. The remaining unhybridized p orbitals form π bonds. Figure 1 plots the C–H bond length against the s character of the carbon hybrid orbital used in the bond. The pKa of the C–H bond reflects how well the conjugate base, a carbanion, stabilizes its lone pair in a hybrid orbital. A student also considers two molecules built from these fragments: propyne, CH3–C≡CH, and acrylonitrile, CH2=CH–C≡N. The unhybridized p orbitals overlap sideways to form π bonds, while hybrid orbitals overlap end-on to form σ bonds. Bond energies refer to the C–C bond in each molecule, and the data are approximate gas-phase values.

qs.q: What are the hybridizations of the three carbon atoms in propyne, CH3–C≡CH, from left to right?
o: sp³, sp², sp
The central carbon has a triple bond, so it is sp, not sp².
sp³, sp, sp
Correct: The CH3 carbon has four σ bonds (sp³); each alkyne carbon has two σ bonds and two π bonds (sp).
sp², sp, sp
The CH3 carbon has four single bonds and is sp³.
sp³, sp³, sp
A carbon in a triple bond is linear (sp), not tetrahedral.
qs.x: The CH3 carbon has four σ bonds (sp³); each alkyne carbon has two σ bonds and two π bonds (sp). Trap: Assigning hybridization by counting hydrogens instead of counting σ bonds plus lone pairs on each carbon.

qs.q: Which statement best explains the trend in C–H bond length in Table 1?
o: Orbitals with more s character hold the electrons closer to the nucleus, giving shorter C–H bonds.
Correct: Greater s character places electron density nearer the carbon nucleus, which shortens and strengthens the C–H bond (106.0 pm for sp versus 109.4 pm for sp³).
Orbitals with more p character extend farther along the bond axis, bringing H closer.
More p character makes the orbital longer and the bond longer, not shorter.
The π bonds in ethyne pull the C–H bonding electrons toward the C≡C bond and shorten C–H.
Π bonds are perpendicular to the C–H σ bond and do not account for the trend.
Carbon becomes less electronegative with more s character, giving a stronger bond.
Electronegativity of carbon increases, not decreases, with s character.
qs.x: Greater s character places electron density nearer the carbon nucleus, which shortens and strengthens the C–H bond (106.0 pm for sp versus 109.4 pm for sp³). Trap: Treating p character as the source of bond shortening, when s character is the factor that draws electrons toward the nucleus.

qs.q: Which feature of the conjugate base best explains why ethyne (pKa ~25) is much more acidic than ethane (pKa ~50)?
o: The carbanion lone pair occupies a p orbital that can delocalize over the triple bond.
The lone pair of the acetylide is in an sp orbital in the plane of the σ framework, not delocalized into the π system.
The sp carbanion has a higher energy because the electrons are held farther from the nucleus.
Electrons in an sp orbital are held closer, not farther.
The carbanion lone pair occupies an sp orbital with 50% s character, which is closer to the nucleus and lower in energy.
Correct: Greater s character stabilizes the lone pair, so the sp carbanion is more stable and its conjugate acid is more acidic.
The C–C triple bond is the weakest of the three, so it is easier to break the C–H bond.
The triple bond is the strongest (839 kJ/mol), and C–H deprotonation does not break the C–C bond.
qs.x: Greater s character stabilizes the lone pair, so the sp carbanion is more stable and its conjugate acid is more acidic. Trap: Attributing acidity to the C–C bond strength or to delocalization instead of the s character of the orbital holding the lone pair.

qs.q: How many σ bonds and π bonds does acrylonitrile, CH2=CH–C≡N, contain?
o: 7 σ and 2 π
The triple bond holds one σ and two π bonds, and the double bond one σ and one π, so π total is 3.
5 σ and 4 π
This counts only 5 σ bonds, omitting a C–H bond or the σ component of a multiple bond.
6 σ and 4 π
This counts 4 π bonds, but there are only three: one in the double bond and two in the triple bond.
6 σ and 3 π
Correct: σ: 3 C–H, 1 C=C, 1 C–C, 1 C≡N = 6; π: 1 in C=C and 2 in C≡N = 3.
qs.x: σ: 3 C–H, 1 C=C, 1 C–C, 1 C≡N = 6; π: 1 in C=C and 2 in C≡N = 3. Trap: Counting every line in a Lewis structure as a σ bond, or forgetting the σ component of each multiple bond.

passages.title: FL08 · Chem/Phys · Passage 9
text: A biochemist calibrates a size-exclusion (gel filtration) column using protein standards of known molecular weight. The column has a void volume V0 = 40.0 mL, determined with blue dextran (2,000 kDa), which is excluded from the pores of the beads, and a total volume Vt = 120 mL. Each protein is run in a neutral buffer with moderate salt concentration, and its elution volume Ve is recorded. The partition coefficient is defined as Kav = (Ve − V0)/(Vt − V0). Table 1 gives the standards, and Figure 1 plots Kav against log10 of the molecular weight, which gives a straight line, Kav = 0.945 − 0.282 log M (M in kDa). The biochemist then applies the column to a purified enzyme of unknown size, which elutes at 70 mL, and to a second protein X, which elutes at 40 mL. SDS-PAGE under reducing conditions of the enzyme shows a single band at 35 kDa.

qs.q: Why do larger proteins elute earlier from a size-exclusion column?
o: They bind more strongly to the beads, which carries them through faster.
SEC separates by size, not by binding; strong binding would delay, not hasten, elution.
They carry more charge, which makes them migrate faster through the column.
SEC is run with moderate salt to suppress charge effects and does not separate by charge.
They diffuse more rapidly than small proteins and so reach the end of the column first.
Larger molecules diffuse more slowly; the order arises from access to pore volume.
They are excluded from the pores in the beads and travel only through the volume between beads.
Correct: Small molecules enter the pores and have access to a larger volume, so they take longer to elute; large molecules are excluded and pass through faster.
qs.x: Small molecules enter the pores and have access to a larger volume, so they take longer to elute; large molecules are excluded and pass through faster. Trap: Thinking that large molecules are retained more, as in many other chromatographic methods, when SEC is the reverse.

qs.q: What is the approximate molecular weight of the enzyme that elutes at 70 mL?
o: About 158 kDa, the nearest standard
This is simply the nearest standard (aldolase, 66 mL), not an interpolated value.
About 67 kDa, the albumin standard
This is albumin, which elutes at 74 mL, later than the enzyme.
About 105 kDa
About 240 kDa, from the wrong axis
This results from reading the wrong axis of Figure 1 when converting Kav to molecular weight.
qs.x: Kav = (70 − 40)/80 = 0.375; log M = (0.945 − 0.375)/0.282 = 2.02, so M ≈ 105 kDa. Trap: Assigning the unknown the mass of the nearest standard instead of interpolating on the log scale.

qs.q: What does the elution of protein X at 40 mL indicate?
o: Its molecular weight is exactly 2,000 kDa, equal to that of blue dextran.
Any protein larger than the exclusion limit elutes at V0; the mass cannot be inferred.
It has no molecular weight because it does not interact with the column.
It has a mass but is simply too large to enter the pores.
Its size exceeds the exclusion limit of the column, so its mass cannot be determined from the calibration.
Correct: Elution at V0 means Kav = 0, so the protein is completely excluded from the pores.
It is a very small molecule that passes through the pores without delay.
Small molecules enter the pores and elute near Vt, not V0.
qs.x: Elution at V0 means Kav = 0, so the protein is completely excluded from the pores. Trap: Assigning a specific large mass to a protein that elutes in the void volume.

qs.q: Albumin (67 kDa) forms a dimer in a different buffer. About what elution volume is expected for the dimer?
o: About 68 mL
About 74 mL
This is the elution volume of the monomer.
About 80 mL
This would be a smaller species that elutes later than the monomer.
About 56 mL
This is the elution volume of ferritin (440 kDa), a much larger protein.
qs.x: Dimer M = 134 kDa, log M = 2.13, Kav = 0.945 − 0.282(2.13) = 0.345, and Ve = 40 + 0.345(80) ≈ 68 mL. Trap: Predicting that a larger complex elutes later, or ignoring the oligomeric state of the protein.

qs.q: The enzyme elutes at 70 mL (about 105 kDa) but shows a single 35 kDa band on reducing SDS-PAGE. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: It is a monomer, because SDS-PAGE shows only one band.
A single band means identical subunits, but the native mass of 105 kDa is three times the subunit mass.
It is a homodimer, because two identical subunits give a single band.
A dimer of 35 kDa subunits would be about 70 kDa and would elute near 74 mL, later than 70 mL.
It is a homotrimer of identical 35 kDa subunits.
Correct: SEC under native conditions reports the mass of the whole complex, while SDS-PAGE under reducing conditions separates subunits; 105/35 = 3 identical subunits.
The SEC result is wrong, because SDS-PAGE is more accurate than gel filtration.
The two methods measure different things: native complex size versus denatured subunit size.
qs.x: SEC under native conditions reports the mass of the whole complex, while SDS-PAGE under reducing conditions separates subunits; 105/35 = 3 identical subunits. Trap: Assuming that SEC and SDS-PAGE must give the same mass, when one reports native size and the other reports subunit size.

passages.title: FL08 · Chem/Phys · Passage 10
text: Chiral molecules rotate the plane of plane-polarized light. The observed rotation α in a polarimeter is related to the specific rotation by α = [α] × l × c, where l is the path length in dm and c is the concentration in g/mL. A chemist prepares the (S)-enantiomer of a chiral secondary alcohol in enantiomerically pure form; its specific rotation is +40.0 °·mL·g⁻¹·dm⁻¹ at 589 nm and 20 °C, so the (R)-enantiomer has a specific rotation of −40.0. All solutions are prepared in ethanol at c = 0.100 g/mL and measured in a 1.00 dm tube unless noted. Ethanol is optically inactive, and the polarimeter is zeroed with a blank tube of pure solvent before each measurement. Table 1 lists the observed rotations of four samples, and Figure 1 shows how α varies with the percentage of the (S)-enantiomer in calibration mixtures of the two enantiomers. The rotation of a mixture is the weighted sum of the rotations of its components.

qs.q: What is the composition of Sample B?
o: Correct: α/α(pure S) = 2.00/4.00 = 50% enantiomeric excess of (S), so (S) = 50% + 50%/2 = 75% and (R) = 25%; this matches the calibration line at +2.00°.
A racemic mixture would show zero rotation, not +2.00°.
This would give 75% ee and α = +3.00°.
This would give 25% ee and α = +1.00°.
qs.x: α/α(pure S) = 2.00/4.00 = 50% enantiomeric excess of (S), so (S) = 50% + 50%/2 = 75% and (R) = 25%; this matches the calibration line at +2.00°. Trap: Reading the ratio of rotations (50%) as the percentage of the major enantiomer rather than the enantiomeric excess.

qs.q: What is the composition of Sample C?
o: This corresponds to a 50% ee and α = −2.00°.
The negative rotation shows an excess of (R), not (S).
This would be a 50% ee of (S), giving a positive rotation.
Correct: The negative rotation means (R) is in excess; ee = 1.00/4.00 = 25%, so (R) = 50% + 12.5% = 62.5%.
qs.x: The negative rotation means (R) is in excess; ee = 1.00/4.00 = 25%, so (R) = 50% + 12.5% = 62.5%. Trap: Interpreting the percent ee as the percent of the major enantiomer, or ignoring the sign of the rotation.

qs.q: Which conclusion about Sample D is valid?
o: It must be a meso compound, because only meso compounds show no optical rotation.
A racemic mixture also gives zero rotation, so the observation is not specific to meso compounds.
It must be a pure enantiomer whose rotation is too small to detect.
A pure enantiomer of this alcohol rotates strongly (±4.00° here).
It must contain no stereocenters, because stereocenters always cause rotation.
A racemic mixture contains stereocenters yet shows no net rotation.
It could be a racemic mixture or an achiral compound, since either gives no net rotation.
Correct: Equal and opposite rotations of a 50:50 mixture cancel; an achiral compound has no rotation at all, so α = 0 does not distinguish them.
qs.x: Equal and opposite rotations of a 50:50 mixture cancel; an achiral compound has no rotation at all, so α = 0 does not distinguish them. Trap: Believing that zero optical rotation proves a compound is achiral.

qs.q: Sample B is diluted to c = 0.050 g/mL and measured in a 2.00 dm tube. What is the expected observed rotation?
o: This accounts for the dilution but not the longer tube.
Correct: [α] of the mixture = 0.50 × 40.0 = +20.0; α = 20.0 × 2.00 dm × 0.050 g/mL = +2.00°, as the doubled path length offsets the halved concentration.
This uses the specific rotation of the pure enantiomer, rather than that of the mixture.
This halves the rotation twice, using both the concentration and the path length incorrectly.
qs.x: [α] of the mixture = 0.50 × 40.0 = +20.0; α = 20.0 × 2.00 dm × 0.050 g/mL = +2.00°, as the doubled path length offsets the halved concentration. Trap: Forgetting that observed rotation scales with both path length and concentration.

graph.title: Figure 1. Observed rotation versus percent (S) in calibration mixtures

passages.title: FL08 · Psych/Soc · Passage 1
text: Upright posture depends on the integration of vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive input. A researcher measured postural sway in 12 healthy adults and in 12 adults with bilateral vestibular hypofunction, a reduced function of the inner-ear balance organs. Each participant stood barefoot on a force platform for 30 s under four conditions: eyes open on a firm surface (EO-Firm), eyes closed on a firm surface (EC-Firm), eyes open on a compliant foam pad (EO-Foam), and eyes closed on foam (EC-Foam). The foam pad distorts the signals that arise from the ankles and soles of the feet. Sway was quantified as the total path length, in centimeters, traveled by the center of pressure. A trial was stopped early if the participant stepped off the platform or grabbed a support rail. Mean sway path lengths are shown in Table 1. In the EC-Foam condition, 5 of the 12 participants with vestibular hypofunction had to end the trial early, whereas none of the healthy participants did.

qs.q: Which condition requires postural control to depend most heavily on vestibular input?
o: EO-Firm, because vision and ankle signals both remain fully available to guide balance
All three systems are available here, so no one system is forced to dominate.
EC-Firm, because removing vision leaves ankle and foot signals fully intact and reliable
Proprioceptive and tactile input from the firm surface can still stabilize posture, so the vestibular system is not the main cue.
EO-Foam, because vision remains available to compensate for the degraded ankle signals
Vision is available to substitute for degraded ankle input, so vestibular reliance is reduced.
EC-Foam, because vision is absent and the foam makes ankle and foot signals unreliable
Correct: With eyes closed and a distorted somatosensory surface, the vestibular system is the only remaining reliable source of balance information.
qs.x: With eyes closed and a distorted somatosensory surface, the vestibular system is the only remaining reliable source of balance information. Trap: Choosing eyes-closed firm surface because it is the usual Romberg test, forgetting the foam also degrades proprioception.

qs.q: In the EC-Foam condition, the mean sway path of the vestibular hypofunction group was approximately how many times that of the healthy group?
o: Correct: 241 / 97 is approximately 2.5.
1.5 would correspond to a path of about 145 cm.
2.0 would correspond to a path of about 194 cm.
3.5 would correspond to a path of about 340 cm.
qs.x: 241 / 97 is approximately 2.5. Trap: Dividing 97 by 241 or subtracting values (144) instead of forming the ratio the stem asks for.

qs.q: A participant tilts the head forward while standing still. Which structures primarily detect this change in head position relative to gravity?
o: The semicircular canals, in which hair cells are bent by endolymph moving during rotation of the head
The canals mainly report angular (rotational) acceleration, not static tilt.
The otolith organs, in which hair cells are covered by a gelatinous layer weighted with calcium carbonate crystals
Correct: The utricle and saccule contain otoliths whose weight shifts with linear acceleration and static head tilt, bending hair cells.
The cochlea, in which hair cells are displaced by traveling waves along the basilar membrane after sound
The cochlea transduces sound, not head position.
The muscle spindles of the neck, in which sensory endings respond to a change in the tension of the tendons
Muscle spindles report muscle length, and tendon tension is reported by Golgi tendon organs, not spindles.
qs.x: The utricle and saccule contain otoliths whose weight shifts with linear acceleration and static head tilt, bending hair cells. Trap: Assigning all balance functions to the semicircular canals instead of splitting rotation (canals) from tilt (otoliths).

qs.q: Moving from EO-Firm to EC-Firm increased sway by 34 cm in the vestibular hypofunction group and by 14 cm in the healthy group. These data best support which conclusion?
o: People with vestibular loss rely more on proprioception than healthy adults do, since their eyes-closed sway grew less
Their sway grew by more (34 cm vs 14 cm), not less, so the data do not indicate greater proprioceptive reliance.
Healthy adults rely less on vision because their vestibular and proprioceptive cues are fully redundant
Healthy adults also swayed more with eyes closed (+14 cm), so they still use vision to some degree.
People with vestibular loss rely more on vision to maintain posture
Correct: Removing vision hurt the vestibular group more, which indicates that they were leaning on vision to compensate for the missing vestibular signal.
Vision is unnecessary for balance in either group, since neither group fell from the firm platform
Both groups swayed more with eyes closed, so vision contributes to balance in both.
qs.x: Removing vision hurt the vestibular group more, which indicates that they were leaning on vision to compensate for the missing vestibular signal. Trap: Reading any sway change as evidence of the other sense without checking its direction.

qs.q: The foam pad is meant to degrade the information carried by receptors that signal changes in muscle length around the ankle. Which receptors are these?
o: Muscle spindles
Correct: Muscle spindles lie within muscles and report stretch (length) and its rate of change.
Golgi tendon organs
Golgi tendon organs signal tension in tendons rather than length.
Pacinian corpuscles
Pacinian corpuscles respond to vibration and deep, rapidly changing pressure.
Merkel cells
Merkel cells respond to sustained light touch and texture.
qs.x: Muscle spindles lie within muscles and report stretch (length) and its rate of change. Trap: Mixing up muscle spindles (length) with Golgi tendon organs (tension), both being proprioceptors.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Mean sway path length (cm)

passages.title: FL08 · Psych/Soc · Passage 2
text: The critical period hypothesis proposes that there is a window early in life during which language exposure is needed for full grammatical mastery. Deaf children born to hearing parents often meet sign language at widely different ages, which makes them a natural test of this idea. Researchers recruited 80 deaf adults who had used American Sign Language (ASL) as their primary language for at least 30 years and grouped them by age of first ASL exposure, with 20 per group. Participants between 45 and 55 years old completed a timed grammaticality judgment task of 100 ASL sentences, half grammatical and half containing a morphological error. Chance performance is 50% correct. Participants first exposed after age 13 had had little accessible language input before then. Results are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. Separately, a signer with a left inferior frontal lesion produced slow, effortful signing of short, ungrammatical phrases but responded appropriately to signed questions.

qs.q: Which statement is best supported by the results?
o: Accuracy declines progressively as age of first exposure increases, with no sharp cutoff
Correct: Means fall steadily from 92 to 81 to 66 to 54, a graded decline consistent with a sensitive period rather than a hard boundary.
Accuracy is unaffected by exposure before age 9, then drops abruptly to chance among later signers
Accuracy already falls from 92 to 81 between the first two groups, and the oldest group (54%) is slightly above, not at, chance.
Accuracy remains above 90% only in signers whose first exposure to ASL came from a deaf parent
Parental hearing status was not measured or compared in the study.
Accuracy depends on the number of years of signing experience, which differs across the four groups
All participants had at least 30 years of ASL use, so experience was roughly equated and cannot explain the pattern.
qs.x: Means fall steadily from 92 to 81 to 66 to 54, a graded decline consistent with a sensitive period rather than a hard boundary. Trap: Reading a sensitive period as an abrupt on/off cutoff rather than a gradual decline.

qs.q: The accuracy of the 14-18 group exceeds chance by what fraction of the amount by which the 0-3 group exceeds chance?
o: About 10%
Correct: (54 - 50) / (92 - 50) = 4 / 42, about 0.095 or roughly 10%.
About 25%
25% would require the later group to score about 60%.
About 44%
44% is 4 divided by 9, not by 42.
About 58%
58% would require a later-group score of roughly 74%.
qs.x: (54 - 50) / (92 - 50) = 4 / 42, about 0.095 or roughly 10%. Trap: Comparing raw scores (54/92 is about 59%) instead of the amount above the 50% chance floor.

qs.q: The signer with a left inferior frontal lesion most likely has damage to which region, and which deficit does this produce?
o: Wernicke's area, producing fluent but meaningless language output with impaired comprehension
Wernicke's lesions lie in the posterior superior temporal lobe and impair comprehension, which this signer retains.
The arcuate fasciculus, producing fluent language with a selective inability to repeat heard speech
Arcuate fasciculus damage (conduction aphasia) spares fluency and comprehension but impairs repetition; the described output is not fluent.
Broca's area, producing nonfluent language output with relatively preserved comprehension
Correct: Broca's area in the left inferior frontal gyrus supports production and grammar; lesions produce halting, agrammatic output with good comprehension, and this holds for signed language too.
The angular gyrus, producing an inability to read and write alongside normal spontaneous speech
Angular gyrus damage is linked to alexia/agraphia, which does not match the signing deficit.
qs.x: Broca's area in the left inferior frontal gyrus supports production and grammar; lesions produce halting, agrammatic output with good comprehension, and this holds for signed language too. Trap: Equating aphasia with Wernicke's because comprehension is mentioned, ignoring the effortful output.

qs.q: Which feature of the design most limits the conclusion that age of exposure causes differences in grammatical ability?
o: Participants were tested between 45 and 55 years of age, so aging itself would erase differences among the groups
The testing ages were similar across groups, so age at test would not differentially erase group differences.
The grammaticality task used 100 sentences, a number too small to allow the group means to be compared
100 items with 20 participants per group is adequate for the observed 38-point range.
Participants could not be randomly assigned to an age of first exposure, so family and schooling factors may be confounded with it
Correct: Age of first exposure is a naturally occurring variable; factors such as parental hearing status, quality of early schooling, or additional disabilities could vary with it.
Participants all used ASL, a visual language, so the findings could never apply to the learning of any language
Generalization to spoken language is a question of external validity, and the study does not claim ASL results are meaningless for other languages.
qs.x: Age of first exposure is a naturally occurring variable; factors such as parental hearing status, quality of early schooling, or additional disabilities could vary with it. Trap: Blaming sample size when the actual problem is lack of random assignment.
