passages.title: FL08 · Psych/Soc · Passage 3
text: The amygdala has been implicated in the rapid evaluation of threat, whereas the hippocampus supports the formation of explicit memories. To compare their roles, researchers tested 10 adults with bilateral amygdala damage, 10 adults with bilateral hippocampal damage, and 10 healthy controls in a fear-conditioning procedure. Participants viewed colored squares on a screen. A blue square (CS+) was repeatedly followed by a loud, aversive tone, whereas a yellow square (CS-) was never followed by the tone. Skin conductance response (SCR), a measure of sweat gland activity, was recorded during each square. After the session, participants were taken to a separate room and asked which square had predicted the tone. Mean SCRs, in microsiemens (uS), and the number of participants who correctly named the CS+ are shown in Table 1. All participants had normal hearing, and all rated the tone as unpleasant. Each square was shown 20 times in random order, and the first two presentations of each square were excluded from the SCR averages to remove orienting responses.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by Table 1?
o: The amygdala is needed for explicit recall of the pairing, whereas the hippocampus is needed for the conditioned physiological response
This reverses the pattern: amygdala patients recalled the pairing (9 of 10) while hippocampal patients did not (3 of 10).
The amygdala is needed for the conditioned physiological response, whereas the hippocampus is needed for explicit recall of the pairing
Correct: Amygdala patients had no differential SCR yet knew the contingency; hippocampal patients had a normal SCR yet could not report it: a double dissociation.
Both structures are needed for the conditioned response, since each lesion group differs from controls on at least one measure
Each lesion group differed from controls on only one measure, which indicates separate roles rather than both being needed for each response.
Neither structure is needed for fear learning, because every group showed a larger SCR to the aversive tone than to silence
Responses to the tone itself were not reported, and the CS+ versus CS- comparison shows an impairment in the amygdala group.
qs.x: Amygdala patients had no differential SCR yet knew the contingency; hippocampal patients had a normal SCR yet could not report it: a double dissociation. Trap: Treating an impairment on any measure as proof that the structure is needed for fear learning in general.

qs.q: The difference between SCR to CS+ and CS- in controls was about how many times the same difference in the amygdala group?
o: A ratio of 4 would require an amygdala-group difference of about 0.18 uS.
Correct: Controls: 0.82 - 0.11 = 0.71; amygdala: 0.14 - 0.10 = 0.04; 0.71 / 0.04 is about 18.
A ratio of 9 would require an amygdala-group difference of about 0.08 uS.
A ratio of 35 would require an amygdala-group difference of about 0.02 uS.
qs.x: Controls: 0.82 - 0.11 = 0.71; amygdala: 0.14 - 0.10 = 0.04; 0.71 / 0.04 is about 18. Trap: Dividing CS+ values (0.82/0.14 is about 6) instead of using the CS+ minus CS- differences.

qs.q: Skin conductance increases during the CS+ because of activation of which division of the nervous system?
o: Sympathetic
Correct: Sweat glands are innervated by sympathetic fibers (cholinergic), so arousal raises skin conductance.
Parasympathetic
The parasympathetic division promotes rest-and-digest functions and does not drive sweating.
Somatic
The somatic division controls skeletal muscle.
Enteric
The enteric division governs the gut.
qs.x: Sweat glands are innervated by sympathetic fibers (cholinergic), so arousal raises skin conductance. Trap: Assuming sympathetic activation always involves norepinephrine receptors, and so dismissing sweat glands as sympathetic targets.

qs.q: Compared with controls, individuals with bilateral amygdala damage would most likely show which impairment?
o: Inability to form new explicit memories of events they experienced
Explicit memory formation relies on the hippocampus, which is intact in this group.
Loss of the ability to recognize familiar faces despite intact vision
Face recognition failure (prosopagnosia) reflects fusiform and related damage.
Reduced ability to recognize fear in other people's facial expressions
Correct: The amygdala contributes to processing threat-related social signals, so lesions impair recognition of fearful faces.
Failure to experience any emotion, including pleasure and sadness
Amygdala lesions blunt fear responses selectively; they do not abolish all emotions.
qs.x: The amygdala contributes to processing threat-related social signals, so lesions impair recognition of fearful faces. Trap: Overgeneralizing amygdala damage to a total loss of emotional experience.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Fear conditioning results

passages.title: FL08 · Psych/Soc · Passage 4
text: Learned helplessness is a pattern of passivity that follows exposure to aversive events that cannot be controlled. In a laboratory study, 60 rats were assigned to three groups of 20. Group E (escapable) received 64 mild tail shocks that could be terminated by pressing a lever. Group Y (yoked) was paired with a Group E rat and received shocks of identical timing and duration, but lever presses had no effect. Group N received no shock but was restrained for the same period. Twenty-four hours later, every rat was placed in a shuttle box in which a floor shock could be escaped by crossing to the other compartment. Rats were given 5 blocks of 6 trials. Escape latency, in seconds, was recorded for each trial, and a trial counted as a failure if the rat did not cross within 30 s. Results are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. Experimenters scoring latencies did not know which pretreatment each rat had received, and all rats had been handled equally before the study.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of including Group Y?
o: To equate the amount and timing of shock across animals while varying only whether the shock was controllable
Correct: Because Group Y received exactly the shocks Group E did, a difference between them can be attributed to controllability.
To determine whether the lever itself, as an object, becomes a conditioned stimulus for later shocks
The lever's conditioned properties were not tested.
To measure the effect of restraint on later behavior when no shock was ever delivered to the animals
Restraint without shock is the purpose of Group N, not Group Y.
To test whether yoked animals learn faster when the lever is paired with a tone rather than shock
No tone or learning-speed manipulation exists in the design.
qs.x: Because Group Y received exactly the shocks Group E did, a difference between them can be attributed to controllability. Trap: Mistaking the yoked group for the no-shock control, which has a different job.

qs.q: By Block 5, the mean latency of Group Y was approximately how many times that of Group E?
o: 2 would imply about 6.4 s.
3 would imply about 9.6 s.
Correct: 16.8 / 3.2 = 5.25, about 5.
13 is the difference in the number of rats failing (15 - 2), not a latency ratio.
qs.x: 16.8 / 3.2 = 5.25, about 5. Trap: Using the 13-rat difference in failures instead of a latency ratio read from the graph.

qs.q: The similar performance of Groups E and N supports which interpretation?
o: Helplessness arises from lack of control over shock, not from shock exposure alone
Correct: Group E got the same shocks as Group Y but escaped normally, and Group N matched it, so controllability is the critical variable.
Helplessness arises from exposure to shock alone, regardless of whether the shock is controllable
Group E received shock and did not become helpless, which contradicts this.
Helplessness arises from restraint, because only restrained animals later failed to escape
All three groups were restrained or placed in the apparatus, yet only Group Y failed.
Helplessness arises from practice, since animals with more trials always show longer latencies
Groups E and N had decreasing latencies across blocks, so more trials did not lengthen latency.
qs.x: Group E got the same shocks as Group Y but escaped normally, and Group N matched it, so controllability is the critical variable. Trap: Attributing the effect to the shock itself rather than to its uncontrollability.

qs.q: In humans, an explanatory style most associated with depression after uncontrollable negative events attributes the cause to which kind of factor?
o: External, stable, and global
An external cause does not implicate the self, which lowers the risk.
Internal, unstable, and specific
An unstable, specific cause limits expected impact to one situation.
External, unstable, and specific
External, unstable, and specific attributions are the most protective style.
Internal, stable, and global
Correct: The reformulated model predicts that attributing failures to oneself (internal), as lasting (stable), and as affecting many areas (global) produces helplessness and depression.
qs.x: The reformulated model predicts that attributing failures to oneself (internal), as lasting (stable), and as affecting many areas (global) produces helplessness and depression. Trap: Selecting 'internal' alone without checking stability and globality.

qs.q: In Group E, pressing the lever to end the shock is best described as which type of learning process?
o: Positive punishment, because the aversive shock is presented after the lever is pressed
Punishment would reduce pressing, not increase it.
Negative reinforcement, because removing an aversive stimulus increases the likelihood of the response
Correct: Terminating shock strengthens pressing: a response followed by removal of an aversive stimulus.
Positive reinforcement, because the animal gains a pleasant stimulus after the lever is pressed
No pleasant stimulus is added; an unpleasant one is removed.
Negative punishment, because a rewarding stimulus is withdrawn after the lever is pressed
Negative punishment removes a pleasant stimulus to decrease behavior, which does not fit.
qs.x: Terminating shock strengthens pressing: a response followed by removal of an aversive stimulus. Trap: Equating negative reinforcement with punishment because both involve something unpleasant.

passages.title: FL08 · Psych/Soc · Passage 5
text: Deindividuation is a state of reduced self-awareness and accountability that can occur when people feel anonymous within a group. A researcher tested whether anonymity increases aggression more in groups than in individuals. Participants were told the study examined the effects of noise on learning. In each session, either one participant (alone) or four participants (group) served as teachers who pressed a button to deliver an unpleasant burst of noise to a learner, a confederate, each time he erred on a word task. Teachers chose how long to hold the button. In the identifiable condition, teachers wore name tags in a brightly lit room and the experimenter recorded who pressed. In the anonymous condition, teachers wore identical hooded coats in a dim room and responses were pooled so individual presses were not recorded. Each of the four cells contained 32 participants. Mean duration per press, in seconds, is shown in Table 1.

qs.q: Which process best explains why press durations were longest among anonymous group members?
o: Increased self-monitoring, which makes people comply more strongly with the group's expectations about aggression
Deindividuation lowers, not raises, self-monitoring.
Reduced self-awareness and accountability, which weakens the restraint that usually comes from personal norms
Correct: Anonymity within a group lowers private self-awareness and perceived accountability, so behavior is guided less by internal standards.
Cognitive dissonance, which makes people justify the noise bursts by raising their liking for the learner
Dissonance would predict attitude change after an act, not more aggression because of anonymity.
Social facilitation, which improves performance on a well-learned task whenever others are watching the individual
Social facilitation depends on evaluation by others, which was removed in the anonymous condition.
qs.x: Anonymity within a group lowers private self-awareness and perceived accountability, so behavior is guided less by internal standards. Trap: Confusing deindividuation with social facilitation because both involve being in the presence of others.

qs.q: Among participants in groups, by approximately what percent did anonymity increase mean press duration relative to the identifiable condition?
o: 43% results from dividing 1.7 by 4.0, the wrong base.
Correct: (4.0 - 2.3) / 2.3 = 0.74, an increase of about 74%.
174% is the new value as a percentage of the old one, not the increase.
1.7% is the raw difference in seconds misread as a percentage.
qs.x: (4.0 - 2.3) / 2.3 = 0.74, an increase of about 74%. Trap: Dividing the 1.7 s difference by the anonymous value (4.0) rather than by the baseline identifiable value.

qs.q: Which pattern in Table 1 indicates that the effect of anonymity depends on group size?
o: Group sessions produced longer presses than alone sessions in both the identifiable and anonymous conditions
This is a main effect of group size; it would occur even without an interaction.
Anonymity raised press duration by 1.7 s in groups but by only 0.3 s for individuals alone
Correct: A difference of differences (1.7 vs 0.3) is an interaction: anonymity matters mostly when people are in a group.
Anonymous participants pressed longer than identifiable participants regardless of whether they were in groups
Anonymous participants alone pressed only 0.3 s longer, a small difference that does not show a consistent effect of anonymity.
Press durations in the alone sessions were shorter than those in the group sessions across all four cells
This restates the group-size main effect and says nothing about whether anonymity's effect changes with group size.
qs.x: A difference of differences (1.7 vs 0.3) is an interaction: anonymity matters mostly when people are in a group. Trap: Reading two main effects as an interaction.

qs.q: Which added condition would best test whether diffusion of responsibility, rather than anonymity itself, explains the long presses in anonymous groups?
o: An alone condition in which participants wear hoods in a dim room and are told their presses will be recorded
This tests recording in the alone setting, so it cannot address group responsibility.
A group condition in which the learner is replaced with a second confederate who performs poorly on the task
Changing the confederate tests a different variable (provocation).
A group condition in which all members wear name tags in a brightly lit room and the learner makes no errors
With no errors there are no presses to measure, so no behavior can be compared.
A group condition in which each member's presses are recorded individually but members still wear hoods in a dim room
Correct: Keeping anonymity of appearance but restoring individual accountability separates visual anonymity from shared responsibility.
qs.x: Keeping anonymity of appearance but restoring individual accountability separates visual anonymity from shared responsibility. Trap: Changing the learner instead of the accountability manipulation.

passages.title: FL08 · Psych/Soc · Passage 6
text: Social learning theory proposes that people acquire behaviors by observing models and the consequences those models receive. In an experiment modeled on classic work in this area, 80 children aged 5 to 6 were randomly assigned, 20 per group, to watch one of four 5-minute films. In three films, an adult model struck an inflatable doll with a mallet while shouting distinctive insults. In the rewarded film, the model was praised and given candy afterward. In the punished film, the model was scolded and spanked. In the no-consequences film, nothing followed the aggression. In the fourth film, the model played calmly with toys. Each child was then left alone for 10 min in a room containing the doll and mallet while observers behind one-way glass counted imitative aggressive acts (spontaneous performance). An experimenter then entered and offered a sticker for each act the child could reproduce from the film (incentive performance). Mean counts are shown in Table 1.

qs.q: The change in the punished group after stickers were offered best illustrates which distinction?
o: Learning can occur only when the observer is directly reinforced, so performance mirrors earlier rewards
Children were never directly reinforced for aggression, yet they learned it by observation.
Learning depends on attention but not on retention, so performance is unaffected by later incentives
Retention was needed to reproduce the acts a week of testing later and the data show it was intact.
Learning can occur without being displayed, so performance depends on motivation as well as acquisition
Correct: Punished-model children had acquired the aggressive acts (6.9 under incentive) but suppressed them until motivated to show them.
Learning is complete once behavior is shown, so performance and acquisition are the same process
If performance and acquisition were the same, incentives would not change the count.
qs.x: Punished-model children had acquired the aggressive acts (6.9 under incentive) but suppressed them until motivated to show them. Trap: Concluding that the children in the punished condition did not learn the acts because they did not perform them.

qs.q: Children in the rewarded and punished films were influenced by consequences that they themselves never received. This is known as:
o: Stimulus generalization
Generalization is responding to stimuli similar to a conditioned stimulus.
Latent learning
Latent learning is learning that is not expressed until a reward appears, without observing a model.
Higher-order conditioning
Higher-order conditioning pairs a new stimulus with an already-conditioned stimulus.
Vicarious reinforcement and punishment
Correct: Observing a model's outcome changes the observer's likelihood of imitating, even without personal reward or punishment.
qs.x: Observing a model's outcome changes the observer's likelihood of imitating, even without personal reward or punishment. Trap: Picking latent learning because the incentive revealed hidden learning, ignoring the stem's focus on observed consequences.

qs.q: By what percent did the mean number of acts in the punished group increase when stickers were offered?
o: 30% results from dividing 2.1 by 6.9.
70% is not derived from either value.
329% is 6.9 as a percentage of 2.1, which includes the original amount.
qs.x: (6.9 - 2.1) / 2.1 = 2.29, a 229% increase. Trap: Reporting 6.9/2.1 (329%) as the increase, forgetting to subtract the baseline.

qs.q: Which is the most important limitation on generalizing these findings to real-world media violence?
o: Hitting an inflatable doll in a lab may not reflect harmful aggression toward real people in daily life
Correct: Aggression toward a toy designed to be hit has limited ecological validity as a measure of real violence.
Random assignment to four films makes it impossible to know whether each group started with the same aggression
Random assignment equates groups on average, which is its purpose.
Counting acts with observers behind one-way glass is certain to alter the behavior of every child in the study
One-way glass is used precisely to minimize observer effects; the claim of certain alteration is unfounded.
Using children aged 5 to 6 means the results could apply only to learning that occurs at those precise ages
Age restricts generalization somewhat, but not to precisely those ages, and the doll issue is more critical.
qs.x: Aggression toward a toy designed to be hit has limited ecological validity as a measure of real violence. Trap: Naming the sample age as the key problem when the measured behavior is the weaker link.

passages.title: FL08 · Psych/Soc · Passage 7
text: Stereotype threat is the concern about confirming a negative stereotype about one's group, which can impair performance on tasks related to the stereotype. A researcher recruited 150 undergraduates who rated math as important to them and assigned them to five groups of 30. All completed a difficult 20-item math test in a quiet room. Women were assigned to one of three instructions. In the control condition, they were told the test was a problem-solving exercise. In the threat condition, they were told that the test had shown gender differences in the past. In the no-difference condition, they were told that the test had shown no gender differences. Men were assigned to the control or threat instructions. Participants also completed a brief measure of anxiety after the test. Mean scores (out of 20) are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. Women in the threat condition also reported higher test anxiety than women in the control condition.

qs.q: The mean score of women in the threat condition was lower than that of women in the control condition by approximately what percent of the control mean?
o: 17% is 3.4 as a percentage of the 20-point maximum, not of the control mean.
34% would be 3.4 treated as a percentage.
41% is not produced by any of the given values.
qs.x: (11.6 - 8.2) / 11.6 = 3.4 / 11.6, about 29%. Trap: Using the 20-point maximum (17%) as the base when the stem asks about the control mean.

qs.q: Which interpretation of the women's results is best supported?
o: The lower performance reflects a fixed difference in ability, because women scored below men in the threat condition
Women with no-difference or control instructions matched men, so ability is not fixed at the lower level.
The lower performance reflects less effort, because women who rated math as important quit the test early
No effort or quitting data are reported, and the participants all valued math.
The lower performance reflects the situation created by the instructions rather than a fixed difference in math ability
Correct: The same women scored as well as men when told there were no gender differences (11.9), so ability itself cannot explain the threat-condition deficit.
The lower performance reflects test anxiety only among men, because men scored lower in the threat condition
Men's scores were essentially unchanged by the threat instructions (11.8 vs 11.5).
qs.x: The same women scored as well as men when told there were no gender differences (11.9), so ability itself cannot explain the threat-condition deficit. Trap: Treating a group difference under one condition as evidence of an inherent ability difference.

qs.q: Which statement about causal inference in this study is correct?
o: Effects of gender on scores are causal because the groups were of equal size, but effects of instructions are not
Equal group size does not make gender causal; random assignment, which applies only to instructions, does.
Effects of the instructions are not causal because the participants knew they were being tested on math skills
Awareness of the topic does not remove the benefit of randomization.
Effects of both gender and instructions are causal because the same 20-item test was given to every group
Using one test for all groups controls the measure, but does not make gender assigned.
Effects of the instructions on women's scores are causal because assignment was random, but effects of gender are not because gender was not assigned
Correct: Random assignment to instruction supports causal inference about instructions; gender is a quasi-independent variable.
qs.x: Random assignment to instruction supports causal inference about instructions; gender is a quasi-independent variable. Trap: Believing equal cell sizes or a shared test confer causal inference for a non-manipulated variable.

qs.q: Which pre-test intervention is most likely to reduce the effect of stereotype threat on performance?
o: Having test-takers write about how the test reveals their ability, which sharpens their focus on the test
Emphasizing that the test diagnoses ability increases threat.
Having test-takers read about past gender differences, which reminds them of the standard to meet
Reminders of the stereotype increase threat.
Having test-takers complete the test under time pressure, which prevents them from thinking about the stereotype
Time pressure adds stress and consumes working memory, which worsens the effect.
Having test-takers write about a personally important value, which broadens their self-concept
Correct: Self-affirmation reduces the threat to self-integrity by reminding the person of other valued aspects of identity.
qs.x: Self-affirmation reduces the threat to self-integrity by reminding the person of other valued aspects of identity. Trap: Assuming that more focus on the test helps performance when that focus is the source of the threat.

qs.q: Women in the threat condition reported higher test anxiety. Which mechanism best links that anxiety to their lower scores?
o: Heightened arousal improves performance on complex tasks, but only up to the point at which scores plateau
Arousal at high levels impairs complex tasks (Yerkes-Dodson), and the stem describes a decline, not a plateau.
Worry about confirming the stereotype uses working memory capacity that is needed to solve the problems
Correct: Stereotype threat is thought to impair performance by consuming working memory with evaluation-related worry.
Anxiety causes participants to attribute their scores to luck, which makes them stop trying on the items
Attribution to luck is not measured, and no data on effort or quitting appear in the study.
Anxiety increases the speed of processing, so women attempt more items and make more careless errors
No data on speed or attempted items are given, and anxiety generally disrupts rather than speeds careful reasoning.
qs.x: Stereotype threat is thought to impair performance by consuming working memory with evaluation-related worry. Trap: Assuming arousal always aids performance.

passages.title: FL08 · Psych/Soc · Passage 8
text: Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek and interpret information in ways that support existing beliefs. To study it in hiring, researchers recruited 90 experienced managers and randomly assigned 30 to each of three conditions. All read the same one-page resume for an analyst position. Only a cover note differed. In the positive condition, a note said that a trusted colleague considered the candidate outstanding. In the negative condition, a note said that a colleague had concerns about the candidate's reliability. In the neutral condition, no note was included. Each manager then selected five interview questions from a list of ten, of which five probed strengths and five probed weaknesses. A question was counted as expectation-consistent if it probed strengths in the positive condition or weaknesses in the negative condition; in the neutral condition, strength questions were counted as a reference. Managers then watched an identical scripted video interview and rated the candidate from 1 to 10. Results are shown in Table 1.

qs.q: The ratings in Table 1, given that all managers saw an identical video, are best explained by which process?
o: Accurate updating on new evidence, because managers weighted the video more heavily than the note
If managers had updated accurately, ratings would converge across conditions.
Ambiguous answers being interpreted so as to fit the expectation created by the cover note
Correct: Identical evidence produced different judgments, indicating that the prior note biased the interpretation of the responses.
Attribution of the candidate's answers to the situation, because the interview was scripted for every manager
Attribution of scripted answers to the situation would apply equally to every condition and would not produce different ratings.
Reduced cognitive load in the neutral condition, because managers with no note could not make comparisons
Cognitive load is not measured, and the neutral rating (6.4) lies between the other two.
qs.x: Identical evidence produced different judgments, indicating that the prior note biased the interpretation of the responses. Trap: Treating different ratings of the same video as differences in the candidate's performance.

qs.q: How many more managers in the positive condition than in the no-note condition chose three or more expectation-consistent questions?
o: 3 is the percentage-point gap divided by 10 or a miscount.
9 is not supported by the table.
Correct: 21 - 15 = 6.
21 is the total in the positive condition, not the difference.
qs.x: 21 - 15 = 6. Trap: Reading the positive-condition count (21) as the difference between conditions.

qs.q: Suppose the managers had instead conducted live interviews and the candidate, faced with weakness-probing questions, performed poorly. This would most clearly illustrate:
o: The halo effect, because one strongly positive trait influences judgments about the candidate's other traits
The halo effect concerns generalizing from a single positive trait, which is not what drove the poor performance.
The fundamental attribution error, because the interviewer blames the candidate's disposition for the poor outcome
The fundamental attribution error might coexist, but the key feature here is the elicitation of the confirming behavior.
The actor-observer bias, because the candidate attributes the performance to the situation rather than ability
Actor-observer bias concerns differences between explaining one's own and others' actions.
A self-fulfilling prophecy, because the interviewer's expectation shaped the behavior that confirmed it
Correct: When expectations elicit the very behavior expected, the prophecy fulfills itself (behavioral confirmation).
qs.x: When expectations elicit the very behavior expected, the prophecy fulfills itself (behavioral confirmation). Trap: Selecting fundamental attribution error because the interviewer blames the candidate, overlooking the interviewer's causal role.

qs.q: Which change to the hiring process would best reduce the influence of the cover note?
o: Allowing each interviewer to adapt questions to the candidate's strengths and weaknesses
Adaptive questioning gives the bias more room to operate.
Telling each interviewer to be careful to rate the candidate without forming an opinion
Simply instructing people to avoid bias has little effect on automatic processes.
Asking every candidate the same pre-set questions and scoring answers with a fixed rubric
Correct: Standardized questions and scoring limit selective information seeking and subjective interpretation.
Giving interviewers a detailed summary of earlier colleagues' impressions to inform the interview
Colleague impressions are the very prior information that produces the bias.
qs.x: Standardized questions and scoring limit selective information seeking and subjective interpretation. Trap: Believing that awareness of bias alone is enough to prevent it.

h: Managers choosing 3 or more expectation-consistent questions

passages.title: FL08 · Psych/Soc · Passage 9
text: Researchers contrasted two explanations of helping. The empathy-altruism hypothesis holds that empathic concern produces helping aimed at relieving another's distress. The negative-state relief model holds that people help to reduce their own distress. Eighty undergraduates were told they were observing, by closed-circuit video, a student named Elaine who received mild electric shocks during a task and was visibly distressed. Participants were asked whether they would take her place for the remaining trials. Before watching, empathy was manipulated: some participants were told that Elaine's values and interests were very similar to their own (high empathy), and others were told that they were very different (low empathy). Ease of escape was also manipulated: participants were told that they would watch only 2 trials (easy escape) or all 10 trials (difficult escape). Each of the four cells contained 20 participants. The number who volunteered to take Elaine's place is shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

qs.q: Which result best supports the empathy-altruism hypothesis?
o: Low-empathy participants helped more when escape was difficult than when escape was easy
Helping that depends on escape being difficult fits the negative-state relief model.
High-empathy participants helped at higher rates than low-empathy participants when escape was difficult
A difference when escape is difficult shows an empathy effect but does not exclude self-interest, since escape was blocked.
Participants in the difficult-escape condition helped more often than those in the easy-escape condition
A main effect of difficulty is consistent with relief of personal distress and pools across empathy conditions.
High-empathy participants helped at similarly high rates whether escape was easy or difficult
Correct: If help flows from concern for the victim, it should persist even when the helper could easily leave: 85% versus 90%.
qs.x: If help flows from concern for the victim, it should persist even when the helper could easily leave: 85% versus 90%. Trap: Picking the option showing high empathy helps more than low empathy, which is true in both models when escape is hard.

qs.q: Which result is best explained by the negative-state relief model?
o: Among high-empathy participants, helping stayed near 85% to 90% even when escape was easy
Helping despite an easy exit is better explained by empathic concern.
Among easy-escape participants, helping was much higher in the high-empathy group than in the low-empathy group
A gap between empathy groups in easy escape is predicted by the empathy-altruism hypothesis.
Among all participants, helping was at least 20% regardless of the empathy or escape condition
A floor of 20% does not distinguish the models.
Among low-empathy participants, helping rose from 20% to 65% when escape became difficult
Correct: When escape is blocked, observing the victim's suffering is aversive, so helping to end it (and one's own distress) becomes the best option.
qs.x: When escape is blocked, observing the victim's suffering is aversive, so helping to end it (and one's own distress) becomes the best option. Trap: Treating any high rate of helping as evidence of self-interest.

qs.q: Among the 40 low-empathy participants, what percent volunteered to take Elaine's place?
o: 20% is only the easy-escape cell.
52.5% would correspond to 21 helpers.
65% is only the difficult-escape cell.
qs.x: (4 + 13) / 40 = 17 / 40 = 42.5%. Trap: Reporting a single cell instead of pooling the two low-empathy cells.

qs.q: Table 1 shows that ease of escape affected helping mainly in one empathy condition. This pattern is best described as:
o: A main effect of empathy only, because high-empathy participants helped more in both escape conditions
Empathy had a clear main effect, but the data also show a difference in the effect of escape across levels of empathy.
A main effect of escape only, because difficult escape produced more helping in both empathy conditions
The escape effect was large only at low empathy (+45) and small at high empathy (+5), so it is not uniform.
An interaction, because the effect of escape depended on the level of empathy
Correct: Escape mattered a lot for low-empathy participants (+45 points) and little for high-empathy ones (+5 points).
No effect of either variable, because the average for easy and difficult escape was the same in every row
Both variables had clear effects, and their rows do not average to the same value.
qs.x: Escape mattered a lot for low-empathy participants (+45 points) and little for high-empathy ones (+5 points). Trap: Naming a main effect when the size of one effect varies with the other variable.

passages.title: FL08 · Psych/Soc · Passage 10
text: Researchers conducted a randomized trial of a sleep-hygiene smartphone app for chronic insomnia. Adults were randomly assigned 1:1 to the active app or to a sham app that looked similar and delivered general health tips. Assignment used a computer-generated sequence concealed from the staff who enrolled participants. Participants were not told which app was active. The outcome was the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI; 0 to 28, higher is worse) at 8 weeks, scored by an assessor unaware of group assignment. Values in Table 1 are for participants who completed 8 weeks. The difference in mean change between groups was -3.8 points (95% confidence interval, -5.1 to -2.5). Participants had met criteria for chronic insomnia for at least 3 months and did not use prescription sleep medication during the study. Figure 1 shows mean ISI over time among completers. Dropout was higher in the sham group, and several sham participants who dropped out reported that the app 'was not helping.'

qs.q: What is the primary advantage of using a sham app rather than a no-treatment control?
o: It guarantees that dropout will be identical across arms, since all participants receive an app of some kind
Dropout was not equal; a sham does not guarantee equal retention.
It eliminates sampling error in the outcome, since both groups use a device that matches in appearance
Sampling error arises from sample variability, not from the control type.
It lets participants remain unaware of their assignment, so expectation and attention effects are balanced across arms
Correct: A sham controls for placebo effects and attention, and supports participant blinding.
It allows investigators to see participants' assignment sooner, since the sham app records usage patterns
Revealing assignment would defeat blinding and is not a benefit.
qs.x: A sham controls for placebo effects and attention, and supports participant blinding. Trap: Believing that a placebo control guarantees equal retention or removes random error.

qs.q: What percent of randomized participants completed week 8?
o: 80% would be 192 completers.
90% would be 216 completers, and is the active arm's rate (108/120).
92% would be about 221 completers.
qs.x: (108 + 96) / 240 = 204 / 240 = 0.85. Trap: Reporting the active arm's completion rate (90%) instead of the overall rate.

qs.q: What does the confidence interval of -5.1 to -2.5 for the difference in mean change indicate?
o: The interval includes 0, so no conclusion can be drawn about whether the active app outperforms the sham
-5.1 to -2.5 does not include 0.
The interval shows that 95% of individual participants improved by between 2.5 and 5.1 points
A CI for a mean difference says nothing about the range of individual responses.
The interval excludes 0, so a difference of no effect is not compatible with the data at the 5% level
Correct: A 95% CI that excludes the null value corresponds to p < 0.05 for the difference.
The interval shows a 95% probability that the next participant will improve by exactly 3.8 points
A CI describes uncertainty in the mean difference, not a prediction for the next participant.
qs.x: A 95% CI that excludes the null value corresponds to p < 0.05 for the difference. Trap: Interpreting a confidence interval as the range containing 95% of individuals.

qs.q: Because dropout was higher in the sham group, which analysis would best preserve the benefits of randomization?
o: Analyzing only the 204 completers so that every analyzed participant received the full 8 weeks (per-protocol)
Completers-only analysis breaks randomization if dropouts differ systematically.
Excluding the sham participants who reported that the app was not helping from the analysis altogether
Excluding participants on the basis of their opinion biases the result in favor of the active app.
Analyzing all 240 participants in the groups to which they were assigned (intention-to-treat)
Correct: Intention-to-treat keeps groups comparable and limits attrition bias.
Replacing each missing sham participant with a new volunteer recruited after the trial had ended
Replacement volunteers were not randomized, so they cannot restore comparability.
qs.x: Intention-to-treat keeps groups comparable and limits attrition bias. Trap: Choosing completers-only because it appears to match 'full treatment'.

qs.q: Baseline ISI scores were 17.2 and 17.0 in the two arms. This similarity is most directly attributable to:
o: Allocation concealment, which guarantees that every participant characteristic is identical across arms
Allocation concealment prevents selection bias, and chance imbalance can still occur.
Random assignment, which tends to balance both known and unknown participant characteristics across arms
Correct: Randomization makes systematic baseline imbalance unlikely, particularly with a large sample.
Assessor blinding, which prevents differences in baseline severity from arising across arms
Blinding of the assessor prevents measurement bias, not baseline imbalance.
Intention-to-treat analysis, which statistically adjusts the baseline scores so that they match
ITT concerns analysis populations and does not alter baseline scores.
qs.x: Randomization makes systematic baseline imbalance unlikely, particularly with a large sample. Trap: Crediting blinding for baseline balance, when blinding addresses bias after assignment.

passages.title: FL09 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 1
text: Histidine hydrochloride (0.1 M) was titrated with NaOH while pH was monitored. The titration curve showed three buffering regions, corresponding to the alpha-carboxyl group (pKa 1.8), the imidazole side chain (pKa 6.0), and the alpha-amino group (pKa 9.2). A student used the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation to calculate the average net charge of histidine at several pH values (Table 1 and Figure 1). The net charge is the sum of the charges on the three groups: the carboxyl group is neutral when protonated and negative when deprotonated, whereas the imidazole and alpha-amino groups are positive when protonated and neutral when deprotonated.

In a second experiment, the student applied histidine at pH 4.0 to a cation-exchange column containing negatively charged sulfonate groups, washed the column, and then eluted the bound amino acid by gradually raising the pH of the buffer. Histidine began to leave the column as the buffer pH approached the value at which its net charge reached zero.

qs.q: According to the pKa values given, at what pH does histidine carry a net charge of zero?
o: pH 5.5, the average of the carboxyl and alpha-amino pKa values
averages the wrong pair of pKa values; at pH 5.5 the net charge is still positive.
pH 7.6, the average of the imidazole and alpha-amino pKa values
Correct: The isoelectric point lies midway between the two pKa values that flank the neutral species, here 6.0 and 9.2, giving (6.0 + 9.2)/2 = 7.6, consistent with Table 1.
pH 3.9, the average of the carboxyl and imidazole pKa values
also uses the wrong pair; the neutral form is not flanked by the carboxyl and imidazole groups.
pH 6.0, the pKa of the imidazole side chain, where it is half protonated
at pH 6.0 Table 1 shows a net charge of +0.50, not zero.
qs.x: The isoelectric point lies midway between the two pKa values that flank the neutral species, here 6.0 and 9.2, giving (6.0 + 9.2)/2 = 7.6, consistent with Table 1. Trap: Averaging the lowest and highest pKa values, or choosing the side-chain pKa, instead of the two pKa values around the neutral species.

qs.q: Why does histidine bind to the cation-exchange column at pH 4.0?
o: It carries a net charge of about -1, so it is attracted to the negative resin
a negative histidine would be repelled by the negatively charged sulfonate groups.
It is neutral at pH 4.0, so it adsorbs to the resin through hydrophobic contacts
histidine is not neutral at pH 4.0 (+1.00 in Table 1), and a neutral molecule would not be retained by charge.
It carries a net charge of about +1, so it is attracted to the negative resin
Correct: Table 1 gives a net charge of +1.00 at pH 4.0 (carboxylate -1, imidazolium +1, ammonium +1), so the cation binds the sulfonate groups by electrostatic attraction.
It carries a net charge of +2, which is the only charge able to displace the sulfonate groups
+2 occurs only near pH 1; no minimum charge is needed to bind the resin.
qs.x: Table 1 gives a net charge of +1.00 at pH 4.0 (carboxylate -1, imidazolium +1, ammonium +1), so the cation binds the sulfonate groups by electrostatic attraction. Trap: Forgetting that the carboxyl group is already deprotonated at pH 4.0 and so counting too many or too few charges.

qs.q: At pH 7.0, what fraction of the imidazole side chains of free histidine is protonated?
o: About 9%
Correct: pH - pKa = 1.0, so [deprotonated]/[protonated] = 10 and the protonated fraction is 1/(1 + 10) = 0.091, or about 9%.
About 50%
50% would apply only when pH equals the pKa (6.0).
About 91%
91% is the deprotonated fraction; the ratio was inverted.
About 1%
1% would require the pH to be 2 units above the pKa.
qs.x: pH - pKa = 1.0, so [deprotonated]/[protonated] = 10 and the protonated fraction is 1/(1 + 10) = 0.091, or about 9%. Trap: Inverting the ratio in the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation and reporting the deprotonated fraction as the protonated one.

qs.q: Which feature of histidine makes it common in enzyme active sites that transfer protons near physiological pH?
o: The imidazole ring is permanently positively charged at all pH values above 2
Table 1 shows the side chain loses its charge as pH rises above about 6.
The imidazole pKa is near neutral, so it can readily gain or lose a proton

Correct: Because the imidazole pKa (about 6, and often closer to 7 inside proteins) is near physiological pH, the side chain exists in both protonated and deprotonated forms and can act as a general acid or base.
The imidazole ring is uncharged and nonpolar, so it excludes water from the active site
the ring is polar and can be charged; it is not a hydrophobic residue.
The imidazole ring forms disulfide bonds that hold substrates in place
disulfide bonds form between cysteine residues, not histidine.
qs.x: Because the imidazole pKa (about 6, and often closer to 7 inside proteins) is near physiological pH, the side chain exists in both protonated and deprotonated forms and can act as a general acid or base. Trap: Assuming histidine side chains are always charged like lysine and arginine, rather than titrating near neutral pH.

qs.q: Which pH range would give the best buffering by the histidine side chain?
o: pH 5 to 7, near the imidazole pKa
Correct: Buffering is greatest within about one pH unit of a pKa; the imidazole pKa is 6.0, and in this region the net charge changes steeply as protons are released.
pH 3 to 4, where the net charge is nearly constant
the net charge plateaus here because no group is near its pKa, so little base is neutralized.
pH 7.6 to 8.6, around the isoelectric point where charge is zero
this range lies between the imidazole and amino pKa values (6.0 and 9.2), so no group is near its pKa and buffering is weak.
pH 10 to 11, where the net charge approaches -1
above about pH 10 the amino group is mostly deprotonated, so few titratable protons remain and buffering is weak.
qs.x: Buffering is greatest within about one pH unit of a pKa; the imidazole pKa is 6.0, and in this region the net charge changes steeply as protons are released. Trap: Choosing the pH of zero net charge as the best buffering region rather than a region near a pKa.
