passages.title: FL09 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 2
text: Researchers studied the role of a kinase, KIN1, in the proliferation of cultured epithelial cells. Cells were transfected with a small interfering RNA (siRNA) designed to match a 21-nucleotide sequence in the KIN1 mRNA, or with a control siRNA of scrambled sequence. At 24, 48, and 72 hours, KIN1 mRNA was measured by quantitative PCR and KIN1 protein was measured by western blot. Both values are expressed as a percentage of the control-siRNA cells (Table 1, Figure 1). Cell numbers were also counted.

In a third experiment, cells received the KIN1 siRNA together with a plasmid encoding KIN1 in which several codons had been changed to synonymous codons at the siRNA target site, leaving the encoded protein unchanged. At 72 hours, cell number in this group was 94% of the control-siRNA value, compared with 52% for cells receiving the KIN1 siRNA alone. The half-life of KIN1 protein in untreated cells was measured to be about 20 hours.

qs.q: At 24 hours, KIN1 mRNA is reduced by 80% but KIN1 protein by only 22%. The best explanation is that:
o: the siRNA acts only on protein, so mRNA levels are an unreliable indicator
siRNA pairs with mRNA, not with protein, so mRNA is the direct target.
the siRNA blocks transcription of the KIN1 gene, which lowers mRNA before protein
siRNA acts after transcription by directing cleavage of the mRNA in the cytoplasm.
KIN1 protein that was made before transfection persists until it is degraded
Correct: The siRNA destroys mRNA, but existing protein falls only as it is turned over; with a half-life near 20 hours, substantial protein remains at 24 hours and declines later (35% at 48 hours).
KIN1 protein is synthesized from a separate pool of mRNA that the siRNA cannot reach
no separate protected pool of mRNA is described, and the protein decline at 48 and 72 hours shows the siRNA is effective.
qs.x: The siRNA destroys mRNA, but existing protein falls only as it is turned over; with a half-life near 20 hours, substantial protein remains at 24 hours and declines later (35% at 48 hours). Trap: Assuming protein must fall as fast as mRNA, forgetting that protein half-life delays the decline.

qs.q: What is the purpose of the plasmid with synonymous codon changes in the third experiment?
o: To rule out off-target effects of the siRNA

Correct: The rescue construct encodes normal KIN1 protein but its mRNA lacks the matching sequence, so the siRNA cannot cleave it; restoring proliferation (94% of control) shows that KIN1 loss, not off-target silencing, causes the defect.
To increase the amount of siRNA that enters the RISC complex
the plasmid encodes KIN1 and does not supply siRNA or RISC components.
To confirm that the siRNA lowers KIN1 mRNA by blocking its translation
the siRNA is described as targeting mRNA sequence; the rescue tests specificity rather than mechanism.
To correct a mutation in the endogenous KIN1 gene
the endogenous gene is not mutated; the cells are wild type apart from the siRNA treatment.
qs.x: The rescue construct encodes normal KIN1 protein but its mRNA lacks the matching sequence, so the siRNA cannot cleave it; restoring proliferation (94% of control) shows that KIN1 loss, not off-target silencing, causes the defect. Trap: Thinking the plasmid delivers more siRNA or repairs the gene rather than serving as a specificity control.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for the rise in KIN1 mRNA between 48 and 72 hours (Table 1)?
o: The siRNA is diluted by cell division and degraded, so silencing wanes
Correct: Transfected siRNA is not replicated in mammalian cells; it is diluted with each division and degraded, so the silencing effect is transient and mRNA recovers.
The siRNA is amplified by RNA polymerase in the cells, so silencing wanes
siRNA does not amplify in mammalian cells, and amplification would deepen rather than reduce silencing.
KIN1 protein loss induces transcription from new copies of the gene
new gene copies are not made, and the protein continues to fall at 72 hours.
The scrambled control siRNA begins to target KIN1 mRNA at later times
the control siRNA has no match to KIN1 and would not lower mRNA in any case.
qs.x: Transfected siRNA is not replicated in mammalian cells; it is diluted with each division and degraded, so the silencing effect is transient and mRNA recovers. Trap: Believing silencing by siRNA is permanent, so any recovery must reflect a change in the gene.

qs.q: Within the RNA-induced silencing complex, the guide strand of a perfectly complementary siRNA most directly causes which event?
o: The ribosome stalls at the start codon of the target mRNA
translation repression by stalling is typical of partial miRNA pairing, not of full complementarity.
Argonaute cleaves the base-paired region of the target mRNA
Correct: Perfect complementarity lets the Argonaute protein in RISC cut the target mRNA, which is then degraded; partial pairing (as with many miRNAs) usually represses translation instead.
The target mRNA is capped at its 5' end and exported
capping and export are normal steps of mRNA maturation in the nucleus and are unrelated to RISC.
The siRNA is polyadenylated and translated into peptide
an siRNA is not an mRNA and is neither polyadenylated nor translated.
qs.x: Perfect complementarity lets the Argonaute protein in RISC cut the target mRNA, which is then degraded; partial pairing (as with many miRNAs) usually represses translation instead. Trap: Mixing up the mechanisms of siRNA (cleavage) and miRNA (translational repression).

graph.title: Figure 1. KIN1 mRNA and protein after KIN1 siRNA

passages.title: FL09 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 3
text: A genetics class compared two inheritance patterns. Human ABO blood type is determined by a single gene with three alleles: IA and IB, which each encode a glycosyltransferase that adds a different sugar to the surface of red blood cells, and i, which encodes a nonfunctional enzyme. IA and IB are dominant to i, so people with type O blood have genotype ii. Dominance relationships describe how the products of the two alleles of a gene combine in a heterozygote, and they are inferred from the phenotypes of offspring in crosses. Red cells of people with genotype IAIB carry both sugars. Plasma contains antibodies against the A or B sugars that the person's own red cells lack.
In snapdragons, a cross between red-flowered and white-flowered plants produces only pink-flowered offspring. Pink flowers contain about half as much red pigment as red flowers.
Students collected blood-type data from five families, each with several children (Table 1). The parental phenotypes are given; students used the children's phenotypes to infer parental genotypes.

qs.q: Family 1 has a fifth child. What is the probability that this child has type O blood?
o: 1/2 is the chance of one parent passing i, not both.
1/8 would require an extra independent 1/2 event that is not part of this cross.
Correct: The type O child requires that each parent carries i, so the mother is IAi and the father is IBi; the chance of receiving i from both is 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.
the parents are both heterozygous carriers of i, so type O is possible.
qs.x: The type O child requires that each parent carries i, so the mother is IAi and the father is IBi; the chance of receiving i from both is 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4. Trap: Using the probability that one parent transmits i instead of multiplying the two parents' contributions.

qs.q: For Family 2 (mother AB, father O), what is the probability that the next child has type A blood?
o: 1/4 would apply if four equally likely phenotypes were possible, but only A and B can occur.
3/4 has no basis here: only two outcomes, type A and type B, can occur, and they are equally likely.
not every child is type A, since the mother passes IB half the time (a type B child was observed).
Correct: The mother gives IA or IB with equal probability and the father gives only i, so children are IAi (type A) or IBi (type B), each with probability 1/2.
qs.x: The mother gives IA or IB with equal probability and the father gives only i, so children are IAi (type A) or IBi (type B), each with probability 1/2. Trap: Treating AB as if one allele hides the other, instead of counting each of the mother's gametes equally.

qs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the inheritance of AB blood type from that of pink snapdragon flowers?
o: AB shows both alleles fully expressed; pink shows an intermediate amount of one product
Correct: IA and IB are codominant: both sugars appear on the same cell. Pink snapdragons show incomplete dominance: the heterozygote makes about half as much red pigment, an intermediate phenotype.
In AB blood the IA allele is incompletely dominant over IB, whereas pink flowers arise from codominance
this reverses the terms; the AB phenotype is codominance and the pink phenotype is incomplete dominance.
AB blood arises when two copies of one allele are inherited, whereas pink flowers require two different alleles
AB blood requires the two different alleles IA and IB, so the description of homozygotes is wrong.
AB blood shows an intermediate phenotype between A and B, whereas pink flowers express both pigments separately
red cells of type AB carry both sugars rather than an intermediate form, and pink flowers do not express red and white pigment separately.
qs.x: IA and IB are codominant: both sugars appear on the same cell. Pink snapdragons show incomplete dominance: the heterozygote makes about half as much red pigment, an intermediate phenotype. Trap: Reversing the definitions of codominance and incomplete dominance.

qs.q: The child with type A blood in Family 3 needs a red-cell transfusion. Which donor red cells could be given safely?
o: Type A or type O
Correct: A type A recipient has anti-B antibodies, so red cells lacking the B sugar (type A and type O) are safe.
Type B or type O
type B cells carry the B sugar and would be attacked by the recipient's anti-B antibodies.
Type AB only
type AB cells also carry the B sugar, and the recipient is not limited to AB donors.
Type A or type AB
type AB cells carry the B sugar and would be agglutinated by the recipient's anti-B antibodies.
qs.x: A type A recipient has anti-B antibodies, so red cells lacking the B sugar (type A and type O) are safe. Trap: Reasoning from the donor's plasma antibodies rather than from the recipient's antibodies against donor red cells.

passages.title: FL09 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 4
text: Researchers incubated primary rat hepatocytes under four conditions to examine how fatty acid synthesis and fatty acid oxidation are coordinated. Cells were treated with insulin or glucagon for 2 hours. In two further groups, insulin-treated cells received either TOFA, an inhibitor of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC), or etomoxir, an irreversible inhibitor of carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I) in the outer mitochondrial membrane. Malonyl-CoA was measured by mass spectrometry. Fatty acid synthesis was measured as incorporation of radiolabeled acetate into lipid, and beta-oxidation was measured as production of radiolabeled acid-soluble products from radiolabeled palmitate. Synthesis and oxidation are expressed relative to the insulin condition (Table 1 and Figure 1).

Glucagon raised cyclic AMP in the cells and increased phosphorylation of ACC by protein kinase A and AMP-activated protein kinase. Phosphorylated ACC has low activity. All dishes received identical amounts of palmitate and acetate, each condition was run in triplicate, and cell viability exceeded 95% at the end of the incubation in every group.

qs.q: Which mechanism best explains the low rate of beta-oxidation in insulin-treated cells?
o: Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I, which limits entry of fatty acyl groups into mitochondria
Correct: High malonyl-CoA (10.0 pmol/mg) inhibits CPT-I, so long-chain fatty acyl groups cannot enter the matrix via the carnitine shuttle and beta-oxidation is low (15).
Malonyl-CoA inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase, which depletes the acetyl-CoA needed for oxidation
malonyl-CoA is the product of ACC and does not deplete acetyl-CoA; oxidation produces acetyl-CoA.
Malonyl-CoA is oxidized in the matrix and competes with palmitoyl-CoA for NAD+
malonyl-CoA does not compete for NAD+ and is not an oxidation substrate in the matrix.
Malonyl-CoA activates CPT-I, which exports fatty acyl groups from the mitochondria
CPT-I imports acyl groups and is inhibited, not activated, by malonyl-CoA.
qs.x: High malonyl-CoA (10.0 pmol/mg) inhibits CPT-I, so long-chain fatty acyl groups cannot enter the matrix via the carnitine shuttle and beta-oxidation is low (15). Trap: Confusing the synthesis intermediate malonyl-CoA with an oxidation substrate instead of a regulator of CPT-I.

qs.q: Why does glucagon lower malonyl-CoA levels in these cells?
o: Phosphorylation activates ACC, which consumes malonyl-CoA
ACC produces malonyl-CoA, and phosphorylation lowers its activity as stated in the passage.
Phosphorylation inactivates ACC, so less malonyl-CoA is produced
Correct: Glucagon raises cAMP and activates PKA (and AMPK), which phosphorylate and inactivate ACC; with less carboxylation of acetyl-CoA, malonyl-CoA falls to 2.0 pmol/mg.
Glucagon increases insulin release, which degrades malonyl-CoA
hepatocytes were cultured with glucagon alone and glucagon opposes insulin action.
Phosphorylation inactivates CPT-I, which increases malonyl-CoA breakdown
CPT-I is inhibited by malonyl-CoA, and the passage describes phosphorylation of ACC rather than CPT-I.
qs.x: Glucagon raises cAMP and activates PKA (and AMPK), which phosphorylate and inactivate ACC; with less carboxylation of acetyl-CoA, malonyl-CoA falls to 2.0 pmol/mg. Trap: Assuming phosphorylation always activates enzymes rather than reading the direction given for ACC.

qs.q: The insulin-plus-etomoxir results (Table 1) are best explained by which statement?
o: CPT-I acts upstream of ACC, so its inhibition raises malonyl-CoA
malonyl-CoA is unchanged, not raised, so CPT-I is not regulating ACC.
CPT-I acts downstream of malonyl-CoA and is not required for synthesis

Correct: Etomoxir blocks CPT-I, so oxidation falls to 3, yet malonyl-CoA (10.0) and synthesis (100) are unchanged because malonyl-CoA is made by ACC upstream of CPT-I and synthesis occurs in the cytosol.
CPT-I is required for cytosolic fatty acid synthesis, so its inhibition would lower synthesis
synthesis stayed at 100, so CPT-I is not needed for it; synthesis occurs in the cytosol.
Etomoxir activates ACC, which keeps malonyl-CoA at 10.0 pmol/mg
malonyl-CoA is the same as in insulin alone, which shows ACC activity was unaffected.
qs.x: Etomoxir blocks CPT-I, so oxidation falls to 3, yet malonyl-CoA (10.0) and synthesis (100) are unchanged because malonyl-CoA is made by ACC upstream of CPT-I and synthesis occurs in the cytosol. Trap: Assuming that blocking one pathway step changes every other measurement in the pathway, regardless of order.

qs.q: Compared with fatty acid synthesis, beta-oxidation of palmitoyl-CoA differs in which respect?
o: It occurs in the cytosol and consumes NADPH
cytosolic NADPH use describes synthesis rather than oxidation.
It occurs in the mitochondrial matrix and consumes ATP for each two-carbon unit added
oxidation removes two-carbon units and does not add them; ATP is used to activate the fatty acid, not per unit.
It occurs in the cytosol and yields NADH and FADH2
oxidation occurs in the matrix, not the cytosol, even though it yields NADH and FADH2.
It occurs in the mitochondrial matrix and yields NADH and FADH2
Correct: Beta-oxidation runs in the mitochondrial matrix and cleaves two-carbon acetyl-CoA units while reducing NAD+ and FAD; synthesis occurs in the cytosol and uses NADPH.
qs.x: Beta-oxidation runs in the mitochondrial matrix and cleaves two-carbon acetyl-CoA units while reducing NAD+ and FAD; synthesis occurs in the cytosol and uses NADPH. Trap: Attributing the location or cofactor of one pathway to the other.

qs.q: How many rounds of the beta-oxidation spiral are needed to convert one palmitoyl-CoA (16 carbons) completely to acetyl-CoA?
o: Correct: Each round removes two carbons; the last round releases two acetyl-CoA units, so a 16-carbon chain needs 7 rounds and yields 8 acetyl-CoA.
8 is the number of acetyl-CoA produced, not the number of rounds.
16 is the number of carbons in the chain.
15 is one less than the number of carbons and is not related to a two-carbon cycle.
qs.x: Each round removes two carbons; the last round releases two acetyl-CoA units, so a 16-carbon chain needs 7 rounds and yields 8 acetyl-CoA. Trap: Counting the acetyl-CoA products (8) instead of the cleavage rounds (7).

graph.title: Figure 1. Fatty acid oxidation by condition
graph.x_label: Condition (1 = insulin, 2 = glucagon, 3 = insulin + TOFA, 4 = insulin + etomoxir)

passages.title: FL09 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 5
text: Researchers examined how intercellular junctions contribute to the barrier and communication properties of a cultured intestinal epithelial monolayer grown on a porous filter. They measured transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), which reflects ion flow between cells, and the flux of radiolabeled mannitol (molecular weight 182) from the apical to the basolateral chamber. To assess cell-to-cell coupling, a single cell was injected with Lucifer yellow (molecular weight 457), and the number of neighboring cells containing dye after 5 minutes was counted. Control monolayers were compared with monolayers treated with EGTA (a calcium chelator) for 30 minutes, with monolayers in which the tight junction protein claudin-4 had been partly depleted, and with monolayers treated with carbenoxolone, an inhibitor of connexin channels (Table 1).

In a separate experiment, a fluorescent dextran of molecular weight 10,000 was injected into single control cells and did not appear in neighboring cells. All monolayers had been grown to confluence for 14 days and had similar cell density at the time of measurement, and each value in Table 1 is a mean of at least six filters.

qs.q: Which junction most directly limits the paracellular movement of mannitol across the monolayer?
o: Tight junctions
Correct: Reducing the tight junction protein claudin-4 or chelating calcium (which disrupts junction assembly) lowers TEER and raises mannitol flux, so tight junctions seal the paracellular space.
Gap junctions
blocking gap junctions with carbenoxolone left TEER (340) and flux (1.1) near control.
Desmosomes
desmosomes anchor cells mechanically through intermediate filaments but do not seal the space between cells.
Hemidesmosomes
hemidesmosomes attach cells to the basement membrane and are not between neighboring cells.
qs.x: Reducing the tight junction protein claudin-4 or chelating calcium (which disrupts junction assembly) lowers TEER and raises mannitol flux, so tight junctions seal the paracellular space. Trap: Choosing a junction that connects cells without recognizing that only tight junctions create the paracellular seal.

qs.q: Carbenoxolone treatment is most consistent with which conclusion?
o: Connexin channels seal the paracellular space, so their block reduces mannitol flux
mannitol flux was 1.1, essentially control, so connexins are not the paracellular seal.
Connexin channels carry ions across the apical membrane, so their block reduces TEER
TEER barely changed (340 versus 350), so the connexin block did not affect ion flow across the monolayer.
Gap junctions pass dye between cells but do not form the barrier
Correct: Dye spread falls from 12 to 1 neighbors while TEER and mannitol flux hardly change, so gap junctions mediate cytoplasmic coupling but not the barrier to paracellular flux.
Connexin channels are needed for tight junction assembly, so their block abolishes TEER
TEER was normal after treatment, so tight junctions remained assembled.
qs.x: Dye spread falls from 12 to 1 neighbors while TEER and mannitol flux hardly change, so gap junctions mediate cytoplasmic coupling but not the barrier to paracellular flux. Trap: Assuming any junction inhibitor must change TEER regardless of the junction's actual role.

qs.q: Why did the 10,000-dalton dextran fail to pass between neighboring cells, while Lucifer yellow did?
o: Gap junction channels admit only molecules larger than about 1,000 daltons
the size limit works in the opposite direction; larger molecules are excluded.
Dextran is positively charged and is repelled by the connexon pore
dextran is a neutral polysaccharide, and the exclusion depends on size.
Dextran is degraded by lysosomes before it can reach the junction
the experiment shows no lysosomal degradation, and the dextran would still have appeared in neighbors if it fit the pore.
Gap junction channels admit molecules smaller than about 1,000 daltons

Correct: A gap junction is formed from paired connexons (each a ring of six connexin subunits), and its channel passes ions and small molecules up to about 1 kDa, so Lucifer yellow (457) passes but a 10-kDa dextran does not.
qs.x: A gap junction is formed from paired connexons (each a ring of six connexin subunits), and its channel passes ions and small molecules up to about 1 kDa, so Lucifer yellow (457) passes but a 10-kDa dextran does not. Trap: Reversing the size limit, thinking larger molecules pass more readily through channels.

qs.q: If tight junctions were disrupted in an intestinal epithelium, which additional consequence would be expected?
o: Desmosome proteins would be unable to bind intermediate filaments
desmosome-intermediate filament attachment does not depend on tight junctions.
Hemidesmosomes would no longer bind the basement membrane
hemidesmosome attachment depends on integrins binding the basement membrane.
Membrane proteins would lose their polar distribution
Correct: Tight junctions also act as a fence that keeps apical and basolateral membrane proteins separate; without them, polarity is lost and directional absorption is impaired.
Gap junction channels would increase in number to compensate
the data show gap junction coupling unchanged in EGTA, with no compensation seen.
qs.x: Tight junctions also act as a fence that keeps apical and basolateral membrane proteins separate; without them, polarity is lost and directional absorption is impaired. Trap: Overlooking the second role of tight junctions in maintaining membrane polarity.

passages.title: FL09 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 6
text: Bacterium B is a marine species that forms surface-attached biofilms. It synthesizes an acyl-homoserine lactone (AHL) autoinducer using the synthase LuxI, and the AHL binds the cytoplasmic receptor LuxR, a transcription factor that activates genes for extracellular polysaccharide production. Researchers compared the wild-type strain with a luxI deletion mutant, a luxR deletion mutant, and the luxI mutant supplemented with 100 nM synthetic AHL. All cultures were grown for 24 hours in microtiter plates. Planktonic growth was measured as optical density at 600 nm (OD600), biofilm biomass by crystal violet staining of surface-attached cells (OD570), and AHL concentration in the supernatant by a bioassay (Table 1). Each condition was tested in six replicate wells at 25 degrees C with gentle shaking, and values are means.

When biofilms and planktonic cultures of the wild-type strain were exposed to the same concentration of an antibiotic for 4 hours, 42% of biofilm cells survived compared with 0.5% of planktonic cells.

qs.q: What do the equal OD600 values in Table 1 indicate?
o: The mutants form biofilm as readily as the wild type
biofilm OD570 is much lower in both mutants (0.30 and 0.28 versus 1.80).
The wild type makes the same amount of AHL as the luxR mutant at each cell density
the wild type makes 85 nM and the luxR mutant 90 nM, which are similar but not the question, and OD600 does not measure AHL.
The biofilm defects of the mutants are not caused by slower planktonic growth
Correct: All strains reach OD600 of 1.2, so growth is similar, and the lower biofilm OD570 of the luxI and luxR mutants reflects a defect in biofilm formation rather than in growth.
Biofilm biomass depends only on the number of planktonic cells
the luxI + AHL strain has the same OD600 but a much higher biofilm OD570 than the luxI mutant, so biomass is not just cell number.
qs.x: All strains reach OD600 of 1.2, so growth is similar, and the lower biofilm OD570 of the luxI and luxR mutants reflects a defect in biofilm formation rather than in growth. Trap: Reading similar planktonic growth as evidence of similar biofilm formation.

qs.q: The luxR mutant produces AHL (90 nM) but forms little biofilm. This result indicates that:
o: LuxR is the synthase that produces AHL
LuxI is the synthase, and the luxR mutant still makes AHL (90 nM).
LuxR is the receptor for AHL
Correct: AHL is present in luxR cells yet biofilm is poor, so the signal cannot be sensed without LuxR, the transcription factor that binds AHL and activates polysaccharide genes.
AHL is not required for biofilm formation in this species
the luxI mutant is rescued by AHL, so AHL is required.
LuxR is an exporter that releases AHL from the cell
the passage describes LuxR as a cytoplasmic transcription factor, not an exporter.
qs.x: AHL is present in luxR cells yet biofilm is poor, so the signal cannot be sensed without LuxR, the transcription factor that binds AHL and activates polysaccharide genes. Trap: Confusing the synthase (LuxI) with the receptor (LuxR) in the quorum-sensing circuit.

qs.q: Why does AHL accumulate to effective levels only at high cell density?
o: Each cell releases AHL, so the extracellular concentration rises with population size, and AHL also induces more luxI expression

Correct: Per-cell AHL production is small, so the concentration crosses the activation threshold only when many cells are present; AHL-LuxR also upregulates luxI, giving positive feedback (autoinduction).
AHL is made only when cells attach to a surface, which occurs at high density
production does not require attachment, and planktonic cells in culture also produce AHL.
AHL is made by only a few cells, and spreads at a rate set by cell division
there is no mention of a specialized subset of cells, and AHL diffuses without needing division.
Cells degrade AHL at low density, which removes the signal until nutrients are exhausted
degradation at low density is not described, and the signal depends on population size, not nutrient exhaustion.
qs.x: Per-cell AHL production is small, so the concentration crosses the activation threshold only when many cells are present; AHL-LuxR also upregulates luxI, giving positive feedback (autoinduction). Trap: Thinking that quorum sensing responds to surface contact instead of the concentration of a shared signal.

qs.q: Which feature of biofilms best explains the higher antibiotic survival of biofilm cells?
o: Biofilm cells carry more copies of the gene for the antibiotic target
the survival difference is physiological and does not depend on gene copy number.
Biofilm cells take up more antibiotic, which activates their repair enzymes
taking up more drug would increase killing rather than survival.
Biofilm cells lose their cell walls, which blocks antibiotics that target peptidoglycan
biofilm cells retain their walls, and loss of walls is not described.
The extracellular matrix slows antibiotic diffusion and many cells grow slowly
Correct: The polysaccharide matrix limits penetration of the drug and cells within the biofilm are often in slow-growth or persister states, so they survive far better (42% versus 0.5%).
qs.x: The polysaccharide matrix limits penetration of the drug and cells within the biofilm are often in slow-growth or persister states, so they survive far better (42% versus 0.5%). Trap: Ascribing biofilm tolerance to genetic resistance rather than to matrix and growth-state effects.

graph.title: Figure 1. Biofilm biomass by strain
graph.x_label: Strain (1 = wild type, 2 = luxI deletion, 3 = luxI deletion + AHL, 4 = luxR deletion)

passages.title: FL09 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 7
text: Researchers studied how signaling molecules specify embryonic cell fates using explants from the animal cap of Xenopus blastulae. Animal cap tissue normally forms epidermis. Explants were cultured for 8 hours in solutions containing different concentrations of activin, a secreted protein that signals through receptors that activate SMAD transcription factors. Expression of three marker genes was then measured by quantitative PCR: keratin (epidermis, an ectodermal derivative), Brachyury (mesoderm), and Sox17 (endoderm). Values are expressed as a percentage of the maximum measured for each marker (Table 1 and Figure 1).

In a second experiment, animal cap cells were dissociated and cultured at low density in the presence or absence of noggin, a protein that binds and inactivates bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs). Dissociated cells without noggin formed epidermis, whereas dissociated cells with noggin formed neural tissue expressing NCAM. In a third experiment, a piece of dorsal lip tissue was grafted to the ventral side of a host embryo, which then developed a second body axis.

qs.q: Which tissue would most likely arise from cells with the marker profile seen at 100 ng/mL activin?
o: The epidermis of the skin
epidermis is ectoderm and keratin is low (2%) at this dose.
Skeletal muscle of the limbs
muscle is mesodermal, and Brachyury is only 30% at this dose, lower than at 20 ng/mL.
The neurons of the spinal cord
neurons are ectodermal and would require BMP inhibition, as seen with noggin.
Pancreatic epithelium
Correct: High Sox17 (85%) marks endoderm, which gives rise to the lining of the gut and respiratory tract and to the liver and pancreas.
qs.x: High Sox17 (85%) marks endoderm, which gives rise to the lining of the gut and respiratory tract and to the liver and pancreas. Trap: Matching the tissue to the marker that is highest at a different concentration.

qs.q: Which conclusion about activin is best supported by Table 1?
o: Activin acts only as an inducer of ectoderm at all concentrations
keratin (ectoderm) falls steadily as activin rises, so activin does not induce ectoderm.
Different concentrations of activin specify different germ layers, as expected for a morphogen
Correct: As concentration increases, the dominant marker shifts from keratin (0) to Brachyury (5-20) to Sox17 (100), showing concentration-dependent fate choice, the defining property of a morphogen.
Activin lowers Brachyury expression at every concentration tested
Brachyury rises from 2% at 0 ng/mL to 90% at 20 ng/mL.
Activin acts only on explants that contain dorsal lip tissue
the explants were animal cap tissue, and dorsal lip tissue is used in a separate experiment.
qs.x: As concentration increases, the dominant marker shifts from keratin (0) to Brachyury (5-20) to Sox17 (100), showing concentration-dependent fate choice, the defining property of a morphogen. Trap: Reading only one marker and overlooking the shift among germ layers with dose.

qs.q: The noggin experiment suggests that, in the absence of BMP signaling, dissociated ectoderm cells would:
o: Adopt a neural fate

Correct: Dissociated cells without noggin form epidermis, with BMP signaling present; when noggin blocks BMPs, they express NCAM and become neural tissue, so neural fate is the outcome when BMP is inhibited.
Adopt an endodermal fate
endoderm required high activin in Table 1, not BMP inhibition.
Become notochord
notochord is dorsal mesoderm, which required activin rather than BMP inhibition.
Undergo apoptosis
no increase in cell death is described; the cells differentiate.
qs.x: Dissociated cells without noggin form epidermis, with BMP signaling present; when noggin blocks BMPs, they express NCAM and become neural tissue, so neural fate is the outcome when BMP is inhibited. Trap: Assuming that blocking a signal prevents differentiation rather than revealing a default neural fate.

qs.q: The graft of dorsal lip tissue producing a second body axis is an example of:
o: Cell autonomous determination, in which the graft alone forms the entire axis
the second axis is largely made of induced host tissue, not the graft alone.
Induction by an organizer that signals to neighboring host cells
Correct: The dorsal lip (Spemann organizer) secretes signals, including BMP inhibitors, that induce host cells to form dorsal structures, so most of the second axis is made from host cells.
Induction of ectoderm by the endoderm to form neural crest
the dorsal lip is mesodermal and the induction described is of neural and dorsal tissue, not neural crest formation by endoderm.
Transdifferentiation of host mesoderm into endoderm
the signals induce a dorsal fate in host tissue, and no conversion to endoderm is described.
qs.x: The dorsal lip (Spemann organizer) secretes signals, including BMP inhibitors, that induce host cells to form dorsal structures, so most of the second axis is made from host cells. Trap: Thinking the grafted tissue itself forms the new structure rather than inducing the host.

qs.q: By what factor does Sox17 expression increase when activin is raised from 20 to 100 ng/mL?
o: About 0.18-fold
0.18 is the inverse ratio, 15/85.
About 5.7-fold
Correct: The ratio of 85% to 15% is 5.67, or about 5.7-fold.
About 85-fold
85-fold would use the value at 100 ng/mL alone as the ratio.
About 70-fold
70-fold is the difference, 85 - 15, not a ratio.
qs.x: The ratio of 85% to 15% is 5.67, or about 5.7-fold. Trap: Inverting the ratio or reporting a difference rather than the fold change.

passages.title: FL09 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 8
text: Sound transduction occurs in the organ of Corti, where hair cells sit on the basilar membrane. Each hair cell has stereocilia projecting into the endolymph, a fluid with high K+ concentration and a positive potential of about +80 mV relative to perilymph. Deflection of stereocilia toward the tallest row opens mechanically gated channels at the tips, K+ enters, and the hair cell depolarizes; voltage-gated Ca2+ channels then open at the base of the cell.

Researchers studied cochlear function in guinea pigs treated for 14 days with high-dose gentamicin, an aminoglycoside antibiotic known to enter hair cells through the mechanotransduction channels and cause cell death. Hearing thresholds at several frequencies were measured before and after treatment using auditory brainstem responses. The site along the basilar membrane that responds maximally to each frequency, expressed as distance from the base of the cochlea, was determined from mapping studies in untreated animals (Table 1 and Figure 1).

qs.q: Why does K+ entry depolarize the hair cell?
o: Endolymph is K+ rich and positive, so K+ flows inward

Correct: Endolymph K+ is high and the endolymph is about +80 mV, so with the hair cell interior near -60 mV there is a large electrical force driving K+ inward; entry of positive charge depolarizes the cell.
Endolymph has a low K+ concentration, so K+ moves inward down its concentration gradient
endolymph is rich in K+, unlike most extracellular fluids.
Mechanically gated channels pump K+ inward using ATP, which adds positive charge
channels open passively to allow flow; they do not pump, and no ATP use is involved in the transduction current.
Hair cell cytoplasm has a higher K+ concentration than endolymph, so K+ is pulled inward by diffusion
the interior of the cell does not have more K+ than the endolymph in this case; the electrochemical force, including the +80 mV potential, drives inward flow.
qs.x: Endolymph K+ is high and the endolymph is about +80 mV, so with the hair cell interior near -60 mV there is a large electrical force driving K+ inward; entry of positive charge depolarizes the cell. Trap: Applying the usual low-K+ extracellular fluid rule to endolymph, which is unusually rich in K+.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, the high-frequency hearing loss after gentamicin most likely reflects damage to hair cells located:
o: Near the apex of the cochlea, where high frequencies are encoded
high frequencies map to the base, not the apex.
Near the apex of the cochlea, where low frequencies are encoded
the apical region encodes low frequencies, and those thresholds changed little (5 dB).
Near the base of the cochlea, where high frequencies are encoded

Correct: Larger shifts occur at 8 and 16 kHz, which map to 9 and 4 mm from the base; so basal hair cells, which encode high frequencies on the stiff, narrow end of the basilar membrane, are most affected.
Uniformly along the cochlea, because all frequencies are affected equally
the shift ranges from 5 dB at 0.5 kHz to 70 dB at 16 kHz, so loss is not uniform.
qs.x: Larger shifts occur at 8 and 16 kHz, which map to 9 and 4 mm from the base; so basal hair cells, which encode high frequencies on the stiff, narrow end of the basilar membrane, are most affected. Trap: Reversing the tonotopic map of the cochlea (low frequencies at the base).

qs.q: Which event follows hair cell depolarization and leads to activation of the auditory nerve?
o: Na+ enters through voltage-gated channels and triggers release of acetylcholine onto spiral ganglion neurons
the hair cell signal depends on Ca2+ entry and the transmitter is glutamate, not acetylcholine.
Ca2+ leaves the cell through voltage-gated channels and triggers release of GABA onto spiral ganglion neurons
Ca2+ enters the cell, which is how it triggers exocytosis, and the transmitter is glutamate.
K+ leaves through mechanically gated channels and triggers an action potential in the hair cell
K+ enters, not leaves, through the mechanically gated channels, and hair cells signal with graded potentials rather than action potentials.
Ca2+ enters through voltage-gated channels and triggers release of glutamate onto spiral ganglion neurons
Correct: Depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels; Ca2+ entry triggers exocytosis of glutamate-containing vesicles, which excites the spiral ganglion neurons.
qs.x: Depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels; Ca2+ entry triggers exocytosis of glutamate-containing vesicles, which excites the spiral ganglion neurons. Trap: Assuming the hair cell fires an action potential rather than releasing transmitter in graded fashion.

qs.q: Gentamicin damages hair cells mainly because it:
o: Blocks the voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, which starves cells of energy
Ca2+ channel block is not described and would not itself kill cells.
Enters through the open mechanotransduction channels and accumulates in the cells
Correct: The passage states the drug enters through the mechanotransduction channels, so cells with active channels accumulate it and die; high-frequency basal cells are affected first.
Raises the K+ concentration in the endolymph, which hyperpolarizes the cells
the drug does not alter endolymph K+, and higher K+ would depolarize rather than hyperpolarize.
Is excluded by the tight junctions, which concentrates it in the perilymph
the drug reaches the hair cells and kills them, which would not happen if it were excluded.
qs.x: The passage states the drug enters through the mechanotransduction channels, so cells with active channels accumulate it and die; high-frequency basal cells are affected first. Trap: Inventing a mechanism not stated in the passage instead of using the entry route given.

h: Distance of maximal response from base (mm)

passages.title: FL09 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 9
text: Clotting is evaluated clinically with two screening tests. The prothrombin time (PT) measures clotting after tissue factor is added to citrated plasma and is sensitive to factors VII, X, V, II, and fibrinogen. The activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) measures clotting after a contact activator is added and is sensitive to factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, and fibrinogen. Reference values are 11-14 seconds for PT and 25-35 seconds for aPTT. The International Normalized Ratio is calculated as INR = (patient PT / mean normal PT)^ISI, where the ISI of the thromboplastin reagent used in this laboratory is 1.0 and the mean normal PT is 12 seconds.

Four patients with bleeding symptoms were tested (Table 1). Patient 1 is a boy with a family history of bleeding into joints. Patient 2 takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. Patient 3 is a woman with easy bruising and a normal family history of joint bleeding. Patient 4 is receiving intravenous unfractionated heparin after surgery.

qs.q: Patient 1 has a normal PT and prolonged aPTT. Which deficiency is most consistent with these results?
o: Factor VII
factor VII deficiency would prolong the PT, as in patient 3.
Vitamin K-dependent factors as a group
a deficiency of vitamin K-dependent factors prolongs the PT, as in patient 2.
Fibrinogen
fibrinogen deficiency would prolong both tests, but the PT is normal here.
Factor VIII
Correct: A prolonged aPTT with a normal PT points to the intrinsic pathway (factors XII, XI, IX, VIII); together with a family history of joint bleeding, hemophilia A (factor VIII) fits.
qs.x: A prolonged aPTT with a normal PT points to the intrinsic pathway (factors XII, XI, IX, VIII); together with a family history of joint bleeding, hemophilia A (factor VIII) fits. Trap: Mixing up which test reflects which pathway when only one is abnormal.

qs.q: Warfarin prolongs the PT in patient 2 because it:
o: Activates antithrombin, which inhibits thrombin and factor Xa
this describes the mechanism of heparin through antithrombin, not warfarin.
Binds calcium, which prevents the activation of platelets and factors
warfarin does not chelate calcium; the citrate in the sample tube does.
Cleaves fibrinogen to fibrin, which exhausts the available fibrinogen
thrombin, not warfarin, cleaves fibrinogen to fibrin.
Blocks vitamin K recycling for factor carboxylation

Correct: Warfarin blocks regeneration of reduced vitamin K, so factors II, VII, IX, and X lack gamma-carboxyglutamate residues needed to bind Ca2+ on phospholipid surfaces; factor VII has the shortest half-life, so the PT rises first.
qs.x: Warfarin blocks regeneration of reduced vitamin K, so factors II, VII, IX, and X lack gamma-carboxyglutamate residues needed to bind Ca2+ on phospholipid surfaces; factor VII has the shortest half-life, so the PT rises first. Trap: Confusing the mechanisms of warfarin (factor synthesis) and heparin (antithrombin activation).

qs.q: What is the INR for patient 2?
o: 0.4 is the inverse ratio, 12/30.
30 is the raw PT in seconds, not the ratio.
1.5 would result from subtracting reference time or using 18/12, which is not the patient's value.
qs.x: INR = (30 / 12)^1.0 = 2.5. Trap: Inverting the PT ratio or reporting the PT itself instead of the ratio.

qs.q: Patient 3 has a prolonged PT and a normal aPTT. A deficiency of which factor would best explain this?
o: Factor VII, which is part of the extrinsic pathway only
Correct: Factor VII acts only in the tissue factor (extrinsic) pathway, so its deficiency prolongs the PT but leaves the aPTT normal.
Factor IX, which is part of the intrinsic pathway only
factor IX deficiency prolongs the aPTT and leaves the PT normal.
Factor X, which would also prolong the aPTT
factor X is in the common pathway, so its deficiency would prolong both tests.
Factor XII, which is part of the contact system only
factor XII deficiency prolongs only the aPTT.
qs.x: Factor VII acts only in the tissue factor (extrinsic) pathway, so its deficiency prolongs the PT but leaves the aPTT normal. Trap: Forgetting that common pathway deficiencies prolong both tests while pathway-specific ones prolong just one.

passages.title: FL09 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 10
text: Plasma cholesterol is carried in lipoproteins. Chylomicrons and very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) deliver triglycerides to tissues, and VLDL remnants are converted to low-density lipoprotein (LDL). LDL particles, which contain apolipoprotein B-100, are taken up by hepatocytes after binding the LDL receptor (LDLR). High-density lipoprotein (HDL) contains apolipoprotein A-I and carries cholesterol from peripheral tissues to the liver.

Researchers compared four groups: control subjects, patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), patients with homozygous FH, and control subjects treated with a statin for 8 weeks. Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase. Table 1 shows mean fasting lipid values and relative hepatic LDLR activity (measured in liver biopsy samples in the first three groups and estimated by LDL clearance in the treated group). In a second analysis, patients with homozygous FH were treated with the same statin dose, and mean LDL cholesterol fell by only 6%. All subjects fasted for 12 hours before blood sampling, and none was taking other lipid-lowering drugs or had diabetes or thyroid disease.

qs.q: Which process is impaired in patients with FH who have defective LDL receptors?
o: Lipoprotein lipase hydrolysis of triglycerides in chylomicrons
lipoprotein lipase acts in tissue capillaries and does not depend on LDLR, and triglycerides are only mildly changed.
LDL uptake by receptor-mediated endocytosis
Correct: LDLR binds apoB-100 on LDL and internalizes it in clathrin-coated vesicles; reduced receptor activity (50% and 2%) leaves LDL in plasma, so LDL-C rises to 220 and 600 mg/dL.
Esterification of cholesterol in HDL by LCAT
LCAT esterifies cholesterol on HDL, and HDL-C changes only modestly.
Secretion of VLDL from the liver as an energy source
VLDL secretion is not impaired in FH, and it is not the cause of LDL accumulation.
qs.x: LDLR binds apoB-100 on LDL and internalizes it in clathrin-coated vesicles; reduced receptor activity (50% and 2%) leaves LDL in plasma, so LDL-C rises to 220 and 600 mg/dL. Trap: Attributing the elevated LDL to a defect in triglyceride transport instead of LDL receptor clearance.

qs.q: Why does LDL-C fall in control subjects given a statin?
o: Lower hepatocyte cholesterol suppresses LDLR expression, which increases LDL uptake
LDLR expression rises, not falls, when intracellular cholesterol is low.
The statin binds LDL particles directly, which targets them for excretion in the bile
statins act on the enzyme in the cell, not on LDL itself.
The statin increases HMG-CoA reductase activity, which makes more HDL
statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase rather than activate it, and HDL is unchanged at 55 mg/dL.
Lower hepatocyte cholesterol activates SREBP-2, which increases LDLR expression and LDL uptake

Correct: By inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol synthesis, statins lower intracellular cholesterol; SREBP-2 then raises LDLR expression (160% in Table 1), so more LDL is cleared.
qs.x: By inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol synthesis, statins lower intracellular cholesterol; SREBP-2 then raises LDLR expression (160% in Table 1), so more LDL is cleared. Trap: Predicting that low cellular cholesterol should lower LDL receptor expression.

qs.q: Why did LDL cholesterol fall by only 6% in statin-treated patients with homozygous FH?
o: Their cells make too much HDL, which blocks statin action
HDL-C is lower in this group (40 mg/dL), and HDL does not block statins.
Their HMG-CoA reductase is insensitive to all statins
the statin works in other groups through the same enzyme, and no insensitivity is described.
Their cells convert statin to LDL, which offsets the benefit
statins are not converted to LDL, which is a lipoprotein.
Their cells have almost no LDL receptors to upregulate
Correct: Statins lower plasma LDL mainly by increasing LDLR; with only 2% receptor activity, little additional receptor expression is possible, so LDL-C remains high.
qs.x: Statins lower plasma LDL mainly by increasing LDLR; with only 2% receptor activity, little additional receptor expression is possible, so LDL-C remains high. Trap: Assuming a drug resistance mechanism instead of using the receptor data in the table.

qs.q: A patient has total cholesterol 240 mg/dL, HDL-C 50 mg/dL, and triglycerides 150 mg/dL. Using the Friedewald equation (LDL-C = total cholesterol - HDL-C - triglycerides/5), what is the estimated LDL-C?
o: 190 mg/dL
190 results from subtracting only HDL-C.
160 mg/dL
Correct: Triglycerides/5 = 30, so LDL-C = 240 - 50 - 30 = 160 mg/dL.
40 mg/dL
40 results from subtracting the full triglyceride value (240 - 50 - 150) without dividing by 5.
90 mg/dL
90 results from subtracting the undivided triglycerides and omitting HDL-C (240 - 150).
qs.x: Triglycerides/5 = 30, so LDL-C = 240 - 50 - 30 = 160 mg/dL. Trap: Forgetting to divide triglycerides by 5 when estimating VLDL cholesterol.

qs.q: A competitive statin binds the active site of HMG-CoA reductase. Compared with the uninhibited enzyme, the statin changes the kinetics of the reaction in which way?
o: The apparent Km decreases and Vmax decreases
a decrease in both Km and Vmax is the signature of uncompetitive inhibition.
The apparent Km is unchanged and Vmax decreases
unchanged Km with decreased Vmax is the signature of noncompetitive inhibition.
The apparent Km increases and Vmax increases
an inhibitor cannot raise Vmax, which stays the same under competitive inhibition.
The apparent Km increases and Vmax is unchanged

Correct: A competitive inhibitor competes with HMG-CoA for the active site, so more substrate is needed to reach half-maximal velocity (higher apparent Km), but sufficiently high substrate overcomes it and Vmax is unchanged.
qs.x: A competitive inhibitor competes with HMG-CoA for the active site, so more substrate is needed to reach half-maximal velocity (higher apparent Km), but sufficiently high substrate overcomes it and Vmax is unchanged. Trap: Mixing up the Km and Vmax changes produced by competitive, noncompetitive, and uncompetitive inhibitors.

graph.title: Figure 1. LDL cholesterol versus LDLR activity

passages.title: FL09 · CARS · Passage 1
text: Philosophers who ask what makes a person at one time the same person as someone at another time often begin with a ship. If every plank of a vessel is replaced over decades, is it still the same vessel? Most people answer yes, and the reason they give is continuity: no single moment of replacement broke the ship's history. The analogy tempts us to think that a person, too, is a continuous thing whose parts may change while the whole persists. But the analogy conceals a difficulty. A ship is an object we identify largely by convention; a person, we assume, is something more definite, the subject of experiences who will actually undergo tomorrow's pains.

John Locke proposed that what unites a person across time is neither an immaterial soul nor a body but consciousness, specifically the ability to remember one's earlier experiences from the inside. The old officer who recalls being the young soldier is the same person as that soldier. Thomas Reid answered with a famous objection. Suppose a boy is flogged for stealing apples, a young officer remembers the flogging, and an old general remembers being the officer but no longer remembers the flogging. Locke's criterion implies that the general is the officer and the officer is the boy, yet the general is not the boy, which violates the transitivity of identity. Later defenders replaced direct memory with chains of overlapping memory, which restores transitivity, but critics note that the repair is suspiciously ad hoc, and that memory presupposes identity rather than constituting it: to count as a genuine memory, an impression must be of an experience that I myself had, so the account seems circular.

Derek Parfit took a bolder path. He imagined a teletransporter that scans a body, destroys it, and builds an exact replica on another planet. Most of us feel that stepping into such a device is a form of death. Parfit argued that this reaction rests on a mistaken picture, on which identity is a deep further fact over and above physical and psychological continuity. If we drop that picture, he suggested, the question "Will the replica be me?" has no determinate answer, and what matters in survival is not identity but psychological connectedness and continuity, which the replica has in full. Parfit found this conclusion liberating; he reported that his own sense of separation from other people seemed to shrink, and that he cared less about his own future in a narrowly selfish way.

Critics are not persuaded that relief should count as evidence. Some argue that Parfit's cases, being technologically impossible, tell us only about our linguistic habits in fantastic situations, not about the nature of persons. Others, drawing on a narrative conception, hold that a person is not a metaphysical substance to be discovered but a life that is told and answered for; to be the same person over time is to be able to take responsibility for earlier actions and to integrate them into a developing story. This view handles ordinary cases well, for it explains why we hold a reformed offender accountable while granting that he has changed. Yet it has trouble with persons who cannot narrate, such as infants or patients with advanced dementia, whom we nonetheless regard as the same individuals who once lived fuller lives. A satisfactory theory, it seems, must account both for the practical significance of identity in ethics and law and for the strange results that thought experiments elicit, and no current proposal does both without cost.

qs.q: The primary purpose of the passage is to:
o: argue that Parfit's reductionism refutes Locke's memory criterion and so resolves the debate over identity
Parfit is presented with criticism, and the passage ends without declaring any view settled.
show through the ship analogy that personal identity is only a matter of linguistic convention
The ship analogy is raised only to show its limits, not to prove identity is conventional.
compare accounts of personal persistence and note a flaw in each
Correct: The passage moves through the ship analogy, Locke, Reid, Parfit, and the narrative view, and ends by saying no current proposal avoids cost.
defend the narrative conception as the one account that fits both ethical practice and thought experiments
The narrative view is criticized for its trouble with infants and dementia, so it is not defended as the only account.
qs.x: The passage moves through the ship analogy, Locke, Reid, Parfit, and the narrative view, and ends by saying no current proposal avoids cost. Trap: Choosing the view discussed most vividly (Parfit) as the author's thesis instead of the survey-and-critique structure.

qs.q: Reid's example of the boy, the officer, and the general is offered primarily to show that:
o: memory is too unreliable a faculty to ground any claim about who a person is
Reid's objection concerns logical structure, not the accuracy of recollection.
an old person cannot be the same individual as the child he once was
The example grants that the three are one man; it does not deny that old and young selves are identical.
a memory-based criterion can make identity fail to be transitive, because the chain of remembering may be broken at one link
Correct: The general is the officer and the officer is the boy, yet the general cannot recall being the boy, so Locke's criterion denies an identity that transitivity requires.
bodily continuity is more important to identity than psychological continuity
The example does not mention the body at all and so does not rank bodily over psychological continuity.
qs.x: The general is the officer and the officer is the boy, yet the general cannot recall being the boy, so Locke's criterion denies an identity that transitivity requires. Trap: Reading the objection as a complaint about faulty memory rather than about the transitivity of identity.

qs.q: Which of the following best expresses the circularity objection to the chain-of-memory account?
o: Chains of overlapping memory cannot be established for persons who have forgotten large parts of their lives.
Overlap between links is exactly what the chain view supplies, and gaps are not the stated problem.
Any chain of memories could be fabricated by a skilled storyteller, so no memory could be trusted as genuine.
The objection is conceptual, not about fabrication or deception.
Memory links preserve transitivity only if the earlier experiences remain equally vivid at each stage of the chain.
Vividness plays no role in the passage's treatment of transitivity.
A genuine memory must be of an experience the rememberer had, so the account assumes the identity it explains.
Correct: The passage says an impression counts as a memory only if it is of an experience I myself had, which already assumes who I am.
qs.x: The passage says an impression counts as a memory only if it is of an experience I myself had, which already assumes who I am. Trap: Mistaking a practical worry about unreliable memory for the logical worry that the criterion assumes what it explains.

qs.q: According to the passage, Parfit would most likely claim that stepping into the teletransporter:
o: ends the traveler's existence, because the replica is made of different matter than the original body
This is the intuition Parfit argues rests on a mistaken picture of identity.
is rational only if one holds that a deep further fact guarantees the replica's identity with the traveler
Parfit rejects the deep further fact, so his view does not depend on it.
is unwise because psychological connectedness cannot hold between a person and a physical duplicate
The passage states the replica has psychological connectedness and continuity in full.
preserves what matters in survival even if identity is lost
Correct: Parfit holds that what matters is psychological connectedness and continuity, which the replica has in full.
qs.x: Parfit holds that what matters is psychological connectedness and continuity, which the replica has in full. Trap: Importing the common intuition that the teletransporter kills the traveler rather than Parfit's reductionist reply.

qs.q: Which situation would the narrative conception described in the passage most readily explain?
o: A woman with advanced dementia is regarded as the same person who once ran a business.
The passage identifies dementia as a difficulty for the narrative view, not a strength.
A traveler who enters a teletransporter is judged not to have survived the trip.
The teletransporter case is Parfit's, and the narrative view is not tied to it.
A man is held responsible for a fraud committed decades ago even though years of reflection and repentance have changed his character.
Correct: The passage says the narrative view explains how a reformed offender is accountable while granting that he has changed.
A soldier who cannot remember an old battle is excused from any blame for it.
Excusing the soldier because he forgot applies a memory criterion, not a narrative of responsibility.
qs.x: The passage says the narrative view explains how a reformed offender is accountable while granting that he has changed. Trap: Picking the dementia case because it was mentioned, when the passage lists it as a weakness.

qs.q: The author mentions the ship of replaced planks in the first paragraph in order to:
o: prove that replacing parts always destroys the identity of an object, however gradual the replacement
Most people say the ship stays the same, so the example does not show destruction of identity.
introduce the appeal of continuity while hinting that persons differ from conventionally identified objects
Correct: The passage says continuity makes us answer yes for the ship, then notes that a person is assumed to be something more definite.
support Locke's claim that consciousness, rather than matter, is what unites a thing across time
The ship has no consciousness, so it cannot illustrate Locke's criterion.
illustrate Parfit's view that identity is a deep further fact over and above physical and psychological continuity
Parfit rejects the further-fact view, so the ship cannot illustrate it.
qs.x: The passage says continuity makes us answer yes for the ship, then notes that a person is assumed to be something more definite. Trap: Treating a framing analogy as a premise in the argument rather than as a setup that the author qualifies.

passages.title: FL09 · CARS · Passage 2
text: When Columbus's ships reached the Caribbean in 1492, they inaugurated a biological transfer so large that historians later gave it a name, the Columbian exchange. Alfred Crosby, who coined the phrase in 1972, argued that the voyages did not merely connect two sets of human societies; they reunited two evolutionary histories that had been separate for millions of years. Horses, cattle, pigs, wheat, and sugarcane crossed the Atlantic westward. Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cassava, and tobacco crossed eastward. In each direction the consequences were far greater than any contemporary observer could have predicted, and in neither direction were they evenly distributed.

The most consequential transfer was not a crop but a set of pathogens. Smallpox, measles, and influenza had circulated for centuries among the dense populations of Eurasia, where repeated exposure had left survivors with partial immunity and made many of these diseases chiefly childhood illnesses. Indigenous Americans, whose ancestors had entered the hemisphere before most of these diseases emerged, had no such history. Epidemics swept through communities, often traveling ahead of the Europeans who carried them, so that early explorers sometimes described landscapes already emptied. Estimates of the population decline vary widely, from fifty to ninety percent over the first century and a half in some regions, and the variation reflects disagreement over the pre-contact baseline, which has to be inferred from sparse evidence. Scholars have therefore been cautious about attributing precise figures to a catastrophe whose scale is nonetheless not in doubt.

A tempting simplification treats the exchange as a story of European agency and American passivity: Europeans carried plants and animals, and Americans received them. Crosby's own framing resisted this reading, and recent historians have pushed against it further. The crops that traveled east transformed Old World diets with a force that rivaled the effects of the American silver that financed empires. The potato, which yields more calories per acre than most European grains and grows in poor soil, supported population growth in northern Europe, and in parts of China maize and sweet potatoes opened hillsides that rice could not use. The same crop's success had a darker side. Ireland's dependence on a narrow range of potato varieties made it vulnerable to blight in the 1840s, a reminder that the exchange also exported fragility.

Other scholars question whether a single label can hold so many processes. Plants moved when farmers recognized their value, and in many cases adoption was driven by ordinary people rather than by imperial plans; livestock moved because settlers wanted them. But enslaved Africans, who were also part of the traffic that the Atlantic system created, did not choose to move, and their agricultural knowledge, notably of rice cultivation, shaped the plantation landscapes of the Americas. To fold the transfer of human beings into a catalogue of species risks flattening a moral difference. Historians who share this worry often prefer to speak of a set of exchanges, with distinct causes and distinct victims, rather than of one.

Even so, the concept has endured because it corrects an older habit of treating political and military events as the primary drivers of history. By asking what a horse or a germ did, historians gained a way of explaining outcomes that conquest narratives alone could not: how a few hundred Spaniards could topple an empire of millions, or why the grasslands of the Americas came to support herds of animals that had not existed there before 1492. Biology, on this view, is not background to history but one of its actors, and an actor with no intentions at all.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: The spread of European pathogens was the only significant consequence of the voyages that followed 1492.
Crops, animals, and enslaved people are also discussed as significant consequences.
Crosby's concept has been abandoned because it hides the role of human agency in the Atlantic world.
Scholars question the label but the concept is said to endure.
American crops contributed more to European prosperity than American silver and so reversed the direction of influence.
The passage says crops rivaled silver, not that they outweighed it or reversed any direction.
The Columbian exchange transformed life in both hemispheres, but its effects were uneven and the concept has limits.
Correct: The passage describes two-way transfers, uneven consequences, and the objection that one label cannot hold many processes.
qs.x: The passage describes two-way transfers, uneven consequences, and the objection that one label cannot hold many processes. Trap: Choosing the most dramatic topic, disease, as the whole point.

qs.q: According to the passage, Indigenous Americans suffered more from smallpox and measles than Eurasians did because:
o: Eurasians had been exposed to these diseases over centuries and had partial immunity
Correct: The passage ties Eurasian survival to repeated exposure and partial immunity, which Indigenous Americans lacked.
Eurasian physicians had developed effective treatments before the voyages of 1492
The passage mentions no treatments.
Eurasian communities were too small and scattered for epidemics to spread widely
It says Eurasia had dense populations.
the Europeans who arrived carried only mild strains that harmed few of their own people
The passage gives no basis for claiming the strains were mild; the point is immunity.
qs.x: The passage ties Eurasian survival to repeated exposure and partial immunity, which Indigenous Americans lacked. Trap: Assuming a technological explanation (medicine) where the passage gives a biological one.

qs.q: Suppose new archaeological evidence showed that the pre-contact population of one region was much smaller than scholars had assumed. According to the passage, the most likely consequence would be that scholars would:
o: conclude that European pathogens had played little part in the region's depopulation
A smaller baseline changes the size of the decline, not the cause.
lower their estimated percentage of decline for that region while still treating the demographic catastrophe as severe
Correct: The passage says estimates vary because the baseline must be inferred, and that the scale of the catastrophe is not in doubt.
abandon the view that disease traveled ahead of the Europeans who carried it
The spread of disease ahead of Europeans is a separate matter from the baseline.
revise the dates of the voyages of Columbus to match the new population figures
The dates of the voyages are independent of population estimates.
qs.x: The passage says estimates vary because the baseline must be inferred, and that the scale of the catastrophe is not in doubt. Trap: Letting a change in one number overturn the whole conclusion, when the passage says the scale is not in doubt.

qs.q: The author discusses Ireland's reliance on a few potato varieties in order to:
o: argue that the potato was less nutritious than European grains grown in poor soil
The passage says potatoes yield more calories per acre than most European grains.
show that an exchanged crop could create fragility as well as benefit
Correct: The passage calls the blight a reminder that the exchange also exported fragility.
demonstrate that Europe was affected less severely by the exchange than the Americas were
The example does not compare the severity of effects across hemispheres.
suggest that Irish farmers resisted the adoption of crops from the Americas
The passage describes heavy dependence on the potato, the opposite of resistance.
qs.x: The passage calls the blight a reminder that the exchange also exported fragility. Trap: Taking a story about a failure of the crop as a claim that the crop was inferior.

qs.q: The scholars who question whether a single label can hold so many processes object chiefly that the label:
o: merges the voluntary spread of plants with the coerced movement of people
Correct: The passage says folding the transfer of human beings into a catalogue of species risks flattening a moral difference.
underestimates how quickly crops moved between hemispheres once farmers heard of them
The passage says nothing about speed of adoption as an objection.
overstates the part Europeans played in carrying livestock to the Americas
The objection is not about who carried livestock.
ignores the fact that pathogens, unlike crops, were never moved deliberately
Pathogens are not discussed in this objection.
qs.x: The passage says folding the transfer of human beings into a catalogue of species risks flattening a moral difference. Trap: Picking a plausible but unmentioned criticism that sounds like a historian's complaint.

qs.q: The closing phrase 'an actor with no intentions at all' most nearly implies that:
o: historians should avoid attributing any importance to human decisions
The author keeps human actors, such as farmers and settlers, in the account.
historical outcomes can be shaped by biological forces acting without human purpose
Correct: The sentence says biology is one of history's actors even though it has no intentions, so effects need not come from plans.
germs and animals moved only when European leaders had planned their transfer in advance
The passage says pathogens often outran Europeans, so they were not planned.
the concept of agency has no place in any account of the Atlantic world
The claim is that biology is an additional actor, not that agency is irrelevant.
qs.x: The sentence says biology is one of history's actors even though it has no intentions, so effects need not come from plans. Trap: Reading a provocative phrase as an extreme claim that removes human agency altogether.

passages.title: FL09 · CARS · Passage 3
text: The Gothic novel of the late eighteenth century is often remembered as a catalogue of props: crumbling castles, secret passages, a villain with a tormented past, a heroine who faints at the right moments. It would be easy to dismiss the form as escapist entertainment, which is what many of its contemporary critics did. But the persistence of Gothic conventions across two centuries suggests that they answer to something other than fashion. A better explanation is that the genre gives shape to anxieties that a society cannot comfortably name. The castle, on this reading, is less a place than a condition: a past that refuses to stay buried.

Consider the form's earliest preoccupations. Writers like Horace Walpole and Ann Radcliffe set their stories in a Catholic southern Europe of the distant past, a setting that allowed Protestant English readers to project onto it fears about tyranny, superstition, and arbitrary authority. The projection was displaced rather than direct: dangers belonged to another country and another century, and so could be indulged without implicating the present. Yet the Gothic's relationship to rationality was never simple. Radcliffe's novels, for instance, typically conclude by explaining each apparent ghost as a natural event, a bit of trickery or a play of light. The reader is permitted a shiver and then returned to a reassuring world in which the unexplained turns out to be explicable. Critics have called this strategy the "explained supernatural," and have argued that it reflects the Enlightenment confidence that fear is a product of ignorance.

Other Gothic writers refused that comfort. Mary Shelley's Frankenstein locates the horror not in a haunted building but in the laboratory, and the monster is not a ghost but a creature made by methods that her contemporaries knew from experiments with galvanism. Here the anxiety is about science itself, about whether the power to make and remake life carries obligations that the maker cannot meet. Similarly, Bram Stoker's Dracula, written at the close of the nineteenth century, sets an ancient predator against a modern apparatus of typewriters, telegraphs, and phonographs, and the novel's heroes defeat him by assembling records into a single narrative. The modern technologies are both a defense and a source of unease, since the same media that assemble evidence can circulate contagion.

How should we interpret readers' pleasure in such fears? One influential view holds that Gothic fiction works as a safety valve: by experiencing terror in a controlled setting, readers discharge tensions that would otherwise attach to real objects. A second view, associated with psychoanalytic critics, claims that the genre dramatizes the return of the repressed, so that the monster stands for what a culture has pushed out of sight, whether sexual desire, colonial violence, or the claims of the dead. The two views are not strictly rivals, but they differ in what they imply about the genre's effects. The safety-valve theory predicts that Gothic fiction should leave readers more content with the order that frightens them in fiction; the return-of-the-repressed theory suggests instead that the fiction unsettles that order by reminding readers of what it excludes.

What neither theory fully explains is why the form has survived without a fixed set of fears. Its monsters have been aristocrats, scientists, immigrants, doubles, and houses, and each era has chosen the figure that most disturbs it. The conventions are the stable element; the anxiety they carry is the variable. That adaptability, more than any particular castle, is what makes the Gothic a durable instrument for a culture's self-examination.

qs.q: Which of the following best summarizes the passage?
o: Gothic fiction is best understood as escapist entertainment whose appeal faded once Enlightenment rationality triumphed.
The passage rejects the escapism view and notes the genre persisted for two centuries.
The supernatural in Gothic novels always proves explicable, which shows the genre's commitment to reason.
Frankenstein and Dracula are cited as works that refuse the explained supernatural.
Psychoanalytic readings of the Gothic are more convincing than any explanation that appeals to the release of tension.
The author calls the two interpretations not strictly rivals and prefers neither.
Gothic fiction has endured because its conventions can carry whatever anxieties an era finds most disturbing.
Correct: The passage argues that the form's conventions are stable while the anxiety they carry varies, which explains its survival.
qs.x: The passage argues that the form's conventions are stable while the anxiety they carry varies, which explains its survival. Trap: Generalizing from Radcliffe's novels to the whole genre.

qs.q: The passage says the 'explained supernatural' in Radcliffe's novels reflects:
o: a wish to suggest that ghosts are real but cannot be proved
Radcliffe's endings explain ghosts as natural events, so they do not suggest ghosts exist.
a Protestant suspicion that Catholic southern Europe was haunted
The setting, not the explanation, is tied to Protestant fears of Catholicism.
an impatience with the conventions of the Gothic novel itself
Radcliffe is working within the Gothic conventions, not impatient with them.
the Enlightenment belief that fear arises from ignorance
Correct: The passage says critics link the strategy to the Enlightenment confidence that fear is a product of ignorance.
qs.x: The passage says critics link the strategy to the Enlightenment confidence that fear is a product of ignorance. Trap: Conflating the Catholic setting with the reason for explaining the supernatural.

qs.q: Which finding would most support the safety-valve view over the return-of-the-repressed view?
o: Gothic novels written in periods of social upheaval contain more varied monsters than those written in calm periods.
Variety of monsters is explained by both theories and does not discriminate between them.
Critics who study Gothic novels closely identify more hidden themes than ordinary readers do.
The number of themes critics find is not a prediction of either theory about readers' contentment.
Readers report greater satisfaction with their social arrangements after finishing a Gothic novel than before.
Correct: The passage says the safety-valve theory predicts readers will be more content with the order that frightens them in fiction.
Readers who finish Gothic novels frequently report a greater awareness of groups their society excludes.
Greater awareness of exclusion is what the return-of-the-repressed view predicts.
qs.x: The passage says the safety-valve theory predicts readers will be more content with the order that frightens them in fiction. Trap: Choosing the result that the rival theory predicts because it also involves readers' reactions.

qs.q: The passage mentions that Dracula's heroes defeat him by assembling records into a single narrative in order to:
o: show that modern media can both protect against a threat and carry it
Correct: The passage says the technologies are both a defense and a source of unease because the same media can circulate contagion.
prove that Stoker rejected science in favor of older forms of knowledge
The heroes win with modern tools, so Stoker does not reject science.
suggest that Dracula is a more rationalist work than Frankenstein
The passage does not compare the two works' rationalism.
claim that typewriters and phonographs were invented to combat fears of contagion
No claim is made about why the devices were invented.
qs.x: The passage says the technologies are both a defense and a source of unease because the same media can circulate contagion. Trap: Reading the heroes' success as an endorsement of technology with no accompanying unease.

qs.q: According to the passage, the distant Catholic settings of Walpole and Radcliffe allowed English readers to:
o: indulge fears of tyranny and superstition without implicating their own society
Correct: The passage says the projection was displaced, so dangers belonged to another country and century.
enter a world of genuine supernatural events that rational explanation could not touch
Radcliffe's endings supply natural explanations.
criticize Catholic doctrine openly under the cover of historical scholarship
The passage speaks of fears projected onto the setting, not of doctrinal criticism or scholarship.
recognize the castle as a symbol of the English aristocracy of their own day
The castle's symbolism is described as a past that will not stay buried, not as the English aristocracy.
qs.x: The passage says the projection was displaced, so dangers belonged to another country and century. Trap: Choosing an answer that sounds historically plausible but is not stated.

qs.q: Which of the following works would the author most likely cite as continuing the Gothic's role as an instrument of cultural self-examination?
o: A comic novel that parodies earlier ghost stories and offers readers no menace or unease at any point
A parody with no menace carries no anxiety, which is the variable element.
A novel in which a household's AI assistant becomes a menace and exposes a family's hidden guilt
Correct: The passage says each era chooses the figure that most disturbs it, here a new technology, while the conventions of menace and a buried past persist.
A biography of a Gothic novelist that sets out the facts of her life in strict chronological order
A biography is not a work of fiction giving shape to anxieties.
A realist novel about a village economy that contains no frightening or disturbing events at all
