A realist novel without fear lacks the conventions that make a work Gothic.
qs.x: The passage says each era chooses the figure that most disturbs it, here a new technology, while the conventions of menace and a buried past persist. Trap: Choosing a work connected to the Gothic in subject matter rather than in function.

passages.title: FL09 · CARS · Passage 4
text: A portrait appears to be a simple thing: a likeness of a person who sat for a painter. Yet in European art from the fifteenth through the nineteenth centuries, the portrait was one of the most reliable ways for people to announce who they were and where they stood. The genre was never merely a record of faces. A sitter chose a costume, a pose, a setting, and often a handful of objects, and each choice made a claim about rank, wealth, or character. To read a portrait is therefore to read a negotiation between painter and sitter, one in which the sitter usually held the purse but the painter held the skill.

The shift from aristocratic to bourgeois patronage shows how the negotiation changed. In the sixteenth century, portraits of rulers and courtiers followed conventions that emphasized lineage and authority: the full-length pose, the column or drape signaling a palace, the hand resting on a sword or a scepter. The face was individual, but the body was an office. When Dutch merchants began to commission portraits in the seventeenth century, they borrowed some of these conventions and discarded others. Their portraits favored sober black clothing, which advertised both prosperity and Protestant restraint, and the collars and cuffs of fine linen, which were costly to launder, did the work that jewels did for princes. Group portraits of civic guards and regents gave the image a communal rather than dynastic meaning: what was being displayed was membership in a body that governed.

Portraiture could also be turned against its sitters. The English painter William Hogarth, working in the eighteenth century, produced portraits of the wealthy alongside satirical prints that mocked the same social aspirations the portraits flattered. Later, in the nineteenth century, the invention of photography democratized the likeness. A carte de visite cost a fraction of a painted portrait, and in the decades after 1860 working families who had never owned a picture of themselves could own several. Some critics predicted that painting would lose its social role. What happened instead was that painted portraiture split. Commissioned portraits retained prestige because their expense was itself the message, while avant-garde artists used the genre to question the very idea of a stable social self.

Historians who study these developments disagree about how far a portrait can be read as evidence. One camp treats the image as a document of social structure, in which a ruffled collar is a reliable index of rank. A second camp, wary of that confidence, points out that sumptuary laws, which regulated who could wear which fabrics, were often ignored, and that sitters sometimes dressed above their station precisely because the portrait was the one place they could do so. On this view the portrait documents not the sitter's class but the sitter's wish about class, an aspiration that the painter was paid to make plausible. The two positions can be reconciled only partly. Even a flattering fiction depends on a shared vocabulary of signs, and a viewer who did not already know what a sword or a velvet curtain meant could not be impressed by them.
What is clear is that the portrait was never socially neutral. It was a tool, and like any tool it could be used to build, to flatter, or to challenge the hierarchies of the society that produced it.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the central claim of the passage?
o: Portrait painting lost its importance once photography could record a likeness more cheaply.
The passage says painted portraiture split and retained prestige.
Dutch merchants in the seventeenth century abandoned the conventions of aristocratic portraits and invented a wholly new form.
The Dutch borrowed some conventions and discarded others, not all.
Portraits let sitters assert social position, though historians disagree about how far they are evidence of rank.
Correct: The passage presents portraits as claims about rank and wealth and then describes two camps about their evidential value.
Sumptuary laws succeeded in keeping portraits an accurate record of the social order of their time.
The passage says sumptuary laws were often ignored.
qs.x: The passage presents portraits as claims about rank and wealth and then describes two camps about their evidential value. Trap: Picking a detail from one paragraph as the thesis of the whole passage.

qs.q: The author mentions fine linen collars and cuffs in Dutch portraits in order to illustrate that:
o: Dutch merchants rejected sober clothing in favor of elaborate ornament and jewels
The passage says portraits favored sober black clothing.
linen cloth was reserved by sumptuary law for civic guards and regents
No law about linen is mentioned.
costly everyday goods could signal prosperity as jewels did for princes
Correct: The passage says linen was costly to launder and did the work that jewels did for princes.
merchants simply copied the full-length pose used in aristocratic portraits
The passage says merchants discarded some aristocratic conventions.
qs.x: The passage says linen was costly to launder and did the work that jewels did for princes. Trap: Overlooking that sober dress and display of wealth coexist in the same portrait.

qs.q: According to the passage, which factor best explains why commissioned painted portraits retained their prestige after photography became widespread?
o: They were more accurate likenesses than photographs, which distorted the sitter's face.
The passage claims no superiority in accuracy for painting.
Their high cost was itself part of what they communicated.
Correct: The passage says commissioned portraits retained prestige because their expense was itself the message.
Photographs remained available only to members of the aristocracy for many decades.
The passage says working families could own several cartes de visite.
Avant-garde artists refused to paint portraits and left the field to commissioned work.
Avant-garde artists used the genre to question the social self, not abandon it.
qs.x: The passage says commissioned portraits retained prestige because their expense was itself the message. Trap: Assuming prestige must rest on a technical advantage rather than on cost as a signal.

qs.q: Which finding would most support the second camp of historians described in the fourth paragraph?
o: Contracts in which painters were told to copy a sitter's actual clothing exactly as worn
Exact copying of real clothing favors the first camp's view of the portrait as document.
Portraits of rulers that consistently show a column or drape signaling a royal palace
The conventions of ruler portraits describe the aristocratic tradition, not a mismatch between sitter and dress.
Estate inventories showing many sitters owned none of the fabrics shown in their portraits
Correct: The second camp holds that portraits show the sitter's wish about class, which fits sitters depicted above their means.
Evidence that sumptuary laws were strictly enforced where the portraits were painted
Strict enforcement would make depicted clothing a reliable index of rank.
qs.x: The second camp holds that portraits show the sitter's wish about class, which fits sitters depicted above their means. Trap: Choosing evidence that fits the first camp because it mentions clothing too.

qs.q: The author's claim that the two positions 'can be reconciled only partly' depends on which assumption?
o: Even an image of aspiration persuades only if viewers recognize the signs it uses.
Correct: The passage says even a flattering fiction relies on a shared vocabulary of signs, so the signs carry social meaning.
Painters seldom understood the conventions used in the portraits they made.
The argument concerns viewers' knowledge, not painters' ignorance.
Sitters who dressed above their station were eventually prosecuted under sumptuary laws.
Prosecution is not discussed and the passage says the laws were often ignored.
Viewers of portraits were generally unaware of the sitter's actual social rank.
Viewers' knowledge of the signs, not of the sitter's real rank, is what the argument needs.
qs.x: The passage says even a flattering fiction relies on a shared vocabulary of signs, so the signs carry social meaning. Trap: Choosing an answer that sounds like a precondition of the second camp without testing what the reconciliation requires.

qs.q: The discussion of Hogarth is used to show that:
o: satirical prints replaced portraits as the favored medium of the wealthy
The passage says nothing about satire replacing portraits.
Hogarth painted portraits chiefly for working families
Hogarth's sitters were the wealthy.
portraiture and the aspirations it flattered could also be turned to satire
Correct: The passage says Hogarth made portraits of the wealthy alongside prints mocking the same aspirations.
photography made satirical portraiture obsolete in the nineteenth century
Photography is discussed later and no claim is made about satire.
qs.x: The passage says Hogarth made portraits of the wealthy alongside prints mocking the same aspirations. Trap: Merging separate examples from different centuries into one causal story.

passages.title: FL09 · CARS · Passage 5
text: Conventional theatre depends on an agreement so familiar that it rarely needs stating: the audience sits in the dark, silent and still, while the actors perform in the light, behaving as though no one were watching. The playwright and director Bertolt Brecht regarded this arrangement as a political problem. An audience lulled into absorption, he argued, comes to experience events on stage as inevitable, and so loses the capacity to ask whether things could be otherwise. His remedy was the alienation effect, a set of techniques that reminded spectators they were watching a construction: visible lighting rigs, actors who stepped out of character to address the house, captions that announced the outcome of a scene before it began. The aim was not to deny the audience pleasure but to convert it into judgment.

Brecht still left the line between stage and house intact; his audience thought, but it did not act. Later experimenters tried to erase the line altogether. In the 1960s, groups such as the Living Theatre invited spectators onto the stage, and in Augusto Boal's Theatre of the Oppressed, developed in Brazil, spectators were encouraged to halt a performance and replace an actor in order to try out a different response to a situation of injustice. Boal called such participants "spect-actors." For him the point was practical: a person who has rehearsed resistance in a theatre is better prepared to attempt it elsewhere. Theatre became a rehearsal for life rather than a reflection of it.

Participation raises problems that these pioneers sometimes underestimated. Audiences do not enter a theatre as blank slates; they bring habits of deference and fear of embarrassment, and a performer who calls on a spectator to join in may in effect compel consent, since refusing in public carries a cost. Critics have noted that some participatory works merely stage the appearance of freedom: the spectator who is invited to "choose" among options the director has already prepared is controlled as surely as one who watches in silence, but now believes otherwise. Participation may also be unevenly distributed. In many performances, the same confident few volunteer while the majority watch the volunteers, so that a form meant to equalize may reproduce the hierarchies of the room.

Defenders reply that the risks are inseparable from the value. A scripted audience response, such as the shouted refrains of some popular theatre or the call-and-response of many religious services, is not usually considered inauthentic because it follows a pattern; the pattern is what allows people to join without fear. By the same logic, participatory theatre need not abolish structure but can design it so that a greater range of people feel able to take part. The philosopher Jacques Ranciere has gone further, arguing that the distinction between active actors and passive viewers is itself a myth. Watching, he claims, is already an activity: the spectator compares, interprets, and composes a meaning from what is seen. If so, the real question is not whether an audience participates but in what ways, and whether the form of the performance honors the thinking that every spectator is already doing.

qs.q: Which of the following best summarizes the passage?
o: Brecht's alienation effect failed because it prevented audiences from forming any judgment of events on stage.
The passage says the aim of the alienation effect was to convert pleasure into judgment.
Theatre has moved from silent spectacle toward participation, which raises questions about what participation requires.
Correct: The passage traces Brecht, Boal, critics, defenders, and Ranciere and ends on how a performance should honor spectators' thinking.
Participatory theatre should be abandoned because audiences cannot join in without being compelled.
The passage presents defenders' replies and does not conclude that participation should be abandoned.
Ranciere's claim that watching is active has been refuted by the experiments of Boal and the Living Theatre.
Ranciere's claim is presented as a further step, not as refuted.
qs.x: The passage traces Brecht, Boal, critics, defenders, and Ranciere and ends on how a performance should honor spectators' thinking. Trap: Taking the critics' paragraph as the author's final verdict.

qs.q: Which practice would Brecht most likely endorse, based on the passage?
o: Dimming the house lights so spectators forget their surroundings
Absorption is what Brecht regarded as the problem.
Casting actors who stay in character without a pause so that the illusion is unbroken
Remaining in character without a pause preserves the illusion that he wished to break.
Projecting a caption before a scene that announces what will happen in it
Correct: The passage lists captions announcing the outcome of a scene as part of the alienation effect.
Hiding the stage machinery so spectators remain absorbed in the story
Visible rigs were part of his techniques, so hiding machinery runs against them.
qs.x: The passage lists captions announcing the outcome of a scene as part of the alienation effect. Trap: Choosing techniques that increase absorption, the opposite of the aim.

qs.q: Boal's approach differs from Brecht's chiefly in that Boal:
o: asked spectators to act within the performance
Correct: The passage says Brecht's audience thought but did not act, while Boal's spect-actors replaced actors on stage.
denied that theatre could serve any political purpose
Both men saw theatre as political.
wanted audiences to become absorbed in the events on stage
Absorption is the condition Brecht criticized and Boal did not seek.
believed spectators should stay silent in order to think
Neither wanted silent spectators to be the ideal; Brecht wanted judgment and Boal action.
qs.x: The passage says Brecht's audience thought but did not act, while Boal's spect-actors replaced actors on stage. Trap: Overlooking that both thinkers had political aims and differed in the role given to spectators.

qs.q: Which of the following most closely parallels the 'choice' criticized in the third paragraph?
o: A museum exhibit that asks visitors to vote between two displays, both selected in advance by the curators
Correct: In both cases participants seem to choose but only among options prepared by those in control.
A town meeting at which any resident may propose a topic for debate
Residents may propose topics, so the options are not fixed in advance.
A concert at which listeners shout song requests that the band then plays
Listeners generate the requests, so the choices are not prepared by the performers.
A classroom in which students design their own experiments
Students design the experiments themselves, so the options are open.
qs.x: In both cases participants seem to choose but only among options prepared by those in control. Trap: Choosing a scene that looks participatory without checking who sets the options.

qs.q: The reference to call-and-response in religious services serves to argue that:
o: audiences always prefer scripted participation to improvised participation
No claim about universal preference is made.
religious services originated participatory theatre
The passage offers the example as an analogy, not as an origin.
unstructured participation is more dangerous than structured participation
The passage does not rank danger in this way.
following a pattern need not make participation inauthentic
Correct: The passage says the pattern is what allows people to join without fear, so structure can enable participation.
qs.x: The passage says the pattern is what allows people to join without fear, so structure can enable participation. Trap: Treating an illustrative analogy as a claim about origins.

qs.q: According to the passage, Ranciere would most likely say that an audience member who sits silently through a performance:
o: has been deceived by the director about her freedom to choose
Deception about choice is the critics' concern about some participatory works, not Ranciere's claim about silent viewers.
is nonetheless engaged in interpreting what she sees
Correct: The passage says that for Ranciere watching is already an activity in which the spectator compares, interprets, and composes meaning.
has chosen to withhold the consent that participation would require of her
The passage does not describe silence as a refusal of consent.
has failed to participate and must be invited onto the stage to do so
Ranciere denies the sharp distinction between active performers and passive viewers, so no invitation is needed for activity.
qs.x: The passage says that for Ranciere watching is already an activity in which the spectator compares, interprets, and composes meaning. Trap: Applying the critics' concern about manufactured choice to a thinker whose argument is that spectators are already active.

passages.title: FL09 · CARS · Passage 6
text: Does the language one speaks shape the way one thinks? The proposal, associated with Edward Sapir and his student Benjamin Lee Whorf, has had a turbulent history. In its strongest form, linguistic determinism, it claims that the categories of a language fix the categories of thought, so that speakers of different languages inhabit different mental worlds and cannot fully understand one another. Whorf's own writings gave this version its popular appeal; his claim that the Hopi language lacks any concept of time seemed to show that a speaker could be conceptually closed to ideas that others find obvious. Later linguists found that Whorf's description of Hopi was inaccurate, and by the 1960s the strong form had few defenders.

The weaker claim, linguistic relativity, survived. It holds only that language influences habitual patterns of attention and memory without making any thought impossible. Because this version predicts differences in degree rather than in kind, it can be tested. The classic experimental approach compares speakers of languages that carve up a domain differently. Color has been the favored domain. Russian requires speakers to choose between two basic terms for light and dark blue, whereas English has a single word. In a well-known set of experiments, Russian speakers discriminated between shades of blue slightly faster when the shades fell on opposite sides of the lexical boundary than when they fell on the same side, and the advantage vanished when participants had to repeat a string of digits while performing the task. The disappearance under verbal interference suggests that the effect depended on the active use of linguistic labels in real-time judgment, rather than on a permanent restructuring of perception.

Other domains have yielded results of a similar kind. Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, an Australian language that uses compass directions in place of left and right, maintain an accurate sense of cardinal orientation even in unfamiliar surroundings, a skill English speakers rarely display. Language here seems to train a habit that the culture requires. Yet critics ask whether the language is the cause. Communities that live in open landscapes may need to track direction, and a language that encodes direction might be a consequence of that need rather than its source. Researchers have tried to separate the two by teaching participants new labels in the laboratory, and some studies find that arbitrary labels do alter later performance, though the effects are often small and short-lived.

A further complication concerns what counts as thought. Infants and nonhuman animals discriminate colors, quantities, and spatial relations well before any language is learned, so language cannot be the only source of such categories. A more modest view holds that language acts as a tool for thinking, one that sharpens certain distinctions by making them cheap to retrieve. On this view the question is not whether language shapes thought in an all-or-nothing way, but under what conditions and for which tasks the habit of naming makes a measurable difference. The debate is not closed, but its terms have shifted from sweeping claims about worldviews to careful measurements of attention, and that shift has been its most productive result.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: The Hopi language shows that some speakers lack any ability to think about time, as Whorf claimed.
The passage says Whorf's description of Hopi was inaccurate.
Experiments on color show that language has no influence on perception, even on rapid judgments.
The Russian experiments found a modest effect, not none.
Whorf's hypothesis has been confirmed by experiments on Russian speakers and on Guugu Yimithirr speakers.
The evidence supports only the weaker claim, and critics question causation.
Strong determinism has been abandoned, while weaker claims about attention are tested with modest results.
Correct: The passage moves from the discredited strong form to experiments on the weaker form with small, conditional effects.
qs.x: The passage moves from the discredited strong form to experiments on the weaker form with small, conditional effects. Trap: Accepting Whorf's famous example without noting the passage's correction.

qs.q: According to the passage, the weaker claim of linguistic relativity can be tested because it:
o: denies that infants and nonhuman animals can discriminate colors before they learn words
Infants and animals are mentioned later as a complication, not as a denial.
depends on an accurate description of the Hopi language and its treatment of time
The Hopi description belongs to the strong form that lost support.
predicts differences in degree rather than absolute limits
Correct: The passage says the weaker version predicts differences in degree rather than in kind, so comparisons can detect them.
applies only to the single domain of color, where labels are easiest to measure
Color is the favored domain, but other domains are tested too.
qs.x: The passage says the weaker version predicts differences in degree rather than in kind, so comparisons can detect them. Trap: Confusing the domain most often studied with the reason for testability.

qs.q: The finding that the Russian speakers' advantage vanished while they repeated digits is best explained if the advantage:
o: reflected a permanent change in the visual system of Russian speakers
A permanent change would not disappear under a temporary verbal load.
relied on verbal labels being actively used during the judgment
Correct: The passage says interference suggests the effect depended on active use of linguistic labels in real time.
was an artifact of Russian speakers' better memory for digits
No difference in digit memory is described.
arose only when participants were unaware of the lexical boundary
Awareness of the boundary is not manipulated in the passage.
qs.x: The passage says interference suggests the effect depended on active use of linguistic labels in real time. Trap: Interpreting the disappearance of an effect as proof the effect was a measurement artifact.

qs.q: Which finding would best address the critics' concern about the Guugu Yimithirr results?
o: Guugu Yimithirr speakers do better on orientation tasks in familiar surroundings than in unfamiliar ones.
Better performance in familiar places does not separate language from environment.
Guugu Yimithirr children learn compass terms later than other words in their vocabulary.
Order of acquisition does not address whether need or language is the cause.
Orientation skill among speakers correlates with their years of formal education.
Education is a different variable and does not hold environment constant.
Speakers in similar open landscapes whose language lacks compass terms show markedly poorer orientation.
Correct: It holds the environment roughly constant while varying language, which helps separate the two explanations.
qs.x: It holds the environment roughly constant while varying language, which helps separate the two explanations. Trap: Choosing a result about the same group that cannot separate cause from environment.

qs.q: The author mentions infants and nonhuman animals in order to:
o: show that language cannot be the only source of conceptual categories
Correct: The passage says these groups discriminate colors, quantities, and spatial relations before any language is learned.
prove that languages do not differ in any meaningful way in how they divide up experience
The passage says language may sharpen distinctions, so differences exist.
argue that teaching new labels in the laboratory has no lasting effect on later performance
Laboratory labels are said to have small, short-lived effects, not none.
support Whorf's claim that thought depends on the grammar of the speaker's language
The point tells against determinism, not for it.
qs.x: The passage says these groups discriminate colors, quantities, and spatial relations before any language is learned. Trap: Reading evidence against determinism as evidence against any influence of language.

qs.q: On the view of language as a 'tool for thinking,' a speaker's vocabulary is best compared to:
o: a locked room in which thoughts are kept so no outside thought can enter
A locked room implies strict determinism, which the passage rejects.
a lens ground to a fixed prescription that distorts everything the speaker sees through it
A fixed distorting lens suggests that language fixes perception.
labeled drawers that make some items quicker to find while the others remain reachable
Correct: The passage says language sharpens certain distinctions by making them cheap to retrieve without making other thoughts impossible.
a library whose books are the only source of information that the speaker can ever consult
A sole source of information again implies determinism.
qs.x: The passage says language sharpens certain distinctions by making them cheap to retrieve without making other thoughts impossible. Trap: Choosing a metaphor that restates the strong claim the passage has dismissed.

passages.title: FL09 · CARS · Passage 7
text: For most of recorded history, educated people assumed that the best age lay behind them. Classical writers placed a golden age at the beginning of time and described subsequent history as decline; medieval Christian thinkers located the decisive events of history in the past, with the future awaiting a single, final judgment. The modern idea of progress, the belief that human affairs can improve cumulatively and that later generations may expect to live better than earlier ones, is a comparatively recent invention. It emerged in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, when advances in natural science provided a model: knowledge, unlike a golden age, could be added to, and each generation could stand on the shoulders of the last.

Enlightenment thinkers extended the model from knowledge to society. Condorcet, writing in hiding during the French Revolution, sketched a history of humanity as a march through ten stages toward the abolition of inequality between nations and the indefinite perfection of the species. Adam Smith's account of commercial society offered a more concrete mechanism: the division of labor increased productivity, which raised the standard of living even of the poorest. In the nineteenth century, Hegel and Marx gave the idea a structure by arguing that history moves according to a logic, one driven by conflict, that makes later stages higher than earlier ones. Whatever their differences, these thinkers shared a conviction that history has a direction and that the direction is upward.

The twentieth century dealt the conviction heavy blows. Industrialized warfare, genocide, and the possibility of nuclear annihilation suggested that technical capacity could grow while moral wisdom did not. Critics such as Walter Benjamin pictured history as a storm that drives an angel backward into the future while wreckage piles at his feet; what the optimist calls progress, he suggested, is the same storm viewed from the standpoint of the victors. Others pointed out that the idea of progress has often served as an ideology: colonial administrators justified conquest as the spread of civilization, and states have demanded present sacrifice for the sake of a better future whose arrival the sacrificed would never witness.

Defenders have since narrowed rather than abandoned the claim. They distinguish between progress as a law of history, which few now defend, and progress as a measurable trend in particular domains. Child mortality, literacy, and life expectancy have improved across much of the world over two centuries, and such gains, the defenders argue, cannot be explained away as ideology. Skeptics reply that selecting indicators already presupposes a standard of the good, and that metrics which improve may be accompanied by losses that no statistic registers, such as the erosion of local forms of life. The disagreement is thus partly empirical and partly about values: even those who accept the numbers may dispute whether they capture what matters.

A sober position may be that progress is real but neither inevitable nor irreversible. Gains in health or in rights have been won through specific institutions and struggles and can be lost when those institutions decay. On this view, to believe in progress is not to predict that tomorrow will be better, but to hold that improvement is possible and that the burden of bringing it about falls on those who would benefit from it.

qs.q: The main point of the passage is that the modern idea of progress:
o: arose from the model of cumulative science, was damaged in the twentieth century, and survives in a narrower form
Correct: The passage traces origins in science, the twentieth century's blows, and the narrowed defense with its disputes.
is a timeless belief that educated people in every period of history have held about their own societies
The passage says earlier writers assumed decline and the idea is recent.
has been shown by statistics on mortality and literacy to be a reliable law governing all of history
The defenders drop the law-of-history claim and the skeptics contest the indicators.
was entirely abandoned among thinkers of the twentieth century after industrialized warfare exposed technical limits
Defenders have narrowed rather than abandoned the claim.
qs.x: The passage traces origins in science, the twentieth century's blows, and the narrowed defense with its disputes. Trap: Choosing a claim that fits one paragraph but contradicts others.

qs.q: According to the passage, natural science served as a model for the idea of progress because:
o: science had shown that history is governed by a logic of conflict
The logic of conflict belongs to Hegel and Marx in the nineteenth century.
scientists were the first to predict that inequality between nations would end
Condorcet's predictions came later and were not made by scientists as such.
knowledge could be added to, unlike a golden age
Correct: The passage says knowledge could be added to and each generation could build on the last.
natural philosophers had already rejected the classical belief in a golden age at the start of time
The passage does not describe natural philosophers rejecting that belief as the reason.
qs.x: The passage says knowledge could be added to and each generation could build on the last. Trap: Mixing the later Enlightenment extension to society with the original scientific model.

qs.q: Benjamin's image of the storm suggests that what is called progress:
o: is a law of history that operates independently of anyone's point of view or experience
The image criticizes the law-of-history view.
results from technical capacity that human beings have never been able to control
Control of technology is not the point of the image.
was misunderstood only by medieval writers who had expected the future to bring judgment
Medieval writers are not part of the image.
looks different to those who profit than to those who suffer
Correct: The passage says the optimist's progress is the same storm viewed from the standpoint of the victors, so it depends on viewpoint.
qs.x: The passage says the optimist's progress is the same storm viewed from the standpoint of the victors, so it depends on viewpoint. Trap: Reading a perspective-dependent image as a claim about uncontrolled technology.

qs.q: Which situation would best illustrate the skeptics' objection about indicators?
o: Two researchers pick different measures of well-being for one region and reach opposite verdicts
Correct: The skeptics say that choosing indicators already presupposes a standard of the good, so different standards give different verdicts.
A study finds that child mortality in the region fell steadily over the last two centuries
A measured fall in mortality is the kind of gain the defenders cite.
A government claims that some of the published indicators were falsified by local officials
Falsification is a question of accuracy, not of standards.
An economist predicts that literacy will keep rising in the region over the next decade
A prediction about literacy does not address which indicators matter.
qs.x: The skeptics say that choosing indicators already presupposes a standard of the good, so different standards give different verdicts. Trap: Choosing an example about data accuracy rather than about values built into the choice of data.

qs.q: Which of the following views is most consistent with the position described in the final paragraph?
o: A historian predicts that living standards will keep rising because history has a direction.
A prediction of inevitable rise is the law-of-history view the author sets aside.
An advocate credits vaccination with saving lives but warns that funding cuts could reverse the gains.
Correct: The final paragraph says gains were won through institutions and can be lost when they decay, and that improvement is possible but not inevitable.
A critic maintains that gains in rights are illusions produced by ideology.
The author accepts that gains in health or rights are real.
A philosopher holds that effort is pointless because progress happens automatically.
An automatic process would make the burden on beneficiaries pointless, contrary to the passage.
qs.x: The final paragraph says gains were won through institutions and can be lost when they decay, and that improvement is possible but not inevitable. Trap: Choosing the optimist's inevitability instead of the author's conditional optimism.

passages.title: FL09 · CARS · Passage 8
text: The word statistics once meant, literally, the science of the state: the collection of numbers about population, trade, and land that governments needed to tax and to wage war. Only in the nineteenth century did the term come to mean a body of mathematical methods for reasoning from uncertain data. The shift was not simply a matter of better mathematics. It required a change in what people thought a number could be. Before the 1800s, a physician or an astronomer who obtained discrepant measurements usually tried to decide which was correct; the idea that variation was itself a phenomenon to be described, and that a distribution of errors could be more informative than any single reading, took time to become natural.

The astronomers led the way. Faced with repeated observations of a star's position that did not agree, Legendre and Gauss developed the method of least squares around 1800, a systematic procedure for choosing the single value that minimized the total squared discrepancy. Gauss and Laplace then showed that errors of observation tended to follow a bell-shaped curve, a result that gave the procedure a theoretical rationale. The curve appeared to be a law of nature, and this impression was strengthened when the Belgian scholar Adolphe Quetelet found similar curves in the heights of soldiers and the rates of crime. He proposed the "average man" as a social ideal, a figure around whom deviations were errors of nature. Quetelet's reading was, in hindsight, a conceptual mistake, since a population average describes no actual person, but it inspired the notion that human affairs could be investigated with the confidence of physical science.

Francis Galton and Karl Pearson, working in Victorian Britain, turned that notion in a different direction. For them, variation was not error around an ideal but the raw material of evolution, and their methods, including correlation and regression, were designed to measure how traits are related across individuals. The motives were not neutral. Galton coined the term eugenics, and Pearson shared his hope that statistical study of heredity could guide human breeding. Many of the central tools of modern statistics thus have origins entangled with a program that is now widely repudiated. Historians of science stress that this does not make the tools invalid, since a method can be sound while the purposes of its first users were not; but it does warn against supposing that mathematical techniques arise from pure reason, untouched by the social setting in which they were developed.

In the twentieth century, Ronald Fisher, working at an agricultural research station, introduced randomized experiments and significance testing to the analysis of crop trials. Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson proposed a competing framework centered on decision rules and error rates, and the two approaches, which their authors regarded as incompatible, were later blended in textbooks into a single routine that neither side would have endorsed. Critics today argue that the hybrid encourages the mechanical use of a threshold for "significance" in place of judgment. If so, the history carries a lesson: methods that began as responses to particular problems can harden into rituals once the problems are forgotten, and a researcher who understands where a technique came from is better placed to know when it does not apply.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Statistics was invented by astronomers and has never been influenced by anything outside mathematics itself.
The passage stresses that techniques do not arise from pure reason.
Quetelet's average man was a valid discovery that guided later work in correlation and regression.
The passage calls Quetelet's reading a conceptual mistake.
Statistical methods grew out of shifting ideas and motives and sometimes harden into routine.
Correct: The passage follows ideas of error, population averages, heredity, and testing, and notes social context and ritual use.
Fisher's methods are superior to those of Neyman and Pearson and should replace the hybrid routine.
The passage does not rank Fisher's methods above the rival framework.
qs.x: The passage follows ideas of error, population averages, heredity, and testing, and notes social context and ritual use. Trap: Overstating a role of one group in a history that spans several.

qs.q: The conceptual change described in the first paragraph is best characterized as a move from:
o: using numbers to tax and wage war toward using them only in astronomical observation
The passage says the word came to mean mathematical methods, not astronomy alone.
collecting data for governments toward discarding data in favor of pure theory
The passage does not say data collection was discarded.
regarding variation as a law of nature toward regarding it as an artifact of measurement
The passage describes the reverse, the curve being seen as a law of nature, only later.
treating discrepant measurements as errors toward treating the pattern of variation as informative
Correct: The passage says earlier investigators tried to decide which discrepant measurement was correct, whereas later ones treated the distribution of errors as informative.
qs.x: The passage says earlier investigators tried to decide which discrepant measurement was correct, whereas later ones treated the distribution of errors as informative. Trap: Mistaking the change in the word's meaning for the change in what numbers could be.

qs.q: Which of the following is most analogous to Quetelet's 'conceptual mistake'?
o: Declaring a species' mean leaf length its true length and each leaf's departure from it a defect
Correct: Like Quetelet, it treats a population average as an ideal and individual deviations as errors of nature.
Using the mean to summarize a month of daily temperatures at one weather station
Summarizing data with a mean does not call deviations errors.
Estimating a star's position by minimizing the squared discrepancy among several observations
Least squares for repeated measurements of one quantity is the legitimate use described.
Reporting the range of heights observed among soldiers in one regiment
Reporting a range makes no claim about an ideal.
qs.x: Like Quetelet, it treats a population average as an ideal and individual deviations as errors of nature. Trap: Choosing an example that merely uses an average rather than treating it as an ideal.

qs.q: The passage suggests that historians of science regard the eugenic motives of Galton and Pearson as:
o: proof that correlation and regression yield invalid results whenever heredity is studied
The passage says the tools are not invalid.
a reason to examine the tools' origins but not to reject them
Correct: The passage says a method can be sound while its first users' purposes were not, but that origins warn against assuming pure reason.
irrelevant to any account of how the tools developed in Victorian Britain
The passage says the social setting matters.
evidence that statistical methods can never be applied to questions of heredity
No claim is made that statistics cannot be applied to heredity.
qs.x: The passage says a method can be sound while its first users' purposes were not, but that origins warn against assuming pure reason. Trap: Letting disapproval of motive stand in for a judgment of the method.

qs.q: Which of the following is the best example of the 'ritual' described in the last paragraph?
o: A researcher declares an effect real whenever p falls below 0.05, regardless of design or effect size.
Correct: The passage says hybrid practice encourages a mechanical threshold in place of judgment.
A researcher randomizes plots in an agricultural trial to avoid bias in treatment assignment.
Randomization is a design principle that Fisher introduced, not a mechanical threshold.
A researcher states in advance the error rates she will tolerate and justifies them.
Specifying and justifying error rates is the exercise of judgment.
A researcher studies the history of a method before deciding whether it fits her data.
Consulting history is what the passage recommends.
qs.x: The passage says hybrid practice encourages a mechanical threshold in place of judgment. Trap: Choosing a careful practice because it mentions the same vocabulary of statistics.

qs.q: Suppose the errors in astronomers' measurements had followed a strongly skewed distribution. According to the passage, which development would have been most directly weakened?
o: Legendre's publication of the method of least squares around 1800
The method itself could still have been proposed as a procedure.
Quetelet's collection of data on the heights of soldiers
Quetelet's data come from human populations rather than measurement errors.
Fisher's use of randomized crop trials
Fisher's randomization concerns experimental design, not error distribution in astronomy.
The theoretical rationale for least squares given by Gauss and Laplace
Correct: The passage says the bell-shaped distribution of errors gave the procedure its theoretical rationale.
qs.x: The passage says the bell-shaped distribution of errors gave the procedure its theoretical rationale. Trap: Choosing the development nearest in time rather than the one logically dependent on the bell curve.

passages.title: FL09 · CARS · Passage 9
text: Arguments about privacy often begin from a picture of a private sphere, a zone of life that others have no business entering. In 1890, the lawyers Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis gave this picture a legal form when they described a "right to be let alone," prompted by newspapers that had begun to publish photographs and gossip about private citizens. The right they proposed protected an inviolate personality, and its model was property: just as a person may exclude trespassers from a house, a person may exclude the public from facts about his domestic life. For decades this property-like conception shaped both law and intuition. Privacy was something one possessed, and a violation was an intrusion.

Modern surveillance challenges that picture because it rarely involves intrusion into a protected place. A person who walks through a city is observed by cameras whose images are in public view; one who makes a phone call generates records held by a company; a person who browses a website leaves traces that no one deliberately sought. Under a traditional doctrine, information knowingly exposed to others carries no expectation of privacy, and if so then each of these exposures seems unprotected. But critics argue that the doctrine treats information as discrete items, to be judged one at a time, and ignores what happens when items are combined. A single trip to a clinic reveals little. A year of location records, assembled, can reveal religious practice, medical conditions, and political associations, and the revelation emerges from the compilation rather than from any one datum. The harm, on this view, lies in aggregation.

Defenders of expanded surveillance respond that security is also a value, and that some information which citizens regard as private is exactly what investigators need to prevent harm. They add that most people consent, in practice, to extensive data collection in exchange for convenience. Privacy advocates answer that consent given to an unreadable contract is a thin fiction, and that the choice is rarely free when the alternative is exclusion from services that ordinary life requires. They also note an effect that is easy to miss: people who believe they are watched modify their behavior, even when they have nothing to hide, avoiding unpopular opinions and unconventional associations. A society may remain nominally free while its members become cautious, and this chilling effect represents a cost that does not appear in any single case of observation.

The philosopher Helen Nissenbaum has proposed that privacy should be understood not as secrecy but as the appropriate flow of information in context. Medical details flow properly from patient to doctor, and the norms of that setting forbid their flow to an employer; the same detail is neither secret nor public in the abstract, but proper or improper according to where it travels. This account explains why a photograph taken in a public square can still be harmful when assembled into a database of faces, and why a worker who tells a colleague about an illness may feel betrayed when the colleague tells the manager. Its weakness is that contexts are not always clear, and norms evolve; a new technology may create a setting for which no norms exist, and in that case the theory has little to say until a convention forms. Still, it shifts the question from "Is this secret?" to "Is this flow consistent with the purposes for which the information was shared?", a question that courts and legislators can at least begin to answer.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Privacy is a value so absolute that no security interest could ever justify observing any citizen at all.
The passage presents the defenders' security argument and does not call privacy absolute.
The right to be let alone has been replaced entirely by an account that treats privacy as simple secrecy.
Nissenbaum explicitly treats privacy as context-based flow, not as secrecy.
Modern surveillance is harmless in practice because most people consent to extensive data collection.
Privacy advocates call consent a thin fiction, and the passage treats the harms as real.
Modern surveillance strains the view of privacy as exclusion and prompts views based on aggregation and context.
Correct: The passage moves from the property-like view to aggregation, chilling effects, and Nissenbaum's contextual account.
qs.x: The passage moves from the property-like view to aggregation, chilling effects, and Nissenbaum's contextual account. Trap: Choosing an extreme position that one side of the dispute might hold.

qs.q: The conception of privacy proposed by Warren and Brandeis is modeled most closely on:
o: an owner's right to exclude others from property
Correct: The passage says its model was property, as a person may exclude trespassers from a house.
a contract between a citizen and the press
No contract is mentioned.
the public's right to be informed about private citizens
The press prompted the argument but the right protects individuals against it.
a state's duty to protect citizens from crime
Crime prevention is a concern of surveillance defenders, not of this conception.
qs.x: The passage says its model was property, as a person may exclude trespassers from a house. Trap: Taking the newspapers that provoked the right as its model.

qs.q: Which situation best illustrates the harm of aggregation described in the passage?
o: A neighbor reads a single postcard that a visitor has left lying open on a hallway table.
A single item read in a private setting is intrusion rather than aggregation.
A data broker combines harmless purchases and locations to infer that a customer is ill.
Correct: The passage says harm emerges from combining items, none of which reveals much alone.
A camera records a person once as she crosses a public street on her way to work.
A single recording in public is the discrete item the traditional doctrine considers.
An employer reads an email that a colleague addressed directly to him about a project.
Reading mail addressed to oneself involves no combination.
qs.x: The passage says harm emerges from combining items, none of which reveals much alone. Trap: Choosing a single invasive act, which is the harm the property view already covers.

qs.q: Which finding would most directly support the chilling effect described in the third paragraph?
o: After a surveillance program expands, crime rates fall in the monitored neighborhoods over several years.
A fall in crime concerns security, not the behavior of law-abiding people.
Users accept lengthy data policies without reading them, because the service would otherwise be unavailable.
Accepting policies relates to consent, not to avoiding unpopular activity.
People who share more personal data online report greater satisfaction with the services they use.
Greater satisfaction is unrelated to changes in behavior under observation.
After publicity about monitoring, users search less for controversial topics though they broke no law.
Correct: The chilling effect is a change in behavior by people who believe they are watched, even with nothing to hide.
qs.x: The chilling effect is a change in behavior by people who believe they are watched, even with nothing to hide. Trap: Choosing evidence about consent when the question is about behavior change.

qs.q: Under Nissenbaum's account, which scenario would most clearly be a privacy violation?
o: A patient describes his symptoms to a doctor in order to receive treatment.
The flow from patient to doctor matches the norms of that context.
A woman tells a friend over dinner about her own illness.
A person sharing her own information with a friend follows the norms of friendship.
A teacher reads a student's essay aloud at the student's request.
The student requested the reading, so the flow fits the purpose of sharing.
A pharmacy sells customers' prescription records to a marketing firm.
Correct: Medical information moves to a setting whose norms do not allow it, which is an inappropriate flow.
qs.x: Medical information moves to a setting whose norms do not allow it, which is an inappropriate flow. Trap: Treating any disclosure of sensitive information as a violation regardless of context.

qs.q: Which of the following best exemplifies the weakness of the contextual account that the author notes?
o: A doctor shares a patient's record with an employer in violation of well-established medical norms.
A clear violation of established norms is the kind of case the theory handles well.
A new platform's users disagree about whether a post may be reposted, and no norm exists.
Correct: The passage says a new technology may create a setting for which no norms exist, leaving the theory with little to say.
A company states plainly in a notice, before the sale, exactly how it will use customers' data.
A plain notice does not involve the absence of norms.
A court cannot decide a case because the facts of the dispute remain unresolved.
A dispute about facts is not a lack of norms.
qs.x: The passage says a new technology may create a setting for which no norms exist, leaving the theory with little to say. Trap: Selecting a hard case about facts instead of one about missing norms.

passages.title: FL09 · Chem/Phys · Passage 1
text: An engineer tests a traction elevator motor on a loaded car. In each trial the car starts from rest, rises a height h, and reaches its final speed v at the top, with the motor supplying the necessary work. Rail friction is negligible except where noted, and g = 10 m/s². Motor work was computed from the work-energy theorem, W(motor) + W(gravity) = ΔKE, and agreed with a power meter reading. Table 1 lists four trials, including one with a lighter 800 kg car. In Figure 1, the engineer compared motor work for the 1,000 kg car as a function of rise height, first with negligible rail friction and then with a constant friction force of unknown magnitude opposing the motion; the final speed was 2 m/s in both series. In Trial C, the motor operated for 20.0 s. In a separate check, the 1,000 kg car descended 10 m at constant speed with the motor connected.

qs.q: In Trial B, what is the net work done on the car during the rise?
o: 102.0 kJ, equal to the work supplied by the motor over the whole rise
102.0 kJ is the motor work alone; gravity does negative work, so the net is far smaller.
2.0 kJ, equal to the gain in kinetic energy of the car
Correct: Net work equals ΔKE = ½(1,000)(2)² = 2,000 J = 2.0 kJ (motor +102.0 kJ, gravity -100 kJ).
100 kJ, equal to the gain in gravitational potential energy of the car
100 kJ is the magnitude of the work done by gravity (mgh), not the net work.
98 kJ, equal to the motor work minus twice the kinetic energy gained
The net work is not obtained by subtracting kinetic energy twice; W(net) = ΔKE exactly.
qs.x: Net work equals ΔKE = ½(1,000)(2)² = 2,000 J = 2.0 kJ (motor +102.0 kJ, gravity -100 kJ). Trap: Confusing the work done by the motor with the net work on the car; net work equals only the change in kinetic energy.

qs.q: Trial D requires 6.0 kJ more motor work than Trial C. This difference is best explained by:
o: the greater gravitational potential energy gained, since the faster car ends at a greater height
Both trials rise 30 m, so the potential energy gain is the same (300 kJ).
a larger friction force on the rails at the higher speed, which the motor must also overcome
The passage states friction is negligible in Table 1, so friction cannot account for the difference.
the larger car mass in Trial D, which raises the weight that the motor must lift through 30 m
Both trials use a 1,000 kg car, so the weight lifted is identical.
the greater final kinetic energy, ½(1,000)(4² - 2²) = 6,000 J
Correct: Both trials have the same mass and height, so mgh is identical (300 kJ); the extra work is ΔKE = ½(1,000)(16 - 4) = 6.0 kJ.
qs.x: Both trials have the same mass and height, so mgh is identical (300 kJ); the extra work is ΔKE = ½(1,000)(16 - 4) = 6.0 kJ. Trap: Attributing the extra work to height or mass when only the final speed changed between the two trials.

qs.q: According to Figure 1, the constant friction force on the car is approximately:
o: 5,000 N would result from reading the 5 kJ gap as a force without dividing by the 10 m distance.
10,500 N is the slope of the friction series (mg + f), not the friction force alone.
Correct: The friction series lies above the frictionless series by 5 kJ per 10 m of rise; f = 5,000 J / 10 m = 500 N (the gap grows 5, 10, 15, 20 kJ).
50 N would require a gap of only 0.5 kJ over 10 m.
qs.x: The friction series lies above the frictionless series by 5 kJ per 10 m of rise; f = 5,000 J / 10 m = 500 N (the gap grows 5, 10, 15, 20 kJ). Trap: Reading the vertical gap as a force; force is the gap divided by distance, i.e. the difference in slopes.

qs.q: In Trial C, what is the average power delivered by the motor?
o: 15.1 W has the right digits but is off by a factor of 1,000 because the work is in kilojoules.
30.2 kW would result from dividing by 10 s rather than 20.0 s.
7.55 kW would result from dividing by 40 s.
qs.x: P = W/t = 302,000 J / 20.0 s = 15,100 W = 15.1 kW. Trap: Forgetting that the table lists work in kilojoules, giving an answer in watts that is 1,000 times too small.

qs.q: In the separate check, the 1,000 kg car descends 10 m at constant speed. The work done by the motor is closest to:
o: +100 kJ would mean the motor adds energy while the car loses potential energy, violating energy balance.
0 J, because the net work on the car is zero
The net work is zero, but the motor work is not zero; it cancels the +100 kJ done by gravity.
-2.0 kJ is a kinetic energy value; no speed change occurs here.
Correct: With constant speed, ΔKE = 0 so W(motor) = -W(gravity) = -mgh = -100 kJ; the motor holds the car back.
qs.x: With constant speed, ΔKE = 0 so W(motor) = -W(gravity) = -mgh = -100 kJ; the motor holds the car back. Trap: Equating zero net work with zero motor work, ignoring that gravity does positive work on the descending car.

passages.title: FL09 · Chem/Phys · Passage 2
text: A student examines the entropy changes that accompany phase transitions using thermodynamic data for three liquids at 1 atm. Table 1 lists each substance's melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion, boiling temperature, and enthalpy of vaporization. At a phase transition temperature the two phases are at equilibrium, so ΔG = 0 and ΔS = ΔH/T. Figure 1 shows the molar entropy of water as it is warmed from 250 K to 400 K at constant pressure; the vertical segments are the transitions at 273 K and 373 K. The student also considers supercooled liquid water at 263 K, assuming that ΔH and ΔS for freezing (the negatives of the fusion values at 273 K) are independent of temperature. All measurements were made at 1 atm, and each liquid is treated as pure. Because entropy is a state function, the entropy of the vapor at 373 K can be found by summing the changes along the heating path. A second part of the study compares the vaporization entropies of the three liquids to the roughly constant value expected when a liquid with little molecular association becomes a gas.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, the entropy change for the melting of one mole of ice at 273 K is closest to:
o: 109 J/(mol·K) is the vaporization value (40,700/373), not fusion.
Correct: ΔS = ΔH/T = 6,010 J/mol / 273 K = +22.0 J/(mol·K).
2.20 J/(mol·K) results from dividing 6.01 kJ (not 6,010 J) by 273 and mis-scaling the units.
A negative value would describe freezing; melting increases the disorder of the system.
qs.x: ΔS = ΔH/T = 6,010 J/mol / 273 K = +22.0 J/(mol·K). Trap: Using kilojoules directly with kelvin, or choosing the vaporization or freezing value instead of the fusion value.

qs.q: In Figure 1, the jump in molar entropy at 373 K is much larger than the jump at 273 K. Which statement best explains this?
o: Vaporization takes place at a higher temperature, and entropy change is directly proportional to temperature
Since ΔS = ΔH/T, a higher T actually lowers ΔS for a given ΔH; the larger ΔH(vap) is the cause.
Melting breaks all intermolecular attractions while vaporization breaks only a few of them
Melting only loosens the lattice; vaporization breaks essentially all attractions, the opposite of this statement.
Heat absorbed during vaporization is smaller, so the surroundings gain less entropy at 373 K
The heat absorbed in vaporization (40.7 kJ/mol) is larger than in fusion (6.01 kJ/mol).
Vaporization frees molecules into a far larger volume with many more accessible microstates than melting does
Correct: Gas molecules occupy a much larger volume and have translational freedom, so ΔS(vap) = 109 J/(mol·K) greatly exceeds ΔS(fus) = 22.0.
qs.x: Gas molecules occupy a much larger volume and have translational freedom, so ΔS(vap) = 109 J/(mol·K) greatly exceeds ΔS(fus) = 22.0. Trap: Reasoning that a higher temperature means a larger entropy change, when ΔS = ΔH/T decreases with T.

qs.q: From Table 1, the vaporization entropy of water (about 109 J/(mol·K)) exceeds that of benzene (about 87 J/(mol·K)). The most reasonable explanation is that:
o: liquid water is more ordered because of extensive hydrogen bonding, so it gains more entropy on vaporizing
Correct: ΔS(vap) = ΔH/T: benzene 30,800/353 = 87 J/(mol·K); water 109. Hydrogen bonding lowers the entropy of liquid water, so the liquid-to-gas gain is larger.
water has a lower molar mass than benzene, so its gas-phase molecules are more disordered
Molar mass is not the determinant here; both gases have large entropies and the difference lies in the liquid.
water boils at a higher temperature than benzene, which makes its vaporization entropy larger
The boiling temperatures (373 K and 353 K) are nearly equal and T is in the denominator of ΔS.
benzene forms hydrogen bonds in the gas phase, which lowers its entropy on vaporizing
Benzene cannot hydrogen bond, and association in the gas would be negligible at 1 atm.
qs.x: ΔS(vap) = ΔH/T: benzene 30,800/353 = 87 J/(mol·K); water 109. Hydrogen bonding lowers the entropy of liquid water, so the liquid-to-gas gain is larger. Trap: Attributing the difference to the gas phase when the ordering of the liquid phase is what differs.

qs.q: For supercooled water freezing at 263 K, using the stated assumptions, which of the following is true?
o: ΔG ≈ +0.22 kJ/mol, so freezing is nonspontaneous because the system's entropy decreases on freezing at this temperature
The sign is wrong: -TΔS = +5.79 kJ is smaller in magnitude than ΔH = -6.01 kJ, so ΔG is negative.
ΔG = 0 kJ/mol, so supercooled water and ice are at equilibrium because ΔH and ΔS share a sign, as at 273 K
ΔG = 0 only at 273 K, the melting point; at 263 K the temperature differs from equilibrium.
ΔG ≈ -0.22 kJ/mol, so freezing is spontaneous because the enthalpy term outweighs the entropy term
Correct: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS = -6,010 - (263)(-22.0) = -6,010 + 5,786 ≈ -224 J/mol; negative, so freezing is spontaneous below 273 K.
ΔG ≈ -6.01 kJ/mol, so freezing is spontaneous because the entropy term is negligible at low temperature
The entropy term (+5.79 kJ/mol) is not negligible; it nearly cancels ΔH, leaving only about -0.22 kJ/mol.
qs.x: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS = -6,010 - (263)(-22.0) = -6,010 + 5,786 ≈ -224 J/mol; negative, so freezing is spontaneous below 273 K. Trap: Believing a decrease in system entropy always makes a process nonspontaneous, ignoring the temperature-dependent balance with ΔH.
