passages.title: FL09 · Chem/Phys · Passage 3
text: A technician characterizes a small hydraulic lift consisting of two cylindrical pistons connected by an incompressible oil. A force F(in) is applied to the small input piston, and the force F(out) that the large output piston can support is measured with a load cell. In an ideal lift, the pressure applied to the enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished, so F(out)/F(in) equals the ratio of the piston areas. Table 1 gives the piston radii, applied input force, and measured output force for three configurations. In Figure 1, F(out) is plotted against F(in) for Configuration 1 along with the ideal prediction. Seals and the fluid itself introduce a small friction loss. Heights of the two pistons are equal, so hydrostatic pressure differences can be ignored. In Configuration 2, the input piston is pushed down 25 cm. Take π ≈ 3.14, and treat the car in the final trial as having weight 10,000 N.

qs.q: In Configuration 1, the pressure that the 200 N input force applies to the fluid is closest to:
o: 4.0 × 10⁴ Pa uses the diameter (0.040 m) as if it were the radius in the area formula.
1.0 × 10⁴ Pa divides force by radius instead of by area.
6.4 × 10⁵ Pa uses a radius of 1.0 cm, which is half the actual value.
qs.x: P = F/A = 200 N / [3.14 × (0.020 m)²] = 200 / 1.256 × 10⁻³ = 1.6 × 10⁵ Pa. Trap: Using diameter in place of radius in A = πr², or dividing force by a length instead of an area.

qs.q: In Configuration 2, how far does the output piston rise when the input piston moves down 25 cm?
o: 25 cm
25 cm would be correct only if the two pistons had equal areas.
4.0 cm
Correct: Incompressible fluid conserves volume: A(in)d(in) = A(out)d(out). The area ratio is (5.0/2.0)² = 6.25, so d(out) = 25/6.25 = 4.0 cm.
156 cm
156 cm multiplies by 6.25; the larger piston moves less, not more.
10 cm
10 cm divides by the radius ratio 2.5 rather than the area ratio 6.25.
qs.x: Incompressible fluid conserves volume: A(in)d(in) = A(out)d(out). The area ratio is (5.0/2.0)² = 6.25, so d(out) = 25/6.25 = 4.0 cm. Trap: Using the ratio of radii instead of the ratio of areas when relating distances moved by the pistons.

qs.q: In Configuration 3, what is the ratio of output work to input work?
o: 6.00 is the measured force ratio; work also depends on the distance ratio.
Correct: Force ratio = 2,400/400 = 6.00; the distance ratio is d(out)/d(in) = 1/6.25. Work ratio = 6.00/6.25 = 0.96, so 4% of the work is lost to friction.
1.00 would describe an ideal lift; the measured force (2,400 N) is below the ideal 2,500 N.
0.16 is the inverse of the area ratio, not the energy efficiency.
qs.x: Force ratio = 2,400/400 = 6.00; the distance ratio is d(out)/d(in) = 1/6.25. Work ratio = 6.00/6.25 = 0.96, so 4% of the work is lost to friction. Trap: Treating the force ratio as the work ratio; a lift multiplies force but divides distance.

qs.q: Using the measured line in Figure 1, the input force needed to hold up the 10,000 N car on the output piston of Configuration 1 is closest to:
o: 400 N is the ideal value; the measured line shows only 9,600 N at 400 N.
380 N would imply more than ideal force multiplication, which a real lift cannot achieve.
4,200 N is off by a factor of 10 from the correct reading of the line.
Correct: The measured slope is 4,800/200 = 24, so F(in) = 10,000/24 ≈ 417 N (about 420 N). Friction makes this larger than the ideal 400 N.
qs.x: The measured slope is 4,800/200 = 24, so F(in) = 10,000/24 ≈ 417 N (about 420 N). Friction makes this larger than the ideal 400 N. Trap: Using the ideal area ratio when the question asks for the measured performance of the real device.

graph.title: Figure 1. Output force versus input force, Configuration 1

passages.title: FL09 · Chem/Phys · Passage 4
text: A proton-exchange-membrane hydrogen fuel cell is operated at 25 °C. Hydrogen gas is oxidized at the anode (H₂ → 2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻), and oxygen is reduced at the cathode (O₂ + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻ → 2 H₂O). Protons cross the membrane, while electrons travel through an external load. The standard cell potential is 1.23 V. A researcher varies the load, so the current drawn from a single cell changes, and records the terminal voltage and the electrical power delivered (Table 1). Figure 1 shows the resulting polarization curve. The measured open-circuit voltage is 1.00 V, below 1.23 V. The researcher assumes all hydrogen consumed supplies current at 100% efficiency, and uses F = 96,500 C/mol e⁻ and 2.0 g/mol for H₂. The cell has an active area of 25 cm², is supplied with pure hydrogen and oxygen at 1 atm, and reaches steady state at each load before readings are recorded. Voltage efficiency is defined as the terminal voltage divided by 1.23 V.

qs.q: At a steady current of 4 A, what mass of hydrogen is consumed per hour?
o: 0.30 g treats each H₂ as delivering one electron instead of two.
0.075 g is the number of moles of H₂, not the mass in grams.
0.60 g assumes four electrons per H₂ (the O₂ stoichiometry).
qs.x: Charge = 4 A × 3,600 s = 14,400 C; moles e⁻ = 14,400/96,500 = 0.149; moles H₂ = 0.0746; mass = 0.0746 × 2.0 = 0.15 g. Trap: Ignoring that each H₂ molecule releases two electrons, or reporting moles as grams.

qs.q: At 6 A, the voltage efficiency of the cell is closest to:
o: Correct: Efficiency = 0.70 V / 1.23 V = 0.569, or about 57%.
70% reads the voltage in volts as a percentage of 1 V rather than dividing by 1.23 V.
43% is the fraction lost (1 - 0.57), not the efficiency.
81% is the open-circuit voltage (1.00 V) divided by 1.23 V, not the value at 6 A.
qs.x: Efficiency = 0.70 V / 1.23 V = 0.569, or about 57%. Trap: Dividing by the wrong reference voltage or reporting the loss instead of the efficiency.

qs.q: Table 1 shows 4.20 W at both 6 A and 10 A, even though the voltage is much lower at 10 A. Which statement explains this?
o: Power depends only on voltage, so the two operating points must share the same internal resistance
Power depends on both current and voltage; internal resistance is not required to be equal.
The cell stores charge at the higher current, which adds to the power delivered to the external load
A fuel cell does not store charge; reactants are fed continuously.
Power equals current times voltage, and the increase in current offsets the drop in voltage, since 0.70 × 6 = 0.42 × 10
Correct: P = IV: 6 × 0.70 = 4.20 W and 10 × 0.42 = 4.20 W, a coincidence of the decreasing voltage and the increasing current around the 8 A maximum.
Power is defined as current squared divided by voltage, which yields equal values at these two points
The relation P = I²/V is not valid; P = IV = I²R = V²/R.
qs.x: P = IV: 6 × 0.70 = 4.20 W and 10 × 0.42 = 4.20 W, a coincidence of the decreasing voltage and the increasing current around the 8 A maximum. Trap: Assuming lower voltage always means lower power, ignoring that P = IV depends on both quantities.

qs.q: The sharpest drop in voltage between 0 and 2 A (1.00 V to 0.85 V) is most consistent with which source of loss?
o: ohmic resistance of the membrane, which dominates at the lowest currents
Ohmic loss is proportional to current and shows as a steady linear decline, not a sharp initial drop.
activation overpotential from slow oxygen reduction at the cathode

Correct: A rapid initial voltage loss at small current reflects the energy barrier of the sluggish oxygen reduction (activation overpotential); ohmic loss grows linearly and mass-transport loss dominates at high current.
depletion of hydrogen at the anode, which limits the supply at the lowest currents
Reactant depletion limits the cell at high current (the steep drop from 8 to 10 A), not at 2 A.
a decrease in the standard cell potential as the current drawn increases
E° is a thermodynamic constant and does not change with current.
qs.x: A rapid initial voltage loss at small current reflects the energy barrier of the sluggish oxygen reduction (activation overpotential); ohmic loss grows linearly and mass-transport loss dominates at high current. Trap: Attributing every voltage loss to resistance rather than distinguishing activation, ohmic, and mass-transport regions.

qs.q: Which description of the electrode processes in the operating cell is correct?
o: Electrons flow through the membrane from the cathode to the anode, and H⁺ is carried through the external circuit
The membrane blocks electrons and ions are not carried by the wire.
Electrons flow through the external circuit from the anode to the cathode, where O₂ is reduced to H₂O using H⁺ that crossed the membrane
Correct: Oxidation occurs at the anode; electrons travel through the wire to the cathode, and the membrane conducts only H⁺, which combines with O₂ and electrons to form water.
Electrons flow through the external circuit from the cathode to the anode, where H₂ is oxidized to supply H⁺
Oxidation of H₂ is at the anode, and electrons leave from the anode, not toward it.
Protons and electrons both flow through the membrane from the anode to the cathode, where O₂ is reduced
The membrane is an electronic insulator; electrons must use the external circuit.
qs.x: Oxidation occurs at the anode; electrons travel through the wire to the cathode, and the membrane conducts only H⁺, which combines with O₂ and electrons to form water. Trap: Letting electrons cross the electrolyte or reversing the direction of electron flow relative to anode and cathode.

graph.title: Figure 1. Polarization curve of a single hydrogen fuel cell

passages.title: FL09 · Chem/Phys · Passage 5
text: Students investigate polarized light with a lamp that emits unpolarized light of intensity 200 W/m² and two ideal linear polarizing filters. The first filter (P1) transmits light polarized along its axis, so the beam leaving P1 has half the incident intensity. The second filter (P2), the analyzer, is rotated by an angle θ relative to P1, and a sensor measures the intensity leaving P2. For polarized light, the transmitted intensity follows Malus's law, I = I₀ cos²θ, where I₀ is the intensity incident on the analyzer. Table 1 shows the measurements for several angles, and Figure 1 displays the data. In a second experiment, P1 and P2 are crossed (θ = 90°) and a third filter (P3) is inserted between them with its axis at 45° to P1. The sensor was calibrated in the dark, and a shroud blocked ambient light so that only the lamp contributed; the lamp output remained stable throughout. Light intensity is proportional to the square of the electric field amplitude.

qs.q: According to Malus's law, what intensity would be expected after P2 at θ = 20°?
o: 88 W/m²
94 W/m²
94 W/m² forgets to square the cosine (100 × cos 20°).
12 W/m²
12 W/m² uses sin²20°, the component blocked rather than transmitted.
83 W/m²
83 W/m² results from linear interpolation between 100 and 75, but the curve is not linear.
qs.x: I = 100 cos²20° = 100 × (0.940)² = 88 W/m². Trap: Omitting the square in Malus's law or interpolating linearly on a cos² curve.

qs.q: When a third filter at 45° to P1 is inserted between crossed P1 and P2, the intensity after P2 is closest to:
o: 0 W/m²
0 would be the result without P3; crossed filters alone block all light.
50 W/m²
50 W/m² is the intensity after P3 only; P2 further reduces it.
12.5 W/m² results from applying a factor of 0.25 at the second step instead of 0.5.
25 W/m²
Correct: After P1: 100. After P3: 100 cos²45° = 50. After P2 (45° from P3): 50 cos²45° = 25 W/m².
qs.x: After P1: 100. After P3: 100 cos²45° = 50. After P2 (45° from P3): 50 cos²45° = 25 W/m². Trap: Concluding that adding a filter can only reduce light, so crossed polarizers still transmit nothing.

qs.q: What is the polarization of the light leaving the analyzer P2 at θ = 60°?
o: Linearly polarized along the axis of P1, with 25% of the intensity incident on it
The light takes on the orientation of the last filter that it passed, not P1.
Linearly polarized along the transmission axis of P2, with 25% of the intensity incident on it
Correct: An ideal polarizer outputs light polarized along its own axis; cos²60° = 0.25 gives the transmitted fraction.
Unpolarized, with 25% of the intensity incident on it
Light passing an ideal linear polarizer is always polarized.
Circularly polarized, with 75% of the intensity incident on it
A linear polarizer does not produce circular polarization; 75% is the blocked fraction.
qs.x: An ideal polarizer outputs light polarized along its own axis; cos²60° = 0.25 gives the transmitted fraction. Trap: Assuming the polarization direction is set by the first filter instead of the last one the light passed.

qs.q: At θ = 60°, the ratio of the transmitted electric field amplitude to the amplitude incident on P2 is:
o: Correct: E(out)/E(in) = cos 60° = 0.50; squaring gives 0.25, the intensity ratio.
0.25 is the intensity ratio, which is the square of the amplitude ratio.
0.75 would result from 1 - 0.25 and is not the amplitude ratio.
0.87 is sin 60°, the blocked component.
qs.x: E(out)/E(in) = cos 60° = 0.50; squaring gives 0.25, the intensity ratio. Trap: Mixing up the intensity ratio (cos²θ) with the amplitude ratio (cosθ).

h: Angle θ between P1 and P2 (degrees)

graph.title: Figure 1. Transmitted intensity versus analyzer angle

passages.title: FL09 · Chem/Phys · Passage 6
text: A science teacher introduces nuclear energy by comparing two processes, the fission of uranium-235 and the deuterium-tritium (D-T) fusion reaction. In the fission example, U-235 absorbs a neutron and splits into Ba-141, Kr-92, and three neutrons. In the fusion example, deuterium and tritium combine to form He-4 and a neutron. Using atomic masses, the teacher computes the mass defect Δm for each reaction and converts it to energy using 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c². The results are in Table 1. Figure 1 plots approximate binding energy per nucleon against mass number for several nuclides. The teacher also notes that a nuclear power plant operating at 1,000 MW thermal output obtains its energy from fission, and uses 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J. All masses are atomic masses in unified atomic mass units, with electron masses accounted for in the balance, and the energy released appears mainly as kinetic energy of the products. Fusion requires plasma temperatures of order 10⁸ K, whereas fission can be started by slow neutrons at ordinary temperatures.

qs.q: Which statement best explains why both reactions in Table 1 release energy?
o: The products have lower binding energy per nucleon than the reactants, so the total mass increases
Lower binding energy per nucleon in the products would require energy input and a mass increase.
The products are more tightly bound per nucleon, so the total mass decreases

Correct: Figure 1 shows binding energy per nucleon rising from A = 2 to a peak near A = 56, and falling for U-235; fusion and fission both move toward the more tightly bound region, converting mass into energy.
The reactants are heavier nuclei in both cases, so any reaction that splits a nucleus releases energy
Fusion does not split nuclei, and splitting light nuclei would absorb energy.
Both reactions emit neutrons, and the kinetic energy of the neutrons is the source of the energy released
Neutron kinetic energy is a result of the energy release, not the underlying source.
qs.x: Figure 1 shows binding energy per nucleon rising from A = 2 to a peak near A = 56, and falling for U-235; fusion and fission both move toward the more tightly bound region, converting mass into energy. Trap: Assuming that splitting or joining nuclei always releases energy, without considering where the product lies on the binding energy curve.

qs.q: From Table 1, how does the energy released per unit mass of fuel for D-T fusion compare with that for U-235 fission?
o: About 0.21 times as large
0.21 is the reciprocal of the ratio; fusion releases more per unit mass.
About 9.9 times as large
9.9 is the ratio of energy per reaction event (173.3/17.6) with fission in the numerator; it ignores the difference in fuel mass.
About 4.7 times as large
Correct: 3.50 MeV/u ÷ 0.737 MeV/u = 4.7.
About equal
The per-mass values 3.50 and 0.737 MeV/u differ by nearly a factor of five.
qs.x: 3.50 MeV/u ÷ 0.737 MeV/u = 4.7. Trap: Comparing energy per reaction event rather than energy per unit mass of fuel.

qs.q: Why does fusion need temperatures near 10⁸ K while fission of U-235 can be triggered by slow neutrons at ordinary temperatures?
o: Fusion releases less energy per reaction, so extra heat must be supplied to reach the mass defect
Energy released does not set the activation requirement; the Coulomb barrier does.
The strong nuclear force acts only at high temperatures, whereas fission relies on the weak force
The strong force is temperature-independent, and fission is not a weak-force process.
Fusing nuclei must overcome the Coulomb repulsion between positive charges, whereas a neutron is uncharged and is not repelled
Correct: Two nuclei both carry positive charge and must be driven close enough for the strong force to bind them; a neutron feels no electrostatic repulsion.
Neutrons have greater mass than the reacting nuclei, so they penetrate the nucleus at any temperature
A neutron is much lighter than a U-235 nucleus; its ability to enter is due to its neutrality.
qs.x: Two nuclei both carry positive charge and must be driven close enough for the strong force to bind them; a neutron feels no electrostatic repulsion. Trap: Thinking that the temperature requirement is about total energy released rather than electrostatic repulsion.

qs.q: A reactor delivers 1,000 MW of thermal power, and each fission releases 173.3 MeV. The number of fissions per second is closest to:
o: 6.3 × 10²¹ treats each fission as releasing only 1 MeV.
Correct: Energy per fission = 173.3 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ = 2.77 × 10⁻¹¹ J; rate = 10⁹ J/s ÷ 2.77 × 10⁻¹¹ J = 3.6 × 10¹⁹ per second.
3.6 × 10¹⁶ uses 10⁶ W rather than 1,000 MW (10⁹ W).
2.8 × 10⁻¹¹ is the energy per fission in joules, not a rate.
qs.x: Energy per fission = 173.3 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ = 2.77 × 10⁻¹¹ J; rate = 10⁹ J/s ÷ 2.77 × 10⁻¹¹ J = 3.6 × 10¹⁹ per second. Trap: Forgetting to convert MW to W or MeV to J before dividing power by energy per event.

qs.q: According to Figure 1, which nuclide among those plotted is the most stable per nucleon, and what does this imply for fusing it with another nucleus?
o: He-4; fusing it would absorb energy, because helium has the highest binding energy per nucleon
He-4 (7.07 MeV) is well below Fe-56 (8.79 MeV) in Figure 1.
U-235; fusing it would release energy, because it has the largest number of nucleons
U-235 (7.59 MeV) is less stable per nucleon, and the number of nucleons does not give stability.
Fe-56; fusing it would absorb energy, because the product would be less tightly bound per nucleon
Correct: The peak near A = 56 (8.79 MeV) marks the most tightly bound nucleus; fusion beyond this point is endothermic.
H-2; fusing it would absorb energy, because it has the lowest binding energy per nucleon
H-2 has the lowest binding energy, so fusing it releases energy rather than absorbing it.
qs.x: The peak near A = 56 (8.79 MeV) marks the most tightly bound nucleus; fusion beyond this point is endothermic. Trap: Equating the heaviest nucleus with the most stable one.

graph.title: Figure 1. Binding energy per nucleon versus mass number (approximate)

passages.title: FL09 · Chem/Phys · Passage 7
text: A chemistry class measures how the solubility of three salts in water depends on temperature, using saturated solutions equilibrated for one hour at each temperature and analyzed by evaporating a weighed sample. Table 1 lists the solubility in grams of solute per 100 g of water for potassium nitrate, sodium chloride, and lithium carbonate, and Figure 1 plots the same data. Students then carry out recrystallization-type exercises with these salts. In Exercise 1, 200 g of water is saturated with KNO₃ at 80 °C and then cooled to 20 °C. In Exercise 2, a mixture of 100 g KNO₃ and 5 g NaCl is dissolved in 100 g of water at 80 °C and cooled to 20 °C. In Exercise 3, a saturated solution of Li₂CO₃ in 100 g of water at 20 °C is heated to 80 °C. Assume the salts dissolve independently and the water mass remains constant.

qs.q: In Exercise 1, the mass of KNO₃ that crystallizes upon cooling is closest to:
o: 137 g is the amount for 100 g of water; the sample contains 200 g.
338 g is the total amount dissolved at 80 °C (2 × 169); some KNO₃ remains dissolved at 20 °C.
63 g is twice the amount that stays dissolved at 20 °C (2 × 31.6).
Correct: Per 100 g water the solubility drops from 169 to 31.6 g, so 137.4 g crystallizes per 100 g; for 200 g of water, 2 × 137.4 = 275 g.
qs.x: Per 100 g water the solubility drops from 169 to 31.6 g, so 137.4 g crystallizes per 100 g; for 200 g of water, 2 × 137.4 = 275 g. Trap: Forgetting to scale by the water mass, or reporting the dissolved amount instead of the amount that crystallizes.

qs.q: The data show that Li₂CO₃ becomes less soluble as temperature rises, whereas KNO₃ becomes more soluble. Which conclusion about the enthalpy of solution (ΔH_soln) is consistent with this?
o: ΔH_soln is negative for Li₂CO₃ and positive for KNO₃
Correct: By Le Chatelier's principle, heating shifts an endothermic dissolution toward more dissolved solute (KNO₃) and an exothermic dissolution toward solid (Li₂CO₃).
ΔH_soln is positive for Li₂CO₃ and negative for KNO₃, since heating favors exothermic dissolution
This reverses the signs; a salt whose solubility falls on heating releases heat on dissolving.
ΔH_soln is negative for both, since both dissolve spontaneously in water
KNO₃ solubility increases with T, indicating endothermic dissolution.
ΔH_soln is positive for both, because solubility is determined by entropy alone
Opposite temperature trends cannot arise from the same sign of ΔH_soln.
qs.x: By Le Chatelier's principle, heating shifts an endothermic dissolution toward more dissolved solute (KNO₃) and an exothermic dissolution toward solid (Li₂CO₃). Trap: Reversing the relationship between temperature dependence of solubility and the sign of ΔH_soln.

qs.q: In Exercise 2, what is the result of cooling the solution to 20 °C?
o: About 100 g of KNO₃ crystallizes together with the 5 g of NaCl impurity
Not all KNO₃ crystallizes; 31.6 g remains in solution, and NaCl is far below saturation.
About 68 g of KNO₃ crystallizes; the NaCl stays dissolved
Correct: At 20 °C only 31.6 g KNO₃ remains in 100 g of water, so 100 - 31.6 = 68.4 g crystallizes; 5 g NaCl is below its solubility (35.9 g), so it remains dissolved.
About 68 g of KNO₃ crystallizes together with the 5 g of NaCl impurity
NaCl would precipitate only if more than 35.9 g were present per 100 g of water.
No KNO₃ crystallizes, because the solution was not saturated at 80 °C
The solution holds 100 g of KNO₃ per 100 g water, which exceeds 31.6 g at 20 °C, so crystals do form on cooling.
qs.x: At 20 °C only 31.6 g KNO₃ remains in 100 g of water, so 100 - 31.6 = 68.4 g crystallizes; 5 g NaCl is below its solubility (35.9 g), so it remains dissolved. Trap: Assuming all solutes precipitate on cooling, ignoring the solubility of each salt at the final temperature.

qs.q: In Exercise 3, heating the saturated Li₂CO₃ solution from 20 °C to 80 °C results in:
o: dissolution of about 0.48 g of additional Li₂CO₃
More dissolving would require solubility to increase with T, but it falls for Li₂CO₃.
no change, since the amount of solute is fixed
The amount of solute is fixed, but the amount that can remain dissolved is not.
precipitation of about 0.48 g of solid Li₂CO₃
Correct: Solubility falls from 1.33 to 0.85 g/100 g water, so 1.33 - 0.85 = 0.48 g must come out of solution.
precipitation of about 0.85 g of solid Li₂CO₃
0.85 g is the amount that remains dissolved at 80 °C, not the amount precipitated.
qs.x: Solubility falls from 1.33 to 0.85 g/100 g water, so 1.33 - 0.85 = 0.48 g must come out of solution. Trap: Assuming heating always increases solubility, as it does for most solids.

graph.title: Figure 1. Solubility of three salts versus temperature

passages.title: FL09 · Chem/Phys · Passage 8
text: A materials chemist studies the phase behavior of carbon dioxide, which is used both as dry ice and as a supercritical solvent. Table 1 lists three characteristic points of CO₂ (the normal sublimation point, the triple point, and the critical point) together with those for water. Figure 1 shows the three phase-boundary curves of CO₂ as pressure versus temperature; the solid-liquid line is nearly vertical, with a slightly positive slope of about 0.02 K per atm. All pressures are absolute, and the boundaries were assembled from vapor pressure and melting measurements on pure CO₂ at several temperatures. In Experiment 1, a block of solid CO₂ at 180 K is warmed to 250 K at a constant pressure of 1.0 atm. In Experiment 2, gaseous CO₂ at 250 K is compressed slowly. In Experiment 3, CO₂ at 320 K is compressed isothermally from 1 atm to 100 atm. The chemist notes that, in contrast to CO₂, liquid water is denser than ice.

qs.q: In Experiment 1, what happens as solid CO₂ is warmed from 180 K to 250 K at 1.0 atm?
o: The solid melts at about 195 K and the liquid boils at about 250 K
A liquid phase cannot exist below 5.11 atm, so there is no melting or boiling step.
The solid melts at 216.6 K and the liquid remains until 250 K
Melting at 216.6 K would require a pressure of at least 5.11 atm.
The solid sublimes at 216.6 K and the gas then condenses to liquid
216.6 K is the triple-point temperature, not the sublimation temperature at 1.0 atm; and warming does not condense a gas.
The solid sublimes directly to a gas at about 195 K, and no liquid forms
Correct: At 1.0 atm the pressure is below the triple point pressure (5.11 atm), so the solid-gas boundary is crossed at 194.7 K and liquid never appears.
qs.x: At 1.0 atm the pressure is below the triple point pressure (5.11 atm), so the solid-gas boundary is crossed at 194.7 K and liquid never appears. Trap: Expecting every solid to melt at atmospheric pressure, ignoring that this pressure is below the triple point pressure.

qs.q: In Experiment 2, the minimum pressure at which the CO₂ gas at 250 K begins to condense to liquid is closest to:
o: 18 atm
Correct: At 250 K the vertical line crosses the liquid-gas curve in Figure 1 at about 17.7 atm; compressing past this pressure produces liquid.
5.1 atm
5.1 atm is the triple-point pressure, but 250 K is well above the triple-point temperature.
73 atm
73 atm is the critical pressure; liquefaction at 250 K occurs well below it.
1.0 atm
1.0 atm is the standard pressure, at which CO₂ is a gas at 250 K.
qs.x: At 250 K the vertical line crosses the liquid-gas curve in Figure 1 at about 17.7 atm; compressing past this pressure produces liquid. Trap: Using the triple point or critical pressure instead of reading the liquid-gas curve at the specified temperature.

qs.q: The positive slope of the solid-liquid line for CO₂ indicates that:
o: increasing pressure lowers the melting point, because solid CO₂ is less dense than liquid CO₂ near the triple point
That behavior (negative slope) belongs to water, where ice is less dense than the liquid.
increasing pressure raises the melting point, because solid CO₂ is denser than liquid CO₂
Correct: Higher pressure favors the denser, smaller-volume phase; a positive dP/dT therefore means the solid is denser, unlike water, whose negative slope reflects less dense ice.
increasing pressure raises the melting point, because liquid CO₂ is denser than the solid phase near the triple point
If the liquid were denser, pressure would favor the liquid and lower the melting point.
the melting point is independent of pressure, because the phases of CO₂ differ only in energy and not in volume
The slope is nonzero, so the melting temperature does depend on pressure.
qs.x: Higher pressure favors the denser, smaller-volume phase; a positive dP/dT therefore means the solid is denser, unlike water, whose negative slope reflects less dense ice. Trap: Applying water's anomalous behavior to every substance.

qs.q: In Experiment 3, as the CO₂ at 320 K is compressed to 100 atm, the sample:
o: condenses to a liquid at about 52 atm, forming two phases
No liquid-gas boundary exists above the critical temperature, so there is no condensation at any pressure.
remains a single supercritical fluid throughout, with no distinct liquid-gas boundary crossed
Correct: 320 K exceeds the critical temperature (304.2 K), so no pressure can produce a distinct liquid phase.
condenses to a solid at about 100 atm, since the pressure is high
The solid-liquid line is far to the left at about 220 K; compression at 320 K does not freeze CO₂.
condenses to a liquid at 73 atm, which is the critical pressure
The critical pressure applies only at 304.2 K; above that temperature there is no condensation.
qs.x: 320 K exceeds the critical temperature (304.2 K), so no pressure can produce a distinct liquid phase. Trap: Assuming that sufficient pressure always liquefies a gas, regardless of temperature.

passages.title: FL09 · Chem/Phys · Passage 9
text: A biochemist separates a mixture of proteins using two electrophoretic methods. In SDS-PAGE, proteins are denatured in sodium dodecyl sulfate and a reducing agent and then run through a 10% polyacrylamide gel toward the anode; migration distance after a fixed time is a linear function of log(molecular mass). Four standards were run alongside two unknown proteins, X and Y (Table 1, Figure 1). In isoelectric focusing (IEF), proteins are placed in a gel containing a stable pH gradient from pH 3 (anode end) to pH 10 (cathode end) and an electric field is applied; each protein migrates until its net charge is zero. The isoelectric points (pI) of X and Y were found to be 8.2 and 4.9. Gels were stained with Coomassie dye after the run, and distances were measured from the bottom of the loading well to the center of each band. In a final experiment, the SDS-PAGE is repeated with a 15% polyacrylamide gel. For the pI experiment, protein X was initially applied at a position where the pH is 6.

qs.q: Based on Table 1 and Figure 1, the molecular mass of protein X is closest to:
o: 37.5 kDa
37.5 kDa is the arithmetic mean of 50 and 25, but the relationship is linear in log of the mass.
25 kDa
25 kDa corresponds to a migration distance of 5.00 cm, farther than X traveled.
35 kDa
Correct: The standard curve is linear in log(mass), and 4.25 cm lies midway between 50 kDa (3.50 cm) and 25 kDa (5.00 cm); the log midpoint corresponds to √(50 × 25) ≈ 35 kDa.
42 kDa
42 kDa would require a distance of about 3.9 cm, which is not the measured 4.25 cm.
qs.x: The standard curve is linear in log(mass), and 4.25 cm lies midway between 50 kDa (3.50 cm) and 25 kDa (5.00 cm); the log midpoint corresponds to √(50 × 25) ≈ 35 kDa. Trap: Interpolating on a linear mass scale rather than the logarithmic scale used by the standard curve.

qs.q: What is the primary role of SDS in the first method?
o: It binds only to positive residues and neutralizes the proteins, so migration depends on shape
SDS binds the polypeptide backbone through hydrophobic interactions and adds negative charge; it doesn't neutralize.
It denatures the proteins and gives them a uniform negative charge per unit mass, so migration depends on size
Correct: SDS coats polypeptides with a nearly constant negative charge per gram, masking intrinsic charge and unfolding them, so sieving by the gel separates by mass.
It cleaves peptide bonds into short fragments of equal length, so all proteins migrate together
SDS does not break peptide bonds; the reducing agent breaks disulfide bonds only.
It creates the pH gradient, so migration continues until the net charge of each protein is zero
The pH gradient of IEF comes from carrier ampholytes; SDS-PAGE has no such gradient.
qs.x: SDS coats polypeptides with a nearly constant negative charge per gram, masking intrinsic charge and unfolding them, so sieving by the gel separates by mass. Trap: Confusing SDS-PAGE (separation by mass) with IEF (separation by charge at the pI).

qs.q: In IEF, protein X (pI 8.2) starts where the pH is 6. Which statement describes its behavior?
o: It carries a net positive charge, migrates toward the cathode, and stops where the pH is 8.2
Correct: At pH 6 < pI the protein is protonated and net positive, so it moves toward the cathode (higher pH) until pH = pI, where the net charge is zero.
It carries a net negative charge, migrates toward the anode, and stops where the pH is 8.2
Net negative charge occurs when pH > pI; at pH 6 the protein is positive.
It carries a net positive charge, migrates toward the anode, and stops where the pH is 6
A positive protein moves toward the cathode, and it does not stop until the pH reaches its pI.
It carries no net charge and remains at pH 6 because it is already within the pH gradient
Net charge is zero only at the pI (8.2), not at pH 6.
qs.x: At pH 6 < pI the protein is protonated and net positive, so it moves toward the cathode (higher pH) until pH = pI, where the net charge is zero. Trap: Mixing up the sign of the charge below and above the pI, or the direction of migration toward electrodes.

qs.q: When the SDS-PAGE is repeated with 15% polyacrylamide rather than 10%, which outcome is expected?
o: All bands migrate longer distances, since the denser gel exerts a greater force on the proteins
Smaller pores hinder movement; they do not enhance it.
The bands do not change position, since SDS makes migration independent of the gel pore size
SDS equalizes charge-to-mass, but the gel sieving effect still determines migration.
Only the small proteins migrate shorter distances, since large proteins do not enter the gel
Both large and small proteins are slowed, and large proteins are retarded more.
All bands migrate shorter distances, with larger proteins impeded to a greater extent
Correct: A higher acrylamide concentration gives smaller pores and more resistance, slowing migration, especially for larger proteins; this increases resolution for smaller proteins.
qs.x: A higher acrylamide concentration gives smaller pores and more resistance, slowing migration, especially for larger proteins; this increases resolution for smaller proteins. Trap: Believing that a denser gel speeds migration, or that the gel plays no role once SDS is added.

qs.q: Protein Y has a pI of 4.9. In a native (non-denaturing) gel at pH 8.6, with no SDS, the net charge of Y and its direction of migration are:
o: positive, migrating toward the anode (positive electrode)
A positive protein would be repelled by the anode; the charge here is negative.
negative, toward the anode
Correct: At pH 8.6 > pI 4.9 the protein carries a net negative charge, and negative species migrate toward the anode (positive electrode).
negative, migrating toward the cathode (negative electrode)
A negatively charged protein is attracted to the positive electrode, the anode.
positive, migrating toward the cathode (negative electrode)
The protein is above its pI, so it is not positively charged.
qs.x: At pH 8.6 > pI 4.9 the protein carries a net negative charge, and negative species migrate toward the anode (positive electrode). Trap: Applying the sign of charge relative to the pI backwards.

graph.title: Figure 1. SDS-PAGE standard curve

passages.title: FL09 · Chem/Phys · Passage 10
text: Peptide bonds link amino acids through a condensation reaction in which the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another lose a molecule of water. In water at neutral pH, the reverse reaction, hydrolysis, is thermodynamically favorable, yet it is extremely slow. A biochemist tests the dipeptide Ala-Gly under several conditions, measuring the percentage hydrolyzed after 24 hours by amino acid analysis (Table 1). In 6 M HCl at 110 °C, hydrolysis is a first-order process in the dipeptide. Figure 1 shows the time course in this medium. The biochemist then examines the proposed mechanism for acid hydrolysis and the form in which each amino acid exists in the final solution. The reactions were run in sealed tubes with equal starting concentrations of dipeptide (0.10 M), and samples were neutralized before analysis to stop the reaction. Assume that the pKa values of a carboxyl group and an ammonium group in free amino acids are about 2 and 9–10.

qs.q: Hydrolysis of Ala-Gly is thermodynamically favorable, yet Table 1 shows less than 0.1% hydrolysis in water at pH 7 over 24 hours. This is best explained by:
o: a positive ΔG for hydrolysis, because water is a poor nucleophile
The premise states that hydrolysis has a favorable ΔG; the slow rate is kinetic.
a negative ΔS for the reaction, which makes hydrolysis nonspontaneous
The stated favorable ΔG means the net spontaneity is not governed by a negative ΔS here.
the absence of the peptidase, which changes the equilibrium position of the reaction
Enzymes accelerate the approach to equilibrium but do not change its position.
a high activation energy, because resonance gives the amide C-N bond partial double-bond character
Correct: Thermodynamic favorability (negative ΔG) does not imply a fast rate; the stabilized, planar amide bond has a high barrier, making uncatalyzed hydrolysis slow.
qs.x: Thermodynamic favorability (negative ΔG) does not imply a fast rate; the stabilized, planar amide bond has a high barrier, making uncatalyzed hydrolysis slow. Trap: Equating a slow reaction with an unfavorable free energy change; kinetic stability is distinct from thermodynamic stability.

qs.q: According to Figure 1, the half-life of Ala-Gly in 6 M HCl at 110 °C is closest to:
o: 3 h
Correct: Half the dipeptide is hydrolyzed (50%) between 2 h (35%) and 4 h (58%), so t½ ≈ 3 h (k ≈ 0.22 h⁻¹, t½ = 0.693/k ≈ 3.2 h).
8 h
At 8 h about 82% has already been hydrolyzed, far beyond one half-life.
At 12 h roughly 93% has been hydrolyzed, which is more than three half-lives.
1 h
At 1 h only about 20% is hydrolyzed, so half the dipeptide has not yet reacted.
qs.x: Half the dipeptide is hydrolyzed (50%) between 2 h (35%) and 4 h (58%), so t½ ≈ 3 h (k ≈ 0.22 h⁻¹, t½ = 0.693/k ≈ 3.2 h). Trap: Choosing the time at which the reaction is nearly complete rather than the time at which 50% has reacted.

qs.q: Which statement describes the role of acid in the hydrolysis mechanism?
o: Protonation of the amide nitrogen makes the nitrogen a stronger nucleophile, so it attacks water
Nitrogen is not the primary basic site, and protonating it does not make it nucleophilic.
Protonation of water generates hydroxide, which is a much stronger nucleophile at low pH
Acid lowers hydroxide concentration; hydroxide is not generated at low pH.
Protonation of the carbonyl oxygen makes the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic, so water can attack it

Correct: The carbonyl oxygen of the amide is the most basic site; protonation increases the carbonyl carbon's positive character, and water adds to form a tetrahedral intermediate, which then expels the amine.
Protonation of the α-carbon breaks the C-N bond directly without a tetrahedral intermediate
The hydrolysis involves nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl; the α-carbon is not protonated.
qs.x: The carbonyl oxygen of the amide is the most basic site; protonation increases the carbonyl carbon's positive character, and water adds to form a tetrahedral intermediate, which then expels the amine. Trap: Proposing protonation of the amide nitrogen, which is not basic because its lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl.

qs.q: After complete hydrolysis in 6 M HCl, the predominant form of the glycine product is:
o: ⁺H₃N-CH₂-COO⁻, a zwitterion with no net charge
The zwitterion predominates near neutral pH, between the two pKa values.
H₂N-CH₂-COO⁻, with a deprotonated amine and a carboxylate
The fully deprotonated anion predominates only at high pH, above about 10.
⁺H₃N-CH₂-COOH, with a protonated amine and a neutral carboxyl group
Correct: In 6 M HCl (pH well below 0) both groups are protonated, because the pH is below the carboxyl pKa of about 2; glycine carries a net +1 charge.
H₂N-CH₂-COOH, with a neutral amine and neutral carboxyl group
A neutral amine with a neutral carboxyl group is a minor form in water at any pH.
qs.x: In 6 M HCl (pH well below 0) both groups are protonated, because the pH is below the carboxyl pKa of about 2; glycine carries a net +1 charge. Trap: Drawing amino acids as zwitterions regardless of the pH of the solution.

graph.title: Figure 1. Hydrolysis of Ala-Gly in 6 M HCl at 110 °C

passages.title: FL09 · Psych/Soc · Passage 1
text: Researchers examined how sleep loss affects emotional functioning. Forty-eight healthy adults (ages 19-30) were randomly assigned to one night of total sleep deprivation (n = 24) or one night of normal sleep at home (n = 24). The next day, participants completed the Profile of Mood States (POMS) negative-affect scale (range 0-60; higher scores indicate worse mood) at four sessions: 8:00, 12:00, 16:00, and 20:00. At 12:00, participants also viewed negative images while undergoing functional MRI. Amygdala reactivity was quantified as percent signal change relative to neutral images, and functional connectivity between the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and the amygdala was expressed as a correlation coefficient. Scorers of the imaging data were blind to group. Group means are shown in Table 1 (standard deviations in parentheses); the difference in mean negative-affect score, averaged over the four sessions, was significant by independent-samples t-test (p < .01). Figure 1 shows negative-affect scores at each session.

qs.q: Approximating the pooled standard deviation as the square root of the average of the two group variances, the effect size (Cohen's d) for the group difference in mean negative-affect score is closest to:
o: 0.6, the 8.8-point mean difference divided by the sum of the two SDs (15.6)
Dividing by the sum of the SDs (15.6) overstates the denominator; d uses a pooled SD, not a sum.
1.1, the 8.8-point mean difference divided by a pooled SD of about 7.8
8.8, the raw difference between the two group means in POMS points
The raw difference is not standardized, so it is not an effect size in SD units.
0.1, the 8.8-point mean difference divided by the average variance (about 61)
Dividing by variance rather than SD gives units of 1/POMS point and a value that is far too small.
qs.x: Pooled SD = sqrt((8.1^2 + 7.5^2)/2) = sqrt(60.9) = 7.8; d = 8.8/7.8 = 1.1. Trap: Reporting the raw mean difference (8.8) as the effect size, or dividing by a sum or variance instead of the pooled SD.

qs.q: Greater amygdala reactivity to negative images in the sleep-deprived group is most consistent with which function of the amygdala?
o: Appraising the emotional significance of stimuli, particularly threatening ones
Correct: The amygdala evaluates emotional salience, particularly threat and negative valence, so heightened reactivity indicates amplified emotional responses.
Consolidating declarative memories of each image into long-term storage in the cortex
Declarative memory consolidation is a hippocampal function, and the study did not measure memory.
Coordinating the motor planning needed to enter ratings on the response device
Motor planning relies on premotor cortex and basal ganglia, not the amygdala.
Regulating body temperature and fluid balance during the long scanning session
Temperature and fluid balance are hypothalamic functions.
qs.x: The amygdala evaluates emotional salience, particularly threat and negative valence, so heightened reactivity indicates amplified emotional responses. Trap: Confusing the amygdala with the hippocampus because both are limbic structures involved in emotional memories.

qs.q: Reduced mPFC-amygdala connectivity in the sleep-deprived group suggests that these participants would be most impaired in which of the following tasks?
o: Reappraising a distressing image to lessen its emotional impact
Correct: Top-down prefrontal control over the amygdala supports emotion regulation such as cognitive reappraisal, so weaker coupling should impair it.
Recognizing familiar faces among a large set of unfamiliar faces shown briefly
Face recognition depends mainly on the fusiform and temporal regions, not on mPFC-amygdala coupling.
Distinguishing a high-pitched tone from a low-pitched tone presented in quiet
Pitch discrimination depends on auditory cortex and the cochlea.
Maintaining balance while standing on an unstable surface with the eyes closed
Balance depends on the vestibular system and cerebellum.
qs.x: Top-down prefrontal control over the amygdala supports emotion regulation such as cognitive reappraisal, so weaker coupling should impair it. Trap: Choosing any task that sounds impaired by poor sleep instead of the one that depends on the specific circuit measured.

qs.q: Random assignment of participants to the two sleep conditions primarily helps the researchers to:
o: Ensure that the sample is representative of all adults in the general population, including older adults and those with sleep disorders
Representativeness comes from random sampling, not random assignment.
Distribute pre-existing differences, such as baseline mood or usual sleep habits, evenly across groups on average
Correct: Random assignment makes the groups equivalent in expectation on both measured and unmeasured characteristics, supporting causal inference.
Prevent participants from knowing, until the end of the study, which sleep condition they were assigned to
Participants cannot be blinded to whether they stayed awake all night.
Guarantee that the mood scale gives consistent scores from one session to the next
Test reliability is a property of the instrument, not of how groups are formed.
qs.x: Random assignment makes the groups equivalent in expectation on both measured and unmeasured characteristics, supporting causal inference. Trap: Mixing up random assignment (internal validity) with random sampling (external validity).

qs.q: According to Figure 1 and Table 1, at which sessions did the gap between the two groups in negative-affect score exceed the overall mean group difference reported in Table 1?
o: The 12:00 gap is 8.2, which is below 8.8.
20:00 only, the last session of the day
The 16:00 gap is 11.2, which also exceeds 8.8, so 20:00 is not the only session.
All four sessions, since the sleep-deprived group is higher throughout
Being higher at every session does not mean every gap exceeds the average gap; the 8:00 and 12:00 gaps are smaller.
16:00 and 20:00 only
Correct: Gaps are 4.2 (8:00), 8.2 (12:00), 11.2 (16:00), and 11.6 (20:00); only the last two exceed 8.8.
qs.x: Gaps are 4.2 (8:00), 8.2 (12:00), 11.2 (16:00), and 11.6 (20:00); only the last two exceed 8.8. Trap: Judging 'larger than average' by direction of the difference rather than computing each session's gap.

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean negative-affect score by session

passages.title: FL09 · Psych/Soc · Passage 2
text: Temperament refers to early-appearing, biologically based differences in emotional and behavioral reactivity. In a longitudinal study, 120 four-month-old infants were exposed in the laboratory to novel stimuli (a moving mobile, unfamiliar voices, and a swab with a faint odor). Trained observers coded motor activity and distress and classified each infant as high-reactive, moderate-reactive, or low-reactive. At age 4 years, children were observed with unfamiliar adults and peers in a playroom. A child was classified as behaviorally inhibited if he or she stayed near the caregiver and showed prolonged wariness. Observers coding the 4-year behavior did not know the infant classification. Of the 120 enrolled families, 100 completed the 4-year session; the 20 families lost to follow-up had, on average, lower household incomes. Table 1 shows the results for the 100 children who completed both phases. Across these children, the correlation between a continuous 4-month reactivity score and a 4-year inhibition score was r = .38.

qs.q: What percentage of the children who completed the 4-year session were classified as behaviorally inhibited?
o: Correct: 12 + 10 + 4 = 26 inhibited out of 100 completers = 26%.
31.7%, the mean of the three group percentages
Averaging percentages ignores the unequal group sizes (20, 40, 40).
60%, the rate among the high-reactive group
60% is the rate in one group only, not the whole sample.
22%, the number inhibited divided by the 120 enrolled infants
Dividing by 120 includes the 20 families lost to follow-up, who have no 4-year data.
qs.x: 12 + 10 + 4 = 26 inhibited out of 100 completers = 26%. Trap: Averaging the three percentages instead of weighting by group size.

qs.q: Approximately what proportion of the variance in 4-year inhibition scores is statistically accounted for by the 4-month reactivity score?
o: 38%, because the proportion equals the correlation coefficient itself
The proportion of variance is r^2, not r.
Correct: Variance explained is r squared: .38 x .38 = .144, or about 14%.
62%, because the remainder is 1 minus the correlation coefficient
1 - r (.62) has no meaning as variance explained; unexplained variance would be 1 - r^2.
3.8%, because the coefficient is divided by 10 to give a percentage
Dividing r by ten is not a valid transformation.
qs.x: Variance explained is r squared: .38 x .38 = .144, or about 14%. Trap: Reading the correlation coefficient as the percentage of variance explained.

qs.q: Eight of the 20 high-reactive children were not classified as inhibited at age 4. This finding is best interpreted as evidence that:
o: Infant temperament has no biological basis and is determined solely by learning
Substantial prediction (60% vs 10%) argues against a purely learned account.
The laboratory reactivity measure is invalid because it did not predict perfectly
Imperfect prediction is expected for any behavioral measure and does not make it invalid.
Inhibition at age 4 is determined only by the parents' own temperament
The study did not measure parental temperament, and the data do not support exclusive parental determination.
Experiences such as caregiving style can moderate how an early temperament is expressed
Correct: A partial, probabilistic link between infant reactivity and later inhibition fits a model in which biology sets tendencies that environment shapes.
qs.x: A partial, probabilistic link between infant reactivity and later inhibition fits a model in which biology sets tendencies that environment shapes. Trap: Treating an imperfect prediction as proof that a measure or a biological account is wrong.

qs.q: The 20 families lost to follow-up had lower incomes on average. This attrition most directly threatens the study's:
o: Generalizability, because lower-income children may be underrepresented among completers
Correct: Systematic dropout of one subgroup means the final sample no longer represents the original population, limiting generalization.
Blinding, because observers could then infer each child's infant classification during the playroom session
Dropout does not unblind observers, who never saw the infant classifications.
Temporal order, because later behavior was measured before infant behavior
Infant measures came first at 4 months, so temporal order is intact.
Construct validity, because inhibition was defined using caregiver proximity
How inhibition is defined is unrelated to who dropped out.
qs.x: Systematic dropout of one subgroup means the final sample no longer represents the original population, limiting generalization. Trap: Confusing attrition (a sampling and external-validity problem) with measurement problems.

passages.title: FL09 · Psych/Soc · Passage 3
text: The social facilitation effect, in which the presence of others alters performance, was tested in a laboratory study. Sixty undergraduates were randomly assigned (n = 20 per group) to complete tasks alone, in front of an audience of three silent observers, or in front of an audience of six. Each participant completed a simple task (sorting cards by color) and a complex task (solving difficult anagrams), in counterbalanced order, while heart rate was recorded. Observers were told to watch the participant's performance closely. Accuracy was measured as the percentage of items answered correctly. Table 1 shows group means, and Figure 1 plots accuracy against audience size. Heart rate was higher in both audience conditions than in the alone condition (p < .01). Participants had no prior experience with the anagram task. Group differences were analyzed with a mixed-design ANOVA, which showed a significant interaction between audience size and task type (p < .001). Participants were run individually in 10-minute sessions, and the observers were confederates following a script.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for why an audience lowered accuracy on the anagram task but raised it on the card-sorting task?
o: Observers provide corrective feedback during the easy task but are unable to assist during the difficult anagram task, so errors accumulate
Observers were silent in every condition, so no feedback was given.
Participants lose motivation on difficult tasks because the audience makes success seem unattainable
Lower motivation would predict worse performance on both tasks, but simple-task accuracy increased.
Arousal strengthens the dominant response, which is correct for an easy task but often incorrect for a difficult, unpracticed task
Correct: Social facilitation theory predicts that arousal enhances well-learned (dominant) responses and impairs poorly learned ones.
An audience reduces arousal on simple tasks, which brings it closer to the optimum for card sorting
Heart rate rose with an audience, so arousal increased rather than decreased.
qs.x: Social facilitation theory predicts that arousal enhances well-learned (dominant) responses and impairs poorly learned ones. Trap: Assuming an audience helps or hurts all performance regardless of task difficulty.

qs.q: From the alone condition to the audience of six, the relative decrease in complex-task accuracy was closest to:
o: 21%, the absolute drop in percentage points
21 is the absolute change in percentage points, not a relative change.
43%, the drop divided by the audience-of-six accuracy
Dividing by the final value (49) instead of the starting value (70) gives 43%.
70%, the accuracy of the alone condition
70 is the baseline accuracy, not a change.
30%, the drop relative to the alone condition
Correct: (70 - 49)/70 = 21/70 = 0.30, a 30% relative decrease.
qs.x: (70 - 49)/70 = 21/70 = 0.30, a 30% relative decrease. Trap: Computing a percent change relative to the endpoint instead of the baseline, or reporting percentage points.

qs.q: Which added condition would best test whether the audience effect depends on being evaluated, as opposed to the mere presence of others?
o: An audience of nine observers, to determine whether accuracy keeps changing as the audience grows
A larger audience varies size, not evaluative potential.
An audience of six who are blindfolded and wearing headphones, so that they are present but cannot evaluate the participant
Correct: Holding presence constant while removing the observers' ability to evaluate isolates evaluation apprehension.
A condition in which heart rate is recorded at more frequent intervals during each of the tasks to improve measurement precision
More frequent heart-rate recording changes measurement, not the social manipulation.
A condition in which participants complete the anagram task before the card-sorting task
Task order is already counterbalanced and unrelated to the evaluation question.
qs.x: Holding presence constant while removing the observers' ability to evaluate isolates evaluation apprehension. Trap: Choosing a manipulation that varies audience size rather than the specific mechanism in question.

qs.q: If participants had practiced the anagram task for several weeks before testing, the audience would most likely:
o: Reduce anagram accuracy, because the audience always impairs complex tasks
Impairment depends on task mastery, not on complexity alone.
Leave anagram accuracy unchanged, because practice eliminates arousal
Practice does not eliminate arousal; audiences still raise it.
Improve anagram accuracy, because the well-learned correct response would now be dominant
Correct: Practice makes correct responses dominant, so audience-induced arousal facilitates rather than impairs performance.
Lower heart rate, because practiced tasks no longer cause physiological arousal
Heart rate rises with an audience regardless of task familiarity in this account.
qs.x: Practice makes correct responses dominant, so audience-induced arousal facilitates rather than impairs performance. Trap: Treating task complexity as fixed rather than dependent on the performer's skill.

qs.q: The increase in heart rate seen in the audience conditions most directly reflects:
o: Greater parasympathetic activity, as acetylcholine released by the vagus nerve speeds the sinoatrial node
Vagal acetylcholine slows the heart, not speeds it.
Lower sympathetic activity, which disinhibits the atrioventricular node
Reduced sympathetic input would slow, not raise, heart rate.
Greater sympathetic activity, as norepinephrine acts on the sinoatrial node to speed pacemaker firing
Correct: Arousal activates the sympathetic division, whose norepinephrine increases heart rate via the sinoatrial node.
Greater somatic motor output, as skeletal muscle contraction pumps blood back to the heart
Somatic motor output does not directly set heart rate through the pacemaker.
qs.x: Arousal activates the sympathetic division, whose norepinephrine increases heart rate via the sinoatrial node. Trap: Mixing up sympathetic and parasympathetic effects on heart rate.

graph.title: Figure 1. Accuracy by audience size and task

passages.title: FL09 · Psych/Soc · Passage 4
text: Habituation and sensitization are simple forms of non-associative learning. In this study, 40 adults sat in a quiet room while skin conductance response (SCR, in microsiemens, uS), a measure of sympathetic arousal, was recorded. All participants heard a moderate 70-dB tone presented once every 30 seconds, in eight blocks of five tones. In Group A (n = 20), the tone was presented alone throughout. In Group B (n = 20), a brief, unexpected 100-dB noise burst was delivered between block 4 and block 5, after which the 70-dB tone resumed. Mean SCR to the tone for each block is shown in Figure 1 and for selected blocks in Table 1. Participants reported no hearing difficulty, and SCR to the 100-dB burst itself did not differ between groups. A repeated-measures ANOVA with block as a within-subjects factor and group as a between-subjects factor showed a significant group x block interaction (p < .01). Participants were assigned to groups at random, and the person scoring the SCR recordings did not know group membership.

qs.q: Which observation in the data best supports interpreting the decline in Group A's response as habituation rather than simple fatigue of the ear's receptors?
o: Group A's SCR fell by more than half between block 1 and block 4
A large decline fits both habituation and fatigue, so it does not discriminate between them.
Group A's SCR remained above zero even at block 8
A nonzero residual response is expected under either account.
Both groups had identical SCR in blocks 1 through 4
Identical early responses show the groups started alike but say nothing about the mechanism.
Group B's response to the same tone rebounded in block 5 after a different, intense stimulus
Correct: If receptors were fatigued, an unrelated stimulus would not restore the response to the same tone; the rebound indicates a central change in responsiveness.
qs.x: If receptors were fatigued, an unrelated stimulus would not restore the response to the same tone; the rebound indicates a central change in responsiveness. Trap: Using the size of the decline as evidence of mechanism when only a restored response distinguishes habituation from fatigue.

qs.q: In block 5, Group B's mean SCR was approximately how many times Group A's?
o: 0.4 times, since Group B's response was lower than Group A's
Group B's response was higher, so the ratio must exceed 1; 0.4 reverses numerator and denominator.
1.6 times, since the groups differed by 1.6 uS
A difference of 1.6 uS does not exist; the actual difference is 0.38 uS and a difference is not a ratio.
2.6 times
Correct: 0.62/0.24 = 2.58, or about 2.6.
3.9 times, since 0.62 divided by 0.16 gives the ratio
0.62/0.16 uses the block 8 value for Group A instead of block 5.
qs.x: 0.62/0.24 = 2.58, or about 2.6. Trap: Dividing by a value from the wrong block or reporting the difference (0.38) instead of the ratio.

qs.q: Which of the following is the best everyday example of sensitization?
o: A new resident stops noticing the sound of a nearby train after several weeks
Ceasing to notice a repeated harmless sound is habituation.
A dog salivates at the sound of a bell that has been paired with food
Salivating to a bell paired with food is classical conditioning.
After a car backfires loudly, a pedestrian startles at ordinary street sounds she had been ignoring
Correct: Sensitization is an increased response to a range of stimuli after a strong or noxious event.
A child learns to avoid a hot stove after being burned once and receiving a reprimand
Avoiding a stove after punishment reflects associative learning, not a generalized change in responsiveness.
qs.x: Sensitization is an increased response to a range of stimuli after a strong or noxious event. Trap: Calling any change in response to a stimulus sensitization, including decreases and associative learning.

qs.q: The drop in Group B's SCR from 0.62 uS (block 5) to 0.30 uS (block 8) is best explained by:
o: Permanent damage to the sympathetic pathway caused by the noise burst
Responses did not disappear; they were still above Group A's, so there is no evidence of damage.
Sensitization from the burst wearing off while habituation to the repeated tone continued
Correct: Sensitization is transient, and ongoing habituation to the benign tone drives the response back down.
Classical conditioning of the 70-dB tone to the noise burst, which strengthens the response
Conditioning would sustain or increase the response, not reduce it.
Extinction of the response to the 100-dB burst because it was no longer presented
Extinction applies to conditioned responses and the burst was never repeated or measured here.
qs.x: Sensitization is transient, and ongoing habituation to the benign tone drives the response back down. Trap: Treating a rebound as a permanent change instead of a transient state superimposed on ongoing habituation.

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean SCR to the 70-dB tone by block

passages.title: FL09 · Psych/Soc · Passage 5
text: Cognitive-developmental theories propose that children's understanding of gender develops in stages: gender labeling (correctly identifying oneself and others as boys or girls), gender stability (understanding that gender stays the same over time), and gender consistency (understanding that gender stays the same despite changes in clothing, hairstyle, or activities). In a cross-sectional study, 150 children in three age groups (n = 50 each) were interviewed with picture cards. To assess consistency, for example, a child viewed a photo of a boy wearing a dress and was asked whether he was a boy or a girl. A child received credit for a stage only if he or she also passed all earlier stages. Table 1 gives the percentage of each age group passing each stage, and Figure 1 plots the same data. Separately, the time children spent playing with toys stereotyped for their own gender was recorded; it was similar across children at all stages (p > .05).

qs.q: How many of the 5- to 6-year-old children passed gender stability but did not pass gender consistency?
o: 22 children, the number who passed gender consistency
22 is the number who passed consistency (44% of 50), not those who failed it.
40 children, the number who passed labeling but not consistency in the 3-4 group
The 3-4 group is a different age group, and the figure is not the one asked for.
41 children, the number who passed gender stability
41 children passed stability, but 22 of them also passed consistency and must be excluded.
19 children, the 38% of the group who passed stability only
Correct: Because credit was cumulative, 82% passed stability and 44% of these also passed consistency; (82 - 44)% of 50 = 38% x 50 = 19.
qs.x: Because credit was cumulative, 82% passed stability and 44% of these also passed consistency; (82 - 44)% of 50 = 38% x 50 = 19. Trap: Reporting the number who passed stability without subtracting those who also passed consistency.

qs.q: Within a cognitive-developmental framework, gender consistency emerges last because it:
o: Depends on the child having been rewarded for gender-typed behavior many times
Reinforcement is the mechanism emphasized by social learning theory, not cognitive-developmental theory.
Requires understanding that an attribute persists despite superficial changes, reasoning akin to conservation in the concrete operational stage
Correct: Recognizing that gender is constant despite changes in appearance parallels conservation, which develops around ages 6-8.
Requires the hormonal changes of puberty to define one's gender and sexual identity in later childhood
Most 7- to 8-year-olds passed consistency, years before puberty.
Demands abstract hypothetical reasoning that appears only in the formal operational stage
Abstract hypothetical reasoning arises in adolescence, but 90% of 7- to 8-year-olds passed.
qs.x: Recognizing that gender is constant despite changes in appearance parallels conservation, which develops around ages 6-8. Trap: Attributing a stage that emerges by about age 7 to puberty or formal operational thought.

qs.q: A limitation of studying three different age groups at one point in time is that:
o: The same children are retested, so practice with the picture cards inflates scores in the older groups
Each child was interviewed once, so there is no retesting or practice effect.
Differences among the age groups may reflect cohort differences rather than development within individual children
Correct: A cross-sectional design cannot follow individuals, so age effects are confounded with cohort and background differences.
Children who drop out between sessions can bias the sample toward more advanced understanding
Attrition between sessions is a feature of longitudinal, not cross-sectional, designs.
Observers may record play behavior differently as they learn which children are in which group
Nothing in the design suggests changing observer coding standards across groups.
qs.x: A cross-sectional design cannot follow individuals, so age effects are confounded with cohort and background differences. Trap: Attributing longitudinal problems (practice, attrition) to a cross-sectional design.

qs.q: The finding that own-gender toy play was similar across children at all stages is more consistent with:
o: Cognitive-developmental theory, which predicts that gender-typed play appears only after gender consistency
Cognitive-developmental theory predicts that stage understanding precedes gender-typed behavior.
Psychoanalytic theory, in which gender-typed play arises only after resolving conflicts with the same-sex parent
The data do not address identification with a parent, and the theory's timeline would not fit toddlers' play.
Social learning theory, in which gender-typed behavior arises from reinforcement and modeling before full understanding of gender
Correct: Gender-typed play was present before children understood gender stability or consistency, which a cognitive-developmental sequence does not predict but social learning permits.
Biological theory, which predicts that play preferences are fixed at birth and cannot be changed by the environment or reinforcement
Similar play across ages does not show immutability; no environmental manipulation occurred.
qs.x: Gender-typed play was present before children understood gender stability or consistency, which a cognitive-developmental sequence does not predict but social learning permits. Trap: Assuming any early-appearing behavior must be purely biological.

qs.q: A 6-year-old girl states firmly that she is a girl but prefers trucks and refuses dresses. Her statements and behavior illustrate:
o: Gender dysphoria, since gender-atypical play indicates that identity differs from assigned sex
Gender-atypical play alone does not indicate that identity differs from assigned sex.
A stable gender identity that is distinct from her gender role preferences
Correct: Gender identity is the internal sense of being male, female, or another gender, while gender role and expression concern behaviors and preferences.
A lack of gender constancy, since she plays with toys associated with boys
Constancy concerns understanding that gender persists over change, which her statement demonstrates.
A sexual orientation, since toy preference predicts later attraction to partners
Toy preference does not determine sexual orientation.
qs.x: Gender identity is the internal sense of being male, female, or another gender, while gender role and expression concern behaviors and preferences. Trap: Equating gender-atypical behavior with a different gender identity or with orientation.

graph.title: Figure 1. Percentage passing each stage by age group

passages.title: FL09 · Psych/Soc · Passage 6
text: The stereotype content model proposes that groups are stereotyped along two dimensions, warmth (friendly, well-intentioned) and competence (capable, skilled), and that each combination elicits a characteristic emotion. In a survey, 120 adults rated four social groups on both dimensions using 7-point scales (1 = not at all, 7 = extremely). To reduce social-desirability pressure, participants were asked how they believe most people in society view each group, rather than how they personally view it. Participants also chose the emotion they thought society most often directs toward each group. Mean ratings and the most frequently chosen emotion are shown in Table 1, and Figure 1 plots warmth against competence for each group. Respondents were recruited online and were balanced by gender and age. Each rating was averaged across respondents, and the standard error of every mean was below 0.15. Groups were presented in random order to prevent order effects, and responses from participants who failed an attention check were excluded.

qs.q: According to Table 1 and the model, which group is perceived as high in competence but low in warmth, and which emotion does this combination elicit?
o: Wealthy professionals; envy
Correct: Wealthy professionals have competence 6.1 and warmth 3.0, the high-competence, low-warmth pattern that elicits envy.
Older adults; pity
Older adults are high in warmth (5.6) and low in competence (3.2).
Middle-class workers; pride
Middle-class workers are high on both dimensions.
People experiencing homelessness; disgust
People experiencing homelessness are low on both dimensions.
qs.x: Wealthy professionals have competence 6.1 and warmth 3.0, the high-competence, low-warmth pattern that elicits envy. Trap: Reversing the two axes and assigning pity to the group that is competent but cold.

qs.q: The pity that participants believed society directs toward older adults is best classified as which component of intergroup bias?
o: Stereotype, because it is a belief about the traits of group members
A stereotype is the cognitive component, such as the belief that older adults are warm but incompetent.
Discrimination, because it is differential treatment of group members
Discrimination is a behavior, and no behavior was measured.
Ethnocentrism, because it is a belief that one's own group is superior to all others
Ethnocentrism refers to judging other groups by one's own group's standards; pity toward older adults does not show that.
Prejudice, because it is an affective response toward members of a group
Correct: Prejudice is the affective (feeling) component; pity is an emotion.
qs.x: Prejudice is the affective (feeling) component; pity is an emotion. Trap: Confusing emotions toward a group (prejudice) with beliefs about it (stereotypes).

qs.q: Which group shows the largest absolute difference between its competence rating and its warmth rating, and what is that difference?
o: Wealthy professionals, 3.1 points
Correct: Gaps: older adults 2.4, wealthy professionals 3.1, middle-class workers 0.1, homeless 0.2; the largest is 3.1.
Older adults, 2.4 points
2.4 is the gap for older adults, which is smaller than 3.1.
People experiencing homelessness, 0.2 points
0.2 is the smallest nonzero gap but not the largest.
Middle-class workers, 0.1 points
0.1 is the gap for the middle-class group and is the smallest of the four.
qs.x: Gaps: older adults 2.4, wealthy professionals 3.1, middle-class workers 0.1, homeless 0.2; the largest is 3.1. Trap: Ignoring the sign of the difference or stopping after the first group computed.

qs.q: Because participants rated how most people in society view each group, the results most directly reflect:
o: Culturally shared stereotypes that participants know, not necessarily their own prejudices
Correct: Asking about societal views measures awareness of cultural stereotype content, which may differ from personal endorsement.
Participants' own implicit attitudes toward each group, measured without social pressure
Implicit attitudes require indirect measures such as the IAT, and these ratings were explicit.
The actual warmth and competence of the members of each group
Ratings reflect perceptions, not objective traits of the groups.
Participants' behavior toward members of each group in real interactions
The survey did not measure behavior.
qs.x: Asking about societal views measures awareness of cultural stereotype content, which may differ from personal endorsement. Trap: Reading perceived societal views as the respondents' personal beliefs.

graph.title: Figure 1. Perceived warmth and competence of four groups

passages.title: FL09 · Psych/Soc · Passage 7
text: Realistic conflict theory predicts that competition for scarce resources breeds intergroup hostility. In a summer program, 60 adolescents who did not know each other were divided into two teams of 30 and housed separately. During days 1-4, the teams competed in tournaments for prizes. Teams were then randomly split, within each team, into three conditions of 20 (10 from each team): (1) contact, in which members of both teams ate meals and watched films together; (2) superordinate goal, in which members of both teams jointly repaired the camp's failed water supply, a task neither team could complete alone; and (3) control, in which team members stayed separated. Outgroup bias was measured on a 7-point scale (higher = more negative toward the other team) at baseline, after the competition, and after a 3-day intervention. Table 1 and Figure 1 show the mean scores. Bias scores were analyzed with a mixed-design ANOVA (condition x phase), and the interaction was significant (p < .001); post hoc tests showed that only the superordinate goal group differed from the control group.

qs.q: In the superordinate goal condition, the reduction in bias from the post-competition level to the post-intervention level was closest to what percentage of the post-competition level?
o: 19%, the change in points multiplied by 10
Multiplying the 1.9-point change by ten is not a percentage of any base.
55%, the post-intervention level as a share of the post-competition level
2.3/4.2 = 55% is the remaining bias, not the reduction.
83%, the change divided by the post-intervention level
Dividing by the final value (2.3) gives 83%, but a percent reduction uses the starting value.
qs.x: (4.2 - 2.3)/4.2 = 1.9/4.2 = 0.45. Trap: Using the wrong denominator or reporting the remaining level instead of the reduction.

qs.q: The contact condition produced little reduction in bias, most likely because:
o: Contact between competing groups always increases hostility regardless of the setting
Contact did not increase bias here (4.1 to 3.9), and contact is not always harmful.
The participants in the contact condition were more biased at baseline than the other participants
Baseline scores were similar (2.0 vs 2.1 and 2.0).
Shared meals and films did not require the groups to cooperate toward a goal that depended on both
Correct: Contact reduces prejudice when it involves cooperative interdependence; passive, parallel contact did not.
Superordinate goals reduce bias only for groups that have never competed
These groups had competed, and the superordinate goal still worked.
qs.x: Contact reduces prejudice when it involves cooperative interdependence; passive, parallel contact did not. Trap: Assuming that any contact, regardless of its structure, should reduce prejudice.

qs.q: The control condition was included mainly to determine whether:
o: The two teams differed in their initial skill at the tournaments
Team skill is not tested by a control group that stays separated.
Participants responded to the questionnaire consistently with their true attitudes
Questionnaire honesty requires other safeguards, not a control group.
Adolescents are more susceptible to bias than adults
No adult group was included, so age comparisons cannot be made.
Bias would have declined on its own as time passed after the competition ended
Correct: A no-intervention group shows the natural course of bias, so changes in other groups can be attributed to the interventions.
qs.x: A no-intervention group shows the natural course of bias, so changes in other groups can be attributed to the interventions. Trap: Reading a control group as a check on measurement or on sample characteristics instead of on natural change.

qs.q: Which of the following is the closest real-world application of the strategy that worked best in this study?
o: Two rival hospital departments are jointly assigned to cut infection rates, a target neither department can reach alone
Correct: A superordinate goal requires cooperation between groups to achieve an outcome that neither can accomplish alone.
Two rival departments hold a quarterly social mixer where staff from both are encouraged to chat and share a meal
A mixer is passive contact, like the contact condition, and was not very effective.
Two rival departments are ranked, with rewards for the better-performing department
Ranking and rewards create competition, which promotes hostility.
Two rival departments are merged and the budget of the smaller one is eliminated
Cutting the smaller department's budget creates a resource conflict, not a shared goal.
qs.x: A superordinate goal requires cooperation between groups to achieve an outcome that neither can accomplish alone. Trap: Treating friendly contact or merging as equivalent to genuine cooperative interdependence.

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean outgroup bias by phase
graph.x_label: Phase (0 = baseline, 1 = after competition, 2 = after intervention)

passages.title: FL09 · Psych/Soc · Passage 8
text: Max Weber described bureaucracy as the most rationalized form of organization, marked by hierarchy, a division of labor, written rules, and impersonal application of procedures. A researcher studied 30 municipal permit offices that varied in how strongly they had standardized their procedures (checklists, written decision rules, and fixed approval chains) and grouped them into three levels of standardization, with 10 offices per level. Processing times and error rates came from public records. Applicants (n = 900) rated the fairness of their treatment (1 = very unfair, 5 = very fair), and employees (n = 300) rated job satisfaction (1-5).
