Offices were not randomly assigned to levels; the most standardized offices tended to be larger and to serve bigger populations. Table 1 lists the mean values at each level. Differences across levels were tested with one-way ANOVAs and were significant (p < .05), although the researchers noted the small number of offices. No statistical adjustment for office size was made.

qs.q: Which finding in Table 1 best fits Weber's concern that rationalization can be dehumanizing for the people within organizations?
o: Processing time decreased as standardization increased
Faster processing reflects efficiency, one of the benefits of rationalization.
Error rate decreased as standardization increased
Fewer errors reflect predictability and calculability, also benefits.
Applicant fairness ratings increased as standardization increased
Higher perceived fairness reflects impersonal treatment, again a benefit.
Employee satisfaction decreased as standardization increased
Correct: Weber's 'iron cage' idea is that rigid rules and routines can constrain workers; falling employee satisfaction is the cost pattern.
qs.x: Weber's 'iron cage' idea is that rigid rules and routines can constrain workers; falling employee satisfaction is the cost pattern. Trap: Picking an efficiency benefit when the question asks for a human cost.

qs.q: From low to high standardization, the error rate fell by approximately what percentage of the low-standardization error rate?
o: 8%, the absolute difference in percentage points
8 is the absolute change in percentage points, not a relative reduction.
33%, the high-standardization error rate as a share of the low rate
4/12 = 33% is the remaining error rate, not the reduction.
50%, the point midway between the two rates
The midpoint of the rates is 8%, which has no relation to a percent reduction.
qs.x: (12 - 4)/12 = 8/12 = 0.67. Trap: Reporting remaining share or percentage points as a relative reduction.

qs.q: Which characteristic of bureaucracy most directly explains the higher fairness ratings at the highly standardized offices?
o: A rigid hierarchy, so that each employee answers to a single supervisor
Hierarchy clarifies authority but does not itself ensure equal treatment of applicants.
A division of labor, so that each employee performs a narrow specialized task very efficiently and repeatedly
Specialization raises efficiency, not necessarily perceived fairness.
Reliance on tradition, so that decisions follow the customs of long-serving staff
Bureaucracy replaces traditional authority with rational-legal authority.
Impersonal application of written rules, so that applicants are treated the same regardless of who they are
Correct: Impersonal, uniform rules reduce favoritism, which applicants perceive as fair.
qs.x: Impersonal, uniform rules reduce favoritism, which applicants perceive as fair. Trap: Choosing a defining feature of bureaucracy that is not the one linked to equal treatment.

qs.q: Which statement is the most important caution about concluding from Table 1 that standardization causes lower error rates?
o: Error rates are measured in percentages, which cannot be compared across offices
Percentages can be compared across groups.
Office size may be a confounding variable, because the most standardized offices were also larger
Correct: When offices were not randomly assigned and standardization co-varies with size, size could explain differences in errors.
Public records are inherently unreliable sources of data about processing times
Nothing in the description questions the reliability of the records.
The sample of 30 offices is too small to calculate a mean for each level
Ten offices per level is small but sufficient for means; the main issue is confounding, not computability.
qs.x: When offices were not randomly assigned and standardization co-varies with size, size could explain differences in errors. Trap: Attributing an observational association to causation without considering confounders.

passages.title: FL09 · Psych/Soc · Passage 9
text: The natural sex ratio at birth (SRB) is about 105 boys per 100 girls. In "Country X," where cultural preference for sons was strong, the government in 2012 banned prenatal sex determination and began cash payments to families with daughters. Researchers analyzed national birth-registry data, calculating SRB (boys per 100 girls) separately for first births and third births at ten-year intervals (Table 1; Figure 1). Third births are informative because couples who already have daughters may be more likely to use sex selection. Registry coverage exceeded 95% in each year. The researchers also noted that the cohort born in 2010 would reach typical marriage ages around 2035. Sex-selective abortion cannot be observed directly in registry data, so the researchers used excess male births as an indirect indicator. Because the registry records millions of births, even small differences in ratios are statistically significant, so the researchers focused on the size of the differences.

qs.q: Which pattern in the data is the strongest evidence that sex selection, rather than biology, raised the sex ratio in the 2000s?
o: Both ratios were above the natural ratio of 105 boys per 100 girls in every year of the study, from 1990 to 2020
Both being slightly above 105 does not distinguish selection; first-birth values were close to the norm.
Third-birth ratios rose far above the biological norm while first-birth ratios remained near it
Correct: A birth-order-specific excess, concentrated where couples already have daughters, is the signature of sex-selective practices.
The third-birth ratio in 2020 was lower than in 2010
A decline in 2020 suggests the ban had an effect but is not evidence about the cause of the earlier increase.
First-birth ratios rose by 2 points between 1990 and 2000
A 2-point rise in first births is small and within normal variation.
qs.x: A birth-order-specific excess, concentrated where couples already have daughters, is the signature of sex-selective practices. Trap: Taking any value above 105 as proof of selection rather than a birth-order-specific pattern.

qs.q: What percentage of third-birth babies were boys in 2010?
o: Correct: 132 boys per 100 girls means 132 boys out of 232 births = 0.569, or about 57%.
32%, the number of boys above 100 per 100 girls
132 - 100 = 32 is a count per 100 girls, not a percentage of births.
51%, the share of boys at the natural ratio
The natural ratio of 105 gives about 51%, and 2010 values are far higher.
66%, the ratio of boys to girls expressed as 132/200
Dividing by 200 assumes 200 total babies; the total is 232.
qs.x: 132 boys per 100 girls means 132 boys out of 232 births = 0.569, or about 57%. Trap: Treating a ratio (boys per 100 girls) as a percentage of all births.

qs.q: The researchers' note about the 2010 birth cohort anticipates which long-term demographic consequence?
o: A rise in the dependency ratio because of a surplus of children relative to working-age adults
The sex-ratio imbalance does not itself create a surplus of children relative to workers.
A shortage of women relative to men at marriage ages, known as a marriage squeeze
Correct: A male-skewed cohort will face fewer potential female partners when it reaches marriage age.
A decline in life expectancy at birth because of excess male mortality in infancy
Life expectancy is not determined by the birth sex ratio; excess male infant mortality is not described.
A rise in international migration of women from poorer regions to Country X
Migration responses are possible but are speculation, not the direct consequence signaled by the cohort note.
qs.x: A male-skewed cohort will face fewer potential female partners when it reaches marriage age. Trap: Choosing a general demographic effect instead of the one tied to cohort sex imbalance.

qs.q: Which feature most limits the conclusion that the 2012 policy caused the decline in third-birth SRB by 2020?
o: The use of national registry data instead of a survey of individual couples
High-coverage registry data are a strength, not a limitation.
The calculation of ratios separately by birth order instead of overall
Separating by birth order is informative and strengthens the inference.
The use of ten-year intervals, which cannot show the exact timing of changes relative to the 2012 policy
Multiple time points are better than one for showing a trend.
No comparison country without the policy, so simultaneous changes such as rising female education cannot be ruled out
Correct: With no comparison group, other concurrent trends can account for the change.
qs.x: With no comparison group, other concurrent trends can account for the change. Trap: Interpreting a before-and-after change as caused by the policy without a comparison group.

graph.title: Figure 1. Sex ratio at birth by birth order

passages.title: FL09 · Psych/Soc · Passage 10
text: Bourdieu proposed that cultural capital, familiarity with the dominant culture's tastes, language, and norms, is transmitted through families and can be converted into educational advantage. Researchers surveyed 480 first-year students at a large public university (240 with at least one parent holding a college degree and 240 without). Students completed a 10-point cultural capital index based on childhood museum visits, reading, and comfort interacting with faculty. The researchers recorded whether each student had been placed in the advanced academic track and collected faculty ratings of how well each student fit the academic environment (1-5). In a regression predicting advanced-track placement that controlled for standardized test scores, cultural capital remained a significant predictor (standardized beta = .24, p < .001), as did parental education (beta = .12, p = .03). Table 1 gives group means, and Figure 1 shows placement by cultural capital quartile. Differences between the two groups on each measure were significant (p < .001). Faculty raters did not know the students' parental education.

qs.q: What percentage of all 480 students were placed in the advanced track?
o: 90%, the sum of the two groups' placement percentages (62 + 28)
Adding two percentages that describe different halves of the sample double counts; the combined rate is their average when group sizes are equal.
62%, the placement rate among students with a college-educated parent
62% applies only to the subgroup of 240 students with a college-educated parent.
Correct: Advanced-track students: 0.62 x 240 = 149 plus 0.28 x 240 = 67, totaling 216 of 480 = 45%.
28%, the placement rate among students whose parents have no college degree
28% applies only to the subgroup of 240 students without a college-educated parent.
qs.x: Advanced-track students: 0.62 x 240 = 149 plus 0.28 x 240 = 67, totaling 216 of 480 = 45%. Trap: Rounding or selecting a single group's rate instead of weighting both groups.

qs.q: The persistence of cultural capital as a predictor after controlling for test scores most strongly suggests that:
o: Standardized test scores had no relationship with track placement
Controlling for scores does not show that scores are unrelated to placement.
Cultural capital is a more valid measure of intelligence than test scores
The data say nothing about cultural capital measuring intelligence.
Track placement depends partly on factors other than measured achievement
Correct: A significant coefficient with achievement held constant implies that placement reflects something beyond tested achievement.
Parental education has no influence on placement once cultural capital is known
Parental education remained significant (beta = .12, p = .03).
qs.x: A significant coefficient with achievement held constant implies that placement reflects something beyond tested achievement. Trap: Reading statistical control as proof that the control variable is irrelevant.

qs.q: According to Figure 1, between which two consecutive quartiles was the increase in placement percentage greatest?
o: Quartile 3 to quartile 4, an increase of 24 percentage points
Correct: Consecutive increases are 16 (1 to 2), 18 (2 to 3), and 24 (3 to 4).
Quartile 1 to quartile 2, an increase of 16 percentage points
The quartile 1 to 2 increase is 16, the smallest.
Quartile 2 to quartile 3, an increase of 22 percentage points
The quartile 2 to 3 increase is 18, not 22, and is smaller than 24.
Quartile 1 to quartile 4, an increase of 58 percentage points
Quartile 1 to 4 is not a consecutive pair.
qs.x: Consecutive increases are 16 (1 to 2), 18 (2 to 3), and 24 (3 to 4). Trap: Reading the endpoints instead of consecutive differences.

qs.q: Which perspective would most likely interpret the track-placement results as schools helping to reproduce class advantage?
o: Functionalism, because schools sort students by ability to fill social roles efficiently
Functionalism would interpret tracking as meritocratic sorting, which the results call into question.
Symbolic interactionism, because individual students construct meaning from daily classroom interactions
Interactionism could describe the fit rating but not the reproduction of class advantage.
Conflict theory, because schools reward the cultural resources of already advantaged families
Correct: Conflict theory stresses how institutions perpetuate inequality, and cultural capital is the mechanism proposed by Bourdieu.
Rational choice theory, because each family weighs costs and benefits of education
Rational choice theory focuses on individual cost-benefit calculations, not structural reproduction.
qs.x: Conflict theory stresses how institutions perpetuate inequality, and cultural capital is the mechanism proposed by Bourdieu. Trap: Choosing functionalism because tracking sounds like sorting by ability.

qs.q: Which of the following is the best example of cultural capital as Bourdieu used the term?
o: A student whose family can pay for private tutoring and test preparation courses
Money for tutoring is economic capital.
A student whose uncle is friends with the dean and can arrange an introduction
Useful connections are social capital.
A student who earned a high score on a standardized mathematics exam
A test score is a measure of achievement, not an inherited cultural resource.
A student who learned at home how to discuss literature and address professors in ways that teachers reward
Correct: Cultural capital is knowledge, tastes, and styles transmitted by families and valued by institutions.
qs.x: Cultural capital is knowledge, tastes, and styles transmitted by families and valued by institutions. Trap: Treating any family advantage as cultural capital.

graph.title: Figure 1. Advanced-track placement by cultural capital quartile

passages.title: FL10 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 1
text: Collagen is a triple helix of three polypeptide chains rich in the repeat Gly-X-Y, where X and Y are often proline or 4-hydroxyproline. Proline hydroxylation occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum after translation and is catalyzed by prolyl 4-hydroxylase, an Fe2+-containing enzyme that also requires alpha-ketoglutarate, O2, and ascorbate (vitamin C). A researcher cultured human dermal fibroblasts for 72 hours under the conditions in Table 1. One culture was derived from a patient with a heterozygous Gly-to-Ser substitution at a single Gly-X-Y triplet of the alpha-1(I) chain (mutant line); the others were normal fibroblasts. 2,2'-Dipyridyl is a membrane-permeant chelator of Fe2+. Secreted collagen was purified from the medium, its hydroxyproline content was measured by amino acid analysis, and its thermal denaturation midpoint (Tm) was determined by circular dichroism. Secretion was expressed relative to normal cells grown with 50 uM ascorbate. Body temperature is 37 degrees C. Under-hydroxylated procollagen that cannot fold into a stable helix is retained in the endoplasmic reticulum and degraded.

qs.q: Which statement best describes the role of ascorbate in the reaction catalyzed by prolyl 4-hydroxylase?
o: It keeps the enzyme's iron in the Fe2+ state so that the enzyme remains catalytically active
Correct: Ascorbate is a reducing agent that regenerates Fe2+ when the iron is oxidized during catalysis; without it the enzyme stalls (the biochemical basis of scurvy).
It binds the Gly-X-Y repeat and holds proline in the conformation needed for hydroxylation
Ascorbate does not bind the substrate; it acts on the enzyme's metal center.
It is decarboxylated alongside oxygen activation, which generates succinate as a byproduct
alpha-Ketoglutarate, not ascorbate, is the co-substrate decarboxylated to succinate.
It supplies the oxygen atom that is added to the proline ring during hydroxylation reactions
O2 is the oxygen source, not ascorbate.
qs.x: Ascorbate is a reducing agent that regenerates Fe2+ when the iron is oxidized during catalysis; without it the enzyme stalls (the biochemical basis of scurvy). Trap: Confusing ascorbate with alpha-ketoglutarate, the co-substrate that is actually consumed, instead of recognizing it as the iron-reducing cofactor.

qs.q: Which conclusion about normal fibroblasts grown without ascorbate is best supported by the data in Table 1?
o: Their collagen is not stably folded at 37 C, so little of it is secreted
Correct: Tm is 31 C, below 37 C, so triple helices would unfold at body temperature and are retained and degraded, matching secretion of only 0.3.
Their collagen is secreted at a normal rate but is rapidly digested once it reaches the medium
Secretion is reduced to 0.3, so the collagen is not secreted normally.
Their collagen gene is transcribed less efficiently, which accounts for the lower hydroxyproline value
Nothing in the table measures transcription; hydroxylation is post-translational.
Their collagen has extra cross-links that raise its Tm above body temperature but prevent export
The Tm is lower, not higher, and cross-linking is not what the table measures.
qs.x: Tm is 31 C, below 37 C, so triple helices would unfold at body temperature and are retained and degraded, matching secretion of only 0.3. Trap: Reading hydroxyproline loss as a transcription defect, when Tm and secretion data point to a post-translational folding problem.

qs.q: The mutant line has nearly normal hydroxyproline content but a Tm of 33 C and low secretion. Which explanation is most consistent with these results?
o: Only glycine fits at the helix center, so serine disrupts packing

Correct: Every third residue must be glycine because it lacks a side chain and sits in the crowded interior of the helix; a bulkier serine distorts the helix even though hydroxylation is normal (94 residues per 1000).
The mutant fibroblasts cannot import ascorbate, so hydroxylation is incomplete in the mutant line
Hydroxyproline content shows ascorbate was used normally.
Serine forms disulfide bonds between chains that lock the helix in a distorted conformation
Serine has a hydroxyl group, not a thiol, and cannot form disulfides.
Serine occupies the proline site and prevents prolyl 4-hydroxylase from modifying neighboring residues
Hydroxyproline is 94 per 1000, so hydroxylation was not blocked.
qs.x: Every third residue must be glycine because it lacks a side chain and sits in the crowded interior of the helix; a bulkier serine distorts the helix even though hydroxylation is normal (94 residues per 1000). Trap: Assuming any collagen defect must reflect a hydroxylation problem, even though this line's hydroxyproline content is normal.

qs.q: Compared with normal cells grown at 50 uM ascorbate, the hydroxyproline content of normal cells grown with no ascorbate is approximately
o: 2.3% lower
96 / 42 is 2.3-fold, which is a ratio rather than a percentage decrease.
44% lower
42 / 96 is 44%, which is the fraction remaining, not the fraction lost.
54% lower
54 is the absolute difference in residues per 1000, not a percentage of the reference value.
56% lower
Correct: (96 - 42) / 96 = 0.56, so the no-ascorbate collagen has about 56% less hydroxyproline.
qs.x: (96 - 42) / 96 = 0.56, so the no-ascorbate collagen has about 56% less hydroxyproline. Trap: Dividing by the wrong base or reporting the remaining fraction (44%) rather than the decrease.

qs.q: A researcher proposes that dipyridyl lowers hydroxyproline by chelating Fe2+ in prolyl 4-hydroxylase rather than by some other toxic effect. Which experiment would best test this hypothesis?
o: Raising the ascorbate concentration to 500 uM in the presence of dipyridyl and measuring cell number
Cell number does not report hydroxylase activity.
Adding excess Fe2+ together with dipyridyl and determining whether hydroxyproline content returns toward 96 residues per 1000
Correct: If dipyridyl acts by sequestering iron, supplying iron in excess should compete for the chelator and rescue hydroxylation; non-rescue would suggest another mechanism.
Growing mutant fibroblasts with dipyridyl and measuring whether their Tm falls below 33 C
This tests the mutant phenotype and does not test the iron-dependence of the chelator.
Measuring the Tm of collagen heated in the medium that contained dipyridyl for 72 hours
Heating collagen in medium tests thermal stability, not the mechanism of dipyridyl.
qs.x: If dipyridyl acts by sequestering iron, supplying iron in excess should compete for the chelator and rescue hydroxylation; non-rescue would suggest another mechanism. Trap: Choosing an experiment that reports a downstream phenotype instead of one that reverses the proposed mechanism.

passages.title: FL10 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 2
text: Nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) is a surveillance pathway that degrades mRNAs containing premature termination codons (PTCs). During splicing, an exon junction complex (EJC) is deposited about 20 to 24 nucleotides upstream of each exon-exon junction. Ribosomes in the first round of translation remove EJCs as they advance. If a ribosome terminates at a stop codon located more than about 50 nucleotides upstream of the final exon-exon junction, a remaining EJC recruits the helicase UPF1, which triggers mRNA decay. A researcher transfected HeLa cells with a three-exon beta-globin minigene. Constructs carried either no mutation (WT), a nonsense mutation at codon 39 in exon 1, or a nonsense mutation at codon 140 in exon 3 (the final exon). Cells received a control siRNA or an siRNA against UPF1, or were treated for 4 hours with cycloheximide, an inhibitor of translation elongation. mRNA was quantified by RT-qPCR and normalized to an unrelated reporter transcript; values are relative to WT with control siRNA.

qs.q: Why is the mRNA carrying the codon 140 nonsense mutation largely spared from NMD?
o: Exon 3 contains an enhancer sequence that blocks deadenylation of the transcript after splicing
No enhancer or deadenylation block is described; the exon-junction rule explains the data.
Nonsense codons in the final exon are read through by suppressor tRNAs that restore full-length protein, so no truncated product is made
Read-through by suppressor tRNAs is not a general mechanism and is not implied by the data.
No exon-exon junction lies downstream of the stop codon, so no EJC remains to signal that the termination is premature
Correct: EJCs are placed only at exon-exon junctions; a stop codon in the last exon has no downstream junction, so the ribosome removes all EJCs before terminating and UPF1 is not recruited.
The stop codon is too close to the 5' cap for UPF1 to be recruited to the terminating ribosome
The codon 140 PTC lies near the 3' end, not near the cap.
qs.x: EJCs are placed only at exon-exon junctions; a stop codon in the last exon has no downstream junction, so the ribosome removes all EJCs before terminating and UPF1 is not recruited. Trap: Thinking NMD depends only on whether a PTC exists, without applying the position rule relative to the last exon-exon junction.

qs.q: The cycloheximide result for the codon 39 construct is best explained by which conclusion?
o: Cycloheximide inhibits UPF1 helicase activity directly, preventing it from unwinding the mRNA
No data show direct inhibition of UPF1; cycloheximide acts on the ribosome.
Cycloheximide increases splicing efficiency, so more minigene mRNA is made from the transgene
Higher splicing would not selectively rescue only the PTC mRNA.
NMD occurs in the nucleus before export, so translation inhibitors change mRNA stability only indirectly
NMD is coupled to translation, which occurs in the cytoplasm.
NMD requires an actively translating ribosome to reach the PTC and displace or read the EJC signal
Correct: Blocking translation raised the PTC mRNA from 0.12 to 0.81, showing decay depends on translation of the message.
qs.x: Blocking translation raised the PTC mRNA from 0.12 to 0.81, showing decay depends on translation of the message. Trap: Attributing a drug's effect to its best-known target in an unrelated pathway instead of inferring from the logic of the experiment that translation is required.

qs.q: By what factor did UPF1 knockdown increase the abundance of the codon 39 PTC mRNA?
o: About 6.5-fold
About 0.15-fold
0.15 is the inverse ratio (0.12 / 0.78).
About 0.66-fold
0.66 is the absolute difference (0.78 - 0.12), not a ratio.
About 8.3-fold
8.3 is 1 / 0.12, which compares WT to the PTC mRNA rather than knockdown to control.
qs.x: 0.78 / 0.12 = 6.5. Trap: Subtracting the two values or inverting the ratio instead of dividing the knockdown value by the control value.

qs.q: Heterozygous carriers of a beta-globin PTC in exon 1 are usually clinically silent, whereas some carriers with PTCs in the final exon have a severe dominant phenotype. Which explanation is most consistent with the data?
o: Final-exon PTCs trigger more efficient NMD, which removes the normal mRNA from the same cell along with the mutant
Final-exon PTCs escape NMD rather than triggering it more efficiently.
Exon 1 mutations are corrected by splicing, whereas final-exon mutations are not removed from the transcript
Splicing does not remove nonsense mutations from exons.
Exon 1 PTC mRNA is stabilized, which dilutes the abnormal protein with extra normal globin from the second allele
The exon 1 PTC mRNA is degraded, not stabilized.
NMD degrades exon 1 PTC mRNA, whereas final-exon PTC mRNA escapes and yields truncated protein

Correct: NMD acts as a safeguard: it degrades exon 1 PTC transcripts (0.12) so truncated protein is rare, whereas final-exon PTC transcripts escape (0.93) and produce a truncated protein that can precipitate and harm the cell.
qs.x: NMD acts as a safeguard: it degrades exon 1 PTC transcripts (0.12) so truncated protein is rare, whereas final-exon PTC transcripts escape (0.93) and produce a truncated protein that can precipitate and harm the cell. Trap: Assuming that a more severe phenotype must come from more efficient decay, when escape from NMD is what allows truncated protein to accumulate.

passages.title: FL10 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 3
text: A genetics clinic evaluates a woman who has had three first-trimester miscarriages and one child with Down syndrome. G-banded karyotyping of her blood lymphocytes shows 45 chromosomes with a single large chromosome that appears to be a fusion of chromosomes 14 and 21, written 45,XX,der(14;21)(q10;q10). This is a Robertsonian translocation: the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes fuse at the centromere, and the tiny short arms, which carry mostly redundant ribosomal RNA genes, are lost. The carrier has two normal copies of the genes on the long arms and is phenotypically normal. At meiosis I the three chromosomes involved (14, 21, and the derivative) can segregate in six ways. Table 1 lists the six possible egg types and the zygote that results when each is fertilized by a normal sperm carrying one chromosome 14 and one chromosome 21. A counselor wants to estimate theoretical risks, assuming the six egg types are formed with equal frequency and that zygotes with monosomy or with trisomy 14 do not survive to birth.

qs.q: Why is the carrier woman phenotypically normal even though her karyotype shows only 45 chromosomes?
o: Robertsonian translocations delete the centromere, which removes the cell's dependence on genes from both chromosomes
The centromeres are fused, not deleted; a derivative chromosome retains one functional centromere.
The derivative chromosome silences one copy of each fused chromosome through X-inactivation-like mechanisms
No X-inactivation-like silencing of autosomes occurs here.
Nearly all genes remain in two copies, and the lost short arms carry redundant sequences

Correct: A Robertsonian translocation is a balanced rearrangement: nearly all euchromatic genes are retained in normal dosage, and loss of the acrocentric short arms is tolerated because rRNA genes are present in many copies on several chromosomes.
The missing chromosome is replaced by a duplicated chromosome 22 that supplies the lost gene products
Chromosome 22 does not compensate for lost genes of other chromosomes.
qs.x: A Robertsonian translocation is a balanced rearrangement: nearly all euchromatic genes are retained in normal dosage, and loss of the acrocentric short arms is tolerated because rRNA genes are present in many copies on several chromosomes. Trap: Equating a lower chromosome number with lost genetic information instead of recognizing a balanced fusion of two chromosomes.

qs.q: Based on the assumptions in the passage, what is the probability that a live-born child of the carrier woman and a normal man has Down syndrome?
o: 2/3 is the fraction of live-born children who are not Down syndrome.
1/2 would result if only types 1 and 3 were viable.
Correct: Only egg types 1, 2, and 3 give viable zygotes; they are equally likely, and only type 3 (one in three) produces Down syndrome among live births.
1/6 is the fraction of all zygotes with Down syndrome, which includes the three nonviable outcomes in the denominator.
qs.x: Only egg types 1, 2, and 3 give viable zygotes; they are equally likely, and only type 3 (one in three) produces Down syndrome among live births. Trap: Using all six egg types as the denominator instead of conditioning on live birth.

qs.q: A different parent carries a Robertsonian translocation that fuses the two copies of chromosome 21, written der(21;21). Assuming only zygotes with at least one copy of 21 genes survive and that the other parent is normal, what fraction of this parent's live-born children are expected to have Down syndrome?
o: One half of them
Half would apply only if a normal egg type also formed, but this carrier has no normal chromosome 21.
None of them
The derivative chromosome carries both copies of the long arm, so its gametes cannot be normal.
One third of them
One third applies to the 14;21 carrier, which also forms normal gametes.
All of them
Correct: Gametes carry either der(21;21) or no chromosome 21; with a normal gamete they give trisomy 21 or monosomy 21, and monosomy 21 is not viable, so every live birth has Down syndrome.
qs.x: Gametes carry either der(21;21) or no chromosome 21; with a normal gamete they give trisomy 21 or monosomy 21, and monosomy 21 is not viable, so every live birth has Down syndrome. Trap: Transferring the one-third risk from the 14;21 carrier to a 21;21 carrier, which cannot make a normal gamete.

qs.q: A child with Down syndrome has a karyotype of 46 chromosomes, including one derivative chromosome fusing a chromosome 14 and a chromosome 21. What does this finding imply for the parents?
o: The child inherited a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 14 that is responsible for Down syndrome
Down syndrome results from extra 21q material, not a deletion on 14.
One parent may carry a balanced translocation, so the recurrence risk exceeds that for a typical trisomy 21

Correct: A translocation Down syndrome karyotype (46 chromosomes) often reflects inheritance from a balanced carrier parent, and parental karyotyping is recommended because recurrence risk can be high.
Both parents must have had nondisjunction at meiosis II, so the recurrence risk is the same as the general population
Standard trisomy 21 from nondisjunction gives 47 chromosomes and a low recurrence risk.
The child's cells arose by mitotic nondisjunction after fertilization, so the parents' karyotypes will be normal
The chromosome count and derivative chromosome do not suggest mitotic nondisjunction.
qs.x: A translocation Down syndrome karyotype (46 chromosomes) often reflects inheritance from a balanced carrier parent, and parental karyotyping is recommended because recurrence risk can be high. Trap: Assuming all Down syndrome has the same recurrence risk without noticing that 46 chromosomes with a derivative points to a translocation.

h: Zygote after fertilization by a normal sperm

passages.title: FL10 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 4
text: The urea cycle converts toxic ammonia to urea in the liver. The first two steps, catalyzed by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) and ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC), occur in the mitochondrial matrix; citrulline is then exported to the cytosol, where argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS) condenses it with aspartate. Three newborns presented on day 3 of life with lethargy and vomiting after beginning protein feeds. Each had a defect in a different urea cycle enzyme (CPS I, OTC, or ASS). Table 1 lists plasma and urine measurements. When carbamoyl phosphate accumulates in the matrix, it can exit to the cytosol and enter pyrimidine synthesis, increasing orotic acid. Patient A was then given a standardized protein load, and plasma ammonia was followed for 6 hours (Figure 1) alongside a healthy infant. Patient A was treated with a protein-restricted diet, arginine, and sodium benzoate. Blood was sampled before feeding and at intervals afterward, and all assays were performed in a single reference laboratory to minimize variability between samples.

qs.q: Which defect most likely accounts for Patient A, based on Table 1?
o: OTC deficiency, because carbamoyl phosphate accumulates and spills into pyrimidine synthesis
Correct: Low citrulline with a 38-fold rise in orotic acid indicates that carbamoyl phosphate is made but not used by OTC, so it is diverted to orotic acid.
CPS I deficiency, because carbamoyl phosphate cannot be made and ammonia therefore builds up
lowers carbamoyl phosphate, so orotic acid is not raised.
ASS deficiency, because aspartate is not condensed with citrulline and orotic acid rises as a result
produces a large rise in citrulline, which Patient A does not show.
Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency, because fumarate cannot be released and citrulline is depleted
A lyase defect, downstream of ASS, would raise argininosuccinate and generally not lower citrulline.
qs.x: Low citrulline with a 38-fold rise in orotic acid indicates that carbamoyl phosphate is made but not used by OTC, so it is diverted to orotic acid. Trap: Concluding that any hyperammonemia with low citrulline is CPS I deficiency without using orotic acid to separate it from OTC deficiency.

qs.q: Plasma glutamine is elevated in all three patients. Which explanation is most reasonable?
o: High ammonia inhibits glutamine synthetase, which leaves glutamine as the only nitrogen carrier left
High ammonia drives, rather than inhibits, glutamine synthesis.
Glutamine is the direct substrate of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and therefore accumulates when it is blocked
CPS I uses free ammonia (with bicarbonate and ATP), not glutamine, in the mitochondrial matrix.
Glutaminase is activated by high ammonia, so glutamine is made from the breakdown of urea in blood
Glutaminase releases ammonia from glutamine; urea is not a source of glutamine.
Glutamine synthetase incorporates excess ammonia into glutamate, so glutamine serves as a nitrogen buffer that tracks the ammonia load
Correct: Glutamine synthetase adds NH4+ to glutamate using ATP, trapping ammonia in a nontoxic form; plasma glutamine therefore tracks the ammonia load.
qs.x: Glutamine synthetase adds NH4+ to glutamate using ATP, trapping ammonia in a nontoxic form; plasma glutamine therefore tracks the ammonia load. Trap: Mixing up glutaminase and glutamine synthetase, which run in opposite directions with respect to ammonia.

qs.q: Sodium benzoate lowers ammonia in these patients. Which mechanism is best supported?
o: Benzoate inhibits glutamine synthetase, which lowers glutamine and therefore reduces ammonia production
Inhibiting glutamine synthetase would raise ammonia rather than lower it.
Benzoate conjugates with glycine to form hippurate, which is excreted in urine, removing nitrogen without the urea cycle
Correct: Glycine carries nitrogen; once it is conjugated to benzoate and cleared as hippurate, it is replaced by new glycine made using ammonia, so nitrogen is removed through a bypass pathway.
Benzoate is converted to urea by arginase, which provides an alternative route for ammonia disposal
Arginase is a urea cycle enzyme and does not use benzoate.
Benzoate activates carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, which restores flux through the first step of the cycle
Benzoate does not activate CPS I; the defect is in the cycle itself.
qs.x: Glycine carries nitrogen; once it is conjugated to benzoate and cleared as hippurate, it is replaced by new glycine made using ammonia, so nitrogen is removed through a bypass pathway. Trap: Assuming a drug that lowers ammonia must repair the defective enzyme rather than provide an alternate nitrogen excretion pathway.

qs.q: At 4 hours after the protein load, Patient A's plasma ammonia was approximately how many times that of the healthy infant?
o: Correct: 720 / 28 = 25.7, or about 26-fold.
29 uses the healthy infant's 0-hour value (720 / 25) instead of the 4-hour value.
0.04 inverts the ratio (28 / 720).
22 pairs Patient A's 2-hour value with the control's 4-hour value (610 / 28).
qs.x: 720 / 28 = 25.7, or about 26-fold. Trap: Reading the wrong time point or inverting the ratio when comparing two curves.

qs.q: Patient C accumulates citrulline. Which statement best explains why the citrulline is found in plasma rather than remaining in the mitochondria?
o: The defective ASS blocks the mitochondrial ornithine transporter, which traps citrulline in the intermembrane space
ASS is a cytosolic enzyme and does not regulate the mitochondrial carrier.
Citrulline is made in the matrix and exported, then accumulates where ASS is deficient
Correct: OTC makes citrulline in the matrix; an ornithine-citrulline carrier exports it, and with ASS deficient the cytosolic pool rises and spills into blood.
Citrulline is produced from aspartate in plasma, so its level depends on aspartate rather than on urea cycle flux
Aspartate is a substrate of ASS, but citrulline is not produced from aspartate in plasma.
Citrulline is synthesized in the cytosol from arginine and cannot enter mitochondria, so it accumulates there
Citrulline is made from ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate in the matrix, not from arginine in the cytosol.
qs.x: OTC makes citrulline in the matrix; an ornithine-citrulline carrier exports it, and with ASS deficient the cytosolic pool rises and spills into blood. Trap: Forgetting that the urea cycle spans two compartments and so misplacing where each intermediate is synthesized or consumed.

passages.title: FL10 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 5
text: Most mitochondrial proteins are encoded in the nucleus and imported after synthesis in the cytosol. Matrix proteins usually carry an N-terminal presequence, an amphipathic alpha helix with positively charged and hydrophobic faces, that is recognized by the TOM complex on the outer membrane and then passes through the TIM23 channel of the inner membrane. Inside the matrix, mitochondrial processing peptidase (MPP), a zinc metalloprotease, removes the presequence. A researcher fused the presequence of a matrix enzyme to GFP and incubated radiolabeled precursor with isolated yeast mitochondria for 20 minutes at 25 degrees C. After import, samples were treated with proteinase K, which digests proteins on the outside of intact membranes, and then analyzed by SDS-PAGE. Protease-protected precursor was scored as imported, and a smaller band was scored as processed by MPP. Conditions included the uncoupler CCCP (which dissipates the electrical potential across the inner membrane), depletion of matrix ATP, EDTA (a metal chelator), and a variant presequence in which three arginines were replaced by glutamate.

qs.q: The loss of import in the presence of CCCP most directly indicates that translocation of the presequence across the inner membrane
o: requires a cytosolic chaperone that is inactivated by uncouplers of oxidative phosphorylation
Nothing in the data implicates a chaperone being inactivated by CCCP.
depends on the membrane potential, which pulls the positively charged presequence toward the negative matrix side
Correct: CCCP dissipates the electrical potential (negative inside the matrix), which electrophoretically drives the positively charged presequence through TIM23; protection falls from 88% to 6%.
requires the outer membrane TOM complex to be disassembled before the precursor can reach the matrix and be pulled across the inner membrane
The TOM complex remains intact and is not disassembled during import.
depends on a proton-motive force that is used by ATP synthase to phosphorylate the imported protein
The potential drives movement of the presequence; no phosphorylation of the precursor is involved.
qs.x: CCCP dissipates the electrical potential (negative inside the matrix), which electrophoretically drives the positively charged presequence through TIM23; protection falls from 88% to 6%. Trap: Linking every effect of an uncoupler to ATP synthesis instead of recognizing that the membrane potential itself drives presequence movement.

qs.q: In the EDTA condition, 87% of the precursor is protease protected but only 3% is processed. What is the most likely interpretation?
o: The precursor remained on the outer surface of the mitochondria, where it was bound to the TOM complex
Surface-bound precursor would be digested by proteinase K, giving low protection.
The precursor entered the matrix, but MPP, a metal-dependent protease, could not remove the presequence despite normal translocation
Correct: Protection from proteinase K means the precursor is inside intact membranes; lack of cleavage fits chelation of the zinc that MPP requires.
EDTA ruptured the mitochondrial membranes, so the protected precursor reflects leaky organelles rather than import
Ruptured membranes would expose the precursor to proteinase K and give low, not high, protection.
EDTA stimulated import by blocking proteinase K, and therefore it prevented the digestion of the precursor
Proteinase K is not blocked by EDTA in this design; protection reflects location, not enzyme inhibition.
qs.x: Protection from proteinase K means the precursor is inside intact membranes; lack of cleavage fits chelation of the zinc that MPP requires. Trap: Treating protease protection and presequence cleavage as the same measurement, when the EDTA row shows they can be uncoupled.

qs.q: A GFP fusion containing a tightly folded domain that cannot be unfolded is not imported. Which statement best explains this observation?
o: The channels thread precursors through in an unfolded state, aided by matrix Hsp70 and ATP

Correct: Import channels accommodate extended polypeptide chains; tightly folded segments stall translocation, and ATP-dependent matrix Hsp70 helps pull the chain inward (ATP depletion lowered import to 22%).
Folded proteins are imported only into the intermembrane space, where TIM23 releases them to the matrix
Matrix proteins are not routed to the intermembrane space in a folded state.
The folded domain masks the presequence from the signal peptidase located in the endoplasmic reticulum
Mitochondrial import does not involve ER signal peptidase.
The folded domain increases the positive charge of the precursor, which prevents it from being drawn through TIM23
The fold does not alter net charge in a way that explains the block.
qs.x: Import channels accommodate extended polypeptide chains; tightly folded segments stall translocation, and ATP-dependent matrix Hsp70 helps pull the chain inward (ATP depletion lowered import to 22%). Trap: Picturing import as passage of folded proteins through large pores, like nuclear import, rather than as threading of unfolded chains.

qs.q: Which feature best allows the cell to sort a protein with a mitochondrial presequence away from one with an endoplasmic reticulum signal sequence?
o: The mitochondrial presequence is added to the C-terminus after folding, whereas the ER signal is at the N-terminus
The presequence is N-terminal and is removed by MPP.
The mitochondrial presequence is recognized by the signal recognition particle, whereas the ER signal sequence is not
SRP recognizes the ER signal sequence, not mitochondrial presequences.
The mitochondrial presequence is hydrophobic and uncharged, whereas the ER signal sequence is rich in acidic residues
The presequence is charged and amphipathic, not hydrophobic and uncharged.
The mitochondrial presequence is amphipathic and positively charged, whereas the ER signal sequence has a central hydrophobic core

Correct: A positively charged amphipathic helix is recognized by TOM receptors, while the hydrophobic core of an ER signal sequence is bound by SRP; the Arg-to-Glu variant (11% imported) shows how much the charge matters.
qs.x: A positively charged amphipathic helix is recognized by TOM receptors, while the hydrophobic core of an ER signal sequence is bound by SRP; the Arg-to-Glu variant (11% imported) shows how much the charge matters. Trap: Remembering that both are N-terminal signals but swapping their chemical properties and receptors.

passages.title: FL10 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 6
text: Bacteriophage lambda infects Escherichia coli and can follow either of two pathways. In the lytic cycle, phage genes are expressed in a cascade that replicates the genome and lyses the cell. In lysogeny, the phage integrates at attB as a prophage and the cI repressor shuts off lytic genes. The decision depends on the CII protein, a transcription activator that is unstable because of host FtsH protease; CII activates transcription of cI. A researcher infected E. coli with lambda variants and counted lysogens by selecting for resistance to superinfection, and determined plaque appearance. Lysogens were also exposed to ultraviolet (UV) light, which damages DNA and activates RecA; activated RecA stimulates auto-cleavage of the cI repressor. In a separate series, wild-type phage were added at different multiplicities of infection (MOI, average phage per cell), and the percentage of infected cells that became lysogens was measured (Figure 1). Table 1 summarizes the other experiments.

qs.q: Why does the cI- mutant form clear rather than turbid plaques?
o: Without cI repressor, the phage cannot adsorb to E. coli, so only a few cells are infected at all
Adsorption does not depend on cI; the mutant infects normally, as 0% lysogens at MOI 5 reflects the lytic outcome.
Without cI repressor, the host RecA protein is inactive, so the phage genome cannot be replicated
RecA is a host protein that is not required for lytic replication.
Without cI repressor, the CII protein is degraded more quickly, which blocks integration of the prophage into the E. coli chromosome at attB
CII acts upstream of cI; cI loss does not accelerate CII degradation.
Without cI repressor, no infected cell can maintain lysogeny, so every infected cell proceeds through the lytic cycle
Correct: A turbid plaque contains surviving lysogens that are immune to superinfection thanks to cI; with no cI, no lysogens survive and the plaque clears.
qs.x: A turbid plaque contains surviving lysogens that are immune to superinfection thanks to cI; with no cI, no lysogens survive and the plaque clears. Trap: Treating a mutation in the repressor as an infection defect instead of recognizing that it removes the ability to establish or maintain lysogeny.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for the increase in lysogeny with increasing MOI in Figure 1?
o: Higher MOI saturates FtsH, which stabilizes cI and prevents the repressor from being cleaved by RecA
FtsH degrades CII, not cI; saturating it would not change cI cleavage.
Higher MOI raises the concentration of RecA, which cleaves lytic proteins and thereby favors integration
RecA cleaves cI, which favors lysis rather than lysogeny.
Several genomes per cell increase the dose of Cro, which represses lytic genes and promotes integration of the prophage at the attB site in the host chromosome
Cro favors the lytic pathway, so more Cro would not promote lysogeny.
Several genomes per cell increase the dose of CII, so enough accumulates despite FtsH degradation to activate cI transcription
Correct: CII is unstable and acts as a dose-dependent sensor of infection; multiple genomes per cell synthesize more CII, promoting cI expression and lysogeny.
qs.x: CII is unstable and acts as a dose-dependent sensor of infection; multiple genomes per cell synthesize more CII, promoting cI expression and lysogeny. Trap: Reversing the roles of Cro (lytic) and cI or CII (lysogenic) when predicting which regulator accumulates at high multiplicity.

qs.q: In Table 1, lysogens exposed to UV lyse efficiently in a recA+ host but not in a recA- host. Which mechanism is most consistent with this result?
o: UV-activated RecA phosphorylates cI, which causes the repressor to bind more tightly to the operators
Phosphorylation of cI is not part of this mechanism, and tighter binding would maintain lysogeny.
UV-activated RecA activates CII, which then switches the prophage from lysogeny to the lytic cycle
CII promotes lysogeny rather than lysis, and RecA does not activate it.
UV-activated RecA promotes auto-cleavage of cI, releasing repression of lytic genes and inducing the prophage
Correct: RecA acts as a co-protease that triggers cI self-cleavage, so Cro and other lytic genes are expressed; without RecA only 2% of cells lyse.
UV light cuts the prophage out of the chromosome directly, and RecA only packages the excised genome
Excision depends on phage Int and Xis after induction, not on direct cutting by UV light.
qs.x: RecA acts as a co-protease that triggers cI self-cleavage, so Cro and other lytic genes are expressed; without RecA only 2% of cells lyse. Trap: Assuming UV induces lysis by directly excising the prophage rather than by inactivating the repressor.

qs.q: Assume that every one of 500 cells is infected at MOI 1. Based on Figure 1, about how many cells enter the lytic cycle?
o: 225 is the number of lysogens (45%) expected at MOI 2, not lytic cells at MOI 1.
100 is the number of lysogens (20% of 500), not lytic cells.
Correct: At MOI 1, 20% become lysogens, so 80% of 500, or 400 cells, enter the lytic cycle.
200 is 40% of 500 and matches no value in Figure 1 at MOI 1.
qs.x: At MOI 1, 20% become lysogens, so 80% of 500, or 400 cells, enter the lytic cycle. Trap: Reporting the lysogenic fraction (100 cells) instead of the complement that undergoes lysis.

graph.title: Lysogeny as a function of multiplicity of infection

passages.title: FL10 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 7
text: Normal human somatic cells divide a limited number of times before entering replicative senescence, in which they remain metabolically active but stop dividing. Telomeres, repeats of TTAGGG at chromosome ends, shorten with each division because DNA polymerase cannot fully replicate the 3' end of the lagging strand. Telomerase, a ribonucleoprotein with a catalytic reverse transcriptase subunit (hTERT) and an RNA template (hTR), extends telomeres but is silent in most somatic cells. Critically short telomeres are recognized as DNA damage and activate p53, which drives arrest. A researcher engineered primary human fibroblasts as shown in Table 1 and passaged them continuously, measuring mean terminal restriction fragment length (a measure of telomere length) at intervals (Figure 1). Telomerase activity was measured by the TRAP assay (relative to control cells). Senescent cells were identified by staining for senescence-associated beta-galactosidase (SA-beta-gal) at population doubling (PD) 55, and the fraction of cells with gamma-H2AX foci at telomeres was scored as a marker of telomere damage.

qs.q: Which statement best explains why telomeres in the control fibroblasts shorten with each division?
o: DNA polymerase cannot synthesize the leading strand at chromosome ends because it only copies in the 3' to 5' direction, which leaves the ends uncopied
DNA polymerase copies 5' to 3' on both strands; the leading strand can be copied to the end.
The RNA component of telomerase is degraded at each division, so repeats are no longer added to the 5' ends
Telomerase is absent in control cells, and it extends the 3' end, not the 5' end.
Telomeric repeats are specifically cut by nucleases whenever the cell passes through the S phase checkpoint
No nuclease activity specific to telomere repeats at S phase is part of the explanation.
DNA polymerase cannot replicate the extreme 3' end of the lagging-strand template after the terminal RNA primer is removed

Correct: The end-replication problem: the lagging strand lacks a primer for the last Okazaki fragment, so the 3' overhang shortens by about 80 bp per division in these cells (9.0 kb to 5.8 kb over 40 PD).
qs.x: The end-replication problem: the lagging strand lacks a primer for the last Okazaki fragment, so the 3' overhang shortens by about 80 bp per division in these cells (9.0 kb to 5.8 kb over 40 PD). Trap: Believing polymerase cannot copy one direction or that active nucleases erase telomeres, rather than the missing primer at the lagging-strand end.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of including the catalytically dead hTERT line?
o: It shows that catalytic activity, not hTERT protein alone, prevents senescence
Correct: The dead enzyme is expressed but cannot add repeats; its senescence at PD 56 (84% SA-beta-gal positive) matches control, so the catalytic activity is required for immortalization.
To show that overexpression of any protein increases the number of population doublings in a cell line
The dead enzyme did not extend lifespan, so this does not support a general effect of protein overexpression.
To show that the hTR template RNA is dispensable for telomerase to elongate telomeres in these cells
The experiment does not test the RNA template; telomerase needs hTR to function.
To show that p53 is activated by the catalytically dead enzyme more strongly than by the control cells
No p53 measurements were made in this comparison.
qs.x: The dead enzyme is expressed but cannot add repeats; its senescence at PD 56 (84% SA-beta-gal positive) matches control, so the catalytic activity is required for immortalization. Trap: Reading the catalytically dead line as a test of an unrelated variable instead of a control for expression versus enzymatic activity.

qs.q: Knockdown of p53 extended the lifespan of control cells to PD 68 but did not make them immortal. Which explanation is most consistent with the data?
o: p53 knockdown activated telomerase, but the enzyme was inactive in the absence of the hTR template
TRAP activity stays at 1, so telomerase was not activated.
Cells divided without p53 arrest, but telomeres kept shortening until a later crisis
Correct: gamma-H2AX foci remain high (55%) in the p53 shRNA line, so telomeres still shorten and signal damage; loss of p53 only removes the arrest response, which delays but does not prevent crisis.
p53 knockdown prevented telomere shortening, but the cells then accumulated another senescence signal
Telomere shortening is a replication phenomenon and continues without p53.
p53 knockdown eliminated the DNA damage signal at telomeres, so the cells no longer needed telomeres
Persistent telomeric foci show that telomere damage remains in the p53 knockdown line.
qs.x: gamma-H2AX foci remain high (55%) in the p53 shRNA line, so telomeres still shorten and signal damage; loss of p53 only removes the arrest response, which delays but does not prevent crisis. Trap: Assuming that bypassing the checkpoint also repairs the underlying telomere problem.

qs.q: Using the slope of the control curve between 0 and 40 population doublings, at about which population doubling would the control telomeres reach 5.0 kb?
o: 40 is the PD at which telomeres are 5.8 kb, which is not yet 5.0 kb.
Correct: The loss is (9.0 - 5.8) / 40 = 0.08 kb per PD, so reaching 5.0 kb requires (9.0 - 5.0) / 0.08 = 50 PD.
62 results from dividing the remaining 5.0 kb by 0.08 instead of the 4.0 kb lost.
30 would apply to a loss of about 0.13 kb per PD, faster than the curve shows.
qs.x: The loss is (9.0 - 5.8) / 40 = 0.08 kb per PD, so reaching 5.0 kb requires (9.0 - 5.0) / 0.08 = 50 PD. Trap: Dividing the final telomere length by the rate instead of the length lost from the starting value.

graph.title: Mean telomere length during serial passage

passages.title: FL10 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 8
text: Heart rate is set by the sinoatrial (SA) node, whose pacemaker cells depolarize spontaneously during phase 4 of the action potential. The vagus nerve releases acetylcholine onto M2 muscarinic receptors on the node, and sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine onto beta-1 adrenergic receptors. In a study of healthy 25-year-old volunteers resting supine, heart rate was measured under pharmacologic blockade (Table 1). Atropine is a muscarinic receptor antagonist and propranolol is a nonselective beta-adrenergic antagonist. In a second protocol, phenylephrine, an alpha-1 agonist that raises arterial pressure without direct effects on the heart, was infused at increasing doses to produce graded increases in mean arterial pressure (MAP), and heart rate was recorded with and without atropine (Figure 1). Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch send signals to the medulla, which adjusts autonomic outflow to the heart. Each value is the mean of ten participants. Participants avoided caffeine and exercise for 24 hours before testing, and heart rate was recorded by continuous electrocardiogram after 10 minutes of rest.

qs.q: Which conclusion about resting autonomic tone is best supported by Table 1?
o: Sympathetic tone dominates at rest, because blocking it lowers heart rate by a larger amount than blocking vagal input raises it
Propranolol lowers rate by 8, which is less than the 20 beat/min rise with atropine.
Parasympathetic tone dominates at rest, because blocking it raises heart rate more than blocking sympathetic input lowers it
Correct: Atropine raises heart rate by 20 beats/min whereas propranolol lowers it by only 8, so vagal slowing is the larger resting influence.
Parasympathetic and sympathetic tone are equal at rest, because the two single drugs change heart rate in opposite directions
The magnitudes differ (20 versus 8), so tone is not equal.
Neither division influences rest heart rate, because the intrinsic rate with both blocked is not different from control
Double blockade gives 104, well above the control of 68, so autonomic input matters.
qs.x: Atropine raises heart rate by 20 beats/min whereas propranolol lowers it by only 8, so vagal slowing is the larger resting influence. Trap: Reading opposite directions of change as equal tone instead of comparing the sizes of the two effects.

qs.q: Which mechanism best explains how acetylcholine slows the SA node?
o: M2 receptors open voltage-gated Na+ channels, which causes a rapid upstroke that shortens the interval between beats
Na+ channel opening would speed, not slow, the rate and is not how M2 receptors act.
M2 receptors block the funny current by closing gap junctions, which isolates the SA node from the atrium
M2 receptors do not close gap junctions; they alter ion channel activity in SA nodal cells.
M2 receptors activate Gs, which raises cAMP and shifts If channels to open at more negative potentials
Gs and increased cAMP describe the sympathetic, beta-1 effect, which speeds the node.
M2 receptors activate Gi-coupled K+ channels and lower cAMP, which hyperpolarizes the cell and slows phase 4 depolarization
Correct: M2 receptors act through Gi: the beta-gamma subunits open GIRK K+ channels (hyperpolarization) and the alpha-i subunit decreases cAMP, lowering If and slowing the pacemaker potential.
qs.x: M2 receptors act through Gi: the beta-gamma subunits open GIRK K+ channels (hyperpolarization) and the alpha-i subunit decreases cAMP, lowering If and slowing the pacemaker potential. Trap: Mixing up Gs (sympathetic, beta-1) and Gi (parasympathetic, M2) signaling in the pacemaker cell.

qs.q: What does the flat atropine curve in Figure 1 indicate about the baroreflex slowing of heart rate seen in the control curve?
o: It is mediated mainly by increased vagal outflow acting on muscarinic receptors rather than by withdrawal of sympathetic drive
Correct: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors, and the slope falls from about -0.8 beats/min per mmHg to almost zero; the reflex slowing therefore depended on vagal activation.
It is mediated mainly by decreased sympathetic outflow, because atropine blocks beta-1 receptors on the SA node
Atropine blocks muscarinic, not beta-1 receptors.
It is mediated mainly by local autoregulation in the heart, because the atropine curve is independent of arterial pressure
The control curve shows the dependence on pressure; local autoregulation is not shown by these data.
It is mediated by direct effects of phenylephrine on the SA node, because the curve is flat after the drug is given, rather than by any change in autonomic outflow
Phenylephrine acts on alpha-1 receptors in vessels and lowers rate only through the reflex, as the control curve shows.
qs.x: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors, and the slope falls from about -0.8 beats/min per mmHg to almost zero; the reflex slowing therefore depended on vagal activation. Trap: Assuming that the drug-sensitive step must be sympathetic withdrawal because the heart rate fell as pressure rose.

qs.q: What is the slope of the control curve in Figure 1 between MAP of 90 and 110 mmHg?
o: +0.8 beats/min per mmHg
The slope is negative; heart rate falls as pressure rises.
-1.25 beats/min per mmHg
-1.25 is the inverse (mmHg change per unit of heart rate change).
-0.8 beats/min per mmHg
-16 beats/min per mmHg
-16 is the change in heart rate without dividing by the 20 mmHg interval.
qs.x: (52 - 68) / (110 - 90) = -16/20 = -0.8. Trap: Reporting the total change in heart rate without dividing by the pressure interval, or inverting the ratio.

qs.q: A patient has recently received a heart transplant, which interrupts autonomic nerves to the donor heart. Compared with the 68 beats/min of the control volunteers, the patient's resting heart rate is expected to be
o: lower, near 60 beats/min, because the sympathetic supply is lost and vagal tone remains
Vagal input is also lost with the transplant, so the vagal tone does not remain.
much lower, because the denervated SA node cannot depolarize spontaneously without vagal input
The SA node depolarizes spontaneously and does not require neural input to fire.
higher, near the intrinsic rate, because vagal tone is lost
Correct: The denervated SA node fires at its intrinsic rate (about 100 beats/min, as in the double-blockade condition), higher than the resting rate of innervated hearts.
unchanged, because the SA node does not depend on autonomic input to generate a rhythm
The double-blockade rate of 104 shows that autonomic input changes the rate.
qs.x: The denervated SA node fires at its intrinsic rate (about 100 beats/min, as in the double-blockade condition), higher than the resting rate of innervated hearts. Trap: Assuming the pacemaker needs nerve input to fire, rather than recognizing that nerves only modulate an intrinsically faster rate.

graph.title: Heart rate during phenylephrine-induced rise in arterial pressure

passages.title: FL10 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 9
text: Gastrin, secretin, and cholecystokinin (CCK) are hormones released by enteroendocrine cells into the blood in response to luminal contents. In a study of healthy volunteers, tubes were placed in the stomach and duodenum, and fasting values were compared with those after specified stimuli. Table 1 gives mean changes in plasma hormone concentration (as multiples of the fasting value) and a physiologic response for each stimulus. G cells in the gastric antrum release gastrin; D cells release somatostatin when luminal pH falls, which inhibits G cells. In a separate experiment, antral pH was clamped at different values and plasma gastrin was measured (Figure 1). Gastrin stimulates acid secretion by parietal cells both directly and through histamine release from enterochromataffin-like (ECL) cells. Secretin is released from S cells of the duodenum, and CCK from I cells. A patient with a gastrin-secreting tumor was also studied and had very high fasting gastrin, and acid output that was not reduced by low antral pH.

qs.q: The rise in secretin after duodenal acid serves which physiologic purpose?
o: It stimulates pancreatic duct cells to secrete bicarbonate that neutralizes acid entering the duodenum
Correct: Secretin is released when duodenal pH is low; the 6.0-fold rise matches the 4-fold increase in pancreatic bicarbonate, protecting duodenal mucosa and raising pH for pancreatic enzymes.
It stimulates parietal cells to secrete more acid so that digestion of protein in the duodenum is accelerated
Secretin inhibits, rather than stimulates, gastric acid secretion.
It stimulates the gallbladder to contract and the sphincter of Oddi to relax to deliver bile salts
Gallbladder contraction and sphincter relaxation are CCK effects (fat infusion row).
It stimulates pancreatic acinar cells to release zymogens that digest the fats delivered from the stomach
Enzyme release from acinar cells is mainly stimulated by CCK, not by secretin.
qs.x: Secretin is released when duodenal pH is low; the 6.0-fold rise matches the 4-fold increase in pancreatic bicarbonate, protecting duodenal mucosa and raising pH for pancreatic enzymes. Trap: Mixing up the targets of secretin (bicarbonate, duct cells) and CCK (enzymes and bile).

qs.q: Which mechanism explains the response of gallbladder emptying to fatty acids?
o: Fatty acids directly depolarize gallbladder smooth muscle through intrinsic reflexes without hormonal input
The data show a strong CCK response, which points to a hormonal mechanism.
Fatty acids stimulate S cells to release secretin, which contracts the gallbladder and raises bicarbonate
Secretin rose only 1.5-fold with fatty acids, and its main effect is on bicarbonate.
Fatty acids stimulate I cells to release CCK, which contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi
Correct: CCK rose 7-fold with duodenal fatty acids; it contracts gallbladder smooth muscle and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi to deliver bile for emulsification.
Fatty acids stimulate G cells to release gastrin, which raises acid output and speeds gallbladder emptying
Gastrin fell slightly (0.8) with fatty acid infusion.
qs.x: CCK rose 7-fold with duodenal fatty acids; it contracts gallbladder smooth muscle and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi to deliver bile for emulsification. Trap: Choosing secretin for any duodenal stimulus without matching the hormone to the nutrient that triggers it.

qs.q: What explains the pattern of plasma gastrin in Figure 1?
o: Acid activates D cells to release somatostatin, which inhibits G cells
Correct: Gastrin is under negative feedback: acid triggers somatostatin, which restrains G cells, and gastrin increases from 12 to 110 pg/mL as pH rises.
Low luminal pH directly stimulates G cells, so gastrin release is greatest when the antrum is most acidic
Gastrin is lowest, not highest, at the most acidic pH in the figure.
High luminal pH stimulates D cells, which release somatostatin that increases gastrin release from the G cells
Somatostatin is released in response to low pH and is inhibitory.
Plasma gastrin tracks parietal cell activity, which falls as the antrum becomes less acidic
The figure shows gastrin falling as acid rises, which would not follow a parietal-cell-driven pattern.
qs.x: Gastrin is under negative feedback: acid triggers somatostatin, which restrains G cells, and gastrin increases from 12 to 110 pg/mL as pH rises. Trap: Assuming that acid always stimulates acid-promoting hormones rather than recognizing negative feedback.

qs.q: The patient with the gastrin-secreting tumor develops fatty, bulky stools. Which mechanism is most likely?
o: Excess acid stimulates pancreatic lipase and bile secretion, which causes fats to be absorbed too quickly by the ileum
Acid inactivates lipase rather than stimulating it.
Excess gastrin increases secretin release, which overstimulates bicarbonate secretion and washes bile salts out of the lumen
Acid in the duodenum raises secretin, but bicarbonate is not overwhelmed in this patient and no washout is described.
Excess acid entering the duodenum inactivates pancreatic lipase and precipitates bile acids, which impairs fat digestion and micelle formation
Correct: With acid output not suppressed, the duodenal pH stays low, below the optimum of pancreatic lipase, and bile acids precipitate, so fat is malabsorbed (steatorrhea).
Excess gastrin directly blocks CCK release from I cells, which prevents gallbladder contraction in response to fat
The case describes no direct effect of gastrin on CCK release.
qs.x: With acid output not suppressed, the duodenal pH stays low, below the optimum of pancreatic lipase, and bile acids precipitate, so fat is malabsorbed (steatorrhea). Trap: Attributing malabsorption to altered hormone interactions rather than to the effect of low duodenal pH on enzymes and bile acids.

qs.q: A patient takes a proton pump inhibitor for several months. Which change in plasma gastrin would be expected, and why?
o: Higher, because the drug directly stimulates G cells through the CCK2 receptor in the antrum
The drug blocks the H+/K+ ATPase of parietal cells and does not stimulate G cells directly.
Unchanged, because gastrin secretion is controlled only by vagal input and is independent of pH
Figure 1 shows a strong dependence of gastrin on pH.
Higher, because less acid in the antrum lowers somatostatin release and removes inhibition of G cells
Correct: By Figure 1, rising antral pH raises gastrin through loss of somatostatin-mediated inhibition; this hypergastrinemia is a known effect of long-term acid suppression.
Lower, because less acid in the stomach reduces the stimulus for gastrin release from G cells
Acid inhibits gastrin release, so less acid does not reduce it.
qs.x: By Figure 1, rising antral pH raises gastrin through loss of somatostatin-mediated inhibition; this hypergastrinemia is a known effect of long-term acid suppression. Trap: Predicting that reducing acid would reduce gastrin, which ignores the negative feedback loop.

graph.title: Plasma gastrin at clamped antral pH

passages.title: FL10 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 10
text: In regions where Plasmodium falciparum malaria is endemic, the sickle cell allele (HbS), a glutamate-to-valine substitution at position 6 of the beta-globin chain, reaches high frequencies. Heterozygotes (AS) generally have normal red cell morphology under ordinary conditions. A researcher followed a birth cohort of 10,000 newborns in a high-transmission region, assuming Hardy-Weinberg proportions at birth, and recorded the percentage of children aged 2 to 5 years with high-density parasitemia and the relative fitness (survival to reproductive age, scaled to a maximum of 1.00). In parasitized AS red cells, hemoglobin deoxygenates more quickly and polymerizes, causing the cells to sickle and to be cleared by the spleen, and parasite proteins display on the cell surface is impaired. Parasite density was estimated from thick blood smears, and genotypes were determined by hemoglobin electrophoresis. Table 1 shows the cohort data. Figure 1 plots the frequency of HbS among adults against the prevalence of malaria in children across six surveyed regions.

qs.q: Which mechanism best explains the lower parasitemia in AS children?
o: AS red cells lack the membrane receptors that merozoites need to enter, which prevents all new infections
AS children still become infected; parasite density, not infection, is lower.
The valine substitution makes hemoglobin unable to bind oxygen, which starves the parasite of the oxygen it requires
HbS still binds oxygen, although it polymerizes in the deoxygenated form.
Heterozygotes produce antibodies against Plasmodium that are absent in AA children at the same ages, which prevents infection altogether in early childhood
The protection is not mediated by a unique antibody response.
Polymerization of HbS in parasitized cells causes sickling and clearance, and impairs display of parasite adhesion proteins
Correct: Under low oxygen in infected cells, HbS polymerizes, the cell sickles and is removed by the spleen, and surface display of PfEMP1 is impaired, which limits parasite growth and cytoadherence.
qs.x: Under low oxygen in infected cells, HbS polymerizes, the cell sickles and is removed by the spleen, and surface display of PfEMP1 is impaired, which limits parasite growth and cytoadherence. Trap: Attributing protection to a loss of function in oxygen binding or to immunity rather than to polymerization in infected cells.

qs.q: Using the relative fitnesses in Table 1, what is the expected equilibrium frequency of the HbS allele?
o: 0.05 would require much weaker selection against AA.
0.84 is the equilibrium frequency of the A allele, not of S.
0.19 results from dividing 0.15 by t (0.80) instead of by s + t.
Correct: With selection coefficients s = 1 - 0.85 = 0.15 against AA and t = 1 - 0.20 = 0.80 against SS, q = s / (s + t) = 0.15 / 0.95 = 0.158, about 0.16.
qs.x: With selection coefficients s = 1 - 0.85 = 0.15 against AA and t = 1 - 0.20 = 0.80 against SS, q = s / (s + t) = 0.15 / 0.95 = 0.158, about 0.16. Trap: Dividing by the selection against SS alone instead of the sum of the two selection coefficients, or reporting the A allele.

qs.q: If malaria were eliminated from a region, what change in HbS frequency would be expected over many generations?
o: A slow decline, because SS individuals would still have low fitness, while most S alleles are masked in heterozygotes
Correct: Without malaria, AS and AA have about equal fitness while SS keep their disadvantage; because most S alleles reside in heterozygotes, selection removes them slowly.
No change, because the allele has no effect on fitness when malaria is absent
SS individuals still have reduced survival, so the allele has fitness effects.
A steady rise, because heterozygotes would be fitter than AA children when no malaria is present
Without malaria, AS has no advantage over AA, so a rise would not be expected.
A rapid disappearance within a few generations, because AS individuals would lose all of their fitness
AS would not lose fitness; they would be similar to AA.
qs.x: Without malaria, AS and AA have about equal fitness while SS keep their disadvantage; because most S alleles reside in heterozygotes, selection removes them slowly. Trap: Expecting the heterozygous advantage to reverse into a strong disadvantage instead of a weak, slow selection against a recessive allele.

qs.q: Why does substitution of valine for glutamate at beta position 6 lead to polymerization of deoxyhemoglobin S?
o: The new hydrophobic valine fits into a hydrophobic pocket on a neighboring deoxy hemoglobin, which promotes fiber formation

Correct: Replacing a polar, charged residue with hydrophobic valine creates a sticky surface patch that binds a complementary pocket on another deoxygenated hemoglobin, so tetramers stack into fibers.
The new valine blocks the heme pocket, which locks hemoglobin in the oxygenated R state and induces precipitation
HbS polymerizes in the deoxygenated T state, not by locking the R state.
The loss of a negatively charged glutamate increases electrostatic repulsion between hemoglobins, which favors aggregation
Removing a negative charge would reduce, not increase, repulsion.
The new valine forms a disulfide bond with a cysteine on a neighboring hemoglobin, which cross-links tetramers
Valine has no sulfhydryl group and cannot form a disulfide bond.
qs.x: Replacing a polar, charged residue with hydrophobic valine creates a sticky surface patch that binds a complementary pocket on another deoxygenated hemoglobin, so tetramers stack into fibers. Trap: Explaining a charge-to-hydrophobic substitution by a covalent cross-link or a change in the oxygen-binding pocket.

graph.title: HbS allele frequency versus malaria prevalence across regions

passages.title: FL10 · CARS · Passage 1
text: Every morning the sun has risen, and every morning we have inferred that it will rise again. David Hume's challenge to this ordinary habit of mind is easy to state and notoriously hard to dispel. Our confidence in the future, he argued, rests on the assumption that the future will resemble the past. But what grounds that assumption? It cannot be demonstrated by reasoning alone, since there is no contradiction in supposing that the course of nature might change tomorrow. And it cannot be established by experience without circularity, since the only experience we have is of past regularities, and to treat these as evidence about the future is precisely to assume the uniformity in question. The inference from observed to unobserved cases, on this view, is a habit of expectation produced by repetition, not a conclusion that reason has earned.

Responses to Hume have tended to divide into two camps. The first accepts that no justification of induction is available and tries to live comfortably with that result. Karl Popper, most famously, argued that science does not in fact proceed by induction at all. Scientists propose bold conjectures and then try to refute them; a theory that survives severe testing is not thereby made probable, merely not yet falsified. Critics reply that this evasion only relocates the problem. If we rely on well-tested theories to build bridges and prescribe drugs, we are betting that they will keep working, and that bet looks like an inductive one.

The second camp seeks a justification that does not beg the question. Some argue that induction is simply part of what we mean by rational inference, so that asking whether induction is reasonable is like asking whether the law is legal. Others, following Hans Reichenbach, offer a pragmatic vindication: if nature has any regularities at all, then induction will eventually find them, whereas no other method can do better, and if nature has none, no method will succeed. Induction is thus the best bet available even if we cannot show it is a good bet. The weakness of this argument is that it guarantees only convergence in the long run, which says little about the reliability of any particular prediction we must make today.

Nelson Goodman sharpened the puzzle in a different direction. Define "grue" as the property of being green if examined before some future date and blue otherwise. Every emerald examined so far is both green and grue, so the evidence supports "all emeralds are green" and "all emeralds are grue" equally well, yet the two hypotheses predict different colors for emeralds examined after the date. The lesson Goodman drew is that the trouble lies not only in justifying the step from past to future but in saying which regularities are projectible at all.
