passages.title: FL10 · Psych/Soc · Passage 4
text: Researchers studied how people explain outcomes. One hundred twenty students completed a difficult 20-item verbal test and were randomly assigned (n = 30 per group) to one of four conditions. In two conditions, students received bogus feedback on their own score (success or failure) and then rated how much the result was caused by internal factors (ability and effort) and external factors (test difficulty and luck) on a 1-9 scale. In the other two conditions, observers watched a recording of a peer taking the test, were told the peer had succeeded or failed, and rated the same causes for the peer. Feedback was assigned at random and was unrelated to actual performance. Mean ratings are shown in Table 1, and internal attribution ratings are plotted in Figure 1. A two-way analysis of variance showed a significant interaction between role (self or observer) and outcome for internal attributions (p < 0.01). All raters completed the ratings in private and were debriefed afterward.

qs.q: In the self conditions, how much higher was the mean internal attribution after success than after failure?
o: 3.2 is the difference in external ratings (6.3 - 3.1).
1.9 is the gap between external and internal ratings after failure (6.3 - 4.4).
0.3 is the observer difference (5.9 - 5.6).
qs.x: 7.2 - 4.4 = 2.8. Trap: Subtracting the external ratings instead of the internal ratings that the question asks about.

qs.q: Observers rated another person's failure as more internally caused (5.9) than actors rated their own failure (4.4). Which concept best captures this difference?
o: Actor-observer difference, a reflection of the fundamental attribution error in judging others' behavior
Correct: People tend to explain others' behavior by dispositions while explaining their own by situations.
Self-serving bias, because observers protect their own self-esteem when judging peers
Self-serving bias would explain actors' favorable self-attributions, not observers' judgments of peers.
Hindsight bias, because observers knew the outcome before rating its cause
Hindsight bias concerns judging an outcome as predictable, not attributing causes.
The halo effect, because observers generalized from one positive trait to others
The halo effect concerns generalizing a positive impression, which is not measured here.
qs.x: People tend to explain others' behavior by dispositions while explaining their own by situations. Trap: Labeling any attribution pattern as self-serving bias without noting that the target is another person.

qs.q: Why was feedback assigned at random and unrelated to actual test performance?
o: To ensure the sample was representative of all college students
Random assignment of conditions is not random sampling.
To ensure group differences in attribution were due to the feedback rather than true ability
Correct: Random, bogus feedback separates the outcome from ability, so attributional differences can be attributed to the feedback received.
To remove the need for success and failure comparison conditions
The comparison between success and failure is still central.
To keep participants unaware of the study hypothesis, as in blinding of researchers
Hiding hypotheses is a separate procedure from randomization.
qs.x: Random, bogus feedback separates the outcome from ability, so attributional differences can be attributed to the feedback received. Trap: Mixing up random assignment, which supports causal inference, with random sampling, which supports generalization.

qs.q: A student consistently attributes failures to stable internal causes and successes to luck. This pattern is:
o: identical to the self-serving pattern shown by actors in the table
The table shows actors credit success to internal causes.
the reverse of the self-serving pattern
Correct: Self-serving bias credits successes internally and failures externally; this student does the opposite, as in pessimistic attributional styles.
an example of the halo effect applied to self-ratings of ability
The halo effect is a different bias.
evidence that the student is an observer rather than an actor in the attributional sense
Actor and observer roles refer to who is being judged, not to this pattern.
qs.x: Self-serving bias credits successes internally and failures externally; this student does the opposite, as in pessimistic attributional styles. Trap: Assuming any attribution style that involves internal causes is self-serving.

qs.q: Observers' mean internal ratings differed little between success (5.6) and failure (5.9). This most likely indicates that observers:
o: attributed outcomes almost entirely to luck and test difficulty
Observers' external ratings (4.6-4.8) were not dominant over internal ratings.
lacked the outcome-dependent shift in attributions that actors showed
Correct: Actors' internal ratings changed by 2.8 points with outcome, whereas observers' changed by only 0.3.
showed a stronger self-serving bias than the actors did
Self-serving bias would increase differences by outcome, not decrease them.
responded more strongly to the feedback manipulation than the actors did
A smaller difference indicates weaker, not stronger, responsiveness.
qs.x: Actors' internal ratings changed by 2.8 points with outcome, whereas observers' changed by only 0.3. Trap: Assuming a small difference means the manipulation produced a bigger effect.

passages.title: FL10 · Psych/Soc · Passage 5
text: Anchoring is the tendency for judgments to stay close to an initially presented number. In an experiment, 160 participants read a description of a three-bedroom house and then estimated its appraised market value. Half were novices (undergraduate students) and half were licensed real estate agents (n = 80 each). Within each group, participants were randomly assigned to see either a low listing price anchor ($180,000) or a high listing price anchor ($320,000) before estimating the value; both anchors were randomly generated by the experimenters and participants were told the listing price was for reference only. All participants estimated in private and received the same house description. Mean estimates are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. The anchoring index is defined as the difference between mean estimates in the high-anchor and low-anchor conditions divided by the difference between the anchors, expressed as a percentage. The effect of anchor was significant in both groups (p < 0.01), and the anchor-by-expertise interaction was also significant (p = 0.02).

qs.q: Estimates that were pulled toward the randomly assigned listing price illustrate which cognitive process?
o: Anchoring and insufficient adjustment away from an initial reference value during estimation
Correct: The numerical anchor biased estimates because adjustments away from it were insufficient.
The availability heuristic, in which estimates depend on how easily examples come to mind
Availability concerns ease of recall, which was not manipulated.
The representativeness heuristic, in which judgments rely on similarity to a prototype
Representativeness concerns similarity to a prototype.
Confirmation bias, in which people seek information consistent with a prior belief
Confirmation bias concerns seeking supportive evidence, which was not measured.
qs.x: The numerical anchor biased estimates because adjustments away from it were insufficient. Trap: Selecting any named heuristic without matching it to what the manipulation actually varied.

qs.q: What was the anchoring index for novices?
o: 80% treats the 80-thousand difference in estimates as a percentage.
43% is the complement of the index (1 - 0.57).
29% is half of 57%, from incorrectly dividing by twice the anchor difference.
qs.x: (285 - 205) / (320 - 180) = 80 / 140 = 0.57. Trap: Using the raw difference in estimates, or its complement, as the index.

qs.q: Compared with novices, the agents' results indicate that expertise:
o: made agents completely immune to anchors because their estimates were more accurate overall
Agents' estimates still differed by 30 thousand across anchors.
increased anchoring because agents' estimates differed from novices' in both conditions
Agents' index is smaller, not larger.
had no relationship to anchoring since both groups showed significant anchor effects
The significant interaction shows the groups differed in the size of the effect.
reduced anchoring but did not eliminate it
Correct: Agents' index was (262 - 232) / 140 = 21%, lower than novices' 57%, but still nonzero.
qs.x: Agents' index was (262 - 232) / 140 = 21%, lower than novices' 57%, but still nonzero. Trap: Concluding that a significant effect in both groups means expertise has no effect.

qs.q: Which modification would best test whether anchoring occurs because participants assume the anchor is informative?
o: Double the number of real estate agents in each condition
A larger sample improves precision but does not address the mechanism.
Replace the house with a used car and keep the same procedure
A different object tests generality, not mechanism.
Have each participant give both a low-anchor and a high-anchor estimate
A within-subjects design changes carryover effects, not the informativeness of the anchor.
Tell participants that the anchor was set by a random coin toss
Correct: If an anchor known to be random still biases estimates, then perceived informativeness is not required; reduced bias would indicate it matters.
qs.x: If an anchor known to be random still biases estimates, then perceived informativeness is not required; reduced bias would indicate it matters. Trap: Choosing a design change that increases power or generality but does not manipulate the proposed mechanism.

passages.title: FL10 · Psych/Soc · Passage 6
text: Researchers examined whether recognition of facial emotion is shared across cultures and how expression is regulated. In Study 1, participants from three samples (a US university, a Japanese university, and a small rural Community R with little exposure to Western media; n = 60 each) viewed 36 posed photographs, six per emotion, and chose one of six emotion labels for each. Mean percent correct is shown in Table 1. Chance performance on each trial is 1 in 6. In Study 2, 40 students from each of the US and Japanese universities watched a disturbing film, either alone or with a high-status experimenter present, while hidden cameras recorded their faces. Trained coders rated spontaneous expression intensity (0-10). Study 2 results are shown in Table 2. Coders were blind to participants' nationality and condition. Participants in Study 2 gave informed consent and were debriefed after the film. In Study 1, photographs were presented in a random order, and each participant completed the task in a quiet room with no time limit. Differences among samples were tested with an analysis of variance (p < 0.01).

qs.q: Which result best supports the claim that the recognition results are not due to guessing?
o: Accuracy was higher in the US sample than in Community R for every emotion
A US advantage shows difference between samples but not that results exceed chance.
Fear was recognized less accurately than happiness in every sample
The ordering of emotions does not test guessing.
Accuracy for every emotion in all three samples was far above the 16.7% expected by chance
Correct: Chance is 1/6 = 16.7%, and the lowest accuracy in the table was 61%.
Japanese participants showed lower expression intensity in front of the experimenter
Study 2 concerns expression, not recognition.
qs.x: Chance is 1/6 = 16.7%, and the lowest accuracy in the table was 61%. Trap: Choosing a true statement from the data that does not actually address the question of chance.

qs.q: The reduced expression intensity of Japanese participants in front of the experimenter is best explained by:
o: an absence of the underlying emotion in Japanese individuals
Alone, Japanese participants showed intensity (7.1) equal to US participants, so the emotion was present.
a failure of Japanese participants to recognize facial emotion
Recognition in Japan was high.
culture-specific display rules
Correct: Display rules are cultural norms about when and how to show emotion; Japanese expression dropped only when a high-status observer was present.
the facial feedback effect, which amplifies expression when others are present
Facial feedback does not predict suppression with an observer present.
qs.x: Display rules are cultural norms about when and how to show emotion; Japanese expression dropped only when a high-status observer was present. Trap: Treating less outward expression as less felt emotion.

qs.q: For which emotion was the gap in accuracy between the US sample and Community R largest?
o: Disgust
Disgust gap was 16.
Anger
Anger gap was 13.
Happiness
Happiness gap was only 7.
Fear
Correct: Gaps were fear 19, disgust 16, anger 13, and happiness 7 percentage points.
qs.x: Gaps were fear 19, disgust 16, anger 13, and happiness 7 percentage points. Trap: Choosing the emotion with the lowest accuracy overall rather than computing the gap, though here the two coincide for fear only.

qs.q: The use of posed, static photographs in Study 1 most limits the conclusions because:
o: they may differ from the dynamic, context-dependent expressions people produce spontaneously
Correct: Posed static images may not reflect natural expressions, which limits ecological validity.
they prevent the computation of percent correct for each emotion
Percent correct can be computed from any forced-choice task.
they make chance performance impossible to determine for a six-choice task
Chance is 1/6 in a six-choice task.
they ensure that participants have already seen all of the expressions before
Prior exposure is not guaranteed by static photographs.
qs.x: Posed static images may not reflect natural expressions, which limits ecological validity. Trap: Confusing a limit on generalizability (ecological validity) with a limit on statistical computation.

passages.title: FL10 · Psych/Soc · Passage 7
text: Urban ecologists study how neighborhood conditions shape residents' outcomes. Researchers analyzed 40 neighborhoods in one city and grouped them into quartiles by poverty rate. A resident survey measured collective efficacy (social cohesion and willingness to intervene for the common good) on a 1-5 scale, and police records provided violent crimes per 1,000 residents. Quartile means are shown in Table 1. Figure 1 plots collective efficacy against crime rate for eight representative neighborhoods. Because residents are not randomly distributed across neighborhoods, the researchers also described a separate housing program in which low-income families were randomly chosen by lottery to receive vouchers for homes in low-poverty neighborhoods; control families received no voucher. Several years later, adolescents in voucher families reported better mental health than control adolescents (p = 0.01), although adult employment did not differ between groups. The correlation between collective efficacy and crime across all 40 neighborhoods was r = -0.88.

qs.q: The finding that neighborhoods with lower collective efficacy had more violence is most consistent with which framework?
o: Labeling theory, which emphasizes the effects of formal designations on identity
Labeling theory concerns reactions that create deviant identities.
Social disorganization theory from the Chicago school, linking weak community ties and informal control to crime
Correct: Social disorganization theory from the Chicago school links weak community ties and informal control to crime.
Differential association theory, which emphasizes learning of deviance through close contacts
Differential association concerns interpersonal learning of norms.
Strain theory, which emphasizes a gap between cultural goals and legitimate means
Strain theory concerns blocked access to goals.
qs.x: Social disorganization theory from the Chicago school links weak community ties and informal control to crime. Trap: Choosing a different well-known theory of deviance because it sounds individual rather than neighborhood-level.

qs.q: How many times higher was the violent crime rate in the highest-poverty quartile than in the lowest-poverty quartile?
o: 10.3 is the difference (12.4 - 2.1), not a ratio.
2.0 is not supported; the lowest-quartile rate is 2.1 per 1,000, not a ratio.
0.17 is the inverse ratio (2.1 / 12.4).
qs.x: 12.4 / 2.1 = 5.9. Trap: Subtracting the rates instead of dividing them, or inverting the ratio.

qs.q: Why can the voucher lottery, but not the neighborhood quartile data, support the claim that neighborhoods influence outcomes?
o: The lottery increased the number of neighborhoods in the sample from 40 to 80
The lottery does not change the number of neighborhoods analyzed.
Random assignment to move reduces self-selection of which families live in which neighborhoods
Correct: Random assignment makes voucher and control families comparable at baseline, so differences can be attributed to moving.
The quartile data cannot show any association between poverty and crime
The quartile data do show an association; they just cannot show causation.
The lottery demonstrated that employment was affected by the neighborhood as much as mental health
Employment did not differ between groups.
qs.x: Random assignment makes voucher and control families comparable at baseline, so differences can be attributed to moving. Trap: Concluding that observational data show no association rather than that they cannot establish causation.

qs.q: Using the first and last points in Figure 1, the approximate slope of the relationship between collective efficacy and crime rate is:
o: +5.7 crimes per 1,000 per unit of collective efficacy
The relationship is negative, so the sign is wrong.
-0.18 crimes per 1,000 per unit of collective efficacy
-0.18 is the inverse (2.1/11.9) of the slope.
-11.9 crimes per 1,000 per unit of collective efficacy
-11.9 is the rise only, not divided by the change in x.
-5.7 crimes per 1,000 per unit of collective efficacy
qs.x: (1.6 - 13.5) / (4.5 - 2.4) = -11.9 / 2.1 = -5.7. Trap: Reporting the change in y without dividing by the change in x.

passages.title: FL10 · Psych/Soc · Passage 8
text: Globalization has increased the movement of workers across borders. A sociologist examined one lower-middle-income country over 15 years. National statistics recorded the number of workers living abroad, total annual remittances (money sent home by emigrants), gross domestic product (GDP), and the domestic unemployment rate. Values are shown in Table 1. Figure 1 plots remittances as a share of GDP and the unemployment rate over time. In interviews with 120 emigrants, most said they left because wages abroad were several times higher than at home, while a minority cited family reunification. Most remittances were spent on household consumption, schooling, and housing. Officials also reported that the proportion of emigrants with university degrees was higher than the proportion in the national workforce. The study was descriptive; there was no comparison country, and the interview sample was recruited through emigrant community associations. Each interview lasted about an hour and was conducted in the emigrant's home language. The sociologist used official statistics for all numerical comparisons, and the unemployment rate was defined as the share of the labor force without work who were seeking it.

qs.q: High domestic unemployment and low wages in the origin country are examples of which type of migration factor?
o: Push factors
Correct: Conditions at the origin that encourage people to leave are push factors; higher wages abroad are pull factors.
Pull factors that attract migrants to a destination country
Pull factors are conditions at the destination.
Intervening obstacles that hinder migration between origin and destination
Intervening obstacles are barriers such as costs and laws.
Chain migration processes in which earlier migrants help later ones
Chain migration refers to network assistance.
qs.x: Conditions at the origin that encourage people to leave are push factors; higher wages abroad are pull factors. Trap: Labeling high foreign wages and low home wages with the same term instead of separating push from pull.

qs.q: Remittances as a percentage of GDP in 2005 were closest to:
o: 1.8% does not follow from any row; 1,980 / 27,000 is about 7.3%.
10.0% is the 2010 and 2015 value.
5.0% is the 2000 value.
qs.x: 1,980 / 27,000 = 0.0733, or 7.3%. Trap: Reading the percentage for a neighboring year rather than computing from the 2005 row.

qs.q: By about what percentage did the average remittance per emigrant worker increase from 2000 to 2015?
o: 35% does not match the per-worker figures (it would require about $12,400 per emigrant in 2015).
158% is the increase in the number of emigrant workers (120 to 310), not in remittance per worker.
258% is the ratio of emigrant numbers expressed as a percentage (310/120), not a per-worker change.
qs.x: 2000: 1,100 / 120 = 9.17 thousand USD; 2015: 4,350 / 310 = 14.03; (14.03 - 9.17) / 9.17 = 53%. Trap: Using the change in total remittances or number of emigrants rather than the per-worker average.

qs.q: A sociologist argues that continued reliance on remittances and the loss of skilled workers leave the country economically dependent on wealthier nations. This argument reflects which perspective?
o: World-systems (dependency) theory, which describes peripheral economies' reliance on core economies
Correct: World-systems and dependency theories describe how peripheral economies depend on core economies.
Structural functionalism, which emphasizes the contribution of each part to social stability
Functionalism concerns stability and function of institutions.
Symbolic interactionism, which emphasizes shared meanings in face-to-face interaction
Symbolic interactionism concerns meanings in micro-level interaction.
Rational choice theory, which emphasizes individuals' cost-benefit calculations in each decision
Rational choice explains individual decisions, not structural dependency.
qs.x: World-systems and dependency theories describe how peripheral economies depend on core economies. Trap: Choosing rational choice because migrants are described as seeking higher wages, though the claim is about structural dependence.

passages.title: FL10 · Psych/Soc · Passage 9
text: Intergenerational mobility describes how children's economic positions relate to their parents'. Researchers linked tax records for 100,000 parent-child pairs in one country. Parents' household income (averaged over ages 40 to 45) and children's household income (averaged over ages 35 to 40) were each ranked into quintiles within their generation. Table 1 shows, for each parental quintile, the percentage of children who ended in each quintile (rows sum to 100). The researchers also calculated, separately for two regions, the percentage of children from bottom-quintile families who reached the top quintile in four birth cohorts. These results are plotted in Figure 1. Sample sizes within each region and cohort exceeded 5,000 pairs, and the standard error for each percentage was below 0.5 percentage points. The study is observational and cannot determine which family or school characteristics produce the patterns. Incomes were adjusted for inflation, and pairs were included only if both parent and child had positive reported income in the averaging years. Quintile boundaries were computed separately for the parent and child generations.

qs.q: According to Table 1, what percentage of children from bottom-quintile families ended above the bottom quintile as adults?
o: 34% is the percentage who stayed in the bottom quintile.
8% is the percentage who reached the top quintile.
Correct: 100 - 34 = 66%; equivalently 26 + 20 + 12 + 8.
92% is the percentage who did not reach the top quintile.
qs.x: 100 - 34 = 66%; equivalently 26 + 20 + 12 + 8. Trap: Reading the first cell of the row rather than summing the other cells.

qs.q: How many times more likely is a child from a top-quintile family to be in the top quintile than a child from a bottom-quintile family?
o: About 5.4 times
Correct: 43 / 8 = 5.4.
About 35 times
35 is the difference in percentage points, not a ratio.
About 1.3 times
1.3 does not follow from the table.
About 0.19 times
0.19 is the inverse ratio (8/43).
qs.x: 43 / 8 = 5.4. Trap: Subtracting percentages and calling it a ratio.

qs.q: Which statement is supported by Figure 1?
o: In the North the chance rose across cohorts, whereas in the South it fell
Both regions declined.
The gap between the regions widened with each successive birth cohort
The gap narrowed, not widened.
In both regions the chance of rising to the top fell across cohorts, and the gap between regions narrowed
Correct: North fell from 12 to 8.5 and South from 7 to 6, so the gap went from 5 to 2.5 points.
In both regions the chance remained constant across all four cohorts
Neither region was constant.
qs.x: North fell from 12 to 8.5 and South from 7 to 6, so the gap went from 5 to 2.5 points. Trap: Describing a falling line as constant because the South's changes look small.

qs.q: Because Table 1 compares children's income positions with their parents' positions, it measures:
o: intragenerational mobility, the change in one person's position over a lifetime
Intragenerational mobility follows the same person over time.
structural mobility, produced by changes in the number of available occupations
Structural mobility concerns shifts in the occupational structure, and quintile ranks remove overall growth.
intergenerational mobility, expressed in relative terms based on income rank
Correct: Linking parents' and children's ranks measures relative intergenerational mobility.
absolute poverty, defined as the lack of income needed for basic needs
Absolute poverty uses a fixed standard, not income ranks.
qs.x: Linking parents' and children's ranks measures relative intergenerational mobility. Trap: Confusing movement across generations with movement within one person's career.

passages.title: FL10 · Psych/Soc · Passage 10
text: A school district offered an after-school tutoring program to students who scored in the lowest 10% on a standardized mathematics test (district mean 70, SD 10). Of 200 low scorers, 100 families chose to enroll their children (tutored group) and 100 did not (untutored group). All 200 students retook an equivalent form of the test at the end of the year. As a comparison, a random sample of 100 students from the whole district, not selected by score, was also retested. The test-retest correlation of the two forms in the district was r = 0.80. Group means are shown in Table 1. Because tutored students were selected based on a low pretest score and had parents who chose to participate, the district's analyst warned that the 7-point gain in the tutored group could not be interpreted as the effect of tutoring alone. The expected posttest mean for a group with a given pretest mean is calculated as the district mean plus r times the difference between the group's pretest mean and the district mean.

qs.q: The 4-point improvement among untutored low scorers is most likely due to:
o: maturation of the selected students that did not occur in the random sample
Maturation would also affect the random sample, which did not change.
a placebo effect resulting from the students' belief that they were being helped
Untutored students received no treatment to create a placebo effect.
practice effects that apply only to students with low pretest scores
Practice would raise the random sample's scores too.
regression to the mean after selection on extreme scores
Correct: Selecting extreme low scorers on an imperfectly reliable test leads their retest scores to move toward the mean, while the unselected group did not change.
qs.x: Selecting extreme low scorers on an imperfectly reliable test leads their retest scores to move toward the mean, while the unselected group did not change. Trap: Attributing the improvement of a group that received no treatment to some treatment-like effect.

qs.q: Using the stated formula, the expected posttest mean for the low scorers because of regression alone is:
o: 52.0 would be expected only if the retest were perfectly reliable (r = 1).
59.2 results from using r = 0.60.
70.0 would be expected if r = 0.
qs.x: 70 + 0.80 x (52 - 70) = 70 - 14.4 = 55.6. Trap: Assuming no regression (r = 1) or complete regression (r = 0).

qs.q: Compared with the untutored low scorers, the tutored low scorers gained an additional:
o: 3 points
Correct: Tutored change (+7) minus untutored change (+4) equals 3 points (59 - 56).
7 points
7 points is the total gain, which includes regression and self-selection.
4 points
4 points is the untutored group's gain.
11 points
11 points adds the two gains.
qs.x: Tutored change (+7) minus untutored change (+4) equals 3 points (59 - 56). Trap: Attributing the entire 7-point gain to tutoring.

qs.q: Which change in design would best allow the district to estimate the effect of tutoring?
o: Randomly assign the low scorers to tutoring or to a no-tutoring comparison group of similar students
Correct: Random assignment among equally low scorers balances regression and parental choice across groups.
Enroll only the students whose parents requested tutoring and compare them with their own earlier scores
A before-after design for self-selected students is vulnerable to regression.
Compare the tutored students with the random district sample instead of with low scorers
The random sample starts at a very different level, so it is not comparable.
Retest the tutored group several times and use the highest score for each student
Using the highest scores biases results upward.
qs.x: Random assignment among equally low scorers balances regression and parental choice across groups. Trap: Using a pretest-posttest comparison within one self-selected group as if it were controlled.

questions.q: At pH 7.4, in a native gel electrophoresis experiment, a protein with an isoelectric point of 9.5 will most likely migrate toward:
o: the anode, because the protein has a net positive charge
positive molecules move toward the cathode, not the anode
the cathode, because the protein has a net negative charge
a negative protein would move toward the anode
neither electrode, because the net charge is zero
zero charge occurs only at pH = pI (9.5)
the cathode, because the protein has a net positive charge
Correct: A pH below the pI protonates the protein, giving a net positive charge, so it moves toward the negative electrode (cathode).
questions.x: A pH below the pI protonates the protein, giving a net positive charge, so it moves toward the negative electrode (cathode). Trap: Mixing up the direction of migration of cations and anions or misreading pH relative to pI.

questions.q: A purified antibody migrates at 150 kDa on SDS-PAGE without a reducing agent. With beta-mercaptoethanol, bands are seen at 50 kDa and 25 kDa. These data are most consistent with an antibody composed of:
o: one 50 kDa and one 25 kDa chain linked by hydrogen bonds
one of each chain sums to 75 kDa, and SDS disrupts hydrogen bonds anyway
two heavy and two light chains linked by disulfide bonds
Correct: Reducing agents break disulfides: 2(50) + 2(25) = 150 kDa, so four chains are held together by disulfide bonds.
three 50 kDa chains linked by disulfide bonds
three 50 kDa chains would not produce a 25 kDa band and total 150 without light chains
one 150 kDa chain with internal peptide bonds cleaved
beta-mercaptoethanol does not cleave peptide bonds
questions.x: Reducing agents break disulfides: 2(50) + 2(25) = 150 kDa, so four chains are held together by disulfide bonds. Trap: Ignoring that the two bands must sum to the total mass in the unreduced state.

questions.q: A template strand has the sequence 3'-TACGGATTC-5'. What is the sequence of the mRNA transcribed from it?
o: 5'-AUGCCUAAG-3'
Correct: mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template and uses uracil: 5'-AUGCCUAAG-3'.
5'-UACGGAUUC-3'
this copies the template without complementing, and the polarity is wrong
3'-AUGCCUAAG-5'
this is complementary but the strand polarity is written backwards
5'-ATGCCTAAG-3'
mRNA contains uracil, not thymine
questions.x: mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template and uses uracil: 5'-AUGCCUAAG-3'. Trap: Writing the template sequence with T replaced by U instead of the complement.

questions.q: Cells lacking telomerase activity are cultured through many divisions. Which outcome is most likely?
o: Telomere lengthening through repeated lagging-strand synthesis at chromosome ends
lagging-strand synthesis causes the end-replication problem rather than lengthening
Loss of centromeres in daughter chromosomes, causing missegregation at anaphase
centromeres are not affected
Increase in Okazaki fragment length, which slows replication of the lagging strand
Okazaki fragment length is unrelated to telomerase
Progressive telomere shortening, eventually leading to senescence or apoptosis
Correct: DNA polymerase cannot fully replicate the 3' end of the lagging strand, so telomeres shorten each division unless telomerase extends them.
questions.x: DNA polymerase cannot fully replicate the 3' end of the lagging strand, so telomeres shorten each division unless telomerase extends them. Trap: Believing that lagging-strand synthesis maintains chromosome ends without telomerase.

questions.q: Three linked genes have recombination frequencies of 12% between A and B, 5% between B and C, and 7% between A and C. What is the gene order?
o: A-B-C
A-B-C would require A-C = 17
A-C-B
Correct: The largest distance (A-B = 12) is the sum of the other two (7 + 5), so C lies between A and B.
B-A-C
B-A-C would require B-C = 19
C-A-B
C-A-B would require C-B = 19, the sum of the other two distances
questions.x: The largest distance (A-B = 12) is the sum of the other two (7 + 5), so C lies between A and B. Trap: Ordering genes by the letters given instead of from the largest distance.

questions.q: In regions where malaria is endemic, the sickle cell allele remains at a substantial frequency in the population. Which concept best explains this?
o: Homozygotes for the sickle cell allele have the highest fitness
homozygous sickle cell individuals have severe disease
The allele is selectively neutral and maintained by genetic drift
strong, repeatable geographic patterns are not typical of drift
Heterozygotes have higher fitness than either homozygote
Correct: Heterozygotes are protected against severe malaria without sickle cell disease, maintaining both alleles (balancing selection).
The allele is maintained by repeated back mutation from the normal allele
mutation rates are too low to maintain the frequency
questions.x: Heterozygotes are protected against severe malaria without sickle cell disease, maintaining both alleles (balancing selection). Trap: Attributing high allele frequency to dominance or neutrality instead of selection.

questions.q: Which change would most likely increase the activity of phosphofructokinase-1 in a hepatocyte?
o: Increased fructose-2,6-bisphosphate
Correct: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is the most potent allosteric activator of PFK-1, promoting glycolysis in the fed state.
Increased citrate
citrate signals abundant biosynthetic precursors and inhibits PFK-1
Increased ATP
high ATP is an allosteric inhibitor
Decreased AMP
AMP activates PFK-1, so a decrease would lower activity
questions.x: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is the most potent allosteric activator of PFK-1, promoting glycolysis in the fed state. Trap: Mistaking inhibitors for activators when the energy charge is considered.

questions.q: Complete beta-oxidation of one molecule of palmitoyl-CoA (16 carbons) produces how many FADH2?
o: 8 is the number of acetyl-CoA
15 is not related to the number of cycles
16 is the number of carbons
Correct: A 16-carbon fatty acid needs 7 cycles of beta-oxidation, each producing one FADH2 and one NADH, plus 8 acetyl-CoA.
questions.x: A 16-carbon fatty acid needs 7 cycles of beta-oxidation, each producing one FADH2 and one NADH, plus 8 acetyl-CoA. Trap: Equating the number of cycles to the number of acetyl-CoA produced.

questions.q: A mutation in the genes encoding claudins disrupts the tight junctions of an epithelium. Which defect would most likely result?
o: Increased paracellular leakage and loss of apical-basolateral protein segregation
Correct: Tight junctions seal the space between cells and keep apical and basolateral proteins separate.
Loss of the ability to anchor cells to the basal lamina through integrin-based contacts
hemidesmosomes anchor cells to the basal lamina
Loss of cytoplasmic communication between adjacent cells through connexin channels
gap junctions allow cytoplasmic communication
Loss of the keratin network inside cells, weakening their resistance to mechanical stress
keratin is a cytoplasmic intermediate filament and is not a claudin
questions.x: Tight junctions seal the space between cells and keep apical and basolateral proteins separate. Trap: Confusing the functions of tight junctions, gap junctions, and desmosomes.

questions.q: A drug blocks reverse transcriptase in cells infected with a retrovirus. Which step is directly prevented?
o: Synthesis of DNA from the viral RNA genome
Correct: Reverse transcriptase copies viral RNA into DNA, which is later integrated into the host genome.
Translation of viral proteins from viral RNA
translation uses host ribosomes and does not require reverse transcriptase
Assembly of virions at the plasma membrane
assembly occurs later and does not require reverse transcriptase
Entry of the virus by receptor-mediated endocytosis
entry occurs before reverse transcription
questions.x: Reverse transcriptase copies viral RNA into DNA, which is later integrated into the host genome. Trap: Assigning the enzyme to translation or assembly steps because they involve viral RNA.

questions.q: Nondisjunction of one homologous pair during meiosis I in a human spermatocyte would result in:
o: four gametes, none of which has the normal chromosome number for that pair
Correct: In meiosis I, homologs fail to separate, so both daughter cells are abnormal, and all four gametes are n+1 or n-1 for that chromosome.
two normal gametes and two with an extra chromosome
two normal gametes arise only from meiosis II nondisjunction, which also gives one n+1 and one n-1 gamete, not two with extra copies
Two gametes with the normal number of chromosomes and two lacking that chromosome
an error in meiosis I affects both daughter cells, so two normal gametes cannot result
one abnormal gamete and three normal gametes
a single abnormal gamete does not match either meiotic division
questions.x: In meiosis I, homologs fail to separate, so both daughter cells are abnormal, and all four gametes are n+1 or n-1 for that chromosome. Trap: Confusing the outcomes of meiosis I and meiosis II nondisjunction.

questions.q: A cell with a loss-of-function mutation in TP53 experiences DNA damage. Compared with a normal cell, it is more likely to:
o: arrest in G1 so that the damage can be repaired
G1 arrest is caused by p53-induced p21
continue through the cell cycle without repair or apoptosis
Correct: p53 normally induces p21 and apoptotic genes after DNA damage; without it, checkpoints fail and mutations can be propagated.
undergo apoptosis through activation of caspases
apoptosis is promoted by p53
increase expression of the CDK inhibitor p21
p21 is a target of p53 and would not increase
questions.x: p53 normally induces p21 and apoptotic genes after DNA damage; without it, checkpoints fail and mutations can be propagated. Trap: Reversing the effect of a loss-of-function mutation in a tumor suppressor.

questions.q: Damage to the dorsal root of a spinal nerve would most likely cause:
o: loss of motor function in the corresponding region, with sensation preserved there
motor deficits result from ventral root damage
loss of both sensation and motor function in the corresponding region of the body
both roots are required to be damaged for loss of both
loss of the autonomic control of the heart and of voluntary movement in the arm
cardiac control uses cranial and sympathetic pathways, not this root
loss of sensation from the corresponding region with preserved motor function
Correct: Sensory neurons carry afferent signals into the cord through the dorsal root; motor neurons leave through the ventral root.
questions.x: Sensory neurons carry afferent signals into the cord through the dorsal root; motor neurons leave through the ventral root. Trap: Reversing the dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) roots.

questions.q: During intense exercise, hemoglobin in the muscle capillaries most likely shows:
o: increased oxygen affinity from increased CO2 and H+, so less oxygen is released
higher CO2 and H+ decrease hemoglobin affinity
decreased oxygen affinity from decreased temperature, so more oxygen is released
exercise increases, not decreases, temperature, and a lower temperature increases affinity
increased oxygen affinity from increased 2,3-BPG, so less oxygen is released
2,3-BPG increases release of oxygen by lowering affinity
decreased oxygen affinity from increased CO2 and H+, releasing more oxygen
Correct: Lower pH, higher CO2, and higher temperature shift the curve to the right (Bohr effect), favoring release of oxygen to tissue.
questions.x: Lower pH, higher CO2, and higher temperature shift the curve to the right (Bohr effect), favoring release of oxygen to tissue. Trap: Shifting the curve in the wrong direction for the Bohr effect.

questions.q: Acidic chyme entering the duodenum stimulates the release of secretin, which acts on the pancreas to:
o: increase bicarbonate secretion to neutralize acid
Correct: Secretin from duodenal S cells promotes bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice, which raises the duodenal pH.
increase secretion of pancreatic lipase only
lipase secretion is stimulated mainly by cholecystokinin
decrease secretion of bicarbonate
bicarbonate is increased, not decreased
stimulate release of gastric acid from parietal cells
gastrin, not secretin, stimulates gastric acid release
questions.x: Secretin from duodenal S cells promotes bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice, which raises the duodenal pH. Trap: Confusing the roles of secretin and cholecystokinin.

questions.q: A ball is thrown horizontally at 20 m/s from the edge of a 45 m cliff. Neglecting air resistance and using g = 10 m/s², how far from the base of the cliff does it land?
o: Correct: Fall time: 45 = ½(10)t², so t = 3 s. Horizontal distance = 20 m/s × 3 s = 60 m.
30 m uses a 1.5 s fall time, which corresponds to dropping 11 m rather than 45 m.
90 m would require a 4.5 s fall time (using h/g).
120 m comes from using t = 6 s, double the correct fall time.
questions.x: Fall time: 45 = ½(10)t², so t = 3 s. Horizontal distance = 20 m/s × 3 s = 60 m. Trap: Mixing up the fall-time formula, for example using t = h/g instead of √(2h/g).

questions.q: A 40 kg child sits 1.5 m from the pivot of a uniform seesaw. At what distance from the pivot on the other side must a 30 kg child sit to balance the seesaw?
o: Correct: At balance the torques are equal: 40(1.5) = 30d, so d = 2.0 m. The lighter child needs a longer lever arm.
1.1 m results from inverting the ratio (1.5 × 30/40).
1.5 m would only balance if the masses were equal.
3.0 m would be correct only if the mass ratio were 2:1.
questions.x: At balance the torques are equal: 40(1.5) = 30d, so d = 2.0 m. The lighter child needs a longer lever arm. Trap: Inverting the mass ratio so the lighter child sits closer to the pivot.

questions.q: What is the approximate absolute pressure at the bottom of a lake at a depth of 10 m? (Density of water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s², atmospheric pressure = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa)
o: 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa is only atmospheric pressure and ignores the water.
9.8 × 10⁴ Pa is the gauge pressure and omits the atmosphere.
3.0 × 10⁵ Pa would be reached at about 20 m depth.
questions.x: P = P_atm + ρgh = 1.0 × 10⁵ + (1000)(9.8)(10) = 1.0 × 10⁵ + 0.98 × 10⁵ ≈ 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Trap: Giving gauge pressure when absolute pressure is asked for.

questions.q: In the circuit, a 12 V battery is connected in series to a 4.0 Ω resistor, which is in series with a parallel combination of a 6.0 Ω resistor and a 3.0 Ω resistor. What is the current through the 6.0 Ω resistor?
o: 1.3 A is the current in the 3.0 Ω resistor (4.0/3.0).
2.0 A is the total current from the battery, which splits between the two parallel branches.
1.0 A would result from an equal split or wrong voltage.
Correct: The parallel pair equals (6 × 3)/(6 + 3) = 2.0 Ω, so the total is 6.0 Ω and I = 2.0 A. The parallel pair has 2.0 A × 2.0 Ω = 4.0 V across it, so I(6 Ω) = 4.0/6.0 = 0.67 A.
questions.x: The parallel pair equals (6 × 3)/(6 + 3) = 2.0 Ω, so the total is 6.0 Ω and I = 2.0 A. The parallel pair has 2.0 A × 2.0 Ω = 4.0 V across it, so I(6 Ω) = 4.0/6.0 = 0.67 A. Trap: Giving the total current instead of the current in one parallel branch.

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor remains connected to a battery while the plate separation is doubled. What happens to the energy stored in the capacitor?
o: It doubles.
Doubling d does not increase C or U; capacitance falls when plates are farther apart.
It is reduced to one quarter of its original value.
A quarter would apply if both C and V were halved, but V is held fixed by the battery.
It is reduced to half its original value.
Correct: C = ε₀A/d, so doubling d halves C. With V fixed by the battery, U = ½CV² is halved.
It stays the same.
U depends on C, which changed.
questions.x: C = ε₀A/d, so doubling d halves C. With V fixed by the battery, U = ½CV² is halved. Trap: Assuming charge is fixed rather than voltage when the battery remains connected.

questions.q: An object is placed 30 cm from a converging lens with focal length 10 cm. Which describes the image?
o: Virtual, upright, and larger than the object
A virtual, upright, magnified image occurs only when the object is inside the focal length.
Real, inverted, and smaller than the object
Correct: 1/v = 1/10 − 1/30 = 1/15, so v = +15 cm (real, on the opposite side). Magnification = −15/30 = −0.5, so the image is inverted and half the size.
Real, inverted, and the same size as the object
A same-size real image occurs when the object is at 2f (20 cm).
Virtual, upright, and smaller than the object
A converging lens makes virtual images only for objects inside f, and these are enlarged.
questions.x: 1/v = 1/10 − 1/30 = 1/15, so v = +15 cm (real, on the opposite side). Magnification = −15/30 = −0.5, so the image is inverted and half the size. Trap: Mixing up the 2f case (same size) with an object beyond 2f (smaller).

questions.q: A pipe closed at one end and open at the other has length 0.85 m. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, what is the fundamental frequency?
o: 100 Hz
Correct: A closed pipe has a node at the closed end and antinode at the open end, so λ = 4L = 3.4 m and f = 340/3.4 = 100 Hz.
200 Hz
200 Hz is the fundamental of a pipe open at both ends (v/2L).
400 Hz
400 Hz is the fundamental if the wavelength were L.
50 Hz
50 Hz would apply to an 1.7 m pipe or λ = 2 × 3.4.
questions.x: A closed pipe has a node at the closed end and antinode at the open end, so λ = 4L = 3.4 m and f = 340/3.4 = 100 Hz. Trap: Using λ = 2L, which applies to a pipe open at both ends.

questions.q: Light of wavelength 400 nm strikes a metal with work function 2.0 eV. Use hc = 1240 eV·nm. What is the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons?
o: 2.0 eV
2.0 eV is the work function, the minimum energy needed to free an electron.
3.1 eV
3.1 eV is the total photon energy, not the kinetic energy left after overcoming the work function.
1.1 eV
Correct: The photon energy is 1240/400 = 3.1 eV, so KEmax = hf − φ = 3.1 − 2.0 = 1.1 eV.
5.1 eV
5.1 eV adds the work function instead of subtracting it.
questions.x: The photon energy is 1240/400 = 3.1 eV, so KEmax = hf − φ = 3.1 − 2.0 = 1.1 eV. Trap: Adding the work function to the photon energy instead of subtracting it.

questions.q: The Ksp of AgCl is 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. What is the equilibrium concentration of Ag⁺ in a saturated solution of AgCl that is also 0.10 M in NaCl?
o: 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M is the solubility in pure water (√Ksp), without the common ion.
1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ M is Ksp itself, not a concentration.
1.8 × 10⁻¹¹ M comes from dividing by 10 instead of dividing by 0.10.
Correct: [Ag⁺] = Ksp/[Cl⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ / 0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M, because of the common-ion effect.
questions.x: [Ag⁺] = Ksp/[Cl⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ / 0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M, because of the common-ion effect. Trap: Using the pure-water solubility (square root of Ksp) despite the common ion present.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide has polar C=O bonds, yet the CO₂ molecule is nonpolar. Which explains this?
o: The molecule is linear, so the two bond dipoles cancel.
Correct: VSEPR predicts linear geometry with two electron domains on carbon; the equal and opposite dipoles give a net dipole moment of zero.
The C=O bonds are actually nonpolar because carbon and oxygen have equal electronegativity.
Oxygen is significantly more electronegative than carbon, so each C=O bond is polar.
The molecule is bent, which gives dipoles that cancel.
A bent shape (like water or SO₂) leaves a net dipole.
Carbon dioxide has lone pairs on carbon that cancel the dipoles.
Carbon in CO₂ has no lone pairs.
questions.x: VSEPR predicts linear geometry with two electron domains on carbon; the equal and opposite dipoles give a net dipole moment of zero. Trap: Assuming that polar bonds always produce a polar molecule.

questions.q: In SDS-PAGE, a mixture of proteins of 15 kDa, 50 kDa, and 150 kDa is separated. Which statement is correct after the run?
o: The 15 kDa protein migrates farthest toward the anode.

Correct: SDS coats proteins with negative charge in proportion to their mass, so separation is determined by size: smaller proteins move through the gel matrix more easily and migrate farther toward the positive electrode.
The 150 kDa protein migrates farthest toward the anode.
Larger proteins are slowed more by the gel pores and so migrate less.
All three proteins migrate the same distance because SDS gives them equal charge.
Equal charge-to-mass ratio does not equalize migration; the gel acts as a sieve.
The proteins migrate toward the cathode, with the smallest protein moving most.
SDS-coated proteins are negatively charged and move to the anode (positive electrode).
questions.x: SDS coats proteins with negative charge in proportion to their mass, so separation is determined by size: smaller proteins move through the gel matrix more easily and migrate farther toward the positive electrode. Trap: Forgetting that SDS-coated proteins have similar charge density, so size alone determines mobility.

questions.q: Alanine is dissolved in a solution of pH 1.0. Which statement describes the predominant form of the amino acid?
o: It is a zwitterion with no net charge.
The zwitterion predominates near the isoelectric point (pH ≈ 6), not at pH 1.
The amino group is protonated and the carboxylate is deprotonated, with net charge −1.
At pH 1 the carboxyl is protonated, so the net charge cannot be −1.
Both the amino group and the carboxyl group are protonated, and the net charge is +1.
Correct: At pH well below the carboxyl pKa (~2.3), the COOH is protonated (neutral) and the amino group (pKa ~9.7) is protonated (+1), so the net charge is +1.
The amino group is neutral and the carboxylic acid is deprotonated, with net charge −1.
At low pH the amine is protonated, and the net charge is not negative.
questions.x: At pH well below the carboxyl pKa (~2.3), the COOH is protonated (neutral) and the amino group (pKa ~9.7) is protonated (+1), so the net charge is +1. Trap: Assuming the zwitterion is the dominant form at any pH.

questions.q: 1-Propanol is treated with pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) in dichloromethane. What is the major organic product?
o: Propanoic acid
Propanoic acid would result from stronger aqueous oxidants such as chromic acid (Jones).
Propanal
Correct: PCC is a mild oxidant that, in anhydrous conditions, stops at the aldehyde stage for a primary alcohol.
Propanone
Propanone is the oxidation product of 2-propanol, a secondary alcohol.
Propene
PCC is not a dehydrating agent, so no alkene forms.
questions.x: PCC is a mild oxidant that, in anhydrous conditions, stops at the aldehyde stage for a primary alcohol. Trap: Over-oxidizing a primary alcohol to the carboxylic acid when a mild oxidant is used.

questions.q: Given C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −394 kJ/mol, and CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −283 kJ/mol, what is ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g)?
o: −111 kJ/mol
Correct: Reverse the second reaction (+283) and add it to the first (−394): −394 + 283 = −111 kJ/mol.
−677 kJ/mol
−677 kJ/mol adds both values without reversing the second equation.
+111 kJ/mol
+111 kJ/mol has the correct magnitude but the wrong sign.
−283 kJ/mol
−283 kJ/mol is the value for oxidizing CO to CO₂, not for forming CO.
questions.x: Reverse the second reaction (+283) and add it to the first (−394): −394 + 283 = −111 kJ/mol. Trap: Forgetting to reverse an equation (and flip the sign of ΔH) when applying Hess's law.

questions.q: The Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), is exothermic. What is the effect of increasing the temperature on the equilibrium constant K and the equilibrium yield of NH₃?
o: K increases, and the equilibrium yield of NH₃ increases.
K and yield rise with temperature for an endothermic reaction only.
K decreases, and the equilibrium yield of NH₃ decreases.
Correct: For an exothermic reaction, heat acts as a product, so adding heat shifts the equilibrium toward reactants. K, which depends only on temperature, decreases, and so does the NH₃ yield.
K is unchanged, and the equilibrium yield of NH₃ decreases.
K is temperature dependent, so it changes when T changes.
K decreases, and the equilibrium yield of NH₃ increases.
K and the equilibrium composition are linked; a smaller K means less product, not more.
questions.x: For an exothermic reaction, heat acts as a product, so adding heat shifts the equilibrium toward reactants. K, which depends only on temperature, decreases, and so does the NH₃ yield. Trap: Thinking K is constant when temperature changes (only concentration changes leave K unchanged).

questions.q: A person rubs her elbow immediately after striking it, and the pain lessens. According to the gate control theory of pain, this occurs because:
o: rubbing destroys the nociceptors in the elbow so pain signals can no longer be generated or transmitted.
Nociceptors are not destroyed by rubbing; their signaling is modulated.
rubbing triggers release of cortisol, which blocks transmission along C fibers.
Cortisol release is a slow hormonal effect and does not explain immediate relief.
activation of large-diameter touch fibers excites inhibitory interneurons that reduce pain transmission in the spinal cord.
Correct: A-beta touch input closes the 'gate' by activating inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn, reducing relay of nociceptive signals.
touch fibers travel to the thalamus faster than pain fibers and cancel the pain signals in the cortex.
The gate operates in the spinal cord, before the thalamus and cortex.
questions.x: A-beta touch input closes the 'gate' by activating inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn, reducing relay of nociceptive signals. Trap: Placing the pain-modulating mechanism in the brain instead of the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.

questions.q: In a signal detection experiment, an observer adopts a stricter criterion for reporting that a faint tone was present, while sensitivity does not change. Compared with before, the observer will have:
o: more hits and more false alarms, with no change in sensitivity.
More of both occurs with a more lenient criterion.
fewer hits and more false alarms, with no change in sensitivity.
The two rates move in the same direction when only the criterion shifts.
fewer hits and fewer false alarms, with no change in sensitivity.
Correct: A stricter criterion makes the observer say 'yes' less often, lowering both hits and false alarms without changing the sensitivity (d').
more hits and fewer false alarms, with no change in sensitivity.
Gaining hits while losing false alarms would require an increase in sensitivity.
questions.x: A stricter criterion makes the observer say 'yes' less often, lowering both hits and false alarms without changing the sensitivity (d'). Trap: Believing that criterion shifts trade hits for false alarms in opposite directions.

questions.q: A patient with bilateral hippocampal damage cannot recall meeting her doctor earlier in the day but improves from day to day on a mirror-tracing task without any memory of having practiced. These findings indicate that:
o: explicit and procedural memory share a single system located in the hippocampus and temporal lobes.
If one system served both, the skill learning would be lost.
procedural memory depends on systems other than those needed for new explicit memories.
Correct: Impaired explicit encoding with intact skill learning shows a dissociation: skills rely on basal ganglia and cerebellum.
the patient has retrograde amnesia only, with intact formation of new memories.
She cannot form new memories, which is anterograde amnesia; retrograde amnesia is loss of old memories.
procedural memories are stored in Wernicke's area and retrieved there.
Wernicke's area is a language comprehension region.
questions.x: Impaired explicit encoding with intact skill learning shows a dissociation: skills rely on basal ganglia and cerebellum. Trap: Assuming all memory types depend on the hippocampus.

questions.q: A 6-year-old watches water poured from a short, wide glass into a tall, thin glass and says that the tall glass now holds more water. According to Piaget, this child is most likely in the:
o: preoperational stage.
Correct: Failure to conserve volume because attention centers on one dimension (height) is typical of the preoperational stage.
sensorimotor stage.
The sensorimotor stage (birth to about age 2) involves object permanence.
concrete operational stage.
Concrete operational children understand conservation.
formal operational stage.
Formal operational thinking involves abstract hypothetical reasoning in adolescence.
questions.x: Failure to conserve volume because attention centers on one dimension (height) is typical of the preoperational stage. Trap: Assigning the stage by age alone without using the conservation clue.

questions.q: A man feels his heart pounding and his hands trembling after a near-collision, and he concludes that he must be afraid. This sequence is most consistent with:
o: the Cannon-Bard theory of emotion.
Cannon-Bard holds that arousal and emotional experience occur simultaneously and independently.
the Yerkes-Dodson law.
The Yerkes-Dodson law relates arousal to performance, not the origin of emotional experience.
the James-Lange theory of emotion.
Correct: James-Lange proposes that perception of bodily arousal produces the emotion; here arousal precedes the emotional labeling.
the opponent-process theory of emotion.
Opponent-process theory is about the aftereffects of emotional experiences, not their onset.
questions.x: James-Lange proposes that perception of bodily arousal produces the emotion; here arousal precedes the emotional labeling. Trap: Choosing the better-known multi-factor theory when the sequence described is simple arousal then feeling.

questions.q: In a twin study of a personality trait, the twin correlation is r = 0.50 for monozygotic pairs and r = 0.20 for dizygotic pairs. Using Falconer's formula, heritability = 2 x (r_MZ - r_DZ), the estimated heritability is:
o: 0.30 is the difference without the factor of 2.
0.70 is the sum of the two values, not the formula's difference.
1.00 would mean the trait is entirely genetic, which these data do not show.
questions.x: 2 x (0.50 - 0.20) = 2 x 0.30 = 0.60. Trap: Omitting the factor of 2 in Falconer's formula.

questions.q: A gambler keeps pulling a slot machine lever even though wins are unpredictable and sporadic. Which reinforcement schedule is operating, and why does it produce this pattern?
o: Fixed ratio, which yields a pause after each reinforcement and then a rapid burst of responding.
Slot machine wins are not tied to a fixed number of pulls.
Variable interval, which yields a slow and steady rate of responding with moderate extinction resistance.
Variable interval depends on time elapsed, not on number of responses.
Variable ratio, which yields a high and steady rate of responding that is resistant to extinction.
Correct: Reinforcement after an unpredictable number of responses is a variable ratio schedule, the most extinction-resistant schedule.
Fixed interval, which yields a scalloped pattern of responding that accelerates before reinforcement.
Fixed interval depends on elapsed time, and rates accelerate before the interval ends.
questions.x: Reinforcement after an unpredictable number of responses is a variable ratio schedule, the most extinction-resistant schedule. Trap: Matching the schedule by name rather than by whether it depends on responses or on time.

questions.q: A viewer who is not interested in the topic of an advertisement for a car is persuaded because the commercial features an attractive celebrity. According to the elaboration likelihood model, this is an example of:
o: the central route to persuasion, which relies on careful evaluation of the argument.
The central route involves careful evaluation of argument quality by a motivated listener.
cognitive dissonance reduction, in which attitudes change to match behavior.
Dissonance reduction involves changing attitudes to remove inconsistency with behavior.
the peripheral route to persuasion, which relies on superficial cues.
Correct: With low motivation, attitudes shift through superficial cues, such as source attractiveness, rather than argument quality.
the sleeper effect, in which a message persuades more after the source is forgotten.
The sleeper effect is persuasion rising over time as the source is forgotten.
questions.x: With low motivation, attitudes shift through superficial cues, such as source attractiveness, rather than argument quality. Trap: Calling a celebrity endorsement central because it is memorable.

questions.q: An experienced pianist plays a well-rehearsed piece. Her performance is likely to be best when she plays in front of a large audience, compared with when she is alone. This is an example of:
o: social facilitation, because an audience raises arousal and enhances well-learned tasks.
Correct: Audience presence raises arousal, which strengthens the dominant response, and for well-learned tasks this is correct, improving performance.
social loafing, because individual effort is reduced when people work together in groups.
Social loafing is reduced effort in a group when contributions are pooled, which is not the situation.
groupthink, because the audience suppresses dissent in favor of consensus.
Groupthink is a decision-making problem in cohesive groups.
deindividuation, because the audience provides anonymity and reduces self-awareness.
The pianist is identifiable to the audience, and deindividuation requires anonymity.
questions.x: Audience presence raises arousal, which strengthens the dominant response, and for well-learned tasks this is correct, improving performance. Trap: Predicting that an audience harms all performance, forgetting the task-difficulty qualifier.

questions.q: A teenager changes her goals and the way she dresses after noticing that her peers regard her as shy and unreliable. This is the best illustration of:
o: the self-serving bias.
The self-serving bias is attributing successes to the self and failures to external causes.
Cooley's looking-glass self.
Correct: The looking-glass self holds that self-concept is based on how we imagine others perceive and judge us.
the actual self matching the ideal self.
The scenario describes change prompted by others' views, with no stated match between actual and ideal self.
the spotlight effect.
The spotlight effect is overestimating how much others notice us, and not formation of the self-concept.
questions.x: The looking-glass self holds that self-concept is based on how we imagine others perceive and judge us. Trap: Choosing the self-concept term that sounds closest without matching the source of the change.

questions.q: A driver who is cut off in traffic concludes that the other driver is selfish and reckless. When the same person later cuts off another car, he explains that he was late for an important meeting. This pattern illustrates:
o: the self-serving bias exclusively, in which people credit successes to themselves and failures to others.
Self-serving bias concerns attributions after success and failure, not the differing explanations for actor and observer.
the actor-observer bias, including the fundamental attribution error when judging others.
Correct: He attributes others' behavior to disposition and his own to the situation, which is the actor-observer difference.
the just-world hypothesis, in which people believe outcomes are deserved.
The just-world hypothesis is the belief that people get what they deserve.
the halo effect, in which one positive trait colors judgments of other traits.
The halo effect is generalizing from one positive trait to other traits.
questions.x: He attributes others' behavior to disposition and his own to the situation, which is the actor-observer difference. Trap: Picking the self-serving bias because the person excuses his own behavior.

questions.q: A researcher recruits adults who volunteer for a new therapy program and compares them with adults who did not volunteer, finding that the volunteers have better outcomes at 6 months. The most serious threat to the validity of concluding that the therapy caused the improvement is:
o: a ceiling effect on all outcome measures, which compresses variability in the scores.
A ceiling effect is not suggested by the description.
observer drift in blinded raters, which gradually changes how outcomes are scored.
Observer drift is a measurement concern that is not described here.
selection bias, because volunteers may differ in motivation from non-volunteers.
Correct: Without random assignment, volunteers may differ systematically, which confounds the therapy effect.
the Hawthorne effect in the non-volunteer group, who changed behavior because they were observed.
The non-volunteers were not enrolled and cannot show a response to being observed.
questions.x: Without random assignment, volunteers may differ systematically, which confounds the therapy effect. Trap: Overlooking that self-selection into a condition prevents causal conclusions.

questions.q: In a country with a high birth rate that has begun to improve sanitation and medical care, death rates fall while birth rates remain high. According to the demographic transition model, the population will most likely:
o: grow rapidly.
Correct: Stage 2 features falling death rates with persistently high birth rates, so natural increase is large.
shrink rapidly.
Shrinkage occurs only if deaths exceed births, as in some late-stage populations.
remain stable.
Stability occurs when birth and death rates are both low and nearly equal (stage 4).
age rapidly with few children.
A rapidly aging population results when birth rates are low, which has not occurred.
questions.x: Stage 2 features falling death rates with persistently high birth rates, so natural increase is large. Trap: Confusing the early stage of the transition with the late stage.

questions.q: A study shows that Black women in the United States experience worse maternal outcomes than would be expected by considering race alone or gender alone. Which concept best describes the framework used to explain this?
o: Anomie, in which social norms fail to regulate behavior during rapid social change.
Anomie refers to normlessness.
Meritocracy, in which rewards are distributed according to individual effort.
Meritocracy is the idea that people are rewarded on merit and does not explain outcomes tied to identity.
Assimilation, in which a minority group adopts the dominant culture.
Assimilation is cultural adoption by minorities, not a theory of combined disadvantage.
Intersectionality, the overlap of social identities that yields distinct disadvantage.
Correct: Intersectionality holds that overlapping categories, such as race and gender, combine to produce unique forms of disadvantage.
questions.x: Intersectionality holds that overlapping categories, such as race and gender, combine to produce unique forms of disadvantage. Trap: Treating race and gender effects as simply additive.

questions.q: A sociologist studies how a group of hospital nurses and patients come to define a 'good patient' through their daily conversations, gestures, and labels. Which perspective is she using?
o: Functionalism, which views society as interdependent parts
Functionalism analyzes how social structures contribute to stability.
Conflict theory, which views society as competition over scarce resources
Conflict theory emphasizes power and competition among groups.
Symbolic interactionism
Correct: Symbolic interactionism focuses on how shared meanings are created and sustained through face-to-face interaction and symbols.
Rational choice theory, which views behavior as cost-benefit calculation
Rational choice theory assumes individuals weigh costs and benefits to maximize utility.
questions.x: Symbolic interactionism focuses on how shared meanings are created and sustained through face-to-face interaction and symbols. Trap: Using the macro-level theories for a micro-level interaction study.

questions.q: At a physiological pH of 7.4, which amino acid side chain is predominantly uncharged and also able to act as a proton donor or acceptor near neutral pH?
o: Lysine
the side chain pKa is about 10.5, so it is protonated and positive at pH 7.4.
Aspartate
the side chain pKa is near 4, so it is deprotonated and negative at pH 7.4.
Histidine
Correct: The imidazole side chain has a pKa near 6, so at pH 7.4 it is mostly deprotonated and neutral, and it buffers near neutrality.
Arginine
its guanidinium group has a pKa above 12 and is always positive at this pH.
questions.x: The imidazole side chain has a pKa near 6, so at pH 7.4 it is mostly deprotonated and neutral, and it buffers near neutrality. Trap: Calling histidine charged at pH 7.4 because it is classified as a basic amino acid.

questions.q: Many collagen mutations that replace a glycine residue with a bulky amino acid cause severe disease. The most likely reason is that glycine:
o: forms disulfide bonds that link the three strands together at regular intervals along the helix
glycine has no thiol group and cannot form disulfides.
is the only residue that can be hydroxylated by prolyl hydroxylase, which stabilizes the helix
hydroxylation involves proline and lysine, not glycine.
is required to start translation of every collagen chain, as the initiator residue at the N-terminus
translation starts with methionine.
fits into the crowded interior of the triple helix because its side chain is only a hydrogen atom
Correct: Every third residue sits at the center of the tight triple helix, where only the smallest side chain fits.
questions.x: Every third residue sits at the center of the tight triple helix, where only the smallest side chain fits. Trap: Assuming glycine matters because of a special chemical reactivity rather than small size.

questions.q: An enzyme has a Km of 4 mM. At a substrate concentration of 12 mM, the reaction velocity is closest to what fraction of Vmax?
o: Correct: v/Vmax = [S]/(Km + [S]) = 12/16 = 0.75.
this occurs when [S] equals Km, or 4 mM.
this results from 8/12, using the wrong denominator.
this requires [S] about nine times Km, or 36 mM.
questions.x: v/Vmax = [S]/(Km + [S]) = 12/16 = 0.75. Trap: Assuming velocity is half of Vmax at any concentration above Km.

questions.q: A tRNA has the anticodon 5'-GAA-3'. Which mRNA codon does it recognize?
o: this is the complement written in the wrong direction.
Correct: Codon and anticodon pair antiparallel, so the complement of GAA read 5' to 3' is UUC.
this is the sequence of the anticodon itself, not its complement.
this is the reverse of the anticodon without complementing.
questions.x: Codon and anticodon pair antiparallel, so the complement of GAA read 5' to 3' is UUC. Trap: Writing the complement 3' to 5' and reading it as 5' to 3'.

questions.q: A linear 8-kb DNA fragment is cut once by a restriction enzyme at 2 kb from its left end and again at 5 kb from the left end. What fragment sizes will be seen after complete digestion?
o: 2 kb, 3 kb, and 3 kb
Correct: Two cuts divide the line into three pieces: 0-2, 2-5, and 5-8 kb.
2 kb and 6 kb
this would result from a single cut at 2 kb.
3 kb and 5 kb
this would result from a single cut at 3 kb.
2 kb, 5 kb, and 8 kb
these are the cut positions, not fragment lengths.
questions.x: Two cuts divide the line into three pieces: 0-2, 2-5, and 5-8 kb. Trap: Reporting the positions of the cuts as fragment sizes.

questions.q: Treatment of cells with a histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor is most likely to cause:
o: decreased histone acetylation, tighter chromatin packing, and gene silencing at many loci
inhibiting the deacetylase prevents loss of acetyl groups.
methylation of CpG islands in all promoters, which shuts off transcription genome-wide
HDAC inhibition does not directly add DNA methylation.
increased histone acetylation, looser chromatin, and increased transcription of many genes
Correct: Acetyl groups neutralize lysine charges and open chromatin; blocking their removal keeps chromatin accessible.
a decrease in transcription due to tighter DNA-histone binding and condensed nucleosomes
acetylation lowers histone affinity for DNA.
questions.x: Acetyl groups neutralize lysine charges and open chromatin; blocking their removal keeps chromatin accessible. Trap: Reversing the roles of acetylation and deacetylation.

questions.q: A species survives a disease outbreak that reduces its population to 20 individuals, and the population then recovers. Compared with the original population, the recovered population will most likely show:
o: increased genetic diversity due to new mutations in the survivors
the diversity of survivors is only a sample of the original diversity.
the same allele frequencies, because selection was strong
the survivors were not necessarily selected for specific alleles; random sampling dominates.
greater heterozygosity due to outbreeding
a small number of founders increases inbreeding and reduces heterozygosity.
reduced genetic diversity, with allele frequencies that differ from the original by chance
Correct: A bottleneck strongly amplifies genetic drift, so many alleles are lost or change randomly in frequency.
questions.x: A bottleneck strongly amplifies genetic drift, so many alleles are lost or change randomly in frequency. Trap: Assuming survivors are a representative sample of the original population.

questions.q: In Labrador retrievers, allele B (black) is dominant to b (brown), and a second gene determines deposition of pigment: ee dogs are yellow regardless of the B gene. In a cross of BbEe x BbEe, what fraction of offspring is yellow?
o: this is the fraction that is bbee only.
Correct: All ee offspring are yellow: 1/4 of offspring are ee, regardless of the B genotype.
this is the fraction that is brown (bbE_).
this is the fraction that is black (B_E_).
questions.x: All ee offspring are yellow: 1/4 of offspring are ee, regardless of the B genotype. Trap: Counting only bbee dogs as yellow.

questions.q: A reaction has a standard free energy change of +20 kJ/mol. It is coupled to the hydrolysis of ATP, whose standard free energy change is -30.5 kJ/mol. What is the standard free energy change of the coupled process?
o: -10.5 kJ/mol
Correct: The values add: +20 + (-30.5) = -10.5 kJ/mol, so the coupled process is spontaneous.
+50.5 kJ/mol
this subtracts the ATP value instead of adding it.
+10.5 kJ/mol
this has the wrong sign for a favorable coupled process.
-50.5 kJ/mol
this adds the magnitudes without regard to sign.
questions.x: The values add: +20 + (-30.5) = -10.5 kJ/mol, so the coupled process is spontaneous. Trap: Adding magnitudes instead of the signed values.

questions.q: During prolonged fasting, the liver converts acetyl-CoA to ketone bodies rather than oxidizing it in the citric acid cycle. The main reason is that:
o: fatty acid oxidation stops, so acetyl-CoA levels fall and ketone bodies are not made
fatty acid oxidation is increased during fasting.
oxaloacetate is diverted to gluconeogenesis, limiting condensation with acetyl-CoA
Correct: With oxaloacetate depleted, citrate synthase cannot use all the acetyl-CoA, which is diverted to ketone body synthesis.
the liver has no mitochondria, so it cannot oxidize fatty acids at all
ketogenesis occurs in liver mitochondria.
high insulin levels stimulate ketogenesis by activating hormone-sensitive lipase
insulin is low in fasting and it inhibits ketogenesis.
questions.x: With oxaloacetate depleted, citrate synthase cannot use all the acetyl-CoA, which is diverted to ketone body synthesis. Trap: Believing that ketone body production reflects low acetyl-CoA availability.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes the path of a newly made secreted protein through the cell?
o: Golgi apparatus, rough ER, lysosome, plasma membrane
the Golgi comes after the ER, and lysosomes are for degradation.
Free cytosolic ribosome, nucleus, Golgi apparatus, plasma membrane
the nucleus is not on the secretory pathway.
Smooth ER, mitochondrion, secretory vesicle, plasma membrane
the mitochondria are not part of the secretory pathway.
Rough ER, Golgi apparatus, secretory vesicle, plasma membrane
Correct: Secreted proteins are made on ribosomes bound to the rough ER, packaged and modified in the Golgi, and exported in vesicles.
questions.x: Secreted proteins are made on ribosomes bound to the rough ER, packaged and modified in the Golgi, and exported in vesicles. Trap: Placing the Golgi apparatus before the ER.

questions.q: Which feature is characteristic of the lysogenic cycle of a bacteriophage?
o: Host cells burst immediately after viral assembly, releasing progeny phage at once
this describes the lytic cycle.
The viral genome is degraded in the cytoplasm by host nucleases soon after entry
lysogeny requires a stable phage genome.
The viral genome integrates into the host chromosome and is replicated along with it
Correct: In the lysogenic cycle the prophage is passed to daughter cells without lysing the host.
Phage coat proteins are produced in large numbers right after infection and assembled
this is the lytic cycle; in lysogeny repressors keep these genes off.
questions.x: In the lysogenic cycle the prophage is passed to daughter cells without lysing the host. Trap: Mixing up the features of the lytic and lysogenic cycles.

questions.q: Which of the following tissues is derived from embryonic mesoderm?
o: The epidermis of the skin
this derives from ectoderm.
The epithelial lining of the lungs
this derives from endoderm.
The neurons of the retina
these derive from neural ectoderm.
Cardiac muscle
Correct: The heart muscle arises from mesoderm, along with skeletal muscle, bone, and blood.
