questions.x: The heart muscle arises from mesoderm, along with skeletal muscle, bone, and blood. Trap: Placing organ epithelia in mesoderm because they are within the body.

questions.q: The effects of cortisol on gene expression take hours, whereas the effects of epinephrine on glycogen breakdown take seconds. This difference is best explained by:
o: cortisol acting through intracellular receptors that alter transcription, while epinephrine acts through surface receptors and second messengers
Correct: Cortisol is a lipophilic steroid that must change gene expression and protein levels, while epinephrine triggers a rapid phosphorylation cascade.
cortisol being secreted by the posterior pituitary
cortisol is produced by the adrenal cortex.
epinephrine entering the nucleus to act on DNA
epinephrine binds membrane receptors.
cortisol binding G protein coupled receptors on the plasma membrane
steroid receptors are intracellular.
questions.x: Cortisol is a lipophilic steroid that must change gene expression and protein levels, while epinephrine triggers a rapid phosphorylation cascade. Trap: Thinking all hormones act through surface receptors.

questions.q: A virus-infected body cell displays viral peptides to cytotoxic T cells. These peptides are presented on:
o: MHC class II molecules
these present extracellular antigens to CD4+ helper T cells and are limited to antigen-presenting cells.
MHC class I molecules
Correct: MHC I is found on nearly all nucleated cells and presents intracellular peptides to CD8+ T cells.
Free antibodies on the surface of the cell
antibodies are produced by plasma cells and are not displays of peptide antigens.
Complement protein C3b
complement marks pathogens for destruction, but does not present peptides to T cells.
questions.x: MHC I is found on nearly all nucleated cells and presents intracellular peptides to CD8+ T cells. Trap: Choosing MHC II because the antigen is from a virus.

questions.q: A 1200 kg car travels around a flat circular curve of radius 30 m. If the coefficient of static friction between the tires and road is 0.60, the maximum speed at which the car can round the curve without skidding is closest to (use g = 10 m/s²):
o: 13 m/s
Correct: Friction supplies the centripetal force: μmg = mv²/r, so v = √(μgr) = √(0.60 × 10 × 30) = √180 ≈ 13 m/s.
17 m/s
17 m/s is √(gr) = √300, which omits the coefficient of friction.
6.0 m/s is μg, which ignores both the radius and the square root.
180 m/s is v² in m²/s², not a speed.
questions.x: Friction supplies the centripetal force: μmg = mv²/r, so v = √(μgr) = √(0.60 × 10 × 30) = √180 ≈ 13 m/s. Trap: Leaving out the square root, so that v² is reported as v.

questions.q: A 2.0 kg object is lifted vertically at constant speed through a height of 3.0 m in 4.0 s. What is the average power delivered to the object (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: 60 W is the work in joules and is not divided by time.
7.5 W uses t = 8.0 s, doubling the time.
30 W uses t = 2.0 s instead of 4.0 s.
questions.x: Work = mgh = (2.0)(10)(3.0) = 60 J, so P = W/t = 60/4.0 = 15 W. Trap: Reporting work as power without dividing by the time interval.

questions.q: Blood flows through a horizontal vessel under a constant pressure difference. If the radius of the vessel is halved (all else constant), laminar flow rate changes by a factor of:
o: 1/2 assumes flow rate is proportional to radius.
1/4 assumes flow rate is proportional to cross-sectional area (r²).
1/8 assumes flow rate is proportional to r³.
Correct: Poiseuille's law gives Q ∝ r⁴, so halving r reduces Q by (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.
questions.x: Poiseuille's law gives Q ∝ r⁴, so halving r reduces Q by (1/2)⁴ = 1/16. Trap: Using the area (r²) dependence from continuity instead of the r⁴ dependence of viscous flow.

questions.q: A 60 W light bulb is designed to operate at 120 V. What is the resistance of the filament during operation?
o: 0.50 Ω is 60/120 = 0.50, which is the current in amperes.
7200 Ω multiplies V² by P instead of dividing.
2.0 Ω is the inverse of the current, 120/60.
Correct: P = V²/R, so R = V²/P = (120)²/60 = 240 Ω.
questions.x: P = V²/R, so R = V²/P = (120)²/60 = 240 Ω. Trap: Confusing the current (P/V) with the resistance.

questions.q: A galvanic cell is made from Zn/Zn²⁺ (E° = −0.76 V) and Cu/Cu²⁺ (E° = +0.34 V) half-cells. What is ΔG° for the overall reaction? (F = 96,500 C/mol)
o: −106 kJ/mol
−106 kJ/mol uses n = 1.
+212 kJ/mol
+212 kJ/mol has the wrong sign; a positive E°cell gives a negative ΔG°.
−212 kJ/mol
−1.1 kJ/mol
−1.1 kJ/mol reflects E°cell alone without n or F.
questions.x: E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V and n = 2, so ΔG° = −nFE° = −(2)(96,500)(1.10) = −212 kJ/mol. Trap: Using n = 1 when two electrons are transferred.

questions.q: A sound has its intensity increased by a factor of 100. By how many decibels does the sound intensity level increase?
o: 20 dB
Correct: ΔL = 10 log(I₂/I₁) = 10 log(100) = 20 dB.
100 dB
100 dB treats the intensity ratio as the number of decibels.
2 dB
2 dB uses log(100) without multiplying by 10.
10 dB
10 dB corresponds to a factor of 10 in intensity.
questions.x: ΔL = 10 log(I₂/I₁) = 10 log(100) = 20 dB. Trap: Forgetting that decibels are logarithmic and multiplying by 10 after taking the log.

questions.q: A concave mirror has a focal length of 10 cm. An object is placed 30 cm in front of the mirror. The image is:
o: virtual, upright, and located 15 cm behind the mirror.
virtual, upright, and located 15 cm behind the mirror. A virtual image forms only when the object is inside the focal length.
real, inverted, and located 30 cm from the mirror.
real, inverted, and located 30 cm from the mirror. An image 30 cm from the mirror would require the object to be at 15 cm; an object at 2f = 20 cm gives an image at 20 cm.
real, inverted, and located 15 cm from the mirror.
Correct: 1/s′ = 1/f − 1/s = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30, so s′ = 15 cm (positive, real). Magnification = −15/30 = −0.5, so the image is inverted and reduced.
real, upright, and located 7.5 cm from the mirror.
real, upright, and located 7.5 cm from the mirror. real images from a single mirror are always inverted.
questions.x: 1/s′ = 1/f − 1/s = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30, so s′ = 15 cm (positive, real). Magnification = −15/30 = −0.5, so the image is inverted and reduced. Trap: Assuming that an object beyond the focal point can form a virtual image.

questions.q: A nucleus of ²³⁸₉₂U undergoes one alpha decay followed by two successive β⁻ decays. The resulting nuclide is:
o: ²³⁰₉₀Th
²³⁰₉₀Th would require two alpha decays followed by two β⁻ decays (A drops by 8, not 4).
²³⁴₉₀Th
²³⁴₉₀Th is the product after alpha decay only.
²³⁴₉₂U
Correct: Alpha decay gives ²³⁴₉₀Th. Each β⁻ increases Z by 1 without changing A, so the final nuclide is ²³⁴₉₂U.
²³⁴₉₄Pu
²³⁴₉₄Pu would result from four beta-minus decays.
questions.x: Alpha decay gives ²³⁴₉₀Th. Each β⁻ increases Z by 1 without changing A, so the final nuclide is ²³⁴₉₂U. Trap: Subtracting two from the atomic number for each beta decay instead of adding one.

questions.q: The Ksp of Ag₂CrO₄ is 1.1 × 10⁻¹². What is its molar solubility in pure water?
o: 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ M is √Ksp, which treats the salt as a 1:1 electrolyte.
1.3 × 10⁻⁴ M is [Ag⁺] = 2s, not the molar solubility.
2.8 × 10⁻¹³ M is Ksp/4, without taking the cube root.
Correct: Ksp = [Ag⁺]²[CrO₄²⁻] = (2s)²(s) = 4s³, so s = (1.1 × 10⁻¹²/4)^(1/3) = 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ M.
questions.x: Ksp = [Ag⁺]²[CrO₄²⁻] = (2s)²(s) = 4s³, so s = (1.1 × 10⁻¹²/4)^(1/3) = 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ M. Trap: Applying the 1:1 formula s = √Ksp to a salt that dissociates into three ions.

questions.q: At room temperature, Br₂ is a liquid while Cl₂ is a gas. The best explanation is that:
o: Br₂ has permanent dipole–dipole interactions.
Br₂ has permanent dipole–dipole interactions. Both are nonpolar diatomic molecules with no permanent dipole.
Br₂ forms hydrogen bonds between molecules.
Br₂ forms hydrogen bonds between molecules. Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to N, O, or F.
Br₂ has a larger, more polarizable electron cloud and therefore stronger London dispersion forces.
Correct: Both are nonpolar, so dispersion forces determine boiling points. Larger molecules with more electrons are more polarizable, giving stronger dispersion forces.
The Br–Br covalent bond is stronger than the Cl–Cl bond.
The Br–Br covalent bond is stronger than the Cl–Cl bond. The Br–Br bond is weaker, and covalent bond strength does not affect boiling points.
questions.x: Both are nonpolar, so dispersion forces determine boiling points. Larger molecules with more electrons are more polarizable, giving stronger dispersion forces. Trap: Attributing a difference between nonpolar molecules to dipoles or covalent bond strength.

questions.q: What is the molecular geometry of XeF₄?
o: Square planar
Correct: Xe has 4 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs (6 electron domains, octahedral electron geometry); the lone pairs occupy opposite positions, so the molecular geometry is square planar.
Tetrahedral
Tetrahedral would apply to four bonding pairs and no lone pairs.
Seesaw
Seesaw applies to four bonding pairs and one lone pair, as in SF₄.
Square pyramidal
Square pyramidal applies to five bonding pairs and one lone pair.
questions.x: Xe has 4 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs (6 electron domains, octahedral electron geometry); the lone pairs occupy opposite positions, so the molecular geometry is square planar. Trap: Counting only the bonded atoms and ignoring the two lone pairs on xenon.

questions.q: A neutral compound has a distribution coefficient K = [organic]/[aqueous] = 4.0 between diethyl ether and water. If 100 mL of aqueous solution is shaken once with 100 mL of ether, what fraction of the compound ends up in the ether layer?
o: 25% is the fraction in the ether if the ratio were 1:4.
20% is the fraction remaining in the water, not in the ether.
Correct: With equal volumes, the amount in each phase is proportional to its concentration: ether:water = 4:1, so 4/5 = 80% is in the ether.
40% halves the correct fraction without justification.
questions.x: With equal volumes, the amount in each phase is proportional to its concentration: ether:water = 4:1, so 4/5 = 80% is in the ether. Trap: Reporting the fraction remaining in the aqueous layer or inverting the ratio.

questions.q: A mixture of proteins is separated by size-exclusion (gel filtration) chromatography. Which protein elutes first?
o: The largest protein, because it is excluded from the pores of the beads.
Correct: Large molecules cannot enter the pores and take a shorter path through the column, so they elute first. Smaller molecules enter pores and are delayed.
The smallest protein, because it moves fastest through the pores.
The smallest protein, because it moves fastest through the pores. small proteins enter pores and take a longer path, so they elute last.
The most positively charged protein, because it binds the beads least.
The most positively charged protein, because it binds the beads least. charge does not determine elution in size-exclusion chromatography.
The most hydrophobic protein, because it is repelled by water.
The most hydrophobic protein, because it is repelled by water. hydrophobicity is the basis of reversed-phase or hydrophobic interaction chromatography, not size exclusion.
questions.x: Large molecules cannot enter the pores and take a shorter path through the column, so they elute first. Smaller molecules enter pores and are delayed. Trap: Assuming that smaller molecules always move through a column faster.

questions.q: Ethyl acetate is heated with excess aqueous NaOH. Which products are formed, and why does the reaction go essentially to completion?
o: Acetic acid and ethanol; the equilibrium is shifted by removing water.
Acetic acid and ethanol; the equilibrium is shifted by removing water. these are the products of acid-catalyzed hydrolysis, which is reversible.
Ethyl acetate and water; no reaction occurs with hydroxide.
Ethyl acetate and water; no reaction occurs with hydroxide. Hydroxide attacks the ester carbonyl carbon readily.
Acetaldehyde and sodium ethoxide; hydroxide reduces the ester.
Acetaldehyde and sodium ethoxide; hydroxide reduces the ester. hydroxide is a nucleophile, not a reducing agent.
Sodium acetate and ethanol; the carboxylic acid is deprotonated by the base, driving the reaction forward.

Correct: Base-promoted ester hydrolysis (saponification) produces a carboxylic acid, which is immediately deprotonated by hydroxide to give the stable carboxylate, making the overall process irreversible.
questions.x: Base-promoted ester hydrolysis (saponification) produces a carboxylic acid, which is immediately deprotonated by hydroxide to give the stable carboxylate, making the overall process irreversible. Trap: Giving the neutral carboxylic acid as the product of a base-promoted hydrolysis.

questions.q: The following initial rate data were obtained for A + B → products: [A] = 0.10 M, [B] = 0.10 M, rate = 2.0 × 10⁻³ M/s; [A] = 0.20 M, [B] = 0.10 M, rate = 4.0 × 10⁻³ M/s; [A] = 0.20 M, [B] = 0.20 M, rate = 1.6 × 10⁻² M/s. What is the overall order of the reaction?
o: 2 treats doubling [B] as doubling the rate, giving 1 + 1.
Correct: Doubling [A] doubles the rate (first order in A). Doubling [B] quadruples the rate (second order in B). Overall order = 1 + 2 = 3.
4 adds the rate-ratio exponents incorrectly (e.g., 2 + 2).
1 counts only the order in A.
questions.x: Doubling [A] doubles the rate (first order in A). Doubling [B] quadruples the rate (second order in B). Overall order = 1 + 2 = 3. Trap: Confusing the factor by which the rate changes (4) with the exponent (2).

questions.q: Olfaction differs from most other senses in that olfactory information:
o: reaches olfactory cortex and limbic structures without a thalamic relay.
Correct: Olfactory receptor neurons synapse in the olfactory bulb, whose output goes directly to olfactory cortex and the amygdala.
is relayed through the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus first.
This is the thalamic relay for vision.
is transduced by mechanoreceptors in the olfactory epithelium of the nose.
Olfactory receptors are chemoreceptors.
is processed only in the contralateral hemisphere of the cortex.
Olfactory projections are largely ipsilateral.
questions.x: Olfactory receptor neurons synapse in the olfactory bulb, whose output goes directly to olfactory cortex and the amygdala. Trap: Assuming that all senses relay through the thalamus.

questions.q: A study fails to detect a significant difference although a true difference exists. Which change would most reduce the probability of this error?
o: Lowering the significance level from 0.05 to 0.01.
This reduces Type I error but raises Type II error.
Increasing the variability of the measurement.
More variability reduces power.
Increasing the sample size.
Correct: This is a Type II error; larger samples increase power.
Testing a smaller group of participants.
Reducing sample size lowers power.
questions.x: This is a Type II error; larger samples increase power. Trap: Confusing Type I and Type II error.

questions.q: A country's Gini coefficient rises from 0.30 to 0.45 over two decades. This indicates that:
o: income is distributed more equally.
This would be a decline in the coefficient.
average income has doubled.
The Gini coefficient says nothing about the average.
poverty has been eliminated.
It does not measure poverty directly.
income is distributed less equally.
Correct: A Gini coefficient rises with greater income inequality, from 0 (equality) to 1.
questions.x: A Gini coefficient rises with greater income inequality, from 0 (equality) to 1. Trap: Thinking a higher index indicates greater equality.

questions.q: A patient speaks slowly with great effort, using short phrases such as 'walk dog now', but understands spoken questions well. The most likely damaged region is:
o: the posterior superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke's area).
This produces fluent but meaningless speech and poor comprehension.
the primary auditory cortex.
Damage mostly impairs hearing, not production.
the occipital cortex.
This is a visual processing region.
the left inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area).
Correct: Damage to Broca's area produces non-fluent speech with relatively intact comprehension.
questions.x: Damage to Broca's area produces non-fluent speech with relatively intact comprehension. Trap: Mixing up the fluency and comprehension patterns of Broca's and Wernicke's aphasia.

questions.q: An EEG recording during sleep shows brief bursts of 12-14 Hz activity (sleep spindles) and large isolated waveforms (K-complexes). This is characteristic of:
o: stage N1.
N1 shows theta waves.
stage N3.
N3 shows high-amplitude delta waves.
stage N2.
Correct: Spindles and K-complexes mark stage N2.
REM sleep.
REM shows low-amplitude mixed-frequency activity similar to wakefulness.
questions.x: Spindles and K-complexes mark stage N2. Trap: Linking spindles with deep sleep.

questions.q: Which of the following is a negative symptom of schizophrenia?
o: Flat affect
Correct: Negative symptoms are absences of normal function, such as flat affect.
Auditory hallucinations
These are positive symptoms.
Delusions of persecution
These are positive symptoms.
Disorganized speech
This is classed as a disorganized symptom.
questions.x: Negative symptoms are absences of normal function, such as flat affect. Trap: Assuming 'negative' means unpleasant.

questions.q: A rat is conditioned to freeze in response to a tone paired with shock. After extinction training, the tone is presented again after a rest of several days, and freezing briefly returns. This is:
o: stimulus generalization.
This is responding to stimuli similar to the CS.
higher-order conditioning.
This uses a conditioned stimulus as the unconditioned stimulus for a new CS.
spontaneous recovery.
Correct: A previously extinguished conditioned response reappears after a rest.
acquisition.
Acquisition is the initial learning of the CS-US pairing.
questions.x: A previously extinguished conditioned response reappears after a rest. Trap: Calling any return of a response 'acquisition'.

questions.q: Which variation of Milgram's obedience paradigm would most likely decrease obedience?
o: The learner is in another room and cannot be seen by the teacher.
Greater distance from the victim increases obedience.
A confederate teacher continues to deliver shocks while the participant watches.
Obedient models increase obedience.
The experimenter gives instructions by telephone.
Correct: Reduced physical presence and authority lowers obedience.
The study is conducted in a prestigious university setting.
Prestige increases perceived authority.
questions.x: Reduced physical presence and authority lowers obedience. Trap: Misjudging how proximity and authority influence obedience.

questions.q: A canvasser first asks residents to display a small pin supporting a cause, and a week later asks them to place a large sign in their yard. The technique is:
o: door-in-the-face.
This begins with an unreasonably large request.
low-ball.
This changes the terms after commitment.
bandwagon.
This appeals to what many others do.
foot-in-the-door.
Correct: Agreement with a small request raises compliance with a larger one.
questions.x: Agreement with a small request raises compliance with a larger one. Trap: Confusing foot-in-the-door with door-in-the-face.

questions.q: A 16-year-old tries out different friend groups, hobbies, and career ideas, and is unsure who he is. According to Erikson, the psychosocial task is:
o: industry versus inferiority.
This stage occurs in school-age children.
intimacy versus isolation.
This stage occurs in young adulthood.
identity versus role confusion.
Correct: Adolescence centers on building a coherent identity.
generativity versus stagnation.
This stage occurs in middle adulthood.
questions.x: Adolescence centers on building a coherent identity. Trap: Misplacing Erikson's stages by age.

questions.q: A person says that a victim of burglary must have been careless, because the world is basically fair and people get what they deserve. This reflects:
o: the just-world hypothesis.
Correct: The belief that the world is fair leads to blaming victims.
the self-serving attribution bias.
This involves crediting oneself for success and blaming others for failure.
the halo effect in judgment.
This generalizes one positive trait to other traits.
the actor-observer bias in attribution.
This concerns different explanations for one's own versus others' behavior.
questions.x: The belief that the world is fair leads to blaming victims. Trap: Choosing attribution biases that do not feature a belief in fairness.

questions.q: A server is polite and formal with diners but swears and jokes in the kitchen. According to Goffman's dramaturgical approach, this illustrates:
o: role strain within a single role.
Role strain is tension among demands within one role.
role conflict between two different roles.
This refers to incompatible demands from different roles.
moving between front stage and back stage.
Correct: Front stage is a performance for an audience; back stage is where the performance is dropped.
social loafing in a work group.
This is reduced effort in a group.
questions.x: Front stage is a performance for an audience; back stage is where the performance is dropped. Trap: Confusing role strain, role conflict, and impression management.

questions.q: A small farming village where residents know one another and are bound by tradition and kinship is best described by Tonnies as:
o: Gemeinschaft.
Correct: Gemeinschaft describes communities with close personal ties.
Gesellschaft.
This describes impersonal societies based on formal relations.
anomie.
This is a state of normlessness described by Durkheim.
a bureaucracy.
This is a formal organization.
questions.x: Gemeinschaft describes communities with close personal ties. Trap: Reversing Gemeinschaft and Gesellschaft.

questions.q: In one year, a city of 500,000 receives 12,000 immigrants and loses 8,000 emigrants. The net migration rate per 1,000 is:
o: This is the emigration rate alone, 8,000 / 500,000 x 1,000.
This is the immigration rate alone.
This adds immigrants and emigrants rather than subtracting.
questions.x: (12,000 - 8,000) / 500,000 x 1,000 = 8. Trap: Using the immigration or emigration rate alone.

questions.q: After a news story about a plane crash, a person overestimates how dangerous flying is. This illustrates:
o: the representativeness heuristic.
This judges category membership by resemblance.
the availability heuristic.
Correct: Vivid, easily recalled examples distort estimates of frequency.
anchoring.
This relies too heavily on an initial value.
confirmation bias.
This favors information that supports prior beliefs.
questions.x: Vivid, easily recalled examples distort estimates of frequency. Trap: Choosing representativeness whenever a judgment is probabilistic.

questions.q: Histidine is often involved in buffering in proteins near physiological pH. This is because the side chain of histidine has:
o: no ionizable groups in its imidazole ring, so it is uncharged at any pH.
The imidazole ring is ionizable.
a pKa near 6, so it can accept or release a proton near neutral pH.
Correct: The imidazole pKa is about 6, so it is partially protonated near pH 6-7 and is an effective buffer in that range.
a pKa near 3.9, so it is fully deprotonated and negatively charged at pH 7.4.
This applies to aspartate.
a pKa near 10.5, so it is mostly protonated and cannot act as a buffer at pH 7.4.
This applies to lysine's amino group.
questions.x: The imidazole pKa is about 6, so it is partially protonated near pH 6-7 and is an effective buffer in that range. Trap: Assigning the pKa of lysine or aspartate to histidine.

questions.q: Proline is commonly found at the ends of alpha helices or in turns rather than in the middle of helices because proline:
o: is too hydrophobic to be found in any form of secondary structure.
Hydrophobicity does not prevent helix formation; many nonpolar residues are in helices.
forms disulfide bonds that cross-link adjacent helices and prevent folding.
Proline has no sulfur.
carries a charged side chain that repels adjacent residues within the helix.
Proline's side chain is nonpolar and uncharged.
lacks an amide hydrogen for hydrogen bonding and has a rigid ring.
Correct: The backbone nitrogen of proline is bonded to the side chain and has no hydrogen to donate, and the fixed phi angle introduces a kink.
questions.x: The backbone nitrogen of proline is bonded to the side chain and has no hydrogen to donate, and the fixed phi angle introduces a kink. Trap: Attributing helix disruption to charge or disulfide bonds rather than to the backbone geometry.

questions.q: A point mutation changes a codon in an mRNA from CAA (glutamine) to UAA. The most likely consequence for the encoded protein is:
o: a truncated protein due to premature termination of translation.
Correct: UAA is a stop codon, so translation stops at that position and the protein is shortened.
a protein with no change at all because the genetic code is degenerate.
Degeneracy applies to synonymous codons, and UAA codes for no amino acid.
a protein of the same length with a single amino acid substituted.
This describes a missense mutation, not a change to a stop codon.
a protein with a frameshift in all codons downstream of the change.
Frameshifts follow insertions or deletions not divisible by three.
questions.x: UAA is a stop codon, so translation stops at that position and the protein is shortened. Trap: Calling any single-base change silent or missense without checking whether the new codon is a stop codon.

questions.q: Shortening of the poly-A tail of a eukaryotic mRNA in the cytoplasm is most likely to:
o: increase mRNA stability by exposing the coding region to ribosomes.
Shortening reduces protection.
cause introns to be retained in the mature mRNA exported from the nucleus.
Splicing occurs in the nucleus and is independent of tail length.
make the mRNA more susceptible to degradation and decrease translation.
Correct: The poly-A tail and its binding proteins protect against exonucleases and promote translation; shortening commits the mRNA to decay.
prevent the 5' cap from being added during transcription.
Capping is cotranscriptional and has already occurred.
questions.x: The poly-A tail and its binding proteins protect against exonucleases and promote translation; shortening commits the mRNA to decay. Trap: Thinking that a shorter tail is more stable or confusing splicing with polyadenylation.

questions.q: A woman who is a carrier of an X-linked recessive disorder has children with an unaffected man. What is the probability that a child of unknown sex is affected?
o: This is the probability for a son only.
Correct: Half of the sons (1/2 of children) are affected with probability 1/2, so 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4; daughters are carriers or unaffected.
This applies a second 1/2 without justification.
The mother's allele can be transmitted to sons, who have only one X.
questions.x: Half of the sons (1/2 of children) are affected with probability 1/2, so 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4; daughters are carriers or unaffected. Trap: Stating the probability for sons as the probability for any child.

questions.q: A small island population was founded by 20 individuals, one of whom carried a rare recessive allele. A century later the allele is common on the island. This is best explained by:
o: the founder effect, a form of genetic drift.
Correct: Small founding samples can poorly represent the source gene pool, and a rare allele can reach high frequency by chance.
gene flow from the mainland.
The scenario describes an isolated population.
directional selection acting against the recessive allele.
Selection against an allele would reduce its frequency.
a high mutation rate on the island.
Mutation is too slow and the explanation relies on chance sampling.
questions.x: Small founding samples can poorly represent the source gene pool, and a rare allele can reach high frequency by chance. Trap: Attributing every change in allele frequency to natural selection.

questions.q: A child with a deficiency of thiamine would be expected to have increased blood levels of pyruvate and lactate because thiamine is a cofactor for:
o: lactate dehydrogenase, which interconverts pyruvate and lactate.
LDH uses NADH, and if inhibited, lactate would fall.
citrate synthase, which condenses acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate.
Citrate synthase uses acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate with no thiamine.
pyruvate kinase, which forms pyruvate at the end of glycolysis.
Pyruvate kinase does not require TPP.
pyruvate dehydrogenase.
Correct: Thiamine pyrophosphate is required by pyruvate dehydrogenase (and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase); a block raises pyruvate, which is converted to lactate.
questions.x: Thiamine pyrophosphate is required by pyruvate dehydrogenase (and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase); a block raises pyruvate, which is converted to lactate. Trap: Linking thiamine with glycolytic enzymes rather than with the dehydrogenase complexes.

questions.q: During prolonged fasting, increased fatty acid oxidation in the liver raises acetyl-CoA. This acetyl-CoA promotes gluconeogenesis by:
o: inhibiting phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase.
This enzyme is induced during fasting.
activating pyruvate dehydrogenase.
Acetyl-CoA inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase, favoring conservation of pyruvate.
activating pyruvate carboxylase.
Correct: Acetyl-CoA is an allosteric activator of pyruvate carboxylase, which converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate, the first gluconeogenic step.
activating phosphofructokinase-1.
Glycolysis is inhibited, not activated, during fasting.
questions.x: Acetyl-CoA is an allosteric activator of pyruvate carboxylase, which converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate, the first gluconeogenic step. Trap: Assuming acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate dehydrogenase because it is its product.

questions.q: Cholera toxin causes severe diarrhea by modifying the alpha subunit of Gs so that it cannot hydrolyze GTP. The direct result in intestinal epithelial cells is:
o: persistent inhibition of adenylyl cyclase and low cAMP in the cell.
This would result from persistent activation of Gi, not Gs.
increased tyrosine phosphorylation by an activated receptor kinase.
This is not the pathway of a G protein-coupled receptor.
increased IP3 formation and release of Ca2+ from the endoplasmic reticulum.
This is the Gq pathway.
persistent activation of adenylyl cyclase and high cAMP.
Correct: A Gs alpha subunit locked in the GTP-bound state continuously stimulates adenylyl cyclase, which raises cAMP and PKA activity, opening the CFTR channel.
questions.x: A Gs alpha subunit locked in the GTP-bound state continuously stimulates adenylyl cyclase, which raises cAMP and PKA activity, opening the CFTR channel. Trap: Mixing up the Gs, Gi, and Gq pathways.

questions.q: Penicillin is most effective against bacteria that are actively growing because it:
o: blocks DNA gyrase, preventing relaxation of positive supercoils during replication.
Fluoroquinolones act in this manner.
inhibits the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA.
This applies to aminoglycosides and tetracyclines.
inhibits cross-linking of peptidoglycan during cell wall synthesis.
Correct: Penicillin blocks transpeptidase, so new wall is weak and cells lyse as they grow and divide.
disrupts the nuclear membrane of the bacterial cell.
Bacteria have no nucleus.
questions.x: Penicillin blocks transpeptidase, so new wall is weak and cells lyse as they grow and divide. Trap: Assuming all antibiotics act on the ribosome.

questions.q: Which of the following tissues is derived from embryonic mesoderm?
o: The epidermis of the skin
The epidermis is ectoderm.
Cardiac muscle
Correct: The heart muscle, skeletal muscle, kidney, bone, and blood are mesodermal derivatives.
The retina
The retina is a neural derivative of ectoderm.
The epithelial lining of the lungs
The respiratory epithelium comes from endoderm.
questions.x: The heart muscle, skeletal muscle, kidney, bone, and blood are mesodermal derivatives. Trap: Assuming that all organs of the trunk are endodermal.

questions.q: A second exposure to the same antigen produces a faster and larger antibody response mainly because:
o: memory B cells formed during the first exposure are activated quickly.
Correct: Memory B and T cells are long-lived and, on re-exposure, differentiate into plasma cells quickly and produce high-affinity IgG.
antibodies from the first response are still produced by the same B cells at the same rate.
The response is faster and larger, not unchanged.
the antigen is now processed by the innate system alone.
Memory is an adaptive process.
natural killer cells have learned to recognize the antigen.
NK cells are part of innate immunity and have no antigen-specific memory.
questions.x: Memory B and T cells are long-lived and, on re-exposure, differentiate into plasma cells quickly and produce high-affinity IgG. Trap: Attributing immunologic memory to innate immune cells.

questions.q: A patient with central diabetes insipidus (deficient ADH secretion) would be expected to excrete:
o: large volumes of dilute urine, with increased plasma osmolarity.
Correct: Without ADH, aquaporin-2 channels are not inserted in the collecting duct, so water is not reabsorbed.
small volumes of dilute urine, with decreased plasma osmolarity.
With low ADH, water is not reabsorbed.
small volumes of concentrated urine, with decreased plasma osmolarity.
This would occur with excess ADH.
large volumes of urine containing glucose, with normal plasma osmolarity.
This describes the osmotic diuresis of diabetes mellitus.
questions.x: Without ADH, aquaporin-2 channels are not inserted in the collecting duct, so water is not reabsorbed. Trap: Confusing diabetes insipidus with diabetes mellitus.

questions.q: A person hyperventilates for several minutes. The expected change in arterial blood is:
o: no change, because the buffer system fully compensates immediately.
Buffers limit but do not prevent the change.
increased PCO2 and decreased pH.
This would occur with hypoventilation.
decreased PCO2 and decreased pH.
Less CO2 means less carbonic acid, so pH rises.
decreased PCO2 and increased pH.
Correct: Excess ventilation removes CO2, which shifts the bicarbonate equilibrium so that H+ falls, giving a respiratory alkalosis.
questions.x: Excess ventilation removes CO2, which shifts the bicarbonate equilibrium so that H+ falls, giving a respiratory alkalosis. Trap: Reversing the effect of CO2 on pH.

questions.q: Which of the following is an effect of sympathetic nervous system stimulation?
o: Constriction of the pupil
This is parasympathetic.
Increased secretion of watery saliva
This is predominantly parasympathetic.
Dilation of the bronchioles
Correct: Sympathetic stimulation increases airflow by dilating the bronchioles, raises heart rate, and decreases digestive activity.
Increased peristalsis
This is parasympathetic.
questions.x: Sympathetic stimulation increases airflow by dilating the bronchioles, raises heart rate, and decreases digestive activity. Trap: Mixing up the functions of the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems.

questions.q: A 2.0 kg cart moving at 3.0 m/s collides with a stationary 1.0 kg cart and the two stick together. What is the speed of the combined carts immediately after the collision?
o: 1.0 m/s divides the momentum by 6 kg.
Correct: Momentum is conserved: (2.0)(3.0) = (3.0)v, so v = 2.0 m/s.
3.0 m/s ignores the added mass.
1.5 m/s is half the initial speed, which would apply only for equal masses.
questions.x: Momentum is conserved: (2.0)(3.0) = (3.0)v, so v = 2.0 m/s. Trap: Assuming the speed is unchanged or splitting it evenly regardless of the masses.

questions.q: A satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius r at speed v. If it is moved to a circular orbit of radius 2r, what is its new speed?
o: v/2 assumes v is inversely proportional to r.
v√2 has the wrong direction; higher orbits are slower.
Correct: Gravity supplies the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r), so doubling r divides v by √2.
2v
2v has the wrong direction and the wrong magnitude.
questions.x: Gravity supplies the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r), so doubling r divides v by √2. Trap: Using v ∝ 1/r instead of v ∝ 1/√r.

questions.q: In a hydraulic lift, the small piston has an area of 2.0 cm² and the large piston has an area of 50 cm². What force on the small piston can support a 1000 N load on the large piston?
o: 1.6 N multiplies by A₁/A₂ twice or mishandles the ratio.
80 N doubles the correct force.
Correct: Pressure is equal in both pistons: F₁ = F₂(A₁/A₂) = 1000 × (2/50) = 40 N.
25,000 N multiplies the load by the area ratio instead of dividing.
questions.x: Pressure is equal in both pistons: F₁ = F₂(A₁/A₂) = 1000 × (2/50) = 40 N. Trap: Using the area ratio in the wrong direction.

questions.q: Water exits a small hole in the side of a large open tank 5.0 m below the water surface. Neglecting viscosity, what is the approximate exit speed?
o: 7.0 m/s is √(gh), missing the factor of 2.
98 m/s
98 m/s is 2gh, without the square root.
Correct: Bernoulli's equation gives v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 5.0) = 9.9 m/s.
49 m/s
49 m/s is gh, without the factor of 2 or the square root.
questions.x: Bernoulli's equation gives v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 5.0) = 9.9 m/s. Trap: Forgetting the factor of 2 or the square root in Torricelli's law.

questions.q: A 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected across a 4.0 Ω resistor and a 2.0 Ω resistor in series. What is the power dissipated in the 4.0 Ω resistor?
o: 36 W is V²/R with the full 12 V across the 4.0 Ω resistor.
8.0 W is the power in the 2.0 Ω resistor.
48 W is V × I with 12 V times 4.0.
questions.x: I = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A, so P = I²R = (2.0)²(4.0) = 16 W. Trap: Using the full battery voltage across a single resistor in a series circuit.

questions.q: A galvanic cell made from Zn/Zn²⁺ and Cu/Cu²⁺ under standard conditions has E°cell = 1.10 V and transfers 2 moles of electrons per mole of reaction. What is ΔG° per mole of reaction?
o: −106 kJ uses n = 1.
+212 kJ has the wrong sign; a positive E° means spontaneous.
−425 kJ uses n = 4.
questions.x: ΔG° = −nFE° = −(2)(96,485)(1.10) = −212 kJ/mol. Trap: Using the wrong n or the wrong sign in ΔG = −nFE.

questions.q: Light travels from glass (n = 1.50) toward an interface with air. What is the critical angle for total internal reflection?
o: 48° is the complement of the critical angle.
Correct: sin θc = n₂/n₁ = 1.00/1.50 = 0.667, so θc = 42°.
34° is arctan(0.667).
90° would be the angle of refraction at the critical angle.
questions.x: sin θc = n₂/n₁ = 1.00/1.50 = 0.667, so θc = 42°. Trap: Using tangent or cosine in place of sine in Snell's law.

questions.q: The intensity of a sound is increased by a factor of 100. By how many decibels does the sound intensity level increase?
o: 20 dB
Correct: Δβ = 10 log(100) = 20 dB.
2 dB
2 dB is log(100), omitting the factor 10.
100 dB
100 dB confuses the intensity ratio with the decibel change.
10 dB
10 dB corresponds to a factor of 10 in intensity.
questions.x: Δβ = 10 log(100) = 20 dB. Trap: Dropping the factor 10 in the decibel formula.

questions.q: Radium-226 (atomic number 88) undergoes alpha decay. What is the daughter nuclide?
o: ²²²₉₀Th
Thorium-222 would have Z = 90, a gain of two protons.
²²⁶₈₉Ac
Actinium-226 has the same mass number, so it would result from beta decay.
²²⁶₈₇Fr
Francium-226 has Z = 87 and is the product of beta-plus decay, not alpha.
²²²₈₆Rn
Correct: An alpha particle (⁴₂He) removes 2 protons and 4 nucleons, giving A = 222 and Z = 86 (radon-222).
questions.x: An alpha particle (⁴₂He) removes 2 protons and 4 nucleons, giving A = 222 and Z = 86 (radon-222). Trap: Mixing up how Z and A change for alpha and beta decays.

questions.q: A buffer contains 0.20 M NH₃ and 0.10 M NH₄Cl. The pKb of NH₃ is 4.74. What is the pH of the buffer?
o: 8.96 inverts the ratio.
9.26 would apply if the concentrations of base and acid were equal.
4.44 is the pOH, not the pH.
questions.x: pOH = pKb + log([NH₄⁺]/[NH₃]) = 4.74 + log(0.50) = 4.44, so pH = 14.00 − 4.44 = 9.56. Trap: Reporting pOH as pH or inverting the buffer ratio.

questions.q: What is the molecular geometry of XeF₄?
o: Tetrahedral
Tetrahedral applies to four bonds and no lone pairs.
Square planar
Correct: Xe has 4 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs, giving octahedral electron geometry; the lone pairs occupy opposite positions and the molecular shape is square planar.
Seesaw
Seesaw applies to four bonds and one lone pair.
Octahedral
Octahedral describes the electron geometry, not the molecular geometry.
questions.x: Xe has 4 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs, giving octahedral electron geometry; the lone pairs occupy opposite positions and the molecular shape is square planar. Trap: Naming the electron geometry rather than the molecular shape.

questions.q: A mixture of three proteins with molecular masses of 150 kDa, 45 kDa, and 12 kDa is passed through a size-exclusion (gel filtration) column. In what order do the proteins elute?
o: 150 kDa, 45 kDa, 12 kDa
Correct: Large proteins are excluded from the pores and travel through the void volume, while small proteins enter the pores and are delayed.
12 kDa, 45 kDa, 150 kDa
That reverses the order, as in a sieve gel such as SDS-PAGE with migration distance.
45 kDa, 150 kDa, 12 kDa
That order does not follow size.
All proteins elute together
Separation depends on size, so they elute at different times.
questions.x: Large proteins are excluded from the pores and travel through the void volume, while small proteins enter the pores and are delayed. Trap: Reversing the order, as in gel electrophoresis where small molecules travel farthest.

questions.q: Optically active (R)-3-bromo-3-methylhexane is dissolved in ethanol and slowly forms an ether. What is the expected stereochemical outcome?
o: A single enantiomer with inverted configuration
Complete inversion is the SN2 outcome, which is not feasible for a tertiary center.
A single enantiomer with retained configuration
Complete retention is not expected without a neighboring group.
A meso compound
A meso compound requires internal symmetry and two stereocenters.
A racemic mixture of ethers
Correct: The tertiary substrate ionizes to a planar carbocation (SN1), which ethanol can attack from either face with equal probability, yielding both enantiomers.
questions.x: The tertiary substrate ionizes to a planar carbocation (SN1), which ethanol can attack from either face with equal probability, yielding both enantiomers. Trap: Applying SN2 inversion to a tertiary halide in a protic solvent.

questions.q: The initial rate of a reaction A + B → products is 2.0 × 10⁻³ M/s when [A] = [B] = 0.10 M. Doubling [A] gives 8.0 × 10⁻³ M/s, and tripling [B] gives 6.0 × 10⁻³ M/s. What is the rate constant?
o: 0.20 M⁻¹ s⁻¹
0.20 M⁻¹ s⁻¹ assumes overall second-order kinetics.
0.020 s⁻¹ assumes overall first-order kinetics.
0.50 M² s
0.50 M² s is the reciprocal of the correct value.
2.0 M⁻² s⁻¹
Correct: Doubling [A] quadruples the rate (second order in A) and tripling [B] triples it (first order in B). Rate = k[A]²[B], so k = 2.0 × 10⁻³/(0.10² × 0.10) = 2.0 M⁻² s⁻¹.
questions.x: Doubling [A] quadruples the rate (second order in A) and tripling [B] triples it (first order in B). Rate = k[A]²[B], so k = 2.0 × 10⁻³/(0.10² × 0.10) = 2.0 M⁻² s⁻¹. Trap: Assuming order from stoichiometric coefficients instead of the initial-rate data.

questions.q: When 0.020 mol of a salt dissolves in 50.0 g of water, the temperature rises by 6.0°C. Taking the specific heat of the solution as 4.184 J/(g·°C) and neglecting the heat capacity of the calorimeter, what is ΔH of dissolution per mole of salt?
o: +63 kJ/mol
+63 kJ/mol has the wrong sign; a temperature rise means an exothermic process.
−1.3 kJ/mol
−1.3 kJ/mol is the total heat and is not divided by moles.
−63 kJ/mol
Correct: q = (50.0)(4.184)(6.0) = 1255 J absorbed by the water, so the dissolution released 1.26 kJ. Per mole: −1.26 kJ/0.020 mol = −63 kJ/mol.
−31 kJ/mol
−31 kJ/mol would result from dividing by 0.040 mol.
questions.x: q = (50.0)(4.184)(6.0) = 1255 J absorbed by the water, so the dissolution released 1.26 kJ. Per mole: −1.26 kJ/0.020 mol = −63 kJ/mol. Trap: Giving the sign of ΔH as the sign of ΔT or forgetting to divide by moles.

questions.q: After staring at a green square for 60 seconds, a person looks at a white wall and briefly sees a red square. This afterimage is best explained by:
o: trichromatic theory alone, because three cone types respond to short, medium, and long wavelengths.
Trichromatic theory explains color matching at the receptor but not complementary afterimages.
opponent-process theory: fatigue of the green side of a red-green channel gives a red rebound.
Correct: Opponent cells signal red or green; after prolonged green stimulation, the fatigued green response yields a relative red signal against white.
dark adaptation, in which rods regenerate rhodopsin during prolonged time in low light.
Dark adaptation concerns sensitivity changes in low light, not colored afterimages.
feature detection by simple cells in the visual cortex, which respond to edges and orientations.
Feature detectors respond to edges and orientation, not afterimage color.
questions.x: Opponent cells signal red or green; after prolonged green stimulation, the fatigued green response yields a relative red signal against white. Trap: Choosing trichromatic theory because it is the better-known color theory, even though it does not predict afterimages.

questions.q: Why can a person with thalamic damage still detect odors?
o: Olfactory receptor axons project directly to the visual cortex in the occipital lobe.
Olfactory axons synapse in the olfactory bulb and not in visual cortex.
Odor detection occurs entirely within the nasal cavity without any involvement of the brain.
Perception of odor requires central processing.
Olfactory bulb neurons project to cortex and limbic areas without a thalamic relay.
Correct: Smell is the only major sense whose primary pathway bypasses the thalamus on its way to cortex.
Taste receptors on the tongue take over the sensory function of detecting odor molecules.
Taste provides a different modality and does not substitute for smell.
questions.x: Smell is the only major sense whose primary pathway bypasses the thalamus on its way to cortex. Trap: Assuming all senses route through the thalamus before cortex.

questions.q: After seeing extensive news coverage of a plane crash, a person overestimates the likelihood of dying in a plane crash relative to driving. This reflects the:
o: representativeness heuristic, judging probability by similarity to a prototype.
The judgment is based on ease of recall rather than resemblance to a category.
confirmation bias, favoring information that supports prior beliefs.
No prior belief or selective search is described.
availability heuristic, judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind.
Correct: Vivid, recent coverage makes plane crashes easy to recall, inflating their perceived probability.
functional fixedness, the inability to see novel uses of an object.
This concerns problem solving with objects.
questions.x: Vivid, recent coverage makes plane crashes easy to recall, inflating their perceived probability. Trap: Picking representativeness because crashes seem 'typical' of danger, rather than recognizing recall ease.

questions.q: A patient with a left-hemisphere stroke speaks slowly with effort and in short phrases, but understands spoken instructions and recognizes her errors. The lesion most likely involves the:
o: left posterior superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke's area).
Damage here causes fluent speech with poor comprehension.
right hemisphere homologue of Broca's area.
Right-sided lesions rarely produce this nonfluent aphasia in right-handed people.
left inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area).
Correct: Nonfluent speech with relatively preserved comprehension is characteristic of Broca's aphasia.
primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe.
Visual cortex damage affects vision, not speech production.
questions.x: Nonfluent speech with relatively preserved comprehension is characteristic of Broca's aphasia. Trap: Mixing up Broca and Wernicke by remembering only that both involve language.

questions.q: A child who enjoys drawing is given prizes for drawing each day. When the prizes stop, the child draws much less than before the prizes began. This is best explained by:
o: extinction of a conditioned fear response once the expected prizes stopped arriving.
No fear conditioning is involved.
the overjustification effect: extrinsic rewards undermined intrinsic motivation.
Correct: The child came to attribute drawing to the reward rather than to interest, so removing the reward reduced the behavior below baseline.
drive reduction, as drawing satisfied a physiological need such as hunger or thirst.
Drawing does not reduce a biological drive such as hunger.
a fixed-ratio schedule producing a pause in responding after each reinforcement.
Drawing fell well below baseline instead of pausing briefly after each reward.
questions.x: The child came to attribute drawing to the reward rather than to interest, so removing the reward reduced the behavior below baseline. Trap: Interpreting the drop as ordinary extinction rather than a decline below the pre-reward baseline.

questions.q: A sleeping participant shows low-amplitude, high-frequency EEG activity, rapid eye movements, and loss of skeletal muscle tone. The participant is most likely in:
o: stage N3 (slow-wave) sleep.
N3 shows high-amplitude, low-frequency delta waves.
REM sleep.
Correct: This combination of a waking-like EEG, rapid eye movements, and muscle atonia defines REM sleep.
stage N2 sleep.
N2 shows sleep spindles and K-complexes without rapid eye movements.
stage N1 sleep.
N1 shows slow rolling eye movements and theta waves, with muscle tone retained.
questions.x: This combination of a waking-like EEG, rapid eye movements, and muscle atonia defines REM sleep. Trap: Choosing N3 because 'deep sleep' is associated with dreaming, when vivid dreaming is typical of REM.

questions.q: According to the dopamine hypothesis, antipsychotic drugs that block D2 receptors are most effective at reducing:
o: flat affect and social withdrawal.
These negative symptoms respond poorly to traditional antipsychotics.
hallucinations and delusions.
Correct: Excess dopaminergic activity is linked to positive symptoms, which respond best to D2 antagonists.
memory loss and slowed processing.
Cognitive deficits are less responsive to D2 blockade.
manic episodes and decreased need for sleep.
These are features of bipolar disorder rather than the core symptoms of schizophrenia.
questions.x: Excess dopaminergic activity is linked to positive symptoms, which respond best to D2 antagonists. Trap: Assuming antipsychotics treat all schizophrenia symptoms equally, including the negative symptoms.

questions.q: A cohesive committee, led by a strong chair, quickly agrees on a plan. Members privately have doubts but do not voice them and believe that everyone else agrees. The plan fails. This is an example of:
o: groupthink, in which pressure for consensus suppresses dissent and critical evaluation.
Correct: Self-censorship and an illusion of unanimity within a cohesive group are hallmarks of groupthink.
social loafing, in which individuals exert less effort in groups.
The issue is suppressed dissent, not reduced effort.
the bystander effect, in which individuals help less when others are present.
No emergency or helping behavior is described.
group polarization, in which a group's decision becomes more extreme than members' initial leanings.
Members' leanings were not described as moving toward an extreme.
questions.x: Self-censorship and an illusion of unanimity within a cohesive group are hallmarks of groupthink. Trap: Selecting group polarization because the group's decision turned out poorly.

questions.q: Residents who agreed to sign a petition for a safer street were later much more willing to display a large 'Drive Carefully' sign in their yards than residents who were asked only about the large sign. This is the:
o: door-in-the-face technique.
This starts with a large request that will be refused and follows with a smaller one.
low-ball technique.
This involves withdrawing an attractive feature after a commitment has been made.
peripheral route of persuasion.
This describes how a message is processed, not a sequence of requests.
foot-in-the-door technique.
Correct: Agreement to a small request increases the likelihood of agreeing to a later larger request, consistent with self-perception and consistency.
questions.x: Agreement to a small request increases the likelihood of agreeing to a later larger request, consistent with self-perception and consistency. Trap: Reversing the order of requests and picking door-in-the-face.

questions.q: According to Bandura, which experience typically produces the strongest increase in a student's self-efficacy for solving physics problems?
o: Successfully solving similar problems on her own
Correct: Mastery experiences are the strongest source of self-efficacy.
Hearing a lecture on the importance of physics
Verbal persuasion is a weaker source of self-efficacy.
Watching a classmate solve a problem that she cannot
Vicarious experience helps, but it is typically less powerful than personal success.
Feeling anxious while taking a quiz
High physiological arousal and anxiety usually reduce self-efficacy.
questions.x: Mastery experiences are the strongest source of self-efficacy. Trap: Choosing encouragement or modeling over a person's own successful performance.

questions.q: In an experiment, participants are told they were randomly assigned by a coin flip to the 'blue' or 'green' group. They then give more money to members of their own group than to the other group. This best illustrates:
o: the fundamental attribution error, attributing others' actions to disposition.
The behavior is a bias in allocation, not an explanation of others' actions.
in-group favoritism, which is predicted by social identity theory.
Correct: Even arbitrary group membership can lead people to favor the in-group to enhance their social identity.
the just-world hypothesis, believing that people get what they deserve.
The allocation was based on group membership.
stereotype threat, in which fear of confirming a stereotype impairs performance.
No performance was assessed.
questions.x: Even arbitrary group membership can lead people to favor the in-group to enhance their social identity. Trap: Believing that favoritism requires a history of conflict or real group differences.

questions.q: A student from a family that regularly attends museums and uses formal speech finds it easier to succeed in an elite university than a student without that background. Which concept does this best illustrate?
o: Cultural capital, nonfinancial assets that confer social advantage.
Correct: Familiarity with the dominant culture's tastes and styles functions as a resource that helps in education and elite settings.
Social capital, advantage derived from networks and relationships.
The advantage described comes from knowledge and style, not from contacts.
Anomie, a state of normlessness during periods of rapid social change.
No normlessness is involved.
Intragenerational mobility, a change in one person's status over her life.
The scenario compares students' backgrounds rather than one person's status over time.
questions.x: Familiarity with the dominant culture's tastes and styles functions as a resource that helps in education and elite settings. Trap: Confusing cultural capital (tastes, knowledge) with social capital (networks).

questions.q: In a period of sudden economic collapse, some researchers observe a rise in suicide rates as norms about aspirations break down. Durkheim would most likely attribute this to:
o: alienation from the products of one's labor.
This is Marx's concept.
rationalization of social life through bureaucracy.
This is Weber's concept.
symbolic interactionism, in which meaning is built through interaction.
This is a theoretical perspective, not an account of suicide.
anomie, a lack of social regulation and normative guidance.
Correct: In Durkheim's analysis, sudden change loosens social regulation, producing anomic suicide.
questions.x: In Durkheim's analysis, sudden change loosens social regulation, producing anomic suicide. Trap: Attributing the concept to Marx or Weber because all three wrote on social change.

questions.q: A city of 500,000 people has 12,000 immigrants and 8,000 emigrants in one year. Its net migration rate per 1,000 population is:
o: A decimal place slip would give 0.8.
This is the net number of migrants in thousands, 4, not a rate per 1,000 population.
This results from a different decimal error and has no basis in the figures.
questions.x: (12,000 - 8,000) / 500,000 = 0.008, or 8 per 1,000. Trap: Giving the net count in thousands (4) or slipping a decimal place when converting to a rate per 1,000.

questions.q: A researcher conducts 20 independent hypothesis tests at alpha = 0.05 in a situation in which none of the null hypotheses is false. About how many significant results are expected by chance?
o: With alpha = 0.05, some false positives are expected even when no effect exists.
This would correspond to alpha of 0.25.
Correct: 20 x 0.05 = 1 expected Type I error.
This would occur only if every test were significant, which is not expected.
questions.x: 20 x 0.05 = 1 expected Type I error. Trap: Assuming that no significant results can occur when the null hypotheses are all true.

questions.q: A proline residue in the middle of an α-helix would most likely:
o: stabilize the helix by adding an extra hydrogen bond between its side chain and the backbone carbonyl four residues earlier
Proline lacks the N-H and cannot add a hydrogen bond.
have no effect on the helix because proline is nonpolar and its side chain is buried in the hydrophobic core
Polarity is not the issue; geometry and missing N-H are.
disrupt the helix, because its ring restricts rotation and its nitrogen lacks a hydrogen for backbone bonding
Correct: Proline's amide nitrogen has no H to donate to the i+4 carbonyl, and its ring constrains the phi angle, producing a kink.
increase the length of the helix through disulfide formation with a cysteine located one turn away in the sequence
Proline has no thiol for disulfide formation.
questions.x: Proline's amide nitrogen has no H to donate to the i+4 carbonyl, and its ring constrains the phi angle, producing a kink. Trap: Considering only side chain polarity.

questions.q: The peptide bond is planar and does not rotate freely primarily because:
o: resonance gives the C-N bond partial double-bond character
Correct: Delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl gives the C-N bond partial double-bond character.
the peptide linkage is a covalent disulfide bond between sulfur atoms of neighboring residues
Disulfides link cysteines, not the backbone.
the bond is stabilized by hydrogen bonds to surrounding water molecules that hold the atoms in one plane
Hydrogen bonding to water doesn't restrict rotation of the bond.
the carbonyl oxygen is protonated at physiological pH, which locks the bond into a single orientation
The carbonyl oxygen is not protonated at pH 7.
questions.x: Delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl gives the C-N bond partial double-bond character. Trap: Confusing backbone planarity with side-chain interactions.

questions.q: A cell line lacks functional DNA ligase. Which finding would be expected in newly replicated DNA?
o: Accumulation of RNA primers only on the leading strand
The leading strand needs only one primer, and ligase is not related to primers.
Accumulation of short fragments on the lagging strand
Correct: DNA ligase seals nicks between Okazaki fragments after primer removal and gap filling, so unjoined fragments accumulate on the lagging strand.
Failure to unwind the parental duplex
Helicase unwinds DNA independent of ligase.
Increased formation of pyrimidine dimers
Pyrimidine dimers are caused by UV light, not ligase loss.
questions.x: DNA ligase seals nicks between Okazaki fragments after primer removal and gap filling, so unjoined fragments accumulate on the lagging strand. Trap: Ligase is needed on both strands but especially on the lagging strand.

questions.q: An aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase attaches the wrong amino acid to a tRNA and lacks proofreading activity. What is the expected result?
o: The ribosome rejects the tRNA because the anticodon is incorrect
The anticodon is correct; the ribosome cannot see the amino acid.
The codon is misread as a stop codon
Stop codons are read by release factors.
The mRNA is degraded by nonsense-mediated decay
Nonsense-mediated decay targets premature stop codons.
The wrong amino acid is incorporated at codons matched by that tRNA's anticodon
Correct: The ribosome recognizes codon-anticodon pairing, not the attached amino acid, so a mischarged tRNA inserts the wrong amino acid at the matching codon.
questions.x: The ribosome recognizes codon-anticodon pairing, not the attached amino acid, so a mischarged tRNA inserts the wrong amino acid at the matching codon. Trap: Believing the ribosome checks the amino acid.

questions.q: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, an autosomal recessive disease affects 1 in 10,000 people. The carrier frequency is closest to:
o: 1/100 is q, the allele frequency.
1 in 50
1/10,000 is the disease frequency.
1/5,000 is a miscalculation of 2q².
questions.x: q² = 0.0001, so q = 0.01; 2pq = 2(0.99)(0.01) ≈ 0.02, or 1 in 50. Trap: Reporting the allele frequency as carrier frequency.

questions.q: Nondisjunction of one pair of sister chromatids in meiosis II in a single primary spermatocyte lineage produces gametes that are:
o: all four with an extra chromosome
Not all four are affected, because only one secondary cell failed.
two with an extra chromosome and two missing a chromosome
That is the outcome of nondisjunction in meiosis I.
two normal, one with an extra chromosome, and one missing a chromosome
Correct: Meiosis I is normal, so both secondary cells are fine; in only one of them the sister chromatids fail to separate, giving one n+1, one n−1, and two normal gametes.
all four normal
One cell's failure produces aneuploid gametes.
questions.x: Meiosis I is normal, so both secondary cells are fine; in only one of them the sister chromatids fail to separate, giving one n+1, one n−1, and two normal gametes. Trap: Confusing the outcomes of meiosis I and meiosis II errors.

questions.q: Thiamine deficiency would most likely cause elevated blood pyruvate and lactate because thiamine pyrophosphate is a cofactor for:
o: the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
Correct: Pyruvate dehydrogenase requires TPP (E1), so deficiency blocks pyruvate conversion to acetyl-CoA, shunting pyruvate to lactate.
pyruvate carboxylase, which converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate in the mitochondria
Pyruvate carboxylase uses biotin.
lactate dehydrogenase, which interconverts pyruvate and lactate using NADH
Lactate dehydrogenase uses NADH.
phosphofructokinase-1, which commits glucose to glycolysis in the liver and muscle
PFK-1 does not require TPP.
questions.x: Pyruvate dehydrogenase requires TPP (E1), so deficiency blocks pyruvate conversion to acetyl-CoA, shunting pyruvate to lactate. Trap: Confusing biotin-dependent and TPP-dependent enzymes.

questions.q: Individuals with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency are susceptible to hemolysis under oxidative stress because their red blood cells:
o: cannot carry out glycolysis and so make no ATP
Glycolysis is intact.
lack mitochondria needed to detoxify peroxide
Red cells lack mitochondria regardless; detoxification uses glutathione.
cannot synthesize heme
Heme synthesis isn't affected by G6PD deficiency.
cannot generate enough NADPH to regenerate reduced glutathione
Correct: G6PD is the first and rate-limiting enzyme of the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, the main source of NADPH in red cells. NADPH maintains glutathione that neutralizes peroxides.
questions.x: G6PD is the first and rate-limiting enzyme of the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, the main source of NADPH in red cells. NADPH maintains glutathione that neutralizes peroxides. Trap: Linking G6PD to glycolysis instead of NADPH production.

questions.q: Cholera toxin causes severe watery diarrhea by locking Gαs in the active state. The immediate intracellular effect is:
o: inhibition of adenylyl cyclase
Gαi, not Gαs, inhibits adenylyl cyclase.
activation of phospholipase C and IP3 production
PLC is activated by Gαq.
closure of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels
Not a direct effect of Gαs.
persistent activation of adenylyl cyclase and elevated cAMP
Correct: Active Gαs stimulates adenylyl cyclase to make cAMP, activating PKA and opening CFTR chloride channels, with water following.
questions.x: Active Gαs stimulates adenylyl cyclase to make cAMP, activating PKA and opening CFTR chloride channels, with water following. Trap: Confusing Gs, Gi, and Gq pathways.

questions.q: Penicillin kills growing bacteria by inhibiting:
o: peptidyl transferase activity of the 50S ribosomal subunit, which blocks peptide bond formation during elongation
That is the target of chloramphenicol.
cross-linking of peptidoglycan by transpeptidases, weakening the wall so that growing cells lyse
Correct: β-lactams inhibit the transpeptidase (penicillin-binding proteins), so the wall cannot withstand turgor in growing cells.
bacterial DNA gyrase, a topoisomerase that relieves the supercoiling that builds up ahead of the replication fork
That is the target of fluoroquinolones.
synthesis of folate, a cofactor that bacteria must make to produce nucleotides for DNA replication
That is the target of sulfonamides.
questions.x: β-lactams inhibit the transpeptidase (penicillin-binding proteins), so the wall cannot withstand turgor in growing cells. Trap: Mixing up antibiotic classes and targets.

questions.q: When a nucleus from a differentiated frog intestinal cell is transplanted into an enucleated egg and can direct development of a tadpole, the experiment shows that:
o: differentiated cells retain the full genome and differences arise from differential gene expression
Correct: The transplanted nucleus is reprogrammed by egg cytoplasm, showing that the genome was retained.
differentiation involves irreversible loss of genes that are not needed in the mature cell type
The success of the experiment shows the opposite.
egg cytoplasm is not needed for development, since the transplanted nucleus directs all of the events
Egg cytoplasm is required to reprogram the nucleus.
mitochondrial DNA determines cell type, because the transferred cytoplasm carries the instructions for differentiation
Mitochondrial DNA is not involved in cell identity.
questions.x: The transplanted nucleus is reprogrammed by egg cytoplasm, showing that the genome was retained. Trap: Believing differentiation changes DNA content.

questions.q: Demyelination in multiple sclerosis slows action potential conduction primarily because:
o: voltage-gated Na+ channels are not found in the axon, so action potentials cannot be regenerated along its length
Na+ channels are present, mostly at nodes.
the resting membrane potential becomes more negative, so a larger depolarization is needed to reach threshold
Resting potential is set by K+ gradients and is not the cause.
depolarizing current leaks across the axonal membrane and does not reach the next node of Ranvier effectively
Correct: Myelin raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, so current spreads to the next node. Without it, charge leaks and conduction slows or fails.
myelin normally increases membrane capacitance, so its loss reduces the stored charge available at each node
Myelin decreases capacitance.
questions.x: Myelin raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, so current spreads to the next node. Without it, charge leaks and conduction slows or fails. Trap: Reversing the effect of myelin on capacitance.

questions.q: A patient has lost ADH secretion after head trauma. Compared with a healthy person, the patient would produce:
o: a large volume of dilute urine and an increased plasma osmolality
Correct: Without ADH, aquaporin-2 is not inserted into the collecting duct, so water is not reabsorbed, producing dilute urine and elevated plasma osmolality.
a small volume of concentrated urine, with a decreased plasma osmolality from water retention
Concentrated urine requires ADH.
a large volume of concentrated urine, because Na+ reabsorption in the collecting duct increases
Urine volume increases but is dilute.
a normal volume of urine with high glucose content, because the filtered load of glucose exceeds its transport maximum
Glucose is not elevated in diabetes insipidus.
questions.x: Without ADH, aquaporin-2 is not inserted into the collecting duct, so water is not reabsorbed, producing dilute urine and elevated plasma osmolality. Trap: Confusing diabetes insipidus with diabetes mellitus.

questions.q: Blockage of the common bile duct by a gallstone would most likely cause:
o: decreased protein digestion in the stomach because pepsin cannot be activated without bile salts
Gastric protein digestion depends on pepsin and acid.
fatty, pale stools due to impaired fat emulsification and absorption
Correct: Bile salts emulsify dietary fat and help form micelles. Without them lipid absorption falls and fat appears in feces (steatorrhea).
impaired carbohydrate digestion by salivary amylase, which depends on bile for its activation in the mouth
Salivary amylase acts in the mouth.
increased gastric acid secretion, because bile retention stimulates the parietal cells through gastrin release
Bile duct obstruction doesn't alter gastric acid.
questions.x: Bile salts emulsify dietary fat and help form micelles. Without them lipid absorption falls and fat appears in feces (steatorrhea). Trap: Linking bile to digestion of all macronutrients.

questions.q: A virus-infected nucleated cell presents viral peptides on MHC class I. Which cell recognizes it and induces its death?
o: A CD4+ helper T cell, which binds the peptide on the MHC class I molecule and kills by releasing cytokines
Helper T cells recognize MHC class II.
A B cell secreting IgM, which binds the viral peptide on the cell surface and lyses the cell with its antibody
B cells make antibodies and do not kill infected cells directly.
An erythrocyte, which binds the infected cell through complement receptors and destroys it by phagocytosis
Erythrocytes do not kill other cells.
A CD8+ cytotoxic T cell, via perforin and granzymes
Correct: CD8 T cells recognize peptide on MHC I with their TCR and kill using perforin and granzymes.
questions.x: CD8 T cells recognize peptide on MHC I with their TCR and kill using perforin and granzymes. Trap: Confusing MHC I and II recognition.

questions.q: A 70 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator that accelerates upward at 2.0 m/s². What does the scale read? (Use g = 9.8 m/s².)
o: 690 N is the weight mg, valid only at constant velocity.
550 N is m(g − a), the reading for downward acceleration.
Correct: N − mg = ma, so N = m(g + a) = 70(11.8) = 826 N, about 830 N.
140 N is only the net force ma.
questions.x: N − mg = ma, so N = m(g + a) = 70(11.8) = 826 N, about 830 N. Trap: Using g − a instead of g + a for an upward acceleration.

questions.q: A 2.0 kg cart moving at 3.0 m/s collides and sticks to a 1.0 kg cart at rest. How much kinetic energy is lost?
o: 6.0 J is the final kinetic energy, not the loss.
9.0 J is the initial kinetic energy.
1.5 J has no basis; it would be half the loss.
Correct: Final speed = 6.0/3.0 = 2.0 m/s; KE_i = 9.0 J, KE_f = ½(3.0)(4.0) = 6.0 J; lost = 3.0 J.
questions.x: Final speed = 6.0/3.0 = 2.0 m/s; KE_i = 9.0 J, KE_f = ½(3.0)(4.0) = 6.0 J; lost = 3.0 J. Trap: Assuming kinetic energy is conserved in an inelastic collision or reporting the final energy as the loss.

questions.q: Water flows at 2.0 m/s through a pipe of radius 3.0 cm into a section of radius 1.5 cm. What is the speed in the narrower section?
o: 4.0 m/s scales speed with radius rather than area.
16 m/s
16 m/s applies the factor of four twice.
Correct: Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂; A scales with r², so halving r quadruples v: 8.0 m/s.
1.0 m/s inverts the relation, as if the speed fell in the narrow section.
questions.x: Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂; A scales with r², so halving r quadruples v: 8.0 m/s. Trap: Using the radius ratio instead of the area ratio in the continuity equation.

questions.q: A 12 V battery is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel combination of a 6.0 Ω and a 12 Ω resistor. What is the current through the 6.0 Ω resistor?
o: 0.5 A is the current through the 12 Ω resistor.
1.5 A is the total current.
2.0 A applies the full 12 V across the 6.0 Ω resistor.
Correct: R_parallel = 4.0 Ω, total = 8.0 Ω, I = 1.5 A; voltage across the parallel branch = 6.0 V, so I = 6.0/6.0 = 1.0 A.
questions.x: R_parallel = 4.0 Ω, total = 8.0 Ω, I = 1.5 A; voltage across the parallel branch = 6.0 V, so I = 6.0/6.0 = 1.0 A. Trap: Applying the battery voltage across a resistor that sees only part of it.

questions.q: A current of 2.0 A flows through aqueous CuSO₄ for 965 s. What mass of copper is deposited? (F = 96,500 C/mol; Cu = 63.5 g/mol.)
o: 1.3 g assumes one electron per copper atom.
0.32 g divides by two twice.
Correct: Q = 1930 C = 0.020 mol e⁻; Cu²⁺ needs 2 e⁻, so 0.010 mol × 63.5 = 0.64 g.
6.4 g has an error of a factor of ten in the moles of electrons.
questions.x: Q = 1930 C = 0.020 mol e⁻; Cu²⁺ needs 2 e⁻, so 0.010 mol × 63.5 = 0.64 g. Trap: Forgetting that Cu²⁺ requires two electrons per atom.

questions.q: An object is placed 30 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Which describes the image?
o: Virtual, upright, 15 cm from the lens
Virtual, upright, 15 cm from the lens would occur only for an object inside the focal length.
Real, inverted, 15 cm from the lens
Correct: 1/d_i = 1/10 − 1/30 = 1/15, so d_i = 15 cm; positive d_i means real and magnification −0.5 means inverted.
Real, inverted, 7.5 cm from the lens
Real, inverted, 7.5 cm from the lens gives the wrong image distance.
Real, upright, 30 cm from the lens
Real, upright, 30 cm from the lens occurs for no real object with a converging lens.
questions.x: 1/d_i = 1/10 − 1/30 = 1/15, so d_i = 15 cm; positive d_i means real and magnification −0.5 means inverted. Trap: Mixing up sign conventions for real versus virtual images.

questions.q: Light in glass (n = 1.5) strikes the glass–air interface. What is the critical angle?
o: Correct: sinθ_c = n_air/n_glass = 1/1.5 = 0.667, so θ_c = 42°.
48° is the complement, found with cosine instead of sine.
56° would correspond to n of about 1.2.
90° is the angle of refraction at the critical angle, not the critical angle.
questions.x: sinθ_c = n_air/n_glass = 1/1.5 = 0.667, so θ_c = 42°. Trap: Using cosine instead of sine in the critical angle relation or confusing it with the refraction angle.

questions.q: A radioisotope has a half-life of 8.0 days. What percentage of a sample remains after 24 days?
o: 25% is the amount after two half-lives.
Correct: 24 days is three half-lives, so (1/2)³ = 12.5%.
50% is the amount remaining after only one half-life.
6.25% is the amount after four half-lives.
questions.x: 24 days is three half-lives, so (1/2)³ = 12.5%. Trap: Miscounting half-lives or treating decay as linear.

questions.q: An electron in a hydrogen atom moves from n = 3 to n = 2. Which wavelength is emitted?
o: 487 nm
487 nm is the n = 4 to 2 transition.
656 nm
122 nm
122 nm is in the ultraviolet, the n = 2 to 1 transition.
1875 nm is the n = 4 to 3 transition.
questions.x: E = 13.6(1/4 − 1/9) = 1.89 eV, so λ = 1240/1.89 = 656 nm. Trap: Using the wrong pair of levels or mixing up emission series.

questions.q: What is the molar solubility of AgCl (Ksp = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) in 0.10 M NaCl?
o: 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M is the solubility in pure water, √Ksp.
1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ M is Ksp itself.
Correct: [Ag⁺] = Ksp/[Cl⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰/0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M, because of the common ion effect.
1.8 × 10⁻¹¹ M multiplies Ksp by 0.10 instead of dividing by the 0.10 M chloride concentration.
questions.x: [Ag⁺] = Ksp/[Cl⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰/0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M, because of the common ion effect. Trap: Using √Ksp even when a common ion is present.

questions.q: What is the molecular geometry of XeF₄?
o: Tetrahedral
Tetrahedral would apply to four bonding pairs and no lone pairs.
Square planar
Correct: Xe has 4 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs (octahedral electron geometry), with the lone pairs opposite each other: square planar.
See-saw
See-saw corresponds to 4 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair.
Octahedral
Octahedral has six bonding pairs, as in SF₆.
questions.x: Xe has 4 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs (octahedral electron geometry), with the lone pairs opposite each other: square planar. Trap: Ignoring lone pairs on the central atom.

questions.q: A mixture of benzoic acid and naphthalene in diethyl ether is shaken with aqueous NaHCO₃. Where is each compound found?
o: Benzoic acid in the ether layer and naphthalene in the aqueous layer
Benzoic acid in the ether layer and naphthalene in the aqueous layer reverses the solubility, as nonpolar naphthalene does not dissolve in water.
Both in the ether layer
Both in the ether layer ignores acid-base reactivity of benzoic acid.
Benzoate in the aqueous layer and naphthalene in the ether layer
Correct: The carboxylic acid is deprotonated to the water-soluble benzoate salt, while neutral naphthalene stays in ether.
Both in the aqueous layer
Both in the aqueous layer is incorrect; naphthalene is nonpolar.
questions.x: The carboxylic acid is deprotonated to the water-soluble benzoate salt, while neutral naphthalene stays in ether. Trap: Forgetting that ionic forms partition into the aqueous layer.

questions.q: Ethyl benzoate is treated with excess LiAlH₄ followed by aqueous acid. What are the products?
o: Benzaldehyde and ethanol
Benzaldehyde and ethanol would be the product of partial reduction, which LiAlH₄ does not stop at.
Benzoic acid and ethanol
Benzoic acid and ethanol is hydrolysis, not reduction.
Benzyl alcohol and ethanol
Correct: LiAlH₄ reduces esters to two alcohols: PhCH₂OH from the acyl portion and EtOH from the alkoxy portion.
Benzyl alcohol only
Benzyl alcohol only ignores the ethanol released from the alkoxy group.
questions.x: LiAlH₄ reduces esters to two alcohols: PhCH₂OH from the acyl portion and EtOH from the alkoxy portion. Trap: Stopping the reduction at the aldehyde stage.

questions.q: The pKa values of alanine are 2.34 (carboxyl) and 9.69 (ammonium). What is its isoelectric point?
o: 2.3 is the carboxyl pKa.
9.7 is the ammonium pKa.
12.0 is the sum, not the average.
Correct: pI = (2.34 + 9.69)/2 = 6.02, where the zwitterion dominates.
questions.x: pI = (2.34 + 9.69)/2 = 6.02, where the zwitterion dominates. Trap: Using a single pKa or summing instead of averaging.

questions.q: Dissolving a salt in 50.0 g of water raises the temperature of the water by 6.0°C. What heat did the water absorb? (c = 4.18 J/g·°C)
o: 0.30 kJ omits the specific heat.
0.072 kJ divides mass by c instead of multiplying.
5.2 kJ
5.2 kJ multiplies by c twice.
1.3 kJ
questions.x: q = mcΔT = 50.0 × 4.18 × 6.0 = 1254 J, or 1.3 kJ. Trap: Omitting c or mis-handling units in q = mcΔT.
