The Hfr cell transfers only plasmid genes and never chromosomal DNA, so recipient cells remain F- after mating.
Hfr strains transfer chromosomal markers, which is the basis of conjugation mapping.
The recipient degrades all transferred DNA through homologous recombination before it can be expressed or replicated.
Homologous recombination integrates the transferred donor DNA; it does not degrade it all.
questions.x: Transfer starts within the integrated F sequence and moves chromosomal genes first; the remaining F genes enter last, if at all. Trap: Treating Hfr transfer like transfer of an autonomous F plasmid.

questions.q: At the time of ovulation in humans, the oocyte is arrested in which stage?
o: Metaphase of meiosis II
Correct: The primary oocyte completes meiosis I just before ovulation and then arrests in metaphase II until fertilization completes meiosis II.
Prophase of meiosis I
Prophase I arrest lasts from fetal life until shortly before ovulation.
Metaphase of meiosis I
The oocyte completes meiosis I before ovulation.
Telophase of meiosis II
Meiosis II is completed only after sperm penetration.
questions.x: The primary oocyte completes meiosis I just before ovulation and then arrests in metaphase II until fertilization completes meiosis II. Trap: Confusing the first arrest point (prophase I) with the one present at ovulation.

questions.q: Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET imaging highlights many tumors. Which feature of tumor metabolism does this reflect?
o: Increased glucose uptake and glycolysis, with trapping of phosphorylated FDG in the cell
Correct: Tumor cells often take up glucose and perform glycolysis at high rates (the Warburg effect). FDG-6-phosphate cannot proceed through glycolysis and stays in the cell.
Decreased glucose uptake, with accumulation of FDG in the mitochondria
Tumors typically take up more glucose, not less.
Increased oxidative phosphorylation, with FDG used as a TCA cycle substrate
FDG-6-phosphate is not oxidized, and tumor ATP often comes from glycolysis despite oxygen.
Increased gluconeogenesis, with FDG exported to the blood
Gluconeogenesis is not a feature of the signal, and phosphorylated FDG does not leave cells.
questions.x: Tumor cells often take up glucose and perform glycolysis at high rates (the Warburg effect). FDG-6-phosphate cannot proceed through glycolysis and stays in the cell. Trap: Assuming an imaging tracer must be metabolized fully like glucose.

questions.q: A patient has an elevated free thyroxine level, a suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone level, and a diffusely enlarged thyroid. Which is the most likely cause?
o: A pituitary adenoma that secretes TSH
A TSH-secreting tumor would produce high TSH, not suppressed TSH.
Destruction of the thyroid by autoantibodies against thyroid peroxidase
Destruction of the gland lowers T4 and raises TSH.
Dietary iodine deficiency
Iodine deficiency lowers T4 and raises TSH.
Antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor
Correct: Stimulating antibodies mimic TSH, increasing T4 and goiter size, and the high T4 suppresses pituitary TSH by negative feedback (Graves disease).
questions.x: Stimulating antibodies mimic TSH, increasing T4 and goiter size, and the high T4 suppresses pituitary TSH by negative feedback (Graves disease). Trap: Forgetting that TSH is suppressed when the thyroid is driven independently of the pituitary.

questions.q: A patient with severe liver disease has low serum albumin and develops peripheral edema. Which change in the Starling forces best explains the edema?
o: Increased interstitial oncotic pressure resists fluid movement into the interstitium.
Higher interstitial oncotic pressure would draw fluid out; the described change would not occur from low plasma albumin.
Decreased capillary hydrostatic pressure favors net movement of fluid into the interstitium.
Lower hydrostatic pressure would reduce filtration.
Decreased capillary oncotic pressure favors net movement of fluid into the interstitium.
Correct: Albumin supplies most of the plasma oncotic pressure, which opposes filtration; with less albumin, filtration exceeds reabsorption, causing edema.
Increased capillary oncotic pressure favors net movement of fluid into the interstitium.
Higher oncotic pressure in capillaries would pull fluid back into them.
questions.x: Albumin supplies most of the plasma oncotic pressure, which opposes filtration; with less albumin, filtration exceeds reabsorption, causing edema. Trap: Choosing hydrostatic pressure when the problem involves a plasma protein deficit.

questions.q: A uniform plank is balanced on a central pivot. A 30 kg child sits 1.5 m to the left of the pivot. At what distance to the right of the pivot must a 45 kg child sit for the plank to remain in rotational equilibrium?
o: This would balance only if the two children had equal weights.
Correct: Net torque is zero: (30)(g)(1.5) = (45)(g)(d), so d = 1.0 m.
This multiplies 1.5 m by the mass ratio 45/30 instead of dividing.
This squares the mass ratio, which does not occur in a torque balance.
questions.x: Net torque is zero: (30)(g)(1.5) = (45)(g)(d), so d = 1.0 m. Trap: Inverting the lever-arm relationship so that the heavier child sits farther from the pivot.

questions.q: A 0.15 kg ball moving at 20 m/s is caught and brought to rest in 0.010 s. What is the magnitude of the average force exerted by the glove on the ball?
o: 30 N, with Δt = 0.10 s
This uses Δt = 0.10 s, a decimal-place error.
This uses Δt = 0.0010 s, a decimal-place error.
600 N, with Δp = 2mv
This doubles the momentum change, as if the ball had rebounded at the same speed.
questions.x: F = Δp/Δt = (0.15)(20)/0.010 = 300 N. Trap: Treating the momentum change as 2mv, which applies only to a rebound, when the ball is simply stopped.

questions.q: Water flows at 1.0 m/s through a horizontal pipe of diameter 4.0 cm that narrows to a diameter of 2.0 cm. By how much is the pressure in the narrow section lower than in the wide section? (ρ = 1,000 kg/m³)
o: This assumes the speed only doubles when the diameter is halved (v2 = 2 m/s).
Correct: Continuity gives v2 = 4.0 m/s, and Bernoulli gives ΔP = ½ρ(v2² − v1²) = ½(1,000)(16 − 1) = 7,500 Pa.
This uses ½ρv2² and forgets to subtract the kinetic term of the wide section.
This omits the factor of ½ in ½ρΔ(v²).
questions.x: Continuity gives v2 = 4.0 m/s, and Bernoulli gives ΔP = ½ρ(v2² − v1²) = ½(1,000)(16 − 1) = 7,500 Pa. Trap: Taking the speed to scale with diameter rather than with cross-sectional area, which scales as diameter squared.

questions.q: A block of wood with density 600 kg/m³ floats in water with 60% of its volume submerged. If the block is placed in oil of density 800 kg/m³, what fraction of its volume will be submerged?
o: This is the fraction submerged in water, where the fluid density is different.
Correct: Floating requires ρ_block × V = ρ_fluid × V_sub, so V_sub/V = 600/800 = 0.75.
This multiplies 0.60 by 0.80 instead of dividing 600 by 800.
A block less dense than the oil still floats and does not sink completely.
questions.x: Floating requires ρ_block × V = ρ_fluid × V_sub, so V_sub/V = 600/800 = 0.75. Trap: Multiplying the density ratios or forgetting that a denser fluid supports the same weight with less displaced volume.

questions.q: A 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected to a 2.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel combination of a 6.0 Ω and a 3.0 Ω resistor. What is the power dissipated in the 6.0 Ω resistor?
o: Correct: The parallel pair equals 2.0 Ω, so the total is 4.0 Ω and I = 3.0 A; the parallel voltage is 3.0 × 2.0 = 6.0 V, and P = V²/R = 36/6 = 6.0 W.
This applies the full 12 V of the battery across the 6.0 Ω resistor.
This uses I²R with the total current of 3.0 A through the 6.0 Ω resistor.
This uses P = I²R with I = 1.0 A and R = 2.0 Ω, the equivalent resistance of the parallel pair, instead of 6.0 Ω.
questions.x: The parallel pair equals 2.0 Ω, so the total is 4.0 Ω and I = 3.0 A; the parallel voltage is 3.0 × 2.0 = 6.0 V, and P = V²/R = 36/6 = 6.0 W. Trap: Using the battery voltage or total current for a single resistor in a mixed series-parallel network.

questions.q: A proton and an alpha particle (mass about 4 times that of the proton, charge 2e) enter the same uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the field with the same speed. What is the ratio of the alpha particle's orbit radius to the proton's?
o: This assumes that the radius depends only on speed and field strength.
This accounts for the mass but not for the doubled charge.
This inverts the ratio of mass to charge.
Correct: r = mv/(qB), so r_α/r_p = (4m/2q)/(m/q) = 2.
questions.x: r = mv/(qB), so r_α/r_p = (4m/2q)/(m/q) = 2. Trap: Forgetting that the orbit radius scales with mass divided by charge, so the charge of the alpha particle partly offsets its mass.

questions.q: A source emitting a 500 Hz tone moves directly toward a stationary observer at 34.3 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency does the observer hear?
o: 550 Hz, for a moving observer
This is the result for an observer moving toward a stationary source at 34.3 m/s, not for a moving source.
454 Hz, for a receding source
This uses v + v_s in the denominator, the result for a receding source.
500 Hz, with no Doppler shift
The frequency changes because the source moves relative to the medium.
556 Hz
questions.x: f' = f·v/(v − v_s) = 500 × 343/(343 − 34.3) = 556 Hz. Trap: Using the observer-motion form of the Doppler equation for a moving source, or choosing the wrong sign for the approach.

questions.q: An object is placed 30 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Which describes the image?
o: Virtual, upright, 15 cm from the lens, half the size of the object
An object beyond the focal point of a converging lens forms a real image.
Real, inverted, 15 cm from the lens, half the size of the object
Correct: 1/di = 1/10 − 1/30 = 1/15, so di = 15 cm (real); m = −di/do = −0.5, so the image is inverted and half as large.
Real, inverted, 7.5 cm from the lens, twice the size of the object
This does not satisfy the thin lens equation or m = −di/do.
Virtual, upright, 7.5 cm from the lens, equal in size to the object
A converging lens forms virtual images only for objects inside the focal length.
questions.x: 1/di = 1/10 − 1/30 = 1/15, so di = 15 cm (real); m = −di/do = −0.5, so the image is inverted and half as large. Trap: Using the thin lens equation without checking whether the object lies beyond or within the focal length.

questions.q: Iodine-131 (Z = 53) decays by β⁻ emission. What is the daughter nuclide?
o: ¹³¹Te
This lowers Z by 1, which would be β⁺ decay or electron capture.
¹²⁷Sb
This lowers A by 4 and Z by 2, as in alpha decay, which β⁻ emission does not do.
¹³¹Xe
Correct: β⁻ decay converts a neutron into a proton, raising Z by 1 with unchanged A: ¹³¹I → ¹³¹Xe + e⁻ + antineutrino.
¹³⁰I
Β⁻ decay does not change the number of protons and neutrons together, so A stays at 131.
questions.x: β⁻ decay converts a neutron into a proton, raising Z by 1 with unchanged A: ¹³¹I → ¹³¹Xe + e⁻ + antineutrino. Trap: Confusing the direction in which Z changes in β⁻ versus β⁺ decay.

questions.q: Which aqueous solution has the highest boiling point, assuming complete dissociation of the ionic solutes?
o: 0.20 m glucose
Glucose does not dissociate, so its effective molality is 0.20 m.
0.10 m CaCl2
Correct: The effective solute molality is i × m: CaCl2 gives 3 × 0.10 = 0.30 m.
0.10 m NaCl
NaCl gives 2 × 0.10 = 0.20 m, below that of CaCl2.
This gives 5 × 0.05 = 0.25 m, still below 0.30 m.
questions.x: The effective solute molality is i × m: CaCl2 gives 3 × 0.10 = 0.30 m. Trap: Comparing stated molalities without multiplying by the van't Hoff factor.

questions.q: Which compound has the highest boiling point?
o: 1-Propanol, CH3CH2CH2OH
Correct: 1-Propanol can donate and accept hydrogen bonds, which are much stronger than the dipole-dipole and dispersion forces of the others.
Methoxyethane, CH3OCH2CH3
It has an oxygen but no O–H group, so it cannot form hydrogen bonds with itself.
Propanal, CH3CH2CHO
It has dipole-dipole attractions but no H-bond donor.
Butane, CH3CH2CH2CH3
It is nonpolar and held together only by dispersion forces.
questions.x: 1-Propanol can donate and accept hydrogen bonds, which are much stronger than the dipole-dipole and dispersion forces of the others. Trap: Judging boiling point from molar mass or polarity instead of the ability to form hydrogen bonds.

questions.q: On a silica gel TLC plate, a compound's spot travels 3.0 cm while the solvent front travels 7.5 cm. What is the compound's Rf value?
o: Correct: Rf = distance spot traveled/distance solvent traveled = 3.0/7.5 = 0.40.
This inverts the ratio; Rf can never exceed 1.
This uses (7.5 − 3.0)/7.5, the fraction of the distance not traveled.
This divides by 10.5 cm, the sum of the two distances.
questions.x: Rf = distance spot traveled/distance solvent traveled = 3.0/7.5 = 0.40. Trap: Inverting the ratio of distances, which gives an impossible Rf greater than 1.

questions.q: Ethylmagnesium bromide is added to acetone, followed by aqueous acid workup. What is the major product?
o: 2-Methyl-2-butanol
Correct: The carbanion-like ethyl group adds to the carbonyl carbon of the ketone, and protonation of the alkoxide gives the tertiary alcohol (CH3)2C(OH)CH2CH3.
2-Butanol
This has only four carbons, but the product must contain five (three from acetone and two from the ethyl group).
3-Pentanol
This requires an aldehyde with a 3-carbon chain, such as propanal, not acetone.
2-Methyl-1-butanol
A Grignard reagent addition to a ketone forms a tertiary alcohol, never a primary alcohol.
questions.x: The carbanion-like ethyl group adds to the carbonyl carbon of the ketone, and protonation of the alkoxide gives the tertiary alcohol (CH3)2C(OH)CH2CH3. Trap: Forgetting that Grignard addition to a ketone forms a tertiary alcohol and that the new C–C bond forms at the carbonyl carbon.

questions.q: For the reaction A + B ⇌ C, K = 50 at a given temperature. A mixture contains [A] = 0.10 M, [B] = 0.20 M, and [C] = 2.0 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?
o: Toward products, because Q = 100 exceeds K
If Q exceeds K, the reaction must reverse to lower Q.
Toward products, because Q = 0.01 is less than K
This inverts Q; the correct value is 100.
It is at equilibrium, because K is greater than 1
K > 1 does not mean the mixture is at equilibrium; Q must equal K.
Toward reactants, because Q = 100 exceeds K
Correct: Q = [C]/([A][B]) = 2.0/(0.10 × 0.20) = 100 > 50, so the system shifts left to reach equilibrium.
questions.x: Q = [C]/([A][B]) = 2.0/(0.10 × 0.20) = 100 > 50, so the system shifts left to reach equilibrium. Trap: Comparing Q and K backward, or inverting the reaction quotient.

questions.q: A catalyst is added to a reaction at constant temperature. Which quantity is unchanged?
o: The rate constant of the forward reaction
The catalyst lowers Ea, which increases the forward rate constant.
The activation energy of the forward reaction
The catalyst provides a pathway with lower activation energy.
The equilibrium constant
Correct: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions equally, so K, ΔH, and ΔG are unchanged.
The time required to reach equilibrium
The catalyst speeds up approach to equilibrium, reducing this time.
questions.x: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions equally, so K, ΔH, and ΔG are unchanged. Trap: Thinking that a catalyst shifts the equilibrium position instead of only the rate at which it is reached.

questions.q: A university requires a first-year seminar intended to teach study skills. Many students report that the seminar is where they made their closest friendships. According to the functionalist perspective, the friendships are best described as:
o: A latent function, because the friendships are an unintended consequence of the seminar's design
Correct: Latent functions are unintended, unannounced consequences of an institution; the friendships are an unplanned benefit.
A manifest function, because the seminar was openly designed to produce friendships among students
Manifest functions are intended and recognized; the seminar's stated aim was study skills.
A latent dysfunction, because they disrupt the seminar's stated purpose of teaching study skills
Nothing suggests friendships harm the seminar, so they are not dysfunctions.
A manifest dysfunction, because they are a recognized and intended harm to the seminar's goals
Friendships were neither intended nor harmful.
questions.x: Latent functions are unintended, unannounced consequences of an institution; the friendships are an unplanned benefit. Trap: Treating any beneficial outcome as manifest, rather than checking whether it was intended.

questions.q: An assembly-line worker performs a single repetitive task, has no say in the design of the final product, and cannot keep or sell what she helps make. Which concept from Marxist theory best describes her situation?
o: Anomie, because the norms that once regulated her work have broken down and left her without guidance
Anomie is Durkheim's concept of normlessness, not Marx's.
False consciousness, because she wrongly believes that her interests are the same as those of the factory owners
False consciousness would require evidence that she misperceives her interests, which the stem does not give.
Alienation from the product of her labor and from the production process
Correct: Marx described alienation as the separation of workers from the products they create, the production process, other workers, and their own potential.
Cultural lag, because the material technology of her factory has advanced faster than the norms for using it
Cultural lag (Ogburn) concerns the pace of material and nonmaterial culture, not worker control.
questions.x: Marx described alienation as the separation of workers from the products they create, the production process, other workers, and their own potential. Trap: Choosing anomie because it is the better-known term for disconnectedness at work.

questions.q: A sociologist using the conflict perspective would most likely argue that sorting students into college-preparatory and vocational tracks:
o: Efficiently matches students' abilities to the occupational roles that society needs filled most urgently
This is the functionalist account, which stresses social efficiency.
Reproduces existing class inequality by channeling advantaged students toward higher-status paths
Correct: Conflict theory emphasizes how institutions maintain the advantages of dominant groups, including through tracking.
Arises from teacher-student interactions in which labels gradually become self-fulfilling for each student
This is the symbolic interactionist account, which focuses on labeling in micro-level interaction.
Reflects a rational, rule-based system that standardizes decisions through formal procedures and records
This describes Weber's bureaucratic rationalization, not a conflict critique of tracking.
questions.x: Conflict theory emphasizes how institutions maintain the advantages of dominant groups, including through tracking. Trap: Attributing the functionalist 'efficient sorting' idea to conflict theory.

questions.q: A country has a crude birth rate of 22 per 1,000, a crude death rate of 7 per 1,000, and negligible net migration. Using the rule of 70, approximately how long will its population take to double?
o: About 47 years
Correct: Natural increase = (22 - 7) / 1,000 = 1.5% per year, and 70 / 1.5 is about 47.
About 15 years
15 comes from using the 15-per-1,000 difference directly as a percentage without converting.
About 32 years
32 comes from using only the birth rate (70 / 2.2).
About 100 years
100 comes from using only the death rate (70 / 0.7).
questions.x: Natural increase = (22 - 7) / 1,000 = 1.5% per year, and 70 / 1.5 is about 47. Trap: Using the crude birth rate alone instead of the rate of natural increase.

questions.q: A country's total fertility rate has been at about the replacement level for 20 years, yet its population continues to grow. The most likely explanation is:
o: A rising crude death rate, which increases the net number of people added each year to the population
A rising death rate would slow growth, not increase it.
A falling life expectancy, which raises the number of births each woman has during her lifetime
Falling life expectancy would not raise births per woman and would reduce growth.
Population momentum, because a large cohort now of childbearing age keeps annual births above annual deaths
Correct: Past high fertility created large young cohorts; as they reach reproductive age, births exceed deaths even at replacement fertility.
A declining proportion of women in the population, which raises the number of births per woman
A smaller share of women would reduce total births, and fertility rate is already fixed at replacement.
questions.x: Past high fertility created large young cohorts; as they reach reproductive age, births exceed deaths even at replacement fertility. Trap: Assuming replacement-level fertility produces an immediately stable population size.

questions.q: In a population of 1,000, 250 people are under 15, 650 are 15 to 64, and 100 are 65 or older. What is the age dependency ratio?
o: About 15 per 100 working-age people
15 counts only older adults (100 / 650).
About 54 per 100 working-age people
Correct: (250 + 100) / 650 = 0.54, or 54 dependents per 100 people aged 15 to 64.
About 35 per 100 working-age people
35 divides the 350 dependents by the whole population (1,000).
About 38 per 100 working-age people
38 counts only children (250 / 650).
questions.x: (250 + 100) / 650 = 0.54, or 54 dependents per 100 people aged 15 to 64. Trap: Dividing dependents by the total population rather than the working-age population.

questions.q: Residents of a neighborhood belong to a community organization whose members come from many income levels and occupations. Through acquaintances there, one resident learns of a job opening outside her usual circle. This is best described as:
o: Bonding social capital, which strengthens ties among members of a similar and close-knit group
Bonding capital is within-group solidarity and would not supply information from outside her circle.
Cultural capital, which consists of knowledge and tastes that signal membership in a social class
Cultural capital concerns class-linked tastes and credentials, not network connections.
Human capital, which consists of the skills and training that increase an individual's productivity
Human capital refers to skills, not to relationships.
Bridging social capital, which connects people across different social groups and supplies new information
Correct: Bridging ties link people across social divisions and supply access to novel information and resources.
questions.x: Bridging ties link people across social divisions and supply access to novel information and resources. Trap: Treating any network benefit as bonding capital.

questions.q: A woman inherits a title of nobility and later earns a medical degree. How should these two statuses be classified?
o: Nobility is an ascribed status, and being a physician is an achieved status
Correct: Ascribed statuses are assigned at birth or involuntarily; achieved statuses are earned through effort or choice.
Nobility is an achieved status, and being a physician is an ascribed status because of the degree
This reverses the two definitions.
Both are ascribed statuses, because social position is fixed at birth in every stratified society
Medical training is earned, so it cannot be ascribed.
Both are achieved statuses, because each is recognized by society after the person has acted
An inherited title is not earned through individual action.
questions.x: Ascribed statuses are assigned at birth or involuntarily; achieved statuses are earned through effort or choice. Trap: Assuming that all statuses recognized by society are earned.

questions.q: According to the Davis-Moore thesis, surgeons are paid much more than most other workers because:
o: Unequal rewards motivate talented people to fill important positions that require long and costly training
Correct: Davis and Moore argued that stratification is functional: unequal rewards ensure that the most important roles are filled by the most capable.
Dominant groups restrict entry to high-paying positions in order to preserve their own privileges
This is a conflict-theory explanation.
Occupational prestige is determined mainly by the cultural capital that children inherit from parents
This is Bourdieu's reproduction argument, not Davis-Moore.
Wage differences are residues of past discrimination, which gradually disappear as markets modernize
This is a different (discrimination and market) argument that does not feature in the thesis.
questions.x: Davis and Moore argued that stratification is functional: unequal rewards ensure that the most important roles are filled by the most capable. Trap: Choosing the conflict explanation because inequality seems to favor the privileged.

questions.q: A listener can just barely detect an increase of 2 g when holding a 50 g weight. If Weber's law holds, approximately what increase would be just noticeable when holding a 200 g weight?
o: 2 g
2 g would imply the difference threshold is constant, which Weber's law rejects.
4 g
4 g would imply the threshold doubles when the weight quadruples.
16 g would imply a fraction of 0.08.
8 g
Correct: Weber's fraction = 2 / 50 = 0.04; 0.04 x 200 = 8 g.
questions.x: Weber's fraction = 2 / 50 = 0.04; 0.04 x 200 = 8 g. Trap: Assuming that the just-noticeable difference stays constant regardless of baseline intensity.

questions.q: A child watches water poured from a short, wide glass into a tall, narrow glass and says the tall glass now holds more water. In Piaget's theory, this response is best explained by:
o: Preoperational thinking, which centers on one dimension, such as height, and lacks conservation
Correct: Preoperational children center on a single salient feature and fail to conserve quantity across changes in appearance.
Sensorimotor thinking, in which the child has not yet formed an understanding of object permanence
Sensorimotor children are infants and toddlers, and conservation tasks are beyond them.
Concrete operational thinking, in which the child can reason only about hypothetical or abstract problems
Concrete operational children succeed at conservation; the limitation described applies to abstraction.
Formal operational thinking, in which the child overgeneralizes abstract rules to concrete situations
Formal operational thinkers reason abstractly and conserve easily.
questions.x: Preoperational children center on a single salient feature and fail to conserve quantity across changes in appearance. Trap: Selecting concrete operational because the task uses physical objects.

questions.q: A student who prepared well performs best with moderate anxiety but performs poorly with very high anxiety. Which idea is most consistent with this pattern?
o: Performance is best at an intermediate level of arousal, as described by the Yerkes-Dodson law
Correct: Yerkes-Dodson describes an inverted-U relation between arousal and performance, especially for complex tasks.
Performance increases steadily as drive increases, as described by drive-reduction theory
A steady increase in performance would not predict a decline at high anxiety.
Physiological arousal follows the conscious experience of emotion, as described by the Cannon-Bard theory
Cannon-Bard says arousal and emotion occur simultaneously and in parallel.
Physiological arousal and emotion are independent and unrelated, as described by the James-Lange theory
James-Lange says that emotion follows arousal, not that they are unrelated.
questions.x: Yerkes-Dodson describes an inverted-U relation between arousal and performance, especially for complex tasks. Trap: Matching any arousal-related theory of emotion to a question about performance.

questions.q: Two siblings share the same genetic risk for major depression. One develops the disorder after a severe job loss, and the other, who has faced no major stressors, does not. Which model best explains this pattern?
o: The dopamine hypothesis, in which excessive dopamine activity in mesolimbic pathways produces the disorder
The dopamine hypothesis is mainly applied to schizophrenia, and the stem points to stress.
The diathesis-stress model, in which an inherited vulnerability produces the disorder only when a stressor is present
Correct: Diathesis-stress holds that a predisposition and an environmental trigger interact to produce a disorder.
The gene-environment correlation model, in which genes lead people to choose the environments they experience
Gene-environment correlation involves genes shaping exposure, which is not described here.
The social-cognitive model, in which the disorder arises entirely from imitating the behavior of observed models
Imitation of models is not the basis of the described difference.
questions.x: Diathesis-stress holds that a predisposition and an environmental trigger interact to produce a disorder. Trap: Reaching for a neurotransmitter hypothesis rather than a stress-vulnerability interaction.

questions.q: A canvasser asks residents to sign a petition for a park cleanup and returns a week later to ask the same residents for a $20 donation. These residents donate more often than residents asked only for the donation. The technique at work is:
o: Door-in-the-face, in which refusing a large request increases compliance with a later, smaller one
Door-in-the-face starts with a large request that is refused.
Foot-in-the-door, in which agreeing to a small request increases compliance with a larger one
Correct: Compliance with a small initial request (the petition) increases the chance of agreeing to a larger request later.
Low-ball, in which commitment persists after the costs of the original agreement are raised
Low-ball involves raising the cost after commitment, which did not occur.
That's-not-all, in which a bonus is added to an offer before the person has responded to it
That's-not-all improves an offer before the target responds, which was not done.
questions.x: Compliance with a small initial request (the petition) increases the chance of agreeing to a larger request later. Trap: Mixing up foot-in-the-door with door-in-the-face because both involve two requests.

questions.q: A drug truly lowers blood pressure, but a trial with 15 patients per arm yields p = 0.12 and the researchers conclude it has no effect. Which error likely occurred, and what would reduce its probability?
o: Type II error; increasing the sample size would increase the statistical power of the trial design
Correct: Failing to reject a false null is a Type II error; larger samples raise power and lower its probability.
Type I error; lowering the significance threshold would reduce the chance of detecting false effects
A Type I error is rejecting a true null, which did not happen here.
Type I error; increasing the sample size would reduce the chance of rejecting a true null hypothesis
Type I error is not the mistake here, because the researchers did not claim an effect.
Type II error; lowering the significance threshold would increase the chance of detecting true effects
Lowering alpha makes rejection harder, which raises the Type II error rate.
questions.x: Failing to reject a false null is a Type II error; larger samples raise power and lower its probability. Trap: Labeling a missed true effect as a Type I error.

questions.q: In an alpha helix, the hydrogen bonds that stabilize the structure form between:
o: The side-chain groups of residues that are adjacent in the sequence and point in the same direction
side chains project outward from the helix and do not form its backbone hydrogen-bond pattern.
The backbone carbonyl oxygen of one residue and the backbone amide hydrogen of a residue four positions along the chain
Correct: Alpha helix hydrogen bonds link the C=O of residue i to the N-H of residue i+4, running parallel to the helix axis.
The backbone carbonyl oxygen and amide hydrogen of residues on separate, antiparallel strands
bonds between separate strands characterize beta sheets, not alpha helices.
The side-chain hydroxyl groups of serine residues and the peptide backbone of the preceding turn
side chains are not required for the regular helical hydrogen-bond pattern.
questions.x: Alpha helix hydrogen bonds link the C=O of residue i to the N-H of residue i+4, running parallel to the helix axis. Trap: Confusing the interstrand hydrogen bonding of beta sheets with the intrastrand bonding of helices.

questions.q: On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, a competitive inhibitor changes the line for the enzyme reaction by:
o: Increasing the y-intercept while leaving the x-intercept unchanged
a higher y-intercept would imply a lower Vmax, as in noncompetitive inhibition.
Decreasing both the slope and the y-intercept
a lower slope and lower intercept would mean a faster enzyme, not an inhibited one.
Increasing the slope while leaving the y-intercept unchanged
Correct: Competitive inhibition raises the apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged, so the slope (Km/Vmax) rises and the y-intercept (1/Vmax) is the same.
Leaving the slope unchanged while shifting the line up
a parallel upward shift is the pattern for uncompetitive inhibition, in which both intercepts change.
questions.x: Competitive inhibition raises the apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged, so the slope (Km/Vmax) rises and the y-intercept (1/Vmax) is the same. Trap: Mixing up which intercept is 1/Vmax and which is -1/Km.

questions.q: Which activity allows DNA polymerase III in E. coli to correct a mismatched nucleotide that it has just added?
o: A 3' to 5' exonuclease activity that removes the terminal nucleotide
Correct: The epsilon subunit has 3' to 5' exonuclease activity that excises a wrongly paired 3' terminal nucleotide so synthesis can resume.
A 5' to 3' exonuclease activity that removes the RNA primer
5' to 3' exonuclease activity (of DNA polymerase I) removes RNA primers and is not proofreading.
A helicase activity that unwinds the daughter strand
helicase unwinds the parental duplex and does not edit the new strand.
A ligase activity that seals the nick after the mismatch
ligase joins fragments and does not remove incorrect bases.
questions.x: The epsilon subunit has 3' to 5' exonuclease activity that excises a wrongly paired 3' terminal nucleotide so synthesis can resume. Trap: Confusing the 3' to 5' proofreading activity with the 5' to 3' activity that removes primers.

questions.q: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases help maintain the accuracy of translation primarily because they:
o: Recognize the codon on the mRNA and select the matching tRNA by base pairing
codon recognition is performed by the anticodon of the tRNA on the ribosome, not by the synthetase.
Catalyze peptide bond formation between adjacent amino acids on the ribosome
peptide bond formation is catalyzed by the rRNA of the large ribosomal subunit.
Attach the right amino acid to its tRNA and edit mischarged ones
Correct: Each synthetase uses ATP to charge a tRNA with its cognate amino acid and has editing activity, so the amino acid carried matches the anticodon.
Select the amino acid at the ribosome by checking codon-anticodon pairing
synthetases act before the tRNA reaches the ribosome, and the ribosome checks codon-anticodon pairing, not the amino acid.
questions.x: Each synthetase uses ATP to charge a tRNA with its cognate amino acid and has editing activity, so the amino acid carried matches the anticodon. Trap: Placing the key step of amino acid selection at the ribosome instead of at the charging reaction.

questions.q: Two unaffected parents have a child with an autosomal recessive disease. What is the probability that an unaffected child of these parents is a carrier?
o: 1/2 ignores that the affected genotype is excluded from the outcomes.
1/4 is the probability of an affected child, or of AA, before conditioning.
Correct: Both parents are carriers (Aa x Aa); among unaffected offspring (AA, Aa, Aa) 2 of 3 are carriers.
3/4 is the probability of being unaffected, not of being a carrier.
questions.x: Both parents are carriers (Aa x Aa); among unaffected offspring (AA, Aa, Aa) 2 of 3 are carriers. Trap: Failing to restrict the denominator to unaffected genotypes.

questions.q: During prolonged fasting, the brain can use ketone bodies, but the liver cannot because the liver:
o: Lacks the enzyme that synthesizes HMG-CoA from acetyl-CoA
the liver makes HMG-CoA in mitochondria as the first step of ketogenesis.
Cannot convert acetyl-CoA to acetoacetate in the matrix
the liver produces acetoacetate from HMG-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix.
Lacks mitochondria in which to oxidize the ketone bodies
hepatocytes have abundant mitochondria.
Lacks the enzyme that activates acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA, thiophorase
Correct: Hepatocytes make ketone bodies but lack succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase), so they cannot use them as fuel.
questions.x: Hepatocytes make ketone bodies but lack succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase), so they cannot use them as fuel. Trap: Believing the liver cannot synthesize ketone bodies or lacks mitochondria.

questions.q: During exercise, epinephrine binding to its receptor on muscle cells ultimately increases glycogen breakdown by:
o: Activating protein phosphatase 1, which dephosphorylates glycogen synthase and activates it
phosphatase activation would favor synthesis rather than breakdown.
Inhibiting adenylyl cyclase, which lowers cAMP and relieves inhibition of phosphorylase
epinephrine activates, not inhibits, adenylyl cyclase through a Gs-coupled receptor.
Activating glucokinase, which traps glucose as glucose-6-phosphate in muscle
glucokinase is a liver enzyme and phosphorylation of glucose does not drive glycogen breakdown.
Activating protein kinase A, which activates phosphorylase kinase and then phosphorylase
Correct: Epinephrine raises cAMP through a Gs protein, activating PKA, which phosphorylates and activates phosphorylase kinase; this activates glycogen phosphorylase to release glucose-1-phosphate.
questions.x: Epinephrine raises cAMP through a Gs protein, activating PKA, which phosphorylates and activates phosphorylase kinase; this activates glycogen phosphorylase to release glucose-1-phosphate. Trap: Mixing up the kinase cascade that promotes breakdown with the phosphatase action that promotes synthesis.

questions.q: Binding of a ligand to a Gs-coupled receptor leads to which sequence of events?
o: GTP is hydrolyzed to GDP on the alpha subunit, which activates adenylyl cyclase and raises cAMP
GTP hydrolysis inactivates the G protein rather than activating it.
GDP is exchanged for GTP on the alpha subunit, which inhibits adenylyl cyclase and lowers cAMP
Gi, not Gs, inhibits adenylyl cyclase.
GDP is exchanged for GTP on the alpha subunit, which activates adenylyl cyclase and raises cAMP
Correct: Ligand-bound receptor acts as a GEF; the alpha subunit swaps GDP for GTP, dissociates, and stimulates adenylyl cyclase to make cAMP.
The receptor phosphorylates itself on tyrosine, which recruits adenylyl cyclase to the membrane
autophosphorylation on tyrosine is a feature of receptor tyrosine kinases, not GPCRs.
questions.x: Ligand-bound receptor acts as a GEF; the alpha subunit swaps GDP for GTP, dissociates, and stimulates adenylyl cyclase to make cAMP. Trap: Reversing the roles of GTP exchange (activation) and GTP hydrolysis (inactivation).

questions.q: A Gram-negative bacterium is generally less susceptible than a Gram-positive bacterium to penicillin G because it:
o: Lacks peptidoglycan in its cell wall
Gram-negative cells have a thin peptidoglycan layer, not none.
Has a thick peptidoglycan layer that binds the drug
the peptidoglycan layer is thin in Gram-negative cells, and it would not protect them by binding the drug.
Has a protective outer membrane
Correct: The outer membrane with porins restricts penicillin G, so less drug reaches the thin peptidoglycan layer and its transpeptidases.
Has teichoic acids that degrade the drug
teichoic acids are in the Gram-positive wall and do not degrade penicillin.
questions.x: The outer membrane with porins restricts penicillin G, so less drug reaches the thin peptidoglycan layer and its transpeptidases. Trap: Thinking Gram-negative organisms lack peptidoglycan.

questions.q: In bacterial conjugation, which structure is required for DNA transfer from the donor to the recipient?
o: A pilus encoded by the F plasmid in the donor cell
Correct: F-plasmid genes encode the sex pilus, which contacts the recipient and brings cells together for transfer of single-stranded DNA.
A bacteriophage capsid carrying donor DNA
a phage capsid describes transduction, not conjugation.
A competence factor that opens pores in the recipient
pore formation by competence factors describes natural transformation.
An endospore that protects the donor DNA
endospores are dormant survival structures and do not transfer DNA.
questions.x: F-plasmid genes encode the sex pilus, which contacts the recipient and brings cells together for transfer of single-stranded DNA. Trap: Mixing up the three modes of horizontal gene transfer.

questions.q: The midcycle surge of luteinizing hormone is triggered by:
o: A high progesterone level from the corpus luteum, which exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus
progesterone is high only after ovulation, from the corpus luteum, and it inhibits LH.
A high estrogen level from the dominant follicle, which exerts positive feedback on the anterior pituitary
Correct: Sustained high estradiol from the mature follicle switches feedback from negative to positive, causing a GnRH-driven LH surge and ovulation.
A fall in FSH from the pituitary, which removes inhibition of GnRH
FSH does not inhibit GnRH, and the surge is driven by rising estrogen.
A high level of inhibin, which exerts positive feedback on the ovary
inhibin suppresses FSH rather than provoking LH release.
questions.x: Sustained high estradiol from the mature follicle switches feedback from negative to positive, causing a GnRH-driven LH surge and ovulation. Trap: Missing that estrogen switches from negative to positive feedback at midcycle.

questions.q: When a rod photoreceptor absorbs light, which change occurs?
o: cGMP is synthesized, cGMP-gated channels open, and the cell depolarizes
the sequence is reversed; cGMP is lowered by light and the channels stay open in the dark.
cGMP is hydrolyzed, cGMP-gated channels close, and the cell hyperpolarizes
Correct: Light isomerizes retinal, activating transducin and phosphodiesterase, which lowers cGMP; channels close, Na+ entry falls, and the rod hyperpolarizes, which reduces glutamate release.
cAMP is hydrolyzed, voltage-gated Na+ channels close, and the cell depolarizes
cAMP does not drive rod phototransduction, and closing channels hyperpolarizes.
cGMP is hydrolyzed, cGMP-gated channels open, and the cell hyperpolarizes
if cGMP falls, cGMP-gated channels close rather than open.
questions.x: Light isomerizes retinal, activating transducin and phosphodiesterase, which lowers cGMP; channels close, Na+ entry falls, and the rod hyperpolarizes, which reduces glutamate release. Trap: Expecting photoreceptors to depolarize in response to light.

questions.q: Compared with insulin, cortisol is more likely to:
o: Bind a membrane receptor and signal through receptor tyrosine kinase phosphorylation
tyrosine kinase signaling describes insulin, not cortisol.
Be stored in secretory vesicles until a stimulus triggers its release
peptide hormones such as insulin are stored in vesicles, whereas steroids are made on demand.
Circulate freely in plasma, since it is highly water soluble
cortisol is lipophilic and circulates mostly bound to transport proteins.
Diffuse through the plasma membrane and alter gene transcription by binding an intracellular receptor
Correct: Cortisol is a lipophilic steroid hormone that crosses the membrane, binds a cytoplasmic receptor, and acts as a transcription factor, producing slower, longer-lasting effects.
questions.x: Cortisol is a lipophilic steroid hormone that crosses the membrane, binds a cytoplasmic receptor, and acts as a transcription factor, producing slower, longer-lasting effects. Trap: Assigning the receptor location of one hormone class to the other.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes the digestion and absorption of dietary triglycerides?
o: Pepsin hydrolyzes fat in the stomach, and fatty acids enter the portal blood bound to albumin
pepsin is a protease, and long-chain fatty acids are repackaged into chylomicrons rather than carried in the portal blood.
Bile salts hydrolyze fats, and glycerol enters the lacteals as free fatty acids
bile salts emulsify but do not hydrolyze, and fatty acids are repackaged into chylomicrons.
Bile salts emulsify fat, pancreatic lipase produces monoglycerides and fatty acids, and chylomicrons carry the resynthesized triglycerides into lacteals
Correct: Bile salts emulsify fat, pancreatic lipase yields 2-monoglycerides and free fatty acids, enterocytes re-esterify them and package them into chylomicrons, which enter lymphatic lacteals.
Pancreatic lipase digests fats in the jejunum, and enterocytes release them directly into portal capillaries
long-chain products are packaged into chylomicrons and enter lacteals, not portal capillaries.
questions.x: Bile salts emulsify fat, pancreatic lipase yields 2-monoglycerides and free fatty acids, enterocytes re-esterify them and package them into chylomicrons, which enter lymphatic lacteals. Trap: Thinking that bile salts digest fats chemically instead of emulsifying them.

questions.q: In a systemic capillary, net filtration of fluid out of the vessel at the arterial end is mainly driven by:
o: Oncotic pressure of plasma proteins exceeding the capillary hydrostatic pressure
oncotic pressure exceeding hydrostatic pressure would draw fluid in, as at the venous end.
Interstitial hydrostatic pressure exceeding capillary hydrostatic pressure
interstitial hydrostatic pressure opposes filtration and is small.
Hydrostatic pressure exceeding oncotic pressure

Correct: At the arterial end the capillary hydrostatic pressure (about 35 mm Hg) exceeds the oncotic pressure (about 25 mm Hg), so fluid leaves; at the venous end oncotic pressure dominates and fluid returns.
Lymphatic suction exceeding the capillary oncotic pressure
lymphatic suction is not the main force, and oncotic pressure favors retention of fluid.
questions.x: At the arterial end the capillary hydrostatic pressure (about 35 mm Hg) exceeds the oncotic pressure (about 25 mm Hg), so fluid leaves; at the venous end oncotic pressure dominates and fluid returns. Trap: Reversing the forces at the arterial and venous ends of a capillary.

questions.q: A uniform 4.0 m plank of mass 10 kg is balanced on a pivot at its center. A 30 kg child sits 1.5 m to the left of the pivot. At what distance to the right of the pivot must a 50 kg child sit for the plank to remain in rotational equilibrium?
o: 2.5 m inverts the mass ratio (50/30 × 1.5).
1.1 m adds an imagined torque from the plank, but its weight acts through the pivot.
0.60 m results from dividing 30 × 1.5 by 75, mixing the masses incorrectly.
Correct: The plank's weight acts at the pivot and produces no torque. Setting torques equal: (30)(1.5) = (50)x, so x = 0.90 m.
questions.x: The plank's weight acts at the pivot and produces no torque. Setting torques equal: (30)(1.5) = (50)x, so x = 0.90 m. Trap: Including the weight of a uniform plank at its center as a torque; it acts at the pivot and contributes zero.

questions.q: A 2.0 kg cart moving at 3.0 m/s collides with a stationary 1.0 kg cart, and the two stick together. What fraction of the initial kinetic energy is lost in the collision?
o: None, because momentum is conserved in the collision
Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is not in a perfectly inelastic collision.
Two-thirds
Two-thirds is the fraction of energy that remains if 6.0 J is mistaken for the loss.
One-half
One-half has no basis here; the final kinetic energy is 6.0 J of the original 9.0 J.
One-third
Correct: Momentum: (2.0)(3.0) = (3.0)v, so v = 2.0 m/s. KE before = 9.0 J; after = ½(3.0)(2.0)² = 6.0 J; 3.0 J (one-third) is lost.
questions.x: Momentum: (2.0)(3.0) = (3.0)v, so v = 2.0 m/s. KE before = 9.0 J; after = ½(3.0)(2.0)² = 6.0 J; 3.0 J (one-third) is lost. Trap: Assuming that conservation of momentum implies conservation of kinetic energy.

questions.q: A 50.0 g sample of metal at 100.0 °C is dropped into 100.0 g of water at 20.0 °C in an insulated calorimeter. The final temperature is 24.0 °C. The specific heat of water is 4.18 J/(g·°C). What is the specific heat of the metal?
o: 0.88 would result from using 25 g for the metal mass.
0.22 would result from doubling the metal mass.
Correct: Heat gained by water = (100.0)(4.18)(4.0) = 1,672 J. The metal lost this heat: c = 1,672 / [(50.0)(76.0)] = 0.44 J/(g·°C).
4.18 J/(g·°C) is the specific heat of water, not of the metal.
questions.x: Heat gained by water = (100.0)(4.18)(4.0) = 1,672 J. The metal lost this heat: c = 1,672 / [(50.0)(76.0)] = 0.44 J/(g·°C). Trap: Using the temperature change of water for the metal, or mixing up the masses of the metal and the water.

questions.q: A uniform wooden block with density 600 kg/m³ floats at rest in fresh water (density 1,000 kg/m³). What fraction of the block's volume is submerged?
o: Correct: Floating means buoyant force equals weight: ρ(water)V(sub)g = ρ(block)Vg, so V(sub)/V = 600/1,000 = 0.60.
40% is the fraction above the water line, not submerged.
The block would be fully submerged only if its density equaled or exceeded that of water.
16% has no connection to the density ratio of the block and the water.
questions.x: Floating means buoyant force equals weight: ρ(water)V(sub)g = ρ(block)Vg, so V(sub)/V = 600/1,000 = 0.60. Trap: Reporting the fraction above the surface instead of the submerged fraction.

questions.q: A household heater rated at 1,200 W operates on a 120 V supply. What is the resistance of its heating element?
o: Correct: P = V²/R, so R = (120)²/1,200 = 14,400/1,200 = 12 Ω (the current is 10 A).
10 is the current in amperes (P/V), not the resistance.
0.10 comes from V/P, which has no physical meaning here.
144 Ω results from dividing V² by 100 instead of by the power.
questions.x: P = V²/R, so R = (120)²/1,200 = 14,400/1,200 = 12 Ω (the current is 10 A). Trap: Confusing the current with resistance or using V/P instead of V²/P.

questions.q: An ambulance siren emits a steady 700 Hz tone as the ambulance travels toward a stationary listener at 30 m/s. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. The frequency heard by the listener is closest to:
o: 762 Hz
762 Hz results from the approximation f₀(1 + v_s/v), which is not exact for a moving source.
643 Hz
643 Hz is the frequency heard after the ambulance passes (receding).
768 Hz
Correct: f = f₀ v/(v - v_s) = 700 × 340/310 = 768 Hz; the source's approach compresses the wavelength.
700 Hz
700 Hz would be heard only if there were no relative motion.
questions.x: f = f₀ v/(v - v_s) = 700 × 340/310 = 768 Hz; the source's approach compresses the wavelength. Trap: Using the receding-source formula or the approximate expression for an approaching source.

questions.q: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a thin converging lens with focal length 10 cm. The image formed is:
o: virtual, upright, and 7.5 cm from the lens, on the object side
A virtual image requires an object inside the focal length (closer than 10 cm).
real, inverted, and 30 cm from the lens, the same size as the object
A 30 cm image distance would require the object to be at 15 cm.
real, inverted, and 15 cm from the lens
Correct: 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = 1/10 - 1/30 = 1/15, so v = +15 cm (real side); m = -v/u = -0.5, so the image is inverted and half the object's size.
virtual, upright, and 15 cm from the lens, on the object side
A positive v indicates a real image formed on the far side of the lens.
questions.x: 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = 1/10 - 1/30 = 1/15, so v = +15 cm (real side); m = -v/u = -0.5, so the image is inverted and half the object's size. Trap: Assigning a virtual, upright image to an object placed outside the focal length of a converging lens.

questions.q: Light of wavelength 400 nm illuminates a metal with a work function of 2.0 eV. Using hc ≈ 1,240 eV·nm, the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected photoelectrons is closest to:
o: 1.1 eV
Correct: Photon energy = 1,240/400 = 3.1 eV; KE(max) = hf - φ = 3.1 - 2.0 = 1.1 eV.
3.1 eV
3.1 eV is the photon energy, before the work function is subtracted.
5.1 eV
5.1 eV would result from adding the work function to the photon energy.
0 eV
Electrons are ejected because 3.1 eV exceeds the 2.0 eV work function.
questions.x: Photon energy = 1,240/400 = 3.1 eV; KE(max) = hf - φ = 3.1 - 2.0 = 1.1 eV. Trap: Reporting the photon energy as the electron kinetic energy.

questions.q: Radium-226 (atomic number 88) undergoes alpha decay. The daughter nuclide is:
o: radon-226 (atomic number 86), with an unchanged mass number
The mass number must drop by 4 in alpha decay.
radon-222 (atomic number 86)
Correct: An alpha particle carries 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so A decreases by 4 and Z by 2: 226 - 4 = 222 and 88 - 2 = 86.
francium-226 (atomic number 87), after emission of a beta particle
Francium-226 would be produced by beta-plus decay or electron capture, not alpha decay.
thorium-230 (atomic number 90), after gaining an alpha particle
Thorium-230 has a higher mass number and atomic number than the parent.
questions.x: An alpha particle carries 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so A decreases by 4 and Z by 2: 226 - 4 = 222 and 88 - 2 = 86. Trap: Changing only the atomic number or confusing alpha emission with beta emission.

questions.q: What is the expected freezing point of a 0.50 m aqueous solution of CaCl₂? (K_f of water = 1.86 °C/m; assume complete dissociation.)
o: Correct: ΔT_f = i K_f m = (3)(1.86)(0.50) = 2.79 °C, so the solution freezes at about -2.8 °C.
-0.93 °C ignores dissociation (i = 1).
-1.86 °C results from using i = 2 (two particles) instead of 3.
-5.6 °C would arise from i = 6.
questions.x: ΔT_f = i K_f m = (3)(1.86)(0.50) = 2.79 °C, so the solution freezes at about -2.8 °C. Trap: Forgetting that CaCl₂ provides three particles per formula unit.

questions.q: An acetic acid/acetate buffer (pKa = 4.76) is prepared with 0.10 M acetate and 0.010 M acetic acid. The pH of this buffer is closest to:
o: 3.76 comes from inverting the ratio.
4.76 would be the pH only if the concentrations of acid and conjugate base were equal.
6.76 would correspond to a ratio of 100.
Correct: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) = 4.76 + log(10) = 5.76.
questions.x: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) = 4.76 + log(10) = 5.76. Trap: Inverting the base-to-acid ratio in the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.

questions.q: Ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) boils at 78 °C, whereas dimethyl ether (CH₃OCH₃), which has the same molecular formula, boils at -24 °C. The best explanation is that:
o: dimethyl ether is more polar, so it has stronger dipole-dipole forces than ethanol does
Ethanol is at least as polar, and its hydrogen bonding is much stronger than dipole-dipole forces.
ethanol has a larger molar mass, so its London dispersion forces are much greater
The two compounds are isomers with identical molar mass.
dimethyl ether molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another, but these bonds are weaker than in ethanol
Dimethyl ether has no H bonded to oxygen and so cannot be a hydrogen bond donor.
ethanol forms hydrogen bonds between molecules, but dimethyl ether does not
Correct: Ethanol has an O-H group, so it can donate and accept hydrogen bonds; dimethyl ether has only an acceptor oxygen, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself.
questions.x: Ethanol has an O-H group, so it can donate and accept hydrogen bonds; dimethyl ether has only an acceptor oxygen, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself. Trap: Attributing boiling point differences to molar mass or polarity when the compounds are isomers.

questions.q: A mixture of benzoic acid and naphthalene in diethyl ether is shaken with aqueous sodium bicarbonate, and the layers are separated. Which statement describes the outcome?
o: Naphthalene is converted to a salt and enters the aqueous layer, while benzoic acid remains in the ether layer
Naphthalene has no acidic proton and cannot form a salt.
Both compounds remain in the ether layer, because neither reacts with a weak base
Bicarbonate is a strong enough base to deprotonate a carboxylic acid.
Benzoic acid is converted to sodium benzoate and enters the aqueous layer, while naphthalene remains in the ether layer
Correct: Bicarbonate deprotonates the carboxylic acid (pKa ≈ 4.2), forming a water-soluble carboxylate salt; neutral, nonpolar naphthalene stays in the organic layer.
Both compounds enter the aqueous layer, because sodium bicarbonate is soluble in water
Water solubility of the base does not make a nonpolar hydrocarbon soluble in water.
questions.x: Bicarbonate deprotonates the carboxylic acid (pKa ≈ 4.2), forming a water-soluble carboxylate salt; neutral, nonpolar naphthalene stays in the organic layer. Trap: Thinking that only strong bases deprotonate carboxylic acids, which would leave both compounds in the organic layer.

questions.q: (R)-2-Bromobutane reacts with sodium cyanide in acetone by an SN2 mechanism. The major product is:
o: (S)-2-methylbutanenitrile, formed with inversion of configuration
Correct: SN2 proceeds by backside attack of cyanide, inverting the stereocenter; with CN replacing Br at the top priority, the descriptor changes from R to S.
(R)-2-methylbutanenitrile, formed with retention of configuration at the stereocenter
Retention would imply frontside attack, which SN2 does not do.
a racemic mixture, formed through a planar carbocation intermediate in the slow step
A carbocation would be required for racemization, which is characteristic of SN1.
(S)-2-methylbutanenitrile, formed with retention of configuration at the stereocenter
The product is S because of inversion; retention would leave R.
questions.x: SN2 proceeds by backside attack of cyanide, inverting the stereocenter; with CN replacing Br at the top priority, the descriptor changes from R to S. Trap: Assuming that the stereochemical descriptor stays the same, or that substitution of a secondary halide always passes through a carbocation.

questions.q: A compound with formula C₄H₈O shows a strong infrared absorption near 1715 cm⁻¹ and no broad absorption near 3300 cm⁻¹ and none near 2720 cm⁻¹. The compound is most likely:
o: 2-butanone
Correct: The 1715 cm⁻¹ band indicates a ketone C=O; the absence of O-H (3300) and aldehyde C-H (2720) bands rules out alcohols and aldehydes.
butanal
Butanal would show an aldehyde C-H stretch near 2720 cm⁻¹.
3-buten-1-ol
3-Buten-1-ol has an alcohol O-H (broad ~3300 cm⁻¹) and no C=O.
cyclobutanol
Cyclobutanol has an O-H group and no C=O absorption.
questions.x: The 1715 cm⁻¹ band indicates a ketone C=O; the absence of O-H (3300) and aldehyde C-H (2720) bands rules out alcohols and aldehydes. Trap: Assigning a carbonyl to an aldehyde without checking for the characteristic aldehyde C-H stretch.

questions.q: A person can just barely distinguish a 50-g weight from a 51-g weight. According to Weber's law, the just-noticeable difference for a 400-g weight is closest to:
o: 1 g, because the just-noticeable difference is constant for all weights
Weber's law says the JND is proportional to the baseline, not constant.
8 g
Correct: The Weber fraction is 1/50 = 2%; 2% of 400 g = 8 g.
4 g, because 400 g is four times the size of the 100-g reference
The baseline weight is 8 times 50 g, not 4 times a 100-g reference.
16 g, because the weight is eight times as large as the reference
Doubling the proportional change gives 16 g, which overstates the 2% fraction.
questions.x: The Weber fraction is 1/50 = 2%; 2% of 400 g = 8 g. Trap: Assuming the JND is a fixed amount rather than a fixed proportion of the baseline.

questions.q: After entering a dark theater, a person sees a dim exit sign better when looking slightly to the side of it than directly at it. This is best explained by:
o: A high density of cones in the peripheral retina, which allows color discrimination in very dim light
Cones need brighter light and are concentrated in the fovea, not the periphery.
A high density of rods in the fovea, which makes the center of the visual field most sensitive to dim light
The fovea contains almost no rods.
Dilation of the pupil, which projects the dim light directly onto the optic disc
The optic disc is the blind spot, which has no photoreceptors.
A high density of rods, which are more light-sensitive than cones, in the peripheral retina compared with the fovea
Correct: Rods function in low light and are concentrated outside the fovea; the fovea is dominated by cones.
questions.x: Rods function in low light and are concentrated outside the fovea; the fovea is dominated by cones. Trap: Assuming the fovea, the center of sharp vision, is also the most sensitive region in dim light.

questions.q: A viewer looks at several separated arcs arranged in a circle and perceives a complete circle. Which Gestalt principle best explains this perception?
o: Closure
Correct: Closure is the tendency to fill gaps to perceive a complete, whole form.
Similarity
Similarity groups elements that look alike, but the arcs' resemblance does not complete the circle.
Figure-ground
Figure-ground concerns separating an object from its background.
Proximity
Proximity groups elements that are near each other, but this does not explain the filled-in gaps.
questions.x: Closure is the tendency to fill gaps to perceive a complete, whole form. Trap: Choosing proximity because the arcs are near each other.

questions.q: A reader sees the phrase 'THE CAT' printed so that the H in 'THE' and the A in 'CAT' are the same ambiguous shape, yet she reads each letter correctly. This best illustrates:
o: Bottom-up processing, in which features are assembled from sensory data without prior knowledge or expectations
Bottom-up processing would give the same interpretation of the identical shape in both words.
Sensory adaptation, in which a constant stimulus gradually becomes less noticeable
Adaptation concerns decreasing responsiveness to constant stimuli.
Top-down processing, in which context and expectations shape the interpretation of sensory input
Correct: The same shape is perceived as different letters depending on the word context, which is knowledge-driven processing.
Transduction, in which light energy is converted into neural signals by photoreceptors
Transduction occurs in the retina and is the same for both letters.
questions.x: The same shape is perceived as different letters depending on the word context, which is knowledge-driven processing. Trap: Ignoring that identical input produced different percepts, which can only be explained by context.

questions.q: Participants study a list of 20 words and then recall them. In one condition they recall immediately; in another they count backward for 30 seconds before recalling. Compared with immediate recall, the delay condition most likely shows:
o: Markedly poorer recall of the first few words, with late-word recall largely unchanged
The primacy effect depends on rehearsal into long-term memory and is not removed by a brief delay.
Better recall of middle words, because interference is lower at the center of the list
Middle words are typically recalled worst, and the delay does not help them.
No change in the shape of the serial position curve, since recall depends on the total number of words
The curve changes shape: the recency portion falls.
Markedly poorer recall of the last few words, with early-word recall largely unchanged
Correct: A distractor task removes the recency effect because the last items are held in short-term memory and are displaced, while primacy reflects long-term encoding.
questions.x: A distractor task removes the recency effect because the last items are held in short-term memory and are displaced, while primacy reflects long-term encoding. Trap: Confusing the primacy effect (long-term memory) with the recency effect (short-term memory).

questions.q: After a stroke, a patient speaks fluently in long sentences that contain made-up words and make no sense, and she cannot follow simple spoken commands. Damage is most likely in:
o: The left inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area)
Broca's area damage produces halting, effortful speech with preserved comprehension.
The posterior superior temporal lobe of the left hemisphere (Wernicke's area)
Correct: Fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension is the pattern of Wernicke's aphasia.
The primary auditory cortex of both hemispheres
Bilateral primary auditory damage would cause hearing deficits, not fluent speech production.
The primary motor cortex controlling the muscles of the mouth and tongue
Primary motor damage would impair articulation, not the content of speech.
questions.x: Fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension is the pattern of Wernicke's aphasia. Trap: Confusing fluent aphasia with nonfluent aphasia.

questions.q: A child watches water poured from a short, wide glass into a tall, thin glass and says the tall glass now holds more water. According to Piaget, this child is most likely in which stage, and why?
o: Sensorimotor, because the child has not yet developed object permanence or symbolic thought
Sensorimotor children are infants, and a child who can talk about glasses is beyond this stage.
Concrete operational, because the child reasons using the reversibility of physical actions and logical rules
Reversibility would let the child see that pouring back restores the original, and concrete operational children pass conservation.
Preoperational, because the child focuses on one dimension (height) and has not mastered conservation
Correct: Failing conservation by centering on one dimension is characteristic of the preoperational stage (about ages 2-7).
Formal operational, because the child is generating hypotheses about the amount of water
Hypothetical reasoning is a formal operational skill and would not produce this error.
questions.x: Failing conservation by centering on one dimension is characteristic of the preoperational stage (about ages 2-7). Trap: Assuming that any child who can talk about quantities has acquired conservation.

questions.q: After using the same locker combination for a year, a student is given a new combination and keeps reciting the old one. This is best described as:
o: Proactive interference, in which previously learned information disrupts recall of new information
Correct: The old combination (learned earlier) interferes with the new one, which is proactive interference.
Retroactive interference, in which newly learned information disrupts recall of old information
Retroactive interference would be forgetting the old combination because of learning the new one.
Anterograde amnesia, in which a brain injury prevents the formation of any new long-term memories
Anterograde amnesia is neurological and would affect memory formation generally, not just this item.
Decay, in which memory traces gradually fade over time because they are not used or rehearsed
Decay concerns fading with disuse; the old combination is being recalled too strongly, not fading.
questions.x: The old combination (learned earlier) interferes with the new one, which is proactive interference. Trap: Reversing proactive and retroactive interference.

questions.q: A disease has a prevalence of 10% in a population of 1000 people. A screening test has 90% sensitivity and 80% specificity. Among those who test positive, what proportion actually have the disease?
o: 50%, because sensitivity and specificity average to 85%
Averaging sensitivity and specificity does not give a predictive value and 50% is not supported by the counts.
Correct: 100 have disease: 90 true positives. 900 are healthy: 20% false positives = 180. PPV = 90/(90 + 180) = 33%.
80%, because specificity gives the proportion of positives that are real
Specificity is the proportion of healthy people testing negative, not a predictive value.
90%, because sensitivity gives the proportion of positives that are real
Sensitivity is the proportion of diseased people who test positive, not the proportion of positives who have disease.
questions.x: 100 have disease: 90 true positives. 900 are healthy: 20% false positives = 180. PPV = 90/(90 + 180) = 33%. Trap: Equating sensitivity with the probability that a positive result is correct, ignoring prevalence.

questions.q: A researcher tests 20 independent hypotheses, all of which are actually true null hypotheses, each at alpha = .05. The probability of obtaining at least one statistically significant result is closest to:
o: 5%, because each test has a 5% false-positive rate
5% is the chance for a single test; across 20 tests the chances accumulate.
Correct: P(at least one) = 1 - 0.95^20 = 1 - 0.36 = 0.64.
36%, because this is the probability that all 20 tests are nonsignificant
0.95^20 = 0.36 is the chance that none is significant, not that at least one is.
100%, because with 20 tests at least one must be significant
The probability is high but not certain.
questions.x: P(at least one) = 1 - 0.95^20 = 1 - 0.36 = 0.64. Trap: Using the per-test error rate as the family-wise error rate.

questions.q: A researcher wants to increase the probability of detecting a true difference between two groups without changing the significance level. The most effective change would be to:
o: Lower alpha from .05 to .01, which makes a result more convincing when it is detected
A stricter alpha reduces power; the question states alpha should not change.
Recruit a more heterogeneous sample, which increases the variability of scores
Greater variability increases the standard error and reduces power.
Increase the sample size in each group, which reduces the standard error of the mean difference
Correct: Larger samples reduce standard error, so a true effect is more likely to reach significance.
Use a one-sample design with a smaller expected effect, which reduces the required measurements
A smaller expected effect is harder to detect, not easier.
questions.x: Larger samples reduce standard error, so a true effect is more likely to reach significance. Trap: Believing that a stricter alpha makes a study stronger, when it lowers power.

questions.q: Depression scores (a continuous measure) are compared among three independent groups of patients receiving cognitive-behavioral therapy, an antidepressant, or a placebo. Which analysis is most appropriate?
o: One-way ANOVA, since it compares means across three independent groups
Correct: ANOVA tests for mean differences among three or more independent groups while controlling the overall Type I error rate.
A paired t-test, because the same measure is used in all groups
A paired t-test applies to two related measurements, but these are independent groups.
A chi-square test of independence, because treatments are categories
Chi-square analyzes categorical outcomes, and depression scores are continuous.
Three separate independent-samples t-tests, each at alpha = .05 and without correction
Three uncorrected t-tests would inflate the overall chance of a false positive.
questions.x: ANOVA tests for mean differences among three or more independent groups while controlling the overall Type I error rate. Trap: Defaulting to repeated t-tests, which inflates the Type I error rate.

questions.q: A woman has adequate food and water but has just been laid off and lives in a neighborhood with frequent break-ins. According to Maslow's hierarchy, which need most likely dominates her motivation?
o: Physiological needs
Her food and water are adequate, so physiological needs are not the priority.
Esteem needs
Esteem needs lie higher in the hierarchy and take priority only when lower needs are met.
Self-actualization
Self-actualization is the highest level and is pursued after lower needs are met.
Safety needs
Correct: Her physiological needs are met, so the next unmet level, safety (security of income and personal safety), dominates.
questions.x: Her physiological needs are met, so the next unmet level, safety (security of income and personal safety), dominates. Trap: Picking the lowest need because the scenario involves hardship.

questions.q: A man seeks help for 3 weeks of depressed mood and loss of interest. He reports that last year he had one week of unusually elevated mood, little need for sleep, grandiose plans, and spending sprees. Which diagnosis is most consistent with his history?
o: Major depressive disorder, because he currently meets criteria for a depressive episode
Major depressive disorder requires no history of mania.
Persistent depressive disorder, because his symptoms involve low mood
Persistent depressive disorder requires a chronic low mood of at least two years and no manic history.
Bipolar disorder, because he has had a manic episode in addition to depression
Correct: A history of a manic episode (a week of elevated mood with decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, and risky spending) points to bipolar disorder.
Generalized anxiety disorder, because his sleep and spending patterns are disrupted
Generalized anxiety disorder involves excessive worry and does not explain elevated mood.
questions.x: A history of a manic episode (a week of elevated mood with decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, and risky spending) points to bipolar disorder. Trap: Diagnosing from the current episode alone and ignoring a past manic episode.

questions.q: A country defines poverty as household income below 50% of the national median, which is $40,000. A household with an income of $18,000 would be classified as:
o: In relative poverty, because its income is below the $20,000 threshold set at half the median
Correct: Fifty percent of $40,000 is $20,000, and $18,000 is below it, so the household is in relative poverty.
In absolute poverty, because its income falls below a fixed amount needed to meet basic survival needs in any society
Absolute poverty is defined by a fixed subsistence standard, not by comparison with the median, and the stem gives no such standard.
Not in poverty, because the income is greater than one third of the national median
The country's threshold is 50% of the median; being above one third is irrelevant.
In relative poverty, because any income below the national median counts as poverty
The country's definition is half of the median, not the median itself.
questions.x: Fifty percent of $40,000 is $20,000, and $18,000 is below it, so the household is in relative poverty. Trap: Applying the median instead of the stated percentage threshold.

questions.q: An enzyme has a Vmax of 50 umol/min and a Km of 2 mM. In the presence of a fixed concentration of a competitive inhibitor, the apparent Km is 6 mM. At a substrate concentration of 6 mM with the inhibitor present, what is the reaction velocity?
o: 50 umol/min
50 umol/min is Vmax, which would be reached only at saturating substrate.
37.5 umol/min
37.5 umol/min is the velocity without the inhibitor (50 x 6 / 8).
25 umol/min
Correct: A competitive inhibitor leaves Vmax unchanged and raises apparent Km; v = Vmax[S]/(Km,app + [S]) = 50(6)/(6 + 6) = 25 umol/min.
12.5 umol/min
12.5 umol/min would require an apparent Km of 18 mM.
questions.x: A competitive inhibitor leaves Vmax unchanged and raises apparent Km; v = Vmax[S]/(Km,app + [S]) = 50(6)/(6 + 6) = 25 umol/min. Trap: Using the uninhibited Km of 2 mM in the equation, which gives the velocity without inhibitor.

questions.q: A protein with an isoelectric point of 9.2 is applied to an ion-exchange column at pH 7.0. Which column would bind the protein?
o: An anion exchanger, because the protein carries a net negative charge at pH 7.0
A net negative charge would occur only above the pI, at pH values higher than 9.2.
A cation exchanger, because the protein carries a net positive charge at pH 7.0
Correct: At a pH below its pI the protein has a net positive charge and binds the negatively charged resin of a cation exchanger.
A cation exchanger, because the protein carries a net negative charge at pH 7.0
A negatively charged protein would bind an anion exchanger, but the protein is positive here.
An anion exchanger, because the protein carries a net positive charge at pH 7.0
Positively charged proteins are repelled by the positively charged groups on an anion exchanger.
questions.x: At a pH below its pI the protein has a net positive charge and binds the negatively charged resin of a cation exchanger. Trap: Reversing the relationship between pH, pI, and net charge.

questions.q: After DNA replication in E. coli, the mismatch repair proteins MutS and MutL correct a mispaired base. How does the system distinguish the newly synthesized strand from the template strand?
o: The new strand carries ribonucleotides at its 5' end that mark it for removal and resynthesis
RNA primers mark Okazaki fragments, but they do not mark mismatches for repair.
The new strand is transiently unmethylated at GATC sites, whereas the parental strand is methylated
Correct: Dam methylase methylates adenine at GATC sequences after replication; the hemimethylated state lets repair proteins identify the new strand for correction.
The new strand is bound by the sliding clamp, which remains bound throughout the entire cell cycle
The clamp does not remain on DNA across the cell cycle and is not the strand marker.
The template strand carries uracil at mismatched positions, which is excised by uracil DNA glycosylase
Uracil excision is base excision repair, which acts without MutS and MutL.
questions.x: Dam methylase methylates adenine at GATC sequences after replication; the hemimethylated state lets repair proteins identify the new strand for correction. Trap: Confusing mismatch repair with base excision repair or primer removal.

questions.q: A researcher begins a PCR with 1,000 copies of a target sequence and assumes 100% efficiency in every cycle. What is the minimum number of cycles needed to exceed 1 x 10^6 copies?
o: 20 cycles would give 1,000 x 2^20, about 10^9 copies.
30 cycles would amplify beyond 10^12 copies.
Correct: Copies double each cycle, so 1,000 x 2^n > 10^6 requires 2^n > 1,000, which is first met at n = 10 (1,024).
7 cycles give 1,000 x 128 = 128,000 copies, which is too few.
questions.x: Copies double each cycle, so 1,000 x 2^n > 10^6 requires 2^n > 1,000, which is first met at n = 10 (1,024). Trap: Dividing 10^6 by 1,000 and then by 2 (or using ln or log10 values) instead of finding n for which 2^n exceeds 1,000.

questions.q: Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder that affects about 1 in 2,500 newborns in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. What is the approximate frequency of carriers?
o: 1 in 50
1 in 50 corresponds to the allele frequency q = 0.02, not to carriers (2pq).
1 in 25
Correct: q squared = 1/2,500, so q = 0.02, p is about 0.98, and carrier frequency 2pq is about 0.04, or 1 in 25.
1 in 2,500 is the frequency of affected homozygotes.
1 in 12
1 in 12 would be 2pq for a more common allele (q about 0.04).
questions.x: q squared = 1/2,500, so q = 0.02, p is about 0.98, and carrier frequency 2pq is about 0.04, or 1 in 25. Trap: Reporting q (1 in 50) as the carrier frequency without multiplying by 2p.
