questions.q: During a prolonged fast, the liver produces ketone bodies that are used by the brain but cannot be used by the liver itself. Which enzyme deficiency in hepatocytes explains this?
o: HMG-CoA synthase, which forms HMG-CoA from acetoacetyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA
HMG-CoA synthase is highly active in liver mitochondria and is needed for ketone production.
Succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase), which activates acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA
Correct: The liver makes acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyrate but lacks thiophorase, so it cannot convert them back to acetyl-CoA; extrahepatic tissues have the enzyme.
Carnitine acyltransferase I, which is required to import fatty acids into mitochondria
Carnitine acyltransferase I is needed to supply the substrate for ketogenesis, so liver has it.
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase, which forms malonyl-CoA from acetyl-CoA
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is a fatty acid synthesis enzyme and is not involved in ketone use.
questions.x: The liver makes acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyrate but lacks thiophorase, so it cannot convert them back to acetyl-CoA; extrahepatic tissues have the enzyme. Trap: Naming an enzyme of ketone synthesis instead of the enzyme needed for ketone utilization.

questions.q: A malnourished patient has elevated blood lactate and pyruvate and low erythrocyte transketolase activity. A deficiency of which vitamin is most likely?
o: Biotin, because pyruvate carboxylase and transketolase both require it for carboxylation reactions
Transketolase is not a carboxylase and has no biotin requirement.
Riboflavin, because pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase both require FAD as a cofactor
Transketolase does not use FAD; thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor shared by both enzymes.
Niacin, because pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase both use NAD+ as the electron acceptor
Transketolase does not use NAD+ as its cofactor.
Thiamine, because pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase both require thiamine pyrophosphate

Correct: Thiamine pyrophosphate is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase, so its deficiency raises pyruvate and lactate and lowers transketolase activity.
questions.x: Thiamine pyrophosphate is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase, so its deficiency raises pyruvate and lactate and lowers transketolase activity. Trap: Selecting a vitamin that serves only one of the two enzymes cited, rather than the cofactor shared by both.

questions.q: Cholera toxin causes severe watery diarrhea by modifying a G protein in intestinal epithelial cells. Which change in the signaling pathway most directly accounts for the secretion of chloride and water?
o: Gq is locked in its active state, which activates phospholipase C and raises cAMP through IP3
Gq acts through IP3 and diacylglycerol and does not raise cAMP directly.
Gs is locked active, so cAMP stays high, PKA is active, and CFTR opens
Correct: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the alpha subunit of Gs, preventing GTP hydrolysis; persistent cAMP production activates PKA, which phosphorylates and opens the CFTR chloride channel.
Gi is locked in its active state, which inhibits adenylyl cyclase and lowers cAMP, which opens CFTR
Gi activation would lower cAMP and not stimulate secretion.
Gs is permanently inactivated, which lowers cAMP and relieves inhibition of the Na+/K+ ATPase
Inactivating Gs would lower cAMP and reduce secretion.
questions.x: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the alpha subunit of Gs, preventing GTP hydrolysis; persistent cAMP production activates PKA, which phosphorylates and opens the CFTR chloride channel. Trap: Mixing up the G protein subtypes and the direction of change in cAMP.

questions.q: In an Hfr x F- cross in E. coli, the recipient cells rarely become F+ (Hfr) even though DNA is transferred. What is the best explanation?
o: The recipient's F- pilus blocks the transfer of F factor genes, while chromosomal genes cross the bridge freely
F- recipient cells do not make F pili, and the donor makes the pilus.
The F genes are last in line, and the mating pair usually separates first
Correct: Transfer starts at the origin inside the integrated F factor, so the remaining F genes are last in line and conjugation usually breaks before they enter the recipient.
The F factor genes are transferred first, but they are degraded by restriction enzymes in the recipient
The F genes are transferred last, not first, because they lie behind the origin of transfer; restriction is not the issue.
The F factor is excised from the donor chromosome before transfer begins, so only chromosomal genes are passed
In an Hfr strain the F factor remains integrated; excision would produce an F' or F+ cell instead.
questions.x: Transfer starts at the origin inside the integrated F factor, so the remaining F genes are last in line and conjugation usually breaks before they enter the recipient. Trap: Assuming that the whole F factor is transferred first because it initiates conjugation.

questions.q: A cell sustains a double-strand break in a chromosome. Why is repair by homologous recombination favored in S and G2 phases but rarely used in G1?
o: It needs an intact sister chromatid as a template, which exists only after DNA replication
Correct: Homologous recombination copies the undamaged sequence from the sister chromatid, which is present only after replication; G1 cells rely on error-prone nonhomologous end joining.
It needs the nuclear envelope to be disassembled, which occurs only after S phase
The nuclear envelope remains intact during repair in S and G2.
It requires Cdk activity to unwind the helix, which is absent in G1
Helix unwinding is not what Cdk activity provides; the missing item is the template.
It requires a second homologous chromosome to be paired in a synaptonemal complex, which forms after replication
The synaptonemal complex is specific to meiosis, not to repair of breaks in somatic cells.
questions.x: Homologous recombination copies the undamaged sequence from the sister chromatid, which is present only after replication; G1 cells rely on error-prone nonhomologous end joining. Trap: Applying meiotic recombination features (synaptonemal complex) to repair in somatic cells.

questions.q: A child with trisomy 21 inherited two different maternal chromosome 21 homologs, as shown by heterozygosity for markers near the centromere. In which stage did the nondisjunction most likely occur?
o: Meiosis II in the mother, because sister chromatids failed to separate
A meiosis II error gives two copies of the same homolog, which would appear homozygous near the centromere.
Mitosis in the early embryo, because sister chromatids failed to separate
A mitotic error would produce mosaicism and would not give two different maternal homologs.
Meiosis I in the mother, because homologs failed to separate
Correct: If two different homologs of maternal origin are present, then homologs failed to segregate at meiosis I; a meiosis II error would produce two identical copies (apart from crossovers).
Meiosis I in the father, because homologs failed to separate
The extra chromosomes came from the mother, as the markers show.
questions.x: If two different homologs of maternal origin are present, then homologs failed to segregate at meiosis I; a meiosis II error would produce two identical copies (apart from crossovers). Trap: Not distinguishing between the two meiotic divisions based on whether the extra chromosomes are identical or different.

questions.q: In a neuron, the extracellular K+ concentration rises from 4 mM to 8 mM, with intracellular K+ unchanged. At 37 C, about how much does the K+ equilibrium potential change?
o: It becomes about 61 mV less negative
61 mV is the change for a 10-fold change in concentration, not a 2-fold change.
It becomes about 9 mV less negative
9 mV would be half of the correct shift, from omitting the logarithm of 2 (0.30).
It becomes about 18 mV less negative
Correct: E_K = 61.5 log([K]out/[K]in); doubling [K]out adds 61.5 x log 2 = 18.5 mV, moving E_K toward zero (depolarization).
It becomes about 18 mV more negative
Raising extracellular K+ decreases the outward gradient and so E_K becomes less negative, not more.
questions.x: E_K = 61.5 log([K]out/[K]in); doubling [K]out adds 61.5 x log 2 = 18.5 mV, moving E_K toward zero (depolarization). Trap: Using 61 mV for a two-fold change instead of 61 x log 2, or getting the sign of the shift wrong.

questions.q: A patient has a diffusely enlarged thyroid, exophthalmos, low serum TSH, and high serum free T4. Which mechanism most likely explains this presentation?
o: A TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma drives the thyroid, which raises T4 and TSH together
A pituitary adenoma would give high TSH, not low TSH.
Iodine deficiency reduces hormone synthesis, so TSH is elevated and the thyroid enlarges
Iodine deficiency causes hypothyroidism with high TSH.
Antibodies block the TSH receptor, so the thyroid produces less hormone and TSH rises
Blocking antibodies would cause hypothyroidism with high TSH.
Antibodies activate the TSH receptor, and excess T4 suppresses TSH
Correct: In Graves disease, stimulating autoantibodies mimic TSH, causing hyperthyroidism and goiter; high T4 suppresses TRH and TSH through negative feedback.
questions.x: In Graves disease, stimulating autoantibodies mimic TSH, causing hyperthyroidism and goiter; high T4 suppresses TRH and TSH through negative feedback. Trap: Expecting TSH to be high whenever the thyroid is enlarged, ignoring the feedback effect of excess T4.

questions.q: A patient with heart failure begins taking spironolactone. Which set of changes in the patient's serum and urine is most likely?
o: Serum K+ falls, and urinary Na+ excretion falls
Natriuresis occurs with the drug, so urinary Na+ excretion rises rather than falls, and K+ is retained rather than lost.
Serum K+ rises, and urinary Na+ excretion falls
Blocking aldosterone reduces Na+ reabsorption, so urinary Na+ does not fall.
Serum K+ rises, and urinary Na+ excretion rises

Correct: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone's mineralocorticoid receptor in principal cells, so fewer ENaC channels and Na+/K+ ATPases are made: less Na+ is reabsorbed (more in urine) and less K+ is secreted (higher serum K+).
Serum K+ falls, and urinary Na+ excretion rises
Aldosterone antagonism reduces K+ secretion, so serum K+ does not fall.
questions.x: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone's mineralocorticoid receptor in principal cells, so fewer ENaC channels and Na+/K+ ATPases are made: less Na+ is reabsorbed (more in urine) and less K+ is secreted (higher serum K+). Trap: Remembering the diuretic effect but not that K+ secretion falls, which makes the drug potassium-sparing.

questions.q: A person is exposed to carbon monoxide in a poorly ventilated room. Which set of findings is expected?
o: Normal PaO2, reduced O2 content, and a left-shifted curve

Correct: CO binds hemoglobin with about 200-fold higher affinity than O2, reducing O2 content, but dissolved O2 and PaO2 are determined by the lungs and are unchanged; CO also increases the O2 affinity of the other subunits, shifting the curve left.
Normal arterial PO2, normal oxygen content of the blood, and a right-shifted oxyhemoglobin curve
The oxygen content is reduced because many heme groups are occupied by CO, and the PaO2 is normal, so the content cannot be normal.
Reduced arterial PO2, normal oxygen content of the blood, and a left-shifted oxyhemoglobin curve
The oxygen content is reduced because CO occupies heme sites, even though PaO2 itself is normal; reduced PaO2 would imply a lung problem.
Reduced arterial PO2, reduced oxygen content of the blood, and a right-shifted oxyhemoglobin curve
PaO2 is not reduced because gas exchange across the alveolar membrane is intact, and a right shift would favor unloading.
questions.x: CO binds hemoglobin with about 200-fold higher affinity than O2, reducing O2 content, but dissolved O2 and PaO2 are determined by the lungs and are unchanged; CO also increases the O2 affinity of the other subunits, shifting the curve left. Trap: Equating low oxygen content with low arterial PO2, when CO leaves the dissolved oxygen unchanged.

questions.q: A massless seesaw is balanced at its center. A 30 kg child sits 2.0 m from the pivot. At what distance from the pivot on the opposite side must a 40 kg child sit for the seesaw to balance?
o: 1.0 m, from halving the distance of the lighter child because the masses differ
The distance scales with the inverse mass ratio (0.75), not with one half.
2.7 m, from dividing the larger mass by the smaller mass and multiplying by 2.0 m
Inverting the ratio of the masses gives 2.7 m; the heavier child sits closer.
1.5 m, from the torque balance 30 x 2.0 = 40 x d, with the heavier child closer
Correct: Torque balance: 30 x 2.0 = 40 x d, so d = 1.5 m.
2.0 m, since a seesaw balances only when both children sit at equal distances
Equal distances balance only equal masses.
questions.x: Torque balance: 30 x 2.0 = 40 x d, so d = 1.5 m. Trap: Inverting the mass ratio in a torque balance.

questions.q: A 0.20 kg ball strikes a wall at 15 m/s and rebounds along the same line at 10 m/s. The contact time is 0.010 s. What is the magnitude of the average force exerted by the wall on the ball?
o: 100 N, from using the difference between the speeds, 5 m/s, as the velocity change
Velocity is a vector, and the direction reverses, so the speeds add.
200 N, from using only the rebound speed to calculate the change in momentum
Using only 2.0 kg·m/s omits the momentum that must first be removed.
300 N, from using only the incoming speed to calculate the change in momentum
The ball's momentum changes from −3.0 to +2.0 kg·m/s; using only 3.0 omits the rebound.
questions.x: Δp = 0.20 x (10 − (−15)) = 5.0 kg·m/s; F = Δp/Δt = 5.0/0.010 = 500 N. Trap: Subtracting the speeds without accounting for the reversal in direction.

questions.q: When 0.050 mol of NaOH reacts completely with excess HCl in a coffee-cup calorimeter containing 200 g of solution, the reaction releases 57 kJ per mole of NaOH. What is the approximate temperature change? (Specific heat = 4.18 J/g·K.)
o: An increase of about 34 K, from using 0.50 mol rather than 0.050 mol of NaOH
The amount is 0.050 mol, which gives 2.85 kJ rather than 28.5 kJ.
An increase of about 3.4 K, from 2.85 kJ absorbed by 200 g of solution at 4.18 J/g·K
Correct: q = 0.050 mol x 57 kJ/mol = 2.85 kJ; ΔT = 2,850 J / (200 g x 4.18 J/g·K) = 3.4 K.
A decrease of about 3.4 K, because the neutralization of a strong acid and base is endothermic
Heat is released by the reaction and absorbed by the solution, which warms.
An increase of about 6.8 K, from doubling the result to account for heat absorbed by the vessel
A coffee-cup calorimeter has negligible heat capacity here, and the 200 g of solution already accounts for the heat absorbed.
questions.x: q = 0.050 mol x 57 kJ/mol = 2.85 kJ; ΔT = 2,850 J / (200 g x 4.18 J/g·K) = 3.4 K. Trap: Mismanaging the mole amount or the sign in calorimetry.

questions.q: A first-order decomposition has a rate constant of 0.0231 min⁻¹. What fraction of the original reactant remains after 90 minutes?
o: 1/4, because the half-life is 45 minutes and two half-lives have passed
A half-life of 45 min would require k = 0.0154 min⁻¹.
1/16, because the half-life is 22.5 minutes and four half-lives have passed
A half-life of 22.5 min would require k = 0.0308 min⁻¹.
Correct: t½ = ln 2/k = 0.693/0.0231 = 30 min; 90 min is three half-lives, so (1/2)³ = 1/8 remains.
1/2, because a first-order reaction loses half of its reactant in any 90 minute period
Half-life is 30 min, not 90 min.
questions.x: t½ = ln 2/k = 0.693/0.0231 = 30 min; 90 min is three half-lives, so (1/2)³ = 1/8 remains. Trap: Miscalculating the half-life from the rate constant.

questions.q: A uniform block with a density of 800 kg/m³ floats at rest in fresh water (density 1,000 kg/m³). What fraction of the block's volume is submerged?
o: 20%, because the fraction above water equals the density ratio of block to water
20% is the fraction above water, not below.
80%, because the density ratio gives the submerged fraction of the volume
Correct: Floating equilibrium: ρ_water V_sub g = ρ_block V g, so V_sub/V = 800/1000 = 0.80.
100%, because any object that floats at rest must be fully surrounded by the fluid
A floating object displaces only its weight in water; the rest is above the surface.
64%, because the buoyant force depends on the square of the density ratio
The fraction is linear in the density ratio.
questions.x: Floating equilibrium: ρ_water V_sub g = ρ_block V g, so V_sub/V = 800/1000 = 0.80. Trap: Reporting the exposed fraction instead of the submerged fraction.

questions.q: Blood flows at 0.30 m/s through an arterial segment of radius 1.0 cm and then enters a stenotic region of radius 0.50 cm. Treating the blood as incompressible, what is its speed in the narrowed region?
o: 0.60 m/s, because the speed doubles when the radius is cut in half
Speed scales with 1/r², so halving the radius quadruples the speed.
1.2 m/s, because the area falls to one-fourth and so the speed rises fourfold
Correct: Continuity: A1v1 = A2v2; area scales with r², so a half radius gives a quarter of the area and four times the speed: 0.30 x 4 = 1.2 m/s.
4.8 m/s, because the speed increases with the inverse fourth power of the radius
The inverse fourth-power dependence applies to Poiseuille flow resistance, not to speed from continuity.
0.075 m/s, because the speed decreases in a narrower vessel
Fluid must speed up in a constriction to maintain the same volume flow.
questions.x: Continuity: A1v1 = A2v2; area scales with r², so a half radius gives a quarter of the area and four times the speed: 0.30 x 4 = 1.2 m/s. Trap: Using the radius ratio instead of the area ratio in the continuity equation.

questions.q: A 6.0 Ω resistor and a 3.0 Ω resistor are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. What is the total current supplied by the battery?
o: 4.0 A, from counting only the current through the 3.0 Ω resistor
The 4.0 A through the 3.0 Ω resistor is only part of the total current.
1.3 A, from adding the resistances as if they were in series
A series combination would give 9.0 Ω, but the resistors share the same voltage in parallel.
2.0 A, from counting only the current through the 6.0 Ω resistor
The 2.0 A through the 6.0 Ω resistor is only part of the total current.
questions.x: R_eq = (6.0 x 3.0)/(6.0 + 3.0) = 2.0 Ω; I = 12/2.0 = 6.0 A (4.0 A + 2.0 A). Trap: Adding branch resistances as though they were in series.

questions.q: A proton (charge 1.6 x 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 2.0 x 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on the proton?
o: 8.0 x 10⁻¹⁴ N, from including a factor of one half as in kinetic energy
The factor of one-half belongs to kinetic energy, not magnetic force.
1.6 x 10⁻¹³ N, from F = qvB with sin 90° = 1, using the given charge and speed
3.2 x 10⁻¹³ N, from doubling the product to account for both field directions
No factor of 2 appears in F = qvB.
Zero, because a magnetic force can never act on a moving charged particle
Magnetic force acts on moving charges; it is zero only when v is parallel to B.
questions.x: F = qvB sin 90° = (1.6 x 10⁻¹⁹)(2.0 x 10⁶)(0.50) = 1.6 x 10⁻¹³ N. Trap: Adding extraneous factors to the magnetic force formula.

questions.q: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Where is the image, and what are its characteristics?
o: 40 cm in front of the mirror; real and inverted
40 cm is the sum of the object distance and the focal length, which is not the mirror equation.
15 cm in front of the mirror; real and inverted
Correct: 1/di = 1/f − 1/do = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30, so di = 15 cm; positive di means a real, inverted image in front of the mirror.
15 cm behind the mirror; virtual and upright
A virtual image forms only when the object is inside the focal length.
7.5 cm in front of the mirror; real and inverted
7.5 cm results from an arithmetic error such as halving the focal-length difference.
questions.x: 1/di = 1/f − 1/do = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30, so di = 15 cm; positive di means a real, inverted image in front of the mirror. Trap: Misusing the mirror equation or confusing real and virtual images.

questions.q: An ambulance siren emits a 700 Hz tone and moves at 34 m/s toward a stationary listener. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. What frequency does the listener hear?
o: 778 Hz, because an approaching source raises the observed frequency
Correct: f' = f v/(v − vs) = 700 x 340/306 = 778 Hz; the frequency is higher for an approaching source.
770 Hz, from multiplying 700 Hz by 1.10 as an approximation
The exact calculation uses 340/(340 − 34), not 1.10.
636 Hz, the frequency heard if the ambulance were moving away
A receding source gives a lower frequency (700 x 340/374 = 636 Hz).
700 Hz, because the frequency of a source is unaffected by the motion
The relative motion changes the received wavelength and frequency.
questions.x: f' = f v/(v − vs) = 700 x 340/306 = 778 Hz; the frequency is higher for an approaching source. Trap: Using the receding-source form of the Doppler equation.

questions.q: Light with a photon energy of 4.0 eV strikes a metal whose work function is 2.5 eV. What is the stopping potential needed to halt the most energetic emitted electrons?
o: 6.5 V, from adding the photon energy and the work function
The work function is subtracted, not added.
2.5 V, from using the work function as the stopping potential
The work function is the energy needed to free the electron, not the leftover kinetic energy.
1.5 V, from the maximum kinetic energy of 1.5 eV divided by the electron charge
Correct: K_max = hf − φ = 4.0 − 2.5 = 1.5 eV, so the stopping potential is 1.5 V.
4.0 V, from using the full photon energy as the stopping potential
Part of the photon energy is used to overcome the work function.
questions.x: K_max = hf − φ = 4.0 − 2.5 = 1.5 eV, so the stopping potential is 1.5 V. Trap: Adding the work function instead of subtracting it.

questions.q: A buffer is prepared with 0.20 M sodium acetate and 0.10 M acetic acid (pKa = 4.76). What is the pH of the buffer?
o: 4.76, because the pH of a buffer always equals the pKa of its weak acid
pH equals pKa only when the acid and base concentrations are equal.
5.36, from using the logarithm of 4 rather than the logarithm of 2
The ratio is 0.20/0.10 = 2, not 4.
5.06, from 4.76 plus the log of the 2:1 base-to-acid ratio, 0.30
4.46, from inverting the ratio of base to acid in the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation
The base is in the numerator; inverting gives 4.46.
questions.x: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) = 4.76 + log 2 = 4.76 + 0.30 = 5.06. Trap: Inverting the base-to-acid ratio in the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.

questions.q: n-Pentane boils at 36 °C, whereas 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane), an isomer of the same formula, boils at 9.5 °C. Which explanation is best?
o: The n-pentane molecule has a permanent dipole, so dipole–dipole forces raise its boiling point
Both are nonpolar; neither has a significant permanent dipole.
The neopentane molecule has a higher molar mass, so more energy is needed to vaporize it
Isomers have identical molar masses.
The n-pentane molecule forms hydrogen bonds, so it is held in the liquid more strongly
Alkanes have no O–H or N–H bonds and cannot hydrogen bond.
The elongated n-pentane molecules have more surface contact, so London dispersion forces are stronger
Correct: Both are nonpolar hydrocarbons with the same molar mass; the more compact neopentane has less surface area and thus weaker dispersion forces.
questions.x: Both are nonpolar hydrocarbons with the same molar mass; the more compact neopentane has less surface area and thus weaker dispersion forces. Trap: Looking for polarity or hydrogen bonding in a nonpolar hydrocarbon.

questions.q: On a silica gel TLC plate, compound A moves 1.5 cm and compound B moves 4.0 cm while the solvent front moves 5.0 cm. Which conclusion is justified?
o: A and B have the same polarity, since both spots are inside the solvent front
Different Rf values show different affinities for the stationary phase.
A is less polar than B, with Rf values of 0.30 and 0.80, since A is carried farther by the solvent
The compound that travels farther is the one that interacts less with silica.
B is less polar than A, with Rf values of 0.80 and 0.30, since B interacts less with the polar silica
Correct: Rf = distance traveled / solvent front distance: A = 1.5/5.0 = 0.30 and B = 4.0/5.0 = 0.80. The polar stationary phase retains polar compounds more strongly.
B is more polar than A, with Rf values of 0.80 and 0.30, since B interacts more with the silica
Greater interaction with silica reduces mobility and Rf.
questions.x: Rf = distance traveled / solvent front distance: A = 1.5/5.0 = 0.30 and B = 4.0/5.0 = 0.80. The polar stationary phase retains polar compounds more strongly. Trap: Reading a larger Rf as higher polarity on silica.

questions.q: Methyl bromide, ethyl bromide, isopropyl bromide, and tert-butyl bromide each react with azide in a polar aprotic solvent by an SN2 mechanism. Which reacts fastest, and why?
o: Methyl bromide, because backside attack at the carbon is least hindered by neighboring substituents
Correct: SN2 rates fall as substitution increases (CH3 > 1° > 2° >> 3°) because steric crowding blocks the backside approach.
Isopropyl bromide, because a secondary carbon balances steric hindrance against carbocation stability
No carbocation forms in the one-step SN2 pathway.
All react at the same rate, because the leaving group is bromide in every case
The leaving group is the same, but the steric environment differs, so the rates differ.
tert-Butyl bromide, because the most substituted carbon best stabilizes the developing positive charge
Carbocation stability governs SN1 rather than SN2 reactions.
questions.x: SN2 rates fall as substitution increases (CH3 > 1° > 2° >> 3°) because steric crowding blocks the backside approach. Trap: Applying SN1 carbocation-stability ordering to an SN2 reaction.

questions.q: A hiker sees a bear, notices her pounding heart and trembling, and then reports feeling afraid. According to the James-Lange theory, the sequence of events is:
o: stimulus, with arousal and conscious emotion occurring simultaneously and independently
Simultaneous, independent arousal and emotion is the Cannon-Bard theory.
stimulus, cognitive appraisal of the situation, then arousal that is labeled as an emotion
Arousal labeled through appraisal is the Schachter-Singer two-factor theory.
stimulus, physiological arousal, then the conscious experience of emotion as a result
Correct: James-Lange holds that the perception of bodily changes constitutes the emotion.
stimulus, conscious fear, then physiological arousal produced by that fear
Emotion first and arousal second is the commonsense view James-Lange rejected.
questions.x: James-Lange holds that the perception of bodily changes constitutes the emotion. Trap: Confusing James-Lange with the commonsense order in which emotion causes the bodily response.

questions.q: A sleeper is easily awakened and shows an EEG with brief 12-14 Hz bursts and occasional large biphasic waves, but no rapid eye movements. The sleeper is in:
o: stage N1
Stage N1 shows theta waves and slow rolling eye movements.
stage N2
Correct: Sleep spindles and K-complexes characterize stage N2 sleep.
stage N3
Stage N3 is dominated by high-amplitude delta waves and is hard to arouse from.
REM sleep
REM shows low-amplitude mixed-frequency activity with rapid eye movements.
questions.x: Sleep spindles and K-complexes characterize stage N2 sleep. Trap: Choosing N3 because large waves are visible, even though spindles and an easy awakening point to N2.

questions.q: Which stage of Selye's general adaptation syndrome is characterized by sustained physiological arousal, with cortisol remaining elevated while the body attempts to cope with an ongoing stressor?
o: Alarm
Alarm is the initial fight-or-flight activation.
Resistance
Correct: In resistance, the body maintains heightened arousal and cortisol while coping continues.
Exhaustion
Exhaustion occurs when resources are depleted and illness risk rises.
Recovery
Recovery is not a stage of the general adaptation syndrome.
questions.x: In resistance, the body maintains heightened arousal and cortisol while coping continues. Trap: Choosing alarm because cortisol is associated with the stress response in general.

questions.q: Two siblings share a genetic vulnerability to depression, but only the one who lost a job develops the disorder. This is best explained by:
o: a purely genetic model, in which siblings with the same alleles must develop the disorder
A purely genetic model predicts both siblings would be affected.
a purely environmental model, in which genetic vulnerability plays no role
The shared vulnerability is stated, so genes are not irrelevant.
a diathesis-stress model, in which vulnerability produces illness only when a stressor occurs
Correct: Diathesis-stress combines predisposition and a triggering stressor.
a learned helplessness model, in which the disorder follows exposure to an uncontrollable shock in a laboratory
Learned helplessness is a laboratory model and does not require a shared genetic vulnerability.
questions.x: Diathesis-stress combines predisposition and a triggering stressor. Trap: Choosing a single-cause model.

questions.q: Which symptom of schizophrenia is classified as a negative symptom?
o: Auditory hallucinations that comment on the person's behavior
Hallucinations are positive symptoms.
Flat affect with little spontaneous speech
Correct: Negative symptoms reflect diminished normal functions, such as blunted emotion and reduced speech.
A fixed false belief that neighbors are monitoring the person
Delusions are positive symptoms.
Tangential speech in which ideas are only loosely connected
Disorganized speech is classified with positive symptoms.
questions.x: Negative symptoms reflect diminished normal functions, such as blunted emotion and reduced speech. Trap: Assuming the most obviously abnormal behaviors are negative symptoms.

questions.q: A shy student avoids parties, receives fewer invitations, and becomes more socially anxious. Which concept from social-cognitive personality theory best describes this loop?
o: Psychosexual fixation at the oral stage
Psychosexual fixation is a Freudian concept unrelated to this loop.
Reciprocal determinism
Correct: Reciprocal determinism describes mutual influence among person, behavior, and environment.
Situationism, which holds that behavior is determined almost entirely by the immediate context
Situationism ignores the role of the person.
Trait stability, which holds that behavior is consistent across all contexts and over time
Trait stability does not describe a feedback loop with the environment.
questions.x: Reciprocal determinism describes mutual influence among person, behavior, and environment. Trap: Choosing situationism because the environment is involved.

questions.q: In studies of obedience, which change would be expected to reduce obedience substantially?
o: The authority figure wears a laboratory coat and speaks calmly and firmly
Visible markers of authority increase obedience.
The study is run at a well-known and prestigious university
Prestige increases obedience.
The authority figure takes responsibility for any harm caused to the learner
Taking responsibility reduces the participant's felt responsibility, increasing obedience.
The authority figure gives commands by telephone instead of being in the room
Correct: Physical distance from the authority reduces obedience.
questions.x: Physical distance from the authority reduces obedience. Trap: Choosing a variable that increases obedience, since all options sound like Milgram's variations.

questions.q: Individuals pull less hard on a rope when in a team than when pulling alone, and no one can identify individual contributions. This is best described as:
o: social facilitation
Social facilitation concerns performance changes due to an audience.
social loafing
Correct: Individuals reduce effort in groups when contributions are not identifiable.
deindividuation
Deindividuation concerns reduced self-awareness and norm adherence in crowds.
the bystander effect
The bystander effect concerns helping in emergencies.
questions.x: Individuals reduce effort in groups when contributions are not identifiable. Trap: Choosing social facilitation because both involve other people affecting performance.

questions.q: Members of a group who each moderately favored a risky investment before meeting end up choosing an even riskier option after discussion. This is an example of:
o: groupthink
Groupthink involves suppression of dissent for cohesion.
group polarization
Correct: Discussion strengthens the group's initial leaning.
regression to the mean
Regression to the mean is a statistical phenomenon.
the false consensus effect
False consensus is overestimating agreement with others.
questions.x: Discussion strengthens the group's initial leaning. Trap: Choosing groupthink because the group made a poor decision.

questions.q: The just noticeable difference for a 200-g weight is 4 g. According to Weber's law, the just noticeable difference for a 500-g weight is:
o: Correct: The Weber fraction is 4/200 = 0.02, and 0.02 x 500 = 10 g.
4 g
4 g assumes JND is constant.
8 g
8 g would be the JND for 400 g.
2.5 g is the result of inverting the ratio.
questions.x: The Weber fraction is 4/200 = 0.02, and 0.02 x 500 = 10 g. Trap: Assuming that the JND is a fixed amount rather than a fixed proportion.

questions.q: A child watches water poured from a short, wide glass into a tall, thin glass and says the tall glass now holds more. According to Piaget, this child:
o: is in the sensorimotor stage and lacks object permanence entirely
Sensorimotor children are infants developing object permanence.
is in the concrete operational stage and has mastered reversibility
Concrete operational children succeed on conservation.
is in the preoperational stage and has not yet achieved conservation
Correct: Failure on conservation tasks characterizes the preoperational stage.
is in the formal operational stage and reasons only about abstract hypotheses
Formal operational thinkers pass conservation tasks easily.
questions.x: Failure on conservation tasks characterizes the preoperational stage. Trap: Choosing concrete operational because the child is school-aged.

questions.q: A teenager comes to see herself as talented after noticing that teachers and classmates respond to her with praise. This process illustrates:
o: the self-serving bias
Self-serving bias concerns credit for success and blame for failure.
the fundamental attribution error
The fundamental attribution error concerns explanations of others' behavior.
the looking-glass self
Correct: Cooley's looking-glass self holds that self-concept develops from imagining how others perceive us.
a self-fulfilling prophecy involving only her own prediction
A self-fulfilling prophecy requires a belief that changes behavior to confirm itself.
questions.x: Cooley's looking-glass self holds that self-concept develops from imagining how others perceive us. Trap: Choosing self-serving bias because the self-image is favorable.

questions.q: A university's manifest function is educating students. Which of the following is a latent function?
o: Granting degrees that certify completion of a course of study
Granting degrees is recognized and intended.
Conducting research that is published in scholarly journals
Research is an intended function.
Training students for professional careers through coursework
Career training is an intended function.
Providing a place for students to meet future spouses and friends
Correct: Latent functions are unintended and often unrecognized consequences of an institution.
questions.x: Latent functions are unintended and often unrecognized consequences of an institution. Trap: Choosing an intended function that seems secondary to education.

questions.q: A household in a wealthy country earns 40% less than the national median but has adequate food and housing. This household is best described as experiencing:
o: absolute poverty
Absolute poverty means lacking basic necessities.
a high Gini coefficient
The Gini coefficient measures inequality for a population, not for one household.
relative poverty
Correct: Relative poverty is defined by comparison with the typical standard of a society.
downward intergenerational mobility
Intergenerational mobility concerns changes relative to parents.
questions.x: Relative poverty is defined by comparison with the typical standard of a society. Trap: Treating any low income as absolute poverty.

questions.q: A researcher raises the significance level from 0.05 to 0.10. Assuming nothing else changes, which effect is expected?
o: The probability of a Type I error increases and that of a Type II error decreases
Correct: A higher alpha makes rejecting the null easier, so false positives rise and false negatives fall.
The probability of a Type I error decreases and that of a Type II error increases
This describes lowering alpha.
The probabilities of both Type I and Type II errors increase
The errors trade off against each other when other factors are fixed.
The probabilities of both Type I and Type II errors remain unchanged
Alpha is the Type I error rate, so it changes.
questions.x: A higher alpha makes rejecting the null easier, so false positives rise and false negatives fall. Trap: Reversing the direction of the tradeoff between Type I and Type II errors.
